title: Thomas Quarry hominins (~773 ka) basal to the Homo sapiens lineage
claim: Hominin fossils from Thomas Quarry I (Casablanca, Morocco), dated to approximately 773,000 years ago, are basal to the Homo sapiens lineage and push the African origin of the last common ancestor of humans and Neanderthals to the older end of the genetic split estimates — with northwest Africa now central to the deep-roots story, linked to other African regions by population movement across the Sahara during wetter phases.
place: Thomas Quarry I, Casablanca, Morocco
grade_reason: Published in Nature with full stratigraphic documentation; the morphological case is detailed, but it is one quarry complex and the LCA attribution rests on the current genetic-split window — corroborated, not verified.
earliest_attestation: Thomas Quarry I fossils, excavated over decades of stratigraphic work; announced as a lineage-basal assemblage in the January 2026 Nature paper

sources.ref: Hublin, Lefèvre, Perini et al. 2026, Nature, doi:10.1038/s41586-025-09914-y — 'Early hominins from Morocco basal to the Homo sapiens lineage'
Genetic split estimates for the sapiens–Neanderthal divergence (~765–550 ka)

competing_hypotheses: The LCA of sapiens and Neanderthals lies toward the younger end of the genetic estimates (~550 ka), with the Thomas Quarry fossils representing a side branch rather than the direct stem
The fossils are correctly placed but undersampled — one quarry complex does not yet establish northwest Africa as the exclusive LCA homeland
The split occurred outside Africa with back-migration (minority position; contradicted by the African fossil and genetic evidence)
falsifiability: A securely dated, directly comparable stem-lineage fossil assemblage elsewhere in Africa older than Thomas Quarry would break the northwest-Africa centrality claim; retraction of the dating on stratigraphic grounds would collapse the age.

title: Tromerosaurus solumons — the mosaic tyrannosaur (Oldman Formation, 2026)
claim: A new tyrannosaurid genus and species, Tromerosaurus solumons, described October 2026 from a partial skeleton excavated in 2010–2011 from the Upper Cretaceous Oldman Formation of Alberta (~76 Ma, Campanian), mixes features of both major tyrannosaurid subfamilies — a mosaic of gracile albertosaurine and robust tyrannosaurine characters — and supports a younger divergence of the two lineages with rapid character acquisition during the Late Cretaceous (Santonian–Maastrichtian). The description also reassigns the 'largest adult Gorgosaurus' specimen to Tromerosaurus.
place: Oldman Formation, Alberta, Canada (exposures associated with the upper Oldman Formation; exact locality in the describing paper)
grade_reason: Peer-reviewed species description (JVP, online first 2 Oct 2026) with holotype diagnosis, maxillary morphometrics, and character-taxon analysis; withheld from VERIFIED because the taxon rests on a single partial skeleton and the albertosaurine-vs-tyrannosaurine placement is analysis-dependent.
earliest_attestation: The fossil itself — partial skeleton (substantial skull portion, vertebrae, both humeri, hind limb material, parts of pelvis) discovered 2010 in the upper Oldman Formation, recovered over the 2010 and 2011 field seasons by University of Alberta expeditions; skull prepared at the University of Alberta Laboratory for Vertebrate Palaeontology; described in print October 2026

sources.ref: Powers et al. 2026, Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology (online first 2 October 2026) — description of Tromerosaurus solumons from the Oldman Formation; holotype UALVP 52981; maxillary morphometrics (anteroposteriorly longer maxillary fenestra, narrower pila promaxillaris than Gorgosaurus libratus); anatomical diagnosis permitting referral of the 'largest adult Gorgosaurus' specimen; parsimony vs Bayesian topology disagreement; younger divergence + rapid character acquisition inference (as reported in the Oct 2026 press cycle)

New Scientist, 19 October 2026 — 'Discovery of T. rex's cousin upends our understanding of tyrannosaur evolution' (early albertosaurine; 'frightful lizard' + Tolkien 'lonely mountain' etymology; Jared Voris's call for deeper 78–79 Ma sampling)

Everything Dinosaur (blog), 5 October 2026 — 'Remarkable New Tyrannosaur Highlights an Evolutionary Puzzle' (author-compiled with images from lead author Mark J. Powers, University of Alberta; ~76 Ma Campanian; JVP venue confirmed)

competing_hypotheses: Bayesian analysis in the describing paper recovers Tromerosaurus inside Tyrannosaurinae rather than Albertosaurinae — the parsimony and Bayesian topologies disagree, so the subfamily placement is method-dependent, not settled

The rapid-divergence reading is the authors' inference from reduced node support values; the 'stepwise growth into T. rex' model it argues against remains the position the paper critiques, not a claim the paper falsifies with a single taxon
The 'T. rex's cousin' popular framing is relationship-by-family, not closeness: Tromerosaurus is an albertosaurine-branch animal ~76 Ma, tens of millions of years before Tyrannosaurus
falsifiability: A re-examination reassigning the holotype to Gorgosaurus or Daspletosaurus on overlapping material, or a phylogenetic re-analysis collapsing the diagnosis into existing taxa, would sink the species; a second independent tyrannosaurid dataset recovering deep divergence timing would weaken the rapid-radiation reading.

title: The first adult T. rex trackway — Hell Creek, North Dakota, described 2026
claim: A peer-reviewed study published in September 2026 in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology (DOI 10.1080/02724634.2026.2706201) (Falkingham, Hups, Tamez-Galvan, Bercovici & Lyson) formally describes 'a large tridactyl trackway from the Upper Cretaceous Hell Creek Formation of North Dakota, likely attributable to an adult Tyrannosaurus rex' — the first known multi-step adult tyrannosaur trackway: four consecutive three-toed prints (left-right-left-right) across ~7 m (23 ft), each print ~1 m long and 0.6–0.8 m wide, stride ~4 m (13 ft), yielding an estimated walking speed of ~3.5–4.5 mph (5.6–7.2 km/h). The prints were found in July 2025 by Colorado high-school science teacher Kent M. Hups (volunteer research associate, Denver Museum of Nature & Science) on Dakota Prairie Grasslands ~2.5 miles northwest of Marmarth, ND, ~33 m below the top of the Hell Creek Formation (~66.5 Ma). High-resolution 3D surface scans were analyzed by lead author Peter Falkingham in England via computer and VR; three exposed prints were scheduled for helicopter removal to the Denver Museum of Nature & Science in autumn 2026. Trackmaker attribution rests on size, narrow-elongate toe shape (theropod, not the broad-toed Edmontosaurus, the only other Hell Creek animal that big), location, and the local abundance of adult T. rex remains; the authors' own wording is 'likely attributable' and the measurements are presented as approximate because the impressions are strongly weathered.
place: Hell Creek Formation near Marmarth, southwestern North Dakota (Dakota Prairie Grasslands)
grade_reason: Peer-reviewed primary description in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology (12 September 2026) with documented measurements, high-resolution 3D scan archive, and a museum deposition plan — withheld from VERIFIED because it is a single study and the trackmaker attribution is explicitly 'likely', not certain.
earliest_attestation: Falkingham, P. L., Hups, K. M., Tamez-Galvan, E. M., Bercovici, A. D. & Lyson, T. R. (2026) 'A large tridactyl trackway from the Upper Cretaceous Hell Creek Formation of North Dakota, likely attributable to an adult Tyrannosaurus rex.' Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology. https://doi.org/10.1080/02724634.2026.2706201 (accepted manuscript, open access via LJMU Research Online; submitted 23 Jan 2026, accepted 13 July 2026; published September 2026).

sources.ref: Falkingham, P. L. et al., Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology (2026), DOI 10.1080/02724634.2026.2706201 — 'A large tridactyl trackway from the Upper Cretaceous Hell Creek Formation of North Dakota, likely attributable to an adult Tyrannosaurus rex' (accepted manuscript, open access)

Denver Museum of Nature & Science press release, via earth.com 2026-10-22 — Kent Hups discovery (July 2025), four prints, ~66.5 Ma, 3.5–4.5 mph walking estimate, three prints helicopter-lifted in early October; Tyler Lyson (DMNS senior curator) on the attribution basis

competing_hypotheses: Trackmaker identity is not certain — the authors' own phrasing is 'likely attributable to an adult Tyrannosaurus rex', and no associated skeleton was found at the site
The walking-speed estimate (~3.5–4.5 mph) is approximate: the prints are strongly weathered and partly deformed, and the authors stress the numbers are coarse
An isolated-track counter-reading (a non-walking origin for the depressions) is ruled out by the four-print left-right-left-right sequence, but the record honestly carries the 'likely' qualifier
falsifiability: A peer-reviewed ichnological re-study re-identifying the four impressions as erosion features or non-tyrannosaurian would overturn the attribution; the trackway's existence stands on the peer-reviewed description and the Denver Museum's 3D scan archive.

title: The K-Pg boundary's microfossil witness: the planktic foraminiferal turnover and the <2,000-year recovery
claim: The planktic foraminiferal turnover at the K-Pg boundary is the extinction's highest-resolution fossil witness. Cretaceous planktic foraminifera vanish at the boundary horizon worldwide, and the first new Paleocene species — Parvularugoglobigerina eugubina, the base of Biochron P0 — appear within thousands of years of the impact: Lowery et al. 2026's 3He recalibration at six boundary sites gives Biochron P0 a duration of 3.5–11.1 kyr (average 6.4 kyr) and puts the first new species under 2,000 years after the Chicxulub impact — replacing the long-accepted ~30 kyr estimate that assumed constant sedimentation across the boundary. The selectivity is real and mechanistic: Rui Ying et al. 2026's EcoGENIE model of the first 100 post-impact years reproduces the fossil pattern — large forams and zooplankton die, small phytoplankton and mixotrophs survive — with impact-driven darkness plus body-size-dependent extinction thresholds doing the work.
place: K-Pg boundary global — stratotype El Kef, Tunisia (plus the six 2026 3He sites spanning Europe, North Africa, the Gulf of Mexico)
grade_reason: Multiple independent boundary sections worldwide record the foram turnover at the horizon; the recovery-timing sub-claim rests on one 2026 peer-reviewed paper (six sites, independent chronometer) — CORROBORATED, not VERIFIED; the mechanistic selectivity claim is single-model, fenced accordingly.
earliest_attestation: The boundary clay itself — Cretaceous planktic forams absent above it; Parvularugoglobigerina eugubina first appears centimeters above the horizon

sources.ref: Lowery, Bralower et al. 2026, Geology 54(3):285–288, DOI 10.1130/G53313.1 — 'New species evolved within a few thousand years of the Chicxulub Impact': 3He sedimentation-rate recalibration at six K-Pg sites; Biochron P0 = 3.5–11.1 kyr (avg 6.4 kyr), first new planktic foram species <2 kyr post-impact; up to 10 new species within Zone P0 (taxonomy varies); the old ~30 kyr estimate assumed constant sedimentation, shown to be invalid across the cataclysm

Rui Ying et al. 2026, Nature, DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-10541-4 — 'Ocean environmental and plankton community responses to abrupt K-Pg climate change within a century (100 years) of the Chicxulub impact': EcoGENIE global ocean ecosystem model; size-dependent extinction rule reproduces the fossil pattern (large forams/zooplankton die, small phytoplankton/mixotrophs survive); darkness + body-size thresholds as the coupled driver. A model, fenced — reproduces, does not attest

The boundary horizon's foram turnover is textbook paleontology: the planktic foram extinction is the primary biostratigraphic marker of the K-Pg boundary (Zone P0 defined by the extinction of Cretaceous species and the first appearance of Parvularugoglobigerina eugubina) — the micropaleontological discipline's standard reference

competing_hypotheses: Keller's extended-decline reading: planktic forams decline below the ejecta layer at multiple sites, interpreted as Deccan-driven stress before the impact (the credentialed-minority case, carried on evt-kpg-extinction-002)

The Signor-Lipps effect: the apparent abruptness of a horizon is partly an observer artifact — the last observed fossil predates the true last occurrence; the turnover's sharpness is read at the limit of sampling
The new-species count within Zone P0 (as many as 10) is taxonomic: which forms count as distinct species varies among researchers (Lowery et al. 2026, stated in the paper)
The Ying et al. 2026 result is a model simulation (EcoGENIE, first 100 years), not a fossil observation — it reproduces the pattern; it does not independently attest it
falsifiability: If Cretaceous planktic forams were shown to cross the boundary in substantial numbers (not as reworked fossils), or if the 3He cosmic-dust-flux calibration underpinning the 2026 timing is shown to vary with the solar system dust input at the boundary, the timing claim reopens.

title: The rock that fell: end-Cretaceous extinction
claim: 66.04 million years ago an asteroid 10–15 km wide struck Chicxulub (Yucatan, 21.40°N 89.52°W), ending the non-avian dinosaurs and ~75% of species. Ruthenium isotopes (Fischer-Gödde et al. 2024) identify a carbonaceous-type impactor from beyond Jupiter; nickel isotopes (Makhatadze et al. 2026) narrow it to a CO (Ornans-class) chondrite. The kill-mechanism evidence has shifted from sulfur aerosols toward fine silicate dust (Senel et al. 2023; Johnson et al. 2026). Deccan Traps volcanism is the main competing cause (Keller camp, 2025 book) — current peer-reviewed consensus holds the impact as the trigger and main driver, Deccan a contributing stressor.
place: Chicxulub, Yucatan Peninsula, Mexico
grade_reason: Independent lines converge: global iridium layer, shocked quartz, impact spherules at 50+ boundary sites, a ~180 km crater drilled and dated to the boundary, and isotope fingerprints of the impactor — all coincident with the extinction horizon.
earliest_attestation: Global K-Pg boundary clay; Chicxulub crater (identified Hildebrand et al. 1991); IODP Expedition 364 peak-ring core (2016)

sources.ref: Alvarez, Alvarez, Asaro & Michel 1980, Science 208:1095–1108 (global iridium anomaly; impactor 10 ± 4 km)
Hildebrand et al. 1991, Geology 19:867–871 (Chicxulub crater: ~180 km, ~1 km buried under Yucatán)
Morgan et al. 2016, Science 354:878–882 (IODP Expedition 364: peak-ring shocked granite uplifted from 8–11 km; gypsum vaporized)
Fischer-Gödde et al. 2024, Science 385:752–756 (Ru isotopes: carbonaceous-type asteroid from beyond Jupiter; comet ruled out)
Makhatadze et al. 2026, Science Advances (Ni isotopes: CO chondrite — one of the rarest meteorite classes)

Keller 2025, The Last Extinction (Diversion Books) — the credentialed minority's Deccan-as-primary case, stated fairly

Baker & Casadevall 2026, PNAS (pre-impact fungal spike — carried via secondary coverage of the May 2026 PNAS paper; fenced: the authors' own reading is ecological stress, not an alternative extinction mechanism)

Rui Ying et al. 2026, Nature, DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-10541-4 — EcoGENIE first-100-years model: size-dependent extinction (large forams/zooplankton die, small phytoplankton/mixotrophs survive); impact-driven darkness + body-size thresholds as the coupled driver. A model — reproduces the fossil pattern, does not attest it

sources.citation: Chiarenza, Mannion et al. 2026, Science Advances (published 21 Oct 2026) — UCL: >7,000 fossils, 400+ living+extinct species, 52 palaeoclimate reconstructions over 245 Myr; crocodylomorphs tracked warm climates throughout (thermal niche conservatism); post-impact climate simulations show tropical/subtropical refugia stayed suitable for crocs under all but the most extreme scenarios, while suitable climates for non-avian dinosaurs shrank far more drastically — the selectivity companion to the extinction record
sources.note: Chained 2026-10-22 (II.8 tenth pass, ep900) — peer-reviewed primary paper via press citation; explains who survived, not whether the impact happened; grade-neutral per the Turin-shroud precedent

competing_hypotheses: Deccan Traps volcanism as the primary driver (Keller camp: forams decline below the ejecta layer at multiple sites; 2025 book; gas-release timing vs. lava volume genuinely unresolved)
Dinosaur diversity already in long-term decline before impact (Sakamoto et al. 2016; contested — Dean et al. 2025 attributes the signal to North American rock-availability bias)
Exact kill-mechanism sequence (heat vs. darkness vs. dust vs. sulfur) — actively being revised 2023–2026 toward silicate dust

Pre-impact ecological stress 30,000–10,000 years before the boundary (Baker & Casadevall 2026, PNAS — pre-impact fungal-abundance spike in three boundary sections, carried via secondary coverage of the May 2026 PNAS paper; does not contest the impact as the extinction driver, proposes a stressed world at arrival)
falsifiability: If the iridium layer, shocked quartz, and spherules were shown to sit stratigraphically above or below the extinction horizon rather than coincident with it, the impact-extinction link would reopen

title: Infernogallus jamesi — the 'hell chicken' and its first complete skull (Hell Creek, 2026)
claim: A new caenagnathid species, Infernogallus jamesi ('hell chicken'), described in Nature Communications 2026 from the Hell Creek Formation (~66 Ma), preserves the first nearly complete skull ever found for the caenagnathid group of toothless, beaked, birdlike theropods — a 26-pound (12-kg) turkey-sized animal whose jaw mechanics point toward a fruit-eating diet, widening the documented dietary range of late-Cretaceous feathered dinosaurs at the K-Pg boundary.
place: Hell Creek Formation, Montana / South Dakota / North Dakota
grade_reason: Peer-reviewed Nature Communications description with the first nearly complete caenagnathid skull (a genuine completeness milestone for a group whose delicate skeletons rarely fossilize); withheld from VERIFIED because the species rests on one specimen and the diet is a mechanics-based inference.
earliest_attestation: The fossil itself — ROM VP 65050, excavated from the Hell Creek Formation; described in print 2026 (Nature Communications 2026, DOI 10.1038/s41467-026-78343-w)

sources.ref: Nature Communications 2026, DOI 10.1038/s41467-026-78343-w — Infernogallus jamesi (ROM VP 65050): first nearly complete caenagnathid skull; 12-kg turkey-sized; Hell Creek ~66 Ma; jaw mechanics consistent with frugivory (as reported in the Oct 2026 press cycle)

Phys.org, 14 October 2026 — 'Toothless 'hell chicken' dinosaur may have had a taste for fruit' (caenagnathid context; skull completeness as the research unlock; ~66 Ma; toothless beak and slender body)

competing_hypotheses: The fruit-eating inference is biomechanical interpretation of the new skull's jaw mechanics, not preserved stomach contents — diet-by-mechanics is one inferential step
A single new species widens the group's documented dietary range; it does not establish that caenagnathids as a whole were frugivores
The 'peaceful herbivore vs fearsome predator' press framing is a narrative compression; the animal's ecological role is inferred from jaw mechanics and size, not observed behavior
falsifiability: A re-examination reassigning the skull to an existing caenagnathid taxon, or biomechanical re-analysis contradicting the jaw-mechanics dietary inference, would downgrade the species or the diet claim; the first-complete-skull finding stands on the specimen's own completeness.

title: The Cambrian explosion: the fossil record's rapid animal diversification, ~541–520 Ma
claim: The fossil record shows a geologically rapid diversification of animal body plans in the early Cambrian, ~541–520 million years ago: most animal phyla first appear in Cambrian strata, preserved in exceptional soft-bodied detail across multiple independent localities worldwide — the Burgess Shale (Canada, 1909, ~508 Ma), Chengjiang (China, 1984, ~518 Ma), Sirius Passet (North Greenland, ~518 Ma), Doushantuo/Weng'an (China), and now the Huayuan biota (China, 2026, ~512 Ma, post-Sinsk extinction). The Cambrian base is fixed at the Fortunian GSSP, Fortune Head, Newfoundland (541 Ma). The small shelly fossils mark the boundary interval. The 'explosion' is a fossil-record pattern; whether it was a biological radiation or a taphonomic unveiling is the live dispute.
place: Fortune Head, Newfoundland (Fortunian GSSP); the Lagerstätten span Canada, China, Greenland
grade_reason: The diversification pattern in the fossil record is multiply attested: five independent Lagerstätten across three continents plus the small shelly fossil record, the Fortunian GSSP, and the 2026 Huayuan and myllokunmingid additions. Held at CORROBORATED, not VERIFIED: the pattern is observed, but the central interpretive claim — biological explosion vs. taphonomic unveiling — is actively disputed by the 2026 evidence (Durbin et al. clocks, Dunn et al. Ediacaran complex animals).
earliest_attestation: Charles Doolittle Walcott's 1909 Burgess Shale discoveries, Stephen Jay Gould's 'Wonderful Life' (1989) for the explosion narrative; the Fortunian GSSP ratified 2007.

sources.ref: Fortunian GSSP, Fortune Head, Newfoundland (ratified 2007) — the Cambrian base at 541 Ma
Walcott 1909 + the Burgess Shale (~508 Ma, British Columbia) — the original soft-bodied Lagerstätte

Hou Xianguang 1984 + the Chengjiang biota (~518 Ma, Yunnan) — the earliest chordate Myllokunmingia; 2026 Nature paper: myllokunmingids carried four camera-type eyes (Xu Xing, Cong Peiyun et al., reported by University of Leicester, Jan 2026)
Sirius Passet biota (~518 Ma, North Greenland) — the northernmost Cambrian Lagerstätte

Han Zeng et al., Nature, Jan 2026 — the Huayuan biota (~512 Ma): 90+ new species, 153 species total, deep-water refuge 1.5 Myr after the Sinsk extinction; Helmetia and Surusicaris shared with Burgess Shale; fossil pelagic tunicates date the ocean carbon pump to the Cambrian (reported Quanta Magazine, May 2026)

Durbin, Anderson, Briggs et al. 2026, Science Advances (doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeg6289) — the taphonomy challenge: the Kheseen Biota (Mongolia) is as well-preserved as Weng'an but contains no animals despite their known existence elsewhere; the Weng'an absence-inference collapses; Tonian-calibrated clocks push animal origins to 800–700 Ma. MODEL, fenced: a clock inference, not an observation (evt-animal-origins-molecular-clock-2026-001)

First-pass review 2026-10-18 (via #535 Dr. Stian Viken — The Explosion Reader): CORROBORATED assigned — the timeline's first Cambrian-explosion record; the fossil-record pattern graded, the interpretation carried as live dispute; no prior cambrian record existed on disk

Swiss Journal of Palaeontology (2026, via scienmag Oct 2026) — Kaotaia globosa (~500 Ma, Kaili Biota, Guizhou): 145 specimens across nearly the full post-embryonic sequence; a head-to-tail increasing growth gradient governing trunk segmentation — Cambrian developmental biology as a measured mechanism

Second-pass review 2026-10-18 (via #544 Dr. Sigrid Aas — The Burrow Reader): CORROBORATED held — no supersession; the Oct-2026 Cambrian press cycle (Yujingia, Kaotaia) adds soft-bodied and developmental exhibits to the pattern without resolving the explosion-vs-unveiling interpretation dispute (the II.7 pattern: chain strengthened, grades held); fenced: the bioscience.com.pk 'Youti yuanshi' 520-Ma larva-brain piece — aggregator only, primary Nature reference unverified, not counted as evidence

Chen, Lirong et al. 2026, Proc. R. Soc. B (doi:10.1098/rspb.2026.1709) — Polyostiosphaera operculata gen. et sp. nov. (Kuanchuanpu Biota, early Cambrian, South China): phosphatized multicellular algae with plug-like opercula sealing apertures over an inner reproductive cell cluster (micro-CT); 'Was the Cambrian explosion merely an explosion of animals?' — the primary-producer complexity exhibit; ECOSYSTEM CONTEXT, not an animal-diversification exhibit; grade-neutral (Turin-shroud precedent)

Song, Baopeng et al. 2026, Nature (3 June 2026, doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10590-9) — High-fidelity modular skeletons authenticate a Cambrian origin for Bryozoa: Protomelission gatehousei + Dayingomelission hexaclitia gen. et sp. nov. (Xiannüdong Formation, ~520 Ma) with phosphatized soft tissues (styles, annular muscles, membranous sacs, ring septa) in modular skeletons; crown-group stenolaemates. Bryozoa was the last major animal phylum without a Cambrian representative — the gap is now closed, and the phylum was already diversifying during the radiation (the authors place the origin possibly pre-Cambrian). Grade-neutral: confirms the CORROBORATED pattern more completely; appended 2026-10-23 (I.7 fourteenth pass, ep954, Turin-shroud precedent)

competing_hypotheses: Abrupt biological radiation: the Gould 'Wonderful Life' reading — most phyla genuinely originate in the early Cambrian, with the pre-Cambrian world nearly empty of animals.

Deep origins + preservation artifact: animal lineages diverged hundreds of Myr earlier (molecular clocks, now revived to 800–700 Ma by Durbin et al. 2026); early animals were small, soft-bodied, and unpreservable — the Cambrian is when hard parts and Burgess-type Lagerstätten make them visible, not when they evolve (evt-animal-origins-molecular-clock-2026-001).

Ediacaran-to-Cambrian continuum: complex triploblastic animals with mouths, anuses, burrowing, and three-dimensional lives already existed at 539 Ma (Dunn et al. 2026) — the boundary is a transition, not a starting gun (evt-jiangchuan-ediacaran-complex-2026-001).
Environmental trigger: the Shuram oxygenation excursion and related oxygen rises enabled larger, active body plans — the environment made the explosion possible rather than inventing the animals.
falsifiability: A well-documented pre-Cambrian assemblage of diverse, clearly animal body-fossils (not traces, not contested microfossils) would collapse the 'explosion' as a biological timing claim; the fossil-record pattern itself would only fall if the Lagerstätten's ages or taxonomic assignments were systematically wrong.

title: Yujingia glutenotunica (2026): the tentacled ancestor that killed the burrowing-worm reading
claim: The 2026 Current Biology paper by Kaiyue He, Degan Shu, Graham Mussini and colleagues describes Yujingia glutenotunica, a ~518-million-year-old fossil from the Maotianshan Shales (Yunnan, China — the Chengjiang biota), interpreted as close to the last common ancestor of the ambulacrarians (modern starfish, sea urchins, and acorn worms). The 8–22 mm animal carried two sets of appendages: feather-like feeding tentacles that captured suspended particles, and a second set for temporary seabed anchoring — an active particle-feeding lifestyle. The paper's central argument: this contradicts the long-standing hypothesis that the ambulacrarian common ancestor was a burrowing worm that filtered food through its throat and gill openings. The authors (incl. Degan Shu, Northwest University) frame it as evidence that ecology — the chordate branch streamlining for movement, the ambulacrarian branch anchoring and specializing for particle feeding — drove the two deuterostome lineages onto divergent body plans.
place: Maotianshan Shales, Yunnan Province, China (Chengjiang biota)
grade_reason: Peer-reviewed primary (Current Biology 2026) with multiple independent press corroborations of the same paper (Cambridge press release, phys.org, scitechdaily, scienmag, geologypage) — the anatomy is photographed and described; the 'last common ancestor' placement is carried as the authors' inference, fenced as interpretation. Held at CORROBORATED, not VERIFIED: a new species from a few specimens makes one paper, and the tree position is an inference, not a second observation.
earliest_attestation: He et al., Current Biology (2026), doi:10.1016/j.cub.2026.08.053; University of Cambridge press material, Sept 2026.

sources.ref: He et al., Current Biology (2026), doi:10.1016/j.cub.2026.08.053 — 'Cambrian fossils illuminate the ambulacrarian common ancestor' (Yujingia glutenotunica, ~518 Ma, Maotianshan Shales)

University of Cambridge press material (Sept 2026), reprinted via geologypage.com (Oct 7, 2026) — Mussini: ecology drove the lineages onto divergent paths; Shu: Yujingia connects primitive tentacle-bearing animals with modern echinoderms and hemichordates
phys.org (Sep 16, 2026) — the Maotianshan Shales' soft-body preservation window: one of the handful of sites where soft Cambrian anatomy survives

Second-pass review 2026-10-18 (via #544 Dr. Sigrid Aas — The Burrow Reader): CORROBORATED assigned — peer-reviewed primary with photographed anatomy; the ancestor placement fenced as tree inference; note: the reading it kills (the burrowing-worm ancestor) is a body-fossil answer to what was partly a trace-fossil question — the Burrow Reader's lane

competing_hypotheses: The burrowing-worm ancestor (the prior hypothesis): the ambulacrarian common ancestor was a worm living in seafloor burrows, filtering food passively through gills or pharynx — the reading Yujingia's tentacles contradict, but the burial position and anchoring appendages keep some version of a benthic ancestor alive.

The tentaculate ancestor (the 2026 paper's reading): active particle-feeding with specialized appendages is ancestral; skeletons and the radial body plan are later specializations of already-feeding animals.

The phylogenetic placement is the claim's load-bearing joint: 'close to the last common ancestor' is a tree inference from a handful of fossils; if Yujingia nests elsewhere in the deuterostome tree, the ecological narrative re-anchors but the tentacle anatomy still stands as an observation.
falsifiability: Re-examination showing the 'feeding tentacles' are taphonomic artifacts or misidentified structures, or a phylogenetic re-analysis nesting Yujingia outside the ambulacrarian stem, would collapse the ancestor claim; the observed anatomy (two appendage sets, tentaculate feeding structures, 8–22 mm size range) is the photographic evidence.

title: Herugavialis cairensis (2026) — the crocodile in the Sphinx's stone
claim: A new genus of ancient crocodile, Herugavialis cairensis, was identified in 2026 from fossils in the Mokattam Formation — the same Middle Eocene (~45 million-year-old) limestone from which the Great Sphinx of Giza was carved. The reclassification (Burke et al., Royal Society Open Science, 7 Oct 2026) moves a 1920s skull (Müller 1927, 'Tomistoma cairense') into its own genus via CT re-analysis; the genus name honors Heru (Horus), after the coincidence that the skull — like the Sphinx — is missing the tip of its snout.
place: Gebel Mokattam, east of Cairo, Egypt (the formation the Sphinx was carved from)
grade_reason: Peer-reviewed taxonomic revision in Royal Society Open Science by an international team (UK, Sweden, Germany, Egypt), based on CT re-examination of museum specimens with the diagnostic characters stated — independent secondary attestation via CNN, The Watchers, and others within days. The genus call is the authors' conclusion; the fossil-in-the-formation fact is multiply attested.
earliest_attestation: Burke, P. et al. 2026, Royal Society Open Science (published 7 Oct 2026); specimen collected from Gebel Mokattam in the 1920s, described by Lorenz Müller in 1927.

sources.ref: Burke, P. et al. 2026, Royal Society Open Science (7 Oct 2026) — the Herugavialis cairensis paper: CT re-analysis of the 1920s Mokattam skull, new genus, named for Heru/Horus after the missing-snout coincidence

CNN 2026-10-06: 'Scientists name ancient crocodile species found in rock that built the Great Sphinx' — Paul Burke (Swedish Museum of Natural History) and Philip Mannion (UCL) as co-leads; 'one of the six species of gharials that we see in the Mediterranean across a 43 million year period'

The Watchers 2026-10: 'Crocodilian fossil from the Sphinx's rock formation reveals a different evolutionary history' — the Müller 1927 Tomistoma classification history and the CT-driven reclassification

competing_hypotheses: The original Müller 1927 reading: Tomistoma cairense — the skull belonged with the false gharial lineage on superficial resemblance (later questioned, exact position uncertain)

The Burke et al. 2026 reading: CT of internal skull anatomy shows sufficient differences from Tomistoma to warrant a new genus — a separate, relatively early branch of gavials, one of six Mediterranean gharial species across 66–23 Ma

The popular confusion to fence: the fossil dates the LIMESTONE, not the carving — a 45-million-year-old rock does not make a 45-million-year-old Sphinx; the monument's date still rests on the 4th-Dynasty evidence lines (radiocarbon, ceramics, inscriptions)
falsifiability: A published phylogenetic re-analysis returning the specimen to Tomistoma, or demonstration that the CT characters used are within Tomistoma's variation, would revise the genus call.

title: The contested Nuvvuagittuq microfossils
claim: Hematite tubes, filaments, and knobs in jasper of the Nuvvuagittuq Supracrustal Belt (Quebec) are microfossils of iron-metabolizing bacteria that lived 3.77–4.28 billion years ago near seafloor hydrothermal vents.
place: Nuvvuagittuq Supracrustal Belt, northern Quebec (Hudson Bay east coast)
grade_reason: Published in Nature (2017) and Science Advances (2022) with a follow-up structure no known abiotic process reproduces; but named skeptics dispute both the biogenicity and the age, and the host-belt chronology is actively being revised. Attested, single-source lineage, contested.
earliest_attestation: Dodd et al. 2017, Nature (hematite tubes as microfossils); Papineau et al. 2022, Science Advances (tree-like stem, metabolic by-products)

sources.ref: Dodd et al. 2017, Nature — hematite tubes/filaments/knobs in NSB jasper as iron-oxidizing microfossils, 3.77–4.28 Ga; Bower: 'I am not convinced the structures are biogenic'
Papineau et al. 2022, Science Advances — cm-scale tree-like hematite stem with parallel branches, hundreds of distorted ellipsoids, metabolic by-products consistent with Fe/S/CO2 metabolism

O'Neil et al. 2025, Science (June 26, 2025) — dual Sm–Nd dating of crosscutting Nuvvuagittuq intrusions to 4.16 Ga; NEW record evt-nuvvuagittuq-belt-oldest-rocks-2025-001 CORROBORATED (the belt as Earth's oldest dated rocks); the 2026 coverage explicitly fences the result: 'establishes a geological clock and ordering, not a fossil, metabolic product or inhabited ecosystem' — the clock is settled, the tubes' biogenicity is not.

competing_hypotheses: The structures are abiotic: hydrothermal fluid flow or metamorphic deformation produced the tubes and filaments (named skeptics: Dina Bower, NASA Goddard; Kelly)
The age is wrong: assigning 3.77–4.28 Ga to the fossil-bearing features is disputed — some argue the structures could be younger than 2.7 Ga in such complex metamorphic rocks
The Nuvvuagittuq age itself is being re-measured: a June 2025 Science study (Sm–Nd, two methods) dated belt intrusions to 4.16 Ga — the host-rock chronology is still moving
falsifiability: If the structures are shown to be metamorphic artifacts, or the host features dated reliably below ~3.5 Ga, the claim as stated falls

title: The oldest rocks on Earth — Nuvvuagittuq at 4.16 Ga (the clock, not the fossil)
claim: The Nuvvuagittuq Supracrustal Belt (northern Quebec) contains the oldest dated rocks on Earth: crosscutting intrusions dated to 4.16 billion years by two independent samarium–neodymium chronometers (O'Neil et al., Science, June 2025), making this the only known intact rock record of the Hadean eon.
place: Nuvvuagittuq Supracrustal Belt, Hudson Bay east coast near Inukjuak, Quebec
grade_reason: Two independent isotopic chronometers converging on the same age in a peer-reviewed Science paper; single-team result on extraordinary-age rocks keeps it at CORROBORATED rather than VERIFIED. The 2026 reporting (ScienceDaily) independently reaffirms the finding and carries the crucial fence: a clock, not a fossil.
earliest_attestation: O'Neil et al. 2025, Science (dual Sm–Nd dating, published June 26, 2025)

sources.ref: O'Neil et al. 2025, Science — dual samarium–neodymium dating of Nuvvuagittuq belt intrusions to 4.16 Ga; the belt's older host rocks must predate the intrusions; Earth's oldest known rocks, the only Hadean rock record

ScienceDaily coverage, August 27, 2026 — reaffirms the 4.16 Ga result; the belt is on Inuit-owned land (Pituvik Landholding Corporation) with restricted access after specimen damage; explicit fence: the paper 'establishes a geological clock and ordering, not a fossil, metabolic product or inhabited ecosystem'

competing_hypotheses: Earlier work had placed belt ages anywhere from ~3.3 to ~4.28 Ga (2008 claim of 4.28 Ga contested); the 2025 study settles the minimum host-rock age via crosscutting intrusions — a rock cut by a 4.16 Ga intrusion must be older than 4.16 Ga
The previous record-holder remains the 4.03 Ga Acasta Gneiss (Northwest Territories) — dethroned by the new measurement

This record is about the ROCKS' age, never the fossils: the 2026 coverage explicitly fences it — 'establishes a geological clock and ordering, not a fossil, metabolic product or inhabited ecosystem' (evt-nuvvuagittuq-microfossils-001 carries the tubes separately, CLAIMED)
falsifiability: An independent chronometer system (e.g. U–Pb on better-constrained phases) returning a significantly younger age for the same intrusions would revise the 4.16 Ga figure; the crosscutting logic itself would need a structural reinterpretation to fall.

title: The contested 3.7 Ga Isua 'stromatolites'
claim: The cone-shaped structures in the 3.7-billion-year-old Isua Greenstone Belt (southwest Greenland) are fossilized microbial stromatolites — life on Earth by 3.7 Ga.
place: Isua supracrustal belt, southwestern Greenland
grade_reason: Single primary paper claims biogenicity; a peer-reviewed Nature reassessment (2018) argues abiotic tectonic deformation is the more plausible explanation; the claimants dispute the sampling; the planned 2019 joint field trip has no published resolution. Contested, not settled.
earliest_attestation: Nutman et al. 2016, Nature (biogenic claim); Allwood et al. 2018, Nature (abiotic reassessment)

sources.ref: Nutman et al. 2016, Nature — cone structures interpreted as stromatolites; four reasons: onlapping sediment, low-temperature dolomite, sedimentary (non-hydrothermal) geochemistry, laminated internal fabric

Allwood et al. 2018, Nature — 3D morphological and geochemical reassessment: structures 'most plausibly explained' by deformation of layered rock under tectonic compression/elongation; no biosignatures found

Allwood/Nutman dispute coverage — Nutman: 'classic comparing-apples-and-oranges scenario' (samples ~0.5 m apart); Allwood's planned joint field trip to settle it; van Zuilen commentary on the outcrop's under-studied geology

Wu & Jiang 2022, Biopetrology 1(2):61-69 — agree the Nutman cones are structural folds (with Zawaski et al. 2020); report two other candidate stromatolite structures with domal/conic laminae, furcation, and discontinuity in the same Isua rocks

October 2026 evidence-state check (third pass): literature search found no peer-reviewed resolution of the Nutman (2016) vs Allwood (2018) sampling dispute; the planned joint field trip has no published outcome; Wu & Jiang 2022's two other Isua candidates have no follow-up found. The 2018 reassessment stands unrebutted in print; Phys.org (Jan 2026) review carries Isua as the contested rival to Strelley Pool.

competing_hypotheses: The structures are tectonic deformation: compressed one way, stretched another, producing stromatolite-mimicking cross-sections in metamorphosed rock (Allwood et al. 2018, Nature)
The two studies sampled different material: Nutman's 'relatively unaltered' patch vs. Allwood's sample <0.5 m from his site — the apples-and-oranges dispute
Wu & Jiang 2022 (Biopetrology) agree the main cones are folds but report two other candidate stromatolite structures in the same Isua rocks — untested claim, no follow-up found
falsifiability: If the biogenicity is demonstrated for the original outcrop (or falsified wholesale), the grade moves — up on independent corroboration, to DEBUNKED as fossils on a demonstrated abiotic mechanism

title: Homo sapiens emerged ~300,000 years ago in Africa
claim: The earliest fossils attributed to Homo sapiens are the Jebel Irhoud (Morocco) remains, dated 315 ± 34 thousand years ago by thermoluminescence — a mosaic of modern facial morphology with an archaic elongated braincase; the evidence now supports a pan-African, gradual emergence rather than a single ~200 ka East African origin.
place: Jebel Irhoud, Morocco (west of Marrakech)
grade_reason: Two independent dating methods (TL on associated flints, ESR/U-series on the Irhoud 3 mandible) plus corroborating fauna and microfauna; the taxon attribution and the emergence model are debated by specialists.
earliest_attestation: Jebel Irhoud fossils, first excavated 1960s, re-excavated and re-dated 2017 (Hublin et al., Nature 2017, doi 10.1038/nature22336; author correction Nature 2018, doi 10.1038/s41586-018-0166-3)

sources.ref: Hublin et al. 2017, Nature 546:289-292, doi 10.1038/nature22336 — new fossils, mosaic morphology, pan-African origin
Richter et al. 2017, Nature 546:293-296, doi 10.1038/nature22335 — thermoluminescence dating 315 ± 34 ka; ESR 286 ± 32 ka
Hublin et al. 2018, Nature 558:E6, doi 10.1038/s41586-018-0166-3 — author correction
Vidal et al. 2022 (Omo Kibish re-dating to 233 ± 22 ka) — the previous 'oldest', now second
Florisbad skull, South Africa (~259 ka), now attributed to H. sapiens on the Irhoud basis

Moraes et al. 2026, Heritage 9(9):369, doi 10.3390/heritage9090369 (13 Sept 2026) — digital facial approximation of the Irhoud composite skull; brain-volume estimate ~1,230 cm³; the 'face' is a five-individual composite from 2017 press-video stills with modern-donor soft tissue (provenance caveat carried)

Jakobsson, Schlebusch et al. 2026, Nature 650(8100):156–163, doi 10.1038/s41586-025-09811-4 — 28 ancient southern-African genomes: ≥200 kyr long-term isolation, deepest split ~310–240 ka, 490 sapiens-specific variants; the genomic anchor for pan-African structured emergence (PubMed 41339558)

competing_hypotheses: Single recent origin ~200 ka in East Africa (the pre-2017 consensus; revised but still held in some textbooks)
The Irhoud hominins are 'protomodern' / highly evolved H. heidelbergensis-grade, not H. sapiens proper (Alison Brooks; Richard Klein's 'protomodern, not modern')
Fully gradual pan-African emergence over ~400 ka with no definable start (current direction of the evidence)
falsifiability: Securely dated fossils with fully modern globular braincases at 400+ ka would push the emergence back; a retraction of the Irhoud dating on stratigraphic grounds would pull it forward.

title: The Bhitardari chert — the oldest directly dated rock with a confirmed biosignature (3.497 Ga)
claim: A carbonaceous chert at Bhitardari (Singhbhum Craton, eastern India) dated 3.497 ± 5 Ma by syn-depositional tuffaceous zircons contains laminated kerogen with biological carbon-isotope depletion (d13C -30.9 per mil) and Raman-confirmed indigenous organics — the tightest radiometric life–age link at ~3.5 Ga.
place: Bhitardari, Singhbhum Craton, eastern India
grade_reason: Peer-reviewed PNAS 2026; four independent lines in one study (field relationships, syn-depositional zircon geochronology, carbon isotopes, Raman) — but a single primary publication awaiting independent replication.
earliest_attestation: Chaudhuri, Harrison et al. 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (August 2026)

sources.ref: Chaudhuri, Harrison et al. 2026, PNAS — Bhitardari banded chert, Singhbhum Craton: eight zircons, four concordant (3497 ± 5 Ma, MSWD 1.2), tuffaceous interpretation; micron-scale alternating carbonaceous/siliceous layers; d13C -30.9 per mil; Raman poorly ordered kerogen; 'to our knowledge, the oldest directly dated rock with a confirmed biosignature'

ScienceAlert 2026-08-20 — lead author Trisrota Chaudhuri (Geological Survey of India): needle-like vs rounded detrital zircon morphology; the embedded-clock distinction; 'life thrived in a chemically extreme world 3.5 billion years ago' (coverage, not a second source)

Phys.org 2026-08 — coverage: stratigraphic relationships + petrographic corroboration of the isotopic value; explicit caveat that independent studies must test whether the zircons truly date deposition and confirm the biological interpretation

competing_hypotheses: The zircons are older detrital grains despite their needle-like morphology, and the age does not date the carbon layer
The d13C depletion is abiotic (Fischer–Tropsch-type or other non-biological fractionation) — the phys.org caveat
The kerogen was introduced later via fractures rather than deposited with the sediment
falsifiability: Independent dating showing the zircons are detrital, or demonstration that the carbon is post-depositional (e.g., migrated kerogen with no stratigraphic control)

title: The Apex chert 'microfossils' are pseudofossils — the 2026 resolution
claim: The filamentous carbon-rich microstructures of the ~3.465 Ga Apex chert (Warrawoona Group, Pilbara, Western Australia), identified by Schopf (1993) as fossil cyanobacteria — until recently accepted as the oldest morphological evidence of life on Earth — are pseudofossils: reorganized carbonaceous matter in hydrothermal chert, not cells.
place: Apex chert, near Marble Bar, Pilbara, Western Australia
grade_reason: Converging independent lines falsify the biogenic interpretation: (1) Brasier et al. 2002, Nature — the fossil-bearing black cherts are hydrothermal feeder-dyke veins cutting across strata, not seafloor beds; shapes/sizes uncharacteristic of cyanobacteria; (2) Wacey/Brasier et al. 2015, PNAS — transmission-electron-microscopy nanoscale maps show the 'microfossils' are stacks of plate-like clay minerals with carbon absorbed on mineral edges (hydrothermal chemistry), lacking the coherent rounded carbon envelopes seen in all authentic microfossils examined with the same technique; (3) Marshall et al. 2026, Nature Geoscience — the microstructures' pale color is incompatible with organic carbon at this metamorphic grade, plus indigeneity analysis; Buick (UW, commentator): the results 'virtually seal the case... that these microstructures are not ancient microfossils of cyanobacteria.' Schopf's promised rebuttal was still unpublished as of October 2026; if it publishes with new evidence, the record reopens per the falsifiability line.
earliest_attestation: Schopf 1993, Science (the cyanobacterial-microfossil claim); closed by Marshall et al. 2026, Nature Geoscience

sources.ref: Schopf 1993, Science 260:640 — eleven species of filamentous prokaryote proposed as authentic Archean microfossils; taken as oldest morphological evidence of life and support for early oxygenic photosynthesis

Brasier et al. 2002, Nature 416:76 — re-mapping of the type material: 'microfossils' sit ~100 m down a hydrothermal dyke complex in metalliferous black/white BaSO4-rich vein cherts; size/shape distribution uncharacteristic of cyanobacteria; reinterpreted as pseudofossils from recrystallizing amorphous-to-spherulitic silica

Wacey, Kilburn, Saunders, Cliff & Brasier 2015, PNAS 112(45):13990 — TEM ultrathin-slice nanoscale maps of size, shape, mineral chemistry and carbon distribution: the Apex structures are branched, tapered worm-like chains of clay-mineral plates with carbon absorbed on edges (chemistry compatible with high-temperature hydrothermal setting); false cellular compartments; no coherent rounded walls — a direct contrast with authentic microfossils examined identically. The late Prof. Brasier's final Apex paper.

Bower et al. (Carnegie Institution, 2016) — Eoleptonema apex re-studied: a cracked quartz grain filled with carbon-rich sheet material, carbon of indeterminate (biological or abiotic) origin but the structure itself not a fossil; 60% of the originally described alleged microfossils found in material younger than the host rock — the indigeneity problem; a new indigeneity test developed

Marshall et al. 2026, Nature Geoscience (online 20 Feb 2026) — 'New study finds apex fossils aren't life': the microstructures' pale color is incompatible with truly organic carbon in rocks of this metamorphic grade ('if they were truly organic, they shouldn't be pale in such metamorphosed rocks' — Buick, UW, commenting); the most important implication 'is that they virtually seal the case that has been building for many years that these microstructures are not ancient microfossils of cyanobacteria' (Buick); Schopf noted he and a colleague had a response in preparation — still unpublished as of Oct 2026. Mars-prospecting caution: Olcott Marshall (KU): if finding convincing evidence for life on early Earth is this hard when we know life exists here, interpreting Mars data demands extra caution.

competing_hypotheses: Schopf's promised 2026 rebuttal to Marshall et al. could reopen the biogenic case if it brings new sub-micrometer evidence — parked pending publication

The carbon's biological origin remains possible even where the structures are pseudofossils (Bower 2016: 'the source of the carbon could have been biological, or abiotic') — carbon biogenicity is a separate, unresolved question from microstructure biogenicity

Authentic Archean microfossils elsewhere (e.g., the Gunflint 1.88 Ga benchmark) are unaffected — the Apex verdict kills one case, not the enterprise (Buick 2026: 'it is still worthwhile searching for Archean microfossils')
falsifiability: Publication of Schopf's prepared response with sub-micrometer evidence of biogenic indigeneity and coherent cell-wall carbon would reopen the record (grade moves up only on that evidence); the current DEBUNKED verdict stands on Brasier 2002 + Wacey 2015 + Marshall 2026.

title: The most widely accepted fossil evidence of life
claim: The oldest widely accepted fossil evidence of life on Earth is the stromatolite reef of the Strelley Pool Chert, Pilbara, Western Australia — layered structures built by microbial communities ~3.43 billion years ago.
place: Strelley Pool Chert, East Pilbara, Western Australia
grade_reason: Multiple independent lines (morphology across tens of km, seven morphologies, growth geometry, cooked organics tied to lamination) published in peer-reviewed literature and independently reported; initial skepticism (Lowe's own doubts, Grotzinger & Rothman 1996) addressed by subsequent work.
earliest_attestation: Lowe 1980 (first description); Allwood et al. 2006, Science (biogenicity case)

sources.ref: Allwood et al. 2006, Science 312:1457 — stromatolite reef facies at Strelley Pool; seven distinct morphologies, growth geometry inconsistent with abiotic processes
Allwood, Grotzinger et al. 2009, Caltech/JPL — organic mat layers contouring the stromatolites edge to edge, Raman-confirmed burial-temperature carbon, mat fragments in storm deposits
New Scientist (2018) — 'the oldest accepted fossils are those from Strelley Pool in the Pilbara region of western Australia ... 3.4 billion years old'

Phys.org, 'How microbial fossils illuminate life's origins' (Jan 2026) — contemporary review: Strelley Pool stromatolites' spatial organization, vertical growth, and internal textures 'consistent with the activity of microbial mats' — 'especially strong candidates for biological origin'; treats Isua 3.7 Ga structures as the contested rival. The 2026 review-consensus state.

Alcheringa review (Oct 2026) — 50 years of microbialite research in Western Australia: Strelley Pool (~3.5 Ga Pilbara) held as the oldest accepted fossil examples; living microbialites at Shark Bay/Lake Clifton under pressure; fossil sites vulnerable to over-collection/degradation (the May 2024 Lake Clifton thrombolite trampling). Review-level synthesis, grade-neutral for the Strelley Pool CORROBORATED standing.

Nerearchaeum marumarumayae (Apr 2026) — Current Biology 10.1016/j.cub.2026.03.041 (Burns, Duggin, Ghosal et al.): first visual evidence of an Asgard archaeon physically interacting with a bacterium via nanotubes, isolated from the modern Shark Bay stromatolite microbial mats — the living analogue of the ancient mats. A model for how the archaeon–bacterium partnership at the root of eukaryogenesis may have looked; organism named with Malgana Traditional Owner consultation. Secondary coverage: phys.org 2026-04-09. Grade-neutral for the Strelley Pool claim (Turin-shroud precedent — strengthens the chain, no supersession)

Wong, Prabhu, Hazen et al. 2025, PNAS 10.1073/pnas.2514534122 (17 Nov 2025) — pyrolysis-GC-MS + supervised machine learning on 406 samples; molecular biosignatures to ~3.3 Ga (Josefsdal Chert, Barberton; Singhbhum Craton 3.51 Ga biogenicity), earliest molecular evidence of photosynthesis ~2.5 Ga (Gamohaan Fm); >90% accuracy biogenic-vs-abiogenic discrimination. Independent detection line at the same horizon as the Strelley Pool morphological record. Grade-neutral for the ~3.43 Ga CLAIMED-free accepted-rung standing (Turin-shroud precedent — strengthens the chain, no supersession)

Alleon et al. (MIT/Sorbonne, reported Sept 2026) — intact Strelley Pool microstructures preserve nitrogen- and oxygen-rich organic molecules only slightly degraded despite exposure to temperatures above 300°C: chemical preservation at Strelley Pool is real, not powdered-sample artifact. Grade-neutral (Turin-shroud precedent) — strengthens the biogenicity case, does not move the grade.

Journal of Microscopy (2026) — near-infrared confocal imaging of far-red photosynthesis (chlorophyll d/f, Halomicronema sp. 'Clifton') in intact Shark Bay microbial mats; modern-analogue photobiology, special issue honoring Guy C. Cox (authors not surfaced in sweep — cited by journal + year, not invented).

competing_hypotheses: Some conical forms could still reflect abiotic evaporative precipitation or chemical garden growth (the Apex Basalt controversy shows how high the bar is)
The 3.7 Ga Isua structures and the Nuvvuagittuq hematite tubes, if biogenic, would push 'earliest' back hundreds of millions of years — both contested
Chemical biosignatures (3.95 Ga Saglek graphite, 4.1 Ga Jack Hills zircon carbon) hint at earlier life but are isotope-only, no fossils, and contested
falsifiability: A demonstrated abiotic mechanism reproducing the full assemblage (seven morphologies, onlap geometry, burial-cooked organics) would collapse the biogenicity case

title: Musango matusadonaensis — Zimbabwe's fifth dinosaur, and the end of the homogeneous southern fauna
claim: A new early sauropodomorph dinosaur species, Musango matusadonaensis, described in 2026 from a partial associated skeleton found on the southern margin of Lake Kariba, Zimbabwe, shows that Late Triassic southern Africa held distinct regional dinosaur communities rather than one homogeneous fauna — a fifth dinosaur named from Zimbabwe, living ~210 million years ago while dinosaurs were diversifying toward Jurassic dominance.
place: Musango Archosaur Site, southern margin of Lake Kariba, Zimbabwe — Pebbly Arkose Formation (approximate regional pin, southern shore)
grade_reason: Peer-reviewed species description in the Journal of Systematic Palaeontology with a stated autapomorphy set, osteohistology, and phylogenetic analysis; withheld from VERIFIED because the taxon rests on one partial specimen without a skull, the sister-taxon support is weak by the authors' own analysis, and no independent replication exists yet.
earliest_attestation: The fossil itself — partial associated skeleton collected from the Musango Archosaur Site, bank of the Nyamasango River near Musango Island, Lake Kariba, Zimbabwe; described in print 2026 (received November 2025, accepted April 2026).

sources.ref: Barrett et al. 2026, Journal of Systematic Palaeontology — 'A new sauropodomorph dinosaur from the Pebbly Arkose Formation (Upper Triassic: Norian) of Kariba, Zimbabwe' (received 28 Nov 2025, accepted 17 Apr 2026; partial associated skeleton: vertebrae, pectoral and pelvic girdle elements, partial fore- and hind limbs; autapomorphies distinct from sympatric Musankwa sanyatiensis; sister-taxon relationship within Unaysauridae with weak support; holotype a small-bodied sub-adult or adult, at least eight years old, growth decelerating)

Natural History Museum, London, Science News, 29 July 2026, James Ashworth — 'Musango: The new Zimbabwean dinosaur discovered from a boat' (fifth dinosaur named from Zimbabwe; ~4.5 m long; same rocks as Musankwa sanyatiensis; ~210 Ma Late Triassic; Barrett: southern Africa was a series of smaller ecosystems, not one fauna; one further undescribed species already in hand)

Phys.org, 10 October 2026, Paul Barrett — 'Zimbabwe's dinosaurs were different from South Africa's: New species offers clues' (bipedal, ~4.5 m, ~220 kg, sub-adult at death; skull not preserved so diet unknown; discovery history: first thought a non-dinosaurian archosaur in the ground, recognized as a dinosaur only after preparation)

competing_hypotheses: The Unaysauridae sister-taxon placement with Musankwa sanyatiensis carries weak phylogenetic support in the describing paper itself — the tree position is provisional, not settled

Diet, skin, and behavior are unpreserved (no skull) — all ecological readings (niche partitioning with Musankwa, waterside life) are inferences from relatives and depositional setting, not direct evidence
The 'distinct regional ecosystems' reading rests on two Zimbabwean taxa plus the wider southern-African record — more taxa from the Pebbly Arkose Formation could revise the faunal picture
falsifiability: A re-examination placing the specimen in Musankwa sanyatiensis or another described taxon, or a revised formation date moving the Pebbly Arkose out of the Norian, would sink the species hypothesis; the 'distinct ecosystems' reading dies if wider sampling shows the same fauna across southern Africa.

title: Drimolen Homo erectus DNH 127 (2026)
claim: In September 2026, a La Trobe-led team published 18 new hominin fossils from Drimolen Main Quarry, South Africa — including DNH 127, the first adult Homo erectus cranial fossil from the site — confirming the species' first appearance in southern Africa at 2.0 million years ago, ~200,000 years earlier than the Dmanisi adults; the same paper documents microevolutionary change in co-occurring Paranthropus robustus (larger teeth and chewing muscles between 2.0 and 1.8 Ma), supporting the subspecies P. robustus ukusa.

grade_reason: Peer-reviewed publication of physical specimens with stratigraphic context, reported independently by multiple science outlets; the specimens are the exhibit.

La Trobe University media release, 30 Sept 2026 (18 new fossils; DNH 127 first adult H. erectus at Drimolen)

SciTechDaily, Oct 2026 — 'Homo erectus Was Outnumbered 10 to One by Another Human Relative' (P. robustus 10:1 ratio at Drimolen)

The 2.0 Ma first-appearance reading depends on the Drimolen deposit dating, which future refinement could shift
