title: Hisarlık is Troy — and the Hittite Wilusa
claim: That the tell at Hisarlık in northwest Anatolia is the Troy of the epic tradition — and the Wilusa of 13th-century BCE Hittite diplomatic texts.
place: Hisarlik (Troy), Tevfikiye, Çanakkale Province, Turkey
grade_reason: Four converging lines: (1) topography — the plain, rivers, and sea at Hisarlık match the Iliad's geography; (2) stratigraphy — a 4,000-year tell with a Late Bronze Age citadel and a burned VIIa; (3) Hittite diplomacy — the Alaksandu treaty (early 13th c. BCE), the Tawagalawa letter, and the Ahhiyawa/Wilusa contention texts, naming people whose names map onto the epic's (Alaksandu/Alexandros); (4) the 1995 Luwian seal — Bronze Age writing found at Troy itself, tying the site to the Hittite sphere. Held below VERIFIED on the named minority dissent (Carpenter; the DOAJ 2024 name-association critique) — honestly carried, not hidden. Convergence, not consensus alone, carries the grade.
earliest_attestation: Schliemann's identification, 1871 — his own claim, refined by every excavator since. The Hittite side: Alaksandu of Wilusa ↔ Alexandros/Paris (equated 1911), Wilusa ↔ (W)Ilios (1924), Taruwisa ↔ Troy (1924), Appaliunas (a Wilusian god) ↔ Apollo (1931).

sources.ref: Dartmouth Aegean Prehistory, Lesson 27 — 'Blegen, Dörpfeld, Schliemann, and many others' accept Hisarlık as Homeric Troy; Carpenter's arguments against noted; Troy VIIa 'perhaps the most likely candidate for the city of Priam'; the layer table (Troy 0 3600–3000 BCE through Troy IX 85 BCE–500 CE).

Penn Gazette / C. Brian Rose (2004): the 13th-century BCE Hittite tablet describing the alliance between the Hittites and 'Aleksandu (Alexandros), the ruler of Wilusa' — Alexandros being another name for Paris; other tablets frame Troy/Ilion as a bone of contention between the Hittites and the Ahhiyawans (Mycenaean Greeks); the 1995 Luwian-inscribed seal from Troy — 'the only piece of writing that has come down to us from Bronze Age Troy.'

Popular Archaeology interview with Dr. Paul Cartledge — Hittite documents of the 13th century referring to Wilusa ('which sounds like the Greeks' (W)Ilion'), Ahhijawa ↔ Achaea, Aleksandu ↔ Alexandros; excavated at Hattusa (Boğazköy) and deciphered.

DOAJ/Gephyra: 'Is Troy the Hittite Wilusa?' — the dissenting paper: the link 'is based on little other than name associations,' none of the equations 'cogent'; the stronghold 'was neither Troy nor the capital of Wilusa.' Carried as the named minority position.
Wikipedia, 'Hissarlik' / 'Late Bronze Age Troy' — the stratigraphic sequence and the scholarly consensus on the identification.

competing_hypotheses: The name-association critique (DOAJ 2024): the Wilusa=(W)Ilios, Alaksandu=Alexandros, Taruwisa=Troy, Appaliunas=Apollo equations rest on phonetic similarity, not proof; the stronghold was 'neither Troy nor the capital of Wilusa'
Carpenter's geographic argument against the Hisarlık localization (carried in the Dartmouth lesson as the standing objection)
The VIh preference: a vocal minority holds Troy VIh (earthquake-destroyed, grander) rather than VIIa as Homer's city
falsifiability: A securely provenienced Hittite text fixing Wilusa's location elsewhere (with excavated confirmation) would collapse the identification; a Troy-side inscription naming the city (W)Ilion in Linear B or Luwian would push it to VERIFIED.

title: The chewing sticks — humanity's first toothbrushes
claim: Chewed twigs with frayed, brush-like ends were used to clean teeth in Mesopotamia by ~3500 BCE and in Egypt by ~3000 BCE; the practice continues today as the miswak (Salvadora persica).
place: Southern Mesopotamia (Babylonian context)
grade_reason: Multiply attested across archaeological finds and the continuous living practice (miswak), but the precise 3500 BCE figure is a widely repeated convention rather than a single excavated-and-dated object.
earliest_attestation: Babylonian use, conventionally ~3500 BCE; Egyptian tomb finds containing tooth sticks, c. 3000 BCE.

sources.ref: Dental-history convention (Central Coast Dental Care; Sure Dental; Scribd 'Ancient Dental Hygiene Practices' citing Journal of Orofacial Research 2012): chew sticks from ~3500 BCE Mesopotamia; Egyptian tomb finds from 3000 BCE
Gurudath et al., Journal of Orofacial Research 2012: the Mesopotamian royal tomb toilet set c. 3000 BCE with golden toothpick; Babylonian chewing-stick origins
Dr. Scott Swank, National Museum of Dentistry (Living on Earth, 2002): the chew stick dates from Babylonian times; still used in parts of Africa and rural America

competing_hypotheses: The 3500 BCE figure is a rounded convention; the securely datable end of the practice is the Egyptian tomb material c. 3000 BCE
falsifiability: Demonstration that the earliest 'chew stick' reports are all 19th/20th-century ethnographic projections with no ancient material or textual leg.

title: The clay envelopes of Uruk, c. 3500-3100 BCE
claim: Hollow clay balls (bullae) enclosing accounting tokens, sealed and seal-impressed, were in use in Uruk-period Mesopotamia c. 3500-3100 BCE as tamper-proof containers of recorded information — the envelope's oldest known ancestor.
place: Uruk (Warka), southern Iraq — the type-site region; examples from multiple Mesopotamian sites
grade_reason: The objects exist in museum collections (~150 recovered); their token contents and seal impressions are documented; the accounting function is the scholarly consensus reading of Schmandt-Besserat's catalogue, held below VERIFIED on the inferential link between form and function.
earliest_attestation: The bullae themselves, Late Uruk-period archaeological deposits, c. 3500-3100 BCE.

sources.ref: ThoughtCo — 'Clay Tokens: Neolithic Seeds of Mesopotamian Writing' (Late Uruk bullae 3500-3100 BCE, ~150 recovered, stamped exteriors, pinched-shut closures)
Schmandt-Besserat, D. — 'An Archaic Recording System and the Origin of Writing' (SMS 1, 1977)
Woods, C. (Oriental Institute) — Royal Ontario Museum lecture on the clay balls as data-storage devices; Nuzi bulla with 49 pebbles + sheep-and-goats contract (archaeology.wiki summary)
MacGinnis / Ziyaret Tepe project — tokens sealed in bullae as certified records from the late fourth millennium (Live Science summary)

competing_hypotheses: Schmandt-Besserat's token-to-writing sequence is a hypothesis, not a closed case — the bullae's exact function is inferred from form and context, and some scholars weigh other accounting roles
The ~150 recovered examples are a survival sample; most bullae were probably broken open in antiquity (their contents' whole point)
The analogy 'envelope' is modern scholarly shorthand — no evidence the makers thought of them as correspondence wrappers; the manifest-not-message reading is an interpretation
falsifiability: Stratigraphic or typological re-dating placing all known bullae after the first proto-cuneiform tablets would break the sequence; proof the tokens were votive rather than accounting would break the function reading.

title: 'The envelope was invented in 1840' — DEBUNKED
claim: The telling that 'the envelope was invented in 1840' (by Edwin Hill and Warren de la Rue, or in the year of the Penny Post).
place: London — where the 1840s telling was born
grade_reason: Three independent pre-1840 envelope lines kill the invention date: (1) clay bullae c. 3500-3100 BCE; (2) centuries of lettersheets and letterlocking — folded, secured letters sent without envelopes — per the Library of Congress; (3) a pre-1840 handmade-envelope trade, with George Wilson's 1840 tiling patent itself presuming envelope-making was already a going process to improve.
earliest_attestation: The 1840s British envelope-machine publicity (Hill/de la Rue patent 1845) as the moment the invention story crystallized around the machine.

sources.ref: Library of Congress, Inside Adams — 'Opening the Envelope' (letterlocking used alongside handmade envelopes; envelopes 'have been around for centuries'; Hill patent 1845)
Baylor University, Texas Collection — 'envelope history' (pre-1840s world of cut-and-fold-your-own; George Wilson 1840 tiling patent; Hill & de la Rue 1845 steam machine; Crystal Palace 1851)
ThoughtCo — Clay Tokens (bullae 3500-3100 BCE) — the sealed-container line

competing_hypotheses: The scoped, honest version of the claim — 'the first machine-made envelope patent dates to 1845' — is true and graded separately (evt-envelope-machine-hill-delarue-1845-001)

Hill and de la Rue's defenders could argue 'invention' here means the standardized diamond-sheet gummed envelope as a commercial product — but the tellings in circulation use 'invented the envelope' without that scoping
falsifiability: The debunk could only be revived if the clay bullae, the lettersheets, and the pre-1840 handmade-envelope trade all proved modern — an archaeological impossibility on three independent lines.

title: The invention of cuneiform writing
claim: Cuneiform writing was invented in southern Mesopotamia (Uruk), with the earliest proto-cuneiform tablets dated c. 3400-3200 BCE — the earliest known true writing system.
place: Uruk
grade_reason: The tablets physically exist in stratified, dated contexts; 'earliest writing' is a genuine tie with Egypt's Abydos U-j tags (both c. 3400-3200 BCE, both administrative), not a settled Sumerian first.
earliest_attestation: Proto-cuneiform tablets from Uruk, Uruk IV-III strata (c. 3400-3200 BCE)

sources.ref: Uruk IV/III proto-cuneiform tablets (CDLI corpus)
Denise Schmandt-Besserat, token-to-tablet research (secondary analysis)
Abydos tomb U-j ivory tags, c. 3400-3200 BCE (Dreyer 1998; contested readings by Kahl 2003 — the inventory-tag function and date range hold)
Robert K. Englund, 'Accounting in proto-cuneiform' (CDLI): Uruk archives are ~85% administrative; Uruk IV tablets all from Uruk, discarded as refuse once checked
Karenleigh A. Overmann, 'Beyond Writing', Cambridge Archaeological Journal 26(2) (2016): the complex-token-to-pictograph derivation 'remains the most controversial aspect of this hypothesis'

Silvia Ferrara, Kathryn Kelley, Mattia Cartolano et al., Antiquity (Nov 2024): designs on pre-literate cylinder seals (c. 4400 BCE onward) identified as graphic-and-contextual precursors of proto-cuneiform signs (e.g. ZATU639) for pottery/textile transport — a parallel origin line for sign shapes alongside Schmandt-Besserat's token sequence

competing_hypotheses: Cuneiform developed from clay-token accounting systems (Schmandt-Besserat) — but split honestly: the plain-token-to-bullae-to-numerical-tablet lineage is the secure half; the claim that complex tokens became the pictographic signs 'remains the most controversial aspect of this hypothesis' (Overmann 2016)
Egyptian hieroglyphs developed independently and nearly simultaneously (Abydos U-j, c. 3400-3200 BCE — a contested tie, not a Sumerian trophy), so there is no single 'first writing'
Writing was invented once and diffused (largely rejected for Uruk/Abydos)
falsifiability: Securely dated writing anywhere predating Uruk IV by centuries, or proof the Uruk tablets are administrative tokens without linguistic content

title: Ötzi's 61 tattoos — the world's oldest preserved (3370–3100 BCE)
claim: Ötzi the Tyrolean Iceman — the naturally mummified man found in the Ötztal Alps in 1991, dated 3370–3100 BCE — bears 61 tattoos (thin parallel black lines and crosses on the spine, left calf, right instep, ankle joints, left wrist, and torso), making him the oldest tattooed human remains discovered to date.
place: Ötztal Alps, Austrian-Italian border (discovery site); body at the South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology, Bolzano
grade_reason: VERIFIED across radiocarbon dating, multispectral imaging, and peer-reviewed publication (Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports). Ötzi's 61 tattoos — groups of thin parallel lines and crosses along the lower spine, left calf, right instep, both ankle joints, left wrist, and right torso — were made with campfire-soot pigment. Their placement along degenerating joints and the spine supports the therapeutic reading: ancient cultures believing tattoos could relieve physical ailments. A 2024 experiment (Deter-Wolf et al., European Journal of Archaeology) confirmed the technique was hand-poking with a pigment-tipped pointed tool, not slicing and rubbing ash — overturning 30 years of conventional wisdom. Ötzi is highly unlikely to be the first tattooed human; he is simply the oldest whose skin survived.
earliest_attestation: Discovery 1991; full tattoo mapping via multispectral imaging (Samadelli et al.)

sources.ref: Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports (via HAL): 'This research conclusively determines that the oldest preserved tattoos known to date belong to the Tyrolean Iceman, also known as Ötzi.'
IFLScience: Ötzi's 61 tattoos (3370–3100 BCE); the lines and crosses; the therapeutic/medicinal reading; the campfire-soot pigment.
Science News (2024): the Deter-Wolf hand-poke experiment — 'the past 30 years of conventional wisdom as to how the Iceman was tattooed is incorrect'; the single-pointed pigment-tipped tool.

falsifiability: Older preserved tattoos on human skin

title: Kani Shaie 2025 — the Uruk expansion reaches the Zagros foothills
claim: In 2025 the Kani Shaie Archaeological Project (KSAP, University of Coimbra CEAACP — co-directed by André Tomé, Steve Renette, Maria da Conceição Lopes, Michael Lewis) excavated a monumental public-or-ritual building of the Uruk period (c. 3300–3100 BCE) on the summit tell at Kani Shaie, in the Basian Basin at the western edge of the Zagros Mountains, Sulaimania province, Iraqi Kurdistan — with an associated fragment of a gold earring, an Uruk-period cylinder seal, and decorative wall cones of Uruk monumental-architecture type — the strongest newly excavated exhibit in a decade for the Uruk expansion's eastern reach.
place: Kani Shaie, Basian Basin, Sulaimania province, Iraqi Kurdistan (approximate — site coordinates not yet published)
grade_reason: The find is documented by the excavation project itself (multi-university team with Iraqi Kurdistan heritage authorities) and reported with project-supplied imagery; the peer-reviewed preliminary publication is pending — documented excavation, awaiting print confirmation. The building's function stays the excavators' provisional interpretation, fenced.
earliest_attestation: The excavated structure and associated artifacts themselves (KSAP 2025 campaign); announced October 2025 via the project/University of Coimbra communications, reported by Labrujulaverde with project-supplied imagery

sources.ref: KSAP/University of Coimbra announcement via Labrujulaverde (Oct 2025): monumental Uruk-period structure, gold earring, Uruk cylinder seal, wall cones — project-supplied imagery

Kani Shaie Archaeological Project (KSAP) — co-directors André Tomé, Steve Renette, Maria da Conceição Lopes, Michael Lewis; Universities of Coimbra, Algarve, Cambridge; Iraqi Kurdistan heritage authorities; campaigns begun 2013

Algaze, G., The Uruk World System (1993; 2nd ed. 2005) — the core-periphery expansion thesis; Stein, G.J. (1999, Rethinking World-Systems) — the distance-parity/trade-diaspora counter-thesis; the frame the new site enters

competing_hypotheses: The building's cultic-or-communal-gathering function is the excavators' provisional interpretation from scale and technical features; definitive confirmation awaits the post-excavation analysis phase

Uruk influence at Kani Shaie as emulation by a local elite (the gold earring's local accumulation-and-display reading) rather than direct Uruk administration — the Algaze core-periphery vs Stein distance-parity question at a new eastern site
The press summary's 'first great urban center of humankind' phrasing for Uruk is popular-press language, not the project's claim — the record keeps the definitional fence from evt-uruk-city-002
falsifiability: Publication of the preliminary results showing the building's levels are not Uruk-period (would move the record); full publication confirming a Uruk-period administrative presence with tablets or sealed archives (would strengthen toward the 'node' reading)

title: Narmer and the unification of Egypt
claim: Narmer (c. 3100 BCE) unified Upper and Lower Egypt, founding the First Dynasty; the Narmer Palette depicts him wearing the crowns of both lands.
place: Hierakonpolis (find spot of the Palette)
grade_reason: Narmer's existence is multiply attested (palette, maceheads, year-labels, the Den seal list, Levantine pottery at Arad and Tel Erani); the identification of Narmer with the legendary Menes and the single-event unification narrative remain debated — the palette's documentary reading is now graded separately at evt-narmer-palette-001 (CLAIMED).
earliest_attestation: Narmer Palette and Narmer macehead from the Hierakonpolis Main Deposit, contemporary; Dreyer's 1993 Abydos year-label of Narmer depicts the same smiting scene (read as evidence for a real event by Wilkinson and Davies & Friedman; contested by Baines and Wengrow); later king lists name Menes as first king

sources.ref: Narmer Palette (Egyptian Museum, Cairo)
Narmer macehead (Hierakonpolis Main Deposit)
Smarthistory — Palette of King Narmer (iconography: both crowns, serpopards, smiting scene, serekh)
Bronk Ramsey et al., Proceedings of the Royal Society A (2013), radiocarbon chronology of early Egypt
UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology (peer-reviewed, open access)

competing_hypotheses: Narmer personally unified Egypt in a conquest, and is the Menes of later king lists (majority view: Petrie's identification, Menes = honorific 'he who endures')
Hor-Aha, Narmer's successor, is the Menes of tradition (minority identification)
Menes is a composite figure cobbled from several early rulers (the king lists of Seti I/Manetho postdate Narmer by ~2,500 years)

Unification was a gradual political process over generations of Dynasty 0 rulers (Ka, Scorpion II); Narmer is one ruler among them and the Palette is ideological, not documentary — this hypothesis is compatible with any of the above identifications
falsifiability: Evidence that Upper and Lower Egypt were already politically unified before Narmer, or that the Palette is a later forgery

title: The Narmer Palette as a documentary record of the unification
claim: The Narmer Palette (siltstone, c. 3100 BCE, found 1897-98 by Quibell and Green in the Main Deposit of the temple of Horus at Hierakonpolis) depicts an actual historical event — Narmer's defeat of a Lower-Egyptian foe and unification of the Two Lands — rather than being a purely symbolic composition.
place: Hierakonpolis (Kom el-Ahmar) — find spot of the Palette, Main Deposit
grade_reason: The palette is a genuine contemporary artifact bearing Narmer's name; the DOCUMENTARY reading — that it records a real event rather than asserting kingship — is the dominant scholarly opinion (Dreyer's year label, Wilkinson, Davies & Friedman) but has named, serious dissent (Kohler, O'Connor, Baines, Wengrow, Millet, Davis, Schulman).
earliest_attestation: The palette itself (Egyptian Museum, Cairo, Gallery 43; siltstone, 64 x 42 cm); found with the Scorpion Macehead and Narmer Macehead in the Main Deposit

sources.ref: Egyptian Museum Cairo — Narmer Palette artefact record (Gallery 43, Ground Floor; Late Predynastic, Dynasty 0; discovered by Quibell and Green 1897-1898 in the temple of Horus at Nekhen)

Smarthistory — Palette of King Narmer (iconography: smiting scene, serpopards, bull destroying a walled city, decapitated/castrated foes, serekh with catfish-and-chisel name, both crowns on one ruler for the first time)
Dreyer 1993 Abydos year-label of Narmer depicting the same smiting scene; Wilkinson and Davies & Friedman read it as evidence the palette records a real event (dominant opinion)
Kohler 2002, p. 505 — the 'subjecting the enemy' motif reaches back to Naqada Ic (~400 years before Narmer); the palette as ritual defeat of chaos, not unification
Baines — the events portrayed are 'tokens of royal achievement'; the chief purpose of the piece is not to record an event but to assert that the king dominates the ordered world
Schulman (following Breasted 1931) — the palette commemorates a Dynasty-0 Libyan conquest; the Palermo Stone shows predynastic kings already wearing the double crown

competing_hypotheses: The palette depicts an actual historical event — Narmer's unification conquest — and Dreyer's 1993 Abydos year-label confirms it (dominant opinion: Dreyer, Wilkinson, Davies & Friedman)

The palette is ideological, not documentary: Kohler's 'subjecting the enemy' motif reaches back to Naqada Ic (~400 years before Narmer) — the ritual defeat of chaos, a fundamental role of the king; O'Connor 2011 argues a complicated religious meaning with nothing to do with unification
Baines: the scenes are 'tokens of royal achievement' from the past; the piece's chief purpose is to assert that the king dominates the ordered world in the name of the gods, not to record an event
Millet: the palette does not represent a historical event at all, but represents the events of the year in which the object was dedicated to the temple

Schulman (following Breasted 1931): the palette commemorates a Libyan conquest from Dynasty 0, earlier than Narmer — the Palermo Stone shows predynastic kings already wearing the double crown of a unified Egypt, so the palette cannot be recording the unification
falsifiability: A contemporary inscription explicitly naming the event the palette depicts (Dreyer's year-label is the closest candidate and is itself contested), or proof the palette is a later copy or forgery

title: The Narmer Palette as 'the first historical document in the world'
claim: The Narmer Palette is the oldest Egyptian — or the first-ever — historical record (Brier & Hobbs: 'The oldest Egyptian historical record'; the Egyptian Museum's own page: it 'has been considered the first historical document in the world').
place: Hierakonpolis (Kom el-Ahmar) — Main Deposit
grade_reason: The superlative fails twice: (1) the Scorpion Macehead and Narmer Macehead were found in the same deposit and are equally old early-kingship depictions, so no 'first' is undisputed; (2) whether the palette is a historical document at all — rather than an ideological charter of kingship — is the live two-camp scholarly debate (evt-narmer-palette-001, CLAIMED). The grade kills the superlative only, never the palette, never Narmer, never the unification debate.
earliest_attestation: The superlative is modern (Brier & Hobbs; the Egyptian Museum's own artefact page); the palette itself is c. 3100 BCE

sources.ref: Brier & Hobbs — the Narmer Palette as 'The oldest Egyptian historical record'
Egyptian Museum Cairo — Narmer Palette artefact page: it 'has been considered the first historical document in the world'

The Narmer Palette scholarly debate — two camps: those who read the palette as a record of an important event vs. those who argue it is an object designed to establish the mythology of united rule (Kohler 2002; O'Connor 2011; Baines; Wengrow; Millet; Davis; Schulman/Breasted)
The Scorpion Macehead and Narmer Macehead, found with the palette in the Main Deposit at Hierakonpolis — equally old, equally early depictions of kingship, sharing the 'first' field

competing_hypotheses: The 'first historical document' reading: the palette is among the earliest surviving objects that can plausibly be read as recording a political event, and the superlative is harmless shorthand for that status
The skeptical reading: applying 'historical document' to an object whose documentary status is the contested question begs the whole debate (see evt-narmer-palette-001's two camps)
falsifiability: A scholarly consensus that (a) the palette records a real event and (b) no equally old Egyptian object can claim the same — neither condition is met

title: The Narmer Palette's making — the 2026 tool-mark study (preliminary)
claim: New 2026 imaging of the Narmer Palette shows tool marks, possible changes to the carved scenes, and evidence of damage and repair — meaning the object has a production history beyond its finished iconography. Dr. Kathryn Piquette (with stonecarver Mick Oakey, Essex Egyptology Group, March 2026 lecture): high-resolution computer-enhanced images of the palette compared against experimental stonecarving on a similar stone slab with replica tools, in an attempt to reverse-engineer the production process. Findings are preliminary, presented as a lecture, and not yet peer-reviewed.
place: Hierakonpolis (the palette's find spot, 1897–98)
grade_reason: Single-team preliminary findings presented in a lecture, not yet peer-reviewed: the imaging and experimental method is documented, but the interpretations (tool marks, scene changes, repair) are unattested elsewhere and await publication.
earliest_attestation: The palette itself (Quibell & Green, 1897–98, Main Deposit, Hierakonpolis); the 2026 imaging study.

sources.ref: Piquette, K. & Oakey, M. — 'New Research on the Making of the Narmer Palette', Essex Egyptology Group lecture (March 2026): experimental stonecarving + computer-enhanced imaging; findings preliminary
EBSCO Research Starters: Narmer Palette — summary of the 2026 finding (tool marks, possible changes to carved scenes, damage and repair)

EBSCO Research Starters, History: Narmer Palette — bibliography entry citing Piquette & Oakey, 'New Research on the Making of the Narmer Palette,' Essex Egyptology Group, Mar 2026 (indexed as of Sept 2026); citation only, no new data, grade-neutral

competing_hypotheses: The standard iconographic reading: the palette's scenes are understood through their finished imagery (unification, ma'at vs isfet); tool marks add manufacture data without changing the established readings
The marks could be from later handling, damage, and repair across 5,000 years of the object's life (including its modern museum history) rather than its original making
Digital imaging and experimental archaeology as a research line: the method is sound, but preliminary lecture findings are not findings until published and peer-reviewed
falsifiability: Full peer-reviewed publication with the enhanced images and experimental comparisons; independent re-examination of the tool-mark attributions.

title: Retainer sacrifice at Umm el-Qaab — the 2026 forensic re-reading
claim: The hundreds of subsidiary burials around the First-Dynasty royal tombs at Umm el-Qaab (Abydos) include victims of retainer sacrifice — people killed to accompany the king in death. The 2026 forensic re-examination (Roselyn Campbell, Purdue University, Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology): 46 skulls surviving from Flinders Petrie's early-20th-century excavations (Duckworth Collection, University of Cambridge) were re-examined with modern forensic methods; 18 of the 46 (39%) carry major fractures judged perimortem and probably fatal — mostly linear fractures (thin cracks without inward displacement, distinct from depressed fractures a mace would leave), plus sharp-force injuries including a chopping wound to one individual's eye. The study supports Petrie's century-old suspicion that the simultaneous burials around the king were killings, while acknowledging the 28 skulls without such injuries are unexplained, and that the skulls are a surviving sample, not the whole buried population.
place: Umm el-Qaab, Abydos, Upper Egypt
grade_reason: Independent forensic determination (modern method, curated collection) of perimortem trauma on a documented sample — a genuine second line beyond Petrie's suspicion — but single-study, sample-only (46 skulls of hundreds buried), and the interpretation, not just the fractures, is what the record grades; the 39% is a share of surviving skulls, not of the population. The Oct-14 Saleem rebuttal keeps the dispute live on sampling grounds; two specialist voices (Ikram: rigorous methodology, endorses; van Dijk: practice still controversial) sit on opposite sides of the interpretation. Grade HELD at CORROBORATED — no upward move while the study is contested by named specialists; no downward move — the fractures are the fractures.
earliest_attestation: Petrie's excavations (early 20th c.); the forensic re-analysis published 2026.

sources.ref: Campbell, R. A. 2026. Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology — forensic re-examination of 46 First-Dynasty skulls from Umm el-Qaab (Duckworth Collection, Cambridge)
Petrie, W. M. F. — early-20th-c. excavations of the Abydos royal tombs and subsidiary burials; plans, photographs, and notes (the original suspicion of simultaneous death)
labrujulaverde.com report (2026-10): 'Egypt's Earliest Kings Were Buried Among Hundreds of Servants — Forensics Finally Finds Signs of Violent Deaths'
Baadsgaard, A., Monge, J. & Zettler, R. 2011. Antiquity — CT analysis of Great Death Pit (PG 1237) skulls at Ur: blows to the head, not poison (the independent parallel)

Saleem, S. 2026 (Times of Lanka, 14 Oct 2026) — expert rebuttal of the Campbell paper: the 46 skulls are a selective 5–15% of the 700–900 subsidiary graves; paraffin-wax coating; macroscopic-only inspection cannot distinguish perimortem trauma from excavation damage; Reisner (1936) + recent DAI excavations show modular phased roofs, not simultaneous burial; calls retainer sacrifice a colonial-era interpretation, appeals for repatriation

The Guardian, 5 Oct 2026 ('Skull fractures suggest servants of Egypt's ancient kings were sacrificed') — Salima Ikram (American University in Cairo, not involved): 'one of the few times that rigorous current methodologies are being used to evaluate these remains'; subsidiary burials declined early Second Dynasty, statuettes replaced people; killing skilled retainers 'not really sustainable' (Ars Technica) — the abandonment mechanism
van Dijk, J. (Egyptologist, not involved, via Live Science Oct 2026) — welcomed the Campbell work but said the practice is still controversial (the live-dispute specialist voice)

competing_hypotheses: Petrie's own original conclusion: he found no sign of fatal wounds and could not prove sacrifice — the modern reading says the excavators saw the injuries and misread them as natural damage (the paper's claim)
Alternative causes of death: suffocation and poisoning leave no bone trace; some of the 28 died naturally or of wounds elsewhere in the skeleton (the reburied bodies cannot be checked)

The Ur parallel (Baadsgaard, Monge & Zettler 2011, Antiquity): CT scans of two Great Death Pit (PG 1237) skulls showed blows to the head, overturning Woolley's poison-sedative reading — independent corroboration that royal retainer sacrifice in this era was violent, not peaceful
The practice ends after the First Dynasty in Egypt (reason unknown); ushebti figurines are proposed as the later symbolic replacement — a competing explanation for why the custom disappears

Saleem's rebuttal (Oct 14, 2026, Times of Lanka): the sample is the flaw — 46 skulls selected from 700–900 graves, wax-coated, macroscopic-only; excavation damage cannot be ruled out; the phased-roof evidence (Reisner 1936, recent DAI work) argues the burials were not simultaneous; the 'sacrifice' reading is a colonial-era interpretation imposed on the collection. The rebuttal is press-published expert opinion, not a peer-reviewed re-analysis — it contests the sample and the interpretation, not the fractures; the falsifiability condition (full-skeleton recovery + independent trauma replication) stands.
falsifiability: A published forensic re-examination of the same collection showing the fractures are postmortem or consistent with excavation damage; recovery and analysis of the reburied bodies showing a different mortality pattern; demonstration that the Duckworth skulls are not from the subsidiary burials.

title: The measured ancient alignments (archaeoastronomy ledger)
claim: A subset of ancient monuments carry sky alignments that survive measurement and dating: Stonehenge's solstitial axis (the Avenue on the summer-solstice sunrise alignment, Neolithic-Bronze Age phases), the Great Pyramid's near-cardinal orientation (arcminute-level precision, 4th Dynasty), Chankillo's thirteen towers as a working solar calendar (4th c. BCE, Peru) — while other claimed alignments fail on measurement or stay contested (Nabta Playa's proposed solstice alignments remain disputed among specialists). The fringe 'impossible knowledge of the heavens' reading is not needed to explain any measured alignment.
place: Stonehenge (family anchor; Chankillo -9.56,-78.23; Giza 29.9792,31.1342; Nabta Playa 22.53,30.75)
grade_reason: The alignments are multiply and independently measured (surveys, theodolite, excavation context); the interpretation of intent is fenced, not graded
earliest_attestation: Stonehenge solstice alignment: recorded in 18th-c. antiquarian literature (Stukeley 1740); measured in 20th-c. archaeoastronomy surveys

sources.ref: Darvill et al. — Stonehenge phase and solstice-axis survey literature (Antiquity)
Spence 2000 Nature — simultaneous-transit method for the pyramid cardinal orientations
Ghezzi & Ruggles 2007 Science — Chankillo: the 13 towers as a solar calendar
Belmonte — archaeoastronomy surveys of ancient Egypt (the peer-reviewed corpus against which fringe readings are measured)
Malville et al. — Nabta Playa megalithic complex (claimed solstice alignments, contested)

competing_hypotheses: All reported alignments are chance coincidences (the noise floor across many monuments)
The fringe reading: alignments this precise imply non-human or lost-high-tech knowledge
Nabta Playa's alignments are real and push African archaeoastronomy earlier
falsifiability: A securely dated monument whose claimed alignment cannot be measured within stated error, or a showing that counted alignments across the full surveyed corpus sit at chance levels

title: The 'candles lit the premodern world' telling
claim: Before electric light, candles were the main source of artificial light for ordinary people in the premodern world.
place: British Isles (control sample)
grade_reason: Convergent kills: the rushlight record (centuries of near-free light for the poor, explicitly contrasted with costly candles), the price record (8s 6d per dozen in 1788; a dedicated 1709 tax), and the wax hierarchy (beeswax reserved for churches and festivals). The candle was a costly good, not the people's light.
earliest_attestation: The modern popular telling has no single origin; it is carried in schoolbooks, period dramas, and museum placards.

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Rushlight' — Cobbett: rushlights 'cost almost nothing to produce and was believed to give a better light than some poorly dipped candles'; Aubrey 1673 earliest printed description; Gilbert White 1789; rural use into the 19th c., WWII revival
Country Life, 'From fish oil to chandeliers' — rushlights the most common early domestic lighting; the 1709 tallow candle tax, from which rushlights were exempt
oldandinteresting.com, tallow candles — England 1788: a dozen candles (ten to the pound) at 8s 6d; tallow's odor, smoke, quick melting; braided wick as a 19th-c. discovery
Lakeville Journal / Colebrook Historical Society, colonial New England lighting — tallow dips; spermaceti candles (one worth three tallow) 'regarded as very expensive' and first used by the wealthy

competing_hypotheses: Tallow candles were common among the urban middle class by the 18th c. — true for a class, not the world
Beeswax candles were genuinely central to church and elite life — a different, luxury market, never the people's light
falsifiability: Household account books showing candles as the cheapest available light for the poor, or production records showing tallow candles cheaper than rushlights or oil.

title: The 'Jesus copied the dying-and-rising gods' claim
claim: Popular internet-level versions of Frazer's 'dying-and-rising god' category claim Jesus was modeled on pagan saviors (Osiris, Tammuz, Attis, Adonis). Scholarship killed this parallel: Jonathan Z. Smith (1987 Encyclopedia of Religion) dismissed the category as 'largely a misnomer based on imaginative reconstructions and exceedingly late or highly ambiguous texts', arguing gods who 'died' did not return and those who returned never truly 'died'. Tryggve Mettinger's 2001 monograph found pre-Christian death-and-return for Baal, Melqart, and Dumuzi — but none match the structure of the Christian claim, and he warned against hypostasizing a single type.
place: Eastern Mediterranean (scholarly debate, not a place)
grade_reason: The category itself was dismantled by scholarship: the individual parallels collapse on details (gods who died stayed dead; those who 'returned' never died; the return mechanisms are vegetation cycles, not resurrection), leaving no genuine pre-Christian structural match for the Christian claim.
earliest_attestation: Frazer, The Golden Bough (1890) assembled the category; J.Z. Smith, 'Dying and Rising Gods' in Eliade's Encyclopedia of Religion (1987); Mettinger, The Riddle of Resurrection (2001)

sources.ref: Jonathan Z. Smith, 'Dying and Rising Gods', Encyclopedia of Religion (1987)
Tryggve N.D. Mettinger, The Riddle of Resurrection (Stockholm, 2001)
Mark S. Smith, The Origins of Biblical Monotheism (Oxford, 2001), 104–131
Marcel Detienne, The Gardens of Adonis (1977)

competing_hypotheses: Mettinger's mediating position: Baal, Melqart, Dumuzi did die and return pre-Christianity — but as distinct phenomena, not one borrowed type
Robert M. Price's view: Christianity owes far more to myth than history; Frazer was 'even half right' (mythicist-adjacent position, named fairly)
M. David Litwa (Iesus Deus): classical mortal-to-divine apotheoses (Heracles, Romulus) are more plausible comparative material than 'dying gods'
falsifiability: A pre-Christian text describing a god dying as a human death and returning bodily to the world of the living in a structure matching the Christian resurrection claim

title: Meretneith's serekhs — the 2026 digital re-reading (First Dynasty female king)
claim: Meretneith of Egypt's First Dynasty (c. 3000–2900 BCE) ruled as a king in her own right — not merely a queen consort — as evidenced by her name written in the royal serekh, the emblem that marked Egyptian rulers. The 2026 re-reading (Susan Kelly et al., Prague Egyptological Studies 2026) digitally enhanced a 1940s photograph of a lost mud stopper from an unknown Saqqara tomb (Walter B. Emery's archive, Egypt Exploration Society, London): the signs in the name portions of the second and third serekhs are consistent with the main sign used to write Meretneith's name, identifying her with the primary mark of rulers. The authors propose a staged political career: the serekh beside Djer's marks co-regency; tomb seals confirm a later regent/king's-mother role; studies estimate she ruled at least 30 years in one capacity or another. The claim is new and awaits scholarly reception.
place: Saqqara (unknown tomb excavated in the 1940s)
grade_reason: Single new reading of a single photograph of a lost artifact: the digital enhancement (Macquarie University) is methodologically documented, but the evidence base is one black-and-white image and the reading has not yet survived scholarly reception. Attested in one new paper; independent confirmation absent.
earliest_attestation: The 1940s photograph of the mud stopper (13 such stoppers excavated from an unknown Saqqara tomb; only one photograph survives, in Emery's EES archive); Emery's original hand-illustration of the signs.

sources.ref: Kelly, S. et al. 2026. 'New technology illuminating ancient evidence: Re-evaluating Meretneith's serekhs and political position', Prague Egyptological Studies (2026) — the digital re-reading of Emery's photograph
Emery, W. B. — 1940s excavation photograph of the mud stopper, Egypt Exploration Society archive, London (the only surviving image of the 13 stoppers)
phys.org / The Conversation republication, 2026-09-15: 'A 5,000-year-old royal mystery: Digital clues point to Meretneith as Egypt's female king'
Meretneith's tomb complex at Abydos (Umm el-Qaab) and associated seals — the material body of evidence for her royal career

competing_hypotheses: Emery's original 1940s reading (first and fourth serekhs Djer, second and third Meretneith) was long rejected by many scholars on the grounds that the poor-quality photograph made confirmation impossible — the 2026 enhancement answers the image-quality objection, not necessarily the epigraphic one
The enhanced reading could still be contested: a single black-and-white photograph of a lost artifact is a fragile evidence base, and digital enhancement can sharpen noise as well as signal
Meretneith as interim ruler or regent only (the traditional conservative reading): her lavish tomb complex and seals prove high status and governance authority, not necessarily independent kingship
The staged-career model (co-regent → regent → king's mother) is the authors' hypothesis from differing text types, not a settled biography
falsifiability: Recovery of the original artifact or its glass-plate negative showing different signs; published scholarly refutation of the enhanced reading; the authors' own framing is a new hypothesis open to the field's response.

title: The Yamnaya steppe migration (~3000–2500 BCE)
claim: Around 3000–2500 BCE, a large-scale population movement carried people of the Yamnaya (Pit-Grave) culture out of the Pontic-Caspian steppe — the grass sea north of the Black Sea, in what is now Ukraine and Russia — into central and northern Europe. The migrants were cattle-and-sheep pastoralists who had adopted wheels and wagons around 3300 BCE. Ancient DNA shows the Corded Ware population of what is now Germany drew about three-quarters of its ancestry from the steppe newcomers — 'the largest migration into Europe in the last 5000 years' (Anthony). The migration is the leading explanation for the spread of Indo-European languages into Europe: the inference from genes to language rests on the migration's magnitude (if the people came in those numbers, their language came with them).
place: Pontic-Caspian steppe (Yamnaya homeland) → central/northern Europe (Corded Ware horizon)
grade_reason: Three independent lines converge: archaeology (Yamnaya kurgans, wagons, material culture flowing west ~3300–2500 BCE), linguistics (shared wheel/transport vocabulary across Indo-European, pointing to a wheeled culture), and ancient DNA (Corded Ware ~75% steppe ancestry). The MIGRATION is corroborated by all three; the language-spread inference is the weakest leg (DNA records no words) and stays CLAIMED within the claim.
earliest_attestation: Haak, W. et al. 2015, Nature 522:207–211 ('Massive migration from the steppe was a source for Indo-European languages in Europe'); Allentoft, M. E. et al. 2015, Nature 522:167–172; archaeological case in Anthony 2007, The Horse, the Wheel, and Language.

sources.ref: Haak, W. et al. 2015, 'Massive migration from the steppe was a source for Indo-European languages in Europe,' Nature 522:207–211 — the core ancient-DNA result: Corded Ware ancestry ~75% steppe/Yamnaya.
Allentoft, M. E. et al. 2015, 'Population genomics of Bronze Age Eurasia,' Nature 522:167–172 — companion ancient-DNA study of the same migration.
Anthony, D. W. 2007, The Horse, the Wheel, and Language: How Bronze-Age Riders from the Eurasian Steppes Shaped the Modern World (Princeton) — archaeology + linguistics case; wagons ~3300 BCE.

Lazaridis, I. et al. 2026, Nature pair of papers (co-authored with David Anthony) — DNA pointing to Eurasian herders ~6400 years ago; homeland refinement toward the Caucasus–Lower Volga / South Caucasus. Science AAAS reporting, 2026.

competing_hypotheses: The Anatolian hypothesis (Renfrew): Indo-European spread with Neolithic farming from Anatolia, not with steppe pastoralists — genes and language are decoupled, and the language family is much older.

The Caucasus–Lower Volga homeland (Lazaridis et al., 2026 Nature papers): early Indo-European was spoken ~4400–4000 BCE further south (South Caucasus/Caucasus-Lower Volga), with the later Yamnaya expansion as the vehicle — a refinement of the steppe model, not its refutation; the debate now concerns where within the broad region the language started.

The language-gene decoupling objection: DNA cannot record a word, and populations can change language without migration (cf. the spread of Latin without mass Italian emigration) — so the migration is certain, the language inference remains the weakest leg.
falsifiability: Ancient genomes showing Corded Ware populations with no steppe admixture; or securely dated steppe languages (if such were ever found) belonging to a non-Indo-European family; or the discovery that the '75% steppe ancestry' signal is an artifact of unrepresentative reference populations.

title: Alulim, first king of Eridu
claim: The Sumerian King List opens with Alulim of Eridu as the first king, reigning a mythical 28,800 years 'before the flood'.
place: Eridu (traditional)
grade_reason: Attested only in the King List tradition; no contemporary inscription or archaeological evidence of Alulim exists.
earliest_attestation: The Sumerian King List itself, copies c. 2100-1800 BCE

sources.ref: Sumerian King List, opening lines (ETCSL t.2.1.1)
Weld-Blundell Prism

competing_hypotheses: Alulim is an eponymous ancestor figure of the Eridu priesthood, not a historical person
A garbled memory of a real early Eridu ruler, with reign length inflated by scribal convention
falsifiability: Contemporary third-millennium evidence for or against a ruler of Eridu by this name; absent such evidence the grade cannot rise above CLAIMED

title: The Babylonian soap recipes (c. 2800/2200 BCE)
claim: The earliest recorded evidence of soap-like materials dates to around 2800 BCE in ancient Babylon: clay tablets carry written soap recipes — the ~2200 BCE formula of water, alkali, and cassia oil, and a Nabonidus-reign (556-539 BCE) recipe of uhulu (ashes), cypress oil, and sesame seed oil.
place: Babylon, Mesopotamia
grade_reason: The recipe tradition is attested in secondary scholarship (Roth; Conchon & Rasmussen, 'An Ancient Cleaner: Soap Production and Use in Antiquity', Chemical Technology in Antiquity) and the Nabonidus-reign recipe is textually specific (uhulu/cypress/sesame). Held at CORROBORATED, not VERIFIED: the early tablets' identity and contents are thinly reported in the literature, and the 'soap-like' label is a modern chemical reading of an ancient material that was used for textiles and medicine, not personal washing.
earliest_attestation: Babylonian clay tablets (excavated at Babylon; recipe texts c. 2200 BCE and 556-539 BCE)

sources.ref: Roth, on Sumerian/Babylonian clay tablets (3rd millennium BCE) — cited in the Invention podcast soap episode: 'with water, I bathed myself with soda... I cleansed myself with soda from a shiny basin'

Conchon & Rasmussen — 'An Ancient Cleaner: Soap Production and Use in Antiquity' (Chemical Technology in Antiquity): Nabonidus-reign recipe (uhulu [ashes], cypress oil, sesame seed oil 'for washing the stones for the servant girls'); caveat that 'details concerning the identity and contents of these tablets have not been reported'

soaphistory.net — 'First Soap': first recorded evidence 'Babylonian clay cylinders dating from 2800 B.C.'; the product 'not necessarily used to wash the body; it might have been used to clean textile fibers such as wool and cotton in preparation for weaving into cloth'
Ebers Papyrus (Egypt, c. 1550 BCE) — animal/vegetable oils with alkaline salts for washing and skin ailments: the Egyptian leg of the early record

competing_hypotheses: The ~2800 BCE date attaches to the Babylon excavation material generally; the securely described written formula is the ~2200 BCE tablet
The product was proto-soap used for wool/textiles and medicine, not body washing — the 'first soap' label overstates continuity with modern soap
falsifiability: Re-examination of the tablets showing the inscriptions describe something else entirely (unrelated workshop accounts, not soap recipes)

title: Gilgamesh, king of Uruk
claim: The Sumerian King List names Gilgamesh as king of Uruk with a 126-year reign; he may be the historical kernel behind the Epic of Gilgamesh.
place: Uruk
grade_reason: Named in the King List and the Tummal building inscription, but no contemporary inscription of a king Gilgamesh survives; the epic is literature, not history.
earliest_attestation: Sumerian King List, copies c. 2100-1800 BCE; Tummal inscription names him as a builder of the Ekur at Nippur

sources.ref: Sumerian King List, Uruk dynasty entry
Tummal inscription
Epic of Gilgamesh (Standard Babylonian version, c. 1200 BCE tablets)

competing_hypotheses: Gilgamesh was a real Early Dynastic king of Uruk whose deeds were mythologized
Gilgamesh is a composite literary hero with no single historical referent
falsifiability: A contemporary inscription of a king named Gilgamesh of Uruk would raise this to CORROBORATED; continued absence keeps it CLAIMED

title: The Step Pyramid of Djoser
claim: Pharaoh Djoser (c. 2670 BCE, Third Dynasty) built the Step Pyramid at Saqqara, designed by his vizier Imhotep — the first monumental stone building in Egypt and a prototype for later pyramids.
place: Saqqara
grade_reason: The monument exists and contemporary inscriptions name Imhotep; the Djoser attribution is strong but partly carried by later king lists.
earliest_attestation: The pyramid itself at Saqqara; inscriptions naming Imhotep in the pyramid complex; later king lists name Djoser

sources.ref: Step Pyramid complex at Saqqara (standing monument)
Imhotep inscriptions in the Djoser complex
UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology
UCL Digital Egypt chronology

competing_hypotheses: Djoser commissioned the pyramid as a single project designed by Imhotep

The complex was built in stages within Djoser's reign (Lauer's reconstruction from 1926-1996 excavations: square mastaba → enlarged horizontally → four-step pyramid → six-step pyramid) — progressive ambition, one architect, one reign
The complex was built in stages across reigns, and the Imhotep legend grew later (he was deified centuries after)
falsifiability: Inscriptions attributing the complex to a different king, or re-dating placing it in a different dynasty

title: Enmebaragesi of Kish
claim: Enmebaragesi, king of Kish (c. 2600 BCE), is the earliest Sumerian king attested outside the King List itself, named in a contemporary alabaster vase inscription.
place: Kish
grade_reason: Named in the King List AND in a contemporary inscription, giving independent attestation beyond the list.
earliest_attestation: Alabaster vase inscription from Nippur, Early Dynastic period; also named in the Tummal inscription (later copy)

sources.ref: Vase inscription naming Enmebaragesi (Nippur, Early Dynastic)
Tummal inscription (later copy preserving the king's building works)
Sumerian King List, Kish dynasty entry

competing_hypotheses: The vase inscription attribution is correct and Enmebaragesi is the first verifiable Sumerian king
The inscription is misattributed or belongs to a namesake, leaving the King List entry as the only source
falsifiability: Re-examination showing the vase inscription names a different king, or proof the King List Kish entries are entirely invented

title: The Harappan (Indus Valley) Civilization
claim: A planned urban civilization covering the Indus river system and beyond — with Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira, Ganweriwala, and Rakhigarhi among its great cities — at its mature height from c. 2600 to 1900 BCE, spread over a larger area than contemporary Mesopotamia or Egypt.
place: Mohenjo-daro, Sindh (representative pin; the civilization spans the Indus-Ghaggar system)
grade_reason: Hundreds of excavated sites across 1,000,000+ km² with consistent urban planning signatures: grid streets, covered drains, standard cubical weights, the Great Bath, the Lothal dockyard.
earliest_attestation: Seals published 1875 (Cunningham); cities identified by Marshall's ASI excavations, 1920s

sources.ref: Kenoyer, J.M. — Ancient Cities of the Indus Valley Civilization (1998)
Possehl, G. — The Indus Civilization: A Contemporary Perspective (2002)
Harappa.com archaeological database (archaeological survey record)
Dholavira excavations, Archaeological Survey of India

competing_hypotheses: How urban it was: some scholars (Possehl) argue for a looser 'civilization' than the Mesopotamian city-state model; the cities' political structure is unknown — no palaces, no royal tombs, no temple complexes have been identified
Decline causes: climate drying (4.2-ka event / monsoon failure, Dixit et al. 2014) vs river course shifts (Lambrick; Agrawal) vs tectonic flooding (Dales, Raikes) — all published, none exclusive
falsifiability: A single secure context showing the 'Harappan' signature to be a modern misattribution of unrelated settlements, or radiocarbon showing the mature phase to lie entirely outside 2600–1900 BCE

title: The Indus Script Is Undeciphered
claim: The Indus civilization's sign system — ~4,000 inscriptions, ~400 signs, mostly 5–6 symbols long, longest 34 — has never been convincingly deciphered. In January 2025 the Tamil Nadu government offered a $1,000,000 prize for a decipherment accepted by archaeological experts; as of this record it stands unclaimed.
place: Mohenjo-daro seals (corpus spans the Indus system)
grade_reason: The 'undeciphered' status is a statement about the state of knowledge (consensus, uncontroversial); whether the signs encode language at all is the open speculation — the Dravidian hypothesis, early-Indo-Aryan hypothesis, and the non-linguistic-signs hypothesis all published, none conclusive.
earliest_attestation: First published Indus seal 1875 (Cunningham); prize announced January 2025 (Tamil Nadu CM M.K. Stalin, centennial of Marshall's excavations)

sources.ref: Asko Parpola — Deciphering the Indus Script (1994): 'the most important system of writing that is undeciphered'
Smithsonian Magazine, Jan 2025: $1M prize report (Stalin announcement)
Archaeology News Online Magazine, Jan 2025: prize report
Rajan, K. & Sivananthan, R. — graffiti/indus-sign comparison study (2024, morphological approach)
Farmer, Sproat & Witzel (2004) — 'The Collapse of the Indus-Script Thesis': signs are non-linguistic symbols

competing_hypotheses: Dravidian hypothesis (Parpola): the signs encode a proto-Dravidian language — most widely defended in the specialist literature
Early Indo-Aryan hypothesis (Jha & Rajaram): announced decipherment in 2000 as Vedic Sanskrit — not accepted by the scholarly consensus
Non-linguistic hypothesis (Farmer, Sproat & Witzel 2004): the signs are religious/political symbols, not a script; statistical properties don't match known scripts
Graffiti continuity (Rajan & Sivananthan 2024): ~60% sign-shape match with Tamil pottery graffiti — morphological similarity only, explicitly not a linguistic claim
falsifiability: A published, expert-accepted decipherment (e.g., a claimed prize winner passing expert review) would collapse the record to CORROBORATED/VERIFIED overnight — this record is explicitly designed to be superseded

title: The tomb of Sekhentiu-Ptah, 'keeper of the king's secrets' — 2026 Saqqara discovery
claim: Excavations at Saqqara's Bubasteum necropolis uncovered an Old Kingdom tomb of the senior official Sekhentiu-Ptah (keeper of the king's secrets, royal chamberlain, priest of Maat, supervisor of the royal library) with three sealed stone sarcophagi found intact in their original positions, an intact false door, painted funerary cartonnage, alabaster ritual tools, a wooden falcon statue, and over 100 ushabti figurines; parts of the complex were looted in antiquity.
place: Bubasteum necropolis, Saqqara, Egypt
grade_reason: Ministry/SCA announcement with specific in-situ finds (three sealed sarcophagi, intact false door); independent press reporting; continued study expected — title readings and reign may refine.
earliest_attestation: Excavated and announced September 2026 (official SCA report 29 Aug 2026); Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities statement via SCA Secretary-General.

sources.ref: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities / SCA statement, Sept 2026 (Bubasteum, Saqqara; three sealed sarcophagi in situ; inscriptions naming Sekhentiu-Ptah and his titles)
Daily Mail reporting of the ministry announcement, Sept 2026: 'keeper of the king's secrets' tomb
crbcnews.com report, 6 Sept 2026 (updated 14 Oct 2026): sealed sarcophagi and painted cartonnage in original conditions

CRBC News, updated 14 Oct 2026: Bubasteum Sekhentiu-Ptah tomb re-report — three sealed sarcophagi, painted cartonnage, intact false door; venue-echo of the 4 Sept 2026 ministry announcement, grade-neutral

competing_hypotheses: The 'keeper of the king's secrets' title translation may be refined by epigraphers
The tomb's original reign attribution awaits inscription analysis
falsifiability: Re-attribution of the tomb to a different owner, or demonstration that the sarcophagi were sealed in modern times

title: The Great Pyramid of Khufu at Giza
claim: The Great Pyramid at Giza was built for Pharaoh Khufu (c. 2560 BCE), the largest of the three Giza pyramids; workers' graffiti inside names Khufu's crews.
place: Giza
grade_reason: The monument stands, Vyse's 1837 relieving-chamber graffiti names Khufu's crews (the 'Friends of Khufu' gang), and the Wadi al-Jarf papyri independently document construction logistics in his reign — multiple independent contemporary sources. The Djedi 2013 hieratic numerals ('121') corroborate construction-phase recording; the Big Void is not evidence for or against the attribution.
earliest_attestation: The pyramid itself; quarry marks and workers' graffiti naming 'the gang, Friends of Khufu' in the relieving chambers above the King's Chamber, discovered 1837 by Howard Vyse's team (the Khufu cartouche claim that grounds the attribution). Djedi Project robot (2010-11; published Journal of Field Robotics, May 2013) filmed red hieratic numerals '121' (the length of the Queen's Chamber southern shaft in cubits, per Miatello) in that shaft's hidden space — numerical mason's marks, NOT a crew-name cartouche, and NOT in a relieving chamber (the 2013 'cartouche in a relieving chamber' shorthand is a conflation; the cartouches are Vyse's 1837 find).

sources.ref: Workers' graffiti in the Great Pyramid relieving chambers (Howard Vyse, 1837: Khufu cartouches, 'Friends of Khufu' gang name)
Wadi al-Jarf papyri (Diary of Merer, contemporary logbook of pyramid construction logistics)
Richardson et al., 'The Djedi Robot Exploration of the Southern Shaft of the Queen's Chamber', Journal of Field Robotics 30(3), May 2013
Procureur et al., 'Precise characterization of a corridor-shaped structure in Khufu's Pyramid by observation of cosmic-ray muons', Nature Communications, 2 March 2023 (North Face Corridor)
UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology
ScanPyramids collaboration 2017, Nature: 'Discovery of a big void in Khufu's Pyramid by observation of cosmic-ray muons' — the ≥30 m Big Void above the Grand Gallery
ScanPyramids 2023, Nature Communications: the ~9 m North Face Corridor behind the chevron blocks, confirmed by endoscope camera

Zahi Hawass, Sharjah International Book Fair, Nov 2025: a new Great Pyramid discovery to be revealed in 2026 ('write a new chapter in the history of the pharaohs'); as of Oct 2026 no published evidence of the reveal — viral 'sealed door opened' stories carry no published evidence

theegyptfiles.com (Sept 2026 review): Hawass's announced ~30 m passage ending at a door still has no published data or announcement as of September 2026 — kept separate from the Italian team's Khafre SAR work and from the ScanPyramids Big Void / North Face Corridor
ScIDEP collaboration 2025 paper + June 2026 conference abstract: muon-telescope prototypes for Khafre still under construction in 2026 — no pyramid data from that instrument yet

FORFOXS Evidence File, Oct 2026: 'The Great Pyramid's Hidden Spaces — What ScanPyramids Actually Found' — Big Void (2017, ~30m, above Grand Gallery) confirmed; North Face Corridor (2023, 9.06m); Aug-2026 SAR retraction does not affect muon findings; status summary, grade-neutral

competing_hypotheses: Built by Khufu's workforce in the mid-26th century BCE (consensus)

The Vyse-forgery claim (Sitchin; Creighton): the 1837 relieving-chamber cartouches were painted by Vyse's team — contradicted by the marks' positions on blocks sealed inside the masonry during construction (inaccessible to paint afterwards), and by the independent Wadi al-Jarf papyri naming Khufu's crews (fringe; contradicts two independent lines)
Alternative builders/dates including ancient-astronaut claims (fringe; contradicted by the graffiti and papyri evidence)
falsifiability: Contemporary inscriptions attributing the pyramid to another king, or secure re-dating of the Wadi al-Jarf papyri away from Khufu's reign

title: The Lagash omitted archive — the royal inscription control on the King List's Early Dynastic sequence
claim: The Lagash royal inscription archive — contemporary Early Dynastic royal records that the Sumerian King List never names — is an independent control on the King List's dynastic scheme: the Treaty of Mesilim (c. 2500 BCE, the king of Kish arbitrating Lagash and Umma's Gu'edena border, the oldest known boundary treaty), the Vulture Stele of Eannatum (c. 2450 BCE, the earliest identified victory monument, with its oath-bound border settlement), the Cone of Enmetena, and the reform cones of Urukagina (c. 2350 BCE). Lagash's inscribed royal line (Ur-Nanshe through Urukagina, ED III) runs parallel in time to the King List's named dynasties of Kish I, Uruk I, Ur I and Kish III — the archive's existence and sequence are established from contemporary inscriptions, not from any later copy.
place: Telloh (Girsu) and Tell al-Hiba (Lagash), Dhi Qar, Iraq
grade_reason: Multiple contemporary (Early Dynastic) royal inscriptions with excavated findspots, independently catalogued in the CDLI/ETCSL corpora; the dynasty's internal sequence is cross-witnessed by year-ordered inscriptions (Ur-Nanshe through Urukagina); the omission from the King List is a fact of the list's content, not an inference. CORROBORATED, not VERIFIED: precise absolute dates of individual reigns remain middle-chronology estimates.
earliest_attestation: Vulture Stele of Eannatum, c. 2450 BCE (contemporary).

sources.ref: Archaeology Magazine (May/June 2016), 'The World's Oldest Writing — Warfare': the Vulture Stele, c. 2450 BCE, earliest identified victory monument; long inscription recounts Lagash-Umma history ending in oath-bound border settlement; Umma's later plunder of Lagash

The Sumerian World (Routledge, via summary): Bänder 1995/Nigro 1998 — Eanatum of Lagash's Early Dynastic stela as the earliest identified victory monument; Ningirsu's battle-net with POWs; the oath formula as a legal instrument on the defeated ruler

Cuneiform law reference corpus: the Urukagina reforms c. 2350 BCE — referenced in other sources, the code text itself never found by archaeologists; the Code of Ur-Nammu (c. 2060 BCE) remains the earliest code with surviving fragments

CDLI/ETCSL corpora (general): the Lagash ED III royal inscriptions (Ur-Nanshe, Eannatum, Enannatum I, Enmetena, Urukagina) as a catalogued contemporary corpus; the Treaty of Mesilim tradition transmitted via the Eannatum/Enmetena inscriptions

Marta Santos Pérez, 'A Historical Synthesis on Lagaš and the archaeological excavations at Tell al-Hiba/Lagaš (Iraq)', Astarté (2024): Tell al-Hiba as a major Sumerian urban centre; dynastic sequence (Gudea, Urukagina); the Nin-Girsu temple tablets and inscriptions documenting Lagash's political organisation

competing_hypotheses: The 'first legal code' reading of Urukagina's reforms as a formal written code — the reforms are attested only as summarized in the cone inscriptions; the code text itself is not extant (fenced as CLAIMED, the telling graded separately)
The treaty of Mesilim's early date (~2500 BCE) — transmitted through later Lagash inscriptions, no contemporary copy survives; the event rests on the Eannatum/Enmetena tradition citing it
falsifiability: Peer-reviewed demonstration that the key Lagash inscriptions are Old Babylonian or later forgeries, or a contemporary Lagash record placing the Lagash dynasty in the King List's sequence as a named dynasty

title: Karnak on a river island — the temple the substrate chose
claim: The temple of Amun-Ra at Karnak (Luxor, Egypt) was built on a fluvial terrace island formed between Nile channels — the only known such high-ground-in-water configuration in the area, recalling the primeval-mound of Egyptian creation myth — with permanent occupation becoming possible only after 2520 BCE +/-420 (Old Kingdom), and subsequent occupants engineering the channels themselves (desert-sand dumping to make land).
place: Karnak, Luxor, Egypt
grade_reason: Peer-reviewed geoarchaeological survey (cores, chronostratigraphy, paleolandscape reconstruction) independently published in Antiquity; the myth-link reading is the authors' stated interpretation, fenced as such.
earliest_attestation: Pennington et al. 2025 (Antiquity) — first comprehensive geoarchaeological survey of the Karnak area; builds on the 2024 Nature Geoscience Nile Valley landscape paper (doi:10.1038/s41561-024-01451-z).

sources.ref: Pennington et al. 2025, Antiquity 99(408):1535-1549, doi:10.15184/aqy.2025.10185 — core-drilling + sediment analysis; island-terrace configuration; 2520 BCE +/-420 occupation threshold; opportunistic/proactive channel engineering

Pennington/Graham et al. 2024, Nature Geoscience (doi:10.1038/s41561-024-01451-z) — climatic/environmental shaping of the Nile Valley over 11,500 years; the substrate-context the Karnak survey builds on

competing_hypotheses: The site choice was religiously/mythologically motivated independent of the geomorphology — the island configuration is coincidence, not cause
The 2520 +/-420 occupation threshold is model-dependent and will move as more cores are dated
falsifiability: A re-dated chronostratigraphy showing permanent occupation well before the terrace stabilized, or a peer-reviewed rebuttal overturning the island configuration

title: The Kingdom of Kush
claim: The Kingdom of Kush — the Nubian kingdom along the Nile from the First Cataract south, with capitals successively at Kerma, Napata (near Jebel Barkal), and Meroë — was a major independent civilization of the ancient Nile Valley, with state-level organization, temple building, iron working, and its own writing, spanning roughly two thousand years.
place: Napata / Jebel Barkal (representative capital; Kerma and Meroë also pinned in media)
grade_reason: Multiply attested in Egyptian, Assyrian, and Kushite sources plus extensive excavation (Reisner 1908–1932, ongoing Sudanese missions); the exact Kerma-to-Napata continuity has some scholarly debate, so it stops short of VERIFIED.
earliest_attestation: Egyptian execration texts and Kerma archaeological horizon (c. 2500–1500 BCE); the kingdom's own record begins in the Napatan period (8th c. BCE).

sources.ref: Kerma excavations: Reisner 1913–1916; Bonnet (Swiss mission) — tumuli, Deffufa, the cemetery-city of 30,000+
Piye's Victory Stela (Jebel Barkal, 1862; Cairo JE 48862) — the Kushite conquest of Egypt in its own words
Assyrian royal annals: Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal prisms — the Kushite pharaohs as named adversaries (external witness)
UNESCO World Heritage: Archaeological Sites of the Island of Meroe (inscribed 2011) — Meroë, Musawwarat es-Sufra, Naqa

competing_hypotheses: Kush as a persistent Egyptian province/dependency rather than an independent civilization — the older European scholarly frame, now largely abandoned

The Meroitic state as primarily a continuation of Egyptian cultural models rather than a distinct civilization — the archaeology shows deep Egyptian influence but also distinct institutions (election of kings, candace queens, iron industry)
falsifiability: Proof that the Napatan/Meroitic material culture is an Egyptian colonial outpost rather than a self-governing kingdom — contradicted by Kushite kings ruling Egypt itself in the 25th Dynasty

title: Ku-Baba, the tavern-keeper who became king
claim: The Sumerian King List's 3rd dynasty of Kish names Ku-Baba — 'the woman tavern-keeper' (munus-kas-de-a), the only female ruler in the entire list — as reigning 100 years and 'establishing the foundation of Kish'; she is also named in the Weidner Chronicle's literary history of kingship.
place: Kish (Tell al-Uhaymir, traditional)
grade_reason: Attested in the King List tradition and the Weidner Chronicle — two witnesses inside the same scribal-literary tradition — with no contemporary inscription or seal naming her; the person cannot rise above CLAIMED.
earliest_attestation: Old Babylonian copies of the Sumerian King List (WB 444 and duplicates); the Weidner Chronicle (early 2nd millennium literary letter) as second witness within the scribal tradition

sources.ref: ETCSL transliteration t.2.1.1 (the Ku-Baba passage, 3rd dynasty of Kish)
Weld-Blundell Prism, Ashmolean AN1923.444 (carrier of the passage)
Weidner Chronicle (ABC 19; literary letter naming Ku-Baba among the kings)

competing_hypotheses: Ku-Baba as a historical ruler whose memory the scribes preserved precisely because she was anomalous
Ku-Baba as a literary figure — the tavern-keeper-made-king as a moral exemplum about kingship's accessibility, composed or amplified by the tradition
falsifiability: A contemporary Early Dynastic inscription or seal impression naming Ku-Baba of Kish (would raise the grade); demonstration that the passage is absent from all pre-Old-Babylonian witnesses and a late interpolation (would lower it)

title: Sixteen tablets against the evil demons
claim: The Utukkū Lemnūtu ('evil demons') is a canonical sixteen-tablet series of bilingual (Sumerian-Akkadian) exorcistic incantations directed against evil demons, ghosts, and other malefactors; some incantations derive from 3rd-millennium BCE compositions, and the series was transmitted for over two millennia as the professional lore of the āšipu (exorcist). The Metropolitan Museum holds tablets 3, 12, and 16; tablet 12 (Seleucid) treats demonic disruption of nature and agriculture with a scapegoat ritual.
place: Nineveh / Assur, Assyria
grade_reason: The series' existence, sixteen-tablet canonical form, bilingual format, and multi-millennium transmission are established by the manuscript record and the modern critical editions; graded as artifact + belief-phenomenon.
earliest_attestation: 3rd-millennium BCE forerunner incantations; canonical series known to Assyrian and Babylonian scholars of the first millennium BCE

sources.ref: Geller, Evil Demons: The Canonical Utukkū Lemnūtu Incantations (SAACT 5, Helsinki 2007)
Geller, Healing Magic and Evil Demons: Canonical Udug-hul Incantations (de Gruyter, BAM 8, 2016)
Metropolitan Museum of Art — Utukku lemnutu tablet 12 (Seleucid; scapegoat ritual) and tablets 3, 16
SBL review: 'a sixteen-tablet series' — sickness/health polarity as the series' organizing presumption
Haus des Beschwörungspriesters (House of the Exorcism Priest), Assur — generations of exorcists' working archive

competing_hypotheses: The exact boundaries of the 'canonical sixteen' vs forerunner tablets (Geller's forerunner volumes map the pre-canonical material)
Whether the sickness/health polarity was the compilers' presumption or a modern reading of the series' emphasis (SBL review's framing)
falsifiability: A first-millennium library catalogue listing the series' supposed companions while omitting Utukkū Lemnūtu would weaken the canonicity claim; the grade covers the artifacts and the attested belief, never the demons.

title: The Yunmin and Iti mastaba — 2026 Saqqara discovery
claim: A joint Egyptian-Spanish mission excavated a late Fifth Dynasty mastaba at the Mariette Cemetery north of Saqqara (reign of Djedkare Isesi, c. 24th century BCE) with two decorated funerary chapels — the main chapel of the senior official Yunmin (judge, court director, chief of the petition-handling scribes) and the southern chapel of his father Iti (scribal official of agricultural lands and offerings) — with reliefs retaining vivid original color.
place: Mariette Cemetery, north Saqqara, Egypt
grade_reason: Announced by the Egyptian antiquities ministry with named mission, named owners, and readable titles; reported independently by international press; excavation still in analysis — final publication pending.
earliest_attestation: Excavated and announced September 2026; the mastaba site had been known since Auguste Mariette's 19th-century excavations but never excavated or documented with modern scientific methods.

sources.ref: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities announcement, Sept 2026 (Egyptian-Spanish mission, Autonomous University of Barcelona + Supreme Council of Antiquities, 2026 excavation season, Mariette Cemetery)
CBS News, Sept 2026: 'Exceptionally well-preserved' tomb of judge and his father
ImNews Africa, 19 Sept 2026: Saqqara excavation reveals Fifth-Dynasty chapels of Egyptian judge and father

Archaeology Magazine (archaeologymag.com), Sept 2026: 'Senior judge's tomb with colorful funerary scenes uncovered at Saqqara' — coverage of the Yunmin/Iti mastaba (Mariette Cemetery, 2026 season), venue-echo of the recorded ministry announcement, grade-neutral
Medium (Adam Jones), Oct 2026: 'Fifth Dynasty Tomb Reveals Colorful Life at Saqqara' — popular restatement of the same 2026-season find, venue-not-evidence

competing_hypotheses: The exact readings of Yunmin's and Iti's titles may be refined in the final publication
The mastaba's original 19th-century discovery context (Mariette) vs. the 2026 documentation differ in methods, not in the monument
falsifiability: Re-reading of the inscriptions attributing the chapels to different owners, or re-dating of the mastaba outside the late Fifth Dynasty

title: Osiris: the murdered, reassembled, enthroned god of the dead
claim: The Egyptian tradition attests Osiris as a god who was murdered (by his brother Seth), dismembered, reassembled by Isis, and enthroned as judge and king of the dead — a death-and-return attested from the Old Kingdom onward, forming the theological core of Egyptian funerary religion.
place: Abydos (Osiris cult center; Osireion)
grade_reason: The belief-phenomenon is multiply attested across ~2,300 years of independent textual layers — Old Kingdom funerary texts, Middle Kingdom Coffin Texts, New Kingdom Book of the Dead, Abydos material culture, and the late classical witness. Grade covers the attestation, never the entities.
earliest_attestation: Pyramid Texts, Pyramid of Unas, 5th Dynasty, c. 2350 BCE; Coffin Texts; Book of the Dead; the Abydos Osireion; Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride, 2nd c. CE

sources.ref: Pyramid Texts of Unas (5th Dynasty, c. 2350 BCE) — Osiris mythos in the oldest religious literature
Coffin Texts; Book of the Dead (Book of Coming Forth by Day)
Abydos Osireion — material cult center of Osiris
Plutarch, De Iside et Osiride (2nd c. CE) — fullest narrative retelling; late outsider witness
Mettinger, Tryggve N.D., The Riddle of Resurrection: 'Dying and Rising Gods' in the Ancient Near East (Coniectanea Biblica OT Series; Eisenbrauns, 2001) — Osiris among the pre-Christian cases

competing_hypotheses: Osiris's 'death' is a kingship ritual rather than a dying-and-rising narrative: the king becomes Osiris at death, but Osiris himself does not 'return' to life among the living

The dismemberment/resurrection reading over-reads the Pyramid Texts — the early texts are fragmentary and funerary-formulaic, and the coherent narrative is mostly Plutarch's late (2nd c. CE) retelling
The maximalist reading: the texts describe a real entity's history — not graded; the attestation rule grades the belief, never the metaphysics
falsifiability: A demonstration that the Pyramid Texts are modern forgeries, or that no pre-Hellenistic Egyptian source describes Osiris's death and enthronement as king of the dead, would overturn the attestation

title: The destruction argument: deletion and destruction, read properly, are evidence
claim: Deletion and destruction, read properly, are historical evidence: what a regime erases proves the hand that feared it (the chisel's mark grades the belief that commissioned the hammer — evt-attestation-rule-001); what catastrophe preserves proves the archive that was there (fire bakes clay to permanence — evt-fire-baked-archives-001; Vesuvius carbonized the only intact ancient library — evt-herculaneum-pherc1667-2026-001); and the measured pattern of what is missing, checked against what should have survived, is itself a record. Destruction is deposition.
place: Multi-site method claim (Ebla, Herculaneum, Alexandria, Baghdad)
grade_reason: Method claim demonstrated across independent cases: Ebla (fire preserves), Herculaneum (catastrophe preserves the only intact ancient library, read 2026), Alexandria (the destruction telling itself debunked as the artifact), Baghdad 1258 (sack attested, legendary telling fenced), damnatio memoriae (erasure as evidence of the eraser).
earliest_attestation: The method is demonstrated in the excavation and manuscript records cited below

sources.ref: Ebla Palace G: fire-baked tablet archives preserved in shelving order (evt-fire-baked-archives-001)
PHerc.1667 read end-to-end without unrolling, June 2026, Vesuvius Challenge — ESRF Grenoble scans + AI ink detection, 22 columns of Greek Stoic text (evt-herculaneum-pherc1667-2026-001)

The single-catastrophic-fire account of Alexandria's library is DEBUNKED — Strabo's library outlives Caesar's 48 BCE fire; no library in five contemporary 391 CE accounts; the 642 story is 13th-century fabrication (evt-library-alexandria-001)

Mongol sack of Baghdad 1258 — siege, sack, and caliph's death multiply attested (evt-baghdad-1258-sack-001); the 'Tigris ran black with ink' telling is later/popular only (evt-baghdad-ink-river-legend-001)

Syria 2015–2025: the measured-destruction exhibit — Casana et al., Heritage, July 2026: 199 sites, 59% looted or destroyed 2015–2025 vs 13% in 2011–2016; mechanical (bulldozer) looting associated with military activity; Ain Dara nearly leveled by 2022 (evt-syria-heritage-destruction-2026-001). The destruction pattern is the record.

Crimea, 16 Oct 2026: Center for Spatial Technologies + CISS interactive satellite map — Russian fortifications (trenches, firing positions) cutting through ~3,000 years of settlement layers along the western coast; a live exhibit of erasure-as-deposition

Hagia Sophia, Oct 16–17, 2026: the third church on the site; the first burned in the 5th c., the second burned in the Nika riots (532) — foundations 2.3 m below the current floor; destruction is deposition, measured in stratigraphy (Diker presentation, Istanbul)
Damnatio memoriae: chiselled-out cartouches and gouged imperial names as evidence of the erasing regime (evt-attestation-rule-001 demonstration chain)
