title: Dumuzi becomes Tammuz: a documented cross-cultural transmission
claim: The Sumerian Dumuzi is the same figure as the Akkadian and Hebrew Tammuz — one god transmitted across languages and empires, his lament cult reaching the Jerusalem Temple court (Ezekiel 8:14).
place: Sumer to Babylonia to Jerusalem (the Dumuzi-Tammuz route)
grade_reason: Same figure across three languages with textual continuity, culminating in a Hebrew-prophetic witness to his Jerusalem cult; independent attestations on both ends of the transmission.
earliest_attestation: Sumerian Dumuzi literature, 3rd millennium BCE (Inanna's Descent, ETCSL t.1.4.1; Dumuzi's Dream)

sources.ref: ETCSL, Inanna's Descent to the Nether World (t.1.4.1); Dumuzi's Dream
Ezekiel 8:14 — women weeping for Tammuz at the north gate of the Temple
Tryggve N.D. Mettinger, The Riddle of Resurrection (2001) — Dumuzi chapter
Private pre-Christian letter likening survival of uprisings to Tammuz's ability to return from the dead (cited Mettinger 2001, p. 201)

competing_hypotheses: The Tammuz of Ezekiel is a local Canaanite fertility figure only coincidentally named, not the Sumerian Dumuzi by transmission (minority; the month-name chain and lament-form continuity weigh against it)
falsifiability: A demonstration that the Sumerian Dumuzi and the Akkadian Tammuz are lexically and cultically distinct figures (no name or lament continuity) would downgrade this to CLAIMED.

title: The preservation paradox: palace fire bakes Ebla's archives to permanence
claim: The cuneiform archives of Palace G at Ebla (Syria) survived for ~4,300 years because the palace burned: sun-dried clay tablets stored on wooden shelves were fire-baked by the palace's destruction (c. 2300 BCE) and collapsed in place, preserving the archive's original shelving order — destruction as the mechanism of preservation.
place: Tell Mardikh (Ebla), Syria — Palace G
grade_reason: Excavation reports multiply attest the fire-baked tablets in their shelving order; the mechanism (sun-dried clay + palace fire = kiln-fired permanence) is demonstrated material science applied to an archaeological fact.
earliest_attestation: The tablets themselves, excavated in situ by Paolo Matthiae's team 1974–75

sources.ref: Ebla Palace G archive: ~1,800 complete tablets, 4,700 fragments, found in situ on collapsed shelves

Wikipedia — Ebla tablets: 'Many of the tablets had not previously been baked, but when all were preserved by the fire that destroyed the palace, their storage method served to fire them almost as thoroughly as if in a kiln' (citing the excavation reports)
Wikipedia — Ebla: 'palace G was burned, baking the clay tablets of the royal archives and preserving them'

competing_hypotheses: The archive survived by accident of shelter rather than fire-baking (rebutted: unbaked tablets do not survive 4,300 years in a Levantine tell)

The preservation is typical, not paradoxical — most Near Eastern tablet archives are fire-baked (true at scale, which strengthens rather than weakens the record: the general rule is that archives survive destruction)
falsifiability: Unbaked tablets from the same archive surviving unbaked elsewhere, or proof the Palace G fire postdates the tablets' deposition

title: The exposed-infant-on-the-river topos: Sargon's basket as the older witness
claim: The birth narrative of Sargon of Akkad — exposed as an infant in a reed basket caulked with bitumen, set on the river, recovered and raised by a water-drawer — is attested in cuneiform copies (Neo-Assyrian, preserving older tradition; Brian Lewis, The Sargon Legend, ASOR 1978). The exposed-infant-on-the-river topos therefore predates the Moses birth narrative (Exodus 2) by roughly a millennium in its attested form. Whether the Exodus writer knew Sargon's legend directly, or both drew on a shared older topos, is a literary judgment, not a provable borrowing.
place: Akkad / Mesopotamia (legend's setting; copies from Nineveh)
grade_reason: The Sargon legend's text exists and carries the topos; the chronological priority of the attested witness is a matter of the tablets, not of interpretation.
earliest_attestation: The Sargon Birth Legend (cuneiform; surviving copies Neo-Assyrian, 7th c. BCE, preserving older tradition)

sources.ref: The Sargon Birth Legend (cuneiform text; Neo-Assyrian copies)
Brian Lewis, The Sargon Legend (American Schools of Oriental Research, 1978)
Exodus 2:1–10 (the Moses birth narrative — the topos's later witness)
Michael Heiser, Naked Bible Podcast 257 analysis: the Sargon legend's current form may post-date the Exodus composition; structural differences between the narratives

competing_hypotheses: Direct literary dependence: the Exodus writer knew the Sargon legend and modeled the birth narrative on it
Shared topos: both narratives draw independently on an older exposed-infant tradition (the genre reading)
Reverse or convergent dating: the Sargon legend's surviving form post-dates the Exodus composition, weakening the priority claim (Heiser's caution)
falsifiability: A securely dated copy of the Sargon legend older than the earliest Exodus composition would settle the priority; a demonstration that the topos is a modern scholarly construct would collapse the record

title: The King List as political charter (the legitimation thesis)
claim: The Sumerian King List was composed and redacted to legitimize contemporary rulers' claims to power over Babylonia — the 'Chronicle of the One Monarchy' in which kingship, a single institution, passes from city to city — rather than to record political history; the Weld-Blundell recension's ending with the Isin dynasty marks it as Isin's turn as rightful inheritor of the Ur III legacy.
place: Isin (whose dynasty the WB 444 recension ends with)
grade_reason: A well-supported scholarly thesis resting on the text's structure (the one-monarchy formula, the Isin ending, documented deliberate edits between recensions) — but the composition act itself is inferred, and the Akkad-origin alternative is live.
earliest_attestation: Inferred from the text's structure and recension history, not from any contemporary statement of purpose; scholarly thesis (Jacobsen 1939; Michalowski 1983)

sources.ref: Sumerian King List overview (list created/redacted to legitimize claims to power; Steinkeller's Akkad-origin argument; WB 444's Isin ending; antediluvian section as Kish-downplaying insertion)
Piotr Michalowski, 'History as Charter: Some Observations on the Sumerian King List', JAOS 103 (1983), pp. 237-248
Thorkild Jacobsen, The Sumerian King List (AS 11, 1939)
Piotr Steinkeller, 'An Ur III Manuscript of the Sumerian King List' (Festschrift Wilcke, 2003)

competing_hypotheses: Steinkeller's Akkad-origin thesis: the list was first created under the Akkad dynasty to position Akkad as direct heir to Kish's hegemony, with later rulers amending it for their own purposes
The list as scribal-school tradition: a literary composition that accreted over centuries (Ur III USKL through Old Babylonian copies) rather than a single commissioned political act
falsifiability: A contemporary inscription stating the list's purpose as straight historiography, or a single Ur III-period exemplar identical in ideology to the Isin recension (which would collapse the deliberate-editing evidence)

title: The King List's dynasties overlapped — the sequential 'one monarchy' is editorial
claim: The Sumerian King List's dynasties did not all rule sequentially: several city-state dynasties were contemporary with each other, so the list's 'kingship was taken to [city]' sequence — the one-monarchy formula — is an editorial arrangement, not a political record of Mesopotamia.
place: Southern Mesopotamia (Kish, Uruk, Ur, Lagash, Mari, Akkad)
grade_reason: Three independent lines: (1) the Sumerian composition 'Gilgamesh and Aga' shows Aga of Kish as Gilgamesh of Uruk's contemporary, while the List files Kish I before Uruk I; (2) the ETCSL composite text's own manuscript variants disagree about dynasty order, boundaries, and reign numbers, proving the sequence was fluid and editorial; (3) contemporary royal inscriptions (Enmetena, the Lagash ruler line) document courts the List's sequence compresses into succession. CORROBORATED, not VERIFIED: some dynastic boundaries rest on thin inscriptional ground and the Jacobsen-preservation minority position is live.
earliest_attestation: The finding is modern scholarship's (Jacobsen 1939; collated variants in ETCSL t.2.1.1); the ancient evidence is the 'Gilgamesh and Aga' composition and contemporary royal inscriptions

sources.ref: ETCSL t.2.1.1 composite text — the manuscript variants: mss. P2+L2 reorder the 10th/11th rulers of Kish ahead of the 8th/9th; P3+BT14, Su1, S, IB add, omit, and reverse dynasties and reigns throughout (re-verified live 2026-10-16)
'Gilgamesh and Aga' (ETCSL t.1.8.1.1): Aga of Kish besieges Uruk while Gilgamesh reigns there — the two kings of the List's supposedly sequential Kish I and Uruk I dynasties as contemporaries
Thorkild Jacobsen, The Sumerian King List (AS 11, 1939) — the compositional and variant analysis; Finkelstein 1963 version comparison (7-8 vs 10 kings)

Piotr Steinkeller, 'An Ur III Manuscript of the Sumerian King List' (2003) — the USKL (Ur III copy) differs structurally from the Old Babylonian recensions, proving editorial reshaping across centuries; the Sargon-Rimush-Manishtusu internal sequence itself contested (Steinkeller's reversal proposal vs the traditional order)

competing_hypotheses: Jacobsen's tradition-preservation thesis: the sequence preserves garbled but genuine dynastic memory, and the parallelism is overstated where the evidence is thin
The list as scribal-school literary composition: the sequence was never meant as chronology at all, so 'parallel' is the wrong axis — it is literature, not a broken calendar
falsifiability: A recension-independent chronology (a king list tradition plus contemporary dating) showing every named dynasty strictly sequential with no overlap — the contemporary evidence would have to stop contradicting the sequence

title: Udug: the word that didn't pick a side
claim: The Sumerian udug (Akkadian utukku) was originally a neutral class-term for spirits — the word itself did not connote good or evil. Gudea of Lagash (c. 2144–2124 BCE) asked a goddess to send him a 'good udug' for protection; exorcism texts invoke the good udug against the evil udug (udug-hul / utukkū lemnūtu), the evil ones blamed as vectors of physical and mental illness. The belief-phenomenon is multiply attested across two millennia of cuneiform texts; the entities are not graded.
place: Lagash (Telloh), southern Mesopotamia
grade_reason: The neutral-to-ambivalent usage is multiply attested in primary texts (Gudea, OB incantations); the evil-udug-as-illness-vector is the canonical series' own premise, graded as belief-phenomenon per the attestation rule.
earliest_attestation: Gudea cylinders (good udug, c. 2144–2124 BCE); Old Babylonian exorcism texts invoking good udug against evil udug

sources.ref: Gudea cylinders (Lagash, c. 2144–2124 BCE) — 'good udug' for protection
Konstantopoulos 2017 (on the udug's originally neutral connotation)
Black & Green 1992, Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia
Cunningham 2007 ('daimon' preferable to 'demon' for the ambivalent udug)
Old Babylonian incantation: 'May the evil udug and the evil galla stand aside. May the good udug and good galla be present.'

competing_hypotheses: Udug as umbrella term for all demons (the word sometimes functions generically, not as a specific being)
The 'udug alone usually connotes the evil udug' usage note — unqualified udug in late texts defaults to evil
falsifiability: Securely dated pre-Gudea attestations using udug as inherently evil would overturn the original-neutrality claim; the grade covers the attestation, never the entities.

title: The "House of Abraham" at Ur — Saddam-era tourist designation with no archaeological basis
claim: A specific excavated house at Tell el-Muqayyar (Ur) is presented to visitors as the house / birthplace of the biblical Abraham.
grade_reason: Woolley himself selected the house 'more or less at random' from Old Babylonian-period dwellings on the assumption Abraham was a wealthy merchant (diggings.co.uk); the houses date to the Ur III / Old Babylonian periods (c. 2112–1600 BCE) and are typical domestic structures of the quarter, not distinguishable as any individual's home (madainproject.com); the 1990s restoration and 'House of the Prophet Abraham' signage were ordered under Saddam Hussein's regime as national-religious heritage branding, following modern political agendas rather than archaeological accuracy; no excavation data links any Ur dwelling to Abraham.
earliest_attestation: Woolley 1920s publicity; signage 1990s

sources.ref: madainproject.com 'House of Abraham (Ur)' — 'entirely speculative and has no basis in archaeology or historical evidence'; Saddam-era 1990s restoration and signage as political heritage campaign

falsifiability: A contemporary inscription or stratified deposit linking a specific Ur dwelling to Abraham would reopen the claim; none exists.

title: Dumuzi/Tammuz: the shepherd-god condemned, dragged down, and portioned between worlds
claim: The Sumerian tradition attests Dumuzi (Akkadian Tammuz) as a shepherd-god condemned to death by Inanna's 'look of death' (igi mu-un-ši-in-bar), seized by the galla-demons, and granted a divided fate — six months in the underworld, six months above (shared with his sister Geshtinanna) — with laments for him attested into the Hebrew Bible (Ezekiel 8:14).
place: Southern Mesopotamia (Nippur — tablet copies; Uruk — Dumuzi's city)
grade_reason: The death is textually ironclad (the 'look of death' passage, ETCSL c.1.4.1:354-358); the return/partition is attested across variant endings and Dumuzi's Dream; the living lament reaches the Hebrew Bible. The grade covers the belief-phenomenon with the half-year crux fenced in competing hypotheses.
earliest_attestation: Inanna's Descent to the Netherworld (ETCSL c.1.4.1); Dumuzi's Dream (ETCSL c.1.4.3); Ezekiel 8:14 (the women weeping for Tammuz at the Temple)

sources.ref: Inanna's Descent to the Netherworld (ETCSL c.1.4.1:354-358) — the 'look of death' and the galla-demons seizing Dumuzi
Dumuzi's Dream (ETCSL c.1.4.3) — the pursuit, death, and the six-months-below/six-months-above decree
Ezekiel 8:14 — the women of Jerusalem 'weeping for Tammuz' in the Temple court (6th c. BCE)
Mettinger, The Riddle of Resurrection (2001) — Dumuzi as a genuine pre-Christian dying-and-rising case against the 1990s consensus

competing_hypotheses: The half-year arrangement is the decisive textual crux: it is drawn from Dumuzi's Dream and variant endings of the Descent, and lacunae in the manuscripts leave the exact decree disputed — the 'resurrection' half of the story is reconstructed across texts, not read in one
Dumuzi's death is a sacred-marriage ritual drama, not a 'dying-and-rising god' narrative: the king's ritual death/rebirth, not the god's

The 1990s consensus position: Dumuzi died but did not return — the return half is a modern scholarly construction (answered by Mettinger 2001: 'the category of dying and rising gods is not a phantom construct')
The maximalist reading: the texts describe a real entity's history — not graded; the attestation rule grades the belief, never the metaphysics
falsifiability: A demonstration that the Descent tablets are forgeries, or that Ezekiel 8:14's 'Tammuz' refers to something other than the Mesopotamian god, would overturn the attestation

title: The Kish I reign spans are mathematically constructed, not chronology
claim: The post-flood First Dynasty of Kish reign lengths in the Sumerian King List (Gushur 1,200 through Aga 625 years, ~24,510 years total) are arithmetically designed numbers — most exact multiples of 60 (1,200 = 20×60, 960 = 16×60, 840 = 14×60, 720 = 12×60, 600 = 10×60, 420 = 7×60, 300 = 5×60), with perfect squares among them (900 = 30² for Zuqaqip, Melem-Kish, Ilku, and Enmebaragesi; 324 = 18² for Meshkiangasher of Uruk I) — a different numerical scheme from the antediluvian set (sars of 3,600, ners of 600, sosses of 60).
place: Kish (Tell al-Uhaymir), Iraq — the manuscripts' findspots vary (Nippur, Larsa, Susa, Sippar)
grade_reason: A peer-reviewed mathematical observation about the transmitted text: the reign figures are verifiable in the manuscripts (ETCSL), and Young's two JNES studies argue the pattern is deliberate design, not transmission noise; it remains a scholarly interpretation of the scribal method, not an excavated fact, so the ceiling is CORROBORATED.
earliest_attestation: Old Babylonian copies of the Sumerian King List, c. 19th–18th c. BCE

sources.ref: Young, Dwight W. (1988). 'A Mathematical Approach to Certain Dynastic Spans in the Sumerian King List.' JNES 47(2): 123–129 (doi:10.1086/373263) — the multiples-of-60 and perfect-squares reading (900 = 30², 324 = 18²)
Young, Dwight W. (1991). 'The Incredible Regnal Spans of Kish I in the Sumerian King List.' JNES 50(1): 23–35 (doi:10.1086/373462) — dedicated study of the Kish I dynasty spans

ETCSL t.2.1.1 composite text, post-flood Kish I section (opened 2026-10-16) — the reign figures as transmitted: 1,200 / 960 / 670 / 420+3mo3.5d / 300 / 840 / 960 / 840 / 900 / 600 / 840 / 720 / 1,500 / 400 / 660 / 900 / 1,200 / 140 / 305 / 900 / 1,200 / 900 / 625; 23 kings, 24,510 years 3 months 3.5 days

Wikipedia Sumerian King List article, Oct-2026 state — restates Young's reading ('various reigns were multiples of 60 ... while others were squares (e.g. Ilku reigned for 900 years (square of 30) while Meshkiangasher ruled for 324 years (square of 18))')

Rowton, M. B. (1960). 'The Date of the Sumerian King List.' JNES 19(2): 156–162 — the parallel argument for the Gutian dynasty (5/6/7-year reigns as sexagesimal round numbers, i.e. 'about 6' = decimal 'about 10')

competing_hypotheses: Young's designed-numbers reading (peer-reviewed, JNES 1988/1991) — the reigns were constructed from sexagesimal round units and squares
Jacobsen 1939's salvage reading — the names are real administrative-list survivals and the long spans exaggerate a shorter truth (20–30-year average replacements)

Recension-level explanation — the figures vary across copies (ETCSL apparatus: 960/900 for Kullassina-bel, 840/240 for Puannum, 1,500/635 for Etana), so the 'formula' may be an emergent product of editorial accumulation rather than a single design
falsifiability: A contemporary Early Dynastic inscription documenting actual Kish I reign lengths in human scale, or demonstration that the multiples-of-60/squares pattern is a cherry-picked coincidence against the full variant corpus

title: The King List's one-at-a-time dynastic sequence is false
claim: The Sumerian King List presents the dynasties of the Early Dynastic period as strictly sequential — kingship held by one city at a time, passed from city to city only when the previous city was 'smitten with weapons'. Contemporary evidence contradicts this: cities the list serializes (Kish, Uruk, Ur, Lagash) held power at the same moment; the list omits the Dynasty of Lagash entirely although its rulers are contemporary with listed kings (Ur-Nanshe(k) of Lagash was roughly contemporaneous with Mes-Anne-pada of Ur; the list's 45 pre-Sargonic rulers cannot have reigned sequentially in the period Lagash's 11 rulers cover); only seven pre-Sargonic SKL kings are attested in contemporary Early Dynastic inscriptions; the ESF-funded ARCANE project's final volume on third-millennium Mesopotamia lists no pre-Sargonic SKL ruler unless corroborated by contemporary inscriptions; recent handbooks warn the SKL should not be used as a historical source for the Early Dynastic period at all. The omission of important cities (Lagash, Larsa) is treated as deliberate.
place: Southern Mesopotamia (Kish, Uruk, Ur, Lagash, Adab, Mari, Akshak)
grade_reason: Contemporary inscriptions and the ARCANE chronological tables contradict the list's sequential presentation: serialized cities were contemporary, Lagash is omitted while contemporary with listed kings, and only seven pre-Sargonic SKL kings have contemporary attestation. This grades the sequentiality claim only — the artifact's existence is CORROBORATED (evt-sumerian-king-list-002), the antediluvian reign lengths are DEBUNKED (evt-skl-antediluvian-reigns-001), the parallel dynasties are CORROBORATED as overlapping (evt-skl-parallel-dynasties-001 — this record is its mirror image: where that record corroborates the overlap, this one debunks the list's claim that no overlap existed), and the legitimation thesis remains CLAIMED (evt-skl-legitimation-charter-001).
earliest_attestation: The Sumerian King List copies themselves (the 'then X was defeated and the kingship was taken to Y' formula); contradicted by contemporary Early Dynastic inscriptions

sources.ref: Sumerian King List overview — ARCANE final volume excludes uncorroborated pre-Sargonic SKL rulers from chronological tables; only seven pre-Sargonic SKL kings attested in contemporary Early Dynastic inscriptions; recent handbooks warn against using the SKL as a historical source for the Early Dynastic period; omission of Lagash and Larsa judged deliberate; strict sequential ordering does no justice to overlapping reigns (Oct-2026 article state)

Steinkeller 2003 (via Oct-2026 archaeological synthesis): the Ur III copy (dedicated to the living divinized Shulgi, ending with Ur-Namma's 18 years) carries no Flood-era opening — the antediluvian section is a later Old Babylonian editorial layer; 'Kish, Uruk, Ur and Lagash often held power at the same moment'; Enmebaragesi the earliest king with a contemporary inscription (debated)

Thorkild Jacobsen, The Sumerian King List (AS 11, 1939): Mes-Anne-pada of Ur roughly contemporaneous with Ur-Nanshe(k) of Lagash — the list's 45 pre-Sargonic rulers cannot have followed one another sequentially in the period covered by Lagash's eleven; treatment of Kish III/Akshak/Kish IV shows the author working from city-specific date lists
Lagash priest-kings absent from the list (political play in the composition); contemporaneous dynasties placed one after another as if sequential
ETCSL transliteration t.2.1.1 (Oxford) — the primary text of the sequential formula itself ('then the flood swept over'; 'then X was defeated and the kingship was taken to Y')

competing_hypotheses: The theological-argument reading: the list was never meant as history but as a theological argument about kingship as a single institution descending from heaven (so 'false as chronology' misses its purpose)
The hegemony-shift reading: the sequence records changes in regional dominance, not exclusive rule — serialized dynasties overlapped but the list tracks who held hegemony
falsifiability: A stratified, independently dated destruction/abandonment sequence matching the list's city order, or contemporary year-name/dated-inscription evidence that the serialized Early Dynastic dynasties were in fact strictly sequential

title: The Code of Ur-Nammu — the earliest extant law code
claim: The Code of Ur-Nammu (c. 2100-2050 BCE), issued in the name of the Ur III king Ur-Nammu (2112-2095 BCE) — or possibly published by his son Shulgi — is the earliest extant written law code: 57 laws in casuistic if-then form, mostly compensation-based (fines rather than lex talionis), preserved on tablets now in the Schøyen Collection and the Istanbul Archaeological Museum.
place: Ur (Tell el-Muqayyar), Iraq
grade_reason: The tablets physically exist and are multiply attested; authorship (Ur-Nammu vs Shulgi) and exact date are debated, so it stops one step short of VERIFIED.
earliest_attestation: Cuneiform tablets: copies found at Ur and Sippar; the 1965 Ur tablets allowed ~30 of the 57 laws to be reconstructed

title: The 'Apiru/'Habiru in the Bronze Age sources
claim: The 'Apiru (Akkadian ḫa-bi-ru / SA.GAZ) appear in Bronze Age texts from the early 2nd millennium through the 12th century BCE — the Amarna letters (c. 1350 BCE, ~60 occurrences), Egyptian New Kingdom administrative records, and the Mari, Nuzi, Alalakh, and Hittite archives — as a social category of displaced persons, mercenaries, laborers, and outsiders. In those texts the term is a status label, not an ethnic self-designation.
place: Tell el-Amarna, Egypt (densest attestation cluster; the term's range runs Mesopotamia–Levant–Egypt)
grade_reason: Multiple independent primary corpora (Amarna cuneiform, Egyptian administrative texts, Hittite/Mari/Nuzi archives) attest the term across ~7 centuries; mainstream scholarship reads it as a social category. Not VERIFIED: no single corpus fixes the term's exact semantic range, and the 'Apiru-to-'Ivri equation remains a separate debated claim.
earliest_attestation: Early 2nd-millennium cuneiform archives (Mari); the Amarna letters, c. 1350 BCE, carry roughly sixty occurrences.

sources.ref: The Amarna letters (EA corpus; e.g. EA 68, 71–74) — Moran, The Amarna Letters (1992)

falsifiability: A philological demonstration that SA.GAZ/ḫa-bi-ru never denotes a social category in any corpus, or proof that the Amarna 'Apiru references are modern forgeries, would reopen this record.

title: The Mesopotamian flood tradition

Direct literary borrowing of Genesis from Gilgamesh is NOT established; scholars argue shared tradition rather than word-for-word copying.
place: Shuruppak (Tell Fara), Ziusudra's city, southern Iraq
grade_reason: The tablets exist, are multiply attested, and the structural parallels are documented by generations of scholars. The MECHANISM (borrowing vs shared tradition vs independent invention) remains disputed, not graded.
earliest_attestation: Sumerian Flood Story (Ziusudra), Nippur, pre-2000 BCE; Atrahasis epic, Old Babylonian, ca. 1630 BCE; Gilgamesh Tablet XI translated by George Smith 1872 (British Museum)

sources.ref: Lambert & Millard, Atra-Hasis: The Babylonian Story of the Flood (1969)

Grade-neutral exhibit: real Mesopotamian flooding, dated after the tradition.

falsifiability: Discovery of a Genesis manuscript older than the Mesopotamian texts, or proof the Mesopotamian flood tablets are modern forgeries

title: The ancient parasols: shade-umbrellas before the rain umbrella
claim: Parasols — umbrellas used as sun-shades and emblems of rank — existed in the ancient Near East and China millennia before the modern rain umbrella: royal parasols in ancient Assyria and Egypt (conventionally ~4,000 years, carried by servants for kings), waterproof oil-paper and silk umbrellas in China (conventionally 11th c. BCE), early folding forms (conventionally c. 21 CE), and the Roman umbraculum as a sun-shade for women and priests.

grade_reason: Multiple independent iconographic and textual traditions — Assyrian royal reliefs, Egyptian tomb paintings, the Roman umbraculum in Latin texts, and the Chinese oil-paper tradition — agree that shade-parasols are ancient; held below VERIFIED because this pass relied on trade-history aggregations (aina.org, umbrella histories) rather than a museum-cataloged primary artifact per claim.

title: The antediluvian reign lengths are schematic, not historical
claim: The Sumerian King List's eight antediluvian kings did not literally reign 28,800 to 43,200 years each (241,200 years total): every reign is expressible in the Sumerian sexagesimal units sars (3,600), ners (600), and sosses (60), none of the eight kings is verified as historical by any contemporary inscription or excavation, and the antediluvian section is absent from some recensions including the Nippur majority copies.
place: Southern Mesopotamia (Eridu, Bad-tibira, Larag, Sippar, Shuruppak — the five antediluvian cities)
grade_reason: The numbers are arithmetically constructed from sexagesimal round units (8/10/12 x 3,600 etc.), no contemporary evidence names any of the eight as historical rulers, and the section's absence from major recensions proves it is a removable editorial layer.
earliest_attestation: Old Babylonian copies of the Sumerian King List (the section is absent from the Nippur majority and from the Ur III USKL)

title: Proto-Sinaitic — the first alphabet (c. 1800 BCE)
claim: The earliest alphabetic writing is the Proto-Sinaitic script, invented c. 19th-16th century BCE — roughly seven centuries before the Phoenician abjad — by Semitic-speaking workers in Egyptian service, working from hieroglyphic signs by the acrophonic principle (the 'Egyptian origin of the Semitic alphabet').
place: Serabit el-Khadim, Sinai Peninsula (turquoise-mining region; Wadi el-Hol on the Theban desert road is the second anchor)
grade_reason: The inscriptions are real, multiply published, and dated by context; Gardiner's 1916 reading of lbʿlt ('to the Lady' = Hathor) is practically universally accepted; but the exact century, the language identification, and WHO held the chisel are all still argued between the leading scholars.
earliest_attestation: Serabit el-Khadim inscriptions, Sinai — discovered winter 1904-1905 by Flinders Petrie (published 1906); decipherment breakthrough by Alan Gardiner 1916 ('The Egyptian Origin of the Semitic Alphabet,' JEA 3); Wadi el-Hol inscriptions discovered 1993, published 1999 (Darnell et al.)

sources.ref: Gardiner, A.H. (1916), 'The Egyptian Origin of the Semitic Alphabet,' Journal of Egyptian Archaeology 3

Darnell, J.C., Dobbs-Allsopp, F.W., Lundberg, M.J., McCarter, P.K., Zuckerman, B. (2005), 'Two Early Alphabetic Inscriptions from the Wadi el-Hôl,' BASOR 340 — the 1999/2005 publication pushing the alphabet's origin to c. 1800-1900 BCE
Goldwasser, O. (2010), 'How the Alphabet Was Born from Hieroglyphs,' Biblical Archaeology Review 36(1) — the Semitic-miners inventor thesis
Rollston, C. — rollstonepigraphy.com: the Serabit corpus, Wadi el-Hol, and the honest-dating work (18th c. BCE argued)
BBC News (15 Nov 1999), 'Oldest alphabet found in Egypt' — contemporary report of the Darnell publication

competing_hypotheses: The Darnells' original 1999 hypothesis: Egyptian scribes and bureaucrats invented the script to communicate with the Semitic-speaking 'Asiatics' in their charge — same rocks, opposite direction of invention

Orly Goldwasser's refinement: the inventors were the Semitic-speaking miners themselves (illiterate or semi-literate), using the acrophonic principle — the house-sign becomes 'b' for bayt — with the Wadi el-Hol forms showing the borrowing in progress

The sceptical position: the corpus is small (~40 inscriptions, many single-sign), the decipherment rests on a handful of readings (Gardiner's lbʿlt), and the 'single invention c. 1800 BCE' consensus may over-read the evidence — Rollston's own caveat work on exact dating stands here
falsifiability: A securely dated alphabetic inscription in an independent tradition that clearly predates the Wadi el-Hol finds, or positive proof that the Wadi el-Hol marks are non-phonetic decoration rather than writing

title: The 'Pythagorean' triples of Old Babylon — Plimpton 322 & YBC 7289, c. 1800 BCE
claim: Old Babylonian scribes (c. 1822-1762 BCE, Larsa, the age of Hammurabi) knew and used the relationship between the sides of right triangles: the Plimpton 322 tablet lists 15 rows of Pythagorean triples (integer sets satisfying a² + b² = c²), and the YBC 7289 school tablet computes the diagonal of a square as 1;24,51,10 in sexagesimal (~1.41421296, i.e. √2 to six sexagesimal places) — the 'diagonal rule' in working use roughly twelve centuries before Pythagoras of Samos was born.
place: Larsa (Tell as-Senkereh), southern Mesopotamia — attributed provenance
grade_reason: The artifacts are multiply documented and their mathematical content (the triples, the √2 approximation) is uncontested; only the tablet's PURPOSE is debated (trig table vs teacher's problem list) — the triples themselves are not in dispute.
earliest_attestation: The tablets themselves — contemporary Old Babylonian artifacts, c. 19th-18th century BCE

sources.ref: Plimpton 322 (Columbia University Rare Book & Manuscript Library) — the artifact
YBC 7289 (Yale Babylonian Collection) — the √2 school tablet
Neugebauer & Sachs, Mathematical Cuneiform Texts (1945) — first publication of Plimpton 322

Robson, 'Neither Sherlock Holmes nor Babylon: a reassessment of Plimpton 322', Historia Mathematica 28(3):167-206 (2001), doi:10.1006/hmat.2001.2317 — the pedagogy reading; the trig-table view 'cannot be correct' given the Old Babylonian concept of angle
Britton, Proust & Shnider, 'Plimpton 322: a review and a different perspective', Archive for History of Exact Sciences 65(5):519-566 (2011)

competing_hypotheses: Mansfield & Wildberger 2017 (Historia Mathematica 44(4):395-419): the tablet is exact sexagesimal trigonometry, predating Hipparchus by a millennium — the trig reading, contested

Robson 2001: the tablet is a teacher's aid for generating reciprocal-pair/right-triangle problems — the pedagogy reading; the column headings read as reciprocal-pair language, and the Old Babylonian period has no concept of angle as the Greeks used it
The older Neugebauer view: a number-theoretic exercise in generating Pythagorean triples; purpose secondary to the mathematics
falsifiability: Proof the tablet is a modern forgery, or a redating outside the Old Babylonian period; or a demonstration that the number columns do not in fact satisfy the triple relationship

title: The Weld-Blundell Prism (WB 444)
claim: The Weld-Blundell Prism is the only relatively undamaged, complete surviving witness of the Sumerian King List: a four-sided baked-clay prism (~20 x 9 cm), inscribed in Sumerian cuneiform in two columns per face, found at Larsa in 1922 and dated to year 11 of Sin-magir of Isin (c. 1800 BCE).

grade_reason: The object exists in the Ashmolean, its inscription is published and multiply photographed, and its internal dating (year 11 of Sin-magir) is read directly from the clay.

Weld-Blundell Prism summary (dimensions, Larsa 1922 find, AN1923.444)

falsifiability: Epigraphic re-examination showing the year formula names a different king, or proof the prism is a modern forgery (its 1922 excavation context and 1923 publication argue against this)

title: The ukkinu: the Babylonian assembly that voted Marduk king
claim: In Enūma Eliš (the Babylonian Epic of Creation, Tablet II–III), the divine assembly is the mechanism of cosmic government: the gods are summoned by ministerial herald (Gaga/Kakka), 'make ready for a feast, at a banquet let them sit, let them eat bread, let them mix wine, that for Marduk, their avenger they may decree the fate.' Drunk at the banquet, the assembled gods invest Marduk — 'they granted him the right to exercise kingship over the gods' (Tablet IV) — and in Tablet VI the same assembly presides as a court: 'Let the great gods be here in Assembly,' Kingu is tried and executed for the uprising, and the fifty great gods take their seats to divide the stations of heaven and netherworld. The council decrees fates (šīmatu), names, and destinies; it is where divine kingship is voted, not born.
place: Nineveh (copies); Babylon (composition)
grade_reason: The epic exists in multiple ancient copies; the assembly/decree vocabulary is documented Akkadian philology.
earliest_attestation: Enūma Eliš Tablets II–IV, VI; copies from Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh (excavated 1849–1851; George Smith's 1876 publication)

sources.ref: Enūma Eliš, Tablets II–III (the feast), IV (the investiture), VI (the assembly court)
W.G. Lambert's edition and translation
Copies from Ashurbanipal's library, Nineveh (7th c. BCE)

competing_hypotheses: The assembly scenes are Babylonian political theater written to legitimize Marduk's elevation under the First Dynasty (the 'propaganda' reading — the council as Marduk's campaign apparatus)
The Enūma Eliš assembly reflects an older pan-Mesopotamian divine-assembly template (cf. the ukkinu in the Anzu epic, Atrahasis) rather than a specifically Babylonian invention
falsifiability: Proof the Nineveh copies are modern forgeries, or that the 'assembly' lines are mistranslated ritual instructions

title: The 'Moses inscription' telling (Serabit el-Khadim, 2025-2026)
claim: The press telling that Proto-Sinaitic inscriptions at the Serabit el-Khadim turquoise mines (c. 1800-1600 BCE) contain the name 'Mose' and may be the handwriting of the biblical Moses — from Michael S. Bar-Ron's draft thesis (Ariel University, 2025), reported by the Daily Mail and National Geographic in August 2025 and recirculated in 2026. The telling grades the press claim, not the inscriptions (which are real and long known).

grade_reason: The reading comes from an unpublished draft thesis whose author states it will be subject to peer review and has already revised it 100+ times; Proto-Sinaitic characters are notoriously hard to decipher; and the biblical identification is not established even if the name-reading were right — 'Mose' is documented as a common Egyptian name in New Kingdom documents.

title: The Bar-Ron Proto-Sinaitic 'Moses' reading (2026)
claim: In 2026, researcher Michael S. Bar-Ron (Ariel University) proposed that two Proto-Sinaitic inscriptions (Sinai 357 and 361) from the turquoise mines at Serabit el-Khadim, Egypt, c. 1800-1600 BCE, read 'zot m'Moshe' ('This is from Moses') and 'ne'um Moshe' ('A saying of Moses') — presented as a possible extra-biblical attestation of the name Moses centuries before the Exodus narratives. The inscriptions are real Middle Bronze Age carvings; the Moses reading is one researcher's proposal, contested by specialists and not peer-reviewed. It does not constitute a verified contemporary attestation of the figure and does not overturn evt-moses-figure-attestation-001.
place: Serabit el-Khadim, Sinai Peninsula, Egypt (turquoise mines)
grade_reason: A real proposal by a named researcher about real Middle Bronze Age inscriptions — but Proto-Sinaitic is undeciphered (letter values, reading direction, word divisions insecure), the reading is rejected by the relevant specialist, and it has not survived peer review. The artifacts grade high; the reading grades CLAIMED. A vote is not evidence — and neither is a reading.

sources.ref: Archaeology Magazine, July 2026 — report of Bar-Ron's proposed 'zot m'Moshe' reading via high-resolution photography and 3D scanning of 20+ proto-Sinaitic inscriptions (as quoted in cogwriter.com, Aug 2025)

attractions.net.au, Oct 2026 — Bar-Ron's Fox News Digital interview: 'zot m'Moshe' / 'ne'um Moshe', inscriptions reference El and curse the Ba'alat cult ('BŠ' — 'for shame'; 'nimosh' — 'let us leave')

title: Hammurabi of Babylon
claim: Hammurabi, sixth king of Babylon's First Dynasty, reigned c. 1792-1750 BCE (middle chronology), unifying southern Mesopotamia under Babylonian rule; his reign is documented by year names, royal inscriptions, and an extensive archive of letters.
place: Babylon
grade_reason: Multiple independent contemporary sources — year names, inscriptions, and diplomatic correspondence — confirm his reign and deeds.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary year names, royal inscriptions, and the Mari archive letters (early 18th century BCE)

sources.ref: Hammurabi year-name lists (contemporary administrative records)
Hammurabi's letters (e.g., the Mari archive correspondence)
Royal inscriptions of Hammurabi

Manning et al. 2016, 'Integrated Tree-Ring-Radiocarbon High-Resolution Timeframe to Resolve Earlier Second Millennium BCE Mesopotamian Chronology' (PLOS ONE 11(7):e0157144) — independent dendro-radiocarbon support for the middle chronology

competing_hypotheses: Middle chronology dating (1792-1750 BCE) is correct — now backed by independent dendro-radiocarbon evidence (Manning et al. 2016)
Low-middle chronology (±8 years lower) is correct — the honest residual dispute; a decisive astronomical anchor would settle it

Low chronology (1728-1686 BCE) and ultra-low (1696-1654 BCE) — largely superseded: incompatible with the dendro-radiocarbon timeframe (ultra-low also refuted by the Venus observations themselves, Huber 2000)
falsifiability: A contemporary source placing a different king on Babylon's throne for those years, or proof the Mari letters are misattributed

title: The middle chronology for Hammurabi and Old Babylon
claim: The middle chronology is the correct absolute chronology for the Old Babylonian period: Hammurabi of Babylon reigned 1792–1750 BCE, the fall of Babylon to Mursili I dates to 1595 BCE, and the fall of Ur to 2004 BCE — against the rival high (Hammurabi 1848–1806), low (1728–1685), and ultra-low/new (1696–1654) chronologies.
place: Babylon, Iraq
grade_reason: Independent physical evidence (dendro-14C, Manning et al. 2016) converges on the same chronology the textual relative-chronology had long made the mainstream default; the rival high/low/ultra-low schemes are excluded by that anchor — though the ultra-low camp's eclipse-based case remains a stated minority position.
earliest_attestation: Relative chronology from Old Babylonian year-name lists and king lists; absolute anchor via dendro-14C in Manning et al. 2016 (PLOS ONE)

sources.ref: Manning, Griggs, Lorentzen, Barjamovic, Bronk Ramsey, Kromer & Wild 2016, 'Integrated Tree-Ring-Radiocarbon High-Resolution Timeframe to Resolve Earlier Second Millennium BCE Mesopotamian Chronology', PLOS ONE — tree-ring sequences integrated with radiocarbon from Kültepe (Waršama Palace) and Acemhöyük (Sarıkaya Palace), tied to Old Assyrian tablets naming Shamshi-Adad I; found 'compatible only with the so-called Middle Chronology'
Old Babylonian year-name lists and king lists (internal relative chronology; Hammurabi year 18 = death of Shamshi-Adad I — the tie between Anatolian timber contexts and Babylonian reigns)
Venus Tablet of Ammisaduqa (Enuma Anu Enlil Tablet 63) — genuine transmitted observational record whose 8/56/64-year cycle degeneracy leaves multiple chronologies selectable; see evt-venus-tablet-002

Gurzadyan 1998, 'Dating the Fall of Babylon' (Univ. of Ghent / Oriental Institute Chicago) — the ultra-low case (fall of Babylon 1499 BCE): pottery evidence, rejection of the extrapolated 56/64-year Venus cycles (8-year cycle only), lunar-eclipse identifications
Gurzadyan 2020, 'The Double Eclipse at the Downfall of Old Babylon' — lunar-eclipse record analysis of the Old Babylonian downfall

Wikipedia, 'Chronology of the ancient Near East' (page updated October 2026 — cross-checked 2026-10-17): middle chronology still 'the most commonly seen solution' with 'far from a consensus' stated; the October 2026 text is consistent with the held record state — no 2026 development on any chronology leg

The Old Assyrian merchant archive at Kaneš (Kültepe): ~23,000 tablets (letters, debt notes, caravan accounts, marriage contracts) plus the Revised Eponym List (Veenhof) — the 125-year limmu (year-eponym) sequence from Ērišum I. The documentary half of the Manning 2016 anchor: the Waršama Palace timbers grew where the merchants lived, and tablets naming Assyrian officials tie the tree-ring sequence to the year-name lists that tie to Shamshi-Adad I (died Hammurabi year 18). The REL's sequence is independently reconstructible across the Karum levels (Kt 92/k 94–96 eponym groups) and converges with the Kültepe building levels — the year-names merchants wrote to keep loans due are the dates the chronology stands on. (Grade-neutral source, appended 2026-10-18 via #512 — Turin-shroud precedent, no grade change.)

Eclipses, Volcanoes, and Eponyms: New Perspectives on the Chronology of the Early Second Millennium BC (Orbis Biblicus et Orientalis, Series Archaeologica 43, 2025, open access) — conference-volume position favoring the Lower Middle Chronology (Hammurabi accession 1784 BCE), an 8-year position inside the record's stated ~8-year residual window; grade-neutral (venue = proceedings, not a peer-reviewed journal anchor), Turin-shroud precedent

competing_hypotheses: Ultra-low / new chronology (Gasche, Gurzadyan): fall of Babylon 1499 BCE — Venus 56/64-year cycles are artefacts of the copy tradition; lunar eclipses (Enuma Anu Enlil records, Tell Muhammad year-names) and pottery point 96 years lower
Low chronology (fall of Babylon 1531 BCE) — favoured by some archaeologists on stratigraphic grounds
High chronology (fall of Babylon 1651 BCE) — best fit to certain astronomical readings, worst fit to the textual distance data historians prefer
Manning's 'resolution' is overstated — the ~8-year residual window and the unrefuted eclipse identifications mean the debate is narrowed, not closed
falsifiability: A securely dated 14C/dendro series from a context tied by sealed year-names to the Old Babylonian kings that lands >30 years off the middle-chronology anchor, or a verified total solar/lunar eclipse matching a low-chronology year-name formula, would falsify the middle chronology.

title: The Code of Hammurabi
claim: Hammurabi promulgated a law code of 282 laws, inscribed on a 2.25-meter dark-igneous stele (traditionally called 'diorite' since Scheil 1902; the Louvre identifies the material as basalt — the lithology is an unresolved scientific question per the peer-reviewed 2026 Comment, Liu & Xu, npj Heritage Science 14:141), covering commerce, family, labor, and criminal justice — one of the oldest and most complete legal codes known.
place: Susa (find spot; originally erected at Babylon or Sippar)
grade_reason: The inscribed stele physically exists and is contemporary with Hammurabi; its text is complete and legible.
earliest_attestation: The diorite stele itself (Louvre, Sb 8), inscribed in Hammurabi's reign

sources.ref: Code of Hammurabi stele (Louvre Sb 8, excavated at Susa 1901-1902)
Laws of Ur-Nammu and Lipit-Ishtar (earlier codes, comparison)

Liu & Xu 2026, npj Heritage Science 14:141 (doi:10.1038/s40494-026-02411-z) — Comment reframing the century-old diorite-vs-basalt controversy over the Louvre stele's material as a testable hypothesis; proposes a noninvasive pXRF/SWIR/Raman protocol; leans basalt on philological-historical review but leaves the question explicitly unresolved pending direct analysis (received 16 Dec 2025, accepted 26 Feb 2026). Grade-neutral: the material question does not touch the code's authenticity or date.

competing_hypotheses: The code was a functioning legal instrument used by judges
The code was primarily royal ideology/justice propaganda, with earlier codes (Ur-Nammu, Lipit-Ishtar) as the real precedents
falsifiability: Proof the stele is a later copy or forgery, or that its legal provisions postdate Hammurabi's reign

title: 'Hammurabi's Code was the first written law code' (the telling, killed)
claim: The popular telling that Hammurabi's Code (c. 1754 BCE) was the first written law code in human history.
place: Babylon (stele findspot: Susa, Iran — carried as 12th-century BCE war booty)
grade_reason: Three centuries before Hammurabi, Ur-Nammu's code stood in writing — and Lipit-Eshtar and Eshnunna came two centuries earlier too. The 'first' telling dies on the tablets themselves.
earliest_attestation: The 'first law code' telling is a modern popularization (textbooks, museum copy); the stele itself makes no such claim

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Code of Ur-Nammu' (earliest extant legal text; three centuries older than Hammurabi; Urukagina's code survives by reference only)
worldhistory.org, 'Code of Ur-Nammu' (c. 2100-2050 BCE; Laws of Eshnunna c. 1930 BCE; Lipit-Ishtar d. c. 1924 BCE — all before Hammurabi)
Schøyen Collection and Istanbul Archaeological Museum tablets of the Code of Ur-Nammu (physical artifacts)

Martha T. Roth, Law Collections from Mesopotamia and Asia Minor (SBL Writings from the Ancient World, 1997) — the standard English edition carrying Ur-Nammu, Lipit-Eshtar, Eshnunna, and Hammurabi side by side

sciencenewstoday.org, 'Hammurabi's Code: The First Written Laws' (c. 2026-10-01) — 'humanity's first great experiment with written law'; killed-telling instance recrawled, graded separately on the record

lawshun.com, 'Babylonian King And The First Codes Of Law' (recrawled 2026-10-21) — "The Code of Hammurabi is widely regarded as the world's first code of law"; killed-telling instance chained, graded separately on the record

travelmate.tech, Louvre audio guide 'Hammurabi Stele Richelieu Wing Hall 3' (recrawled 2026-10-24) — 'the so-called Code of Hammurabi — the earliest collection of written laws in the history of man'; killed-telling instance chained, graded separately on the record

competing_hypotheses: The honest root of the telling: Hammurabi's is the earliest COMPLETE and most famous code, and the most influential on later law — first in fame and completeness, not first in time

The Urukagina reform decrees (c. 24th century BCE) survive only by reference, not in text — so 'earliest extant text' belongs to Ur-Nammu, 'earliest code by reference' to Urukagina; neither belongs to Hammurabi

The minimalist reading: no pre-Hammurabi legal compilation counts as a 'code' in the modern sense — but the same critique applies to Hammurabi's own stele (exemplary-judgments thesis), so it cannot rescue the telling
falsifiability: A demonstration that the Ur-Nammu, Lipit-Eshtar, Eshnunna, and Urukagina tablets are misdated or modern forgeries — no such challenge exists in the literature

title: The Tell el-Koua Second Intermediate Period settlement (2026)
claim: In June 2026, Egypt's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities announced the discovery of a Second Intermediate Period settlement at the Tell el-Koua site in the Wadi Tumilat region — the ancient corridor linking the eastern Nile Delta with Egypt's eastern frontier. The site includes 15th Dynasty (Hyksos-period) tombs and evidence of occupation continuing into the 18th Dynasty, spanning the transition from Hyksos rule to the New Kingdom — the era that has long figured in scholarly debates over the historical setting of the Exodus. This is context for the Hyksos-expulsion hypothesis, never evidence of the Exodus itself.
place: Tell el-Koua, Wadi Tumilat, eastern Delta, Egypt
grade_reason: Announced by the Egyptian ministry and reported by the press; the facts are the site and its dating, both documented. Graded on the discovery, with the Exodus framing explicitly fenced as press context, not evidence — the site proves a town existed in the corridor, never that anyone left through it.
earliest_attestation: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities announcement, late June 2026

sources.ref: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities announcement, late June 2026 — Tell el-Koua settlement: 15th Dynasty tombs, occupation into the 18th Dynasty; 10 mudbrick tombs, homes, ovens, grain silos, walled neighborhood; scarab amulets, bronze tools, pottery, alabaster cosmetic containers, human and animal remains; 98-by-197-ft residential complex with halls, kilns, silos; first crouched burials outside the mudbrick tombs at the site

NY Post, 27 July 2026 — 'Ancient Egyptian settlement discovered from era that fueled Exodus debate' (the press framing fenced as context: the Hyksos period 'may provide historical context' for the biblical account, per scholars)

competing_hypotheses: The site documents the Hyksos-to-New-Kingdom transition that some scholars invoke as the Exodus's historical background (the context the press reported)
The site has no bearing on the Exodus question (its evidence is settlement archaeology, not departure archaeology)
falsifiability: Full excavation report altering the dating or character of the site would revise the record; the discovery itself is ministry-announced and press-reported

title: The Theran (Santorini) eruption
claim: That the island of Thera in the Aegean erupted catastrophically in the Late Bronze Age — an eruption ~60x Mount St. Helens that buried the town of Akrotiri, collapsed the volcanic center into a caldera, and sent tsunamis toward Minoan Crete ~110 km south.
place: Santorini (Thera), Aegean Sea
grade_reason: The eruption is multiply attested (volcanic deposits, buried town, ice cores, tsunamites); the exact year is still contested, so VERIFIED is parked.
earliest_attestation: Tephra and pumice layers across the eastern Mediterranean; Akrotiri buried in life position; Greenland ice-core sulfate spike; tsunamites on Cretan coasts

sources.ref: Friedrich et al. 2006, Science 312:548 — olive branch buried alive in pumice, wiggle-matched to 1627–1600 BCE (95.4%)
Pearson et al. 2018, Science Advances — IntCal recalibration widening the window to 1600–1525 BCE
Marinatos 1939 — hypothesis linking the eruption's memory to the Atlantis legend (hypothesis, not verification)

competing_hypotheses: The high chronology (~1620s BCE): radiocarbon + wiggle-match point a century before the traditional archaeological date
The low/traditional chronology (~1500 BCE): Egyptian-linked pottery chronology; IntCal recalibration is the contested middle
On consequences: whether the eruption ended Minoan civilization (competing evidence: Crete's palaces decline gradually, not in one ash cloud)
falsifiability: Proof that the tephra layers are from another volcano, or that the buried Akrotiri dates to a different millennium.

title: The Venus Tablet of Ammisaduqa
claim: Twenty cuneiform copies in six groups (oldest copied at Babylon c. 720-704 BCE under Sargon II; main copy K.160 recovered from Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh) preserve 21 years of Venus's heliacal risings and settings — first and last visibility before sunrise and after sunset — originally observed during the reign of the Babylonian king Ammisaduqa, fourth king after Hammurabi. It is the principal relative anchor for Old Babylonian absolute chronology.
place: Babylon (copies); principal copy recovered at Nineveh
grade_reason: The artifact is multiply attested — 20 copies in 6 groups — but the astronomical content is a heavily copied tradition: copying corruptions are probable and the entries for years 13 and 21 are not physically possible, so the observations are CLAIMED as transmitted, the tablet's existence is CORROBORATED.
earliest_attestation: Observations attributed to the reign of Ammisaduqa (mid-17th century BCE, middle chronology); surviving copies are 7th-century BCE. Earliest published: Rawlinson & Smith, 1870, as Enuma Anu Enlil Tablet 63.

sources.ref: British Museum tablet K.160 (the 'Venus tablet K.160'), recovered from the library at Nineveh
Reiner, E. & Pingree, D. (1975), Babylonian Planetary Omens, Part 1: The Venus Tablet of Ammisaduqa (Bibliotheca Mesopotamica) — the fundamental modern edition
Langdon, S., Fotheringham, J.K. & Schoch, C. (1928), The Venus Tablets of Ammizaduga (Oxford)
Gurzadyan, V.G. (2003), 'The Venus Tablet and refraction' (Akkadica 124) — atmospheric refraction corrections; Gurzadyan (2000) argues the 56/64-year Venus cycle cannot be traced in the tablet

de Jong, T. & Foertmeyer, V., 'The Venus observations of Ammisaduqa reanalysed' (JEOL) — physical-model reanalysis; ~2 years of enhanced atmospheric extinction, possibly the Thera eruption signature (unconfirmed)
Weir, J.D. (1982), 'The Venus Tablets — a Fresh Approach' (Journal for the History of Astronomy 13); Weir (1998), 'The Pattern of Venus Tablet Solutions' — tabular overview of the candidate solutions

competing_hypotheses: The tablet preserves genuine mid-17th-century BCE Venus observations, corrupted in transmission but astronomically usable (Kugler 1912 onward; the basis for all five chronology solutions)

The tablet is partly a late compilation or reconstruction rather than continuous observation — usable only in its broad 8-year pattern, not in detail (Gurzadyan 2000: the 56/64-year cycle cannot be traced in the data)
Only the 8-year Venus cycle is reliable; the detail entries are too corrupted to support any absolute anchor (Gasche/Gurzadyan position)
falsifiability: Proof the tablets are modern forgeries (no such evidence exists), or demonstration that all 20 copies descend from one corrupt late source with no genuine observational original behind them
