title: The Fall of Babylon to Mursili I (1595 BCE, middle chronology)
claim: The First Dynasty of Babylon ended when the Hittite king Mursili I marched down the Euphrates, sacked Babylon, and carried off the cult statue of Marduk from the Esagila; the last Amorite king, Samsu-Ditana, fell. In the middle chronology the sack dates to 1595 BCE; the date is one of the absolute anchors of Old Babylonian chronology (1651 / 1595 / 1531 / 1499 BCE across the four schemes).
place: Babylon, Iraq
grade_reason: The raid is independently attested in two traditions (Babylonian chronicles and Hittite royal inscriptions) and the aftermath — a real settlement hiatus in Babylon's own archives — is archaeologically visible. The absolute year is an inference from the chronology scheme, not a contemporary statement, so the event sits below VERIFIED: the raid is attested, the 1595 date is our reckoning.
earliest_attestation: Babylonian chronicle tradition (the Chronicle of Early Kings: Mursili's raid and the removal of the Marduk statue); the Hittite Edict of Telepinu (Mursili I's reign and its end); the Merkes/Babylon text gap marking the settlement hiatus after the fall

sources.ref: Chronicle of Early Kings (Babylonian chronicle): Mursili's raid on Babylon, the taking of the Marduk statue, the Kassite succession under Agum II
Edict of Telepinu (Hittite): Mursili I's reign, the campaign against Babylon, his assassination on his return
Babylonian King List A: the First Dynasty ends with Samsu-Ditana; the Kassite dynasty begins (Gandaš)

Academia.edu / 'Babylon in the Second Millennium BCE: New Insights on the Transitions from Old Babylonian to Kassite and Isin II Periods' (~2025): the Merkes-area text gap marking the transition — a settlement hiatus coinciding with the suggested Fall of Babylon (1595 MC), followed by resettlement under the early Kassite kings (Pedersén 2005 Archive und Bibliotheken von Babylon text census)
Manning, Griggs, Lorentzen, Barjamovic, Bronk Ramsey, Kromer & Wild 2016, PLOS ONE — the dendro-14C anchor that selects the middle-chronology 1595 over 1531/1499

competing_hypotheses: Middle chronology: 1595 BCE (the held position — Manning 2016 compatible-only)
Low chronology: 1531 BCE — the 64-year offset, archaeology-preferred by some excavators
Ultra-low / new chronology: 1499 BCE — Gurzadyan's eclipse-based case
High chronology: 1651 BCE — best fit to certain Venus-tablet readings, worst fit to the textual distances
The Mursili raid as a Hittite-Kassite joint operation — proposed, unproven; the texts name only Mursili
falsifiability: A contemporary dated source placing Samsu-Ditana or a successor on Babylon's throne in the years immediately after 1595 BCE; or a securely dated cuneiform record of the Marduk statue's return that predates Agum II's reign

title: The Kassite Dynasty of Babylon (c. 1595–1155 BCE)
claim: The Kassite dynasty ruled Babylon from c. 1595 to 1155 BCE — roughly 440 years, the longest dynasty in Mesopotamian history: a stable, literate great-power era (the Amarna age: Kadashman-Enlil I and Burna-Buriaš II corresponding with Egypt's Amenhotep III), not a dark age. Kassite kings kept Akkadian as the language of administration and cuneiform as its script, copied Hammurabi's Code for six centuries, and left the kudurru boundary stones as their own documentary record.
place: Babylon, Iraq
grade_reason: Multiple independent lines converge: the Kassite king list (Babylonian King List A), ~hundreds of surviving kudurru stones with royal names, the Amarna correspondence (external witness), Chronicle P, and the terminal Elamite conquest attested on both sides. The 'dark age' telling is the only casualty — the dynasty is one of the best-documented long reigns in the ancient Near East, yet it has no dedicated scholarly synthesis in English. Below VERIFIED: the early-dynasty decades (Gandaš–Agum II, the Sealand overlap) are thinly documented.
earliest_attestation: Babylonian King List A; the kudurru boundary stones (oldest major witness: the Louvre Meli-Shipak kudurru granting land to Marduk-apla-iddina I); the Amarna letters (EA 1–11: Kadashman-Enlil I, Burna-Buriaš II); Chronicle P (Kassite–Assyrian conflicts)

sources.ref: Babylonian King List A: the Kassite dynasty — 36 kings, 576 traditional years

Kudurru boundary stones (e.g., the Meli-Shipak kudurru, Louvre AO 6684; the corpus catalogued in Brinkman 1976, 'Materials and Studies for Kassite History') — the dynasty's own legal-visual documentary record
Amarna letters EA 1–11: Kassite kings Kadashman-Enlil I and Burna-Buriaš II in correspondence with Amenhotep III/Akhenaten — external attestation of the Kassite great-power status
Chronicle P: the Kassite–Middle Assyrian conflicts; the Assyrian interregnum inside the Kassite period
The 1155 BCE Elamite overthrow: Shutruk-Nahhunte's own inscriptions on the trophies carried to Susa (including Hammurabi's Code stele, Louvre Sb 8) — the end of the dynasty attested by its conqueror
Wikipedia 'Kassite dynasty' consensus page (status Oct 2026): 1595–1155 BCE brackets, Zagros origin, Sealand parallel, assimilation of the later kings

competing_hypotheses: The traditional reading: the Kassites were foreign mountaineers who inherited a ruined city — the 'dark age' framing (outdated, but still the textbook shorthand)

The revisionist reading (held): a continuous, conservative administration that preserved Old Babylonian culture — the 576-year King List A tradition (overlapping reigns) as legitimation, not arithmetic

The Sealand dynasty as the true 'First' post-Amorite power: the Second Dynasty of Uruk/Sealand held the south for ~368 years in parallel; the Kassite unification of Sumer-and-Akkad came only with Ulam-Buriaš and Agum III in the early 15th century BCE
The Kassites as a small foreign elite over a Babylonian population — vs. full assimilation (eight of the last kings carry Akkadian names; Kassite princesses married into the Assyrian royal house)
falsifiability: A contemporary source showing Babylon under non-Kassite rule for a substantial part of the 15th–12th centuries BCE (the Assyrian interregnum is already accounted for); or demonstration that the kudurru corpus is a late antiquarian fabrication (no such evidence exists)

title: The Temple menorah burned olive oil
claim: The seven-branched menorah of the Temple in Jerusalem burned pure beaten olive oil — seven oil lamps on a gold lampstand — not wax candles.
place: Jerusalem (the Temple)
grade_reason: Attested within the Hebrew textual tradition only — Exodus 27:20 ('pure oil olive beaten for the light'), Leviticus 24:2, and Josephus's eyewitness-adjacent account — with the Arch of Titus relief confirming the seven-branched form externally; no surviving Temple lampstand exists to inspect, and no contemporary inscription names the fuel.
earliest_attestation: Exodus 25:31-37 (seven lamps on the gold lampstand) and Exodus 27:20 (pure beaten olive oil for the light); Leviticus 24:2; Josephus, Antiquities 3.7.7 (three of the seven lights burned by day)

sources.ref: Exodus 25:31-37; 27:20-21 — the gold lampstand with seven lamps; 'pure oil of pressed olives for the light, so that the lamps may be kept burning'
Leviticus 24:2 — the command to bring pure beaten olive oil for the lamps
Josephus, Antiquities 3.7.7 — three of the seven lights burned in the daytime (reported via Bible commentaries citing the text)
The Arch of Titus, Rome (c. 81 CE) — the triumphal relief showing the seven-branched menorah carried as spoil from the 70 CE sack; contemporary external depiction of the form

competing_hypotheses: The menorah's lamps were a later overlay on a pre-existing fire-cult object, and the oil prescription is editorial rather than descriptive
The Second Temple menorah differed in fuel or form from the tabernacle prescription (the text prescribes; practice is unattested)
falsifiability: A surviving Temple lampstand with wax-candle fixtures, or a contemporary inscription describing wax as the Temple fuel, would overturn the reading

title: The Crossing of the Yam Suf (Exodus 14)
claim: In Exodus 14, Moses stretches out his hand over the yam suf and the sea parts — the waters standing as walls on the right hand and on the left while Israel crosses on dry ground, and the returning water drowns Pharaoh's army.
place: Eastern Nile Delta candidate zone — Ballah Lakes / Lake Timsah / Lake of Tanis (disputed; no agreed pin)
grade_reason: Attested across multiple tradition-internal witnesses, but with no independent contemporary attestation and no archaeological footprint; even the water's identity (a sea vs reed marshes) is disputed within scholarship.
earliest_attestation: Exodus 14 (composed centuries after the events it describes, per scholarly consensus). Tradition-internal echoes: Psalms 106:9, 114:3; Wisdom 19:7-8; Josephus, Antiquities 2.16.

sources.ref: Exodus 14 (the narrative; yam suf rendered 'Red Sea' in the Septuagint's Greek thalassa erythra)
Psalms 106:9, 114:3; Wisdom 19:7-8 (tradition-internal echoes)
Josephus, Antiquities 2.16 (1st-c. CE tradition-internal account)
Merneptah Stele c. 1207 BCE (attests 'Israel' in Canaan; says nothing about a crossing — the silence is on the record)
Hoffmeier, 'The Location of the Re(e)d Sea' (Ancient Israel in Sinai, 2005): yam suf = eastern-Delta reed lakes (Ballah Lakes / pa-tjufy), not the Gulf of Suez
Drews & Han (2010), PLoS ONE 5(8): e12481 — models the mechanism only, never the event

competing_hypotheses: Kernel-of-truth: a smaller group's escape from Egypt grown in the telling (Hyksos-expulsion echo and other candidates)
Literary composition of the exilic or post-exilic period, with no historical core
A naturalistic event (wind setdown) behind a theologized account — the mechanism models of evt-wind-setdown-mechanism-001
The Septuagint's 'Red Sea' rendering relocated the scene from Delta reed-marshes to the open sea; the original story knew only the marshes
falsifiability: A contemporary Egyptian or Canaanite record of the crossing — or of an army lost in the water — would raise the grade. The grade stays CLAIMED until any independent contemporary evidence appears either way.

title: The Exodus
claim: The biblical tradition holds that the Israelites, enslaved in Egypt, departed under Moses, crossed the sea, and wandered the wilderness before entering Canaan.
place: Sinai / Nile Delta (route traditionally placed here; unattested)
grade_reason: A central tradition of the Hebrew Bible, but with no contemporary extra-biblical attestation and no archaeological trace of a mass migration as described. The Merneptah Stele (c. 1207 BCE) proves 'Israel' existed as a people in Canaan by then — a terminus ante quem, not a confirmation.
earliest_attestation: The Exodus narratives (Exodus-Deuteronomy); no contemporary Egyptian source mentions the event

sources.ref: Exodus-Deuteronomy narratives
Merneptah stele (terminus ante quem for 'Israel' in Canaan, c. 1207 BCE; people-determinative)
Santa Clara University timeline: Exodus c. 1280 BCE paired with composition dates
Finkelstein & Silberman, The Bible Unearthed (2001): narrative reached final form in the 26th Dynasty (late 7th-early 6th c. BCE)
Hoffmeier (maximalist): concedes no direct archaeological evidence for the Exodus as described
Egyptian royal-propaganda caveat: monuments routinely omit defeats (e.g., Kadesh spun as triumph)

competing_hypotheses: A historical core: a small group of Semitic laborers escaped Egypt and their story was nationalized (e.g., Hoffmeier)
No historical exodus; Israel emerged indigenously within Canaan (Finkelstein's 'Canaanite origins' model)
The narrative encodes memories of the Hyksos expulsion (c. 1550 BCE) — Redford; or a deliberate 'counterhistory' (Assmann)
A composite cultural memory assembled over centuries, finalized in the 7th-6th c. BCE (Finkelstein & Silberman)
falsifiability: A contemporary Egyptian inscription describing the departure would raise the grade; the current silence is ambiguous (Egyptian monuments omit defeats), so silence alone cannot lower it further

title: The Exodus narrative is literally accurate in every detail as written
claim: The Exodus narrative (Exodus 1-15) is literally accurate word-for-word as written: the ten plagues occurred as described, the census figure of 603,550 fighting men (Numbers 1:46) is a literal headcount, and a departure of roughly two million people from Egypt is historically accurate as stated.
place: Sinai / Nile Delta (route traditionally placed here; unattested)
grade_reason: The literalist reading fails at scale: the text's own arithmetic intends 603,550 as a literal headcount (2025 HIPHIL paper); a two-million-person migration through the Sinai would leave archaeological traces and leaves none (Finkelstein & Silberman); the internal chronology is symbolic (2666 AM, 480 = 12x40); Canaan was Egyptian territory at the supposed date. This is the 267th DEBUNKED family.
earliest_attestation: The Exodus narratives (Exodus-Deuteronomy); the literalist reading as a doctrine is modern (19th-20th c. fundamentalism), not ancient

sources.ref: HIPHIL Novum 10 (2025), issue 1: eleph=1,000 algebra — summing the tribal counts in Numbers 1, the writer's own totals prove eleph was intended as 1,000, not 'clan'

Finkelstein & Silberman, The Bible Unearthed (2001), pp. 61-63: even a considerably smaller group than 600,000 warriors could not pass through the Sinai/Negev without leaving traces; no such traces exist

Wikipedia, 'Sources and parallels of the Exodus': scholarly consensus — symbolic chronology (Tabernacle in Anno Mundi 2666, two-thirds of a 4,000-year era; 480 years = 12x40 symbolic generations), Canaan under Egyptian control ('escaping from Egypt to Egypt'), no Jericho destruction layer, 'the lack of evidence has led scholars to conclude that the Exodus story does not represent a specific historical moment'
Merneptah stele (c. 1207 BCE): 'Israel' in Canaan by then — terminus ante quem; says nothing about an exodus
Hoffmeier (maximalist): concedes no direct archaeological evidence for the Exodus as described (via 'The Historicity of the Exodus')
Finkelstein & Silberman, The Bible Unearthed (2001): the exodus narrative may encode vague memories of the Hyksos expulsion (c. 1550 BCE), refashioned centuries later
ABC News poll, Feb 2004 (n=1,011): 64% said the Red Sea parting story is literally true word-for-word — the belief ledger, graded as attestation not evidence

competing_hypotheses: The eleph-clan hypothesis (Mendenhall 1958, Humphreys, Rendsburg): eleph as clan/military unit, reducing the force to ~5,500 men — a live reading option, but the 2025 HIPHIL algebra shows the Numbers writer's own sums intend 1,000
A historical kernel: a small group of Semitic laborers escaped Egypt and their story was nationalized (Hoffmeier) — untouched by this verdict
No historical exodus; Israel emerged indigenously within Canaan (Finkelstein's Canaanite-origins model) — untouched by this verdict
The narrative encodes memories of the Hyksos expulsion (Redford) or a deliberate counterhistory (Assmann) — untouched by this verdict
Absence-of-evidence limits: the eastern Delta is under-excavated; nomadic groups leave few traces (Hoffmeier's caveat; biblia.work review)
falsifiability: A stratified Late Bronze Age Sinai/Negev occupation record consistent with a migrating population of ~10^5-10^6 people, or a contemporary Egyptian record of the plagues and mass departure, would falsify this verdict.

title: Baal's return: death at Mot's hands, the rains coming back
claim: The Ugaritic Baal Cycle (KTU 1.1–1.6, c. 1400–1200 BCE) attests the storm-god Baal's death at the hands of Mot (Death) and his return — with Anat's slaughter of Mot and the restoration of the rains — a pre-Christian dying-and-rising narrative in which the god's death is the dry season and his return the weather.
place: Ugarit (Ras Shamra, Syria)
grade_reason: The tablets are securely dated pre-Christian by centuries; the death-and-return narrative is read from the texts themselves, with the storm-god/rain logic intrinsic to the narrative. Mettinger's rehabilitation counts Baal among the genuine pre-Christian cases.
earliest_attestation: The Baal Cycle, KTU 1.1–1.6 (Ugarit, Ras Shamra)

sources.ref: The Baal Cycle (KTU 1.1–1.6), Ugarit, c. 1400–1200 BCE — Baal's death at Mot's hands, Anat's vengeance, the return of the rains
Mettinger, The Riddle of Resurrection (2001) — Baal as a genuine pre-Christian dying-and-rising case
Day, John — on Baal's death-and-resurrection behind Hosea 5:12–6:3 (the imagery's afterlife in the Hebrew Bible)

competing_hypotheses: Baal's 'death' is a seasonal allegory (disappearing-deity, not dying-and-rising-deity, in Mettinger's own taxonomy of distinctions) — the return is the rains, not a resurrection
The cycle is a palace/temple cult drama whose performance context, not narrative alone, carried the 'return' — the texts are fragmentary and the ending reconstructed
The Hosea connection: J. Day reads Baal's death-and-resurrection behind Hosea 5:12–6:3 — a biblical reuse of the imagery, disputed
The maximalist reading: the texts describe a real entity's history — not graded; the attestation rule grades the belief, never the metaphysics
falsifiability: A redating of the Ugarit tablets to post-Christian times, or a demonstration that no tablet describes Baal's death and return, would overturn the attestation

title: El's assembly at Ugarit: the council of the sons of El
claim: At Late Bronze Age Ugarit (14th–12th c. BCE), the divine assembly is a documented institution: El presides over the mphrt bn il ('the assembly of the sons of El') — the seventy sons of El (cf. Deut 32:8's 'seventy'), deliberating kingship, war, and fate. The Baal Cycle's council scenes (KTU 1.2 i, iii–iv) show the assembly in session: El presiding from his tent at the source of the cosmic rivers, Yam's messengers demanding Baal's surrender before the seated gods, Athirat interceding with El for Baal's palace, the vote-style deliberation by which divine authority moves. The assembly is not metaphor; it is the pantheon's government.
place: Ugarit (Ras Shamra), northern Levant coast
grade_reason: The tablets exist, are multiply attested, and the assembly vocabulary (mphrt bn il) is documented philology.
earliest_attestation: KTU (Die keilalphabetischen Texte aus Ugarit) 1.2 i–iv; 1.40 (list of the seventy); excavated 1929 onwards

sources.ref: KTU³ (Dietrich/Loretz/Sanmartín), esp. KTU 1.2 i–iv; KTU 1.40
Charles Virolleaud, critical edition of the Baal Cycle (1938)
Lowell K. Handy, Among the Host of Heaven (1994)
Mark S. Smith, The Origins of Biblical Monotheism (Oxford, 2001)
E. Theodore Mullen Jr., The Divine Council in Canaanite and Early Hebrew Literature

competing_hypotheses: The Ugaritic assembly is royal-court ideology projected upward (Handy 1994: the Syro-Palestinian pantheon as royal bureaucracy) rather than a 'government' in any functional sense
El's council is already in decline within the texts — an aging El being eclipsed by Baal, so the assembly scenes are transitional, not normative
falsifiability: Proof the tablets are modern forgeries or the 'assembly' passages are mistranslations of mundane ritual language

title: The name 'Moses' as Egyptian (contested)
claim: The personal name 'Moses' (Hebrew Mosheh) is of Egyptian origin — the standard scholarly reading deriving it from Egyptian msi/ms ('child, born of, son'), the common element of New Kingdom theophoric names (Thutmose, Ramose, Ahmose, Ptahmose, Ramesses). The Hebrew etymology given in Exodus 2:10 ('because I drew him out of the water', from mashah 'drew out') is a folk etymology — Hebrew wordplay on an Egyptian-sounding name, not the name's origin.
place: Egypt/Levant onomastics (the name, not the person)
grade_reason: The Egyptian derivation is the long-standing majority position (Lepsius 19th c. to Hoffmeier 2016's 'widespread agreement'), but it is contested within peer-reviewed scholarship: Kitchen (2003) and Hoffmeier (2016) themselves expressed doubts; Redford (2009) argues the Hebrew shin-for-Egyptian-s rendering cannot be 2nd-millennium phoneticism (Ex 1:11 renders the s in 'Ramses' as Samek); Schneider's reassessment concludes the name is 'not likely of Egyptian origin' — most probably a NW Semitic name of uncertain etymology, with Mosheh consistent with an Iron Age I-or-later form. The folk-etymology status of Exod 2:10's explanation is broadly shared; the origin question itself is not settled.
earliest_attestation: Egyptian theophoric -mose names throughout the New Kingdom (c. 1550-1070 BCE); the Hebrew form in the biblical text; the etymological question enters scholarship with Lepsius (19th c.)

sources.ref: James Hoffmeier (2016), cited for 'widespread agreement that at the root of the name of the great Hebrew leader is the Egyptian word msi, which was a very common element in theophoric names throughout the New Kingdom (e.g., Amenmose, Thutmose, Ahmose, Ptahmose, Ramose, Ramesses)' and derives from the Egyptian verb 'to give birth'
Louis Feldman (2004): the name 'is almost certainly Egyptian, from the root msy, meaning "to be born", as in Tuthmosis ("Tuth is born") and Rameses ("Re is born")'

Ernest Klein, A Comprehensive Etymological Dictionary of the English Language (via etymonline): 'Most scholars see in it the Hebraization of Egyptian mes, mesu "child, son," which is often used in theophorous names'; Ex. 2:10 read as Hebrew sound-wordplay on mashah 'he drew out'

Thomas Schneider, 'Moses the Egyptian? A Reassessment of the Etymology of the Name "Moses"' (peer-reviewed reassessment): concludes the name is 'not likely of Egyptian origin' — most probably a NW Semitic personal name of uncertain etymology; Mosheh consistent with an Iron Age I (or later) form via the Canaanite a>o shift; 'Moses the Egyptian would indeed be a later construct'; Kitchen (2003) and Hoffmeier (2016) cited for expressed doubts; Redford (2009: 175) cited for the sibilant objection
Exodus 2:10 (the folk etymology: 'she called his name Moses, and said, Because I drew him out of the water')

National Geographic 2025-08-07 (Serabit el-Khadim coverage): Joshua Huddlestun cited — 'Mose' appears as a personal name in New Kingdom letters and legal documents (a land-inheritance plaintiff named Mose); Liane Feldman (Princeton): the name may well be Egyptian and is less distinctive than it appears. Grade-neutral: supports the Egyptian-name plausibility already in the record while weakening any distinctive-identification reading of the name.

competing_hypotheses: Dropped-theophoric theory: Moses = [Deity]-mose with the divine element later removed when he aligned with his former Semitic identity
NW Semitic origin: a Northwest Semitic personal name of uncertain etymology (Schneider's conclusion)
Syriac mshy 'to collect, to glean' as the semantic option behind the Exod 2:10 wordplay
falsifiability: A securely dated pre-Exodus Egyptian attestation of 'Mose' standing alone as a complete personal name in a non-theophoric context would strengthen the Egyptian reading; a NW Semitic onomastic parallel with the same consonantal form and matching sibilant would strengthen Schneider's.

title: The 2026 Samuha (Kayalıpınar) royal archive announcement
claim: Türkiye's Ministry of Culture and Tourism announced on 8 October 2026 that archaeologists recovered 131 cuneiform tablets and fragments at Kayalıpınar (ancient Samuha) in the 2026 season, bringing the reported royal archive total to 184 tablets and fragments with 53 found in 2025; the texts are attributed to King Tudhaliya II's reign and include Hittite and Hurrian, covering military, administrative, ritual, and royal-household affairs; excavators call it the most extensive Hittite royal archive found in the 21st century and one of the largest concentrations of Hittite documents outside Hattusa; translation and excavation are ongoing.
place: Kayalıpınar (ancient Samuha), Türkiye
grade_reason: Announced by a state ministry and reported by multiple independent outlets with consistent figures; fenced as an announced find — the objects' contents and full dating await the peer-reviewed edition, so this is the announcement, not the archive's content.
earliest_attestation: Türkiye Ministry of Culture and Tourism announcement, 8 October 2026 (press; peer-reviewed edition pending)

sources.ref: Heritage Daily, 8 Oct 2026: '184 cuneiform tablets discovered in Hittite royal archive'
The Debrief, 13 Oct 2026: 'Archaeologists Uncover a Hittite Royal Archive of 184 Cuneiform Tablets'

competing_hypotheses: The archive's scale or dating may be revised once the tablets are fully cleaned, joined, and edited
falsifiability: A retraction or correction by the excavation team or the ministry revising the tablet count or attribution; the peer-reviewed edition contradicting the announcement

title: The Shasu of Yhw in the Egyptian lists
claim: Two New Kingdom Egyptian temple topographical lists contain 't3 sh3sw yhw3' — 'the land of the Shasu of Yhw' — the oldest extra-biblical occurrence of the divine name YHWH in human records. The Soleb list (temple of Amenhotep III, Nubia, c. 1400 BCE) carries the name among the Shasu lists; the Amarah West list (Ramesses II, c. 1300 BCE) repeats the 'Shasu of Yhw' entry and separately names 'the land of the Shasu of Seir' (t3 sh3sw s3rr). Egypt knew a group called the Shasu attached to the name Yhw, located in the Seir/Edom/Midian region — the biblical tradition's own homeland of YHWH (cf. Deut 33:2, Judg 5:4, Hab 3:3, 1 Kgs 19). This grades the NAME's antiquity and geography, never the Exodus.
place: Soleb, Nubia (Sudan) — temple of Amenhotep III; also Amarah West, Nubia — temple of Ramesses II
grade_reason: Two independent Egyptian temple lists, ~150 years apart, both carry the yhw entry among the Shasu lists; the reading is long-established in the scholarly literature (Leclant 1960, Goedicke 1965). Graded as belief-phenomenon attestation per the attestation rule: it proves Egypt recorded the name in the southern wilderness, never that a deity did anything. It says nothing about the Exodus itself.
earliest_attestation: The Soleb topographical column (Amenhotep III, c. 1400 BCE); the reading published by Leclant 1960 and refined by Goedicke 1965

sources.ref: Soleb topographical list (Amenhotep III, c. 1400 BCE) — column naming 't3 sh3sw yhw3' ('the land of the Shasu of Yhw'); published by Jean Leclant 1960
Amarah West topographical list (Ramesses II, c. 1300 BCE) — 't3 sh3sw yhw3' and 't3 sh3sw s3rr' ('the land of the Shasu of Seir')
Goedicke 1965 — the yhw reading confirmed and discussed

AncientBibleHistory (groups.io), Sept 2026 — secondary discussion summarizing the Soleb/Amarah West evidence: Shasu as West Semitic pastoral nomads, Yhw placed in the southern wilderness of northwestern Arabia/Edom, coupled with Seir at Amarah West

competing_hypotheses: The yhw of the lists is the deity-name YHWH — the oldest extra-biblical occurrence (the standard reading since Goedicke 1965)
yhw is a place-name, not a deity-name (minority position; the reading debate)
The lists reflect 14th/13th-c. Egyptian knowledge of southern nomad groups and say nothing about Moses, the Exodus, or Israel's origins
falsifiability: A definitive re-reading of both lists removing the yhw entry, or proof the lists are later restorations, would lower the grade; the name is in the stone, not in dispute since Goedicke — the interpretation is where the fight is

title: Adonis: the mourned youth, the withering gardens, the witnessed return
claim: The tradition attests Adonis as a youth-god mourned in the annual Adonia festival (rooftop laments, the withering 'gardens of Adonis') and celebrated in return — with a pre-Hellenistic Phoenician pedigree: the Damu/Adon of Byblos, the male deity beside the Lady of Byblos in the Amarna letters, and early-Christian witnesses (Origen, Jerome) who describe the festival without claiming it as theirs.
place: Byblos (Gebal, Lebanon) — the Adonis river, the Lady of Byblos
grade_reason: The festival laments and the mourning are multiply attested in the classical record; the pre-Hellenistic pedigree is argued with named evidence (Amarna, Byblian inscriptions) but stays fenced as argued-per-link. Grade covers the belief-phenomenon, never the entities.
earliest_attestation: Amarna letters EA 84 ('my DA.MU') and EA 129 ('my living god'), 14th c. BCE; the Adonia festivals in Greek and Roman sources; Origen and Jerome (3rd–4th c. CE)

sources.ref: The Adonia festivals — Greek and Roman sources on the rooftop laments and the 'gardens of Adonis'
Origen; Jerome (3rd–4th c. CE) — early-Christian witnesses to the Adonis festival, connecting it with the Tammuz of Ezekiel 8:14
Amarna letters EA 84, EA 129 (14th c. BCE) — the male deity of Byblos ('my DA.MU', 'my living god'); 10th-c. Byblian inscriptions — the pedigree chain
Mettinger, The Riddle of Resurrection (2001) — Adonis 'may well have been' a pre-Christian dying-and-rising god; the Damu/Adon reconstruction

competing_hypotheses: The Adonis 'return' is the weakest half of the case: the Adonia's celebration-of-return is late (Greek/Roman) and the resurrection reading may be a retrojection onto the lament festival

The Damu/Adon→Adonis pedigree (Mettinger via the Amarna EA 84/129 'my DA.MU' / 'my living god') rests on logographic scribal convention — the continuity between Late Bronze Age Byblos and the Hellenistic Adonis is argued, not proven
The Tammuz-of-Ezekiel-8:14 = Adonis equation (Origen, Jerome) is an ancient Christian reading, not a documentary identity — kept as an attested ancient reading, not as fact
The maximalist reading: the texts describe a real entity's history — not graded; the attestation rule grades the belief, never the metaphysics
falsifiability: A demonstration that the Adonia festival never included a return/celebration phase, or that the Byblos pedigree is broken (the Amarna 'DA.MU' referring to a different deity), would weaken the attestation

title: The divine council: a shared West Semitic concept
claim: The idea of a heavenly council of gods is attested in Late Bronze Age Ugaritic texts (the assembly of El, KTU, 13th–12th c. BCE) and in the Hebrew Bible (Psalm 82's 'council of El', Job, 1 Kings 22, Daniel 7) — same cultural world, with Israelite writers reshaping the vocabulary around YHWH's sovereignty. Deuteronomy 32:8's Qumran/Septuagint reading ('sons of God' / 'angels of God') against the Masoretic 'sons of Israel' shows the concept was live and edited.
place: Ugarit (Ras Shamra), northern Levant coast
grade_reason: Both the Ugaritic tablets and the biblical texts exist and are independently attested; the shared vocabulary (council of El) is documented by philology.
earliest_attestation: Ugaritic tablets from Ras Shamra (KTU³, Dietrich/Loretz/Sanmartín); excavated 1929 onwards

sources.ref: KTU³ (Die keilalphabetischen Texte aus Ugarit), ed. Dietrich, Loretz, Sanmartín
Mark S. Smith, The Origins of Biblical Monotheism (Oxford, 2001); The Early History of God (2002)
E. Theodore Mullen Jr., The Divine Council in Canaanite and Early Hebrew Literature
Deuteronomy 32:8 — 4QDeutj (Qumran), Septuagint, Masoretic Text

competing_hypotheses: Psalm 82's 'gods' are human rulers, not a heavenly council (long reception history; minority modern view)
The council scenes are independent Israelite invention with no Ugaritic influence (weak against the philological matches)
Direct borrowing of the whole pantheon structure (overstates; convergence + differentiation is the documented pattern)
falsifiability: Proof the Ugaritic tablets are misdated or forged, or a Psalm 82 manuscript tradition with no council reading at all periods

title: The Shiloh favissa: ritual repository of sacrificial remains
claim: The subterranean ritual repository (favissa) at Tel Shiloh contains roughly 10,000 animal bones interspersed with cultic chalices, votive bowls, and ceremonial vessels — systematically buried sacred paraphernalia from Late Bronze Age sacrificial activity, re-analyzed in an exhaustive September 2026 reassessment published via the Enoch Seminar & Biblical Archaeology surveys.
place: Tel Shiloh (Khirbet Seilun), West Bank
grade_reason: The deposit is real and excavated; the bone counts and cultic vessels are published excavation data; the 2026 reassessment is a scholarly re-analysis confirming ritual decommissioning practice.
earliest_attestation: The favissa exposed in the Finkelstein-era excavations (1981–84); faunal and excavation records re-analyzed and published September 23, 2026

sources.ref: Enoch Seminar & Biblical Archaeology surveys, September 2026 reassessment (favissa, ~10,000 bones, ritual decommissioning)
Fox News Digital / jubileecast: three MBA storage jars with charred olives, wheat, lentils; ritual deposit above (10,000 bones, 8 gold/silver objects)

competing_hypotheses: The favissa's cultic interpretation is accepted by both confessional and mainstream archaeologists; dispute centers only on which cultic tradition it serves
falsifiability: Published independent faunal re-analysis contradicting the ritual-decommissioning interpretation

title: The denominator rule: where VIII.d's silence ends and VIII.f's destruction begins
claim: The timeline's two negative-evidence rules — VIII.d (silence is ambiguous: absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, and not evidence either) and VIII.f (deletion and destruction, read properly, are evidence) — are not rivals. They are one rule applied with and without a denominator. The baseline is the denominator: the expected survival rate for a given medium in a given climate under a given regime's archiving and destroying habits. Where the baseline is a GUESS, VIII.d retains jurisdiction — silence stays ambiguous (Herculaneum: ~1,800 scrolls found, library size unknown, so 'what else the villa held' is not evidence). Where the baseline is a MEASUREMENT, VIII.f operates — the pattern of what is missing, checked against what should have survived, is itself a record. The Kadesh case is the crossover exhibit: Egyptian royal inscriptions never record defeats (the regime baseline — Ramses II's battle reliefs claim victory), so the monuments' silence about the stalemate is VIII.d silence; but once the regime baseline is stated, that systematic silence becomes an VIII.f-pattern — the equal-terms treaty DOES survive on temple walls (Karnak, Ramesseum) in the Hittite and Egyptian versions alike, so the boasting is measurable policy, not news. The Oxyrhynchus case is the climate exhibit: ~500,000 papyrus fragments from the rubbish mounds vs almost none from Rome's damp soil — taphonomy, not literacy; Rome's papyrus 'silence' is evidence of groundwater, not of lesser bureaucracy. The honesty fence that keeps this from becoming a universal solvent: the baseline itself must be evidenced, not assumed. 'Of course nothing survived — it all burned' is unfalsifiable when the regime's archiving rate is unknown; the Alexandria single-fire telling died precisely on this (the expected survival was asserted, not measured — evt-library-alexandria-001 DEBUNKED). When the baseline is a guess, VIII.d governs; when it is a measurement, VIII.f governs; and the work of the historian is moving cases across that line by measuring denominators.
place: Oxyrhynchus (climate exhibit); Kadesh/Qadesh (regime exhibit); Herculaneum (denominator exhibit)
grade_reason: Method claim demonstrated across independent cases sharing one evidentiary logic: the Oxyrhynchus/Rome climate contrast, the Ebla medium contrast, the Kadesh regime-baseline crossover, and the Herculaneum denominator bound — each an independent line, each requiring the same denominator work.
earliest_attestation: The rule is synthesized 2026-10-16 from the timeline's own records: evt-silence-argument-002 (VIII.d) and evt-destruction-argument-001 (VIII.f). The taphonomic components are standard archaeological method (medium survival rates); the denominator formulation is this pass's synthesis.

sources.ref: evt-silence-argument-002 — the VIII.d rule (Kadesh two-sided record; Egyptian royal monuments never record defeats; McGrew 2013 independent formulation; the expected-evidence refinement)
evt-destruction-argument-001 — the VIII.f rule (the chisel's mark; fire-baked clay; the measured pattern of what is missing checked against what should have survived)

Oxyrhynchus papyri: ~500,000+ fragments from the town's rubbish mounds (Grenfell & Hunt excavations 1896–1907 onward); dry desert conditions as the preservation mechanism — the standard taphonomic contrast with damp-soil sites
Ebla Palace G: fire-baked tablet archives preserved in shelving order (evt-fire-baked-archives-001) — the medium-baseline demonstration: sun-dried clay survives the fire that should destroy it
PHerc.1667 read end-to-end without unrolling, June 2026, Vesuvius Challenge — the denominator exhibit: ~1,800 scrolls recovered, total villa library size unknown

Kadesh treaty: equal-terms Egyptian version on temple walls (Karnak, Ramesseum) alongside the Hittite Akkadian version — the regime-baseline crossover (battle reliefs claim victory per royal-inscription policy; the treaty records parity)
evt-library-alexandria-001 DEBUNKED — the asserted-but-unmeasured baseline that failed: the single-fire telling

Oxyrhynchus April 2026: University of Barcelona Oxyrhynchus Archaeological Mission (Nov 2025–Feb 2026 campaign, Al-Bahnasa necropolis) recovered a papyrus of Homer's Iliad Book II (Catalogue of Ships) from inside a Roman-era mummy's wrappings — the first Greek literary (non-magical) papyrus found in a mummy-wrapping context (phys.org, 20 Apr 2026) — the climate-baseline exhibit keeps being measured: new deposition contexts arrive in 2026, same dry-soil mechanism

PHerc.1667 read end-to-end, announced 25 June 2026 at the Biblioteca Nazionale di Napoli (Vesuvius Challenge; reported across the October 2026 press cycle, e.g. Gizmodo Science Fair 2026 writeup) — exhibit detail: first Herculaneum scroll ever virtually unwrapped and read end to end without physical opening; 22 columns of Greek over ~4.6 feet (1.4 m) of papyrus, a Stoic treatise on ethics; scans by high-resolution phase-contrast X-ray microtomography at ESRF Grenoble; machine-learning ink detection trained on carbon-ink-vs-carbonized-papyrus; transcriptions examined by papyrologists; data, code and transcriptions released openly under CC licence. The denominator exhibit, measured: the scroll carried a pre-read 'readability score of zero' and survived every 19th/20th-century opening attempt by being given up on.

Herculaneum denominator bound, re-confirmed October 2026: ~1,800 carbonized scrolls the measured population, of which ~300 intact scrolls remain sealed and unread (some outlets report ~600 unopened — press-level variance across the October 2026 coverage, fenced as unadjudicated). The total size of the Villa of the Papyri's original collection is still unknown in print — so 'what else the villa held' remains VIII.d territory: the baseline is a guess, and VIII.d retains jurisdiction. No 2026 publication changes the measured/guessed line.

competing_hypotheses: The denominator is itself unattainable in most ancient cases, so the synthesis collapses back into VIII.d's rule — the baseline is nearly always a guess, making VIII.f the rare special case
Regime and climate baselines smuggle in presentist models of ancient behavior — what 'should have survived' assumes we know ancient archiving rates, which for most societies we do not

The Kadesh crossover over-reads: Egyptian royal inscriptions DO sometimes record setbacks obliquely (the 'revolt' framing), so the 'never record defeats' baseline is itself an overstatement needing its own denominator
falsifiability: A case where a measured, evidenced baseline (medium survival rate + regime archiving rate + climate) exists and the silence still yields no readable pattern — or a case where the denominator is a pure guess and the pattern reads cleanly anyway, breaking the jurisdiction claim.

title: Marco Polo brought noodles to Italy from China
claim: Marco Polo, returning to Venice in 1295 from his years in Asia, brought noodles home from China, thereby introducing pasta to Italy.
place: Venice (the claimed homecoming, 1295)
grade_reason: The claimed event is contradicted three ways: pasta was made and exported in Italy a century before Polo's return (al-Idrisi 1154, Genoese inventories), Polo's own book contains no noodle-bringing passage and compares foreign food to familiar 'lasagne', and the story's earliest traceable form is a 1929 American pasta-trade article, not any medieval source.
earliest_attestation: The Macaroni Journal, October 1929 — the U.S. pasta industry's trade journal: the earliest form of the story the food-history literature has produced (a piece about Polo arriving at a destination 'seeming more South Pacific than Chinese' and finding natives drying strands of dough; later retellings add a sailor named Spaghetti). No earlier attestation traced.

sources.ref: Macaroni Journal, October 1929 (U.S. pasta-industry trade journal) — earliest traceable form of the legend
Marco Polo, Description of the World (dictated c. 1298–1299): contains no passage about bringing noodles home; the Fansur chapter compares sago-flour dishes to 'lasagne'
John Dickie, Delizia! The Epic History of the Italians and Their Food (2007) — documents the myth as modern manufacture
Jen Lin-Liu, On the Noodle Road (2013); NPR interview 20 July 2013
al-Idrisi, Nuzhat al-mushtaq (Book of Roger), 1154: Trabia (Sicily) itriyya industry — pasta already in Italy 141 years before Polo's return
Genoese notarial records: 13th-century inventories listing macaroni (commonly cited 1279; some retellings give 1244 or 1284; Spaghetti Museum, Pontedassio)

competing_hypotheses: Silk Road transmission at an earlier date: pasta/drying technology reached the Mediterranean via Arab traders and nomadic intermediaries (the Persian rishta thread) centuries before Polo — no single introducer
True core in Polo's observations: Polo described Chinese noodles to a European audience (the 'lasagne' comparison is real) and later popular storytelling upgraded description into introduction
falsifiability: A pre-1929 text attributing noodle-bringing to Polo, or a passage in the Description of the World describing noodles carried home — either would revive the claim

title: Battle of Kadesh (c. 1274 BCE): the battle both kings claimed to win
claim: In year 5 of Ramesses II (c. 1274 BCE), Egyptian and Hittite armies fought at Kadesh on the Orontes (Tell Nebi Mend, south of Lake Homs, modern Syria) — one of the largest chariot battles of the Late Bronze Age. Both empires' records agree a battle happened; they do not agree on who won. The Egyptian version (the Poem and the Bulletin, inscribed at Karnak, Luxor, Abydos, Abu Simbel, the Ramesseum) tells it as a personal triumph of the pharaoh, who was deceived by Hittite spies, ambushed, and rallied his forces. The Hittite tradition tells it as a checked Egyptian invasion: Kadesh was never captured, and Ramesses withdrew south to Egypt. The modern scholarly reading is a stalemate: Ramesses survived near-disaster and drove the Hittites from the field on the second day, but failed to take the city — and Kadesh and Amurru, the disputed territory the battle was fought over, stayed Hittite. Egypt's 'victory' is a single-tradition claim.

title: The silence argument (VIII.d): absence of evidence is not evidence of absence — but it is not evidence either
claim: The synthesis-docket argument d ('Silence is ambiguous — Kadesh. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, but it is not evidence either'), stated as the timeline's method rule with its Kadesh exhibit and its honest refinement. The rule: (1) Silence is not evidence. Egyptian royal monuments never recorded defeats — Ramses II's Kadesh walls are proof of the mechanism — so the absence of an Egyptian record for an event (e.g., the Exodus, evt-exodus-001) is expected silence and moves no grade either way. (2) Silence IS informative where evidence would be expected: the expected-evidence refinement. The Babylonian chronicle series records Nebuchadnezzar's campaigns year by year through his 11th year (594 BCE); its silence on the 586/587 BCE destruction of Jerusalem is silence at the tablets' edge, not silence inside the coverage — an honest, narrow distinction the record carries. And the Kadesh correction: if we had only Ramesses's wall, 'Egypt won' would be the record. The Hittite account exists, and the 1258 BCE treaty between equals exposes the stalemate. The rule's discipline is the schema's falsifiability line: a claim cannot be rescued by 'absence of evidence' unless it states what evidence WOULD exist if it were true — the standard the timeline's contact-proof-bar record (evt-contact-proof-bar-001) states in advance. (3) The failure mode, named: 'absence of evidence' used as an apologetic blanket that excuses every failed prediction. That is the rule misused, and the misuse is itself a pattern the map can mark.

title: Treaty of Kadesh (c. 1258 BCE): the earliest surviving international peace treaty
claim: In year 21 of Ramesses II (c. 1258 BCE), Egypt and Hatti signed the Treaty of Kadesh between Ramesses II and the Hittite king Hattusili III (Muwatalli II's brother and successor) — sixteen years after the Battle of Kadesh, and ending the borderland conflicts in Syria. The treaty was written on a silver tablet; a Hittite cuneiform clay copy was excavated at Hattusa (now in the Istanbul Archaeology Museum), and an Egyptian version survives on papyrus and temple walls (Karnak, Ramesseum). Its terms: mutual non-aggression, mutual defense against external enemies, and extradition of fugitives. It is widely described as the earliest known surviving international peace treaty; a replica hangs at the United Nations headquarters. The treaty's existence is evidence that the Kadesh-era stalemate held: it is a treaty between equals, not a victor imposing terms.

geo_precision: region — the treaty is a document, not a site; pin carries the contested region

grade_reason: VERIFIED: the treaty survives in two independent primary textual traditions (Hittite clay copy from Hattusa, Egyptian papyrus + temple inscriptions) preserving the same agreement, dated internally to year 21 of Ramesses II. The 'earliest treaty' superlative is the standard description, honestly fenced with 'known/surviving'.

title: The cowrie as currency
claim: The money cowrie (Monetaria moneta, syn. Cypraea moneta), harvested chiefly in the Maldives, circulated as a genuine currency across the Indian Ocean world and West Africa for centuries: a Bengal standard (3,840 shells to the rupee in the 19th century), a regular West African market currency from the 16th to the 19th century, and the 'sine qua non' of the European slave trade's purchasing price — before collapsing under 19th-century inflation when European traders flooded West Africa with cheaper Zanzibar cowries.
place: Maldives (harvest) → Bengal → Bight of Benin/West Africa (circulation)
grade_reason: Multiple independent documentary lines (customs/import quantities, European merchant accounts, the 1986 Hogendorn & Johnson monograph, Johnson's 1970 JAH pair, colonial price schedules) converge on the same system; the inflation-collapse mechanism is documented, not inferred.
earliest_attestation: Chinese bronze cowrie imitations, Shang dynasty (archaeological, 2nd millennium BCE); Maldivian cowrie trade described by medieval Arab geographers; 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica 'Shell-money' article summarizes the 19th-century state

Citéco (Cité de l'Économie) — cowrie as currency 'more than three millennia', 13th-c.-BC Chinese bronze cowrie motifs, Maldives origin, Ghana/Mali/Songhai unit of account

competing_hypotheses: The 'primitive money' anthropological reading: cowries as a pre-monetary stage superseded by 'real' money — contested by the system's own sophistication (standardized rates, arbitrage, fiduciary circulation)

falsifiability: Port/customs records showing no large-scale Maldives→West Africa cowrie shipments in the 16th–19th centuries, or evidence the shells circulated only as ornament with no price function

title: The yazatas of the Avesta

The Yashts (hymns 5, 8, 10, 13–19) are dedicated to individual yazatas; the Yasna liturgy invokes them collectively.

grade_reason: The belief-phenomenon is multiply attested: the Avestan texts exist in a manuscript tradition, name the yazatas individually, and are studied by an independent scholarly discipline. Per the attestation rule this grades the belief, never the beings.
earliest_attestation: The Gathas (Yasna 28–34, 43–51, Old Avestan) for the tradition's core; the individual Yashts (Young Avestan) for the developed yazata hymns

title: 'The face that launched a thousand ships' — Helen's abduction as the war's cause
claim: That the Trojan War was caused by Paris's abduction (or elopement) of Helen of Sparta — 'the face that launched a thousand ships' as a historical casus belli.
place: Hisarlik (Troy), Tevfikiye, Çanakkale Province, Turkey
grade_reason: CLAIMED: attested only in the epic tradition; no independent evidence that Helen of Sparta existed as a historical person, let alone that her abduction caused a war. The 'thousand ships' is Marlowe 1604, not Bronze Age evidence. The competing trade-route reading is honestly carried as SPECULATION — reasoned but unattested — not smuggled in as fact. The grade is on the cause, not on the poems: the Iliad's premise is real and ancient; its historicity is not.
earliest_attestation: The epic tradition — the Iliad's premise (composed c. 8th c. BCE). 'The face that launched a thousand ships' is NOT Homer: it is Christopher Marlowe, Doctor Faustus (1604) — 'Was this the face that launch'd a thousand ships?'

sources.ref: Homer, Iliad (public domain) — the war's premise: the abduction/elopement as casus belli; the epic tradition's own account.
Christopher Marlowe, Doctor Faustus (1604) — 'Was this the face that launch'd a thousand ships, / And burnt the topless towers of Ilium?' The line is Marlowe's invention, not Homer's.

Penn Gazette / C. Brian Rose — the Alaksandu treaty naming 'Aleksandu (Alexandros), the ruler of Wilusa' (Alexandros = Paris in the epic); 'proving there is real history behind the myth' — the treaty attests a ruler, never an abduction.

competing_hypotheses: The materialist reading: Dardanelles trade-route politics — a Mycenaean interest in the straits' tolls — as the war's real engine. SPECULATION: reasoned, unattested, no Bronze Age document states it
The euhemerist reading: a real abduction of a real queen, inflated by the epic tradition. Unattested beyond the poems
The myth-only reading: Helen as a goddess-figure (daughter of Zeus) from the start — the war's cause is theology, not history
falsifiability: A Bronze Age record naming Helen — a Hittite or Linear B attestation of a Spartan queen — would move the person to CORROBORATED; proof the abduction premise is a later poetic invention would drop the cause to SPECULATION.

title: The Trojan Horse — the Greeks took Troy in a giant wooden horse
claim: That the Greeks captured Troy by concealing soldiers inside a giant wooden horse, which the Trojans dragged through their own gates, after which the soldiers emerged at night and opened the gates — the horse mechanism as history, as literally described.
place: Hisarlik (Troy), Tevfikiye, Çanakkale Province, Turkey
grade_reason: Single literary tradition (Odyssey 8's brief song, four centuries later; Aeneid 2's full account, a millennium later) with zero archaeological corroboration — Troy VIIa shows a burned, fought-over city (~1180 BCE), not a mechanism. Four live mechanism readings: (1) a battering ram or siege engine draped in damp horse-hides (D'Angour); (2) a ship (the 'hippos'-as-ship reading); (3) an earthquake metaphor (Poseidon = god of horses and earthquakes; Troy VI's seismic damage is real); (4) poetic invention (the majority reading). None proved; none has falsified the others. The attestation is real and ancient; the mechanism is CLAIMED — held below DEBUNKED per the silence argument: the tell proves a fire, never a horse, and silence about the horse is not evidence against every possible mechanism.
earliest_attestation: Homer's Odyssey, Book 8 (Demodocus's song — fewer than sixty lines), composed c. 8th c. BCE, some four to five centuries after the claimed event. The Iliad never mentions the horse; Laocoön and Sinon are not in Homer. The full account is Virgil's Aeneid, Book 2 (~19 BCE) — a millennium after the event. 'Timeo Danaos et dona ferentes' (beware Greeks bearing gifts) is Virgil's line, not Homer's.

sources.ref: Homer, Odyssey Book 8 — Demodocus's song (public domain): the earliest literary attestation of the horse, brief and embedded in a song-within-a-song.
Virgil, Aeneid Book 2 (~19 BCE) — the first full account of the episode, including Laocoön, Sinon, and 'timeo Danaos et dona ferentes'; composed roughly a millennium after the claimed event.

IFLScience, 'Did The Famous Trojan Horse Really Exist?' — Dr Armand D'Angour (Oxford): Troy was indeed burned down, 'but the wooden horse is an imaginative fable, perhaps inspired by the way ancient siege-engines were clothed with damp horse-hides to stop them being set alight'; Homer mentions the horse only in passing in the Odyssey, the first substantial description is the Aeneid.
The Tab / History Today (Julia Kindt): the live mechanism theories — siege tower or battering ram, an earthquake (horses = Poseidon, god of horses and earthquakes), or a ship carrying Greek soldiers.

Dartmouth Aegean Prehistory, Lesson 27 — Troy VIIa: 'perhaps the most likely candidate for the city of Priam'; destruction in a general conflagration ~1180 BCE; no mechanism attested in the stratigraphy.

competing_hypotheses: The siege-engine reading: the 'horse' as a battering ram or siege tower draped in damp horse-hides against fire (D'Angour) — the mechanism the stratigraphy can almost accommodate
The ship reading: 'hippos' as a ship name/type — the Greeks sailed in, not marched in
The earthquake reading: Poseidon the horse-god as the earth-shaker; a seismic event breached the walls (Troy VI's earthquake damage is the precedent)
The poetic-invention reading: the horse as an imaginative fable — the majority scholarly position (IFLScience)
falsifiability: A contemporaneous Bronze Age record of the ruse — a Hittite tablet, a Linear B entry, an inscription — naming the horse stratagem at Wilusa would move this to CORROBORATED. Conversely, textual proof that the Odyssey 8 horse passage is a post-Homeric interpolation would drop the earliest attestation and push this toward SPECULATION.

title: Troy VIIa burned ~1180 BCE — a city destroyed, an attacker unnamed
claim: That Troy VIIa — the Late Bronze Age city at Hisarlık — suffered violent destruction by fire around 1180 BCE, with evidence of attack (arrowheads, unburied dead, emergency food stores, a packed lower town). The agent of destruction (Greek attackers, earthquake, or both) is contested.
place: Hisarlik (Troy), Tevfikiye, Çanakkale Province, Turkey
grade_reason: CORROBORATED on the destruction: a general conflagration destroying both citadel and extramural buildings (Dartmouth Lesson 27), with attack signatures — Mycenaean arrowheads embedded in the walls, unburied skeletons, buried food rations, Korfmann's subdivided lower-city homes packed for siege. Held below VERIFIED: the date rests on relative ceramic dating (no absolute anchor), and the agent is genuinely contested — siege, earthquake, or both; the 'Greeks did it' reading is SPECULATION on the current evidence. The ~1180 date landing near Eratosthenes's 1184 is convergence, not proof — stated honestly.
earliest_attestation: The stratigraphy itself (Blegen 1932–1938; Korfmann 1988–2005) — the burn layer is the primary document. The epic tradition's war-date reckonings are later Greek chronography, not attestation of this layer.

sources.ref: Dartmouth Aegean Prehistory, Lesson 27 — Troy VIIa: occupied from ~1300/1280 BCE to ~1180 BCE (LH IIIB imports in, LH IIIC sherds out); Blegen's dating debate (1240 → 1270; Nylander 1200–1190); 'Troy VIIa perished in a general conflagration which destroyed both the buildings within the citadel and those outside'; the Greek war-date reckonings (Eratosthenes 1184, Parian Marble 1209/8, Herodotus ~1250, Douris 1334/3); the VIh minority and Wood 1985.
Wikipedia, 'Late Bronze Age Troy' — Troy VIIa 1300–1180 BCE; the layer table (Troy VI 1750–1300, VIIa 1300–1180, VIIb 1180–950).

Korfmann excavations 1988–2005 (via secondary summaries): the lower city packed with subdivided homes, buried food rations, unburied skeletons, Mycenaean arrowheads in the walls — the siege signatures.

competing_hypotheses: The Greek-siege reading: Mycenaean attackers (the epic's claim) — unproven; no inscription names them
The earthquake reading: Troy VI's seismic destruction is the precedent; a quake may have finished or preceded VIIa's violence
The VIh preference: a vocal minority holds earthquake-destroyed Troy VIh (grander, ~1250 BCE) as Homer's city, not VIIa (Wood 1985 balanced appraisal carried in the Dartmouth lesson)
falsifiability: Dendrochronological or radiocarbon re-dating shifting VIIa's destruction outside ~1250–1150 BCE would force re-evaluation; a contemporaneous inscription naming the attackers would settle the agent; proof the destruction horizon is seismic-only would move the 'attack' reading down.

title: 'The Phoenicians invented the alphabet' — the schoolbook claim
claim: The Phoenicians invented the alphabet around 1050 BCE — the schoolbook version: the Phoenician abjad as the first true alphabet.
place: The Levantine coast (Byblos, Tyre, Sidon — the Phoenician cities that did the standardizing, not the inventing)
grade_reason: The Proto-Sinaitic inscriptions (Serabit el-Khadim, Wadi el-Hol) put alphabetic writing at c. 1800 BCE — roughly seven centuries before the Phoenician abjad. The Phoenicians adapted and standardized an existing alphabet; they did not invent it. Christopher Rollston (2022): 'There is a wide misconception in the general public that the Phoenicians invented the alphabet. They didn't. They adapted and standardized the alphabet several centuries after it was invented.'
earliest_attestation: The claim as stated is a modern textbook formulation; the Proto-Sinaitic evidence that kills it dates to 1905-1916 (Petrie's finds, Gardiner's decipherment)

sources.ref: Rollston, C. (2022), 'Oldest Canaanite Sentence Found,' Bible History Daily / BAS — 'a wide misconception in the general public that the Phoenicians invented the alphabet. They didn't.'
Naveh, J. (1982), Early History of the Alphabet — the standard history of the transmission
Companion record evt-proto-sinaitic-alphabet-001 (CORROBORATED) — the ~1800 BCE evidence that does the killing

competing_hypotheses: The charitable reading: 'invented' as popular shorthand for the Phoenician achievement — the standardized 22-letter consonantal abjad, its fixed letter order and names (aleph, bet...), and its transmission through the Levantine trade network to Aramaic, Hebrew, and Greek. On this reading the sentence is imprecise, not false — the record keeps this as the fair defence

The minimalist transmission case: some scholars (the Sass/Naveh debates) dispute the dating and mechanics of the Greek adoption — but none of them disputes that the alphabetic principle predates Phoenicia by centuries
falsifiability: The grade is closed unless the entire Proto-Sinaitic corpus — Petrie's 1905-1906 finds, Gardiner's 1916 decipherment, the Wadi el-Hol inscriptions published 1999/2005 — is shown to be fraudulent or misdated by ~700 years. Extraordinary evidence would be required.

title: The Yellow River's first prehistoric diversion (~3000–2600 BP): the Taihang-foothill course

falsifiability: A dated, peer-reviewed stratigraphic reconstruction showing no such northward channel in the 3000–2600 BP window along the Taihang foothills would retire this exhibit; the argument's other exhibits stand independently.
