competing_hypotheses: Traditional unitary 6th-century authorship: Daniel the exile wrote the whole book in Babylon
Middle position: Persian-period court tales with Maccabean visions appended
The court tales as Hellenistic-period compositions throughout
falsifiability: A securely dated pre-3rd-century-BCE manuscript of Daniel 7-12, or a Persian/Babylonian record naming a king 'Darius the Mede', would overturn the dating. Fenced inside the record: Daniel's 'Belshazzar son of Nebuchadnezzar' (5:2, 5:22) is wrong on the father (the cylinders name Nabonidus) and on the title (mar sarri, never king); 'Darius the Mede' (5:31) appears in no Persian or Babylonian source — the candidates (Ugbaru/Gubaru the governor, Cyrus himself, Cyaxares II) are identifications, none of them an attested king.

title: The Decalogue in two versions: Exodus 20 vs Deuteronomy 5
claim: The Ten Commandments exist on the documentary record in at least two different versions inside the canonical Hebrew Bible itself: Exodus 20:2-17 and Deuteronomy 5:6-21. The versions differ materially: the Sabbath commandment's rationale (Ex 20:11 — God rested after six days of creation; Deut 5:15 — 'remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt'), the order of the coveting commandment's objects (Ex 20:17: 'your neighbor's house... your neighbor's wife'; Deut 5:21: 'your neighbor's wife... your neighbor's house'), and the wording of the preamble's closing. The 'word-for-word' telling of the Decalogue — one fixed dictation, transmitted unchanged — fails on the documentary record before any archaeology is consulted. The words on the stone, as written, come in two drafts.
place: Mount Sinai (the tradition's own geography for the giving; the comparison is documentary, not excavated)
grade_reason: The difference is verifiable by reading: any two printed Bibles show it. The Nash Papyrus (evt-nash-papyrus-001) independently witnesses the Second-Temple plurality by harmonizing both. No scholar of any camp disputes the variants; the dispute is only what they mean.
earliest_attestation: The biblical texts themselves (Exodus 20:2-17; Deuteronomy 5:6-21) — the variants are visible in every printed edition.

sources.ref: Exodus 20:2-17 and Deuteronomy 5:6-21 in any printed edition (e.g., BHS) — the Sabbath rationale and the coveting order differ on the page

Cambridge University Library, 'The ten commandments' (Lines of Thought) — the Nash Papyrus 'contains the Ten Commandments... The text of the Ten Commandments preserved on the papyrus is different from that found in the Bible, suggesting that even this fundamental religious text has changed'

competing_hypotheses: The differences are Moses' second-address recapitulation, not a textual problem — the harmonizing reading (the tradition's own account in Deuteronomy as 'the second law'). The record fences it as a reading, not a document: the two texts still differ

Deuteronomy's version reflects the exilic or Deuteronomic redactional layer — the documentary-hypothesis reading. The record does not grade source-critical layer assignments; the documentary fact is the difference
falsifiability: A single manuscript tradition in which Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5 read identically would falsify this record; none exists. Held below VERIFIED: the record grades a textual fact, and textual facts carry the edition-history caveat.

title: The Tower of Babel was Etemenanki
claim: The tower of Genesis 11:1–9 — built in 'the land of Shinar' at 'Babel' — is the ziggurat Etemenanki at Babylon. This is the mainstream scholarly identification.
place: Etemenanki, Babylon (Al Hillah, Iraq)
grade_reason: The mainstream identification, converging on place (Shinar/Babylon), name (Babel), and the tower's fame — but no ancient text makes the equation explicit; it is scholarship's inference, not a document's statement.
earliest_attestation: Genesis 11:1–9 (the narrative); the Etemenanki identification from 1876 (Smith's Esagila translation) through George 1992/2011

sources.ref: Genesis 11:1–9
Akkadian Bāb-ili / Babilu 'gate of god(s)' (Sumerian Ka.dingir.ra) — Genesis 11:9's balal 'confuse' is the text's own Hebrew folk-etymology
Esagila tablet (Louvre AO 6555) + Koldewey excavations — the building the identification points at
Tower of Babel Stele (Schøyen MS 2063, now Iraq Museum) — George 2011; the labeled seven-stage 'great ziggurat of Babylon'

competing_hypotheses: The Babel story is etiological folklore about language diversity, attached to no specific building
The story conflates multiple Mesopotamian towers (Etemenanki, Borsippa) into one archetype
The 'confusion of tongues' reflects the multilingual reality of the Neo-Babylonian empire, not a single event
falsifiability: Evidence the Genesis narrative predates any ziggurat, or a contemporary text identifying a different tower as the story's referent

title: The Babylonian Exile
claim: Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon captured Jerusalem (597 BCE; Babylonian Chronicle) and destroyed the First Temple (586/587 BCE; biblical chronology), deporting Judah's elite to Babylon; returns began under Cyrus (538 BCE decree tradition), but Judahite communities persisted in Babylonia and the Temple was not rebuilt until Darius I (516/515 BCE).
place: Babylon (destination of the deportees)
grade_reason: Babylonian administrative and chronicle texts independently confirm the capture, the deportations, and the exiled king's presence in Babylon; the 586/587 destruction rests on the biblical record plus Jerusalem's destruction layers.
earliest_attestation: The Babylonian Chronicle (contemporary cuneiform); the Lachish letters (c. 588 BCE); Jehoiachin's ration tablets from Babylon (c. 592 BCE)

sources.ref: Babylonian Chronicle BM 21946 (Wiseman 1956): 7th year of Nebuchadnezzar, 2 Adar — capture of the 'city of Judah', seizure of Jehoiachin, Zedekiah installed; 2 Kings 24:8-17 gives the same event from inside
Lachish ostraca (letters from the Babylonian invasion, c. 588 BCE) — 'Azekah we do not see'
Jehoiachin ration tablets (Weidner 1939, Babylon administrative texts): 'Yaukin, king of the land of Judah' on Babylonian rations
2 Kings 25; Jeremiah 52 (destruction narrative — the only detailed account; no cuneiform coverage)
Nabonidus Chronicle: Babylon falls to Cyrus, October 539 BCE
Ezra 1 / Ezra 6 (return tradition; Second Temple completed under Darius I, 516/515 BCE, Ezra 6)

Pearce & Wunsch (2014), Documents of Judean Exiles and West Semites in Babylonia (Al-Yahudu, 'town of Judah', ~100 tablets, 572-477 BCE) + Murashu archive (5th c. BCE Nippur) — Judahite life in Babylonia long after 538

competing_hypotheses: A large-scale deportation as described, with a substantial exilic community in Babylon (consensus)
The deportations were smaller and the 'empty land' motif is exaggerated; most Judahites remained
falsifiability: Babylonian records showing no deportation or no Jehoiachin in Babylon would overturn the corroboration

title: The Jehoiachin ration tablets (Babylon, 592 BCE)
claim: Babylonian palace ration tablets from Nebuchadnezzar II's 13th year (592 BCE) record oil rations to 'Ya'ukin, king of the land of Judah' (Yaukin = Jehoiachin), his five sons, and other Judeans — the Babylonian administration's own record of the exiled king, five years after the 597 deportation.
place: Babylon, southern palace area near the Ishtar Gate (findspot)
grade_reason: Excavated Babylonian administrative tablets, multiply represented within a ~300-tablet palace archive; a single archive, so the grade holds at CORROBORATED rather than VERIFIED.
earliest_attestation: The tablets themselves: palace-storehouse ration receipts, Babylon, c. 595-570 BCE

sources.ref: Ernst Weidner, 'Jojachin, Koenig von Juda, in babylonischen Keilschrifttexten,' Melanges syriens II (1939): 923-935 — editio princeps

The ration tablets (primary): ~300 palace-store receipts, Babylon; entry of Nebuchadnezzar's 13th year: 10 sila of oil to 'Ya'ukin, king of the land of Yahudu' (Akkadian Ya-`u-kinu, sar mat Ya-hudu), plus 2.5 sila for his five sons; other Judeans, Ashkelonite princes, Egyptian and Ionian craftsmen on the same lists
Excavation context: Robert Koldewey's Babylon expedition (1899-1917), palace-storehouse fill near the Ishtar Gate; tablets now in the Vorderasiatisches Museum, Berlin
Babylonian Chronicle BM 21946: the 597 BCE capture that put Jehoiachin in Babylon — the chronicle context for the ration lists
Ezekiel's dating formula ('in the Nth year of the exile of King Jehoiachin') — a second, independent tradition counting time from the same king's deportation

competing_hypotheses: The standard reading: Jehoiachin maintained in Babylonian custody at royal expense, his royal title preserved by the palace clerks (mainstream)
The rations reflect a diplomatic pension or honored-guest maintenance rather than imprisonment — the tablets specify the ration, not his legal status
falsifiability: A re-reading of the name Ya'ukin as someone else, or proof the tablets are modern forgeries — unlikely, given the excavated context

title: 'Yahweh' — the scholarly reconstruction of the divine-name pronunciation
claim: The scholarly reconstruction of the Tetragrammaton's pronunciation is 'Yahweh' — the best current reading of how ancient Hebrew speakers said YHWH.
place: Jerusalem — locus of the divine-name tradition
grade_reason: Multiple independent lines (theophoric name forms, Lachish Letters, Greek transcriptions, Masoretic vowel-pattern analysis) converge on the Yahweh reading; held below VERIFIED since no audio of the ancient pronunciation exists.
earliest_attestation: Modern scholarly consensus — reconstructed from theophoric names (Yeho-/Yahu- prefixes), the Lachish Letters (pre-586 BCE), and Greek transcriptions (e.g., Iao/Iabe) in ancient sources.

sources.ref: Encyclopedia Judaica, vol. 7: the name was pronounced 'Yahweh' regularly at least until 586 B.C., 'as is clear from the Lachish Letters written shortly before this date'
The Jewish Encyclopedia (1901), 'Tetragrammaton': distinguishes the unpronounced written form from the 'Yahweh' scholarly reading of the ancient pronunciation

competing_hypotheses: Encyclopedia Judaica's stronger claim: the true pronunciation 'was never lost' and was regularly spoken at least until 586 BCE (Lachish Letters); 'reconstruction' undersells the continuity of the reading tradition
Minority: the original pronunciation is irrecoverable and 'Yahweh' is one plausible vocalization among several (e.g., Yahwoh)
falsifiability: A contemporary pre-exilic Hebrew transcription voweled differently would demote the reconstruction; the consensus rests on converging independent lines, not a single attestation.

title: The 'empty land' telling
claim: The popular reading that Nebuchadnezzar's 586/587 BCE conquest emptied the land of Judah entirely — 'the land enjoyed its sabbaths' (2 Chronicles 36:21) taken as literal demography: everybody deported, nobody left.
place: Mizpah (Tell en-Nasbeh) — Babylonian administrative center after 586 BCE
grade_reason: Archaeology (Mizpah, Benjamin surveys, Ein Gedi, Mosa, Tell el-Ful) proves settlement continuity through the exilic period; no scholar defends literal emptiness — the live debate is the depopulation level (Faust ~15% vs Lipschits ~1/3 survival), not whether anyone remained.
earliest_attestation: 2 Chronicles 36:20-21 — composed 4th c. BCE, two centuries after the events; a theological historiography, not a census.

sources.ref: Hans M. Barstad, The Myth of the Empty Land (Oslo: Scandinavian University Press, 1996) — continuity at Mizpah, Ein Gedi, Mosa, Tell el-Ful
Oded Lipschits, The Fall and Rise of Jerusalem: Judah under Babylonian Rule (Eisenbrauns, 2005) — ~one-third survival estimate; Mizpah as Babylonian administrative center
Avraham Faust, Judah in the Neo-Babylonian Period: The Archaeology of Desolation (SBL, 2012) — critical counter: ~15% survival, 'relative emptiness' but not literal; Benjamin consensus reexamined
Lipschits & Blenkinsopp eds., Judah and the Judeans in the Neo-Babylonian Period (Eisenbrauns, 2003) — the debate volume
2 Kings 25:12; Jeremiah 39:10; 52:16 — the Bible's own counter-testimony: 'the poorest of the land' left behind as vinedressers and farmers
Mizpah (Tell en-Nasbeh) excavations — continued occupation and administrative function through the exilic period

competing_hypotheses: Maximal continuity (Barstad): the conquest peripherally affected Judah's infrastructure; no significant discontinuity of life
'Relative emptiness' (Faust): ~85% population loss, but the land was not literally empty — Benjamin continuity overstated by the consensus
The Chronicler's theological reading (Jonker 2007): the 'sabbath rest' is ideology — a New Israel narrative — not demography
falsifiability: A complete, survey-wide settlement hiatus across Benjamin and the Judean hills for 586–538 BCE would falsify; the surveys show the opposite

title: Judaism's formation: from Judahite kingdom to portable religion
claim: Between the 6th century BCE (exile, First Temple destruction) and the 2nd century BCE (Maccabees), Judahite religion transformed into Judaism — a Torah-centered, synagogue-bearing identity carried in exile and diaspora; the word 'Judaism' (Ioudaismos) first appears in print in 2 Maccabees (2:21; 8:1; 14:38), late 2nd century BCE.
place: Jerusalem (with Elephantine at 24.08 N, 32.89 E and Babylon at 32.54 N, 44.43 E as diaspora nodes)
grade_reason: The people and their practice are multiply attested in contemporary administrative records (Elephantine papyri, Yehud coins, ration tablets) independent of the later literary tradition; the belief-phenomenon is graded, not the metaphysics.
earliest_attestation: Babylonian-era cuneiform (Jehoiachin ration tablets, Al-Yahudu texts); the Elephantine Aramaic papyri (Passover Papyrus 419 BCE; Petition to Bagoas 407 BCE); Yehud coinage inscribed YHD (c. 350–333 BCE); 2 Maccabees for the word 'Judaism' (late 2nd c. BCE)

sources.ref: Elephantine papyri: the Jewish temple at Yeb, Passover Papyrus (419 BCE), Petition to Bagoas (407 BCE) — Porten 1968; Kraeling 1953
Yehud coinage: small silver coins inscribed YHD/YHWD in Paleo-Hebrew and Aramaic, minted c. 350 BCE onward; Gitler et al. typological corpus (2023); MDPI archaeometallurgy (2023)
2 Maccabees 2:21; 8:1; 14:38 — earliest printed use of Ioudaismos (Skarsaune: hellenismos → Ioudaismos, the first 'isms' as identity responses)
Cohen, Shaye J. D. — the meaning of 'Ioudaios' evolves through the Second Temple period; 2 Maccabees marks the cultural-religious emphasis
Theophrastus (4th c. BCE, via Josephus C. Apion 1.166): earliest Greek mention of the Ioudaioi as 'a nation of philosophers'

competing_hypotheses: Judaism's core formed in the exile itself (6th c. BCE): the Deuteronomistic and Priestly traditions as the exile's literary products
Judaism as we know it is a Hasmonean/Hellenistic-period construction (2nd c. BCE), with earlier Yehud as a Persian temple-state, not yet 'Judaism'
Continuity model: unbroken development from First-Temple Judahite religion through Ezra–Nehemiah to the Second Temple, no sharp break
falsifiability: Documentary evidence that Torah-centered practice, synagogue worship, or the Ioudaios identity predates the exile in the form claimed by tradition would sharpen or shift the bracket

title: The Eclipse of Thales — the battle interrupted, 28 May 585 BCE
claim: A solar eclipse interrupted the battle between the Lydians and the Medes near the Halys river, prompting the armies to break off fighting and make peace (Herodotus 1.74). Modern retrocalculation fixes it to 28 May 585 BCE (proleptic Julian).
place: Battle on the Halys (Kızılırmak) frontier, Anatolia
grade_reason: Herodotus's battle narrative converges with Pliny's independent Olympiad date and modern retrocalculation; the eclipse itself is the firmest event in the Thales tradition.
earliest_attestation: Herodotus, Histories 1.74 (c. 440-430 BCE) — roughly 150 years after the event

sources.ref: Herodotus, Histories 1.74 (battle interrupted by the eclipse)
Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia 2.53 (4th year of the 48th Olympiad)
Stephenson & Fatoohi, retrocalculation of the 585 BCE eclipse (totality path over Asia Minor)
Querejeta, 'On the Eclipse of Thales' (Culture and Cosmos 15.1) — survey of the date debate

competing_hypotheses: Herodotus embroidered a real eclipse into the battle narrative; the date is right but the peacemaking detail is formulaic
The prediction story (see evt-thales-001) is a later accretion; the eclipse itself is independent of Thales
falsifiability: A retrocalculation showing the 585 BCE totality band missed the Halys battlefield entirely, or a contemporary source contradicting the Lydian-Mede peace

title: The Eclipse of Thales — the battle interrupted, 28 May 585 BCE
claim: A solar eclipse interrupted the battle between the Lydians and the Medes near the Halys river, prompting the armies to break off fighting and make peace (Herodotus 1.74). Modern retrocalculation fixes it to 28 May 585 BCE (proleptic Julian). The eclipse itself is firm; everything about Thales's foreknowledge is the legend (see evt-thales-001).
place: Battle on the Halys (Kızılırmak) frontier, Anatolia
grade_reason: Herodotus's battle narrative converges with Pliny's independent Olympiad date and modern retrocalculation; the eclipse itself is the firmest event in the Thales tradition. The prediction story is fenced OUT of this record: Worthen's finding stands — Herodotus is the sole source for the prediction, while the doxographical tradition that actually read Thales claims only causal understanding, never prediction. Neugebauer denied a 6th-century prediction was possible; the Saros cycle cannot fix a solar eclipse's locality; no eclipse prediction is attested anywhere before the Seleucid era. Grade CORROBORATED held from -001; the evidence chain, not the grade, is what this supersession refines.
earliest_attestation: Herodotus, Histories 1.74 (c. 440-430 BCE) — roughly 150 years after the event

sources.ref: Herodotus, Histories 1.74 (battle interrupted by the eclipse; ὁρίσας ἐνιαυτόν — he marked out the YEAR)
Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia 2.53 (4th year of the 48th Olympiad)
Stephenson & Fatoohi, retrocalculation of the 585 BCE eclipse (totality path over Asia Minor)
Querejeta, 'On the Eclipse of Thales' (Culture and Cosmos 15.1) — survey of the date debate; the translation controversy (year vs day)
Worthen, 'Herodotus's Report on Thales' Eclipse' (Electronic Antiquity 3.7) — Herodotus likely the sole source of the prediction; the doxographical tradition claims only causal understanding

'How Ancient Greeks Explained and Predicted Eclipses' (brewminate.com, 2026) — the 'Thales Problem': astronomy confirms an appropriate eclipse occurred, but cannot place armies under the shadow or identify a prediction
Panchenko, 'Thales's Prediction of a Solar Eclipse' (JHA 25, 1994) — the Saros-based defense of a year-prediction, heard and fenced as the live counter-argument

competing_hypotheses: Herodotus embroidered a real eclipse into the battle narrative; the date is right but the peacemaking detail is formulaic

The 28 May 585 BCE identification rests on ΔT (Earth-rotation) uncertainty and an unknown battlefield location — the astronomy confirms an appropriate eclipse occurred, not that named armies stood under the shadow
The 'prediction' is a later inflation: Herodotus's Greek says Thales marked out the YEAR (ὁρίσας ἐνιαυτόν); Cicero, Pliny, and Diogenes Laertius inflated it to the day
Alternative eclipse dates (21 Sep 582, 16 Mar 581 BCE) have named defenders but are too limited over Anatolia to turn day dramatically into night
falsifiability: A retrocalculation showing the 585 BCE totality band missed the Halys battlefield entirely (beyond ΔT margins), or a contemporary source contradicting the Lydian-Mede peace

title: The al-Yahudu archive (Judean exiles in Babylonia, 572-477 BCE)
claim: The al-Yahudu archive — roughly 200 cuneiform tablets (572-477 BCE), 103 published by Pearce & Wunsch (2014) — documents Judean exiles as tenant farmers, taxpayers, litigants, and merchants in Babylonian villages including al-Yahudu ('Judah-town'): an exiled community living ordinary economic lives, not languishing in chains.
place: al-Yahudu ('Judah-town'), Babylonia — actual village location unknown; the tablets are unprovenanced
grade_reason: A substantial internally-dated archive with Judean theophoric names (Gedalyahu, Hanan, Shaltiel, Netanyahu) across promissory notes, leases, tax receipts, a lawsuit, and a marriage agreement; capped at CORROBORATED because the tablets are unprovenanced (antiquities market), which bars VERIFIED.
earliest_attestation: The tablets themselves (Neo-Babylonian and Persian-period cuneiform business documents)

sources.ref: Laurie E. Pearce & Cornelia Wunsch, Documents of Judean Exiles and West Semites in Babylonia in the Collection of David Sofer (CUSAS 28, CDL Press, 2014) — editio princeps: 103 cuneiform texts, 'insights into the social and economic life of the Judeans (along with other groups forcibly settled in Mesopotamia by Nebuchadnezzar II) in their community of Al Yahudu (Jewtown)'
The tablets (document): ~200 known total; Judean theophoric names; the Samak-Yama family traceable over five generations; land-for-service tenure as susanu Yahudaya (Judean state dependents)

PROVENANCE CAVEAT: unprovenanced — entered the antiquities market by unknown means (possibly looting); held in private collections, primarily the David and Cindy Sofer Collection; some later acquired by the British Museum. Stated on the record.

'By the Rivers of Babylon' exhibit, Bible Lands Museum Jerusalem (opened Oct 2026, ~100 al-Yahudu tablets from the private David Sofer collection, first public display; curator Dr. Filip Vukosavovic) — the archive's first mass public exhibition; PROVENANCE FENCE CARRIED: antiquities-market tablets, findspot unknown — the exhibit publicizes the evidence, it does not add excavated context

Pre-opening coverage (Times of Israel / Evangelical Focus, 16-17 Oct 2026) — GRADE-NEUTRAL detail append, no supersession (Turin-shroud precedent): exhibit opens Sunday 18 Oct 2026, scheduled to run at least one year; animated Mesopotamian-village centerpiece; the Samak-Yama family's four-generation paper trail (inheritance to five great-grandchildren); Judean theophoric names incl. Natanyahu; handful of Aramaic epigraphs; press head-counts ("80,000 chose to stay", "1,500 to Lebanon/Syria in 587 BCE") carried as press figures, not evidence; Wikipedia's Al-Yahudu article updated Oct 2026 to cite the exhibit opening

competing_hypotheses: The mainstream reading: the tablets are the business records of the real exilic community — Judean theophoric names, land-for-service tenure as Babylonian state dependents (susanu Yahudaya)

The provenance caveat: market tablets could in principle be modern forgeries — but internal consistency across ~200 tablets (dating formulas, prosopography, the Samak-Yama family over five generations) argues strongly against it
falsifiability: Excavation of a provenanced al-Yahudu village archive confirming the readings would raise the grade; demonstration of forgery would collapse it. The grade is capped by provenance, not by content.

title: Pythagoras of Samos
claim: Pythagoras (c. 570-495 BCE) founded a religious-philosophical community at Croton; the Pythagorean theorem tradition is attached to his name, though no writings of his survive.
place: Samos (birthplace, traditional)
grade_reason: No contemporary or near-contemporary writings; the detailed life is built from sources many centuries later, and the theorem was known in Babylon a millennium earlier.
earliest_attestation: Heraclitus and Herodotus mention him (5th century BCE); the detailed biographies (Diogenes Laertius, Porphyry, Iamblichus) are 700+ years later

sources.ref: Herodotus 2.81, 4.95 (earliest literary mentions)
Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Philosophers (3rd c. CE, much later)
Wikidata entity for Pythagoras (CC0, derivative)

competing_hypotheses: Pythagoras was a historical charismatic founder whose community preserved mathematical and religious teachings
The 'Pythagoras' of the biographies is largely a construct of later Pythagorean schools projecting doctrines backward
falsifiability: A contemporary 6th-century inscription or text naming Pythagoras of Samos as a teacher would raise the grade

title: Pythagoras of Samos — the name on the theorem (attribution autopsy)
claim: Pythagoras of Samos (c. 570-495 BCE) founded a religious-philosophical community at Croton; the Pythagorean theorem tradition is attached to his name. The attachment is late doxography: no source within five centuries of Pythagoras connects him to the theorem — the attribution rides Proclus's 5th-century CE commentary on Euclid I.47, citing the lost History of Geometry of Eudemus (4th c. BCE), roughly a thousand years after Pythagoras; the ox-sacrifice-on-discovery legend comes through Apollodorus via Diogenes Laertius 8.12. Plato and Aristotle never connect Pythagoras to the theorem. Burkert's Lore and Science in Ancient Pythagoreanism (1972): the earliest brotherhood was a religious community, and the 'mathematical Pythagoras' is largely later construction. The relationship itself was in working use in Old Babylon ~1,200 years before his birth (evt-pythagorean-triples-babylon-001); Euclid's Elements I.47 (c. 300 BCE) is the earliest fully verifiable proof and does not name Pythagoras.
place: Samos (birthplace, traditional)
grade_reason: The figure's historicity is thinly attested but real (Heraclitus, Herodotus); every mathematical attribution is late doxography, and the theorem's priority now sits on the Old Babylonian tablets — the name on the theorem is a 2,000-year-old misattribution that the record keeps fenced, not repeated.
earliest_attestation: Heraclitus and Herodotus mention Pythagoras (5th century BCE) — neither connects him to the theorem; the detailed biographies (Diogenes Laertius, Porphyry, Iamblichus) are 700+ years later

sources.ref: Herodotus 2.81, 4.95 (earliest literary mentions — no theorem connection)
Proclus, Commentary on Euclid I.47 (5th c. CE), citing Eudemus's History of Geometry — the attribution chain
Diogenes Laertius 8.12 (via Apollodorus) — the ox-sacrifice-on-discovery legend
Euclid, Elements I.47 (c. 300 BCE) — the earliest fully verifiable proof; names no discoverer
Burkert, Lore and Science in Ancient Pythagoreanism (1972) — the religious-brotherhood-first reading; the mathematical Pythagoras as later construction

competing_hypotheses: Pythagoras was a historical charismatic founder whose community preserved mathematical and religious teachings — the brotherhood's later mathematics projected back onto the founder
The 'Pythagoras' of the biographies is largely a construct of later Pythagorean schools projecting doctrines backward (Burkert's reading)
A lost Pythagorean proof existed and Euclid I.47 descends from it — possible, unattested, unprovable either way
falsifiability: A contemporary 6th-century inscription or text naming Pythagoras of Samos as a teacher would raise the grade; a pre-Euclidean Greek proof text naming him would change the attribution grade

title: The Buddha (Siddhartha Gautama)
claim: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, taught the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path in northern India; tradition dates him 563-483 BCE, though modern scholarship favors c. 480-400 BCE.
place: Lumbini (traditional birthplace)
grade_reason: Ashoka's pillar gives 3rd-century BCE state-level attestation of the Buddha and his birthplace; the life details come from much later texts.
earliest_attestation: Ashoka's Lumbini pillar inscription (c. 249 BCE) marking the birthplace; Pali canon texts compiled centuries after his death

sources.ref: Ashoka's Lumbini (Rummindei) pillar edict (c. 249 BCE)
Pali Canon (compiled 1st c. BCE and later, Sri Lanka)
Bechert (ed.), The Dating of the Historical Buddha (1988 symposium volume)

competing_hypotheses: The Buddha was a historical teacher in the 5th century BCE whose movement is reliably traced to him
The Buddha narratives are largely hagiographic with a thin historical core (a minority of scholars)
falsifiability: The dating dispute is live: new epigraphic or radiocarbon evidence fixing 6th-5th century BCE northern Indian chronology would narrow the range

title: Cyrus the Great
claim: Cyrus II of Persia (reigned c. 559-530 BCE) conquered Media, Lydia, and Babylon, founding the Achaemenid Empire. The Jewish return tradition credits Cyrus with a decree permitting the exiles to return (Ezra 1; Aramaic version in Ezra 6); the Cyrus Cylinder itself does not mention Judah or the Jews.
place: Pasargadae (Cyrus's capital)
grade_reason: Multiple independent contemporary sources — the Cylinder, the Babylonian chronicle tradition, and Greek accounts — confirm his conquests and reign; the return-decree tradition rests on Ezra, not the Cylinder.
earliest_attestation: The Cyrus Cylinder (539/538 BCE); the Nabonidus Chronicle (contemporary Babylonian); Herodotus Histories Book 1

sources.ref: Cyrus Cylinder, BM 90920 (British Museum) — genuine artifact; ll. 30-32 restore only Mesopotamian sanctuaries east of the Tigris; names no Jews, no Judah
Nabonidus Chronicle (Babylonian, contemporary) — fall of Babylon, October 539 BCE
Herodotus, Histories 1.46-216 (independent Greek account)
Ezra 1 (Hebrew decree tradition) vs Ezra 6:3-5 (Aramaic version) — the two versions differ substantially; wording-authenticity debated, but the tradition is held to reflect real Persian practice
Kuhrt 1983; Finkel 2013; Grabbe — the cylinder as Babylonian royal formula, not a general repatriation policy (see evt-cyrus-cylinder-charter-001)

competing_hypotheses: Ezra's decree reflects a genuine Cyrus order toward Judah (consensus holds it reflects real Persian practice)
One or both decree versions are a post hoc fabrication (wording-authenticity debated; the cylinder gives no support either way)
falsifiability: Contemporary sources placing a different king over Persia in those years, or proof the Cylinder is not Cyrus's

title: Confucius
claim: Confucius (Kong Qiu, 551-479 BCE) of Lu taught ethics centered on ren (humaneness) and li (ritual propriety); his disciples compiled his sayings in the Analects, which became foundational to East Asian thought.
place: Qufu, Lu state (traditional)
grade_reason: Attested in the Analects tradition and in Sima Qian's biography with Lu-state context; no contemporary inscription, and the Analects has debated layers.
earliest_attestation: The Analects (compiled by disciples, 5th-3rd c. BCE); Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian (c. 109-91 BCE) biography

sources.ref: The Analects (Lunyu)
Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian, 'Biography of Confucius' (c. 100 BCE)
Zuo Zhuan (contemporary-ish Spring and Autumn chronicle of Lu)

competing_hypotheses: Confucius was a historical teacher whose sayings the Analects broadly preserves (consensus)
Confucius is a composite sage-figure assembled by Warring States schools (minority skeptical view)
falsifiability: Contemporary 6th-5th century BCE texts from Lu naming Kong Qiu as a teacher would strengthen historicity; proof the Analects is a Han forgery would collapse it

title: The Achaemenid Empire — Persia, 550–330 BCE
claim: The Achaemenid Empire (c. 550–330 BCE), founded by Cyrus the Great, was the largest empire the ancient world had seen — about 5.5 million km² at greatest extent under Darius I and Xerxes I, spanning three continents, administered through satrapies, linked by the Royal Road and a state postal system, and documented in its own trilingual royal inscriptions and tens of thousands of administrative clay tablets.
place: Persepolis, Fars, Iran (empire-wide record; pinned at the ceremonial capital)
grade_reason: Multiple independent primary and contemporary sources: the Behistun trilingual inscription, the Persepolis Fortification tablets (administrative clay archive), Babylonian and Egyptian administrative documents, and Greek historiography — the state's reality is uncontested in scholarship.
earliest_attestation: Behistun inscription of Darius I, c. 522–486 BCE — trilingual (Old Persian, Elamite, Babylonian) royal account carved on Mount Behistun

sources.ref: Behistun inscription of Darius I (c. 522–486 BCE) — trilingual Old Persian/Elamite/Babylonian royal account; the king's own list of the lands he ruled
Persepolis Fortification tablets — thousands of Elamite administrative clay tablets recording rations, wages, travel permits, and personnel; the empire's own paperwork
Babylonian and Egyptian administrative documents naming Persian satraps and taxation — independent provincial attestation
Herodotus, Histories (5th c. BCE) — Greek-side account of the empire's scale, satrapies, and the Royal Road
Multiple secondary aggregators converge on ~5.5M km² at greatest extent under Darius I/Xerxes I (e.g., empire-size surveys citing the satrapy lists)

competing_hypotheses: The 5.5M km² figure is a modeled maximum from frontier lists and satrapy rosters, not a surveyed boundary — the extent is approximate, the state's existence is not

The 'tolerant empire' reading leans on royal self-presentation (Behistun, the Cyrus Cylinder); the rebellions Darius lists in Behistun itself show the empire was held by force as well as administration
Some historians argue the empire's coherence is overstated and the satrapies were looser than the paperwork suggests
falsifiability: Proof the Behistun inscription and the Persepolis Fortification tablets are modern forgeries, or a contemporary document showing the satrapy administration never existed

title: The Cyrus Cylinder as 'first declaration of human rights'
claim: The Cyrus Cylinder is the world's first declaration of human rights, in which Cyrus the Great freed the Jewish exiles from Babylon and granted religious freedom to all peoples of his empire.
place: Babylon (findspot of the cylinder)
grade_reason: The cylinder is genuine, but it is a traditional Babylonian royal foundation text, not a rights charter; its restoration passage names only Mesopotamian sanctuaries and never mentions Jews, Judah, or a general release of exiles.
earliest_attestation: Cyrus Cylinder, BM 90920 (Rassam 1879 find), Akkadian cuneiform foundation-deposit text

sources.ref: Cyrus Cylinder, BM 90920 (British Museum); ll. 30-32 restoration passage — sanctuaries east of the Tigris (Agade, Eshnunna, Zamban, Me-Turnu, Der, Gutium region); names no Jews, no Judah

Amélie Kuhrt (1983), 'The Cyrus Cylinder and Achaemenid Imperial Policy': the piety passage as literary device contrasting Cyrus with the 'impious' Nabonidus; privileges to strategic cities following earlier Assyrian practice, not a general repatriation policy
Irving Finkel (2013), The Cyrus Cylinder (British Museum): the restoration lines concern Mesopotamian sanctuaries only and 'make no reference to the Judean refugees'
Lester L. Grabbe: Persian religious policy 'not that different from the basic practice of the Assyrians and Babylonians before them' — tolerating, not promoting, local cults
Shah of Iran's 1971 2,500-year celebrations: origin of the 'first declaration of Human Rights' framing

2026 instance of the same telling family (DEBUNKED held, no supersession — the family kills the reading, not each retelling): usfandomstareveryday.com, c. Feb-Mar 2026 — "Scholars have translated its inscriptions, revealing Cyrus the Great's decree to restore the exiled Jewish people to their homeland" — the cylinder's ll. 30-32 name no Jews, no Judah; the restoration passage concerns Mesopotamian sanctuaries east of the Tigris (Ashur, Susa, Agade, Eshnunna, Zamban, Me-Turnu, Der, Gutium). The piece's "challenges Islamic teachings" framing is polemics, not evidence.

Nathan Steinmeyer (Sept 13, 2026), 'The Cyrus Cylinder,' Bible History Daily / Biblical Archaeology Society: restates the held scholarly position for the 2026 record — the cylinder is a foundation inscription (buried, 'meant to be read by the gods alone'), never speaks of Jerusalem or the Judeans (Babylonian cult centers only), and follows the earlier royal-inscription tradition (Kuhrt 1983; Esarhaddon precedent; 2009–2010 British Museum duplicate fragments from a tablet, likely a scribal-office copy per Finkel 2012). Grade-neutral restatement — DEBUNKED held, no supersession (Turin-shroud precedent).

YouTube documentary 'The Cyrus Cylinder Myth: Was It Really the First Human Rights Charter?' (~2026-10-12) — reads all 45 lines, dates the 'first human rights charter' label to the 1971 Pahlavi 2,500-year celebrations, cites Walker / Arnold & Michalowski / Kuhrt (1983) / Finkel — a popular restatement of this record's held DEBUNKED grade, no new evidence (venue exhibit, grade-neutral, chained per the Turin-shroud precedent)

UNESCO 43rd General Conference resolution (Samarkand, 2026-11-06; sponsors Iran, Tajikistan, Iraq) recognizing the Cylinder as 'the earliest written expression of freedom, justice, tolerance, and respect for cultural diversity' — an institutional/political act, not evidence; the scholarly autopsy (Kuhrt 1983; Finkel) stands — the official language outruns the grade (venue note, grade-neutral)

competing_hypotheses: The cylinder reflects a genuine general Persian policy of repatriating deported peoples, of which Judah's return was one instance (the Ezra tradition as the Judah-specific version of the decree)
The cylinder is Cyrus co-opting Babylonian priestly idiom for Babylonian consumption only; the Ezra decree tradition is independent
falsifiability: A cylinder passage naming Judah or a general release of exiles would overturn the debunking; the extant text has none

title: The Cyrus edict of return (Ezra's decree tradition)
claim: Cyrus the Great issued a decree in his first year (538 BCE) permitting the Jewish exiles in Babylonia to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the Temple, with royal support.
place: Babylon (where the decree tradition originates)
grade_reason: Attested in the biblical tradition only; no contemporary Persian copy of the decree survives, and the two versions differ substantially — though the Aramaic memorandum carries genuine Persian chancellery form.
earliest_attestation: Ezra 1:2-4 (Hebrew) and Ezra 6:3-5 (Aramaic); the biblical book of Ezra, composed centuries after the events it describes

sources.ref: Ezra 1:2-4 (Hebrew proclamation): universal scope, Yahweh-theology, voluntary local funding for returnees

Ezra 6:3-5 (Aramaic archive memorandum): temple dimensions (60 x 60 cubits), construction method, costs from the royal treasury, restitution of the gold and silver vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken — widely accepted as genuine Persian chancellery form
Ezra 6:6-12 (Darius's decree): proceeds on the premise that a Cyrus decree existed — the search of the Ecbatana archive is narrated as finding it

Elias Bickerman, 'The Edict of Cyrus in Ezra 1,' JBL 65 (1946): 'Ezra 1 preserves a genuine edict of Cyrus, which had the same formula and the same modes of promulgation, by herald and through poster, as the Roman edictum'
Kuhrt 1983; Grabbe: the cylinder confirms a genuine imperial restoration policy, so the Ezra wording is a localized, theological adaptation of real Persian practice — not dismissible as fiction
Philip R. Davies 1992 (minimalist position): the proclamation as largely post-exilic invention to legitimize Judean land and temple claims

competing_hypotheses: A genuine Cyrus decree toward Judah, reflecting real Persian restoration policy (Bickerman 1946; the mainstream synthesis with Kuhrt/Grabbe)
An authentic administrative core — the Aramaic memorandum of Ezra 6 — with a theologized Hebrew paraphrase (Ezra 1) by the Chronicler: the mainstream middle position
A post-exilic literary composition legitimizing the return and the rebuilt temple (Davies/Thompson minimalists)
falsifiability: A contemporary Persian cuneiform copy of the decree naming Judah would raise the grade to CORROBORATED or VERIFIED; proof the Aramaic memorandum's chancellery form is a later forgery would collapse the middle position

title: The Boyce thesis: Zoroastrian angelology → Second Temple Jewish angelology
claim: Mary Boyce's thesis: the angelology of post-exilic Judaism — the named, ranked heavenly court of the Second Temple period (the archangels, the watchers) — was developed after the pattern of the Zoroastrian Amesha Spentas and yazatas, under the influence of Persian-period contact (c. 538–332 BCE), when Judah lived under Achaemenid rule and Jews 'entertained warm feelings thereafter for the Persians,' making them receptive to Zoroastrian influence (Boyce, Zoroastrians: Their Religious Beliefs and Practices, 1979; crystallized in Boyce & Grenet, A History of Zoroastrianism vol. 3, 1991, pp. 404–405).
place: Jerusalem / Yehud (the Persian-period Jewish province where the influence is claimed to have landed)
grade_reason: Reasoned from real contact and real structural resemblance, but no ancient source attests the borrowing, the direction of dependence is disputed, and the Avestan redaction chronology (Young Avestan, Sasanian codification) lets critics reverse the arrow. Reasoned, unattested: SPECULATION.
earliest_attestation: The scholarly thesis: Mary Boyce, Zoroastrians: Their Religious Beliefs and Practices (1979), and Boyce & Grenet, A History of Zoroastrianism, vol. 3 (1991), pp. 404–405. No ancient source attests the borrowing.

sources.ref: Mary Boyce & Frantz Grenet, A History of Zoroastrianism, vol. 3 (1991), pp. 404–405 — the crystallized influence thesis (post-exilic Jewish angelology after the pattern of the Amesha Spentas)
Albert de Jong, Traditions of the Magi (1997) — the redaction-chronology caution: the Avesta's layered dating complicates any claimed Persian→Jewish arrow
evt-malakhim-001 — already carries this thesis as a competing hypothesis ('contested; the direction and extent of influence are debated'); this record grades the thesis itself

competing_hypotheses: Parallel development: Jewish angelology grew from native Israelite sources (the divine council, the mal'akhim) under the pressures of exile theology, without Persian borrowing
Reverse or shared-source direction: the Persian and Jewish systems both drew on older common Near Eastern material, or the dependence runs the other way
Minimalism: the resemblances are real but superficial — court hierarchies are what bureaucracies look like, in heaven as in Persepolis (the structural-convergence reading)
falsifiability: A pre-exilic Jewish angelology already containing the named, ranked archangel court — with pre-Persian-period attestation — would kill the dependence claim; so would a secure demonstration that the developed Avestan yazata system postdates the Second Temple angelology it is supposed to have influenced.

title: The Abrahamic offshoots tree: a shared patriarch, claimed by three traditions
claim: Judaism, Christianity, and Islam each ground their origins in the figure of Abraham — the shared 'Abrahamic' lineage is a genuine feature of each tradition's own foundational texts (Hebrew Bible, New Testament, Qur'an), not a modern scholarly invention. The tree is the map of that shared tradition-claim; it is not a verified genealogy of a verified person.
place: Jerusalem / the shared sacred geography
grade_reason: The claim that all three traditions ground themselves in Abraham is multiply attested in each tradition's foundational documents — a belief-phenomenon graded on attestation, not metaphysics. The trunk (Abraham the person) stays CLAIMED; this grade covers the tree as tradition-map only.
earliest_attestation: Genesis 17 (covenant with Abraham) in the biblical tradition; Romans 4 / Galatians 3 (Paul's Abraham) 1st c. CE; Qur'an 2:135, 3:67, 2:124-129 (Ibrahim) 7th c. CE

sources.ref: Genesis 17; 25 (covenant, the sons)
Paul's epistles: Romans 4, Galatians 3 (1st c. CE) — Abraham as father of Gentile believers
Qur'an 2:135, 3:67 ('Abraham was not a Jew, nor a Christian'), 2:124-129 (Ka'ba foundations), 14:35-41
F.E. Peters, The Monotheists (Princeton, 2003) — the Abrahamic family as analytic category
Seed records: evt-abraham-001 (trunk, CLAIMED), evt-judaism-001, evt-christianity-emergence-001, evt-islam-origin-001, evt-quran-manuscripts-001 (branches, CORROBORATED)

competing_hypotheses: The tree is essentially correct as a tradition-map: the shared Abraham claim is the documented mechanism by which the three traditions understood themselves

The 'Abrahamic' category is a modern scholarly construct that flattens the traditions' real differences — the three Abrahams (covenant patriarch, Pauline archetype, Qur'anic hanif) are not the same figure and the branches developed largely independently
The trunk is entirely unverifiable, so the tree is a map of literary inheritance, not history — graded honestly as CLAIMED for the person, CORROBORATED for the attestation
falsifiability: Any one tradition's foundational texts lacking an Abraham claim would downgrade the tree; evidence that the 'shared Abraham' framing originated only in modern scholarship would debunk the 'not a modern invention' clause

title: Adon to Adonis: the Semitic root behind the Greek god
claim: The Greek Adonis derives from the Semitic title adon ('lord') — the Byblos cult's god, carried into the Greek world; his explicit resurrection references are largely of the Christian era.
place: Byblos (origin) to the Greek world (transmission)
grade_reason: The linguistic root and the Byblos-to-Greece transmission are documented; the dying-and-rising reading of Adonis is the debated part, honestly dated late.
earliest_attestation: Byblos cult of the Baal of Gebal/Adonis, 1st millennium BCE; Greek Adonia attested by the 3rd c. BCE

sources.ref: Theocritus, Idyll 15 (Adonia festival, 3rd c. BCE)
Roland de Vaux (1933) — critique of Frazer's dying-and-rising category, late-dating of Adonis resurrection
Marcel Detienne, The Gardens of Adonis (1972/1977) — the Adonia festival in its Greek context
Tryggve N.D. Mettinger, The Riddle of Resurrection (2001) — Adonis chapter ('may well have been' a dying-and-rising god)

competing_hypotheses: Adonis as originally Greek, with the Semitic connection a later syncretism (minority; the adon root and Byblos priority weigh against it)
De Vaux: resurrection references are late borrowings from the Osiris cult (3rd c. CE Alexandria); Will: they are Christian-era misreadings of the evidence
falsifiability: A pre-Christian Greek text narrating Adonis's resurrection as cult doctrine would move the dying-and-rising reading from debated to attested.

title: Attis: the Phrygian lament and the argued return
claim: The Phrygian/Gallo-Roman tradition attests Attis as a dying-and-rising figure of the Cybele cult, with the Hilaria festival of March 25 celebrated as his return/rebirth — but the 'resurrection' half of the story is the weakest of the five columns, largely a later Roman reading of an older Phrygian lament tradition.
place: Phrygia (central Anatolia)
grade_reason: Single-tradition, late, and Roman-overlayed attestation: the lament is attested, the 'rising' half is argued rather than witnessed. The grade stays CLAIMED — the team's honesty about the weakest column.
earliest_attestation: Phrygian cult material; Roman-period sources on the Cybele-Attis rites and the Hilaria (March 25)

sources.ref: Phrygian cult material — Attis in the Cybele cult; the self-castration and pine traditions
Roman-period sources on the March rites: the arbor intrat (March 22) and the Hilaria (March 25)

competing_hypotheses: Attis does not 'return' at all in the older Phrygian material: he dies (self-castration, pine transformation) and is mourned — the Hilaria's 'rebirth' is a Roman-period overlay
The pine cult (the arbor intrat, March 22) and the Hilaria (March 25) were separate rites later merged by Roman syncretism — the 'dying-and-rising' reading is the merge, not the original
Mettinger leaves Attis outside his five defended cases — the category rehabilitation does not carry Attis; this record follows that restraint
The maximalist reading: the texts describe a real entity's history — not graded; the attestation rule grades the belief, never the metaphysics
falsifiability: A pre-Roman Phrygian source describing Attis's return/rebirth would raise the grade; a demonstration that the Hilaria never concerned Attis would drop it to SPECULATION

title: "Liubo was chess" — the identity claim
claim: Liubo, the Han-dynasty Chinese board game, was an early form of chess (i.e., the same game family, not merely a predecessor or inspiration).
place: Han China (liubo's attested range)
grade_reason: Liubo is a documented distinct game (TLV board, racing/capture mechanics, divination use) with no chess pieces, chess moves, or chess board; even Needham framed it as a possible 'pre-game' inspiration, not as chess. The identity claim has no scholarly defense.
earliest_attestation: The claim is modern; liubo itself is attested in Han tombs (e.g. Mawangdui) and texts. Needham (1962) — the chief champion of a Chinese route — treated the liubo-family board only as a possible divination 'pre-game' inspiration for chess, never as chess itself.

sources.ref: Joseph Needham, Science and Civilisation in China, Vol.4 Part 1 (CUP, 1962), pp. 314–334 — the liubo-family board as possible divination-board 'pre-game', not as chess
Excavated liubo sets (Han tombs, e.g. Mawangdui): TLV-pattern board, twelve-piece racing/capture mechanics, no chess armies

ChessBase, 'On the origins of chess (3/7): Chinese origin of chess' — the serious China-origin argument runs through Xiang Jing (569 CE) and Needham's divination hypothesis, not through liubo-identity

competing_hypotheses: Needham's divination-route hypothesis: a Chinese yin-yang divination board was 'vulgarized' into the military symbolism that became chaturanga (SPECULATION — serious, unresolved)
David Li's thesis: xiangqi predates and generated the Western game (live minority position, CLAIMED)
falsifiability: A liubo text or excavated set showing the six-piece chess-family army structure, 8×8 field, or shatranj-like movement rules.

title: Dead Sea Scrolls
claim: ~900 manuscripts / tens of thousands of fragments from eleven Qumran caves (Bedouin discovery of Cave 1's seven scrolls incl. the Great Isaiah Scroll, 1947); c. 250 BCE-68 CE (paleography, stratified archaeology, radiocarbon converge).
place: (varies by record — see sources)
grade_reason: PROVES multiple variant textual traditions of the Hebrew Bible coexisted in the Second Temple period (Emanuel Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, 1992/2001) and organized Jewish sectarianism (Community Rule, Damascus Document, pesharim). DOES NOT PROVE eyewitness records of patriarchs, the Exodus, or any First Temple event. The Qumran-Essene link is CORROBORATED, not settled (Norman Golb's Jerusalem-origin hypothesis named fairly). Via Geza Vermes, The Dead Sea Scrolls in English (1962).
earliest_attestation: (see sources)

sources.ref: Geza Vermes, The Dead Sea Scrolls in English (1962; rev. 1975)
Emanuel Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible (1992; 2nd ed. 2001)

ERC 'Tracing Scribes and Scrolls' project (2026–2031, €2.5M) — Mladen Popović (Univ. of Groningen) + Israel Antiquities Authority + European labs: chemical-signature database (parchment, collagen, inks) + palaeography/codicology/AI for scroll provenance. Grade-neutral: documents the 2026 research program, moves no manuscript grade (the Turin-shroud precedent).

Marcello Fidanzio (Universita della Svizzera Italiana) — material analysis of the Great Isaiah Scroll reported Jan 2026 (Times of Israel via United with Israel, 4 Jan 2026): first 8 parchment sheets vs final 9 differ in manufacture, folding patterns, layout, and repairs — the 7.34m manuscript began life as two independent scrolls later joined into one. Manufacturing history, not authenticity; the scroll's 2nd-c.-BCE date unchallenged.

Eshbal Ratzon (Tel Aviv Univ.), 'The Qumran 364-day calendar,' Tarbiz (published Sept 2026, reported newsy-today): the sect practiced the rigid solar calendar — 52 exact weeks, festivals fixed to weekday — then abandoned it as the ~1.25-day/yr drift made the agricultural festivals seasonally untenable. Resolves the practiced-vs-ideal debate.

CSNTM multispectral-imaging project (Sept 2026, csntm.org): state-of-the-art imaging of dozens of purported DSS fragments in the Martin Schoyen collection (31 Dead Sea Scroll artifacts) with the Oslo Cathedral School Rare Book & Manuscript Library — most fragments show modern-forgery characteristics; some show physical characteristics of genuine 1st-c.-CE fragments; MS 4612-1 possibly the first known pre-2002 forgery (Justnes). Strengthens the forgery-detection side of the DSS manuscript story.

University of Manchester / John Rylands Library (announced Jan 2021; Joan Taylor et al.): four Dead Sea Scroll fragments in the JRL collection, photographed with multispectral imaging; one fragment preserves 4 lines with 'Shabbat' legible, possibly Ezekiel 46:1-3 — grade-neutral context (Turin-shroud precedent): the finding predates the record; the Oct-2026 press cycle recycles it as news.
Dead Sea Discoveries 33(3) (2026) thematic issue 'Fifty Years After Milik's Enoch' (Goff & Uusimaki intro online Oct 1, 2026; Dugan on fragment-joining; Ratzon & Hadad on 4Q319 calendar)

competing_hypotheses: Qumran-Essene link (CORROBORATED mainstream) vs. Golb's Jerusalem-origin hypothesis
falsifiability: New primary documents could refine or overturn any of these records; grades move only on evidence.

title: Elephantine Papyri
claim: The Judean military colony at Yeb/Elephantine (Upper Egypt) left ~100 Aramaic papyri and ostraca (495-399 BCE), including the Passover letter of 419 BCE (TAD A4.1) and the 407 BCE petitions to rebuild the Yahw temple destroyed in 410 BCE (TAD A4.7/A4.8).
place: (varies by record — see sources)
grade_reason: PROVES a functioning Yahw temple with sacrificial cult outside Jerusalem in the 5th c. BCE and lived Judean religion under Achaemenid rule (Bezalel Porten, Archives from Elephantine, 1968; Porten & Yardeni, TAD, 1986-1999). DOES NOT PROVE normative monotheism (the colony honored other deities) or anything about patriarchs or the Exodus. Three independent archives, internally dated, cross-consistent.
earliest_attestation: (see sources)

sources.ref: Bezalel Porten, Archives from Elephantine (1968)
Porten & Ada Yardeni, Textbook of Aramaic Documents from Ancient Egypt, 4 vols. (1986-1999)

falsifiability: New primary documents could refine or overturn any of these records; grades move only on evidence.

title: The Deucalion flood
claim: The Greek Deucalion flood: Deucalion and Pyrrha survive a Zeus-sent flood in a chest/ark (larnax), land on Parnassus, and repopulate the world by casting stones ('the bones of the mother'). Attested in Pindar (Olympian 9), Apollodorus (Library 1.7.2), and Ovid (Metamorphoses 1.313-415) — a literary tradition, not a dated event. It shares the ark/bird/landfall skeleton of the Mesopotamian story at a structural level, via the common ancient Near Eastern/Mediterranean flood-memory pool, not direct copying.
place: Mount Parnassus, Phocis (mythic landfall)
grade_reason: The tradition is textually attested across centuries and authors. No contemporary corroboration as an event; graded as a CLAIMED tradition.
earliest_attestation: Pindar, Olympian 9.41-56 (476 BCE); Apollodorus, Library 1.7.2; Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.313-415

sources.ref: Pindar, Olympian 9.41-56
Apollodorus, Library 1.7.2-3
Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.313-415

competing_hypotheses: Borrowing: the Greek version adapted the Mesopotamian story (possible via trade/literacy contacts)
Shared memory pool: flood stories are common around great rivers and remembered catastrophes (majority view for the general motif)
falsifiability: N/A as event claim — this record grades the attestation of the tradition only

title: Ioudaismos First Use
claim: The Greek word Ioudaismos first occurs in surviving literature in 2 Maccabees — 2:21 and 8:1 (the epitomist's preface; admitting to Judas Maccabeus's forces only those 'who had remained in Judaism'), set against Hellenismos; recurs 2 Macc 14:38, 4 Macc 4:26, Galatians 1:13-14. 2 Maccabees dates to the late 2nd c. BCE (c. 124 BCE).
place: (varies by record — see sources)
grade_reason: PROVES a named, self-aware 'Judaism' consciously opposed to 'Hellenism' by the Hasmonean era. DOES NOT PROVE the coinage date (an earlier unattested use can't be ruled out) or that it meant 'religion' in the modern sense (Steve Mason, 'Jews, Judaeans, Judaizing, Judaism,' JSJ 38 (2007):457-512, reads it dynamically as 'Judaizing'; John J. Collins counters it denotes distinct cultural content — honestly underdetermined: only four pre-Christian attestations). Rests on a single text tradition; no independent contemporary source attests the word.
earliest_attestation: (see sources)

sources.ref: Steve Mason, 'Jews, Judaeans, Judaizing, Judaism,' JSJ 38 (2007):457-512

competing_hypotheses: Mason's 'Judaizing' dynamic reading vs. Collins's distinct-cultural-content reading
falsifiability: New primary documents could refine or overturn any of these records; grades move only on evidence.

title: Ketef Hinnom Amulets
claim: Two tiny rolled silver amulets (KH1, KH2) with paleo-Hebrew variants of the priestly blessing (Numbers 6:24-26), excavated 1979 from burial-cave repository 24 at Ketef Hinnom, Jerusalem (Gabriel Barkay's team; first published Biblical Archaeology Review 9.4, 1983).
place: (varies by record — see sources)
grade_reason: PROVES the blessing's text circulated as a liturgical amulet in Jerusalem by ~600 BCE on the conventional dating (paleography + stratigraphy; Barkay, Vaughn, Lundberg & Zuckerman, BASOR 334, 2004, 41-71). DOES NOT PROVE the Pentateuch's composition date or Moses. The dating is contested (Renz & Roellig, Handbuch der althebraeischen Epigraphik I, 1995; later-origin minority unexcluded); the object's existence and text are not.
earliest_attestation: (see sources)

sources.ref: Barkay et al., 'The Amulets from Ketef Hinnom: A New Edition and Evaluation,' BASOR 334 (2004)
Johannes Renz & Wolfgang Roellig, Handbuch der althebraeischen Epigraphik I (1995)

2026 imaging refinements of the Ketef Hinnom silver scrolls — reflectance transformation imaging (RTI) and 3D scanning of the tarnished silver surfaces, rendering letters previously marked illegible readable and refining earlier transcriptions (reported 2026 via truthstodiefor.com — an advocacy site; the underlying imaging techniques and the refined readings are the technical fact, the site's apologetic framing fenced). The 1979 Barkay controlled-excavation provenance (sealed Chamber 25 repository) is what defeats the forgery question; the imaging defeats only the legibility question.

competing_hypotheses: The conventional late-7th/early-6th c. BCE dating vs. a later-origin minority — the amulets' existence and text are VERIFIED regardless
falsifiability: New primary documents could refine or overturn any of these records; grades move only on evidence.

title: Mishnah
claim: The Mishnah — 63 tractates in six Sedarim, the earliest systematic rabbinic legal work, redacting Tannaitic traditions; rabbinic tradition attributes redaction to Judah ha-Nasi, c. 200 CE (scholarly consensus ~190-220 CE).
place: (varies by record — see sources)
grade_reason: PROVES the shape of 1st-2nd c. CE rabbinic practice and law (Sabbath, purity, tithes, festivals, civil damages) — the documentary baseline of rabbinic Judaism. DOES NOT PROVE anything contemporary about the biblical period (the Sinai-chain claim in Avot 1 is theological, not historical). The Judah ha-Nasi attribution rests on later tradition — CORROBORATED. Via Jacob Neusner, Judaism: The Evidence of the Mishnah (1981); Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Mishnah'.
earliest_attestation: (see sources)

sources.ref: Jacob Neusner, Judaism: The Evidence of the Mishnah (1981)
Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Mishnah'

falsifiability: New primary documents could refine or overturn any of these records; grades move only on evidence.

title: Moses's horns: qaran to cornuta
claim: Exodus 34:29's Hebrew says Moses's face qaran ('was radiant,' 'shone'); Jerome's Vulgate (late 4th c. CE) rendered it cornuta est ('was horned'); Michelangelo's Moses (1513-1515, San Pietro in Vincoli, Rome) wears the Latin's horns — a fifteen-hundred-year-old translation choice, in marble.
place: San Pietro in Vincoli, Rome (the statue); the Hebrew belongs to the Exodus tradition
grade_reason: Both readings are multiply attested; the marble statue is a documented material witness to which reading the Latin West received.
earliest_attestation: Hebrew qaran in the Masoretic Text; Latin cornuta est in Jerome's Vulgate; the horns in marble from 1513-1515

sources.ref: Exodus 34:29-35 — Hebrew qaran ('shone/was radiant'), vv. 30, 35 fixing the sense by repetition
Jerome, Vulgate: 'cornuta esset facies sua' — the Latin reading the medieval West inherited
Michelangelo, Moses (1513-1515), tomb of Julius II, San Pietro in Vincoli — the horns as sculpted

Lee M. Jefferson, 'The Horns of Moses,' Biblical Archaeology Society, Bible History Daily (first published May 2023; updated 4 Feb 2026): Jerome's cornuta read as the best Latin available, not malice; the LXX's Ex 34:29 reading as dedoxastai ('glorified') — a third witness at the crossing; Moses depicted hornless for centuries after the Vulgate, earliest horned depiction the 11th-c. Aelfric Paraphrase; the anti-Jewish weaponization of the horns from the 13th c. onward (Mellinkoff 1970, The Horned Moses in Medieval Art and Thought).

media.caption: Michelangelo's Moses (1513-1515) with horns — a reconstruction-free photograph of the Vulgate's reading in stone

competing_hypotheses: Jerome read qaran as qeren ('horn') deliberately: the 'horns of power' as a positive ancient-Near-Eastern symbol (the horned crowns of Mesopotamian gods), making cornuta a theological choice, not an error
The radiant reading is itself interpretive: qaran's root qrн is rare, and the 'shining' sense is fixed by context and the parallel in v.30, 35
Michelangelo followed the Vulgate because it was the Church's Bible, whatever the Hebrew said — the statue witnesses the Latin tradition, not the translation debate
falsifiability: A pre-Vulgate Latin or Greek witness reading 'horned' at Exodus 34:29, or a Hebrew manuscript tradition reading qeren ('horn') at this verse

title: Sacrificed Son Unnamed
claim: The Qur'an names the son Abraham was commanded to sacrifice as Ishmael
place: (varies by record — see sources)
grade_reason: Qur'an 37:102-107 names no son — the text says only 'O my son'. Early Islamic exegesis was genuinely divided: al-Tabari's Jami' al-Bayan records both views and inclines to Isaac on philological grounds; reports attributed to Ibn 'Abbas exist on both sides (al-Dhahabi attributes the Isaac-reports to Ka'b al-Ahbar); the Ishmael reading became the majority only later (Ibn Taymiyya, Ibn Kathir, 14th c.). The 'Qur'an names Ishmael' telling is a misreading compounded by a later consensus retrojected onto the text.
earliest_attestation: (see sources)

sources.ref: Qur'an 37:102-107 (Arabic text: no son named)
Al-Tabari, Jami' al-Bayan (c. 883-923)
Reem Firestone, 'The Other Ishmael in Islamic Scripture and Tradition' (almuslih.org, n. 19): 'the Qur'an does not specifically name the intended sacrifice'

competing_hypotheses: The belief-phenomenon (Ishmael as the sacrificed son in later Muslim devotion) is graded separately — beliefs leave artifacts; the misreading of the text is what this record kills
falsifiability: New primary documents could refine or overturn any of these records; grades move only on evidence.

title: The Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim (5th c. BCE - 110 BCE)
claim: A Yahwistic sanctuary stood on Mount Gerizim's summit from the Persian period (5th century BCE), massively expanded under the Hellenistic kings into a city and sacred precinct, and was destroyed by John Hyrcanus I c. 110 BCE.
place: Mount Gerizim summit, Samaria
grade_reason: The excavated sanctuary (precinct, inscriptions, thousands of finds) + Josephus's destruction account + the Delos dedications converge; the Persian start-date is the single contested element.
earliest_attestation: Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 13.254-256 (c. 93-94 CE) records Hyrcanus's destruction; the precinct's Persian-phase stratigraphy from excavation

sources.ref: Magen, Y., Mount Gerizim Excavations vols. I-II (Judea and Samaria Publications) — the sacred precinct, finds, and inscriptions
Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 13.254-256 (Hyrcanus destroys the Gerizim temple, c. 110 BCE)
Sauter, M., 'The Temple on Mount Gerizim—In the Bible and Archaeology', BAR (8 Sept 2026) — explainer of Gudme 2019 + Magen; venue only
The two Samaritan dedicatory inscriptions on Delos (2nd c. BCE) — 'Israelites who make offerings on Mount Gerizim'

competing_hypotheses: The Gerizim sanctuary began as a shared Yahwistic high place, only later exclusively 'Samaritan'
The precinct's earliest phase is Hellenistic, not Persian (the non-peer-reviewed critique's position)
falsifiability: Peer-reviewed evidence that the summit complex was not a temple (no altar, no votive inscriptions), or a re-dating of the precinct entirely into the Hellenistic period

title: Yehud Coinage
claim: Small silver fractional coins inscribed YHD (the Achaemenid province 'Judah/Yehud'), many imitating Athenian owl types; Persian-period series mid-4th c. BCE (c. 350-333 BCE), die typology extending to ~30 BCE.
place: (varies by record — see sources)
grade_reason: PROVES a Persian-administered province named Yehud with a functioning local mint — Judah was a real, governed Achaemenid unit, not a literary memory. DOES NOT PROVE the Davidic kingdom or a united monarchy (imperial provincial issues; early types likely struck in Philistia on commission). Leo Mildenberg, 'Yehud' (1979); Gitler, Lorber & Fontanille, The Yehud Coinage (2023) — ~2,000 specimens, 44 types, 198 obverse/282 reverse dies. Die-linked sequences, hoard-distributed — the timeline's own receipts, fenced for Dr. Rosa Delgado's numismatic beat.
earliest_attestation: (see sources)

sources.ref: Leo Mildenberg, 'Yehud: A Preliminary Study of the Provincial Coinage of Judaea' (1979)
Gitler, Lorber & Fontanille, The Yehud Coinage (Israel Numismatic Society, 2023)
Economou, Michael (2026), 'The Paleo-Hebrew Script in Achaemenid, Hellenistic and Early Roman Jewish Coinage', European Hebrew Journal 1(2):314-332 (paleography of paleo-Hebrew on Yehud coinage)

competing_hypotheses: Early Philistia-commissioned striking vs. local Yehud mint — honestly underdetermined
falsifiability: New primary documents could refine or overturn any of these records; grades move only on evidence.

title: The '300 vs Millions' reading of Thermopylae — DEBUNKED
claim: At Thermopylae, 300 Spartans alone faced millions of Persian soldiers — the pop version of the battle (the school shorthand, Frank Miller's 1998 graphic novel, Zack Snyder's 2007 film): three hundred men against an army counted in the millions.
place: Thermopylae (the Hot Gates), Phthiotis, Greece — the reading is about this pass
grade_reason: Killed twice from the ancient record itself: (1) the Persian 'millions' — Herodotus 7.186's 2,641,610 is rejected by modern scholarship as logistically impossible (modern consensus ~200–250,000 for the whole invasion force; Ctesias, the only other ancient witness to the battle's scale, says 80,000 fought at Thermopylae); (2) the '300 alone' — Herodotus's own contingent list (7.202) totals ~5,200–7,000 Greeks on the first two days, and on the last day 700 Thespians stayed and died with the 300 Spartans (7.222), plus 400 Thebans and likely helots. The odds were still enormous; the numbers are not.
earliest_attestation: Herodotus, Histories VII.186 (the 2.6-million figure; c. 450s–420s BCE) — the ancient root of the modern myth; the pop form is 20th-century

sources.ref: Herodotus, Histories VII.186 — 1,700,000 infantry + 80,000 cavalry + 20,000 in chariots/camels + 517,610 in the fleet = 2,317,610 fighting men brought 'as far as Thermopylae'; 2,641,610 total with support/allies — the famous 2.6 million
Ctesias (via later fragments) — 800,000 as the total army Xerxes assembled; 80,000 Persians fought at Thermopylae — the only other ancient figure for the battle itself
Simonides (contemporary poet) — 4 million; the ancient inflation had multiple versions

Modern scholarly consensus (e.g., via the Battle of Thermopylae survey literature): the ancient millions rejected as unrealistic; modern estimates ~200–250,000 for the total invasion force, the Thermopylae force probably the majority (~200,000 by one estimate; range 120,000–300,000 across modern scholars)
Herodotus VII.202–203 — his own Greek contingent list, totaling ~5,200 hoplites (plus Locrians and Malians, ~7,000 with all contingents) on the first two days
Herodotus VII.222 — the 700 Thespians 'very willingly stayed' to die with Leonidas; VII.233 — the 400 Thebans; helot attendants reported in the later tradition
Herodotus VII.206 — Sparta sent only 300, claiming it was their avantgarde (prophasis) — the '300' was a token force, not the army

Belief ecology: Frank Miller's '300' (1998 graphic novel) and Zack Snyder's '300' (2007 film) — the millions-vs-300 image's modern engine; no published Pew/Gallup/YouGov survey asks the question, so no belief number is attached

competing_hypotheses: Herodotus's numbers are internally consistent arithmetic — he shows his work by corps — so some argue they preserve a genuine Persian claim or a deliberate psychological-warfare narrative rather than a scribal error
The Greek contingent totals are also transmitted, not muster rolls: Herodotus's 5,200 and Diodorus's higher figures disagree, so the 'seven thousand' is an honest range, not a census
Defenders of large Persian numbers argue the logistics were managed by sea supply (3,000 supply ships in Herodotus); the counter is that the sea-supply figures come from the same rejected arithmetic
falsifiability: A contemporary Persian administrative document (in the class of the Persepolis Fortification tablets) mustering millions for the 480 expedition, or archaeological evidence of a camp and logistics footprint sized for millions

title: The Battle of Thermopylae, 480 BCE
claim: In late August/early September 480 BCE, a Greek allied force under the Spartan king Leonidas I held the pass of Thermopylae against the Persian invasion army of Xerxes I for two full days of battle; after the mountain path was betrayed, the rear guard — 300 Spartans, 700 Thespians, and others — was annihilated on the third day and the pass was forced.
place: Thermopylae (the Hot Gates), Phthiotis, Greece
grade_reason: Attested in Herodotus's near-contemporary account built from veteran interviews, corroborated across the later Greek tradition (Diodorus, etc.); no contemporary Persian-side record names the battle, so it stops at CORROBORATED.
earliest_attestation: Herodotus, Histories Book VII (written c. 450s–420s BCE, ~50 years after the battle; Herodotus interviewed Greek veterans of the Persian Wars)

sources.ref: Herodotus, Histories VII.201–239 — the battle narrative: the pass, the two days, the betrayal by Ephialtes, the last stand

Herodotus VII.202–203 — the Greek contingent list (300 Spartans, 500 Tegeans, 500 Mantineans, 120 Orchomenians, 1,000 other Arcadians, 400 Corinthians, 200 Phliasians, 80 Mycenaeans, 700 Thespians, 400 Thebans, 1,000 Phocians, plus Locrians and Malians)
Herodotus VII.222 — the Thespians 'very willingly stayed' with Leonidas on the last day
Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca historica XI — later Greek corroboration of the battle tradition

competing_hypotheses: The exact date within the late-summer 480 window is traditional, fixed by the Olympic/Carneian festival calendar in Herodotus's account — the year is solid, the week is reckoning
The casualty figures on both sides (Herodotus's Persian dead, the Greek rearguard's ~2,000) are transmitted, not counted — the loss happened, the ledger is ancient
The Thebans' role (400 men who stayed, then surrendered) is Herodotus's version and is contested in detail, though their presence is not
falsifiability: Contemporary Persian administrative or royal evidence that Xerxes's 480 invasion never reached central Greece, or proof the battle is a later invention with no 5th-c. root

title: The Murasu archive (Judean descendants in Babylonia, 455-403 BCE)
claim: The Murasu archive — roughly 800 legal texts from Nippur (455-403 BCE, excavated 1893) — records the business of a single family across four generations, with some 80 distinctively Judean personal names among its clients: the exiles' descendants, still identifiably Judean a century-plus after the fall, as tenants and entrepreneurs in Persian-period Babylonia. A large Judean community stayed and thrived rather than returning.
place: Nippur (excavation site)
grade_reason: Excavated, massive (~800 texts), internally dated across 28 Nippur-area settlements; the Judean marker is onomastic (names), which caps the community-identity reading at CORROBORATED.
earliest_attestation: The tablets themselves: excavated legal archive, Nippur, 5th century BCE

sources.ref: The Murasu archive (document): ~800 legal texts and fragments, Nippur; records of a single business family over four generations, 455-403 BCE; excavated 1893 under John Henry Haynes (University of Pennsylvania expedition); held at the Penn Museum, Istanbul, and elsewhere
~80 distinctively Judean personal names (Shabbatai, Minyamin, Haggai; yah/yaw theophorics) in contracts and land-for-service deals across ~28 Nippur-area settlements
M. W. Stolper's editions and studies of the archive (the standard publication of the corpus)

competing_hypotheses: The mainstream reading: Judean theophoric names (Shabbatai, Minyamin, Haggai; yah/yaw elements) mark genuine Judean descent — the community that stayed (mainstream)
The onomastics caveat: names are cultural fashion, not identity proof — a Judean name could be worn by an assimilated Babylonian. The grade is capped by this caveat, not by the archive
falsifiability: The archive is too large, too excavated, and too internally consistent to be a fabrication; the falsifiable part is the identity reading — a prosopographic study showing the Judean-named clients were not a community would weaken it

title: The dating of the Jewish-Samaritan 'schism' (the single-break telling)
claim: Jews and Samaritans split at one datable moment: Nehemiah 13:28's priest expelled for marrying Sanballat's daughter, or Josephus's Manasseh-and-Sanballat temple-founding story (Ant. 11.302-347).
place: Mount Gerizim / Jerusalem (the two claimants)
grade_reason: The tradition narrates a break; the archaeology shows centuries of shared sanctuary use; no contemporary inscription or single datable event marks the split.
earliest_attestation: Nehemiah 13:28 (Persian-period text, edited over time); Josephus, Ant. 11.302-347 (c. 93-94 CE)

sources.ref: Nehemiah 13:28 (the priest with the foreign wife, expelled)
Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 11.302-347 (Sanballat, Manasseh, and the Gerizim temple founding)
Magen, Y., Mount Gerizim Excavations — a sanctuary both communities' era shared for centuries
Knoppers, G., Jews and Samaritans (2013) — the slow-process scholarship

competing_hypotheses: The schism was a slow process (centuries of divergence), not a dated event
The 'schism' is partly a modern scholarly construct retrojected onto ancient tensions
falsifiability: A contemporary inscription or administrative record naming the moment of institutional separation

title: The Kingdom of Aksum
claim: That the Kingdom of Aksum — centered on Axum in the Ethiopian highlands, c. 400 BCE–c. 960 CE, at its height spanning the Red Sea into Himyar (Yemen) — was a literate, minting, trading empire: trilingual royal inscriptions (Ge'ez, Sabaean, Greek), giant granite stelae, the first sub-Saharan African minted coinage (gold/silver/bronze), the Red Sea trade hub at Adulis, and the 4th-century CE conversion to Christianity under King Ezana.
place: Axum (Aksum), Tigray Region, Ethiopia
grade_reason: Multiply attested from independent sides: the king's own trilingual inscriptions, a Roman emperor's letter, the coin series with the conversion signal in the metal, and the stelae. Stops short of VERIFIED only on the conventional termini (no dated foundation charter, no dated end); the core (the 4th-century Christian Aksumite state) is as secure as ancient African history gets.
earliest_attestation: Ezana Stone (trilingual: Ge'ez, Sabaean, Greek), standing at Axum, UNESCO 1980; Ezana's Ge'ez inscriptions at Meroë; Aksumite coinage from c. 270 CE (sun/moon symbols, replaced by the cross post-conversion); the giant stelae field; Constantius II's letter to Ezana and Saizana requesting Frumentius be sent to Alexandria

sources.ref: The Ezana Stone — trilingual stele at Axum documenting Ezana's conversion and campaigns incl. Meroë (4th c. CE)
Rufinus, Ecclesiastical History — Frumentius converts the child-king Ezana
Constantius II's letter to Ezana and Saizana (c. 356 CE) — requests Frumentius be sent to Alexandria for doctrinal examination
Munro-Hay, Stuart — Aksum: An African Civilisation of Late Antiquity (1991); 'most famous of the Aksumite kings before Kaleb'
Stephanie L. Black — study of fourth-century inscriptions identifying Ezana as Ethiopia's first Christian king

competing_hypotheses: On Ezana's Meroë campaign: proof the Aksumites destroyed the Kingdom of Kush (some authorities) vs military aid to quell a Nuba revolt (others) vs Meroë already in economic decline by c. 300 CE (archaeological position) — conclusive evidence currently unavailable
The diplomatic vs spiritual reading of the conversion (Aaron Butts: strategic alignment with Byzantium + domestic consolidation) — not a grade question; motives are unattested
falsifiability: Proof that the Ezana Stone inscriptions are later fabrications, or that the Aksumite coin series is misattributed.

title: Socrates's daimonion: the sign that only ever said no
claim: Plato's Apology (31c-d, 40a-b) and Xenophon's Memorabilia (1.1.2-4) attest that Socrates experienced a daimonion — 'a divine thing,' a voice or sign that came to him since childhood and always held him back from actions he was about to take, never urging him forward. The same charge appears in the indictment at Apology 24b-c ('introducing new daimonia'). The attestation is graded as belief-phenomenon: the texts attest what Socrates reported and what Athens heard, not the sign's metaphysical status.
place: Athens
grade_reason: Two independent near-contemporary witnesses (Plato and Xenophon, who disagreed with each other freely) report the same phenomenon with the same prohibitive-only character; the indictment's 'new daimonia' charge corroborates the public notoriety of the claim.
earliest_attestation: Plato, Apology 31c-d, 40a-b; Xenophon, Memorabilia 1.1.2-4, Apology 12-13

sources.ref: Plato, Apology 31c-d, 40a-b (Perseus Project / Tufts)
Xenophon, Memorabilia 1.1.2-4; Xenophon, Apology 12-13 (Perseus Project / Tufts)
Plutarch, De genio Socratis — the ancient reception and debate over what the sign was

competing_hypotheses: The daimonion was a literary device Plato used to dignify Socrates's prudence and explain his political abstention
The daimonion describes a genuine psychological phenomenon — an auditory-hallucination or conscience-experience Socrates interpreted in religious terms
