The daimonion was a deliberate theological provocation, an innovation claim meant to distinguish Socratic piety from civic religion
falsifiability: Proof that the Apology passages are later insertions (no such evidence exists in the manuscript tradition)

title: Eros the great daimon: the middle term of the cosmos
claim: In the Symposium (202d-203a), Diotima teaches Socrates that Eros is neither god nor mortal but a 'great daimon' (daimon megas) — an intermediary power whose work is to interpret and convey between gods and men: carrying prayers and sacrifices upward and commands and rewards downward, 'filling the space between' so that the whole is bound together. This is the most explicit classical statement of the daimon as the middle term of the cosmos.
place: Athens (composition); dramatic setting: Agathon's house, Athens
grade_reason: The text is securely transmitted; the daimon-intermediary doctrine is stated explicitly and consistently, and its function-language echoes Hesiod's guardians.
earliest_attestation: Plato, Symposium 202d-203a (R.G. Bury commentary, Perseus / Tufts)

sources.ref: Plato, Symposium 202d-203a (Perseus Project / Tufts; R.G. Bury commentary)
F.E. Brenk, 'In Mist Apparelled' (1977) — the daimon as intermediary in classical religion

competing_hypotheses: Diotima is a fictional mouthpiece and the 'great daimon' doctrine is Plato's invention, not a report of lived Greek religion (counter: the intermediary function matches Hesiod's guardians and the widespread folk daimon-belief)
The passage describes Eros alone, not a general daimon-class; the generalization to all daimones is the commentators' work
falsifiability: A manuscript tradition showing the 202d-203a passage is interpolated (no such variant exists)

title: Alexander the Great
claim: Alexander III of Macedon (356-323 BCE) conquered the Persian Empire from Greece to India in twelve years, founding cities including Alexandria and spreading Hellenistic culture across three continents.
place: Pella (birthplace and capital of Macedon)
grade_reason: Contemporary Babylonian records, coinage, and inscriptions confirm his existence, dates, and conquests; multiple independent traditions agree on the campaign outline.
earliest_attestation: Babylonian astronomical diaries (contemporary, record his death 11 June 323 BCE); coins and inscriptions in his name; the primary histories (Callisthenes, Ptolemy) are lost and survive via Arrian, Plutarch, Diodorus

sources.ref: Babylonian astronomical diaries (death of Alexander, 323 BCE)
Contemporary coinage and inscriptions in Alexander's name
Arrian, Anabasis (2nd c. CE, based on Ptolemy and Aristobulus)
The 20/21 September 331 BCE lunar eclipse (Plutarch, Life of Alexander 31.8, 'eleven days before Gaugamela') — an independent astronomical anchor on the campaign chronology

The lost primary histories: Callisthenes (court historian), Ptolemy I and Aristobulus (participants); surviving only through Arrian/Plutarch (2nd c. CE) and the 'Vulgate' line Cleitarchus -> Diodorus/Curtius/Justin — the narrative texture is ~400 years removed

competing_hypotheses: The campaign narrative of Arrian/Plutarch is broadly reliable (consensus)
The 'great man' narrative is inflated by court historians; the conquest's speed owed more to Persian imperial fragility

The source-tradition split (16:46 pass): the 'official' line (Arrian via Ptolemy/Aristobulus) vs. the 'Vulgate' line (Cleitarchus via Diodorus/Curtius/Justin) disagree on texture and some events while agreeing on the outline — the dates are anchored independently (Babylonian diaries, Gaugamela eclipse), the speeches and motives are literary
'Twelve years' is conventional rounding: 13 years of reign (336-323 BCE), 11 of eastern campaign (334-323 BCE)
falsifiability: Contemporary evidence contradicting the campaign's basic geography or chronology; none exists

title: The Mieza Royal Gymnasium identified as Aristotle's school where Alexander was tutored (Sept 2026 announcement)
claim: The excavated royal complex at ancient Mieza, northern Greece — the Didaskaleion (teaching area) with lecture rooms and stone benches, a three-part banquet complex with mosaic floors, palaestra, stadium and 200-meter running track — is the royal school where Aristotle tutored the young Alexander (c. 343–340 BCE). The Hellenic Ministry of Culture announced the identification in early September 2026 from the ongoing excavation led by Angeliki Kottaridi (work began 2024 under a Ministry–Municipality of Naoussa agreement). The complex dates to Philip II's reign; its architecture closely resembles Philip's palace at Aigai. Independent scholars (Graham Wrightson, Jeanne Reames) publicly endorsed the identification; Miltiades Hatzopoulos cautioned it is probably right but awaits a peer-reviewed publication of the evidence.
place: Mieza (ancient town; Royal Gymnasium / Didaskaleion complex), near Naoussa, northern Greece — ~43 km from Pella
grade_reason: The announcement itself and the excavation are documented by the excavating authority (Hellenic Ministry of Culture, Sept 2026) and multiple independent news reports with on-the-record archaeologists; the building remains are archaeologically real. The IDENTIFICATION is the ministry/excavator's claim — it awaits peer-reviewed publication (Hatzopoulos's caveat) — so the announcement event is CORROBORATED while the identification stays a claim pending the paper. VERIFIED is not reached. Wrightson's 'one stylus belonged to Alexander' remark is reported as a dream, not evidence.
earliest_attestation: Ancient literary tradition that Aristotle taught Alexander at Mieza (Plutarch, Alexander 7–8); excavation announcement September 2026

sources.ref: Hellenic Ministry of Culture — announcement of the Mieza Royal Gymnasium / Didaskaleion findings, early September 2026 (excavation led by honorary curator of antiquities Angeliki Kottaridi, since 2024)

PEOPLE (Sept 29, 2026): newly uncovered mosaics and ruins strengthening the identification; on-the-record comment from Jeanne Reames (Univ. of Nebraska) — 'all the evidence suggests' this is the school

Graham Wrightson (South Dakota State Univ.) on the four styluses — 'allows us to dream that one belonged to Alexander' (reported as aspiration, not evidence); Miltiades Hatzopoulos — probably the right place, but no peer-reviewed paper yet (the caution)
Daily Galaxy (Sept 30, 2026) summary of the ministry's release: lecture hall, banquet spaces, athletic facilities, architectural decorations

competing_hypotheses: The Mieza Royal Gymnasium is Aristotle's school where Alexander was tutored (Kottaridi/Ministry of Culture 2026; endorsed by Wrightson, Reames — the standing position)

The complex is a royal educational facility of the right period but the Aristotle–Alexander identification is unproven pending peer-reviewed publication (Hatzopoulos's caution — the identification is not yet independently established)
falsifiability: Peer-reviewed publication of the excavation evidence confirming or rejecting the identification; an alternative identification of the complex's function from the epigraphy or stratigraphy

title: Alexander's consultation of the oracle of Zeus-Ammon at Siwa (331 BCE)
claim: In early 331 BCE, Alexander the Great marched across the Libyan desert from the Mediterranean coast to the Siwa oasis and consulted the oracle of Zeus-Ammon at the Ammoneion (Oracle Temple, Aghurmi), where the priests publicly greeted him as the son of the god.
place: Oracle Temple of Zeus-Ammon (Ammoneion), Aghurmi, Siwa Oasis, Matrouh Governorate, Egypt
grade_reason: Four independent surviving traditions (Arrian, Plutarch, Diodorus, Curtius) agree on the essentials — the desert march, the consultation, the public greeting as son of the god — plus a near-contemporary fragment (Callisthenes via Strabo) and corroborating material evidence: a genuine oracle temple at Aghurmi whose fame demonstrably grew after 331, and Alexander's subsequent son-of-Ammon titulary and posthumous ram's-horns iconography. No contemporary attestation survives, so VERIFIED is not reached.
earliest_attestation: Callisthenes of Olynthus (contemporary court historian, lost), preserved via Strabo 17.1.43 on the son-of-Zeus claim. Earliest surviving full accounts: Diodorus 17.49-51, Curtius 4.7, Plutarch Alex. 26-27, Arrian Anab. 3.3-4 (all 1st-2nd c. CE, built on the lost Ptolemy/Aristobulus/Cleitarchus memoirs).

sources.ref: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 3.3-4 (based on Ptolemy and Aristobulus; Arrian explicitly flags which embellishments came from which source, 3.3.5-6)
Plutarch, Life of Alexander 26-27 (public greeting 'as a father greeting his son'; private consultation; alleged letter to Olympias)
Diodorus Siculus 17.49-51 (the journey; oracular answers: vengeance on Philip's murderers, dominion of the world)
Curtius Rufus 4.7 (the consultation; the priest's 'son of Ammon' greeting)
Justin 11.11
Strabo 17.1.43, preserving Callisthenes on the son-of-Zeus claim
Robin Lane Fox, Alexander the Great (1973): the visit as 'the strangest strand in Alexander's life and legend'
The Oracle Temple (Ammoneion) at Aghurmi, Siwa Oasis — 26th-Dynasty fabric, Amasis reliefs, Graeco-Roman annexes (archaeological)

competing_hypotheses: The visit is as reported: a genuine religious consultation by a king steeped in the Heracles/Perseus pilgrimage tradition (consensus).
The visit was political legitimation theater: the pharaoh presents himself at the Amun temple; in the local idiom the 'son of Ra/Ammon' greeting meant 'king'. Not in contradiction with the first.

Skeptical reading: the march happened, but the oracular content and the 'son of Zeus' greeting are court embellishment transmitted through self-serving memoirs (Ptolemy, Aristobulus); no independent contemporary witness survives.
The miracles — rain in a waterless desert, ravens or snakes finding the lost track — are folklore embroidery, not history (Arrian himself declines to vouch for them).
falsifiability: A contemporary Egyptian or Persian administrative document contradicting the visit, or proof the Ammoneion had no oracle function in the 4th century BCE — no such evidence exists.

title: Alexandria-on-the-Tigris (Charax Spasinou) — location confirmed at Jebel Khayyaber
claim: Alexander the Great founded the port city of Alexandria-on-the-Tigris in 324 BCE on his return from the Indus Valley; the city (later renamed Charax Spasinou) stood at Jebel Khayyaber in southern Iraq, and its location — first proposed by John Hansman in 1965 — was confirmed in early 2026 by the Charax Spasinou Project (Stefan Hauser, University of Konstanz) using aerial/drone photography, caesium-magnetometer geophysics, and over 500 km² of surface survey, revealing a planned grid, harbor/canal works, and residential blocks among the largest in the ancient world.
place: Jebel Khayabir (spelled 'Khayyaber' in some 2026 reporting), Al-Qurna District, Basra Governorate, southern Iraq — the Alexandria-on-the-Tigris / Charax Spasinou site
grade_reason: The 324 BCE foundation is attested in the ancient campaign tradition; the location is now independently confirmed by multi-method archaeological survey (drone/aerial, caesium magnetometer, 500+ km² surface survey) reporting a fully planned metropolis consistent with the literary city. No contemporary inscription naming Alexander at the site has yet been published, so VERIFIED is not reached.
earliest_attestation: Ancient written sources on the 324 BCE foundation (Arrian; the campaign tradition); site identification proposed by John Hansman, 1965

sources.ref: Stefan R. Hauser / Charax Spasinou Project, University of Konstanz — press release, January 2026; synthesis in Hauser 2025, Economies of the Edge (Heidelberg UP)

Archaeology Magazine, 'New Research Confirms Location of Lost City Founded by Alexander the Great' (Feb 2026, print July/August 2026): aerial photo of the walls at Jebel Khayyaber; grid, canals, insulae; temple complexes and industrial districts
Hansman, John (1965): first modern identification of Charax Spasinou at Jebel Khayyaber
Fassbinder/Lambers 2019 magnetometer study (prior geophysical basis)

competing_hypotheses: The identification is correct (Hansman 1965; Hauser 2016–2026 survey program) — the standing position
The grid and harbor works are later (Characene/Parthian redevelopment) with only the foundation episode belonging to Alexander — the 324 BCE core claim is the ancient tradition's, not the survey's
falsifiability: Excavation producing a foundation inscription or stratified sequence inconsistent with the 324 BCE foundation / Hansman identification

title: The death of Alexander at Babylon and the lost tomb
claim: Alexander III died at Babylon on 11 June 323 BCE (29 Ajaru), after about ten days of fever, at age 32. The medical cause is unattested: poisoning, malaria, typhoid, West Nile virus, Guillain-Barre syndrome, and pancreatitis are all modern retro-diagnoses from symptom lists written ~400 years later. His body was carried to Memphis then Alexandria by Ptolemy I; the tomb survived into the Roman period (Augustus visited it) and is now lost — the famous 'Alexander Sarcophagus' from Sidon is not his (it belonged to Abdalonymus, king of Sidon).
place: Babylon (death place); Alexandria, Egypt (tomb — location lost)
grade_reason: The death at Babylon in June 323 BCE is anchored by a contemporary Babylonian diary and agreed by all independent traditions — VERIFIED by convergence. The cause is unattested: the ancient symptom list is second-hand and ~400 years removed, and every modern diagnosis is a retro-diagnosis competing with five others on the same thin evidence — SPECULATION by doctrine ('reasoned but unattested'). The tomb's location is simply unknown, and the record says so instead of grading a location.
earliest_attestation: Babylonian astronomical diary -323 B (contemporary, rev.: 'The king died'); Arrian 7.25-27 (2nd c. CE, from the Ephemerides journal + Ptolemy/Aristobulus); Plutarch Alex. 76-77 (1st/2nd c. CE)

sources.ref: Babylonian astronomical diary No. -323 B (Sachs & Hunger, Astronomical Diaries and Related Texts from Babylonia, vol. III): contemporary record of the king's death, 29 Ajaru
Arrian, Anabasis 7.25-27: the ten-day fever narrative, drawn from the Ephemerides (royal journal) and the lost memoirs of Ptolemy and Aristobulus
Plutarch, Life of Alexander 76-77: fever account and explicit dismissal of the poisoning story
Diodorus 17.117-118; Curtius 10.5 (the Vulgate tradition via Cleitarchus): alternative, more sensational narratives of the death
Suetonius, Augustus 18; Dio 51.16: Augustus visits Alexander's tomb in Alexandria — the tomb still existed in the Roman period
Hall, Katherine (2018), Ancient History Bulletin: Guillain-Barre ascending-paralysis retro-diagnosis (accounts for the 'body showed no decay for six days' claim — he may not have been dead yet)
Marr & Calisher (2003), Emerging Infectious Diseases: West Nile virus hypothesis; Engels (1978): malaria hypothesis — both as modern retro-diagnoses

competing_hypotheses: Natural illness (fever of unknown origin; the ancient narrative's own position)
Poisoning by Antipater's agents via Cassander and Iolaus (the Alexander Romance tradition; doubted already by Plutarch — the timing and the surviving fellow-drinkers argue against it — and by Arrian)
Ascending paralysis / Guillain-Barre (Hall 2018: explains the reported delayed decay; implies he may have been declared dead while still alive — a chilling and untestable possibility)
Malaria (Engels 1978), typhoid, West Nile virus (Marr & Calisher 2003), gallstone pancreatitis (2024): modern medical retro-diagnoses, none testable, all SPECULATION

The body's journey to Alexandria (Ptolemy's interception of the cortege in Syria, c. 321 BCE) is the accepted tradition (Diodorus, Curtius, Pausanias); the tomb was a real, visitable monument into the Roman period, then the location was lost — no graded location claim exists on the timeline
falsifiability: A contemporary document contradicting the Babylonian diary's death notice; or a verified, excavated tomb with inscriptions naming Alexander III. None exists.

Arrian, Anabasis 7.25-27: the ten-day fever narrative, drawn from the Ephemerides (royal journal) and the lost memoirs of Ptolemy and Aristobulus
Plutarch, Life of Alexander 76-77: fever account and explicit dismissal of the poisoning story
Diodorus 17.117-118; Curtius 10.5 (the Vulgate tradition via Cleitarchus): alternative, more sensational narratives of the death
Suetonius, Augustus 18; Dio 51.16: Augustus visits Alexander's tomb in Alexandria — the tomb still existed in the Roman period
Hall, Katherine (2018), Ancient History Bulletin: Guillain-Barre ascending-paralysis retro-diagnosis (accounts for the 'body showed no decay for six days' claim — he may not have been dead yet)
Marr & Calisher (2003), Emerging Infectious Diseases: West Nile virus hypothesis; Engels (1978): malaria hypothesis — both as modern retro-diagnoses

Zhou AL et al. (2025), 'Decoding Alexander the Great's gastrointestinal cause of death using artificial wisdom: An artificial intelligence-human inquiry into a medical mystery,' World J Gastroenterol 31(46):111669. ChatGPT-4 Pro's differential (typhoid, malaria, WNV encephalitis, pancreatitis, poison) cross-checked by two human clinicians — the AI hallucinated citations and was corrected by the humans; final human-reviewed conclusion: C. jejuni-induced Guillain-Barre syndrome most credible. First scholarly engagement with Hall's line since 2019; reinforces it.

2026 evidence-state survey: no 2025–2026 publication challenges the Gaugamela diary/eclipse anchor (331 BCE) or locates the tomb; Kasta tumulus (Amphipolis) peribolos fully exposed May 2026 (Greek Ministry of Culture) with no occupant identified — no Alexander attribution; Mieza 'School of Aristotle' excavation announcements (Sept 2026) carry no inscription and no attribution finding.

Greek Ministry of Culture statement (May 2026, reported via vema.com.au): Kasta tumulus (Amphipolis) to open to the public in early 2028 — conservation and partial restoration ongoing, visitor facilities and a small museum under construction; minister Lina Mendoni: aiming 'to deliver the monument, safe and in its entirety, at the beginning of 2028.' The opening is an administrative event, not an attribution finding: the five sets of scattered remains (woman aged 60+, two men 35-40, a newborn, one cremated adult) remain unidentified; the excavator's Hephaestion suggestion and press 'mother/wife/friend' readings carry no inscription.

Hellenic Ministry of Culture announcement (Sept 2026, via Smithsonian Magazine 28 Sept 2026): Mieza Royal Gymnasium (near Naoussa) excavation — mosaic-decorated Didaskaleion (teaching area), palaestra, stadium, 200m xystus; four writing styluses, coins, pottery; excavator Angeliki Kottaridi's attribution (Aristotle taught the teenage Alexander here) vs Miltiades Hatzopoulos's caution that no scientific paper has yet been published. The site's identity is the excavator's stated hypothesis, not a published finding; no inscription names Aristotle or Alexander. Looser press tellings ('school discovered', myteachnology) carry the same announced facts with weaker hedging — venue-not-evidence, fenced.

competing_hypotheses: Natural illness (fever of unknown origin; the ancient narrative's own position)
Poisoning by Antipater's agents via Cassander and Iolaus (the Alexander Romance tradition; doubted already by Plutarch — the timing and the surviving fellow-drinkers argue against it — and by Arrian)

Ascending paralysis / Guillain-Barre (Hall 2018: explains the reported delayed decay; implies he may have been declared dead while still alive — a chilling and untestable possibility); reinforced 2025 by Zhou et al.'s AI-human inquiry (WJG 31(46):111669) — the human reviewers converged on C. jejuni-induced GBS as the most credible cause, independently landing on Hall's core diagnosis

Malaria (Engels 1978), typhoid, West Nile virus (Marr & Calisher 2003), gallstone pancreatitis (2024): modern medical retro-diagnoses, none testable, all SPECULATION — the 2025 WJG paper is an 'artificial wisdom' exercise on the same symptom lists, not new evidence

The body's journey to Alexandria (Ptolemy's interception of the cortege in Syria, c. 321 BCE) is the accepted tradition (Diodorus, Curtius, Pausanias); the tomb was a real, visitable monument into the Roman period, then the location was lost — no graded location claim exists on the timeline; a 2025/26 social-media video claiming 'Siwa DNA proved Alexander's GBS markers' is unverifiable clickbait with no scholarly source (GBS susceptibility is not a DNA test result; no such excavation or sequencing is published)
falsifiability: A contemporary document contradicting the Babylonian diary's death notice; or a verified, excavated tomb with inscriptions naming Alexander III. None exists.

title: The 300-year source gap behind Alexander's life
claim: No contemporary continuous account of Alexander's life survives. The five surviving full-length ancient narratives — Diodorus (1st c. BCE), Curtius Rufus (1st c. CE), Plutarch (c. 46–c. 120 CE), Arrian (c. 86–160 CE), and Justin's epitome of Pompeius Trogus (2nd/3rd c. CE) — were all written centuries after Alexander's death in 323 BCE, each drawing on lost eyewitness and near-eyewitness works: Callisthenes (court historian), Ptolemy, Aristobulus, Onesicritus, and Nearchus, which survive only as fragments quoted in later authors. The historical Alexander is therefore reconstructed through intermediaries, and every statement about him must be weighted by the distance of its chain.
place: Alexandria, Egypt (composition center of the lost traditions and the Romance; the Library as the symbol of what survived and what burned)
grade_reason: The dates of composition of the five continuous accounts are uncontested manuscript-chronology facts, and the fragment-only survival of the eyewitness memoirs is the standing position of the field (Nawotka et al. 2019; standard handbooks). VERIFIED by convergence of independent bibliographical evidence — not by any single excavation.
earliest_attestation: Babylonian astronomical diary -323 B (contemporary death notice); the eyewitness memoirs survive only as fragments (FGrH/Fragmente der griechischen Historiker)

sources.ref: Nawotka, Rollinger, Wiesehöfer, Wojciechowska (eds.), The Historiography of Alexander the Great (Harrassowitz, Classica et Orientalia 20, 2019): 'the most serious problem facing modern Alexander the Great studies: that of inadequate sources'; surviving accounts 'at least three hundred years younger than Alexander'; the search for Callisthenes, Onesicritus, Aristobulus, Ptolemy fragments and papyri
Arrian, Anabasis, preface: stated reliance on Ptolemy and Aristobulus as the most trustworthy because they wrote while Alexander lived (the one ancient source-consciousness on record)
Plutarch, Life of Alexander 1.1-3: 'I am writing biography, not history' — the ancient disclaimer on his own genre

competing_hypotheses: The lost sources survive sufficiently through quotation (Arrian's stated reliance on Ptolemy and Aristobulus) to give a near-eyewitness core
The fragmentary tradition is so mediated that the 'historical Alexander' is largely a Hellenistic construction — the maximalist skepticism position
falsifiability: The discovery of a complete contemporary narrative (e.g., a surviving copy of Callisthenes or Ptolemy) would close the gap; a verified, complete eyewitness history would supersede this record.

title: The pagan-to-Christianity borrowing claim (dying-and-rising)
claim: Early Christianity borrowed its death-and-resurrection narrative from the pagan dying-and-rising gods of the surrounding world (Osiris, Tammuz/Adonis, Attis, Baal).
place: Eastern Mediterranean (the Hellenistic religious marketplace)
grade_reason: No documentary chain connects any pre-Christian dying-and-rising cult to the early Christian resurrection narrative; Mettinger, who rehabilitated the category, found 'no prima facie evidence' of the link.
earliest_attestation: Frazer, The Golden Bough (1906-1915), Adonis/Attis/Osiris volume; popularized via Joseph Campbell and the 'Christ myth' literature

sources.ref: Frazer, The Golden Bough, 3rd ed. (1906-1915), Adonis/Attis/Osiris volume
Jonathan Z. Smith, 'Dying and Rising Gods', Encyclopedia of Religion (1987)
Jonathan Z. Smith, Drudgery Divine (University of Chicago Press, 1990)
Tryggve N.D. Mettinger, The Riddle of Resurrection (Almqvist & Wiksell, 2001), p. 221
Hendel, review of Mettinger, Journal of the American Oriental Society (2003)

competing_hypotheses: Jewish-internal development: Daniel 12:2, 2 Maccabees 7, and Pharisaic resurrection doctrine (evt-jewish-resurrection-lineage-001) supply the proximate, textually chained source

General Hellenistic conceptual substrate: continuities between Near Eastern dying-and-rising gods, mystery cults, and early Christian theology 'complexly interwoven' but not a simple borrowing (Burkert; Hendel's review)
falsifiability: A pre- or early-Christian text citing a dying-and-rising myth as precedent for Jesus's resurrection, or a Pauline-era writer acknowledging the parallel as a source, would upgrade the claim to CLAIMED.

title: The Great Library of Alexandria — the institution
claim: The Great Library of Alexandria was a real institution: part of the Mouseion (Place of the Muses) founded under Ptolemy I Soter and brought to fruition under Ptolemy II Philadelphus, advised by Demetrius of Phaleron, that aggressively acquired scrolls (Galens ship-search account), produced the Pinakes of Callimachus (a 120-book catalogue), and employed Zenodotus, Apollonius of Rhodes, Eratosthenes, Aristarchus of Samothrace, and Hero — with a daughter library established at the Serapeum under Ptolemy III.
place: Alexandria, Egypt (Brucheion royal quarter, traditional; no excavated building securely identified)
grade_reason: The institution is attested across independent literary lines (Strabo's eyewitness description, Athenaeus, Galen's acquisition accounts, the scholarly canon of librarians) plus the Serapeum daughter library; held below VERIFIED because the scroll-count figures are literary inflation and no excavated building is securely the Library.
earliest_attestation: The Letter of Aristeas (2nd c. BCE — itself a Jewish forgery pushing the Septuagint story, but an early witness to the library's fame, claiming 200,000+ scrolls); Strabo, Geography 17.1.8 (c. 25 BCE — an eyewitness description of the Mouseion and library still functioning).

sources.ref: Strabo, Geography 17.1.8 (c. 25 BCE) — describes the Mouseion and its library still functioning ~23 years after Caesar's fire

The Letter of Aristeas (2nd c. BCE) — earliest description of the library's ambition; claims 200,000+ scrolls; itself judged a forgery (Septuagint propaganda), so its numbers are not evidence of the numbers
Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 5.203e — the 490,000 + 42,800 scroll figures (literary, untested)
Galen on the Ptolemaic ship-search — every ship entering Alexandria searched for books, copied, originals kept
The head-librarian succession: Zenodotus, Callimachus (Pinakes), Apollonius of Rhodes, Eratosthenes, Aristarchus of Samothrace — multiply attested across ancient sources

competing_hypotheses: The 'universal library' ambition is a Hellenistic boast projected backward by literary sources — the real collection was large but ordinary, and the Septuagint-translation story is sectarian legend
The Library as an institution barely outlived the Ptolemaic funding — the scholarly program ended in the 2nd c. BCE civil wars, and 'the Library' afterward was a building with a diminished collection
falsifiability: Excavation of the Brucheion quarter definitively proving no such institution existed (impossible now — the royal quarter is under modern Alexandria and the sea), or contemporary Ptolemaic documents contradicting the scholarly payroll.

title: Manetho's Osarseph account (via Josephus)
claim: The 3rd-century BCE Egyptian priest-historian Manetho wrote an account, preserved in Josephus's Contra Apion (1.26-31), in which a renegade Egyptian priest named Osarseph (Osarsiph) led a group of polluted/lepers who seized Egypt for a time, were expelled, and — at the end of the story — Osarseph took the name Moses.
place: Avaris (Tell el-Dab'a, per Manetho's setting)
grade_reason: The account is multiply attested through Josephus's quotation; the quoted content's inverting relationship to the Exodus narrative is recognized by mainstream scholarship.
earliest_attestation: Josephus, Contra Apion 1.26-31, quoting Manetho's Aegyptiaca (early 1st c. CE composition, quoting a 3rd-c. BCE text)

sources.ref: Josephus, Contra Apion 1.26-31 (the quotation itself; Josephus cites Manetho to refute him)
Wikipedia, 'Osarseph' — three proposed interpretations (Amarna memory, Hyksos memory, anti-Jewish propaganda); Assmann's composite-folk-memory proposition
Jan Assmann, Moses the Egyptian: The Memory of Egypt in Western Monotheism (Harvard UP, 1997)

Israel Knohl's identification of Osarseph with Irsu (the Shasu who seized power in Egypt after Queen Twosret, per Papyrus Harris I and the Elephantine Stele; defeated and expelled by Setnakhte) — reported via TheTorah.com (2021) and the Osarseph summary page; the competing Chancellor Bay identification is 'usually rejected by scholars' (Albertz & Becking); the hypothesis that the Osarseph tale is a 1st-c. BCE anti-Jewish interpolation into Manetho (Cook) is noted as unresolved

Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, 29 Jun 2026: Tell el-Ku'a (Ismailia, southern edge of the Wadi Tumilat) — complete walled Second Intermediate Period settlement: residential compound ~30x60m behind a mudbrick wall, kilns and grain silos, ten mudbrick tombs attributed to the Fifteenth (Hyksos) Dynasty, Tell el-Yahudiyeh pottery; occupation continuing into the mid-Eighteenth Dynasty. August 2026: SIP residential area at Kom el-Khilgan (Dakahlia).
sources.note: Appended 2026-10-19 (IV.27 sixth pass): grade-neutral — restates the held gradual-infiltration Hyksos picture (the tale's 'Hyksos' element sits in composite legend, distinct non-overlapping periods); no grade mover. Turin-shroud precedent.

sources.ref: vlakov.substack.com, "The 'Priest of Set' Charge Against Moses," ~2026-09-20 — essay recap of Manetho's Osarseph account (via Josephus, Contra Apion 1.26-31) and Josephus's refutation; venue recap, not new research

competing_hypotheses: The story preserves a garbled memory of the Amarna period (pharaoh Amenophis, religious conflict)
The story preserves a memory of the Hyksos (the name Avaris; Osarseph as Hyksos-era)
The story is Hellenistic anti-Jewish propaganda with no historical kernel
Assmann's composite: folk memory combining Amarna, Hyksos, and other experiences
falsifiability: A complete pre-Josephan manuscript of Manetho contradicting Josephus's quotation; or demonstration that Josephus invented the passage (unlikely — he cites it to attack it)

title: The Maya hieroglyphic script — deciphered
claim: The Maya hieroglyphic script is a fully functional logosyllabic writing system that records spoken Mayan languages, and it has been substantially deciphered — the great majority of its signs can now be read.
place: Maya lowlands (southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, western Honduras, El Salvador)
grade_reason: Convergent independent readings: thousands of texts read by independent scholars agree; predictive readings confirmed by new finds (e.g., San Bartolo murals, 2001); phonetic complements make the readings testable, not interpretive.
earliest_attestation: Long Count inscriptions, Late Preclassic onward; the codex corpus (Dresden, Madrid, Paris) copied in the Postclassic

sources.ref: Knorozov, Yuri V. — 'Ancient Writing of Central America' (Sovetskaya Etnografiya, 1952): the phonetic break — Landa's 'alphabet' read as syllabic signs
Kelley, David H. — 'Phoneticism in the Maya Script' (1962): first Western corroboration of the phonetic reading
Proskouriakoff, Tatiana — Piedras Negras date pattern (1960): monuments record dynastic history, not astronomy alone
Berlin, Heinrich — emblem glyphs (1958): polity name-signs, enabling political geography
Coe, Michael D. — Breaking the Maya Code (1992): the decipherment history
The Dresden, Madrid, and Paris codices (bark-paper books; Dresden Codex, Sächsische Landesbibliothek)

competing_hypotheses: Thompson-era ideographic orthodoxy (pre-1960s): glyphs as pure idea-signs — superseded, kept on the record as the position the evidence defeated
The remaining ~10% of unread signs may still contain a non-linguistic decorative or calendrical component — a live minority refinement, not a rival
falsifiability: A newly found Maya text that consistently resists the established phonetic readings, or a demonstration that the phonetic complements are coincidental rather than systematic

title: The Samaritan tenth commandment: Mount Gerizim
claim: The Samaritan Pentateuch's Decalogue carries a tenth commandment absent from the Jewish and Christian versions: a commandment to build an altar on Mount Gerizim (commanded, the Samaritan text says, as Moses received it), constructed from the Deuteronomy 27:4 altar-command with 'Gerizim' in place of 'Ebal.' The Samaritan tradition thus holds that the Ten Commandments number ten differently — the same covenant, a different tenth word. The 'word-for-word' telling of the Decalogue fails a second time: the commandments were counted differently by living communities, not only copied differently by scribes.
place: Mount Gerizim (the Samaritan Decalogue's tenth word; the comparison is documentary across living traditions)
grade_reason: The Samaritan tenth commandment is documented in the Samaritan Pentateuch's Decalogue recensions and in the community's practice; no scholar of any camp disputes that the Samaritan version differs. The dispute is only direction (insertion vs preservation), which the record fences.
earliest_attestation: The Samaritan Pentateuch manuscripts (Exodus 20 / Deuteronomy 5 in the Samaritan recension); the living Samaritan liturgy on Mount Gerizim.

sources.ref: The Samaritan Pentateuch, Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5 recensions — the Gerizim altar commandment (Deut 27:4 'Gerizim' reading) interpolated as the tenth word
Encyclopaedia Judaica / standard Samaritan-studies reference — the Samaritan Decalogue's tenth commandment concerning Mount Gerizim, documented across Samaritan manuscripts

competing_hypotheses: The Gerizim commandment is a Samaritan sectarian insertion — the majority scholarly reading. The record holds it as one attested version among versions, not as the older text
The Gerizim commandment preserves the original — the minority reading. The record does not adjudicate originality; the documentary fact is the plurality
falsifiability: A Samaritan manuscript tradition without the Gerizim commandment would falsify this record; none is known. Held below VERIFIED: the record grades a version-plurality fact across traditions, not a single excavated artifact.

title: Saqqara Bird glider claim
claim: The Saqqara Bird (sycamore-wood carving, ~200 BCE) is a model of a glider, proving ancient Egyptians understood aerodynamics.
place: Saqqara necropolis, Egypt (now Egyptian Museum, Cairo)
grade_reason: Rejected by mainstream science: Richard P. Hallion judged it 'far too heavy and unstable itself to fly'; Levitt & Gross note replicas only glide when rebuilt in balsa wood WITH a horizontal stabilizer the original lacks; a 2023 CFD simulation (Institute of Aerospace Technology, Bremen, from a 3D scan) found low glide ratio, center of mass behind the neutral point (pitch-unstable), and asymmetric lift causing uncontrolled roll — 'not consistent with... ancient knowledge of aerodynamics.'
earliest_attestation: Excavated 1898 at Saqqara; rediscovered in storage 1969 by Khalil Messiha, who proposed the glider reading

sources.ref: Saqqara Bird article: Messiha's hypothesis, Hallion's verdict, Levitt & Gross on the balsa-plus-stabilizer problem, and the 2023 Bremen CFD study
Kevin Desmond (history of airplanes): no evidence found for the aerodynamics claim

competing_hypotheses: A child's toy or funerary bird carving — the original excavators catalogued it as a bird in 1898
A masthead fitting for the sacred boats of the Opet Festival (reliefs at the Temple of Khonsu, Karnak)
A primitive boomerang for waterfowl hunting
falsifiability: A flight-capable replica built from the original's actual materials (sycamore, not balsa) and geometry (no added horizontal stabilizer) would reopen the question. Every test to date fails without those two modifications.

title: The Translation Rule (VIII.i synthesis)
claim: A claim's evidence grade can turn on a translation choice: the earliest surviving witness to a text is often a translation, and the translation is a new, separately dated claim — so the timeline grades the crossing, not just the source. Where the Hebrew says one thing and the Greek, Latin, or English says another, the grade follows the word.
place: Jerusalem (oracle) / Alexandria (Septuagint) / Bethlehem (Vulgate) — the rule spans the crossings
grade_reason: Three independent, multiply-attested crossings (almah/parthenos, qaran/cornuta, kamelos/kamilos) each show the grade moving at the translation, not the source.
earliest_attestation: Demonstrated in the 2026 VIII.i synthesis pass; the exhibits are ancient

sources.ref: Isaiah 7:14 — Hebrew ha-almah vs LXX parthenos; HALOT; the GOARCH almah etymology survey
Exodus 34:29 — Hebrew qaran vs Vulgate cornuta; Michelangelo's Moses (1513-1515, San Pietro in Vincoli, Rome) as the material witness
Matthew 19:24 // Mark 10:25 // Luke 18:25 — kamelos vs kamilos variant; Metzger, Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament ('an attempt to soften the rigor of the statement')

competing_hypotheses: Translations are transparent conduits: meaning survives the crossing intact, and grading the source text suffices
All translation is betrayal: no cross-language claim can be graded at all (rejected — the variants are themselves dated documents, which is what makes the crossing gradable)
The original-language reading is always recoverable, so the translation layer is grade-neutral
falsifiability: A demonstrated case where a major doctrine's textual basis reads identically in the earliest Hebrew/Aramaic and in every ancient translation, with no variant at any crossing, would bound the rule's scope

title: The Pharos of Alexandria (early 3rd c. BCE)
claim: The Pharos of Alexandria — the great lighthouse on the island of Pharos off Alexandria, Egypt — was a purpose-built monumental navigational tower constructed in the early 3rd century BCE (commissioned under Ptolemy I Soter, traditionally completed under Ptolemy II Philadelphus), attributed to the architect Sostratus of Cnidus; it stood in three tiers (square base, octagonal middle, cylindrical top), burned a furnace-fed beacon by night (with a polished-bronze mirror reported for day), endured earthquakes from 956 CE onward with the 1303 Crete quake decisive, and its stones were reused for the Citadel of Qaitbay built on the site in 1477.
place: Island of Pharos, Alexandria, Egypt (site of the Citadel of Qaitbay)
grade_reason: Multiply attested across independent lines: classical literary tradition (Strabo, Pliny), a millennium of Arabic and European eyewitness descriptions, and the underwater archaeological record (Empereur 1994-present, 2025 block raisings). Exact height and summit details stay estimates.
earliest_attestation: Classical: Strabo (Geography 17.1.6, 1st c. BCE/CE) and Pliny the Elder (Natural History 36.83) on Sostratus; Arabic travelers' accounts (e.g. al-Idrisi, al-Balawi) on the medieval tower; archaeology: Jean-Yves Empereur's CEAlex underwater survey from 1994 (>3,300 objects documented, including tower blocks), 2025 block-raising program.

sources.ref: Strabo, Geography 17.1.6 — the Pharos tower on the island, its beacon fires (classical literary attestation)
Pliny the Elder, Natural History 36.83 — Sostratus of Cnidus as builder, the dedicatory-inscription anecdote (classical literary attestation)

archaeologymag.com (2025) — CEAlex/Empereur: Sostratus of Cnidus attribution, >100 m height, earthquake of 1303 rendering it inoperable, Qaitbay fortress 1477 on the same site, systematic underwater work since 1994
dailygalaxy.com (2026) — 80-ton stones raised; commissioned by Ptolemy I, designed by Sostratus; 1303 Crete quake; remains quarried, Qaitbay Citadel 1477 on the site
airial.travel Pharos of Alexandria — height estimates 100-140 m; three tapering tiers; bronze mirror/fire; earthquakes 956-1303 CE; 'pharos' as the root of 'lighthouse' in several languages

competing_hypotheses: Height estimates range ~100-140 m across sources (350 ft / 110 m in some modern accounts; the exact figure is an estimate, never a measurement)
Commissioning under Ptolemy I vs. completion under Ptolemy II — the two traditions differ; the record carries both, not one
The summit arrangement — statue of Zeus/Poseidon vs. furnace-and-mirror only — rests on late literary and numismatic evidence, not on surviving structure
falsifiability: Empereur's underwater block survey proving the tower blocks are later medieval spolia with no Ptolemaic origin, or a pre-Ptolemaic monumental tower elsewhere predating the Pharos as the type, would overturn the archetype claim; the exact height can never be 'verified' and stays an estimate.

title: Baghdad battery
claim: The 'Baghdad battery' vessels (Khujut Rabu'a, near Baghdad) were ancient electric batteries, proving knowledge of electrochemistry ~2,000 years before Volta.
place: Khujut Rabu'a, northeast of Baghdad, Iraq
grade_reason: The artifacts exist (one Ctesiphon jar at the MET), but the battery function is unsupported: Prof. Elizabeth Stone (Stony Brook), returning from Iraq in 2012, stated she does 'not know a single archaeologist who believed that these were batteries'; no wires, terminals, or acid residues; the jars closely resemble known scroll-storage vessels from Seleucia.
earliest_attestation: Excavated 1936 at Khujut Rabu'a (dig led by Sherif Yousif and Jawad al-Saffar); published as a battery hypothesis by Wilhelm König (assistant/director, Baghdad Antiquities Administration)

sources.ref: Baghdad Battery article: physical description, dating dispute (Simpson), resemblance to Seleucia scroll vessels
Elizabeth Stone (2012): no archaeologist she knows believes they were batteries

competing_hypotheses: Storage vessels for sacred scrolls from nearby Seleucia — the Seleucia vessels are almost identical in form minus the metals; papyrus/parchment inside would have rotted away
Ordinary ceramic vessels whose metal inserts served a mundane purpose; no wires, terminals, or electrochemical residues found
falsifiability: Residue analysis showing acidic electrolyte remains, wiring, or connected multi-cell assemblies would reopen the question. After decades of attention, none has been produced; no archaeologist defends the battery function.

title: The three Genesis 5 number traditions
claim: The Adam-to-Noah genealogy's begetting ages differ systematically across the Masoretic Text, the Samaritan Pentateuch, and the Septuagint, yielding three different Adam-to-Flood totals — 1656, 1307, and 2242 years — while the patriarchs' total lifespans mostly agree.
place: Textual tradition: Jerusalem (MT), Samaria (Samaritan Pentateuch), Alexandria (LXX)
grade_reason: The three number-sets are read directly from the three manuscript traditions; every witness inspected (Ellicott, Barnes, Lange, Peake, ICDST) reports the same divergence, and the divergence sits in the begetting ages while total lifespans mostly agree.
earliest_attestation: The divergent number-sets are visible in the manuscript traditions themselves (LXX, Samaritan Pentateuch, Masoretic Text), and are tabulated in classical commentaries: Ellicott, Barnes, Lange, Peake.

sources.ref: Ellicott's Commentary for English Readers, Genesis 5 — the three-authority table (Hebrew 1656, Samaritan 1307, LXX 2262)
Barnes Notes on Genesis 5 — Hebrew/Samaritan/Septuagint/Josephus comparison table (deluge totals 1656/1307/2262/2256)
Lange's Commentary, Genesis 5 — Creation-to-Flood 1656 (Hebrew) / 1307 (Samaritan) / 2242 (Septuagint); post-Flood-to-Abraham 365 / 1015 / 1245
ICDST tabulation — begetting ages and flood dates in the MT, Jubilees, and Samaritan Pentateuch (dl.icdst.org PDF)

competing_hypotheses: One of the three traditions preserves the original numbers and the other two were altered — commentators disagree on which (Barnes argues the Hebrew carries preponderating authority; others argue LXX priority)
The numbers are schematic theology (a ten-generation structure paralleling the Cainite list in Genesis 4) and were never meant as a calendar
falsifiability: A pre-divergence manuscript witness showing uniform begetting ages across all three traditions, or a single tradition internally reconciling the three totals

title: Eratosthenes measures the Earth (c. 240 BCE)
claim: Around 240 BCE, Eratosthenes of Cyrene — librarian at Alexandria — measured the Earth's circumference using the summer-solstice shadows at Syene and Alexandria: the 7.2° shadow angle (1/50 of a circle) times the 5,000-stadia intercity distance gave ~250,000 stadia.
place: Alexandria (with Syene/Aswan)
grade_reason: Multiple independent sources agree on the method (solstice shadows, 1/50 of a circle, 5,000 stadia by bematists, 250,000/252,000 stadia total), the ~240 BCE date, the Cleomedes/Strabo transmission, and the two cancelling false assumptions (Syene not exactly on the Tropic, not exactly due south). The accuracy is fenced: 'historians believe that Eratosthenes' conclusion was between .5% and 17% off the mark' (Gizmodo) — the Egyptian-stade reading gives ~1%, the Attic-stade reading ~16%. The method is sound; the ruler is uncertain.
earliest_attestation: Cleomedes' Meteora (1st c. CE); Strabo's Geography (reports 252,000 stadia)

sources.ref: IFLScience: 'Eratosthenes measured the angle and worked out it was about 1/50th of a circumference, so knowing that the distance between Alexandria and Syene was 5,000 stadia, the full circumference of the Earth must be 50 times that... 250,000 stadia.' Caveats: 'We do not know the exact length of a stadia... that puts the circumference between about 38,624 kilometers and 46,671 kilometers' vs the true 40,075 km. The method relied on the simplified account of Cleomedes (1st c. CE).

Wikipedia, 'Eratosthenes': 'The distance between Alexandria and Syene was reported to be about 5,000 stadia, as measured by professional bematists. Eratosthenes multiplied this number by 50 and arrived at a total of roughly 250,000 stadia.' His two false assumptions 'fortuitously cancelled each other out' — Syene 1° north of the Tropic, 3° east of Alexandria.

Gizmodo: 'Due to the uncertain distance that stadia represents (and particularly which stadia he was using), historians believe that Eratosthenes' conclusion was between .5% and 17% off the mark... many scholars think it likely that he was using the Egyptian stadia (157.5 m), being in Egypt at the time. This would make his estimate only about 1% too small.'

Scribd, 'Eratosthenes: Measuring Earth's Circumference': 'Seventeen hundred years after Eratosthenes's death, while Christopher Columbus studied what Eratosthenes had written about the size of the Earth, he chose to believe, based on a map by Toscanelli, that the Earth's circumference was one-third smaller.'

competing_hypotheses: The 'almost exactly right' telling (fenced: with the Egyptian stade of 157.5 m the result is ~39,690 km — about 1% off the true 40,075 km; with the Attic stade of ~185 m it is ~46,620 km — about 16% off. The accuracy claim depends entirely on which stade he used, which is unknown)
falsifiability: Evidence that the Cleomedes/Strabo accounts are fabrications, or that the measurement belongs to another scholar

title: Jewish reception: almah was the young woman next door
claim: Pre-Christian Jewish reading of Isaiah 7:14 was non-messianic and contemporary: Targum Jonathan renders 'the young woman is pregnant' (Aramaic 'ulaymta, no virginity term) with no messianic language at 7:14 (though it reads 9:5-6 and 11:1 messianically); Rashi reads the almah as Isaiah's own wife ('My wife will conceive this year. This was the fourth year of Ahaz') and rejects the Hezekiah identification on chronology; Ibn Ezra agrees. The 2nd-c. CE Jewish Greek revisers (Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion) all render neanis ('young woman'), correcting the LXX's parthenos. The 'virgin' reading enters via the Septuagint, which Matthew 1:23 quotes.
place: Jerusalem (oracle); Alexandria (LXX)
grade_reason: Multiply attested across independent Jewish witnesses spanning a millennium; converges with modern lexicons (BDB/HALOT) and the NABRE/JPS notes.
earliest_attestation: Targum Jonathan on Isaiah 7:14; Aquila/Symmachus/Theodotion Greek renderings; Rashi's commentary

sources.ref: Targum Jonathan Isa 7:14 ('ulaymta); the Three's neanis; Rashi ('My wife will conceive this year'); Soncino Isaiah p.35 summary — surveyed 2026-10-18
NABRE footnote: 'Hebrew almah designates a young woman of marriageable age without specific reference to virginity... this translation underlies Mt 1:23'

competing_hypotheses: The LXX translators read the Hebrew rightly and parthenos is faithful (pre-Christian Jewish-witness argument)
falsifiability: A pre-Christian Jewish source reading 7:14 messianically with a virginity term

title: The Nazca Geoglyphs
claim: The Nazca lines and geoglyphs — ~800 straight lines, 300 geometric figures, and dozens of biomorphic figures (hummingbird, spider, monkey, condor) up to hundreds of meters long on the coastal pampa of southern Peru — are human-made works created by the pre-Incan Nazca culture (c. 200 BCE–700 CE) by clearing dark, sun-oxidized surface stones to expose the pale gypsiferous subsoil beneath; shallow grooves only a few centimeters deep, preserved by the hyper-arid climate.
place: Nazca pampa, Ica region, Peru
grade_reason: Multiple independent lines — a century of aerial and ground survey, excavation, pottery-motif links to the Nazca culture, and the 2024 AI survey — agree the geoglyphs are indigenous human-made works; no credible source disputes authorship.
earliest_attestation: Peruvian archaeologist Toribio Mejía Xesspe noted the figures in 1927; scientific study began with Paul Kosok's 1939 aerial observations (Long Island University).

sources.ref: UNESCO World Heritage Centre — 'Lines and Geoglyphs of Nasca and Palpa' (inscribed 1994)
Paul Kosok (1939) aerial observations — launched scientific study of the pampa
Maria Reiche (1941–1998) — four decades of ground survey, mapping, preservation; Reiche's astronomical-calendar thesis for the lines
Gerald Hawkins (1968) — archaeoastronomical computer analysis found no statistically significant celestial correlation; Reiche's calendar thesis not sustained
Johan Reinhard — water-cult/fertility ritual hypothesis (mountain-deity ethnographic-archaeological work)

Sakai, M. et al. (2024) 'AI-accelerated Nazca survey nearly doubles the number of known figurative geoglyphs and sheds light on their purpose', PNAS 121(40), e2407652121 — 303 new figurative geoglyphs in six months (Yamagata University + IBM Research); relief-type geoglyphs as trail-side 'billboards', line-type for community ceremony
Anthony Aveni — Between the Lines (statistical rebuttal of celestial alignments; processional/ritual walkway readings)

competing_hypotheses: Purpose: water/fertility ritual imploring the gods for rain in the hyper-arid desert (Reinhard) — the leading archaeological reading
Purpose: sacred processional pathways walked in community ceremony (Aveni; Sakai 2024: line-type = collective ritual, relief-type = trail-side information)
Purpose: astronomical calendar / 'largest astronomy book in the world' (Kosok–Reiche) — statistically refuted by Hawkins 1968 and Aveni
Purpose: precursor of Inca ceque sacred-pathway systems radiating from shrines
falsifiability: Proof that the geoglyphs are modern forgeries on a mass scale (e.g., 20th-century construction) would overturn authorship; absent that, the indigenous-human origin stands

title: The oldest extant paper: Fangmatan, early 2nd c. BCE
claim: Paper was already being made in China by the early 2nd century BCE — the Fangmatan Tomb 5 map fragment is the oldest extant sheet of paper on Earth.
place: Fangmatan, near Tianshui, Gansu
grade_reason: A surviving artifact in excavated context (Tomb 5, early Western Han), identified as paper by fiber analysis, with the map drawn on it; the early-Han Xuanquan and Zhongyan paper fragments corroborate repeated utilitarian papermaking before 105 CE. Held below VERIFIED on the absolute-date line (tomb-context, not radiocarbon dating) and because the 'oldest extant' superlative is hostage to future finds.
earliest_attestation: The fragment itself, excavated 1986, Fangmatan Tomb 5, near Tianshui, Gansu — the artifact is the attestation

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Fangmatan' — Tomb 5 excavated 1986, early Western Han (early 2nd c. BCE); occupant buried with a paper map on his chest; water damage left a single 5.6 x 2.6 cm fragment; the map is drawn on the oldest extant piece of paper (citing Yi & Liu 2010, p.64; Behr 2007, p.113)

China Development Gateway (Xinhua), Nov 2016 — Li Xiaocen (Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology) on the fragment: uneven fiber distribution under the microscope; yellow, rough surface, randomly yet densely interlaced fibers; traits of an ancient paper-making technology very different from Cai Lun's, still used by ethnic minorities in Tibet, Yunnan and Xinjiang

hal.science hal-03221031 — 'A Study of Ancient Paper Fragments from an Eastern Han Dynasty Tomb in Minfeng County, Xinjiang': the Niya paper (flaxlike fibers, no screen pattern, watering method) consistent with the techniques of early Han paper such as the Xuanquan paper from Gansu and the Zhongyan paper from Shaanxi — repeated, distinctively primitive Han papermaking

competing_hypotheses: The fragment could be an exceptional one-off rather than evidence of an established craft — but the 2006 c. 8 BCE specimens and the Xuanquan/Zhongyan strips show paper in repeated, utilitarian use across the Han, which reads as a craft, not an accident
Some historians reserve the word 'paper' for the Cai Lun-process sheet and class the earlier fragments as 'proto-paper' — a terminological fence, not an evidential dispute
falsifiability: Re-dating of Tomb 5 to post-105 CE, or a laboratory finding that the fragment is not felted plant-fiber paper, would demote the grade; a pre-Western-Han paper find would retire the 'oldest extant' superlative, not the grade.

title: Parchment was invented at Pergamum under a papyrus embargo
claim: Parchment — prepared animal skin used as a writing surface — was INVENTED at Pergamum in the 2nd c. BCE, when King Eumenes II's scribes, cut off from Egyptian papyrus by Ptolemy's export ban during the Alexandria-Pergamum library rivalry, were forced to invent the material (the 'pergamena' story, from Pliny NH 13.21 citing Varro).
place: Pergamum (Bergama, Turkey) — the claimed site of the invention
grade_reason: Two independent kills: (1) animal-skin writing surfaces predate Eumenes II by two millennia — Egyptian examples from the 24th c. BCE (NTU history-of-the-book), leather writing c. 2500 BCE Egypt, Herodotus (5th c. BCE) describing books written on skins; McClintock & Strong (1870): Pliny, 'without good grounds, places the invention as late as 196 B.C.' (2) The embargo itself is single-source Pliny-via-Varro — no independent attestation of Ptolemy's export ban exists. The name 'parchment' (pergamena) is genuinely Pergamene; the invention is not.
earliest_attestation: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 13.21 (1st c. CE), citing Varro: 'when owing to the rivalry between King Ptolemy and King Eumenes about their libraries, Ptolemy suppressed the export of paper, parchment was invented at Pergamum.' No earlier source; no independent source.

sources.ref: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 13.21, citing Varro — the single source for the invention story ('parchment was invented at Pergamum' after Ptolemy's export suppression); the claim under test
NTU History of the Book blog — earliest documents on animal skin from the 24th c. BCE in ancient Egypt, two millennia before Eumenes II

McClintock & Strong, Cyclopedia of Biblical, Theological and Ecclesiastical Literature (1870), 'Parchment' — 'Pliny, without good grounds, places the invention as late as 196 B.C.'; skins used 'at least as early as 500 years B.C.', Herodotus on skin books

Kenyon (1932), via the Lochac College of Scribes parchment paper — parchment documents (Avroman 88/22 BC; Dura-Europos 189-196 BC) already in circulation before the Pergamum refinement, and parchment 'in use before the time of the Pergamum library'

Reed (1975) — the Pergamene contribution was REFINEMENT, not invention: the simplified liquor bath and stretched-state drying that made the durable, smooth, uniformly opaque sheet (cited via the Lochac summary)

competing_hypotheses: The embargo never happened — it is Pliny-via-Varro's single-source telling, and the 'invention' is the Roman story of Pergamene REFINEMENT misremembered as invention
The rivalry was real but the material story is retrofitted — Pergamum's workshops improved a known product, and the imperial anecdotists turned a manufacturing upgrade into an origin myth
falsifiability: A pre-Pergamene documentary record of skin writing destroys it — such records exist in abundance, which is why the grade is DEBUNKED and not merely CLAIMED.

title: The Pergamum Library — Alexandria's Hellenistic rival
claim: Pergamum under Eumenes II (197-158 BCE) built the ancient world's great rival to the Alexandrian library — ~200,000 scrolls by literary report, in a library building excavated in the 1880s (Carl Conze's team) with wall niches for the rolls — and the Pergamene workshop refined parchment (pergamena) into a durable, smooth writing surface; the 'Antony gave Cleopatra the 200,000 Pergamene scrolls' episode (Plutarch, Antony 58.9) is single-source and untested.
place: Pergamum (Bergama, Turkey) — the acropolis library building near the sanctuary of Athena
grade_reason: The institution converges across Strabo, the excavated building with its roll-niches, and the Roman literary tradition; held below VERIFIED because the 200,000 figure and the Antony gift are single-line literary reports, not independently tested.
earliest_attestation: Strabo on Pergamum's library; Plutarch, Antony 58.9 (c. 100 CE) for the Cleopatra gift; Pliny NH 13.21 for the parchment-invention story (DEBUNKED as invention — separate record).

sources.ref: Strabo, Geography — Pergamum's library as the Hellenistic rival to Alexandria
Plutarch, Antony 58.9 — Antony gave Cleopatra 200,000 rolls from the Pergamene library (single-source; carried at CLAIMED)
Carl Conze's 1880s excavations — the Pergamene acropolis library building with wall niches for scroll rolls, near the sanctuary of Athena
Reed (1975) — the Pergamene refinement of parchment manufacture: the simplified liquor bath and stretched-state drying that produced durable, smooth, uniform sheets

competing_hypotheses: The 200,000-scroll figure and the Antony gift are literary embroidery — Plutarch's Cleopatra gift is a moralizing set piece about Antony plundering one library to please a queen

The Pergamum-Alexandria 'rivalry' was an invention of the same Roman authors who told the parchment story — the cities' real relationship was dynastic alliance (the Attalids as Pergamene kings, Roman clients)
falsifiability: Proof the excavated 'library' building was something else, or a contemporary source listing Pergamum's collection as small — neither exists; the building's niches and Strabo's testimony converge.

title: The Jewish-internal resurrection lineage (Daniel, 2 Maccabees, Josephus)
claim: Bodily resurrection belief was already documented inside Second Temple Judaism before Christianity: Daniel 12:2 (c. 165 BCE), 2 Maccabees 7 (c. 124 BCE), and Josephus's report of Pharisaic doctrine (Jewish War 2.163) — the proximate, textually chained source of the early Christian resurrection concept.
place: Jerusalem / Judea
grade_reason: Three independent witnesses in a documentary chain — apocalypse, martyrology, and a historian's report of a living school's doctrine — all pre- or contemporary with Christian origins.
earliest_attestation: Daniel 12:2 — 'multitudes who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake'

sources.ref: Daniel 12:2 (Maccabean-era apocalyptic; also Isaiah 24-27, the 'Isaianic Apocalypse', earlier mythic substrate)
2 Maccabees 7 (the martyred brothers' resurrection hope, c. 124 BCE)
Josephus, Jewish War 2.163 (the Pharisees' doctrine of resurrection)

competing_hypotheses: The chain is a Jewish mask for older Near Eastern dying-and-rising influence (the 'complexly interwoven' substrate position — possible but unattested as a transmission chain)
Daniel 12 reflects Zoroastrian influence (the Sasanian redaction-chronology caution applies; pre-Sasanian dating of the influence is debated)
falsifiability: Evidence that Daniel 12:2 and 2 Maccabees 7 postdate Christian origins, or that Pharisaic resurrection doctrine is a Josephan invention, would collapse the chain.

title: The cruse of oil: Hanukkah's eight-day miracle telling
claim: When the Temple in Jerusalem was rededicated in 164 BCE, a single cruse of pure oil bearing the High Priest's seal burned for eight days instead of one — the oil miracle is the original account of Hanukkah.
place: Jerusalem — the Temple
grade_reason: Attested only in a sixth-century CE aggadah; absent from 1 Maccabees, 2 Maccabees, Josephus, the Jerusalem Talmud, and the Al HaNissim prayer — every source closer to the event.
earliest_attestation: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 21b — a sixth-century CE aggadah, roughly five to six centuries after the event

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 21b — 'When the Greeks entered the Temple, they desecrated all the oils... they could only find one jar of oil with the High Priest's seal, with enough to last for one day. A miracle happened, and it lasted for eight' (sixth-century CE aggadah)

Wikipedia 'Miracle of the cruse of oil' — 'Contemporary accounts of the revolt, including 1 Maccabees, 2 Maccabees, and writings by Josephus, do not mention the miracle of the oil, attributing the eight-day holiday instead to the military victory and the rededication of the Temple. The story is also absent in the Jerusalem Talmud.'

The Algemeiner, 'The Myths of Hanukkah' (2020) — the miracle 'is first described in the Talmud (Shabbat 21b), completed about 600 years after the events described in the books of the Maccabees'; Al HaNissim 'talks about Matisyahu and his sons defeating the Greeks... But no miracle'
1 Maccabees 4:36-59 — the rededication account, no oil (negative attestation)
Josephus, Antiquities 12.316-325 — the rededication account, no oil (negative attestation)

competing_hypotheses: The miracle is a late aggadic reading that gives theological meaning to an eight-day festival whose sources explain it by victory and rededication
The Scholion to Megillat Taanit's Kislev-25 entry may carry an earlier form of the telling — but its dating is contested, so it cannot anchor the claim earlier than the Bavli
falsifiability: A pre-Bavli source (e.g. a securely dated Dead Sea or early rabbinic text) narrating the eight-day cruse would promote the grade; proof that Shabbat 21b's story is a later editorial insertion with no earlier tradition would push it toward DEBUNKED.

title: The Temple rededication of 164 BCE — the festival before the miracle story
claim: In 164 BCE, on the 25th of Kislev, the Maccabees rededicated the Jerusalem Temple after defeating the Seleucids and celebrated for eight days — the festival that became Hanukkah.
place: Jerusalem — the Temple
grade_reason: Three independent ancient witnesses (1 Maccabees, 2 Maccabees, Josephus) agree on the rededication and the eight-day festival; none mentions an oil miracle.
earliest_attestation: 1 Maccabees 4:36-59 (written ~100 BCE)

sources.ref: 1 Maccabees 4:36-59 — the rededication, the 25th of Kislev, the eight-day celebration; no oil miracle
2 Maccabees 10:1-8 — the eight-day celebration 'in the manner of the feast of booths' (Sukkot); no oil miracle
Josephus, Antiquities 12.316-325 — the rededication, the eight-day 'Festival of Lights'; no oil miracle
Al HaNissim prayer — prays of Matisyahu and his sons defeating the Greeks, God's deliverance, purifying the Temple, lighting lights — but no miracle

competing_hypotheses: The eight-day length deliberately mirrors Solomon's Temple dedication (2 Chron 7:8-9) rather than recording the campaign's exact duration
The festival absorbed an earlier winter-solstice observance — a calendrical, not military, origin
falsifiability: A contemporary Seleucid record showing the Temple un-rededicated through 163 BCE, or proof 1 Maccabees is a wholly fictional composition, would collapse the grade.

title: The Nash Papyrus: the oldest Decalogue, and it is not the Masoretic one
claim: The Nash Papyrus (Cambridge University Library, MS Or.233) is a second-century BCE (c. 150-100 BCE) Hebrew manuscript containing the Decalogue followed by the start of the Shema (Deut 6:4-5). Four fragments, 24 lines, acquired from an Egyptian antiquities dealer by W. L. Nash (1898/1902, published by S. A. Cooke 1903); before the Dead Sea Scrolls it was the oldest Hebrew biblical text known. Its Decalogue harmonizes Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5, accords closely with the Septuagint's Exodus 20, orders the later commandments Adultery-Murder-Steal (the LXX order, not the Masoretic Murder-Adultery-Steal), and omits the phrase 'house of bondage' (used in both Masoretic versions) — plausibly a reflection of its Egyptian composition setting. The manuscript is not a scroll but a single sheet, likely a phylactery/tefillin extract or a liturgical copy matching the Second-Temple daily recitation (m. Tamid 5:1). The oldest Decalogue we own does not match the Masoretic text in any hymnal.
place: Cambridge University Library, Cambridge, UK (MS Or.233; alleged Fayyum, Egypt provenance fenced)
grade_reason: Artifact held and published by Cambridge; dating and text-description converge across independent encyclopedia entries (Jewish Virtual Library / Encyclopaedia Judaica, encyclopedia.com, Cambridge's own Lines of Thought exhibition, historyofinformation.com) and the original Cooke publication. The variant facts (harmonization, LXX order, 'house of bondage' omission) are reported identically in all of them. CORROBORATED, not VERIFIED: provenance unknown.
earliest_attestation: The papyrus itself (2nd c. BCE); S. A. Cooke, 'A Pre-Masoretic Biblical Papyrus,' Proceedings of the Society of Biblical Archaeology 25 (1903): 34-56.

sources.ref: Cambridge University Library, 'The ten commandments' (Lines of Thought exhibition) — Nash Papyrus, Egypt, 2nd c. BCE; the text 'is different from that found in the Bible, suggesting that even this fundamental religious text has changed'; MS Or.233

Jewish Virtual Library / Encyclopaedia Judaica, 'Nash Papyrus' — 2nd-c. BCE, 24 lines, Decalogue + Shema, published Cooke 1903; text accords with the Septuagint of Exodus 20; daily-liturgy reading per m. Tamid 5:1

historyofinformation.com, 'Nash Papyrus' — acquired 1898 by W. L. Nash, presented to Cambridge; Cook 1903 first description; re-dated to c. 150-100 BCE; harmonizes Ex 20 + Deut 5; Adultery-Murder-Steal order = LXX order; omits 'house of bondage'

competing_hypotheses: The harmonized text is a liturgical conflation rather than a witness to a variant Hebrew Vorlage — the reading-context hypothesis (m. Tamid 5:1 daily recitation). The record holds both readings: either way, the transmitted Decalogue was plural in the Second Temple period
Provenance is unknown (allegedly Fayyum, Egypt) — the Egyptian-orthography explanation for 'house of bondage' omission is plausible but unproven; the omission is documented fact regardless
falsifiability: Redating the papyrus securely outside the 2nd c. BCE, or a demonstrated forgery finding, would supersede this record. Held below VERIFIED: provenance is unknown and the reading-context function is inferred, not proven.

title: The word-for-word Decalogue transmission telling
claim: The Ten Commandments have been transmitted word-for-word identical from Moses to the present day, with no variation, no alternate versions, and no textual development. FALSE: the documentary record carries the Decalogue in multiple differing versions — Exodus 20 vs Deuteronomy 5 (different Sabbath rationales, different wording), the Nash Papyrus (2nd c. BCE, a harmonized pre-Masoretic text that matches neither), and the Samaritan tenth commandment (Mount Gerizim, absent from Jewish and Christian versions). The 'word-for-word' telling is the 293rd DEBUNKED family: the identical-transmission telling.
place: Jerusalem (textual tradition; witnesses span Egypt, Samaria, Qumran)
grade_reason: The telling dies on the documents: Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5 give different Sabbath rationales and different wording for the same commandments (verifiable by reading any two printed Bibles — evt-decalogue-two-versions-001, CORROBORATED); the Nash Papyrus (2nd c. BCE) carries a harmonized Decalogue matching neither canonical version (evt-nash-papyrus-001, CORROBORATED); the Samaritan Pentateuch adds a tenth commandment (Mount Gerizim) absent from Jewish and Christian texts (evt-samaritan-decalogue-gerizim-001, CORROBORATED). Three independent witnesses, three different Decalogues. DEBUNKED as a transmission claim; the telling's persistence is graded as a belief phenomenon, not an evidence claim.
earliest_attestation: The variant Decalogue texts themselves (Exodus 20 vs Deuteronomy 5; Nash Papyrus 2nd c. BCE; Samaritan Pentateuch).

sources.citation: Nash Papyrus (Cambridge MS Or.233) — S. A. Cooke 1903; Albright 1937 dating
Samaritan Pentateuch Decalogue — Mount Gerizim tenth commandment

competing_hypotheses: The variations are scribal accidents around a stable original — but the Nash Papyrus's harmonization and the Samaritan tenth commandment are deliberate recensional differences, not accidents; the record grades the plurality, not the accident theory.
falsifiability: A single uniform Decalogue text across all ancient witnesses (Masoretic, Nash, Samaritan, Septuagint, Qumran) would falsify; the witnesses disagree.

title: The Silk Road trade network (c. 130 BCE – c. 1500 CE)
claim: A long-lived, braided network of overland and maritime trade routes connected China, Central Asia, Persia, India, and the Mediterranean world for roughly sixteen centuries — many routes, not one road.
place: Samarkand (the road-city that taxed it)
grade_reason: Multiply attested across independent traditions (Han documents, Sogdian merchant letters, Persian/Arabic geographies, Italian merchant handbooks) and physically excavated at the oasis cities; the exact structure and volume remain debated.
earliest_attestation: Han sources on Zhang Qian's missions to the Western Regions (Shiji 123, c. 100 BCE) for the opening; the Sogdian Ancient Letters (c. 313 CE) for the merchant system in operation

sources.ref: Sima Qian, Shiji 123 (c. 100 BCE) — Zhang Qian's missions 138–115 BCE, the Han opening of the western routes
The Sogdian Ancient Letters (c. 313 CE), Stein's 1907 Dunhuang watchtower find — merchant houses operating the network in their own words
Francesco Pegolotti, Pratica della mercatura (c. 1340) — the 14th-century route to China with station-by-station costs
UNESCO Silk Roads Programme (1988–); the Chang'an–Tianshan corridor World Heritage inscription (2014, 33 sites)
Valerie Hansen, The Silk Road: A New History (2012) — the 'many routes' thesis; Beckwith, Empires of the Silk Road — the regional-exchange caution

competing_hypotheses: The maximalist highway reading (one great continuous route, Rome to Chang'an) — the popular version; fails on the relay structure: goods moved hand-to-hand in stages, no merchant traveled the whole distance

The minimalist reading (Beckwith and others): long-distance bulk trade was thinner than the myth; most exchange was regional, and 'the Silk Road' as a unified system is a modern narrative overlay on local circuits
The nomad-centered reading: the steppe nomads were the true system — the carriers, protectors, and taxers — with the oasis cities as their service stations; the road was their infrastructure
falsifiability: Excavation of the full oasis-city sequence yielding no long-distance trade goods at all, or documentary proof that all east-west movement in the period was coastal-maritime, would falsify the overland network as a system

title: The Aztecs built the pyramids of Teotihuacan
claim: The Mexica (Aztecs) built the pyramids of Teotihuacan — the Pyramid of the Sun, the Pyramid of the Moon, and the Temple of the Feathered Serpent.
place: Teotihuacan, Valley of Mexico
grade_reason: Two independent kills: (1) chronology — the civic core burned c. 550 CE, ~775 years before the 1325 founding of Tenochtitlan; (2) the Mexica's own attribution — they coined the Nahuatl name Teotihuacan ('place where gods were born') centuries after the fall and credited the gods, never themselves.
earliest_attestation: Modern popular conflation — no ancient source supports it. The Mexica's own tradition (Florentine Codex Book X, Sahagun) attributes the ruins to the gods, never to themselves.

sources.ref: Wikipedia, Teotihuacan — 'The name Teotihuacan was given by the Nahuatl-speaking Aztecs centuries after the fall of the city around 550 CE' (glossed 'birthplace of the gods' / 'place where gods were born'; Thelma D. Sullivan: 'place of those who have the road of the gods')

Scientific American, 'Decoding Mexico's City of Gods' — 'Sometime in the 14th century, the first Mexica found their way into the valley'; they named the Avenue of the Dead and the two pyramids and called the city Teotihuacan, 'the place where gods are born'
Bernardino de Sahagun, Florentine Codex, Book X — the Mexica Fifth-Sun creation account set at Teotihuacan (the gods, not the Mexica, as builders)
George L. Cowgill, Ancient Teotihuacan (Cambridge University Press, 2015) — the 550 CE burning and the multiethnic-builder debate

competing_hypotheses: The Mexica made genuine pilgrimages and ritual use of the ruins (true — pilgrimage is not construction)
A Mexica-era restoration layer could be misread as construction (no such layer documented in the monumental core)
The early-20th-century Tollan debate placed the chronicles' Tollan at Teotihuacan (resolved: Tollan is a generic Nahua term for any large settlement, per current scholarship)
falsifiability: A Mexica-period (14th–16th c.) construction inscription, or a sealed-context Mexica artifact layer beneath the Pyramid of the Sun's construction fill

title: Seven years' bad luck for a broken mirror — the Roman attribution
claim: The folklore that breaking a mirror brings seven years of bad luck is said to be Roman in origin — the Romans supposedly believed the gods watched mortal souls through mirrors, and that the body renewed itself every seven years, so the bad luck would expire at the next renewal. The Roman attribution is asserted by modern pop outlets; no primary Latin source is cited by any of them, so it sits one grade below folklore-with-a-trail.
place: Rome (claimed origin; unproven)
grade_reason: The belief's existence as folklore is undoubted; the Roman origin story is widely asserted but unsourced in every source consulted — grade carries the attribution, not the folklore itself.
earliest_attestation: Modern pop treatments (Discover Magazine 2024, Google Arts & Culture '18 Superstitions', sc.edu 2021, Brewminate) — all asserting a Roman origin without citing a Roman text.

sources.ref: Discover Magazine, 'Black Cats and Broken Mirrors' (2024) — Roman origin, seven-year body renewal
Google Arts & Culture, '18 Superstitions from Around the World' — Roman contribution of the seven-years notion
sc.edu, 'How did the superstition... start' (2021) — Greek soul-reflection + Roman manufacture, seven-year renewal

competing_hypotheses: The Roman attribution is a 19th/20th-century antiquarian invention that hardened into 'fact' by repetition (the classic etiological-myth lifecycle)
The belief has multiple independent roots (Narcissus/reflection-as-soul ideas across cultures) and the Roman version is only one tributary
falsifiability: A primary Latin text describing seven years of bad luck for a broken mirror would raise the Roman attribution to CORROBORATED; a documented 19th-century coinage would drop it to SPECULATION.

title: The gougu rule — China's own right-triangle tradition
claim: The Chinese gougu (勾股) tradition carries the right-triangle relationship under its own name: the Zhou Bi Suan Jing preserves the 3-4-5 triangle and the gou-gu-xian (勾股弦) rule, and Zhao Shuang's 3rd-century CE commentary gives a dissection diagram — right triangles arranged inside a square, areas compared — a visual demonstration of the theorem in a non-Euclidean style.
place: China (textual tradition; no findspot)
grade_reason: The tradition and the diagram are real and documented, but the earliest layer's date is disputed and no transmission chain connects it to the Babylonian, Indian, or Greek traditions.
earliest_attestation: The received Zhou Bi Suan Jing (Han); Zhao Shuang commentary (c. 250 CE) for the dissection diagram

sources.ref: Zhou Bi Suan Jing (received text, Han) — the gougu passages
Zhao Shuang commentary (c. 3rd c. CE) — the dissection diagram
Cullen, Astronomy and Mathematics in Ancient China: The Zhou Bi Suan Jing (Cambridge, 1996)

competing_hypotheses: The Zhou-era setting of the Zhou Bi dialogue (Duke of Zhou, 11th c. BCE) is traditional; the received text is Han-era (c. 100 BCE-100 CE), so the early date is the tradition's claim, not the manuscript's
Independent invention: the gougu rule arises from the same practical problems (astronomy, surveying) with no documented contact with the western traditions
falsifiability: A demonstration that the gougu passages are late interpolations, or a documented transmission route, would re-grade the record

title: Jinn in pre-Islamic Arabia: the Palmyrene ginnayê and the poets
claim: Beings named as jinn (or the Aramaic ginnayê) were attested in Arabia before Islam: Palmyrene inscriptions dedicate offerings to the 'good and rewarding gods' ginnayê, and pre-Islamic poetic tradition ascribes poetic inspiration and soothsaying to jinn companions.
place: Palmyra region (inscriptions); the Arabian Peninsula (poetic tradition)
grade_reason: Epigraphic attestation (the carved dedications) plus an independent poetic-tradition strand — graded as the belief-phenomenon, never the beings.
earliest_attestation: The Beth Fasi'el inscription near Palmyra dedicating tribute to the Ginnaye ('the good and rewarding gods'); pre-Islamic Arabic poetry (the jinn-inspired poet / kahin tradition); the Arabic root j-n-n ('to conceal') with Semitic cognates.

sources.ref: Beth Fasi'el inscription near Palmyra — dedication to the Ginnaye
Pre-Islamic Arabic poetry as transmitted in Islamic-era compilations (jinn-inspiration topos)
Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Jinni' — pre-Islamic belief in poet/soothsayer inspiration
