competing_hypotheses: The Palmyrene ginnayê derive from Roman genii (etymological proposal: ginnayê < genius), with only a convergent resemblance to the Arabic jinn
The poetic jinn-inspiration topos is largely a later Islamic-era literary construction retrojected onto the jahiliyya poets
falsifiability: A re-reading of the Beth Fasi'el inscription disproving the ginnayê reading, or proof the inspiration topos appears only in post-Islamic fabrications with no authentic pre-Islamic kernel

title: Magdala — the archaeology of Mary's hometown
claim: The town of Magdala (Migdal; Josephus's Tarichaea) on the Sea of Galilee's western shore has yielded a first-century Jewish town destroyed in 67 CE (Vespasian's campaign): a synagogue discovered in 2009 with the carved Magdala Stone (its seven-branched menorah, at the time of the IAA excavation report, the earliest known Second Temple-period menorah depiction outside Jerusalem), mosaic floors, mikvaot, and harbor works — and in September-October 2026 the excavation of a second first-century synagogue at the site (University of Haifa), reported as making Magdala the only known site with two Second Temple-period synagogues (the superlative is press framing, fenced; the excavation itself is the graded claim).
place: Magdala/Migdal, Sea of Galilee
grade_reason: Excavated, published, and independently visitable; the 2026 second-synagogue report is news-grade but the excavation it reports is a real dig.
earliest_attestation: The 2009 IAA excavation report (Avshalom-Gorni & Najar)

sources.ref: IAA excavation report, Avshalom-Gorni & Najar (2009+) — the synagogue, the Magdala Stone
Josephus, Jewish War 3.462 (Tarichaea)
arkeonews, Sept 2026 — the second-synagogue excavation (University of Haifa)
TBN Watchman Newscast, Oct 2026 — the second-synagogue report (Christian-media framing, fenced)

competing_hypotheses: The Tarichaea=Magdala identification is near-universal but technically inferential
The 'Jesus taught in this synagogue' claim (Matt 4:23, 9:35) is unattested for this specific building
falsifiability: Stratigraphic re-dating of either synagogue to post-70 CE, or identification of the 'second synagogue' as a non-synagogue building

title: The Roman lead-pipe water system (the foil)
claim: Roman cities distributed water through lead pipes (fistulae); lead levels in Roman tap water were measurably elevated (about 100 times natural background), though modern sediment-core analysis finds the contamination was unlikely to have been truly harmful.
place: Rome, Italy
grade_reason: Multiply attested: Frontinus's firsthand treatise, surviving stamped lead fistulae across the Empire (e.g. Portus, Pompeii), and Delile et al. 2014's sediment-core Pb-isotope record matching the pipe lead to mines in Spain, France, England, and Germany. Held at CORROBORATED rather than VERIFIED on the remaining interpretive margin around exact ingested doses.
earliest_attestation: Sextus Julius Frontinus, De aquaeductu (De aquis urbis Romae), c. 97 CE — the water commissioner's own treatise documenting the nine aqueducts; Vitruvius, De architectura 8.6, on lead vs earthen pipes.

sources.ref: Delile, Hugo et al., 'Lead in ancient Rome's city waters,' PNAS 111(18):6594-6599, 2014 — Pb-isotope fingerprinting ties water lead to foreign mines (Spain, France, England, Germany); calcium-carbonate crust insulation; 'unlikely to have been truly harmful'
Frontinus, De aquaeductu, c. 97 CE — documents the nine aqueducts, their maintenance, and water quality administration
Vitruvius, De architectura 8.6.10-11 — warns that water through lead pipes 'must be injurious' (white lead forms) and that earthen pipes are more wholesome; notes lead workers' pallor

competing_hypotheses: The pipes-as-smoking-gun reading (Gilfillan 1965 and popularizers): the elevated lead in the 2014 sediment cores proves mass poisoning — rejected by the study's own authors on the calcium-carbonate insulation and continuous-flow evidence

The terracotta-preference reading: Vitruvius's warning (De architectura 8.6.10-11) shows Romans knew lead pipes were inferior, so earthen pipes were preferred where feasible — but the fistulae network was vast and lead remained standard for urban distribution
falsifiability: Excavation showing Roman urban distribution used no lead pipes, or sediment analysis showing no anthropogenic lead in Imperial-era water sediment — the 2014 study confirmed both the lead and its measurable-but-unlikely-harmful level.

title: Teotihuacan, the Classic-period metropolis of central Mexico
claim: Teotihuacan was a vast planned city in the Valley of Mexico, founded c. 100 BCE: at its zenith (c. 150–450 CE) it held 100,000–200,000 people, making it one of the largest cities in the world and the largest in the pre-Columbian Americas; its monumental core — the Pyramid of the Sun, the Pyramid of the Moon, the Avenue of the Dead, the Feathered Serpent Temple — was sacked and systematically burned c. 550 CE, and the city was abandoned by c. 750 CE.
place: Teotihuacan, Valley of Mexico
grade_reason: The city stands: 21–30 km² of excavated urban fabric, a monumental core dated by stratigraphy and radiocarbon across a century of independent campaigns (Millon's mapping project, INAH excavations, UNESCO 1987) — multiple independent lines, not one excavation.
earliest_attestation: The archaeology itself is the earliest witness — 21–30 km² of excavated urban fabric. Earliest surviving external written mention: Maya hieroglyphic texts of the Classic period render the city as 'puh', 'Place of Reeds'.

sources.ref: Rene Millon, Urbanization at Teotihuacan (University of Texas Press, 1973) — the Teotihuacan Mapping Project
George L. Cowgill, Ancient Teotihuacan: Early Urbanism in Central Mexico (Cambridge University Press, 2015)
Saburo Sugiyama, Human Sacrifice, Militarism, and Rulership (Cambridge University Press, 2005) — Feathered Serpent dedicatory sacrifices (~200 victims)
Sergio Gomez Chavez, Proyecto Tlalocan field reports, INAH 2003–2018 — the Feathered Serpent tunnel and its offerings
UNESCO World Heritage inscription 1987 — 'Pre-Hispanic City of Teotihuacan'

competing_hypotheses: Foundation c. 100 BCE (standard) vs c. 200 BCE (earlier urban growth accounts)
Peak population 100,000 (conservative) vs 150,000 vs 250,000 (upper estimates)
Builders: Totonac vs Otomi vs a multiethnic coalition — the ethnic identity of the founders is genuinely unknown, and the city's original name is unknown
falsifiability: Sealed-context radiocarbon or stratigraphic dates placing the monumental architecture outside c. 100 BCE–750 CE, or demonstration that the excavated fabric is modern reconstruction

title: The gladiator's missio — mercy in the arena
claim: A defeated gladiator could appeal for mercy by raising an index finger (ad digitum); the munus's editor then granted or refused 'missio' (release), following the crowd's expressed wishes.
place: Amphitheatres of the Roman world (Colosseum as the type site)
grade_reason: Multiple independent Roman sources describe the mechanism (Martial's ad digitum formula, the shout vocabulary Mitte!/Iugula!, the editor's decision, the missio term, the sine missione exception); held below VERIFIED because the crowd-vs-editor decision mechanics rest on literary and later accounts rather than a single procedural document.
earliest_attestation: Martial, De Spectaculis 29 (1st c. CE): the law 'when the prize was set up, to fight until the finger was raised (ad digitum)'

sources.ref: Martial, De Spectaculis 29 — 'when the prize was set up, to fight until the finger was raised (ad digitum)'; Caesar 'obeyed his own law'
The crowd vocabulary: 'Mitte!' (let him go) / 'Iugula!' (kill him); 'Habet, hoc habet!' (he's had it) — the attested shout lexicon
The editor muneris (games' sponsor) as the decider; the emperor as the most conspicuous editor at Rome
Munus sine missione — bouts without release, the documented exception (Augustus-era restrictions tradition)
Cavillargues medallion — 'STANTES MISSI' (released standing): the mercy granted, commemorated

competing_hypotheses: Crowd participation may have been more ritual than decisive — the editor's political calculus (pleasing the crowd while protecting his investment in trained gladiators) is the real mechanism, so 'the crowd decided' can be overstated
The 'morituri te salutant' salute may have been a criminals' formula, not the gladiators' (Suetonius, Claudius 21) — carried to fence the ceremony, not adjudicated here
falsifiability: Contemporary evidence that defeated gladiators had no formal mercy procedure, or that 'missio' meant something other than release from the bout

title: The Sepulchre road toward Calvary (Stasolla's hypothesis, 2026)
claim: A broad stepped road uncovered in the Holy Sepulchre excavations, from the early-Roman phase before Hadrian's 2nd-century rebuilding, may have ascended toward the area of Calvary — providing access to a place of public executions. Stasolla's own words: 'One possibility – at present no more than a hypothesis.'
place: Church of the Holy Sepulchre, Jerusalem (traditional)
grade_reason: Attested by the excavator herself as an explicit hypothesis — single-source, unreviewed, with the excavator's own fence that it is no more than a possibility.
earliest_attestation: Excavator's hypothesis reported via press, c. 16 October 2026 (Stasolla, Sapienza)

sources.ref: catholiconline.news, ~16 Oct 2026: Stasolla 'suggested that the road may have provided access to an area used for public executions'; quoting her directly: 'One possibility – at present no more than a hypothesis – is that this was a suburban road ascending toward the area of the Calvary, assuming that the site functioned as a place of public executions.' Researchers also considered, and downweighted, the Hadrian-era construction-material-transport explanation (the broad step complicates cart movement).
Stasolla's context: 'What is certain is that the place of execution must have been public and accessible' — consistent with Roman crucifixion practice as deliberately public spectacle.

competing_hypotheses: The road served Hadrian's 2nd-century construction program (transport of building material) — downweighted by the excavator because the broad step would have complicated cart movement, not ruled out
An ordinary suburban road unrelated to executions; the Calvary association is the researcher's reach toward the site's tradition
falsifiability: Absolute dating of the road's construction/uses to the post-Hadrianic period, or excavation evidence that the area was not used for executions in the early-Roman phase, would close the hypothesis

title: The invention of glassblowing (c. 50–25 BCE, Levant)
claim: Glassblowing was invented in the coastal Levant in the final quarter of the 1st century BCE.
place: Jerusalem (Jewish Quarter excavations)
grade_reason: CORROBORATED: the invention event is archaeologically attested — the earliest glassblowing debris comes from a sealed Herodian-period context in Jerusalem, with Judean glass production sites also found in Galilee — but the inventor is anonymous, so it stays below VERIFIED.
earliest_attestation: Workshop debris in the Jewish Quarter, Jerusalem — a fill layer inside a ritual bath sealed by Herodian street paving (Herod the Great / Herod Archelaus era, under Augustus)

sources.ref: Phys.org / Corning Museum of Glass reporting: glassblowing invented toward the end of the 1st century BCE in the coastal Levant (Syria, Lebanon, Israel, Palestine, Jordan); earliest evidence Jerusalem, final quarter of 1st c. BCE, Herod the Great / Herod Archelaus under Augustus; the tube-reworking recycling experiment

Wikipedia 'History of glass': glass blowing discovered on the Syro-Judean coast during the 1st century BCE; first evidence in the Jewish Quarter of Jerusalem, in fill inside a ritual bath overlain by Herodian street paving; Judean glass sites in Galilee

Penn Museum, 'Roman Glass': no Latin word for glass until ~65 BCE; scarcely a century after blown glass was invented it was in virtually every Roman house; Syrian and Judaean craftsmen shipped to Italy as spoils of war ~10 BCE

David Whitehouse, 'Looking Through Roman Glass', Archaeology Magazine (1997): glassblowing discovered in the Syro-Palestinian region during the first century B.C.; vessels commonplace empire-wide by the first century A.D.

competing_hypotheses: Independent invention elsewhere (no earlier blown vessel is known anywhere)
The recycling-experiment origin: the Jerusalem evidence suggests furnace workers were reworking heated glass-tube ends — someone blew into a tube and changed the industry
falsifiability: A blown glass vessel securely dated earlier than the Jerusalem floor, from outside the Levant

title: The Library of Alexandria — the single-catastrophic-fire claim
claim: The Great Library of Alexandria was destroyed in a single catastrophic fire (Julius Caesar's fire of 48 BCE being the most-cited candidate).
place: Alexandria, Egypt (Brucheion quarter, traditional)
grade_reason: Every named destruction event fails as a single-fire explanation: Strabo's library outlives Caesar's fire, five contemporary accounts of 391 CE mention no library, the 642 story is a 13th-century fabrication, and the institution declined over centuries through defunding and unreplaced scrolls.
earliest_attestation: Seneca (1st c. CE, quoting Livy) on Caesar's harbor fire; no ancient source describes a single destruction of the Library itself.

sources.ref: Strabo, Geography 17.1.8 (c. 25 BCE) — describes the Mouseion and its library still functioning ~23 years after Caesar's fire
Caesar, Civil War 3.111 — describes burning ships in the harbor; says nothing about the Library
Five contemporary accounts of the Serapeum's destruction, 391 CE — none mention a library burning
Bar Hebraeus (13th c.) — the Caliph Omar story; fabricating ~600 years after the 642 conquest
Luciano Canfora, The Vanished Library (1987) — gradual-decline synthesis
Bernard Lewis — the Omar story as later fabrication

competing_hypotheses: Caesar's fire destroyed a harbor warehouse of export scrolls (the ancient damage that grew into the myth)
The Library's core collection declined as Ptolemaic funding collapsed and expelled scholars left; scrolls rotted unreplaced — a maintenance failure, not a fire
The Mouseion survived in diminished form into the 3rd c. CE (Aurelian's 270 CE campaign damaged the quarter)
falsifiability: A contemporary account describing the main Library burning in a single event, or an ancient source listing the destruction as one date — none exists in the record.

title: Jesus of Nazareth
claim: Jesus of Nazareth, a Jewish teacher in Roman Galilee and Judea, was crucified under Pontius Pilate (c. 30 CE); his followers proclaimed his resurrection, founding the movement that became Christianity.
place: Nazareth (traditional)
grade_reason: Multiple independent attestations within a century - Pauline letters (20-30 years out), the Gospels, Josephus's two passages (one near-universally authentic, one majority-partial), Tacitus's hostile Roman notice, Suetonius, and Pliny - agree on a historical figure crucified under Pilate; the prefect's own name is in stone at Caesarea. No contemporary inscription or Roman record of Jesus survives, so the ceiling is CORROBORATED, not VERIFIED.
earliest_attestation: Paul's letters (c. 50s CE, earliest); the Gospel of Mark (c. 70 CE); Josephus, Antiquities 18 and 20 (c. 93 CE, partially interpolated); Tacitus, Annals 15.44 (c. 116 CE). NB: these are composition dates — the earliest surviving physical witnesses are centuries later: P52 (2nd c., disputed exact date), P46/P66/P75 (c. 200–250 CE). See evt-p52-fragments-001 for the transmission gap.

sources.ref: Paul's letters (1 Thessalonians, Galatians, 1 Corinthians — c. 50s CE)
Gospel of Mark (c. 70 CE)
Josephus, Antiquities 18.63-64 and 20.200 (c. 93 CE; Testimonium partly interpolated)
Tacitus, Annals 15.44 (c. 116 CE, independent Roman attestation)
OpenBible.info geocoding (Nazareth, Capernaum, Jerusalem)
The transmission gap: no autograph survives; earliest NT copies are 2nd-3rd c. papyri (see evt-p52-fragments-001)
Josephus, Antiquities 20.200 - 'the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James' (authenticity accepted by the overwhelming majority of scholars)
The Testimonium Flavianum (Antiquities 18.63-64): authentic core + Christian interpolations - assessed as its own record, evt-testimonium-flavianum-001

Tacitus, Annals 15.44 (c. 116 CE): 'Christus ... suffered the extreme penalty during the reign of Tiberius at the hands of one of our procurators, Pontius Pilatus' - a hostile Roman witness (calls Christianity a 'destructive superstition')
Suetonius, Life of Claudius 25.4 ('Chrestus' - Jews expelled from Rome, c. 49 CE); Pliny the Younger, Letters 10.96-97 to Trajan (Christians in Bithynia, c. 112 CE)

Pilate Stone (Caesarea Maritima, 1961, Frova excavations): '[Pon]tius Pilatus [praef]ectus Iuda[ea]e' - the only non-literary confirmation of Pilate's existence; settles the title as prefect, not procurator (Tacitus's word is the anachronism). Israel Museum, Jerusalem

Gregor et al. (2025) — re-analysis of Carrier's Bayesian historicity argument reported in the secondary literature (cited via the 'On the Historicity of Jesus' survey, accessed Oct 2026): Carrier's reference class of pre-10th-century-BCE figures was challenged as producing false negatives; with post-10th-century-BCE samples (closer to Jesus' period) the computed historicity probability moved from Carrier's 33% to 99% on the corrected class. Carried secondhand — the primary paper was not read in this pass; the point recorded is the peer-reviewed direction of the 2025 exchange, not the headline number. Added 2026-10-16 (III.21 second pass).

Gathercole, S., 'The undisputed Pauline letters presuppose a historical and human Jesus', Journal for the Study of the Historical Jesus (2025, per the secondary survey) — a direct peer-reviewed counter to the mythicist reading of Paul as describing a purely celestial figure. Carried secondhand; primary not read in this pass. Added 2026-10-16 (III.21 second pass).

McGrath, J., 'The Obsolete Paradigm Of A Purely Mythical Jesus' (Patheos, Aug 2026) summarizing the JSNT (Journal for the Study of the New Testament) review of a 2026 volume engaging Carrier's mythicist case — carried secondhand, the primary review not read in this pass: the review's verdict (the historicity paradigm 'alive and well', mythicism 'obsolete in 2026 as it was prior') recorded as the peer-reviewed direction of the 2026 exchange, not evidence. Added 2026-10-18 (III.21 fifth pass).

competing_hypotheses: Jesus was a historical apocalyptic preacher whose followers preserved his teachings (mainstream scholarly consensus - e.g., Ehrman 2012, Sanders, Vermes)

Jesus is a mythic figure with no historical core (mythicist minority, e.g., Carrier, Price) - stated fairly, rejected by the mainstream; the honest counterpoint is that all sources are non-contemporary
The minimalist objection that the 2025 Gregor re-analysis merely trades Carrier's prior for another (reported as contested — carried secondhand, not adjudicated in this pass)

The 2026 Holy Sepulchre excavation (quarry → garden → rock-cut tombs, consistent with John's setting) is grade-neutral on the person question: it documents the world, never the man (see evt-holy-sepulchre-excavation-2026-001 CORROBORATED; the 'tomb found' press telling DEBUNKED at evt-holy-sepulchre-tomb-found-telling-001)
falsifiability: A contemporary Roman or Jewish source naming Jesus of Nazareth would raise this to VERIFIED; the grade honestly reflects the gap between attestation and contemporaneity

title: The claim that Jesus of Nazareth was born on December 25
claim: Jesus of Nazareth was born on December 25 — that the calendar date of his birth is known and is the 25th of December.
place: Bethlehem (traditional)
grade_reason: The date dies on the documents, not on skepticism: no Gospel gives a date, the December 25 date first appears c. 336 CE as a liturgical assignment, and the 'stolen from a pagan solstice festival' story it is usually paired with has thin evidence (Hijmans).
earliest_attestation: No Gospel gives a month, day, or year. The December 25 date first appears in the Chronograph of 354 (Philocalian Calendar), whose Depositio Martirum ('VIII kal. Ian. natus Christus in Betleem Iudeae') was compiled c. 336 CE — three centuries after the event.

sources.ref: The Gospels of Matthew and Luke: the nativity narratives name no month, day, or year

Chronograph of 354 (Philocalian Calendar), Depositio Martirum: 'VIII kal. Ian. natus Christus in Betleem Iudeae' — earliest undisputed attestation of December 25 as Christ's birth date; depositio compiled c. 336
Nothaft, C. P. E., 'The Origins of the Christmas Date: Some Recent Trends in Historical Research' — surveys the two main hypotheses (History of Religions vs calculation)

Hijmans, S. E. (2003 article; 2009 Groningen dissertation, 583-95): the evidence for a December 25 festival of Sol Invictus is thin; none of Sol's recorded festivals fell on the winter solstice (Aug 8/9, Aug 28, Oct 19/22, Dec 11)
Simmons, E., 'The Origins of Christmas and the Date of Christ's Birth,' JETS 58.2 (2015), 299-324
Forbes, B. D., Christmas: A Candid History (University of California Press, 2007)

competing_hypotheses: The calculation hypothesis (Duchesne): Dec 25 was derived by symbolic arithmetic — March 25 (annunciation / creation) plus nine months — predating Sol Invictus's popularity; the Hippolytus Commentary-on-Daniel passage (c. 204) as possible early attestation, though the passage's authenticity is contested as a possible later interpolation

The History-of-Religions thesis (Usener 1889): the date annexed a pagan winter-solstice festival (Sol Invictus, Aurelian 274); held below the evidence — Hijmans shows the Dec-25 Sol festival evidence is thin, and the first to claim Christians copied pagans was the anti-Christian emperor Julian
The simple shepherds argument: Luke's shepherds keeping watch in the fields points away from midwinter — circumstantial, not decisive
falsifiability: A contemporary or near-contemporary (1st-2nd c.) source dating the birth to December 25 would overturn the grade; the current earliest attestation of the date is c. 336 CE

title: The James ossuary inscription
claim: The Aramaic inscription 'Ya'akov bar Yosef akhui di Yeshua' (James, son of Joseph, brother of Jesus) on the James ossuary is an authentic 1st-century inscription identifying the family of Jesus of Nazareth.
place: Reported as found near Silwan, Jerusalem (unverifiable — antiquities-market provenance)
grade_reason: The limestone box is an authentic ancient ossuary, but the inscription — the claim that matters — is DEBUNKED per the strongest evidence: the 2003 IAA scientific committee verdict (modern forgery, patina artificially applied) and the Geological Survey of Israel's isotopic analysis showing the letters' patina could not have formed under natural Judean conditions in 2000 years. The forgery objections (Krumbein 2006; Harrell cleanser hypothesis) are named as minority positions, not consensus.
earliest_attestation: Inscription brought to scholarly attention by André Lemaire (2002); ossuary obtained by collector Oded Golan, who said he purchased it in the 1970s through the antiquities market — no controlled excavation provenance

sources.ref: Israel Antiquities Authority committee report, 18 June 2003: inscription declared a modern forgery; inscription carved through the natural rock varnish

Geological Survey of Israel (Dr. Amos Bein, 22 June 2003): oxygen-isotope analysis — letters' patina significantly different from authentic ossuary patinas; could not have formed under Judean conditions of the last 2000 years
ARCHAEOLOGY (Archaeological Institute of America), 'Ossuary Dethroned' (24 July 2003): IAA verdict and police confiscation context

Minority contest: Krumbein (2006, defense-called patina expert) — inscription ancient, patina removed by cleaning; Harrell — cleanser explains δ18O discrepancy. Named in competing hypotheses, not consensus

Oct-2026 press recycle (aggregator re-report ~Oct 7, 2026): 'the most important archaeological discovery ever linked to Jesus Christ's era' — no new evidence; the piece itself restates the 2003 IAA verdict, the 2012 acquittal, and the judge's caveat. Venue flagged advocacy-adjacent; grade-neutral (Turin-shroud precedent)

competing_hypotheses: The ossuary box is a genuine 1st-century artifact; the inscription is an authentic family record (minority position, e.g. Krumbein's 2006 patina analysis; Harrell's cleanser explanation of the isotopic discrepancy)
The box is genuine but the inscription was cut in modern times onto the ancient box (IAA committee 2003 verdict, supported by the Geological Survey of Israel)

Even if the inscription is ancient, the names James, Joseph, and Jesus were all extremely common in 1st-century Judea, so the identification with the New Testament family is not established by the inscription alone
falsifiability: A controlled-excavation parallel, or peer-reviewed material analysis showing the letter patina formed continuously with the surface patina over two millennia, would reopen the question. The minority patina analyses have not carried a peer-reviewed consensus.

title: Cova Dones Roman sanctuary — the Domina inscriptions (announced 2026-10-20)
claim: At Cova Dones (Millares, Valencia, Spain), the DONARQ project has documented at least 120 Latin inscriptions in an underground Roman sanctuary chamber more than 200 m below the surface — the largest Latin cave-inscription corpus known in the Roman Empire, surpassing La Griega (107). Most are dated by the team to the 1st–2nd centuries CE. Five votive inscriptions are dedicated to a goddess reverentially called Domina ('the Lady'), whose specific epithet (possibly water-connected) is still being read; preliminary readings indicate some women inscribed their own vows, and in-situ offerings include spindle whorls, rings, a bracelet, chalice-shaped vessels and a Roman coin of Claudius found in the 2024 campaign.
place: Cova Dones, Millares, Valencia, Spain
geo_anchor: textual (published site location; coordinates not surveyed in this pass)
grade_reason: House standard for named-institution excavation announcements (cf. Saudi Heritage Commission 2026 records): named project (DONARQ), named universities, named epigraphers, specific counts and named comparanda, artifacts documented in situ — the corpus's existence and scale are CORROBORATED. Two sub-claims are graded lower and fenced: (1) the 'well-organized, structured cult' reading is the team's interpretation of the inscriptions' concentration — CLAIMED as interpretation; (2) the suggestion that the site's recorded name Cova de les Dones ('Cave of the Women') preserves a fossilized memory of the cult is explicitly offered by the team as a possibility — SPECULATION. The Domina epithet is unread as of the announcement; no peer-reviewed edition exists yet, so no part of this record is VERIFIED.
earliest_attestation: DONARQ project announcement via University of Southampton / University of Zaragoza / University of Alicante, 20 October 2026 (phys.org syndication of the university release). The Roman sanctuary itself was first revealed in 2024; only ~15 inscriptions were previously known.

sources.ref: University of Southampton news release, syndicated as 'Largest collection of Roman cave inscriptions discovered in Spain', phys.org, 2026-10-20 — DONARQ project led by Dr. Aitor Ruiz-Redondo (Zaragoza/Southampton) and Dr. Virginia Barciela (Alicante); epigraphy by Dr. Silvia Alfayé (Zaragoza) and Dr. Sergio García-Dils (UNED-Seville); quotes, counts (>=120 inscriptions; 5 Domina votives), La Griega comparison (107, one female name), offerings in situ, Claudius coin (2024 campaign)

Ancient Pages, 'Archaeologists Uncover Largest Collection Of Roman Cave Inscriptions, Revealing Ancient Women's Cult', 2026-10-20/22 — secondary restatement of the same university release (NOT an independent source; counted as venue echo, not corroboration)

competing_hypotheses: The team's reading: a structured cult of a single goddess (Domina) in which women were active dedicants, unusual for Roman cave sanctuaries (supported by 5 Domina votives + female-associated offerings in situ).
Weaker reading: women were present among a broader dedicant population and the Domina cluster is one sector's local emphasis — the concentration argument needs the full published corpus to test.
The name-origin suggestion (Cova de les Dones as fossilized cult memory) is a possibility raised by the team, not a finding — medieval/early-modern naming could have independent causes.
falsifiability: Publication of the full epigraphic corpus: if the Domina dedications or the female dedicants dissolve on full reading (misread names, joins, or re-dating), the cult claim falls; if the corpus confirms >=120 inscriptions with the Domina cluster intact, the grade can rise toward VERIFIED.

title: The folding fan was invented in Japan (~9th c.) and traveled Japan→China
claim: The folding fan (sensu/ōgi) was invented in Japan around the 9th century, in the hi-ogi form of thin cypress slats riveted at one end — and from Japan the folding fan traveled to China, not the reverse.
place: Heian-kyo (Kyoto), Japan
grade_reason: CORROBORATED — independent lines agree: Kyoto Women's University (Google Arts & Culture) dates the invention to ~9th c. and the China export to the 10th (wasen); USC Pacific Asia Museum gives 9th c.; the haes-producties survey documents 10th-c. literary attestation and Song-court records. Held below VERIFIED — the 9th-c. date rests on court tradition and scholarship, not a surviving 9th-c. artifact.
earliest_attestation: Japanese court use, Heian period; Japanese dictionary c. 935 listing Uchiwa and Ogi; Song-dynasty Chinese court records of folding-fan gifts

sources.ref: Kyoto Women's University, Lifestyle Design Laboratory (Google Arts & Culture, 'Kyō-sensu — Folding Fans from Kyoto'): 'The folding fan was invented in Japan around the 9th century... Japanese folding fans were exported to mainland China in the 10th century and were known as wasen in China'
USC Pacific Asia Museum (Google Arts & Culture, 'Fans of East Asia'): 'In the 9th century, the first folding fans, known as Sensu, emerged in Japan'

'History — Japanese Fans' (haes-producties.nl): earliest literary references to the folding fan in both Japan and China date from the 10th century; Japanese dictionary c. 935 lists Uchiwa and Ogi; Song-dynasty records of folding fans as gifts at the Chinese court; Choho-era (999–1003) sumptuary laws on fans

anart4life.com ('The mystical appeal of Japanese fans'): oldest known surviving fans are Chinese woven bamboo hand screens (tomb c. 2nd c. BCE); Japan's fixed uchiwa arrived from China in the Nara period; the folding sensu emerged 6th–9th c. in Japan and was introduced back to China

competing_hypotheses: The haes-producties chronology: earliest literary references date from the 10th century (a Japanese dictionary c. 935 lists Uchiwa and Ogi), Song-dynasty records note folding-fan gifts at the Chinese court — consistent with a 9th-c. invention, but the paper trail starts later than the consensus date
The bat-wing legend (reported in The Free Library's fan history): the fold was inspired by bat wings — carried as legend, not attestation

The rigid uchiwa (round paper fan) predates the folding fan in Japan and arrived from China (oldest known fans from a Chinese tomb c. 2nd c. BCE) — the folding mechanism is the Japanese innovation, not the fan itself
falsifiability: A securely dated pre-9th-century folding fan from outside Japan, or a Chinese textual attestation of a folding fan predating Japanese use

title: Mary Magdalene — the canonical figure
claim: Mary of Magdala is attested in the earliest Christian writings as a follower of Jesus: named among the women who 'provided for them out of their resources' (Luke 8:1-3, with the note that seven demons had gone out of her), named at the crucifixion (Mark 15:40; John 19:25), named at the burial (Mark 15:47), named first at the tomb in all four gospels (Mark 16:1; Matt 28:1; Luke 24:10; John 20:1), and in John 20:11-18 the first person commissioned to carry the resurrection claim ('go to my brothers'). 'Magdalene' is a place-name: Mary of Magdala/Migdal, the fishing town on the Sea of Galilee (Josephus, Jewish War 3.462, Tarichaea).
place: Magdala/Migdal, Sea of Galilee
grade_reason: Multiply attested across the earliest narrative sources, including the embarrassment-grade detail that a woman is the first commissioned witness.
earliest_attestation: The Gospel of Mark (c. 70 CE); Paul's letters (c. 50s CE) do not name her

sources.ref: Luke 8:1-3 (the women who provided; the seven demons note)
Mark 15:40, 15:47, 16:1 (cross, burial, tomb)
John 19:25, 20:1-18 (cross; first witness, the commission)
Josephus, Jewish War 3.462 (Tarichaea/Magdala)

competing_hypotheses: The Magdalene is a composite literary figure assembled by the evangelists
The figure is entirely a narrative function with no historical referent (carried fairly; the mythicist lane)
falsifiability: A pre-Markan textual witness naming a different 'Mary of Magdala' tradition, or proof the Markan tomb narratives are second-century compositions

title: The emergence of Christianity
claim: In the mid-1st century CE, the Jesus movement spread from Judea/Galilee through the eastern Roman Empire as distinct Christian communities, documented by Paul's letters and noted by Roman officials by the early 2nd century.
place: Jerusalem (traditionally the movement's origin)
grade_reason: Contemporary 1st-century letters document the communities, and independent Roman officials (Pliny, Tacitus) confirm Christianity's spread and persecution by the early 2nd century.
earliest_attestation: Paul's letters (c. 50s CE); Acts of the Apostles; Pliny the Younger, Epistles 10.96 (c. 112 CE); Tacitus, Annals 15.44 (c. 116 CE)

sources.ref: Paul's letters (c. 50s CE)
Pliny the Younger, Epistles 10.96 to Trajan (c. 112 CE)
Tacitus, Annals 15.44 (Neronian persecution, c. 116 CE)
Dura-Europos house church (archaeology of 3rd-c. Christian worship, later but material)

competing_hypotheses: A Jewish renewal movement that rapidly Gentilized after Paul (consensus outline)
The Jerusalem church and the Pauline mission were more distinct movements than Acts suggests (scholarly debate)
falsifiability: 1st-century evidence showing no Christian communities outside Judea by 100 CE would overturn the spread narrative

title: 'Red sky at night, shepherd's delight' (verified folk meteorology)
claim: 'Red sky at night, shepherd's delight; red sky in the morning, shepherd's warning' — a red sunset presages fair weather the next day, and a red sunrise presages foul weather, because mid-latitude weather systems move from west to east.
place: England (mid-latitude saying; biblical and Shakespearean attestations)
grade_reason: The mechanism is documented across independent sources: high-pressure air traps dust and aerosols, which scatter blue wavelengths (Rayleigh scattering) leaving red; with mid-latitude systems moving west to east, a red sunset means high pressure (fair weather) approaching from the west, while a red sunrise means the high pressure has passed eastward and low pressure follows. Wikipedia's weather-lore survey, BBC Science Focus, and the Met Office (via the Gazette) all confirm the physical basis with the mid-latitude scope fence.
earliest_attestation: Matthew 16:2-3 — 'When it is evening, ye say, It will be fair weather: for the sky is red. And in the morning, It will be foul weather: for the sky is red and threatening.'

sources.ref: Wikipedia 'Weather lore' — 'Red sky at night': 'When weather systems predominantly move from west to east, a red sky at night indicates that the high pressure air (and better weather) is westwards. In the morning the light is eastwards, and so a red sky then indicates the high pressure (and better weather) has already passed, and an area of low pressure is following behind.' Notes the Rayleigh scattering mechanism and the Australian reversal.

BBC Science Focus Magazine, 'Is there any truth behind the saying red sky at night, shepherd's delight?': 'a red sunset does typically presage clear skies the following day. However, this only holds true in regions where weather systems mostly travel from west to east, which includes most mid-latitude areas such as the UK.' Explains the pressure–particle–scattering mechanism for both the evening and morning cases.

Matthew 16:2-3 (authorized 1903 translation, via Farm Collector): 'When it is evening, ye say, It will be fair weather: for the sky is red. And in the morning, It will be foul weather: for the sky is red and threatening.' — the saying's oldest attestation, ~2,000 years of currency
Shakespeare, Venus and Adonis, lines 453-456 (1593): 'Like a red morn that ever yet betoken'd, Wreck to the seaman, tempest to the field...' — the saying in Elizabethan English

competing_hypotheses: The saying as pure coincidence or confirmation bias (refuted by the physical mechanism: the correlation follows from Rayleigh scattering plus the west-to-east motion of mid-latitude systems, not from selective memory)

The saying as universal (fenced: it holds only where weather systems predominantly move west to east — the tropics and southern-hemisphere reversals break it, as the weather-lore literature notes for Australian readers)
falsifiability: A meteorological analysis showing no correlation between sunset/sunrise redness and next-day weather in mid-latitudes, or a physical account contradicting the pressure-scattering mechanism

title: 'This is my body': the institution narrative, earliest written form (~55 CE)
claim: The words of institution ('this is my body... this cup is the new covenant in my blood') are quadruply attested: 1 Cor 11:23-25 (~55 CE, the earliest written account, already a fixed liturgical formula predating the gospels), Mark 14:22-25, Matt 26:26-29, Luke 22:19-20. Whether ipsissima verba or early-church formulation is debated; an early meal tradition is not in doubt.
grade_reason: Multiple independent attestations with the earliest in fixed liturgical form within ~25 years of the crucifixion
competing_hypotheses: The wording is Jesus's own (traditional)
The wording is early-church liturgical formulation retrojected into the narrative (form-critical)
falsifiability: A pre-55 CE manuscript lacking the formula would revise the dating

title: The Great Fire of Rome, July 64 CE
claim: The Great Fire of Rome broke out in the night of 18–19 July 64 CE (reign of Nero) and burned for six days and seven nights (Tacitus; Dio says nine days), devastating the city.
place: Rome, Italy — the 14 Augustan regions
grade_reason: The fire as an event is independently attested by three ancient historians writing in three different centuries' removes (Tacitus ~116, Suetonius ~121, Dio ~229), with Nero's relief measures (Antium return, opened gardens/palaces, grain-price reduction) and the subsequent Christian persecution (Tacitus 15.44) as the independently witnessed political facts. The cause — not the occurrence — is what the sources contest.
earliest_attestation: Tacitus, Annals 15.38–44 (written c. 116–120 CE, ~50 years after); Suetonius, Nero 38; Dio Cassius, Roman History 62.16–18. No contemporary surviving account.

sources.ref: Tacitus, Annals 15.38–44 — the fire's outbreak (shops at the Circus Maximus), spread, Nero at Antium and his return, relief measures (opened gardens and buildings, grain-price cut), the rumor of the private-stage performance (15.39), the Christian scapegoating (15.44); the cause hedged as uncertain (incertum an dolo principis)
Suetonius, Nero 38 — the fire watched from the tower of Maecenas, 'the Sack of Ilium' in stage costume; the arson asserted more flatly (men with tow and torches on Nero's orders)

Dio Cassius, Roman History 62.16–18 — the fire's course, the arson asserted (soldiers setting fires by order), Nero singing the 'Capture of Troy' from the palace roof in lyre-player's costume; duration 9 days
HISTORY.com, 'Did Nero Really Fiddle While Rome Burned?' — fire began July 64, 10 of 14 districts burned, Nero at Antium 35 miles away, relief measures, Christians blamed
Live Science / Prof. Anthony Drake — Rome 64: 10 of 14 districts burned, thousands displaced in a city of 500,000–1M; rumor mechanics and the cithara correction

competing_hypotheses: The standard account (Tacitus Annals 15.38–44): the fire began in the shops around the Circus Maximus, on the side adjoining the Palatine and Caelian hills, and was driven by wind through the dense timber districts; 10 of the 14 Augustan regions were affected — 3 destroyed, 7 badly damaged.

The arson-by-Nero position: Suetonius (Nero 38) and Dio Cassius (62.18) report, more flatly than Tacitus, that the fire was started on Nero's orders (to clear ground for the Domus Aurea); some ancient writers claimed his men were seen with torches. Tacitus himself hedges: whether it was accidental or 'by the treachery of the emperor' is uncertain (incertum an dolo principis).

The modern scholarly middle position: the fire's scale is not disputed; the cause is not provable from the surviving sources. Modern readings (e.g. the firebreak thesis: the alleged 'arsonists' were vigiles and Praetorians creating firebreaks, unwelcome but necessary) treat the ancient blame narrative as partly political — Nero's unpopularity with the senatorial class and the Christians shaped the transmission.
falsifiability: A contemporary inscription or dated document fixing a different year, or dendrochronological/archaeological evidence from Rome contradicting a city-wide conflagration in 64 CE, would overturn the grade.

title: Nero fiddled while Rome burned — the anachronistic legend
claim: Nero fiddled while Rome burned — the popular image of the emperor playing the violin during the Great Fire of Rome (July 64 CE).
place: Rome, Italy — the rumor's claimed scene
grade_reason: Three independent kills. (1) THE ANACHRONISM: the viol class of instruments, to which the fiddle belongs, was not developed until the 11th century (HISTORY.com, citing music historians); bowed instruments would not become popular for another 1,000 years (Live Science / Drake). If Nero played anything it would have been a cithara — a portable seven-string harp — not a fiddle. (2) TACITUS HEDGED: the source-critical fact — Tacitus reports the singing as a rumor (pervaserat rumor), in an indirect statement, 'unconfirmed by eyewitness accounts' (HISTORY.com). The most authoritative ancient source never states it as fact. (3) HE WASN'T THERE: Nero was at his villa at Antium, ~35 miles from Rome, when the fire broke out; he returned and organized relief (opened palaces and gardens, cut grain prices). The fiddle never existed, the singing was rumor, the player was 35 miles away.
earliest_attestation: Tacitus, Annals 15.39: the rumor (pervaserat rumor) that Nero mounted his private stage (domesticam scaenam) and sang of the destruction of Troy (cecinisse Troianum excidium) — reported as RUMOR, unconfirmed by eyewitnesses, in an indirect statement. Suetonius, Nero 38 and Dio 62.18 report the performance more flatly (singing the Sack of Ilium / Capture of Troy in stage costume). None of the three mentions a fiddle; none is presented by Tacitus as established fact.

sources.ref: Tacitus, Annals 15.39 (Latin text via Open Book Publishers commentary): 'pervaserat rumor ipso tempore flagrantis urbis inisse eum domesticam scaenam et cecinisse Troianum excidium' — the rumor of the private-stage performance of the Fall of Troy; reported as rumor only, in indirect statement
Suetonius, Nero 38 — the 'Sack of Ilium' sung in stage costume while watching from the Maecenas tower (singing, not fiddling)
Dio Cassius 62.18 — Nero on the palace roof in lyre-player's costume singing the 'Capture of Troy' (the costume detail, not a fiddle)

HISTORY.com, 'Did Nero Really Fiddle While Rome Burned?' — viol class not developed until the 11th century; cithara the plausible instrument; Tacitus's rumor 'unconfirmed by eyewitness accounts'; Nero at Antium, relief measures
Live Science / Prof. Anthony Drake — bowed instruments 'would not become popular for another 1,000 years'; cithara correction; Nero's relief efforts and exhaustion

competing_hypotheses: The popular-culture position: Nero played a fiddle as Rome burned — indifference in musical form. This is the version in the schoolbooks and the cartoons.
The source-critical position (this record): the 'fiddle' is an invention of later centuries; the ancient claim was a rumor of singing, and Tacitus reports it as rumor only.

The hostile-transmission position: later Christian and senatorial writers, hostile to Nero, elaborated the performance story to fix his image as a theatrical tyrant — the elaboration tells us about the transmission, not about July 64.
falsifiability: A contemporary (64 CE) source — a letter, graffito, or inscription — recording Nero playing a bowed string instrument during the fire would overturn the grade. The violin family's documented 16th-century Italian origin makes this effectively impossible.

title: The Roman persecution of Christians
claim: The Roman state persecuted Christians across three centuries — episodic and regional, never continuous — documented by contemporary and near-contemporary sources: Tacitus on the Neronian scapegoating of 64 CE, the Pliny–Trajan exchange of c. 112 CE, the Decian universal-sacrifice edict and its 45 surviving libelli certificates of 250 CE, and the Diocletianic Great Persecution of 303–311 CE, closed by Galerius's 311 Edict of Toleration and the Milan letters of 313.
place: Rome (Neronian persecution); the phenomenon spans the empire, 64–313 CE
grade_reason: Multiple independent primary sources across three centuries agree on the phenomenon; the exact death counts and Eusebius's 'ten persecutions' schema are later historiographical construction, so the ceiling stays CORROBORATED.
earliest_attestation: Tacitus, Annals 15.44 (c. 116 CE, on the events of 64 CE); Pliny, Epistles 10.96–97 (c. 112 CE, the in-office exchange)

sources.ref: Tacitus, Annals 15.44 (Neronian scapegoating, 64 CE)
Pliny the Younger, Epistles 10.96–97 (the Bithynian inquiry and Trajan's rescript, c. 112 CE)
45 Decian libelli (sacrifice certificates, 250 CE; archaeology)
Letter of the Churches of Vienne and Lyons (177 CE; the Blandina account)
Lactantius, De Mortibus Persecutorum (Great Persecution; Galerius's deathbed plea, c. 311–315 CE — partisan author, carried as such)
Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History (partisan contemporary; the 'ten persecutions' schema is his construction)
Edict of Serdica / Galerius's Edict of Toleration (311 CE)
Edict of Milan letters (313 CE; via Lactantius 48 / Eusebius — toleration, not establishment)
Ehrman blog, 'When Emperors Became More Involved in Christian Persecutions' (secondary; carries J. Rives's Decius revisionism)

competing_hypotheses: The maximalist tradition: millions martyred under a continuous imperial campaign (fences the death arithmetic — the documents never sustained it)
The minimalist reading: persecutions were local, episodic, often mob-driven, with the imperial center restraining rather than leading (Trajan's rescript: do not hunt them)

The Rives revisionism: Decius's 250 CE edict was universal religious-loyalty enforcement in an imperial crisis, Christians caught by it rather than targeted by it (carried fairly — the libelli prove the mechanism, not the motive)
Eusebius's expanded 1st–2nd-century persecutor list (Domitian et al.) vs the mainstream view that Nero stands nearly alone in the 1st century
falsifiability: A contemporary imperial rescript forbidding anti-Christian action across these reigns, or proof that the Tacitus notice or the Pliny letters are later insertions

title: Jairus's daughter: 'the child is not dead but sleeping' (triple tradition)
claim: The raising of Jairus's daughter is triple-tradition (Mark 5:21-43; Matt 9:18-26; Luke 8:40-56): Jairus named (Mark/Luke), the daughter twelve years old, Peter/James/John taken inside, the mockers expelled, 'not dead but sleeping' (Mark 5:39), the Aramaic 'talitha koum' (Mark 5:41). The girl herself is NEVER named in any gospel, nor is her mother — the family cannot be traced further. Meier grants the raising stories a claim to historicity on multiple attestation; mainstream form-criticism treats the miracle element with reserve.
grade_reason: Triple attestation of the pericope as an early tradition; the event itself and the unnamed family are beyond verification
competing_hypotheses: Early tradition of a historical wonder-working event
Legendary formation around a wisdom saying about sleep/death
falsifiability: No independent attestation exists to test against

title: Joseph of Arimathea: the council member who buried Jesus
claim: Joseph of Arimathea — 'a respected member of the council' (Mark 15:43) — buries Jesus in all four gospels (Mark 15:43-46; Matt 27:57-60; Luke 23:50-53; John 19:38-42) plus the Gospel of Peter. For historicity: Brown/Meier argue via the criterion of embarrassment (an awkward Sanhedrin burial for the early church, a named checkable Jerusalem figure). Against: Crossan/Ehrman argue Mark created him to solve the body-disposal problem, since Roman practice left crucified corpses unburied. A 2004 JSHJ study splits the difference: Mark likely found the name in earlier tradition. Verdict: plausible, not proven. The Grail legends around him (Glastonbury, the blood-cup) are later accretions with no 1st-century root.
grade_reason: Fourfold gospel attestation plus Gospel of Peter, but genuine scholarly split on historicity; Grail accretions fenced off as later
competing_hypotheses: Historical Jerusalem councillor (Brown/Meier)
Markan creation to solve the burial problem (Crossan/Ehrman)
falsifiability: Contemporary non-Christian attestation would raise the grade; none exists

title: The women at the tomb: the least convenient, most consistent witnesses
claim: All four gospels agree the first witnesses of the empty tomb were women (Mary Magdalene named in all four; Mark 16:1-8; Matt 28:1-10; Luke 24:1-12; John 20:1-18) — witnesses whose testimony did not count in a first-century court. By the criterion of embarrassment, this is the strongest internal evidence that a memory rather than pure invention sits beneath the narratives: no inventor optimizing for ancient credibility chooses female witnesses.
grade_reason: Fourfold attestation of the least convenient possible witnesses; granted even by skeptical scholars
earliest_attestation: Mark 16:1-8
competing_hypotheses: Theological motif of the marginalized as first witnesses (literary)
falsifiability: A gospel tradition with male first-witnesses would weaken the embarrassment argument; none exists

title: The Murabba'at deeds — the revolt's legal paper trail
claim: The Wadi Murabba'at caves yielded legal documents of the Bar Kokhba administration's own calendar and bureaucracy: land leases dated 'year one / year two of the Redemption of Israel' — e.g. Mur 24E, a five-year tenancy at Herodium dated Shevat 20 of year two (~Jan/Feb 134 CE), 'of the Redemption of Israel by Shimeon ben Kosba, the nasi of Israel' — alongside the revolt-era divorce corpus: the Aramaic 'Masada get' (Joseph son of Naqsan to Miriam daughter of Jonathan, 'year six' = 72 CE, presented at Masada) and the Shelamzion document from Nahal Se'elim ('year three of the freedom of Israel' = 135 CE, naming Bar Kokhba 'nasi of Israel'). A Jewish legal system was operating under the revolt, in Aramaic, in its own year-count.
place: Wadi Murabba'at, ~11 km north of En-Gedi (Judean Desert)
grade_reason: The deeds exist in excavation contexts, their internal year-counts converge with the revolt's externally attested dates, and the legal formulas match known Second Temple–period Jewish documentary practice.
earliest_attestation: The documents themselves (72 CE, 134 CE, 135 CE).

sources.ref: Mur 24E (Wadi Murabba'at) — land lease, Shevat 20, year two of the Redemption of Israel (~Jan/Feb 134 CE), 'Shimeon ben Kosba, the nasi of Israel'
The Masada get (72 CE) and the Shelamzion divorce/Nahal Se'elim document (135 CE) — Posen Library, 'Early Jewish Divorce Documents'
Benoit, Milik & de Vaux, Les grottes de Murabba'at (DJD II, 1961)

competing_hypotheses: The 'Redemption of Israel' dating is the rebel administration's own era — evidence of a functioning state apparatus, not just a military uprising
The year-count reflects a legal fiction maintained by scribes even where rebel control was thin — the documents prove the claim of administration, not its territorial reach
The Shelamzion document's alternative reading — an acknowledgment of ketubah receipt rather than a woman-initiated divorce (the wife-initiated-divorce reading would be a rare attestation)
falsifiability: Proof the Murabba'at documents are modern forgeries; or that their year-counts postdate the revolt (antedating by later scribes).

title: 'Nero's sunglasses' — the emerald misreading (DEBUNKED)
claim: The Emperor Nero wore the first sunglasses — he watched the gladiatorial games through an emerald, which corrected or shaded his vision.
place: Rome (the arena Nero watched)
grade_reason: DEBUNKED as eyewear: Pliny's sentence describes watching through (or in) an emerald with no optics, no frame, no correction — the 'first sunglasses' reading imports 2,000 years of invention into five Latin words. The honest readings are a concave emerald used as a mirror or a luxury viewing stone; neither is spectacles, and neither is sunglasses.
earliest_attestation: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 37.16.64 (c. 77 CE): Nero 'used to watch the gladiatorial shows in an emerald' (smaragdo spectabat) — a single sentence with no mention of correction, shading, framing, or any device held to the eyes

sources.ref: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 37.16.64 — 'Nero... used to watch the gladiatorial shows in an emerald' (smaragdo); the full extent of the ancient evidence for the claim

Eyeglass-retailer histories (e.g. VCC2020, Millennium Eye Center) repeating the modern telling: 'Emperor Nero couldn't see gladiator fights very well without his magnifying emerald' — the telling this record grades

competing_hypotheses: Pliny's emerald was a mirror: Nero watched the reflected image, the green stone serving as a darkened reflective surface
Pliny's line is about luxury display (watching through a jewel), not optics at all — the emerald as status object
falsifiability: An artifact or text showing a framed, wearable, vision-correcting or light-shading device in 1st-century Rome

title: Pliny's sapo: soap's first Latin word (77-79 CE)
claim: The Latin word sapo (soap) appears first in a European language in Pliny the Elder's Natural History (77-79 CE): he describes soap manufactured from tallow and ashes as an invention of the Gauls ('Galliarum hoc inventum'), used principally as a hair pomade — and notes, disapprovingly, that among the Gauls and Germans men use it more than women.
place: Gaul (the manufacture Pliny describes)
grade_reason: A directly surviving primary text, precisely book-chapter locatable, reporting both the manufacture (tallow + ashes) and the Celtic origin — held at CORROBORATED rather than VERIFIED because it rests on one author, and Pliny is reporting foreign manufacture he did not observe himself. The hair-pomade-only use is the documented Roman-era reality: the word arrived in Latin from Celtic/Germanic, not from any Roman hill.
earliest_attestation: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia 28.51.191

sources.ref: Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia 28.51.191 — 'Prodest et sapo, Galliarum hoc inventum rutilandis capillis' (soap, an invention of the Gauls, for reddening hair); discussed as hair pomade, men likelier users among Gauls and Germans

Soap history survey (Wikipedia 'History of soap'): the word 'soap' (Latin sapo) 'appears first in a European language in Pliny the Elder's Historia Naturalis, which discusses the manufacture of soap from tallow and ashes, but the only use he mentions for it is as a pomade for hair'

competing_hypotheses: Pliny's passage may describe a Germanic/Celtic borrowing that Latin absorbed — the loanword etymology vs the Mount Sapo toponym theory (the latter DEBUNKED, evt-mount-sapo-legend-001)
Zosimos of Panopolis (c. 300 CE) later describes soap and soap-making in Greek — the Latin first-occurrence claim is about the word, not the chemistry
falsifiability: An earlier surviving Latin text using sapo

title: The magnetic compass was invented in China — the Han spoon tradition and the Song nautical needle, ~150 years before Europe's first mention (c. 80 CE - 1088 CE)
claim: The magnetic compass was invented in China, centuries before any European mention: a lodestone 'south-pointing spoon' (sinan) tradition in the Han era, a magnetized-needle compass for navigation by the Song dynasty, while Europe's first surviving description of the mariner's compass is Alexander Neckam's De naturis rerum, c. 1180-1190 — roughly a century and a half later.
place: Kaifeng / Song China (compass textual tradition)
grade_reason: The navigational-priority claim rests on a five-century textual chain of dated, surviving texts (Lunheng c. 80 CE; Wujing Zongyao 1040-1044; Shen Kuo ~1088; Zhu Yu 1111-1117), Needham's analysis (Science and Civilisation in China, vol. IV pt 1) treating Shen Kuo as the fixed point 'a century before the earliest European mention,' and Kreutz's scholarly-consensus margin of ~150 years over Neckam (~1180-1190). Held below VERIFIED because the Han spoon element — the linchpin of the 'invented in Han China' wording — is itself only CLAIMED: the Lunheng passage never says 'magnet,' no physical spoon survives (the 1951 Wang reconstruction model was never based on a recovered artifact and has been challenged by modern Chinese historians of science, e.g. Jiang Xiaoyuan), and modern skeptics (Meynard & Zhang 2026) accept the Han lodestone spoon and Song compass while rejecting only the exaggerated antiquity. The grade applies to Chinese invention and navigational priority; it does not assert the spoon was a working compass, nor a transmission path.
earliest_attestation: Wang Chong's Lunheng (c. 70-80 CE) 'south-pointing spoon' passage — though the passage does not explicitly mention magnetism; the lodestone reading is scholarly inference (Chen-Cheng Yih: 'widely considered' the earliest form of the magnetic compass).

sources.ref: Wikipedia 'History of the compass': Han lodestone devices (divination/geomancy); Wang Chong's Lunheng (70-80 CE) spoon passage — 'does not explicitly mention magnetism,' 'speculated to be a lodestone'; Chen-Cheng Yih — 'widely considered to be the earliest form of the magnetic compass'; Wujing Zongyao (1040-1044, south-pointing fish); Shen Kuo Dream Pool Essays (1088, first incontestable magnetized-needle reference); Zhu Yu Pingzhou Table Talks (written 1111-1117, first maritime use); Kreutz — Chinese navigational invention pre-dates first European mention by 150 years

Meynard & Zhang, 'The Chinese Compass: How the Jesuits Created and Spread the Myth,' Journal of Jesuit Studies 13 (2026), 96-116: accepts Han lodestone spoon + Song nautical compass as real; Needham cited — Chinese pilots used the compass by ~1090, possibly ~850; 'we hardly know enough' on the China-Arab transmission question

Needham, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. IV pt 1, pp. 249-250 (quoted via Wikipedia Talk:Shen Kuo): Shen Kuo's Meng Chhi Pi Than (~1088) is 'our fixed point,' 'a century before the earliest European mention of the magnetic compass'

OpenEdition/Artefact journal: skeptical scholarship arguing Needham's 'compass-based navigation' was misleading — the Song water-bowl pointer 'could not have acted as a useable and reliable sea-going navigational aid'; traditional Chinese navigation not obviously compass-based

Sixth Tone: historian Jiang Xiaoyuan (Shanghai Jiao Tong University) — 'a physical model was never recovered' of the spoon compass; recommends removing it from history textbooks; modern Chinese scholarly skepticism of the sinan model

competing_hypotheses: The revisionist navigation line (Artefact journal, modern scholarship): Needham's 'compass-based navigation' framing overstates the case — the Song floating pointer was too primitive to be a reliable sea-going navigational aid, and traditional Chinese navigation was not 'compass-based' in the modern sense. Date priority is not overturned by this; navigational utility is qualified.

The independent-invention line: the European dry-pivot compass may have been invented independently of the Chinese needle (Arab transmission via the Indian Ocean and the crusaders is one candidate route; independent European invention is another). Needham himself concluded 'we hardly know enough' on the transmission question — the transmission path remains SPECULATION.

The transmission line: Chinese compass knowledge reached the Arab/Indian Ocean world (first Islamic-world mention, 1232) and from there Europe; the similar dry-pivot forms support a shared ancestry. Also unproven on primary evidence — carried honestly, not decided.
falsifiability: A securely dated European or other non-Chinese compass description that predates Shen Kuo (1088) would overturn the Chinese navigational-priority claim; a recovered Han-dynasty magnetic spoon would raise the spoon element from CLAIMED to CORROBORATED or better.

title: Gamaliel: the historical teacher behind a composed speech (Acts 5)
claim: Gamaliel I is a real historical figure (Mishnah; Josephus Ant. 20; Acts 22:3 as Paul's teacher). But his Acts 5:34-40 speech — the one that freed the apostles from the Sanhedrin — is widely judged Lukan composition: set ~30s CE, it cites the revolt of Theudas BEFORE Judas of Galilee, yet Josephus dates Theudas to 44-46 CE and Judas to 6 CE. The person is historical; the freeing speech is a literary set-piece, not a transcript.
grade_reason: Person independently attested; the speech's Theudas/Judas inversion is a documented anachronism
competing_hypotheses: Lukan free composition using a remembered name (majority)
Preserved memory of Gamaliel's intervention (minority)
falsifiability: None available; the anachronism is the evidence

title: The 'Both Genealogies Are Literal Compatible Pedigrees' Telling
claim: Matthew 1 and Luke 3 are both complete, literal, historically compatible family trees of Jesus.
place: Jerusalem (compositional setting of the harmonization question)
grade_reason: The two lists diverge completely after David — different names, different counts (Matthew's schematic 14-14-14), omitting names Matthew 1 itself skips (Ahaziah, Joash, Amaziah) — and the harmonizations require mechanisms the texts never state. Killed on the documents.
earliest_attestation: The modern telling has roots in early harmonizing exegesis (Julius Africanus, Eusebius); its current popular form in confessional apologetics

sources.ref: Matthew 1:1-17 and Luke 3:23-38 compared name-for-name (the divergence is in the texts)
The lists' own omissions: Matthew 1:8 skips three kings between Joram and Uzziah (Ahaziah, Joash, Amaziah) — telescoping visible in the text
Raymond E. Brown, The Birth of the Messiah (Doubleday, 1977/1993) — the genealogies as theological constructs
Cusack (2026), 'The Genealogies of Jesus: Matthew, Luke, Jewish Tradition, and the Apocryphal Gospels', IJRISS (genealogies as legal/tribal/theological legitimacy; divergence restated)
sources.note: 2026-10-21 eighth-pass chain: 2026 literature noted; no grade movement

competing_hypotheses: Matthew traces Joseph's line and Luke traces Mary's line (the traditional harmonization)
Matthew gives the royal/legal line and Luke the biological line
The evangelists drew on different received traditions, each theologically shaped
falsifiability: Independent attestation of the intermediate names in either list from contemporary inscriptions, or a demonstration that the two lists can be reconciled without appealing to unnamed adoptions, levirate marriages, or textual error

title: The 'other disciple known to the high priest' (John 18:15-16)
claim: John 18:15-16 names an 'other disciple who was known to the high priest' who got Peter into the courtyard. Johannine-only attestation. Proposed identifications (Beloved Disciple/John son of Zebedee per Irenaeus — the strongest internal case via John 20:2; the Last Supper householder; an unnamed Jerusalem disciple) are all conjectural; Kok's objection stands (a Galilean fisherman with that social capital is hard to picture). Augustine's verdict holds: Scripture is silent — nothing above speculation.
grade_reason: Single-source, unidentified figure; every identification is conjectural
competing_hypotheses: The Beloved Disciple (Irenaeus/Culpepper/Keener)
An unnamed Jerusalem disciple
Johannine literary device
falsifiability: Independent attestation would raise the grade; none exists

title: Blood and water from the side (John 19:34-35): attested, read as theology
claim: John 19:34 (the soldier's spear; blood and water flow) with 19:35's explicit eyewitness claim is securely attested. Mainstream scholarship reads it theologically, not forensically: the water as the Holy Spirit given now that Jesus is glorified (cf. John 7:39), the blood as the Passover-lamb sacrificial motif (cf. m. Pesahim 5:3-5 on free-flowing sacrificial blood). Medical readings (pericardial fluid) exist but are secondary; the evangelist's interest is christological.
grade_reason: Secure attestation with explicit eyewitness framing; the theological reading is the scholarly consensus
competing_hypotheses: Theological symbolism (majority)
Medical/forensic description (minority)
falsifiability: Textual; the attestation is not in doubt, only the reading

title: Nicodemus: the Johannine-only ruler of the Jews
claim: Nicodemus — 'a ruler of the Jews' (John 3:1) — appears only in John (3:1-21; 7:50-51; 19:38-42), absent from all three Synoptics. The proposed identification with the Talmudic Nicodemus ben Gurion is rejected by most scholars on dating/age grounds. Majority scholarly view: a representative Johannine figure (the sympathetic-but-secret insider), not an independently attested historical person.
grade_reason: Single-source attestation in the latest gospel; scholarly majority reads him as symbolic
earliest_attestation: John 3:1-21
competing_hypotheses: Historical Jerusalem aristocrat (minority)
Johannine literary figure (majority)
falsifiability: Independent attestation would raise the grade; none exists

title: The Testimonium Flavianum (Josephus on Jesus)
claim: Josephus's Antiquities of the Jews, Book 18 (written c. 93-94 CE), contains an authentic first-century core mentioning Jesus — his execution under Pontius Pilate and the survival of his followers — with later Christian interpolations overlaid on that core.
place: Rome (where Josephus wrote the Antiquities; the claim's subject is Roman Judea and Galilee)
grade_raw: CORROBORATED (authentic Josephan core) / DEBUNKED (Christian-phrase overlays as Josephan authorship)
grade_reason: The passage cannot be fully authentic as it stands: a non-Christian Jew would not write 'He was the Messiah,' the narrative flow breaks around the passage, and the 1935-style scholarly tally favors a partially interpolated text. But the authentic core (a Jesus, condemned by Pilate, followers surviving him) fits Josephus's style and subject matter, and the independently authentic James passage (Ant 20.200) proves Josephus referred to Jesus anyway - so the whole-passage forgery thesis has to explain away two passages, not one.
earliest_attestation: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews 18.63-64, written c. 93-94 CE in Rome; earliest surviving quotation: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History (c. 324 CE)

sources.ref: Josephus, Antiquities 18.63-64 (Testimonium Flavianum)

Feldman survey of the literature (1937-1980): 87 articles; 39 of 52 surveyed scholars support partial authenticity (4 entirely genuine, 6 mostly genuine, 20 with some interpolations, 9 with several; 13 total interpolation)
John P. Meier, A Marginal Jew (1991): three Christian interpolations identified - 'He was the Messiah,' 'if indeed one ought to call him a man,' and the resurrection/prophecies passage

Josephus, Antiquities 20.200 - 'the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James': authenticity accepted by the overwhelming majority of modern scholars; the highest-authenticity Josephus reference to Christianity
Minority positions on record: Ken Olson's Eusebian-authorship thesis (1999/2013); Louis Feldman's 2012 move to wholesale interpolation (Brill, persuaded by Olson + Origen's silence)

competing_hypotheses: Partial interpolation (majority): authentic Josephan core with later Christian additions; Meier's three-interpolation reconstruction is the standard working text
Total interpolation (minority): Eusebius or a 4th-century Christian composed the whole passage; the citation gap before Eusebius is the strongest argument
Full authenticity: the passage is exactly as Josephus wrote it - near-universally rejected
The James passage is itself an interpolation (Carrier's 'Jesus son of Damneus' reading) - the far minority, negatively evaluated in the scholarship
falsifiability: A pre-4th-century manuscript of Antiquities 18 lacking the passage would kill the partial-authenticity consensus; a pre-Eusebian quotation of the full Christian phrasing would kill the interpolation thesis. Either discovery is possible in principle.

title: The Babatha archive — a Jewish woman's legal papers, 94–132 CE
claim: A leather pouch holding 35 legal documents — wedding contracts (ketubot), property transfers, land registration, loans, guardianship petitions and summonses — written in Nabatean Aramaic, Judean Aramaic, and Greek and dated c. 94–132 CE, belonged to Babatha bat Shimon, a Jewish woman of Mahoza (Maoza) on the southeastern shore of the Dead Sea (the Nabatean kingdom until 106 CE, then the Roman province of Arabia). She carried the pouch with her when she fled to the Cave of Letters at Nahal Hever with other refugees at the end of the Bar Kokhba revolt (132–135 CE), and hid it in a crevice; she and the others died in the cave. Yigael Yadin's expedition found the pouch in 1961. The documents show a woman litigating, lending, inheriting and registering property under Roman bureaucracy.
place: Cave of Letters, Nahal Hever (Judean Desert); Babatha's Mahoza on the southeastern Dead Sea shore (modern Jordan)
grade_reason: The archive exists, was excavated in controlled archaeological context (1961), is internally dated across four decades, and is multiply documented; the documents' legal formulas match known 2nd-century Roman-provincial practice.
earliest_attestation: The documents themselves, dated 94–132 CE; excavated in controlled context 1961.

sources.ref: The Babatha archive (P. Yadin 1–35), Cave of Letters, Nahal Hever — Israel Museum / Israel Antiquities Authority; discovered 1961, Yadin expedition
Lewis, N. (ed.), The Documents from the Bar Kokhba Period in the Cave of Letters (Greek Papyri), 1989
Jewish Review of Books, 'Businesswomen Before Bar Kokhba' (Babatha archive overview: 35 documents, 94–132 CE, Nabatean Aramaic/Judean Aramaic/Greek)
OUPblog, 'Ancient legal papyri bring lost world to life' (2017) — the Judean Desert legal papyri, 100 BCE–200 CE

Esler, Philip F. (2026), 'Babatha, En-Gedi and the Bar Kokhba revolt: A new approach using evidence from the Cave of Letters', Biblical Theology Bulletin 56(1):18-32 (P. Yadin 27 as draft receipt; revolt outbreak re-dating)

competing_hypotheses: The archive represents the papers of a typical upper-middle-class Jewish household of the period — Babatha's business activity was normal, not exceptional
Selection bias: these are the papers she chose to carry in flight — her most title-critical documents — so the archive overrepresents property and guardianship disputes relative to daily life
That Babatha fled at the very end of the revolt and died in the cave (the starvation/siege reading) vs. dying before Roman forces penetrated the refuge
falsifiability: Linguistic or material anachronism in the documents proving modern forgery; or evidence the 1961 pouch context was planted rather than excavated.

title: The earliest New Testament manuscript fragments
claim: The oldest surviving physical copies of New Testament texts are 2nd–3rd century Greek papyrus fragments from Egypt, headed by P52 (Rylands Gr. P. 457, a fragment of John 18). No autograph — no authorial original — of any New Testament text survives.
place: John Rylands Library, Manchester (current holding; findspot in Egypt unknown)
grade_reason: The fragments exist in major libraries and are multiply attested; radiocarbon work (e.g., on the Isaiah Scroll parallel) corroborates paleographic ranges. But the precise ~125 CE date of P52 is contested and rests on paleography alone, never confirmed by physical dating.
earliest_attestation: The fragments themselves: P52 (John 18:31–33, 37–38; editio princeps Roberts 1935); P90, P104 (2nd c.); P46 (Pauline epistles, c. 200 CE); P66, P75 (John; Luke–John; c. 175–225 CE)

sources.ref: P52 — Rylands Greek Papyrus 457, John Rylands Library, Manchester (editio princeps: C. H. Roberts, 1935)
Brent Nongbri, 'The Use and Abuse of P52' (HTR 98:1, 2005) — the paleographic date cannot be fixed precisely; the range extends into the 3rd century
Orsini & Clarysse — propose 125–175 CE for P52 on comparator documents (P. Flor. 1.1, 153 CE; PSI V 446, 132–137 CE)
John Rylands Library's own statement: 'Recent research points to a date nearer to 200 AD'; carbon-dating has not been used (destructive)
Chester Beatty papyri P45/P46/P47 and Bodmer papyri P66/P75 (2nd–3rd c.; >140 NT papyri known as of 2021)
Codex Sinaiticus (c. 330–350 CE) — the earliest surviving copy of the complete New Testament

1QIsaa, the Great Isaiah Scroll (c. 125 BCE; radiocarbon + paleography agree) — the Hebrew-Bible parallel: >2,600 small differences from the Masoretic text, mostly spelling/grammar, a few sense-changing

competing_hypotheses: P52 dates c. 125 CE and tightly constrains the Gospel of John to the 1st century (Roberts's original position; traditional)

P52's paleographic range extends into the 3rd century and its dating cannot constrain the Gospel's composition tightly — the 'earliest fragment' argument proves less than it is used to prove (Nongbri 2005)
The traditional dates are broadly right and the exact year doesn't matter: a 2nd-century John fragment still kills late-2nd-century composition dates for the Gospel (consensus middle)
falsifiability: An autograph (authorial original) of any New Testament text would falsify the 'no originals survive' half of the claim; a securely dated 1st-century NT fragment would move the frontier earlier and supersede P52's lead.

title: The real history of the padded horse collar: Chinese origin, gradual European adoption
claim: The padded horse collar originated in China (Han-era depictions, documented in Joseph Needham's Science and Civilisation in China research), diffused westward, and was in European use by the High Middle Ages; the European shift from ox to horse draught was then gradual and governed by economics — relative animal prices, fodder (oat) costs, and land regimes (John Langdon, Horses, Oxen and Technological Innovation, 1986) — not a sudden collar-triggered breakthrough.
place: China (Han-era collar origin) → medieval Europe (diffusion, gradual adoption)
grade_reason: Multiply attested across independent lines: Chinese depictions and texts (Needham), European iconography, and Langdon's economic analysis of the ox-to-horse mix; held below VERIFIED on the exact diffusion route and the precise arrival timing in Europe.
earliest_attestation: Han-dynasty Chinese depictions and texts (per Needham's SCC documentation); European iconographic evidence from the early second millennium CE

sources.ref: Joseph Needham et al., Science and Civilisation in China — padded horse collar attested in Han-era China; European arrival c. 9th–10th century
John Langdon, Horses, Oxen and Technological Innovation (1986) — gradual, price-driven English adoption
Thomas E. Lambert, 'The Horse Versus the Ox during Medieval Times' (2023, Univ. of Louisville) — horse/ox cost comparison

competing_hypotheses: Independent European invention of the padded collar (rejected on the iconographic sequence: Chinese depictions predate European ones by centuries)
A rapid White-style adoption after the collar's arrival (rejected by Langdon's price and manorial data, which show a slow, mixed, region-by-region transition)
The claim that the ox was simply 'worse' — the Lambert 2023 comparison: horses ~50% faster but far costlier to feed; on poor land and in poor economies the ox remained rational
falsifiability: A securely dated European padded collar pre-dating any Chinese attestation, or English manorial data showing a sudden, price-independent ox-to-horse flip

title: Cai Lun's 105 CE presentation (the real event)
claim: In 105 CE (the first year of Yuanxing), the Han court official Cai Lun presented an improved papermaking process — using tree bark (likely mulberry), hemp waste, old rags, and fishing nets — to Emperor He, and the court adopted it; the paper was thereafter called 'Cai Hou paper' (Caihou zhi).
place: Luoyang (Eastern Han capital, the imperial court)
grade_reason: The event is attested in the standard dynastic history with a named reign year, named materials, and the named aftermath ('Cai Hou paper'); held below VERIFIED because the Hou Hanshu is a 5th-century compilation writing three centuries after the event.
earliest_attestation: Hou Hanshu 78/68:2513-14 (Fan Ye, 5th c.) — the standard history's biography of Cai Lun; the 'Cai Hou paper' (Caihou zhi) naming tradition

sources.ref: Hou Hanshu 78/68:2513-14 (Fan Ye, Liu-Song dynasty) — the biography passage: writings of old were bamboo and silk (silk costly, bamboo heavy); Cai Lun devises paper from tree bark, hemp tops, rags, and fishing nets; presents it in Yuanxing 1 (105); the emperor praises his ability; paper used everywhere thereafter, called 'Cai Hou paper' (text via Wikipedia, 'Cai Lun')

acclaimedfigures.com, 'Cai Lun Biography' (Dec 2025) — synthesizes Britannica, the Met Museum, and the Silk Road Foundation: eunuch official, director of imperial workshops under Emperor He, presents improved paper in 105; the method spreads across China by the 3rd c., Korea/Japan by the 7th, the Islamic world via Samarkand (Talas 751), Europe by the 12th

competing_hypotheses: Cai Lun was the manager who systematized a craft already circulating in the palace workshops, not the lone bench-worker inventor — the passage credits him with devising the improvement ('Lun nai zaoyi'), which allows a managerial reading
The adoption claim may exaggerate the speed of uptake; bamboo and silk remained standard for decades — the presentation is firm, the 'everywhere thereafter' is the historian's flourish
falsifiability: A contemporary Han document contradicting the 105 presentation, or proof the biography's papermaking passage is a later interpolation, would demote the grade.

title: The Cai Lun invented paper in 105 CE (DEBUNKED)
claim: Paper was invented by the Han court official Cai Lun in 105 CE.
place: Luoyang (Eastern Han capital, where the invention is said to have happened)
