grade_reason: Three independent kills: (1) the Fangmatan Tomb 5 map fragment — early Western Han, early 2nd c. BCE, the oldest extant sheet of paper, laid on a burial chest 200+ years before 105 CE; (2) Li Xiaocen's 2012 microscopic re-examination — a distinct paper-pouring method, not Cai Lun's dip-mould, ~250 years older than his process; (3) the 2006 Fangmatan specimen re-dating — paper bearing written Chinese characters from c. 8 BCE, paper already in military use more than a century before Cai Lun. The historiography's own verdict: Cai Lun systematized and improved the skill and fixed a recipe — he did not invent it.
earliest_attestation: The traditional reading of the Hou Hanshu 78/68:2513-14 passage (Fan Ye, 5th c.); carried into modern reference works — e.g. Encyclopaedia Britannica's 'Cai Lun (Chinese Inventor)' entry — and China's Four Great Inventions framing

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Cai Lun' — the Hou Hanshu 78/68:2513-14 passage: bamboo heavy, silk costly; Cai Lun devises paper from tree bark, hemp waste, old rags, fishing nets; presents it in the first year of Yuanxing (105); the emperor praises it; paper henceforth called 'Cai Hou paper'

Wikipedia, 'Fangmatan' — Tomb 5 excavated 1986, early Western Han (early 2nd c. BCE); paper map fragment 5.6 x 2.6 cm laid on the occupant's chest; drawn on the oldest extant piece of paper (citing Yi & Liu 2010, p.64; Behr 2007, p.113)

China Development Gateway (Xinhua), Nov 2016 — Li Xiaocen (Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology) on the 1986 Fangmatan scrap: uneven fiber distribution under the microscope, the paper-pouring process distinct from Cai Lun's method, ~250 years before Cai Lun

Wikipedia, 'History of paper' — 2006 Fangmatan specimens bearing written Chinese characters re-dated to c. 8 BCE (paper in military use more than 100 years before Cai Lun); 'Cai Lun's contribution was to improve this skill systematically and scientifically, fix a recipe for papermaking'

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Cai Lun (Chinese Inventor)' — the reference-work version of the invention credit, carried into textbooks and the Four Great Inventions list (cited via simple.wikipedia's references)

competing_hypotheses: The fair defense of the schoolbook: 'invention' means the systematized, economical recipe that actually traveled and displaced bamboo and silk — the real achievement, honestly stated
The Hou Hanshu author credited Cai Lun with a process improvement; later readers inflated the passage into an origin story
falsifiability: Proof that every pre-105 paper fragment is misidentified (not paper) or misdated (not pre-105) would restore the claim. A pre-Western-Han paper find would push paper earlier still — a refinement, not a rescue.

title: The Bar Kokhba letters — the revolt's own correspondence, 132–135 CE
claim: Roughly fifteen letters attributed to Shimon bar Kosiba (Bar Kokhba) survive in two groups: a Wadi Murabba'at group (early 1950s, via the antiquities market; published by the de Vaux expedition) and a Nahal Hever Cave of Letters group (1960–61, Yadin expedition, found in a tied bundle in a waterskin). They are addressed to subordinates — Yehonathan ben Be'ayan and Masabala, sitting at En-Gedi — and deal with military discipline, agricultural supplies, taxation, and the movement of people; most are in Aramaic, five in Hebrew, two in Greek; they are not internally dated. They sign the leader 'Shimeon ben Kosba, nasi (prince) of Israel' — the only contemporary voice of the revolt's leadership.
place: Cave of Letters, Nahal Hever (main group); Wadi Murabba'at group ~11 km north of En-Gedi
grade_reason: The letters exist as physical documents in controlled excavation contexts (Murabba'at 1950s, Nahal Hever 1960–61), their language mix matches the period's documentary practice, and they converge with the revolt's independently attested dates — though they are undated internally, which fences the grade below VERIFIED.
earliest_attestation: The letters themselves, 132–135 CE (contemporary with the events).

sources.ref: The Bar Kokhba letters (5/6Hev, Murabba'at) — Israel Antiquities Authority / Shrine of the Book; excavated contexts: Wadi Murabba'at (early 1950s), Cave of Letters (1960–61)
Biblical Archaeology Society, 'What Is the Bar-Kokhba Revolt?' — the revolt reconstructed from contemporary documents, coins, caves and tunnels (2026)
Archeobiblion, 'Bar Kokhba: the correspondence' — the two archive groups, ~15 letters, Aramaic/Hebrew/Greek, the 'nasi of Israel' signature
Yadin, Y. Bar-Kokhba: The Rediscovery of the Legendary Hero of the Second Jewish Revolt against Rome (1971)
Esler, Philip F. (2026), 'Babatha, En-Gedi and the Bar Kokhba revolt', Biblical Theology Bulletin 56(1):18-32 (Bar Kokhba opened with the capture of En-Gedi)

competing_hypotheses: The letters are authentic administration of the revolt — a structured revolutionary government with its own calendar, taxation and discipline (the mainstream reading)
The letters were dictated, not autograph — several different hands wrote them, so 'Bar Kokhba's letters' means letters issued in his name, which matters for what they prove about the man himself
The harsh tone (threats to Yehonathan at En-Gedi) reads as military discipline under pressure, not as evidence for or against later rabbinic traditions about his character
falsifiability: Material or linguistic proof that the letters are modern forgeries; or a contemporary Roman document showing the 'nasi of Israel' administration did not exist.

title: The great inversion: when daimōn became 'demon'
claim: In the 2nd-3rd centuries CE, Christian writers redefined daimones — previously neutral or benevolent intermediary beings in Greek usage — as wholly evil supernatural beings hostile to God and man: Justin Martyr (2 Apology 5) identifies the pagan daimones as the fallen angels of Genesis 6 who enslave mankind; Tatian and Origen (Contra Celsum) carry the identification forward. This is a semantic inversion inside the Christian tradition, not a discovery about the Greek texts: the English word 'demon' descends from the redefined Christian usage, while Hesiod, Plato, and Xenophon attest the earlier, non-evil range. Graded as belief-phenomenon: the redefinition is multiply attested; the beings' status is never adjudicated.
place: Rome, Alexandria, Caesarea (the writers' cities); the Greek texts they redefine are pan-Hellenic
grade_reason: The Christian texts exist and are explicit: the identification of daimones with the fallen angels is stated, and the contrast with Hesiod's and Plato's usage is a matter of lexical record, not interpretation.
earliest_attestation: Justin Martyr, 2 Apology 5; Tatian, Oration to the Greeks 7-18; Origen, Contra Celsum 4.92-99, 7.64-70

sources.ref: Justin Martyr, 2 Apology 5 (the fallen-angel identification of the daimones)
Origen, Contra Celsum (the polemic that fixes the redefinition)
The semantic history of daimōn → 'demon' in the lexical record (LSJ; Lampe's Patristic Lexicon)

competing_hypotheses: The redefinition was continuous with an already-developing negative drift in daimōn usage in Hellenistic popular religion (the word was already acquiring sinister overtones before the Christians)
The Christian writers were describing genuinely hostile entities and the earlier 'benevolent' daimon was the euphemism (a metaphysical claim the attestation rule cannot grade)
falsifiability: A 2nd-century Christian text using daimones in the older benevolent sense without polemic (would show the inversion was slower and less programmatic)

title: The Gospel of Mary — a 2nd-century text about her, not by her
claim: The Gospel of Mary survives in a 5th-century Coptic codex (Papyrus Berolinensis 8502, bought in Cairo 1896, published 1955) plus two 3rd-century Greek fragments (P. Oxyrhynchus 3525; P. Rylands 463): a 2nd-century revelation dialogue in which the risen Savior gives Mary (understood as the Magdalene) private teaching, Peter challenges her authority ('Did he really speak with a woman privately, without our knowledge? Should we turn about and all listen to her?'), and Levi defends her. It was not written by Mary Magdalene and dates a century-plus after the events it describes.
place: Berlin (Papyrus Berolinensis 8502 repository)
grade_raw: CORROBORATED (the text, its date, its contents) / DEBUNKED (Magdalene authorship)
grade_reason: The manuscript witnesses are dated and published; a 2nd-century text cannot be the 1st-century woman's own writing.
earliest_attestation: P. Rylands 463 / P. Oxyrhynchus 3525 (3rd-century Greek fragments)

sources.ref: Papyrus Berolinensis 8502 (5th-c. Coptic codex)
P. Oxy. 3525 and P. Ryl. 463 (3rd-c. Greek fragments)
Gospel of Mary 17-18 (Peter's challenge; Levi's defense)

competing_hypotheses: The maximalist reading: Mary's own circle preserved her teaching and the text carries genuine 1st-century memory
The rivalry-document reading: the Peter-Levi exchange attests real early-Christian authority disputes, not Magdalene biography
falsifiability: A 1st-century manuscript of the text, or a contemporary attestation of Magdalene literacy and authorship

title: The Martyrdom of Polycarp
claim: The letter of the church of Smyrna recounting the arrest, trial, and burning of bishop Polycarp in the stadium is a substantially authentic second-century document, not a later forgery. The core narrative is genuine; the dove emerging from the wound appears only in some manuscripts as a later insertion; the exact date (155/156 CE under Antoninus Pius vs. 167 CE under Marcus Aurelius) remains debated among scholars.
place: Smyrna (Izmir), stadium — the execution site per the letter
grade_reason: The letter's epistolary form, early circulation, and Eusebius's 4th-century quotation anchor it in the second century; mainstream scholarship accepts substantial authenticity.
earliest_attestation: The letter itself (Martyrdom of Polycarp), circulated with instructions for annual liturgical reading; quoted at length by Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 4.15 (early 4th c.)

sources.ref: Martyrdom of Polycarp (the Smyrna letter)
Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 4.15
Barnes 1968 (date under Antoninus Pius)

competing_hypotheses: The letter is substantially genuine, the earliest full martyr narrative outside the New Testament (mainstream: Barnes 1968; Frend)
The letter is a later composition modeling ideal martyrdom theology (skeptical minority)
The core is genuine but the narrative has been theologically edited in transmission
falsifiability: Discovery of the letter's dependence on a later source (e.g., verbatim dependence on Eusebius rather than the reverse), or a manuscript tradition showing the whole text composed after 300 CE

title: The Scillitan Martyrs (180 CE)
claim: The Acts of the Scillitan Martyrs — the record of the trial and execution of Speratus and six companions at Carthage on 17 July 180 CE — are substantially authentic proconsular court records, the earliest surviving Christian text written in Latin.
place: Carthage — the trial before the proconsul; Scilli the martyrs' home town
grade_reason: Consular dating fixes the document to 180 CE; the spare bureaucratic style matches Roman court procedure and shows no legendary overlay.
earliest_attestation: The acta themselves, surviving in Latin (and a later Greek version); the earliest Latin Christian document

sources.ref: Acts of the Scillitan Martyrs (Latin acta)
Tertullian's contemporary North African context (secondary witness to the milieu)

competing_hypotheses: The acts are genuine court records with minimal Christian editing (mainstream)
The acts are substantially genuine but with light Christian redaction of the replies
falsifiability: Manuscript evidence showing the Latin text composed centuries later, or proof the trial records were fabricated as propaganda

title: The Alexander Romance: the legend's literary afterlife
claim: The Alexander Romance (Pseudo-Callisthenes), composed at Alexandria c. 3rd century CE, is a work of fiction about Alexander — opening with the claim that his true father was the Egyptian sorcerer-king Nectanebo, not Philip II — which became the most influential Alexander narrative in the East. It survives in dozens of recensions across some eighty versions (Greek, Latin, Syriac, Arabic, Persian, Armenian, Ethiopic, medieval vernaculars). Byzantine chroniclers (e.g., John Malalas; the Excerpta latina Barbari, 8th c.) treated it as a historical source. As a literary tradition its existence and influence are multiply documented; as a source for the historical Alexander it is graded DEBUNKED.
place: Alexandria, Egypt (composition); recensions across Europe, the Near East, and the Indian Ocean world
grade_raw: CORROBORATED (the literary tradition: composition, recensions, Byzantine use) / DEBUNKED (as a historical source for Alexander's life)
grade_reason: The manuscript tradition is multiply attested (recension alpha onward; the Armenian witnesses preserving passages lost in Greek). Byzantine use as history is documented in the chronicles themselves. The DEBUNKED half rests on the absence of any corroboration for the Romance's exclusive episodes in the five ancient accounts or the fragmentary eyewitness tradition — a fiction the field recognizes as fiction.
earliest_attestation: Pseudo-Callisthenes recension alpha (3rd c. CE); Armenian translation preserving lost passages; Wolohojian (1969) standard English translation

sources.ref: Pseudo-Callisthenes, The Romance of Alexander the Great, trans. Albert Mugrdich Wolohojian (Columbia UP, 1969): standard English translation; the Armenian witnesses preserve passages lost in the surviving Greek

'Alexander Romance and Byzantine world chronicles: history cross-fertilized by fiction and the reverse' (2017): comparative textual analysis — Byzantine chroniclers (Malalas, Excerpta latina Barbari) incorporated Pseudo-Callisthenian motifs (Nectanebo's transformation, divine heritage, fantastic geography) as factual history

Ionescu, Dan-Tudor, 'Alexander the Great in the Persian legends: from the Pseudo-Callisthenes's Greek Romance to the Sikandar of Firdousi's Shah-Nameh': the Greek Romance (Alexandria, 3rd c. CE) → the Persian Sikandar; Ferdowsi (completed 1010) as the first complete exemplar of the Pseudo-Callisthenes tradition in Persian

competing_hypotheses: The Romance preserves genuine early-tradition material (the Persian 'mercenaries' source hypothesis) embedded in the fiction — a minority position carried honestly
The Romance is wholly a Hellenistic-Egyptian literary invention with no historical core beyond the names
falsifiability: A contemporary document confirming any Romance-exclusive episode (the Nectanebo paternity, the glass-bell dive, the Kandake embassy) as historical fact; none exists — the Romance's own earliest manuscripts postdate Alexander by five centuries.

title: The Babylonian Talmud — layered corpus, thin manuscript record
claim: The Babylonian Talmud is a layered rabbinic corpus — the Mishnah (redacted c. 200 CE) wrapped in the Babylonian Gemara, whose Amoraic arguments span c. 200–500 CE with Savoraic redaction and Geonic closure (c. 500–650 CE). Its surviving manuscript record is late and thin: the oldest surviving dated copy is Florence, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Plut. II.1.7–9 (dated 1175 CE), and Munich, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Cod.hebr. 95 (1342) is the only complete manuscript of the Babylonian Talmud; earlier witnesses survive only as Cairo Genizah fragments and citations in later works. The printed standard (Vilna/Romm 1880–1886) carries the censor's erasures — the 1553 Roman burnings under Julius III and the Russian expurgations are part of the record's own history.
place: Babylonia (Sura / Pumbedita academies; manuscripts in Florence, Munich, Cairo)
grade_reason: The dated manuscripts (Florence 1175, Munich 95) are catalogued, photographed, and independently studied artifacts — the documentary facts are VERIFIED-as-documents. The layered composition (Mishnah → Amoraic Gemara → Savoraic redaction → Geonic closure) is the scholarly consensus reconstruction of a text with no contemporary external attestation of its editors — so the corpus-level claim stays CORROBORATED, not VERIFIED. The Talmud proves the shape of its own centuries of argument; it does not prove anything contemporary about the Second Temple period it remembers (the Mishnah record's honesty rule, extended).
earliest_attestation: Florence Plut. II.1.7–9 (1175 CE) as a dated artifact; the Genizah fragments as earlier undated witnesses; the corpus's own traditions date its layers centuries earlier (theological-traditional, not historical evidence)

sources.ref: Munich, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Cod.hebr. 95 (dated 1342) — the only complete manuscript of the Babylonian Talmud
Florence, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Plut. II.1.7–9 (dated 1175) — oldest surviving dated manuscript of the Babylonian Talmud
Cairo Genizah Talmud fragments (Cambridge Taylor-Schechter collection et al.) — earlier partial witnesses
Günter Stemberger, Introduction to the Talmud and Midrash (2nd ed. 1996) — the layering: Tannaim / Amoraim / Savoraim / Geonim
The 1553 Roman burnings (Campo de' Fiori, 9 Sept 1553, under Julius III) and the Vilna/Romm edition's censor-approved expurgations — the censorship archaeology of the printed text

competing_hypotheses: The Geonic closure is later than the Savoraic redaction (the academies kept editing into the 8th c.) — the closure date is the live scholarly dispute
David Halivni's source-critical reconstruction: the Amoraic layer contains recoverable earlier sources, not just attributed sayings — the layering is recoverable, not merely schematic
falsifiability: A securely dated complete manuscript earlier than Florence 1175; or codicological proof that the Munich 95 colophon date (1342) is false; or a securely dated Gemara citation predating the Amoraic attribution it carries

title: The Passion of Perpetua and Felicity (203 CE)
claim: The Passion of Perpetua and Felicity records the imprisonment and execution (7 March 203 CE, Carthage) of the noblewoman Perpetua — whose own prison diary (chapters 3–10) is one of the earliest surviving writings by a Christian woman — alongside her slave Felicity; the framing introduction/conclusion are by a later editor, and the authenticity of the diary portion is the mainstream position.
place: Carthage — prison and amphitheater per the Passio
grade_reason: Internal evidence (the diary's distinct first-person voice, the frame's separate editorial voice, early liturgical use) supports the mainstream two-layer reading.
earliest_attestation: The Passio itself (Latin, with an early Greek version); quoted and honored in North African liturgy within a generation

sources.ref: Passio Sanctarum Perpetuae et Felicitatis (Latin)
The early Greek version (secondary witness to the text's circulation)

competing_hypotheses: The diary is Perpetua's own writing, framed by an editor (mainstream: Frend; Salisbury)
The whole text, diary included, is a later literary composition (skeptical minority)
falsifiability: Evidence the Latin style is uniformly late, or proof the diary was composed by the same hand as the frame narrative

title: Origen's Hexapla (six-column comparative edition)
claim: Origen of Alexandria compiled at Caesarea Maritima, before c. 240 CE, a six-column comparative edition of the Hebrew Bible: (1) the Hebrew in Hebrew characters, (2) the Hebrew transliterated into Greek (the Secunda), (3) Aquila, (4) Symmachus, (5) the Septuagint with asterisked additions (mainly from Theodotion) marking where the Greek had nothing for the Hebrew and obeloi marking where the Greek had no Hebrew beneath it, (6) Theodotion. The asterisked and obelized differences are openly marked, not silently rewritten.
place: Caesarea Maritima (compilation); surviving witnesses at Cairo and Milan
grade_reason: The edition's existence, column structure, critical signs, and Caesarean origin are independently attested (Eusebius, the two palimpsest witnesses, Field) and the Hexaplaric revision is documented in living Septuagint research; the ~240 CE date is traditional-inference, not inscribed.
earliest_attestation: Eusebius of Caesarea, Ecclesiastical History 6.16 (early 4th c.), describing Origen's collection of the Hebrew and the editions of 'the seventy' and Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion 'arranged opposite one another in parallel columns, together with the Hebrew texts'; the Hexapla itself survives in fragments

sources.ref: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 6.16 (the six-column arrangement, the Nicopolis and Jericho 'fifth, sixth, seventh' editions)
Cairo Genizah palimpsest T-S 12.182 — surviving Hexapla fragments
Milan Ambrosian palimpsest (O.39 sup.), recovered by Giovanni Mercati 1895
Frederick Field, Origenis Hexaplorum quae supersunt (1875)
University of Helsinki, 'The Septuagint and Its Ancient Versions' — the B-text's later 'Hexaplaric' revision: Hebraizing additions done on the basis of Origen's Hexapla

competing_hypotheses: The surviving fragments preserve the Tetrapla (four-column) rather than the Hexapla — distinguished by column count, the Hexapla identification stands on the evidence
falsifiability: A contemporary Caesarean witness describing a wholly different edition by Origen, or demonstration that the palimpsest fragments belong to a later compilation

title: Camel or rope: the kamelos/kamilos variant
claim: In the 'eye of the needle' saying (Matthew 19:24 // Mark 10:25 // Luke 18:25), the mainstream Greek witnesses read kamelos ('camel'); a kamilos ('rope, ship's cable') variant appears in later witnesses, traced to Cyril of Alexandria (5th c. CE); Metzger characterizes it as 'an attempt to soften the rigor of the statement.' The variant is documented transmission-drift; the 'rope was the original' telling is rejected by the manuscript evidence.
place: Jerusalem/Judea (the saying); Alexandria (Cyril's variant)
grade_reason: The variant's existence, its late attestation, and the direction (camel to rope as softening) all follow the documented manuscript record.
earliest_attestation: The kamelos reading in the 4th-c. uncials; the kamilos variant first in 9th-c.-and-later witnesses and the fathers' speculations (Cyril, and Origen before him)

sources.ref: Codex Vaticanus, Sinaiticus (4th c.), Alexandrinus (5th c.): kamelos — the mainstream ancient reading
Metzger, Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament: the kamilos evidence 'an attempt to soften the rigor of the statement'
Cyril of Alexandria (5th c.) as the variant's patristic source; Origen's earlier speculation noted
The Babylonian Talmud's 'elephant through the eye of a needle' as the Semitic impossibility-hyperbole parallel — the largest animal, not the nearest thread

kiwihellenist (Nov 2023), 'The camel, the rope, and the needle's eye': philological survey — kamilos 'rope' first appears in the 400s CE, vanishingly rare, never used in a sentence by any ancient/medieval writer, always in lexicographical contexts defined via Cyril of Alexandria's phrasing; the sole possible epigraphic use (the Anarbazos inscription) is speculative and proves nothing about the 1st c.; conclusion: kamilos was 'coined specifically to contrive a variant interpretation of the gospels,' exactly as Liddell & Scott suggested ('Perh(aps) coined as an emendation of the phrase' at Matt 19.24). Supports the record's Metzger-direction reading.

Pirtea, Adrian (2021), 'To Pass a Rope Through the Eye of a Needle: The Influence of Byzantine Catenae and Homiliaries on the Greek, Church Slavonic, and Old Romanian Readings of Matthew 19,24' (Festschrift for Christoph Koch): the reception history of the rejected reading — earliest manuscript witnesses of kamilon: GA 1424 (s. IX), Vatican gr. 354 (a. 949), Family 13 (10th-15th c.); the Old Armenian (malowx 'rope, cable') and Old Georgian (sabeli; Khanmeti Gospels 'rope of a ship's mechanism') daughter versions attest 'rope' in all three synoptic verses; Byzantine catenae/homiliaries as the dissemination mechanism into Church Slavonic and Old Romanian
sources.grade_note: grade-neutral chain strengthening (Turin-shroud precedent) — deepens the late/secondary/daughter-version-carried character; CORROBORATED held

competing_hypotheses: Kamilos was original and kamelos the error: the words were pronounced alike, and dictation-copying could corrupt either direction (the error could run rope-to-camel as easily as camel-to-rope)
The Aramaic behind the Greek carried the wordplay (gamal/gamil), making the Greek fork a translation artifact of a Semitic pun
The variant is theologically neutral: rope-through-a-needle remains hyperbole for impossibility, so the doctrine never turned on it (unlike almah/parthenos)
falsifiability: A pre-9th-century Greek witness reading kamilos at Matthew 19:24, or a demonstrated Aramaic Vorlage with 'rope'

title: The alchemists' successful transmutation of base metals into gold
claim: Medieval and early-modern alchemists succeeded in transmuting base metals into gold (chrysopoeia) — that they actually produced real gold from lead, iron, copper or mercury by alchemical or chemical means, before the twentieth century.
place: Strasbourg (Sethon projection, July 1602, before Dr Jacob Zwinger); Cologne (August 1603)
grade_reason: Three independent kills: (1) the documented projection-frauds and illusions — hidden gold, copper-displacement 'transmutations', the Helvetius 1666 confidence trick; (2) the physics — Lavoisier's 1789 conservation of mass and Dalton's atomic theory make chemical transmutation impossible, since changing an element means changing the proton count, which is a nuclear not a chemical act; (3) the only genuine gold-making is nuclear (Rutherford 1919 -> McMillan 1937 -> Sherr/Bainbridge/Anderson 1941 -> Seaborg 1980), and it is uneconomical by orders of magnitude. The claim fails on every leg.
earliest_attestation: The early-modern 'projection' performances (e.g. Sethon's July 1602 Strasbourg projection before Dr Jacob Zwinger; the August 1603 Cologne projection) — the 'successes' are event-reports from credulous or interested witnesses, never controlled assays.

sources.ref: Principe, The Aspiring Adept (1998) — the Sethon/Sendivogius episode and the projection economy of early-modern courts

1926 Science account of the classic 'copper water' case — an iron vessel immersed in copper-salt solution takes a real copper coating, reported for centuries as an iron-into-copper transmutation; displacement chemistry, not transmutation

Scientific American, 'Fact or Fiction?: Lead Can Be Turned into Gold' — the bismuth-to-gold experiment (1980, Bevalac, ~$5,000/hr beam time, ~a day of beam time; Seaborg: 'more than one quadrillion dollars per ounce' vs ~$560/oz gold in 1980) as the nuclear counterexample
Indiana Public Media, 'Modern Alchemy: Lab-Made Gold' — Sherr, Bainbridge & Anderson 1941 (mercury + neutrons -> radioactive gold, Phys. Rev. 60:147) as the first actual gold-making
Discover Magazine, 'Turning Lead Into Gold' — McMillan 1937 deuteron-beam artificial gold isotopes; Loveland on the decades of accelerator-made gold before Seaborg

competing_hypotheses: Many practitioners were self-deceived rather than fraudulent — the copper-water displacement case fooled working chemists for centuries, and illusions can be honest
The spiritual-hermetic reading: the gold was always a metaphor for perfection, and the literal chrysopoeia claim is a later misreading of the tradition
A few honest practitioners advanced real chemistry while believing the goal was near — the debunked result does not debunk their methods
falsifiability: A surviving pre-1900 alchemical 'gold' sample from a documented projection, assayed as genuine gold and shown to have been produced in the projection itself. No such sample exists; the fraud literature documents the opposite.

title: The 'great horse' study (Ameen et al. 2021) — the bones against the image
claim: The 'great horse' zooarchaeological study (Ameen et al. 2021, published/announced January 2022): 1,965 horse remains from 171 English sites, AD 300–1650 — the first large-scale osteoarchaeological assessment of medieval English horse size, showing medieval horses were markedly smaller than modern riding and draft horses, with the largest animals of the high medieval period reaching about 15–16 hands.
place: England (171 sites; study led by University of Exeter, AHRC-funded)
grade_reason: Peer-reviewed large-scale sample with published methods; held below VERIFIED because the study's own authors fence their inference — size alone cannot identify a war horse.
earliest_attestation: Ameen et al., International Journal of Osteoarchaeology (2021), DOI 10.1002/oa.3038

sources.ref: Ameen, C. et al., 'In search of the 'great horse': A zooarchaeological assessment of horses from England (AD 300–1650)', International Journal of Osteoarchaeology (2021), DOI 10.1002/oa.3038 — lead author Carly Ameen, PI Oliver H. Creighton, Alan Outram, University of Exeter; AHRC-funded; 1,965 remains, 171 sites
Science Daily release, 10 Jan 2022: 'Medieval warhorses were surprisingly small in stature'
Gizmodo coverage: 'none in the almost 2,000 we studied would be able to be modern police horses' (Outram); shire horses (18 hands) cast in film roles but much larger than any medieval specimen

competing_hypotheses: English-only sample: Continental (e.g. Spanish, Hungarian) breeding lines may have run larger
The study explicitly cautions that size alone cannot confidently identify a war horse in the archaeological record — the 'great horse' is a document category, not an osteological one
falsifiability: Re-analysis of the same sample with different height-estimation methods overturning the size distributions, or a comparable multi-site sample showing substantially larger medieval horses

title: The philosophers' stone as a historical goal
claim: For roughly sixteen centuries, a continuous tradition of practitioners — from Zosimos of Panopolis (c. 300 CE) through the Arabic Jabirian corpus, the Latin Pseudo-Geber Summa perfectionis (c. 1280-1310), the Rosarium philosophorum (1550) to Sendivogius's Novum lumen chymicum (1604) — sought a transmuting agent, the philosophers' stone, that would perfect base metals into gold. The GOAL and the PRACTICE are historically real; only the claimed RESULT is debunked.
place: Panopolis (Akhmim), Roman Egypt — Zosimos's ground
grade_reason: Multiply attested across ~1,600 years and three civilizations' manuscript traditions — Greek, Arabic, Latin — with surviving texts, annotated copies in Newton's and Lavoisier's libraries, and documented court demonstrations. Per the doctrine's attestation rule (master-list item 25): we grade the BELIEF, not the entity; the phenomenon is verified, the metaphysics untouched.
earliest_attestation: Zosimos of Panopolis, Chemeu, c. 300 CE — the earliest surviving alchemical author, writing in Greek in Roman Egypt.

sources.ref: Zosimos of Panopolis, Chemeu (c. 300 CE) — the earliest surviving alchemical corpus, in Greek
Pseudo-Geber, Summa perfectionis (c. 1280-1310, attributed to Jabir ibn Hayyan; likely Paul of Taranto) — the Latin corpus that carried the stone's laboratory program into the Latin West

Sendivogius, Novum lumen chymicum (1604) — 56+ editions over two centuries in Latin, German, French, English, Russian and Dutch; Sir Isaac Newton's annotated copy (British Library); Antoine Lavoisier's bookplated copy (Cornell)
Wikipedia, Michael Sendivogius — the Polish court's transmutation demonstrations (e.g. before Sigismund III Vasa) and the TV-afterlife of the legend

competing_hypotheses: The stone as pure metaphor: the spiritual-hermetic reading holds the whole corpus was always about inner perfection, never laboratory metal
The stone as fraud-technology: the manuals were written to sell secrets and patronage, and the 'tradition' is a confidence economy with texts as props
The continuity is overstated: the Greek, Arabic and Latin traditions are substantially independent inventions, not one 1,600-year conversation
falsifiability: Absence of the stone-goal from any one of the three manuscript streams (Greek, Arabic, Latin) would collapse the continuity claim. All three carry it.

title: The Sogdian Ancient Letters (c. 313 CE)
claim: A cache of personal letters written in Sogdian (an Iranian language of the Samarkand region) by merchants stranded in China, found in a ruined Han watchtower near Dunhuang — the voice of the merchant houses that ran the network: debts, partners, camels, and a lost loan, 3,000 km from home.
place: Dunhuang, Gansu — the Han watchtower where Stein found them
grade_reason: The physical letters exist, were found archaeologically in context, and are read in the original script; only the precise dating and some passage readings are debated.
earliest_attestation: The letters themselves, c. 310–313 CE; found 1907 by Aurel Stein in a Han-era watchtower at Dunhuang

sources.ref: The Ancient Letters (British Library): Sogdian text in Aramaic-derived script; one letter in Brahmi, one fragment in Bactrian — found in situ in the watchtower, 1907
W. B. Henning's decipherment and translations (the foundational edition); subsequent re-editions
The 'Lady 1' letter describing the famine and death in Luoyang after 311 CE — the crisis the merchants lived through

competing_hypotheses: The crisis-moment reading: the letters were written during wartime chaos in China (311–313 CE) and may represent the merchant system under extreme stress, not its normal operation
Paleographic debates over specific passages (Henning's readings vs. later editors) — the gist (debts, partnerships, caravan losses) is undisputed; the fine details of the accounts are contested
falsifiability: Proof that the letters are modern forgeries (the find context, script, and linguistic strata rule this out) or a re-dating that breaks the Luoyang-311 anchor would force revision

title: The stirrup's Asian origin and westward transmission
claim: The stirrup was invented in East Asia no later than the 4th century CE and reached Europe by the 6th–7th centuries via the steppe peoples (above all the Avars), with Frankish adoption following in the late 8th–early 9th centuries.
place: Nanjing, China (earliest known representation; the transmission runs west across the steppe to the Carpathian Basin)
grade_reason: The artifacts exist and multiply attest the arc — Chinese tombs to Avar graves to Byzantine manuals — but the exact route, the inventor, and the Strategikon's date stay unproven.
earliest_attestation: Ceramic horse figurine with paired triangular stirrups from a First Jin Dynasty tomb near Nanjing, 322 CE (representation); actual stirrups: gold-plated bronze stirrup from an Anyang grave, same era

sources.ref: 322 CE Jin-dynasty ceramic horse figurine, Nanjing (paired triangular stirrups)
Tomb of Feng Sufu (d. 415 CE), Northern Yan — first directly-dated stirrups (mulberry wood, gilded bronze, iron plates, lacquer)
111 early Avar-age apple-shaped cast-iron stirrups from 55 burial sites in Hungary and environs (excavated by 2005)
Strategikon attributed to Emperor Maurice (575–628) — 'attached to the saddles should be two iron steps [skala]' (dating of the manual disputed, 8th–9th c. alternative)

KPU Pressbooks — MEDIEVAL TECHNOLOGIES: The Stirrup (Hemming): East Asia no later than 300 CE; Europe mid-6th c.; Byzantine army by end of 6th c.; Franks from the neighboring Avars late 8th–early 9th c.

competing_hypotheses: Bálint's revision: too few well-dated finds exist to identify a single Inner Asian route via the Avars
White's emphasis on the Byzantine milieu as the stirrup's European entry point (taken up and scrutinized by Bálint)
A Central Asian origin earlier than China (the c. 100 CE engraving — single depiction, insufficient alone)
falsifiability: A securely-dated European stirrup predating the 6th century, or proof the Jin-dynasty figurines are misdated or the Avar grave associations are intrusive

title: The Eastern Roman Empire (the 'Byzantine' state), 330–1453
claim: A continuous Roman state centered on Constantinople existed from the city's dedication (11 May 330 CE) to the Ottoman conquest of the city (29 May 1453 CE) — an Eastern Roman Empire of eleven centuries, with continuous imperial administration, law, coinage, and historical writing across the span.
place: Constantinople (modern Istanbul)
grade_reason: Uncontested in scholarship; the state's continuous existence across the span is attested by an unbroken chain of contemporary administrative, literary, numismatic, and diplomatic sources, plus the conquest accounts of its end.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary: the Theodosian Code (438), Procopius's Wars (c. 550), Theophanes's Chronicle (9th c.), Anna Komnene's Alexiad (12th c.), imperial coinage throughout, Ottoman conquest accounts (1453)

sources.ref: Procopius, Wars (c. 550)
Theophanes the Confessor, Chronicle (9th c.)
Anna Komnene, Alexiad (c. 1148)
Imperial coinage, 330–1453 (continuous minting record)
Treadgold, Warren (1997), A History of the Byzantine State and Society, Stanford UP
Herrin, Judith (2007), Byzantium: The Surprising Life of a Medieval Empire, Princeton UP

competing_hypotheses: Periodization debates: scholars date the state's 'medieval' character from Heraclius's reforms (7th c.) or the Iconoclast era — a dispute about character, not existence
The 'fall of Rome in 476' convention, which treats the Western collapse as the end of the Roman Empire — this record carries the Eastern continuity against that convention
falsifiability: A documented break in the imperial succession with no institutional continuity, or proof the administrative and legal tradition was founded anew after 330

title: The Rhomaioi: the empire called itself Roman
claim: The people of the Eastern Roman Empire self-identified as Romans (Romaioi/Rhomaioi) and called their state Romania — Romanland — the Empire of the Romans (hê Rhômaíôn Basileía), from Late Antiquity to 1453.
place: Constantinople (modern Istanbul)
grade_reason: The self-identification is attested in the empire's own documents across the span and independently by external sources (the Qur'anic usage, the Sultanate of Rûm's name, the Ottoman Kayser-i Rum title); stops short of VERIFIED on the weaker sub-claims of Kaldellis's ethnicity thesis, which the reviewers flag as partly conjectural.
earliest_attestation: Imperial titulature and chancery documents throughout; Anna Komnene's Alexiad; the Qur'an's Sura 30 (Ar-Rum, c. 615–616 CE) refers to the contemporary Eastern Empire as 'the Romans'

sources.ref: Browning, Robert (1992), The Byzantine Empire (revised ed.) — 'The Byzantines did not call themselves Byzantines, but Romaioi — Romans'
Kaldellis, Anthony (2019), Romanland: Ethnicity and Empire in Byzantium, Harvard UP — the empire as an ethnically Roman state; barrage of primary sources for Roman self-identification
Qur'an, Sura 30 (Ar-Rum), c. 615–616 CE — external contemporary attestation: the 7th-century Eastern Empire is 'the Romans'
Kazhdan & Constable (1982), People and Power in Byzantium

competing_hypotheses: Kaldellis's stronger thesis (Romanland as an ethnically Roman nation-state) — reviewed as broadly persuasive but with conjectural demography (ResearchGate review of Romanland)
The classicizing minority usage: Byzantine authors also called themselves 'Ausones' in literary Greek — a learned affectation, not the identity claim
falsifiability: A contemporary self-document in which the imperial chancery or the population-at-large calls the state 'Byzantium' or its people 'Byzantines' as an endonym before 1557

title: The first celebration of Christmas on December 25 (Rome, by 336 CE)
claim: By 336 CE, the church at Rome was celebrating Christ's nativity on December 25 — the first undisputed attestation of Christmas on that date.
place: Rome
grade_reason: The liturgical fact is documented: the Roman depositio lists the nativity at December 25 by c. 336, and the list's structure treats the nativity as the year's opening entry.
earliest_attestation: Chronograph of 354 (Philocalian Calendar), Depositio Martirum, headed: 'VIII kal. Ian. natus Christus in Betleem Iudeae' (December 25: Christ born in Bethlehem of Judea); the depositio is arranged December 25 to December 25, marking the nativity as the start of the ecclesiastical year.

sources.ref: Chronograph of 354 (Philocalian Calendar), Depositio Martirum: 'VIII kal. Ian. natus Christus in Betleem Iudeae'; Depositio Episcoporum (bishop list ending before 336)
Nothaft, C. P. E., 'The Origins of the Christmas Date: Some Recent Trends in Historical Research' — the depositio as terminus ad quem 336
Simmons, E., 'The Origins of Christmas and the Date of Christ's Birth,' JETS 58.2 (2015): 'the earliest undisputed evidence we possess for celebration of Christ's nativity on December 25th'

competing_hypotheses: The 336 dating is a terminus ad quem from the depositio episcoporum's bishop list (which ends before 336); the observance could be older and undocumented — local Roman celebration before 336 cannot be excluded on the documents
The Hippolytus Commentary-on-Daniel passage (c. 204) as a genuine earlier attestation of the Dec-25 date — carried as contested (possible later interpolation)
falsifiability: Evidence that the depositio martirum's December-25 nativity entry is a later interpolation would drop the grade; an earlier securely dated attestation would raise it.

title: The Aramaic incantation bowls: two thousand buried pleas
claim: In late-antique Babylonia (4th–7th c. CE), Jewish (and Mandaic, and Syriac) households buried earthenware bowls face-down under thresholds, inscribed with Aramaic incantations binding demons — including Lilith and the lilith-classes — quoting the Hebrew Bible, the Targum, and the liturgy. ~2,000 such bowls are known; the published corpora (Montgomery 1913, Nippur; Naveh & Shaked 1985; Naveh & Shaked 1993; Shaked et al. 2013) establish the practice as the material record of lived protective belief.
place: Nippur and Sasanian Babylonia (Iraq)
grade_reason: The artifacts exist by the thousands, the texts are published and translated by multiple independent scholars, and the practice (burial under thresholds, face-down) is archaeologically consistent. The grade covers the artifacts and the lived belief they attest; never the demons they bind.
earliest_attestation: The bowls themselves: earthenware, inscribed in spiral text, buried under domestic thresholds; excavated (Nippur) and unprovenanced market finds alike

sources.ref: Montgomery, James A., Aramaic Incantation Texts from Nippur (1913) — 40 bowls, the founding corpus
Naveh, Joseph & Shaked, Shaul, Amulets and Magic Bowls (1985) — the legible Aramaic amulets plus 13 unpublished bowls
Naveh, Joseph & Shaked, Shaul, Magic Spells and Formulae: Aramaic Incantations of Late Antiquity (1993)
Shaked, Shaul et al., Aramaic Bowl Spells (Brill, 2013)
Hunter, Erica C.D., iconography studies — the Ktar-Lilith female-demon figure drawings on the bowls
National Library of Israel bowl research (Gross & Vilozny) — the bowls as products of competing scribal circles, quoting biblical, Targumic, and liturgical texts

Atamni, Madi, Amar, Saabni & El-Sana (2026), 'Beyond Labels: Visual Invariance in Self-supervised Learning for Aramaic Bowls Document Analysis and Recognition' — ICDAR 2026 (doi:10.1007/978-3-032-36023-6_27, online 26-Aug-2026) — self-supervised visual learning for Aramaic bowl script recognition; machine reading of the bowls, grade-neutral (the Turin-shroud precedent), grade held

Fein, Sari, 'Amulets and Ancestors: Jewish Women's Reproductive Agency in Late Antiquity', AABNER 5, no. 2 (Autumn 2025): 129-163, doi:10.35068/aabner.v5i2.1127 — the Museu da Farmácia Lisbon Jewish Aramaic bowl (Inv. 10895, 5th-8th c. CE): a fertility incantation for Mihranahid daughter of Ahat deploying Gen 30:22 ('And God remembered Rachel...') as imitative magic — a published 5th-8th-c. bowl using the biblical barren-matriarch tradition as a client-side technology; the bowls' users commissioned scripture as a tool, not just a text.

competing_hypotheses: The bowls as normative Judaism: they quote the Bible, Targum, and liturgy — but Gross & Vilozny argue the producers were a market of competing scribal circles, some rabbinic, some closer to neighboring traditions — not a single 'Jewish' practice
The bowls as anti-demonic insurance written by professionals for clients — the 'Gia Bar Imma' commission model (NLI) — vs. domestic folk production
The maximalist reading: the bindings worked — not graded; the attestation rule grades the plea, never the demon
falsifiability: A demonstration that the dated corpora are modern forgeries would overturn the record; the looted provenance of many market bowls affects context, not the paleographic dating, which rests on excavated parallels.

title: The Indian origin of chess: chaturanga → chatrang → shatranj
claim: Modern chess descends from the Indian game chaturanga (6th century CE), transmitted westward through Persian chatrang and Arab shatranj into medieval Europe.
place: Gupta Empire, northern India (traditional)
grade_reason: Four independent witness lines — Sanskrit literary, Persian literary, Arabic treatise, and the continuous European adoption trail — converge on the India → Persia → Arab → Europe route; no single contemporary 6th-century Indian artifact survives, so it stops short of VERIFIED.
earliest_attestation: Subandhu's Sanskrit romance Vasavadatta (dated 400–650 CE), referencing chaturanga; Persian Chatrangnamak tradition (earliest surviving ms 1323, claiming a 6th-c. Sasanian transmission under Khosrow I); the Arabic chess treatise of al-Adli in Baghdad, c. 840 CE, which treats the Indian game as the source the Persians altered.

sources.ref: Subandhu, Vasavadatta (400–650 CE), earliest literary reference to chaturanga (Murray 1913, p.51)
Chatrangnamak (Middle Persian tradition; earliest surviving ms 1323; Meissenburg narrows composition to c. 700–800, with claimed 6th-c. oral transmission)
Firdausi, Shahnama — the Buzurjmihr/Buzurjmihr chess legend (Sasanian-era transmission story; e.g. Met folio ca. 1330–40)
al-Adli, chess treatise, Baghdad c. 840 CE — quoted as stating the Persians altered some rules of Indian chess when they took it over
H.J.R. Murray, A History of Chess (Oxford, 1913) — the founding synthesis of the Indian-origin thesis

competing_hypotheses: The Iranian hypothesis: the earliest securely documented form of the game is late-Sasanian chatrang; the India→Iran direction of transmission is inferred, not proven (CAIS-SOAS reassessment)

The Chinese origin: Needham's 1962 divination-board hypothesis and David Li's 'Genealogy of Chess' thesis; first securely dated Chinese reference is the Xiang Jing (569 CE), later than the Indian literary references
A broader syncretic origin in the Greco-Bactrian / Central Asian cultural zone (Samsin; Josten) rather than a single point of invention
falsifiability: A securely dated pre-400 CE chess-family board or piece-set from a non-Indian context with chess-like armies and movement, or decisive philology showing the Vasavadatta chaturanga reference is a later interpolation.

title: Nalanda Mahavihara — the ancient university
claim: From c. 427 CE (Gupta foundation under Kumaragupta I) into the late 12th century CE, Nalanda in Magadha (Bihar) was one of the ancient world's great residential universities: a mahavihara complex with multiple monasteries, temples, lecture halls, and a major manuscript library tradition (Dharmaganja), drawing students from across Asia — attested by the Chinese pilgrims Xuanzang (at Nalanda 630–643) and Yijing (675–685), by excavated architecture (ASI campaigns from 1915), and by UNESCO's 2016 World Heritage inscription.
place: Nalanda Mahavihara, Bihar, India (near Rajgir)
grade_reason: The institution is multiply attested across independent traditions — contemporary Chinese eyewitness accounts (Xuanzang, Yijing), excavated architecture and inscriptions (ASI), and the Tibetan transmission record — but foundation dates, population figures, and the library buildings' form rest on later tradition, so the grade stops short of VERIFIED.
earliest_attestation: Xuanzang (Hiuen Tsang), Great Tang Records on the Western Regions (Da Tang Xiyu Ji), 7th c. CE — eyewitness account of 630–643; Yijing (I-tsing), 675–685; Kumaragupta I seals (archaeological, 5th c.)

sources.ref: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji (Great Tang Records on the Western Regions), 7th c. — eyewitness 630–643 (8 compounds, 10 temples, meditation halls; admissions examination)
Yijing (I-tsing), account of Nalanda 675–685 — >3,000 monks resident; curriculum (Vinaya, Sanskrit grammar, logic, medicine)
Kumaragupta I seals from the Nalanda excavations — 5th-c. Gupta foundation attestation
Archaeological Survey of India excavations (1915–1937, 1974–1982) — 9+ viharas, stupas, temples, drainage systems; destruction layers
Taranatha, History of Buddhism in India (1608) — Tibetan tradition: the three-building Dharmaganja library (Ratnasagara, Ratnodadhi, Ratnaganj), the nine-storey building
UNESCO World Heritage inscription, 'Archaeological Site of Nalanda Mahavihara' (2016)

competing_hypotheses: The exact foundation date: c. 427 CE via Kumaragupta I seals is the standard reading, but the earliest structural layers and the Tibetan tradition (Nagarjuna associations) keep a precise founding genuinely debated

Population figures are pilgrim-account numbers, not counts: Xuanzang's biographer gives ~10,000 residents, Xuanzang himself says 'some thousand brethren', Yijing gives >3,000 monks — the middle (several thousand) is the honest range

The nine-storey library (Ratnasagara) and the three-building Dharmaganja (Ratnasagara, Ratnodadhi, Ratnaganj) rest on the later Tibetan tradition via Taranatha, not on excavated library buildings — the institution is solid, the architecture of its libraries is tradition

The 'world's first university' superlative is rhetorical framing, not a graded claim: Taxila (Takshashila) and other centres predate it as learning institutions; Nalanda's distinction is scale and residential organisation, not absolute firstness
falsifiability: A dated inscriptional or stratigraphic sequence showing no large monastic complex at the site before the 10th century, or proof that the Chinese pilgrim accounts are later fabrications

title: The sack of Rome by Attila the Hun (the belief that Attila captured and sacked Rome)
claim: Attila the Hun sacked Rome — that is, his Huns captured and sacked the city of Rome itself.
place: Mincio river, near Mantua (meeting site); Rome (the city never taken)
grade_reason: Attila's 452 Italian campaign halted at the River Po; Leo I's embassy at the Mincio secured his withdrawal; the ancient sources never describe a sack of Rome by Attila, who died in 453 without entering the city. The sacks belong to Alaric (410) and Gaiseric (455).
earliest_attestation: The conflation lives in later popular retellings; the ancient sources (Prosper of Aquitaine, Priscus, Jordanes) describe the 452 Italian campaign, the Mincio meeting, and the withdrawal — never a sack of Rome by Attila.

sources.ref: Prosper of Aquitaine — short, reliable contemporary description of the 452 meeting at the Mincio near Mantua: Leo I (with Consul Avienus and Prefect Trigetius, at Valentinian III's wish) obtained Attila's promise to withdraw from Italy and negotiate peace
Priscus (fragments) — reports Attila's superstitious fear of Alaric's fate (Alaric died shortly after sacking Rome in 410) gave him pause at the Po
Jordanes, Getica — the 452 campaign narrative and the tradition of Leo's embassy

Wikipedia, 'Attila' (invasion of Italy and death section, citing the above) — Attila halted at the River Po; Leo's embassy at the Mincio; withdrawal; death in 453 of a nasal hemorrhage on his wedding night to Ildico

Encyclopaedia/Infoplease via FactMonster, 'Attila' — 'Attila turned back and invaded (452) N Italy but abandoned his plan to take Rome itself... withdrawal... appears to have been motivated by a shortage of provisions and the outbreak of pestilence'
Peter Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005) — famine, pestilence, and Marcian's Danube campaign as the withdrawal's real causes, carried as the modern interpretation
Christopher Kelly, The End of Empire: Attila the Hun and the Fall of Rome (2008) — the material-strategic reading of the 452 turn-back, carried as the modern interpretation
The sacks that did happen: Alaric's Visigoths, 410; Gaiseric's Vandals, 455 (Leo I negotiated sanctuary with Gaiseric but could not prevent the sack)

competing_hypotheses: The pious-fable tradition (Raphael's Vatican fresco, the saints-with-flaming-swords story): Leo's diplomacy alone, by miracle, turned Attila back — a later ecclesiastical elaboration, not the campaign's documented cause
The material-strategic reading: provisions failure, pestilence in Attila's camp, and Eastern Roman forces moving across the Danube behind him — the modern consensus causes
falsifiability: A contemporary 5th-century account describing Attila's Huns inside Rome, or Roman administrative records of a 452 Attila sack (e.g., a breach in the Aurelian Walls, a ransom ledger), would revive the claim.

title: The droit du seigneur: the medieval lord's 'right of the first night'
claim: In medieval Europe, feudal lords held a legal right — known as the droit du seigneur or jus primae noctis — entitling them to spend the wedding night with their vassals' brides.
place: Bologna, Italy (Gratian's seat — the seat of medieval canon law, where the right should appear and does not)
grade_reason: Two independent kills: (1) the empty medieval record — across thousands of surviving charters, custumals, lawbooks, and court judgments, the legal right never appears (1911 Britannica: 'For the existence of the custom in a legalized form there is no trustworthy evidence'; Boureau: 'No law, no custom, no lord ever held such a right'); (2) the manufactured trail — the story's documentary birth is early-modern (Boece 1527, invented king; Acta Sanctorum 1643+; Voltaire 1756; Beaumarchais 1784), not medieval, exactly the 'old ugly times' pattern Barbero describes: 'not even a single medieval author' used the trope, while Renaissance writers invented it as something from the barbaric past.
earliest_attestation: No medieval attestation of any kind: no statute, charter, lawbook, manorial roll, or court judgment anywhere in medieval Europe records such a right. The first historian to record it is Hector Boece in 1527 (Scotland), who attributes it to a legendary king, Ewen (Evenus III), and says it was abolished by Malcolm III under St Margaret's influence — Boece's King Ewen was probably invented (Alain Boureau). The phrase in its modern sense belongs to the 18th century: Voltaire's attacks on feudal abuses and Beaumarchais's The Marriage of Figaro (1784), whose Count's abolished right drives the plot.

sources.ref: Alain Boureau, The Lord's First Night: The Myth of the Droit de Cuissage (University of Chicago Press, 1998) — the full autopsy: no law, no custom, no lord ever held such a right; Boece's King Ewen probably invented; the Jangnoma-shaped legend industry of the 19th century

1911 Encyclopedia Britannica, 'Jus Primae Noctis' — 'For the existence of the custom in a legalized form there is no trustworthy evidence. That some such abuse of power may have been occasionally exercised by brutal nobles in the lawless days of the early middle ages is only too likely, but the jus, it seems, is a myth, invented no earlier than the 16th or 17th century.' Also records the Council of Carthage 398 continence custom and Louis Veuillot's 1854 treatment

Wikipedia, 'Droit du seigneur' / 'Primae noctis' — Hector Boece 1527 (first historian to record; Scotland; Malcolm III abolition story; merchet instituted in its place); Melissa/Francesco Campitelli 1624 ordinance episode ('historicity and legal basis remain unverified'); Acta Sanctorum mentions from 1643; play connection to Beaumarchais

historymedieval.com, 'Primae Noctis Myth' (updated Jan 2026) — 'While there is little historical evidence to confirm this practice ever took place'; carries Boureau's verdict and Vasily Polenov's 1874 Le droit du Seigneur as belief-art

Alessandro Barbero (via UCCR) — 'no testimonies to its diffusion in medieval Europe,' no secular or ecclesiastical directives; 'not even a single medieval author' used the trope while modern scriptwriters do; the legend begins in the 16th century 'as something that happened during the old ugly times'

competing_hypotheses: The right existed somewhere but went unrecorded — impossible to exclude absolutely, but the silence spans the very document classes that recorded every other seigneurial due (charters, custumals, manorial rolls), and medieval literature itself — famously frank about sex (Boccaccio, the fabliaux) — never once uses the trope (Alessandro Barbero's point)

The right existed as unwritten custom rather than codified law — fails on the same silence, and on the chronology: every 'evidence' offered is early-modern (Boece 1527, the Acta Sanctorum from 1643, the Melissa ordinance 1624), centuries after the alleged practice

The tradition was manufactured by 18th-century Enlightenment anti-feudal polemic (Voltaire's 1756 essay, Beaumarchais's 1784 Figaro) recycling the 16th-century Boece story — the reading the documentary trail supports
falsifiability: Produce one medieval source — a statute, charter, custumal, or court judgment dated before 1500 — that institutes, records, or enforces a lord's right to the wedding night as a legal right. One parchment moves the grade; there are none.

title: The medieval non-bather: "medieval people never bathed"
claim: Medieval Europeans (c. 500-1500 CE) rarely or never bathed — regular bathing was essentially unknown in medieval Europe, and public bathhouses were a Roman-era relic that did not exist in medieval cities.
place: Medieval Europe (exemplified by Paris)
grade_reason: Multiple independent primary/contemporary sources — monastic rules, guild statutes, royal ordinances, chronicles, and surviving bathhouses across four regions — document public and private bathing as ordinary medieval practice; the universal 'never' is a modern construction.
earliest_attestation: The universal-non-bathing reading is an early-modern/modern projection (Victorian 'Dark Ages' shorthand); medieval sources describe bathing as ordinary practice — see evt-medieval-bathhouses-001.

sources.ref: Rule of St. Benedict, Ch. 36 (c. 530) — 'Let the use of the bath be offered to the sick as often as it is useful'
Livre des métiers (Étienne Boileau, Paris, 1268) — guild statutes of the étuviers, professional bathhouse-keepers
Henry II's 39 Ordinances for the stewholders of Southwark (1161) — Bishop of Winchester's licensed bathhouses
Primary Chronicle / Tale of Bygone Years (c. 1113) — the Apostle Andrew passage describing Slavic wooden bathhouses as routine practice

Ellen Wurtzel, 'Passionate Encounters, Public Healing: Medieval Urban Bathhouses in Northern France' (2023, Oberlin Digital Commons) — 13th-16th c. urban bathhouse resurgence from medical treatises, trial records, archives
Katherine Ashenburg, The Dirt on Clean: An Unsanitized History (2007) — documents the 1348 Paris-medical-faculty plague verdict on baths
Georges Vigarello, Concepts of Cleanliness (1988, orig. Le propre et le sale, 1985) — the hygiene low point by modern standards was the 17th-18th centuries, not the Middle Ages

competing_hypotheses: Bathing frequency did decline by the early-modern period (16th-18th c.), and the myth projects that genuine later decline backward onto the Middle Ages
The ascetic saints' writings record genuine abstinence — but as mortification against a bathing norm (like hair shirts), not as typical behavior
falsifiability: Credible evidence that bathing infrastructure and practice were absent throughout medieval Europe — e.g., medieval cities with no bath references at all in their records

title: The spice-covered rot: "medieval cooks used spices to hide rotten meat"
claim: In medieval Europe, cooks used expensive imported spices to disguise or mask the taste of rotten or spoiled meat.
place: Medieval Europe (the schoolbook tradition's setting)
grade_reason: Multiple independent lines — food historians' audits of the recipe corpus, the economics of who could afford spices, and the documented preservative economy of salt/vinegar/smoke — all show spices as elite display cooking on fresh meat, not a spoilage disguise.
earliest_attestation: The universal rot-masking reading is a modern popular-history construction; medieval recipe books describe spices used on fresh meat at feasts — see evt-spices-status-medieval-001.

sources.ref: Paul Freedman, Out of the East: Spices and the Medieval Imagination (Yale University Press, 2008) — the rot-masking reading as urban legend: those rich enough to afford spices could afford fresh meat; spices not as good at preservation as salt and smoke; spices as symbols of beauty, affluence, taste, and grace

Jack Turner, Spice: The History of a Temptation (Knopf, 2004) — 'puts to sleep the nostrum about rotting food'; spices as food of the wealthy, medicine, and status display from Augustus to the Renaissance
Forme of Cury (c. 1390, British Library Add MS 5016) — royal English cookbook: heavy spicing on court dishes, meats described as fresh
Le Ménagier de Paris (1393) — household manual: spices added late to sauces (the instruction contradicts the simmer-in-to-hide model)

Constance Hieatt & Sharon Butler, Pleyn Delit: Medieval Cookery for Modern Cooks — much medieval cooking, rich and poor alike, bland by modern standards; highly spiced dishes a minority even at feasts

competing_hypotheses: The rot-masking reading confuses the early-modern decline-era practice of heavily saucing over-salted or long-hung game with a medieval-wide practice
The myth projects the genuine 19th-century colonial-administrator complaint about 'native' food hygiene onto medieval Europe
Some spice use did follow humoral dietetics (hot spices correcting 'cold' meat) — a medical theory, not a spoilage confession
falsifiability: A medieval cookbook or household manual instructing cooks to add imported spices specifically to meat described as spoiled or putrid — distinct from saucing, hanging, or humoral correction

title: Why Teotihuacan fell (the cause of the 6th-century decline)
claim: A specific historical cause explains Teotihuacan's 6th-century decline — the deliberate burning of the civic core c. 550 CE and the city's abandonment by c. 750 CE.
place: Teotihuacan, Valley of Mexico
grade_reason: The burning is archaeologically firm (CORROBORATED as an event, inside evt-teotihuacan-001); every proposed cause is reasoned from the ash layer, not attested — an honest gap, like the life-origin mechanism. SPECULATION by design.
earliest_attestation: The ash layer itself — the archaeology is the only witness; no surviving text names a cause.

sources.ref: George L. Cowgill, Ancient Teotihuacan (Cambridge University Press, 2015) — the burning horizon and the cause debate
Wikipedia, Teotihuacan — 'its major monuments were sacked and systematically burned around 550 CE'; 'Its collapse might be related to the extreme weather events of 535–536'

HISTORY.com, Teotihuacan — 'Around 600 A.D., major buildings were deliberately burned and artworks and religious sculptures were destroyed, suggesting an uprising from the poor against the ruling elite'

competing_hypotheses: Internal uprising: the burning targeted elite and ceremonial structures while leaving residential compounds largely intact — revolt from below
External invasion: no fortifications and no identified invader, but the selective destruction could be sack
Climate stress: the extreme weather events of 535–536 as a trigger for the system's failure
A compound of all three — the current default among specialists, which is not an attested cause
falsifiability: A contemporary written account (Teotihuacan or foreign) naming the cause; or sealed-context dates moving the burning horizon centuries outside 550–600 CE

title: The Birmingham Mingana folios' radiocarbon date (568–645 CE)
claim: The two Birmingham (Mingana Collection) Qur'anic folios — Suras 18–20 in Hijazi script on sheep/goat parchment — were radiocarbon-dated by the Oxford Radiocarbon Accelerator Unit to 568–645 CE at 95.4% probability, making the parchment contemporary with or pre-dating the traditional compilation; the written text matches the standard Qur'anic text with no significant variations.
place: Cadbury Research Library, University of Birmingham, UK (Mingana Collection, acquired from the Middle East)
grade_reason: The Oxford radiocarbon measurement is a rigorous primary lab result on the parchment itself; the folios' text matches the standard Qur'an; the skin-vs-hand caveat is carried inside the record.
earliest_attestation: The folios themselves (undated); identified by Alba Fedeli (PhD researcher, University of Birmingham), announced July 2015

sources.ref: Oxford University Radiocarbon Accelerator Unit measurement: 568–645 CE at 95.4% probability (sheep/goat parchment), announced July 2015
University of Birmingham institutional announcement and Susan Worrall / David Thomas statements (the folios' discovery, the ink-dating limitation)
Alba Fedeli's paleographic identification of the folios and their Hijazi script (the discovery pathway)

competing_hypotheses: The parchment is old but the writing is later: radiocarbon dates the animal's death, not the hand that wrote — parchment was reused and stored, so the text could postdate the skin by decades
A later copyist wrote the standard text on old parchment — possible in principle, untestable without ink-dating methods that currently do not exist for carbon inks (Worrall's stated reason)
falsifiability: A demonstrated contamination source in the Oxford measurement, or a successful ink-dating method showing the writing is centuries later than the skin

title: The early Qur'anic manuscript record
claim: A substantial Qur'anic text existed in written form within decades of Muhammad's death: the Birmingham Mingana 1572a folios (parchment radiocarbon-dated 568-645 CE, containing Surahs 18-20 in present-day sequence), the Sanaa palimpsest DAM 01-27.1 (parchment before 671 CE at 99% probability; upper text Uthmanic, lower erased text a non-Uthmanic variant tradition), and the Codex Parisino-petropolitanus (BnF Arabe 328ab, ~45% of the Qur'an, 7th-8th c.) all substantially match the canonical text — while the Sanaa lower text proves textual plurality existed before effective standardization.
place: Sanaa, Yemen (Great Mosque, 1972 find) / Birmingham, UK (Mingana Collection)
grade_reason: Multiple independent physical witnesses (radiocarbon-dated parchment + Hijazi paleography + monumental inscriptions + external chronicles) converge on a substantially fixed Qur'anic text within decades of 632 CE — while the Sanaa lower text keeps the grade honest: one non-Uthmanic tradition demonstrably existed before standardization.
earliest_attestation: Parchment radiocarbon ranges: Birmingham Mingana 1572a (Oxford Radiocarbon Accelerator Unit, 1456/1461 ± 21 BP, calibrated 568-645 CE, 95.4%); Sanaa palimpsest DAM 01-27.1 (before 671 CE at 99%, before 646 at 75% — Sadeghi & Goudarzi 2012); Tübingen fragment Ms M a VI 165 (649-675 CE, 95%)

sources.ref: Birmingham Mingana 1572a: radiocarbon OxA-29418 (Oxford, 2015), Hijazi script, Surahs 18-20
Sanaa palimpsest DAM 01-27.1: upper text Uthmanic; lower text (scriptio inferior) edition Sadeghi & Goudarzi 2012; multispectral recovery at Stanford
Codex Parisino-petropolitanus, BnF Arabe 328(ab): ~70 folios Paris + 46 St. Petersburg + Vatican + Khalili; ~45% of the Qur'an
Dome of the Rock inscriptions (691 CE): first monumental Qur'anic text in public

competing_hypotheses: The traditional account: revelation in Mecca/Medina 610-632, Uthmanic standardization c. 650 — the early manuscripts are copies of that standard

The manuscripts are physical copies of an already-circulating text whose pre-Muhammad oral/liturgical formation remains debated; revisionist positions (Wansbrough, Crone) argue the text crystallized later in a wider Near Eastern milieu
Paleography note: parchment dates are the death-date of the animal, not the writing — a later scribe could write on old parchment; the Hijazi script and Dome of the Rock anchor constrain this
falsifiability: A dated 7th-century Qur'an manuscript showing a substantially different arrangement of surahs or doctrine, or proof the radiocarbon samples were contaminated or the lower-text edition is a misreading

title: The early Qur'anic text substantially fixed before 700 CE (rasm closure)
claim: The early Qur'anic text was substantially fixed before 700 CE: the consonantal skeleton (rasm) reached closure by the end of the 7th century — multiple independent lines converge on a single written archetype within decades of the traditional Uthmanic date, while the vocalized/readings layer froze much later.
place: Sanaa, Yemen (Great Mosque, 1972 find) / Birmingham, UK (Mingana Collection) / Paris (BnF)
grade_reason: Four independent lines converge: (1) radiocarbon-dated parchment (Birmingham 568-645, Sanaa before-671, Tübingen 649-675), (2) Cook 2004's stemma — the regional codices' variants form a tree, i.e. one archetype, (3) van Putten 2019's shared-orthography proof of a written archetype, (4) Sinai 2014's two-part assessment finding no evidence incompatible with conventional dating. The grade stays CORROBORATED, not VERIFIED: the rasm is what closed — the vocalization/readings layer did not (the Seven canonical readings were fixed by Ibn Mujahid in 324/936 and are only rarely evident in first-two-century manuscripts; regional and dotting variants lived on for centuries). The 'fixed by Uthman in 650, crisp and final' telling is the tradition's version; the manuscripts support 'the skeleton closed by ~700, the readings froze in the 10th century.'
earliest_attestation: Radiocarbon ranges: Birmingham Mingana 1572a (Oxford Radiocarbon Accelerator Unit, OxA-29418, 1456/1461 ± 21 BP, calibrated 568-645 CE, 95.4%); Sanaa palimpsest DAM 01-27.1 (before 671 CE at 99%, before 646 at 75% — Sadeghi & Goudarzi 2012); Tübingen Ms M a VI 165 (649-675 CE, 95%); stemmatic argument: Cook 2004, Graeco-Arabica 9-10 (regional variants of the Uthmanic codices form a tree → single archetype); van Putten 2019, BSOAS 82(2):271-288 (shared orthographic idiosyncrasies — e.g. the 'grace of God' spelling — across Uthmanic-type manuscripts prove a written archetype); Sinai 2014 Part I, BSOAS 77(2):273-292 + Part II, BSOAS 77(3):509-521 (systematic assessment of the late-7th-c. closure hypothesis: neither epigraphic nor literary evidence is incompatible with the conventional dating; the emergent-canon counter-position heard and answered); Sidky 2021 (four regional exemplar codices; the Syrian codex traced to Hims, not Damascus)

sources.ref: Cook, M. (2004) 'The Stemma of the Regional Codices of the Koran,' Graeco-Arabica 9-10 — regional variants form a tree, single archetype (generally Uthman)
van Putten, M. (2019) "The 'Grace of God' as evidence for a written Uthmanic archetype," BSOAS 82(2):271-288 — shared orthographic idiosyncrasies prove a written archetype
Sinai, N. (2014) 'When did the consonantal skeleton of the Quran reach closure? Part I,' BSOAS 77(2):273-292; Part II, BSOAS 77(3):509-521 — systematic assessment of the c.700-closure hypothesis
Sadeghi, B. & Goudarzi, M. (2012) 'San'a' 1 and the Origins of the Qur'an,' Der Islam 87(1-2):1-129 — the Sanaa lower text as early companion tradition
Birmingham Mingana 1572a: radiocarbon OxA-29418 (Oxford, 2015), Hijazi script, Surahs 18-20; Codex Parisino-petropolitanus, BnF Arabe 328(ab), ~45% of the Qur'an, 7th-8th c.
Dome of the Rock inscriptions (691 CE): first monumental Qur'anic text in public

BiSaME project (DFG, 2026–2029, Hamburg + Staatsbibliothek Berlin, Fedeli & Eich): the first systematic ensemble biography of the Great Mosque of Sanaa manuscript collection — computer vision/AI/paleography/philology; 2026 evidence-state context, no new dating yet

Al-Fanar: Jurnal Ilmu Al-Qur'an dan Tafsir, Vol. 9 No. 1 (2026), pp. 13–25: interdisciplinary review of radiocarbon dating in early-Qur'an historiography (Birmingham, Sanaa, Tübingen) — secondary synthesis, confirms the parchment-vs-text fence

competing_hypotheses: The traditional account: revelation in Mecca/Medina 610-632, Uthmanic standardization c. 650 — the codices as copies of that standard (graded as traditional narrative, not manuscript proof)
Wansbrough 1977: the text compiled two to three centuries after the Prophet (the revisionist pole)
Burton 1977: the text compiled by the Prophet himself (the early pole)
Donner 2008 'emergent canon model': closure around 700 CE rather than c. 650 (the position Sinai 2014 systematically assesses)

Motzki 2001 methodological caution: fragmentary manuscripts alone do not prove the earliest codices matched later ones exactly — answered by the stemmatic/orthographic arguments, not by more manuscripts

The Sanaa lower text (Sadeghi & Goudarzi 2012): a non-Uthmanic companion tradition before standardization — early plurality, then effective standardization (explicitly NOT evidence against the rasm-closure claim)
falsifiability: A dated 7th-century Qur'an manuscript showing a substantially different arrangement of surahs or doctrine; proof the radiocarbon samples were contaminated; or a published refutation of the Cook/van Putten tree showing the regional codices do NOT descend from one archetype

title: Muhammad
claim: Muhammad (c. 570-632 CE) of Mecca proclaimed the Qur'anic revelation, united the Arabian tribes, and founded the community (umma) at Medina in 622 CE — the event from which the Islamic calendar counts.
place: Mecca (traditional)
grade_reason: Near-contemporary non-Muslim sources (634, 640 CE) confirm an Arab prophet in Arabia; the detailed biography comes from Islamic sources written a century-plus later.
earliest_attestation: Doctrina Iacobi (634 CE, earliest external reference to an Arab prophet); Thomas the Presbyter chronicle (640 CE); Ibn Ishaq's Sira (d. 767 CE, surviving in Ibn Hisham's recension)

sources.ref: Doctrina Iacobi (634 CE, earliest external mention — 'a prophet has appeared, coming with the Saracens'; Anthony 2014, Der Islam 91.2:243-265 — the 'keys of paradise' motif studied in its late-antique context)
Thomas the Presbyter, Chronicle (640 CE — 'the Arabs of Muhammad', tayyaye d-Mhmt)
PERF 558 (643 CE — bilingual Greek-Arabic receipt, the earliest Arabic-language papyrus of the conquest era; documentary witness, not tradition)
Sebeos, Armenian History (c. 660s — external account naming 'Mahmet', sparse details)
Hoyland, R.G., Seeing Islam As Others Saw It (1997; new Gorgias edition with 2020s foreword — the non-Muslim documentary survey; method: external witnesses first)
Ibn Ishaq / Ibn Hisham, Sira (8th c., traditional biography)
Constitution of Medina (preserved in the Sira tradition; debated authenticity — Anthony/Hobson line treats it as early documentary residue; Shoemaker 2022 line doubts it)

competing_hypotheses: The sira tradition preserves the broad outline of a historical Muhammad (mainstream consensus — e.g. Hoyland 1997/2015, Anthony 2014/2020, Tolan 2025)

The traditional biography is largely a 8th-9th century construction; the historical core is minimal (revisionist position: Wansbrough 1977, Crone & Cook 1977; radicalized by the Inarah school — Ohlig/Popp/Luxenberg; contested in print through 2026 — Hobson, 'Was the Prophet Muhammad really Jesus?' ihya journal 2026, arguing the Constitution of Medina + Qur'an for a pre-632 Muhammad and a 620s Qur'an against Shoemaker 2022 and the Inarah dating)

The Qur'anic text's own dating (620s per Hobson 2026 reading vs 691-c.705 per Shoemaker 2022 vs late 8th c. per Wansbrough 1977) is a live scholarly dispute — carried by evt-quran-manuscripts-002 (CORROBORATED: the rasm closed by ~700 CE; the canon froze in the 10th c.)
falsifiability: Earlier, contradictory contemporary accounts of 7th-century Arabia, or proof the Doctrina Iacobi passage is interpolated

title: The 591 conflation: three women fused into one Magdalene
claim: On 21 September 591, Pope Gregory the Great (Homily 33 on the Gospels) identified Mary Magdalene with the 'sinful woman' of Luke 7:36-50 and with Mary of Bethany (John 12): 'she whom Luke calls the sinful woman, whom John calls Mary, we believe to be the Mary from whom seven devils were ejected according to Mark.' The fusion created the penitent-prostitute Magdalene of fourteen centuries of Western art and devotion. No canonical text makes the identification; the Eastern churches never adopted it; the 1969 General Roman Calendar reform (Mysterii Paschalis) separated the celebrations again (July 22, St Mary Magdalene; the Bethany commemoration removed), and in 2016 the July 22 memorial was elevated to a feast, the apostles' own liturgical rank.
place: Rome (Homily 33 preached in Rome)
grade_raw: CORROBORATED (the 591 homily as a dated event) / DEBUNKED (the three-women identification as history)
grade_reason: The homily is a dated, quoted primary source; the identification it asserts contradicts the texts it claims to read and was officially undone in 1969.
earliest_attestation: Gregory the Great, Homiliarum in Evangelia 33 (591)

sources.ref: Gregory the Great, Homily 33 on the Gospels (591) — the fusion sentence
Luke 7:36-50 vs Luke 8:1-3 — the texts name different women
General Roman Calendar reform, Mysterii Paschalis (14 Feb 1969) — the feasts separated
Congregation for Divine Worship decree (3 June 2016) — July 22 elevated to a feast

competing_hypotheses: The confessional defense: Gregory read a legitimate spiritual unity, not a historical identity
The Eastern position: the fusion never happened east of Rome — Magdalene stayed 'apostle to the apostles'
falsifiability: A pre-591 Latin text making the same three-way identification, or a canonical manuscript variant naming Magdalene in Luke 7

title: The khipu as the Inca empire's information technology
claim: The khipu — cords of cotton or camelid wool, hung from a primary cord and tied with systematic knots encoding decimal numbers, with information also carried in cord color, fiber type, ply direction, knot type, and attachment position — was the Inca empire's (Tawantinsuyu's) standard system for recording census data, tribute, storehouse accounts, and other administrative information, read and maintained by trained specialists, the quipucamayocs.
place: Cuzco, Peru — imperial capital; khipu use was empire-wide across Tawantinsuyu (~2 million sq km)
grade_reason: Hundreds of surviving artifacts converge with colonial eyewitness testimony, independent decimal-system decoding (Locke, the Aschers), and a living Andean tradition still observed in the 1990s — three independent lines on the same claim.
earliest_attestation: Colonial Spanish chronicles (mid-16th c.: Cieza de Leon, Polo de Ondegardo, Guaman Poma) describing the quipucamayoc system; surviving khipus from Inca-period contexts.

sources.ref: Marcia and Robert Ascher, 'Code of the Quipu' (1981): analysis of several hundred khipus — most information numeric, decimal knot clusters (simple, long, figure-of-eight knots), powers of ten by position
Leland Locke (1912): demonstration that khipu knots record a full base-10 numerical system
