title: The Dhul-Qarnayn identification question
claim: The Qur'an's 'Dhu al-Qarnayn' ('the Two-Horned One,' Surah 18:83–101) — a builder of an iron wall against Gog and Magog — has been traditionally identified with Alexander since the 8th century (al-Tabari and later commentators), drawing on the Syriac Alexander Legend's Christianized Alexander and Pseudo-Callisthenian material; Ferdowsi's Shahnameh (completed 1010) carries the Persian 'Iskandar' further. The identification-tradition is attested across a millennium of texts. Whether the Qur'anic figure IS Alexander is disputed (minority proposals include Cyrus the Great); the identity itself is unresolved and graded SPECULATION.
place: The tradition is textual, not geographic: the Syriac Legend (northern Mesopotamia milieu), al-Tabari (Baghdad), Ferdowsi (Tus, Khorasan)
grade_raw: CORROBORATED (the identification-tradition as a literary phenomenon, 8th c.–present) / SPECULATION (the identity of the Qur'anic figure)
grade_reason: The attestation half is CORROBORATED by the Syriac text itself, Tabari's commentary, and Ferdowsi's Iskandar passages — independent witnesses to the same identification over centuries. The identity half stays SPECULATION because the identification is interpretive, not documentary: nothing in the Qur'anic text names Alexander, and the horns motif exists in multiple Near Eastern traditions.
earliest_attestation: The Syriac Alexander Legend (Neṣḥānā d-Aleksandrōs, c. 629–630 CE, dated by its Heraclius-era allusions); al-Tabari's Tafsir (9th c.); Ferdowsi's Shahnameh (completed 1010)

sources.ref: The Syriac Alexander Legend (Neṣḥānā d-Aleksandrōs), c. 629–630 CE: the Christianized Alexander building the gate against Gog and Magog — the bridge text between the Greek Romance tradition and the Islamic Dhu al-Qarnayn
al-Tabari, Jami' al-Bayan (9th c.): the classical tafsir carrying the Alexander identification

Ionescu, Dan-Tudor, 'Alexander the Great in the Persian legends': early Islamic scholarship from the 8th century 'began to conflate Dhū'l-Qarnayn with Alexander, notably in al-Tabari's works, reflecting cross-cultural influences between Persian and Arabic literature'; Iranian Zoroastrian texts portray Alexander negatively — the same king, opposite legend
Qur'an 18:83–101 (the Dhu al-Qarnayn pericope): the primary text — the figure is unnamed by the Qur'an itself

competing_hypotheses: Dhu al-Qarnayn = Alexander (the traditional identification: horns = the Ammon horns of Hellenistic coin portraits)
Dhu al-Qarnayn = Cyrus the Great (minority modern proposal, contested)
Dhu al-Qarnayn as a composite figure (Syriac legend + biblical + local traditions) — the identification question may be ill-posed
falsifiability: No single document can settle the identity; the tradition-grade would fall only if the 8th-century identification were shown to be a modern fabrication — it is not, the attestations are genuine.

title: The 'blind Homer wrote the epics' schoolbook picture
claim: The historical Homer was a blind poet who personally composed the Iliad and the Odyssey as written works — the lone blind genius of the schoolroom busts.
place: Chios / Ionia — the traditional homeland of the blind bard (the seven-cities tradition)
grade_reason: The claim dies on the record. (1) No contemporary evidence exists for Homer's blindness or for single written authorship — every biographical tradition is centuries late, and the Homeric Lives contradict each other on his birthplace, dates, and manner of death. (2) The blindness has a traceable genealogy: the blind bard of Chios in the Hymn to Apollo, Demodocus the blind bard of Odyssey 8 read as self-portrait, and the folk-etymology ho me horon ('he who does not see') — a legend manufactured from a character and a pun, never from evidence; the scholarly readings of the name (homeros = 'hostage/surety'; Nagy's 'he who fits the Song together') point to a generic function, not a man with no eyesight. (3) Parry's formulaic analysis (1928) plus the 1933–35 Yugoslav fieldwork demonstrated the poems' composition mechanism is oral-traditional, not written composition by one hand — the 'wrote it' half of the picture is as dead as the 'blind' half. Fences hold: the blindness as cultural image (the busts, the statues), the unitarian monumental-composer thesis as a live scholarly position, and the epics' own greatness — untouched.
earliest_attestation: The blindness: the Homeric Hymn to Apollo, lines 172–173 (the blind bard of Chios), cited by Thucydides (History of the Peloponnesian War 3.104) as Homer's own self-description; the Homeric Lives (Pseudo-Herodotus, Pseudo-Plutarch) — Hellenistic/Roman and mutually contradictory. The written-authorship: the default assumption until Milman Parry's 1928 Harvard theses began the oral-formulaic demolition.

sources.ref: Wikipedia-adjacent Homer overview (poetrynook.com/poet/homer): the blind-bard tradition — Demodocus in Odyssey 8 read as self-referential; homeros = 'hostage/surety'; the Cymean-dialect meaning 'blind'; the Delian Hymn to Apollo cited by Thucydides 3.104; Ephorus; the false etymology ho me horon ('he who does not see')

The Handy Mythology Answer Book (papertrell.com): Demodocus of Phaeacia as the self-portrait; 'Homer' mythologized as 'a blind bard who more than makes up for physical sight with powers of insight'; the epics as 'probably the works of more than one person, composed in various stages between 900 and 700 B.C.E.'; the Homeric question

Wikipedia 'Homeric Question' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeric_Question): the name-as-generic-function readings (Nagy, Durante); the Homeridae hypothesis; the competing 'blind' derivations; the Wolf 1795 analyst/unitarian split and Parry–Lord as the bridge to the traditional composer

competing_hypotheses: The unitarian position (Whitman, Kirk): a single monumental composer shaped one or both epics out of the oral tradition — a claim about authorship and shaping, NOT about blindness or writing; this record kills only the blind-genius-with-a-stylus picture
The blind bard of Chios in the Homeric Hymn to Apollo as an ancient authorial persona — a real literary tradition, fenced as a cultural phenomenon; graded is the historical claim, not the tradition

The competing etymologies of the name: homeros = 'hostage/surety' (Greek homophony); 'he who fits the Song together' (Nagy); 'he who puts the voice in tune' (homereo); the Cumaean dialect meaning 'blind' — attested readings of a name, none of which is evidence of a man's eyesight

The sincerely-held ancient belief (Thucydides citing the Hymn; Ephorus; the Lives) — sincerity of belief is belief ecology, not evidence; the Lives were composed centuries after any historical Homer, and they disagree with each other
falsifiability: A contemporary or near-contemporary record of the poet's life — e.g., an 8th- or 7th-century BCE inscription, administrative text, or dedicatory artifact naming Homer as a blind individual and author of the poems — or manuscript evidence of single written composition (authorial drafts, a dated autograph tradition).

title: The Persian panemone — the first practical windmills (700–900 AD)
claim: The first practical windmills were the Persian panemone — vertical-axis machines with lightweight wooden sails on a central vertical shaft, built in the Sistan region (modern Iran/Afghanistan) around 700–900 AD, first for pumping water and later for grinding grain.
place: Sistan, eastern Iran / western Afghanistan; Nashtifan, Razavi Khorasan Province, Iran
grade_reason: VERIFIED: the Persian panemone is the earliest recorded working windmill design. Vertical lightweight wooden sails attached by horizontal struts to a central vertical shaft; first built to pump water, subsequently modified to grind grain. The 9th-century Sistan mills are documented by Muslim geographers; the design spread across the Islamic world to India and China. At Nashtifan in northeastern Iran, about 30 such mills — 50 to 60 feet high, wooden blades rotating on a vertical axis between high walls of red clay and straw — have stood for over a thousand years and still grind grain in the 'storm's sting' wind that gave the village its name. Earlier wind-powered devices (Heron's organ, Tibetan prayer wheels) are toys or design concepts, not practical windmills; the panemone is the first machine that did real work.
earliest_attestation: 9th-century Muslim geographers; the Nashtifan tradition

sources.ref: Wikipedia 'Panemone windmill': the earliest recorded windmill design, Persian, 700–900 AD; vertical sails on a central shaft; water-pumping first, grain-grinding after; the spread across the Islamic world.
Green Prophet (Nashtifan): ~30 mills, 1,000+ years, still grinding; the 'storm's sting' wind; the vertical-axis design predating European mills.

falsifiability: Earlier documented practical windmills

title: Tariq ibn Ziyad burned his ships at Gibraltar (711) — DEBUNKED
claim: Tariq ibn Ziyad, after landing in Iberia in 711, burned his ships (or had them scuttled) to deny his men any retreat, then delivered the famous khutba: 'the sea is behind you, the enemy before you.'
place: Gibraltar (Jabal Tariq) — the claimed landing site of the burned fleet
grade_reason: Killed twice from the record itself: (1) no early attestation — the earliest substantial Arabic account (Ibn Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr, 9th c.) describes Julian's vessels 'crossing and recrossing' — a working ferry, not a pyre — and says nothing of destruction; the full speech does not exist in print before Ibn Khallikan's 13th-century Wafayat al-A'yan and al-Maqqari's 17th-century Nafh al-tib; (2) Wikipedia's own khutba article labels the speech 'of dubious authenticity', and Tahera Qutbuddin's analysis places it in the standard Arabic battle-oration genre of 'the troops' desperation as a rhetorical strategy' — a literary topos, not a dispatch.
earliest_attestation: No 8th- or 9th-century source reports a burning; the full khutba is first written down in Ibn Khallikan's Wafayat al-A'yan (completed 1274) and al-Maqqari's Nafh al-tib (early 17th c.).

sources.ref: Ibn Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr wa'l-Maghrib (9th c.) — the earliest substantial Arabic account: reports ~7,000 men and vessels 'crossing and recrossing'; no fleet destruction, no speech
Ibn Habib (9th-c., Andalusian) — records a Tariq exhortation (faith, enemy's vulnerability) without the full dramatic rhetoric and without burned ships
Ibn Khallikan, Wafayat al-A'yan (completed 1274) — the full khutba's first known written home, ~563 years after 711
Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Maqqari, Nafh al-tib (early 17th c.) — the full speech again, drawing on medieval traditions; absent from the earliest conquest chronicles

Tahera Qutbuddin — analysis of the khutba as Arabic battle oration: the 'desperation of the troops' as a rhetorical strategy, in the company of Asim ibn Amr at al-Qadisiyyah and Abu Sufyan at Yarmuk; the speech enumerates worldly rewards, unlike Ali's orations
Wikipedia, 'Khutba of Tariq Ibn Ziyad' — 'A khutba of dubious authenticity' — transmission: Ibn Khallikan's Wafayat al-A'yan and al-Maqqari's Nafh at-Tib

Wikipedia, 'Muslim conquest of the Iberian Peninsula' — the khutba is a 'khutba of dubious authenticity' delivered upon 'the legendary burning of the ships'; Ibn Abd al-Hakam's vessels 'crossing and recrossing'

competing_hypotheses: Ibn Habib (9th c., Andalusian) records a genuine Tariq exhortation — a shorter, faith-and-vulnerability address — so the 13th/17th-century khutba may be an elaboration of a real address, with the ship-burning a later dramatic import

The burning may preserve a real order to disable the transports, transformed by retelling into a blaze; note Cortés at Veracruz 1519 really did scuttle his ships — the motif may have migrated across the Atlantic-facing conquest stories
falsifiability: A contemporary witness — the Latin Chronicle of 754, an 8th-century papyrus or inscription, or an archaeological horizon at Gibraltar consistent with a burned 711 fleet — would reopen the grade.

title: Tariq's 711 crossing and the Battle of Guadalete — CORROBORATED
claim: In 711, the Umayyad commander Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed the Strait with about 7,000 men — mostly Berbers — aboard vessels associated with Julian of Ceuta, landed at Gibraltar (Jabal Tariq, 'Mount Tariq'), and defeated the Visigothic king Roderic at Guadalete, opening the Muslim conquest of Iberia.
place: Gibraltar (Jabal Tariq) — the crossing's landing point, named for the commander
grade_reason: The crossing and the Guadalete victory are attested on both sides of the religious divide — the Latin Chronicle of 754 and the 9th-century Arabic tradition agree on the event; held below VERIFIED because force size (~7,000), the Julian ferry contract, and the exact battlefield rest on the later Arabic tradition alone.
earliest_attestation: Latin Chronicle of 754 — the earliest near-contemporary account of the conquest; Ibn Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr (9th c.) — the earliest substantial Arabic account of the crossing's logistics.

sources.ref: Chronicle of 754 (Latin, Mozarabic) — the earliest near-contemporary account of the 711 conquest
Ibn Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr wa'l-Maghrib (9th c.) — reports the ~7,000-man force and vessels 'crossing and recrossing'; the ferry logic that refutes the burning
Ibn al-Qutiyya (10th c.) — the Julian tradition's second anchor
Wikipedia, 'Muslim conquest of the Iberian Peninsula' — crossing, force size, Guadalete in July 711, the 712 reinforcement under Musa ibn Nusayr

competing_hypotheses: Julian (Ilyan) of Ceuta's own historicity is debated — he appears in the 9th-century Arabic tradition (Ibn Abd al-Hakam, Ibn al-Qutiyya) but not in the Latin Chronicle of 754; his ferry role is parked at CLAIMED
The battle's exact site (Guadalete river vs. the lagoon of Janda) is contested; the victory itself is not
falsifiability: A contemporary 8th-century inscription or coinage contradicting the crossing year, or a 711-dated document placing Roderic elsewhere alive after July, would force a re-grade.

title: Charles Martel's cavalry funding and the Church lands
claim: Charles Martel (mayor of the palace 715–741) built Frankish military power in part on mounted warriors and funded it in part through church-land grants (precaria); the documented record shows the reforms and the seizures, but no contemporary source ties either to the stirrup.
place: Tours/Poitiers, Francia (732 — the battle Brunner's thesis keys to)
grade_reason: Martel's military reforms and church-land precaria are independently documented; the stirrup link is absent from the record, so this foil survives White's kill intact.
earliest_attestation: Heinrich Brunner's 19th-century military analysis (White's source for the cavalry argument); Pepin the Short's 758 demand of horses as tribute from the Saxons (evidence of a cavalry-dependent army one generation on)

sources.ref: Heinrich Brunner (19th c.) — the shift to mounted warfare after Tours 732; Pepin's 758 Saxon horse-tribute; the Muslim-incursion prompting of church-land confiscation for cavalry support (as summarized in the Great Stirrup Controversy article)

Rebus Community — History of Applied Science & Technology, ch. 5: Charlemagne (not Martel) placed increased emphasis on cavalry for rapid-response missions; feudal dominance of mounted aristocrats follows the post-Charlemagne royal collapse

competing_hypotheses: Martel's cavalry already existed and developed gradually — White's 'sudden stirrup revolution' is the artifact, not the army
The church-land policy was fiscal and political, not a military-technology funding mechanism
Tours 732 as a cavalry watershed (Brunner/White) vs a defensive Frankish infantry victory in the older historiography
falsifiability: Contemporary 8th-century Frankish records explicitly linking Martel's cavalry funding to stirrup adoption, or proving the precaria system predated the military need

title: The 2026 al-Juhfah miqat excavation
claim: The Saudi Heritage Commission's first scientific excavation season at Miqat al-Juhfah (2026, with the University of Exeter) documented the Hijrah-era pilgrimage station: 1,700+ artifacts, six pottery kilns, a water channel, and 13 tombstones (some Umayyad/Abbasid), with imported goods from the Levant, Egypt, and Abyssinia — the pilgrimage route's infrastructure in the material record.
place: Miqat al-Juhfah, 187 km NW of Mecca
grade_reason: A documented excavation season by the national authority with a university partner: the artifacts, kilns, channel, and dated tombstones are reported as finds, not tradition.
earliest_attestation: Saudi Heritage Commission announcement, 2026; archaeologymag.com report, 11 June 2026

sources.ref: Saudi Heritage Commission / University of Exeter — first excavation season report, 2026
The Gulf Gazette — Heritage Commission dispatch, 2026

competing_hypotheses: The site's material record reflects its documented early-Islamic pilgrimage-station function
Individual artifact datings await peer-reviewed publication before they can weigh on any specific historical claim
falsifiability: Peer-reviewed publication contradicting the excavation's finds, or proof the 2026 report fabricated the assemblage

title: The Donation of Constantine — a forgery
claim: The Constitutum Constantini is an authentic imperial decree issued by Constantine the Great in the 4th century (dated in the document to March 30, consulships naming Constantine's fourth term and Gallicanus), granting Pope Sylvester I and his successors: spiritual supremacy over the four great sees and all churches, the imperial insignia (diadem, tiara, pallium, scepter), the Lateran palace, the city of Rome, and all the provinces, places and cities of Italy and the western regions.
place: Rome (composition: Roman scriptorium, mid-to-late 8th century)
grade_reason: Zero attestation before the 8th century; the Latin carries 8th-century vocabulary impossible in a 4th-century imperial chancery; the document dates itself with two consuls who never served together; Valla's 1440 proof, Cusa's 1433 prior doubt, and Pecock's 1450s independent confirmation converge, and modern scholarship is unanimous.
earliest_attestation: No 4th-, 5th-, 6th- or 7th-century witness of any kind exists. First surviving witness: the 9th-century Pseudo-Isidorian (False) Decretals collection; no pope used it in the 9th or 10th centuries; first papal official citation by Leo IX, c. 1050 (controversy with the Byzantines, per the 1911 Britannica).

sources.ref: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), 'Donation of Constantine': 'without doubt a forgery, fabricated somewhere between the years 750 and 850'; Valla (1440) proved it 'with certainty'; Nicholas of Cusa (De concordantia catholica III.ii, 1433) called it dictamen apocryphum; Reginald Pecock independently reached the same conclusion (1450-57); Baronius's Annales (ad an. 324) admitted the forgery

1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Donation of Constantine': forged at Rome between the middle and end of the 8th century; included in the 9th-century False Decretals; no papal use in the 9th-10th centuries; first official use by Leo IX c. 1050

Wikipedia, 'Donation of Constantine': consul-dating error (Constantine's fourth term 315 paired with Gallicanus 317 — never served together); narrative built on the 5th-century Acts of Sylvester; content details (Lateran palace, Rome, Italy, the western provinces, landed estates across the empire)

competing_hypotheses: Modern majority : an 8th-century Roman forgery, likely produced in the Lateran or its orbit during the 750s, to buttress papal claims in Italy during the Frankish-alliance era
A minority transmission reading once proposed a Greek original later translated — abandoned; the document's Latin anachronisms are Latin anachronisms
falsifiability: A 4th-century manuscript witness or any contemporary 4th-century reference to the document's existence would revive it; none exists, and the philology of the text's own vocabulary is independently fatal.

title: The sira transmission gap
claim: The earliest surviving biography of Muhammad — Ibn Hisham's recension (d. 833/834 CE) of Ibn Ishaq's Sirat Rasul Allah (d. 767/768 CE, original lost) — postdates the events it describes by roughly 120–200 years; no biography of Muhammad from the 600s survives, and the Qur'an itself contains no narrative biography (no birth story, no childhood, no year-by-year life).
place: Fustat (Old Cairo), Egypt — where Ibn Hisham produced the recension
grade_reason: The dated recension chain is multiply attested: the lost Ibn Ishaq original (d. 767/768), the Ibn Hisham recension (d. 833/834) with its recognizable interpolations (Guillaume 1955), and the al-Tabari quotations supplying omitted passages. The gap is a dated-text fact, not an inference; the Qur'an's biographical reticence is textual fact.
earliest_attestation: Ibn Hisham's recension of the Sirat Rasul Allah (d. 833/834 CE) — the earliest extant full biography; the Ibn Ishaq original (d. 767/768) survives only through it and through quotations in al-Tabari.

sources.ref: A. Guillaume, The Life of Muhammad: A Translation of Ibn Ishaq's Sirat Rasul Allah (Oxford University Press, 1955), preface pp. xvii, xxxi — the original text of the Sirat Rasul Allah did not survive; Ibn Hisham 'abbreviated, annotated, and sometimes altered' it, his interpolations recognizable; al-Tabari passages citing Ibn Ishaq supply what Ibn Hisham omitted.

Wikipedia, 'Al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah (Ibn Ishaq)' — summary of the transmission: Ibn Ishaq d. 767/768, original lost, Ibn Hisham (Basra; Fustat, d. 833) recension the earliest substantial surviving biography.

Tarif Khalidi, Arabic Historical Thought in the Classical Period (1994), p. 17 — the early sira as 'a Sira of primitive devotion... The guiding principle is inclusion rather than exclusion' (quoted via the Center for Islamic Pluralism's survey of the historical-Muhammad literature, which also records: 'The oldest Sira is that of Ibn Ishaq (c. 704–767), and it has been the source of all subsequent biographical writings'; the original is lost and survives through Ibn Hisham's redaction, d. 833).

competing_hypotheses: Traditionalist: the oral-isnad transmission preserved the substance reliably; the gap does not void the outline — the sira is broadly trustworthy for the main events of the life
Revisionist (Wansbrough/Crone-Cook lineage): the sira is Abbasid-era literary construction in a sectarian milieu; even the outline is suspect — the gap is a symptom, not a cause
falsifiability: A securely dated 7th-century biography manuscript, or proof that Ibn Hisham's recension was composed before 700 CE.

title: Cahokia: the earthen city of the Mississippi floodplain
claim: At its peak around 1050-1150 CE, Cahokia — the pre-eminent center of the Mississippian culture (800-1350 CE) — was a city of 10,000-20,000+ people covering ~1,600 hectares with ~120 earthen mounds; Monks Mound, its central pyramid, is the largest prehistoric earthen structure in the New World, and the city ran a solar observatory (Woodhenge) and a continent-spanning trade network. This is the timeline's first pre-Columbian North American record.
place: Cahokia Mounds, Collinsville, Illinois (Monks Mound)
grade_reason: The city is multiply attested archaeologically (earthworks, burials, trade goods, chronology) and by an international heritage register; VERIFIED is parked only on the exact peak population, which ranges 10,000-50,000 across the literature.
earliest_attestation: The earthworks themselves; Monks Mound's construction sequence and radiocarbon dates from the excavation record (14 construction stages)

sources.ref: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site listing (1982): largest pre-Columbian settlement north of Mexico; 10,000-20,000 people at peak 1050-1150; Monks Mound the largest prehistoric earthen structure in the New World, 30 m high on a ~6-hectare base, built in 14 stages; Woodhenge astronomical observatory
Monks Mound engineering record: ~22 million cubic feet of earth, dug by hand and carried in baskets, base over 14 acres (316 x 241 m), 100 ft tall; summit building of the paramount chief

Timothy R. Pauketat, Cahokia: Ancient America's Great City on the Mississippi (2009): the city's rise, the Grand Plaza, the palisade, the copper workshop at Mound 34 — the material basis for the higher population estimates (up to 40,000) that UNESCO's conservative figure sits beneath
Benson et al. 2009, American Antiquity 74(3): Cahokia's boom and bust — the environmental/archaeological data on the city's decline by c. 1400

competing_hypotheses: The higher population estimates (30,000-40,000+, from Pauketat and others): same city, larger headcount — the dispute is about the number, not the existence
Cahokia as a theocratic chiefdom vs. an early state: archaeologists dispute the political vocabulary while agreeing on the scale
The cause of abandonment by c. 1400: environmental strain (Benson et al.), social breakdown, or migration — no single cause is established
falsifiability: Stratigraphic proof that Monks Mound was built by post-contact Europeans, or a published radiocarbon series placing the mounds outside the pre-Columbian window

title: 'Lilith was Adam's first wife' (the Genesis claim)
claim: 'Lilith was Adam's first wife' is a biblical statement (Genesis).
place: Medieval Jewish literary culture (textual origin)
grade_reason: The name occurs once in the entire Hebrew Bible (Isaiah 34:14); Genesis never names her. The first-wife story is first told in the medieval Alphabet of Ben Sira — a satirical work, ~2,000 years after Isaiah — which assembled older pieces (the demon name, birth-protection amulets, the two-creation-accounts puzzle) into a narrative that had not previously existed (Payton).
earliest_attestation: Alphabet of Ben Sira (8th–10th c. CE, anonymous, satirical): God forms Lilith from earth as he formed Adam; they quarrel over precedence; she speaks the divine name and departs

sources.ref: Alphabet of Ben Sira (8th–10th c. CE) — the first 'Adam's first wife' narrative (Snvi, Snsvi, Smnglof; the quarrel; the Ineffable Name; the departure)
Payton, Jeremy (2026): the legend assembles older pieces ~2,000 years after Isaiah; the book is satirical and unrelated to the biblical Sirach
Jewish Encyclopedia, s.v. Lilith — the Ben Sira account as Adam's concubine and mother of demons; the Gen. R. xx / b. Eruvin 18b Adam's-130-years tradition
Genesis 1–2; Isaiah 34:14 — the texts the claim misreads (the name's sole biblical occurrence; Genesis's silence)

competing_hypotheses: The popular reading: the two Genesis creation accounts (Gen 1's simultaneous creation; Gen 2's rib) imply a first wife — the Alphabet of Ben Sira supplied the name to resolve the contradiction; the contradiction itself is real, the Lilith solution is medieval
The Zohar/Kabbalah developed Lilith further (Samael's consort; mother of demons) — real medieval mysticism, not biblical text
The maximalist reading: the story preserves ancient memory — against the documentary record, which first attaches the name to Adam ~2,000 years after Isaiah
falsifiability: A pre-medieval (pre-8th c. CE) text naming Lilith as Adam's wife would overturn the grade.

title: The Classic Maya 'collapse' — no vanishing, a transformation
claim: The Classic Maya civilization mysteriously vanished — its people disappeared in a single, unexplained collapse.
place: Southern Maya lowlands (Petén, Guatemala; adjacent Chiapas, Belize)
grade_reason: The 'vanishing' is a 19th-century explorer's framing: what ended was the institution of divine kingship in the southern lowlands — monument carving stops, palaces burn or are abandoned — while Maya-speaking communities persist continuously to the present (~7 million speakers today); the transformation was multi-causal and regionally staggered, not one mysterious night.
earliest_attestation: Archaeological: the cessation of dated monument erection in the southern lowlands; colonial-period Relaciones; modern demographic record

sources.ref: Demarest, Arthur — Ancient Maya: The Rise and Fall of a Rainforest Civilization (Cambridge, 2004): the multi-causal, regionally staggered model of the Terminal Classic transformation
Archaeological record: last dated southern-lowland monuments c. 900–909 CE (Tonina 909 CE); Postclassic centers (Chichen Itza, Mayapan) continue — no single collapse horizon
Living record: Maya languages spoken today (Yucatec, K'iche', Q'eqchi', Tzotzil, Tzeltal, etc.) — ~7 million speakers; continuity is the default state of the evidence

competing_hypotheses: The maximalist version: a sudden civilization-ending catastrophe (invasion, plague, super-drought) — graded against the multi-century, regionally staggered evidence
The minimalist version: 'collapse' is the wrong word entirely; the Maya world transformed continuously and the Terminal Classic is one phase of it (continuous-transformation school)
falsifiability: Evidence of a total, synchronous depopulation of the Maya world in a short span — with no surviving Maya-descended communities — would support the vanishing; the opposite is what exists

title: The Theology of Aristotle: Plotinus in Arabic dress, shelved under Aristotle for a millennium
claim: The Arabic philosophical text known as the Theology of Aristotle (Uthulujiya Aristu), which circulated for roughly a millennium as a work of Aristotle and shaped Islamic, Jewish, and Christian philosophy, is a creative Arabic paraphrase of Plotinus's Enneads (books IV-VI, on Soul, Intellect, and the One), produced in 9th-century Baghdad in the circle of al-Kindi. Its own preface names the layers: 'the book of Aristotle the philosopher, called in Greek Theologia... The exposition of Porphyry of Syria, translated into Arabic by Ibn Na'ima al-Himsi, and corrected for Ahmad ibn al-Mu'tasim by al-Kindi' - Ahmad being the son of the Abbasid caliph who reigned 833-842, which dates the production to the 830s-840s. The work was the single most important conduit by which Neoplatonism reached the Islamic world, read by al-Kindi, al-Farabi, Avicenna (who wrote comments on it and may have doubted its authenticity), and later by Latin scholastics and Safavid thinkers.
place: Baghdad, Abbasid Iraq (production; al-Kindi's circle)
grade_raw: CORROBORATED (the Arabic text: its Plotinian content, 9th-century Baghdad production, and the Ibn Na'ima/al-Kindi transmission layers named in its own preface) / DEBUNKED (the Aristotelian attribution - 'certainly untrue'; conventionally 'Pseudo-Aristotle')
grade_reason: The manuscript tradition and the preface colophon multiply attest the text, its date, and its makers; the philosophical scholarship (Zimmermann 1986, Adamson 2002, SEP) unanimously identifies the content as Plotinus's Enneads IV-VI, not Aristotle - the attribution fails on content, not on doubt.
earliest_attestation: The Arabic manuscripts themselves (vulgate version); the preface colophon naming Ibn Na'ima al-Himsi and al-Kindi

sources.ref: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Theology of Aristotle' (Summer 2019 ed.): the Arabic version produced in the circle of al-Kindi; Zimmermann 1986 the major provenance study, conclusions accepted in subsequent work; the Greek exemplar earlier than our oldest Greek Enneads manuscripts (contains Enn. IV.7.8 via Eusebius, absent from all Greek mss); preface colophon quoted verbatim

Peter Adamson, 'Aristotelianism and the Soul in the Arabic Plotinus': the Theology is a paraphrase of parts of Plotinus's Enneads, authored by a member of al-Kindi's circle in 9th-century Baghdad; Avicenna's notes on the text survive and he may have doubted its authenticity

Peter Adamson, The Arabic Plotinus: A Philosophical Study of the 'Theology of Aristotle' (Duckworth, 2002): the first book-length study; the translation 'the single most important conduit by which Neoplatonism reached the Islamic world'; the paraphrase's creative liberties (new paragraphs, Plotinus harmonized with Aristotle, adapted for Islamic/Christian theological context)

competing_hypotheses: The longer version of the Theology has uncertain authorship - Shlomo Pines proposed an Isma'ili origin, Paul Fenton an Egyptian-Jewish derivation (the vulgate version's Kindian-circle origin is the settled part)
Avicenna may have doubted the text's Aristotelian authenticity while still writing comments on it - the one medieval reader who may have seen through the alias
falsifiability: For the CORROBORATED half: a manuscript trail showing pre-9th-century Arabic circulation or a Greek exemplar contradicting the paraphrase relationship. For the DEBUNKED half: the attribution is closed - no serious scholar defends Aristotelian authorship; only new evidence of an actual lost Aristotelian Theologia could reopen it.

title: The Varangian (Scandinavian) contribution to the formation of the Rus' polity
claim: The Rus' — the people whose name Russia, Ukraine and Belarus all trace their statehood to — began as a polity whose founding elite and early identity were Scandinavian (Norse/Varangian), arriving via the Baltic–Volga–Dnieper river arteries in the 9th century, before assimilating into the East Slavic majority.
place: Staraya Ladoga and the Volkhov–Dnieper river routes (region: NW Russia / Ukraine)
grade_reason: Multiple independent lines converge on a Scandinavian founding core: a contemporary 839 Frankish identification of the Rhos as Swedes, the 944/945 treaty's overwhelmingly Norse name-list (primary text preserved in the Chronicle), a 10th-century Byzantine emperor recording Norse river-names, and 850s–860s Scandinavian strata at Gorodishche/Ladoga.
earliest_attestation: Annales Bertiniani, s.a. 839 — the Frankish court at Ingelheim identifies envoys of the Rhos' king (chacanus) as Sueones (Swedes).

sources.ref: Annales Bertiniani, s.a. 839 (Latin text, e.g. Waitz MGH edition) — the Rhos identified as Sueones

Rus'-Byzantine Treaty 944/945 as preserved in the Primary Chronicle — 76 plenipotentiaries, overwhelming majority Old Norse names (Igor = Ingvar, Olga = Helga, Akun = Hákon, Uleb = Óleifr; only 3 Slavic names in the ruling family: Svjatoslav, Volodislav, Predslava) — via Melnikova 2003 and Feldbrugge 2008
Constantine VII Porphyrogennetos, De Administrando Imperio, ch. 9 — the Dnieper rapids named in both Slavic (Slavonic) and Rhos' (Norse) languages
Rurikovo Gorodishche (Novgorod) / Staraya Ladoga archaeology — Scandinavian settlement strata of the 850s–860s (cited in the CORE historiography review via Noonan)
V. Thomsen, The Relations between Ancient Russia and Scandinavia (1877) — Finnic Ruotsi etymology for the name Rus'
J. Shepard & S. Franklin, The Emergence of Rus 750–1200 (1996) — modern synthesis

competing_hypotheses: Soviet anti-Normanism (Boris Rybakov): the Kievan state was essentially East Slavic, hiring only a Varangian military retinue; the Scandinavian role was minimal — the name-list and 839 evidence make the hardline zero-influence reading DEBUNKED (see evt-varangian-zero-influence-001).
The southern Rus' question: Byzantine and Arabic writers knew a Rus' before 862, located south of the Varangian zone — whether this was the same ethnonym is unresolved.

Pritsak/Noonan multi-ethnic trade-union model: ethnicity is the wrong question — the Rus' began as a polyglot commercial-political confederation controlling the Baltic–Mediterranean trade routes, with a Scandinavian core.
The Ruotsi etymology is the leading derivation (Finnic for Swedes) but not uncontested: Roslagen (rejected — named only in the 13th c.), Reidgotar, and other derivations were tried and abandoned.
falsifiability: A securely dated 9th-century East Slavic (not Norse) documentary source showing a Slavic-led Rus' polity before the Scandinavian strata — e.g. a Slavic name-list replacing the 944 Norse majority — would overturn the grade.

title: The hardline claim that the Scandinavians played NO role in the formation of the Rus'
claim: The Scandinavians (Varangians/Norse) played NO role in the formation of the Rus' polity — the early Rus' were entirely East Slavic in origin and identity, and any Norse presence was non-existent or historiographically irrelevant.
place: Kiev (the polity the claim is about)
grade_reason: Three independent kills: (1) the 944/945 treaty's 76 plenipotentiaries carry overwhelmingly Old Norse names (Igor=Ingvar, Olga=Helga, Akun=Hákon, Uleb=Óleifr) — impossible if no Scandinavian elite existed; (2) the Frankish court at Ingelheim in 839 identified the Rhos' envoys as Sueones (Swedes); (3) Constantine VII records Norse names for the Dnieper rapids alongside Slavic ones.
earliest_attestation: Soviet official historiography, 1930s–1980s — anti-Normanism as doctrine, adopted partly in response to Nazi propaganda casting the Kievan Rus' as a Germanic-founded state (Waldman & Mason 2005: the Soviet wishful-thinking theories 'are more likely the product of wishful thinking than of fact').

sources.ref: Annales Bertiniani, s.a. 839 — the Rhos' envoys identified as Sueones at Ingelheim
Rus'-Byzantine Treaty 944/945, preserved in the Primary Chronicle — 76 names, overwhelming majority Old Norse (Melnikova 2003; Feldbrugge 2008)
Constantine VII, De Administrando Imperio ch. 9 — Norse (Rhos') names for the Dnieper rapids
C. Waldman & C. Mason (2005) — Soviet anti-Normanist theories as 'the product of wishful thinking'

competing_hypotheses: The modern moderate anti-Normanist position: Norse influence existed but was minor — the Kievan state was essentially an East Slavic creation (this milder reading is NOT the target of this record; it survives as a live scholarly position).

The Soviet official-school position (Rybakov): the cultural level of the Varangians could not have warranted an invitation from the culturally advanced Slavs — the invitation story was a pro-Scandinavian manipulation (this reading's political context is itself part of the record).
The Pritsak/Noonan position: 'ethnic origin' is the wrong question entirely — the Rus' began as a multi-ethnic trade union.
falsifiability: Would require explaining away three independent attestations simultaneously: the Frankish identification of the Rhos as Swedes (839), the overwhelmingly Norse 944/945 treaty name-list, and the Norse Dnieper-rapids names in Constantine VII — no credible re-reading does this.

title: Al-Kindi's frequency analysis (c. 850 CE)
claim: Abu Yusuf al-Kindi's treatise Risalah fi Istikhraj al-Mu'amma ('On Deciphering Cryptographic Messages'), written c. 850 CE in Baghdad, is the oldest surviving work describing frequency analysis — the statistical method of breaking substitution ciphers by counting symbol frequencies and matching them against known letter frequencies of the language. It is the first documented systematic method of cryptanalysis: the first time anyone wrote down that a cipher dissolves into arithmetic.
place: Baghdad, Abbasid Caliphate
grade_reason: The manuscript survives, is multiply edited and translated, and contains al-Kindi's own statistical study of Arabic letter frequencies; the 'first documented' framing is explicitly scoped — a lost earlier text would move the grade, not destroy it.
earliest_attestation: The treatise itself (manuscript tradition; edited and published in Arabic by Mrayati et al., 1987, in nine volumes; English translations circulate). Al-Kindi (801-873) is multiply attested as author of ~290 works.

sources.ref: Mrayati et al. (eds.), Arabic Origins of Cryptology vol. 1 — analytical study of the edited al-Kindi manuscript: statistical study of Arabic letter frequencies, originality of contributions

IJCSIS Vol. 15 No. 1 (2017): survey of medieval Arabic cryptologists — al-Kindi's Risalah fi Istikhraj al-Mu'amma, ca 850 AD, 'the oldest existent book on cryptology'; frequency analysis; al-Khalil's lost Kitab al-Mu'amma noted

competing_hypotheses: The lost earlier works: al-Khalil ibn Ahmad's Kitab al-Mu'amma (8th c.) is reported to have covered cryptanalytic method ('probable word') but the book does not survive — the documented-first claim is about surviving texts, not about who thought of it first
Ibn Wahshiyya's 855 CE work on the 'riddles of ancient scripts' dealt in cipher alphabets, not analysis methods — different claim, graded separately
falsifiability: The discovery and authentication of an older surviving cryptanalysis text describing frequency analysis; or proof that the attributed manuscript is a later fabrication.

title: The False Decretals — the forgery's transmission machine
claim: The Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals (the False Decretals), a 9th-century Frankish collection (c. 847-852) of some 100 forged decretals and synodal acts, contains the first surviving witness of the Donation of Constantine; two centuries later the Donation entered Gratian's Decretum (12th century, via a pupil) and thus became part of canon law — the transmission machine that carried the forgery into law.
place: Reims, Francia (Pseudo-Isidorian collection's working milieu)
grade_reason: The collection's existence, dating, and contents are multiply attested; its role as the Donation's first surviving witness and transmission path into the Decretum is stated by the 1911 Britannica and the Catholic Encyclopedia 1913; held at CORROBORATED on the motive questions (Roman import vs local composition).
earliest_attestation: The Pseudo-Isidorian collection itself, c. 847-852: first surviving textual witness of the Donation.

sources.ref: 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Donation of Constantine': included in the 9th-century False Decretals; two centuries later incorporated in the Decretum by a pupil of Gratian; 'enrolled among the decrees of the canon law' in Gibbon's day

Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), 'Donation of Constantine': the Donation's introduction and conclusion imitate authentic imperial-period writings, while other formulæ belong to other periods — the source-analysis work (Grauert and others) on the forger's materials

competing_hypotheses: The authorship question: the collection is attributed to 'Isidore Mercator' of Reims-era France; the Donation itself was likely imported into the collection rather than composed by its compilers — the forgery's Roman origin is the majority reading

The motive reading: the collection's main purpose was defending bishops against metropolitans and secular courts (the universal-monarchy reading is the maximalist version); both readings agree it invented precedents
falsifiability: An earlier surviving manuscript witness of the Donation (pre-847) would push the transmission date back; none has been found.

title: Al-Qarawiyyin of Fez: the 859 foundation and the 'oldest university' dispute
claim: The University of al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, Morocco — founded as a mosque by Fatima al-Fihri in 857-859, later a madrasa, incorporated into Morocco's modern state university system in 1963 — is the oldest existing, continually operating degree-awarding higher learning institution in the world.
place: Fez (Fès), Morocco — the al-Qarawiyyin complex
grade_reason: The 859 foundation, the centuries of continuous operation as mosque-madrasa, and the 1963 university-status reorganization are independently documented; UNESCO and Guinness World Records cite it as the oldest university or oldest continually operating higher learning institution. Held below VERIFIED on the live definitional dispute over 'university.'
earliest_attestation: The foundation by Fatima al-Fihri in 857-859 (traditional); the 1963-1965 Moroccan state reorganization as a modern university (documented).

sources.ref: Guinness World Records — citation of al-Qarawiyyin as the oldest higher learning institution / oldest university
UNESCO recognition of the al-Qarawiyyin complex
Moroccan state university system incorporation 1963; official renaming 1965

competing_hypotheses: Many scholars distinguish the madrasa from the 'university' (a distinctly European invention) and date al-Qarawiyyin's transformation to its 1963 modern reorganization — under that definition the 859 claim is misframed
Other institutions (e.g. the Zaytouna mosque-school in Tunis, founded 703) have older foundation dates; al-Qarawiyyin does not win on raw age even under the broadest definition
The Bologna/Paris 'oldest university' counter-claim rests on the European corporate-charter definition, which al-Qarawiyyin's champions reject as criterion-shopping
falsifiability: A documented break in the institution's continuous operation, or evidence that the 1963 reorganization created an entirely new institution with no continuity to the mosque-madrasa

title: The 'invitation of the Varangians' in 862 (the Chronicle's Rurik narrative)
claim: In the year 862, the East Slavic and Finnic tribes of the northwest (Slovenes, Krivichi, Chud, Ves', Merya) — after expelling their Varangian tribute-takers and falling into internecine strife — sent envoys across the sea inviting the Varangians to rule over them; three brothers came, Rurik, Sineus and Truvor, and Rurik settled at Novgorod, Sineus at Beloozero and Truvor at Izborsk.
place: Novgorod (the Chronicle's settlement of Rurik)
grade_reason: Single-source, 12th-century narrative written ~250 years after the claimed event, shaped as an invitation legend with worldwide folklore parallels; the ethnographic detail (named tribes, the tribute-expulsion prelude) is plausible but unattested anywhere outside the Chronicle.
earliest_attestation: The Russian Primary Chronicle (Povest' vremennykh let), compiled at the Kiev Caves Monastery c. 1113; earliest surviving manuscript copy (Laurentian Codex) 1377.

sources.ref: Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian Text, s.a. 859–862 (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor trans.) — the tribute, the expulsion, the invitation, the three brothers
Boris Rybakov — the invitation as late folkloric insertion; Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor on the controversy volume
John H. Lind (2006) — the PVL compiler's ethnographic problem; N1L preserving an older and sometimes contradicting text
The Normanist-theory historiography review (CORE) — 'the whole issue of the ethnic origin of Rus' is not essential'; Pritsak and Noonan on the multi-ethnic trade union

competing_hypotheses: Rybakov's reading: the invitation is a late insertion and a folklore motif — Nestor (or the Kiev-Caves compiler) biased toward the pro-Scandinavian party of Sviatopolk; Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor note it 'has inspired a larger volume of controversial literature than any other disputed point in Russian history.'

Lind 2006: the compiler, himself a Slavic-speaking Rus', needed to explain a Varangian name on a Slavic-speaking people — the story solves his ethnographic problem; 'ethnicity' is a modern construct the 9th century would not recognise.
The Novgorod First Chronicle (younger version, N1L) preserves an older text than the PVL and sometimes directly contradicts it.

The Rorik of Jutland / Frisian-identification hypothesis: some scholars identify Rurik with the Danish chieftain Rorik known from Frankish annals — an unproven identification, not the invitation itself.
falsifiability: A 9th–10th-century source (Byzantine, Arabic, or Latin) describing a Slavic-initiated invitation to Varangian princes would raise the grade; the absence of any such attestation keeps it here.

title: The Diamond Sutra of 868 CE — the oldest dated printed book
claim: A woodblock-printed scroll of the Diamond Sutra, printed in China in 868 CE, is the oldest complete printed book in the world that carries a date — printed nearly six centuries before Gutenberg's Bible.
place: Mogao Caves, Dunhuang (Cave 17, the Library Cave)
grade_reason: The object exists, is dated by its own printed colophon to a precise day, was produced by a mature woodblock technique, and is multiply documented from discovery (1900) to purchase (1907) to the present British Library holding.
earliest_attestation: The colophon printed on the scroll itself (May 868 CE)

sources.ref: The Diamond Sutra, woodblock print scroll, Or.8210/P.2, British Library (Stein collection) — colophon: 'Reverently made for universal free distribution by Wang Jie on behalf of his two parents'
Smithsonian Magazine, 'Five Things to Know About the Diamond Sutra' (May 11, 2016) — 'acknowledged as the oldest dated printed book in existence'

UNESCO World Heritage documentation, Mogao Caves — cave 17 (the Library Cave) discovered 1900 by the caretaker Wang Yuanlu, sealed c. 1000 CE; Stein's 1907 acquisition of the scroll for the British Museum/Library

competing_hypotheses: The older Mugujeonggwang Dharani scroll (Bulguksa, Korea, 704–751 CE) is the oldest surviving woodblock print — true, but it bears no date; the Diamond Sutra is the oldest DATED printed book, a distinct and historically decisive claim

The colophon date could theoretically reflect an earlier printing batch — the scroll's design maturity suggests a longer ancestry for the technique, which strengthens rather than weakens the 'before Gutenberg' conclusion
falsifiability: An independently authenticated printed book bearing an earlier printed date would take the title; radiocarbon/ink analysis showing the scroll is a modern forgery would collapse the record

title: The Bimaristan Hospitals (872-1284 CE)
claim: The bimaristan: the medieval Islamic hospital as an institution — endowed by waqf (charitable trust), free to rich and poor, male and female, Muslim and non-Muslim, with separate wards (surgery, medicine, eye, mental), pharmacies, lecture halls, running water, and paid discharge stipends. Founded first at al-Fustat (c. 872, Ibn Tulun), institutionalized at the Nuri hospital of Damascus (c. 1154, Nur al-Din Zanki), and monumentalized at the Mansuri hospital of Cairo (completed 1284, al-Mansur Qalawun).
place: Damascus (al-Nuri bimaristan, survives); al-Mansuri in Cairo, city precision
grade_reason: Three independent witness-types converge: surviving architecture (al-Nuri), legal endowment deeds with the open-access clauses, and contemporary eyewitness accounts (Ibn Jubayr 1184); the Mansuri's million-dirham endowment and ~15th-century operation are documented.
earliest_attestation: Waqf endowment deeds (notably Qalawun's 1284 dedication: 'for the soldier and the prince, the large and the small, the free and the slave, for men and women'); Ibn Jubayr's 1184 eyewitness account of the Nuri hospital's registers and physician rounds

sources.ref: Waqf deed of the al-Mansuri hospital (1284): open-access dedication clause; four entrances with fountains; separate wards; dispensary; teaching room
Ibn Jubayr (1184): eyewitness account — the Nuri hospital's patient registers, morning physician rounds, ~15 dinar daily budget
al-Nuri bimaristan, Damascus (c. 1154): surviving building; major hospital into the 15th century

competing_hypotheses: Genuine institutional innovation: the waqf endowment + ward specialization + teaching + free care combination has no ancient parallel at this scale

Continuity from Gundeshapur (Sasanian academy-hospital): the Muslim world scaled and institutionalized the model via waqf law — carry fairly; the honest position is innovation-through-institutionalization, not ex nihilo invention
falsifiability: The institution stands on surviving buildings (the Nuri bimaristan in Damascus), endowment law, and independent travelers' accounts; it would collapse only if the waqf deeds proved forgeries — they have not been challenged

title: Alfred's candle clock
claim: Alfred the Great measured his devotional hours with a candle marked in divisions, burning inside an ox-horn lantern — the origin of the 'Alfred invented the candle clock' telling.
place: Wessex (Alfred's court)
grade_reason: Single-source attestation (Asser, c. 893, panegyric) with no independent corroboration of the horn lantern or the invention claim; the 'invented the candle clock' reading goes beyond what Asser describes.
earliest_attestation: Asser, Life of King Alfred, c. 893 — sole source; no independent corroboration.

sources.ref: Asser, Life of King Alfred (J.A. Giles translation, via orthodoxengland.org.uk) — Alfred resolved to devote half his service to God, 'measured accurately by a candle, which burned inside an ox-horn lantern'
answers.com compilation — 'King Alfred the Great. Source: Bishop Asser, Life of King Alfred' as the attribution for the candle-clock telling

competing_hypotheses: Asser invented or embellished the episode as hagiographic color — the Life is panegyric, and the candle serves the 'devoted king' portrait
Candle/incense clocks in China predate Alfred by centuries — the 'invention' telling is Eurocentric regardless of whether Alfred kept one
falsifiability: A second contemporary source describing Alfred's horn lantern, or textual evidence the passage is an interpolation.

title: The medieval Inquisition's actual targets — and its own law on witches
claim: The medieval Inquisition (established 1231 under Gregory IX) was a court directed against heretics — principally Cathars (Albigensians) and Waldensians — and its own law books treated witchcraft skeptically: Canon Episcopi (c. 906, incorporated into Gratian's Decretum c. 1140) declared that belief in night-flight witchcraft was a demonic delusion, not a crime to prosecute.
place: Languedoc, southern France (Cathar inquisition's main theater)
grade_reason: Multiply attested from independent lines: the Canon Episcopi's text is a primary canon-law source; the medieval inquisition's heretic-targeting is the consensus of specialist historiography; the 1484/1486 turn is dated by primary documents (the bull, the Malleus). Held at CORROBORATED rather than VERIFIED on the full targets list (regional variation) — the skepticism doctrine itself is VERIFIED-grade.
earliest_attestation: Canon Episcopi (c. 906, in Regino of Prum's De ecclesiasticis disciplinis), carried into Gratian's Decretum, C.26 q.5: those who believe in the night flight with Diana are infidels misled by the devil.

sources.ref: Canon Episcopi (c. 906), in Gratian's Decretum C.26 q.5 — belief in night flight with Diana declared a demonic delusion
Gregory IX, Ille humani generis (1231): the papal inquisition's founding commission against heresy (Cathars, Waldensians)
Brian P. Levack, The Witch-Hunt in Early Modern Europe: the witch-hunt era 1450-1750, peak 1560-1630, largely secular/Protestant courts

competing_hypotheses: The heresy-target breadth: Cathars and Waldensians are the best-documented targets; the inquisition also pursued Fraticelli, flagellants, and individual dissenters in various regions — the targets list is longer than two names, but witches are not on the medieval list.

The late-medieval turn: the 1484 papal bull Summis desiderantes affectibus and the 1486 Malleus Maleficarum mark the shift — by the end of the 15th century some ecclesiastical courts did begin treating witchcraft as heresy. That is the beginning of the early-modern hunts, not the medieval institution's normal business.

The skeptic-inquisitors: Spanish Inquisition figures like Salazar y Frias (1610 Logrono investigations, 1614 edict of grace) actively reversed witchcraft convictions — the Inquisition's own records make it one of the institutions that *stopped* witch-burnings in its jurisdiction.
falsifiability: A 13th- or 14th-century inquisitorial manual with witchcraft as a standard prosecution category, or court registers showing systematic medieval witch trials, would force revision; none exist.

title: Kilwa Kisiwani — the Swahili coast's gold-port city-state
claim: Kilwa Kisiwani, on an island off the Tanzanian coast, was a major Swahili city-state from the 11th–15th centuries, built on customs revenue from the gold trade running from the Zimbabwe plateau via Sofala — minting its own gold coins, building in coral stone, and ranked by Ibn Battuta in 1331 as one of the most beautiful cities he had seen.
place: Kilwa Kisiwani, Lindi Region, Tanzania
grade_reason: An eyewitness account by a demanding traveler, the standing coral-stone architecture, the mint's own coin evidence, and systematic excavations converge — held at CORROBORATED on the foundation date and exact sultanate extents.
earliest_attestation: The Kilwa Chronicle (16th-c. histories) and the coins themselves; contemporary eyewitness: Ibn Battuta's Rihla, 1331 visit; excavations by Kirkman and Chittick (British Institute in Eastern Africa, 1950s–60s)

sources.ref: Ibn Battuta, Rihla (1331 visit): 'one of the most beautiful and well-constructed towns in the world' — the dressed stone, the mosque already ~400 years old, the palace, the piety of the people
The Great Mosque: earliest section 1131–1170 (coral limestone blocks, nine hexagonal tree-trunk columns); the 14th-c. domed extension under al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman
Kilwa-minted gold coins from the 11th c. onward — some found as far as Great Zimbabwe and the Maldives: the customs economy's own paperwork
Chittick's excavations: Husuni Kubwa (the palace, unrivaled in East African architectural sophistication) and Husuni Ndogo (the market) as the 14th-c. building program
Portuguese accounts: Cabral 1500 (the 100-room palace of coral stone); the 1502–1505 sack that broke the coast's independent trade era

competing_hypotheses: The Shirazi founding legend (Ali ibn al-Hassan Shirazi, c. 975, buying the island with cloth): a genuine migration memory or a later legitimacy genealogy — carried as CLAIMED, not graded over
Battuta's praise may inflate (he was a court guest of al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman) — the archaeology is the independent check, and it confirms the wealth
falsifiability: Excavation showing no pre-Portuguese stone architecture, or coin hoards contradicting the gold-trade chronology, would collapse the commercial reading

title: St Swithin's Day and the forty days (myth)
claim: If it rains on St Swithin's Day (15 July), it will rain for the next forty days; if it is fair, forty days of fair weather follow.
place: Winchester, England (St Swithin's Old Minster — the legend's origin)
grade_reason: The Met Office states that 'since the start of records in 1861, there has never been a record of 40 dry or 40 wet days in a row following St Swithin's Day.' The legend was put to the test on 55 occasions when it rained on St Swithin's Day, and forty days of rain followed on none of them; the closest approach in the modern record was 34 days at Cassley, Highland. Companion saints'-day prophecies fail the same test.
earliest_attestation: The 15 July 971 reburial legend (St Swithin, Bishop of Winchester 852–862, moved from the churchyard into the Old Minster; the forty-day storm as the saint's anger); first written weather-prophecy trace in a 13th/14th-century Emmanuel College manuscript

sources.ref: Met Office (via multiple outlets): 'since the start of records in 1861, there has never been a record of 40 dry or 40 wet days in a row following St Swithin's Day'; 'Numerous studies have been carried out on past weather observations and none of them have proved the legend true.'

St George's News (2004): the legend 'put to the test on 55 occasions when it has been wet on St Swithun's Day, and 40 days of rain did not follow any of them'; 'there are several saints' days that are supposed to be followed by periods of wet or fine weather... And it doesn't happen on any of these, either.'

Channel 4 News: the 15 July 971 reburial, the forty-day storm as the bishop's displeasure; 'the Met Office has put the legend to the test on 55 occasions when it has been wet on St Swithin's Day, and 40 days of rain did not follow' (citing Jane Struthers, Red Sky at Night: The Book of Lost Country Wisdom)
BBC (via Mumsnet summary, 2025): 'The closest we have got in the modern record was in Cassley, Highland, which once experienced rain on St Swithin's Day and on the following 34 days.'
The rhyme: 'St Swithin's day if thou dost rain / For 40 days it will remain / St Swithin's day if thou be fair / For 40 days 'twill rain no more.'

competing_hypotheses: The prophecy as a garbled memory of the jet-stream's mid-July locking (there is a real, weak tendency for mid-July patterns to persist — but forty days of unbroken rain or shine has never occurred in the instrumental record, so the specific claim still fails)
The prophecy as pure hagiographic legend with no meteorological content (consistent with the evidence, but the record grades the weather claim, not the hagiography)
falsifiability: The Met Office station record showing forty consecutive wet or dry days following a corresponding St Swithin's Day — the exact test the Met Office ran, which found zero occurrences since 1861

title: Al-Zahrawi's Kitab al-Tasrif (c. 1000 CE)
claim: Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi (936-c.1013, Cordoba) compiled Kitab al-Tasrif (c. 1000 CE), a 30-treatise medical encyclopedia whose surgical treatise was the first work in Arabic to describe and illustrate surgical instruments — about 200 of them, many of his own design: cauterization irons, lithotrites for bladder stones, obstetrical forceps, catgut absorbable sutures, arterial ligation instruments.
place: Cordoba, Umayyad al-Andalus
grade_reason: Multiply attested: 50+ surviving Arabic manuscripts, five Latin translations, 500 years as the surgical manual of Salerno and Montpellier, and Guy de Chauliac's Chirurgia Magna (1363) cites al-Zahrawi over 200 times — an independent contemporary witness to his authority.
earliest_attestation: Kitab al-Tasrif manuscripts, 11th century onward; the surgical treatise translated into Latin by Gerard of Cremona (d. 1187)

sources.ref: Campbell, D. (1974) + European Scientific Journal special issue: the Tasrif's surgical treatise, ~200 illustrated instruments, earliest known teaching illustrations
Gerard of Cremona's 12th-century Latin translation; used five centuries at Salerno, Montpellier, and other European schools
Guy de Chauliac, Chirurgia Magna (1363): cites al-Zahrawi 200+ times — the 'Restorer of European Surgery' leaning on the Cordoban's instruments

competing_hypotheses: The instruments are largely al-Zahrawi's own innovations (his own claim, and the mainstream reading: the illustrations are original and the techniques are described from practice)

The instruments refine earlier Hellenistic/Roman and Byzantine designs — carry fairly: some have antecedents (cauterization is ancient); the FIRST ILLUSTRATED surgical manual is the key, not the absolute novelty of every tool
falsifiability: Would be weakened if the instruments proved to be copyist additions (they appear consistently across the manuscript tradition); the 200-instrument figure would shrink if counts are shown to double-count variants

title: The Norse settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows, c. 1000 CE
claim: Norse seafarers established a short-lived settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows, on Newfoundland's Great Northern Peninsula, around the year 1000 CE — a European presence in North America roughly five centuries before Columbus.
place: L'Anse aux Meadows National Historic Site, Great Northern Peninsula, Newfoundland
grade_reason: Independent lines converge: Norse-style turf buildings and artifacts (iron rivets, jasper fire-strikers, bronze ringed pin, soapstone spindle whorl, iron-working slag) excavated from sealed contexts; metal-cut wood dated to the exact year 1021 CE via the global 992-993 CE solar-storm 14C marker; butternuts (Juglans cinerea, not native north of New Brunswick) proving travel farther south; the saga tradition independently describes the same voyages.
earliest_attestation: Eiríks saga rauða and Grænlendinga saga (13th-14th c. manuscripts preserving older oral tradition); archaeological confirmation from 1960.

sources.ref: Anne Stine Ingstad, excavations 1961-1968 (site identified with Helge Ingstad, 1960)
Kuitems, M. et al. (2021), 'Evidence for European presence in the Americas in AD 1021', Nature 601
Eiríks saga rauða; Grænlendinga saga (Vinland sagas)
UNESCO World Heritage inscription, 1978

competing_hypotheses: The site was a short-lived base camp (exploration, boat repair, iron production), not a colony — the settlement's brief duration is the consensus, not a rival

Vinland itself lay farther south (the butternuts and wild grapes of the sagas point to the Gulf of St. Lawrence / New Brunswick); L'Anse aux Meadows is the confirmed gateway, not necessarily the saga's Vinland
The 1021 date fixes one felling season; the site may have seen intermittent use across a few decades — the exact span is open
falsifiability: Demonstration that the excavated Norse-style artifacts and metal-cut wood are misattributed (e.g., a non-Norse iron-working tradition in pre-contact Newfoundland) would collapse the identification; no such evidence exists.

title: Maria Argyropoulina's golden fork at Venice (1004) and Peter Damian's condemnation
claim: In 1004, the Byzantine noblewoman Maria Argyropoulina, marrying into Venice's ruling Orseolo family, refused to touch her food with her fingers and instead ate with a small golden two-pronged fork, scandalizing Venice. The theologian St. Peter Damian (1007-1072) recorded the episode in his letters and condemned her 'artificial metal forks' as decadent luxury, interpreting her early death from plague as divine punishment for that vanity.
place: Venice, Republic of Venice (the Orseolo marriage)
grade_reason: CORROBORATED as the earliest recorded table-fork controversy: the episode is attested by Damian's letters and carried across independent secondary sources. The divine-punishment reading is Damian's moralizing and is graded as attestation of belief, not as metaphysics (the attestation rule).
earliest_attestation: St. Peter Damian's collected letters, late 11th century (secondary account, decades after the event)

sources.ref: St. Peter Damian, letters (collected); cited in National Geographic History Jan/Feb 2022, p. 17
PopSci: 'The thousand-year story of how the fork crossed Europe, and onto your plate today' (2025)
Wikipedia: 'Fork' (Peter Damian as 'excessive delicacy'; Maria Argyropoulina 985-1007, sister of Emperor Romanos III Argyros)
925-1000.com forum: forks & spoons history (Maria Agyropoulaina 1004/5, small gold fork at Venice)

competing_hypotheses: Elements of Maria's story may have been conflated over generations with Theodora Ducina, another Byzantine bride whose legend also carries a luxury-moralism tradition (Plottwist/Turned-Tables analysis)
Damian's account may be moralist embroidery rather than reportage — a cleric turning a cultural difference into a divine warning
The 'plague as punishment' reading is theology, not epidemiology; Maria's death is the fact, the punishment is the frame
falsifiability: A Venetian record contradicting the Orseolo-Argyropoulina marriage, or proof that Damian's letters are misdated or mistranscribed on this point

title: The Tale of Genji
claim: The Tale of Genji (Genji Monogatari) — 54 chapters of sustained prose fiction with interior characterization, court intrigue, and psychological realism — was composed by the Heian court lady Murasaki Shikibu (sobriquet; c. 973 – c. 1014/1031) c. 1008–1021, making it the earliest surviving work of extended prose fiction meeting the criteria most literary historians use to define the novel: it predates Cervantes's Don Quixote (1605) by roughly six centuries.
place: Ishiyamadera temple, Otsu (traditional composition site per legend) / Heian-kyo (Kyoto), Japan — the legend puts the first inspiration at Ishiyamadera; the court life it describes is Heian-kyo
grade_reason: Multiple independent near-contemporary attestations converge: the author's own diary (c. 1008, internal-evidence dating) and a second diarist's acquisition record (1021). The work survives complete; the superlative rests on the dated artifact, not on a claim.
earliest_attestation: Murasaki Shikibu Nikki (diary, entries dated c. 1008–1010 by internal evidence): the author refers to the tale and to her 'Murasaki' nickname, drawn from the heroine, being already in use — the tale was circulating at court by 1008. Second independent witness: the Sarashina Nikki (c. 1021): the author records her joy at acquiring a complete copy.

sources.ref: Murasaki Shikibu Nikki (c. 1008–1010): diary entries — the tale referenced, the 'Murasaki' nickname in use, the Emperor's read-aloud of the opening chapter
Sarashina Nikki (c. 1021): the author's diary entry recording acquisition of a complete copy ('over 50 chapters,' a character from the work's end)
Arthur Waley (trans.), The Tale of Genji, Project Gutenberg ed. (via sites.google.com World Literature I textbook: author c. 973–1014, date c. 11th century, court context)
HISTORY.com, 'What Is the World's Oldest Novel?' — Genji 'widely regarded as the world's first novel' (54 chapters, Heian setting, psychological realism as the defining criterion)

competing_hypotheses: The Greek-romance claim: Chariton's Callirhoe (1st c. CE) and Apuleius's The Golden Ass (2nd c. CE) are older extended prose fiction — if 'novel' means only 'long prose narrative,' the superlative belongs to them, not Genji; the majority literary-historical position distinguishes the romance form from the novel on grounds of interior psychology

The definitional objection (Watt 1957 'formal realism'): only the 17th–18th-century European novel, and by stricter readings only Don Quixote, fully qualifies — on that definition Genji is 'a novel-like precursor'; the majority position treats this as moving the goalposts

Multiple-authorship: Yosano Akiko and later stylometric work (Tyler) propose a second hand — possibly Murasaki's daughter Daini no Sanmi — for the late chapters (42–54); the majority holds that most of the text is Murasaki's, the exact share unsettled unless an archive discovery lands
falsifiability: A securely dated earlier work with sustained interior characterization in prose; or proof the 1008 diary entries are misdated wholesale. The authorship-share dispute could move the 'single author' detail; it cannot move the work's date or existence.

title: Bi Sheng's movable type (1041–1048 CE)
claim: Bi Sheng, a commoner of the Northern Song dynasty, invented movable type printing using fired-clay characters, more than four centuries before Gutenberg — described in detail by his contemporary Shen Kuo in the Dream Pool Essays (~1088).
place: Yingshan County, Hubei (Bi Sheng's home; invention in the Song capital region)
grade_reason: The account is detailed, technical, and internally consistent, written by a reliable near-contemporary who knew the inventor's milieu — but it is single-tradition literary attestation: no Bi Sheng type piece survives, and no independent witness describes the method.
earliest_attestation: Shen Kuo, Mengxi Bitan (Dream Pool Essays), c. 1088 — the only surviving account of Bi Sheng's method

sources.ref: Shen Kuo, Dream Pool Essays (Mengxi Bitan), c. 1088 — full technical description: clay characters 'as thin as the edge of a coin', baked hard, set in an iron frame with pine-resin/wax/paper-ash paste, two alternating formes
Bi Sheng tomb, Yingshan County, Hubei (discovered 1990) — tombstone records death 1051, four sons, three grandsons
Thomas Carter, The Invention of Printing in China and Its Spread Westward (1955) — English transmission of the Shen Kuo passage

competing_hypotheses: Shen Kuo's account could be exaggerated or partly secondhand — he wrote decades after Bi Sheng's death; the engineering detail is the best answer to this (it reads like observation, not legend)
Wooden movable type (Wang Zhen, 1313) and metal movable type (Korea, 13th c.; Hua Sui, 1490) are better-attested continuations — they prove the principle was workable, not that Bi Sheng was first
falsifiability: A dated earlier movable-type artifact would revise priority; evidence that Shen Kuo fabricated the account would collapse the record to SPECULATION

title: The East–West Schism of 1054: the excommunications that did not, by themselves, split Christianity
claim: The Christian Church divided into two churches — Roman Catholic (West) and Eastern Orthodox (East) — in a single event in 1054, when Cardinal Humbert laid a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia and Patriarch Michael Cerularius was excommunicated in return.
place: Hagia Sophia, Constantinople (Istanbul)
grade_reason: The July 1054 excommunications are CORROBORATED as documented events (surviving texts), but the claim under review — that Christianity 'split in 1054' as a single event — is the conventional simplification: the historiographical consensus (Ware and the subsequent literature) holds the schism was a centuries-long process, ordinary Christians largely unaware, contemporary chroniclers unimpressed, and 1204 (the sack of Constantinople) the likelier point of no return. The event is documented; the single-day-division reading stays CLAIMED.
earliest_attestation: The bull of excommunication of 16 July 1054 (text survives); the synodal act of 20 July 1054 excommunicating the legates (text survives)

sources.ref: The bull of excommunication, 16 July 1054 (text preserved; laid on the altar of Hagia Sophia by Cardinal Humbert and two legates)
Synodal act of Constantinople, 20 July 1054 (counter-excommunication of the legates)

Timothy Ware, 'The Great Schism' (Orthodox Church of the Mother of God histories) — 'It is this incident which has conventionally been taken to mark the beginning of the great schism... But the schism, as historians now generally recognize, is not really an event whose beginning can be exactly dated. It was something that came about gradually'

Wikipedia, East-West Schism (survey of the modern literature): 'There was no single event that marked the breakdown. Rather, the two churches slid into and out of schism over a period of several centuries, punctuated with temporary reconciliations'; 'Even after 1054 friendly relations between East and West continued' (quoting Ware); contemporary chroniclers did not consider the event significant

Father Bill's Orthodox Blog, '55. Orthodoxy and Other Faiths: Roman Catholicism, Part Two — The Great Schism' (2018): Humbert did not excommunicate the other Eastern patriarchs; the Pope was dead at the time, so technically the anathema did not count; the Photian Schism precedent; communion continued in parts of the Middle East and Aegean after 1054
Seed records: evt-abrahamic-tree-001 (the tree as attestation map, CORROBORATED — internal splits explicitly not yet mapped, now mapped in part here)

competing_hypotheses: The 'single event' reading: 16 July 1054 is the date of the Great Schism; the mutual excommunications of July 1054 ended communion between East and West (the conventional textbook telling)

The process reading (historiographical consensus): there was no single moment of rupture — East and West slid into and out of schism over several centuries, punctuated by temporary reconciliations; 1054 was one episode in a long estrangement (cultural, political, theological: papal claims, the filioque), and contemporary chroniclers treated the 1054 incident as insignificant
The 1204 reading: the real point of no return was the Fourth Crusade's sack of Constantinople (1204), which made the separation a lived, irreversible enmity rather than a canonical dispute
falsifiability: The record would be upgraded toward CORROBORATED if evidence showed communion between Rome and Constantinople's churches ceased abruptly and permanently in the years immediately after 1054; it would move toward DEBUNKED if the July 1054 bull itself proved to be a later forgery

sources.ref: Kolbjørn Skaare (University of Oslo), 1978: the coin is a Norwegian silver penny minted 1065–1080, reign of Olaf Kyrre (1067–1093); in circulation through the 12th–13th centuries

Maine State Museum: the coin donated 1974 with ~30,000 Goddard-site artifacts (Guy Mellgren's 18 August 1957 collection); described as 'the only pre-Columbian Norse artifact generally regarded as genuine found within the United States'
