title: The Bayeux comet — the earliest known European depiction of Halley's Comet
claim: The Bayeux embroidery's comet panel (scenes 32, under the Latin caption ISTI MIRANT STELLA — 'these men marvel at the star') depicts the April 1066 apparition of what is now called Halley's Comet — and is the earliest known European pictorial depiction of the comet.
place: Bayeux Museum, Normandy, France (the panel); the apparition observed over England, April 1066
grade_reason: Three independent witnesses converge: the stitched panel itself (the comet above the marveling men), the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle's 1066 comet over England, and the Chinese annals' two-month observation. NASA: the Bayeux panel 'depicts a comet that has been identified as the first illustration of Halley's Comet.' DLR calls it 'likely the oldest depiction of Halley's Comet.' Held at CORROBORATED, not VERIFIED: 'earliest known' is survival-dependent (a destroyed earlier image would move the grade), and the Zuqnin Chronicle (760) already anchors the earliest known depiction anywhere — non-European. The European record opens with this stitching.
earliest_attestation: Bayeux embroidery panel, scenes 32 (stitched c. 1070) — the stitched comet above the marveling men

sources.ref: NASA — '955 Years Ago: Halley's Comet and the Battle of Hastings' ('depicts a comet that has been identified as the first illustration of Halley's Comet'; April 1066 over England; Chinese two-month observation)
DLR (German Aerospace Center) — 'The Bayeux Tapestry — oldest depiction of Halley's Comet' ('likely the oldest depiction of Halley's Comet')
The Art Newspaper (2026) — 'The tapestry features the first European depiction of Halley's Comet'; earlier non-European depiction in the Chronicle of Zuqnin (760); next image Giotto 1305
Gizmodo (Public Domain Review, 'Flowers of the Sky') — 'A scene from the Bayeux Tapestry shows men staring at Halley's Comet (c1066), and is the first known picture of the comet'
Heritage Daily (2026, arXiv Portegies Zwart & Lewis) — 'appears on the Bayeux Tapestry, the oldest known visual representation of the comet'

competing_hypotheses: The 'omens' reading: the panel records a period belief (comets as portents of a king's death — Harold's), not an astronomical observation; the record grades the depiction, not the omen reading, and the belief phenomenon is fenced as real

The Chronicle of Zuqnin caveat: the Syriac monastery chronicle depicts a comet at the 760 apparition (the comet now called Halley) — the earliest known depiction anywhere is therefore non-European, per The Art Newspaper; the Bayeux panel is the earliest known European one (Giotto's Padua Arena Chapel 1305 is the next)

Whether the Bayeux embroiders read the 1066 comet as Halley at all: the identification is modern (the orbital math, not the caption); the apparition itself is independently anchored — Chinese records tracked it for two months, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle places it over England in April 1066
falsifiability: An earlier verified European depiction of the 1066 (or any) Halley apparition — none is known; or a documentary proof that the stitched panel depicts a different celestial event (a meteor, a supernova) — no rival identification has the orbit math

title: The Bayeux Tapestry — the artifact
claim: The Bayeux 'Tapestry' (c. 1070) is a ~70-meter embroidered linen cloth depicting the events of 1066 — the Norman Conquest of England — made in England to a Norman brief (traditionally attributed to Bishop Odo's commission, Canterbury workshop) as a piece of Norman propaganda.
place: Musée de la Tapisserie de Bayeux, Normandy, France (long-term home; the work is named for the city it resides in, not where it was made)
grade_reason: The object exists, is measurable, and is stylistically anchored: ~70 m of linen, wool-embroidered in stem stitch and laid-and-couched work, depicting the 1066 conquest in ~58–75 episodes with Latin tituli. The 1476 cathedral inventory anchors its presence; the English manufacture is corroborated by the manuscript tradition, the tituli spellings, and the opus-anglicanum technique (NYRB/Mallinson 2008: 'designed in England and embroidered in England by English craftswomen').
earliest_attestation: The embroidery itself (Bayeux Museum / Musée de la Tapisserie de Bayeux); first documentary mention 1476 (Bayeux Cathedral inventory)

sources.ref: Smarthistory — The Bayeux Tapestry ('c. 1070, embroidered wool on linen'; 'Although it is called the Bayeux Tapestry... the imagery and inscriptions are embroidered using wool yarn sewed onto linen cloth')
History.com — 'What Makes the Bayeux Tapestry a Medieval Wonder?' (embroidered, not woven on a loom; Canterbury origin; Old English lettering; Norman-propaganda reading)
Columbia Encyclopedia (FactMonster) — 'This so-called tapestry is in fact an embroidery'; 230 ft × 20 in (70 m × 51 cm); 'embroidered in worsteds of eight colors in couching and stem stitch'
NYRB letters (Mallinson, 2008) — 'It was, of course, made to a Norman brief, but was designed in England and embroidered in England by English craftswomen'
Smithsonian Magazine (AP/Bayeux Museum, 2021) — 'Though the work is widely known as a tapestry, it technically counts as a work of embroidery'; Bayeux Museum on the propaganda function

competing_hypotheses: The Canterbury attribution is near-consensus, not proof: the Old English spellings in the Latin tituli, the opus-anglicanum stitch technique, and the illuminated-manuscript stylistic matches make England the evidence-supported origin; the 'Matilda and her ladies' tradition (the Matilda Tapestry legend) is the debunked rival provenance

The missing end — the embroidery breaks off at the Battle of Hastings; Montfaucon's 1729 engravings show the loss predates the 18th century — the traditional assumption is that it ended with William's coronation on Christmas Day 1066, unprovable

The exact display context is argued: Norton's 2019 JBA analysis (the LiveScience-reported work) matches the embroidery's physical and narrative structure to the nave of the 11th-century Bayeux Cathedral
falsifiability: A documented provenance placing the commission elsewhere than the Norman-English 1066–1082 window (e.g., a verifiable later workshop signature in the stitching) — none exists; the object, the 1476 inventory, and the manuscript-stylistic evidence all converge

title: The Bayeux Tapestry is not a tapestry

grade_reason: The fiber testifies against the label: the Bayeux images are wool yarn sewn onto linen cloth — embroidery, not tapestry. LiveScience's Norton summary: 'The Bayeux Tapestry is not technically a tapestry, as its design is embroidered onto the linen rather than woven.' Columbia: 'embroidered in worsteds of eight colors in couching and stem stitch.' There is no loom-woven imagery in the object. The name survives by habit, not by technique.
earliest_attestation: The object's own fiber: wool yarn stitched (stem stitch, laid-and-couched work) onto a plain-weave linen ground — every technical examination finds embroidery, never loom-woven imagery

sources.ref: LiveScience / Norton (JBA) — 'The Bayeux Tapestry is not technically a tapestry, as its design is embroidered onto the linen rather than woven'
Smarthistory — 'Although it is called the Bayeux Tapestry... the images are not woven into the cloth; instead, the imagery and inscriptions are embroidered using wool yarn sewed onto linen cloth'

The Matilda legend is a separate misconception (the queen and her ladies-in-waiting as the makers); it is dead on the English-provenance evidence and is fenced out of this record — it dies on its own evidence, not this one

title: The Domesday Book (1086) — the first great count
claim: The Domesday Book (1086) is a real, surviving, comprehensive survey of landholding in England — the largest single record of its kind from the Middle Ages, and the foundation of medieval English demography.
place: The National Archives, Kew, England (holding institution); survey coverage: England
grade_reason: The manuscripts exist, are physically dated to 1086, and their contents — ~13,000 settlements, landholders, ploughs, livestock, and population-derived values — are internally consistent with the fiscal purpose recorded in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle's 1085 entry ('he sent his men all over England... not one ox, nor one cow, nor one pig was left out'). The oldest and largest census-like record of the Middle Ages.
earliest_attestation: The two manuscript volumes themselves (Great Domesday and Little Domesday), held by The National Archives, Kew.

sources.ref: Domesday Book, Great and Little Domesday volumes (1086), The National Archives, Kew — the manuscripts themselves

Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, entry for 1085 (Gloucester): the Christmas court order for the survey — 'so very narrowly, that there was no single hide nor yard of land, nor indeed one ox nor one cow nor one pig which was left out'
The National Archives, Domesday Book research guides: ~13,000 places recorded; the survey's fiscal-administrative purpose and coverage limits

competing_hypotheses: Coverage limits: London, Winchester, and parts of the north-east (Durham, Northumberland) are excluded; the north was under-surveyed after the Harrying — so 'comprehensive' is graded only for its coverage area

The counting question: the survey lists landholders, tenants, and resources, not a headcount — population estimates (roughly 1.5-2 million) are scholarly derivations from multipliers, graded separately and not here
falsifiability: Manuscript evidence that the volumes were compiled later as forgeries, or systematic internal inconsistency in the survey's fiscal logic, would downgrade this.

title: Shen Kuo's Dream Pool Essays (~1088) — the first clearly-dated, named-author account of magnetic declination, four centuries before Europe wrote it down
claim: Shen Kuo (1031-1095), in his Mengxi Bitan (Dream Pool Essays, compiled c. 1086-1088), wrote the first clearly-dated, named-author account of magnetic declination: the magnetized needle 'is always displaced slightly east rather than pointing due south.' Europe did not document the phenomenon until roughly four centuries later.
place: Dream Torrent Garden, Runzhou (modern Zhenjiang), Song China — where Shen Kuo compiled the essays
grade_reason: The Mengxi Bitan is an extant, securely dated text by the named author Shen Kuo (1031-1095), and the passage is unambiguous: needles rubbed with lodestone 'are always displaced slightly east rather than pointing due south' (Needham's translation, Science and Civilisation in China vol. IV pt 1, pp. 249-250; the Education About Asia translation renders it 'the needle often inclines to the southeast direction, not pointing to due south'). Shen Kuo adds the silk-fibre suspension method and notes some needles point north — 'No one can explain the principles of these things.' The core claim (Shen Kuo wrote declination down in 1088) is textually proven. Fenced: 'first in the world' is NOT asserted absolutely — the ~880 anonymous geomantic text is a candidate earlier account, so Shen Kuo is the first clearly-dated named author, not the proven first documenter. Europe's lag is measured: Columbus's 18 September 1492 journal note and Hartmann's 1510 determination (reported 1544) are documented, ~4-4.5 centuries later.
earliest_attestation: Shen Kuo's own text, Mengxi Bitan (Dream Pool Essays), extant and securely attributed.

sources.ref: Wikipedia 'Shen Kuo': Dream Pool Essays (Mengxi Bitan, compiled ~1086-1088) — 'made the first known explicit reference to the magnetic compass-needle and the concept of true north'; needles magnetized by rubbing with lodestone, best hung by a single silk fibre; 'always displaced slightly east rather than pointing due south' — the first known explicit reference to magnetic declination

Needham, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. IV pt 1, pp. 249-250 (quoted via Wikipedia Talk:Shen Kuo): full translation of the declination passage; Shen Kuo's Meng Chhi Pi Than (~1088) is 'our fixed point'

Education About Asia: Shen Kuo (1088) in translation — 'Diviners can make a needle point to the south by rubbing it with a magnetic stone. However, the needle often inclines to the southeast direction, not pointing to due south'
Wikipedia 'History of the compass': declination texts Kuan Shih Ti Li Chih Meng (~880) predating Shen Kuo — the anonymous-earlier fence

Wikipedia 'History of geomagnetism': Georg Hartmann's March 4, 1544 letter to Duke Albrecht of Prussia (~1510 determination); Scientific American (Nov 20, 1869) — Columbus noticed September 18, 1492 that the compass 'pointed due north' where in Europe it 'pointed northeast'

competing_hypotheses: The anonymous-earlier line: the geomantic text Kuan Shih Ti Li Chih Meng (~880) is argued to encode declination knowledge before Shen Kuo. The text is fragmentary and anonymous; Shen Kuo remains the first clearly-dated named author. Both readings are carried: 'first explicit named-author reference' (Shen Kuo) vs. 'first clear account in an anonymous text' (~880).

The European-latency line: Europe had the compass from ~1190 but did not write declination down — Columbus's journal notes the anomaly on 18 September 1492 (unprinted); Georg Hartmann determined it at Rome ~1510 and reported it in a March 4, 1544 letter to Duke Albrecht of Prussia. German sundials carried declination corrections by the mid-15th century. Nobody disputes the gap; its cause (noticed vs. not noticed vs. not published) is open.
falsifiability: A clearly-dated, named-author text predating 1086 that documents declination explicitly would demote the 'first' element; the phenomenon-description element is textually secure and not falsifiable short of textual corruption evidence.

title: The University of Bologna's 1088 founding date

place: Bologna, Italy
grade_reason: The 1088 date is a commemorative back-computation from the 1888 centenary, not a documented founding: no surviving record fixes a founding to 1088, and the first documentary milestones belong to the 12th century.

Paul Grendler: 'it is not likely that enough instruction and organization existed to merit the term university before the 1150s, and it might not have happened before the 1180s'
Authentica Habita (Frederick I Barbarossa, Diet of Roncaglia, November 1158) — the earliest imperial charter protecting scholars at Bologna

Law teaching at Bologna had genuinely coalesced by the late 11th century (Irnerius c. 1050-after 1125), so 1088 is approximately right even if not documented

title: The Two Deaths That Weren't: 'al-Ghazali/Mongols Ended Islamic Science'
claim: The popular two-cause story: Islamic scientific research effectively ENDED with (a) al-Ghazali's critique of philosophy (Tahafut al-Falasifa, 1095; d. 1111) and/or (b) the Mongol sack of Baghdad (1258) — so that nothing significant in science happened in the Islamic world after those events.
place: Maragha, East Azerbaijan, Iran (site of the observatory founded 1259, one year after the sack of Baghdad — the fact that falsifies the claim)
grade_reason: The claim requires an ending; the record shows an afterlife. Al-Ghazali explicitly exempted the demonstrative sciences (his own second introduction to the Tahafut); post-Ghazali philosophy-science continued (al-Razi, Suhrawardi, Tusi, Mulla Sadra); the Mongols themselves funded the Maragha observatory in 1259; and Islamic astronomical devices sit inside Copernicus's 1543 masterwork. The 1111 and 1258 'deaths' are periodization, not events.
earliest_attestation: The claim as popularized: 19th-century European historiography (Renan's L'Islamisme et la science, 1883) — the al-Ghazali-as-assassin story; the 1258 cutoff as 'the end' is a later textbook convenience.

sources.ref: al-Ghazali — Tahafut al-Falasifa, second introduction (eclipses rest on 'geometrical and arithmetical demonstrations'; disputing them is 'a disservice to religion') — Marmura trans. (BYU Press, 1997), pp. 5-7; excerpt at vaticanobservatory.org
Griffel, F. — Al-Ghazali's Philosophical Theology (2009): Tahafut targeted metaphysics (eternity of the world, divine knowledge, resurrection), not the empirical sciences

Saliba, G. — Islamic Science and the Making of the European Renaissance (MIT Press, 2007): ch. 7, 'Age of Decline: The Fecundity of Astronomical Thought' — most creative Arabic astronomy AFTER the supposed endings; Swerdlow endorsement on the endorsement page
Ragep, F.J. (2014, 2016, 2017): on the Maragha school and transmission to Copernicus
Maragheh observatory: founded 1259 under Hulagu Khan, waqf-funded, director al-Tusi, active ~58 years — Wikipedia 'Maragheh observatory' (crawled 2026-10-13) with refs [2][4][6][7]

Huff, T.E. (2008, Middle East Quarterly review of Saliba): the serious counter-position — no major innovations in Muslim astronomy after Shatir (14th c.), in motion after Ibn Bajja (12th c.), in optics after the early 14th c.; the real divergence 16th-17th c. — carried as the honest dissent, not the claim

competing_hypotheses: The decline thesis (older historiography: Renan, Munk, popular versions): al-Ghazali's attack on philosophy strangled rational inquiry; the sack finished what he started — the claim this record debunks
The revisionist position (Pines, Saliba, Gutas, Griffel): philosophical and scientific work continued and innovated for centuries; the 'endings' are periodization choices, not facts

The institutional-late-decline position (Huff 1993/2003/2017): no strangling by al-Ghazali and no 1258 cutoff — but a real drying-up of innovation much later (16th-17th c.), driven by institutional and economic structures, not theology. Carried fairly: this is a serious position, and it also contradicts the 1111/1258 story

The salvage caveat: the 1258 sack really did destroy real libraries and kill real scholars; it was a catastrophe for Baghdad's books. What it did not do was end Islamic science as such — the observatory built by the same khan one year later is the receipt.
falsifiability: Already falsified. It would require that no significant scientific work postdates 1111/1258; a single institution (Maragha, 1259, funded by the Mongols themselves) and a single transmitted device (the Tusi couple inside Copernicus's De revolutionibus) suffice to falsify the absolute claim.

title: The 'Dutch invented the windmill' myth (DEBUNKED)
claim: The Dutch invented the windmill.
place: Netherlands (the claimed origin)
grade_reason: DEBUNKED: practical windmills predate the Dutch by three centuries. The earliest recorded working windmill design is the Persian panemone — vertical lightweight wooden sails on a central vertical shaft — invented around 700–900 AD in the Sistan region (modern Iran/Afghanistan), first built to pump water and later modified to grind grain. Muslim geographers describe 9th-century vertical-axle windmills in Sistan; the design spread across the Islamic world to India and China. The legendary Abu Lu'lu'a account (pre-644) may be a 10th-century amendment, but the 9th-century evidence is clear. The vertical-axis European windmill appeared in northwestern Europe only in the 12th century — a separate reinvention, not a Dutch invention. The Dutch achievement was real but different: they perfected the horizontal-axis smock mill and deployed it at unmatched scale for grain, drainage, and industry. They industrialized the windmill; they did not invent it.
earliest_attestation: Popular telling, early modern onward

sources.ref: Wikipedia 'Windmill': the Persian panemone 700–900 AD; the 9th-century Sistan vertical-axle mills described by Muslim geographers; the 12th-century northwestern European vertical windmill.
Wikipedia 'Panemone windmill': the earliest recorded windmill design, Persian, 700–900 AD; the Abu Lu'lu'a legend and its possible 10th-century amendment; the spread across the Islamic world.
Green Prophet (Nashtifan): ~30 windmills, 50–60 feet high, vertical axis between clay-and-straw walls, 1,000+ years old, still grinding grain; the design predating the Dutch by centuries.

falsifiability: Documented earlier windmills

title: The 'cathedral glass flows' myth (DEBUNKED)
claim: Medieval cathedral window glass has flowed downward over the centuries — old panes are thicker at the bottom because glass is a slow-moving liquid.
place: European cathedrals (Westminster Abbey, Sainte-Chapelle studied)
grade_reason: DEBUNKED: the physics kills it twice. Zanotto (1998, Am. J. Phys. 66:392-395) calculated the room-temperature relaxation time of window glass at ~10^32 years — far longer than the age of the universe; Zanotto & Gupta (1999) revised the estimate downward and still found flow impossible on human timescales; a recent Mauro-team recalculation for medieval Westminster Abbey glass found ~1 nanometer of flow per billion years. The thick bottoms are manufacturing, not gravity: crown-glass disks were uneven (thicker toward the bullseye/edge), and glaziers deliberately set the heavy side down for stability and to keep water out of the lead cames.
earliest_attestation: Popular telling, 19th–20th century (textbooks, cathedral tour guides)

sources.ref: Edgar D. Zanotto, 'Do cathedral glasses flow?', American Journal of Physics 66(5):392-395 (1998) — relaxation time ~10^32 years at room temperature
E. D. Zanotto & P. K. Gupta, 'Do cathedral glasses flow? — Additional remarks', Am. J. Phys. 67:260-262 (1999) — revised estimate, still confirms no flow on human timescales

American Ceramic Society news report on the Mauro team's Westminster Abbey calculation: medieval glass flows ~1 nm per billion years — 'the long-lasting myth about the flow of glasses at room temperature is still just that: a myth'
Cambridge DoITPoMS, 'Do cathedral glasses flow?' — the manufacturing explanation: cylinder/crown process, non-uniform thickness, glaziers fitting thick sides down
Wikipedia 'Crown glass (window)': the crown process — blown globe spun into a disk, thickest toward the bullseye/edge, cut panes mounted in lead lattice

Scientific American, 'Fact or Fiction?: Glass Is a (Supercooled) Liquid' — Ediger (UW–Madison): glass is an amorphous solid; the belief's carriers named as tour guides, internet rumors, and high-school chemistry teachers

competing_hypotheses: The honest nuance: glass is an amorphous solid with a liquid-like atomic structure — the 'frozen liquid' reading survives as a description of structure, never as a claim of flow
Occasional panes found thick-side-up or thick on the side are explained by installation carelessness, which the flow theory cannot explain
falsifiability: A measured thickness change in an undisturbed pane over decades, or a flow-rate calculation for medieval compositions matching the observed change

title: Great Zimbabwe — the Shona stone city
claim: Great Zimbabwe, on the Zimbabwe plateau, was a stone-built African city and capital of a gold-trading state, constructed in the 11th–15th centuries CE by the ancestors of the Shona/Karanga people — the largest ancient stone construction south of the Sahara.
place: Great Zimbabwe, Masvingo, Zimbabwe
grade_reason: The standing architecture is multiply attested by independent excavations (1905, 1929–31, later surveys), stratigraphy, and radiocarbon; authorship is uncontested in archaeology — no credible rival attestation exists.
earliest_attestation: Portuguese traders' accounts, 16th century (earlier European notice: Carl Mauch 1871, searching for the biblical Ophir); indigenous occupation of the site long before

sources.ref: David Randall-MacIver, Medieval Rhodesia (1905): excavated artifacts matched Shona/Karanga material culture in use around the site; 'unquestionably African in every detail'
Gertrude Caton-Thompson, The Zimbabwe Culture: Ruins and Reactions (1931): stratigraphic excavation; the city a medieval Shona-culture capital
UNESCO World Heritage listing 1986 — the standing dry-stone architecture (Great Enclosure walls up to ~11 m, mortarless) as the evidence of indigenous construction
Imported Persian, Arab, and Chinese ceramics and beads in sealed contexts — the Sofala/Kilwa gold road to the Indian Ocean (the trade the city taxed and lived on)
Shona oral tradition and the Bantu etymology: 'zimbabwe' = 'houses of stone' / sacred houses

competing_hypotheses: Construction phases and precise founding dates remain debated within the 11th–15th c. range — the grade is on authorship and the city's reality, never on exact dates
Population estimates (often cited up to ~18,000 at apogee) are modeled, not counted — the figure is an estimate, not a census
falsifiability: Sealed-context artifacts or texts showing non-African construction technology, foreign-language inscriptions predating the Shona occupation, or radiocarbon placing the walls outside the medieval window

title: Medieval European public bathhouses
claim: Medieval European cities had public bathhouses — licensed, guilded establishments operating across the 12th-16th centuries.
place: Paris (the 1268 étuviers guild statutes)
grade_reason: Multiple independent primary/contemporary documentary sources (monastic rule, royal ordinances, guild statutes, chronicles, medical and household literature) across four regions, plus surviving bathhouse archaeology — the documentary lines converge.
earliest_attestation: Rule of St. Benedict, Ch. 36 (c. 530) presumes a working monastic bath system; the first secular documentary line is Henry II's 1161 Southwark stew ordinances.

sources.ref: Rule of St. Benedict, Ch. 36 (c. 530) — bath use offered to the sick, rarely to the healthy
Henry II's 39 Ordinances Touching the Government of the Stewholders in Southwark (1161) — licensed bathhouses under the Bishop of Winchester
London 1417 ordinance — banned stews within the city walls, expressly allowing private bathhouses
Livre des métiers (Étienne Boileau, Paris, 1268) — guild statutes of the étuviers (professional bathhouse-keepers)
Primary Chronicle / Tale of Bygone Years (c. 1113) — Apostle Andrew passage: Slavic wooden bathhouses heated 'to extreme heat' as routine practice
Tacuinum Sanitatis (Latin translation c. 1250) — bath practice in the medical literature
Le Ménagier de Paris (1393) — soap/herb-bath recipes for the household
Caliphal Baths of Córdoba (10th c., al-Hakam II) and El Bañuelo, Granada (11th c., used as a bathhouse into the 16th c.) — surviving Islamic hammams
Janna Coomans (Utrecht University) + Germanisches Nationalmuseum — German/Netherlands urban Badstuben with licensed 'baders' practicing basic medicine
Ellen Wurtzel (2023) — 13th-16th c. resurgence of urban bathhouses in Paris and northern France from medical treatises, trial records, archives

competing_hypotheses: The moral-panic reading: the étuves were dens of prostitution rather than bathing (the 1560 Estates General of Orléans ban) — the bathing they hosted is still documented, so the reading narrows the function, not the existence
falsifiability: Showing the documentary references are fabrications, or that the surviving structures (Córdoba, El Bañuelo) were not bathhouses

title: Spices as medieval status: the pepper that meant money
claim: In medieval Europe, imported spices functioned primarily as luxury goods consumed for social display — elite dining used expensive spices the way a modern household uses a luxury car: as a public statement of wealth.
place: Medieval Europe (the elite table)
grade_reason: The elite recipe corpus documents heavy spicing as feast display on fresh food, and the food historians' economic analysis places imported spices firmly in the luxury register — multiple independent lines, same conclusion; held below VERIFIED pending a dedicated price-roll citation this run.
earliest_attestation: The medieval cookbooks themselves (Forme of Cury c. 1390, Le Viandier, Le Ménagier de Paris 1393) — elite display cooking on the page; Paul Freedman, Out of the East (2008) as the modern synthesis.

sources.ref: Paul Freedman, Out of the East: Spices and the Medieval Imagination (Yale University Press, 2008) — spices as symbols of beauty, affluence, taste, and grace; the elite demand that drove commerce and conquest
Jack Turner, Spice: The History of a Temptation (Knopf, 2004) — 'for a handful of peppercorns, you could have someone killed': the wealth-power nexus of the spice economy
Forme of Cury (c. 1390, British Library Add MS 5016) — the royal cookbook's display sauces; spicing as court fashion
Le Ménagier de Paris (1393) — bourgeois household manual: spices as the mark of a well-appointed table

competing_hypotheses: The humoral-medicine reading: spices were consumed chiefly as 'hot' correctives in Galenic dietetics, with status as a side effect
The religious-austerity counter-reading: clerical moralists' condemnations of spice gluttony prove overconsumption rather than display intent — a competing explanation of the same consumption
falsifiability: Medieval price and recipe evidence showing imported spices priced within reach of common households and consumed as staples rather than as feast-day display

title: The Bologna studium: Europe's first university corporation
claim: In the 12th century Bologna developed the first European studium in the corporate sense: Irnerius's law school and the glossators, imperial protection of wandering scholars, and the student guilds (universitates/nations) that became the university.
place: Bologna, Italy (the law schools; the Authentica issued at the Diet of Roncaglia)
grade_reason: Multiple independent lines converge: the glossator tradition around Irnerius and the Four Doctors, the 1158 Authentica Habita as a dated imperial document addressed to scholars at Bologna, and the late-12th-century student universitates. Held below VERIFIED because the emergence was gradual, not a dated act.
earliest_attestation: The imperial constitution Authentica Habita, issued by Frederick I Barbarossa at the Diet of Roncaglia in November 1158, addressed to scholars — documented privilege of safe residence and judicial jurisdiction for wandering students and masters.

sources.ref: Authentica Habita (1158) — Pearl Kibre, Scholarly Privileges in the Middle Ages (Mediaeval Academy of America, 1962): the Privilegium scholasticum, 'the most famous and influential of its kind'
The glossator tradition: Irnerius and the Four Doctors of Bologna
The student universitates/nations of late-12th-century Bologna (the Natio Germanica Bononiae and others)

competing_hypotheses: The earliest phase was informal master-pupil teaching, not yet a corporation — the corporate form crystallized only in the late 12th century
Paris, Oxford, and Salerno have rival claims to the earliest institutional form of the medieval university
falsifiability: Evidence that the 12th-century law school was a single later fabrication, or a pre-1158 document showing the studium had already vanished

title: Angkor Wat — the temple and its continuous life
claim: Angkor Wat — the world's largest religious complex (162.6 hectares, ~401.8 acres) — was built between c. 1113 and c. 1150 CE during the reign of the Khmer king Suryavarman II as a Hindu state temple dedicated to Vishnu (likely also his mausoleum), and has remained in continuous religious use ever since, converting to Theravada Buddhist use from the late 13th century onward into the present day.
place: Angkor Wat, Siem Reap, Cambodia
grade_reason: The monument exists (measured 162.6 ha, largest religious complex in the world); contemporary inscriptions fix Suryavarman II's reign; an independent 13th-century Chinese eyewitness (Zhou Daguan, 1296–97) describes the functioning capital within living memory of construction; and its continuous religious use is observable into the present — Angkor Wat has remained an active Buddhist center into the modern era.
earliest_attestation: Khmer inscriptions of the Angkorian period (Sanskrit and Old Khmer); the earliest surviving full description of the complex is Zhou Daguan's 'The Customs of Cambodia' (1296–97), a Chinese envoy's eyewitness account written within a century and a half of construction.

sources.desc: 162.6 hectares; constructed 1113–1150 CE under Suryavarman II as Hindu temple dedicated to Vishnu; state temple and likely intended mausoleum; Mount Meru layout, west orientation; gradually transformed into Theravada Buddhist temple from late 13th century onward; 'has remained a Buddhist monastery and an active center of Buddhist worship into the present day'; on the Cambodian national flag
sources.ref: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angkor_Wat

sources.desc: Construction began first half of 12th century by Suryavarman II (reigned 1113–c. 1150); original name Vrah Visnuloka ('sacred dwelling of Vishnu'); the urban macro-complex context — Khmer capital's hundreds of thousands in the 12th–13th centuries, water-engineering landscape
sources.ref: nationalgeographic.com — 'Angkor Wat, the world's biggest religious complex, is sacred to two faiths'

sources.desc: Eyewitness description of Angkor by a Chinese envoy, 1296–97 — the capital described as a functioning, inhabited imperial city within living memory of the temple's construction
sources.ref: Zhou Daguan, 'The Customs of Cambodia' (Zhenla fengtu ji), 1296–97

competing_hypotheses: The exact construction start year is not attested to the year — the range c. 1113–c. 1150 rests on Suryavarman II's reign dates (reigned 1113–c. 1150), not a foundation inscription
The mausoleum reading is scholarly inference ('generally considered'); the state-temple function is the firm ground
falsifiability: A foundation inscription or documented stratigraphic phase predating or postdating the 12th century, contradicting Suryavarman II's commission; proof the standing fabric is modern.

title: Gratian's Decretum: the medieval law books and what they do not contain
claim: Gratian's Decretum (Concordia discordantium canonum, compiled c. 1140 at Bologna) founded medieval canon law; the glossators' Corpus Juris Canonici (completed 1582) regulated marriage, clergy, heresy, and procedure for four centuries — and this entire corpus, thousands of canons and glosses, contains no droit du seigneur, no jus primae noctis, and no seigneurial wedding-night right of any kind.
place: Bologna, Italy (Gratian's school; the manuscripts live in the Biblioteca dell'Archiginnasio and across Europe)
grade_reason: The corpus exists and is multiply attested — hundreds of surviving manuscripts, Friedberg's edition, the 1582 printed standard — and its silence on the wedding-night right is complete across the full canon, the glosses, and the diocesan statutes downstream of it.
earliest_attestation: Manuscript copies of the Decretum from the mid-12th century survive in the hundreds; the text is edited in Friedberg's Corpus Iuris Canonici (1879–1881).

sources.ref: Gratian, Concordia discordantium canonum (c. 1140) — edited in Emil Friedberg, Corpus Iuris Canonici, vol. I (Leipzig, 1879)
Anders Winroth, The Making of Gratian's Decretum (Cambridge UP, 2000) — the two-recensions thesis; the founding text of medieval canon law
Corpus Juris Canonici, standard printed form 1582 (Gregory XIII) — the five-part corpus: Decretum, Liber Extra (1234), Liber Sextus (1298), Clementinae (1317), Extravagantes

competing_hypotheses: A provincial or diocesan statute recorded the right and was lost — possible for small customs, but the Corpus's comprehensiveness on marriage dues (every tithe, fee, and fine is itemized elsewhere) makes a missing 'wedding night' vanishingly unlikely

The right belonged to secular custom and would never appear in canon law — true as far as it goes, but the custumals and secular charters are equally silent, so the silence is pan-legal, not canonical
falsifiability: A canon in the Decretum, the Decretals, or the Sext granting or recognizing a lord's wedding-night right would falsify the claim — and would have falsified the DEBUNKED grade on evt-droit-du-seigneur-001 instead.

title: Angkor Wat was never abandoned — the continuous-use record
claim: Angkor Wat was never abandoned: it converted to Theravada Buddhist use from the late 13th century onward and has remained a continuously active religious center into the present day — the Khmers never 'lost' it.
place: Angkor Wat, Siem Reap, Cambodia
grade_reason: Angkor Wat's Buddhist conversion from the late 13th century is documented; the temple is observable as an active religious center in every period since — including through the colonial era — and 'has remained a Buddhist monastery and an active center of Buddhist worship into the present day.' Held at CORROBORATED rather than VERIFIED because the inscriptional coverage between the 14th and 19th centuries is thin — the continuity rests on the living tradition plus the temple's documented modern status, not unbroken year-by-year attestation. The broader capital's decline is fenced: this record is the temple, not the city.
earliest_attestation: Zhou Daguan's 'The Customs of Cambodia' (1296–97) describes a functioning imperial capital at the moment of the Buddhist transition; the temple's continuous monastic status is documented into the colonial period and the present.

sources.desc: 'From the late 13th century onward, the complex was gradually transformed into a Buddhist temple as Khmer kings adopted Buddhism. Angkor Wat has remained a Buddhist monastery and an active center of Buddhist worship into the present day.' 'From the late 13th century onward, Angkor Wat became predominantly associated with Theravāda Buddhism. It was adapted for Buddhist worship and has remained in continuous religious use.'
sources.ref: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angkor_Wat

sources.desc: Eyewitness account of the functioning Angkorian capital in 1296–97 — the temple's religious world described at the moment of the Buddhist transition, within a century and a half of construction
sources.ref: Zhou Daguan, 'The Customs of Cambodia' (Zhenla fengtu ji), 1296–97

sources.desc: 'Angkor was never lost to the Khmer people, who continuously lived, worshipped and farmed in and around the temple complexes' — the Khmer-side continuity framing; local guides' 'led' Mouhot to Angkor in 1860 (the guided-visit detail)
sources.ref: wondersofcambodia.com — 'Henri Mouhot and the Rediscovery of Angkor'

competing_hypotheses: The broader capital of Angkor did lose population after the 15th century (the court's move south toward Phnom Penh; the chronicle date 1431 is traditional) — that is the capital, not the temple; the two are fenced

The inscriptional record between the 14th century and the colonial period has gaps — hence CORROBORATED, not VERIFIED; the continuity is carried by the living tradition plus the temple's present-day monastic status, not by unbroken year-by-year documentation
falsifiability: Inscriptional or documentary evidence of a centuries-long dormancy in Angkor Wat's religious use (desecration, abandonment as a working temple) between the 14th century and the colonial period.

title: No blood-of-Christ relic has verified 1st-century provenance
claim: No blood-of-Christ relic anywhere has verified 1st-century provenance. The Bruges Holy Blood has a 1150 tradition (Thierry of Alsace) but no documentary record before 1256; most historians link it to the 1204 sack of Constantinople, and the crystal tube is a Byzantine perfume bottle. The Mantua relic's chain is likewise medieval. The claim of a 1st-century blood relic is therefore DEBUNKED as a provenance claim — what exists are medieval devotional objects.
grade_reason: Documentary gap of 1100+ years with a known alternative origin (1204 Constantinople loot); the vessel itself is Byzantine secular work
earliest_attestation: Bruges documentary record, 1256
competing_hypotheses: A genuine 1st-century relic with lost documentation (unfalsifiable, no evidence)
falsifiability: A documented 1st-century chain of custody would overturn; none exists

title: The Trabia itriyya industry — pasta in Sicily before Polo
claim: By 1154, the town of Trabia near Palermo (Sicily) produced thread-like dried pasta (itriyya) in industrial quantities and exported it by ship to Calabria and to Muslim and Christian lands — 141 years before Marco Polo's return from China.
place: Trabia, Sicily
grade_reason: The geographer's 1154 text exists and is the standard scholarly citation, and 13th-century Genoese inventories corroborate pasta's Italian presence before Polo — but al-Idrisi never explicitly writes 'dried'; the drying is historians' inference from long-distance export (fresh dough could not survive the voyage), and the Genoese inventory dates vary across retellings (1244/1279/1284).
earliest_attestation: Muhammad al-Idrisi, Nuzhat al-mushtaq fi ikhtiraq al-afaq (the Book of Roger), 1154, composed at Roger II of Sicily's court in Palermo.

sources.ref: al-Idrisi, Nuzhat al-mushtaq (1154) — the Trabia itriyya passage
Genoese notarial documents (1240, 1279, 1284 per the Spaghetti Museum, Pontedassio; the commonly cited 1279 estate inventory listing macaroni — a few retellings vary the year)
HowStuffWorks, 'Did Marco Polo bring pasta from China?' — durum-wheat and Idrisi summary
Culinary Lore via Cucina Toscana, 'The International Origins of Pasta' — the pre-Polo documentary chain

competing_hypotheses: The passage describes fresh, not dried, itriyya, and the export claim is the geographer's exaggeration — Sicily's pasta industry grew later
The drying technology arrived from the east (rishta/Arab trade networks) rather than being invented in Sicily — the industry's existence is Sicilian, its technique's origin is not
falsifiability: Proof that the Trabia passage is a later interpolation into al-Idrisi's text, or a contemporary 12th-century source contradicting a Sicilian pasta trade — either would downgrade the record

title: Henry II's Assize of Clarendon (1166) — the jury of presentment
claim: Henry II's Assize of Clarendon (1166) established the jury of presentment: twelve lawful men of each hundred and four of each vill, sworn to report under oath those accused or notoriously suspect of robbery, murder, or theft. This jury of twelve — plus the civil-assize recognitions (novel disseisin, mort d'ancestor, darrein presentment) — is the documented seed of the English jury system, forty-nine years before Magna Carta.
place: Clarendon, Wiltshire, England (traditional site of the council)
grade_reason: The assize's own Latin text survives and describes the twelve-man sworn inquiry; the Northampton assize (1176) and subsequent plea-roll practice confirm the system operated. Held below VERIFIED on the debate over how much Henry formalized vs invented (the pre-Conquest hundred-jury precedent is real).
earliest_attestation: The Assize's own text (Latin; Stubbs, Select Charters, via Wikisource): clause 1 — inquiry 'through the several counties and through the several hundreds by twelve more lawful men of the hundred and by four more lawful men of each vill, upon oath'; clause 2 — those found by the oath to be arrested 'and go to the judgment of water'.

sources.ref: Assize of Clarendon, 1166 — Latin text (Stubbs, Select Charters, 9th ed., pp. 170-173; translation via Wikisource): clause 1, twelve lawful men of the hundred + four of the vill; clause 2, the accused go to the judgment of water
Assize of Northampton, 1176 — extending Clarendon; added arson, forgery; six itinerant justice circuits
R.D. Groot, 'The jury of presentment before 1215', American Journal of Legal History 26 (1982), pp. 1-24 — the scholarly account of the pre-charter jury

competing_hypotheses: The Anglo-Saxon/Norman-precedent reading: juries of accusation existed in the hundred before the Conquest; Henry's assize formalized and systematized rather than invented them

The 'presentment only' caveat: the 1166 jury ACCUSED (it did not determine guilt) — guilt was decided by ordeal or battle; the trial-by-jury of fact-finding grows out of this but is not identical to it
falsifiability: Evidence that the Assize of Clarendon is a later fabrication (the Latin text survives in Stubbs's Select Charters tradition) or that its 'twelve lawful men' were never sworn in practice (the Northampton assize and the itinerant justices' plea rolls show the system operating)

title: Alexander Neckam's De naturis rerum (c. 1180-1190) — the earliest surviving European description of the mariner's compass, recorded as existing seamen's practice
claim: Alexander Neckam (1157-1217), in De naturis rerum (book ii, ch. 89/98 'De vi attractiva,' written c. 1180-1190), gives the earliest surviving European literary description of the mariner's compass: sailors in cloudy weather 'touch the magnet with a needle,' which 'whirls round in a circle until, when its motion ceases, the point looks direct to the north.' Neckam describes it as existing seamen's practice, not his own invention.
place: Oxford / St Albans, England — Neckam's teaching world; the sailors he describes are the Channel seamen
grade_reason: Two Neckam texts survive and are securely attributed: De naturis rerum (the north-pointing needle passage, confirmed in Thomas Wright's 1863 Rolls Series edition) and De utensilibus (~1190). The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica's 'Compass' article confirms this is 'the earliest definite mention as yet known of the use of the mariner's compass in the middle ages' and notes that Neckam 'merely records what had apparently become the regular practice of at least many seamen of the Catholic world' — describing existing practice, not claiming invention. Guiot de Provins's poem (~1190s-1204) corroborates the period's seamen using the lodestone. Fenced honestly: the *pivoted* needle detail is not asserted categorically (d'Avezac's emendation is contested); De utensilibus's 'placed upon a dart' passage may even contain an inadvertent observation of variation ('looks northeast' for north).
earliest_attestation: Neckam's own surviving manuscripts; Thomas Wright's 1863 Rolls Series edition confirms the text.

sources.ref: IEEE REACH Early Maritime Navigation background (teacher resource): Neckam's De Naturis Rerum passage translated — 'The sailors, moreover, as they sail over the sea, when in cloudy weather they can no longer profit by the light of the sun... they touch the magnet with a needle. This then whirls round in a circle until, when its motion ceases, the point looks direct to the north'; De Utensilibus — needle 'placed upon a dart' that 'looks northeast' (possible inadvertent variation observation)

1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Compass': De utensilibus (Neckam, 12th c.) is the 'earliest definite mention as yet known of the use of the mariner's compass in the middle ages' — needle on a pivot; Neckam 'merely records what had apparently become the regular practice of at least many seamen of the Catholic world'
1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Alexander Neckam': the earliest European notices of the magnet as a guide to seamen — outside China, the earliest surviving notices in any civilization
arXiv 2209.02371 (Martín Asín et al.): dates Neckam's De utensilibus 'around 1190'; Latin/translation of the pivot passage; quotes Guiot de Provins's Bible (~1204) and later European witnesses
Cambridge scholarly note (core.cambridge.org): d'Avezac's reading of De utensilibus as describing a pivoted needle depends on emending copyist errors — caution against categorical pivot claims

competing_hypotheses: The pivot question: d'Avezac's reading of Neckam's De utensilibus as describing a *pivoted* needle rests on emending copyist errors (suppositam→superpositam, orientem→septentrionem) — a Cambridge scholarly note (core.cambridge.org) cautions against stating the pivoted detail categorically. The description element is VERIFIED; the pivot detail is fenced.

The Guiot witness: Guiot de Provins's poem La Bible (~1190s-1204) independently describes sailors using the lodestone — the European witness is not Neckam alone, which strengthens the 'existing practice' reading over an inventor narrative.
falsifiability: A surviving, securely dated European compass description predating ~1180 would demote the 'earliest' element; none is known. The text itself is multiply transmitted.

title: The blood-catching Grail is a ~1200 literary invention (Robert de Boron)
claim: The Holy Grail as a vessel of Christ's blood originates in literature, not 1st-century tradition: Chrétien de Troyes' Perceval (~1190) has a graal as a serving dish — no blood, not holy. Robert de Boron's Joseph d'Arimathie (~1190-1200) is FIRST to make it the Last Supper cup used to catch Christ's blood. Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival (~1210) makes the grail a stone (lapsit exillis), not a cup at all. The blood-catching grail is twelve centuries younger than the Last Supper.
grade_reason: Established literary history; the invention point is documented in the texts themselves
earliest_attestation: Robert de Boron, Joseph d'Arimathie, ~1200
competing_hypotheses: None in scholarship; the literary sequence is established
falsifiability: A pre-1190 blood-grail text would revise; none exists

title: The Pray Codex's shroud image (c. 1192–1195)
claim: The Hungarian Pray Codex (c. 1192–1195, the first book in Hungarian, National Széchényi Library, Budapest) contains an Entombment illumination showing a burial cloth with distinctive marks — including an L-pattern resembling the Shroud of Turin's burn holes, a long narrow cloth, hands crossed over the body without visible thumbs — attesting a Shroud-like image-tradition roughly 160 years before the Shroud's first undisputed documentation at Lirey (c. 1355).
place: Budapest (National Széchényi Library)
grade_reason: The manuscript is securely dated to 1192–1195, the illumination exists, and its particulars (L-pattern marks, hidden thumbs, crossed hands) are described in the published literature; what is CORROBORATED is the image-tradition's existence and date, not its identification with the Turin Shroud.
earliest_attestation: The codex itself (National Széchényi Library, Budapest); the illumination's particulars described in the literature since the 20th century

sources.ref: The Hungarian Pray Codex (c. 1192–1195), Entombment illumination
Lejeune, J. — first-hand study of the codex in Budapest (presented at the 1993 CIELT Rome symposium): the correspondences with the Shroud's particulars
Markwardt, J., The Hidden History of the Shroud of Turin (2021) — the 1192–1195 dating and the illumination's particulars (carried as the sindonology reading, not as neutral scholarship)
The Shroud's first undisputed documentation: Lirey, France, c. 1355 (the terminus the illumination predates)

competing_hypotheses: The illumination depicts the Turin Shroud itself (the sindonology reading — the artist had the Constantinople relic before his eyes; unfalsified, graded CLAIMED as an identification)
The marks are conventional medieval shroud iconography and the resemblance is coincidental (the skeptical reading — unfalsified)
falsifiability: Demonstration that the L-pattern marks are a standard medieval artistic convention for burial cloths would collapse the identification reading; the depiction itself (dated codex, L-pattern marks) stands regardless.

title: The 'libraries burned for months' claim (Nalanda)
claim: After Bakhtiyar Khilji's 1193 sack of Nalanda, the university's manuscript libraries (Dharmaganja) burned continuously for months — told as three months, six months, nine months, or 'several' months depending on the telling, often paired with 'nine million manuscripts'.
place: Nalanda Mahavihara, Bihar, India
grade_reason: Seventy-fifth DEBUNKED family. The only named near-contemporary source, the Tabaqat-i Nasiri, carries no burn duration in the translated passage the retellings quote; the month-figures appear only in modern retellings and cannot agree among themselves (three, six, nine, 'several' months — a diagnostic signature of unattested numbers). The 'nine million manuscripts' is a pop inflation with no traceable contemporary provenance. The 13th-c. Tibetan witnesses (Chag Lotsawa 1235, Dharmasvamin 1234–36) describe a damaged-but-functioning Nalanda, not a site extinguished in one fire.
earliest_attestation: No pre-modern attestation traced. The widely-quoted Raverty excerpt of the Tabaqat-i Nasiri's Bihar campaign passage describes the assault, the killing of the shaven-headed inhabitants, and the book collections — with no library-fire duration and no month-count (this run could not verify the full Persian text; what the retellings quote carries no duration). The month figures (3/6/9/'several') appear only in modern retellings — Indian exam-prep banks (testbook), blogs, popular histories — variously misattributed to the Tabaqat or vaguely to 'Tibetan sources', none producing the text.

sources.ref: Minhaj-i Siraj, Tabaqat-i Nasiri (c. 1260), Raverty translation — the Bihar campaign passage: assault, the shaven-headed inhabitants, the books; the quoted passage carries NO fire duration (the absence is the evidence)

Testbook exam-prep banks ('Nalanda Vihar was destroyed by: Bakhtiyar Khalji — books burned for 3 months'; 'In which year was Nalanda University finally destroyed? — burnt for months') — the pop telling, captured as belief ecology
lankaweb.com 2019 retelling ('burning continued for over six months'); myindiamyglory.com ('nine months' form) — the unstable month-figures documented across tellings

Rahula Shribhadra / Dharmasvamin material (Wikipedia 'Rahula Shribhadra', citing Tibetan sources) — Nalanda 1234–36: damaged but functioning, <100 monks; the positive record against the one-fire extinction frame

competing_hypotheses: That the durations preserve a genuine lost tradition (Taranatha or another Tibetan witness) whose original text has not been traced in the tellings — possible in principle, but no telling produces the text, and an unattested number that won't sit still is not evidence

That a large library fire really did smoulder for an extended period and the month-counts are folk roundings of that — conceded as physically possible, but possibility is not attestation, and the doctrine grades attestation, not plausibility
falsifiability: A pre-1500 source — Persian, Tibetan, or Chinese — stating a Nalanda library-fire duration in months

title: The 1190s–1200s sack of the Bihar monasteries (Khilji)
claim: In the 1190s–1200s CE, the Turkic general Bakhtiyar Khilji's campaigns in Bihar sacked the great Buddhist monastic universities — Nalanda, Vikramashila, and Odantapuri — killing many monks and damaging the institutions; the near-contemporary Persian chronicle Tabaqat-i Nasiri (Minhaj-i Siraj, c. 1260) describes the Bihar campaign's assault, the killing of the shaven-headed inhabitants, and the discovery of the great book collections.
place: Nalanda / Bihar monastic belt, India
grade_reason: The Bihar monastic sackings are attested in the near-contemporary Tabaqat-i Nasiri and converge with the Tibetan witnesses of Nalanda's damaged-but-functioning remnant (Chag Lotsawa 1235, Dharmasvamin 1234–36); but the passage's exact target identification (Nalanda vs Odantapuri), the single-year date, and casualty figures stay contested, so the grade stops at CORROBORATED.
earliest_attestation: Minhaj-i Siraj, Tabaqat-i Nasiri (c. 1260) — near-contemporary Persian chronicle, Raverty's English translation of the Bihar campaign passage

sources.ref: Minhaj-i Siraj, Tabaqat-i Nasiri (c. 1260) — Raverty translation: the Bihar campaign passage (assault on the 'fortress of Bihar', shaven-headed inhabitants slain, the great book collections discovered)
Dharmasvamin's account (1234–1236, via Tibetan transmission) — Nalanda c. 1236: 80 small viharas mostly abandoned/damaged by the Turushkas, 2 functional, <100 monks, 90-year abbot Rahula Shribhadra
Chag Lotsawa's pilgrimage account (c. 1235) — found the 90-year-old teacher Rahula Shribhadra instructing ~70 students at damaged Nalanda
Taranatha, History of Buddhism in India (1608) — Tibetan tradition on the invasions and the flight of monks to Tibet/Nepal
Arun Shourie, 'How history was made up at Nalanda' (The Indian Express, 28 June 2014) — on the ransacking's description in the contemporary Tabaqat-i Nasiri and Taranatha's 'mine of learning'

competing_hypotheses: Identification question: Minhaj's translated passage describes the 'fortress of Bihar' (Kila-i-Bihar) — some historians identify this with Odantapuri rather than Nalanda proper; the three universities' sackings are treated together in later tradition, but the primary passage's named target is debated
The exact year: 1193 vs 1197 vs 1200 appear across secondary tellings; the campaign span is firm, the single-year precision is not

Revisionist minority (e.g., popular-critical readings): argues the primary passage does not name Nalanda explicitly and that Vikramashila/Nalanda attributions were hardened by later historiography — carried fairly, but against the mainstream scholarly consensus that treats the Bihar monasteries' destruction as established
falsifiability: A contemporary 13th-century account of the Bihar monasteries flourishing untouched after 1200, or proof that the Tabaqat passage is a later interpolation

title: The torture was the procedure: the law-of-proof thesis
claim: Continental Europe's judicial torture was not lawless cruelty but a formal, rule-bound evidentiary stage of the Romano-canonical inquisitorial procedure: the law of proof required two eyewitnesses or the accused's confession for conviction, so torture existed to produce the confession — permitted only on 'half proof' (one eyewitness or sufficient circumstantial indicia), governed by codified safeguards (the Carolina 1532, the ordonnance criminelle 1670), and it died when the law of proof was reformed rather than when a book was read.
place: Regensburg (the Carolina, Diet of 1532); the procedure's theater is the Empire and France
grade_reason: The specialist consensus (Langbein 1977/2006, the definitive account): the two-witness-or-confession rule is documented in the glossators; the half-proof threshold and safeguards are documented in the Carolina's articles and the 1670 ordonnance; the 1808 code's termination of the classical procedure is dated. Held at CORROBORATED rather than VERIFIED because it is a historiographical thesis about causation, not a single dated event.
earliest_attestation: The 13th-century Italian glossators' law of proof (two unimpeachable eyewitnesses, 'clear as the noonday sun', or the accused's confession); codified safeguards in the Constitutio Criminalis Carolina (Diet of Regensburg, 1532).

sources.ref: Constitutio Criminalis Carolina (1532), proclaimed at the Diet of Regensburg — 219 articles; the interrogation-under-torture rules with the indicia threshold, the surgeon's duty, ratification, and appeal
Ordonnance criminelle de 1670 (Saint-Germain-en-Laye; registered 26 Aug 1670, in force 1 Jan 1671) — the question préparatoire / question préalable as formal evidentiary stages

John H. Langbein, Torture and the Law of Proof: Europe and England in the Ancien Régime (Univ. of Chicago Press, 1977; 2nd ed. 2006) — the definitive account: torture as the institutional consequence of the two-witness-or-confession rule
French Code d'instruction criminelle (16 November 1808) — terminates the classical inquisitorial procedure in German territories

competing_hypotheses: The Foucauldian reading (Discipline and Punish, 1975): the decline of torture belongs to a larger shift in the economy of punishment — from the spectacular suffering of the body to the disciplined soul — with the procedure's rules as epiphenomena of power.
The humanitarian-persuasion reading: Beccaria (1764), Voltaire (after the 1762 Calas affair), and Montesquieu persuaded Europe out of torture — the abolition as a victory of ideas.

The practical-failure reading: officials stopped trusting torture because it produced false confessions (Denmark's 1695 royal commission found it ineffective) — abolition as administrative learning, not proof-reform.
falsifiability: A body of pre-13th-century systematic judicial-torture regulation, or evidence that the Carolina's torture articles were dead letter everywhere (routine judicial violation of the half-proof threshold), would weaken the thesis; Langbein's account is the specialist consensus, not a court transcript.

title: Al-Jazari's Book of Ingenious Devices (1206 CE)
claim: Ismail al-Jazari (d. 1206), chief engineer at the Artuqid court of Diyar Bakr (Amid), compiled al-Jami' bayn al-'ilm wa al-'amal al-nafi' fi sina'at al-hiyal ('The Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices', presented 1206): 50+ illustrated machines including the elephant clock, castle clock, musical automata with programmable peg-and-cam mechanisms, the double-action suction pump, the camshaft, and the crankshaft with crank-slider mechanism — the rotary-to-reciprocating conversion at the heart of every modern engine.
place: Amid (Diyarbakir), Artuqid Diyar Bakr
grade_reason: Multiply attested in the manuscript tradition (the Topkapi 1206 copy plus later illustrated copies) and independently verified by reconstruction: the diagrams encode buildable geometry — the strongest possible attestation for a machine treatise.
earliest_attestation: Multiple illustrated manuscript copies (Topkapi Palace Ms. Ahmet III 3472, 1206-dated); Donald R. Hill's 1974 English translation; working reconstructions by modern engineers from the diagrams

sources.ref: Topkapi Palace Ms. Ahmet III 3472 (1206): the presentation copy, illustrated
Hill, D.R. (1974): English translation of the Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices
Modern working reconstructions of the elephant clock, pumps, and automata from the diagrams (museums worldwide)

competing_hypotheses: Original innovations by al-Jazari: crankshaft, camshaft, and programmable automata are absent from his predecessors' works — his own text names the improvements over the Banu Musa and others

Sophisticated refinement: he builds on the Banu Musa brothers' 9th-century devices and Hellenistic automata traditions (he cites them); the honest position is master-builder originality, not isolated invention
Leonardo-influence hypothesis (da Vinci influenced by al-Jazari via Arabic texts): proposed, unproven — carried as speculation, not graded
falsifiability: The devices are reconstructible: modern engineers have built working replicas from the 800-year-old diagrams; a reconstruction failing the geometry would force a re-grade — none has

title: The Mongol Empire at its greatest extent (c. 1279–1294) — the largest contiguous land empire in history
claim: At its greatest extent, around 1279–1294, the Mongol Empire was the largest contiguous land empire in history: roughly 23.5–24 million square kilometers (~9.1 million square miles), about 17.8% of Earth's land surface, with on the order of 110 million subjects — about a quarter of humanity under one administration.
place: Karakorum (capital 1235–1271); the empire at height stretched from the Sea of Japan to Eastern Europe and the Levant
grade_reason: Multiple independent atlases and scholarly syntheses converge on the ~23.5–24 million km² maximal extent and the largest-contiguous-empire superlative; the claim is held at CORROBORATED (not VERIFIED) because pre-modern borders are approximate and the population figure is a modeled estimate, not a count.
earliest_attestation: The Secret History of the Mongols (c. 1228–1240s, Mongolian) for the founding; Persian (Juvayni, Rashid al-Din) and Chinese (Yuan administrative) records for the empire at its height.

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Mongol Empire' — 'The Mongol Empire was the largest contiguous empire in history'; infobox area series: 1206: 4,000,000 km²; 1227: 13,500,000 km²; 1294: 23,500,000 km² (9,100,000 sq mi)
historyandmystery.org, 'History's Largest Contiguous Land Empire Was the Mongol Empire' — 24 million km² (9.27 million sq mi), ~17.81% of Earth's total land surface at peak
Wikipedia, 'Outline of the Mongol Empire' — 'The Mongol Empire at its greatest extent in 1279'
Timothy May, The Mongol Empire (Edinburgh University Press, 2018) — modern scholarly synthesis of the empire's extent and administration, carried as the current reference
The Secret History of the Mongols — the Mongol-side founding narrative (the horde's own book)

competing_hypotheses: The British Empire exceeded the Mongol Empire in total land area — but not as a contiguous landmass, which is the qualifier the claim carries
The 1279 peak date: some reckonings place the practical maximum under Möngke or the fragmented-but-nominal unity of 1294; the figures agree within ~1 million km²
falsifiability: A rigorously surveyed pre-modern border reconstruction showing a larger contiguous land empire (e.g., a corrected Russian Empire figure above ~24 million km² of contiguous territory) would take the superlative.

title: Magna Carta, Clause 39 (the 'peers' clause)
claim: Clause 39 of the 1215 Magna Carta, sealed at Runnymede (15 June 1215), provides that no free man shall be seized, imprisoned, stripped of rights or possessions, outlawed, exiled, or destroyed except by the lawful judgment of his equals or by the law of the land. The clause's actual historical content is a baronial guarantee against arbitrary royal action — judgment by fellow barons in the feudal court — not a grant of trial by jury to the population.
place: Runnymede, Surrey, England (traditional site of the sealing)
grade_reason: The text survives in four contemporary engrossments; the clause's baronial, non-jury meaning is the scholarly consensus across the charter's 800th-anniversary literature.
earliest_attestation: Four surviving engrossments of the 1215 charter (British Library (2), Lincoln Cathedral, Salisbury Cathedral); the operative clause in Latin: 'nullus liber homo capiatur, vel imprisonetur, aut disseisiatur, aut utlagetur, aut exuletur, aut aliquo modo destruatur, nec super eum ibimus, nec super eum mittemus, nisi per legale judicium parium suorum vel per legem terre.'

sources.ref: The four 1215 engrossments — British Library (Cotton MS Augustus II.106; Add MS 48386), Lincoln Cathedral, Salisbury Cathedral; Latin text of clause 39

Library of Congress, 'Trial by Jury — Magna Carta: Muse and Mentor' exhibit: 'The origins of the jury trial precede the creation of Magna Carta... Magna Carta did not institute the jury system in the modern sense'

Daniel Klerman (USC Gould, via Metropolitan News): clause 39's 'judgment of his peers' meant the old feudal court — barons judged by fellow barons — 'this is not trial by jury'; jury trials in criminal cases were unknown in 1215 (cases were resolved by ordeal or battle)
Scholarship summarized for the charter's 700th anniversary: Coke's interpretation of chapter 29 was anachronistic — a 17th-century reading of a 13th-century text; the Latin wording is ambiguous

competing_hypotheses: The Cokean/17th-century reading: clause 39 (chapter 29 of the 1225 charter) as a guarantee of trial by jury — the reading that powered the Levellers, Lilburne's 1640s pleadings, and the American founding; carried here as reception-history, graded separately in evt-magna-carta-created-jury-001

The 'due process' lineage reading: whatever 1215 meant, clause 39/29 became the anchor of due-process jurisprudence in the Anglo-American tradition (e.g. the Fifth Amendment) — the text's later function vs its 1215 meaning
falsifiability: An engrossment carrying a clause 39 that promises jury trial in recognizably modern terms; or 13th-century evidence that 'pares sui' was read by contemporaries as a body of commoners sworn to find facts rather than baronial co-tenants

title: The claim that Magna Carta created trial by jury
claim: Magna Carta (1215) created, invented, or first granted the right to trial by jury — that before Runnymede there was no jury, and the charter gave England (and by inheritance, America) the jury as a new institution.
place: Runnymede, Surrey, England (the myth's alleged birthplace)
grade_reason: Three independent kills from the record itself: (1) the clause's own words — 'judicium parium' is baronial feudal justice, fellow vassals judging vassals, not a sworn jury of fact-finders (Klerman); (2) the chronology — juries of presentment existed by Henry II's Assize of Clarendon (1166), 49 years before Runnymede (companion record evt-henry-ii-assize-1166-001); (3) the reading's provenance — the jury gloss is Coke's 17th-century anachronism, corrected by the 700th-anniversary scholarship.
earliest_attestation: The myth has no medieval attestation — no 13th- or 14th-century source reads clause 39 as creating the jury. It enters as a 17th-century common-law fiction (Coke), is repeated by Lilburne (1640s), Blackstone, and into textbooks and civics teaching.

sources.ref: Library of Congress, 'Trial by Jury — Magna Carta: Muse and Mentor': 'The origins of the jury trial precede the creation of Magna Carta' and 'Magna Carta did not institute the jury system in the modern sense'
Daniel Klerman (USC Gould): 'this is not trial by jury' — jury trials were unknown in criminal cases in 1215; criminal cases were resolved by ordeal or battle
The Economist (via endofyourarm.com summary): Magna Carta 'did not... spawn democracy... or trial by jury (which was already in use)'
700th-anniversary scholarship summary: Coke's interpretation of chapter 29 was anachronistic — a 17th-century reading of a 13th-century text

competing_hypotheses: The 17th-century-reception reading (Coke, the Levellers, Lilburne): chapter 29 of the 1225 charter as the jury's charter — historically false as a claim about 1215, but a real and potent political fiction that shaped the 1640s and the American founding; fenced out of the grade

The softer 'inspired' reading: the charter's due-process intent inspired later generations to view the jury as a safeguard of freedom (the Library of Congress exhibit's own line) — inspiration is reception-history, not invention
falsifiability: A 13th-century reading of clause 39 as creating or mandating the jury; or evidence that no jury of any form existed in England before 15 June 1215

title: The end of the ordeal in England (1215–1219) — how the jury got its courtroom
claim: In 1215, the Fourth Lateran Council (Canon 18) forbade clergy to take part in trials by ordeal — priests could no longer bless the water or the iron. With the rite's divine machinery removed, England abandoned the ordeal: the plea rolls contain no trial by ordeal after 1219, when Henry III's regency issued instructions to the itinerant justices ordering a new method of proof — the jury. The ordeal-to-jury turn was papal-and-crown work, not the charter's.
place: London, England (seat of the 1219 instructions; the ordeal-to-jury turn)
grade_reason: Canon 18's text is primary and explicit; the English plea-roll record shows no ordeal after 1219; Henry III's 1219 instructions are documented. Held below VERIFIED on the causal weight of the Council vs pre-existing decline, and on the exact mechanics of the 1219 instructions.
earliest_attestation: Lateran IV, Canon 18 (1215): clerics may neither pronounce nor execute death sentences, nor take part in judicial tests and trials by ordeal; English royal writs of 1219 instructing the eyre justices; the plea rolls' absence of ordeal cases after 1219.

sources.ref: Fourth Lateran Council, 1215, Canon 18 — De indicio sanguinis et duelli clericis interdicto: clerics 'neither pronounce nor execute a sentence of death... nor take part in matters connected with judicial tests and trials by ordeal'

Trial-by-ordeal scholarship (Wikipedia synthesis): 'In 1215, clergy were forbidden to participate in ordeals by the Fourth Lateran Council. The English plea rolls contain no cases of trial by ordeal after 1219, when Henry III recognized its abolition.'
Legal-history account (Mercatus working paper): ordeals abandoned where their religious trappings evaporated — Denmark 1216, England 1219, Scotland 1230, Italy 1231
LawLessons.ca / JusticeEducation.ca: Henry III issued an edict in 1219 encouraging trial by judge and jury — twelve worthy local citizens using common sense and knowledge of the people and events

competing_hypotheses: The gradual-decline reading: English practice had been moving away from the ordeal before 1215, and the Council ratified a shift already underway rather than causing it

The continental divergence: most of Europe filled the gap with the inquisitorial procedure and judicial torture, not the jury — the jury was England's contingent choice, not the inevitable successor (carried in competing hypotheses, not graded)
falsifiability: Plea-roll ordeal cases in England after 1219; or evidence the ordeal persisted in England with priests' blessings after Canon 18

title: The Wandering Jew (1228) is not Cain
claim: The 'wandering man who cannot die' legend first recorded in 1228 (Roger of Wendover's Flores Historiarum, via an Armenian archbishop at St Albans; incorporated into Matthew Paris's Chronica Majora) concerns Cartaphilus, Pilate's doorkeeper — not Cain. Christ's sentence, 'I will go, but thou shalt remain waiting until I come,' launched 800 years of folklore (renamed Ahasuerus the cobbler in the 1602 German chapbook). Conflating this figure with Cain is a popular error; the legend says nothing about Cain at all.
place: St Albans (recording); Jerusalem (narrative)
grade_reason: Multiply attested in the chronicle record; the Cain-conflation is DEBUNKED by the legend's own dramatis personae.
earliest_attestation: Roger of Wendover, Flores Historiarum (1228); Matthew Paris, Chronica Majora

sources.ref: Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Wandering Jew' — 1228, Cartaphilus, 1602 Ahasuerus
Britannica 9th ed. entry detail (1902encyclopedia transcription)

falsifiability: A pre-1228 witness to the Cartaphilus story, or a version naming Cain

title: Ibn al-Nafis Describes Pulmonary Circulation (1242 CE)
claim: In his Sharh Tashrih al-Qanun ('Commentary on the Anatomy of the Canon of Avicenna', c. 1242 CE), the Damascus physician Ibn al-Nafis (1213-1288) described the pulmonary circulation: blood passes from the right ventricle through the lungs to the left ventricle, explicitly denying Galen's 'invisible pores' in the interventricular septum; he also described the coronary arteries and predicted small passages (manafidh) between pulmonary artery and vein — about 300 years before Servetus and Harvey.
place: Damascus (Ibn al-Nafis's city; he later headed the al-Mansuri hospital in Cairo)
grade_reason: One manuscript but a century of scholarly absorption: Meyerhof's 1924-1935 editions, Spink & Lewis 1973 English translation, and mainstream acceptance in medical-history literature (textbook-level). VERIFIED is withheld because the attestation chain rests on a single surviving copy.
earliest_attestation: Sharh Tashrih al-Qanun manuscript, discovered 1924 by Egyptian physician Muhyo al-Deen Tatawi (Altawi) in the Prussian State Library, Berlin; translated by orientalist Max Meyerhof into German, French, and English

sources.ref: Meyerhof, M. (1935): edition and translation of Sharh Tashrih al-Qanun; first modern publication of the pulmonary-circulation passages
Spink, M.S. & Lewis, G.L. (1973): Arabic Surgical Treatises translation series; English rendering of the anatomical commentary
JBIMA review: 'Ibn al-Nafis — The First Who Described the Pulmonary Blood Circulation' — the coronary-vessel and manafidh (capillary) passages translated

competing_hypotheses: Independent 13th-century discovery by Ibn al-Nafis, subsequently lost to the Latin West (the mainstream reading: the work survives in a single manuscript, and the Latin medical tradition shows no knowledge of it)
Transmission hypothesis: Servetus or Colombo may have known an Arabic-derived account — proposed but unproven; no documented chain exists, so it is not graded

Single-manuscript skepticism: the whole claim chain rests on one rediscovered copy (Prussian State Library); the discovery is accepted because the Arabic text, once translated, was unambiguous and was absorbed into mainstream medical history — the audit is the century of scrutiny since 1924
falsifiability: A forgery finding on the manuscript, or proof the pulmonary-circulation passages were interpolated by a later hand, would collapse the grade; corroboration grows if further copies surface

title: The Tusi Couple's Road to Copernicus
claim: Late Islamic astronomical devices — above all Nasir al-Din al-Tusi's 'Tusi couple' (Tadhkira fi 'ilm al-hay'a) and the planetary models of the 14th-century Damascene astronomer Ibn al-Shatir — appear inside Nicolaus Copernicus's De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (1543), used by Copernicus in his reformulation of mathematical astronomy.
place: Maragha, East Azerbaijan, Iran (observatory site); the devices travel to Copernicus via routes still debated (Byzantine, Hebrew, Iberian)
grade_reason: Multiple independent witnesses converge: Hartner 1973 diagram-notation match; Swerdlow & Neugebauer 1984 on Ibn al-Shatir's models inside De revolutionibus; surviving Byzantine Greek Tusi-couple manuscripts (Vat. gr. 211); the Hebrew Meyasher 'Aqov. But the exact transmission chain is unidentified (Wikipedia 'Tusi couple': 'an exact chain of transmission has not yet been identified'), so VERIFIED is withheld.
earliest_attestation: Hartner, W. (1973) — 'Copernicus, the Man, the Work, and its History': the Tusi-couple diagram in Copernicus matches Tadhkira; Latin notation follows Arabic (alif->A)

sources.ref: Hartner, W. (1973): Tusi-couple diagram in De revolutionibus III.4 matches Tadhkira; Latin notation follows Arabic alif->A, ba->B (JSTOR 986460)
Swerdlow, N. & Neugebauer, O. (1984) — Mathematical Astronomy in Copernicus's De Revolutionibus: Ibn al-Shatir's lunar/mercury models nearly identical to Copernicus's
Saliba, G. (2007): Maragha models were equant-elimination devices for geocentrism; Copernicus's step was heliocentric redeployment
Neugebauer, O. (1975: 11, 1035, 1456) — Vaticanus Graecus MS 211 (pre-1308, Chioniades tradition) contains the Tusi couple in Greek: the device reached Byzantium within decades
Wikipedia 'Tusi couple' (crawled 2026-10-13): coined by Kennedy 1966; 'growing consensus' Copernicus became aware 'in some way'; exact chain unidentified — the honest gap named, not hidden
phys.org 2025-04 (al-Mansouri study): Ibn al-Shatir's solar model maximum equation 2;2,6 deg parallels Copernicus's solar calculations

competing_hypotheses: Direct transmission (Hartner 1973; Swerdlow & Neugebauer 1984; Saliba 2007): Copernicus knew Arabic astronomical material — the diagram notation mirrors Arabic lettering (alif->A, ba->B), and models like the lunar theory match Ibn al-Shatir nearly identically

Indirect transmission: knowledge arrived via Byzantine Greek (Chioniades' translations; Vat. gr. 211 pre-1308), Hebrew (Abner of Burgos's Meyasher 'Aqov, c. 1270-1340), or Iberian translators — without a surviving Latin translation of the Arabic texts
Independent reinvention: the same geometrical problem admits the same solution; similarity is convergence, not contact

Copernicus-as-redeployer (Saliba 2007): Maragha models were built to 'save' geocentrism by eliminating the equant; Copernicus's move was to take the same devices and hold the sun fixed instead — the devices traveled, the cosmology was his
falsifiability: Would be weakened if a complete Latin translation stream were ruled out and the diagram matches were shown to be generic geometry; would be strengthened toward VERIFIED by a documented copy-chain. The exact chain remains unidentified, so the grade stays at CORROBORATED.

title: The Mongol Sack of Baghdad (1258)
