claim: The Mongol army under Hülegü besieged Baghdad in January 1258, took the city in February, massacred its population over roughly a week, and killed the Abbasid caliph al-Musta'sim — ending the Abbasid Caliphate's five centuries as a territorial power.
place: Baghdad, Iraq (Abbasid capital)
grade_reason: The siege, sack, and caliph's death are multiply attested across hostile and friendly traditions (Mongol-commissioned Persian, Arabic chronicles) within decades of the event; casualty figures and the caliph's death-method stay contested and are not smuggled into the event grade.
earliest_attestation: 'Ata-Malik Juvayni, Tarikh-i Jahan-gusha (c. 1260) — near-contemporary Persian account written under Mongol patronage; Rashid al-Din, Jami' al-Tawarikh (c. 1300-1310); Arabic chronicles incl. Ibn Kathir (14th c.)

sources.ref: Juvayni, Tarikh-i Jahan-gusha (c. 1260) — near-contemporary Persian account under Mongol patronage
Rashid al-Din, Jami' al-Tawarikh (c. 1300-1310) — Ilkhanid court chronicle
Ibn Kathir, al-Bidaya wa al-Nihaya (14th c.) — Arabic chronicle tradition
Morgan, David — The Mongols (modern scholarly synthesis; death-toll discussion incl. Sicker 2000 p. 111, Wassaf)

competing_hypotheses: The death toll is wildly contested: Sicker's ~90,000 (the low scholarly estimate) vs. popular figures of 200,000–1,000,000 (Wassaf, later tradition) — the numbers are graded separately, never as part of the event grade
The caliph's exact manner of death varies across accounts (carpet-trampling per most accounts; starvation/imprisonment in others) — the death is attested, the method is single-tradition per version
Some modern readings stress that Baghdad's political weight had already shrunk to a city-state by 1258 — the sack ended a symbol, not a functioning empire
falsifiability: Contemporary 1258 documentation of an intact Baghdad, or proof that the Juvayni/Rashid al-Din accounts are later fabrications

title: The ink-black Tigris: Baghdad 1258's legendary river
claim: After the Mongol sack of Baghdad in 1258, so many books from the House of Wisdom were thrown into the Tigris that the river's water ran black with ink (and, in some tellings, red with blood).
place: Baghdad, Tigris River
grade_reason: The telling is attested in later and popular accounts (which agree on the image) but no contemporary 13th-century witness was documented in this pass; the sack itself is CORROBORATED separately, so this record grades the telling, not the sack.
earliest_attestation: Later and popular accounts only — no contemporary 13th-century witness documented in this pass; current write-ups frame it explicitly as folklore/legend

sources.ref: The Golden Age of Islam: When Baghdad Lit the World (Aug 2026): 'according to popular accounts, so many manuscripts were thrown into the Tigris that its waters ran black with ink'

Bayt al-Hikmah: The Lost Library That Once Lit the World: 'According to folklore, so many burned manuscripts were thrown into the Tigris that the river's water turned black from the ink and soot. Whether this actually happened, however, is a matter of debate.'

competing_hypotheses: The telling preserves a genuine contemporary observation now lost to us (possible but undocumented in this pass)
The black-ink image is a later literary flourish that grew with retelling (the attestation trail runs through popular/late accounts, never a 13th-century witness found in this pass)
falsifiability: A contemporary 13th-century account describing the books' disposal would raise this to CORROBORATED; a documented source-study tracing the telling to a specific late invention would hold it here or lower it

title: The House of Wisdom Destroyed (1258)
claim: The Bayt al-Hikma (House of Wisdom) — Baghdad's grand Abbasid institution of translation and learning — was destroyed by the Mongols in the 1258 sack, its library burned and its books thrown into the Tigris.
place: Baghdad, Iraq (Abbasid capital)
grade_reason: The institution existed (Ibn al-Nadim); the specific claim that the Mongols destroyed it in 1258 is late-tradition only, contested by the documented 9th-century decline and the modern source-critical challenge to the grand-university image — the building's fate, not the institution's existence, is what stays CLAIMED.
earliest_attestation: The institution's existence is attested by Ibn al-Nadim, al-Fihrist (d. 995); its 1258 destruction is attested only in the later popular tradition

sources.ref: Ibn al-Nadim, al-Fihrist (d. 995) — the primary source for the Bayt al-Hikma's existence and holdings
Current House of Wisdom historiography — the 19th/20th-c. Orientalist-construction challenge to the grand-university image (translation errors, retrospective projection)
al-Wasiti's 1237 illustrations to the Maqamat al-Hariri — Baghdad manuscript culture alive a generation before the sack

competing_hypotheses: The institution's own ending is undocumented: it had been declining since the 9th century (administrative functions moved to Samarra under al-Mu'tasim; later caliphs maintained but did not renew it), and no contemporary source records its specific destruction in 1258

Recent historians challenge the grand-university image itself: the narrative of the House of Wisdom as a major academic institution with departments and organized debate was constructed over the 19th and early 20th centuries by Orientalist scholars through translation errors and retrospective projection (per the current House of Wisdom historiography) — the sources (above all Ibn al-Nadim's al-Fihrist, d. 995) support a caliphal library/translation bureau, not a university
The 'total loss' framing is weakened by al-Tusi's rescue of volumes to Maragheh and the survival of Baghdad manuscript traditions into the 13th century (e.g. al-Wasiti's 1237 illustrations)
falsifiability: A contemporary 1258 source naming the Bayt al-Hikma's destruction would raise the grade; so would archaeological identification of the building

title: The Tigris Ran Black with Ink (1258)
claim: During the 1258 Mongol sack of Baghdad, so many books and manuscripts were thrown into the Tigris River that its waters ran black with ink (and, in the paired version, red with the blood of the slain).
place: Baghdad — the Tigris at the city
grade_reason: Attested, but late: the ink-black river is a 14th-century-and-after tale, absent from the near-contemporary accounts; it is a detail about the sack, not evidence of it, and stays CLAIMED until a contemporary attestation appears.
earliest_attestation: No contemporary (1258) source records the ink-black river; the tale belongs to the 14th-century-and-later chronicle tradition

sources.ref: 14th-century-and-later chronicle tradition (tales of book destruction in the Tigris; origin of the ink-black detail per the Siege of Baghdad historiography)
Juvayni, Tarikh-i Jahan-gusha (c. 1260) — the near-contemporary account that does NOT carry the ink detail (the silence, honestly recorded)
Nasir al-Din al-Tusi's rescue of books to Maragheh (tradition: thousands of volumes saved in advance — the 'total loss' framing fails on the record)

competing_hypotheses: The detail is a literary trope of conquest literature — rivers discolored by catastrophe appear across medieval chronicles in both directions (red with blood, black with ink); the image may be conventional rather than observed
The sack's book-destruction is real (libraries were looted and burned per contemporary accounts) — the dispute is only the specific river detail, not the cultural loss
falsifiability: A contemporary 1258 source (Juvayni or equivalent) explicitly describing the ink-black river would raise the grade; physical evidence is unrecoverable either way

title: The Turin Shroud linen
claim: The linen of the Turin Shroud is the burial cloth of Jesus of Nazareth, woven in the 1st century CE.
place: Turin Cathedral, Italy (cloth kept; sample taken 1988)
grade_reason: Three independent AMS labs converged on AD 1260-1390 for the LINEN (Damon et al., Nature 1989, 95% confidence; labs still stand by it; Lirey's 1354 documentary appearance corroborates). A 1st-century burial cloth cannot be woven of 14th-century flax. The 2026 peer-reviewed metagenomic study (Barcaccia et al., Sci Rep) found the cloth's DNA to be a contamination mosaic dominated by its own 1978 sampler — it says nothing about age, and changes nothing about the linen date.
earliest_attestation: The cloth's first certain historical record is the second half of the 14th century (Lirey, France, 1354) — consistent with the radiocarbon result

sources.ref: Damon, P.E. et al., 'Radiocarbon Dating of the Shroud of Turin', Nature (1989): 1260-1390 CE at 95% confidence; 'conclusive evidence that the linen of the Shroud of Turin is mediaeval'

Raw-data release (British Museum, 2017, after legal request); Casabianca et al. 2019 statistical re-analysis — heterogeneity in the data, procedure should be reconsidered (caveat carried, does not overturn the medieval result)
Statistical heterogeneity in the three labs' data: Riani, Atkinson & Corbellini (2013)
First certain historical record: Lirey, France, mid-14th century — corroborates the radiocarbon window from the documentary side

Barcaccia et al., 'DNA Traces on the Shroud of Turin: Metagenomics of the 1978 Official Sample Collection', Scientific Reports (2026), doi:10.1038/s41598-026-60684-7 — first PCR-free metagenomic sequencing of the 1978 official samples: the strongest human DNA in three clean profiles matched the 1978 sampler himself (Pierluigi Baima Bollone, co-author, d. Nov 2025), plus a contamination mosaic of human, animal (cat, dog, cattle, pig), plant (incl. maize, banana, peanut — post-Columbian species, a contamination fingerprint), fungal, and archaeal DNA. The authors state explicitly the study does not determine age or authenticity; Scientific American (2026) reported experts' verdict that it 'doesn't show the relic's origins'. Added 2026-10-16 (III.21 second pass).

Freer-Waters & Jull (2026) — direct examination of the surviving Arizona fragments of the 1988 sample: textilely consistent with the main Shroud (flax, z-twisted yarns, 3/1 herringbone twill, matching thread counts); no signs of repair, no obvious contamination. The study did NOT perform new carbon dating — it tested the integrity of the surviving material from the old sample, and closes the repair-patch objection for the examined fragments (not for the whole strip). Record: evt-shroud-arizona-fragments-2026-001. Added 2026-10-16 (III.21 third pass).

competing_hypotheses: The sampled corner was a medieval reweave/repair patch, not representative of the main cloth (the shroud-research community's principal objection)
Contamination (fire, handling, candle smoke) shifted the radiocarbon age younger — contested, as the three labs applied standard contamination corrections and three control samples dated correctly
The 1988 result stands for the linen: medieval artifact; the image's origin is a separate, ungraded question

The 2026 'Indian origin of Jesus' press telling (sensationalist coverage of the metagenomic study's Indian-haplogroup DNA traces) — the paper reports handling-contamination, not origin; the haplogroup mix describes who and what touched a much-handled cloth, and the authors make no provenance claim for the artifact itself
falsifiability: Re-sampling the main body of the cloth from multiple locations, with independent blind analysis converging on a 1st-century date, would reopen the claim. The custodians have not authorized further sampling.

title: The invention of eyeglasses in Italy, c. 1268–1289 (anonymous)
claim: Eyeglasses were invented in Italy, between about 1268 and 1289, by a maker whose name the record does not preserve; the art spread by the early 14th century.
place: Pisa / Venice, Italy (the two documented early centers)
grade_reason: CORROBORATED: no single contemporary source names the inventor, but independent near-contemporary witnesses converge on the same decade — Rivalto's 1306 sermon, Redi's 1299 manuscript, the Pisa Dominican chronicle's account of Alessandro della Spina (d. 1313) re-making the art 'first made by someone else' and sharing it freely, Bernard Gordon's 1305 medical reference (Montpellier), and Venetian guild regulations governing spectacle sales by 1301. The earliest pictorial evidence is Tommaso da Modena's 1352 portrait of Cardinal Hugh de Provence.
earliest_attestation: Fra Giordano da Rivalto, sermon 23 February 1306 (Pisa): the art of making glasses invented within the last twenty years; the inventor unnamed. Francesco Redi (1676) cites a 1299 manuscript calling spectacles 'lately invented.'

sources.ref: Francesco Redi's 1676 letters (via mrcophth.com): the 1299 manuscript ('glasses... lately invented for the comfort of the old souls who have become weak-sighted') and Fra Giordano da Rivalto's 1305/1306 sermon ('not yet twenty years since the art of making glasses was invented'); Alessandro della Spina's obituary (d. 1313) — 'he made glasses and freely taught the art to others; glasses had previously been made by someone else'
FixMyGlasses history of glasses: Venice guild regulations governing the sale of eyeglasses by 1301; Tommaso da Modena's 1352 portrait of Cardinal Hugh de Provence as the earliest pictorial evidence

competing_hypotheses: A single identifiable inventor whose name was deliberately suppressed (the Pisa chronicle's 'someone else, who was unwilling to share them' reading)
Near-simultaneous independent invention in Venice and Pisa, with the guild record (Venice, 1301) and the Dominican record (Pisa, 1306/1313) as two centers rather than one origin
falsifiability: A securely dated eyeglass artifact or text from before 1268, or proof the 1299 manuscript and the 1306 sermon are forgeries

title: 'Jehovah' as the original pronunciation of the divine name
claim: 'Jehovah' is the original pronunciation of the Hebrew divine name — the way ancient Israelites spoke YHWH.
place: Jerusalem — locus of the divine-name tradition
grade_reason: Multiple independent encyclopedic authorities (Britannica, Jewish Encyclopedia 1901, Encyclopedia Judaica, Harper's Bible Dictionary) agree 'Jehovah' is an artificial hybrid of YHWH's consonants with the vowels of 'Adonai,' never used by the Jews.
earliest_attestation: The misreading itself is a late invention: Jewish Encyclopedia (1901): 'comparatively recent invention'; the pre-Masoretic and ancient sources (Theodoret, Jerome, Origen, Philo) report the Tetragrammaton was written but not pronounced.

sources.ref: Encyclopaedia Britannica ('Yahweh' article): 'The Masoretes ... replaced the vowels of the name YHWH with the vowel signs of Adonai or Elohim. Thus the artificial name Jehovah came into being.'
The Jewish Encyclopedia (1901), 'Jehovah': 'A mispronunciation (introduced by Christian theologians, but almost entirely disregarded by the Jews) of the Hebrew Yhwh ... grammatically impossible.'
Harper's Bible Dictionary (1985), 'tetragrammaton': 'The hybrid word Jehovah is a combination of the vowels of Adonai with the consonants of the tetragrammaton.'
Webster's New Collegiate Dictionary (1973): 'Jehovah — False reading of the Hebrew YAHWEH.'

competing_hypotheses: Encyclopedia Judaica's position: the true pronunciation was never lost — it was regularly pronounced 'Yahweh' at least until 586 BCE, as shown by the Lachish Letters; the ancient reading tradition preserved it even as public pronunciation was avoided
falsifiability: A pre-Masoretic Hebrew inscription or transcription actually voweled as 'Jehovah' would reopen it; none exists in the consulted record.

title: The fall-blade's two-century head start: Halifax and the Scottish Maiden
claim: Fall-blade beheading machines predated the 1792 French guillotine by centuries: the Halifax Gibbet (England) and the Scottish Maiden (Edinburgh, 1564) are documented precedents.
place: Halifax, West Yorkshire (Gibbet); Edinburgh Mercat Cross (Maiden) — pins carried jointly, region precision for the pair
grade_reason: Two independent machines, two independent paper trails. Halifax: the wooden structure (two uprights, horizontal beam, 4.5 m; 3.5 kg axe head on a sliding wooden block), the execution register 1541–1650, the 1532 Weiditz woodcut and 1577 Holinshed illustration as independent pictorial corroboration. Edinburgh: the Maiden — built 1564 on the order of the Provost and Magistrates, in use April 1565 to 1710 (last execution 30 June 1716, John Hamilton), 150+ executed including the Marquess of Argyll (1661) and his son (1685), now in the National Museum of Scotland; the treasurer's accounts record moving and assembling the machine. The Morton-commission story is itself debunked inside this record: the machine was commissioned in 1564, seven years before Morton became Regent — Hume's 1644 telling is the legend's birth certificate, not its evidence. Held below VERIFIED on two honest uncertainties: the exact origin date of the Gibbet (the 1280 execution's method is unknown), and the open historical question of whether the French designers knew of these machines (one secondary source notes it is uncertain whether Guillotin was familiar with the Gibbet).
earliest_attestation: The Halifax execution register (names from 1541 to 1650; the plaque lists 52 executed by the device); a Hans Weiditz 1532 woodcut showing a Gibbet-like device; Holinshed's Chronicles (1577) showing a similar machine at an Irish execution in 1307; Edinburgh City Treasurer accounts recording the Maiden's construction, transport, assembly, and dismantling.

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Guillotine' — Halifax Gibbet description (4.5 m wooden structure, 3.5 kg axe head, sliding block); first recorded Halifax execution 1280 (method uncertain); Maiden constructed 1564, in use April 1565–1710; Morton executed 1581; Morton-commission legend from Hume of Godscroft 1644
Wikipedia, 'Halifax Gibbet' — register 1541–1650; dismantled after 1650; 1974 full-size replica on original stone base; plaque with 52 names; Weiditz 1532 woodcut; Holinshed 1577 illustration

Wikipedia, 'Maiden (guillotine)' — Edinburgh treasurer accounts (transport/assembly); dismantlable oak construction; 150+ executed 1564–1716; Argyll executions 1661/1685; last execution 30 June 1716 (John Hamilton); now National Museum of Scotland
visitnesm.org.uk, 'The Gibbet and the Maiden' — Halifax wool-trade context; 53 executed by the gibbet; blade axe-shaped, never sharpened, relied on weight and drop

competing_hypotheses: The 'French invention from nothing' reading — dies on the Gibbet and the Maiden

The Morton-commission legend: James Douglas, 4th Earl of Morton, commissioned the Maiden after seeing the Halifax Gibbet — the 1644 Hume of Godscroft story, unsupported by the 1564 commission record (Provost and Magistrates of Edinburgh, seven years before Morton became Regent); dies on chronology
falsifiability: A demonstration that the Halifax register, the Weiditz woodcut, and the Edinburgh treasurer accounts all postdate 1792 or are forgeries — the accounts are mundane municipal paperwork, the least romantic evidence class.

title: Venice confines glassmaking to Murano (8 November 1291)
claim: On 8 November 1291, Venice confined most of its glassmaking industry to the island of Murano.
place: Murano, Venetian Lagoon
grade_reason: VERIFIED: the law is an archival record with a precise date, and the industry's centuries-long concentration on Murano is independently attested by the guild records, the 1295 no-leaving law, and Murano's documented dominance of European glassmaking through the Renaissance.
earliest_attestation: The Venetian law of 8 November 1291

sources.ref: Wikipedia 'Murano glass': 'A law dated November 8, 1291 confined most of Venice's glassmaking industry to the island of Murano'; furnaces as fire hazard in a city of wooden structures; the move also kept the technology and glassmakers confined and monitored
The Italian Tribune, 'The History of Venetian Glass in Italy': 1291 order by La Serenissima; historians' dual reading — fire hazard vs isolating craftsmen to protect trade secrets

competing_hypotheses: The stated reading: fire safety — furnaces in a wooden city were a genuine hazard

The secrecy reading: the consolidation was equally about keeping the maestri and their techniques on one monitored island (the 1271 import ban, the 1295 no-leaving law, and the Council of Ten's later oversight support this)
falsifiability: A contradictory archival record, or evidence the law was never enforced (instead the industry demonstrably concentrated on Murano for centuries)

title: The Ottoman Empire (c. 1299–1922)
claim: The Ottoman Empire existed as a continuous state from c. 1299 (Osman I) until 1 November 1922 (the Grand National Assembly's abolition of the sultanate) — roughly six hundred and twenty years, one of the longest-lived states in recorded history.
place: Istanbul (seat of the Sublime Porte; founded as Ottoman state in Bithynia, northwestern Anatolia)
grade_reason: The state is multiply attested in its own vast chancery archive and in every contemporary neighboring power's records for six centuries; its beginning and legal end are both documented to the file.
earliest_attestation: Earliest surviving Ottoman chancery documents (14th c.); the empire's own Tahrir registers, firmans, and the Başbakanlık (Prime Ministry) Ottoman Archives — estimated ~100 million documents; multiply attested by Byzantine, Venetian, Genoese, Papal, and European diplomatic records from the 14th century onward.

sources.ref: Başbakanlık Osmanlı Arşivleri (Prime Ministry Ottoman Archives), Istanbul — ~100 million documents
Grand National Assembly resolution of 1 November 1922 — abolition of the sultanate
İnalcık, Halil — 'The Ottoman Empire: The Classical Age, 1300-1600' (Weidenfeld, 1973) — the documentary-state argument
Contemporary external attestations: Byzantine chronicles, Venetian relazioni, Genoese and Papal records from the 14th century onward

competing_hypotheses: The 1299 date is traditional rather than documentary — the empire's own earliest chancery records date from later; some historians anchor the founding to Osman I's documented campaigns (1302 Bapheus) rather than a coronation year

Some periodizations end the 'imperial' story at 1918 (Mudros) or 1920 (Sevres), treating 1920-1922 as a terminal interregnum rather than imperial rule — the 1 Nov 1922 legal abolition remains the formal terminus
falsifiability: Contemporaneous 14th-century documentation showing no polity under Osman I's successors, or proof that the 1922-abolition documents are forgeries.

title: The fibula (14th c. BCE) — the safety pin's ancestor
claim: The ancient fibula is the safety pin's ancestor: the Mycenaean violin-bow fibula (14th c. BCE) combined a single wire, a spring, a sharp point, and a hooked catch — the same four elements as Hunt's 1849 Dress-Pin — and the type ran for millennia through the Roman bow fibulae.
place: Greek Peloponnese (Mycenaean heartland; violin-bow fibula introduction)
grade_reason: Independently attested in archaeological typology (Peschiera, Unter-Radl types), museum scholarship (Metropolitan Museum Journal), and art-historical survey (Smarthistory) — three independent lines on the same construction principle.
earliest_attestation: Mycenaean violin-bow fibulae (Drahtbügel), 14th c. BCE

sources.ref: Wikipedia "Fibula (brooch)" — Historical development: violin bow fibulae (Drahtbügel) appear in the late Bronze Age; introduced 14th c. BC by the Mycenaeans on the Greek Peloponnese
Metropolitan Museum of Art Journal v.35 (2000) — Dandridge, on the crossbow fibula's construction: basic form is a safety pin from a single wire
Smarthistory — "Fibulae" (Herbert Kuhn typology; thousands of specimens in museum collections)

competing_hypotheses: The exact continuity from Mycenaean fibulae to the Roman period is typologically rich but regionally complex; the claim is about the principle, not an unbroken single lineage
The fibula's decorative elaboration (crossbow fibulae, enamel, gold) sometimes obscures the shared engineering
falsifiability: Dated stratigraphic re-analysis pushing the first fibulae after 1849 — impossible; held at CORROBORATED only because exact earliest-dated specimens carry typological dating ranges

title: The 'died at thirty' myth
claim: The typical (average) person in medieval Europe died at about age 30 — most medieval people were dead by their thirties.
place: England (the IPM data's coverage)
grade_reason: The number ~30 is a REAL statistic misread as a death age. It is life expectancy AT BIRTH — a population mean dominated by extreme infant/child mortality (in the Roman Empire up to a third of infants died before one; in Sweden 1750-1780 40% of children died before 15, per parish records). The conditional figure tells the truth: in medieval England, landowning boys with life expectancy at birth of 31.3 years had life expectancy at age 25 of +25.7 years — they lived to ~51 on average, and many into their 70s and 80s. The myth takes a mean and mistakes it for a biography.
earliest_attestation: The statistic's source data: the Inquisitions Post Mortem (English landholders, c. 1300-1500), analyzed in Josiah C. Russell, British Medieval Population (1958).

sources.ref: Josiah C. Russell, British Medieval Population (1958): Inquisitions Post Mortem data — life expectancy at birth for landowning males ~31.3 years, but life expectancy at age 25 of ~25.7 additional years (average age ~50.7 for those reaching 25)

Max Roser, Esteban Ortiz-Ospina, Hannah Ritchie, 'Life Expectancy' (Our World in Data, first published 2013, revised 2019): premodern life expectancy ~30 in all regions; the increase since is driven largely by falling child mortality (CC-BY)

Max Roser, 'Mortality in the past: every second child died' (Our World in Data, 2023): historical child-mortality evidence — ~one-quarter of infants died in their first year, ~half of all children before the end of puberty across many premodern societies

E.A. Wrigley & R.S. Schofield, The Population History of England, 1541-1871 (1981): life-table method; even in the early-modern era, survivors of childhood had decades of life remaining — the demographic mechanism predates medicine

competing_hypotheses: The 'healthy worker' objection: the landowning class in the IPM data was healthier than peasants, so e(25) may be slightly lower for the poorest — but the direction of the correction is the same for all strata: surviving childhood added decades

The 'Rome comparison' caution: in the Roman Empire up to a third of infants died before age one and perhaps half of children before age ten, dragging life expectancy at birth even lower (~20s) — yet the same skew mechanism applies
falsifiability: A medieval cohort life table in which the modal age at death for those surviving childhood was ~30 — i.e., half the population dying in its thirties despite surviving infancy.

title: The predecessor's Atlantic expedition
claim: Mansa Musa's predecessor equipped a first fleet of 200 ships, then 2,000 ships (1,000 for men, 1,000 for water and provisions) to cross the Atlantic Ocean, and never returned; Musa became king after the fleet vanished.
place: West African Atlantic coast (departure point uncertain)
grade_reason: Attested in one near-contemporary tradition — Musa's own account as recorded by al-Umari — with no independent corroboration and no returns; the popular name 'Abu Bakr II' is a modern misattribution, not a listed mansa.
earliest_attestation: al-Umari, Masalik al-absar, from Ibn Amir Hajib's conversations with Musa in Cairo, 1324

sources.ref: al-Umari, Masalik al-absar, from Ibn Amir Hajib (Levition & Hopkins, Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History, 1981)
Ibn Khaldun on the Mali succession
Tarikh al-Sudan (17th c.) — the mansa sequence (no 'Abu Bakr II')

competing_hypotheses: The predecessor is conventionally named 'Abu Bakr II' ('the Voyager King') in popular accounts, but no such mansa appears in the Mali king lists — Musa's own account, as recorded by al-Umari, names no one, only 'the king who was my predecessor'
The account is Musa's story told to Ibn Amir Hajib in Cairo — a self-reported succession narrative, which serves Musa's legitimacy as well as describing an expedition
falsifiability: A contemporary West African or Arabic source describing the predecessor's reign and succession that contradicts the expedition story, or evidence that al-Umari invented the conversation

title: 'Mansa Musa, the richest man in history'
claim: Mansa Musa was the richest person in history — worth about $400 billion in modern money.
place: Niani, Mali Empire (capital)
grade_reason: The wealth was real and vast — Mali's gold flow is corroborated by the hajj accounts — but the RANKING has no evidence base: Celebrity Net Worth's $400B is a modern estimate, economists agree it is 'impossible to pin down to a number' (BBC 2019), and rival rich-lists put other rulers far higher.
earliest_attestation: The '$400 billion' figure originates with Celebrity Net Worth (2012), a popular-website estimate, not a published economic study

sources.ref: BBC News, 'Is Mansa Musa the richest man who ever lived?' (2019) — Celebrity Net Worth 2012 origin; Ware: 'almost impossible to get a sense of just how wealthy and powerful he truly was'; 'economic historians agree that his wealth is impossible to pin down to a number'
al-Umari via Ibn Amir Hajib — Musa borrowing gold and going into debt on the return journey (merchant Siraj al-Din)

competing_hypotheses: He was 'richer than anyone could describe' (Rudolph Ware, UC Berkeley, BBC 2019) — the honest superlative: real, enormous, but not ranked
Money.com/Celebrity Net Worth's own '10 richest' list puts Augustus at $4.6tn and Zhao Xu as 'incalculable' — the lists disagree with each other, which is the point

The wealth was the empire's, not a personal balance sheet — al-Umari reports Musa borrowing gold on the return journey and going into debt to Siraj al-Din; 'richest' depends on whether you count tribute flows as net worth
falsifiability: A single, consistently applied methodology that can rank historical sovereigns' wealth on one metric (share of world economy, gold flow, purchasing power) without the rankings contradicting each other

title: The Kebra Nagast as 14th-century compilation
claim: That the Kebra Nagast (The Glory of the Kings) — the Ge'ez national epic narrating the Queen of Sheba (Makeda), Solomon, their son Menelik I, and the migration of the Ark of the Covenant to Ethiopia — is a 14th-century CE compilation written to legitimize the restored Solomonic dynasty, not an eyewitness account from the 10th century BCE.
place: Axum (Aksum), Tigray Region, Ethiopia — composition circle
grade_reason: The 14th-century compilation date is multiply convergent: the colophon testimony, the dynastic-legitimation reading (Marcus: 'the Kebra Negest's prime goal was to legitimize the ascendancy of Emperor Yekuno Amlak'), Ullendorff's 1967 Schweich Lecture reading ('the repository of Ethiopian national and religious feelings'), and Munro-Hay's observation that no Ethiopian monarch claimed Solomonic descent before the 13th century. The book's power is real; its antiquity is not.
earliest_attestation: The colophon itself (Arabic Year of Mercy 409 = 1225 CE translation claim); the Solomonic dynasty's 1270 restoration it serves; the 1955 Ethiopian constitution, which wrote its genealogy in as law

sources.ref: Colophon testimony + Conti Rossini / Littmann / Cerulli — composition period 1314–1321/22 (via Wikipedia, citing the scholarship)
Harold Marcus, A History of Ethiopia, p. 17 — 'a pastiche of legends conflated early in the fourteenth century by six Tigrayan scribes' to legitimize Yekuno Amlak
Edward Ullendorff, 1967 Schweich Lectures — 'The Kebra Nagast is not merely a literary work, but it is the repository of Ethiopian national and religious feelings'
Stuart Munro-Hay — no record of Ethiopian monarchs claiming descent from Solomon before the 13th century
Columbia World Epics project / Sites.Google course unit — date c. 14th c. CE; written into the 1955 Ethiopian constitution as historical truth

competing_hypotheses: The colophon's story (Coptic original → Arabic 1225 → Ge'ez) — many scholars doubt a Coptic version ever existed; no evidence past the Arabic vorlage
Shahid (1976): sixth-century core honoring King Caleb's war with Yusuf — the text's last chapter is Caleb-era, but the colophon does not support a 6th-c. date for the whole
Leeman (2005): the pre-Ezra Israelite material (dietary law, Ark worship) suggests a much older centerpiece — a live minority position, carried as text-criticism, not settled
falsifiability: A securely dated pre-14th-century manuscript of the full narrative would reopen the question; none exists.

title: The Kebra Nagast as ancient eyewitness account (DEBUNKED)
claim: That the Kebra Nagast is an ancient text — an eyewitness-era account reaching back to the 10th century BCE, contemporary with Solomon and the Queen of Sheba — whose antiquity vouches for the Ark's migration to Ethiopia as recorded history.
place: Axum (Aksum), Tigray Region, Ethiopia — composition circle
grade_reason: The ancient-date reading dies on the book's own testimony: its colophon anchors the compilation to the 14th century (Conti Rossini/Littmann/Cerulli: 1314–1321/22; Marcus: six Tigrayan scribes, early 1300s), composed to legitimize Yekuno Amlak's 1270 restoration. Munro-Hay: no Ethiopian monarch claimed Solomonic descent before the 13th century. A text cannot be an eyewitness to events 2,300 years before it was written.
earliest_attestation: The manuscript tradition itself — in its existing form at least seven hundred years old, i.e., 14th c. — attests the claim's AGE as a tradition, not the claim's truth as history

sources.ref: Colophon testimony (Arabic Year of Mercy 409 / 1225 CE translation chain) — the book dates itself to the 13th–14th c.
Harold Marcus, A History of Ethiopia, p. 17 — six Tigrayan scribes, early 14th c., blending oral traditions, biblical texts, apocrypha, Jewish and Islamic commentaries
Stuart Munro-Hay — no pre-13th-century Solomonic-descent claims in the monarchic record

competing_hypotheses: The Coptic-original theory in the colophon — scholars doubt a Coptic version ever existed; no manuscript past the Arabic vorlage
Leeman (2005): a genuinely old centerpiece with pre-Ezra material — this keeps the TEXT's components debatable; it does not make the received book a 10th-c.-BCE document
falsifiability: This claim was falsified by the manuscript and colophon evidence itself: the book's own colophon places the compilation in the 13th–14th c., and no pre-14th-century witness to the received narrative exists.

title: Mansa Musa's Hajj of 1324
claim: In 1324, Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire (r. c. 1312–1337), traveled from his capital to Mecca with a vast caravan, distributing such quantities of gold in Cairo that the gold price there fell.
place: Cairo, Egypt
grade_reason: Multiple independent traditions attest the visit and the gold spending: al-Umari's near-contemporary account, Ibn Khaldun, the Sudanese chronicles, and a European map drawn within 50 years depicting the king from the story.
earliest_attestation: Shihab al-Umari, Masalik al-absar, written from the account of Ibn Amir Hajib (the Cairo district governor who met Musa), within decades of the visit

sources.ref: al-Umari, Masalik al-absar (via Ibn Amir Hajib; Levition & Hopkins, Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History, 1981, pp. 269-273)
Ibn Khaldun, Kitab al-Ibar
al-Maqrizi on the gold-price depression in Cairo
Tarikh al-Sudan (17th c., from earlier Timbuktu scholarship)
Catalan Atlas, 1375 (Bibliothèque nationale de France) — 'Rex Melli' enthroned with gold orb and sceptre

competing_hypotheses: The caravan-size figures (60,000 people, 80 camels, 12,000 slaves, 21,000 kg gold in modern retellings; BBC 'You're Dead to Me' 2026) vary between accounts and are best read as tradition figures, not a manifest
The gold-price depression is reported by the Arabic sources; modern economists treat its scale and duration ('12 years' in popular retellings) as attested narrative, not a measured series
falsifiability: A contemporary Mamluk administrative or market record contradicting the visit, or proof that al-Umari's account fabricates the meeting with Ibn Amir Hajib

title: The Black Death (1347–1352): Yersinia pestis and the 30–50% toll
claim: The Black Death pandemic of 1347–1352 — the first and most lethal wave of the second plague pandemic — was caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis (the bubonic-plague pathogen), entered the Mediterranean in 1347 on trade ships from the Black Sea, and killed an estimated 30–50% of Europe's population (~25–30 million people; the literature ranges 25–60% depending on region).
place: Lake Issyk-Kul, Chu Valley, Kyrgyzstan (origin of the source strain, Spyrou et al. 2022) — spread to all of Europe 1347–1352
grade_reason: Convergent independent lines: dozens of contemporary chronicles across independent traditions (Latin, Byzantine, Arabic, Russian) agree on timing, symptoms (buboes), and catastrophic mortality; demography corroborates the 30–50% range; ancient DNA from plague-pit victims (East Smithfield; Issyk-Kul) confirms Y. pestis as the pathogen; Spyrou et al. 2022 (Nature) placed the source strain's diversification node at Issyk-Kul 1338. Single chroniclers' absolute numbers stay CLAIMED; the cause and the range are CORROBORATED.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary chronicles across Europe and the Near East (1347+); Boccaccio's Decameron preface; London burial ledgers; East Smithfield cemetery (consecrated 1348–50). Pathogen attestation: Haensch et al. 2010 (PLOS Pathogens); Bos et al. 2011 (Nature).

sources.ref: Haensch, S. et al. (2010) 'Distinct clones of Yersinia pestis caused the Black Death', PLoS Pathogens 6, e1001134 — Y. pestis DNA from Black Death victims, including the East Smithfield cemetery, London; the study that ended the not-plague debate

Bos, K. et al. (2011) 'A draft genome of Yersinia pestis from victims of the Black Death', Nature 480, 506–509 — complete medieval Y. pestis genome; confirmed the ancient strain as direct ancestor of modern plague lineages

Spyrou, M. et al. (2022) 'The source of the Black Death in fourteenth-century central Eurasia', Nature 606, 718–724 — ancient Y. pestis DNA from teeth of 1338–39 Issyk-Kul cemetery victims (Chu Valley, Kyrgyzstan); the strain sits at the node of the Black Death diversification event — the pandemic's origin placed in Central Asia
Schuenemann, V. J. et al. (2011) 'Targeted enrichment of ancient pathogens yielding the pPCP1 plasmid of Yersinia pestis from victims of the Black Death', PNAS 108, E746–E752
Bramanti, B. & Hänsch, S. (2013) — Aschheim, Bavaria cemetery aDNA confirmed Y. pestis as the agent of the first (Justinianic) pandemic, PLOS Pathogens
Benedictow, O. J. (2004) The Black Death 1346–1353: The Complete History (Boydell) — demographic synthesis
Cowal, L. et al. (2008) The Black Death Cemetery, East Smithfield, London (Museum of London Archaeology Service)

competing_hypotheses: Anthrax as the cause (Graham Twigg, 1984) — refuted by aDNA
Ebola-like/viral hemorrhagic fever as the cause (S. Scott & C. Duncan, Biology of Plagues, 2001, Cambridge UP) — refuted by aDNA
Samuel Cohn's non-Yersinia arguments (2003) — symptom-transmission mismatches; answered by the ancient genomes
Origin debates: the medieval source region was unknown until 2022 (competing hypotheses: China, Central Asia, near the Black Sea documentation point)

Death-toll range disputes: regional studies give 25–60%; Benedictow's upper-range figures vs. more conservative demographic reconstructions (Slavin's English parish work suggests ~40–60% in England; other regions lower)
falsifiability: Recovery of pre-1347 European plague-pit remains bearing a non-Yersinia pathogen with complete genomes would overturn the cause; a coherent demographic record showing <10% European mortality would overturn the toll range.

title: The forty days that gave the world 'quarantine'
claim: The word 'quarantine' comes from the Venetian Republic's forty-day (quaranta giorni) isolation of suspect ships.
place: Lazzaretto Nuovo, Venetian Lagoon
grade_reason: The etymology is solidly attested across independent secondary sources: Italian quarantena = forty days; the Venice sequence (1348 thirty-day hold → 1403 forty-day extension → 1423 Lazzaretto Vecchio → 1468 institutional decree at the Lazzaretto Nuovo) is carried consistently (Global Campus of Human Rights repository paper; Proto Magazine's plague timeline; italyheaven.co.uk's Lazzaretto Nuovo history). Held below VERIFIED for two honest reasons: (1) secondary sources disagree on the first-hold year (1348 vs 1370), and (2) the 'Venice invented quarantine' superlative fails — Ragusa legislated first in 1377. What Venice verifiably gave the world is the word, the forty-day standard, and the lazaretto as an institution — the teze cargo-sanitization sheds, the fumigation with juniper and rosemary, the health passes. The Ragusan priority is carried as a competing hypothesis, not hidden.
earliest_attestation: Venetian Senate decrees: the 1348 hold, the 1403 extension to forty days, the 1423 creation of the Lazzaretto Vecchio on Santa Maria di Nazareth ('Nazaretum' — the name that became 'Lazzaretto'), the 1468 decree for the Lazzaretto Nuovo; Benedetto Bordone's 1528 Isolario showing both lazzaretti

sources.ref: Global Campus of Human Rights repository, 'Pandemic Management During the Republic of Venice' — 1423 Senate creation of the hospital on Santa Maria di Nazareth ('Nazaretum' → 'Lazzaretto'); Lazzaretto Vecchio vs Lazzaretto Nuovo; the 1468 decree institutionalizing quarantine ('from quarantena, meaning 40 days'); suspect ships held at the Lazzaretto Nuovo pending clearance; teze cargo-sanitization sheds; fumigation with juniper and rosemary

Proto Magazine, 'From the Black Death to SARS' — 1348: Venice 'introduces one of the earliest formal systems of quarantine, requiring ships, goods and people to wait 40 (quaranta, in Italian) days'; 1423: 'Rise of Lazarettos'; notes the miasma theory behind the practice and the flea-die-off side effect

italyheaven.co.uk, 'Lazzarettto Nuovo: Venice Island Excursions' — 'the word quarantine actually comes from the Italian for forty (days, at one time the proscribed duration of isolation)'; suspect ships and crews held for a disease-check period; the ill removed to Lazzaretto Vecchio

Public Radio East / NPR, 'A History Of Quarantines, From Bubonic Plague To Typhoid Mary' — Venice's 40-day waiting period as quarrantinario 'from the Italian word for 40'; notes the isolation later shrank to trentinario (30 days) while the original name stuck

competing_hypotheses: The Ragusa-first reading: the Republic of Ragusa (Dubrovnik) enacted the first formal quarantine law in 1377 — a thirty-day (trentino) isolation — so the first legislation is Ragusan while the word and the institutional model are Venetian
The biblical-forty reading: the forty days echoes Lent, the Flood, the desert — the number's cultural resonance helped it stick, though the Venetian decrees cite plague practice, not scripture
falsifiability: Venetian archival research showing the forty-day period was never legislated before 1468, or that the word derives from a different root, would move the grade. A Ragusan document using 'quarantena' before 1403 would hand the word's origin to Dubrovnik.

title: Jikji (1377) — the oldest extant book printed with movable metal type
claim: The Korean Buddhist anthology Jikji, printed in 1377 at Heungdeoksa temple in Cheongju, is the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type — 78 years before Gutenberg's Bible.
place: Cheongju, Korea (Heungdeoksa temple site); volume held in Paris
grade_reason: The object exists, is dated by its own printed colophon to 1377, is confirmed as movable-metal-type printing, and its status is certified by UNESCO's Memory of the World listing.
earliest_attestation: The printed colophon of the metal-type edition (July 1377)

sources.ref: Jikji (Baegun hwasang chorok buljo jikji simche yojeol), metal-type edition, 1377 — 38 of 41 volumes extant, held by the Bibliothèque nationale de France (Richelieu Oriental)
UNESCO Memory of the World Register, 2001 — inscription of Jikji as the oldest extant book printed with movable metal type

Korean movable metal type tradition: Goryeo-era cast bronze type of the 13th century, documented in Korean printing histories (the Wang Zhen 1313 account of wooden type; Hua Sui's bronze type 1490 for the Chinese continuation)
Heritage (2023), vol. 3, pp. 2559-2581 — ink-tone analysis identifying the Gongin version of the 'Song of Enlightenment' (September 1239 imprint) as metal-type printing, 138 years before the Jikji

competing_hypotheses: A wood-type edition of Jikji printed in the same year survives more completely — the metal-type edition's priority is stated in its colophon and the printing technology is verifiable from the type marks
The 1377 date depends on the reign-year conversion (King U, 10th year) — standard and uncontested in Korean historiography

The 2023 'Gongin-version Song of Enlightenment' claim (Heritage 2023, vol. 3, pp. 2559-2581): a Korean treasure designated 2012, imprint-dated September 1239, argued via ink-tone analysis to be metal-type — if confirmed as the oldest extant metal-type book, 'oldest extant' moves from the Jikji; the Jikji keeps UNESCO's consensus position pending resolution
falsifiability: An authenticated earlier movable-metal-type printed book would take the title; proof the colophon was added later would reopen the dating

title: The Mamluk 52-Card Pack — Europe's Deck Ancestor
claim: The European 52-card pack descends from the Islamic world's Mamluk cards: a 52-card deck in four suits (cups, coins, swords, polo sticks) with ten pip cards and three court cards — malik (king), na'ib malik (viceroy), thani na'ib (second viceroy) — the 'na'ib' being the probable origin of the early Italian word naibi for playing cards.
place: Istanbul, Türkiye (Topkapi Palace)
grade_reason: The Topkapi fragments exist and match the European 52-card structure point for point — four suits, ten pips, three courts with na'ib nomenclature — and the 1377 European references describe the same template; held below VERIFIED because fragment dating varies across cataloguers and the transmission route is reconstructed, not documented.
earliest_attestation: John of Rheinfelden, 'De moribus et disciplina humanae conversationis id est ludus cartularum' (Basel, 1377) — the oldest surviving detailed European description; Signoria of Florence, 23 March 1377

sources.ref: Topkapi Palace Museum, Mamluk 'muluk wa-nuwwab' card fragments (c. 1400, catalogued Depaulis)
John of Rheinfelden, De moribus et disciplina humanae conversationis (Basel, 1377)
L. A. Smith, 'The Playing Cards of the Mamluks' (1939); Thierry Depaulis, Mamluk cards research (2013)
Simon Wintle, Early History of Playing Cards & Timeline (1996) — na'ib→naibi note

competing_hypotheses: Direct Chinese-to-Europe transmission via the Silk Road/Mongol intermediaries without the Mamluk intermediary (minority; the suit/court structure points to the Mamluk form)
Independent European invention in the 14th century (no contemporary evidence for it; every structural element tracks eastward)
Persian ganjifa as the nearer ancestor (possible intermediate; the evidence is thinner than for the Mamluk form)
falsifiability: A complete European 52-card pack predating the Mamluk fragments, or proof the Topkapi cards are modern forgeries

title: The 1378 iconoclast: al-Maqrizi's account of the Sphinx's nose
claim: The Great Sphinx's nose was chiseled off in 1378 CE by Muhammad Sa'im al-Dahr, a Sufi iconoclast who was angered by local villagers making offerings to the Sphinx; he was seized and killed by the same villagers after the act.
place: Great Sphinx of Giza, Giza Plateau, Egypt
grade_reason: Single-source attestation: one medieval historian, writing decades after the event, is the entire documentary base. That is the textbook definition of CLAIMED — attested but single-source. Lehner's competing material reading keeps the grade honest and low.
earliest_attestation: al-Maqrizi (Taqi al-Din Ahmad ibn Ali al-Maqrizi, d. 1442), 15th-century Egyptian historian — the only near-source for the 1378 episode, writing roughly 50 years after the alleged event.

sources.ref: al-Maqrizi (d. 1442), 'al-Khitat' / historical writings — the 1378 account of Muhammad Sa'im al-Dahr defacing the Sphinx and being killed by villagers (as summarized in the modern historiography)

Smithsonian Journeys, Sarah Erdman (Sept 2022) — 'The medieval Egyptian historian al-Maqrizi wrote that the nose was actually destroyed by a 14th-century Sufi dervish named Muhammad Sa'im al-Dahr... While scholars debate the theory...'
Mark Lehner's Sphinx geological survey — chisel-mark analysis suggesting the nose may have been removed between the 3rd and 10th century (competing material reading, via the modern summaries)

competing_hypotheses: Lehner's earlier date: archaeologist Mark Lehner's study of the chisel marks suggests the nose may have been removed as early as the 3rd to 10th century CE — an expert material reading against the textual account
The Napoleonic cannon story: DEBUNKED in evt-sphinx-nose-napoleon-001 — kept here only so the record shows what it displaced
Natural weathering and stone failure: the Sphinx's soft middle strata (the body's 'melting' layers) make mechanical damage easy — but the tool marks on the face point to human hands, not weather
falsifiability: An earlier dated image of the Sphinx without its nose (pre-1378) would falsify the 1378 attribution; so would any 14th-century document contradicting al-Maqrizi. A second independent textual witness would move the grade up; none is known.

title: The Chinese bristle toothbrush (15th century, conventionally)
claim: A toothbrush with hog bristles set into a bone or bamboo handle was in use in China by the 15th century; European travelers carried the design west in the 17th century.
place: China (Ming context, conventionally)
grade_reason: The design tradition is multiply described and its westward transmission documented; the precise century wanders across sources, so VERIFIED stays parked on the dating.
earliest_attestation: Chinese writings mentioning bristle brushes, conventionally 13th–15th century; European adoption of hog/horse-hair brushes in the 17th century.

sources.ref: Dr. Scott Swank, National Museum of Dentistry, via HowStuffWorks: 'recorded in China circa 1500 — straight bamboo handles pierced with trimmed hog bristles set at a right angle to the brush'
Dr. Scott Swank, National Museum of Dentistry (Living on Earth, 2002): 'beginning about 1400 years ago, people in China made toothbrush bristles by plucking the neck hairs of the Siberian wild boar'
Dental-history convention: 15th-century China, bone/bamboo handles, hog's-neck bristles; European adaptation with horsehair/feathers (CK Dental; Sure Dental)

competing_hypotheses: The bristle brush is older (Tang 7th c. or 600–900 tellings) and the 15th-century date reflects when the design reached Europe's notice, not its invention
The brush is younger than convention and the 15th-century date is itself a rounded inheritance
falsifiability: A securely dated pre-1400 Chinese bristle brush would move the date earlier; proof that no bristle brush predates the European 17th-century specimens would collapse the Chinese priority.

title: The treasure ships: '44 zhang' (400-foot) claim
claim: Zheng He's largest 'treasure ships' (baochuan) were 44.4 zhang long and 18 zhang wide — roughly 400+ feet, with nine masts — the largest wooden ships ever built.
place: Nanjing, China (Longjiang treasure-shipyard site; 1962 rudder-post find)
grade_reason: Single late literary source (a 1597 novel) for the exact figure; no excavated hull, no contemporary shipyard dimension sheet; the archaeological evidence supports 'very large' but not the specific 44-zhang number. Attested once, by fiction, for a number everyone quotes as fact.
earliest_attestation: Luo Maodeng, Xiyang ji (Romance of the Western Ocean), 1597 — a historical novel; historicity of the ship measurements disputed

sources.ref: Luo Maodeng, Xiyang ji (1597) — the 44 × 18 zhang figure; disputed historicity
Ma Huan, Yingya shenglan (c. 1451) — records the large treasure ships of the fourth voyage; the earliest documentation of the type
1962 Nanjing rudder-post find: 36-foot timber steering post, Ming-era wood, sized for a ship of 540–600 feet — suggestive, not decisive
2005 broken stone tablet: 2,000-liao and 1,500-liao sea ships recorded for the early voyages (via web.archive.org travel-silkroad summary)
Xu Gongsheng's construal: large-size treasure ships as imperial ceremonial vessels; main ship type the 2,000-liao sea ship

competing_hypotheses: The '44 zhang' figure comes from Luo Maodeng's Xiyang ji, a late-Ming historical NOVEL, not a shipyard record — its historicity on measurements is disputed among scholars (Shi Ping, Chinese Historical Review)

The 2005 broken stone tablet at Longjiang records the fleet's main sea ships as 2,000-liao and 1,500-liao vessels — much smaller than the 44-zhang imperial treasure ships; Xu Gongsheng's construal: the giant 44-zhang ships were a small number of imperial ceremonial vessels, and Ma Huan's dimensions cover those few
The moderate reconstruction: ~70 m (230 ft) for the largest type — still far larger than any contemporary European ship, and still unmatched as a fleet
falsifiability: An excavated baochuan hull with measurable dimensions, or a shipyard record contemporaneous with the voyages, would settle it either way; the 1962 Nanjing rudder-post timber (36-ft steering post, Ming-era wood) is suggestive of very large ships but does not verify the 44-zhang figure

title: Zheng He's seven treasure voyages (1405–1433)
claim: Between 1405 and 1433 the Ming court dispatched seven large maritime expeditions under the eunuch admiral Zheng He, sailing from Nanjing through Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean to Calicut (India), Hormuz and the Persian Gulf, the Red Sea, and the east coast of Africa (Malindi) — the largest wooden fleets assembled before the industrial age, on tribute-diplomacy and trade missions.
place: Nanjing, China (Longjiang shipyard, departure point)
grade_reason: Multiply and independently attested in contemporary primary sources: the official Ming Veritable Records, three first-person crew accounts (Ma Huan sailed on four voyages, Fei Xin on three), and contemporary stone inscriptions in China and Sri Lanka.
earliest_attestation: Ming Veritable Records (Ming shilu) entries for the reigns of Yongle and Xuande; Liuhe (Longjiang) inscription 1407; Galle (Sri Lanka) trilingual inscription 1411

sources.ref: Ming shilu (Veritable Records of the Ming Dynasty) — official court record of the expeditions
Ma Huan, Yingya shenglan (The Overall Survey of the Ocean's Shores), c. 1451 — first-person account of voyages 4–7; first text to record the treasure ships and their dimensions
Fei Xin, Xingcha shenglan (c. 1436) — crew member's account
Liuhe/Longjiang inscription, Nanjing, 1407; Changle inscription 1431; Galle trilingual inscription (Chinese, Tamil, Persian), Sri Lanka, 1411
Columbia University, Asia for Educators: The Ming Voyages (http://afe.easia.columbia.edu/special/china_1000ce_mingvoyages.htm)

competing_hypotheses: The fleet-size and crew figures (e.g. 317 ships, 27,870 men for the first voyage) come largely from the Ming shi, compiled centuries later — the scale is broadly corroborated but exact numbers are less secure than the voyages themselves
On motive: pure tribute-diplomacy vs. commercial/trade mission vs. imperial prestige theater — the documentary record supports tribute and trade together; the exact mix is debated
falsifiability: A contemporary Ming document or inscription denying the expeditions occurred, or proof that the Liuhe, Changle, and Galle inscriptions are modern forgeries — none exists

title: Machu Picchu
claim: An Inca settlement on a mountain ridge at ~2,430 m above the Urubamba River, built c. 1420-1450 and occupied until the 1530s; the majority scholarly reading (Rowe; Burger) is that it was a royal estate of the Inca ruler Pachacuti (reigned c. 1438-1471), housing some 500-750 people including Pachacuti's lineage, religious specialists, and skilled yanacona artisans. The Spanish never found or plundered it.
place: Machu Picchu ridge, Urubamba Province, Peru
grade_reason: The site is an extensively documented archaeological fact: standing masonry, surveyed terraces, excavated burials with radiocarbon dates, and a century of continuous scholarship.
earliest_attestation: The site itself (standing Inca masonry); no pre-1911 Inca reference to it survives, and the conquistadors' documents note a place called 'Piccho' without record of a visit.

sources.ref: Burger et al. 2021, AMS radiocarbon study of 26 individuals from the site's cemeteries (Antiquity)
John Howland Rowe — the Pachacuti-estate attribution
Richard L. Burger & Lucy C. Salazar — the estate reading's principal modern defenders
UNESCO World Heritage inscription, 1983
Gonzales & Bauer 2021, 'The Ancient Inca Town Named Huayna Picchu' (Ñawpa Pacha, Journal of the Institute of Andean Studies) — on the site's pre-Bingham name

competing_hypotheses: The Pachacuti royal-estate reading (Rowe; Burger & Salazar) — the majority position, grounded in the site's small elite population, royal masonry, and chronology
The sacred/ritual-center reading — the site's position relative to sacred landscape features and astronomical alignments (Reinhard) is consistent with estate-plus-sanctuary function
The purpose is ultimately undocumented — no Inca source names the site's function, and 'estate' remains an inference from architecture and demographics, not a text
falsifiability: A dated Inca or colonial document naming the site and contradicting the estate reading, or AMS dates placing occupation outside the imperial period

title: Gutenberg's integrated printing system
claim: In Mainz in the 1440s-1450s, Johannes Gutenberg built the first integrated European printing system: reusable metal type cast in a hand mold, a suitable metal alloy, oil-based ink, and an adapted screw press — and with it produced the 42-line Bible (completed late 1455).
place: Mainz, Electorate of Mainz
grade_reason: The system is demonstrated by its surviving products and the near-contemporary paper trail: the 42-line Bible (c. 1454-1455; ~180 copies, over 40 substantially complete surviving in BnF, British Library, Library of Congress), the hand-mold method of casting uniform interchangeable type, the oil-based ink that adhered to metal, and the screw-press adaptation of wine/olive presses (Lehmann-Haupt via Britannica; Clemson STS synthesis; LoC). Gutenberg's goldsmith training explains the alloy and mold; the epochal act was the combination into a practical manufacturing process — method 'virtually unchanged for six centuries' until computer typesetting. Held at CORROBORATED rather than VERIFIED because Gutenberg's own workshop records are lost and the 1439 experiments are known only through later legal documents.
earliest_attestation: The products themselves — the 42-line Bible and the surviving Mainz fragments — plus the 1455 legal/financial record (the Fust dispute) and Piccolomini's March 1455 letter describing printed Bible quires at Frankfurt.

sources.ref: Library of Congress, 'The Gutenberg Bible' — printing completed late 1455 at Mainz; Gutenberg 'generally credited for inventing the process of making uniform and interchangeable metal types and for solving the many problems of finding the right materials and methods for printing'; ~180 copies

Clemson Open Textbook (STS), 'The First Moveable Type Printing Press' — hand mold for mass casting, metal alloy, oil-based ink adhering to metal, screw press adapted from wine presses; 42-line Bible by 1455 as the proof of the manufacturing process

Lehmann-Haupt, H.E. (1995), 'Johannes Gutenberg', Encyclopaedia Britannica 15th ed. (via Maine lecture notes) — the mould for casting movable type in large numbers, the new metal alloy, the press adapted from wine presses, the oil-based ink

competing_hypotheses: New research suggests standardized movable type in Europe was 'a more complex evolutionary process spread over multiple locations' (per the Wikipedia synthesis) — the system may have had co-inventors we cannot name

Gutenberg's Bible may not have been his first printed work: indulgences printed as early as 1452 (at Cusa's request; none survive) precede it — the Bible is the first major work, not necessarily the first impression
falsifiability: A contemporary document showing the 42-line Bible printed by another hand, or Gutenberg's type shown to be wood-carved rather than cast, would downgrade the system claim.

title: Valla's 1440 proof: the philologist who broke the Donation
claim: In 1439-1440 Lorenzo Valla, in his Declamatio 'De falso credita et ementita Constantini donatione' (dedicated to Alfonso V of Naples), proved by philological analysis that the Constitutum Constantini could not have been written in the 4th century: the Latin carries vocabulary impossible for a 4th-century imperial chancery, and the document's own internal dating is self-contradictory.
place: Naples (Valla wrote in the service of Alfonso V of Aragon)
grade_reason: The treatise survives in manuscript and print; its method and conclusion are independently confirmed by Cusa's prior doubt, Pecock's independent confirmation, the Catholic Encyclopedia 1913, the 1911 Britannica.
earliest_attestation: The treatise itself, surviving in manuscript with its dedication to Alfonso V of Naples; first print 1518 (Mainz).

sources.ref: Lorenzo Valla, De falso credita et ementita Constantini donatione declamatio (1439-1440; first printed Mainz, 1518) — the declamatio itself

Fiveable AP Euro, 'Lorenzo Valla': 'proved the Donation of Constantine was a medieval forgery, not a 4th-century document'; philology as the dating-and-authenticating method; Valla's work challenged the Church's institutional power; written while employed by King Alfonso of Naples

The AP-exam standard examples of Valla's linguistic arguments: the medieval word *banna* where a Roman would write *vexillum*; the diadem described as gold and jewels when a 4th-century diadem was made of cloth (per the QuestionAI analysis of Valla's arguments)

competing_hypotheses: The priority question: Nicholas of Cusa had called it apocryphal earlier (De concordantia catholica, 1433) and Reginald Pecock reached the same conclusion independently (1450-57) — Valla's is the first *demonstration*, not the first doubt
Valla's enemies read the treatise as an anti-papal attack; modern scholarship reads it as philology — the proof stands regardless of his patron's (Alfonso's) political interests
falsifiability: A demonstration that Valla's linguistic data is wrong — i.e., that the cited anachronistic usages were genuinely current in 4th-century imperial Latin — would weaken it; 586 years of scholarship have produced none, and the consensus has only hardened.

title: "Gutenberg invented printing"
claim: Johannes Gutenberg of Mainz invented printing — the first person in the world to develop a method of printing text.
place: Mainz (Holy Roman Empire)
grade_reason: The dated Chinese woodblock print of 868 CE and the Korean movable-metal-type book of 1377 each predate Mainz by centuries; the claim 'first in the world' is disproven by the objects themselves.
earliest_attestation: The Mainz workshop's printed works and the court record of the 1455 Fust v. Gutenberg suit (the invention's transmission-era documentation)

sources.ref: Gutenberg Bible (42-line Bible), Mainz, 1454–55 — ~180 copies printed, ~49 extant; the masterpiece of the Mainz workshop
The Diamond Sutra (868 CE) and Bi Sheng's movable type (1041–48 CE) — the prior art, carried in evt-diamond-sutra-001 and evt-bi-sheng-movable-type-001

Fiveable AP European History study guide, unit 1.4 — lists 'Gutenberg invented printing itself' as a common misconception: 'Printing existed earlier, including in China. Gutenberg's contribution in Europe was a fast, practical movable-type press in the 1450s.'

competing_hypotheses: The fair version of the claim: Gutenberg's achievement was the first practical EUROPEAN movable-metal-type press with oil-based ink and a press mechanism that made mass production economical — a genuine world-historical innovation, just not the invention of printing
Whether any printing technique traveled from China to Europe before Mainz (SPECULATION — no evidence of the transmission route; Gutenberg's system is treated as an independent development)
falsifiability: Authentication of a printed book earlier than the Diamond Sutra would not save the claim; only evidence that the Chinese dates are all wrong could revive it

title: The Tarot as a 15th-Century Milanese Game
claim: The tarot deck began as a 15th-century northern-Italian aristocratic card game (tarocchi) — 78 cards: 56 suit cards plus 22 trump cards — documented by surviving hand-painted luxury decks made for the Milanese court.
place: Milan, Italy
grade_reason: Multiple surviving hand-painted decks from the Milanese court (Morgan, Carrara, Colleoni), documented attributions (Bembo/Zavattari workshop), and Dummett's (1980) structural history converge; held below VERIFIED because the single inventor is unproven.
earliest_attestation: Visconti-Sforza tarocchi cards — the Pierpont Morgan Library set (MS M.630.1-35, 35 cards, Milan c. 1450–1480) plus Accademia Carrara and Casa Colleoni survivors

sources.ref: Morgan Library & Museum, Visconti-Sforza Tarot Cards (MS M.630.1-35), Milan c. 1450–1480
Michael Dummett, The Game of Tarot (1980); The Visconti-Sforza Tarot Cards (1986)
Kit Stone, 'Tarot in Late Enlightenment France' (Oct 2024) — tarot's game history before the occult era

competing_hypotheses: Bologna rather than Milan as the city of origin (both northern-Italian aristocratic circles; Milan has the surviving decks)
Duke Filippo Maria Visconti of Milan as the individual inventor (c. 1441, Kit Stone 2024 — plausible but unproven; attribution, not evidence)
The tarot as a natural evolution of existing 14th-century trick-taking games with an added permanent trump series (Dummett's structural account)
falsifiability: Dated tarot artifacts or documents older than the 1430s, or proof the Visconti-Sforza decks are later forgeries

title: The First Documented Coffee Drinking — Yemeni Sufi monasteries, 15th century
claim: Coffee as a brewed drink is first documented in the Sufi monasteries of Yemen in the mid-15th century; the earliest named adopter is Sheikh Jamal al-Din al-Dhabhani, mufti of Aden (d. 1470), reported as the first to take up the drink c. 1454.
place: Aden, Yemen
grade_reason: Multiple independent attestations of 15th-c. Yemeni Sufi coffee drinking; held below VERIFIED because the earliest narrative compiler (al-Jaziri, 1587) writes a century after the fact.
earliest_attestation: Abd al-Qadir al-Jaziri, Umdat al-safwa fi hill al-qahwa (1587) — the earliest surviving compilation tracing coffee's history and legal controversies, reporting the al-Dhabhani adoption c. 1454 and the spread from Yemen northward to Mecca, Medina, Cairo, Damascus, Baghdad, and Constantinople.

sources.ref: Abd al-Qadir al-Jaziri, Umdat al-safwa fi hill al-qahwa (1587) — reports al-Dhabhani, mufti of Aden (d. 1470), as the first adopter of coffee c. 1454, noting its properties (drove away fatigue and lethargy)
Sufi monastery use in 15th-c. Yemen — well established by the late 15th century (general scholarly consensus; no confirmed evidence of coffee as a drink before the 15th century)
2020 Arabica genetic-diversity study — confirms the Yemeni cultivation story: the vast majority of the world's Arabica originates from early Yemeni cultivated varieties

competing_hypotheses: Turkish sources (e.g. Brisel's Kahvaler Kitab) push discovery back to 1258 — circumstantial ceramic/ewer evidence cited, not documentary
The 10th-c. 'bunchum' of al-Razi is sometimes claimed as coffee — later accounts say it was made from a root, not coffee beans
Ethiopian chewing of raw coffee berries predates brewing — a practice, not the drink
falsifiability: A dated, authenticated pre-1450 document describing brewed coffee would push the date back and refine this record; genetic/archaeological evidence of pre-Yemeni brewing would do the same

title: Flavio Gioja 'invented the compass at Amalfi in 1302' — the inventor who was a misplaced comma (legend killed at the Latin)
claim: That Flavio Gioja (Gioia) of Amalfi invented the magnetic compass in 1302 — the schoolbook 'inventor' of the mariner's compass. The claim is an attribution legend built on a 16th-century Latin misreading; the person most likely never existed.
place: Amalfi, Italy — the attributed invention place (the statue stands there)
grade_reason: The attribution chain is fully documented and self-destroying: (1) Flavius Blondus (~1450) wrote only that use of the magnet was known at Amalfi, origin unknown; (2) Baptista Pio (1511) repeated it 'as related by Flavius' ('a Flavio dicitur' — 'as Flavius says'); (3) Lilio Gyraldus (1540) misread the phrase as 'by a certain Flavius'; (4) the 17th century solidified the misreading into an inventor named 'Flavio Gioja' and an invention date of 1302 (Amir Aczel, The Riddle of the Compass, 2001: the whole riddle turns on 'the correct interpretation of a single Latin phrase'; multiple sources note he 'may have never existed'). Independent kill: two surviving European compass descriptions predate 1302 anyway — Neckam ~1190 (VERIFIED, evt-compass-europe-neckam-1190-001) and Petrus Peregrinus's Epistola de magnete (1269) — so even a real Gioja could not be the inventor. Fenced: Amalfi's genuine early *use* of the floating magnet (1911 Britannica) survives the grade; it is the invention and the person that die.
earliest_attestation: Flavius Blondus, Italia illustrata (~1450) — which says only that the magnet's use was known at Amalfi, origin unknown.

sources.ref: Wikipedia 'Flavio Gioja': 'Ioannes Gira Amalphensis' (c. 1300-?); 'It is also likely that Flavio Gioja did not exist at all'; the name 'Flavio' is a translation error (probably Giovanni); the misplaced-comma story (Pio 1511: 'In Amalfi... the use of the magnet was invented, according to Flavio' misread as 'invented by Flavio')

1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Compass': the Gioja legend genealogy — Flavius Blondus (1450) wrote only that use of the magnet was known at Amalfi, origin unknown; Baptista Pio (1511) repeated it 'as related by Flavius'; Lilio Gyraldus (1540) misunderstood 'a Flavio dicitur' as 'by a certain Flavius'; the legend took shape in the 17th century as invention in 1302 by 'Flavio Gioja of Amalfi'; Italian sailors used the floating magnet 'probably introduced... by traders belonging to the port of Amalfi'

Amir Aczel, The Riddle of the Compass (2001) (review via Science News/thefreelibrary.com): the Flavio Gioia of 1302 'may have never existed,' with the riddle turning on 'the correct interpretation of a single Latin phrase' in a 16th-c commentary on Lucretius

Naples Life, Death & Miracle — Amalfi page: 'Flavio Gioia, in spite of the nice statue in Amalfi (photo), most likely never existed'; confusion from Flavio Biondo (1392-1463) reporting the compass as an Amalfitan invention, passed on as 'a Flavio dicitur'; Scipione Mazzella (~1600) located him in Gioia, Puglia

competing_hypotheses: The statue line: Amalfi has a statue of 'Flavio Gioia' and Italian schoolbooks long repeated the invention date 1302. The statue commemorates the legend, not the document — treated as belief-phenomenon, not evidence.

The genuine-Amalfitan line: the 1911 Britannica notes Italian sailors — 'probably introduced... by traders belonging to the port of Amalfi' — used the floating magnet early. Amalfi's real compass connection is early *use*, not invention, and not by a documented person named Flavio.
falsifiability: A contemporary (c. 1300) document naming a Flavio Gioja of Amalfi as compass inventor would revive the claim; five centuries of scholarship have produced none.

title: The 'millions burned as witches' — the nine-million figure
claim: Millions of people were executed as witches during the Middle Ages, primarily by the medieval Inquisition — the popular "millions burned as witches" figure (often nine million).
place: Europe (witch-hunt era 1450-1750); myth's birthplace: 19th-century Germany and the United States
grade_reason: Three independent kills: (1) SCALE — the scholarly estimates (Levack: ~90,000 prosecutions, ~45,000 executions 1450-1750; Oxford Handbook: ~100,000 tried, ~60,000 executed) converge on tens of thousands, two orders of magnitude below "millions." (2) ERA — the hunts peak 1560-1630, early modern and largely secular/Protestant courts (Germany, Switzerland, Scotland, England), not the Middle Ages. (3) INSTITUTION — the medieval Inquisition targeted heretics, not witches: Canon Episcopi (c. 906, carried in Gratian's Decretum) declared belief in night-flight witchcraft a delusion; inquisitorial courts were often the skeptics (Spain's 1614 reversal ended witch-burnings).
earliest_attestation: Matilda Joslyn Gage, Woman, Church and State (1893) — the earliest documented mass-circulation of the "nine million" figure (repeated from German authors per the scholarly reception history); the millions figure has no earlier counting basis.

sources.ref: Brian P. Levack, The Witch-Hunt in Early Modern Europe (2006): ~90,000 prosecutions, ~45,000 executions across Europe 1450-1750
Oxford Handbook of Witchcraft in Early Modern Europe and Colonial America (Levack ed.): ~100,000 tried, ~60,000 executed
Wikipedia, 'Feminist interpretations of witch trials in the early modern period': Gage (1893) repeated the erroneous nine-million figure from German authors

competing_hypotheses: The honest count debate: Levack (2006): ~90,000 prosecutions, ~45,000 executions across Europe 1450-1750; Oxford Handbook of Witchcraft: ~100,000 tried, ~60,000 executed; outlier high estimates reach ~100,000 executions. All converge on the tens-of-thousands order of magnitude — two orders below "millions".

The nine-million transmission chain: Gage's Woman, Church and State (1893) repeated the figure from German authors (per the documented reception history); one account traces the root to Gottfried Christian Voigt's 1784 extrapolation from a single badly-hit German town. The exact first link is not fully settled — but every proposed origin is an extrapolation, not a count.

The Salem-adjacent inflation mechanism: witch-hunt mythology absorbed the medieval Inquisition and the early-modern secular hunts into one undifferentiated "burning times," then multiplied the era's worst single-year tolls across centuries.
falsifiability: Contemporary court records showing executions in the hundreds-of-thousands per decade, sustained across the hunt era, would force a revision. The actual registers — where they survive — run to the low tens of thousands total.

title: Orban's great bombard, 1452-1453
claim: The Hungarian iron-founder Orban (d. 1453), after offering his services to Constantine XI in 1452, cast a giant bronze bombard for Mehmed II at Adrianople — an approximately 8-meter gun firing stone shot of around half a ton to over a ton — which was dragged some 150 miles to Constantinople by teams of oxen and pounded the Theodosian walls through the 53-day siege.
place: Adrianople (Edirne) — the casting; the gun was dragged to Constantinople
grade_reason: The casting, the transport by ox-teams, and the bombard's wall-breaking role are attested across independent traditions (Doukas, Kritovoulos, Tursun Beg, Barbaro); exact dimensions and the founder's biography vary by source and stay fenced.
earliest_attestation: Doukas (c. 1462) for the founder and the Byzantine-offer story; Michael Kritovoulos and Tursun Beg for the artillery's role in the siege; the Dardanelles Gun (cast 1464, Royal Armouries) as the surviving design descendant

sources.ref: Doukas, Historia Turco-Byzantina (c. 1462) — the founder and the Byzantine-offer story
Michael Kritovoulos, History of Mehmed the Conqueror — the artillery's siege role
Tursun Beg, Târîh-i Ebü'l-Feth — Ottoman account of the siege artillery
Nicolò Barbaro, siege diary — the bombardment from the walls
Dardanelles Gun, cast 1464 (Royal Armouries) — surviving design descendant of Orban's bombard

competing_hypotheses: The rejection anecdote: Doukas is the source for Orban first offering himself to the Byzantines and being turned away over price and materials — a single-source, moralizing-chronicler telling; the lightsource critique (story 'leans on a chronicler who loved a good moral') is fair. Held at CLAIMED inside this record, never higher
Orban's origins: Hungarian per most modern authors; German ancestry and Wallachian roots also proposed; Laonikos Chalkokondyles called him 'Dacian' — the sources genuinely disagree
Orban's death: 'said to have died' when one of his great cannons burst from overuse mid-siege — reported, not attested; held at CLAIMED
The monster-gun numbers: 27 feet / 1,200-1,500-pound shot / 3-hour reload / 5-8 shots per day — the figures vary by source; the ratio (enormous, slow, wall-breaking) is what the sources agree on
falsifiability: Ottoman foundry or fiscal records contradicting the Adrianople commission, or proof that Doukas invented the Orban episode wholesale — the artillery's siege role is independently attested beyond Doukas, so the founder could fall while the bombard stands

title: The Fall of Constantinople, 29 May 1453
claim: On 29 May 1453, after a 53-day siege (6 April - 29 May), the Ottoman army of Sultan Mehmed II stormed Constantinople, ending the Eastern Roman Empire's eleven-century continuous existence and making the city the Ottoman capital.
place: Constantinople (modern Istanbul)
grade_reason: Multiply attested by independent contemporary sources from every side of the walls — Venetian, Genoese, Byzantine, and Ottoman — plus an unbroken modern scholarly consensus (Runciman 1965; Philippides & Hanak 2011; Crowley 2005; Kaldellis 2026).
earliest_attestation: Contemporary and near-contemporary, from all sides: Nicolò Barbaro's siege diary (Venetian eyewitness, 1453); Leonard of Chios's letter to Pope Nicholas V (1453); George Sphrantzes's Chronicon Minus (Byzantine court eyewitness); Tursun Beg's Târîh-i Ebü'l-Feth (Ottoman official historian)

sources.ref: Nicolò Barbaro, Giornale dell'Assedio di Costantinopoli (1453) — Venetian eyewitness diary
Leonard of Chios, letter to Pope Nicholas V (1453)
George Sphrantzes, Chronicon Minus (c. 1470s) — Byzantine court eyewitness
Tursun Beg, Târîh-i Ebü'l-Feth — Ottoman official history
Doukas, Historia Turco-Byzantina (c. 1462)
Michael Kritovoulos (Kritoboulos), History of Mehmed the Conqueror (c. 1453-1467)
Runciman, Steven (1965), The Fall of Constantinople 1453, Cambridge UP
Philippides, M. & Hanak, W. (2011), The Siege and the Fall of Constantinople in 1453, Ashgate

competing_hypotheses: Periodization convention: '1453 ended the Middle Ages' is a historiographical convenience, not an evidential claim — the grade here covers the fall, never the period label
