Force-size debates: Ottoman army estimates range from ~80,000 to much higher; defender estimates ~7,000-10,000 — the sources agree on the outcome and the lopsided ratio, not the absolutes
falsifiability: A contemporary account from any of the four source traditions (Venetian, Genoese, Byzantine, Ottoman) contradicting the fall — none exists; all agree the city was stormed on 29 May 1453

title: The Marble Emperor legend (Constantine XI)
claim: Constantine XI Palaiologos did not die when Constantinople fell on 29 May 1453; instead an angel rescued him, turned him into marble, and hid him in a cave beneath the Golden Gate of Constantinople, where he sleeps awaiting God's call to awaken and reconquer the city for Christendom.
place: Constantinople — the Golden Gate (Yedikule) of the legend
grade_reason: The emperor's death in the final assault is the near-universal tradition across independent Greek and Ottoman sources; no contemporary source in any tradition attests the angel, the marble, or the cave. The legend is centuries-deep folk belief, not evidence.
earliest_attestation: The death: near-universal tradition across Greek (Doukas, Kritovoulos, Sphrantzes) and Ottoman (Tursun Beg) sources, 1453-1470s. The marble legend: Greek demotic folk-song tradition of the Halosis (fall), documented by scholars from the 19th century onward — centuries after the event, never contemporary.

sources.ref: Michael Kritovoulos, History of Mehmed the Conqueror — the last charge tradition
Doukas, Historia Turco-Byzantina — the death tradition
Tursun Beg, Târîh-i Ebü'l-Feth — Ottoman account of the fall
Greek demotic folk-song tradition of the Halosis (the fall) — the Marble Emperor (Marmaromenos Vasilias) legend's attested home; documented in 19th-c. collections onward

competing_hypotheses: The honest unknown: no known surviving eyewitness to the exact moment of the emperor's death; the body-identification story (a corpse in silk stockings with an eagle embroidery, decapitated and paraded) failed to gather recognition from the citizens — the uncertainty is real, but it does not support the marble version

Kritovoulos's tradition: 'The city is fallen and I am still alive' — the emperor tore off his imperial ornaments and led a last charge, dying fighting; the near-universal account across Greek and Ottoman sources
The 'Constantine symmetry': the city's founding under Constantine the Great and its loss under another Constantine read as fulfilled destiny — a literary frame, not evidence for the marble claim
falsifiability: A contemporary (1453-1460s) attestation of the angel, the marble transformation, or the Golden Gate cave in any of the four source traditions — none exists in Venetian, Genoese, Byzantine, or Ottoman accounts

title: Columbus's real error: the size of the Earth, not its shape
claim: The learned opposition to Columbus's 1492 plan was not about the Earth's shape — which everyone at the table knew was round — but about its size: Columbus argued the Ocean Sea was crossable because he had shrunk the planet by roughly a quarter; the experts were right and he was wrong.
place: Salamanca, Spain (the examining faculty)
grade_reason: The mechanism is documented end to end: al-Farghani's correct 56.67 Arabic-miles-per-degree (~111.1 km/degree, circumference ~39,986 km, within 90 km of modern value) was mangled by d'Ailly's Roman-mile revision into a 25% smaller planet, and Columbus sailed on the mangled number. Carl Sagan's summary stands: Columbus used the smallest possible Earth and the greatest eastward extension of Asia available, 'and then exaggerated even those.' The experts' objection — the ocean is too wide — was the true reading of the planet, and the Americas saved him from it. Grade fenced: covers only the shape-vs-size reading of the debate, not Columbus's conduct or the voyage's consequences.
earliest_attestation: Cardinal Pierre d'Ailly, Imago Mundi (early 15th c.), citing the 9th-century Persian astronomer al-Farghani (Alfraganus): one degree of longitude at the equator = 56.67 miles. Columbus adopted d'Ailly's figures — but d'Ailly had converted al-Farghani's long Arabic miles (~1,960 m) into short Roman miles, producing the 'dwarf Earth' of ~30,194 km circumference vs the true ~40,008 km. Columbus further used the smallest available Earth and the largest available Asia (Esdras: six-sevenths of the world dry land).

sources.ref: Scientific analysis of d'Ailly's mile conversion: al-Farghani's 56.67 miles/degree in Arabic miles (~1,960 m) = 111.1 km per degree, circumference ~39,986 km; d'Ailly's Roman-mile revision dropped it to 83.872 km/degree and a 30,194 km 'dwarf Earth' — a 25% gap Columbus adopted and built his case on

Columbus's arithmetic: one degree of longitude treated as 56.66 miles → Earth circumference ~20,400 miles (a ~25% underestimate vs 24,901 miles); his Canaries-to-China estimate: ~3,000 miles. He sailed to where he thought the Orient was; the Americas were in the way

Carl Sagan, Cosmos (1980): Columbus 'used the smallest possible circumference of the Earth and the greatest eastward extension of Asia he could find in all the books available to him, and then exaggerated even those. Had the Americas not been in the way, Columbus' expeditions would have failed utterly'

Constant Contact / Columbus miscalculation overview: Columbus read d'Ailly's Imago Mundi; the 56.7 miles-per-degree figure was in longer Arabic miles, not shorter Roman miles; hence ~19,000 vs ~24,901 miles

competing_hypotheses: The narrower honest reading: the Salamanca experts' size estimates were also imperfect, and Columbus's voyage survived only because a continent sat where his arithmetic said Asia should be. The record corrects the myth without canonizing either side.
falsifiability: Falsifiable by showing the Salamanca faculty's surviving objections concerned sphericity rather than distance — they do not; they concerned the voyage's feasibility. Corroborated by the arithmetic itself: the Arabic-mile vs Roman-mile confusion is a checkable conversion error, and Columbus's 3,000-mile Canaries-to-China estimate vs the true ~10,000+ miles is a matter of record.

title: The real shinobi of Iga and Kōka
claim: Professional shinobi existed: Iga and Kōka families produced trained intelligence and infiltration operatives hired by daimyō in 1485–1581; the Tenshō Iga War (1579/1581) destroyed the Iga sōkoku ikki as an independent power; survivors served Tokugawa Ieyasu; the craft was codified in the Bansenshukai (1676).
place: Iga (Mie Prefecture) — the Iga sōkoku ikki
grade_reason: Multiple independent attestations of the operatives' existence (1487 shogunal records, the 1579/1581 campaigns, Tokugawa employment including Hattori Hanzō, the 1676 compendium); the exact content of the craft rests on later compendia, stopping the grade at CORROBORATED.
earliest_attestation: Go Kagami Furoku and the Nochi Kagami supplement: Iga men serving as shinobi in Ashikaga Yoshihisa's camp at Magari, 1487

sources.ref: Iga ikki (Wikipedia, compiled with cited sources) — the 1487 Nochi Kagami supplement ('shinobi whose names were famous throughout the land'); the failed 1579 Nobukatsu invasion; Nobunaga's 1581 five/six-direction assault; Turnbull quoted on the 1579 defeat as 'one of the greatest triumphs of unconventional warfare over traditional samurai tactics in the whole of Japanese history'

Iga-ryū (Wikipedia, compiled with cited sources) — Iga-mono first appear in the historical record in 1487; the 1581 conquest; Hattori Hanzō's guidance of Tokugawa Ieyasu's 1582 escape through Iga; 200 Iga men settled in Edo's Yotsuya as Tokugawa guards
Bansenshukai (1676), Fujibayashi Yasutake — the Edo-period compendium of ninjutsu: climbing equipment, disguise, espionage craft, concealable armor (primary source, post-dates the operational heyday)

competing_hypotheses: The romantic reading: a secret clan of superhuman assassins — graded separately and DEBUNKED in evt-ninja-pop-image-001

The minimalist reading: 'shinobi' was simply what you called any samurai-class scout or retainer on an infiltration errand — the Iga/Kōka regions may have produced a specialization, but the 1676 Bansenshukai's systematization postdates the Sengoku heyday by a century
falsifiability: Proof that the 1487 Iga-shinobi references in the shogunal records, or the Tenshō Iga War accounts, are Edo-period fabrications; or that the Bansenshukai is a modern forgery

title: Aixa's "weep like a woman" rebuke to Boabdil (1492)
claim: As Boabdil departed into exile in 1492, pausing at the hill called El Suspiro del Moro to look back at Granada, his mother Aixa (Aisha al-Hurra) rebuked him with words to the effect of "Weep like a woman for what you could not defend as a man" (Spanish: "Llora como mujer lo que no supiste defender como hombre").
place: El Suspiro del Moro, near Padul, Granada (traditional site of the alleged scene)
grade_reason: No contemporary (15th-century) attestation of the quote or the scene exists; the near-contemporary eyewitness record of the surrender describes a different ceremony entirely. The earliest traceable forms sit in fictionalizing romance literature a century-plus later, and the canonical wording is Irving's 1829 English — a literary scene, not a documented utterance.
earliest_attestation: No 15th-century attestation known. Earliest traceable forms sit in the early-modern morisco romance tradition (Perez de Hita, 1595/1619, writing through a fictitious Arabic narrator); the canonical Anglophone wording is Washington Irving's Chronicle of the Conquest of Granada (1829).

sources.ref: Eyewitness letter to the bishop of Leon, 8 January 1492 (six days after the surrender) — describes the surrender ceremony at the Genil in detail; records no hill-top farewell and no maternal rebuke
Christopher Columbus, journal prologue 1492 ("on the 2nd January I saw the royal banners ... planted ... on the towers of the Alhambra") — contemporary record of the surrender, no quote

Gines Perez de Hita, Historia de los bandos de los Zegries y los Abencerrajes (1595), 2nd part Guerras civiles de Granada (1619) — the morisco romance tradition that fictionalized the fall of Granada in chivalric idiom

Washington Irving, A Chronicle of the Conquest of Granada (1829) — canonical Anglophone form: "You do well ... to weep like a woman for what you failed to defend like a man"; Irving also fixed the hill's name as "El ultimo suspiro del Moro"
Edward Bulwer Lytton, Leila, or The Siege of Granada (1838) — repeats the rebuke as "the reproach which history has preserved"; the 1900 Nuttall Encyclopedia entry for Boabdil repeats it as fact

competing_hypotheses: Aixa said something like it in private and it entered oral tradition before print — unattested, unfalsifiable; the documentary record contains no trace
The scene is entirely literary invention from the morisco romance tradition, canonized by Irving
falsifiability: A pre-1600 source attesting the quote or the hill-top farewell scene would overturn this grade

title: The claim that Columbus discovered the Americas in 1492
claim: Christopher Columbus discovered the Americas in 1492 — i.e., he was the first European to reach them.
place: San Salvador Island, Bahamas (traditional Guanahani landfall, 12 Oct 1492)
grade_reason: Two independent kills. (1) The Norse reached North America ~470 years earlier — VERIFIED at L'Anse aux Meadows (1021 CE, metal-cut timber). (2) The Americas were inhabited for millennia before any European arrived, so 'discovery' of the land is a framing, not a fact. What Columbus did — initiate sustained, consequential European contact, the Columbian Exchange — is historically pivotal but is not discovery.
earliest_attestation: The 'discovery' framing crystallized in the 19th century (Washington Irving's 1828 biography; U.S. quadricentennial 1892); Columbus's own journal (via Las Casas's abstract) never claims a first landing.

sources.ref: L'Anse aux Meadows archaeology: Norse settlement c. 1000 CE, felled timber dated 1021 CE (Kuitems et al. 2021, Nature)
Vinland sagas: Eiríks saga rauða, Grænlendinga saga
Columbus's journal (Bartolomé de las Casas abstract); the four voyages 1492-1504; death at Valladolid 1506 believing he had reached Asia
Archaeological consensus: human presence in the Americas for 15,000+ years before 1492

competing_hypotheses: 'First to initiate sustained European contact' — the accurate significance claim, replacing the discovery claim
'Discovery for Europe' — Irving's framing: a statement about European knowledge, not about the land; true as European intellectual history, false as first arrival
The landfall-island identification itself is disputed (San Salvador vs. Samana Cay vs. others) — a separate open question that does not affect the grade
falsifiability: The Norse leg is in principle revisable (if L'Anse aux Meadows were ever re-attributed, which no evidence supports); the Indigenous-presence leg is not — inhabited land cannot be 'discovered' by a later arrival under any evidence.

title: The surrender of Granada (2 January 1492)
claim: Muhammad XII of Granada (Boabdil) surrendered the Nasrid kingdom — the last Muslim polity of Iberia — to Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile on 2 January 1492, under the Capitulations of Santa Fe signed 25 November 1491. He received a fief at Laujar de Andarax in the Alpujarras, which he sold in 1493 before crossing to Fez.
place: The Alhambra, Granada
grade_reason: Multiple independent contemporary sources — the signed treaty text, a private eyewitness letter six days after the event, and Columbus's contemporary journal entry — converge on the date, the ceremony, and the terms.
earliest_attestation: The Capitulations of Santa Fe, 25 November 1491 (Archivo General de Simancas); eyewitness letter to the bishop of Leon, 8 January 1492; Columbus's journal prologue, 1492.

sources.ref: Capitulations of Santa Fe, 25 November 1491 (Archivo General de Simancas) — the surrender treaty: religious tolerance and fair treatment for Granada's Muslims in return for capitulation

Eyewitness letter to the bishop of Leon, 8 January 1492 — private contemporary account of the handover ceremony at the Genil (Boabdil with 80-100 horsemen); also records that Ferdinand and Isabella declined Boabdil's offer to kiss their hands, at his mother's insistence
Christopher Columbus, journal prologue, 1492 ("on the 2nd January I saw the royal banners of Your Highnesses planted by force of arms on the towers of the Alhambra")

Granada War historiography (Prescott 1837; Harvey, Islamic Spain 1250 to 1500) — the eight-month siege of April 1491-January 1492, the secret negotiations, the Alpujarras fief and 1493 crossing to Fez

competing_hypotheses: The Granada War historiography's bribery-and-treachery narrative (one of Boabdil's advisers working for Castile) colors the surrender's causes but not its occurrence
None on the occurrence itself — the date and ceremony are uncontested
falsifiability: A contemporary source placing the surrender on a materially different date or denying the Capitulations' terms

title: The 1492 'transfusion' of Pope Innocent VIII
claim: Pope Innocent VIII (Giovanni Battista Cybo/Cibo, d. 25 July 1492) received the first recorded blood transfusion in history — the blood of three young boys transfused into the dying pontiff on the suggestion of a Jewish physician.
place: Rome, Vatican
grade_reason: Sole-source hostile gossip from an explicitly unreliable chronicler; the 'transfusion into the pope' leg is a later misreading of a blood-letting account; and a transfusion was conceptually impossible in 1492 — circulation was unknown until Harvey 1628.
earliest_attestation: Stefano Infessura, Diarium urbis Romae (contemporary Roman diary, partly Latin, partly Romanesco; Infessura d. c. 1500)

sources.ref: Stefano Infessura, Diarium urbis Romae — the boys' blood-letting account (three ten-year-old boys, a ducat each, boys die, physician flees, pope not healed)

Wikipedia, 'Innocent VIII' — 'A possibly apocryphal story stated that Innocent's physician drew the blood from three young boys to transfuse it into the Pope but the treatment failed and all four involved died.'
Scientific American guest blog, 'Blood Lust: The Early History of Transfusion' — 'skeptical historians rightly doubt that there is much truth behind this politicized papal story'

New Catholic Dictionary (via DBpedia 2014) on Infessura — 'he inserted every fragment of the most preposterous and malevolent gossip current in Roman society, and is therefore not considered a reliable chronicler'; Infessura belonged to the antipapal faction of the Roman Academy

Phil Learoyd, 'The Early History of Blood Transfusion' (historyofbloodtransfusion.co.uk, 2023) — argues the 'transfusion' reading stems from a later misinterpretation (Villari) of Infessura's blood-letting account; notes circulation was unknown

William Harvey, De Motu Cordis (1628) — blood circulation unknown until 136 years after 1492; no concept of circulation and no method of intravenous access existed in 1492, making a transfusion anachronistic by definition

competing_hypotheses: A failed remedy of some kind was attempted on the dying pope (the gossip's core: a physician bled boys and fled)
The 'transfusion' wording is Villari's later misinterpretation of Infessura's blood-letting account (Learoyd 2023)
The story is pure antipapal factional gossip, weaponizing a Jewish physician and dead children against the dying pontiff
falsifiability: A second, independent contemporary source confirming a deliberate vein-to-vein (or vessel-to-mouth) blood transfer in Rome in 1492 — no such source exists, and the anachronism makes the search nearly closed

title: The post-1492 depopulation of the Americas (the Great Dying)
claim: In the century after 1492, European colonization and introduced disease caused a massive demographic collapse in the Americas — roughly 90% of the pre-contact population died by ~1600 — on a scale that left ~56 million hectares of farmland to revert to forest.
place: The Americas (hemisphere-wide claim)
grade_reason: The collapse is multiply documented (tribute records, missionary accounts, pollen/charcoal archaeology), but the record's headline numbers — 60.5M, 90%, 56M ha — all come from one 2019 study's modeling chain, and the climate-link attribution is a hypothesis, not a measured fact.
earliest_attestation: Colonial tribute rolls, missionary accounts, and the archaeological/palynological record; the modern quantitative synthesis is Koch et al. 2019

sources.ref: Koch, Brierley, Maslin & Lewis, 2019, Quaternary Science Reviews: pre-1492 population estimated ~60.5M; ~90% died by 1600; ~56M ha of farmland reverted to forest; atmospheric CO2 fell 7-10 ppm, contributing to the coldest phase of the Little Ice Age (~0.15 C cooling)
Denevan (ed.), The Native Population of the Americas in 1492 (1976, rev. 1992): 43-65M — the edited-volume consensus range the field argued over for decades
Antarctic ice-core CO2 record: the 16th-century CO2 minimum coincides with the depopulation window; Koch et al. attribute ~half of the observed dip to New World reforestation

competing_hypotheses: The low counters (Kroeber's ~8.4M tradition, revived in various forms): same collapse, smaller starting point — the dispute is about the baseline, not the event
The multi-cause Little Ice Age position (volcanic eruptions, solar minimum, orbital forcing): the depopulation-reforestation CO2 dip as a contributing factor, not the sole driver
Ruddiman's earlier anthropogenic hypothesis (2003): human land-use effects on climate beginning millennia earlier — a broader frame in which the 16th-century dip is one episode, not the beginning
falsifiability: A published population reconstruction showing no post-1492 discontinuity in the ice-core-linked land-use record, or demographic evidence that the pre-contact population was under 10 million with no 16th-century collapse

title: The 'pristine wilderness' myth of the Americas in 1492
claim: The belief that in 1492 the Americas were a sparsely populated wilderness, 'a world of barely perceptible human disturbance' — an almost untouched, Edenic land untrammeled by man.
place: The Americas (the claim covers the hemisphere)
grade_reason: The scholarly record contradicts the claim on every leg: populations were large, forests were managed (fire, terra preta, milpa), earthworks and cities (Cahokia, Upano) are on the ground, and Denevan's closing argument — that human presence was LESS visible in 1750 than in 1492 — shows the 'wilderness' the romantics admired was the aftermath, not the original.
earliest_attestation: The claim as a scholarly refutation: William M. Denevan, 'The Pristine Myth: The Landscape of the Americas in 1492', Annals of the Association of American Geographers 82(3), September 1992, pp. 369-385

sources.ref: Denevan 1992 abstract: 'There is substantial evidence, however, that the Native American landscape of the early sixteenth century was a humanized landscape almost everywhere. Populations were large. Forest composition had been modified, grasslands had been created, wildlife disrupted, and erosion was severe in places. Earthworks, roads, fields, and settlements were ubiquitous. With Indian depopulation in the wake of Old World disease, the environment recovered in many areas.'
Denevan's Amazonia field record: prehistoric raised fields, causeways, and canals reported in Scientific American (1967) and Science (1970); terra preta (anthropogenic dark earth) across Amazonia
Upano Valley laser mapping (Science, January 2024): a ~6,000-year-old urban complex under the Ecuadorian Amazon — the largest and oldest yet found
Charles C. Mann, 1491: New Revelations of the Americas Before Columbus — the popular synthesis: 'Columbus set foot in a hemisphere thoroughly dominated by humankind'

competing_hypotheses: The minimalist remnant: some regions genuinely carried low densities (parts of the Arctic, deserts) — the DEBUNKED grade kills the hemisphere-wide wilderness claim, never the local reality

The Meggers-era 'counterfeit paradise' position (Betty J. Meggers, Smithsonian): Amazonia could not support dense populations — superseded by the terra preta and earthwork evidence, carried here as the position the evidence overcame
falsifiability: A continent-wide survey of pre-1492 landscapes showing no pre-contact modification — no earthworks, no anthropogenic soils, no managed forests; every line of evidence has gone the opposite way

title: The "toothbrush was invented in China in 1498" telling
claim: The toothbrush was invented in China in 1498, during the reign of the Hongzhi Emperor.
place: China (Hongzhi reign, 1488–1505, conventionally)
grade_reason: No contemporary source attests the year 1498; the date is a modern reference-book convention, and the literature cannot agree whether the brush is 7th-, 13th-, or 15th-century. Two independent kills: documentary absence + the wandering date.
earliest_attestation: Modern reference-work convention; no contemporary Ming source for the year has been located (realrareantiques.com: 'We have not found a contemporary source for it, and it should be treated with caution').

sources.ref: realrareantiques.com, 'Hongzhi Emperor (r. 1487–1505)' — 'A widely repeated modern claim credits the Hongzhi reign with the invention of the bristle toothbrush, in 1498. We have not found a contemporary source for it, and it should be treated with caution.'
Dr. Scott Swank, National Museum of Dentistry, via HowStuffWorks: 'The first device that we would consider the precursor to the modern toothbrush is recorded in China circa 1500' — 'circa', not 1498

The wandering date in the literature: Tang-dynasty 7th c., 600–900, 13th-c. first written mention, c. 1500, 15th–16th c. — a precise year that moves by eight centuries across sources has no document behind it

competing_hypotheses: The brush genuinely dates to the Hongzhi reign and 1498 is a reasonable conventional midpoint — but convention is not evidence
An imperial-workshop origin (the Hongzhi Emperor personally commissioned it) — a further unattested elaboration of the same telling
falsifiability: A contemporary Ming document — court record, workshop order, or traveler's diary — explicitly dating a bristle toothbrush to 1498 would restore the year (the brush itself needs no defense).

title: Letterlocking — the letter as its own envelope
claim: Before cheap pre-made envelopes, letters were routinely folded, secured, and sent without any envelope at all — the technique of 'letterlocking' — used alongside handmade envelopes for centuries.
place: Early modern Europe (exemplars in European archives)
grade_reason: The Library of Congress's own exhibit states the technique as institutional knowledge, grounded in surviving artifacts; it is the second of the three independent pre-1840 envelope lines. Held below VERIFIED — the grade rests on one institutional summary plus the physical archive rather than the peer-reviewed letterlocking literature.
earliest_attestation: Surviving folded-and-sealed letters in European archives, early modern period onward.

sources.ref: Library of Congress, Inside Adams — 'Opening the Envelope' (letterlocking: 'a technique in which a letter is folded, secured, and sent without the use of an envelope,' used alongside handmade envelopes; mass production ended it)
Baylor University, Texas Collection — 'envelope history' (pre-1840s cut-and-fold-your-own world)

competing_hypotheses: Letterlocking scholarship sometimes treats the fold as primarily tamper-evident rather than privacy-securing — carried as the competing functional reading; the record grades the technique's existence, not the motive
The envelope's eventual victory was economic (mass production) rather than functional (security) — the LoC's own framing, carried as the honest reading
falsifiability: If the entire surviving corpus of folded letters proved to be modern constructions, the technique's documentary basis would fail — it rests on the physical archive itself.

title: The pointed personal knives that came before the table knife
claim: Before the table knife, the European dining knife was a pointed personal implement — each diner carried his own sharp knife, used it to cut what he had seized with his hand, and the same point served as toothpick, lance for the mouth, and occasional weapon.
place: Europe (dining practice)
grade_reason: Multiple descriptive accounts agree: in the pre-fork era each man had his own knife, seized the joint with his hand, cut off what he wished, and the dish passed on. Knives were kept sharp for their dual role as weapon and eating implement; tooth-picking with the point was a documented bad habit (the habit Richelieu is supposed to have corrected). CORROBORATED on descriptive attestation; the exact ubiquity by country is not dated per-household.
earliest_attestation: 17th-century table-practice accounts; the WSU 'Knives and Forks' description of pre-fork practice

sources.ref: Washington State University Clark collection, 'Knives and Forks': 'each man had his own knife, and at dinner seized the joint with his hand, and cut off what he wished'
Tegan Jones / TodayIFoundOut via Gizmodo (2013): knives as weapon-and-implement; wine-and-ale punctured mouths; the fork's spread reduced the need for a point

competing_hypotheses: That specialist table knives existed earlier in some households — held as weaker variant; the documented norm is personal pointed knives
falsifiability: A dated household inventory or table-setting record showing blunt dedicated table knives as the norm before 1600

title: The Venetian mirror monopoly
claim: In the 16th century, Venetian glassmakers on Murano mastered glass backed with a tin-mercury amalgam, giving Europe's only crystal-clear mirrors — and a Venetian export monopoly lasting ~150 years, guarded by laws forbidding glassmakers from leaving and by trade-secrets oaths enforced on penalty of death.
place: Murano, Venice, Italy
grade_reason: The technique, the Murano confinement, and the export dominance are multiply attested in trade and guild history; the death-penalty enforcement detail rides on period sources rather than modern documentation.
earliest_attestation: Venetian guild records; the 1295 law forbidding glassmakers from leaving the city; 15th–16th-century Venetian mirror production.

sources.ref: Furniture Library, 'The History of Mirror: Through A Glass, Darkly' — tin-mercury amalgam, ~150 years of Venetian supremacy, trade secrets on penalty of death
IPM, 'Mirror, Mirror' (2019) — 16th-century Venice tin-and-mercury backing, much clearer reflection
Martino Interiors / MURANO GLASS doc — 1295 law forbidding glassmakers from leaving; monopoly lasting centuries
Italian Tribune, history of Venetian glass — Angelo Barovier's cristallo, Murano as Europe's only mirror producer

competing_hypotheses: The 'penalty of death' framing is part of Venice's own deterrence theater — historians debate how often it was literally enforced
The monopoly's end is dated variously (1665 French recruitment of Venetian glassmakers vs gradual Bohemian competition into the 18th century)
falsifiability: Venetian guild records showing no restriction on glassmaker travel, or pre-16th-century Venetian glass mirrors equal in clarity, would break the claim.

title: The scale of the transatlantic slave trade: 12.5 million embarked, 10.7 million disembarked
claim: Between 1501 and 1867, slaving vessels embarked about 12.5 million African captives on the transatlantic crossing; about 10.7 million disembarked alive in the Americas. About 1.8 million died in the Middle Passage. Just 4% of the embarkations were destined for what became the United States.
place: the Atlantic crossing corridor (Africa to the Americas)
grade_reason: Built on ~35,000 documented voyages (~80% of the trade by the compilers' own accounting, with published imputation for the rest), converging across ship logs, financial records, and customs/court archives from all trading nations (Portugal ~5.8M, Britain ~3.3M, France ~1.4M, Spain ~1.1M, Netherlands ~0.55M, US ~0.31M, Denmark ~0.11M per the database's country breakouts). The 12.5M/10.7M/1.8M triad (Eltis & Richardson 2010) is the field's consensus estimate, not a single-author figure. Stops short of VERIFIED because ~20% of voyages are imputed, not documented.
earliest_attestation: Ship logs, manifests, merchant ledgers, admiralty and customs records, and post-1808 court prosecution records of illegal slave trading — the documentary base assembled since the 1970s.

sources.ref: David Eltis & David Richardson, Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade (Yale University Press, 2010) — pp. 2-5: 12.5 million embarked, 10.7 million disembarked
Voyages: The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database (Rice University / Emory), ~35,000 documented voyages 1514-1866, ~80% coverage with published imputation
Philip Misevich, Daniel Domingues, David Eltis, Nafees M. Khan & Nicholas Radburn, 'A Digital Archive of Slave Voyages' (The Conversation via Smithsonian Magazine, May 2017)

Sowande' M. Mustakeem, cartographic analysis drawing on Eltis & Richardson 2010 — '1.8 million, more than 14 percent, of the 12.5 million who embarked never disembarked' (OpenEdition, Slaveries journal)

competing_hypotheses: Philip Curtin's 1969 census (~9.5 million) — superseded by the larger documentary base of the TSTD
The ~15-20 million popular figures — never grounded in voyage documentation; see evt-goree-door-throughput-001
Intra-American re-exports inflating destination counts — the database tracks embarkations, not later internal sales
falsifiability: Discovery of a comparable independent documentary corpus yielding an embarkation total materially different from 12.5 million; demonstration that the imputation model for missing voyages is systematically biased in one direction.

title: 'Here be dragons' — the convention that never existed
claim: 'Here be dragons' (hic sunt dracones) was a standard warning that medieval and Renaissance cartographers inscribed on unexplored or dangerous regions of their maps.
place: New York Public Library, Rare Book Division, New York City (the phrase's surviving habitat)
grade_reason: The phrase survives on exactly ONE accepted historical object — the Hunt–Lenox Globe (c. 1508–1510), 'HC SVNT DRACONES' below the equator on the eastern Asian coast. No medieval mappamundi, portolan chart, or earlier globe carries it; the classical cartographers' actual formula was 'hic sunt leones' (here are lions). The 'medieval practice' is a modern invention wearing period costume.
earliest_attestation: Hunt–Lenox Globe, c. 1508–1510 — the only accepted surviving historical object bearing the phrase; no medieval mappamundi or earlier chart carries it

sources.ref: NYPL — The Hunt-Lenox Globe (institution page: 'one of only two medieval or Renaissance-era maps or globes known to bear the famous motto Hic Sunt Dracones')

Wikipedia — 'Here be dragons' ('the only known historical use of this phrase... is on the Hunt-Lenox Globe'; 'the phrase itself is largely an anachronism'; the classical medieval phrase was 'hic sunt leones')
Geography Realm — 'The Map Myth of Here Be Dragons' (survey of known instances: the Lenox Globe as the only documented example; the Ostrich Egg Globe as the contested second)

competing_hypotheses: The medieval equivalent was 'hic sunt leones' ('here are lions') — the classical Roman phrase cartographers actually used to mark unknown territory, which suggests the dragons phrase may be a late corruption or replacement of a real convention

NYPL's own reading: the globe's inscription, placed just below the equator on the eastern coast of Asia, 'may have originally referenced the Komodo dragons that inhabit portions of the Indonesian archipelago' — i.e. the phrase may mark a specific reported fauna, not a general terror of the unknown
falsifiability: A pre-1508 map, chart, or mappamundi bearing 'hic sunt dracones' (or a vernacular equivalent) in an unexplored region, verified by independent scholarly transcription — the scholarly survey to date has found none

title: The Lenox Globe — the apple with dragons
claim: The Hunt–Lenox Globe (c. 1508–1510) is the second-oldest known terrestrial globe after Martin Behaim's Erdapfel (1492); a hollow red-copper engraved globe, ca. 112 mm in diameter, housed in the NYPL Rare Book Division; and the only accepted historical object bearing the inscription 'HC SVNT DRACONES' ('here be dragons'), placed just below the equator on the eastern coast of Asia.
place: New York Public Library, Rare Book Division (Stephen A. Schwarzman Building)
grade_reason: The object exists, is publicly held and photographed, and its inscription is multiply transcribed by independent scholars; held below VERIFIED because its precise date (1508 vs 1510) varies between institutions and its maker is unknown.
earliest_attestation: The globe itself, c. 1508–1510 (copper engraving by an unknown creator; 'the earliest such surviving engraving from the period right after the discovery of the New World' per NYPL); purchased in Paris in 1855 by architect Richard Morris Hunt 'for a song', recognized by bookdealer Henry Stevens, donated to the Lenox Library

sources.ref: NYPL — The Hunt-Lenox Globe ('one of the earliest surviving terrestrial globes,' 'one of the oldest known cartographic depictions of the Americas,' 'one of only two medieval or Renaissance-era maps or globes known to bear the famous motto')

Wikipedia — Hunt–Lenox Globe (second-oldest terrestrial globe after the Erdapfel; hollow red copper, ca. 112 mm; 'the only known example of an historical map actually using the phrase HC SVNT DRACONES')
Henry Stevens's 1870 recollections via the Wikipedia synthesis (Hunt dining-room provenance; Julius Erasmus Hilgard dating assistance)

competing_hypotheses: Stefaan Missinne's fringe theory: the Lenox Globe was not engraved at all but cast from the Ostrich Egg Globe (claimed c. 1504) 'using a very specific and unusual technique' — treated as fringe, not peer-consensus, and carried here only as the belief-ecology around the 'second instance' claim

The Ostrich Egg Globe (two joined ostrich-egg halves, North America as two islands, 'Hic Sunt Dracones' above the Southeast Asian coast) as a second bearing object — contested authorship and dating; if accepted it would make the Lenox Globe the third-oldest rather than the second
falsifiability: A second accepted pre-1510 globe bearing the phrase would downgrade the 'only accepted object' superlative; a peer-reviewed dating study moving the globe before 1504 would promote the date side of this record

title: Luther Nailed the 95 Theses to the Church Door
claim: On 31 October 1517 (the eve of All Saints' Day), Martin Luther nailed his 95 Theses on indulgences to the door of All Saints' Church (the Schlosskirche) in Wittenberg — the dramatic hammer scene that popular tradition holds to be the first act of the Reformation.
place: All Saints' Church (Schlosskirche), Wittenberg, Germany
grade_reason: Attested but single-source and late: the only witness is Melanchthon (1546), who was not in Wittenberg in 1517, and Luther never corroborates his own legend; but routine posting of disputation theses on the Schlosskirche door (the university's notice board) was standard practice, so a routine posting may well have happened — hence CLAIMED, not DEBUNKED.
earliest_attestation: Philipp Melanchthon's preface to the second volume of Luther's Latin works (1546), 29 years after the alleged event — the ONLY source for the posting.

sources.ref: Melanchthon, preface to Tomus secundus of Luther's Latin works (1546): 'he affixed them publicly to the door of the church which is next to the castle of Wittenberg, the eve of the Feast of All Saints, in the year 1517' — sole attestation

Erwin Iserloh, 'Luthers Thesenanschlag — Tatsache oder Legende?', Trierer Theologische Zeitschrift 70 (1961), 303–312 — the legend thesis, reaffirmed in his later work (Luther zwischen Reform und Reformation, 1962)
Luther's letter to Archbishop Albert of Mainz, 31 Oct 1517, enclosing the theses — proves mailing, not nailing; the contemporary paper trail carries the letter, never the door
Luther's own complete silence on the posting across letters, Table Talk, and reminiscences — the act is never mentioned by the alleged actor himself (the negative evidence, honestly recorded)
La Civilta Cattolica survey (History or Legend) — notes Melanchthon was 17 and a student at Tubingen in 1517, arriving in Wittenberg only in 1518; not an eyewitness

competing_hypotheses: A routine posting genuinely happened: disputation theses were routinely affixed to the Schlosskirche door as the university's notice board, and Luther's theses were composed as propositions for disputation — the hammer drama is the late accretion, the posting itself plausible
The posting is a wholesale legend: Iserloh's position — no contemporary evidence exists, and Melanchthon's 1546 narrative retrofits the origin story the young church needed
falsifiability: A contemporary 1517 source (letter, diary, printer's note, university record) describing the posting would raise the grade to CORROBORATED; a 1517-dated refutation of it would sink it to DEBUNKED

title: The Theses Went Viral on the Press
claim: Luther's 95 Theses were printed and spread across Germany and beyond within weeks and months of October 1517 — Nuremberg (December 1517), Leipzig and Basel (January 1518), with a German translation in January 1518 — largely without Luther's involvement: the printing press, not the hammer, made the theses famous.
place: Wittenberg to Nuremberg, Leipzig, Basel — the early print corridor
grade_reason: Multiply attested: the dated letter survives, and multiple independent printed editions with colophons survive in libraries; held below VERIFIED only on exact print-run figures, which are estimates.
earliest_attestation: Surviving printed editions: Nuremberg (Dec 1517), Leipzig and Basel (Jan 1518); Luther's letter to Albert of Mainz, 31 Oct 1517

sources.ref: Surviving printed editions of the 95 Theses: Nuremberg (December 1517), Leipzig (January 1518), Basel (January 1518) — multiple independent surviving witnesses to the rapid print circulation
Luther's letter to Archbishop Albert of Mainz, 31 October 1517, enclosing the theses (also sent the same day to Bishop Jerome Schulz of Brandenburg) — the documented act of publication
German translation of the theses (January 1518) — the move from Latin disputation text to vernacular reading material, the true transmission event

competing_hypotheses: Luther expected a small academic stir: he composed the theses as disputation propositions for local scholars and mailed them to his superiors; the press turned a local argument into a continental one without his direction
The 'viral' framing is modern shorthand: the sixteenth-century transmission was fast but elite-first (Latin), then vernacular; the German translation of January 1518 is the real mass-diffusion event
falsifiability: Provenance-examination showing the December 1517 Nuremberg edition to be a later forgery, or discovery of evidence that Luther himself organized the print run

title: The handful-of-conquistadors myth
claim: Hernán Cortés conquered the Aztec Empire with about five hundred Spaniards — a handful of Europeans toppling a great empire by their own arms.
place: Tenochtitlan (present-day Mexico City)
grade_reason: The conquering force was overwhelmingly indigenous: the final assault on Tenochtitlan was carried out with roughly 200,000 native allies against ~900 Spaniards — Cortés's own figure — and Restall's archival audit shows Africans equaled or exceeded the Spanish conquistadors in number; native sources saw a civil war in which the Spaniards played an important but secondary role.
earliest_attestation: The conquest narratives themselves — Cortés's Cartas de relación (1519–1526), Bernal Díaz del Castillo's Historia verdadera (written c. 1568, published 1632), and the later popular histories that foregrounded Spanish arms.

sources.ref: Matthew Restall, Seven Myths of the Spanish Conquest (Oxford University Press, 2003), ch. 3: 'The Myth of the White Conquistador' — the actual military operations were undertaken by indigenous allies outnumbering the Spanish by many hundreds to one
WorldCat/OCLC 51022823 + Stanford SearchWorks record for Seven Myths of the Spanish Conquest (Restall, 2003, OUP) — bibliographic verification

Hernán Cortés, letter to Charles V (the third carta de relación, 1522) — his own report that the final assault was carried out with 'we Spaniards only some nine hundred' against allied forces 'numbering more than 150,000'
Wikipedia, 'Siege of Tenochtitlan' — force figures for 1521: 900–1,300 Spanish infantry plus ~200,000 native allies, with cited references
Wikipedia, 'Seven Myths of the Spanish Conquest' — summary of Restall's chapter: the final assault was carried out with 200,000 native allies, and Africans equaled or exceeded the Spaniards in number

competing_hypotheses: The Spanish contribution — steel, horses, siege engineering (the 13 brigantines), and tactical leadership — was disproportionately decisive even within a mostly-indigenous force
The absolute figures are inflated on all sides (Cortés had reasons to inflate both the allied numbers and his own smallness); the ratio, not the absolute counts, is what the sources agree on
falsifiability: Contemporary muster rolls or logistics records showing the 1521 assault was conducted primarily by Spanish troops would refute the indigenous-coalition account and revive the myth.

title: The siege of Tenochtitlan, 1521
claim: From late May to 13 August 1521, a Spanish–indigenous coalition besieged and took Tenochtitlan, the Triple Alliance capital, after a smallpox epidemic had devastated the city; Cuauhtémoc was captured on 13 August 1521 and the Mexica state fell.
place: Tenochtitlan (present-day Mexico City)
grade_reason: Spanish letters, the Nahuatl accounts, and the epidemic record converge on the siege dates, the coalition's composition, and smallpox's decisive role; indigenous casualty figures vary widely by source and stay honest.
earliest_attestation: Cortés's third carta de relación (1522); Bernal Díaz del Castillo's Historia verdadera; the Florentine Codex, Book 12 (Nahuatl account, c. 1555–1585).

sources.ref: Florentine Codex, Book 12 (Fray Bernardino de Sahagún — the Nahuatl-side account of the conquest)
Wikipedia, 'Siege of Tenochtitlan' — siege dates, the 13 brigantines, the Chapultepec aqueduct cut, 900–1,300 Spaniards plus ~200,000 native allies
Wikipedia, 'Cuitláhuac' — the 10th Huey Tlatoani's 80-day reign (1520) and death from smallpox
MedicalXpress / AP (2020), '500 years ago, another epidemic swept Mexico: smallpox' — the huey zahuatl epidemic: introduced via Narváez's men in 1520, Cuitláhuac's death, the disease's decisive role
globalsecurity.org, 'The Spanish Conquest' — Cortés exploited the hostile tribes' divisions, using tribe against tribe

competing_hypotheses: The siege as a Spanish military achievement (the traditional historiography — Cortés at the center, allies as auxiliaries)
The siege as a Mexica–Tlaxcalan war in which the Spanish were catalysts rather than the main force (the revisionist reading: Restall, Townsend)
falsifiability: Contemporary Mexica-dated records placing the city's fall in a different year, or under a different attacker, would reopen the whole account.

title: The 'Catherine de' Medici introduced the fork to France in 1533' myth
claim: Catherine de' Medici introduced the table fork to France when she traveled there in 1533 to marry the future Henri II, acting as the fork's emissary to the French court.
place: The French court, Paris (the alleged introduction)
grade_reason: DEBUNKED — 220th DEBUNKED family. Three kills: (1) Francis I, Catherine's father-in-law, dined at elite Italian tables and encountered — even imported — Italian culinary practice long before 1533; (2) the fork was already circulating in Italian elite circles (56 silver forks in the Medici kitchen by the 1400s) — the 'introduction' credits Catherine with a transmission that predates her; (3) the popular timeline itself grades her French campaign as a failed promotion — the myth refutes itself. No period source names her as the fork's introducer.
earliest_attestation: Modern popular-history tellings; no period (16th-century) source names Catherine as the fork's introducer

sources.ref: History Expose / Factinate: 'Foodie Fashions: Debunked!' — the idea that Catherine introduced the fork from Italy to France 'is a routinely discredited myth'; historians note her father-in-law Francis I dined at elite Italian tables and encountered their culinary practices long before her arrival

National Geographic History Jan/Feb 2022 fork timeline: 'Traveling to France to marry Henry II in 1533, Catherine de Médicis became the emissary of the fork in the royal court. She ran into immediate resistance... tries (and fails) to promote it' — the popular version frames her campaign as a failed promotion, not a successful introduction

PopSci: 'The thousand-year story of how the fork crossed Europe' — forks common in Italy by the 14th c.; Florence's Medici kitchen held 56 silver forks by the 1400s; the fork's European spread ran through Italy's wealthy merchant classes in the 16th century

competing_hypotheses: Catherine popularized Italian table manners and cuisine generally — fenced: the fork specifically vs. Italian culinary influence broadly
The 'two women' popular version (Catherine + one other) credits 16th-century Italian influence generally — the mechanism is Italian merchants and travelers, not a queen's trousseau
falsifiability: A 1533-era French record — court inventory, letter, or account — naming Catherine as the fork's introducer to France; none has been produced

title: The Goree Door-of-No-Return throughput: 15-20 million through one house
claim: Fifteen to twenty million enslaved Africans passed through the House of Slaves on Goree Island, Senegal, through its 'Door of No Return,' on the way to the Americas — making the house the trade's principal departure point.
place: Goree Island, Senegal — House of Slaves
grade_reason: Arithmetic: the entire transatlantic trade embarked ~12.5 million Africans from all of Africa (evt-middle-passage-scale-001). A claim that 15-20 million passed through one building on one island exceeds the total of the whole trade by 20-60%. Documentary: Curtin estimated ~50,000 spent time on the island, ~26,000 exported; Araujo (2020) ~33,000; the island was never a key departure point (the Senegal and Gambia river mouths were), and the House of Slaves was built 1775-1778 by a wealthy merchant as one of the island's finest homes — not as a slave warehouse. The 'Door of No Return' cannot have been the mass loading point: rocks prevented safe docking; the beach was the loading place.
earliest_attestation: Portuguese record of slave trading at Goree, 1536; the '15-20 million' figure comes from the House of Slaves' own memorial literature under curator Joseph Ndiaye (1962-2009), not from any documentary source.

sources.ref: Chronicle of Higher Education, 'Debating the History of Slavery on Senegal's Goree Island' — the museum's literature puts 15-20 million through the House of Slaves; Curtin on the 50,000 vs 20 million

HNN (History News Network), 'The Myth of Goree Island' — Curtin's assessment: island was never a key departure point; ~50,000, not 20 million; House built 1775-1778 by a wealthy merchant; door's rocks, beach as loading point
RIA Scolony blog, 'Goree Island, House of Slaves and the Door of No Return' — Ndiaye's 10-15M figures vs Araujo's documentation; Curtin ~26,000; 40-45,000 (1677-1818)
Ana Lucia Araujo (2020) — ~33,000 trafficked through Goree (cited via historytools.org summary)
Voyages: The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database — 12.5 million embarked across the entire trade (the denominator that kills the 15-20M claim)

competing_hypotheses: Philip Curtin's estimate of ~26,000 exported via Goree (reconstructed from company records and the trade's own documentation)
Ana Lucia Araujo's 2020 estimate of ~33,000 trafficked through Goree (mid-15th to mid-19th c.)
Other scholarly estimates of 40,000-45,000 (1677-1818) — all orders of magnitude below the millions claimed
falsifiability: A documentary corpus (voyage records, company ledgers) showing Goree embarkations in the millions — against the database's ~35,000 voyages, which place the whole trade at 12.5 million.

title: The deathbed copy: the legend and the one letter
claim: A finished printed copy of De revolutionibus reached Nicolaus Copernicus on the day of his death (24 May 1543) — the legend of the dying astronomer presented with his book as he lay on his deathbed. The ENTIRE claim rests on one primary source: a letter from Canon Tiedemann Giese to Rheticus, written weeks after the death (recorded via Koestler 1963, citing Prowe 1883-84, vol. 1, pt. 2, p. 554): 'For many days he had been deprived of his memory and mental vigour; he only saw his completed book at the last moment, on the day he died.' Christie's catalog states 'a finished copy of the De revolutionibus only reached Copernicus on the eve of his death, his reaction to this addition is unknown.' Jagiellonian classics scholar Jacek Partyka (2023) calls it 'legend' and wryly doubts Copernicus could have approved anything. Copernicus was apoplectic and possibly unconscious; what he actually perceived is unknown.
place: Frauenburg (Frombork), Poland — Copernicus's death
grade_reason: Single-source attestation through a long transmission chain, with the witness himself describing days of lost memory and vigour; no independent corroboration of what Copernicus perceived. The legend's facts are fenced exactly where the one letter draws them.
earliest_attestation: Single source: Tiedemann Giese's letter to Rheticus, weeks after 24 May 1543. Recorded via Koestler (1963) citing Prowe (1883-84). No independent witness.

sources.ref: Tiedemann Giese to Rheticus, weeks after 24 May 1543 (via Koestler 1963, citing Prowe, Nicolaus Copernicus, 1883-84, vol. 1, pt. 2, p. 554): 'he only saw his completed book at the last moment, on the day he died'
Christie's lot notes: 'a finished copy of the De revolutionibus only reached Copernicus on the eve of his death, his reaction to this addition is unknown'

Astronomy.com (2023): Jagiellonian scholar Jacek Partyka — 'According to legend, Copernicus was presented with a copy of the published book as he lay on his deathbed'; Edward Rosen (1995) scathing on Koestler's account

competing_hypotheses: The romantic version: he held the book, understood it, and died content — unknowable on the evidence; Giese's letter says only that he 'saw' it at the last moment, and describes days of lost memory and vigour
Edward Rosen (1995) was 'particularly scathing' about Koestler's Sleepwalkers account of these events — the transmission chain (Giese -> Prowe -> Koestler) is itself a scholarly contested chain
falsifiability: No contemporary evidence could falsify what a dying man perceived; the grade stays CLAIMED unless a second independent witness emerges or the Giese letter is shown to be inauthentic.

title: De revolutionibus (1543): the book as printed
claim: Nicolaus Copernicus's De revolutionibus orbium coelestium was printed at Nuremberg by Johannes Petreius in 1543. Rheticus delivered the manuscript in 1542 and supervised the printing, then left for a Leipzig mathematics professorship before completion; Andreas Osiander took over. Osiander added the unsigned instrumentalist preface Ad lectorem ('To the Reader Concerning the Hypotheses of this Work' — 'these hypotheses need not be true nor even probable; if they provide a calculus consistent with the observations, that alone is enough') without Copernicus's authorization: the standard scholarly position is that it was added unsigned and long mistaken for Copernicus's own (evidence: Rheticus crossed it out in his copy and would 'rough up the fellow' if he knew; Giese protested to the Nuremberg city council; Schreiber's note; Praetorius learned of Osiander's authorship from Rheticus and wrote his name in the margin; Kepler methodically exposed Osiander as the author in the 1609 introduction to Astronomia nova). Owen Gingerich's census located 269 surviving copies and estimates the print run at 400-500 copies — usual for the period. The book was 'suspended until corrected' by the Index Decree of 5 March 1616.
place: Nuremberg (Johannes Petreius's press, 1543)
grade_reason: The 1543 imprint, the surviving manuscript, the Rheticus/Giese/Schreiber/Praetorius contemporary evidence of Osiander's unauthorized preface, Kepler's 1609 exposure, and Gingerich's 269-copy census with the 400-500 print-run estimate — multiple independent documentary and bibliographic lines.
earliest_attestation: The 1543 Nuremberg printing itself (Johannes Petreius); Copernicus's manuscript survives at the Jagiellonian Library, Krakow. Osiander's authorship of the preface exposed by Kepler in Astronomia nova (1609); Rheticus's and Praetorius's marginal evidence contemporaneous.

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'De revolutionibus orbium coelestium' — Nuremberg 1543, Petreius; Rheticus's delivery and Leipzig departure; Osiander's takeover; the Rheticus/Giese/Schreiber/Praetorius evidence; Kepler's 1609 exposure; Gingerich's 269-copy census and 400-500 estimate

Christie's lot notes (via quoted Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy / Gingerich): 269 surviving copies, print run 'quite usual for the period' at 400-500; 'orbium coelestium' as probable late Osiander addition
Kepler, Astronomia nova (1609), introduction — methodical exposure of Osiander as the preface's author

competing_hypotheses: Whether Osiander's preface shielded the book from censure or delayed Copernican reception — debated; the preface's EFFECT is contested while its unauthorized authorship is the scholarly consensus
Christie's lot notes report the title's final words 'orbium coelestium' were 'probably also a late addition by Osiander' — reported, not certain, and carried here as such
The 'initial print run of 400 failing to sell out' shorthand — rests on the weak end of Gingerich's 400-500 estimate and a sales inference the census data doesn't cleanly support
falsifiability: A pre-1543 printed edition, or evidence Copernicus authorized Osiander's preface, would revise the record; the manuscript, the 1543 imprint, the crossed-out prefaces in contemporary copies, and Kepler's 1609 exposure form a closed documentary loop.

title: The Ottoman 'continuous decline' thesis
claim: The Ottoman Empire entered a continuous, unbroken decline starting in the late 16th century (after Suleiman the Magnificent's death in 1566), decaying steadily in military, fiscal, and administrative power for ~350 years until 1922 — the traditional 'decline thesis.'
place: Istanbul (historiographical debate centered on the Porte's archive and European Orientalist historiography)
grade_reason: The thesis confuses a literary genre with an economic diagnosis: Ottomanists showed the nasihatname complaints were a trope present even in Suleiman's 'golden age' (Howard, Abou-El-Haj), while the archives document adaptation — 'transformation, not decline' (Faroqhi, İnalcık). A 350-year unbroken decline that produces a 623-year state refutes itself; the thesis is 'discarded' (Tezcan 2010).
earliest_attestation: The thesis's raw material: Ottoman nasihatname ('advice for kings') literature, 16th-17th c. — the complaints themselves are real documents; the reading of them as objective evidence of decline is the 20th-c. error.

sources.ref: Jane Hathaway, The Arab Lands under Ottoman Rule, 1516-1800 (Pearson, 2008), pp. 7-8 — 'deconstruction of the so-called Ottoman decline thesis'
Baki Tezcan, The Second Ottoman Empire: Political and Social Transformation in the Early Modern World (Cambridge UP, 2010), p. 9 — the conventional narrative 'has been discarded'
Halil İnalcık, 'Military and Fiscal Transformation in the Ottoman Empire, 1600-1700' — the period titled as transformation, not decline

Douglas Howard and Rifa'at Ali Abou-El-Haj — the nasihatname critique: 'complaint about the times' as literary trope, writers not uninfluenced by their own biases; present even during Suleiman's golden age
Rifa'at Ali Abou-El-Haj, Formation of the Modern State: The Ottoman Empire, Sixteenth to Eighteenth Centuries (SUNY, 1991)
Wikipedia, 'Ottoman decline thesis' — summary of the deconstruction literature

competing_hypotheses: The revisionist 'transformation' thesis: crisis and adaptation, not decay — 17th-18th c. institutional change under a military-fiscal state (Faroqhi, İnalcık, Abou-El-Haj, Tezcan)

The honest middle: no 350-year decay, but real late-era crises — 19th-century fiscal collapse, military defeats, and the empire's eventual outliving by war; decline as teleology vs. decline as dated crises
falsifiability: Already falsified by the archival record: 17th-century military-fiscal adaptation, monetization, decentralization policies, and three centuries of state continuity after the supposed terminal date.

title: 'The Byzantine Empire' — the name is 1557, not 330
claim: The empire we call 'Byzantine' called itself 'Byzantine' — that 'the Byzantine Empire' was its own name and it was a civilization separate from Rome.
place: Augsburg (publication place of Wolf's Corpus, Germany)
grade_reason: The name is a documented 1557 coinage applied 104 years after the empire's end; the empire's own endonym is multiply attested as Roman (see evt-rhomaioi-001). No pre-1557 source uses 'Byzantine' as a self-name.
earliest_attestation: Hieronymus Wolf (1516–1580), Corpus Historiae Byzantinae (1557) — the first systematic application of 'Byzantine' to the medieval Greek state; popularized in the 18th–19th c. (Montesquieu's Considerations, 1734; 19th-c. scholarship)

sources.ref: Hieronymus Wolf, Corpus Historiae Byzantinae (1557)
Kaldellis, Anthony (2019), Romanland: Ethnicity and Empire in Byzantium, Harvard UP
Browning, Robert (1992), The Byzantine Empire
Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Byzantine Empire' — the inhabitants 'referred to themselves as Romans'

competing_hypotheses: The neutral reading: 'Byzantine' is a harmless modern historiographical convenience — scholars use it to distinguish the Greek-speaking medieval phase from the Latin classical phase; the empire's Roman identity is usually footnoted
The minority position that the name is authentically ancient — no support: before 1557 no source, Western or Eastern, applies 'Byzantine' to the state
falsifiability: A pre-1557 source — imperial document, inscription, coin, or the empire's own literature — using 'Byzantine'/'Byzantines' as the state's or people's name

title: Shakespeare of Stratford wrote the canon — the documentary case
claim: William Shakespeare of Stratford-upon-Avon (1564-1616) wrote the plays and poems attributed to him.
place: Stratford-upon-Avon & London (the Globe), England
grade_reason: The historical record is unequivocal in ascribing the canon to a William Shakespeare: 23+ lifetime references name him specifically as a writer, his name stands on the poems' title pages and at least 16 plays published in his lifetime, fellow actors Heminges and Condell assembled the 1623 First Folio, Jonson's Folio eulogy names the 'Sweet Swan of Avon,' and the 1612 Belott-Mountjoy deposition carries his signed testimony. No autograph play manuscript survives, which holds the grade below VERIFIED.
earliest_attestation: 1592 — Robert Greene's Groatsworth of Wit attacks Shakespeare as an actor turned playwright ('Shake-scene'); 1593-94 title pages of the poems name William Shakespeare; 1598 title pages of Richard II and Richard III name 'William Shake-speare'

sources.ref: Robert Greene, Groatsworth of Wit (1592) — 'Shake-scene' attack, contemporary
Title pages: Venus and Adonis (1593), Lucrece (1594), Richard II & Richard III (1598) — 'William Shakespeare' as author
Francis Meres, Palladis Tamia (1598) — names Shakespeare as playwright and poet, lists 12 plays
Heminges & Condell, Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies (First Folio, 1623)
Ben Jonson, eulogy in the First Folio (1623) — 'Sweet Swan of Avon'
Belott v. Mountjoy deposition (1612) — Shakespeare's signed legal testimony as witness
Wikipedia, 'Shakespeare authorship question' — survey of the documentary case and scholarly consensus

competing_hypotheses: The anti-Stratfordian thesis: a hidden aristocrat or courtier (Francis Bacon, Christopher Marlowe, Edward de Vere, Mary Sidney, Queen Elizabeth I, or another of 80+ proposed candidates) wrote the works and used Shakespeare's name as a front
The collaborative reality: some plays were co-written (Fletcher, Middleton) — which concerns shared authorship, not front-men, and leaves Shakespeare's principal authorship intact
falsifiability: A contemporary document showing someone else contracted or paid for the plays under Shakespeare's name, or a contemporary expression of doubt — none exists in 170 years of searching.

title: Gesner's 1565 lead-holder: the first pencil drawing
claim: In 1565, Conrad Gesner (Conrad von Gesner) published, in his book on fossils, a drawing of a strip of graphite held inside a tube of wood — the first depiction of a lead-holder / wood pencil.
place: Zurich, Switzerland
grade_reason: Independently attested by the digitized-book record (Biodiversity Heritage Library) and multiple histories; held below VERIFIED because this pass consulted the attestations secondhand, not the 1565 edition itself.
earliest_attestation: Gesner's 1565 publication, held digitized by the Biodiversity Heritage Library.

sources.ref: NPR / KHSU 'Trace The Remarkable History Of The Humble Pencil' (2016): 'In 1565, Swiss naturalist Conrad Gessner published a drawing of a strip of graphite inside a tube of wood — the first depiction of a wood pencil.'

MRS Bulletin (Cambridge, 1994), 'Leading Up To The Pencil': 'In 1565 the German-Swiss naturalist Konrad von Gesner first wrote about a new writing instrument composed of a chip of black lead inserted into a wooden holder.'

competing_hypotheses: The drawing as an illustration of a known workshop practice Gesner did not invent — first depiction is not first invention
The Keswick-graphite 1564 storm legend as the material cause — the storm story itself is labeled legend by its own tellers
falsifiability: An earlier published depiction of a lead-holder, or proof the 1565 drawing is a later insertion, would overturn this.

title: The Delft tower experiment, 1586 — the documented drop Galileo never did
claim: In 1586, Simon Stevin and Jan Cornets de Groot (the father of Hugo de Groot) carried two lead balls - one ten times heavier than the other - up the Nieuwe Kerk tower in Delft, dropped them 30 feet onto a wooden platform, and heard a single bang: the balls fell at the same rate, disproving Aristotle's weight-proportional fall theory.
place: Nieuwe Kerk, Delft, Netherlands
grade_reason: Contemporary self-published account naming a witness and the place, consistent with Stevin's statics program; held below VERIFIED because the only source is Stevin's own book and the measurement was human ears hearing one bang.
earliest_attestation: Simon Stevin, De Beghinselen der Weeghconst ('The Principles of the Art of Weighing'), 1586 - Stevin's own contemporary published report of the experiment.

sources.ref: Simon Stevin, De Beghinselen der Weeghconst (1586): 'Let us take ... two balls of lead, the one ten times bigger and heavier than the other, and let them drop together from 30 feet high ... This proves that Aristotle is wrong.'
St Andrews MacTutor History of Mathematics biography of Simon Stevin - experiment dated 1586, report preceded Galileo's first gravity treatise by 3 years
E. J. Dijksterhuis, The Principal Works of Simon Stevin (1955-1966) - the scholarly edition of Stevin's Dutch text

competing_hypotheses: The experiment is known only from Stevin's own published report - no independent contemporary replication is documented, and modern reconstructions ask how clean a 30-foot drop with human ears could really be
The passage's exact authorship and whether de Groot was co-experimenter or witness is a matter of Stevin's own framing ('as the highly educated Jan Cornets de Groot ... and I have done')
falsifiability: Contemporary evidence (de Groot family records, Delft civic records) contradicting the experiment, or proof that the Weeghconst passage was a later interpolation, would overturn this record.

title: The Leaning Tower drop — the experiment Galileo never ran
claim: Galileo Galilei, while professor of mathematics at the University of Pisa (c. 1589-1592), publicly dropped balls of different weights from the Leaning Tower of Pisa to demonstrate that they fall at the same rate, disproving Aristotle in front of his colleagues and students.
place: Leaning Tower of Pisa, Pisa, Italy
grade_reason: No account by Galileo himself exists in his writings, letters, or notes; the story first appears in a hagiographic biography written 12 years after his death; most historians treat the event as a thought experiment at best, not a physical test.
earliest_attestation: Vincenzo Viviani's Racconto istorico (biography of Galileo), written 1654 - twelve years after Galileo's 1642 death - and published posthumously in 1717.

sources.ref: Vincenzo Viviani, Racconto istorico della vita del Sig.r Galileo Galilei (1654; publ. 1717) - sole origin of the tower story
Lane Cooper (1935) - showed Viviani's story unsupported by any evidence in Galileo's own papers
Palmieri 1989, 'Galileo, Viviani and the Tower of Pisa', Studies in History and Philosophy of Science, Vol. 20, No. 4, pp. 435-451 - Viviani's biography unreliable as modern history of science
Museo Galileo (Florence) - the tower story treated as dubious; Galileo's own writings contain no account of it
Galileo's Two New Sciences (1638) - presents inclined-plane experiments (Third Day, 'a full hundred times'), never a Pisa drop

competing_hypotheses: Stillman Drake (the leading 20th-century Galileo scholar) inclined toward believing Viviani's story true - the dissent is named, but it rests on Viviani's word against the entire silence of Galileo's own papers
Galileo may have performed informal, unrecorded drop tests (e.g. from towers at Padua or Florence) that never became the Pisa story - reasoned, unattested; DEBUNKED as an event, not as a possibility
Viviani may have conflated Galileo's documented thought experiments about falling bodies (in De motu) with a staged demonstration

The antecedent tradition matters: John Philoponus (6th c.), Benedetto Varchi's report of two Italian experimenters (1544), Domingo de Soto (1551), Giambattista Benedetti (1553) had all questioned Aristotle's weight-speed proportionality before Galileo was born
falsifiability: A contemporary document - a letter, university record, or notebook entry from 1589-1592 - attesting the Pisa demonstration would overturn this record; Viviani's posthumous 1654 account alone cannot.

title: The tine evolution: two tines to three to four
claim: The European table fork evolved from two tines to three to four. The two-prong fork dominated through the 17th century (the earliest two-prong fork bearing an English hallmark, engraved with the Earl of Rutland's coat of arms, dates to 1632 and is held by the V&A). Between the 17th and 18th centuries the tines increased from two to three and then to four — the widely spaced two-prong fork could not spear peas and grains, and from the late 17th to mid-18th century the fork's profile changed from flat to slightly curved to accommodate scooping. The four-tine design became current in the early 19th century; two-tine forks nevertheless lasted in British common usage into the 20th century.
place: London, England (the V&A's 1632 hallmarked fork)
grade_reason: CORROBORATED: multiply attested by museum artifacts (the V&A's 1632 hallmarked fork), cutlery scholarship, and period sources (Coryate 1611). Held below VERIFIED only on the exact transition dates, which vary by source and region.
earliest_attestation: Period cutlery and museum artifacts; the 1632 Earl of Rutland hallmarked two-prong fork (Victoria and Albert Museum, London)

sources.ref: Scribd: 'The Evolution of the Fork' — 1632 Earl of Rutland hallmarked two-prong fork (V&A); tines increased 2→3→4 between the 17th and 18th c.; flat-to-curved profile, late 17th to mid-18th c.; Thomas Coryate, 'Coryat's Crudities' (1611)
Encyclopedia.com: 'Cutlery' — early European forks bronze/silver, two tines; tines varied 2→4 in late 16th/early 17th c.; two-tined fork lasted in British common usage until the 20th c.
Wikipedia: 'Fork' — four-tine design became current in the early 19th century

Fast Company: 'A tool of the devil' — 17th c. addition of third then fourth tine; curving the tines; Scandinavia the last European holdout, end of 17th c.; Charles I's 1633 'It is decent to use a fork'; Queen Elizabeth I preferring fingers

competing_hypotheses: Exact dates of the three-to-four transition vary by source and by region — Britain, Scandinavia, and North America adopted on different schedules
The 'why': practicality (peas slipping through) vs. fashion — both carried as drivers
falsifiability: A securely dated pre-1600 four-tine European table fork would overturn the progression; none is attested

title: The 'wampum was Indian money' telling
claim: The popular telling that wampum — the white and purple shell beads of the Eastern Woodlands — was 'Indian money', a currency of Indigenous societies, is false. In Munsee, Haudenosaunee, and neighboring societies the beads were not used as money: they served spiritual and ceremonial purposes, signified authority, sealed diplomacy, and were woven into belts whose designs acted as mnemonic devices for history, law, and tradition. The currency reading is the colonists' projection, not the makers' practice.
place: Eastern Woodlands / coastal New England and New Netherland
grade_reason: The Indigenous-side evidence is convergent and direct: 17th-c. Dutch observation, Haudenosaunee educators' own statements, and Ceci's archaeological finding that treaty/condolence belts were curated, not traded — against zero pre-contact monetary evidence.
earliest_attestation: Dutch traders' 1620s observations of wampum's place in Munsee culture (noted as ceremonial/diplomatic, not monetary); modern statement: Philipse Manor Hall / Smithsonian National Numismatic Collection exhibit text

sources.ref: Philipse Manor Hall — 'Wampum and Colonial Currency' (citing the Smithsonian National Numismatic Collection): 'Centuries of misinformation spread the idea, still repeated today, that wampum acted as currency in the Indigenous cultures of the Eastern Woodlands... they were not used as money in Munsee society or in those of neighboring Indigenous cultures'

Rogue Art Historian — 'Law You Can Hold: Wampum, Sovereignty, and the Refusal to Disappear' — Haudenosaunee Guide for Educators: Europeans' legal-tender use was appropriation; 'Haudenosaunee themselves did not use wampum as money'; Ceci's archaeological study: condolence strings and treaty belts curated, not freely traded
Cronon, William (via veridelisi synthesis) — wampum as 'medium of gift giving' among Indigenous societies rather than medium of commerce

JSTOR Daily — 'Wampum was Massachusetts' First Legal Currency' — Bradley: wampum's success as cross-cultural communication ('show respect, negotiate and seal agreements'); beads cut from seashells, value by belt length and quality

competing_hypotheses: The numismatic-conventional reading (older literature): wampum as 'the common Indian currency' — the telling this record grades

The gift-economy refinement (Cronon): among Indigenous societies wampum functioned as a medium of gift-giving and diplomacy rather than commerce — consistent with the DEBUNKED verdict on the money claim
falsifiability: A pre-contact Indigenous price schedule, account, or legal code denominating obligations in wampum — none has been found; the colonial legal-tender phase (separate record) is the documented money use

title: Cawdrey's Table Alphabeticall, 1604 — the first English dictionary
claim: In 1604 the schoolmaster Robert Cawdrey published A Table Alphabeticall in London: the first monolingual English dictionary — 120 pages, 2,543 headwords with brief (often single-word) definitions, written 'for the benefit and help of ladies, gentlewomen, or any other unskillful persons.'
place: London, England (published 1604; Cawdrey was living in Coventry)
grade_reason: The artifact survives: the sole surviving copy of the 1604 first edition is held at the Bodleian Library, Oxford, and was republished by the Bodleian in 2007 with an introduction by John Simpson (chief editor of the OED's second edition). The OED's own historical introduction treats Cawdrey's 1604 volume as the acorn of the tradition ('like placing the original acorn beside the oak that has grown out of it').
earliest_attestation: The 1604 title page itself: 'A table alphabeticall conteyning and teaching the true writing, and vnderstanding of hard vsuall English wordes... gathered for the benefit & helpe of ladies, gentlewomen, or any other vnskilfull persons.'

sources.ref: Wikipedia — 'A Table Alphabeticall': first monolingual English dictionary, London 1604; 120 pages, 2,543 words with brief definitions; claimed purpose 'for the benefit and help of unskillful persons'; sole surviving copy at the Bodleian Library, Oxford.
Wikipedia — 'Robert Cawdrey': Cawdrey, assisted by his son Thomas, created the first monolingual English dictionary while living in Coventry; first six entries quoted (abandon, abash, abba...).

Bodleian Library Publishing / readings.com.au (2015): the 1604 Table Alphabeticall republished from the sole surviving Bodleian copy with John Simpson's introduction; 'for the benefit of Ladies, Gentlewomen or any other unskilfull persons.'

competing_hypotheses: Whether 2,543 or 2,499 headwords in the first edition (sources vary; Wikipedia's article reports 2,543 while the Robert Cawdrey article reports 2,499 for the first edition — the fourth edition 1617 defined 3,264)
Whether a 120-page list of mostly brief definitions deserves the name 'dictionary' — the scholarly consensus (OED's historical introduction, the Bodleian's 2007 reprint) says yes
falsifiability: The existence of an earlier monolingual English dictionary (there is none in the record; Cawdrey is the consensus origin) or proof the 1604 imprint is misdated would overturn it.

title: Don Quixote was the first novel ever written
claim: Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes — first part published 1605, second part 1615 — was the first novel ever written.
place: Madrid, Spain (1605 first-part printing, Juan de la Cuesta)
grade_reason: The dates kill the superlative, not the book. Genji's c. 1008–1021 attestation is near-contemporary and independent (two diarists); Quixote's is 1605. Six centuries of fiction separate the two.
earliest_attestation: The 1605 Madrid edition itself; the 1614 Tarragona edition of Avellaneda's Segundo tomo (the unauthorized sequel that forced Cervantes's Part II); Cervantes's contemporary dedications, prologues, and the 2015 Cervantes-remains findings carry the biography, not the publication.

sources.ref: El ingenioso hidalgo don Quixote de la Mancha, Part I (Madrid: Francisco de Robles / Juan de la Cuesta, 1605); Part II (1615) — the dated artifacts

Avellaneda's Segundo tomo del ingenioso hidalgo don Quixote de la Mancha (Tarragona, 1614) — unauthorized sequel; independent external witness that Part I was in circulation by 1614, and that Cervantes answered it inside his own Part II
Intellicurean, 'the novel' (2026): 'the book that literary history calls the first modern novel' — the qualifier as the field states it
2002 Norwegian Book Clubs poll of 100 authors from 54 countries: Don Quixote named the best literary work ever written — the reputation is real; the 'first novel' superlative is the inflation

competing_hypotheses: The majority scholarly position: Quixote is the first MODERN novel (metafiction, unreliable narrator, interior psychology) — the qualifier 'modern' carries the entire honest version of the claim; without it the superlative is six centuries late

The Greek-romance objection: if the bar is merely 'extended prose fiction,' even Genji is not first — Chariton's Callirhoe (1st c. CE) and Apuleius's Golden Ass (2nd c. CE) predate it; the superlative then requires an even narrower definition, which is not how the popular claim is stated
falsifiability: Already falsified: The Tale of Genji (evt-tale-of-genji-001) is securely attested at c. 1008–1021 — six centuries before Quixote's first part. Only a redefinition of 'novel' that excludes Genji could resurrect the bare claim, and the popular statement carries no such qualifier.

title: DEBUNKED: 'Galileo invented the telescope'
claim: The textbook sentence 'Galileo invented the telescope' is false. Galileo Galilei never claimed to have invented the telescope — he learned of the Dutch device from his friend Paolo Sarpi in Venice (who received the Hague newsletter in November 1608), built his own improved instruments from August 1609 (up to ~20-30x), and was the FIRST to turn a telescope to systematic astronomical observation: the four moons of Jupiter (January 1610), the mountains of the Moon, the phases of Venus — published in Sidereus Nuncius (March 1610).
