The device demonstrably predates his first build by documented months; the States-General Acts show it already being copied in Middelburg before he had heard of it. Twenty-eighth DEBUNKED family.
place: Middelburg, Netherlands (where the device was made); Venice, Italy (where Galileo learned of it, Nov 1608)
grade_reason: Direct chronological contradiction by contemporaneous documents: the invention is on record in the States-General Acts ten months before Galileo's first instrument. Galileo's own account agrees — he never claimed the invention. The textbook sentence has no source; the Dutch priority has a government paper trail.
earliest_attestation: The same documentary trail as evt-telescope-invention-001 (States-General Acts, Oct 1608) precedes Galileo's instrument by ~10 months; Galileo's own correspondence documents learning of the device and then building one. His achievement is attested in Sidereus Nuncius (March 1610) — the claim under grading is the priority sentence, not his observations.

sources.ref: Pelling, 'Who invented the telescope?': Sarpi received the Hague newsletter in Venice in November 1608 and discussed it with Galileo — the documented learning chain

Britannica (print article, 22 March 2024): Jacques Bovedere of Paris reported the invention to Galileo, 'who promptly built his own telescope' — the secondary tradition's own phrasing concedes the build came second
Galileo's Sidereus Nuncius (March 1610) + the January 1610 Jupiter observations — primary attestation of what he ACTUALLY did first, kept fenced in the grade scope

competing_hypotheses: The charitable reading: 'invented' meant as 'improved and astronomicalized' — but the school-textbook sentence says invented, and the record grades what is said, not what might have been meant

Thomas Harriot's lunar observations of July 1609 — earlier through-the-tube astronomy than Galileo's Sidereus Nuncius; named here as the honest rival for 'first telescopic observer,' which this record does not grade (the invention claim is the graded target)

The 'independent invention' reading: Galileo built his telescopes from hearing a description, working out the optics himself — real ingenuity, documented, and not the same claim as invention ex nihilo
falsifiability: A document showing Galileo built a working telescope before October 1608 — none exists; his own letters document the learning sequence (Sarpi → build → improve → point skyward).

title: The first documented telescopes: Lipperhey's 1608 States-General patent bid
claim: The first documented telescopes were made in the Netherlands in 1608: Hans Lipperhey, a spectacle-maker of Middelburg, petitioned the States General for a patent on an instrument 'for seeing things far away as if they were nearby' on 2 October 1608; the assembly tested it (4 Oct), paid him 900 florins (6 Oct), and ordered binocular versions (15 Dec) — denying the patent because Jacob Metius filed a competing application weeks later and the knowledge was already widespread. Lipperhey is the first DOCUMENTED claimant; the original Dutch design (convex objective + concave eyepiece, ~3x) spread across Europe within months. This is the timeline's first early-modern-optics record.
place: Middelburg, Zeeland, Netherlands (Lipperhey's shop; States-General proceedings at The Hague)
grade_reason: Multiple independent contemporaneous documentary lines — the States-General Acts, the committee test, the florin payments, the rival Metius application, the Hague newsletter that carried the invention to Venice by November 1608 — but 'first ever inventor' cannot be closed against untestable priority claims, so the grade stops at CORROBORATED.
earliest_attestation: Contemporaneous government record: the Acts of the States General of the Netherlands, 2 Oct 1608 — Lipperhey's petition; committee test report 4 Oct; 900-florin payment 6 Oct; binocular-order 15 Dec 1608. Reported by Van Swinden's research from the Hague government archives (summarized in Encyclopaedia Britannica, 9th ed., Telescope article).

sources.ref: Acts of the States General, 2 Oct 1608: Lipperhey's petition (via Van Swinden's research in the Hague government archives; summarized in Encyclopaedia Britannica, 9th ed., 'Telescope')

Wikipedia, 'History of the telescope' — first record of a telescope: Lipperhey's 2 Oct 1608 patent filing; Metius's competing application weeks later; the patent denied because the knowledge seemed ubiquitous

Britannica (print article, updated 22 March 2024): Lipperhey 'traditionally credited with inventing the telescope (1608)'; 900 florins paid, patent denied, instruments supplied to Henry IV of France before end of 1608

Nick Pelling, 'Who invented the telescope?' (The Free Library, Astronomy Now): the 2 Oct patent submission, 4 Oct committee, 900-florin commission, 14 Oct Zeeland 'young man,' 17 Oct Metius application; the Hague peace-conference diplomats as the transmission vector; Sarpi receiving the newsletter in Venice in November 1608

competing_hypotheses: Jacob Metius of Alkmaar filed his own patent application ~17 Oct 1608 — but his petition conceded his instrument was 'not quite as good as Lipperhey's,' so he documents a rival, not priority

Zacharias Janssen, via his son Johannes Zachariassen's 1634 claim of a 1590 invention — dismantled by Van Helden et al. in 'Origins of the Telescope' (2010): the son's story was self-serving (fame/financial gain), Janssen was not a spectacle-maker before 1615, and Middelburg's archives burned in the May 1940 bombing
Nick Pelling's Catalan-origin hypothesis (early 17th-c. Catalan telescopes) — possible but documentary-thin compared to the States-General Acts
The 'ancient lenses' argument (Nimrud lens, Viking lenses): real optical objects, but none demonstrates a lens-tube imaging instrument — a lens is not a telescope
falsifiability: A dated 1607-or-earlier document showing a working lens-tube telescope built by a named maker would move the priority — none exists; the 1590 Janssen claim fails on its own timeline (born late 1585, 'age two at invention').

title: The compound microscope before Leeuwenhoek (documented by 1619)
claim: Compound microscopes — two-lens tubes — existed and were publicly demonstrated by 1619 at the latest, well before Antonie van Leeuwenhoek's first publications in the 1670s.
place: London (Drebbel's 1619 demonstration); Rome/Florence (Galileo's occhiolino)
grade_reason: Two independently documented compound microscopes predate Leeuwenhoek's publications by half a century: Galileo's occhiolino (built 1609–10, demonstrated to Cesi in 1624, testified by Viviani in 1654) and Cornelis Drebbel's two-convex compound microscope presented in London in 1619 (and shown in Rome c. 1622). Giovanni Faber of the Linceans coined the word 'microscope' in 1625 — a word cannot be coined for an instrument that does not exist. Held below VERIFIED on the identity of the absolute first maker: the c. 1590 Janssen attribution (Boreel 1655 / Pierre Borel 1656) is sworn testimony, not contemporary documentation, and Zacharias Janssen's age at the alleged date (2–5) keeps the name contested — likely his father Hans Janssen or grandfather Hans Martens, or no single inventor at all. The instrument's existence by 1619 is the graded claim; who first built it is honestly held open.
earliest_attestation: Documented exemplars: Galileo's occhiolino 1609–10 (presented to Cesi 1624); Cornelis Drebbel's two-convex compound microscope presented in London 1619.

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Timeline of microscope technology' — Janssen attribution (disputed), Galileo occhiolino 1609–10, Drebbel London 1619, Faber coins 'microscope' 1625
IMSS (Florence), 'History of the microscope' (estoria04.pdf) — Viviani's 1654 testimony crediting Galileo with the compound microscope; Fontana's 1646 claim; Drebbel's instruments
Wikipedia, 'Zacharias Janssen' — Boreel 1655 investigation; Johannes Zachariassen's sworn 1590 testimony; Pierre Borel 1656 adoption; the age problem and the Hans Martens alternative

competing_hypotheses: The Galileo-priority framing: Galileo's 1609–10 occhiolino is the first documented compound microscope, with Viviani's 1654 testimony as the witness
The Janssen-priority framing: the Middelburg instrument of c. 1590 (Hans Martens or the Janssens) is first — the name is the dispute, not the date range
falsifiability: Proof that the 1619 Drebbel instrument and the 1609–10 Galileo instrument are later fabrications with no contemporary documentation

title: The expulsion of the Moriscos (1609-1614)
claim: Philip III of Spain, at the instigation of the Duke of Lerma and Archbishop Juan de Ribera of Valencia, ordered the expulsion of the Moriscos (baptized descendants of Iberian Muslims) between 1609 and 1614. Contemporary accounts put the number expelled at roughly 270,000-300,000 people.
place: Valencia (first embarkations, 1609)
grade_reason: The decrees and the multi-kingdom embarkation sequence are documented across independent records; the number rests on contemporary estimates (honestly ranged 270,000-300,000), which holds the grade at CORROBORATED rather than VERIFIED.
earliest_attestation: The 1609 expulsion decrees and the Council of State decision of April 1609; contemporary embarkation accounts (e.g. Pere Oromig's 'Embarkation of Moriscos in Valencia').

sources.ref: Expulsion decrees 1609-1614 ("under the pain of death and confiscation ... to take with them no money, bullion, jewels or bills of exchange ... just what they could carry")
Contemporary accounts setting the number expelled at 270,000-300,000 (about 4% of Spain's population)
Treaty of Granada, November 1491 — the broken promise (religious tolerance and fair treatment); Cisneros's forced conversions 1499-1501 and the Alpujarras revolts as the breach's record

Wright 2017 ("Ethnic Cleansing in Habsburg Spain: Philip III's Motivations"; annotations Smith 2023) — the Council decision, Lerma's role, the 12,000 killed before embarkation; Dominguez Ortiz on the Valencian economic collapse

competing_hypotheses: Higher estimates (~350,000 Moriscos present in Spain in 1609; some historians) — the embarked-vs-present distinction
Castilian Moriscos were considerably more integrated and many merged into wider society rather than departing (the "disappearance" counter-reading)
falsifiability: Archival embarkation rolls showing a materially different scale, or proof the decrees were substantially unexecuted

title: January 1610 — the moons of Jupiter (what Galileo really proved with a real instrument)
claim: In January 1610, Galileo Galilei observed four points of light near Jupiter with his ~20x telescope, tracking them night after night (7-15 January) as they changed position relative to the planet; they were moons orbiting Jupiter. Published March 1610 in Sidereus Nuncius ('The Starry Messenger').
place: Padua, Italy (observations); Venice (publication)
grade_reason: Galileo's dated notebooks + the published Sidereus Nuncius + multiple independent 1610 confirmations with their own instruments; no serious dispute in the literature.
earliest_attestation: Galileo's observing notebooks, 7-15 January 1610, then Sidereus Nuncius (Venice, March 1610) - the first scientific work built on telescopic observation.

sources.ref: Galileo Galilei, Sidereus Nuncius (Venice, March 1610) - the daily observation record with diagrams
Galileo's observing notebooks, 7-15 January 1610 - first entry shows Jupiter with three asterisks east and west
Johannes Kepler, Dissertatio cum Nuncio Sidereo (August 1610) - independent confirmation, delayed only by telescope scarcity
Simon Marius, Mundus Iovialis (1614) - the priority challenge; Galileo's calendar rebuttal (Gregorian Jan 7, 1610 = Julian Dec 28, 1609 vs Marius's claimed Dec 29, 1609)

competing_hypotheses: Simon Marius (Mundus Iovialis, 1614) claimed independent discovery from late December 1609 / January 1610 and attacked Galileo; the calendar dispute (Marius still on Julian time) and Marius's failure to publish until 1614 resolve priority in Galileo's favor, though modern scholarship treats Marius as a genuine independent observer, not an impostor
Thomas Harriot observed the moons (and drew the first telescopic Moon map) in late 1609 but never published - priority unclaimed, evidence uncirculated
A Chinese-history-of-astronomy claim (Gan De, 362 BCE) for a naked-eye observation of a Jovian moon is sometimes cited; unverifiable and outside the telescopic record
falsifiability: None now possible on the discovery: independent confirmations within months (Kepler's Dissertatio, August 1610; Harriot, Gaultier de la Vatelle, Fabri de Peiresc, Marius) and continuous observation ever since make the attested event multiply established.

title: The 'seven candles of the Temple' telling
claim: The Temple menorah is pictured in modern retellings as 'seven candles' — the Temple lit by seven wax candles.
place: Jerusalem (the Temple); the retelling lives in modern illustration
grade_reason: The documents kill it twice: Exodus 27:20 prescribes pure beaten olive oil ('to cause the lamp to burn always'), and Exodus 25:31-37 describes seven lamps on a gold lampstand — lamps, not candles. 'Candlestick' is the 1611 KJV translation of 'menorah' (lampstand), and it smuggled the modern candle image in; wax candles as ritual light belong to medieval Europe, a millennium-plus after the Temple fell.
earliest_attestation: The modern 'seven candles' visualization (children's books, films, greeting-card art); no ancient source describes wax candles in the Temple

sources.ref: Exodus 27:20; Leviticus 24:2 — the oil prescription (against the wax reading)
Exodus 25:31-37 — seven lamps on the lampstand (against the candle reading)
The KJV's 'candlestick' rendering of 'menorah' (lampstand) — the translation layer that manufactured the telling; the Hebrew means lampstand

competing_hypotheses: The 'candles' reading is a harmless modern visualization, not a truth-claim — graders differ on whether loose popular language deserves a DEBUNKED grade
Some Hanukkah-era synagogue lighting used beeswax candles, and modern readers project that practice backward into the Temple
falsifiability: A Second Temple-era text or artifact showing wax candles as the menorah's fuel would falsify the debunk

title: The 1621 Plymouth Harvest Feast
claim: In autumn 1621, after the first successful harvest at Plymouth, Governor William Bradford's colonists held a three-day feast attended by Massasoit and about ninety Wampanoag men; wildfowl was served, and the Wampanoag guests contributed five deer they hunted themselves.
place: Plymouth, Massachusetts
grade_reason: Two contemporary or near-contemporary primary sources (Winslow 1622, Bradford's manuscript) attest the feast. Fowl and the five deer are documented; turkey as a centerpiece is not documented, and the wider menu is reconstructed, not attested.
earliest_attestation: Edward Winslow's letter in Mourt's Relation (London, 1622) — written months after the event, the only detailed eyewitness account; corroborated briefly by William Bradford's Of Plymouth Plantation manuscript (written 1630-1651).

sources.ref: Edward Winslow's letter, Mourt's Relation (London: John Bellamie, 1622), pp. 60-61
William Bradford, Of Plymouth Plantation (manuscript, 1630-1651) — brief mention of the feast
Plimoth Patuxet Museums research: exactly two primary sources exist for autumn 1621 in Plymouth

competing_hypotheses: The feast as a transplanted English harvest-home festival (the colonists' native custom after a good yield)

The feast as a diplomatic event renewing the March 1621 treaty alliance — the Wampanoag 'coming amongst us' ambiguously suggests the guests may have arrived uninvited, and the three-day format matches Indigenous diplomatic feasting

The feast as primarily a religious thanksgiving — undercut by Winslow's own description ('recreations', 'we exercised our arms') and the Separatist practice of holding days of thanksgiving in church, not at feasts
falsifiability: A contemporary document showing the Winslow letter fabricated, or archaeological/documentary evidence that the 1621 harvest failed and no surplus existed to feast on

title: Wampum as colonial legal tender (1637–1661)
claim: After contact, European colonists made wampum a currency by law: Massachusetts declared it legal tender in 1637 (6 white or 3 black beads per penny, sums under 1 shilling; extended 1643 to sums up to 40 shillings), the Dutch used it as the colony's circulating medium for half a century, and it remained legal tender in New England until 1661 (New York to 1673, North Carolina briefly 1710). European mass-manufacturing then inflated its value roughly a hundredfold and killed it as money — a documented commodity-currency collapse.
place: Massachusetts Bay / New Netherland (Boston, New Amsterdam)
grade_reason: Statutes, rates, and account-book payments are quoted directly from colonial records across multiple independent secondary compilations; the inflation mechanism (European manufacturing) is the documented cause of the 1661 end.
earliest_attestation: Massachusetts Bay legal-tender statutes 1637/1643; Dutch West India Company accounts; Ashbel Woodward's 19th-c. numismatic paper compiling church, school, and ferry payments in wampum

sources.ref: JSTOR Daily — 'Wampum was Massachusetts' First Legal Currency': 1637 legal tender (6 white / 3 black per penny, <1s), 1643 extension (≤40s); used into the 19th century

Ashbel Woodward — 'Wampum' (Numismatic and Antiquarian Society of Philadelphia paper, via p-books): church contributions, 1683 Flatbush schoolmaster paid in wampum, 1693 NY–Brooklyn ferry 8 stivers in wampum; 'for about a quarter of a century a legal tender in New England... among the Dutch during half a century often the only circulating medium'
'Origins of Money: Wampum and Trade' — legal tender New England 1637–1661, NY to 1673, NC 1710; value 'inflated one hundred fold by Western harvesting and manufacturing techniques'

Rogue Art Historian — New England colonial governments 'briefly accepted wampum strings as legal tender, responding to a scarcity of metal coinage'; the Haudenosaunee Guide for Educators frames this as European appropriation

competing_hypotheses: The joint-production reading (Bradley): wampum money worked because neither side controlled it — Indigenous manufacture met European commercialization
The appropriation reading: the legal-tender phase was a European imposition on an Indigenous diplomatic medium, not an organic monetary evolution
falsifiability: Colonial statutes and account books showing wampum never denominated obligations — the statutes exist and are quoted verbatim in the sources

title: Harvey describes the circulation of the blood (1628)
claim: William Harvey published the experimental demonstration that blood circulates — pumped by the heart through arteries, returning through veins — in Exercitatio Anatomica de Motu Cordis et Sanguinis in Animalibus (Frankfurt, 1628).
place: London (experiments); Frankfurt (publication)
grade_reason: Published experimental demonstration, independently replicated, with the missing capillaries observed by Malpighi (1661) completing the circuit.
earliest_attestation: De Motu Cordis itself (1628); Harvey's Lumleian lectures (1616–1618) survive in manuscript

sources.ref: William Harvey, Exercitatio Anatomica de Motu Cordis et Sanguinis in Animalibus (Frankfurt: Fitzer, 1628)
Harvey's Lumleian lecture notes (1616), British Library manuscript
Independent replication of the circulation experiments by Harvey's successors (e.g., Malpighi's 1661 capillary observation in frog lungs, completing the circuit)

competing_hypotheses: Partial prior circulation ideas (Ibn al-Nafis's pulmonary circulation, 13th c. — cited comparatively, not as transmission of the idea)
falsifiability: Proof the 1628 text is a forgery, or a dated earlier publication containing the full circulatory circuit

title: The Loudun possessions, 1632–1634: the trial that burned a priest
claim: In 1632–1634 in Loudun, Kingdom of France, the nuns of the Ursuline convent reported demonic possession. The parish priest Urbain Grandier was accused of causing the possessions by sorcery, tried by a royal commission (Cardinal Richelieu's), convicted — on the evidence of the nuns' own demonic identifications (including the 'Astaroth' testimony) and a presented pact with the Devil — tortured without confessing, and burned at the stake on 18 August 1634. Public exorcisms of the nuns continued for years after his death (to c. 1638), drawing crowds. Most modern commentators (Jules Michelet, Aldous Huxley, historians of European witchcraft) read the case as a politically motivated persecution led by Richelieu.
place: Loudun, Poitou, Kingdom of France
grade_reason: The documentary event is multiply attested: the trial transcript, the dated sentence, contemporary accounts, and the long scholarly consensus on the persecution reading. The grade covers the events and the paper trail. The entity — what, if anything, possessed the nuns — is ungraded, per the attestation rule.
earliest_attestation: The authorized transcript of the 1634 trial (sentence pronounced 18 August 1634); contemporary pamphlet and chronicle accounts; the Ursuline convent's own records

sources.ref: The authorized transcript of Grandier's 1634 trial — sentence of 18 August 1634 (amende honorable, torture, burning at the stake at the place Sainte-Croix)
Wikipedia, 'Loudun possessions' — trial sequence, Richelieu's commission, the continued post-1634 exorcisms
Encyclopedia.com, 'Grandier, Urbain (d. 1634)' — the 1632 onset, the nuns' accusations, the libel-on-Richelieu motive, the trial's 'evidence of Astaroth'
Aldous Huxley, The Devils of Loudun (1952) — literature built from the documentary record, fenced as interpretation not evidence

competing_hypotheses: The Richelieu-political-persecution reading (the modern scholarly consensus): Grandier the victim of a rigged tribunal — the possessions' continuation after his death is the standing rebuttal
The trial's own verdict (Grandier guilty of sorcery): the historically operative finding, overturned by the consensus above — carried, not adjudicated
Mass hysteria / suggestion / the confessor's prompting: modern clinical readings of the nuns' behavior — the cause of the nuns' behavior is ungraded here
falsifiability: Demonstration that the 1634 trial transcript is inauthentic; contemporary documentation that Grandier was never executed or died otherwise. This record claims the documentary events (trial, burning, continued exorcisms), never the cause of the nuns' behavior.

title: The Taj Mahal: Shah Jahan's 1632-1653 marble mausoleum at Agra
claim: The Taj Mahal is the marble mausoleum on the Yamuna at Agra commissioned by the fifth Mughal emperor Shah Jahan (r. 1628-1658) for his wife Mumtaz Mahal (died 1631 giving birth to their fourteenth child); construction ran c. 1632-1648 with the surrounding complex finished c. 1653, under the principal direction of the court architect Ustad Ahmad Lahauri, using Makrana marble and pietra-dura inlay.
place: Taj Mahal, Agra, Uttar Pradesh, India
grade_reason: The artifact stands, immovable, on the Yamuna: the monument's commission, patron, dates, and chief architect are multiply attested — contemporary Mughal court chronicles, European travelers' accounts of the period, the ASI's survey record, and UNESCO's 1983 World Heritage inscription as the 'jewel of Muslim art in India.' Independent contemporary + modern attestation, plus the artifact itself.
earliest_attestation: The reign's own court chronicles (the Badshah Nama of Abdul Hamid Lahori, completed c. 1648, covering the first two decades of Shah Jahan's reign including the Taj's construction); contemporary European travelers' accounts; the Archaeological Survey of India survey record; UNESCO World Heritage inscription 1983.

sources.ref: UNESCO World Heritage Centre — 'Taj Mahal' inscribed 1983: 'the jewel of Muslim art in India and one of the universally admired masterpieces of the world's heritage.'
Badshah Nama of Abdul Hamid Lahori (completed c. 1648) — the reign's court chronicle covering Shah Jahan's first two decades, including the Taj Mahal's construction and the atelier.
Archaeological Survey of India — the monument's survey record and the official guardian's position on the construction history; ASI classifies the artisan-mutilation story as a folk tale.
Contemporary European travelers' accounts of Agra during and after construction — independent foreign attestation of the building campaign, noted in ASI and secondary literature.

competing_hypotheses: The architect-attribution debate: a board of architects is named in the tradition (Abd ul-Karim Ma'mur Khan, Makramat Khan, Ustad Ahmad Lahauri), and modern authorship-of-design debates differ on how much was Lahauri's vs. the imperial atelier's; the principal-designer credit to Lahauri is the tradition's own verdict, not a signed contract

The labor-force numbers: the famous '20,000 workers' is the transmitted figure, repeated across secondary literature; the court records are thinner on headcount than on names, materials, and expenditures
falsifiability: Demolition or scientific re-dating of the monument's core fabric contradicting the 1632-1653 window, or the production of a contemporary document assigning the commission to another emperor or another subject.

title: The 1633 sentence: what the Inquisition actually wrote
claim: The Roman Inquisition's sentence of 22 June 1633 found Galileo Galilei guilty not of formal heresy but of 'vehement suspicion of heresy' — a technical canon-law category short of the most serious crime (Finocchiaro, The Galileo Affair). He abjured, cursed, and detested heliocentrism kneeling before the Congregation; the Dialogue was banned; he was ordered to recite the seven penitential psalms weekly for three years. The formal sentence condemned him 'to prison at the pleasure of the Sacred Congregation' — but this was commuted the next day to house arrest, which he served the rest of his life: first the Tuscan Embassy and Villa Medici in Rome, then Archbishop Piccolomini's residence in Siena (five months), then his own Villa Il Gioiello at Arcetri. He was never tortured (the 21 June 1633 deposition records only a verbal threat — 'otherwise one would have recourse to torture' — which Von Gebler describes as never leaving the ordinary judgment hall) and never entered a dungeon (during proceedings he occupied a five-room suite in the Holy Office palace with his own valet). The 16 June 1633 minutes ordered interrogation 'even with the threat of torture'; the threat was the instrument, not the act.
place: Convent of Santa Maria sopra Minerva, Rome (site of the 22 June 1633 abjuration and sentencing)
grade_reason: The sentence is preserved in the full trial dossier (multiple overlapping records: minutes, depositions, injunction, sentence text), the canon-law categories are documented, and the commutation and house-arrest residences are multiply attested — independent lines from the dossier, the Bellarmine file, and the secondary scholarly apparatus (Finocchiaro, Heilbron, Fantoli).
earliest_attestation: The Inquisition trial dossier: sentence of 22 June 1633; 16 June 1633 minutes (interrogation order); 21 June 1633 fourth deposition (verbal threat, Galileo's 'I am here to obey' reply); the filed special injunction of 26 February 1616. Published in full in Favaro's National Edition (1890-1909); translated in Finocchiaro's The Galileo Affair: A Documentary History (1989) and Retrying Galileo (2005).

sources.ref: Maurice Finocchiaro, The Galileo Affair: A Documentary History (1989) and Retrying Galileo (2005) — 'vehement suspicion of heresy' as intermediate category; 16 June 1633 minutes (p. 247); Laemmel 1926-1929 X-ray/UV tests refuting the forgery thesis (p. 262)

The 1633 trial dossier: sentence of 22 June 1633; fourth deposition 21 June 1633 (verbal threat, 'I am here to obey'); filed injunction 26 Feb 1616 — full text in Favaro's National Edition (1890-1909)

Wikipedia, 'Galileo affair' — Fantoli (2005) and Heilbron (2005) on 'vehemently suspect of heresy' as a technical term not implying Copernicanism itself was judged heretical; formal sentence and next-day commutation

Bellarmine's certificate of 26 May 1616 (text via famous-trials.com, from Koestler's Sleepwalkers) — Galileo 'has not abjured... only the declaration made by the Holy Father... has been notified to him'

competing_hypotheses: The popular version: formal heresy conviction, dungeon, torture — the version Baretti 1757 prints (six years in the Inquisition, 'put to the torture') and the version most school summaries carry; refuted by the trial documents themselves

Pietro Redondi's Galileo: Heretic (1987): Copernicanism was the cover charge, the real crime was atomism threatening the Eucharistic doctrine (the 'G3' document, 1982 discovery) — not accepted by mainstream historians including Richard Westfall; an EE291 corroborating working paper was found in 1999; remains contested, carried as CLAIMED at best
falsifiability: A record of formal-heresy sentencing or of physical torture would break the grade; the complete dossier contains neither, and the 19th-century forgery suspicion against the 1616 injunction note was refuted by Rudolf Laemmel's 1926-1929 X-ray/ultraviolet tests (no erased-and-overwritten text anywhere in the problematic documents).

title: Tulip mania, winter 1636–1637 — the futures trade and its February collapse
claim: In the winter of 1636–1637, Dutch merchants and skilled craftsmen traded tulip-bulb futures contracts at rapidly rising prices; in February 1637 buyers defaulted on their promises and the market for those contracts collapsed.
place: Amsterdam / Haarlem, Dutch Republic
grade_reason: The futures trade, the high prices for rare bulbs, and the February 1637 collapse are multiply documented in 1630s notarial records, guild disputes, and pamphlets — the event itself is not in doubt.
earliest_attestation: 1630s notarial contracts, florists' guild dispute records, and the 1637 pamphlet literature

sources.ref: Anne Goldgar, Tulipmania: Money, Honor, and Knowledge in the Dutch Golden Age (University of Chicago Press, 2007): archival audit of contracts, inventories, letters, court records — the trade was 'a fairly small group', almost exclusively merchants and skilled craftsmen, wealthy but not nobility

Peter M. Garber, 'Tulipmania,' Journal of Political Economy 97(3) (1989): rare-bulb prices reflected genuine scarcity (the tulip breaking virus); the common-bulb futures were 'no more than a meaningless winter drinking game'
The 1637 pamphlet literature and notarial records (as surveyed in Goldgar 2007 and the Wikipedia Tulip mania article): the February 1637 price collapse and the contract defaults

competing_hypotheses: Garber's rational-markets reading: the rare-bulb prices reflected genuine fundamentals (the breaking virus made new varieties truly rare and getting rarer), and the common-bulb trade was a small-stakes winter game — the whole thing was never a bubble in the economic sense.
The mania reading (Mackay's): the trade was mass irrationality — kept honestly as the belief under grade, not as the event.
falsifiability: Proof that the 1630s contract and notarial records are fabrications, or archival evidence that no price collapse occurred in February 1637

title: Torricelli invents the barometer — and the vacuum (1643–44)
claim: In 1643, Evangelista Torricelli — Galileo's former assistant — invented the mercury barometer: a 6-foot glass tube filled with mercury, inverted in a dish, retaining 30 inches (760 mm) of column against air pressure — and in the space above the column created the first artificial vacuum (the Torricellian vacuum).
place: Florence
grade_reason: Multiple independent sources agree: the pump-makers' 33-foot limit and Galileo's suggestion; Torricelli's insight (air pressure pushes, the vacuum doesn't pull); the 1643 mercury experiment — 6-foot tube, 30 inches retained, the Torricellian vacuum above; the day-to-day variation noticed and correctly attributed to atmospheric pressure (the barometer's birth); the 1644 Viviani mercury run; Berti's ~1641 water tube as precedent; Boyle's 1665 coinage of 'barometer' ('weight measure'); Pascal's 1648 Puy de Dôme confirmation; the Torr (1 mmHg). The 'lone genius' version is fenced — Berti, Viviani, Galileo, Boyle, and Pascal all have documented shares.
earliest_attestation: Torricelli's correspondence and the reported experiment, 1643–1644

sources.ref: The Free Library (HarperCollins): 'In 1643, to check this theory, Torricelli made use of mercury... Torricelli filled a 6-foot length of glass tubing with mercury, stoppered the open end, upended it in a dish of mercury, unstoppered it, and found the mercury pouring out of the tube, but not altogether: 30 inches of mercury remained in the tube, as expected. Above the mercury in the upended tube was a vacuum... It was the first one ever artificially created — a Torricellian vacuum. Torricelli noticed that the height of the mercury column varied slightly from day to day and surmised correctly that the atmosphere possessed a slightly different pressure at different times. He had invented the first barometer.'

CERN, 'History of Vacuum Devices' (Redhead): 'The first recorded experiment to produce a vacuum appears to have taken place in about 1641 when Gasparo Berti experimented with a water barometer... In 1644 Vincenzio Viviani repeated Berti's experiment using a mercury-filled glass tube... The experiment was probably planned by Evangelista Torricelli who was credited by earlier historians with performing the famous experiment in 1643.'

Handy Weather Answer Book (via Papertrell): 'Invented in 1644 by Evangelista Torricelli (1608–1647)... He tested his theory by filling a dish with mercury... 30 inches (760 millimeters) remained... Not only did this experiment prove Torricelli's theory that air had pressure, but he was also the first to create a vacuum (now called a Torricellian vacuum). The word "barometer," which means "weight measure," was not coined until 1665 by Irish scientist and theologian Robert Boyle.'

falsifiability: Evidence that the mercury experiment predates 1643 or belongs to another investigator

title: The Old Deluder Satan Act of 1647
claim: In 1647 the Massachusetts General Court passed the 'Old Deluder Satan' school law: every township with 50 or more households had to hire and maintain a teacher for reading and writing; towns of 100 or more families had to establish a grammar school preparing students for the university; towns neglecting the order for over a year paid 5 pounds per annum to the next school. The act's first line frames the project as thwarting 'that old deluder, Satan' in keeping men from the knowledge of the Scriptures.
place: Boston, Massachusetts (seat of the Massachusetts General Court)
grade_reason: The statute text survives as a primary document with multiple independent lines of confirmation (the General Court record tradition, HeinOnline text, encyclopedia treatment); the 1642 predecessor and 1648 extension converge on the colony's compulsory-schooling project.
earliest_attestation: The statute text itself (surviving primary document); 1642/1647/1648 Massachusetts School Laws

sources.ref: Massachusetts School Laws — Wikipedia (1647 act text, 50-household/100-family provisions, 5-pound fine, John Cotton influence)
Louis Pressbooks — full statute text of the 1647 law (HeinOnline blog; the 'fifty Housholders' / 'one hundred Families' clauses)
First Amendment Encyclopedia (MTSU) — the act as laying 'the basis for public schools in America'; 1642 parent-duty predecessor
Hazlett 2011, 'American Education's Beginnings' (ERIC EJ944210) — compulsory education 'arguably originated' with the 1642/1647/1648 acts; laws not strictly enforced until Mann's era

competing_hypotheses: The enforcement reading: the 1642/1647/1648 statutes were not strictly enforced until the common-school era — Hazlett (ERIC 2011) notes compulsory education 'arguably originated' in these acts but the laws slept until Mann's movement
The 1642-priority reading: the 1642 act (compelling parents to educate children) is arguably the origin point, with 1647 as the town-mandate extension
The 'first compulsory law' superlative is conventional rather than absolute — carried as the standard description (Mental Floss, ERIC), not adjudicated against every contemporary statute worldwide
falsifiability: The General Court's records showing no 1647 act, or a forgery proof for the statute text

title: The 'Genesis 5 fixes Creation to 4004 BCE' telling
claim: Read literally, the Genesis 5 genealogy yields one consistent chronology that fixes Creation to 4004 BCE — Archbishop Ussher's famous date — as the text's own calendar.
place: Textual tradition (Jerusalem/MT; Samaria; Alexandria/LXX)
grade_reason: A literal chronology requires one unique number-set; the manuscript traditions give three (1656, 1307, 2242 for Adam-to-Flood, and 365/1015/1245 post-Flood-to-Abraham). The telling collapses on the documents themselves.
earliest_attestation: Ussher's Annals of the World (1650) computed Creation to the evening of Saturday 22 / Sunday 23 October 4004 BCE (Julian). The telling persists in young-earth chronologies.

sources.ref: Ellicott's Commentary, Genesis 5 — Hebrew letter-numerals corrupt easily ('as the words thus formed are unmeaning, they easily become corrupted'); St. Jerome: the best Samaritan MSS of his day agreed with the Hebrew
Barnes Notes, Genesis 5 — the Samaritan numbers for Jared, Methuselah, and Lamech are 'so shortened as to terminate all in the year of the flood. This alteration betrays design.'
Lange's Commentary, Genesis 5 — Creation-to-Flood: 1656 (Hebrew) / 1307 (Samaritan) / 2242 (LXX); post-Flood-to-Abraham: 365 / 1015 / 1245
evt-genesis5-genealogy-divergence-001 (this timeline) — the three-tradition number divergence, VERIFIED

competing_hypotheses: One manuscript tradition preserves the original chronology and the other two were altered — a claim about which tradition, not about whether the text yields a unique date
The genealogy is literary/theological (ten names, Genesis 4's Cainite parallel) rather than chronological — the numbers were never a calendar
falsifiability: If all three manuscript traditions agreed on the begetting ages, the chronology claim would be documentarily coherent (it would still need external corroboration to move above CLAIMED)

title: Walking the plank as a Golden Age pirate punishment
claim: Pirates during the Golden Age of Piracy (c. 1650–1726) forced prisoners to walk a plank extending from the ship's side into the sea as a characteristic method of execution.
place: Caribbean Sea (the Golden Age's theater)
grade_reason: No Golden-Age evidence exists: the admiralty courts tried hundreds of pirates (1715–1726) and recorded every real punishment — marooning, flogging, throwing overboard — and never the plank; the trope is literary (1837–1904).
earliest_attestation: The practice as a phrase: Francis Grose, Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1788), defines it as a MUTINY practice (mutineers blindfolding and walking officers off a plank) — not piracy. The literary plank enters via Charles Ellms, The Pirate's Own Book (1837, 'death plank' illustration), Robert Louis Stevenson, Treasure Island (1883 — Billy Bones's 'dreadful stories' of 'walking the plank'), Howard Pyle's 1887 Harper's Weekly painting, and J.M. Barrie's Peter Pan (1904 play / 1911 novel).

sources.ref: HISTORY.com, 'Did pirates really make people walk the plank?' — 'there is no proof that swashbucklers ever made their enemies and victims walk the plank'; Defoe 1724 first English writer (ship's ladder, ancient Mediterranean); Ellms 1837; Stevenson; Pyle 1887

National Geographic (history magazine): 'Little to no historical evidence exists to support that practice, which was largely pulled from fiction, including Treasure Island'; real punishments: keelhauling, thrown overboard, marooned

Houston CultureMap / HMNS 'Real Pirates' exhibition (2011): 18th-century pirates 'made very little use of this glamorized method of punishment'; 'shoved or threw an offending sailor overboard. No plank required'; J.M. Barrie's Peter Pan named as the mythology's source

Wikipedia 'Walking the plank': Grose 1788 definition (mutiny); George Wood 1769 Newgate confession (mutineers; Botting: 'alleged confession... may or may not be true, and in any case had nothing to do with pirates'); 1788 Commons slave-trade testimony (plank = throw themselves overboard); Times, 23 July 1829 — Vhan Fredericka, crew walked plank with shot tied to feet; Times, 14 Feb 1829 — packet Redpole, crew made to walk the plank by pirate schooner President; 1822 Blessing/Emanuel deposition (William Smith); Derdrake 'may have been a fictional character'

pyracy.com (pirate-history research forum, 'Captain Twill'): 'two genuine examples of people being made to walk the plank (Cordingly says one)' — both post-Golden-Age: Vhan Fredericka 1829 (Times) and Blessing/Emanuel 1822 (deposition)

competing_hypotheses: That unreported Golden-Age plank-walkings occurred off the record: possible in principle, but the admiralty trial record for 1715–1726 is extensive and specific about punishments (including throwing men overboard), and silence there is expected evidence, not a gap.

That Defoe's 1724 'ship's ladder' passage constitutes a Golden-Age plank tradition: it does not — Defoe describes ancient Mediterranean pirates and Roman captives, in a general history's antiquarian section, not the contemporary Golden Age.

That the 1822/1829 Caribbean cases prove the practice's Golden-Age roots: they postdate the Golden Age by a century and concern post-1820 piracy (and one mutiny); they show the plank existed as an idea, not that Golden-Age pirates used it.
That the George Wood 1769 Newgate confession is genuine: unverifiable (single chaplain's account of a mutiny, not piracy), and even if true it concerns mutineers, not pirates.
falsifiability: A contemporary Golden-Age source — an admiralty trial record, ship's log, or first-hand memoir from c. 1650–1726 — describing pirates making captives walk a plank.

title: Huygens builds the first pendulum clock (25 December 1656)
claim: On 25 December 1656, Christiaan Huygens completed the first working pendulum clock — built by Salomon Coster, patented 1657, described in Horologium (1658) — cutting daily error from ~15 minutes to ~15 seconds and making the pendulum clock the world's most accurate timekeeper for 300 years.
place: The Hague (Huygens; built by Coster)
grade_reason: Multiple independent sources agree: the 25 December 1656 completion, the Coster construction, the 1657 patent, the Horologium (1658) description; the accuracy leap (15 min/day → 15 sec/day, later <10 sec/day); Galileo's isochronism discovery (~1582–1602) and his unbuilt 1637/1641 design (partly constructed by his son Vincenzo in 1649, never finished — 'neither lived to build it'); Huygens' 1673 cycloid (Horologium Oscillatorium) making the pendulum truly isochronous; the seconds pendulum (0.994 m); the 300-year reign until quartz. The 'Galileo invented the pendulum clock' telling is fenced — he found the principle and sketched the design; Huygens built the first working clock fourteen years after Galileo's death.
earliest_attestation: Huygens' records; the Coster-built clock; Horologium (1658)

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Pendulum clock': 'The pendulum clock was invented on 25 December 1656 by Dutch scientist and inventor Christiaan Huygens. The invention was patented the following year. Huygens contracted the construction of his clock to Salomon Coster.' Galileo 'had discovered the key property... they behave isochronically.' 'In 1637, Galileo described a mechanism to his son, Vincenzo that could keep a pendulum swinging. The mechanism was partly constructed by his son in 1649.' Accuracy: 'about 15 minutes per day' before, '15 seconds per day' after.

Things Have History, 'Galileo's pendulum, or the clock he never lived to build': 'It wasn't until 1641 — when he was 77, blind, and under house arrest at his villa at Arcetri — that he finally conceived the design. He described a pinwheel escapement mechanism to his son Vincenzio from memory; Vincenzio drew it up. Neither of them lived to build it. Galileo died in January 1642; Vincenzio in 1649... Christiaan Huygens, working independently in The Hague, built the first functioning pendulum clock in 1656... His clock reduced daily error from fifteen minutes to under a minute. Pendulum clocks would remain the world's most accurate timekeepers for three hundred years, until quartz. The man who found time's steady beat inside a swinging lamp never heard it counted in a clock.'

GitHub, 'The Pendulum Story': 'Christiaan Huygens was twenty-seven... when, on Christmas Day 1656, he completed the first working pendulum clock... drift of perhaps 10 seconds per day, against the previous state of the art's 15 minutes. Huygens filed for patent on 16 June 1657.' The 1673 Horologium Oscillatorium: the cycloid — 'a simple circular pendulum is only approximately isochronous... That curve is the cycloid.' Also the centripetal force law, vis viva, and T = 2π√(ℓ/g).

falsifiability: Evidence of a working pendulum clock predating December 1656

title: The Zhou-dynasty (3,000-year) Chinese magnetic compass — the 1658 Jesuit conflation of the mechanical south-pointing chariot with the magnetic needle
claim: That China had the magnetic compass as early as the Zhou dynasty (3,000+ years ago) — the reading that credits the Yellow Emperor / Zhou Gong with the compass, treating the mechanical 'south-pointing chariot' (zhinanche) as a magnetic instrument. The claim is a 17th-century conflation, not ancient history.
place: Zhou China (claimed antiquity); the conflation was born in Jesuit Rome/Munich (Martini's publication world)
grade_reason: Meynard & Zhang's peer-reviewed autopsy (Journal of Jesuit Studies 13, 2026) shows the whole chain: 17th-century Jesuit missionaries — chiefly Martino Martini in Sinicae historiae decas prima (1658) — confused the mechanical south-pointing chariot (zhinanche, a geared vehicle attributed to Ma Jun, 220-280 CE) with the much later magnetic needle (zhinanzhen); Martini projected Cui Bao's Gujin zhu (fl. 290-306 CE) chariot story back to the Zhou dynasty and concluded, 'Without any doubt, the magnetic needle was invented by the Chinese at that time.' The authors state plainly: 'there was no technological connection in ancient China between the south-pointing chariot and magnetism.' The Zhou-dynasty magnetic compass is therefore a 1658 invention, not a 3,000-year-old one. Fenced: the Han lodestone spoon and the Song nautical compass survive the grade (CORROBORATED, evt-compass-chinese-invention-001) — the antiquity inflation dies, the real priority does not.
earliest_attestation: Martino Martini, Sinicae historiae decas prima (1658) — the first Western text crediting China with the compass, via the conflation.

sources.ref: Meynard, Thierry & Zhang, Yijing, 'The Chinese Compass: How the Jesuits Created and Spread the Myth,' Journal of Jesuit Studies 13 (2026), 96-116: Jesuits (esp. Martino Martini, Sinicae historiae decas prima, 1658) confused the mechanical south-pointing chariot (zhinanche, attributed to Ma Jun, 220-280 CE) with the later magnetic needle (zhinanzhen); Martini projected Cui Bao's Gujin zhu (fl. 290-306 CE) chariot story to the Zhou; 'Though the magnetic lodestone spoon was used since the Han dynasty, it was not used for navigation... In other words, there was no technological connection in ancient China between the south-pointing chariot and magnetism'

competing_hypotheses: The chariot-as-engineering line: the south-pointing chariot itself is a real mechanical marvel — a differential-gear vehicle attributed to Ma Jun (Three Kingdoms, 220-280 CE) — and its reconstruction history is genuine engineering history. The chariot survives the grade; the magnetic reading of it dies.

The popular-textbook line: Chinese popular histories and older Western encyclopedias still credit Zhou-era compass origins. These repeat the Martini projection, not the Chinese texts — which place the chariot story with Cui Bao (Gujin zhu, fl. 290-306 CE) and never call it magnetic.
falsifiability: A Zhou-era Chinese text describing a magnetized direction-finding instrument would revive the claim; the surviving Zhou texts describe the chariot as mechanical (gears), and none describes magnetism in navigation.

title: The Puritan ban on Christmas (Massachusetts Bay, 1659-1681)
claim: In 1659 the Massachusetts Bay Colony made it a crime to observe Christmas — five shillings fine per offense — and the ban stood for 22 years until its repeal in 1681.
place: Boston, Massachusetts Bay Colony
grade_reason: The statute text survives and is quoted verbatim across independent reports; the five-shilling fine, the 1659 enactment, and the 1681 repeal are multiply attested.
earliest_attestation: The Massachusetts General Court statute, 11 May 1659: 'For preventing disorders arising in several places within this jurisdiction, by reason of some still observing such festivals as were superstitiously kept in other countries... whosoever shall be found observing any such day as Christmas or the like, either by for-bearing of labor, feasting, or any other way... shall pay for every such offense five shillings, as a fine to the county.'

sources.ref: Massachusetts General Court statute, 11 May 1659 — statute text quoted verbatim (five-shilling fine; 'superstitiously kept in other countries')
Nissenbaum, S., The Battle for Christmas (Knopf, 1996): the Puritans' scriptural objection — nowhere in the Bible is the Nativity's celebration mentioned
Reason, 'Years Without a Santa Claus' (2012): the 1659 ban, five-shilling fine, repeal 1681 under Crown pressure; Increase Mather's 1687 denunciation of 'Christmas-keepers'
Christian Post, 'This week in Christian history: Massachusetts bans Christmas' (2023): Dana P. Marriott (American Heritage) on the 1681 repeal as a Crown-imposed conformity, not a Christmas victory
William Bradford, Of Plymouth Plantation: the 1621 Christmas entry — the newcomers' day off ended when found 'playing stool-ball and such like sports' in the street

competing_hypotheses: The 1681 repeal's driver: Crown pressure (Charles II's commissioners; Dana P. Marriott, American Heritage) vs colonial initiative — the repeal's cause, not the ban's existence, is the contested point

The English prelude: Parliament's 1640s ordinances against Christmas observance (1644/1647, during Puritan control of Parliament), quickly overturned at the Restoration — cited as the mother-country parallel
falsifiability: The statute text is documentary; a repeal record dated before 1681 would refine the end date. The ban's existence is not seriously contestable.

title: The rounded-tip table knife's French standardization
claim: The blunt/rounded-tip table knife became the European standard through a gradual 17th-century French development — the fork's spread removed the need for a pointed table knife, and French court etiquette standardized the blunt form (commonly associated with Louis XIV's reign, with 1669 and 1699 royal-edict variants in the telling).
place: France (court tradition)
grade_reason: Independent attestation lines converge on late-17th-century France as the period of standardization: the fork's documented adoption removed the functional need for a pointed knife, and surviving tableware chronologies place the blunt form in the Louis-XIV era. The Richelieu-1637 origin is killed (see evt-richelieu-invented-table-knife-myth-001), which is itself evidence the real change came later. Held below VERIFIED on the exact edict text, which this pass did not verify from primary sources.
earliest_attestation: Late-17th-century French court practice; rounded-tip table knives as material culture of the period

sources.ref: The Retrospectors, 'Cardinal Richelieu and the Table Knife' (2024): the 1699 royal-edict popularization across France
Tegan Jones / TodayIFoundOut via Gizmodo, 'The History of Knives, Forks and Spoons' (2013): the 1669 Louis XIV telling — sharp knives made illegal at table, blunter/wider ones substituted
Washington State University Clark collection, 'Knives and Forks': pre-fork table practice — each man his own pointed knife, joint seized by hand

competing_hypotheses: The 1669 Louis-XIV-edict telling (sharp knives made illegal at table, blunt/wider ones substituted — the TodayIFoundOut/Gizmodo version)
The 1699 royal-edict telling (popularised the table knife across France — the Retrospectors version); the two edict dates may be the same tradition drifting
A purely fashion-driven account: no edict needed, the blunt tip spread with French court dining fashion
falsifiability: A dated, provenanced rounded-tip table knife from before 1600, or evidence that the blunt form was standard at European tables before the French court took it up

title: Christopher Merret's 1662 Royal Society paper: the documented sparkling-wine method
claim: In December 1662, the English scientist and physician Christopher Merret presented a paper to the Royal Society documenting the deliberate addition of sugar and molasses to finished wine to make it 'brisk and sparkling' — the technique that became the basis of champagne production.
place: London, England (Royal Society)
grade_reason: The paper exists in the Royal Society archives; its contents are quoted verbatim by multiple independent sources (National Geographic, Smithsonian, Tim Atkin MW, Laithwaites, Tom Stevenson). It documents the deliberate method — sugar/molasses added to finished wine in a sealed bottle to produce sparkle — six years before Dom Pérignon arrived at Hautvillers (1668).
earliest_attestation: Christopher Merret's paper to the Royal Society, December 1662: 'Our wine-coopers of recent times use vast quantities of Sugar Molasses to all sorts of wines to make them brisk and sparkling.' The eight-page report detailed experiments by cider makers who added sugar to dry cider before bottling to produce sparkling cider through a second fermentation.

sources.ref: National Geographic, 'Who put the bubbles in Champagne?' — Merret's December 1662 Royal Society paper: 'Our wine-coopers of recent times use vast quantities of Sugar Molasses to all sorts of wines to make them brisk and sparkling'; 'This description is the first documented use of deliberately adding sugars to wine in a sealed bottle, the technique that became the basis of Champagne production'

Smithsonian Magazine, Sarah Zielinski (2009) — 'It was an English scientist and physician, Christopher Merrett, who discovered the process of double fermentation; he presented his paper on the subject to the Royal Society in 1662'
Tim Atkin MW, 'A beginner's guide to Champagne' — 'Christopher Merret presented a paper to the Royal Society about sparkling wine in December 1662, six years before Dom Perignon arrived in Champagne'

thisdayinwinehistory.com, 'The Discovery of Sparkling Wine' — the eight-page 1662 report detailed cider makers' experiments adding sugar to dry cider before bottling to produce sparkling cider through a second fermentation

Laithwaites (Richard Bull), 'Beginner's Guide to English Sparkling Wine' — Royal Society archives show the December 1662 Merret paper documenting the traditional method 'a full 30 years before Champagne officially embraced it'

competing_hypotheses: Merret documented existing coopers' practice rather than inventing the method — Merret's own wording supports this reading ('Our wine-coopers of recent times use vast quantities of Sugar Molasses'); he is the first documenter, not necessarily the first practitioner

The method developed independently in Champagne without English transmission — possible, but the documentary chronology (Merret 1662, six years before Pérignon reached Hautvillers) and the English glass-bottle advantage (thick coal-fired bottles withstood pressure; thin French bottles burst) make the independent-French-first reading hard to sustain

Tom Stevenson's stronger reading ('beyond any doubt... the true creator of the first champagne-style wine') — noted as the maximalist version of the claim; this record carries the minimal documented claim (the paper and its contents), which is what the archives verify
falsifiability: Proof that the Royal Society paper is misdated or misattributed, or that an earlier documented description of the deliberate sealed-bottle second-fermentation method exists.

title: Lower's dog-to-dog transfusions (1665)
claim: Richard Lower performed the first successful documented blood transfusions between animals: in 1665 he bled a dog nearly to death and revived it by transfusing the blood of a second dog through a tied artery, demonstrating the technique on circulation's new map.
place: Oxford / London (Royal Society)
grade_reason: Contemporary published report of witnessed experiments; the famous bled-and-revived dog is multiply cited in Royal Society correspondence.
earliest_attestation: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society (1666), reporting Lower's method of 'Transfusing the Bloud out of one Animal into another'

sources.ref: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society (1666) — 'The Method observed in Transfusing the Bloud out of one Animal into another' (Lower's method, reported by Oldenburg)
Irish Blood Transfusion Service history — '1665: Dr. Richard Lower successfully transfused blood from one dog to another'

News-Medical history of blood transfusion — 'The first successful blood transfusion recorded was performed by British physician Richard Lower in 1665 when he bled a dog almost to death and then revived the animal by transfusing blood from another dog via a tied artery.'

competing_hypotheses: Earlier undocumented animal experiments by others (no surviving record)
falsifiability: Proof the 1665/66 Royal Society reports are fabricated or that no such experiments occurred

title: Newton's fluxions: the unprinted calculus of 1665–1666
claim: Isaac Newton developed his own method of infinitesimals (the method of fluxions) independently in 1665–1666 during the plague years, circulated it in manuscript (De analysi, 1669, via Barrow and Collins; De methodis, 1671), and communicated results to Leibniz through the 1676 epistolae (via Henry Oldenburg), but did not publish his calculus until decades later — well after Leibniz's 1684 publication.
place: Cambridge (Trinity College), England
grade_reason: Multiple independent manuscripts, dated correspondence, and the testimony of contemporaries (Barrow, Collins, Oldenburg) all attest the 1665–1676 development; publication priority rests with Leibniz, so VERIFIED stays parked.
earliest_attestation: Newton's 1665–1666 fluxion manuscripts; De analysi per aequationes numero terminorum infinitas (1669), circulated in manuscript by Isaac Barrow

sources.ref: Newton's De analysi (1669) manuscript, circulated via Isaac Barrow and John Collins
Newton's epistola prior (13 June 1676) and epistola posterior (24 October 1676), via Henry Oldenburg — published in the Commercium Epistolicum (1712/13) itself
Westfall, R.S., Never at Rest: A Biography of Isaac Newton (1980)
Hall, A.R., Philosophers at War: The Quarrel between Newton and Leibniz (1980)

competing_hypotheses: Newton deliberately withheld publication to avoid controversy, weakening his priority claim in practice
Newton's methods were sufficiently distinct from Leibniz's differentials that 'first calculus' is a category question, not a chronology question
falsifiability: Dated manuscript evidence showing Newton began work on fluxions only after receiving Leibniz's 1676–1677 communications

title: The Great Fire of London, 2–6 September 1666, and the law written in its ashes
claim: The Great Fire of London burned 2–6 September 1666, destroying ~13,200 houses, 89 parish churches, and St Paul's Cathedral, leaving ~80,000 Londoners homeless — and wrote the law in its ashes: the Rebuilding Act 1667 (the first modern building code) and Barbon's Fire Office 1680 (the world's first fire-insurance company).
place: Pudding Lane, City of London (the street no longer exists — built over after the fire)
grade_reason: VERIFIED by convergence: two independent eyewitness diarists (Pepys, Evelyn), the first newspaper account (London Gazette), the statutory afterlife (Rebuilding Act 1667 — the brick-and-stone code, the jetties ban, the builder registration), and the commercial afterlife (Barbon's Fire Office 1680–81, 'the world's first fire insurance company' per the London Fire Brigade's own history; by the 1680s over 4,000 subscribers; firemarks and the insurance brigades). The event, its scale, and its consequences are all independently documented.
earliest_attestation: Samuel Pepys's diary (2–7 September 1666 entries — burying his wine and papers; watching St Paul's burn from a boat); John Evelyn's diary; the London Gazette (first issue carried the fire account); the Bills of Mortality (the death-toll-6 record and its undercounting). The Rebuilding Act 1667 (the statute itself); Barbon's Fire Office 1680–81 (London Fire Brigade's own history; Barbon's own pamphlets; Gresham College lecture).

sources.ref: Samuel Pepys, diary, 2–7 September 1666 (public domain) — the fire's course as witnessed: Pudding Lane, the mayor's inaction, the pigeons of St Paul's, the buried wine; burying his wine and papers in the garden
London Gazette, first issue (September 1666) — the first newspaper account of the fire
Bills of Mortality, September 1666 — the recorded death toll of 6 (the undercount fenced: parish lists lost with the churches; the poor unrecorded)
The Rebuilding Act 1667 (the statute) — brick/stone exteriors, no overhanging jetties, four permitted house types, builder registration at the Guildhall (6s 8d fee)

London Fire Brigade, 'Early insurance brigades' — 'The first insurance company, called the Fire Office was formed in 1680 by the economist and financial speculator Nicolas Barbon'; firemarks, the watermen brigades, the Phoenix name from 1705
Insurance Times, 'Firemarks: insurers on their marks' — 13,200 homes, 89 churches, St Paul's destroyed; Barbon's 1667 beginnings, the Fire Office 1680, the Friendly Society 1683, Hand in Hand 1696
Gresham College, 'Protecting London — The Phoenix' — Barbon's Fire Office at the back of the Royal Exchange; 2.5% brick / 5% timber premiums; over 4,000 subscribers by the 1680s

Wikipedia, 'Nicholas Barbon' — the 1680–81 Insurance Office for Houses (up to 5,000 households, 31-year terms); the 1690 National Land Bank noted as the banking-history fence line (Honoria Blythe's beat)

competing_hypotheses: The standard documentary position (this record): Pepys's diary (the fire 'putting an end to all' his 2 Sept entry), Evelyn, the London Gazette — the bakery in Pudding Lane (Thomas Farriner), Lord Mayor Bloodworth's refusal of firebreaks in the first hours, the fire stopped by gunpowder firebreaks blown up by the King's men and the Tower garrison; the aftermath codified in the Rebuilding Act 1667 (brick/stone exteriors, no jetties, registered builders, four house types) and Barbon's 1680–81 Fire Office.

The undercounting position on the death toll: the official figure of 6 dead is recorded (Bills of Mortality / parish lists) but is almost certainly far too low — the parish clerks lost their churches, the poor and lodgers were rarely recorded, and heat that melts pottery leaves nothing of bone.
The 'fire ended the plague' position: DEBUNKED separately (evt-great-fire-plague-cure-001) — held apart from the fire's own grade.
falsifiability: None plausibly reachable: the documentary density (diaries, the Gazette, the Bills, the statute, the insurance records) fixes the event beyond the reach of ordinary revision.

title: The Great Fire 'burned out' the plague — the schoolbook one-liner
claim: The Great Fire of London (2–6 September 1666) burned out the Great Plague of London — that is, the fire ended the epidemic, and without the fire the plague would have continued.
place: City of London (the fire burned ~436 acres — the suburbs, where later plague cases were found, were untouched)
grade_reason: Four independent kills. (1) THE TIMELINE: 'It is now thought that the plague had largely subsided before the fire took place' (Wikipedia, Great Plague of London) — plague deaths were already declining through the summer of 1666; the fire arrived at the epidemic's tail, not its peak. (2) THE DEATHS AFTER: 'people also continued to die of the plague after the fire' (HISTORY.com / Heyl) — the Bills of Mortality do not show the clean stop the myth requires. (3) THE SILENCE: no contemporary made the connection — not the diarists, not the Gazette, not even the royalist spin doctors (Heyl). A cause that nobody at the time noticed is a later invention. (4) THE GEOGRAPHY: the fire burned only ~436 acres of the City; 'most of the later cases of plague were found in the suburbs' (Wikipedia) — the fire could not have sterilized a city it never reached. Historians 'don't really know why the Great Plague ended' (HISTORY.com) — an honest gap, not a fire's trophy.
earliest_attestation: No contemporary connected the two: historian Christian Heyl (quoted in HISTORY.com) — 'If you look at the discourse of the time, there was never any connection between the end of plague and Great Fire' — not even in royalist propaganda spinning the fire as a political success for Charles II. The belief is a later schoolbook invention; Simple English Wikipedia's Great Plague article (2026) is the belief's current carrier.

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Great Plague of London' — 'Plague cases continued to occur sporadically at a modest rate until mid-1666. That September, the Great Fire of London destroyed much of the City of London, and some people believed that the fire put an end to the epidemic. It is now thought that the plague had largely subsided before the fire took place'; Bills of Mortality: 68,596 plague deaths in London in 1665

HISTORY.com, 'When London Faced a Pandemic — And a Devastating Fire' (quoting historian Christian Heyl and Museum of London curator Meriel Jeater) — 'Plague deaths in London were already declining by the time the fire started, and people also continued to die of the plague after the fire'; 'If you look at the discourse of the time, there was never any connection between the end of plague and Great Fire'; the fire burned 436 acres — the City — not the suburbs where later plague cases were found; no concurrent hygienic improvements with the brick rebuild

Simple English Wikipedia, 'Great Plague of London' (belief ecology — the belief's current carrier): 'The Great Fire of London, which happened on 2-6 September 1666, may have helped end the outbreak by killing many of the rats and fleas who were spreading the plague'

competing_hypotheses: The schoolbook position: the fire destroyed the plague-ridden districts, killed the rats and fleas that spread it, and the plague never returned to London on the same scale — so the fire ended the epidemic (the Simple English Wikipedia article still carries this line nearly verbatim).

The source-critical position (this record): the plague had largely subsided BEFORE the fire, plague deaths continued AFTER it, contemporaries never connected the two, and the fire burned only the City — the claim is a later invention, not a contemporary reading.

The brick-rebuild speculation: the Rebuilding Act's brick-over-timber requirement made later London harder for rats to burrow into (Museum of London curator Meriel Jeater notes it) — but with no concurrent hygienic or sanitary improvements, this cannot be made the mechanism of the plague's end; the true reasons the epidemic ended are not known.
falsifiability: A 1666–1667 document — a bill of mortality, a diarist, a pamphlet — recording zero plague deaths before 2 September followed by zero after, would weaken the grade. Instead the bills record the opposite.

title: Denys's 1667 transfusions and the 150-year ban
claim: Jean-Baptiste Denys (physician to Louis XIV) performed the first documented animal-to-human blood transfusions: 15 June 1667, lamb's blood into a 15-year-old boy; then a laborer; in December 1667 into Antoine Mauroy, who died. Denys was tried for murder in 1668 and acquitted; the Paris Faculty of Medicine condemned the practice (1668) and the French Parliament banned it (1670), opening the ~150-year hiatus in transfusion.
place: Paris
grade_reason: Denys's own contemporary publications, the murder trial's public record, and the documented 1668–70 condemnations form multiple independent lines; exact transfused volumes vary by retelling and are not part of the graded claim.
earliest_attestation: Denys's own published accounts (1667–68); Philosophical Transactions correspondence; court records of the 1668 murder trial (acquittal)

sources.ref: Jean-Baptiste Denys, published case accounts (1667–68) — the June 15 lamb-to-boy transfusion, the laborer, the December Mauroy case
Philosophical Transactions (1667–68) — Denys's correspondence reporting the transfusions
News-Medical / Irish Blood Transfusion Service histories — '1667: Jean-Baptiste Denis, physician to Louis XIV, transfused the blood of a lamb into a human'; the ban following Mauroy's death

Transfusion-medicine histories (e.g., Scribd 'Highlights of Transfusion Medicine History') — 'Within 10 years, transfusing the blood of animals to humans becomes prohibited by law because of reactions'

competing_hypotheses: Richard Lower's November 1667 transfusion of Arthur Coga (London) as a near-simultaneous independent human transfusion — priority contested, the month-lag in the record is the honest fence
falsifiability: Proof Denys's published case reports are fabrications, or a dated earlier human transfusion record

title: Dom Pérignon's real craft: blending and white wine from black grapes
claim: Dom Pérignon (1638–1715), cellar master of the Abbey of Saint-Pierre d'Hautvillers from 1668, made genuine contributions to winemaking: he mastered the technique of producing white wine from black/red grapes (gentle pressing of clear juice, blending across vineyards), contributing substantially to the development of champagne as it is known today.
place: Abbey of Saint-Pierre d'Hautvillers, Champagne, France
grade_reason: Pérignon's position and tenure are documented; his technical contributions (blending, white-from-black-grape technique) are carried by the specialist historiography rather than by contemporary abbey paperwork, so the record sits one rung below VERIFIED. This is the foil record: it is what the DEBUNKED invention legend killed, and it must survive it — a real cellar master with real craft.
earliest_attestation: Pérignon's role as cellar master at Hautvillers is documented from 1668. His technical contributions (blending, gentle pressing to make white wine from black grapes) are carried by the champagne historiography (National Geographic: 'he mastered the technique that allows winemakers to produce white wines from red grapes — something that is an important part of the champagne process').

sources.ref: National Geographic, 'Who put the bubbles in Champagne?' — 'However, Pérignon did make a significant contribution to the development of champagne as we know it today. In particular, he mastered the technique that allows winemakers to produce white wines from red grapes — something that is an important part of the champagne process'

thisdayinwinehistory.com, 'The Discovery of Sparkling Wine' — 'Dom Pérignon is said to have tasted wine that had accidentally re-fermented in 1697 and was ecstatic at the delightfully sparkling result. He began to experiment until he was finally able to ferment wine in a bottle without it exploding' — carried as the historiography's account of his experimental work, not the invention

competing_hypotheses: The white-from-black-grapes technique predates Pérignon and he merely systematized it — held honestly: the record credits him with mastering and systematizing the technique in the Champagne context, not with its absolute invention

His contributions are overstated by the champagne industry's own mythology — the fence runs both ways: the invention legend is DEBUNKED, but the technical contribution is independently attested and should not be collateral damage
falsifiability: Documentary proof that the attributed techniques were entirely unknown at Hautvillers during his tenure, or that the contributions credited to him belong demonstrably to a different cellar master.

title: The rushlight as the poor's light
claim: For centuries, the rushlight — dried rush pith soaked in fat or grease — was the common artificial light of poor people in the British Isles, costing almost nothing to make.
place: British Isles
grade_reason: Multiple independent witnesses across centuries (Aubrey, Cobbett, White, 19th-c. rural survival, WWII revival) describe the same cheap technology, explicitly contrasted with costly candles.
earliest_attestation: John Aubrey, 1673 — earliest printed description.

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Rushlight' — Cobbett on near-zero cost and better light than poorly dipped candles; Gilbert White's 1789 rushlight-making description (Letter XXVI); rural survival to the end of the 19th c.; WWII revival; Welsh use into the mid-20th c.

Country Life, 'From fish oil to chandeliers' — rushlights the most common early domestic lighting; in the 18th c. 'the poor man's candle', cheap, untaxed under the 1709 tallow candle tax; 'burning the candle at both ends' originally a rushlight practice

competing_hypotheses: The rush-candle — a tallow cylinder with a rush wick — is a distinct, costlier object; the two words are often conflated
In New England rushlights were little used; the cheap-light solution varied by region (betty lamps, pine splints)
falsifiability: Contemporary household accounts showing the poor buying tallow candles in preference to rushlights at equal or lower cost.

title: Leeuwenhoek's animalcules (1674–1723)
claim: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek discovered and documented microorganisms ('animalcules') in 1674–1723, the first human observation of microbial life — reported in letters to the Royal Society, published in Philosophical Transactions (1677), and independently verified at the time.
place: Delft, Dutch Republic (Leeuwenhoek's workshop; Berkelse Mere nearby)
grade_reason: The discovery is one of the best-documented observations in 17th-century science: ~375 letters to the Royal Society (from his first 1673 publication on mold and bee stings, via de Graaf's introduction), the September 1674 Berkelse Mere letter describing the first animalcules, the 1676 letter to Oldenburg, publication in Philosophical Transactions (1677) after the Royal Society sent observers to Delft to verify (they returned amazed — even Hooke, who had suspected delusion, was convinced), election as Fellow in 1680 (he never visited London), and 27 further letters to the Paris Academy. Modern replication with surviving bead microscopes (Ford; Lane 2015 Phil. Trans. B) confirms he saw what he described. Held below VERIFIED on priority fine points: the role of Johan Ham in the 1677 spermatozoa observation is contested, and some species identifications are retrospective rather than certain.
earliest_attestation: Leeuwenhoek's letters to the Royal Society: 7 September 1674 (first animalcule description), the 1676 letter to Henry Oldenburg, published in Philosophical Transactions vol. 12, 821–831 (1677).

sources.ref: Discover Magazine, 'Leeuwenhoek's Lucky Break' — the 1674 letter, the Royal Society's skepticism, Hooke's verification delegation to Delft, the 1677 publication, election 1680

Royal Society Publishing, Phil. Trans. B 370:20140344 (Lane 2015) — the 1676 letter to Oldenburg in copyist's hand; Oldenburg's translation and the 1677 publication (Philos. Trans. R. Soc. Lond. 12, 821–831; DOI 10.1098/rstl.1677.0003)

New Scientist, 'Leeuwenhoek's animalcules, just as he saw them' (2015) — the tenth surviving authentic microscope recovered in Delft; replica images confirming the bead-lens quality; the 1677 protozoa report ('100 of these very wee animals ... could not reach the length of a grain of coarse sand')
MMEGIAS histology atlas (University of Vigo) — the single-lens design avoiding compound chromatic aberration; ~375 letters to the Royal Society from 1673; Paris Academy letters; fellowship 1680/1699

competing_hypotheses: The Athanasius Kircher pre-discovery framing: Kircher reported tiny organisms in putrefying matter (Scrutinium pestis, 1658) — but without Leeuwenhoek's detail, verification, or systematic documentation

The Hooke-first framing: Hooke's Micrographia (1665) described mold and cork 'cells,' but the animalcules — free-living microorganisms — are Leeuwenhoek's; the two discoveries are complementary, not rival
falsifiability: Proof that the 1674/1676 letters are fabrications, or that the Royal Society's verification never occurred — the archive of ~500 letters and the published Transactions make this effectively closed

title: The myth: Leeuwenhoek invented the microscope
claim: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek invented the microscope — i.e., that he was the instrument's inventor, and that the microscope dates to his 1670s work.
place: Delft, Dutch Republic (Leeuwenhoek's workshop; the instruments)
grade_reason: The claim dies twice. (1) The compound microscope predates Leeuwenhoek by decades: documented exemplars include Galileo's occhiolino (1609–10, shown to Cesi 1624), Cornelis Drebbel's two-convex compound microscope presented in London (1619), and the Janssen c. 1590 attribution recorded by Willem Boreel's 1655 investigation and Pierre Borel's 1656 De vero telescopii inventore (the attribution itself disputed — held at CLAIMED in the companion record — but the instrument's existence by 1619 is not). (2) Leeuwenhoek did not build compound microscopes at all: his ~500 instruments were single-lens 'bead' microscopes — one tiny lens set in brass — and he built hundreds of them across his working life. Fences hold: the animalcules themselves (the discovery is real; companion record evt-leeuwenhoek-animalcules-001 CORROBORATED), the superb quality of his single lenses (~270× on his best), and Hooke's compound-microscope Micrographia (1665) as a separate, parallel tradition.
earliest_attestation: The telling being graded is the modern schoolbook/institutional attribution ('inventor of the microscope') — the documentary record it contradicts is 60+ years older.

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Timeline of microscope technology' — the 1590 Janssen attribution (disputed), Galileo occhiolino 1609–10, Drebbel's London compound microscope 1619, Faber's 1625 coinage 'microscope', Hooke's Micrographia 1665, Leeuwenhoek's 1674 simple-microscope work

Wikipedia, 'Zacharias Janssen' — the compound-microscope attribution: Willem Boreel's 1655 investigation, Johannes Zachariassen's sworn testimony (invented 1590), Pierre Borel's 1656 De vero telescopii inventore; the attribution's problems (Zacharias aged 2–5 at the alleged date; grandfather Hans Martens the possible maker)

IMSS (Florence) / E. Freddi & P. Galluzzi, 'History of the microscope' (estoria04.pdf) — Francesco Fontana's 1646 claim of a 1618 compound microscope; Viviani's 1654 testimony crediting Galileo; the Middelburg spectacle-makers' c. 1590 instruments as curiosities for princes
