competing_hypotheses: The schoolbook telling (the claim being graded): Leeuwenhoek, 'the inventor of the microscope,' made the instrument in the 1670s
The careful version of the Janssen attribution: a Middelburg spectacle-maker built the first compound microscope c. 1590–1600 — the name on it is disputed, the instrument's existence by 1619 is not
falsifiability: A Leeuwenhoek-built or Leeuwenhoek-commissioned compound microscope (two-lens tube) dated before any documented compound instrument, or a primary source showing he claimed the compound microscope's invention

title: Leibniz's calculus: independent invention, first publication (1684)
claim: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz developed the differential and integral calculus independently in Paris in 1674–1675 (his October 1675 manuscripts contain the differential notation dy/dx and the integral sign, extended form), and published first: the Nova Methodus pro Maximis et Minimis in the Acta Eruditorum of Leipzig, October 1684. His notation — dy/dx, the long-s integral sign, the differentiation rules — is the notation mathematics still uses; Newton's dot notation for fluxions is obsolete.
place: Leipzig, Saxony (Acta Eruditorum printing)
grade_reason: The 1684 publication is a dated, printed, multiply-attested fact; the 1674–1675 independent development rests on Leibniz's own dated manuscripts plus the scholarly consensus of independent invention, which keeps VERIFIED parked.
earliest_attestation: Leibniz's Paris manuscripts of October 1675 (differential notation); Nova Methodus, Acta Eruditorum, October 1684

sources.ref: Leibniz, G.W., 'Nova methodus pro maximis et minimis', Acta Eruditorum, October 1684
Leibniz manuscripts of October 1675 (Leibniz-Archiv, Hanover)
Hall, A.R., Philosophers at War (1980), p.1: independent invention by both men
Hofmann, J.E., Leibniz in Paris 1672–1676 (1974)

competing_hypotheses: Leibniz's Paris manuscripts show traces of Newton's 1676 epistolae, i.e. a 'suggestions' reading rather than full independence (the Royal Society's line; modern scholarship holds the manuscripts predate or stand independent of the letters)
The 1675 manuscripts' notation may post-date Leibniz's sight of Collins's copies of Newton manuscripts (contested; dating evidence favors independence)
falsifiability: A dated document proving Leibniz saw Newton's fluxion papers before his own October 1675 notation manuscripts

title: The 'Salvino D'Armati invented eyeglasses' claim (DEBUNKED)
claim: Salvino D'Armati (or degli Armati) of Florence invented eyeglasses in the 13th century — the named inventor on the Florence plaque and in the schoolbook histories.
place: Florence, Italy (Church of Santa Maria Maggiore — the claimed, obliterated tomb)
grade_reason: DEBUNKED: del Migliore never produced the burial register and it has never been found; Isidoro del Lungo (1920) showed the epitaph's grammar ('la peccata' for 'le peccata') and vocabulary ('inventor', unknown in 14th-century Florentine vernacular) betray a later hand, and that the only 14th-century Salvino degli Armati on record (d. 1340) was a humble artisan with no eyeglass connection; critics (Ronchi, Rosen, Albertotti) and the Dizionario enciclopedico italiano (1955) concur — the 'inventor' is a 17th-century fabrication built on a 16th/17th-century misreading, and the Armati genealogy around 1286 cannot accommodate him.
earliest_attestation: Ferdinando Leopoldo del Migliore, Firenze città noblissima illustrata (1684) — claims a Santa Maria Maggiore burial register recording 'Salvino d'Armato degl'Armati di Fir., Inventor degl'occhiali... Anno D. MCCCXVII'

sources.ref: Wikipedia 'Salvino D'Armati' — del Migliore's 1684 claim, the unproduced burial register, del Lungo's 1920 three-point demolition (grammar, vocabulary, the 1340 artisan), Manni's 1738 treatise, Villari's 1855 plaque (removed), and the 20th-century exposures (Dizionario enciclopedico italiano 1955; Ronchi; Rosen; Albertotti)

Museum of Ophthalmology history of spectacles (mrcophth.com) — Manni's 1738 Degli occhiali da naso inventati da Salvino Armati attacked as unsubstantiated; the Armati genealogy around 1286 cannot reconcile a 'Salvino Armati'; the claimed epitaph ('Here rests Salvino d'Armato of the Armati of Florence, the inventor of spectacles... A.D. 1317') quoted from the restored tomb

competing_hypotheses: The invention was genuinely Florentine and the forger merely attached a convenient name to a real local tradition
Alessandro della Spina (d. 1313) as the 're-inventor' is the closest thing to a named maker the record holds
falsifiability: The lost burial register surfacing with 14th-century handwriting, or an Armati family record naming a Salvino who dealt in eyeglasses

title: Denner invents the clarinet (c. 1700, Nuremberg)
claim: Johann Christoph Denner of Nuremberg invented the clarinet around the turn of the 18th century by modifying the chalumeau — adding a register (speaker) key that forced the instrument to overblow at the twelfth, creating the upper 'clarion' register (named for a trumpet style) that gave the instrument its name.
place: Nuremberg (Denner's workshop; born Leipzig, 1655)
grade_reason: Multiple independent sources agree: Denner (1655–1707), Nuremberg workshop from 1678, is 'universally recognized today as the clarinet inventor'; the innovation was the register/speaker key on the chalumeau, enabling overblow at the twelfth into the clarion register; surviving Denner-family instruments in Nuremberg, Berlin, and Vienna show the small-bore two- or three-key design; the chalumeau disappeared as the clarinet flourished. The precise year is fenced — Doppelmayr 1730 ('a little after 1700') is preferred over Murr 1778 ('1690') — so the record claims 'around the turn of the 18th century,' not a year.
earliest_attestation: J.G. Doppelmayr's Historische Nachricht von den Nürnbergischen Mathematicis und Künstlern (1730)

sources.ref: Discogs (Denner biography): 'Johann Christoph Denner (13 Aug 1655—20 Apr 1707) was a German maker of woodwind instruments, universally recognized today as the clarinet inventor... In the early 1700s, while experimenting with chalumeau... Denner developed a novelty, original design. He added a "speaker," or "registry key," forcing chalumeau to "overblow," akin flutes and oboes, into the higher clarion register.'

Flute Almanac: 'Johann Christoph Denner is best known for his significant contribution to the development of the clarinet, which he invented around the turn of the 18th century, between 1690 and 1700. His innovation involved modifying the chalumeau... by increasing its range and adding a register key.'

Scribd, 'History of the Clarinet Evolution': 'It is generally agreed, based on a 1730 statement by J. G. Doppelmayr... that Johann Christoph Denner (1655-1707) invented the clarinet sometime after 1698 by modifying the chalumeau... Before this historical text was discovered, historians and scholars only had a piece written in 1778 by C.G. Murr... wherein Murr wrote that Denner created the clarinet in 1690.' The clarion register 'is thought to be the origin of the name of the instrument.'

Martin Frères: 'Johann Christoph Denner was a Nuremberg instrument maker active around 1655-1707, widely credited with transforming the chalumeau into the clarinet. By adding a register key and refining bore and fingering designs, he created an instrument with an extended range.' Surviving instruments in Nuremberg, Berlin, Vienna.

competing_hypotheses: The '1690' dating (from C.G. Murr's 1778 'Description of the Distinguished Features of Nuremberg' — predates the discovery of the Doppelmayr statement and is no longer the preferred dating)
falsifiability: A dated instrument or document proving a clarinet predating the 1690s, or evidence the register-key innovation belongs to another maker

title: The idiom-origin audit (method)
claim: An idiom's history is graded on two separate claims: the earliest printed attestation (the anchor, graded on its documentation) and the origin story that explains the phrase (a separate claim, graded on its own evidence). The most confidently told origin stories are the ones that fail at the dates.
place: English-language print culture (London anchor)
grade_reason: Demonstrated across six independently documented exhibits (nine-yards, rule-of-thumb, posh, crap, mad-as-a-hatter, let-them-eat-cake), each with published scholarship showing the story failing at the dates.
earliest_attestation: Demonstrated in the 2026 VIII.i idiom pass; the exhibits are centuries of English print

sources.ref: Kelly, Henry Ansgar (1994). 'Rule of Thumb and the Folklaw of the Husband's Stick', Journal of Legal Education 44(3):341-365 — the model demolition

Fred R. Shapiro / Ben Zimmer (Yale Alumni Magazine; Visual Thesaurus 'Word Routes') — the antedating method on 'the whole nine yards': 1962, then 1956/57 Kentucky Happy Hunting Ground, then 1946-51 Lexington KY, plus the 1912 'whole six yards'
Ben Yagoda, Gobsmacked! — the OED on 'posh': 'no evidence has been found for the existence of such tickets' (P.O.S.H.)
OED (2d ed., 1989) via Men and Masculinities 5(1), 2002 — earliest known 'rule of thumb': Sir William Hope, The Compleat Fencing-Master (1692)
TheCollector (Oct 10, 2026) — OED: first waste-sense 'crap' recorded 1846, when Thomas Crapper (b. 1836) was ten

competing_hypotheses: An idiom's origin story is reliable if it is old and widely repeated
Earliest printed attestation is only an artifact of what got digitized, so antedating proves nothing (rejected — it proves the story's postdating, which is the point)
falsifiability: A case where a famous, confidently-told origin story survives a full antedating check with its earliest prints — demonstrating that stories are reliable evidence of origins

title: TELLING (DEBUNKED): 'rule of thumb' = wife-beating law
claim: TELLING (DEBUNKED): the phrase 'rule of thumb' originates from an English common-law rule permitting a husband to beat his wife with a stick no thicker than his thumb.
place: London (legal and fencing print culture)
grade_reason: Henry Ansgar Kelly's 1994 Journal of Legal Education paper (44(3):341-365) surveyed the legal record and found no such law; the phrase never occurs in legal history; the first domestic-violence context is a 1782 satirical cartoon (The Rambler, 'Mr. Justice Thumb in the Act of Flagellation') about a Judge Buller rumor, not a rule.
earliest_attestation: Sir William Hope, The Compleat Fencing-Master (2d ed., 1692): 'What he doth, he doth by rule of thumb, and not by art' (OED 2d ed.)

sources.ref: Kelly, Henry Ansgar (1994). 'Rule of Thumb and the Folklaw of the Husband's Stick', Journal of Legal Education 44(3):341-365

Men and Masculinities 5(1), July 2002 — Kelly's demolition summarized: earliest known reference 1692 Hope; first recorded domestic-violence appearance the 1 Feb 1782 Rambler cartoon satirizing the Buller rumor

Cecil Adams, The Straight Dope — 'A couple of 19th-century U.S. trial opinions referred to an 'ancient law'... but rejected said law'; 'While this alleged rule involved a thumb, it wasn't the origin of 'rule of thumb''
Patricia T. O'Conner — 'one of the most persistent myths of political correctness'

competing_hypotheses: Blackstone's 'reasonable instrument' passage plus isolated judicial remarks (State v Rhodes, 1868; Bradley v State, 1824) — the courts rejected the thumb rule where it appeared
The phrase as a body-based measure (thumb = inch; cf. French pouce), consistent with the 1692 fencing-manual usage
falsifiability: A statute or judgment explicitly codifying a thumb-width standard for domestic discipline would resurrect the telling

title: Dom Pérignon invented champagne (4 August 1693)
claim: The Benedictine monk Dom Pérignon invented champagne (sparkling wine) on 4 August 1693 at the Abbey of Saint-Pierre d'Hautvillers, exclaiming 'Come quickly, I am drinking the stars!'
place: Abbey of Saint-Pierre d'Hautvillers, Champagne, France (the legend's theater)
grade_reason: Two independent kills: (1) the empty contemporary record — Pérignon's documented work ran the opposite direction: as cellar master he researched how to AVOID making sparkling wine, because secondary fermentation in the bottle caused explosions, the infamous le vin du diable ('the devil's wine'); (2) the manufactured trail — the invention legend was built in the 1820s by Dom Grossard, and the famous stars quotation only surfaces in an 1880s champagne advertisement (National Geographic; thisdayinwinehistory). Meanwhile the deliberate sugar-addition method that became the basis of Champagne production was documented in London in December 1662 by Christopher Merret — six years before Pérignon even arrived at Hautvillers (National Geographic, Smithsonian, Tim Atkin MW).
earliest_attestation: No contemporary attestation of any kind: no document from Pérignon's lifetime credits him with inventing sparkling wine, and the 'Come quickly, I am drinking the stars!' exclamation is first traced to an advertisement of the 1880s — nearly 200 years later. The legend itself originates in the 1820s, when Dom Grossard, one of Pérignon's successors at the Abbey of Saint-Pierre d'Hautvillers, falsely attributed the invention to the 17th-century cellar master (National Geographic, citing the champagne historiography).

sources.ref: National Geographic, 'Who put the bubbles in Champagne?' — the full autopsy: Pérignon did not invent champagne; the legend originated in the 1820s with Dom Grossard's false attribution; Merret's December 1662 Royal Society paper ('Our wine-coopers of recent times use vast quantities of Sugar Molasses to all sorts of wines to make them brisk and sparkling') is the first documented use of deliberately adding sugars to wine in a sealed bottle; Pérignon devoted his time to avoiding sparkling wine; English thick glass bottles withstood the pressure

Smithsonian Magazine, Sarah Zielinski (2009), 'Inventing Your Way to a Better Champagne Experience' — 'It was an English scientist and physician, Christopher Merrett, who discovered the process of double fermentation; he presented his paper on the subject to the Royal Society in 1662. (The Benedictine monk Dom Pérignon often erroneously gets credited with Merrett's discovery.)'

Tim Atkin MW, 'A beginner's guide to Champagne' (Observer Food Monthly) — 'Dom Pérignon didn't invent bubbles; we did. Christopher Merret presented a paper to the Royal Society about sparkling wine in December 1662, six years before Dom Perignon arrived in Champagne.'

thisdayinwinehistory.com, 'The Discovery of Sparkling Wine' — the stars quotation has no evidence Pérignon ever said it; earliest reference in an 1880s advertisement, ~200 years after the fact; 'Dom Pérignon initially attempted to remove the bubbles to prevent them from splitting underneath the stresses of the secondary fermentation'

Laithwaites (Richard Bull), 'Beginner's Guide to English Sparkling Wine' (updated 22 May 2026) — 'Royal Society archives show that in December 1662, an Englishman named Christopher Merret delivered a paper detailing how to add sugars and molasses to finished wines to make them 'brisk and sparkling.' This documented the traditional method a full 30 years before Champagne officially embraced it!'

Tom Stevenson, A World Encyclopaedia of Champagne and Sparkling Wine (1998), via The Free Library / Eileen Murphy — Stevenson published the Merret document: 'The documentary evidence describing the addition of sugar to a finished wine to induce a second fermentation for the specific purpose of making it sparkle does exist... it is in London. There is absolutely no evidence that Dom Perignon made a single bottle of sparkling wine. The French didn't like sparkling wine.'

competing_hypotheses: Pérignon invented champagne in some partial sense — e.g., he developed techniques (stronger corks, bottle handling) that later made sparkling production reliable; fails because no contemporary document attributes any sparkling-wine invention to him, and his documented work bent the opposite way
The 1693 date is a harmless founding myth with a grain of truth — held honestly: the grain is that Pérignon was a real, innovative cellar master at Hautvillers; the falsehood is the invention

Sparkling champagne was a purely French invention with a later English footnote — fails on the documentary chronology: Merret 1662 precedes Pérignon's 1668 arrival at Hautvillers, and the Royal Society paper describes the deliberate method
falsifiability: Produce one document from before 1750 — a letter, account book, abbey record, or Pérignon's own writing — crediting Dom Pérignon with the invention of sparkling wine. One parchment moves the grade; there are none.

title: The Cornish wreckers' false lights (the systematic-luring legend)
claim: Cornish wreckers in the 18th and 19th centuries routinely and systematically lured ships onto the rocks with deliberately displayed false lights (the 'lights tied to donkeys' tails' image) as an organized criminal industry — wrecking as deliberate murder-by-deception.
place: Cornwall, England (Mounts Bay sample)
grade_reason: Pearce's systematic 2010 study of 155 recorded Mounts Bay wrecks (1738-1860) found only 11 reports of direct attack (7%) while 77% of cases involved lifesaving activity; wrecking decomposed into three activities with direct attack-and-plunder the rarest; the 'deliberately luring ships onto the rocks' image is explicitly judged a myth.
earliest_attestation: The folk-devil image was 'firmly entrenched by the mid-eighteenth century' (Deacon's review of Pearce); the systematic scholarly refutation is Pearce 2010.

sources.ref: Cathryn J. Pearce, 'Cornish Wrecking 1700-1860: Reality and Popular Myth' (Boydell Press, 2010) — first comprehensive systematic inquiry; shows the image of Cornish wreckers as villains deliberately luring ships onto the rocks is a myth (PhD, Greenwich Maritime Institute)

Bernard Deacon's review of Pearce — the 'folk devil' firmly entrenched by the mid-18th c.; Pearce breaks wrecking into three activities; of 155 Mounts Bay wrecks 1738-1860 only 11 attack reports (7%) vs 77% lifesaving; sources: manor wreck presentments, EIC letter books, wreck case papers, salvage accounts, assize records, Trinity House correspondence

William Blackstone, Commentaries on the Laws of England, vol. I (3rd ed., 1768), p. 294 — on 26 Geo. II c. 19: plundering vessels in distress or wrecked, preventing escape, wounding with intent to destroy, or 'putting out false lights in order to bring any vessel into danger, are all declared to be capital felonies' (evidence of the FEAR, not the prevalence; the statute was repealed 1854)
26 Geo. II c. 19 — Stealing Shipwrecked Goods Act 1753 (royal assent 15 May 1753; repealed by Merchant Shipping Repeal Act 1854)

competing_hypotheses: Individual false-light incidents may have occurred; the DEBUNKED grade kills the SYSTEMATIC, ROUTINE, ORGANIZED reading, not the possibility of isolated incidents
The myth may preserve a distorted memory of genuine disputes over salvage law and the customary 'harvest' of washed-ashore goods
Some violent wrecking incidents are documented; Pearce counts them as rare, not representative
falsifiability: Contemporary court or Admiralty records showing false-light luring as a prosecuted, repeated, organized practice across multiple Cornish communities would revive the claim; Pearce's 155-wreck Mounts Bay sample (1738-1860) found the opposite pattern.

title: The real Cornish wrecking economy (1700-1860)
claim: Cornish wrecking in 1700-1860 was a real, multi-faceted coastal salvage economy: (1) rare direct attack and plunder of vessels, (2) the frequent 'harvesting' of wrecked goods from beaches and shorelines, and (3) salvage of goods washed ashore from wrecks that might lie many miles over the horizon — governed by a developing wreck law (the right to salvage goods washed on shore) and carried out by poor and gentry alike, with lifesaving activity far more common in the record than violence.
place: Cornwall, England
grade_reason: Converging independent source families — manor courts, company letter books, case papers, salvage accounts, assize records, Trinity House correspondence — all document the same three-activity salvage economy; held below VERIFIED as a historiographical synthesis (2010) rather than a single dated event.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary sources compiled by Pearce 2010: manor wreck presentments, East India Company letter books, wreck case papers, salvage accounts, family papers, broadsheets, Trinity House correspondence, assize records, diaries, newspapers, government reports; statute record 26 Geo. II c. 19 (1753).

sources.ref: Cathryn J. Pearce, 'Cornish Wrecking 1700-1860: Reality and Popular Myth' (Boydell Press, 2010) — three activities of wrecking; development of wreck law; poor and gentry alike involved; 155 Mounts Bay wrecks 1738-1860: 11 attack reports (7%), 77% lifesaving
26 Geo. II c. 19 — Stealing Shipwrecked Goods Act 1753 ('An Act for enforcing the Laws against Persons who shall steal or detain shipwrecked Goods'), royal assent 15 May 1753; repealed 1854
Wreck and Salvage Act 1846 — repeal schedule listing the 1753 Act among 13 repealed wreck statutes

competing_hypotheses: The salvage economy shaded into criminality at the margins; Pearce's 7% attack rate shows violence was real but rare, not absent

Local customary 'rights' to wrecked goods were progressively criminalized by central authority — the 1753 Act and later Merchant Shipping Acts represent that centralization, not an invention of new crime
falsifiability: A contemporary coastal-community source showing that beach harvesting and salvage were not customary practiced economies but inventions of the 19th-century record would overturn this; Pearce's multi-source archive makes that unlikely.

title: Cristofori invents the piano (documented 1700; named 1711)
claim: Bartolomeo Cristofori invented the piano in Florence around 1700 — first documented in the 1700 Medici instrument inventory ('arpicimbalo... newly invented by Bartolomeo Cristofori,' a harpsichord-like instrument with hammers and dampers), and first named 'pianoforte' in Scipione Maffei's 1711 article ('gravicembalo col piano, e forte').
place: Florence (the Medici court)
grade_reason: Multiple independent sources agree: the 1700 Medici inventory entry ('newly invented by Bartolomeo Cristofori,' hammers and dampers, two keyboards, four octaves); Meccoli's marginal note ('invented by Master Bartolomeo Christofani of Padua in the year 1700'); Maffei's 1711 Giornale de' letterati d'Italia article giving the name 'gravicembalo col piano, e forte' with a diagram of the action; the three surviving instruments (1720 Metropolitan Museum New York — the oldest surviving piano; 1722 Rome; 1726 Leipzig); the documented action innovations (escapement, check, dampers, isolated soundboard, thicker tenser strings, paired strings, soft pedal). The 1709 variant is fenced as a statement about completed instruments, not the invention date.
earliest_attestation: The 1700 Medici instrument inventory; Federigo Meccoli's marginal note dating the invention to 1700

sources.ref: Italy On This Day: 'An inventory of Medici instruments from 1700 described an "arpicimbalo", which resembled a harpsichord but which created sounds through hammers and dampers rather than the plucking mechanism... It was said to be "newly invented by Bartolomeo Cristofori". In 1711, Scipione Maffei... referred to Cristofori's "gravicembalo col piano, e forte" (harpsichord with soft and loud), the first time it was called by its eventual name, pianoforte. A Florentine court musician, Federigo Meccoli, noted that the "arpi cimbalo del piano e forte" was first made by Cristofori in 1700, which is regarded as the birth date for the piano.' Three survivors: 1720 Met New York, 1722 Rome, 1726 Leipzig. Bach dismissed an early model; Silbermann built on Cristofori's blueprint from 1730.

Timenote: Meccoli's marginal note — 'These are the ways in which it is possible to play the Arpicimbalo del piano e forte, invented by Master Bartolomeo Christofani [sic] of Padua in the year 1700' (transl. Stewart Pollens). By 1711 Cristofori had built three pianos.

Wikipedia, 'Fortepiano': 'The first reliable record of his invention appears in the inventory of the Medici family (who were Cristofori's patrons), dated 1700.' The 1720 Met instrument 'is the oldest surviving piano.' Maffei's 1711 article included a diagram of the action; the 1725 German translation 'was perhaps the triggering event in the spread of the fortepiano to German-speaking countries.'

1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Pianoforte': Maffei's description appeared in the Giornale dei letterati d'Italia, 1711; 'in 1709 Christofori had completed four "gravecembali col piano e forte"' — the source of the 1709 dating variant.

competing_hypotheses: The '1709' dating (found in the 1911 Britannica: 'in 1709 Christofori had completed four gravecembali col piano e forte' — a statement about completed instruments, not the invention's documentary birthdate, which is 1700)
falsifiability: A dated instrument or document proving a piano predating 1700, or evidence the 1700 inventory entry refers to a different instrument

title: The black-clad ninja assassin
claim: Historical Japanese ninja (shinobi) wore distinctive all-black outfits (the classic black shinobi shōzoku) and fought primarily as stealth assassins relying on thrown shuriken.
place: Edo/Tokyo — the theater district where the image was born
grade_reason: No period document records the black uniform; the image's documentary trail runs through the theater (kuroko/bunraku stagehands) and 19th-c. woodblock art, while the historical record shows shinobi working in civilian disguise.
earliest_attestation: Kabuki/kuroko stage convention (18th c.); Hokusai's early-19th-c. black-clad ninja imagery

sources.ref: Kuroko (Wikipedia) — black costume as the theatrical convention for invisibility; historian Stephen Turnbull's suggestion that the black-ninja stereotype derives from kabuki/kuroko

Matt Alt, via Kotaku (2013) — Hokusai credited with the first image of the ninja in the classic black suit, early 19th c.; the word 'ninja' itself does not appear until the 1800s; prior vocabulary: shinobi, 'a dude from Iga'
Jennifer R. Povey, 'No, Ninjas Do Not Wear Black' (Medium, 2022) — the kuroko prop-handler explanation; black is poor night camouflage; real operatives dressed as civilians

Ninja (geishaworld wiki, compiled from published sources) — 'there is no written evidence for such a costume'; the black-clothing notion is 'likely rooted in artistic convention'; operative clothing was civilian dress, with concealable light armor (kusari karuta, tenugui) between layers

competing_hypotheses: A few writers have speculated that dark robes (one formulation: slightly tainted with red to hide bloodstains) could have been sensible infiltration wear — but the literature presents this as speculation, not evidence
The historical shinobi did carry throwing implements; the dispute is about the uniform and the assassin-as-job-description, not the tools
falsifiability: A period (pre-1868) Japanese document, woodblock print, or excavated garment reliably depicting an all-black shinobi uniform in operational use

title: The phonetic-khipu claim: were khipus writing?
claim: Inca khipus encoded spoken language phonetically — a logosyllabic writing system in which pendant cords represent syllables — rather than recording numbers only.
place: San Juan de Collata, Peruvian Andes (approximate; highland village context)
grade_reason: One researcher's published decipherment of two lineage names from two colonial-era khipus, not replicated on independent material and not consensus; the baseline (most imperial khipus are numerical) stands.
earliest_attestation: Sabine Hyland, University of St Andrews, Current Anthropology (2017): analysis of two khipus held by the village of San Juan de Collata, Peru — 95 distinct symbols from combinations of color, fiber type, and ply direction; proposed phonetic decipherment of two lineage names (Alluka, read from final three cords ay-ew-ka; Yakapar on the second khipu).

sources.ref: Sabine Hyland, Current Anthropology (2017): 95 symbols (color x fiber x ply); phonetic decipherment of the Alluka ('ay-ew-ka') and Yakapar lineage names on two 18th-century Collata khipus
New Scientist (2018): Hyland's reading method — 'anka' (blue, in the regional dialect) mapped to a blue S-ply llama-wool cord for the 'ka' syllable
Galen Brokaw (Montana State, uninvolved scholar): 'groundbreaking if true — the challenge is to find more sources, more extensive evidence' (Discover, 2018)

Gary Urton (Harvard, National Geographic reporting): 'time is a big problem — whether or not we can take these findings and project them into the past, that remains the big question' — on whether Collata findings apply to the Inca period
Marcia and Robert Ascher (1981): the consensus baseline — most surviving khipus' information is numeric and readable as such

competing_hypotheses: The Collata logosyllabic system is a colonial-era innovation, developed under contact with alphabetic writing — not a survival of Inca-period practice
The final strings encode kinship or office by conventional signs without full phoneticity — names can be marked without a writing system
The consensus position: imperial khipus were overwhelmingly numerical accounting devices (Ascher & Ascher), with narrative capacity unproven
falsifiability: Independent replication of the phonetic reading on a second khipu set whose named lineages are attested in archival documents (a blinded test), or demonstration that the Alluka/Yakapar matches fail on other khipus with known names

title: The 1712/1713 verdict against Leibniz: a verdict that invalidates itself
claim: The Royal Society's 1712/1713 report, the Commercium Epistolicum (published 8 January 1713), fairly adjudicated the calculus priority dispute between Newton and Leibniz and stands as valid evidence that Leibniz plagiarized Newton.
place: London, Royal Society
grade_reason: The verdict's own process disqualifies it: Newton, as Royal Society president, appointed the committee, controlled the documentary selection, and wrote the report himself (anonymously) — the plaintiff was the judge, the jury, and the author. The committee never solicited Leibniz's version; he saw the verdict only in autumn 1714. Modern scholarship (Hall 1980) holds both men invented the calculus independently.
earliest_attestation: Commercium Epistolicum D. Johannis Collinsii et aliorum de analysi promota (London, 1712/1713)

sources.ref: Commercium Epistolicum (London, 1712/1713) — the report itself
Newton's drafts of the report, in his own hand (Cambridge/Portsmouth papers)
Leibniz–Newton calculus controversy — summary of the committee's composition, Newton's authorship, and Leibniz's autumn-1714 sighting (Wikipedia, aggregating Hall, Westfall)
Hall, A.R., Philosophers at War (1980): the consensus statement of independent invention

competing_hypotheses: The committee genuinely believed the documentary record supported Newton and wrote accordingly (Hall 1980 grants Newton may have believed his own case)
The report's documentary selection is honest even if the process was one-sided — the letters it prints are real
falsifiability: Leibniz's own papers from 1675 proving dependence on Newton's manuscripts — none exists; or evidence the committee solicited Leibniz's testimony — the record shows it did not

title: Newcomen's atmospheric engine (1712): the first successful steam engine
claim: Thomas Newcomen's first commercially successful atmospheric steam engine was erected in 1712 at the Conygree Coalworks near Dudley (Tipton, in the West Midlands) to pump water from a flooded coal mine — the practical steam engine that pumped the mines of the early 18th century.
place: Conygree Coalworks, Tipton, West Midlands (near Dudley Castle)
grade_reason: Independent institutional lines converge on the 1712 Conygree installation (ASME landmark documentation, Newcomen Society, Black Country Living Museum's 1986 working replica erected a mile or two from the original site); held below VERIFIED on the thinness of surviving contemporary documentation and the exact-site ambiguity.
earliest_attestation: The 1712 Conygree (Tipton, near Dudley Castle) engine — reported in engineering-history literature from the Newcomen Society tradition and J. T. Desaguliers's 1717 course of experimental philosophy

sources.ref: ASME Engineering History Landmark documentation: Newcomen atmospheric engine — first success 1712 near Dudley Castle, Tipton; ~600 engines built; operated under Savery patent
Newcomen Memorial Engine / Newcomen atmospheric engine research tradition — first successful engine considered the Dudley Castle engine of 1712; 104 engines by 1733; Conygree Coalworks, Tipton
Black Country Living Museum — full-scale 1986 working replica of the 1712 Newcomen engine, erected near the original site
Chris Upton (Birmingham Post, via Free Library) — 1712: Newcomen and partner John Calley erected the engine to pump Lord Dudley's coal mines; the 'atmospheric engine' naming

competing_hypotheses: Thomas Savery's 1698 'Miner's Friend' steam pump preceded Newcomen and shared the commercial field under Savery's broad patent — a pump, not a beam engine, and commercially marginal for mine drainage
An earlier experimental Newcomen engine may have run in Devon c. 1710–1711 — the 1712 Conygree engine is the first successful installation, not necessarily the first trial
falsifiability: A contemporary 1712 document showing the Conygree installation never operated, or an earlier commercially successful steam engine with a verifiable installation record

title: The 'prompt £20,000 prize' version of the Harrison story
claim: John Harrison's marine chronometer H4 won the longitude problem, and the Board of Longitude promptly awarded him the full £20,000 Longitude Prize under the 1714 Longitude Act.
place: Greenwich / London (Board of Longitude, Royal Observatory, Parliament)
grade_reason: The ledger kills the prompt-full-award reading: the Board demanded replication (two copies of H4) before the final £10,000, paid Harrison in stages, and Parliament's 1773 Act was a benevolence award 'in spite of the Board, instead of from it' — the £20,000 was never formally awarded to anyone. Scope fenced: the grade kills the prompt-award version only — never the Jamaica trial's success, never the man's achievement, never the real £23,065.
earliest_attestation: The Longitude rewards ledger (Derek Howse appendix; Wikipedia 'Longitude rewards'): staged payments £250 (1737) → £2,000 (1741–55) → £2,865 (1760–65) → £7,500 (1765, for H4's performance) → £8,750 by Act of Parliament (1773); total ~£23,065; the £20,000 never formally awarded to anyone.

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Longitude rewards' — Howse appendix payment chain, £23,065 total over ~36 years; full £20,000 never awarded to anyone

Dava Sobel, Longitude (1995), via the Board's 24 April 1773 minutes as reported: 'this amount nearly totaled the remainder of the longitude prize due him, but it was not the coveted prize. Rather, the sum was a bounty awarded by the benevolence of Parliament — in spite of the Board of Longitude, instead of from it'
Spacedaily/explorersweb long-form accounts: the Kew 1772 trial, George III's intervention, the 1773 Act of Parliament

competing_hypotheses: Sobel's popular telling (Longitude, 1995): Harrison 'won' the prize against a corrupt establishment — the emotional spine of the bestseller and the 2000 Granada film
Betts's scholarly rebalance (Time Restored, 2006): the Board was cautious, not corrupt — large public prize, rival method on the table, replication required by the Act's own terms
The textbook one-liner: 'Harrison solved longitude and won £20,000' — true about the solving, wrong about the awarding
falsifiability: A Board-of-Longitude minute or Treasury warrant recording a formal £20,000 award to Harrison under the Act's terms would overturn this; the ledger's thirty-six-year disbursement trail is what currently stands.

title: The world's first lightship: the Nore, 1731-1732
claim: The world's first lightship — a floating lighthouse — was moored at the Nore sandbank at the mouth of the Thames Estuary in 1731-1732: the private venture of Captain Robert Hamblin (shipowner of King's Lynn), the vessel built by David Avery, operating on a 1730 patent from George II; Trinity House revoked the original patent as an infringement of its powers, and the Admiralty allowed tolls to be levied while the vessel became Trinity House property.
place: The Nore sandbank, Thames Estuary, England (approx station area)
grade_reason: Multiple independent secondary sources plus a 1929 abstract of the actual 1730 patent grant converge on Hamblin/Avery/Nore; the 'world's first' phrasing is Trinity House's own tradition and is carried with the 1629 unanswered proposal as a competing earlier that was never built. Held below VERIFIED because the loop has not inspected the primary patent records themselves, and the placement year spreads 1731-1732 (1734 in one outlier source).
earliest_attestation: The patent grant itself, 14 July 1730, as abstracted in Nature 124:76 (13 July 1929), 'Calendar of Patent Records'; George II's 1730 patent for 'the first English lightship' (Grupp 1956:30, via US lightship history)

sources.ref: Nature 124, 76 (13 July 1929), 'Calendar of Patent Records' — patent granted to Captain Robert Hamblin of Lynn, 14 July 1730, for 'a new method for distinguishing of lights'; 'Hamblin also financed the first light-ship, which was established at the Nore in 1732 by David Avery'
Elder Brethren of Trinity House (history section) — 'The Nore lightship was established as the world's first floating light in 1732'

Lightship (history) — 'In 1731, David Avery and Robert Hamblin placed the earliest British lightship at The Nore near the mouth of the River Thames. This was a private venture that operated profitably'
History of lighthouses — 'The Nore lightship was established as the world's first floating light in 1732'

US lightship history (media.defense.gov; Grupp 1956:30) — 1629 unanswered petition to Charles I for a Goodwin Sands lightship; 'In 1730, upon receiving a formal request from Robert Hamblin, George II granted a patent for the first English lightship'
Docklands History Group, 'Trinity House' talk (1999) — 'The first effective lightship was built by David Avery on the Thames at the Nore in 1732 under licence from Trinity House'
FamilySearch Wiki, 'Trinity House' — 'its first lightship was placed at the Nore in 1732'

competing_hypotheses: A 1629 petition to Charles I sought a lightship at the Goodwin Sands — it went unanswered (Grupp 1956:30); an unbuilt proposal does not displace the Nore claim, but it shows the idea predated Hamblin
Roman-era fire beacons placed on ships are attested in some records — precedents for the concept, not a stationed, maintained lightship
The LHC source gives 'invented by Robert Hamblin in 1734' — a late outlier date, carried as a source disagreement, not a rival claim
The Hamblin/Avery division of labour (patent-holder/financier vs builder) varies across tellings; Nature's 1929 abstract has Hamblin financing and Avery establishing
falsifiability: Discovery of a built, stationed, functioning lightship with documentary attestation predating 1731, or proof that the Nore vessel was never stationed (e.g. Trinity House records showing no vessel, no tolls)

title: 'Lightships were safe — they never dragged, never sank'
claim: Lightships were a safe, uneventful duty: anchored vessels that sat quietly on station and were never in serious danger — the romantic assumption that the boats just sat there.
place: South Goodwin Sands, off Deal, Kent (LV-90 loss, Nov 1954)
grade_reason: Killed by the documented casualty record: South Goodwin LV-90 (1954, 7 crew), wartime sinkings (TH's own 1945 fleet count acknowledges them), the Olympic ramming (1934), the 1944 hurricane loss, the U-boat sinking (1918), and anchor-dragging incidents — lightship duty was officially 'the most dangerous duty' in lighthouse organizations. Scope: kills the 'safe/never in danger' reading only; the lightship institution itself is CORROBORATED in evt-nore-lightship-1732-001.
earliest_attestation: The romantic assumption lives in museum-plaque language and maritime nostalgia writing; the documentary killers are the casualty records cited below

sources.ref: List of lightvessels of Great Britain — 'South Goodwin ... 27 Nov 1954 ... Sank in a storm in 1954 with the loss of all lives except one'

JaySea Archaeology / goodwinsands.org.uk — LV-90 (South Goodwin, commissioned 1937, LV number 90), lost night of 26-27 Nov 1954: hurricane-force winds, separated from her anchor chain, unpowered, seven crew lost; the sole survivor was Ronald Murton, a bird-migration observer, not crew

Lighthouse Digest (via goodwinsands.org.uk) — 'Being a crewman stationed on a lightship was considered the most dangerous duty by nearly every lighthouse organization in the world ... regardless of the weather, a lightship was not allowed to leave its station'
Dominic Winter auction footnote (Trinity House WWII bell) — 'At the end of the Second World War (i.e. 1945), TH had, in theory, 43 lightships but some had been sunk and/or damaged during the War'
Lightvessel LV-95 (Inner Dowsing) — 'on the Varne station, she unknowingly dragged anchor in a gale' on 1 December 1966, found 2 nautical miles off-station
Swansea & Port Talbot docks history — English & Welsh Grounds lightvessel sprang a leak in a severe gale, 24 August 1953; Barry lifeboat stood by

US lightship losses (Lighthouse Digest via goodwinsands.org.uk) — Nantucket LV-117 rammed by RMS Olympic 1934; Vineyard Lightship sunk by a September 1944 hurricane with her entire crew; Diamond Shoals lightship sunk by a German U-boat in 1918

competing_hypotheses: The myth's carrier is museum-nostalgia framing — the quiet, picturesque lightship in harbour photos — which hides the station-keeping reality
Survivor bias: most stations held most nights, so the institution looked placid between disasters; the record counts the disasters
falsifiability: Would require the 1954 wreck record, the wartime sinkings, and the documented American losses all to be false — multiple independent casualty records would have to be fabricated

title: Norden's 1737 plates: the Sphinx already noseless
claim: Frederic Louis Norden's Egypt plates — drawn in Egypt in 1737, engraved and published posthumously in 'Voyage d'Egypte et de Nubie' (Copenhagen, 1755) — constitute a dated eyewitness image record of the Sphinx that predates both the Napoleonic myth (1798) and photography (1840s), and functions as documentary evidence: the 1737 plate shows the Sphinx already noseless.
place: Great Sphinx of Giza, Giza Plateau, Egypt (the plate's subject)
grade_reason: The plates exist, are multiply held in libraries, carry a 1755 imprint, and are independently corroborated: Pococke's 1743-45 drawings likewise show the nose gone, and the stone's physical state matches. This is the engraving-as-testimony doctrine made concrete — a dated hand, no retouching possible, falsifying a claim 61 years younger than the drawing.
earliest_attestation: Norden's own travel account and plates, 'Voyage d'Egypte et de Nubie', Copenhagen 1755 (French edition; English translation London 1757).

sources.ref: Frederic Louis Norden, 'Voyage d'Egypte et de Nubie', Copenhagen 1755 (posthumous; Royal Danish Academy of Sciences) — the plates of the Sphinx, noseless
historytools.org, 'The Enigma of the Great Sphinx's Missing Nose' — Norden's 'extraordinarily detailed drawing clearly depicts the Sphinx without a nose'
Richard Pococke, 'A Description of the East' (1743-45) — independent near-contemporary drawn views showing the Sphinx without its nose

media.caption: Norden's 1737 view of the Sphinx, clearly noseless (Wikimedia Commons, via historytools.org)

competing_hypotheses: The plate is a faithful record: Norden was an officer and cartographer, his views systematically detailed, and the absence of the nose corroborates every later image — the strongest reading, and the team's working one

The plate could show a conventional or reconstructed view: Norden's editors engraved from his drawings after his death (1742); but the engravings track his on-the-spot measurements, and the noselessness matches Pococke's independent 1743-45 drawings

One plate is a thin archive: true — and the method's strength is convergence; the Sphinx's noselessness is additionally confirmed by Pococke, by 19th-century lithographs, and by the physical state of the stone itself
falsifiability: Show that the 1755 plates do not derive from 1737 on-site observation (e.g., that they are studio inventions), or produce a dated pre-1737 image showing the Sphinx WITH a nose — which would narrow, not widen, the myth's kill.

title: Prussia 1754: the first abolition of judicial torture
claim: Frederick II of Prussia abolished judicial torture by cabinet order in 1754 — the first European abolition of the practice, a decade before Beccaria's book.
place: Berlin, Prussia (the cabinet orders)
grade_reason: A documented act of state with a stable scholarly dating: the 1740 restriction order and the 1754 abolition order are the standard account (Langbein); the sequence predates Beccaria's 1764 book by a decade, which is the chronological fact that kills the single-cause myth.
earliest_attestation: Frederick II's cabinet orders: the 1740 restriction of torture and the 1754 abolition order — documented acts of state.

sources.ref: Frederick II of Prussia: cabinet order of 3 June 1740 restricting judicial torture; cabinet order of 1754 abolishing it — documented acts of state; standard dating per Langbein, Torture and the Law of Proof
Scholarly account of Frederick II's judicial and legal reforms (abolition of torture and corporal punishment, judicial centralization) — original German sources

competing_hypotheses: The dating caveat: Frederick's 3 June 1740 order restricted torture (high treason and murder with strong suspicion only); the 1754 cabinet order abolished it. Some accounts blur the two steps — the restriction is 1740, the abolition is 1754.

The paper-vs-practice caveat: extralegal coercion and corporal punishment persisted in Prussian practice after 1754; the grade certifies the legal abolition, not the disappearance of every coercive practice.

The Carolina irony: the 1532 Carolina's formal safeguards on torture were the most elaborate in Europe — and Prussia, a Carolina jurisdiction, was the first to scrap the whole edifice rather than reform it.
falsifiability: A pre-1754 Prussian cabinet order fully reinstating torture, or evidence the 1754 order was never issued, would force revision; the 1740/1754 sequence is the standard scholarly account.

title: Celsius's 1742 paper: the reversed scale and the birth of pressure-calibrated thermometry
claim: In 1742, Anders Celsius's paper 'Observations of two persistent degrees on a thermometer' established a mercury thermometer calibrated on two fixed points — with the melting point of ice shown to be essentially pressure-independent and the boiling point of water calibrated at the mean barometric pressure at mean sea level.
place: Uppsala, Sweden (Celsius's observatory; the 1742 paper)
grade_reason: The 1742 paper is a documented publication, and its content is corroborated across the standard histories: (1) Celsius demonstrated that the melting point of ice is essentially unaffected by air pressure — a genuine fixed point; (2) he determined with remarkable precision how the boiling point of water varies with atmospheric pressure and proposed calibrating his scale's zero point (the boiling point on his reversed scale) at the mean barometric pressure at mean sea level — the conceptual seed of what the BIPM's 10th CGPM defined in 1954 as one standard atmosphere (1,013,250 dynes/cm² = 101.325 kPa). Held at CORROBORATED rather than VERIFIED because the paper is known through the standard historiography and encyclopedic transmission rather than multiple independent primary sources consulted directly in this pass. The grade covers the paper and its science, never the schoolbook claim about the scale's orientation — that claim is dead in the companion record.
earliest_attestation: Celsius's paper 'Observations of two persistent degrees on a thermometer' (1742), reporting the experiments

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Degree Celsius' — History section: the 1742 paper's content — melting-point pressure independence, boiling-point pressure dependence, calibration at mean sea-level pressure; the 1954 CGPM one-atmosphere definition

competing_hypotheses: None on the paper's existence or contents. On priority of the forward orientation, see evt-celsius-scale-inverted-myth-001
falsifiability: Showing the 1742 paper does not exist, is misdated, or describes a different scale than the boiling-zero / freezing-100 instrument

title: The myth: Celsius invented the Celsius scale as we use it (0 freezing, 100 boiling)
claim: Anders Celsius invented the Celsius temperature scale with 0° representing the freezing point of water and 100° representing the boiling point of water — the scale as it hangs on every classroom wall.
place: Uppsala, Sweden (Celsius's observatory; the 1742 paper)
grade_reason: Celsius's own 1742 paper documents the reverse of the modern scale: 0 represented the boiling point of water, 100 the freezing point. The modern orientation is documented elsewhere, later: Jean-Pierre Christin published the inverted scale on 19 May 1743 (the 'Thermometer of Lyon,' built by Pierre Casati); Linnaeus used the reversed version from 1744 (thermometer by Daniel Ekström), with the first known forward-scale temperature readings in his 16 Dec 1745 Hortus Upsaliensis letter to Samuel Nauclér; Mårten Strömer (Celsius's own student) also built forward-oriented instruments in Uppsala. The name survived; the orientation did not. The schoolbook telling is false as a claim about Celsius's invention. Fences hold: Celsius's real 1742 achievements — the pressure-independence of ice's melting point, the pressure-calibration of boiling at mean sea level (the seed of the standard atmosphere) — survive in the companion record, untouched.
earliest_attestation: Celsius's 1742 paper 'Observations of two persistent degrees on a thermometer' — the telling being graded here is the modern schoolbook attribution (0 = freezing, 100 = boiling, invented by Celsius)

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Degree Celsius' — History section: Celsius's 1742 reversed original (0 boiling, 100 freezing); Christin's 19 May 1743 inversion and the Thermometer of Lyon (Pierre Casati); Linnaeus's 1744 reversed-scale thermometer by Daniel Ekström; the 16 Dec 1745 Hortus Upsaliensis letter to Samuel Nauclér; Mårten Strömer
Wikipedia 'Celsius' (Simple English) — 'In 1742, Anders Celsius made a "reversed" version of the modern Celsius temperature scale' (archival classroom mirror, rachel.education.gov.ck)
University of North Carolina Asheville ATMS 320, 'History of the Thermometer' lecture slides (Godfrey) — the 1742 / 1744 / 1743 chronology in a meteorology curriculum

Testbook exam Q&A bank — the schoolbook telling being graded: 'Celsius invented the Celsius (Centigrade) temperature scale... 0 represents the freezing point of water, and 100 represents the boiling point'

competing_hypotheses: The co-attribution framing: the modern orientation emerged in 1743–1745 from several workers at once (Christin in Lyon, Linnaeus and Strömer in Sweden) — pre-modern-communications simultaneous invention, so no single inventor owns the orientation
The Christin-first framing: Jean-Pierre Christin's 19 May 1743 Thermometer of Lyon is the first published forward-oriented scale, making him the inventor of the modern form outright
The Strömer framing: Mårten Strömer's Uppsala build (1744–45) is the instrument that actually carried the forward scale into Swedish practice
falsifiability: A Celsius-published or Celsius-built forward-oriented thermometer (0 freezing, 100 boiling) dated before 19 May 1743

title: Jonas Hanway popularizes the umbrella in London (c. 1750-1786)
claim: Jonas Hanway (1712-1786) was the first Englishman who habitually carried an umbrella in London rain — beginning c. 1750 and persisting for about thirty years despite public mockery, notably from hackney coachmen who saw umbrellas as a threat to their fares; by his death umbrellas were commonplace in London, and men even called their umbrellas a 'Hanway'.
place: London
grade_reason: Multiple independent attestations converge: the 1911 Britannica's 'first Englishman who habitually carried an umbrella'; Sangster's trade history (30 years of carrying, the mockery, the hackney coachmen's hostility, Wolfe's 1752 letter); Portsmouth Cathedral's biography (first man to carry his own umbrella around London, with the umbrella's physical description). Held below VERIFIED on the single-biography provenance of some details (the 30-year figure, the ebony-handle description).
earliest_attestation: Pugh's life of Hanway (via Sangster 1868); 1911 Britannica 'Umbrella'; contemporary context in Wolfe's 1752 Paris letter

sources.ref: 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Umbrella' (public domain): 'The traveller Jonas Hanway, who died in 1786, is credited with having been the first Englishman who habitually carried an umbrella'
William Sangster, Umbrellas and Their History (1868): ~30 years of carrying (hence c. 1750); derision from hackney coachmen; Wolfe's 1752 Paris letter; the small parapluie defending his face and wig

Portsmouth Cathedral, Life of Jonas Hanway: 'the first man to carry his own umbrella around London'; umbrella described — ebony handle with small fruits and flowers, pale green silk outside, straw-coloured satin lining, folding to the length of a man's hand
acrosswalls.org Hanway notes: Female Tatler 12 Dec 1709 coffee-house umbrella (pre-Hanway London umbrellas); 'men even called their umbrellas a Hanway'

competing_hypotheses: The 'thirty years' figure traces to Pugh's biography of Hanway via Sangster — one biographical line, not a dated series of sightings
The 'first Englishman' credit is the 1911 Britannica's conventional phrasing; the boundary between 'first' and 'first to do it openly and persistently' is thin on the surviving evidence
falsifiability: A dated source showing habitual male umbrella-carrying in London before 1750, or proof that Pugh's account of Hanway's umbrella use was invented

title: 'The first stapler was made for King Louis XV' — DEBUNKED
claim: The telling that 'the first stapler was made in the 18th century for King Louis XV of France, with handmade staples each inscribed with the insignia of the royal court.'
place: Versailles, France — where the telling places the stapler
grade_reason: Two independent kills: (1) the man who spread the story retracted it after his own research — collector Curtis A. Scaglione traces the tale to a 1997 Swingline company letter, finds 'no evidence to support or validate this stapler ever existed at all,' and shows the embellishments (gold staples, 'kept it to himself') were added later by other writers; (2) material culture: dozens of Louis XV documents examined show single sheets folded with red wax seals bearing the royal insignia — no multi-page documents, no puncture holes, no fasteners ever observed.
earliest_attestation: The story's traceable source: a 1997 Swingline Company letter to collector Curtis A. Scaglione ('The earliest stapling machine we know of was one built during the 18th Century for King Louis XV of France. The individual staples were handmade and inscribed with the insignia of the Royal Court.')

sources.ref: Curtis A. Scaglione, 'Fastener History' (Fact, Fiction, and Folklore) — officemuseum.online: origin traced to 1997 Swingline letter; retraction: 'no evidence to support or validate this stapler ever existed at all'; embellishments identified; documents examined — single sheets, folded, red wax seals, no punctures

Discover Magazine, 'They Invented it' (Fenella Saunders) — repeats the telling ('One of the first known staplers belonged to King Louis XV of France. Each staple was decorated with the royal insignia') — belief ecology, not evidence

University at Buffalo, 'Keeping it all together: The history of the stapler' — 'Legend has it that the first known stapler device was made in the 18th century as a regal gift for Louis XV' — frames it as legend

competing_hypotheses: The scoped, honest version — '18th-century French offices used handmade metal paper fasteners of some kind' — is unattested as well this pass; no surviving example or contemporary description located
A genuine royal fastening device could surface with provenance and would be graded on its own evidence — the debunk kills the story's transmission, not the possibility of an artifact
falsifiability: A surviving 18th-century fastening device with documented French royal provenance, or a contemporary (pre-1800) description of such a device, would reopen the claim.

title: The Encyclopédie (1751–1772): the Enlightenment's printing war
claim: Denis Diderot and Jean le Rond d'Alembert's Encyclopédie, ou dictionnaire raisonné des sciences, des arts et des métiers (1751–1772) — 28 folio volumes (17 of text, 11 of plates), some 72,000 articles — systematically organized all human knowledge with the mechanical arts given the same dignity as the liberal ones, was suppressed in 1759, and was completed anyway: the Enlightenment's masterwork and its printing war.
place: Paris, France (Le Breton's print shop; the volumes were printed in Paris and Neuchâtel)
grade_reason: Multiple independent primary attestation of the strongest kind: the 28 published volumes themselves, the contemporary subscriber and police records, the 1759 suppression decree, and the surviving correspondence of the editors. The book is its own evidence.
earliest_attestation: The published volumes themselves (1751 onward) — thousands of surviving copies in libraries worldwide; contemporary press coverage, subscriber lists, and the 1759 Conseil du Roi suppression decree.

sources.ref: The 28 published volumes (1751–1772) — the artifact itself, thousands of surviving copies
The 1759 Conseil du Roi suppression decree — the state's own record of the book it tried to kill
Diderot's correspondence and Malesherbes's protection (the censor who warned the editors before raids) — the contemporary paper trail of the clandestine completion

competing_hypotheses: The conservative reading: the Encyclopédie was a commercial venture that got rich selling scandal — true as a claim about the business (its subscribers made it one of the century's great publishing successes), and fenced off from this grade, which covers the publication record

The censorship worked: the 1759 suppression (after the Damiens affair's fallout and the Helvétius scandal) genuinely silenced the project — false; Diderot finished the remaining volumes in secret with the tacit protection of Malesherbes, the censor himself
falsifiability: The claim is the publication record; it is falsified by the non-existence of the volumes — they exist, on shelves, in thousands. Individual article attributions (which contributor wrote what) are a separate, finer question and not covered by this grade.

title: The Liberty Bell (State House Bell)
claim: The Liberty Bell — originally the Pennsylvania State House bell — was ordered in 1751 by Assembly Speaker Isaac Norris from the London firm of Lester and Pack (later the Whitechapel Bell Foundry), cast with the inscription 'Proclaim LIBERTY Throughout all the Land unto all the Inhabitants Thereof' (Leviticus 25:10). It arrived in Philadelphia in September 1752, cracked on its first test strike, and was twice recast in 1753 by Philadelphia workmen John Pass and John Stow, whose surnames appear on the bell. It hung in the State House (now Independence Hall) steeple, was used to summon lawmakers and mark proclamations, weighs about 2,080 pounds, was dubbed the 'Liberty Bell' by abolitionist societies in the 1830s, and today stands in the Liberty Bell Center, Independence National Historical Park.
place: Liberty Bell Center, Independence National Historical Park, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
grade_reason: Multiply attested by the commissioning documents, the bell's own surviving inscription naming Pass & Stow and 1753, the Whitechapel order record, and continuous institutional custody (State House to Liberty Bell Center).
earliest_attestation: Pennsylvania Assembly minutes (order, 1751); the bell's own inscription (Pass & Stow, 1753); Whitechapel/Assembly correspondence

sources.ref: National Park Service — 'The Liberty Bell Story' (Independence National Historical Park film/description): Whitechapel casting 1751, first crack on arrival 1752, Pass & Stow 1753 recasting, inscription text, ~2,000 lbs, elm yoke

Wikipedia 'Liberty Bell' — Lester and Pack commission, first crack on ringing after arrival, two Pass & Stow recastings, Leviticus 25:10 inscription, abolitionist naming 1830s, 1847 short story origin of the July 4, 1776 association
American Anti-Slavery Society newspaper (1839) — first 'Liberty Bell' naming via the abolitionist image

competing_hypotheses: Commission year: NPS and most sources say ordered 1751; some summaries say commissioned 1752 — the order and the casting straddle the turn of the year

Whether the bell rang on July 8, 1776: no contemporary account names it, but most historians believe it was among the bells rung at the Declaration's first public reading — carried as probable, not proven
falsifiability: Assembly records showing no such order, or metallurgical proof the bell is not the Pass & Stow recasting — no such evidence exists; the bell's inscription and the foundry paperwork agree

title: Schönbrunn 1752 — the zoo that predates London
claim: Tiergarten Schönbrunn (Vienna), founded 1752, is the oldest zoo in the world still in operation.
place: Tiergarten Schönbrunn, Vienna (coordinates via map.geocode, FULL_ADDRESS match)
grade_reason: Three independent confirmations converge: the zoo's own official history, UNESCO's World Heritage designation of the palace-and-gardens ensemble, and standard encyclopedic sources — all agree on 1752 (public 1779) and continuous operation to the present. The foil to the London-first myth: the documented older institution.
earliest_attestation: 1752 imperial menagerie (Francis I); 1779 general public opening; UNESCO WHS listing for the palace gardens including the zoo.

sources.ref: Schönbrunn Zoo official history — founded 1752, public 1779, 'oldest zoo in the world still in operation'
UNESCO World Heritage Centre — Palace and Gardens of Schönbrunn
tourism-review.com — 'world's oldest zoo is in Austria' (article1326)

competing_hypotheses: A smaller animal park existed on the site from 1540 — the 1752 founding is the imperial menagerie, not the first animals on the ground
The 'oldest zoo' qualifier rests on continuous operation; the distinction is carried honestly as 'still in operation', not 'oldest menagerie ever'
falsifiability: Documented closure of the institution between 1752 and present, or an earlier continuously operating zoo with public access.

title: Beccaria's book did not end judicial torture — the single-cause myth
claim: Cesare Beccaria's 1764 book 'On Crimes and Punishments' (Dei delitti e delle pene) ended judicial torture in Europe — the single-book origin story of the abolition.
place: Europe (the abolition century: Prussia 1754 → Milan 1764 → France 1780/1788)
grade_reason: Three kills: (1) CHRONOLOGY — Prussia abolished judicial torture in 1754, a decade before Beccaria's 1764 book; (2) MECHANISM — abolition was a decades-long, multi-state administrative reform driven by the reformed law of proof (Langbein), not a book's magic; (3) the book's real influence (Tuscany 1786, the French debate, Catherine's Nakaz) survives and is fenced — the grade kills only the single-cause origin story.
earliest_attestation: The abolition-first timeline: Frederick II's Prussian cabinet-order abolition of judicial torture, 1754 — ten years before Beccaria's 1764 publication.

sources.ref: Frederick II of Prussia, cabinet-order abolition of judicial torture, 1754 (following the 1740 restriction order) — standard scholarly dating; Langbein, Torture and the Law of Proof
Cesare Beccaria, Dei delitti e delle pene (1764), Milan — the book's publication and its documented reception (22 translations by 1800, Tuscany's 1786 code, the French reform debate)
Louis XVI's abolitions: question préparatoire (1780), question préalable (1788) — both postdate the book; the ordonnance criminelle abrogated 9 October 1789
John H. Langbein, Torture and the Law of Proof: Europe and England in the Ancien Régime (Univ. of Chicago Press, 1977; 2nd ed. 2006) — abolition tracked the reformed law of proof, not persuasion

competing_hypotheses: The real-influence position: Beccaria's book genuinely mattered — it was translated into 22 languages by 1800, shaped Tuscany's 1786 Leopoldina code, fed the French reform debate and Catherine II's Nakaz (1767). The book was a cause of later abolitions, just not the first one.

The post-book abolition position: France's question préparatoire (1780) and question préalable (1788) abolitions, Sweden (1772), Austria (1787), Tuscany (1786) all came after 1764 — defenders of the single-cause reading credit the book with the cascade, while conceding Prussia as the exception.

The sensibilities position: abolition tracked a broader 18th-century shift in elite feeling about the body and pain (the 'inventing human rights' argument) — Beccaria as the voice of a change already underway rather than its author.
falsifiability: Evidence that no European state abolished judicial torture before 1764, and that Beccaria's book directly caused the Prussian, Swedish, Tuscan, Austrian, and French abolitions, would force revision; the Prussian 1754 abolition alone defeats the single-cause claim.

title: Johnson's Dictionary, 1755 — the nine-year monument that wasn't the first
claim: On 15 April 1755 Samuel Johnson published A Dictionary of the English Language: the product of nine years' work — about 2,300 pages, close to 43,000 entries, and the first English dictionary built on extensive literary quotations (over 100,000) from Shakespeare, Milton, Swift, Pope and others. The standard English dictionary until the OED, 150 years later.
place: London, England (published 15 April 1755)
grade_reason: The book's existence, date, scale, and method are multiply attested: the 1755 first edition survives in numerous copies; the nine-year composition and quotation method (books marked by Johnson and six scribes, over 100,000 quotations) are documented in the Preface and contemporary accounts; the famous definitions (lexicographer as 'a harmless drudge,' 'to make dictionaries is dull work,' the oats definition) are printed in the work itself.
earliest_attestation: The 1755 two-volume first edition itself; Johnson's Preface ('It is the fate of those who toil at the lower employments of life...'); the famous definitions on the page: 'Lexicographer. n.s. A writer of dictionaries; a harmless drudge, that busies himself in tracing the original, and detailing the signification of words.'

sources.ref: MoneyWeek — '15 April 1755: Samuel Johnson publishes his Dictionary': nine years of work, 2,300 pages, 'close to 43,000 entries, or around 80% of the English words in use'; the 'harmless drudge' and oats definitions quoted.

Karen Swallow Prior (Substack, Oct 2026): Johnson's process — reading and marking books with a team of about six scribes, 'more than 100,000 quotations to support the definitions of over 40,000 words'; nine years; the 'harmless drudge' lexicographer definition quoted in full.

Wikipedia — 'Dictionary of the English Language': Johnson's humor and prejudice in definitions documented (excise, lexicographer, oats, monsieur, patron); the meticulousness 'heretofore unseen' in completeness of definitions.

competing_hypotheses: Whether the entry count is 42,773 or 'close to 43,000' (commonly cited both ways; the record reports ~43,000)
The humor-prejudice readings of famous definitions (oats, lexicographer, patron) — the definitions are on the page; their intent is the debate
falsifiability: Proof the 1755 edition did not exist or was misdated would overturn it — the book is one of the most reprinted works in English bibliography.

title: The myth of the first English dictionary: not Johnson, but Cawdrey (1604)
claim: Samuel Johnson wrote the first English dictionary — that no English dictionary existed before Johnson's A Dictionary of the English Language, and that the English dictionary tradition begins with Johnson's 1755 work.
place: London, England (Johnson's Dictionary published 1755; Cawdrey's Table Alphabeticall published 1604, while Cawdrey lived in Coventry)
grade_reason: Killed one way, conclusively: Robert Cawdrey's A Table Alphabeticall, conteyning and teaching the true writing, and understanding of hard usually English words — a 120-page monolingual English dictionary of 2,543 headwords — was published in London in 1604, 151 years before Johnson's Dictionary. The OED's own historical introduction treats it as the acorn to its oak; the Bodleian Library holds the sole surviving first-edition copy and republished it in 2007 with an introduction by OED chief editor John Simpson. Between Cawdrey and Johnson lies a century and a half of continuous English dictionary-making.
earliest_attestation: The belief itself is the textbook and popular shorthand that makes Johnson's 1755 work the origin story; readings.com.au's 2015 Cawdrey edition notes directly: 'Contrary to popular belief, the author of the first English dictionary is not Samuel Johnson, but Robert Cawdrey.'

sources.ref: Wikipedia — 'A Table Alphabeticall': 'A Table Alphabeticall is the first monolingual dictionary in the English language by Robert Cawdrey and first published in London in 1604.' 120 pages, 2,543 words; sole surviving copy at the Bodleian Library, Oxford.

readings.com.au — 'The First English Dictionary 1604: Robert Cawdrey's A Table Alphabeticall' (Bodleian Library Publishing, 2015): 'Contrary to popular belief, the author of the first English dictionary is not Samuel Johnson, but Robert Cawdrey, who published his Table Alphabeticall in 1604 — nearly 150 years before Johnson's dictionary.'
Wikipedia — 'Early English dictionaries': Cawdrey's 1604 work 'is generally regarded as the first genuine dictionary in English.'

competing_hypotheses: The reading that Cawdrey's Table Alphabeticall is not a 'real' dictionary (only 2,543 headwords, mostly brief synonyms) — a defensible position, but it is the standard scholarly consensus (OED's own historical introduction, Bodleian 2007 reprint) that it is the first monolingual English dictionary

Bailey's 1721 Universal Etymological English Dictionary as the true immediate predecessor — Johnson himself worked from Bailey; the 1721 folio contained 40,000+ words and was the dominant English dictionary of Johnson's youth
falsifiability: If no English wordbook before 1755 could be produced, the myth would stand. Instead the shelves are full: Cawdrey 1604, Henry Cockeram's English Dictionarie 1623, Thomas Blount's Glossographia 1656, Edward Phillips's New World of English Words 1658, John Kersey's New English Dictionary 1702, Bailey 1721.

title: The lunar-distance rival method
claim: The lunar-distance method — measuring the Moon's position against known stars and comparing with tabulated predictions to recover Greenwich time — was a genuine, workable rival solution to the longitude problem, championed by Astronomer Royal Nevil Maskelyne, with Tobias Mayer's lunar tables at its core; the Board of Longitude paid Mayer's widow £3,000 and Leonhard Euler £300 for the lunar-table work, and Maskelyne's Nautical Almanac (from 1767) put the method in sailors' hands.
place: Greenwich Observatory (Royal Observatory, home of the Nautical Almanac)
grade_reason: Multiply attested in the Board's own financial records and the published Almanac tradition; the foil record — it explains why the Board treated Harrison's clock as one method among two, not as an obvious winner. Carried below VERIFIED because 'workable rival' is a historiographical judgment, not a measurement.
earliest_attestation: Board of Longitude reward records: £3,000 to Mayer's widow, £300 to Euler for contributions to the lunar-distance method (Howse appendix).

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Longitude rewards' — Mayer's widow £3,000, Euler £300 (Howse appendix)
Wikipedia, 'John Harrison' — Maskelyne's lunar-distance advocacy, the Nautical Almanac 1767, Maskelyne's 1761 St. Helena expedition

competing_hypotheses: Sobel's telling: the lunar-distance method was the establishment's weapon for stonewalling Harrison's superior technology

Betts's telling: it was a legitimate scientific alternative, successfully used at sea — including by Maskelyne himself on his 1761 St. Helena expedition — and the Board's caution was partly honest scientific pluralism

The later verdict of history: the chronometer won the practical race (by 1825+ most British naval vessels carried marine chronometers), but lunar distances remained the backup method into the 19th century
falsifiability: Board minutes showing the lunar-table rewards were fictitious, or evidence the Nautical Almanac's tables were unusable at sea, would overturn this.

title: "E pur si muove" — the whisper that wasn't
claim: After abjuring heliocentrism before the Roman Inquisition on 22 June 1633, Galileo Galilei muttered "E pur si muove" ("And yet it moves") — the defiant whisper under the recantation. No contemporary source contains it. The earliest documented print attribution is 115 years later: Giuseppe Baretti's The Italian Library (London, 1757), which presents a garbled version ("stamping with his foot, in a contemplative mood") alongside claims the trial documents themselves refute (six years' imprisonment, torture). Vincenzo Viviani, Galileo's own disciple and first biographer (1655-56), never mentions it; the Inquisition trial record never mentions it. A 1911 '1643 painting' showing the words was exposed as a near-copy of an 1837 painting. Scholars treat the whisper as an 18th-century invention.
place: Santa Maria sopra Minerva, Rome (site of the 22 June 1633 abjuration — where the whisper allegedly happened)
grade_reason: Zero contemporary attestation across the full trial dossier and Viviani's biography; first appearance 115 years post-mortem in a source that is wrong on its other trial facts (six-year imprisonment, torture — both false); the supporting '1643 painting' is a 19th-century-style copy whose experts place it post-1837.
earliest_attestation: Giuseppe Baretti, The Italian Library (London, 1757): 'The moment he was set at liberty, he looked up to the sky and down to the ground, and, stamping with his foot, in a contemplative mood, said, Eppur si muove; that is, still it moves, meaning the earth.' — per Antonio Favaro's 1911 determination after four decades of research (reported in Scientific American).

sources.ref: Antonio Favaro's 1911 determination of Baretti 1757 as earliest print mention (after four decades of research culminating in the National Edition) — reported in Scientific American

Wikipedia, 'And yet it moves' — first reported in English print in 1757; the van Belle painting episode (dated 1643/45, near-identical to Van Maldeghem 1837, experts doubt pre-19th c., whereabouts unknown)
The full trial dossier (Favaro's National Edition, 1890-1909) and Vincenzo Viviani's 1655-56 biography: silence on the utterance in both

competing_hypotheses: Stephen Hawking's suggestion that the episode might have occurred at the Siena-to-Arcetri transfer — pure speculation with no documentary support

The painting episode (van Belle 1911, dated 1643/45, attributed to Murillo) briefly revived the anecdote — refuted: near-identical to Eugene van Maldeghem's 1837 painting, art experts doubt it predates the 19th century, whereabouts now unknown
falsifiability: A contemporary 1633-or-earlier document (letter, deposition, biography) recording the utterance would revive it; none exists despite the fully preserved trial dossier. The silence of Viviani's 1655-56 biography, written by the man who lived with Galileo, is decisive.

title: 'Melvil Dewey invented the index card' — DEBUNKED
claim: The telling that 'Melvil Dewey invented the index card in 1876' — that the index card began with Dewey and the American library movement.
place: Amherst, Massachusetts — where the telling places the invention (Dewey's 1876 pamphlet)
grade_reason: Three independent kills: (1) the man's own preface names a predecessor — Natale Battezzati's card system, 'the most fruitful source of ideas'; (2) Linnaeus's standardized paper slips of the mid-1760s (~7.5x13 cm, unbound, shufflable — Charmantier & Muller-Wille 2012), a century before Dewey; (3) the 1791 Bureau de Bibliographie playing-card catalogs — over a million confiscated playing cards filled and sent to Paris within three years (Library of Congress blog).
earliest_attestation: The telling's popular form: library-science lore and exam-bank shorthand crediting Dewey's 1876 pamphlet year. Dewey's own 1876 preface to 'A Classification and Subject Index for Cataloguing and Arranging the Books and Pamphlets of a Library' cites the card system of Italian publisher Natale Battezzati as 'the most fruitful source of ideas' — the claimed inventor names a predecessor.

sources.ref: Melvil Dewey, 'A Classification and Subject Index for Cataloguing and Arranging the Books and Pamphlets of a Library' (1876) — preface cites Natale Battezzati's card system as 'the most fruitful source of ideas'; Project Gutenberg ebook 12513 (public domain)

Isabelle Charmantier & Staffan Muller-Wille, 'Carl Linnaeus's Botanical Paper Slips (1767-1773)' — mid-1760s standardized slips ~7.5x13 cm, uniform format, never bound in a fixed order; the authors' own caveat: 'the invention was entirely inadvertent'

Library of Congress blog, 'Inquiring Minds: The Unheralded Story of the Card Catalog' (2017) — 1791 instructions to catalog confiscated aristocratic/clerical libraries on blank-backed playing cards; 'within three years, over a million cards were sent to overwhelmed offices in Paris'

liswiki.org, 'History of the card catalog' — Bureau de Bibliographie practice (Jackson 1974; Hopkins 1992): title transcribed, filing word underlined, collation, cards strung through the lower-left corner; Sharp 1935 on the 1876 'modern form' via the Library Bureau

competing_hypotheses: The scoped honest version — 'Dewey standardized and commercialized the index card, making it the industry's agreed unit' — survives and is graded separately in evt-dewey-library-bureau-cards-001
The modern 75×125 mm (3×5 inch) card IS largely Dewey-era standardization; the telling dies on the invention claim, not the standardization
falsifiability: A demonstrated 19th-century documentary tradition attributing the index card's invention to Dewey in his own lifetime would reopen it; instead his own preface disclaims it.

title: Linnaeus's paper slips (mid-1760s) — the card before the catalog
claim: Carl Linnaeus used standardized, unbound paper slips (~7.5x13 cm) in the mid-1760s for organizing taxonomic data — a paper tool functionally identical to modern index cards.
