place: Uppsala, Sweden — Linnaeus's home; the slips survive in Stockholm collections
grade_reason: The objects exist and were studied at first hand by historians: standard size (~7.5x13 cm), uniform format (genus name at top), never bound in a fixed order, shufflable. Held below VERIFIED on the authors' own honesty fences — no independent evidence Linnaeus filed them alphabetically, and the 'invention' was inadvertent, never a system he designed or taught.
earliest_attestation: The surviving slips themselves, held by the Natural History Museum, Stockholm; studied by Charmantier & Muller-Wille (2012).

sources.ref: Isabelle Charmantier & Staffan Muller-Wille, 'Carl Linnaeus's Botanical Paper Slips (1767-1773)' — slip dimensions, uniform format, unbound storage, and the mid-1760s dating while preparing Systema naturae 12th edition

Staffan Muller-Wille (University of Exeter), BSHS 2009 presentation, reported by Phys.org — 'Towards the end of his career, in the mid-1760s, Linnaeus took this further, inventing a paper tool that has since become very common: index cards'
LSE Research Online, 'Indexing nature' (Muller-Wille) — the 1764 Museum Ludovicae Ulricae cards kept by the Natural History Museum, Stockholm, exhibited 1995

competing_hypotheses: Charmantier & Muller-Wille's own caveat: 'there is much that speaks for this claim, but there are equally arguments against it' — the authors propose the 'invention was entirely inadvertent' and Linnaeus never rationalized or advertised it as a system

The earlier 1752-1764 royal-collection slips (with Solander, ~10.5x17 cm) were used vertically as an unbound manuscript for a particular book project (MLU), not as a shufflable card file — the card-like practice is specifically the mid-1760s Systema naturae 12th-edition work
falsifiability: A re-dating of the slips to the post-Linnaean period, or evidence they were bound/ordered by the archivists rather than produced as loose slips, would weaken the claim.

title: The H4 Jamaica trial, 1761–1762
claim: On the Board of Longitude's official sea trial from Portsmouth to Kingston, Jamaica (HMS Deptford, 18 November 1761 – 19 January 1762, 81 days 5 hours), John Harrison's H4 lost approximately 5.1 seconds after correction for its known daily rate — a longitude error of 1.25 minutes (about one nautical mile), far inside the half-degree (30 nautical miles) required by the 1714 Longitude Act for the £20,000 reward.
place: Kingston, Jamaica (arrival; the voyage ran Portsmouth → Kingston)
grade_reason: The measurement comes from the Board's own commissioned trial — the Board never disputed the 5.1-second figure, only what to infer from it; held below VERIFIED because the rate-correction method (fixed daily rate carried over 81 days) was exactly what the following decade's dispute was about (Maskelyne's 'cancellation of errors' objection, the Greenwich re-test).
earliest_attestation: The Board of Longitude's own trial records and the Deptford's ship logs, 1761–1762 (Robertson, Master of the Academy at Portsmouth, fixed the watch's daily rate at 24/9 seconds per day before departure).

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'John Harrison' — trial account citing R.T. Gould, The Marine Chronometer (1923) and Jonathan Betts, Time Restored (2006)
thingshavehistory.com, 'John Harrison's H4 and the Longitude Prize' (H4 = 13 cm silver watch, 5 beats/sec, citing Royal Museums Greenwich)
Board of Longitude minutes / the Deptford trial documentation (rate-fixing by Robertson, Kingston measurement)

competing_hypotheses: The Board's later position: a single trial proves nothing — the accuracy might have been luck, and H4's known-rate correction assumes what the second trial (Barbados 1764) had to confirm independently
The popular Sobel telling: the Jamaica result closed the case; the Board's subsequent demands were obstruction
Betts's scholarly rebalance (Time Restored, 2006): the Board acted as cautious administrators holding a large public prize, with a working rival method (lunar distances) on the table
falsifiability: A contemporary ship's log or Board minute recording a materially different rate at Kingston, or proof the known-longitude reference used at Kingston was wrong by more than the margin.

title: Prussian schools were designed to produce obedient soldiers
claim: The Prussian school system was designed — from Frederick the Great's 1763 Generallandschulreglement onward — to produce obedient soldiers: a factory-model education 'deliberately designed to produce mediocre intellects... and to ensure docile and incomplete citizens' (Gatto), the template for modern schooling's bells, rows, and 45-minute periods.
place: Berlin, Prussia
grade_reason: The design claim dies on the documents: the 1763 decree's stated aims were Christian formation, literacy, and productive subjects (ages 5-13/14, tax-funded, Hecker's program) — no military-obedience design; the soldier narrative postdates the design by 43 years and rides modern polemic, not historians of education.
earliest_attestation: The soldier-factory form is modern polemic (Gatto's Underground History; YouTube pipeline 2026); the 1763 decree is the documented primary instrument

sources.ref: Wikipedia — Prussian education system (Generallandschulreglement 1763, Hecker, ages 5-13/14 tax-funded compulsory; the critics' obedience claim carried as contested)
Academy of Ideas — the Gatto form of the claim ('deliberately designed to produce mediocre intellects... docile and incomplete citizens,' Weapons of Mass Instruction)
ushistoryscene — Mann's 1844 tour and the Prussian 'common schools' model (the genuine Prussian influence on American schooling: the model, not the motive)

competing_hypotheses: The discipline-ethos reading (conceded): the 1763 decree and the Volksschule really did impose a strict ethos of duty, sobriety, and discipline — the soldier-factory claim confuses a real authoritarian flavor with a military design

The post-Jena reading: the militarized reading belongs to the post-1806 discourse (Fichte's 1808 Addresses to the German Nation, the Stein/Hardenberg reforms) — real, but 43 years after the 1763 design, and a repurposing, not the design

The model-not-motive reading: Mann's 1844 Seventh Report admired the Prussian system's universality, tax funding, and teacher training — the American import was the model, and even Gatto's polemic concedes the influence while inventing the motive
falsifiability: The 1763 decree text showing military-obedience training as a stated design aim, or an 18th-century Prussian source stating the schools were built for the army

title: Rousseau's 'great princess' and the brioche (1765)
claim: In his Confessions, Book 6 (first six books written c. 1765, published posthumously 1782), Jean-Jacques Rousseau recounts that an unnamed 'great princess,' told that the peasants had no bread, replied 'Qu'ils mangent de la brioche' ('Then let them eat brioches') — the true paper trail of the 'let them eat cake' anecdote.
place: Paris, France (where Rousseau set the anecdote and wrote the manuscript)
grade_reason: The text exists, is securely attributed, and says what it says — the anecdote is in Book 6 in every edition. Multiple independent histories of the 'let them eat cake' myth (Wikipedia's sourced article, Britannica, Fraser) converge on this manuscript as the anecdote's origin point.
earliest_attestation: Rousseau's Confessions manuscript, Book 6 — the anecdote's first recorded appearance in any form; published 1782.

sources.ref: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Confessions, Book 6 — the 'great princess' / 'Qu'ils mangent de la brioche' passage
Publication history: first six books written c. 1765, published posthumously 1782
The 16th-century German folklore variants of the same anecdote pattern (noblewoman proposes sweetened bread) — the story predates the princess, whoever she was

competing_hypotheses: Rousseau invented the anecdote — the Confessions are not considered entirely factual, and the episode (Rousseau, too elegantly dressed to enter a bakery with his stolen wine, recalling the princess's 'last resort') reads as literary construction

The 'great princess' was a real figure — candidates proposed over the years include Marie-Thérèse of Spain (Louis XIV's queen), one of Louis XVI's aunts, or others; none proven, and the 16th-century folklore variants of the story mean the pattern predates any named princess
The anecdote circulated orally before Rousseau wrote it — possible; Rousseau claims to recall it from c. 1740, but the only attestation is the Confessions manuscript itself
falsifiability: The record is a text record — it is superseded only by a better manuscript history (e.g., a documented earlier appearance of the anecdote with the named princess). The grade covers the TEXT's attestation, never the truth of the princess.

title: "James Watt invented the steam engine"
claim: James Watt (1736–1819) invented the steam engine.
place: Britain (the schoolbook tradition's setting)
grade_reason: Three independent kills: (1) chronology — Newcomen's commercially successful atmospheric engine of 1712 predates Watt's patent by 57 years and Watt's own birth; (2) the patent's own title — 'A New Invented Method of Lessening the Consumption of Steam and Fuel in Fire Engines,' an improvement on existing fire engines, not an invention of the engine; (3) Watt's entry point — he was asked to repair a model Newcomen engine at Glasgow University, meaning the engine he 'invented' was already on his workbench.
earliest_attestation: The unqualified 'inventor of the steam engine' title is a popular-history and exam-bank construction; no technical history of the engine credits Watt with the invention

sources.ref: ASME Engineering History Landmark: Newcomen atmospheric engine — first success 1712 near Dudley Castle; over 2,000 Newcomen-type engines installed before the Watt era

UK Letters Patent No. 913, 5 January 1769 — James Watt's own title: 'A New Invented Method of Lessening the Consumption of Steam and Fuel in Fire Engines' (the title confesses the improvement reading)

Age of Revolution / Science Museum tradition: James Watt, instrument maker at Glasgow University, asked to repair a model Newcomen engine — the separate condenser born from diagnosing the existing engine's inefficiency
Medium/science-history literature: 'Obviously no, he did not' — the explicit correction that 'inventor of the steam engine' is a title histories sometimes bestow upon Watt without warrant
Belief ecology (the myth in the wild): answers.com's muddled Q&A ('He invented the steam engine'; 'invented by James Watt in 1712') — the confusion itself is the evidence of the myth's circulation

competing_hypotheses: Watt as co-inventor of 'the modern steam engine' — defensible only with the qualifier; without it, the 57-year priority of Newcomen's working engine kills it
The reading confuses the unit of invention (the engine) with the unit of improvement (the separate condenser) — Watt's genuine invention inside a pre-existing machine
falsifiability: Proof that no working steam engine existed before Watt's 1769 patent — impossible against Newcomen's 1712 installation and the 2,000+ atmospheric engines that followed

title: Watt's separate condenser, Patent No. 913 (5 January 1769)
claim: On 5 January 1769 James Watt received UK Letters Patent No. 913 for the separate condenser — 'A New Invented Method of Lessening the Consumption of Steam and Fuel in Fire Engines' — the improvement that kept the working cylinder hot while condensing steam in a separate chamber, cutting fuel consumption by roughly two-thirds and making the steam engine a general-purpose industrial power source.
place: Great Britain (patent enrolled at the Patent Office, London; developed at Glasgow)
grade_reason: The patent itself is a surviving primary legal document with the inventor's name, the date, and a title that states exactly what was invented — a method of lessening consumption in fire engines, not the engine.
earliest_attestation: UK Letters Patent No. 913 (5 January 1769) — primary legal document with the title confessing the improvement reading

sources.ref: UK Letters Patent No. 913, 5 January 1769 — 'A New Invented Method of Lessening the Consumption of Steam and Fuel in Fire Engines' (primary document)
Age of Revolution: Boulton & Watt engine — Watt's Glasgow repair commission, the 1769 patent, the 1775 Boulton partnership, Murdoch's installations, engines for mines, mills, distilleries, waterworks

History of technology literature: separate condenser cut fuel consumption by approximately two-thirds vs Newcomen; Boulton & Watt's engine counter and sealed-box coal-savings billing; ~449 engines manufactured during the patent period

competing_hypotheses: The exact efficiency gain (~two-thirds) is a period comparison against Newcomen engines of the day — modern reconstructions and historians range the improvement with the engine's vintage and condition
The separate condenser as sole authorship: Watt's workshop relied on Roebuck's capital, Boulton's commercialization, and Murdoch's installations — the invention is Watt's, the empire was joint
falsifiability: A surviving Patent Office record contradicting the 1769 enrollment, or a contemporary document showing the separate condenser predating Watt

title: The 'eraser was invented in 1770' telling — DEBUNKED by bread
claim: The telling that the eraser was invented in 1770 — that Nairne's rubber cube was the beginning of erasing — is false. Erasing predates rubber by centuries. Before rubber erasers, tablets of wax were used to erase lead or charcoal marks from paper; bits of rough stone such as sandstone or pumice removed small errors from parchment or papyrus written in ink; and crustless bread was the standard pencil-mark eraser — a Meiji-period (1868–1912) Tokyo student recalled: 'Bread erasers were used in place of rubber erasers, and so they would give them to us with no restriction on amount.' The bread-crumb eraser is itself the probable source of Nairne's 'accidental pickup' tradition. What 1770 invented was the rubber eraser — not the eraser.
place: London (telling's home market)
grade_reason: Multiple independent kills: (1) bread-crumb erasers in documented use before and long after rubber — including a first-person Meiji-era account of bread erasers as school issue; (2) wax tablets for lead/charcoal; (3) sandstone/pumice for ink on parchment/papyrus. 1770 marks the rubber eraser's arrival, not erasing's.
earliest_attestation: The telling: modern popular histories compressing 'first rubber eraser' to 'first eraser'; the refutation: documented bread/wax/pumice practice plus Meiji-era first-person account

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Eraser' — History section: wax tablets, sandstone/pumice, crustless bread; Meiji-period Tokyo student testimony on bread erasers
ThoughtCo, 'The History of Pencils, Markers, Pens, and Erasers': 'Before rubber, breadcrumbs had been used to erase pencil marks'

competing_hypotheses: The telling survives because rubber became the metonym: 'rubber' means eraser in British English, so the material's 1770 arrival feels like the object's invention.
falsifiability: Evidence that no erasing practice existed before 1770 — the bread, wax, and pumice attestations already rule this out.

title: Nairne's widely marketed rubber eraser, 1770
claim: In 1770 the English optician and scientific instrument maker Edward Nairne developed the first widely marketed rubber eraser — natural-rubber cubes sold at three shillings per half-inch cube from his shop opposite the Royal Exchange. The event is documented in Joseph Priestley's footnote of 15 April 1770: 'I have seen a substance excellently adapted to the purpose of wiping from paper the mark of black-lead-pencil. ... It is sold by Mr. Nairne, Mathematical Instrument-Maker, opposite the Royal-Exchange.' Until then the material was known as gum elastic or caoutchouc; the word 'rubber' was in general use in 1770 for anything used to rub and attached to the new material sometime between 1770 and 1778.
place: Royal Exchange, London (Nairne's shop)
grade_reason: Priestley's dated 1770 footnote is contemporary attestation; Nairne's commercial sale at a documented price is independently carried across reference sources. The 'accidental pickup' anecdote is carried as tradition, not evidence.
earliest_attestation: Joseph Priestley, footnote in 'A Familiar Introduction to the Theory and Practice of Perspective' (London, April 15, 1770)

sources.ref: Joseph Priestley, 'A Familiar Introduction to the Theory and Practice of Perspective' (1770), footnote: 'I have seen a substance excellently adapted to the purpose of wiping from paper the mark of black-lead-pencil. ... It is sold by Mr. Nairne, Mathematical Instrument-Maker, opposite the Royal-Exchange.'
Wikipedia, 'Eraser' — History section: Nairne, three shillings per half-inch cube; 'rubber' 1770–1778 word history; bread-crumb and wax/pumice predecessors
NPR Skunk Bear (wamc.org), 'Trace The Remarkable History Of The Humble Pencil': Priestley's 1770 observation and the naming of 'rubber'

competing_hypotheses: The 'accidental pickup' story (Nairne reached for bread crumbs, grabbed rubber instead) is tradition attributed to Nairne — colorful, unverifiable as event, not needed for the grade.
Edward 'Naime'/'Naime' spellings in low-quality secondary sources — the Wikipedia and ThoughtCo spellings ('Nairne') are the instrument-maker's documented name.
falsifiability: A dated 1770-or-earlier reference to a commercially marketed rubber eraser predating Nairne's — none has surfaced.

title: The Jenner-was-first myth (DEBUNKED)
claim: Edward Jenner was NOT the first person to use cowpox to protect against smallpox. The documented predecessors include Benjamin Jesty (1774, Dorset — 22 years before Jenner), Peter Plett (1791, Holstein — 5 years before), and others named in the literature (Bose 1769, Fewster's 1760s observations, Sevel, Jensen, Rendall).
place: Berkeley, Gloucestershire, England (Jenner's 1796 experiment)
grade_reason: Three independent kills: (1) Jesty's 1774 family inoculation, examined and cross-examined in London in 1805 with the son re-challenged against smallpox on the spot; (2) Plett's 1791 Holstein vaccinations, reported to Kiel and published via von Heinze; (3) the wider pre-Jenner list in Plett, Plett & Jenner 2006 (Bose 1769, Fewster, Sevel, Jensen, Rendall). The 'first to use cowpox' reading is dead; what survives is Jenner's real achievement — systematic documentation, experimental challenge, publication, and global dissemination.
earliest_attestation: Jesty: 1805 Original Vaccine Pock Institute examination (of the 1774 event); Plett: 1802 von Heinze interview (of the 1791 event); Jenner: the 1798 Inquiry (of the 1796 experiment)

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Benjamin Jesty' — the 1774 inoculation, 22 years before Jenner
Wikipedia, 'Peter Plett' — the 1791 vaccinations, 5 years before Jenner

Plett, P.C., Plett, P., & Jenner, E. (2006). 'Peter Plett and other discoverers of cowpox vaccination before Edward Jenner.' Sudhoffs Archiv 90(2): 219–232 — 'at least six people in England, Denmark and Germany (Bose in 1769, Sevel, Jensen and Jesty in 1774, Rendall, Plett in 1791)'
Country Life, 'Curious questions: Who administered the first vaccination?' — the popular form of the question

competing_hypotheses: 'First' is legitimately reserved for Jenner as the first to document systematically, challenge immunity experimentally, publish, and drive global adoption — the priority claim survives only in that fenced sense
The pre-Jenner uses were one-off folk practices that never became a transmissible method — true, but that does not rescue the 'first to use' phrasing
falsifiability: Proof that Jesty's and Plett's documented inoculations never happened (e.g., fraud proven in the 1805 examination records), which would restore Jenner's priority

title: Benjamin Jesty's 1774 cowpox inoculation
claim: In 1774, Dorset farmer Benjamin Jesty inoculated his wife Elizabeth and his two eldest sons, Robert (3) and Benjamin (2), with cowpox lymph taken from a cow at Chetnole — twenty-two years before Jenner's 1796 experiment.
place: Chetnole / Worth Matravers, Dorset, England
grade_reason: The 1774 inoculation is multiply attested (the 1805 institutional examination with the son re-challenged for smallpox on the spot, the gravestone, the local-history tradition); held below VERIFIED because the documentation is retrospective and second-generation.
earliest_attestation: Jesty's sworn-style examination before 12 medical officers of the Original Vaccine Pock Institute, Soho, 1805 (published in the Edinburgh Medical and Surgical Journal); Worth Matravers gravestone inscription

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Benjamin Jesty' — 1805 examination, the 1774 inoculation, the gold lancets, the gravestone
Edinburgh Medical and Surgical Journal (c. 1805–1806) — published verbal evidence of the 1805 examination
Artsreach, 'Tales From the Village: Yetminster' — the Yetminster local-history account (Chetnole cow, darning needle, wife's inflamed arm)

competing_hypotheses: The 1805 testimony embellished a folk-memory tradition under institutional examination
Jesty's priority is genuine and the under-documentation is explained by his non-publication and social status (farmer, not physician)
falsifiability: Contemporary 1774 records (parish, surgeon's, or family) explicitly denying the inoculation, or proof the 1805 examination was fabricated

title: The deleted anti-slavery paragraph of the Declaration
claim: Thomas Jefferson's original draft of the Declaration of Independence contained a full paragraph condemning the slave trade — arraigning George III for forcing "that execrable commerce" on the colonies — and Congress deleted the entire paragraph in the Committee of the Whole on July 3-4, 1776, at the objection of South Carolina and Georgia (with the northern states, Jefferson noted, also "pretty considerable carriers" of enslaved people).
place: Independence Hall, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
grade_reason: The Library of Congress exhibits the evidence directly: the first printed version's transcription shows the full slavery paragraph deleted, with the statement that "the entire paragraph on slavery and the slave trade was deleted by Congress sitting in the Committee of the Whole on July 3-4, 1776." Jefferson's own contemporary account names the objectors. The deletion is one of the best-documented edits in the American founding archive.
earliest_attestation: Jefferson's rough draft of the Declaration (preserved) and his "Notes of Proceedings in Congress" recording the deletion.

sources.ref: Library of Congress, 'Creating the United States' exhibition: 'The entire paragraph on slavery and the slave trade was deleted by Congress sitting in the Committee of the Whole on July 3-4, 1776'; Jefferson reported in his Notes of Proceedings that the clause 'reprobating the enslaving the inhabitants of Africa, was struck out in complaisance to South Carolina & Georgia, who had never attempted to restrain the importation of slaves'

HISTORY.com, 'Why Thomas Jefferson's Anti-Slavery Passage Was Removed from the Declaration of Independence': Jefferson's autobiography (1821) blames South Carolina and Georgia while noting 'our Northern brethren also I believe felt a little tender under these censures; for tho' their people have very few slaves themselves, yet they had been pretty considerable carriers of them to others'

Hypatia Bradlaugh, 'The Slave Struggle in America,' Lecture II (public domain): 'In Jefferson's draft for the Declaration of Independence he arraigned George III. for forcing upon the American colonies that "execrable commerce." This clause was struck out by Congress, "in complaisance," Mr. Jefferson declared, "to South Carolina and Georgia"'

competing_hypotheses: Interpretation debates (not evidential disputes): whether keeping the passage would have changed anything, and whether Jefferson's anti-slavery draft language is reconciled with his own enslavement of people at Monticello — interpretation, carried as such, not graded over
falsifiability: Would require the draft's text without the passage or a Congress record showing no deletion — both the draft text and the LoC transcription of the printed original show the passage and its absence.

title: Ned Ludd — real person or figurehead?
claim: Ned Ludd — Captain/General/King Ludd — was a real historical person: an Anstey, Leicestershire weaver's apprentice who, in 1779, smashed two stocking frames in a fit of rage after being whipped for idleness (or taunted by youths), and whose name the 1811–1813 frame-breakers adopted as their leader.
place: Anstey, Leicestershire, England
grade_reason: The figurehead use is beyond dispute (letters signed 'Ned Lud' / 'General Lud'; the TNA proclamation), but no independent evidence of the 1779 incident or the man exists — the story's earliest tellings are 1811 newspaper and local-history items, three decades after the fact, and the details shift between tellings (whipped for idleness vs taunted; Ludd vs Ludlam; Anstey vs Sherwood Forest).
earliest_attestation: The Nottingham Review, 20 December 1811 (the earliest traceable telling); John Blackner, 'History of Nottingham' (1811) gives the 'Ludlam' variant

sources.ref: Wikipedia — Ned Ludd ('Ned Ludd is the legendary, fictitious person to whom the Luddites in England attributed the name of their movement'; story traced to The Nottingham Review, 20 December 1811)
HISTORY — 'Who Were the Luddites?' ('There's no evidence Ludd actually existed — like Robin Hood, he was said to reside in Sherwood Forest')
Smithsonian — 'What the Luddites Really Fought Against' ('In fact, no such person existed. Ludd was a fiction concocted from an incident that supposedly had taken place 22 years earlier')
The National Archives — 'The proclamation of Ned Ludd' (HO 42/118, 23 December 1811) — 'Ned Lud' as the signature of an organized correspondence, whatever its author

competing_hypotheses: The legendary-figurehead reading: Ned Ludd is apocryphal/fictitious, a folkloric character appropriated as a pseudonym — the attested use of 'General Ludd' in letters and proclamations is VERIFIED; the man's existence is not

The Ludlam variant: John Blackner's 1811 'History of Nottingham' gives a boy called 'Ludlam' told by his framework-knitter father to 'square his needles,' who took a hammer to the frames — a parallel folk tale, not independent confirmation
falsifiability: A parish register, apprenticeship indenture, or independent contemporary account tying the 1779 Anstey frame-smashing to a real named person

title: William Addis and the mass-produced toothbrush (1780)
claim: In 1780, William Addis of England made a bone-handled toothbrush with swine bristles (the prison-prototype story) and, after release, began mass-producing toothbrushes in England; the family firm (Wisdom Toothbrush) continued into the 1990s.
place: London, England
grade_reason: The manufacture and the firm's long continuity are documented trade history; the prison-prototype details rest on company tradition, so VERIFIED stays parked.
earliest_attestation: The Addis/Wisdom company tradition; 19th-century trade history of English brush-making.

sources.ref: Dr. Scott Swank, National Museum of Dentistry, via HowStuffWorks: Addis in 1780, jailed for starting a riot, fashioned a brush from a bone and hog's bristles from a jailer, then began mass-producing them in England
Dental-history convention: the first mass-produced toothbrush, designed by William Addis of England in 1780; Wisdom Toothbrush family-owned until the 1990s (Central Coast Dental Care; Sure Dental)
The 1844 first three-row bristle brush (Dr. Meyer L. Rhein) and the 1857 first US toothbrush patent (H. N. Wadsworth) — the post-Addis paper trail (dental-history timelines)

competing_hypotheses: The prison narrative (jailed for starting a riot; found a bone; begged hog's bristles from a jailer) is a family/company tradition whose details are unattested in contemporary records — Swank: 'I have no reason to doubt the story as a whole... it could have become a bit embellished over time'
falsifiability: Business records showing the Addis firm was founded by a successor, not William, or that mass-produced English bristle brushes predate 1780 in the trade record.

title: The Tarot as the Egyptian 'Book of Thoth'
claim: The tarot deck is an ancient Egyptian artifact — the 'Book of Thoth,' the esoteric wisdom of the Egyptian temples preserved in card form and carried to Europe by the Romani people.
place: Paris (publication site)
grade_reason: The claim has a dated birth certificate — de Gébelin's 1781 essay, which offered no evidence — and a documented true origin: the tarot is a 15th-century Milanese card game (evt-tarot-milan-game-001).
earliest_attestation: Antoine Court de Gébelin, 'Le Monde primitif' vol. VIII (1781) — essay on the tarot; Comte de Mellet's companion essay in the same volume supplied the Hebrew-letter link

sources.ref: Antoine Court de Gébelin, Le Monde primitif vol. VIII (1781) — the tarot essay; Donald Tyson's English translation notes
Michael Dummett, The Game of Tarot (1980) — the documented Italian origin
Kit Stone, 'Tarot in Late Enlightenment France' (Journal Article, Oct 2024) — context of the 1781 invention
Morgan Library & Museum, Visconti-Sforza Tarot Cards (MS M.630.1-35) — the physical refutation

competing_hypotheses: The claim is true in a metaphorical or initiatory sense but not historically (the occultist defense)

Tarot symbolism independently encodes universal archetypes, so the Egyptian reading is a legitimate later interpretation regardless of origin (the Jungian reading — graded as interpretation, never as history)
falsifiability: A pre-1781 document connecting tarot to Egypt, or any Egyptian artifact of the 22-trump structure — none has ever been produced

title: The Washington dentures: the materials record
claim: George Washington's surviving dentures were constructed from hippopotamus, walrus, and probably elephant ivory; cow, horse, and human teeth; and lead, brass, silver, and gold alloys — with no wood as a tooth material.
place: Mount Vernon, Virginia (the surviving complete set); New York Academy of Medicine (Greenwood 1789 set)
grade_reason: The objects exist, are multiply held, and are consistent: Mount Vernon's FAQ (primary institutional record), the Greenwood 1789 inscribed set at the New York Academy of Medicine, and the curator's published statements all converge on the same material list. By his 1789 inauguration Washington had one real tooth left (Mount Vernon); his last tooth was kept by dentist John Greenwood with the inscription 'the last one which grew in his head.'
earliest_attestation: Four dentures belonging to Washington survive in museum collections (Mount Vernon holds the only complete set; the New York Academy of Medicine holds a Greenwood 1789 lower set; the National Museum of Dentistry holds one; a fifth set is believed entombed with Washington). Each is constructed differently, 'as though the dentist(s) who made them were continually experimenting' (Mount Vernon FAQ).

sources.ref: George Washington's Mount Vernon — Washington's Dentures FAQ: four dentures, the only surviving complete set on display, full materials list
STAT (2017): New York Academy of Medicine — Greenwood 1789 'Under jaw' set with inscription 'First one made by J. Greenwood 1789'; the 'last one which grew in his head' tooth case

DVIDS (2022): by age 57 a full set despite hygiene (tooth powder, tongue scraping, mouthwash); Washington kept pulled teeth in a locked desk drawer; payments to dentists documented across letters and diaries

competing_hypotheses: None on the materials: the surviving objects are multiply examined and consistent across institutions; the only disputed sub-question (the sourcing of the human teeth) is carried in evt-washington-teeth-purchase-1784-001
falsifiability: Materials analysis (XRF, dental forensics) of the surviving dentures contradicting the documented material list, or a contemporary invoice/letter describing wooden teeth for Washington.

title: The first free flight — Pilatre de Rozier and d'Arlandes, 21 November 1783
claim: On 21 November 1783, Jean-Francois Pilatre de Rozier and the Marquis d'Arlandes made the first untethered crewed balloon flight — the first confirmed human flight of any kind — in a Montgolfier hot-air balloon, taking off from the garden of the Chateau de la Muette in the Bois de Boulogne (Paris) and flying ~25 minutes, ~9 km, to the Butte-aux-Cailles, before a crowd that included Louis XVI and Benjamin Franklin.
place: Chateau de la Muette, Bois de Boulogne → Butte-aux-Cailles, Paris
grade_reason: Universally attested contemporary event: the Versailles animal flight (19 September 1783) as the rehearsal, the tethered tests in October, and the 21 November free flight witnessed by the King and Franklin. The champagne toast afterward began the balloonists' tradition that survives to this day.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary Parisian accounts, 1783; the Montgolfier demonstration program (June–November 1783)

sources.ref: Wikipedia 'Francois Laurent d'Arlandes': de Rozier and d'Arlandes made the first crewed free balloon flight on 21 November 1783 in a Montgolfier balloon; took off 1:54 pm from the Chateau de la Muette; 25 minutes, ~5.5 miles (9 km), 3,000 feet, landing at the Butte-aux-Cailles; champagne tradition
HISTORY.com, 'Men fly over Paris in hot air balloon' (21 Nov 1783): first untethered hot-air balloon flight, 5.5 miles over Paris in ~25 minutes; Montgolfier brothers as inventors

competing_hypotheses: Bartolomeu de Gusmao's 1709 small unmanned hot-air balloon in the Portuguese royal palace predates the Montgolfiers by 74 years — a demonstration, not a crewed flight; the 'first human flight' stands on 1783. Carried comparatively, not as a rival.
falsifiability: A documented untethered crewed flight before 21 November 1783

title: The Bramah Challenge Lock stood unpicked for 67 years (VERIFIED)
claim: Joseph Bramah's Challenge Lock stood unpicked for 67 years — from the 1784 patent to Alfred Charles Hobbs's opening of it at the Great Exhibition of 1851.
place: 124 Piccadilly, London (shop window); opened at the Great Exhibition, Crystal Palace, Hyde Park
grade_reason: Multiple independent contemporary sources: the 2 September 1851 arbitration verdict ('Mr. Hobbs has fairly picked or opened the lock'), the Morning Chronicle report of 10 September 1851 recording the 200-guinea payment with Bramah's detailed protest, and the artifact itself — the Challenge Lock (Science Museum Group object 1972-290) — whose rebuild after Hobbs's picking is visible in the mechanism.
earliest_attestation: The challenge board itself (1790): 'The artist who can make an instrument that will pick or open this lock shall receive 200 guineas the moment it is produced'; the 1851 arbitration verdict and the Morning Chronicle report of 10 September 1851.

sources.ref: Wikipedia — Bramah lock (patent 1784; 124 Piccadilly; challenge board from 1790; 200-guinea inscription; Hobbs opened the lock at the Great Exhibition 1851, ~51 hours over 16 days; arbitration dispute; lock in the Science Museum)
Science Museum Group Collection — Bramah padlock and key (object 1972-290): 'Bramah padlock and key (1801) — the challenge lock of Lock Controversy of 1851'
Science Museum Group Collection — Alfred Charles Hobbs (1812–1891), American locksmith: 'Hobbs was the first pick Bramah's lock'

Daniel Lucian, 'Bramah's Challenge Lock' — committee verdict 2 September 1851 ('Mr. Hobbs has fairly picked or opened the lock'); Bramah's objections (unwitnessed stages, multiple instruments vs 'an instrument', fixed apparatus); payment of 200 guineas announced in the Morning Chronicle, 10 September 1851, with Bramah's detailed protest
IFSEC Global — 'Unlocking 100 years': 67 years unpicked; Hobbs opened it in 1851

competing_hypotheses: The '67 years' counts from the 1784 patent; the window display with the 200-guinea inscription dates from 1790 (61 years of public challenge). Both counts are carried; the verdict holds on either.
Some accounts give 52 hours over 14 days (Gizmodo/British Library) vs 51 hours over 16 days (Wikipedia/SMG-aligned sources); the duration variance does not touch the opening itself.
falsifiability: A documented picking attempt before 1851, or proof the 2 September 1851 arbitration verdict and the Morning Chronicle report are fabrications — neither has been produced in 175 years.

title: Franklin's bifocals, 1784
claim: Benjamin Franklin invented bifocals — lenses with two optical powers in one frame — describing the invention in a 1784 letter from Passy to George Whatley.
place: Passy (Paris), France — where Franklin wrote the 1784 letter
grade_reason: VERIFIED: the inventor's own dated letter describes the invention and the motive (presbyopia plus myopia, constant changing of glasses) in his own hand; the letter survives in the documentary record and is multiply reproduced in Franklin's papers.
earliest_attestation: Benjamin Franklin, letter to George Whatley, 23 May 1784 (Passy, France): describes his 'double spectacles' — the upper half for distance, the lower for reading — invented because he grew tired of changing glasses

sources.ref: Benjamin Franklin, letter to George Whatley, 23 May 1784 (Passy) — 'I have only to move my eyes up or down, as I want to see distinctly far or near'
Indiana Public Media 'A Moment of Science' (2019): Franklin invented bifocals in the 1780s — had his reading glasses cut in half and fused with his distance glasses

competing_hypotheses: Franklin described but did not himself construct the first pair (the letter is certain; the workbench attribution is the softer element)
An earlier unnamed London optician built double spectacles first and Franklin popularized the form
falsifiability: Proof the 1784 letter is forged, or a securely dated double-power lens predating 1784

title: The 1784 ledger: nine teeth, 122 shillings
claim: In 1784, Washington's plantation ledger records a cash payment of 122 shillings (£6.10) to several enslaved people for nine teeth, on account of the French dentist Jean-Pierre Le Mayeur.
place: Mount Vernon plantation, Virginia (the ledger)
grade_reason: The ledger entry is a documented primary record, multiply cited in independent secondary treatments (Wikipedia with citations, Poynter 2026, Popular Science 2019, STAT 2017). Held below VERIFIED on the single-document base; the LINKAGE of the nine teeth to Washington's own mouth is the fenced unknown — stated as CLAIMED, never assumed.
earliest_attestation: The Mount Vernon plantation ledger notation: 'By cash pd Negroes for 9 Teeth on Acct of Dr. Lemoin' (Le Mayeur). Reported in the Wikipedia synthesis of the ledger, Poynter's 2026 fact-check, and Popular Science's 2019 treatment. It is unknown whether the sellers were coerced, and unknown whether they ever received the money (enslaved people were routinely cheated by overseers).

sources.ref: Mount Vernon plantation ledger, 1784: 'By cash pd Negroes for 9 Teeth on Acct of Dr. Lemoin' — via Wikipedia synthesis with citations

Poynter fact-check (2026): surviving financial records show the 1784 payment; 'it is possible that the teeth came from enslaved people... but the evidence is unclear'; none of Washington's dentures from this period include human teeth
Popular Science (2019): the ledger notation and its reading; Le Mayeur's known practice of paying individuals for healthy teeth

competing_hypotheses: The teeth entered Washington's own dentures (cannot be proven: his surviving human-teeth dentures date to 1789 (Greenwood), with no sourcing record)

The teeth were used by Le Mayeur for another patient or a different denture set (fenced honestly: none of Washington's dentures from the 1784 period include human teeth; Le Mayeur's records of his Mount Vernon services do not survive)
falsifiability: Examination of the original ledger page contradicting the transcription, or documentary proof of where the nine teeth went (Le Mayeur's lost records).

title: The Bastille's 'hundreds of political prisoners' (myth)
claim: The popular claim that the Bastille held hundreds of political prisoners, liberated by the storming of 14 July 1789.
place: Place de la Bastille, Paris
grade_reason: The fortress's own inventory shows seven prisoners, none a political leader: four forgers, one mentally ill Irishman, one would-be regicide of 1759, and one aristocrat held by his family's lettre de cachet. The Marquis de Sade — the one famous political-adjacent prisoner — had been transferred out ten days earlier. A decision to replace the fortress with an open public space had already been made before the storming.
earliest_attestation: The prisoner's inventory of 14 July 1789, recovered from the fortress's own records; the myth in Latude's Mémoires (1787) and Linguet's Mémoires de la Bastille (1783)

sources.ref: Bastille fortress's own records: seven prisoners on 14 July 1789 — four forgers held under Grand Châtelet warrants; James F.X. Whyte, an Irish-born 'lunatic' suspected of spying, held at his family's request; Auguste-Claude Tavernier, who had attempted to assassinate Louis XV thirty years earlier; and the Comte de Solages, a 'deviant' aristocrat suspected of murder, held by his father via lettre de cachet (via Wikipedia 'Storming of the Bastille', citing Godechot)

1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Bastille': 'At the time of its capture only seven prisoners were found in it.' Also notes the horror tales found currency in the revolutionary excitement but 'historical evidence... tends to strip of their more dreadful features, and even in many cases to refute altogether.' (public domain)
Bastille archives discovered 1840 by François Ravaisson in the Arsenal vaults (via 1911 Britannica) — the registers that let later scholarship audit the legend

title: The namesake who never invented it — Dr. Guillotin and the machine that stole his name
claim: Joseph-Ignace Guillotin invented the guillotine — the machine as his personal invention.
place: Paris (where Guillotin made his December 1789 Assembly motion, Louis designed the machine, and Schmidt built it; first use at the Place de Grève, 25 April 1792)
grade_reason: Three independent kills on the inventor attribution. (1) THE PAPERWORK NAMES OTHER MEN: the design is credited to Antoine Louis, the Paris Academy of Surgery's secretary, and the first machine was built by Tobias Schmidt — so firmly that the machine's first nickname was the 'Louisette'/'Louison.' (2) GUILLOTIN'S DOCUMENTED ROLE IS ADVOCACY: his December 1789 appearance before the National Assembly argued for a decapitating machine as the standard, equal method of execution; on 3 June 1791 the Assembly decreed it the sole legal means of criminal execution. Advocate, not maker. (3) THE NAMESAKE REJECTED THE NAME: Guillotin opposed capital punishment, was embarrassed by the association for the rest of his life, and his family petitioned the government to rename the machine — refused, they changed their own family name instead. A man does not flee a machine he proudly invented.
earliest_attestation: The popular form travels in the name itself — every encyclopedia entry is filed under 'guillotine.' The contemporary counter-attestation is the machine's first nickname: the 'Louisette'/'Louison,' after Antoine Louis, and Guillotin's own documented role as proposer (his December 1789 Assembly motion), not designer or builder.

sources.ref: Smithsonian Magazine, Kat Eschner (28 Mar 2017), 'The Guillotine's Namesake Was Against Capital Punishment' — Guillotin 'did not in fact invent the machine his name is associated with — that was Dr. Antoine Louis, writes History.com'; machine first nicknamed 'Louison' or 'Louisette'; Guillotin popularized it; December 1789 Assembly appearance ('Now with my machine I take off your head in the twinkling of an eye'); 3 June 1791 decree (sole means of legal criminal execution, per Cavendish); namesake opposed capital punishment

competing_hypotheses: The fair formulation: Guillotin was the machine's parliamentary advocate, not its maker — his December 1789 motion made decapitation-by-machine the single legal method (decreed 3 June 1791); the design is credited to Antoine Louis and the build to Tobias Schmidt, and the machine's first nickname was the 'Louisette'/'Louison'

The name-license reading: the 'guillotine' name stuck by popular mockery of Guillotin's enthusiastic advocacy ('with my machine I take off your head in the twinkling of an eye'), while the man himself spent the rest of his life regretting the association and opposing capital punishment
falsifiability: A contemporary 1790–1792 document crediting Guillotin with the design or construction — the design memoranda name Antoine Louis (secretary of the Paris Academy of Surgery) and the build is credited to Tobias Schmidt, the German harpsichord maker in Paris.

title: DEBUNKED: Marie Antoinette said 'Let them eat cake'
claim: Marie Antoinette, queen of France, when told that the French peasants had no bread, replied "Let them eat cake" (French: "Qu'ils mangent de la brioche") — the remark that became the universal shorthand for aristocratic indifference on the eve of the Revolution.
place: Versailles, France (where the claim sets the remark)

sources.ref: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Confessions, Book 6 (first six books written c. 1765, published 1782): the 'great princess' anecdote — 'Qu'ils mangent de la brioche'
Encyclopaedia Britannica: the phrase first connected to Marie Antoinette in print in 1843, fifty years after her 1793 execution
Antonia Fraser, Marie Antoinette: The Journey (2001): no reference to the remark in the queen's trial records, correspondence, or the 1780s pamphlet attacks on her

competing_hypotheses: The libelle-press theory: the remark was pinned on her by revolutionary pamphleteers of the 1780s-90s as political propaganda — possible as a mechanism, but no pre-1843 print attribution has been found, so the theory carries the mechanism honestly and the date as a limit

Rousseau's 'great princess' was a real earlier figure (Marie-Thérèse of Spain, Louis XVI's aunts, or others have been proposed) — carried as proposed, unproven; the anecdote's provenance dies in Rousseau's text either way

falsifiability: A contemporary document — written before 1789 and naming Marie Antoinette as the speaker — recording the remark. None exists; the 1780s libelle literature, her correspondence, and her 1793 trial records (surveyed by Antonia Fraser) all omit it.

title: The makers: Louis's design, Schmidt's build, Pelletier's morning — 25 April 1792

grade_reason: Multiple independent lines converge. Antoine Louis, secretary of the Paris Academy of Surgery, is credited with the design across secondary scholarship (History.com via Smithsonian; Wikipedia; TopWar's account). Tobias Schmidt, the German harpsichord maker working in Paris, is credited with the build. The 25 April 1792 first use on Nicolas-Jacques Pelletier (a common-law convict) is consistently dated and placed at the Place de Grève. The machine's continued service to 1977 (public executions ended 1939, after the Weidmann execution at Versailles) is the long institutional tail of the same device.
earliest_attestation: The machine's first nickname — the 'Louisette'/'Louison' — is the contemporary counter-attestation to the Guillotin attribution: the era's own vocabulary named the designer, not the advocate.

sources.ref: Smithsonian Magazine, Kat Eschner (28 Mar 2017) — Louis designed, Schmidt built; first use context; 3 June 1791 decree; service history per Cavendish
Wikipedia, 'Guillotine' — 25 April 1792 first use (Nicolas-Jacques Pelletier, Place de Grève); service to 1977; public executions ended 1939 (Eugen Weidmann, Versailles)

title: Chappe's optical telegraph (1791–1794)
claim: Claude Chappe (1763–1805), with his brothers, invented the optical semaphore telegraph; the first public demonstration ran on 2 March 1791 (Brûlon to Parcé, 16 km); the Legislative Assembly adopted the machine in 1792; Chappe was appointed ingénieur-télégraphiste and built the Paris–Lille line (230 km), which carried official military dispatches in 1794.
place: Brûlon, Sarthe, France (the 1791 demonstration site; Paris–Lille line terminals)
grade_reason: Multiple independent attestations converge: the 1791 demonstration (dated message, municipal officials at both ends, recorded in the standard biographical record), the 1792 Legislative Assembly adoption (1911 Britannica), the ingénieur-télégraphiste appointment and the built Paris–Lille line, and the 1794 Condé-sur-l'Escaut dispatch (graded separately). The machine's French name — the Télégraphe Chappe — and Chappe's own coinage of 'semaphore' (1801) and 'telegraph' attach the invention to its maker.
earliest_attestation: The March 1791 Brûlon–Parcé demonstration and the 1792–1793 Legislative Assembly/National Convention records; 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica's Chappe entry (public domain) as the standard biographical account

sources.ref: 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Chappe, Claude' (public domain): 'He was the inventor of an optical telegraph which was widely used in France until it was superseded by the electric telegraph... The machine was adopted by the Legislative Assembly in 1792, and in the following year Chappe was appointed ingénieur-télégraphe'

Wikipedia, 'Optical telegraph': the 2 March 1791 Brûlon–Parcé demonstration ('If you succeed, you will soon bask in glory'); summer 1792 appointment as Ingénieur-Télégraphiste and the Paris–Lille line; 'semaphore' coined by Chappe in 1801

Shannon Selin, 'Napoleonic Telecommunications: The Chappe Semaphore Telegraph' (2020): 'The Napoleonic telegraph system was invented by Claude Chappe'; the 1791 demonstration, the 24 March 1792 Assembly address, Ignace Chappe's election

The 'army method' reading: rivals in Chappe's lifetime charged plagiarism from military semaphore practice — the charge that drove his melancholia; no contemporary ruling credited a rival inventor

title: The revolutionary playing-card catalog (1791) — a million cards to Paris

title: The death of Mozart, 5 December 1791

Sophie Haibel (sister-in-law), later recollections: severe swelling, lucidity to the end

title: 'Napoleon invented the semaphore' — the authorship myth
claim: Napoleon Bonaparte invented the semaphore (optical) telegraph — the 'Napoleonic semaphore' label as an authorship claim.
place: Paris (the popular telling's home — where the Assembly adopted Chappe's machine in 1792, seven years before the 18 Brumaire coup)
grade_reason: Three independent kills on the authorship claim. (1) CHRONOLOGY: the invention is dated and paper-trailed 1790–1794 — the 2 March 1791 demonstration, the 24 March 1792 Assembly address, the 1792/93 ingénieur-télégraphiste appointment — all under the revolutionary government; Napoleon seized power in 1799. An 1804 emperor cannot have invented a 1791 machine. (2) THE NAME: France calls it the Télégraphe Chappe, and the words 'semaphore' (1801) and 'telegraph' were coined by and for Chappe — an inventor's name is stamped on his machine in the Army's own vocabulary. (3) EVERY SOURCE CREDITS HIM ONLY WITH USE: the standard accounts — including the Napoleonic-era histories — record Napoleon 'making good use of the Chappe telegraph' (Italy campaign, imperial coordination); no source of any era credits him with the invention.
earliest_attestation: The popular form travels in the label itself: Wikipedia notes semaphore telegraphs are 'also called "Chappe telegraphs" or "Napoleonic semaphore"'; the army's own paper — the word 'telegraph' coined for Chappe's machine, the French name Télégraphe Chappe — is the contemporary counter-attestation

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Optical telegraph': semaphore telegraphs 'also called "Chappe telegraphs" or "Napoleonic semaphore"'; 'the word semaphore was coined in 1801 by the French inventor of the semaphore line itself, Claude Chappe'; the system 'was used by Napoleon to coordinate his empire and army' (use, not invention)
Wikipedia, 'Claude Chappe': 1763–1805, the 1794 Paris–Lille messages, 'the system was widely copied by other European states, and was used by Napoleon to coordinate his empire and army'
1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Chappe, Claude' (public domain): inventor of the optical telegraph; adopted by the Legislative Assembly 1792; appointed ingénieur-télégraphe 1793

Sam Hallas, 'Short History of Telegraphy — Part 1': 'Just such a system was invented in the 1790s by Frenchman Claude Chappe... Napoleon made good use of the Chappe telegraph in his invasion of Italy' — the use/invention distinction stated in one breath

competing_hypotheses: The fair formulation: Napoleon was the semaphore's heaviest user and great expander — the Italy campaigns, the imperial coordination lines — but the system was a Revolutionary inheritance, not his invention (the association is real; the authorship is not)
The name-license reading: 'Napoleonic semaphore' names the era of its great military use, like 'Napoleonic law' names the Code he commissioned — a period label, not an inventor's credit
falsifiability: A contemporary 1790–1794 document in which Napoleon (then an artillery officer in the south) originated, designed, or commissioned the optical system — the Assembly papers name only the Chappe brothers

title: Salieri and Mozart: the documented courtesy

place: Vienna, Austria
grade_reason: Attested in Mozart's own correspondence and in the documented teaching record; the exact warmth of the relationship is a matter of interpretation, which holds the record below VERIFIED.

title: The legend that Salieri poisoned Mozart
claim: Antonio Salieri poisoned Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart out of professional jealousy, as depicted in Peter Shaffer's 1979 play Amadeus and Milos Forman's 1984 film.
place: Vienna, Austria — the rumor's city and the play's stage
grade_reason: Three independent kills: (1) no contemporary primary-source origin — the rumor's first durable form is a work of fiction (Pushkin 1830); (2) the witnessed symptoms (fever, rash, edema) match an infectious outbreak and do not match poison signatures, corroborated by the 2009 Vienna death-register epidemiology; (3) scholarly consensus (Grove, Britannica) states there is no foundation for the claim, and Salieri denied it during his competent years.
earliest_attestation: Post-1791 Viennese rumor, unattributed and undocumented at the time; the first durable attestation is Alexander Pushkin's 1830 play "Mozart and Salieri," which dramatized the hearsay as a tragedy of envy — literature, not history

sources.ref: Hektoen International ('Mozart and Salieri: From Pushkin to Shaffer'): Pushkin's 1830 play as the myth's literary birth; the Don Giovanni-whistle anecdote is suspect (Salieri was in Paris during the 1787 Prague premiere)
Mozart Portal ('Did Salieri Poison Mozart? The Myth and the Evidence'): five-point debunk — symptom mismatch, no autopsy, Salieri's denials, contemporary epidemic accounts, Grove/Britannica consensus
Norton/Grove Concise Encyclopedia of Music: "He [Mozart] was not poisoned"; Britannica: "no foundation for the belief that Salieri tried to poison Mozart"
Wikipedia 'Antonio Salieri': the rumor has been disproved — Mozart's symptoms did not indicate poisoning; the two were at least mutually respectful peers

Carried honestly — it explains the rumor's 1820s fuel, but a recanted secondhand confession from a distressed old man is not evidence of a 1791 murder.

The genuine-rivalry position: competition for court favor was real; carried honestly — rivalry is not homicide, and the documented courtesy (Magic Flute attendance, teaching Mozart's son) contradicts a murderer's profile.
falsifiability: A contemporary (1791) primary document establishing poisoning — an attending physician's report, a police or court inquiry, or a confession in Salieri's own hand from his competent years. No such document exists.

title: The death the machine never dealt him — Guillotin, 1814, of a carbuncle
claim: Joseph-Ignace Guillotin was executed by the guillotine — killed by the machine that bears his name.
place: Père-Lachaise Cemetery, Paris — Guillotin's burial; the myth dies at the graveside
grade_reason: Two independent kills. (1) THE DEATH RECORD: Guillotin died at home in Paris in 1814, aged 75, of natural causes (a carbuncle), and is buried in Père-Lachaise Cemetery — documented across Wikipedia (citing Donegan's 1990 JRSM biography) and the Smithsonian (Eschner 2017, citing Cavendish's History Today piece, which notes his funeral 'occurred on this day in 1814' while his family was lobbying to rename the machine). A man cannot be guillotined in 1793 and die at home in 1814. (2) THE CONFUSION'S FINGERPRINT: the error has a documented source — a different person, J.M.V. Guillotin, a doctor of Lyon, really was executed by the guillotine, and the shared surname seeded the legend. With the inventor attribution already dead (evt-guillotin-invented-guillotine-001), the 'inventor destroyed by his invention' moral has nothing left to stand on: he didn't invent it, and it didn't kill him.
earliest_attestation: The popular form travels as a joke and a moral — 'the inventor died by his own machine' — repeated without a source. The documentary record gives the opposite: Guillotin's funeral occurred in 1814 (Cavendish, History Today, via Smithsonian), and Wikipedia's article records his death at home in Paris in 1814, aged 75, of a carbuncle, burial in Père-Lachaise.

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Joseph-Ignace Guillotin' — died at home in Paris 1814, aged 75, natural causes (carbuncle); buried Père-Lachaise; family petitioned to rename (refused), changed own name; J.M.V. Guillotin of Lyon executed by the guillotine — the coincidence behind the error
Smithsonian Magazine, Kat Eschner (28 Mar 2017) — funeral in 1814; family lobbying to rename; 'contrary to popular myth, he died of natural causes, not by beheading'
ThoughtCo, 'A History of the Guillotine in Europe' — 'contrary to legend, Doctor Joseph Ignace Guillotin was not executed by his own machine; he lived until 1814, and died of biological causes'

competing_hypotheses: The ironic-justice reading: the inventor destroyed by his invention — dies with the inventor attribution (fenced to evt-guillotin-invented-guillotine-001)
The confusion reading: a different Guillotin — J.M.V. Guillotin, a doctor of Lyon — WAS executed by the guillotine, and the shared surname seeded the error
falsifiability: A contemporary 1793–1794 execution record naming Joseph-Ignace Guillotin among the condemned — no such record exists; the executed Guillotin is a different man (J.M.V. Guillotin of Lyon).

title: The 'Captain Bligh the sadistic tyrant' reading (DEBUNKED)
claim: William Bligh, captain of HMS Bounty, was a sadistic tyrant whose cruelty drove his crew to mutiny on 28 April 1789.
place: Near Tofua, Tonga — where the mutiny's story was born
grade_reason: The punishment ledger (below the Navy average, not above it), the Admiralty's own 1790 honourable acquittal, and the documented two-stage manufacture of the image (1794 family advocacy, then 1935 film inventions) kill the sadistic-tyrant reading; what survives is a foul-tempered, verbally abusive captain — a different, lesser charge.
earliest_attestation: Edward Christian's Appendix to the 1794 'Minutes of the Proceedings on the Court-Martial' — the Christian family's advocacy publication, interviewing mutineer-sympathetic witnesses five years after the event.

sources.ref: Bligh's Bounty log (Mitchell Library, State Library of NSW) — punishment entries for the 1787-1789 voyage

Caroline Alexander, The Bounty (2003): 229 lashes administered over 17 months aboard the Bounty, against 278 lashes in three and a half weeks aboard HMS Brunswick by one of the captains who sat on the mutineers' court-martial
Greg Dening, Mr Bligh's Bad Language (1992): Bligh's flogging rate of less than one in ten seamen was exceptionally low for the period; his violence was more verbal than physical (Alan Frost)
Court-martial of William Bligh for the loss of HMS Bounty, October 1790 — honourable acquittal, the Admiralty's own verdict on his conduct
1935 MGM Mutiny on the Bounty (Frank Lloyd, Charles Laughton as Bligh): stages a keelhauling and the flogging of a dead man — neither happened; keelhauling was not a Royal Navy punishment

competing_hypotheses: Bligh's temper and verbal abuse were genuinely extreme and the lash-count understates his cruelty (the Christian-family position, 1794 — conceded in part by Dening and Frost, who document the tongue while acquitting the lash)
The tyrant image is substantially the film industry's (1935 Laughton), not the family's — the 1794 Appendix argued injustice, the 1935 film invented sadism
Both readings are partial: a below-average flogger with an above-average tongue — the two facts are compatible, and the mutiny needs the Tahiti shore-leave context, not just the captain
falsifiability: A Bounty punishment ledger showing above-average flogging, or a contemporary (pre-1794) account describing systematic cruelty, would revive the reading; none has surfaced in two centuries of archive work.

title: Conté's 1795 recipe: clay, graphite, and the hardness dial
claim: In 1795, Nicolas-Jacques Conté patented the process of making pencil lead from powdered graphite mixed with wet clay, shaped into rods and fired — the mixture ratio controlling the lead's hardness — freeing continental pencil-makers from dependence on British graphite.
place: Paris, France
grade_reason: Consistently attested across independent histories (NPR, ThoughtCo, MRS Bulletin) with the wartime-commission mechanism documented; held below VERIFIED on the commission-to-patent chain and on this pass's secondhand sourcing.
earliest_attestation: French patent record, 1795; the process still in use in modified form.

sources.ref: NPR / KHSU (2016): 'In 1794, Revolutionary France was at war with Britain and completely cut off from high-quality English graphite. The minister of war asked engineer Nicolas-Jacques Conté to find a solution. Conté ground up impure, low-quality graphite, mixed it with wet clay, shaped the mixture into rods and then baked them.'

ThoughtCo, 'Writing Instrument History': 'The breakthrough in pencil technology came when French chemist Nicolas Conte developed and patented the process used to make pencils in 1795. He used a mixture of clay and graphite that was fired before it was put in a wooden case.'

competing_hypotheses: The process as Conté's wartime-commission solution (1794 commission by the French minister of war) vs the 1795 patent as the formal invention — the two dates are one episode, carried honestly
The Thoreau improvements (mid-1840s American refinements of the Conté process) as the practically important version for fine leads
falsifiability: A pre-1794 fired clay-graphite lead process, or proof Conté's patent was never practiced, would overturn this.

title: Paris 1794 — the first public scientific zoo
claim: The Ménagerie du Jardin des Plantes in Paris, officially inaugurated in 1794, was the first modern public scientific zoo.
place: Ménagerie du Jardin des Plantes, 75005 Paris (coordinates via map.geocode, FULL_ADDRESS match)
grade_reason: The Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle's own official history confirms the 1794 decree, the Versailles royal-ménagerie stock, and the free-public scientific mission; independent secondary sources (aboutzoos.info) agree ('France's oldest public zoo', 'second oldest zoo according to modern zoological tradition'). Held below VERIFIED on the single institutional-history base for the founding detail.
earliest_attestation: 1794 revolutionary decree; the Muséum's own official history.

sources.ref: Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle — History of the Menagerie, the zoo of the Jardin des Plantes (1794 decree, 58 animals, free to all)
aboutzoos.info — Paris, La Ménagerie du Jardin des Plantes (France's oldest public zoo)

competing_hypotheses: Schönbrunn (1752, public 1779) is the older institution — Paris's distinction is the revolutionary public-scientific model, not raw age
The 1794 inauguration date is the decree date (16 May 1794, Comité de Salut Public); animals arrived in waves — the record documents the act of founding, not a single opening day
falsifiability: The Muséum's own history being contradicted by an earlier public-scientific zoo charter (Schönbrunn's is an imperial menagerie opened to the public, a different institutional model — the distinction is carried honestly).

title: The Paris–Lille line's first dispatch (1794)
claim: The first military dispatches over the Paris–Lille semaphore line carried news of the French recapture of Condé-sur-l'Escaut from the Austrians in 1794 — the victory known in Paris less than an hour after it occurred.
place: The Paris–Lille semaphore line (230 km); news terminus Condé-sur-l'Escaut (~50.45N, 3.59E)
grade_reason: Multiple secondary sources converge on the core event — a 1794 French victory at Condé-sur-l'Escaut flashed to Paris within the hour over the new line — but they diverge on the exact day and which capture was 'first', so the record holds at CORROBORATED until a dated primary dispatch or operator's logbook pins it.
earliest_attestation: The line's own operation, summer 1794; the standard modern accounts (Wikipedia's Optical telegraph and Chappe telegraph articles; thearticle.com's French telegraph history)

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Optical telegraph': 'In 1794, it brought news of a French capture of Condé-sur-l'Escaut from the Austrians less than an hour after it occurred'

Wikipedia, 'Chappe telegraph': 'The first military use of the system was made to report the recapture from Austrian forces of the cities of Le Quesnoy on 15 August 1794 and the town of Condé-sur-l'Escaut on 30 August 1794. The news of these victories was known by the National Convention in Paris within a few minutes'
thearticle.com, 'How the mechanical telegraph shaped the history of France': the first line inaugurated mid-August 1794; 'The first news carried by the line was the recapture of Conde-sur-Lescaut'

competing_hypotheses: The variant-dating reading: some accounts date the first military use to Le Quesnoy (15 August 1794) and Condé to 30 August 1794, the Convention learning of the victories 'within a few minutes' — carried honestly as the dating variance
The inauguration reading: mid-August 1794 inauguration with Condé as the first carried news — consistent with the above, varying only in which victory counted as 'first'
falsifiability: A Convention or War Ministry record showing the Paris–Lille line carried no dispatches before 1795, or a dated operator's logbook contradicting the Condé carriage

title: Edward Jenner's 1796 experiment and the 1798 Inquiry (the foil)
claim: On 14 May 1796, Edward Jenner inoculated 8-year-old James Phipps with cowpox matter from the hand of the dairymaid Sarah Nelmes; on 1 July he challenged Phipps with smallpox matter and no disease followed. He self-published An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae in 1798 after the Royal Society declined the paper, named the method 'vaccination' (from vacca, cow), and drove its global adoption — earning £10,000 (1802) and £20,000 (1807) from Parliament.
place: Berkeley, Gloucestershire, England
grade_reason: The experiment, the challenge, the naming, and the publication are all in the primary record (the Inquiry itself) with the Royal Society refusal and Parliament rewards independently documented; held at CORROBORATED rather than VERIFIED on the thinness of the single-case experiment and the retrospective telling around it.
earliest_attestation: Jenner, E. (1798). An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae — the primary record of the experiment

sources.ref: Jenner, E. (1798). An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae (self-published, after Royal Society declined)
Wikipedia, 'Benjamin Jesty' — Parliament awards: Jenner £10,000 (1802), £20,000 (1807); Pearson's testimony on Jesty's priority
digpodcast.org, 'The OG Vaccine: Smallpox, Cowpox, and the Procedure that Changed the World' — the Phipps/Nelmes experiment narrative

competing_hypotheses: The Phipps challenge's ethics are indefensible by modern standards — documented fact, not a grade challenge
Jenner's promotion was partly commercial self-interest — true, and irrelevant to whether the method worked
falsifiability: Proof the 1796 Phipps experiment records were fabricated, or contemporary evidence the method's spread predated and bypassed Jenner's publication entirely

title: Phrenology (skull-bump faculty mapping)
claim: The shape of the skull reveals the strengths of the mind: 27 (later 35) mental faculties can be read from the bumps on a person's cranium, allowing diagnosis of character and ability by palpation.
place: Vienna, Austria (Gall's lecture halls)
grade_reason: The diagnostic system is disproven: skull bumps do not reflect cortical development (the skull's outer table follows its own growth), and every faculty-to-region mapping was refuted — first by Flourens's 1824 lesion experiments showing functional loss from cortical ablation, then by Broca (1861) locating speech in a region Gall had assigned to something else entirely.
earliest_attestation: Franz Joseph Gall's Vienna lecture series (1796); publications with Johann Spurzheim, 1810-1819.

sources.ref: F.J. Gall & J. Spurzheim, Anatomie et physiologie du système nerveux en général, et du cerveau en particulier (1810-1819)
Pierre Flourens, Recherches expérimentales sur les propriétés et les fonctions du système nerveux (1824) — lesion experiments
Paul Broca (1861) on the Leborgne ('Tan') case — speech located in the inferior frontal gyrus, not where Gall's faculty maps put it

competing_hypotheses: Gall's localization intuition (different faculties, different brain regions) was directionally right even as every one of his mapped locations was wrong
The 19th-century phrenological establishment (Spurzheim, Combe) made the doctrine a mass social technology — head-reading parlors, employee screening — independent of its truth
falsifiability: Cranial topography predicting cognitive faculties under controlled blinded testing — attempted throughout the 19th century and never demonstrated above chance.

title: The rival 'first skyscraper' candidates: the 93-year candidate map
claim: The 'first skyscraper' title has at least four documented earlier or rival candidates, each holding a different 'first' under a different definition: the Ditherington Flax Mill (1797), Oriel Chambers (1864), the Equitable Life Building (1870), and the Rand McNally Building (1890).
grade_reason: Each candidate is attested by institutional, documentary sources that converge: Historic England (Ditherington), RIBA (Oriel Chambers), the elevator historical record (Equitable Life), and the structural-historical literature (Rand McNally). The record makes no claim about who 'deserves' the title — it is an attestation map, and attestation maps are CORROBORATED by definition.
earliest_attestation: The buildings themselves and their institutional records: Historic England on the Ditherington Flax Mill (world's first iron-framed building, 'grandfather of skyscrapers', Grade I listed); RIBA on Oriel Chambers (1864, Peter Ellis — earliest cast-iron-framed glass curtain walling in England, Grade I listed); the Equitable Life Building's passenger-elevator record (1870, George B. Post); the Rand McNally Building (1890) as the first entirely self-supporting steel-framed skyscraper.

sources.ref: Historic England / Wikipedia 'Shrewsbury Flaxmill Maltings' — 'the first iron-framed building in the world', 'the grandfather of skyscrapers'; built 1797, architect Charles Bage; Grade I listed
RIBA (ribapix) — Oriel Chambers, Water Street, Liverpool (1864, Peter Ellis): 'the earliest use of curtain walling with a cast-iron frame in England'; Grade I listed
Wikipedia 'Oriel Chambers' — 'the world's first building featuring a metal-framed glass curtain wall'; 1864; Grade I listed

Wikipedia 'List of firsts in architecture' — Equitable Life Building (Manhattan), first office building to use passenger elevators (1870); Home Insurance Building 'widely considered to be the first true skyscraper' (1884)
Wikipedia 'Early skyscrapers' — the 1890 Rand McNally Building, 'the first entirely self-supporting, steel-framed skyscraper'

competing_hypotheses: The Chicago-primacy position: none of the earlier buildings was a 'skyscraper' in the functional sense — tall office buildings served by elevators and designed for urban commerce — so the Home Insurance Building keeps the title under the definition that matters (the 'skyscraper as building type' reading).

The cumulative-invention position: the skyscraper was not invented once but assembled piece by piece across ninety-three years — iron frame (1797), curtain wall (1864), elevator (1870), steel frame (1885/1890). Under this reading the title 'first' is a category error, and each candidate is the first OF SOMETHING.
falsifiability: Evidence that any one of these buildings did not exist, did not have its attested feature (iron frame, curtain wall, elevator, self-supporting steel frame), or postdates the Home Insurance Building would remove it from the candidate map — but the map records DOCUMENTED candidates, not a winner.

title: Napoleon's soldiers shot off the Sphinx's nose (1798)
claim: Napoleon Bonaparte's soldiers shot the nose off the Great Sphinx of Giza with cannon fire during the French invasion of Egypt in 1798.
place: Great Sphinx of Giza, Giza Plateau, Egypt
grade_reason: Killed twice by dated evidence: (1) Frederic Louis Norden's 1737 drawings, engraved and published in 1755, show the Sphinx already without its nose — 61 years before the French campaign; (2) Napoleon's troops were never in position anyway — the battle was fought at Imbaba, hours' march from the plateau (Bassam el-Shamaa, 2009). The myth's mechanism is the 20th-century pub-story + cinema pipeline, most recently Ridley Scott's Napoleon (2023), whose own consultant Michael Broers confirmed 'nothing like that happened' and the director kept the scene anyway as 'a fast way of saying he took Egypt'.
earliest_attestation: No contemporary attestation: the story appears only in much later retellings. Scholarly tracing (artnet, citing the myth's historiography) dates the Napoleonic version's appearance to around the dawn of the 20th century — a full century after the campaign.

sources.ref: historytools.org, 'The Enigma of the Great Sphinx's Missing Nose' — Norden's 1737 drawing 'clearly depicts the Sphinx without a nose, confirming that this feature was already missing by the early 18th century'

artnet / Verity Babbs (Nov 2023), 'How Ridley Scott's Napoleon Repeats One of Art History's Biggest Conspiracies' — drawings by Norden in 1737 (displayed 1744) show the nose already lost; Broers/Schott exchange; myth traced to the dawn of the 20th century
Smithsonian Journeys, Sarah Erdman (Sept 2022), 'What happened to the Sphinx's nose?' — Norden's 1737 sketches depict no nose; al-Maqrizi's 14th-century account
allbuzznews.com, Megan Levine (2026-10-09), '20 Pyramid Myths Hollywood Helped Spread' — Norden drew the Sphinx noseless in 1737, 32 years before Napoleon was born

competing_hypotheses: The nose was chiseled off in 1378 by the Sufi iconoclast Muhammad Sa'im al-Dahr (al-Maqrizi's 15th-century account; single-source, hence CLAIMED in evt-saim-al-dahr-1378-001)
The nose was removed earlier still — archaeologist Mark Lehner's study of the chisel marks suggests a 3rd-to-10th-century date
Natural erosion and falling debris did the work over the limestone's five millennia (the soft-middle-layer geology makes mechanical damage easy, but the tool marks point to human hands)
falsifiability: Produce one document, letter, order, or image dated 1798-1801 attesting French artillery damage to the Sphinx's face. One contemporaneous parchment moves the grade; there are none.

title: The Mount Sapo naming legend (soap's false etymology)
claim: Soap takes its name from Mount Sapo (or Sappo), a supposed Roman hill where animals were sacrificed to the gods; rain washed the sacrifices' fat and ashes down the slope into the Tiber, where laundresses discovered the mixture cleaned their clothes.
place: Rome (the legend's claimed setting — no such place)
grade_reason: Three independent kills: (1) no such place exists in any classical, late-antique, or medieval source — the location and the 'ancient Roman legend' are both unattested; the story only appears in articles about the history of soap. (2) Roman animal sacrifice would not yield soap-making quantities of fat: the edible meat and fat went to humans; the gods got bones and inedible entrails. (3) Latin sapo is documented as a loan from Celtic/Germanic (Pliny's own account ties it to the Gauls), not from a Roman toponym.
earliest_attestation: 19th-century soap-trade/popular histories (no classical source)

sources.ref: soaphistory.net — 'First Soap': 'there is no such place and no evidence for the apocryphal story'

Stuff You Missed in History Class — 'A History of Soap': Mount Sappo 'is not a real place'; the legend 'only seems to show up in articles about the history of soap'; no Roman document references it; sacrificial animals would not have yielded the fat needed; heavy dilution by rain and river

Soap history survey (Wikipedia 'History of soap', citing primary literature): 'The location of Mount Sapo is unknown, as is the source of the "ancient Roman legend"... Roman animal sacrifices usually burned only the bones and inedible entrails... would not have included enough fat to make much soap. The legend about Mount Sapo is probably apocryphal.'

competing_hypotheses: A variant names Mount 'Sapo' as the site where temple fires burned — same structural story, same zero attestation
The honest root: Latin sapo was borrowed from a Celtic or Germanic word, cognate with Latin sebum (tallow) — the Pliny record
The legend may have been cooked up in 19th-century soap-trade literature as an origin story for advertising
falsifiability: A classical, late-antique, or medieval Latin text naming a Mons Sapo or a sacrifice-to-soap origin

title: The 'Richelieu invented the table knife' telling
claim: Cardinal Richelieu (1585-1642) invented the blunt-tipped table knife around 1637 — the schoolbook telling that he ordered all table knives' points ground off at his own table after seeing a dinner guest pick his teeth with a pointed knife.
place: Paris (the telling's claimed setting)
grade_reason: Two independent kills: (1) the documentary absence — no 17th-century source records the incident; the anecdote's own phrasing in reference works is 'attributed by tradition', the tell-tale grammar of an unattested retelling; (2) the chronology — the rounded-tip table knife is a later, gradual French development (the fork's spread removed the need for a pointed knife; court etiquette standardized the blunt form under Louis XIV, with 1669/1699 edict variants in the telling), which puts the real transition decades after Richelieu's death in 1642. The grade kills the invention claim only — never the blunt tips, never the tooth-picking habit, never the man.
earliest_attestation: No 17th-century source; the anecdote is an 18th/19th-century retelling, 'attributed by tradition'
