sources.ref: The tradition's standard phrasing ('attributed by tradition to Cardinal Richelieu around 1637, reputedly to cure dinner guests of the habit of...') — the 'by tradition' qualifier is itself the evidence of no attestation
The Retrospectors, 'Cardinal Richelieu and the Table Knife' (2024): dates the alleged incident to 13 May 1637; traces the telling, the tooth-picking context, and the 1699 royal-edict popularization
Rhodri Marsden, 'interesting objects: The table knife' (The Independent, 2015)
Henry Petroski, The Evolution of Useful Things (1992): the gradualist account — forks, pins, clips and zippers evolve by accumulation, not by single-inventor moments

competing_hypotheses: The telling conflates a real habit with a fabricated origin: tooth-picking with knives was a documented bad habit, but the grounding-order is an 18th/19th-century retelling with no 17th-century witness
The Louis-XIV-edict variant (1669 / 1699): the change belongs to the later French court, not to Richelieu's table
falsifiability: A contemporary 17th-century source (household order, memoir, letter) documenting Richelieu's 1637 knife-grounding order

title: The 'valid firman' defense of the Elgin removal
claim: Lord Elgin held a valid Ottoman firman (royal decree) that legally authorized the removal of the Parthenon sculptures from the Parthenon itself — that the surviving document authorizes taking statues and reliefs off the building, not merely drawing, casting, measuring, and excavating around it.
place: The Parthenon, Athenian Acropolis
grade_reason: Two independent kills. (1) Content: the surviving text authorizes drawing, casting, measuring, excavation of gravel, and taking 'a few pieces of stone' with 'no harm' to figures and edifices — not removing reliefs from the building (St. Clair's own 1967 content analysis: the Sultan did not allow the removal and export of statues and reliefs; Elgin's associates conceded before the 1816 committee the act was 'probably illegal'). (2) Provenance: no Ottoman original or archival entry has ever been found for a document of this kind (Korka 2019; Aygen and Sakin). The popular 'valid permit' reading is therefore disproven on its own cited document.
earliest_attestation: The 1801 Italian translation in Lord Elgin's papers (translated by Pisani, the British Embassy dragoman); Philip Hunt's later English rendering; laid before the 1816 Select Committee.

sources.ref: William St. Clair, 'Lord Elgin and the Marbles' (1967) — content analysis of the Italian translation
William St. Clair, 'Imperial Appropriations of the Parthenon', in J.H. Merryman (ed.), 'Imperialism, Art and Restitution' (2006)
David Rudenstine, 'A Tale of Three Documents: Lord Elgin and the Missing Historic 1801 Ottoman Document', Cardozo Law Review 22:5-6 (2001)
Eleni Korka et al., 'The Legality of the Removal of the Parthenon Marbles', Cardozo AELJ (2023)
The 1801 Italian translation of the document (Elgin's papers; British Museum archives)

competing_hypotheses: The British Museum / Policy Exchange position — Elgin acted with the Sultan's authority, the Sultan being the legal ruler, and the 1816 purchase vested clean title — is carried as the institutional counter-position on legality; it does not dispute the text of the surviving document.

St. Clair / Eldem's defense of the Italian translation's AUTHENTICITY (that it is a genuine professional rendering of a real Ottoman document, back-translated convincingly into Ottoman Turkish) is carried honestly — it is a separate question from what the document AUTHORIZED, and the grade kills only the authorization reading.

Rudenstine's stronger claim (Cardozo Law Review 2001) — that no firman ever existed and the surviving Italian version may be a forgery — is carried as the maximalist rival; the grade holds without endorsing it: even if the document is genuine, its text does not authorize the removal.
falsifiability: Discovery of the Ottoman original in the imperial archives expressly authorizing the removal of the Parthenon reliefs and statues — the archives record firmans of this period meticulously, and none has been found.

title: The Parthenon sculptures' removal and 1816 purchase
claim: Sculptures from the Parthenon on the Athenian Acropolis (carved c. 447-432 BCE) were removed between 1801 and 1812 by agents of Thomas Bruce, 7th Earl of Elgin; the collection was sold to the British Parliament in 1816 for 35,000 pounds and has been held in the British Museum since.
place: The Parthenon, Athenian Acropolis (sculptures now in the British Museum, London)
grade_reason: The removal (1801-1812) and the 1816 parliamentary purchase are multiply attested in contemporary primary sources — Elgin's letters, the Select Committee proceedings, the accession records.
earliest_attestation: Lord Elgin's correspondence, 1801-1812; the 1816 Parliamentary Select Committee proceedings on the purchase; the British Museum's accession registers.

sources.ref: 1816 Parliamentary Select Committee report on the Elgin purchase
Elgin's correspondence, 1801-1812
British Museum accession records, Duveen Gallery collection
Policy Exchange, 'The Elgin Marbles' (2023) — the British Museum's legal-title position

competing_hypotheses: The removal was wider in scope than the Parthenon alone — pieces from the Propylaea, the Erechtheion, and other Acropolis structures were also taken — is carried as a documented extension, not a rival to the Parthenon claim.

The British Museum's legal-title position (Elgin acted with Ottoman authority; the 1816 Act of Parliament vested lawful title in the Trustees) is carried as the counter-position on LEGALITY — it does not dispute the removal-and-purchase chain itself, which is the subject of this record.
falsifiability: Parliamentary records showing no 1816 purchase, or contemporary evidence that the sculptures reached London by a different route — neither exists; the removal-and-purchase chain is multiply attested in Elgin's own letters, committee testimony, and museum records.

title: Luke Howard names the clouds (December 1802)
claim: In December 1802, the London pharmacist and amateur meteorologist Luke Howard presented 'On the Modification of Clouds' to the Askesian Society, establishing the Latin cloud nomenclature — cirrus, cumulus, stratus (and nimbus) — that remains the basis of cloud classification today.
place: London (the Askesian Society)
grade_reason: Multiple independent sources agree on the December 1802 lecture, the three principal forms (cirrus 'wisp of hair,' cumulus 'heap,' stratus 'layer,' plus nimbus 'rain cloud' and the compounds), the 1803 Essay publication, the Latin-as-shared-language mechanism, and the system's continuity into the modern International Cloud Atlas. The Royal Society: 'in 1802 he established the terminology for different cloud formations that is still in use today.' The Lamarck rival system (1802, French) is documented and fenced — Howard won the nomenclature, not the attempt.
earliest_attestation: Howard's December 1802 Askesian Society lecture; the 1803 Essay with his own cloud drawings

sources.ref: Weather.com, 'The man who named the clouds' (2026): 'On a December evening in 1802, a reserved London pharmacist by the name of Luke Howard stood before a small group of amateur thinkers and proposed... Presenting his paper, "On the Modification of Clouds," to London's Askesian Society, he introduced a surprisingly practical Latin naming system' — cirrus ('wisp of hair'), cumulus ('heap'), stratus ('layer'), plus nimbus ('rain cloud').

Royal Society, 'Capital climate': 'Most famously, in 1802 he established the terminology for different cloud formations that is still in use today... the use of Latin terms was Howard's way of ensuring non-English-speaking scientists could adopt the new nomenclature.' Also his urban heat island discovery (The Climate of London, 1818).

Wikipedia, 'Luke Howard (meteorologist)': 'In his late twenties, Luke Howard wrote the Essay on the Modification of Clouds, which was published in 1803... Howard named the three principal categories of clouds – cumulus, stratus, and cirrus, as well as a series of intermediate and compound modifications.' Called 'the father of meteorology.'

The Handy Weather Answer Book (via Papertrell): 'The French naturalist Jean Lamarck (1744–1829) was the first to propose a system for classifying clouds in 1802. His work, however, did not receive wide recognition. A year later, the Englishman Luke Howard (1772–1864) developed a cloud classification system that has been generally accepted and is still in use today.'

competing_hypotheses: Howard as sole inventor ex nihilo (fenced: Jean Lamarck proposed a rival French cloud classification in the same year, 1802 — it lost to Howard's Latin, which is why the 'first' is framed as 'established the nomenclature in use today' rather than 'first to attempt classification')
falsifiability: Archival evidence that Howard's lecture did not occur in December 1802, or that the cirrus/cumulus/stratus terms predate him in another author's system

title: The 'short Napoleon' myth
claim: Napoleon Bonaparte was unusually short — about 5 feet 2 inches (English measure).
place: London (caricature press) / Paris (measurement origin)
grade_reason: The '5 feet 2 inches' figure is real — but it is 5 pieds 2 pouces in French units (pied du roi 32.48 cm), converting to ~168-169 cm English, average for French men of the era. The shortness is a conversion error weaponized by British propaganda, not a measurement.
earliest_attestation: British wartime caricature (Gillray et al., c. 1803) depicting Napoleon as tiny; later English-language biographies carrying '5 feet 2 inches' without unit conversion.

sources.ref: Autopsy report, Saint Helena, 6 May 1821 — 5 pieds 2 pouces (French)
National Geographic, 'Was Napoleon even short?' — pied vs English foot analysis, Gillray's size manipulation per art historian Constance McPhee, Imperial Guard height-requirement contrast effect

YouGov Eurotrack, 'How does Europe remember Napoleon?' (fieldwork 7-22 Sept 2023; n=2144 GB / 2134 Germany / 1000 France / 1010 Denmark / 1015 Sweden / 1056 Spain / 1008 Italy) — 'physically short' selected among top-3 descriptors: Germany 52%, GB 37%, Italy 35%, France 29%, Sweden 27%, Denmark 26%, Spain 25%
British Museum print collection — Gillray-era satirical prints (e.g. 1803 tiny-Napoleon-in-cage satire)

competing_hypotheses: The unit-confusion origin alone: the British read '5 feet 2 inches' in French units as English units — an honest conversion error amplified by repetition
The propaganda-primary origin: James Gillray's caricatures and the 'Little Boney' nickname built the image deliberately, with the unit error as a convenient carrier
The contrast effect: Napoleon was often seen among the physically large Imperial Guard grenadiers, making an average man look small
falsifiability: Already falsified: the French-unit reading converts to ~168-169 cm English. Would require proof the pied du roi equaled the English foot.

title: Beaufort devises the wind force scale (1805)
claim: In 1805, Francis Beaufort — then a Royal Navy officer serving aboard HMS Woolwich — devised the Beaufort wind force scale: thirteen classes (0–12) describing wind strength by its effects on a frigate's sails, from 'just sufficient to give steerage' to 'that which no canvas sails could withstand.'
place: Aboard HMS Woolwich (at sea)
grade_reason: Multiple independent sources agree on the 1805 devising (HMS Woolwich), the January 1806 journal entry ('nothing gives a more indefinite representation of the wind and the weather than the previously used expressions like moderate wind'), the 13-class sail-based design with no wind-speed numbers, the refinement through the 1830s, the first use on the Beagle's 1831–1836 voyage under FitzRoy, the Admiralty's late-1830s mandate (1838), and the 1853 Brussels international adoption. The Defoe-and-others lineage is documented and fenced — Beaufort won the standardization, not the first attempt.
earliest_attestation: Beaufort's private journal, January 1806

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Beaufort scale': 'The scale was devised in 1805 by Francis Beaufort (later Rear Admiral), a hydrographer and a Royal Navy officer, while serving on HMS Woolwich, and refined until he was Hydrographer of the Navy in the 1830s, when it was adopted officially. It was first used during the 1831–1836 "Darwin voyage" of HMS Beagle under Captain Robert FitzRoy... The initial scale of 13 classes (zero to 12) did not reference wind speed numbers, but related qualitative wind conditions to effects on the sails of a frigate... from "just sufficient to give steerage" to "that which no canvas sails could withstand". The scale was made a standard for ship's log entries on Royal Navy vessels in the late 1830s and, in 1853, the Beaufort scale was accepted as generally applicable at the First International Meteorological Conference in Brussels.'

Heidorn, 'The Weather Legacy of Admiral Sir Francis Beaufort': 'In his journal for January of 1806, then-Commander Beaufort wrote, "From now on I shall evaluate the force of the wind in accordance with the following scale, since nothing gives a more indefinite representation of the wind and the weather than the previously used expressions like moderate wind or cloudy weather."' The scale 'he conceived in 1805 and the British Navy adopted in 1838.'

competing_hypotheses: Beaufort as sole inventor ex nihilo (fenced: the scale 'had a long and complex evolution from the previous work of others (including Daniel Defoe the century before)' — Beaufort standardized the scale, he did not conjure it from nothing)
falsifiability: Archival evidence that Beaufort's scale predates or postdates 1805, or that the 13-class sail-based system originated with another author

title: Chancel's chemical matches (1805) — the dipping predecessor
claim: In 1805, Paris, Jean-Louis Chancel produced the first chemical match in commercial form: a splint tipped with potassium chlorate, sulfur, sugar, and rubber, ignited by dipping it into a bottle of concentrated sulfuric acid (the oxy-muriatic or 'dipping' chemical match). Walker was already making variations on Chancel's matches for local hunters before his friction-match accident.
place: Paris, France (Chancel's workshop)
grade_reason: Widely and consistently attested in match historiography as the chemical-match predecessor Walker's work varied; held at CORROBORATED because the 1805 date is carried by secondary sources rather than a dated primary document.
earliest_attestation: Jean-Louis Chancel, Paris, 1805 (secondary literature; Walker Wikipedia article notes Walker's pre-1826 work on Chancel variations)

sources.ref: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Walker_(inventor) — 'He had already been creating variations on Jean Chancel's dipping chemical matches'
Stockton local history: Walker's pre-1826 experiments with chemical lighting mixtures (Cleveland & Teesside Local History Society)

competing_hypotheses: Chancel's matches are sometimes dated loosely to 1805–1812 in secondary sources; 1805 is the standard attribution, carried at medium confidence
Chancel's match was chemical ignition, not friction — it belongs to a different technical lineage than Walker's, and is kept separate on the timeline
falsifiability: A dated publication or patent record showing Chancel's chemical match in a different year, or primary evidence that the 1805 attribution is a retrospective confusion

title: Frederic Tudor's ice trade (VERIFIED)
claim: Frederic Tudor of Boston created the global natural-ice trade, shipping New England ice to the Caribbean from 1806 and to India from 1833.
place: Boston, Massachusetts (origin); Martinique; Calcutta, India
grade_reason: Multiply attested: Frederic Tudor (1783–1864), the 'Ice King,' started the trade in 1806 by shipping New England pond ice to Martinique — widely ridiculed at first, with early failures and imprisonment for debt; he persisted, devising sawdust insulation (a waste product of the New England lumber industry) and building ice houses; by 1820 he was steadily shipping to the Caribbean; in 1833 he began shipping to Calcutta, India — 16,000 miles, a four-month voyage — packing 180 tons, losing 80 to melt, and still profiting; India became his most lucrative market for two decades; the trade widened to England (Wenham Ice famous in London), South America, China, and Australia; ice houses stood in southern US cities, Caribbean islands, and Indian ports (Chennai's Ice House, now Vivekananda House, survives); the ice harvesters Thoreau saw at Walden Pond in 1846–47 worked for Tudor; the trade enabled refrigerator cars and the Chicago/Cincinnati meat-packing industry; Tudor's family continued the business until artificial ice production surpassed natural harvesting. The market-creation angle is documented: Tudor taught tropical customers to want ice, bar to bar, iced drinks and ice cream — selling to people who had never seen it.
earliest_attestation: Tudor's first Martinique shipment, 1806

sources.ref: Wikipedia: 'The trade was started by the New England businessman Frederic Tudor in 1806. Tudor shipped ice to the Caribbean island of Martinique... During the 1830s and 1840s the ice trade expanded further, with shipments reaching England, India, South America, China and Australia. Tudor made a fortune from the India trade, while brand names such as Wenham Ice became famous in London.'
ThoughtCo: Tudor's 1806 ridicule, debtor's prison, sawdust insulation, the late-1830s India expansion, the Walden Pond harvesters, the family business continuing until artificial ice won.
FEE: the 1833 Calcutta run — 16,000 miles, four months, 180 tons packed, 80 melted, still profitable; two decades as his most lucrative market; Weightman's Frozen Water Trade (2002).
StoryTrails: Chennai's Ice House (now Vivekananda House) on Marina Beach; the bar-to-bar market creation; sawdust insulation; the transport network.

falsifiability: Tudor's shipping records proven forged

title: The British Orders in Council (1807–1812)
claim: Britain's 1807 Orders in Council — retaliatory trade restrictions requiring neutral shipping to clear British ports — strangled American commerce with Europe; they were suspended 16 June 1812, two days before the United States declared war on 18 June 1812, and provisionally repealed 23 June 1812, the news reaching Madison only on 12 August 1812.
place: London, England (Parliament — the acts and their suspension)
grade_reason: The Orders and their suspension/repeal dates are documented parliamentary acts, convergently reported by the secondary scholarship (Hickey 1989; Hitsman 1999; Mahon 1991 via the Orders in Council article). Held below VERIFIED — this record rests on secondary scholarship's account of the primary acts, not on the primary texts themselves.
earliest_attestation: The Orders in Council themselves, 1807 (British acts of state); Castlereagh's 16 June 1812 suspension announcement in Parliament

sources.ref: Orders in Council (1807), Wikipedia — Repeal section: suspension 16 June 1812 (Castlereagh, Parliament, two days before the US declaration); provisional repeal 23 June 1812; news reached London of the declaration 29 July; repeal news reached Madison 12 August 1812 (citing Hickey 1989; Hitsman 1999; Mahon 1991)
UPenn course materials, 'The War of 1812' — timeline: Orders suspended June 16, war declared June 18, repeal news to Madison August 12, 'better communications would have avoided war'

peacehistory-usfp.org, 'The War of 1812' — the spring-1812 conciliation sequence: Chesapeake affair settled, British navy ordered to keep clear of the American coast, Orders repealed in June; Madison's June 1 war message claiming no 'conciliatory dispositions'

competing_hypotheses: The repeal would have prevented the war if the news had crossed the Atlantic faster — the 'two ships passing in the night' reading (Madison's own later belief: the declaration 'would have been stayed')
Madison would have proceeded anyway — the War Hawks wanted Canada and the concessions were brushed aside as meaningless gestures (Hickey's reading via peacehistory-usfp.org)
The Orders' suspension was a tactical British concession, not a genuine policy reversal (the post-Perceval Liverpool ministry's political reading)
falsifiability: Would require the parliamentary record to show a different suspension date, or the repeal-date chain to break. The secondary scholarship (Hickey 1989; Hitsman 1999; Mahon 1991) converges on the dates.

title: The tin can (Durand, 1810)
claim: English merchant Peter Durand patented the tinplate food can in 1810 (British Patent 3,372, 25 August 1810), adapting Nicolas Appert's heat-preservation process to iron canisters coated in tin; Donkin, Hall & Gamble bought the rights and opened the world's first commercial cannery in London in 1813.
place: London (patent enrolled; first cannery at Bermondsey, opened 1813)
grade_reason: The patent document itself is the primary source; the 1813 cannery is multiply attested in business history.
earliest_attestation: British Patent 3,372 (1810); Donkin, Hall & Gamble business records, 1813

sources.ref: British Patent 3,372, granted to Peter Durand, 25 August 1810 — tinplate canisters for preserving animal and vegetable food

Researchpod, "Lifting the lid on the tin can opener" — Durand's 1810 patent; rights purchased by Donkin, Hall & Gamble; world's first canning factory in London, 1813; wrought-iron cans, hammer-and-chisel opening, the 1820s label advising 'cut round the top near the outer edge with a chisel and hammer'

Smithsonian Magazine (Kat Eschner, 24 Aug 2017) — Durand's 1810 patent building on Appert; early cans six per hour rising to sixty by the 1840s; wrought-iron cans up to 3/16 in thick; hammer and chisel as the manufacturer's suggested method

competing_hypotheses: Nicolas Appert deserves the invention credit — his glass-jar process (c. 1809, published 1810) is the real breakthrough; Durand only moved the container to tin
Durand was a front for Appert in a cross-Channel patent maneuver (a recurring secondary-source suggestion, not established by primary documents)
falsifiability: A dated tinplate can manufactured before 1810, or proof the 1810 patent document is spurious

title: The Luddite movement, 1811–1817
claim: The Luddite movement (1811–1817) was a protest movement of English textile workers — framework knitters in Nottinghamshire/Leicestershire/Derbyshire, croppers in the West Riding of Yorkshire, handloom weavers — who conducted organized, often nocturnal raids to destroy specific textile machinery they held responsible for cutting wages, de-skilling work, and breaking standard labor practices; the movement began at Arnold, Nottinghamshire, on 11 March 1811, spread to Yorkshire and Lancashire in 1812, and was suppressed by legal and military force culminating in the York Special Commission of January 1813.
place: Arnold, Nottinghamshire, England
grade_reason: The movement's existence, its regional structure, its targets, and the state's reply are established by primary documents: the Luddites' own letters and proclamations (Binfield corpus; HO 42/118), the 1812 Frame-Breaking Act (capital offense), the York Special Commission records (over 60 charged, 17 hanged January 1813, ~30 acquitted), and Byron's 27 February 1812 Lords speech against the bill.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary Luddite writings from 1811 onward, collected in Kevin Binfield's 'Writings of the Luddites' (2004); the TNA HO 42/118 'Ned Lud's Proclamation' of 23 December 1811; the York Special Commission trial records, January 1813

sources.ref: Kevin Binfield (ed.), 'Writings of the Luddites' (Johns Hopkins UP, 2004) — the corpus of Luddite letters, songs, and proclamations
The National Archives — 'The proclamation of Ned Ludd' (HO 42/118, 23 December 1811)
HISTORY — 'The Original Luddites Raged Against the Machine of the Industrial Revolution' (on the York Special Commission: over 60 charged, 17 hanged January 1813)
Wikipedia — Luddite (Destruction of Stocking Frames, etc. Act 1812; Byron's 27 February 1812 maiden speech in the Lords)
University of Huddersfield news archive — 'The Luddites go online' (West Riding croppers, Rawfolds Mill, York Gaol January 1813)
E. P. Thompson, 'The Making of the English Working Class' (1963) — the moral-economy reading of Luddism
Eric Hobsbawm, 'The Machine Breakers' (1952); 'Labouring Men' — 'collective bargaining by riot'
Malcolm I. Thomis, 'The Luddites: Machine-Breaking in Regency England' (1970) — machine-breaking as worker tactic, not anti-machinery hostility

competing_hypotheses: Hobsbawm's 'collective bargaining by riot' reading: machine-wrecking as a traditional, instrumental trade-union tactic that sometimes won wage concessions
Thompson's reading: the workers' sense of lost rights, diminished status, and injustice — the loss of a moral economy — as the primary driver, not machines per se
The official-reading of 1812-13: an insurrectionary crime wave requiring repression (the Frame-Breaking Act, 12,000 troops, the York show trials)
falsifiability: A demonstration that the 1811–1813 disturbances were unrelated coordinated events with no shared name, aims, or correspondence

title: 'The Luddites were anti-technology'
claim: The Luddites were opposed to technology itself — blind enemies of progress who smashed machines because they feared or hated machinery, the modern dictionary-shorthand meaning of 'luddite'.
place: Arnold, Nottinghamshire, England
grade_reason: The anti-technology reading dies on the Luddites' own documents: they targeted specific machines wielded by specific employers to cut wages and evade standard labor practices (Thomis 1970), were themselves skilled machine operators, demanded negotiation in their letters, and used machine-breaking — a century-old protest tactic predating the movement — selectively, not indiscriminately.
earliest_attestation: The re-reading is modern (the word's generalized pejorative use); the original meaning is recoverable from the movement's own 1811–1813 writings

sources.ref: Kevin Binfield (ed.), 'Writings of the Luddites' (Johns Hopkins UP, 2004) — Luddite letters demand fair prices and negotiation alongside threats
The National Archives — 'The proclamation of Ned Ludd' (HO 42/118, 23 December 1811) — the threat is aimed at informers and enemies of 'the Cause', not at machinery in the abstract
Malcolm I. Thomis, 'The Luddites' (1970): machine attacks 'did not imply any necessary hostility to machinery as such'
Eric Hobsbawm, 'Labouring Men: Studies in the History of Labour' — machine-breaking as 'collective bargaining by riot'

Wikipedia — Luddites ('Luddites were not opposed to the use of machines per se (many were skilled operators in the textile industry); they attacked manufacturers who were trying to circumvent standard labour practices')

HISTORY — 'Who Were the Luddites?' (HISTORY: 'Luddite is now a blanket term used to describe people who dislike new technology, but its origins date back to an early 19th-century labor movement that railed against the ways mechanized manufacturers and their unskilled laborers undermined the skilled craftsmen of the day')

competing_hypotheses: Hobsbawm's counter-reading: 'collective bargaining by riot' — wrecking as an instrumental trade-union tactic, 'in none of these cases was there any question of hostility to machines as such'
Thomis's counter-reading (1970): 'These attacks on machines did not imply any necessary hostility to machinery as such; machinery was just a conveniently exposed target'
The romantic counter-myth: Pynchon (1984) that a dark, mythic, 'against progress, against time itself' element coexisted with the pragmatism — a character reading, not a factual one
falsifiability: A Luddite letter or proclamation opposing a machine on the grounds that machinery itself is evil or progress must stop, rather than on wages, deskilling, or broken labor standards

title: 'The French burned Moscow'
claim: The French army set the 1812 Moscow fire as policy — that is, Napoleon or his commanders ordered the burning of the city.
place: Moscow
grade_reason: Killed twice: (1) the Russian-initiation record — Rostopchin's letter to Bagration asking him to 'turn the city to ashes', the removed fire equipment, the released convicts, his 1823 Paris denial pamphlet followed by his admission; (2) French interest — Napoleon wanted Moscow intact as winter quarters and as a bargaining chip, and executed alleged arsonists on the spot.
earliest_attestation: Napoleon's accusations against Rostopchin, September-October 1812 (including the European brochure campaign describing the governor-general's 'deceit and cruelty'); French officers' reports of Russian agents with incendiaries

sources.ref: Mikaberidze, Alexander. The Burning of Moscow: Napoleon's Trial by Fire 1812 (Pen & Sword, 2014) — majority-historian consensus: Russian initiation
Rostopchin, Fyodor — Wikipedia biography: 1823 Paris pamphlet denying the arson, 'subsequently admitted to his role in ordering the city's destruction'
Rostopchin's letter to Bagration (1812): asking him to 'turn the city to ashes so that the enemy army does not get bread shops and food warehouses'

competing_hypotheses: French soldiers' looting and campfires spread the fires accidentally (French spread without French orders — the fenced middle ground)
The fires were entirely spontaneous in an abandoned wooden city (the maximal French-exculpatory position)
The fire was a single coordinated Russian operation ordered in detail by Rostopchin (the maximal Russian-patriotic position — his actual order-chain is documented but its completeness is debated)
falsifiability: Already falsified: a French order to burn Moscow would have to surface in the Grande Armée's own orders, bulletins, or the commanders' memoirs — the one army with a motive to keep the city intact. Rostopchin's documented order-chain stands as the positive case.

title: 'General Winter defeated Napoleon'
claim: The Grande Armée was destroyed in 1812 primarily by the Russian winter — that is, the extreme cold, rather than hunger, disease, desertion, and the Russian army, was the main cause of the army's destruction.
place: Western Russia (Niemen to Moscow to Berezina)
grade_reason: Killed four ways: (1) the timeline — the army lost most of its strength June-October to hunger, disease, desertion, and battles, before any serious cold (Zamoyski 2004); (2) the propaganda origin — the 29th Bulletin blamed the cold to protect the Emperor's reputation, and Caulaincourt's memoirs carried it; (3) the weather — October 1812 was mild, first snows fell after the army left Moscow on 19 October, and -30°C arrived only in late November at the Berezina; (4) the 2025 Vilnius teeth study found paratyphoid and relapsing fever, not cold, in the dead of the retreat.
earliest_attestation: Napoleon's 29th Bulletin, 3 December 1812 — attributes the disaster to the cold; Caulaincourt's memoirs (published 1935) carry the winter narrative

sources.ref: Zamoyski, Adam. Moscow 1812: Napoleon's Fatal March (HarperCollins, 2004)
Napoleon's 29th Bulletin, 3 December 1812 — the original cold-weather alibi

Barbieri et al., 'Paratyphoid fever and relapsing fever in 1812 Napoleon's devastated army', Current Biology (2025), 10.1016/j.cub.2025.09.047 — aDNA from 13 French soldiers' teeth at Vilnius: Salmonella enterica enterica (paratyphoid) + Borrelia recurrentis (relapsing fever); no typhus or trench fever
Minard, Charles Joseph. 'Carte figurative des pertes successives en hommes de l'Armée Française dans la campagne de Russie 1812-1813' (1869) — the famous casualty visualization

competing_hypotheses: The winter was the decisive factor and the other causes are revisionist exaggeration (the traditional 19th-century French position after the 29th Bulletin)
The cold was the primary killer of an already-weakened army — primary vs contributing is a judgment call on a multi-causal collapse
Kutuzov's generalship was the primary cause (the Russian nationalist position — Zamoyski 2004 disputes this too, finding Kutuzov indecisive)
falsifiability: Would require evidence that the army was substantially intact through October and that cold-caused deaths (not hunger, disease, desertion, battle) dominated the losses. The campaign returns, Zamoyski's narrative, and the Vilnius teeth show the opposite.

title: The destruction of the Grande Armée, 1812
claim: The 1812 Russian campaign destroyed the Grande Armée as a fighting force: of the several hundred thousand men who crossed the Niemen in June 1812, only tens of thousands recrossed in fighting condition by December — the largest army Europe had yet seen, annihilated.
place: Western Russia (Niemen to Moscow to Berezina)
grade_reason: The annihilation itself is attested across French, Russian, and neutral sources and visualized in Minard's famous 1869 chart (422,000 crossed, ~100,000 reached Moscow, ~10,000 recrossed in fighting condition); held below VERIFIED because the exact force size (~500,000-650,000) and death toll (~380,000) vary between historians.
earliest_attestation: French army returns and muster rolls, 1812-13; Minard's 1869 chart from the official returns

sources.ref: Minard, Charles Joseph. 'Carte figurative des pertes successives en hommes de l'Armée Française dans la campagne de Russie 1812-1813' (1869)
Zamoyski, Adam. Moscow 1812: Napoleon's Fatal March (HarperCollins, 2004)

competing_hypotheses: Higher loss estimates: some modern historians put total deaths above 400,000 against an invasion force above 600,000 (the exact force size and death toll vary by historian)
The 'army' that returned included large numbers of stragglers and non-combatants — 'fighting condition' is the metric that matters, and Minard's 10,000 figure covers only the tracked force
falsifiability: A contemporary complete muster showing the army largely intact in December 1812 would falsify the scale; no such record exists.

title: The Burning of Moscow, September 1812
claim: Moscow burned 14-18 September 1812 (Old Style 2-6 September), beginning the day French troops entered the evacuated city; roughly three-quarters of the mostly wooden city was destroyed over five days.
place: Moscow
grade_reason: Multiply and independently attested as an event: French military accounts, Russian civilian and official accounts, and the physical destruction of the city itself.
earliest_attestation: French officers' letters and journals from Moscow, September 1812; Rostopchin's own correspondence; Russian civilian accounts

sources.ref: Zamoyski, Adam. Moscow 1812: Napoleon's Fatal March (HarperCollins, 2004)
Mikaberidze, Alexander. The Burning of Moscow: Napoleon's Trial by Fire 1812 (Pen & Sword, 2014)
Rostopchin, Fyodor — 'La vérité sur l'incendie de Moscou', Paris pamphlet, 1823, and subsequent admission

competing_hypotheses: The fire was an accident of an abandoned wooden city occupied by careless soldiers (the French exculpatory position in later years)
The fire was entirely French-ordered scorched denial (the Soviet-era Russian popular position)
Spontaneous ignition from unattended hearths, stoves, and bakeries with no human agency
falsifiability: Already falsified alternative 'no fire': the burned city, French orders responding to it, and Rostopchin's own papers all attest the event.

title: The War of 1812
claim: The United States declared war on Great Britain on 18 June 1812; the war ended with the Treaty of Ghent (signed 24 December 1814, ratified 16 February 1815), with the Battle of New Orleans fought 8 January 1815 — after the treaty was signed.
place: United States / British North America / the Atlantic (war theater); Ghent, Belgium (treaty)
grade_reason: Multiple independent primary/contemporary sources converge: the 18 June 1812 declaration, the signed Ghent treaty text (24 December 1814), the 16 February 1815 Senate ratification, and the New Orleans battle returns (8 January 1815).
earliest_attestation: The 18 June 1812 declaration of war (Congressional vote); the Treaty of Ghent's signed text, 24 December 1814

sources.ref: US Naval History & Heritage Command, 'Stalemate: Treaty of Ghent Ends War of 1812 in a Draw' — treaty timeline, New Orleans 8 January 1815, ratification 16 February 1815, proclaimed 18 February 1815
americanhistorycentral.com, 'Treaty of Ghent' — negotiations, the treaty's terms (no impressment, no maritime rights addressed), New Orleans after the signature

competing_hypotheses: The war as a 'second war of independence' (American nationalist framing — the national honor reading)
The war as an expansionist failure (the Canada land-grab reading — the invasions of 1812–1814 all failed)
The war as unnecessary (the 'our first unnecessary war' reading — British conciliation was underway when the declaration was issued)
falsifiability: Would require the declaration, treaty, and ratification records to be other than dated — multiple independent primary sources converge on the same dates.

title: 'The War of 1812 was fought to stop impressment'
claim: The War of 1812 was fought primarily to stop the British practice of impressment — that is, impressment was the war's principal cause.
place: Washington, D.C. (war message, declaration) / Ghent (treaty)
grade_reason: Killed three ways: (1) Madison's 1 June 1812 war message lists British trade restrictions, ship seizures, and the western frontier alongside impressment — never impressment alone; (2) the Orders in Council were suspended 16 June 1812, two days before the 18 June declaration — the war's principal economic cause had been removed before the first shot; (3) the Treaty of Ghent (24 December 1814) never mentions impressment — the alleged cause does not appear in the peace that ended the war.
earliest_attestation: The documentary record the shorthand simplifies: Madison's war message to Congress, 1 June 1812 (trade restrictions, impressment, seizures, frontier); the schoolbook single-cause version is 19th–20th century

sources.ref: Madison, James. Message to Congress, 1 June 1812 — the war message names British trade restrictions, impressment, seizures, and the western frontier

Orders in Council (1807), Wikipedia — Repeal section: suspended 16 June 1812 (Castlereagh announcement in Parliament, two days before the US declaration), provisionally repealed 23 June 1812; news reached Madison 12 August 1812 (citing Hickey 1989, The War of 1812; Hitsman 1999; Mahon 1991)

peacehistory-usfp.org, 'The War of 1812' — April–June 1812 British conciliation record: Madison himself later believed the declaration 'would have been stayed' had he known of the British measures; Hickey on the Madison administration brushing aside accommodations

Treaty of Ghent — eleven articles; no mention of impressment, maritime rights, or trade (americanhistorycentral; US Naval History & Heritage Command, 'Stalemate: Treaty of Ghent Ends War of 1812 in a Draw'; alexluyckx blog citing the Avalon Project's treaty text)

competing_hypotheses: Impressment was the dominant popular grievance even if not the sole war aim — the schoolbook shorthand tracks the flag, not the cabinet's reasoning

Madison's war message lists impressment alongside trade restrictions, ship seizures, and the western frontier — the declaration itself was multi-causal, and the single-cause claim is a later simplification
The War Hawks' real prize was Canada and the end of British backing for Indian resistance — impressment was the moral flag flown over an expansionist war
falsifiability: Would require evidence that impressment was the sole listed cause in Madison's 1 June 1812 message, that the Orders in Council were still in force on 18 June 1812, or that the Treaty of Ghent addressed impressment. The records show the opposite on all three.

title: 'The Star-Spangled Banner has always been the national anthem'
claim: The Star-Spangled Banner has always been the national anthem of the United States — since the founding era, effectively from 1776 onward.
place: Washington, D.C. (Congress, 3 March 1931)
grade_reason: Killed three ways: (1) the song was written in September 1814 — 38 years after 1776, for a specific War of 1812 battle, not the founding; (2) Congress made it the official national anthem only on 3 March 1931 (46 Stat. 1508, codified at 36 U.S.C. § 301, signed by President Herbert Hoover) — 117 years after the writing, 155 years after the Declaration; (3) before 1931, 'Hail, Columbia' and 'My Country, 'Tis of Thee' served as the de facto anthems at official functions.
earliest_attestation: The 'always the anthem' reading is a schoolbook/textbook assumption; the documented adoption trail runs 1889 (Navy) → 1916 (Wilson, armed forces) → 1931 (Congress, the nation)

sources.ref: LibreTexts (citing the documentary record) — recognized for official use by the Navy 1889 and by President Wilson 1916; made national anthem by congressional resolution 3 March 1931 (46 Stat. 1508, codified at 36 U.S.C. § 301), signed by Hoover; 'Hail, Columbia' served at official functions for most of the 19th century; 'My Country, 'Tis of Thee' also served as a de facto anthem
HISTORY.com — adopted as the national anthem on March 3, 1931; Wilson 1916 official-events designation as the stepping stone
The Morgan Library & Museum, 2014 — 'Not until 1931 was The Star-Spangled Banner declared the nation's official anthem by an act of Congress'

competing_hypotheses: The belief's carrier is the schoolbook assumption that a nation's anthem is as old as the nation — the 1931 adoption date is the corrective, not a rival theory
'Hail, Columbia' (1798) and 'My Country, 'Tis of Thee' (1831) served as de facto anthems at official functions for most of the 19th century — the 'always' reading ignores the documented predecessors
falsifiability: Would require a congressional or executive act making the Banner the national anthem before 1931, or evidence that 'Hail, Columbia' never served officially; the 46 Stat. 1508 record stands against it.

title: Key writes 'Defence of Fort M'Henry' (The Star-Spangled Banner), 13–16 September 1814
claim: On the morning of 14 September 1814, after watching the British bombardment of Fort McHenry from detention aboard a British vessel, Francis Scott Key wrote the poem 'Defence of Fort M'Henry' — the words that became 'The Star-Spangled Banner' — setting them to the tune 'To Anacreon in Heaven' (commonly attributed to John Stafford Smith, c. 1770).
place: Fort McHenry, Baltimore, Maryland (written aboard a detained cartel vessel in the Patapsco during the bombardment)
grade_reason: Multiply attested primary evidence: Key's surviving manuscript, the next-day broadside with the tune notation, same-week newspaper printings, the 1814 Carrs sheet-music first edition, and the documented British bombardment record (Armistead's report, ship logs).
earliest_attestation: Key's own draft (untitled, unsigned, written on the back of a letter) — surviving manuscript held by the Maryland Center for History and Culture; the next-day broadside 'Defence of Fort M'Henry' (notation 'Tune – Anacreon in Heaven'); Baltimore newspapers within days; the first printed edition (Baltimore: Carrs Music Store, [1814]) held by the Morgan Library & Museum, James Fuld Music Collection

sources.ref: Veteran's Today (citing the record) — Key watched the 25-hour bombardment 13–14 Sept 1814; finished manuscript untitled/unsigned at the Indian Queen Hotel 16 Sept; printed as broadside 'Defence of Fort M'Henry' the next day with 'Tune – Anacreon in Heaven'; Key had previously used the tune for his 1805 'When the Warrior Returns'

The Morgan Library & Museum, 2014 press release — rare first edition: 'The Star Spangled Banner [Music by John Stafford; words by Francis Scott Key]. Baltimore: Carrs Music Store, [1814]'; tune composed for the Anacreontic Society, Crown and Anchor Tavern, Strand; not declared official anthem until 1931

ChoralWiki / CPDL — anthem recognized for official use by the Navy 1889, by President Wilson 1916; made national anthem by congressional resolution 3 March 1931 (46 Stat. 1508, codified at 36 U.S.C. § 301), signed by Hoover

HISTORY.com — Key detained aboard the ship negotiating Dr. William Beanes's release; bombardment watched from ~8 miles; poem penned at dawn; set to Stafford Smith's 'To Anacreon in Heaven'; Wilson 1916 designation; adopted 3 March 1931

competing_hypotheses: The poem was drafted substantially aboard the cartel ship during the bombardment night vs. completed at the Indian Queen Hotel, Baltimore, on 16 September (both attested; the draft-on-the-back-of-a-letter origin is near-universal in the record)
The tune's composer — John Stafford Smith is the common attribution; the Anacreontic Society's authorship tradition is documented but the exact pen is not provable to a single name
falsifiability: A dated contemporary document placing Key elsewhere during 13–16 September 1814, or a pre-September 1814 printing of the poem, would overturn the record; none exists.

title: Cambronne's 'La Garde meurt, elle ne se rend pas!'
claim: When the British called on the last square of the Imperial Old Guard to surrender at Waterloo, General Pierre Cambronne answered with the noble sentence 'La Garde meurt, elle ne se rend pas!' ('The Guard dies, it does not surrender!').
place: Waterloo battlefield, Walloon Brabant, Belgium
grade_reason: Three independent kills: (1) the directional silence of the battlefield — no British or French witness of 18 June 1815 records the sentence, and the print trail starts in Paris with a journalist who was not there; (2) Cambronne's own lifelong denials; (3) the British counter-tradition that Halkett's men captured him before he could reply at all.
earliest_attestation: No battlefield witness ever attested it; the print trail begins with journalist Michel-Nicolas Balisson de Rougemont's version in the Journal général de France (the Wikipedia 'Arnouph Deshayes de Cambronne' article explicitly traces the phrase's popularization to Rougemont, later quoted by Victor Hugo in Les Misérables, 1862)

sources.ref: Michel-Nicolas Balisson de Rougemont, Journal général de France (the sentence's Paris print debut — not a battlefield account)
Victor Hugo, Les Misérables (1862) — popularized the legend 47 years after the event
Cambronne's own denials (he stated he could not have said such a thing and remained alive)
Letters to The Times, June 1932 — Colonel Hugh Halkett's claim that he captured Cambronne before any reply was made
Peter Hofschroer — Cambronne surrendered to the Osnabrück Landwehr Battalion (possibly first to a man named Führing), wounded and thrown from his horse
Andrew Roberts, Waterloo: June 18, 1815 — 'A myth was soon created that he had in fact replied: La Garde meurt, elle ne se rend pas'

competing_hypotheses: The sentence was said by another general of the Guard, Claude-Étienne Michel, during the last stand (letters to The Times, June 1932) — kept as an ungraded alternative, not a replacement certainty
The 'Merde!' one-word version (le mot de Cambronne) — graded separately at CLAIMED in evt-cambronne-merde-word-001
falsifiability: A contemporary battlefield witness's letter, diary, or dispatch quoting the sentence would revive it; no such source is known after 211 years of searching.

title: Cambronne's one-word reply — 'le mot de Cambronne'
claim: When the British insisted on the surrender of the last Old Guard square at Waterloo, General Cambronne answered with a single scatological word: 'Merde!'
place: Waterloo battlefield, Walloon Brabant, Belgium
grade_reason: Attested only through a literary tradition 47 years after the fact, and explicitly denied by the only man who could have said it — so it cannot rise above CLAIMED, and it cannot be killed by anything short of a better-attested alternative.
earliest_attestation: The version is reported by secondary sources as a battlefield tradition; its immortalization is Victor Hugo's in Les Misérables (1862), 47 years after the event

sources.ref: Victor Hugo, Les Misérables (1862) — 'Brave Frenchmen, will you not surrender?' Cambronne answered, 'Merde!'
Edmond Rostand, L'Aiglon (1900) — repeats the word
Mark Adkin's assessment (via napoleonistyka): Cambronne was 'very much the rough spoken, hard as nails ex-ranker — a soldier's soldier. For this reason perhaps Merde! is the more likely'
Cambronne's own denials (he denied both the noble sentence and the one-word response)
The French euphemism industry: 'le mot de Cambronne', the verb 'cambronniser'

competing_hypotheses: Cambronne said nothing at all — Halkett's brigade captured him before any exchange (Times letters, June 1932; Hofschroer's Osnabrücker account has him wounded and dazed)
The noise and confusion of battle swallowed whatever was said — the Waterloo Association's honest position that perhaps both word and phrase were used, but not necessarily both by Cambronne
falsifiability: A contemporary battlefield dispatch or a British officer's letter of June 1815 reporting the word would promote it; a battlefield witness explicitly denying any reply was given would demote it toward SPECULATION.

title: The Tambora-year motive for the Laufmaschine
claim: Karl Drais invented the Laufmaschine in response to the horse-feed crisis of the Year Without a Summer (1816), when the April 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora caused crop failures that starved horses across Europe.
place: Mannheim / the Baden crisis of 1816
grade_reason: The crisis is verified history (Tambora April 1815; 1816 crop failures and horse slaughter attested in the ADFC biography); but the inventor's motive is unattested in any Drais document, and his 1813/14 four-wheeled human-powered vehicles predate Tambora — so the link stays CLAIMED, not CORROBORATED.
earliest_attestation: The causal narrative is asserted in the modern Drais biographical tradition (notably the ADFC/Lessing biography); no statement of motive by Drais himself is on record.

sources.ref: ADFC Mannheim biography of Karl Drais: sequence of poor harvests from 1812, Tambora April 1815, summer-1816 snow, crops failed, 'horses were slaughtered for lack of food even for the people'; the velocipede as 'a high potential alternative to horse-based traffic'
Drais's own earlier work: two four-wheeled human-powered vehicles (1813/1814), presented in Vienna — predating Tambora, the honest counterpoint to a pure crisis-motive reading

competing_hypotheses: Drais's motive was engineering curiosity in the horseless-carriage line of his own earlier work, not the crisis
The crisis created the market for the machine, not the idea — the motive is biographers' inference, stated as fact
falsifiability: A Drais letter, memorandum, or contemporary interview stating his motive — for or against the crisis explanation.

title: The Battle of Waterloo (18 June 1815)
claim: On 18 June 1815, near Waterloo in present-day Belgium, Napoleon Bonaparte's Armée du Nord was defeated by the Anglo-Allied army under the Duke of Wellington and the Prussian army under Gebhard von Blücher; it was Napoleon's last battle, and he abdicated four days later.
place: Waterloo battlefield, Walloon Brabant, Belgium
grade_reason: The event is multiply and independently attested by hostile traditions (British dispatch, Prussian reports, French accounts) written within days, and corroborated by the battlefield archaeology.
earliest_attestation: Wellington's dispatch to Lord Bathurst, dated 19 June 1815, written the morning after the battle

sources.ref: Wellington's Waterloo dispatch, 19 June 1815 (The National Archives)
Gneisenau's reports and Prussian staff accounts, June 1815
Napoleon's own bulletins and later St Helena accounts
Andrew Roberts, Waterloo: June 18, 1815 — The Battle for Modern Europe (2015)
The battlefield archaeology (Mont-Saint-Jean, Hougoumont, Plancenoit)

competing_hypotheses: Casualty and strength figures vary across traditions (French ~72,000 vs Allied ~68,000 at the opening; combined casualties ~45,000–50,000) — the numbers are honestly ranged, not the event
falsifiability: No plausible falsifier survives; the grade would collapse only if the converging contemporary dispatch record were shown to be a fabrication.

title: The Laufmaschine's first ride (12 June 1817)
claim: Karl Drais rode the first documented two-wheeled steerable vehicle — the Laufmaschine — from Mannheim to the Schwetzinger Relaishaus (Rheinau) and back on 12 June 1817, about 7 km each way, the round trip in a little more than an hour, establishing the two-wheeler principle basic to the bicycle and the motorcycle.
place: Mannheim, Grand Duchy of Baden
grade_reason: The ride is multiply attested in contemporary and near-contemporary sources (Drais's reports, the Baden decree, the French patent, Johnson's licensed-style copies); held below VERIFIED on small variance in reported distance and time across retellings.
earliest_attestation: Drais's own reports and contemporary notices of the 1817 demonstration; the 1818 Baden protection decree and January 1818 French patent; Denis Johnson's improved London model, late 1818.

sources.ref: ADFC (Allgemeiner Deutscher Fahrrad-Club), Kreisverband Mannheim: 'Karl Drais — the new biography' (2006/2010/2014) — 12 June 1817 first ride, Mannheim to Schwetzinger Relaishaus, 'a little more than an hour' round trip; Baden 1818 decree; Johnson 1818
Wikipedia, 'Karl Drais' — Laufmaschine, first ride 12 June 1817, ~7 km, French patent January 1818, the 1819 craze and municipal bans

competing_hypotheses: The distance/time figures are later rounding of a shorter demonstration ride
The 'big bang for horseless transport' framing is the bicycle industry's retrospective myth-making
falsifiability: A dated two-wheeled steerable vehicle predating June 1817 (the 'Comte de Sivrac' 1792 célérifère claim fails this test — the two-wheeled célérifère never existed).

title: Blundell's human-to-human transfusions (1818)
claim: James Blundell (British obstetrician) performed the first documented successful human-to-human blood transfusions: 1818, for postpartum hemorrhage — the patient's husband as donor, about four ounces, delivered by syringe. Between 1825 and 1830 he performed ten transfusions, five of which he reported as beneficial, publishing the results and devising transfusion instruments.
place: London (Guy's Hospital)
grade_reason: Contemporary published case reports with instruments, indications, and outcomes over a decade; the 5-of-10 figure is his own accounting, honestly partial.
earliest_attestation: Blundell's own published reports (1818 onward); the 1825–1830 case series

sources.ref: James Blundell, published case reports 1818–1830 (Medico-Chirurgical Transactions; the Lancet) — the 1818 postpartum-hemorrhage transfusion, the ten-case series

Transfusion-medicine histories — '1818: James Blundell performs the first successful transfusion of human blood to a patient for the treatment of postpartum hemorrhage... Between 1825 and 1830, he performs 10 transfusions, five of which prove beneficial'
Irish Blood Transfusion Service history — '1818: The first human to human blood transfusion took place in London'

competing_hypotheses: Philip Syng Physick's unpublished 1795 Philadelphia transfusion (unpublished — the documentary rule keeps it out of the grade)
falsifiability: Proof Blundell's published case series is fabricated, or a dated earlier published human-to-human transfusion

title: Fresnel's lighthouse lens: invented 1819-1822, first lit at Cordouan 25 July 1823
claim: Augustin-Jean Fresnel invented the stepped annular lighthouse lens for the French Commission des Phares (1819-1822): his lentilles a echelons replaced the parabolic reflectors then in use; the revolving eight-panel first-order apparatus passed its official public test atop the unfinished Arc de Triomphe on 20 August 1822 (witnessed by Louis XVIII and his entourage from 32 km away); the world's first lighthouse Fresnel lens was lit at the Cordouan lighthouse on 25 July 1823. The invention carried a documented 74-year prehistory: Buffon had proposed a stepped lens in 1748 (for burning glasses, single piece), Condorcet had suggested assembling annular sections separately on a frame in 1790, Rogers had focused a lighthouse beam with a conventional lens at Portland Bill in 1789, and Brewster had advocated a Condorcet-style lens for British lighthouses by 1820.
place: Cordouan lighthouse, Gironde estuary, France
grade_reason: Multiple independent secondary sources (the Fresnel biography record, the translated Arago obituary, Smithsonian, lighthouse-history surveys) converge on the 1819-1823 sequence and the Cordouan first lighting; the Buffon/Condorcet/Rogers/Brewster prehistory is independently documented. Held below VERIFIED because the loop has not inspected the primary commission records or Fresnel's 1822 memoir themselves.
earliest_attestation: Fresnel's 1822 memoir on the lighthouse lens system (memoire sur un nouveau systeme d'eclairage des phares); the Commission des Phares records, 1819-1822

sources.ref: Augustin-Jean Fresnel biography — 21 June 1819 secondment to the Commission des Phares; end-August 1819 lentilles a echelons recommendation; 13 April 1821 public demonstration; 20 August 1822 Arc de Triomphe test witnessed by Louis XVIII from 32 km; 25 July 1823 first lighting at Cordouan

Arago obituary of Fresnel (translated, arXiv) — Buffon imagined dividing a convex lens surface into annular zones displaced parallel to the axis; Fresnel 'found — which no one before him had found — the means of making it feasible, in having the rings of the same stepped lens executed separately,' correcting spherical aberration by ring curvature

Fresnel lens history — Buffon 1748 first to replace a convex lens with concentric annular prisms (single piece); Condorcet 1790 suggested separate sections assembled on a frame (intended for burning glasses, not lighthouses); Rogers 1788 first lighthouse lens (Portland Bill 1789); Brewster 1811/1820 advocacy
Smithsonian (via taggedwiki) — 'the first Fresnel lens was used in 1823 in the Cordouan lighthouse at the mouth of the Gironde estuary; its light could be seen from more than 20 miles (32 km) out'

The Pursuit of History — first Fresnel lens operational at Tour de Cordouan 25 July 1823; Fresnel's fixed lens 1824; Navesink Twin Lights 1841 first in the United States; Cordouan's original lens replaced 1854; ~10,000 Fresnel lenses in service within a century

competing_hypotheses: The prehistory was for burning glasses, not lighthouses, and no pre-Fresnel proposal was ever built or made to work in a lighthouse: the honest reading is independent reinvention plus the feasibility breakthrough (separate prisms, corrected spherical aberration), not derivation
The Arc de Triomphe test is dated 20 August 1822 in the main sources; one secondary telling (Risky Regencies) gives April 1822 — a source disagreement, not a rival claim
Rogers's 1788/1789 Trinity House lens is the first lighthouse lens of any kind — fenced: it is a lens, not a Fresnel (stepped) lens, and its heavy glass absorbed much of the light
falsifiability: Discovery of a working stepped lighthouse lens predating 1822, or primary commission records showing the Cordouan installation was not the first

title: Starke's Travels on the Continent (1820) — the first modern travel guide
claim: Mariana Starke's Travels on the Continent, written for the use and particular information of travellers, published by John Murray in 1820, was the first modern travel guide — practical itineraries, journey times, inn and restaurant assessments (the 'daggers of admiration' ratings), maps and archaeological plans, updated across editions.
place: London (John Murray, publisher)
grade_reason: The 1820 first edition is a documented artifact (Cambridge UP reprint from the original text); a 2024 scholarly chapter explicitly describes it as 'may accurately be described as the first modern travel guide,' citing its practical apparatus — ratings, itineraries, maps, updated editions.
earliest_attestation: The 1820 first edition itself (John Murray, London)

sources.ref: Springer Nature chapter, 'Inventing the Travel Guide: Mariana Starke's Advice for the Independent Traveller' (2024): Starke's Travels on the Continent (1820) 'may accurately be described as the first modern travel guide,' written for the new class of affluent British middle-class travellers; notes John Murray II 'unscrupulously plagiarised her work in Murray's Handbooks,' and that Karl Baedeker's guides copied

Cambridge University Press reprint listing (Cambridge Library Collection): first published 1820; updated information from late-1810s research; covers most of mainland Europe with itineraries, journey times, sightseeing and inn recommendations; health-travel advice

Mimesis journal article on Starke and the Grand Tour: the 1820 Murray collaboration — Travels on the Continent, 300 pages in a pocketable 19cm format, with an Advertisement reassuring readers about post-1814 road safety

competing_hypotheses: 'First guidebook ever' (over-reading: Edmund Boyce's The Belgian traveller (1819) and earlier works predate 1820 — the record's claim is specifically 'first modern travel guide,' i.e., the modern apparatus, not the first travel book)
Murray's Handbooks (1836) were the first true guidebooks (undermined by the Springer chapter's finding that Murray plagiarised Starke's work in the Handbooks) — and Baedeker's guides copied both
falsifiability: An earlier-published guidebook (pre-1820) with the same modern apparatus — star/dagger-style ratings, practical itineraries, maps, and updated editions

title: Napoleon's actual height
claim: Napoleon Bonaparte's height was approximately 169 cm (about 5 feet 6 to 5 feet 7 inches in English measure), average to slightly above average for French men of his era.
place: Longwood, Saint Helena
grade_reason: A single primary post-mortem measurement in French units converts to ~168-169 cm; contemporary descriptions and period clothing evidence are consistent — held at CORROBORATED (single autopsy, variable conversions 168-170 cm) rather than VERIFIED.
earliest_attestation: Autopsy report, 6 May 1821: 5 pieds 2 pouces (French units). Contemporary descriptions during his life generally describe him as average in stature.

sources.ref: Autopsy report, Saint Helena, 6 May 1821 (Antommarchi et al.) — 5 pieds 2 pouces
National Geographic, 'Was Napoleon even short? Inside the history of discrimination against short men' (unit conversion + autopsy context + Gillray analysis)
YouGov Eurotrack, 'How does Europe remember Napoleon?' (Sept 2023, fieldwork 7-22 Sept 2023) — notes 5'6.5" (168 cm) as average height for the time
Uniform and clothing evidence (standard sizing of the period, not specially tailored for an unusually short man)

competing_hypotheses: The 1840 exhumation measurements give slightly different figures; conversions of the autopsy figure range 168-170 cm depending on the exact value used for the pied du roi
Some secondary sources report 5'7" English from valet-derived figures — within the same average band, not a disagreement of substance
falsifiability: A contemporary French-language record measuring him below ~165 cm in a verified pied-du-roi unit, or discovery that the 1821 autopsy record is fabricated

title: DEBUNKED: 'no one proposed the stepped lens before Fresnel'
claim: The stepped/annular lighthouse lens — the Fresnel lens — was entirely Augustin-Jean Fresnel's own unanticipated idea: no one had proposed a stepped lens before him. (The ex nihilo lone-genius version of the invention.)
place: Paris, France (the telling's home)
grade_reason: Two independent kills, both published and dated: Buffon proposed the stepped lens in 1748 (Memoires de l'Academie royale des sciences — concentric annular prisms as steps in a single piece of glass), and Condorcet proposed assembling the annular sections separately on a frame in 1790. Both were intended for burning glasses, not lighthouses, which fences the kill: it destroys the 'unanticipated idea' version only, never Fresnel's independent invention or his genuine breakthrough — making the idea feasible and building the first working lighthouse optic (Cordouan, 25 July 1823).
earliest_attestation: The schoolbook and museum-plaque shorthand 'Fresnel invented the Fresnel lens' read as a lone-genius claim (no single primary originator; the fiction lives in the telling, not in a document)

sources.ref: Fresnel lens history — 'In 1748, Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon was the first to replace a convex lens with a series of concentric annular prisms, ground as steps in a single piece of glass, to reduce weight and absorption'

Fresnel lens history — 'In 1790, the Marquis de Condorcet suggested that it would be easier to make the annular sections separately and assemble them on a frame' (intended, like Buffon's, for burning glasses, not lighthouses)

Arago obituary of Fresnel (translated, arXiv) — 'Buffon had imagined dividing the convex surface of a lens into several annular zones... Fresnel, who had the same idea, found — which no one before him had found — the means of making it feasible, in having the rings of the same stepped lens executed separately'
Brewster 1811/1820 proposals and advocacy — a third independent pre-Fresnel thread (carried as context that the stepped-lens idea was 'in the air')

competing_hypotheses: The honest version: Fresnel independently reinvented the stepped lens and — his genuine, unshared achievement — found the means to make it feasible (separate prisms, corrected spherical aberration) and built the first working lighthouse optic; the ex nihilo version is the fiction, the reinvention is the fact

The exact construction Fresnel used (annular sections assembled separately on a frame) was explicitly Condorcet's 1790 suggestion — the one precedent that touches the construction itself, not just the concept
falsifiability: No falsifier can rescue the ex nihilo version: the 1748 and 1790 proposals are published and dated. What the record WOULD change is if evidence emerged that Fresnel derived his design from Buffon/Condorcet rather than reinventing it — that would change the story's shape, not the grade

title: The telling that died: 'the mechanical pencil is modern' (234th family)
claim: DEBUNKED: the mechanical pencil is a 20th-century invention — killed twice: (1) the 1822 British patent (Mordan & Hawkins, #4742) is a documented 203-year-old propelling-pencil patent with manufactured, hallmarked survivors; (2) the 19th century ran a whole propelling-pencil industry — 160+ British patents 1822–1874, the 1877 spring-loaded mechanism, and the 1791 Pandora example — before the 20th-century brands existed.
place: London, England
grade_reason: Two independent kills from the documentary record: the patent file and its manufactured survivors, and the 19th-century patent industry. The fences hold: the kill is on the invention claim, never on the 20th century's genuine refinements (thin leads, the .046-inch Eversharp standard, spring mechanisms).
earliest_attestation: The telling is the unexamined assumption in popular histories that begin the mechanical pencil's story with 20th-century brands; no published survey measures the belief — stated plainly.

sources.ref: Yore Write!, 'S. Mordan & Co.': first patent (#4742) in England, 1822, jointly with John Isaac Hawkins — the kill document.

Wikipedia, 'Mechanical pencil': 'Between 1822 and 1874, more than 160 patents were registered pertaining to a variety of improvements to mechanical pencils. The first spring-loaded mechanical pencil was patented in 1877.' — the kill industry.
Wikipedia, 'Sampson Mordan': manufactured silver mechanical pencils from 1823–1837 (SMGR) and as S. Mordan & Co. until the factory's 1941 bombing — the survivors.

competing_hypotheses: The 20th-century refinement story is the true story misremembered: Eversharp/Sharp-era thin-lead and drafting pencils are genuinely modern — the invention is old, the refinements are not
The American vs British priority question — the American pencil industry's own origin stories (Thoreau, Faber 1861) concern wooden pencils, not the mechanical mechanism
falsifiability: A showing that the 1822 grant was not a propelling mechanism after all, plus the disappearance of the 1822–1874 patent record, would be required — the bar is deliberately high.

title: The 1822 patent: the mechanical pencil's birthday
claim: In 1822, Sampson Mordan and John Isaac Hawkins filed in Great Britain the first patent for a refillable metal pencil with an internal mechanism for propelling the graphite lead forward during use (the 'ever-pointed pencil'); Mordan bought out Hawkins and manufactured the pencils with Gabriel Riddle (1823–1837, SMGR hallmark), then as S. Mordan & Co. into the 20th century.
place: London, England
grade_reason: Multiply attested across independent secondary sources (Wikipedia, dealer/manufacturer histories, Grace's Guide) with surviving marked examples in the antiques trade; held below VERIFIED because the patent specification itself was not primary-inspected this pass.
earliest_attestation: British patent record, 1822; 1826 advertisement 'BY HIS MAJESTY'S ROYAL LETTERS PATENT. MORDAN & CO.'S PATENT EVER-POINTED PENCILS.'

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Sampson Mordan': 'In 1822, Mordan and his co-inventor John Isaac Hawkins filed the first patent in Great Britain for a metal pencil with an internal mechanism for propelling the graphite lead shaft forward during use.'

Wikipedia, 'Mechanical pencil': 'The first patent for a refillable pencil with lead-propelling mechanism was issued to Sampson Mordan and John Isaac Hawkins in Britain in 1822.'; also notes the 1791 Pandora example and 160+ patents 1822–1874.

Yore Write!, 'S. Mordan & Co.': Mordan 'filed the first patent (#4742) in England, in 1822, jointly with John Isaac Hawkins'; Mordan bought out Hawkins, partnered with Gabriel Riddle; earliest pencils hallmarked SMGR.
Grace's Guide to British Industrial History: '1822 Mordan patented his first ever pointed or propelling pencil on which the fortunes of his firm were based' (with the Hawkins/Riddle priority note).

competing_hypotheses: Grace's Guide note: 'There is an opinion that the propelling pencil was invented by John Isaac Hawkins with Sampson Mordan and that Gabriel Riddle was a manufacturer' — the three-man priority question
The unpatented leadholder tradition (Gesner 1565 → 1791 Pandora example) as prior art the patent improved on rather than invented from nothing
falsifiability: An earlier dated propelling-pencil patent, or proof the 1822 grant was never manufactured (refuted by surviving hallmarked examples), would overturn this.

title: Walker's friction match (1826/1827) — the first practical friction match
claim: John Walker of Stockton-on-Tees invented the first practical, commercially successful friction match in 1826 (accidental ignition: a dipped stick scraped against his hearth), and sold the first recorded box on 7 April 1827 — recorded in his sales ledger as 'Sulphurata Hyper-Oxygenata Frict', batch 'No. 30', to a Mr. Hixon, a solicitor. The splints were sulfur-dipped, tipped with antimony trisulfide and potassium chlorate in gumwater, sold 1s 2d per 100 with a tin and a folded piece of sandpaper. Walker never patented the invention ('I doubt not it will be a benefit to the public, so let them have it'), despite encouragement from Michael Faraday; Samuel Jones of London copied the design in 1829 as 'Lucifers'. Walker died 1 May 1859 in Stockton, uncredited in his lifetime.
place: Stockton-on-Tees, County Durham, England (59 High Street chemist's shop)
grade_reason: The 1827 sale is a primary ledger record; the 1826 invention is the consistent local and museum tradition; the no-patent fact and the Jones 1829 copy are consistently attested. Held at CORROBORATED on the inferential 1826 date — the sale itself is primary.
earliest_attestation: Walker's sales ledger, 7 April 1827 ('Sulphurata Hyper-Oxygenata Frict', batch No. 30)

sources.ref: Tees Valley Museums — 'John Walker and the friction match' (invention 1826, first sale 7 April 1827, Faraday's urging, death 1 May 1859 uncredited)
stocktonteesside.co.uk — 'John Walker of Stockton-on-Tees — Inventor of the Friction Match' (first sale 7 April 1827 to Mr. Hixon; no patent despite Faraday; Jones 'Lucifers' 1829)
Cleveland & Teesside Local History Society — 'John Walker Sells Friction Matches – 1827' (59 High Street; 'Sulphurata Hyper-Oxygenata Frict'; 'friction lights' from Sept 1827)
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Walker_(inventor) — invention 1826 or 1827; 'I doubt not it will be a benefit to the public, so let them have it'; Walker never used 'Congreves'/'Lucifers' as names

competing_hypotheses: The 1826 invention date is inferential (the 'No. 30' batch number on the April 1827 sale note may imply 1826 manufacture) — hence CORROBORATED, not VERIFIED

The 'Congreves' name: Stockton tradition says Walker named the matches 'Congreves' after Sir William Congreve; the Walker Wikipedia scholarship says he never called them 'matches', 'lucifers', or 'Congreves' — using 'friction lights' (from Sept 1827) and 'attrition lights' (1828). Both carried honestly
Whether Walker's refusal to patent was public-spirited principle or commercial complacency (Stockton tradition: he was 'already comfortably well off') — motive unsettled, outcome documented
falsifiability: A dated friction-match record from another maker predating April 1827, or Walker's own notes (none survive — the formulation was recovered by later chemical analysis of his products)

title: The 'Victorian secret language of the fan' myth
claim: Victorian (and Regency) women communicated through a codified, widely-used secret 'language of the fan' — a fixed system of fan positions and gestures carrying specific messages ('fan in the left hand in front of the face = I desire your acquaintance', 'touching the handle to the lips = kiss me', etc.).
place: Paris and London (the alleged practice)
grade_reason: DEBUNKED — 221st DEBUNKED family. Two kills: (1) the codebook was manufactured as advertising — Country Life: Jean-Pierre Duvelleroy (Paris fan house 1827, London shop at 121 New Bond Street, supplier to Queen Victoria) published 'Le Langage de l'Eventail' as an advertising ploy, detailing 23 gestures, many loosely based on flamenco dancing; The National independently reports the system as born with Duvelleroy, with the specific gesture meanings his. (2) No evidence of wide adoption — Country Life: 'little evidence that complex signing systems involving the use of fans were widely adopted', citing the practical difficulties (time-consuming, required undivided attention and shared mastery, far from private). A manufacturer's pamphlet is not a social practice.
earliest_attestation: No period evidence of a widely-used fan-gesture code; the pamphlet system is Duvelleroy's own publication

sources.ref: Country Life, 'Curious Questions: Did English ladies really have a secret language of fans?': Duvelleroy's pamphlet 'as an advertising ploy' detailing 23 movements; 'little evidence that complex signing systems involving the use of fans were widely adopted'; contrasted with the genuinely widespread language of flowers

The National, 'Tracing the evolution of hand-held fans': 'in 1827, Jean-Pierre Duvelleroy launched his fan house in Paris... The notion of a "fan language" was born. According to Duvelleroy, if a woman fans slowly, it signifies that she is married, and if her fanning is fast, it means she is engaged. If she carries it in her right hand in front of her face, it means "follow me", and if she twirls it in her left hand, it means "we're being watched"'

The Free Library ('Antiques & Collecting'): lists the standard popular version of the code (left-hand-before-face = desire for acquaintance, right cheek = yes, left cheek = no, handle to lips = kiss me) — the belief's canonical form, carried as belief ecology, not evidence

competing_hypotheses: Fans were genuinely used in flirtation and social signaling (untested, improvised gestures — graded separately from any codified system)
The pamphlet system itself was a printed novelty (the Duvelleroy pamphlet existed as an artifact; the artifact is real, the practice is not)
The language of flowers WAS a genuinely widely-understood code — kept as the contrast case: one codebook caught on, the other did not
falsifiability: A diary, letter, novel, or conduct book from 1780–1900 describing an actual encounter conducted via the codified fan system (as opposed to describing the pamphlet itself)

title: Poenaru's 1827 fountain-pen patent
claim: Petrache Poenaru registered a French patent on 25 May 1827 (brevet no. 3208) for a 'plume portable sans fin, qui s'alimente elle-meme avec de l'ancre' — a portable pen that recharges itself with ink, built from a large swan's quill used as an ink reservoir.
place: Paris, France — where Poenaru studied at the École Polytechnique and registered the invention
grade_reason: Multiply reported from the brevet itself (Wikipedia cites the 25 May 1827 brevet PDF, code 3208, with the French description) and corroborated by trade histories naming it the first patent for a pen holding its own ink supply; held below VERIFIED on the thin transmission of a single surviving document plus the non-survival of the pen.
earliest_attestation: French Ministry of the Interior Manufacture Department registration, 25 May 1827 (Brevets d'Invention Nr. 3208)

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Petrache Poenaru' — registration 25 May 1827, code 3208, 'plume portable sans fin, qui s'alimente elle-meme avec de l'ancre'; swan's quill reservoir; École Polytechnique context

Antique Trader, 'Putting pen to paper with distinction' — 'The first patent for a pen holding its own ink supply was issued in 1827 to Romanian Petrache Poenaru... made from a large swan quill... still messy, like its traditional dipping pen predecessors, and it still needed frequent refilling'

competing_hypotheses: That Poenaru's pen was still messy and needed frequent refilling (Antique Trader) — true, and honestly scoped: the 1827 pen is the first PATENTED self-inking pen, not the first reliable one

That deeper predecessors (al-Mu'izz's 973 commission, Schwenter's 17th-century reservoir quill) deserve the 'first' credit — named here, each to be graded on its own evidence; they are not patent-tradition fountain pens
falsifiability: A demonstration that brevet 3208 does not exist or describes a different device; held below VERIFIED because the pen itself does not survive and the record rides multiply-reported secondary transmission of the brevet

title: 'The match is a Swedish invention' — DEBUNKED (225th family)
claim: The claim that the match is a Swedish invention is DEBUNKED as a blanket statement. The friction match was English: John Walker's Stockton-on-Tees matches were on sale from 7 April 1827, seventeen years before Gustaf Erik Pasch's 1844 Swedish safety-match patent — and Chancel's Paris chemical matches (1805) preceded both. What Sweden genuinely contributed was the SAFETY match: Pasch's 1844 separated design (red phosphorus on the striking surface, not in the head) plus the Lundström brothers' commercial manufacture from Jönköping (1845–47 development, 1855 Paris award). 'Swedish match' is a brand and an industrial monopoly (Jönköpings & Vulcans Tändsticksfabriks AB 1903 → Swedish Match), not an invention credit for the match itself.
place: Stockholm, Sweden (the myth's home — Pasch's city; the fiction belongs where the truth was partial)
