grade_reason: Two kills, both documentary: (1) chronology — Walker's friction match (recorded sale 7 April 1827) predates the Swedish safety-match patent (1844) by seventeen years, and Chancel's chemical matches (1805) precede both; (2) category error — Sweden invented the safety match (Pasch 1844 + Lundström manufacture), not the match; 'Swedish match' names a monopoly and a brand. Grade kills the blanket claim only: the Walker, Chancel, Pasch, Lundström, and white-phosphorus records all stand untouched.
earliest_attestation: Walker's sales ledger 7 April 1827 (primary) vs Pasch's Swedish patent 1844 (patent record)

sources.ref: Tees Valley Museums — Walker first sale 7 April 1827
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustaf_Erik_Pasch — Pasch granted safety-match patent 1844
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safety_matches — Lundström manufacture; Jönköpings & Vulcans Tändsticksfabriks AB 1903; Swedish Match lineage

competing_hypotheses: None on the chronology: Walker's 1827 sale and Pasch's 1844 patent are both documented; the 17-year gap is arithmetic, not interpretation

The myth's ecology: Swedish Match branding, the Jönköping monopoly, and the genuine Swedish safety-match contribution make the claim plausible enough to survive — hence this record exists to kill it cleanly
falsifiability: A dated Swedish friction-match record predating Walker's April 1827 sale

title: The claim that Columbus sailed to prove the Earth was round
claim: Christopher Columbus sailed west to prove the Earth was round, against scholars and churchmen who believed it was flat.
place: Salamanca, Spain (the 1486-87 commission)
grade_reason: Educated Europeans had known the Earth was spherical since antiquity and taught it through the Middle Ages; the Salamanca commission's actual objection — that Columbus grossly underestimated the westward distance to Asia — was correct on the evidence. The flat-earth council is Irving's 1828 invention, not a 1492 event.
earliest_attestation: Washington Irving (1828); the myth's manufacture traced by Jeffrey Burton Russell, 'Inventing the Flat Earth' (1991).

sources.ref: Eratosthenes of Cyrene, c. 240 BCE: measured Earth's circumference within a few percent of the true value
Medieval curriculum: Bede, Aquinas, Macrobius — spherical Earth taught as standard; the university scholars at Salamanca (1486-87) rejected Columbus over DISTANCE, not shape
Jeffrey Burton Russell (1991), 'Inventing the Flat Earth: Columbus and Modern Historians' — the myth's 19th-century manufacture
Columbus's Toscanelli/Marinus-based estimate (~3,000 nautical miles to Asia vs. actual ~10,600): the experts were right about the distance; he was lucky the Americas were in the way

competing_hypotheses: A few patristic writers (Lactantius, Cosmas Indicopleustes) did argue a flat Earth — real, but never the medieval scholarly consensus; the myth needs the consensus to be false, and it wasn't
'Columbus debated the size, not the shape' — the accurate frame, carried as the replacement narrative
falsifiability: A contemporary 1486-87 record showing the Salamanca commission actually disputed Earth's sphericity (rather than the distance estimate) would revive the Irving version; the surviving record shows the opposite.

title: Joseph Henry's wire: the science before the patent (1828–1835)
claim: Joseph Henry — at the Albany Academy, 1826–1832 — built the scientific core the telegraph ran on: the high-intensity multi-turn insulated electromagnet (1828), the 1831 'magnetic telegraph' demonstration ringing a bell through a mile of wire, and the 1835 mercury-dipping electrical relay. He refused to patent, choosing open science.
place: Albany, New York (the Albany Academy)
grade_reason: Independent secondary attestation of the experiments (Wikipedia's synthesis of Henry's papers; Union College's 1997 exhibit assessment; the Smithsonian's Henry records) plus Morse's own correspondence crediting Henry as his teacher in electromagnetism (HISTORY.com; Library of Congress). Held at CORROBORATED rather than VERIFIED: Henry's deliberate non-patenting means there is no patent-office primary record of the kind the Morse and Cooke–Wheatstone systems carry — the science is documented in his notes and the Smithsonian, not in a granted patent.
earliest_attestation: Henry's Albany Academy lecture notes and published descriptions, 1828–31; the Smithsonian's Henry collection

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Electric telegraph': Henry 1828 multi-turn electromagnet; 1831 Albany mile-of-wire 'magnetic telegraph'; 1835 mercury-dipping relay (with Davy)

Union College exhibit: 'the first person to send a message over an electric wire (nearly 20 years before Samuel F. B. Morse)'; mentored Morse on the telegraph and Bell on the telephone; the henry unit
HISTORY.com: Morse 'learned more about the topic from American physicist Joseph Henry'

competing_hypotheses: The counterfactual reading: had Henry patented (as Morse later did), the American telegraph's scientific core would legally have been his — ungraded, since he explicitly chose not to
The Sturgeon-priority note: William Sturgeon's 1825 electromagnet preceded Henry's 1828 improvement — Henry's was the intensity that made long-wire telegraphy practical, not the first electromagnet
falsifiability: Henry's own published descriptions and the Smithsonian's holdings being shown as misattributed or fabricated; Morse's correspondence explicitly credits learning electromagnetism from Henry

title: 'Elias Howe invented the sewing machine' — the sole-invention telling
claim: Elias Howe alone invented the sewing machine — the 1846 lockstitch patent (U.S. 4,750) was the invention of the sewing machine itself, with no prior inventors of working sewing machines.
place: United States (the popular telling)
grade_reason: Three independent chronological kills: Thomas Saint's 1790 patent predates Howe by 56 years; Thimonnier's 1830 functional machine predates him by 16 years; Hunt's 1834 working lockstitch predates him by 12 years.
earliest_attestation: The sole-invention telling is a popular-summary reading of Howe's 1846 patent (Smithsonian NMAH caption notes 'contrary to popular belief, he was not the first to conceive of the idea of a sewing machine')

sources.ref: Alamy/Smithsonian NMAH caption — 'Contrary to popular belief, he was not the first to conceive of the idea of a sewing machine' (Kill 1 framing)
thoughtco.com — History of Sewing Machines: Saint's 1790 patent (Kill 1: chronological — 56 years before Howe)
Smithsonian Magazine — Thimonnier's 1830 functional chain-stitch machine and tailor riot (Kill 2: chronological — 16 years before Howe)
garmenco.org — Walter Hunt's 1834 unpatented lockstitch machine (Kill 3: chronological — 12 years before Howe; Hunt also invented the safety pin)

competing_hypotheses: The narrowed telling — 'Howe patented the lockstitch mechanism that all later machines infringed' — is VERIFIED and never attacked by this kill
falsifiability: Proof that no working sewing machine predated Howe's 1846 filing — defeated by the three kills.

title: Thimonnier's sewing machine: the first functional machine and the tailor riot
claim: French tailor Barthélemy Thimonnier patented a working sewing machine in 1830; his chain-stitch machine (barbed needle, foot treadle, spring return) was put into production in a Paris workshop making army uniforms, and the machines were destroyed by a mob of tailors fearing for their livelihoods.
place: Paris, France (Thimonnier's workshop)
grade_reason: The 1830 patent and the functional machine are multiply attested; the riot's exact year and machine count vary between sources.
earliest_attestation: French patent 1830; Smithsonian Magazine history of the sewing machine; Sewing Machine News 1880 illustration of Thimonnier's machine

sources.ref: Smithsonian Magazine — 'The Many, Many Designs of the Sewing Machine'
Getty Images/SSPL — Thimonnier's chain-stitch machine, 1830 (photo caption record)
France: A Reference Guide from Renaissance to the Present (Thimonnier entry, 1884)

competing_hypotheses: The 1831 destruction date with 80 machines (Getty/SSPL) vs the 1841 date (garmenco.org) — one tradition may conflate two separate tailor attacks (Smithsonian notes a second attack)
falsifiability: French patent records showing no 1830 Thimonnier filing, or proof the preserved machines postdate the patent.

title: 'Morse invented the telegraph' — the sole-inventor myth
claim: The electric telegraph was invented single-handedly by Samuel F. B. Morse — one man, one invention, c. 1832–1844.
place: Washington, D.C. (the Capitol rotunda, where the 1844 line terminated and the stamp's version of the story begins)
grade_reason: Four independent kills on the SOLE-inventor reading. (1) HENRY WAS FIRST: Joseph Henry demonstrated the 'magnetic telegraph' at Albany Academy in 1831 — ringing a bell through a mile of wire — and Morse learned electromagnetism from Henry (HISTORY.com); Union College's assessment: Henry was 'the first person to send a message over an electric wire (nearly 20 years before Morse)'. (2) COOKE & WHEATSTONE WERE FIRST COMMERCIAL AND FIRST PATENTED: English patent 10 June 1837; working trial Euston–Camden 25 July 1837; the world's first commercial telegraph, Paddington–West Drayton 1839 — all before Morse's US patents (1840) and his 1844 line; Morse's 1838 English patent application was opposed by Cooke & Wheatstone as covering already-existing ideas. (3) THE CODE WASN'T EVEN MORSE'S: Alfred Vail's own 1845 'Early History' documents that the telegraphic code was 'originated and applied to the telegraph in the latter part of January, 1838, by Alfred Vail' — and Vail designed the practical hand key; the partnership agreement gave Vail half the foreign-patent proceeds. (4) THE FIELD WAS CROWDED BEFORE MORSE: Ronalds's 1816 static telegraph (the first published work on electric telegraphy, Admiralty-rejected as 'wholly unnecessary'), Schilling 1832, the operative Gauss & Weber telegraph 1833 (Göttingen), Davy's 1837 Regent's Park demonstration and 1838 patent — independent workers, independent evidence.
earliest_attestation: The sole-inventor form: the 19th-century American popular telling and its schoolbook afterlife; the strongest period defense is the Scientific American / Paris Moniteur formulation — principles not his, practical application his

sources.ref: HISTORY.com, 'Morse Code & Telegraph: Invention & Samuel Morse': 'the credit for inventing the telegraph generally falls to two sets of researchers: William Cooke and Charles Wheatstone in England, and Samuel Morse, Leonard Gale and Alfred Vail in the United States'; 'Morse... learned more about the topic from American physicist Joseph Henry'

Library of Congress, Samuel F. B. Morse Papers: 'Henry's experiments, Gale's assistance, and, soon after, hiring the young technician Alfred Vail were keys to Morse's success'; Morse met Wheatstone in England and judged his system 'ingenious' but his own 'simpler, more efficient, and easier to use'
Union College exhibit on Joseph Henry: 'the first person to send a message over an electric wire (nearly 20 years before Samuel F. B. Morse)'; Henry mentored Morse on the telegraph

Wikipedia, 'Telegraphy' / 'Electric telegraph': Cooke & Wheatstone patent 10 June 1837; first commercial telegraph Paddington–West Drayton (13 mi); Gauss & Weber 1833 first operative system; Ronalds 1816 rejected by the Admiralty
Alfred Vail, 'Early History of the Electro-magnetic Telegraph' (1845): 'the telegraphic code was originated and applied to the telegraph in the latter part of January, 1838, by Alfred Vail'

King's College London, Wheatstone exhibition: June 1837 patent; July 1837 Euston–Camden trial; 9 July 1839 Paddington–West Drayton permanent line; 1840 'first successful commercial application of the electric telegraph in the world'; Morse's 1838 English patent application opposed by Cooke & Wheatstone
ThoughtCo, 'Samuel Morse and the Invention of the Telegraph': the popular American form — 'The credit for this invention belongs to Samuel Finley Breese Morse' (the telling under grade)

competing_hypotheses: The 'assembler' reading: Morse assembled existing science (Volta, Oersted, Sturgeon, Henry) into the winning commercial system — carried as the fairest contemporary formulation (the Paris Moniteur's 19th-century verdict: the principles were discovered by others; Morse transferred them from 'speculative science' into practical application)

The plural-invention reading: the telegraph had several independent inventors (Ronalds 1816, Schilling 1832, Gauss & Weber 1833, Davy 1837, Cooke & Wheatstone 1837, Morse/Gale/Vail 1837–1844) — carried as the documentary consensus
falsifiability: Contemporary 1830s evidence that Morse originated the electromagnetic principle itself — e.g., a Morse notebook deriving the electromagnet independently of Henry's published 1828–31 work, or a working Morse system predating Henry's 1831 mile-of-wire demonstration

title: White phosphorus, phossy jaw, and the 1906 Berne Convention
claim: White phosphorus — the active ingredient of most strike-anywhere matches from the 1840s to the 1910s (Charles Sauria's 1831 French substitution of white phosphorus for antimony sulfide in the Walker formula started the industry) — poisoned its workforce. The first case of phossy jaw (phosphorus necrosis of the jaw) was diagnosed in 1839 by Vienna physician Friedrich Wilhelm Lorinser in a Viennese matchstick maker; in 1844 he reported 22 cases and established white phosphorus's toxicity in matches. The disease fed the London matchgirls' strike of 1888 (Bryant & May); William Booth and the Salvation Army opened a red-phosphorus match factory in 1891. The International Convention respecting the Prohibition of the Use of White (Yellow) Phosphorus in the Manufacture of Matches — the Berne Convention — was concluded 26 September 1906 and entered into force 1 January 1912, banning manufacture, import, and sale; it remains in force for 48 states (Switzerland depositary). Edward J. Phelan later said the ILO 'may in one sense be traced to the Berne Convention of 1906'.
place: Bern, Switzerland (Berne Convention, 1906)
grade_reason: Lorinser's 1839/1844 work, the 1888 strike, the 1891 Salvation Army factory, and the 1906 convention (concluded 26 September 1906, in force 1 January 1912) are all consistently attested; held at CORROBORATED rather than VERIFIED as the match-worker disease record is medical-historical rather than multi-primary.
earliest_attestation: Lorinser's 1839 diagnosis, Vienna; 1844 report of 22 cases

sources.ref: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phossy_jaw — Lorinser 1839 first case (Vienna matchstick maker, 5-year exposure); 1844 report of 22 cases; white phosphorus active ingredient 1840s–1910s; 1888 matchgirls' strike; Salvation Army 1891 red-phosphorus factory; Berne 1906
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berne_Convention_(1906) — concluded 26 September 1906; in force 1 January 1912; 48 states; Switzerland depositary; Phelan 1925 ILO remark
Scribd 'Evolution of Ethereal Matches' — Sauria's 1831 white-phosphorus substitution; 'from 1845 match-makers exposed to its fumes succumbed to necrosis'

competing_hypotheses: The 1888 matchgirls' strike did not end white-phosphorus use — the strike's grievances included pay and fines alongside the phosphorus conditions; the ban took the 1906 convention plus national implementation over the following years
The Salvation Army's 1891 red-phosphorus factory used the safer but more expensive process — economics, not chemistry, was the barrier to replacement
falsifiability: A dated medical or industrial record showing white phosphorus in matches was understood and regulated before Lorinser 1839, or evidence the Berne Convention did not drive the phase-out

title: Walter Hunt's 1834 lockstitch machine: built, never patented
claim: New York inventor Walter Hunt built a working lockstitch sewing machine in 1834 — the first American lockstitch machine, with an eye-pointed needle and shuttle interlocking two threads — but never patented it, reportedly fearing it would put seamstresses out of work.
place: New York City, USA (Hunt's workshop)
grade_reason: Multiply attested that Hunt built a working lockstitch machine before Howe and declined to patent it; the 'unemployment fear' motive is the traditional telling, honestly flagged as such.
earliest_attestation: Hunt's machine attested through later patent-war testimony and sewing-machine histories (19th c.); the same Walter Hunt patented the safety pin (U.S. 6,281, 1849) — see evt-hunt-safety-pin-patent-1849-001 (Sylvie Barlow #271 beat)

sources.ref: garmenco.org — History of the Sewing Machine (documents Hunt 1834 unpatented lockstitch)
Scribd — History of Sewing Machine Inventions (Hunt 1834, never patented, unemployment fear)
hooptalent.com — Who Invented the Sewing Machine (Hunt's eye-pointed needle and shuttle as the core mechanism)

competing_hypotheses: Hunt's motive for not patenting is told as unemployment fear; an alternative reading is simple commercial non-interest or distraction (Hunt was a prolific inventor of other things)
falsifiability: A genuine 1834-era Hunt patent filing, or proof the surviving Hunt machines are misdated post-1846 copies.

title: The Liberty Bell's crack is NOT from its first ringing
claim: The famous crack visible on the Liberty Bell today dates to the bell's first ringing — i.e., the bell has carried the same crack since it was first struck in Philadelphia in 1752.
place: Liberty Bell Center, Independence National Historical Park, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
grade_reason: Killed twice by the documents. First: the 1752 first-strike crack was melted away — the bell was recast twice by Pass & Stow in 1753, so no crack from the first ringing can survive in the present metal. Second: the visible crack is a 19th-century injury — it 'acquired its distinctive large crack sometime in the first half of the 19th century' (1835 Marshall tolling is the widespread tradition), was widened and stop-drilled in 1846 after ringing for Washington's birthday, and the bell has not rung since. The schoolbook telling collapses three separate cracks (1752, the 19th-century injury, the 1846 widening) into one.
earliest_attestation: No contemporary documentation fixes the moment; the 1835 Marshall story is later tradition; the 1846 Washington's-birthday widening and stop-drilling repair are the documented end of its ringing life

sources.ref: Wikipedia 'Liberty Bell' — first cracked when rung after arrival, twice recast by Pass & Stow; 'acquired its distinctive large crack sometime in the first half of the 19th century'; 1835 Marshall story; 1846 repair; not rung since

National Park Service — 'The Liberty Bell Story': 'By 1846 a thin crack began to affect the sound of the bell. The bell was repaired in 1846 and rang for a George Washington birthday celebration, but the bell cracked again and has not been rung since. No one knows why the bell cracked either time.'

OnThisDay.com Liberty Bell photo archive (INHP Library and Archives): 'The bell cracked on its first test ring so it was then melted down and recast by local metalworkers John Pass and John Stow'; 'The bell's famous crack formed in the 1830s. Efforts were made to repair the bell in 1846 by widening the crack but these failed.'

competing_hypotheses: The 1835 Marshall tradition: a widespread story holds the final crack opened while tolling for Chief Justice John Marshall's death (July 1835) — tradition, not documentation
The exact metallurgical cause of the 19th-century crack is honestly unknown — the NPS's own telling: 'No one knows why the bell cracked either time'
falsifiability: Metallurgical continuity between the 1752 cracked metal and the present bell — impossible: the 1752 bell was melted down and recast twice by Pass & Stow (1753); the metal carrying the first crack no longer exists

title: 'Liebig invented the mirror in 1835' — the quiz telling
claim: The telling that 'Justus von Liebig invented the mirror in 1835' — repeated in quiz formats and trivia — is false: glass mirrors existed centuries before Liebig (14th-century Italy; the Venetian tin-mercury mirrors of the 16th century). Liebig's 1835 contribution was the chemical silvering PROCESS, not the mirror.
place: Giessen, Germany (Liebig, 1835)
grade_reason: Chronology kill: glass mirrors predate Liebig by at least five centuries; his documented contribution is the silvering process.
earliest_attestation: The telling: modern trivia/quiz formats (e.g. SSC CHSL 2024 exam question, 'created the first mirror'). The refutation: 14th-century Italian glass mirrors (The Handy Physics Answer Book) and 16th-century Venetian tin-mercury mirrors.

sources.ref: The Handy Physics Answer Book — 'The earliest glass mirrors, backed with shiny metal, appeared in Italy during the fourteenth century'
Testbook SSC CHSL 2024 question — the myth's own telling: 'created the first mirror' attributed to Liebig
evt-liebig-silvering-1835-001 — the actual 1835 contribution, for contrast

competing_hypotheses: That 'invented the mirror' is loose shorthand for 'invented the modern mirror-making process' — the honest root of the telling, and why it persists
falsifiability: No honest falsifier — the chronology is settled; only a redefinition of 'invented' ('invented the silvering process') would salvage a true reading, which is the myth's own escape hatch.

title: Liebig's 1835 chemical silvering
claim: In 1835, the German chemist Justus von Liebig developed a process for depositing metallic silver on glass by reducing ammoniated silver nitrate with an aldehyde/sugar — the chemical silvering that replaced poisonous tin-mercury amalgam mirror-making and made the modern looking glass cheap.
place: Giessen, Germany (Liebig's university)
grade_reason: The 1835 date and the chemistry are consistently attested across technical and historical sources; the primary 1835 paper was not inspected this pass, so VERIFIED is withheld.
earliest_attestation: Liebig's 1835 publication on depositing metallic silver on glass.

sources.ref: NZIC, 'Silver Mirroring' — silver produced chemically by reducing a silver salt solution; Liebig-era process lineage
BenchChem, 'A Historical Perspective on the Elusive Silver Hydroxide' — 'In 1835, Justus von Liebig developed a method for depositing a thin layer of metallic silver onto glass'
Gizmodo (2017) — Liebig's 1835 breakthrough: 'Add some sugar to ammoniated silver nitrate, pour it onto glass, and blammo: you've got yourself a mirror'

competing_hypotheses: The process was soon improved and industrialized by others (notably the 1840s German silvering industry), so 'Liebig's process' as manufactured was a collective refinement
Some attributions split credit with the French development work of the same period
falsifiability: A contemporary 1835-dated publication by Liebig that contains no silvering work, or an earlier published silvering process, would revise the attribution.

title: The Great Moon Hoax of 1835 — six days of lunar life in the New York Sun
claim: The New York Sun published six articles, 25–31 August 1835, reporting lunar life — bison, blue single-horned goats, miniature zebras, unicorns, bipedal tail-less beavers, and the winged Vespertilio-homo — discovered by Sir John Herschel at the Cape of Good Hope with a 24-foot, 7-ton lens, ostensibly written by his fictitious companion Dr. Andrew Grant and reprinted from the Edinburgh Journal of Science.
place: New York City — the Sun's office (claim); Cape of Good Hope (the fictional observatory)
grade_reason: The six articles exist and are multiply documented in the Sun's own columns and the European reprints; the Locke authorship is the mainstream scholarly attribution but rests on an 1840 private letter, never a public admission.
earliest_attestation: The Sun, New York, August–September 1835 — the articles themselves, six installments

sources.ref: Wikipedia 'Great Moon Hoax' (citing the Sun's own columns): headline 'GREAT ASTRONOMICAL DISCOVERIES, LATELY MADE BY SIR JOHN HERSCHEL... At the Cape of Good Hope. [From Supplement to the Edinburgh Journal of Science]'; Dr. Andrew Grant as ostensible author-companion; creatures catalogued (bison, single-horned goats, mini zebras, unicorns, bipedal tail-less beavers, Vespertilio-homo who built temples); lens '24 feet in diameter and 7 tons in weight'; observations terminated by the Sun making the lens a burning glass

Smithsonian Magazine ('The Great Moon Hoax Was Simply a Sign of Its Time'): the 24-foot lens claim, the lunar fauna progression across installments, the man-bats 'scientifically denominated Vespertilio-homo'; Herschel's real Cape expedition as the news hook the hoax rode

EarthSky (Aug 25, 2020): six articles from 25 August 1835; Herschel attribution; Richard Adams Locke the attributed author; the Edinburgh Journal of Science 'had been out of commission for some years'; papers across Europe reprinted the story
Smithsonian Libraries lithographs (Leopoldo Galluzzo, Naples 1836, 'Altre scoverte fatte nella luna dal Sigr. Herschel') — the European reprint industry as physical provenance of the story's travel

competing_hypotheses: The authorship: the Locke attribution is the consensus but is built on the 1840 letter and the Bennett finger-pointing, not a signed confession — a strict source audit keeps one rung of doubt open.

The Sun's Sept 16, 1835 admission: Wikipedia dates the admission there; Gizmodo's account says the Sun never admitted to the hoax at all — the admission's exact form is contested, the articles' fabrication is not.
falsifiability: A pre-August-1835 Edinburgh Journal of Science issue carrying the Herschel lunar series, or Herschel's Cape notebooks recording a 24-foot lens

title: The legend that nobody questioned the Moon Hoax
claim: The 1835 Moon Hoax fooled New York wholesale: nobody questioned the articles, the public believed them entirely, and the hoax permanently doubled the Sun's circulation, establishing it as the world's most-read paper.
place: New York City — the city that supposedly was fooled whole
grade_reason: Three independent kills: the Herald named it a hoax on the series' last day; Poe, a practicing hoax-writer, saw through it instantly; and the circulation-doubling leg is flagged as 'certainly exaggerated in popular accounts' by the documentary record.
earliest_attestation: The popular retelling itself: the 'all New York believed it' and 'circulation doubled permanently' forms — attestation of the BELIEF (the legend), not of the fact

sources.ref: Interesting Engineering ('The Great Moon Hoax of 1835: The Birth of Fake News?'): James Gordon Bennett's Herald, back in print 31 August 1835 after the office fire, published 'The Astronomical Hoax Explained' — accused the Sun of fabricating the story, identified Locke as its true author, and pointed out that the Edinburgh Journal of Science was no longer being published

iHeart / Stuff You Missed in History Class (Great Moon Hoax, Part 2): by the fifth installment 'most of the other papers had started denouncing the entirety of this series as a hoax'; Locke's August 31 nebulous denial letter to the Herald; a Philadelphia paper reprinted the letter beside a real-estate auction advertisement for Herschel-discovered lunar property — the joke was already being run with within the series' own week
Wikipedia 'Great Moon Hoax': 'the degree to which the hoax increased the paper's circulation has certainly been exaggerated in popular accounts of the event'

Untapped Cities ('The Great Moon Hoax: NYC Penny Papers and Man-Bats in Space'): Edgar Allan Poe saw the series as a ripoff of his own June 1835 story and recognized the game instantly; 'by the end of the summer, however, newspapers that had initially republished the story were now calling it a hoax'

competing_hypotheses: The soft version: the skepticism was thin — Bennett's Herald had been burned out for most of the series, and Herschel himself later grew tired of answering believers' questions, so many readers genuinely believed. Carried honestly; it softens the wholesale form but cannot carry the 'nobody questioned it' leg.

The circulation claim's defenders: the Sun did boast 19,360 copies in a day (28 August) and the paper's rise was real — the dispute is the PERMANENCE and the scale of the hoax's role, not the boast itself.
falsifiability: Already falsified: the Aug 31, 1835 debunk and the circulation-legend audit both predate the legend.

title: The mythicist hypothesis (the Christ-myth theory)
claim: Jesus of Nazareth never existed as a historical person: the Gospel Jesus is a wholly mythic construction — assembled from Jewish scripture, dying-and-rising god motifs, and early Christian theology — with no human core (the 'Christ myth' or mythicist position).
place: Berlin (Bauer's 1841 Christ-myth writings)
grade_reason: A reasoned interpretation of the same attested sources — not an evidence-free fantasy — held by a small minority of scholars and rejected by the overwhelming mainstream; the hypothesis is coherent but unattested as a mechanism.
earliest_attestation: Bruno Bauer's Christ-myth writings (1841); revived form: Richard Carrier, On the Historicity of Jesus (Sheffield Phoenix Press, 2014)

sources.ref: Richard Carrier, On the Historicity of Jesus (2014) — the peer-reviewed, Bayesian statement of the mythicist case
Robert M. Price, The Christ-Myth Theory and Its Problems (2011); Earl Doherty, The Jesus Puzzle (1999)
Bart D. Ehrman, Did Jesus Exist? (2012) — the mainstream rebuttal; Maurice Casey, Jesus: Evidence and Argument or Mythicist Myths? (2014)
The mainstream consensus statement it argues against: the only two events of 'almost universal assent' — baptism by John, crucifixion under Pilate — per the historical-Jesus research consensus

competing_hypotheses: The mainstream historicist position: a historical apocalyptic preacher lies behind the traditions; baptism and crucifixion are 'almost universally' assented; the rest is scholarly disagreement (Ehrman 2012, Casey 2014, Sanders, Meier's A Marginal Jew)
The agnostic-minimalist middle: the sources establish the tradition's early existence, not the biography's detail — historicity of the figure assumed, biography largely unrecoverable
falsifiability: A contemporary (1st-century, Roman or Jewish) attestation of Jesus of Nazareth would falsify the hypothesis outright; silence alone cannot verify it, and convergence of independent early sources cannot falsify it.

title: Poe's own moon hoax — 'Hans Pfaall,' June 1835
claim: Edgar Allan Poe published 'The Unparalleled Adventure of One Hans Pfaall' — the first installment of his own moon hoax — in the June 1835 Southern Literary Messenger, a month before Locke's Sun series, and afterward charged that the Sun's hoax plagiarized his story.
place: New York (the Sun) and Richmond (the Southern Literary Messenger)
grade_reason: The June 1835 Messenger publication and Poe's repeated plagiarism charge are both documented; held below VERIFIED on the influence question — whether Locke actually used Poe's story — which the scholarship leaves open.
earliest_attestation: Southern Literary Messenger, June 1835 — 'The Unparalleled Adventure of One Hans Pfaall'

sources.ref: Smithsonian Magazine ('The Great Moon Hoax Was Simply a Sign of Its Time'): Poe's 'The Unparalleled Adventure of One Hans Pfaall' published in the June 1835 Southern Literary Messenger, shortly before Locke's Sun series; 'Poe later accused Locke of stealing his idea. That isn't certain'
Wikipedia 'Great Moon Hoax': Poe claimed the story was a plagiarism of his earlier work; his 1846 'Literati of New York City' biographical sketch of Locke in Godey's Lady's Book

Wikipedia 'The Unparalleled Adventure of One Hans Pfaall': the original story appeared in the June 1835 Southern Literary Messenger, a month before the Sun's 'Great Moon Hoax' in August; the story was reprinted Sept 2–5, 1835 in the New York Transcript as 'Lunar Discoveries, Extraordinary Aerial Voyage'
Saturday Evening Post ('The Great Moon Hoax of 1835', Aug 2020): 'the editor of the piece was... Richard Adams Locke' — Poe's Moon story was edited by the man he would later accuse

Wikipedia 'The Balloon-Hoax': Poe's 1844 Sun balloon hoax and his decade-long complaint that the Moon Hoax had plagiarized Hans Pfaall and made 'tremendous profits' from his story (chronicled in Goodman's The Sun and the Moon, 2008)

competing_hypotheses: The influence question (Smithsonian: 'That isn't certain'): the man-bat conceit and the satiric tone differ; Locke may have arrived at the hoax independently, and Poe's grievance may be the loser's reading of a coincidence. Carried honestly — the PUBLICATION is documented, the INFLUENCE is the disputed leg.

The Saturday Evening Post's wrinkle: the Hans Pfaall piece's editor at the Messenger was Richard Adams Locke himself — which makes the plagiarism charge either iron-clad or ironic, depending on the reader.
falsifiability: A June-1835 or earlier Messenger issue without the story, or evidence the Sun series predates Poe's publication

title: The Marsh test for arsenic (1836)
claim: In 1836 the Scottish chemist James Marsh published a sensitive test for arsenic: the sample is treated with arsenic-free zinc and sulphuric acid, any arsenic present forming arsine gas, which is led through a heated tube where it decomposes, leaving a mirror-like deposit of metallic arsenic on a cold porcelain or glass surface. The test could detect minute traces in exhumed matter and became forensic toxicology's first decisive instrument.
place: Royal Arsenal, Woolwich, London (Marsh's workplace; paper published in Edinburgh)
grade_reason: The paper, the procedure, and the forensic adoption are multiply documented in primary and secondary sources; the chemistry is not in dispute. The famous failure modes (antimony, impure zinc) are themselves documented and graded as limitations.
earliest_attestation: Marsh (1836) paper; occasioned by an 1833 poisoning trial in which his decomposed sample failed to convince a jury

sources.ref: Marsh, J. (1836), 'Account of a method of separating small quantities of arsenic from substances with which it may be mixed', Edinburgh New Philosophical Journal 21
Science History Institute, 'Prefiguring the Arsenic Wars' (the Marsh test's gradual acceptance; early Marsh-test nulls at Tulle vs Orfila's positive)

competing_hypotheses: Known failure modes carried as limitations, not rivals: antimony can produce a similar mirror; arsenic impurities in the zinc reagents can produce false positives (the exact objection raised at Tulle in 1840)
falsifiability: The method is documented chemistry with a published procedure and a century of use; the grade covers the method's existence and forensic adoption, not the infallibility of any single application.

title: Cooke & Wheatstone: the first commercial telegraph (1837–1839)
claim: Cooke & Wheatstone's electric telegraph — patented 10 June 1837, trialed Euston–Camden 25 July 1837 — produced the world's first commercial telegraph line: Paddington to West Drayton (13 miles), opened July 1839 on the Great Western Railway.
place: Paddington Station, London (the 1839 line's London terminus)
grade_reason: Multiple independent primary attestation: the patent record (No. 8345, 10 June 1837), the GWR contract and Cooke's cost accounts, King's College London's Wheatstone exhibition archive, J. J. Fahie's 'Heroes of the Telegraph' contemporary account of the 25 July 1837 trial (Wheatstone at Euston, Cooke at Camden, Robert Stephenson watching), and Wikipedia's synthesis of the same primary sources. The 1839 line's daily operation and the 1840 Blackwall deployment are independently documented.
earliest_attestation: English patent 10 June 1837 (No. 8345); the GWR agreement finalized April–May 1838; contemporary press and company records

sources.ref: King's College London, Wheatstone exhibition: patent June 1837; 25 July 1837 trial; 9 July 1839 Paddington–West Drayton line; 'first successful commercial application of the electric telegraph in the world' (Blackwall, 1840); Morse's 1838 English patent application opposed by Cooke & Wheatstone
J. J. Fahie, 'A History of Electric Telegraphy' (via public-library.uk): 25 July 1837 trial account — Wheatstone at Euston, Cooke at Camden, Stephenson observing; the five-needle mechanism

Wikipedia, 'Cooke and Wheatstone telegraph': 1838 Paddington–West Drayton as 'the first commercial telegraph in the world'; five-needle six-wire system; the 1843 Slough extension and first public telegraph service
Cooke's cost accounts (via electrictelegraph.co.uk / Kieve): £2,817 10s. for laying the Paddington line; GWR agreement finalized April–May 1838

competing_hypotheses: The 'first successful commercial application' wording (telegraphy.eu): the July 1840 London & Blackwall Railway opening is sometimes named as the first *successful* commercial deployment — the Paddington line's claim rests on its daily 1839–40 operation
The Morse-priority counterclaim (19th c.): Morse's supporters argued the American system's simplicity made it the 'real' invention — a commercial-judgment argument, not a chronological one
falsifiability: Evidence that no such patent existed, that the 1837 trial did not occur, or that the 1839 line did not operate — the patent office record, the GWR contract (Cooke's £2,817 10s. costs), and King's College's Wheatstone archive would all have to be fabricated

title: Horace Mann invented the public school
claim: Horace Mann (1796-1859) invented the American public school — that is, before Mann's reforms as Secretary of the Massachusetts Board of Education (1837-1848), there were no public schools in America, and the public school is his invention.
place: Boston, Massachusetts
grade_reason: The invention claim dies on the documents: public, town-supported schooling predated Mann by two centuries (Boston Latin 1635, Dedham's taxpayer-funded school 1644, the 1647 Old Deluder Satan Act), and compulsory-schooling statutes predated him by the same margin.
earliest_attestation: The 'Father of American Education' honorific in modern reference works; the textbook one-liner is 20th-century

sources.ref: Wikipedia — Horace Mann (Secretary of the Massachusetts Board of Education 1837-1848; 'The Father of American Education')
Fiveable APUSH exam guide — Mann as 'the reason he gets called the Father of the American Public School System' (belief ecology)
Quizlet/U.S. education history flashcard sets — Boston Latin School founded 1635; Dedham 1 Jan 1644 authorized the first taxpayer-funded public school
EdWeek — 'The Foundation of Universal Education' (Carl F. Kaestle: nowhere was schooling entirely tax-supported and compulsory in the colonial era; 1852 Massachusetts compulsory-attendance law)

competing_hypotheses: The honorific reading: Mann is called the 'Father of American Education' (Wikipedia) as a champion and systemizer of the common school — an honorific, not a priority claim

The revisionist reading: the common-school movement was a multi-actor phenomenon (Barnard, Beecher, the state boards) and Mann's centrality is partly an artifact of his own superb public relations (the 12 annual reports)
The strong-invention reading (the claim graded here): the schoolbook one-liner that public schooling began with Mann
falsifiability: A document showing Massachusetts had no tax-supported or town-maintained schools before 1837

title: Horace Mann's common-school reforms (1837-1848)
claim: Horace Mann, as first Secretary of the Massachusetts Board of Education (1837-1848), campaigned for free, tax-funded, non-sectarian common schools open to all children: he established the first public normal school (Lexington, 1839) to train teachers, pushed standardized curricula, age-graded classrooms, written examinations and report cards, founded The Common School Journal (1838), and wrote 12 annual reports that carried the common-school model nationwide; most U.S. states adopted a version of the Massachusetts system.
place: Boston, Massachusetts
grade_reason: The reform record is multiply attested in Mann's own contemporary reports and the Board's paper trail; held below VERIFIED because this run's pass used secondary aggregators rather than the primary report texts.
earliest_attestation: Mann's 12 annual reports to the Massachusetts Board of Education, 1837-1848 (contemporary primary documents)

sources.ref: Wikipedia — Horace Mann (1st Secretary of the Massachusetts Board of Education 1837-1848; 12 annual reports; normal schools adopted by most states)
resourcesforhistoryteachers (pbworks) — 1837 secretaryship, Common School Journal 1838, normal schools, school-year lengthening, funding campaigns
ushistoryscene — Mann's 1844 European tour and the Prussian 'common schools' model; 1852 Massachusetts compulsory-attendance law
nodaway.org — Mann 'Father of the Common School Movement' dedication text (Lexington normal school 1839; standardized curricula; tax-supported funding)

competing_hypotheses: The multi-actor reading: Henry Barnard and Catharine Beecher share the movement's credit — Wikipedia's own account names them as major advocates alongside Mann
The limits reading: Mann's reforms were resisted in his lifetime (the tax fight, the sectarian fight) and the free-universal system arrived decades after he left office

The Prussian reading: Mann's 1844 European tour and Seventh Report show the Prussian model's influence — the universal, tax-funded, teacher-training system he admired was imported as a model, not invented (ushistoryscene; Mann's Report of an Educational Tour 1844)
falsifiability: Board minutes contradicting the secretaryship, or proof the 12 reports and the 1839 normal school are misattributed

title: The Morse system: the single wire that won the world (1837–1844)
claim: The Morse/Gale/Vail single-wire telegraph system — dots-and-dashes code, practical hand key, embossing receiver — was developed 1837–1844 and connected Washington to Baltimore on 24 May 1844 ('What hath God wrought'), becoming the system that won the world.
place: Baltimore, Maryland (the 24 May 1844 line: Washington, D.C. → Baltimore)
grade_reason: Multiple independent attestation: the 1840 patents (US Patent Office), the 1843 congressional appropriation, the 24 May 1844 demonstration and its press coverage, Vail's own 1845 history, the Library of Congress Morse Papers, and the commercial record (Magnetic Telegraph Company licensing; Western Union's 1851 formation; 4,000+ offices by 1866). Held at CORROBORATED rather than VERIFIED on the scientific-originality question: the system's physics rest on Henry's prior, unpatented 1828–31 work, and the code itself is Vail's (Jan 1838) — the 'Morse' system is a genuine American engineering achievement with multiple authors.
earliest_attestation: Morse's 1837 caveat; US patents 20 June 1840 ('Recording Electric Telegraph' and 'Telegraph Symbols'), based on the 1837 caveat; the 24 May 1844 demonstration, widely reported

sources.ref: Library of Congress, Morse Papers: 1837 caveat, 1840 patents, $30,000 appropriation 23 Feb 1843, 1844 demonstration details
HISTORY.com: single-circuit system of key, battery, wire, receiver; Morse/Gale/Vail collaboration
Vail (1845): code originated Jan 1838 by Alfred Vail; Vail's hand key; partnership terms (Vail half of foreign proceeds)

competing_hypotheses: The Vail-priority reading of the code itself: the practical code originated with Vail (Jan 1838), not Morse — the system is 'Morse' by patent and branding, plural by authorship
The Henry-withheld reading: had Henry patented rather than publishing openly, the American system's scientific core would have been his — the counterfactual is ungraded
falsifiability: Evidence that the 1844 line did not operate or that the system attributed to Morse/Gale/Vail was someone else's — the patents, the congressional record, and the Magnetic Telegraph Company's licensing (50+ companies by the early 1850s; Western Union 1851) would all have to be fabricated

title: Vulcanization: Goodyear's process, Hancock's patent, the band's enabling science
claim: Vulcanization — heating natural rubber with sulfur to make it durable, elastic, and temperature-stable — was discovered by Charles Goodyear (1839) and patented by him in the US (patent 3,633, 15 June 1844); Thomas Hancock independently developed the process and patented it in Britain about eight weeks before Goodyear filed there, and is credited today as an independent co-inventor. The Goodyear Tire & Rubber Company (founded 1898 by Frank Seiberling in Akron, Ohio) was named for Goodyear, never founded by him; he died 1 July 1860 about $200,000 in debt.
place: Connecticut — the Lower Naugatuck Valley rubber works (Goodyear's manufacturing ground); the 1839 stove incident is traditionally placed at Woburn, Massachusetts
grade_reason: Independent secondary attestation of the patents and the filing order (ACS, Rubber News, encyclopedia entries), but the 'reverse-engineered the samples' mechanism and the exact stove-incident details rest on secondary reporting — held below VERIFIED.
earliest_attestation: US Patent 3,633 (Goodyear, 1844); Hancock's British vulcanization patent (1843); the ACS centenary account of the sample shipment and the British filing race.

sources.ref: American Chemical Society (C&EN), 'Lessons learned from Charles Goodyear and the Committee on Patents and Related Matters' — 1839 stove discovery; samples sent to England; 'an English competitor was able to reverse engineer Goodyear's discovery and beat him to the British patent office'; Goodyear died 1860 deeply in debt

Rubber News column (2014), 'Happy anniversary to scientist's revolutionary discovery' — Goodyear 'filed his patent in England eight weeks after Thomas Hancock did and lost out'; Hancock credited in some sources as independent co-inventor

ThoughtCo (Mary Bellis, 2018), 'Vulcanized Rubber' — Goodyear US patent 3,633 for vulcanized rubber; 'On March 17, 1845, the first rubber band was patented by Stephen Perry of London, made from vulcanized rubber'

competing_hypotheses: The solo-inventor telling — 'Goodyear invented vulcanization' with no Hancock — survives in schoolbook shorthand; it dies on the British patent record

That Hancock reverse-engineered Goodyear's samples (the ACS account: Goodyear sent vulcanized samples to England seeking investors; Hancock analyzed them and beat him to the British patent office) versus truly independent discovery — carried honestly; either way the joint-credit verdict stands
The exact 1839 stove-incident date is multiply told (several origin stories circulate; Goodyear himself pointed to lengthy experimentation) — the discovery year is secure, the day is not
falsifiability: A showing that Hancock's 1843 British patent does not exist or covers a different process, or that Goodyear filed in Britain first — the filing order is on the patent record.

title: 'Paperweights are an ancient art' — the myth
claim: Glass paperweights — the glass dome weight as a desk object — are an ancient art, with the object itself dating back to antiquity (ancient Egypt, Rome, or the old world).
place: Paris, France — the trade center of the 1840s paperweight boom
grade_reason: Three kills: (1) no glass paperweight predates the 1840s — the earliest datable examples are French (Baccarat, Saint-Louis, Clichy) and Venetian, all mid-1840s; (2) the telling conflates the millefiori TECHNIQUE (centuries old — Murano 16th c., Roman murrine before) with the OBJECT (the glass dome weight), which is modern; (3) the 'Venetian antique' framing is 19th-century dealer/collector romance, contradicted by the documented 1840s invention boom.
earliest_attestation: The telling circulates in trivia-site and antique-dealer copy in the 20th/21st century; the earliest datable glass paperweights are mid-1840s French/Venetian (see companion records).

sources.ref: Antique Trader, 'The Zen of Glass Paperweights' — glass paperweights originated in France around 1845 (Baccarat, Saint Louis, Clichy), developed as affordable objets d'art/gift items, exhibited at the 1851 Great Exhibition
L. H. Selman Fine Glass Paperweights, 'Why Collect' — by 1845 France was the undeniable paperweight center of the world; after about 1860 the art all but disappeared for eighty years

Christopher Proudlove (Free Online Library) — Pietro Bigaglia of an old Venetian glass family 'generally credited with the manufacture of the first glass paperweight in 1845'; Venetian millefiori cane work since the 15th century

Carters price guide (Baccarat paperweights) — the competing 'Venice-first' tradition: paperweights 'evolved in Venice in the early nineteenth century, and spread to France via Bohemia about 1845' — both tellings agree on the 1840s, never antiquity

competing_hypotheses: The honest scoped telling that survives: the glass paperweight is a 19th-century invention (1840s, France/Venice), which this record covers separately

That non-glass weights held papyri and scrolls down in antiquity — true of any heavy object, but no ancient object identifiable as a glass paperweight exists; the claim under review is about the glass dome weight, not the function of holding paper
falsifiability: A datable glass paperweight object (distinct from a mere glass lump or millefiori bead) with a secure pre-1800 provenance — none has ever been produced; the object's earliest documented examples are all 1840s.

title: The 1840 Lafarge arsenic trial at Tulle
claim: Marie Lafarge was convicted of murdering her husband Charles by arsenic poisoning at the Tulle assizes on 19 September 1840, in a trial dominated by forensic chemistry: the Marsh test for arsenic, applied by Mathieu Orfila as the deciding expert. The trial is widely described as the first murder trial decided by forensic toxicological evidence.
place: Tulle, Corrèze, France (assize court; crime at Le Glandier)
grade_reason: Split by doctrine. The CONVICTION is VERIFIED: a court-record event of 19 September 1840, multiply reported (sentence of life with hard labor, commuted by Louis-Philippe). The 'first trial decided by forensic chemistry' reading is CORROBORATED: independently stated in modern secondary literature (Bertomeu-Sánchez 2006; Science History Institute; the trial record's own evidence chain), though an absolute 'first' is hard to prove — fenced, not asserted. The GUILT (that Marie actually poisoned Charles) is CLAIMED: arsenic was found in the body by Orfila's controlled tests, and a witness (Anna Brun) reported seeing white powder stirred into the victim's food; but the evidence is a single forensic chain with real contemporary contamination debate (Raspail's objections were never adjudicated — he arrived four hours too late for the jury), and the accused maintained innocence to her death.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary daily newspaper coverage of the Tulle assizes (summer-autumn 1840); trial record of the Corrèze assize court

sources.ref: Assize court record, Tulle, 3-19 September 1840 (conviction and sentence; commutation by King Louis-Philippe)
Contemporary daily press coverage of the Lafarge affair (cause célèbre, pan-European press interest)

Bertomeu-Sánchez, J.R. (2006), 'Sense and sensitivity: Mateu Orfila, the Marsh test and the Lafarge affair', in Bertomeu-Sánchez & Nieto-Galan (eds.), M. Orfila and his times, Science History Publications
Bertomeu-Sánchez, J.R. (2015), La verdad sobre el caso Lafarge, El Serbal
Science History Institute, 'Prefiguring the Arsenic Wars' (Orfila's Tulle tests, the soil/reagent controls, Raspail's critique of Orfila's methods)
Adler, L. (1986), L'Amour à l'arsenic: histoire de Marie Lafarge, Denoël
Lafarge, M. (1841), Mémoires de madame Lafarge (self-serving primary source; innocence maintained)

competing_hypotheses: The natural-death line: Charles died of cholera or cholera-like illness, common in the region in 1840, and the arsenic readings were contamination or error
The contamination line (Raspail): arsenic in the zinc reagents, the copper vessels used to boil the cadaver, and the cemetery soil could all have produced the readings; the test proved nothing
The railroaded line: Marie was convicted by Orfila's institutional authority and the press's fascination, not by the evidence — she protested her innocence until her death in 1852
falsifiability: A documented earlier murder conviction resting principally on chemical evidence would demote the 'first' reading; proof that the tested samples were tampered with would move the poisoning claim to DEBUNKED.

title: The Penny Black (1 May 1840)
claim: The Penny Black was the world's first adhesive postage stamp used in a public postal system, issued in the United Kingdom on 1 May 1840 (valid for use from 6 May). It bore the profile of the young Queen Victoria, was printed by Perkins Bacon (68,808,000 printed), and was the instrument of Rowland Hill's 1837 postal reform: a flat rate of one penny per half-ounce regardless of distance, prepaid by the sender — replacing the old system under which the recipient paid, charged by the sheet and by distance travelled.
place: London, United Kingdom (issue; Perkins Bacon printing)
grade_reason: Multiply and independently attested: Hill's 1837 reform pamphlet and parliamentary record, the 1840 issue and Perkins Bacon print run, and the surviving stamps themselves (about 1.3 million still exist) — the artifact and its paper trail converge.
earliest_attestation: Rowland Hill's 1837 pamphlet 'Post Office Reform: Its Importance and Practicability'; parliamentary enquiry record (February 1837); Perkins Bacon print records

sources.ref: Hill, R. (1837), 'Post Office Reform: Its Importance and Practicability' (the reform pamphlet)
Parliamentary enquiry into the Post Office, February 1837 (Hill's testimony on the pre-paid stamp)
Perkins Bacon print records, London 1840 (68,808,000 printed)
Surviving Penny Black stamps, c. 1.3 million extant (the artifact as its own evidence)
Penny Black — Wikipedia (issue dates, print figures, Hill reform summary; secondary aggregator)

competing_hypotheses: The design-competition story: Hill and Henry Cole announced a competition (2,600 entries, all rejected) and chose a rough design featuring the young Victoria's profile — the 'competition' framing vs the chosen-design reality

Earlier adhesive-stamp suggestions: the idea had been proposed in the Austrian Empire, Sweden, and possibly Greece — the first-suggestion claim vs the first-in-public-use claim, which the grade rests on
falsifiability: An earlier adhesive stamp verifiably used in a public postal system — a suggestion or a private issue would not suffice.

title: "Pyramids are Egypt's monopoly"
claim: Pyramids are an Egyptian monopoly: Egypt has the most pyramids in the world, and the pyramid-building tradition belongs to Egyptian civilization alone.
place: The claim is a global belief about pyramid distribution; pin carried at Meroë, the counter-evidence's representative site
grade_reason: The numbers are decisive and have been stable in the archaeological literature for a century: ~255 catalogued Nubian pyramids against 118–138 Egyptian. The Kushite building program also outlasted Egypt's by ~2,000 years. The monopoly claim is false on count and on tradition.
earliest_attestation: The 19th-century European archaeological and popular frame (Lepsius, Baedeker, the museum gallery); the modern textbook/tourism sentence 'Egypt, land of the pyramids'

sources.ref: The archaeological corpus itself: ~255 Nubian pyramids (Reisner 1908–1932 corpus; UNESCO 2011 Meroe listing) vs. 118–138 Egyptian pyramids
The Vintage News 2016 summary of the standard figures: 255 Sudan / 118–138 Egypt — reflecting the established literature, not a reclassification
National Geographic on the Nubian pyramid tradition: c. 900 BCE–400 CE, versus Egyptian royal pyramid construction ending c. 1500 BCE

competing_hypotheses: The definition-of-pyramid escape hatch: restrict 'pyramid' to the classic Old Kingdom royal tomb form, which would hand the count back to Egypt — rejected, because the claim as believed by the public is about pyramids in general, and the Nubian structures are pyramids by every functional definition (royal tombs, pyramidal superstructure)
falsifiability: A full inventory showing Egypt's pyramid count exceeding Sudan's — impossible against the catalogued ~255 standing Nubian structures vs. 118–138 Egyptian

title: The recipient-pays root: before 1840, the addressee paid
claim: Before Rowland Hill's 1840 uniform penny postage, recipients — not senders — usually paid for the post. Britain's prepaid-postage revolution (the Penny Black, issued 1 May 1840, valid from 6 May) flipped the default so the sender paid. Business reply mail and the international reply coupon are therefore the formalized return of the older recipient-pays idea: a prepaid-reply instrument lets the party expecting the reply bear the cost, inside a system where sender-pays is now the default.
place: London, United Kingdom — 1840 postal reform
grade_reason: The Smithsonian National Postal Museum's own account states the pre-1840 recipient-pays norm and the May 1840 flip; Rowland Hill / Penny Black mechanics are multiply attested; held below VERIFIED on the secondary transmission in this pass.
earliest_attestation: Smithsonian National Postal Museum (via Smithsonian Magazine): 'Before Great Britain introduced prepaid postage in May 1840... Recipients — not senders — paid for postage'

sources.ref: Smithsonian Magazine (citing the Smithsonian National Postal Museum), 'First Known Piece of Mail Sent Using a Stamp Goes to Auction' — 'Before Great Britain introduced prepaid postage in May 1840, sending mail was cumbersome... Recipients — not senders — paid for postage'; the Penny Black issued 1 May 1840, valid from 6 May

Mark Smith, 'An invention that put its stamp on communication' (Free Online Library) — the Penny Black launched May 1840; 'Before then, postal charges were based on distance and number of sheets in the letter, and the recipient usually paid for the post, not the sender'

competing_hypotheses: That recipient-pays was universal before 1840 — it was the usual arrangement, with exceptions (franking, prepaid schemes); carried as the honestly scoped reading
That the Mulready prepaid envelopes (1 May 1840) rather than the Penny Black mark the flip — both launched together; the flip is the system change, not one object
falsifiability: Contemporary rate tables showing senders as the default payers before 1840 in Britain

title: 'Thomas Cook invented tourism' (myth)
claim: Thomas Cook invented tourism — the 5 July 1841 Leicester–Loughborough excursion created the travel and leisure industry.
place: Leicester, England (the 'birthplace of tourism' claim's origin point)
grade_reason: Organized leisure travel predates Cook by centuries: the Grand Tour (c. 1660–1840s), the English spa towns, and commercial guidebooks — Mariana Starke's Travels on the Continent (1820, John Murray) and Murray's Hand-Books (1836) — all predate the 1841 excursion, and ERIH places Cook as 'one of several' mid-century entrepreneurs who popularised railway travel. Cook's genuine innovation was the chartered group excursion at a fixed per-head price, the escorted tour, and the package-holiday business — not tourism itself.
earliest_attestation: The retrospective 'birthplace of tourism' framing (e.g., Story of Leicester's 'birthplace of popular tourism' accolade); the underlying excursion is attested in 1841

sources.ref: ERIH biography of Thomas Cook: 'Thomas Cook was one of several entrepreneurs who in the mid-nineteenth century popularised railway travel throughout Europe through publications and through the organisation of excursions and holidays' — the 'one of several' directly contradicts the lone-inventor framing

Wikipedia 'Thomas Cook': the pre-existing travel world Cook entered — his later commercial milestones show the actual shape of his innovation (1845 first profit-making excursion, 1846 Scotland, 1851 Great Exhibition 165,000, Cook's Excursionist monthly magazine, the continental coupon system from the 1855 Paris Exhibition)

The pre-existing travel infrastructure, via the team's own tourism beat (Dr. Verity Hollis, #174): the Grand Tour (c. 1660–1840s), the English spa towns, and published guidebooks — Mariana Starke's Travels on the Continent (1820, John Murray) and Murray's Hand-Books (1836) — all predate the 1841 excursion; the excursion was a new business model applied to an old human habit

competing_hypotheses: Cook invented the package holiday (the narrower, defensible claim: his 1845 commercial tours, the 1855 coupon system, and the escorted-tour model were genuine innovations — that is the excursion and business record, not the invention claim)

Cook invented mass tourism (the popular shorthand — defensible only if 'mass' is defined as railway-scale group excursions at a fixed per-head price, which is the excursion record, not the invention claim)
falsifiability: Evidence that no organized leisure travel, guidebooks, group excursions, or travel businesses existed anywhere before July 1841

title: De Moleyns's 1841 patent — the lamp's birth certificate
claim: In 1841, Frederick de Moleyns of England was granted the first patent for an incandescent lamp: a design using powdered charcoal heated between two coils of platinum wire in vacuo.
place: London, England (British patent register)
grade_reason: The patent grant is multiply attested in the institutional chronologies (Bright 1949 via the UK National Archives; the same chronology the Edison solo-inventor debunk rests on); held below VERIFIED because the primary patent document was accessed here through secondary aggregators, and the surviving record carries the device only to the patent stage — no working surviving de Moleyns lamp is documented.
earliest_attestation: The 1841 British patent grant itself; carried in Bright 1949's 'Chronology of the incandescent lamp and thermionic valve' (p39), preserved via the UK National Archives web archive.

sources.ref: UK National Archives web archive — 'Appendix 2: Chronology of the incandescent lamp and thermionic valve' (citing Bright 1949, p39: '1841 — de Moleyns made lamp by dropping powdered charcoal between two coils of platinum wire in vacuo')
historydraft.com — 'The First patent for an Incandescent Lamp' (1841, England; de Moleyns granted the first incandescent-lamp patent, platinum wires in a vacuum bulb, carbon used)

Encyclopedia (Wikipedia-derived) — 'Incandescent lamp': 'In 1841 Frederick de Moleyns of England was granted the first patent for an incandescent lamp, with a design using powdered charcoal heated between two platinum wires'

competing_hypotheses: The patent was never reduced to a practical working lamp — practical priority belongs to the later carbon-filament workers (Swan's 1860s lamps and 1878 patent, Edison's 1879 system)
The 'first patent' superlative rests on the surviving register; lost or unsealed earlier filings cannot be excluded in principle
falsifiability: A dated pre-1841 incandescent-lamp patent in the registers, or proof the 1841 grant was never issued to de Moleyns

title: Mackay 1841 — the popularizer of the tulip-mania ruin narrative
claim: Charles Mackay's 1841 book Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds created the popular form of the tulip-mania story — the version every subsequent popular account descends from: all levels of society swept in, fortunes ruined, Dutch commerce shocked.
place: London (publication)
grade_reason: The book's existence, its 1841 date, its claims, its continuous print run, and its dominance of the popular narrative are all independently verifiable — it is the documented source of the ruin version.
earliest_attestation: Mackay 1841 itself — the book exists, the tulip chapter exists, and its claims ('the rage among the Dutch to possess them was so great that the ordinary industry of the country was neglected'; merchants 'reduced almost to beggary') are on the page

sources.ref: Charles Mackay, Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds (1841), tulip-mania chapter: the chimney-sweeps-to-nobility narrative, the ruined fortunes, the 'severe shock' to Dutch commerce

The citation trail: Mackay's account 'unchallenged, and mostly unexamined, until the 1980s' — cited by Galbraith (A Short History of Financial Euphoria), invoked in dot-com and 2008 commentary, quoted by the Dutch central bank president on Bitcoin (2013)

Anne Goldgar (2007) on Mackay's sources: most period accounts 'are based on one or two contemporary pieces of propaganda and a prodigious amount of plagiarism' — Mackay treated 17th-c. satirical pamphlets as fact (Smithsonian interview: 'I couldn't find anybody that went bankrupt')

competing_hypotheses: Mackay amplified rather than invented: 17th-c. satirical pamphlets already carried the ruin framing as moral commentary — Mackay's sin was treating satire as reportage, not inventing the story from nothing.
The Galbraith lineage: mid-20th-c. economists canonized Mackay's version as an economic case study, giving a literary artifact the authority of data.
falsifiability: A pre-1841 popular account carrying the full ruin narrative (nation-wide participation, mass bankruptcies, lasting economic shock) in the same form — the pamphlets carry the moral, Mackay carried the economics

title: 1841: Poe's 'Rue Morgue' founds detective fiction
claim: Edgar Allan Poe's "The Murders in the Rue Morgue" (Graham's Magazine, April 1841) is the first detective story — the founding document of detective fiction, with the locked-room murder, the eccentric reasoning detective (C. Auguste Dupin), and the admiring narrator as the genre's DNA.
place: Philadelphia (Graham's Magazine) / Paris (the story's fictional setting)
grade_reason: The 1841 magazine publication is a dated, archived primary document — the claim needs no reconstruction. Multiple independent lines (the trilogy itself, the genre historians' consensus from Chesterton to P.D. James, and Doyle's own in-canon acknowledgment of the Dupin lineage) converge on the same first document.
earliest_attestation: The magazine publication itself, April 1841 — the document is the claim's own evidence. Lineage attestation: Doyle's own canon cites the descent — in 'A Study in Scarlet' (1887) Holmes dismisses Dupin ('In my opinion, Dupin was a very inferior fellow...'), the genre's founder acknowledged by the genre's most famous inheritor; Doyle repeatedly named Poe as a literary influence.

sources.ref: Graham's Magazine, April 1841 — the first publication of 'The Murders in the Rue Morgue'
'The Mystery of Marie Rogêt' (1842) and 'The Purloined Letter' (1844) — the complete Dupin trilogy, the genre's founding corpus
Arthur Conan Doyle, 'A Study in Scarlet' (1887) — Holmes's Dupin comparison, the in-canon lineage acknowledgment

competing_hypotheses: Proto-claims: E.T.A. Hoffmann's Das Fräulein von Scuderi (1819/1820) and Voltaire's Zadig (1747) contain ratiocination episodes — but neither establishes the detective-story FORM (crime, investigation, solution delivered by a reasoning figure); the genre historians' consensus keeps 1841
The Chinese route: Judge Dee / the gong'an tradition (earliest translated centuries later) — parallel, not the Western genre's document lineage
falsifiability: An earlier published work containing the detective-story form — a crime investigated by a reasoning detective figure delivering a deductive solution — dated and documented before April 1841.

title: 'Slocum invented the stapler in 1841' — DEBUNKED
claim: Samuel Slocum of Poughkeepsie, New York, received U.S. Patent 2,275 on September 30, 1841, for a 'machine for sticking pins in paper' — and this machine is often misidentified as the first stapler.
place: Poughkeepsie, New York — Slocum's pin works
grade_reason: The patent's own drawing and description show a machine that stuck rows of pins into folded paper to package them for sale — 'not a paper fastener at all.' Slocum's life's work was pin manufacturing (solid-head pins, 'Poughkeepsie Pins'); the stapler credit is a category error that the primary document refutes.
earliest_attestation: U.S. Patent 2,275 (30 Sept 1841), 'machine for sticking pins in paper' — examined by collector-historian Curtis A. Scaglione from the patent drawing and description.

sources.ref: Curtis A. Scaglione, 'Fastener History' — officemuseum.online: patent drawing/description examined — 'not a paper fastener at all, but a machine that stuck a number of pins to paper for the purpose of packaging them in quantity'; pin-sticking machine in use by 1841 (Chauncey Depew, One Hundred Years of American Commerce, via Stanford Library)
Wikipedia, 'Samuel Slocum' — the 30 Sept 1841 patent (#2275) 'is often believed to be the first stapler. In fact, this patent... is for a device used for packaging pins'

competing_hypotheses: The misreading is understandable: it was a machine, it drove things into paper, and 'Poughkeepsie Pins' marketing language is ambiguous at a distance
Some retellings credit Slocum with 'the U.S. stapler in 1841' — the patent drawing and description settle that the product was pins, packaged for sale
falsifiability: The patent document itself is the killer — it describes sticking pins into paper for packaging; a different specification would change the grade.

title: Cook's first railway excursion, 5 July 1841
claim: On 5 July 1841, Thomas Cook chartered a special train from the Midland Counties Railway and carried some 485–500 members of the Leicester Temperance Society from Leicester Campbell Street station to Loughborough and back for one shilling each — the first publicly advertised special railway excursion.
place: Leicester, England (Campbell Street station)
grade_reason: Multiple independent secondary sources agree on the date, route, fare, party, and purpose; the 'first' is qualified to 'first publicly advertised special railway excursion' because ERIH documents similar trips on the Liverpool & Manchester Railway after 1830.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary 1841 temperance-press reporting of the excursion, via the standard secondary accounts; Cook's own retrospective account of the June 1841 Market Harborough–Leicester walk that sparked the idea

sources.ref: Wikipedia 'Thomas Cook': the June 1841 walk from Market Harborough to Leicester, the 'thought flashed through my brain' quotation, the 5 July 1841 excursion — 485 members of the Leicester Temperance Society, Leicester Campbell Street to Loughborough, one shilling each, train hired from the Midland Counties Railway; later commercial milestones (1845 Liverpool/Caernarfon/Snowdon with a 60-page guidebook, 1846 Scotland, 165,000 to the Great Exhibition 1851, Cook's Excursionist, the continental coupon system from 1855)

Story of Leicester, 'Thomas Cook's Leicester': Leicester as 'the birthplace of popular tourism'; the 5 July 1841 first rail excursion — 485 passengers including Cook's seven-year-old son John Mason Cook, open tub-style carriages, a band, return at 10:30pm; statue outside London Road station

ERIH biography of Thomas Cook: 5 July 1841 excursion for 500 temperance society members at one shilling for the 20 km journey; notes it 'has often been called the first railway excursion, although similar trips were organised on the Liverpool & Manchester Railway soon after its opening in 1830'; 1845 first commercial trip with a 60-page guidebook

Alliance House Foundation, 'Thomas Cook — The Temperance Traveller': the excursion as 'the first publically advertised excursion train in England'; the 175th-anniversary framing; 150,000+ to the Great Exhibition in 1851

competing_hypotheses: The excursion was the first railway excursion of any kind (over-reading: ERIH notes similar trips were organised on the Liverpool & Manchester Railway soon after its opening in 1830)
The headcount was 570 (a 2003 railway-society bulletin) rather than the commonly cited 485
falsifiability: Midland Counties Railway charter records or contemporary July 1841 press showing the excursion never ran, ran on a different date, or was not Cook's organizing

title: The tulip crash that bankrupted a nation — the ruin reading of 1637
claim: The 1637 collapse of tulip prices devastated the economy of the Dutch Republic — ruining fortunes across the nation and inflicting a severe, years-long shock on Dutch commerce.
place: The Dutch Republic (claim) vs the archive (Amsterdam/Haarlem)
grade_reason: Three independent kills: Goldgar's archival audit finds hundreds of traders and almost no bankruptcies; the futures contracts moved no money, so there were no losses to transmit; and the Dutch economy shows no 1637 downturn — the Republic stayed the world's richest economy.
earliest_attestation: Charles Mackay, Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds (1841) — attestation of the BELIEF (all levels of society, merchants 'reduced almost to beggary', commerce suffering 'a severe shock'), not of the fact

sources.ref: Anne Goldgar, Tulipmania (2007): archival audit — trade limited to a few hundred merchants/craftsmen; 'fewer than half a dozen' experienced financial troubles in the period, and even of these it is not clear tulips were to blame; 'no real effect on the economy whatsoever' (HISTORY.com interview)

The futures-contract structure itself (Goldgar 2007; Wikipedia Tulip mania, citing the scholarship): money had not changed hands between buyers and sellers, so profits were never realized — the collapse could not transmit losses to the wider economy

The Dutch economy's continued primacy: the Republic remained one of the world's leading economic and financial powers with the highest per-capita income in the world from about 1600 to about 1720 — no 1637 downturn in the record

competing_hypotheses: Garber's stronger position: the event was never an economic bubble at all — the ruin reading dies twice, once as a claim about the economy and once as a claim about the prices.

The efficient-market-hypothesis readings since the 1980s: rational explanations for the rise and fall (Thirty Years' War lull, hyacinth-type introduction pricing, the voidable-contract expectation) — the mania may be partly a framing artifact.
falsifiability: Notarial records showing mass bankruptcies clearly attributable to tulips in 1637–1638, or fiscal records showing a Dutch economic downturn beginning in 1637 — the archive has been searched for a century and produced neither

title: The showman, minus the sentence — Barnum's documented career
claim: Phineas Taylor Barnum (1810–1891) was the American showman of the American Museum in New York (1842–1865 fire), the admitted humbug-promoter (the Feejee Mermaid, Joice Heth, Tom Thumb, Jumbo), and the man who built and exhibited his own replica of the Cardiff Giant in 1869–1870 after David Hannum refused to sell.
place: New York City — Barnum's American Museum (1842–1865); the Cardiff Giant replica exhibited here 1869–1870
grade_reason: Multiply attested in Barnum's own published autobiography, contemporary press, and the court record — the Cardiff Giant lawsuit's ruling is a matter of record, not memory. Held below VERIFIED because Barnum was his own principal biographer and shaped the legend (the 'I was born a showman' persona) — the autobiography is a primary source with a motive, so the grade stays at CORROBORATED for the self-authored layers.
earliest_attestation: Barnum's own 1855 autobiography 'The Life of P. T. Barnum' — the showman as his own documentarian, admitting humbugs in print; contemporary newspapers and playbills; the Cardiff Giant court record (Hannum v. Barnum, 1870), in which the judge ruled Barnum's 'original' claim was true because both giants were fakes.

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'There's a sucker born every minute' — Barnum (1810–1891) background; the American Museum; the Cardiff Giant affair as the attribution's vehicle
The Independent (Lafayette), 'Too Good To Be True' — Barnum's American Museum, the refused offers to Hannum, the replica, the 1870 ruling

competing_hypotheses: The 'Greatest Showman' reading: the 2017 film's Barnum — the dreamer who invented the circus to celebrate difference. Barnum was a genuine promoter of talent (Tom Thumb, Jenny Lind), but the film's arc inverts his business: his 19th-century show sold curiosity as oddity, and he never claimed the film's pieties.

The pure-con-man reading: Barnum as nothing but a fraud. Against it: he advertised his humbugs as humbugs to audiences willing to pay for the puzzle, sued and won the Cardiff Giant case on the facts, and left a documented paper trail (his autobiography 'The Life of P. T. Barnum,' 1855, openly catalogues his own deceptions).
falsifiability: Evidence that the American Museum, the named attractions, or the Cardiff Giant replica episode did not occur as documented — against Barnum's autobiography, the newspapers, and the court record.

title: Crawford Long's ether surgeries, 1842 (published 1849)
claim: On 30 March 1842, in Jefferson, Georgia, surgeon Crawford W. Long removed a tumor from the neck of James M. Venable under inhaled sulfuric ether — with earlier 'ether frolic' observation (pain-free bruises while inhaling) as the insight, and further ether operations through 1842 (a second tumor operation 6 June, a toe amputation 3 July). He published the account in the Southern Medical and Surgical Journal in December 1849.
place: Jefferson, Georgia (Long's office)
grade_reason: Long's own published account with named certificates, the surviving 1849 original in the US National Library of Medicine, and the long institutional afterlife (Doctors' Day, the 1926 Statuary Hall statue, the 1940 stamp, the Crawford W. Long Museum) — held at CORROBORATED rather than VERIFIED on the single-source structure of the evidence and the 1840s historiographical dispute.
earliest_attestation: Long's 1849 article itself, with certificates from Venable, two witnesses present at the operation, and Venable's family — plus Long's 1854 appeal to Congress via Senator Dawson.

sources.ref: Long's 1849 account (original, via NIH/Archive.org): the 30 March 1842 operation ('the patient gave no evidence of suffering'), the 6 June second operation, the 3 July toe amputation, the certificates of patient and witnesses, the seven-year-delay explanation ('through negligence... my friends think I would be doing myself injustice').

The Conversation/MedicalXpress (2019): the ether-frolic origin, the six witnesses, the 1990s historiographical diminishing (Osler 1912's 'but it was not until October 16, 1846' framing), Friedman's and Friedland's chapter on Long.

Alamy photo-archive record (scholarly summary): 'recognized as the first physician to have administered ether anesthesia for surgery' (March 30, 1842, James M. Venable); the 1849 publication held at the US National Library of Medicine; the 1854 Dawson Congressional presentation.

competing_hypotheses: That the documentary record is thin enough that the 'first ever' superlative remains contested (Long's own contemporaries and later historians diminished or doubted the claim as recently as the 1990s — the claim is CORROBORATED, not VERIFIED).
That Long's delay (seven years to publication) forfeited the historical credit — the sociological judgment, graded separately from the documentary fact of the 1842 operations.
falsifiability: Exposure of the 1849 account as fabricated (e.g. the certificates shown to be forged, or Venable's own denial on the record).

title: Poe's 'Balloon-Hoax' — the Atlantic crossing that never happened (13 April 1844)
