claim: Edgar Allan Poe's 'Balloon-Hoax' — printed as a news extra in the New York Sun on 13 April 1844 with the headline 'THE ATLANTIC CROSSED IN THREE DAYS!' — reported that Monck Mason's steering balloon 'Victoria' had crossed the Atlantic in 75 hours and landed on Sullivan's Island, South Carolina. No such flight occurred: the Victoria never existed, the passengers were invented (the real novelist William Harrison Ainsworth was listed among them), and the Sun printed a retraction on 15 April 1844.
place: New York Sun building (publication); purported landing at Sullivan's Island, South Carolina
grade_reason: The hoax is proven by its own paper trail: the Sun printed the 'extra' on 13 April 1844 and its own retraction on 15 April — 'we are inclined to believe that the intelligence is erroneous.' The first real Atlantic balloon crossing came 134 years later (Double Eagle II, August 1978). DEBUNKED as NEWS — the hoax EVENT (that Poe and the Sun printed it) is VERIFIED on the same documents.
earliest_attestation: New York Sun, 13 April 1844 — 'ASTOUNDING NEWS! BY EXPRESS VIA NORFOLK: THE ATLANTIC CROSSED IN THREE DAYS!'

sources.ref: Wikipedia 'The Balloon-Hoax': publication history — 13 April 1844 extra with headline text; retraction printed 15 April 1844 ('we are inclined to believe that the intelligence is erroneous'); Thomas Monck Mason's 1836 book as source material; real William Harrison Ainsworth listed as passenger

Museum of Hoaxes, 'The Great Balloon Hoax (1844)': Sun extra 13 April 1844; quickly revealed as Poe-authored hoax; Victoria illustration redrawn from the 1843 'Remarks on the Ellipsoidal Balloon' frontispiece; Poe on the Sun building steps that day telling crowds it was a hoax

Smithsonian Magazine, 'A Brief History of Trans-Atlantic Balloon Crossings' (11 Aug 2017): Poe 'authored a hoax about a successful crossing in 1844 — and actually fooled The New York Sun'; 14 failed trans-Atlantic missions before the 1978 success

competing_hypotheses: The authorship question: Poe's authorship is near-universal in the scholarship, but the April 15 retraction's author 'has not been determined and is perhaps Poe himself' — the retraction's authorship stays a fence, not a threat to the hoax finding.

The inspiration line: Poe drew on Thomas Monck Mason's real 1836 London-to-Weilburg balloon voyage (described in Mason's 1837 'Account of the Late Aeronautical Expedition from London to Weilburg') and on the 1843 anonymous pamphlet 'Remarks on the Ellipsoidal Balloon' (frontispiece illustration redrawn for the Victoria). The story is fabrication built on real ballooning — which is why it worked.
falsifiability: A landing record, customs entry, or corroborating eyewitness from Sullivan's Island, April 1844, for the Victoria's passengers

title: Rynd's hollow needle: the first known hypodermic injection (1844)
claim: On 3 June 1844, Dublin surgeon Francis Rynd used a thin hollow needle to inject a solution of morphine (fifteen grains of acetate of morphia in one drachm of creosote) under the skin of Margaret Cox, a 59-year-old neuralgia patient at the Meath Hospital, to the supra-orbital, temporal, malar and buccal nerves — the first known hypodermic injection.
place: Meath Hospital, Dublin, Ireland
grade_reason: Rynd's own contemporary-published account gives patient, date, dosage, instrument and outcome ('In the space of a minute all pain ... had ceased'); the secondary literature agrees it is 'the first known hypodermic injection' (Wikipedia, MDDI). Held at CORROBORATED rather than VERIFIED on the single-primary-source structure and on Rynd's 1861-delayed elaboration of the instrument.
earliest_attestation: Rynd, F. (1845). Dublin Medical Press, 12 March 1845 — Rynd's own account of the 3 June 1844 injection (quoted at length in Wikipedia, 'Francis Rynd')

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Francis Rynd' — the 12 March 1845 Dublin Medical Press report quoted at length: Margaret Cox, aetat. 59, the 3 June 1844 injection, 'the first known hypodermic injection'

Medical Independent, 'Through the eye of the needle: A remarkable medical life' — Rynd's training under Sir Philip Crampton at the Meath Hospital, the 1844 invention, 'the greatest boon to medicine since the discovery of chloroform'
MDDI Online, 'The Hypodermic Syringe: Greatest Medical Device of All Time?' — 'The hollow metal needle was invented in 1844 by Irish physician Francis Rynd'

competing_hypotheses: Rynd's device was a gravity-fed trocar-and-cannula arrangement, not a true syringe — the 'first injection' belongs to him, the 'first syringe' to the 1853 pair (the standard division)
Earlier unrecorded hollow-needle injections occurred before 1844 (possible but unattested — the grade rests on 'first known', not 'first')
falsifiability: Proof the Dublin Medical Press report was fabricated, or a documented earlier hypodermic injection

title: Pasch's safety match (1844) — the separated design
claim: Swedish chemist Gustaf Erik Pasch (1788–1862), professor at the Karolinska Institute and student of Berzelius, was granted the first patent on the safety match in 1844. His design moved the phosphorus from the match head to a specially prepared striking surface: the head contained only potassium chlorate (no phosphorus), and ignition required striking on the red-phosphorus surface. Manufacturing at J.S. Bagge & Co.'s chemical factory in Stockholm failed — the striking surface was poor quality and red phosphorus was prohibitively expensive — and production ceased.
place: Stockholm, Sweden (J.S. Bagge & Co.'s chemical factory)
grade_reason: The 1844 patent and the Bagge & Co. failure are consistently attested; held at CORROBORATED on patent-record basis rather than multi-source primary documentation.
earliest_attestation: Swedish patent grant to Gustaf Erik Pasch, 1844

sources.ref: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustaf_Erik_Pasch — 1844 patent; Berzelius red-phosphorus idea; Bagge & Co. failure on cost and surface quality

competing_hypotheses: Berzelius had the red-phosphorus substitution idea first but could not make a reliable match; Pasch's contribution was the working separation design, honestly credited to both
Pasch's 1844 patent is the Swedish filing; the priority for the separated safety match rests on the patent grant, not on commercial production (which failed)
falsifiability: A dated safety-match patent or reliably dated commercial separated match predating 1844

title: Horace Wells: nitrous oxide 1844, the failed Boston demo, and the 1848 death
claim: On 11 December 1844 (the day after witnessing Samuel Cooley's painless bruised leg at a Gardner Quincy Colton laughing-gas exhibition), Hartford dentist Horace Wells had his own wisdom tooth painlessly extracted under nitrous oxide, used the gas on 12–15 dental patients, and in January 1845 demonstrated it publicly in Boston before John Collins Warren and medical students — the demonstration failed when the gas was removed too soon and the patient groaned, earning cries of 'humbug.' Wells died by suicide under chloroform in New York's Tombs Prison on 24 January 1848; the ADA (1864) and AMA (1870) later declared him the real discoverer of anesthesia.
place: Hartford, Connecticut (Wells's practice); Boston demonstration at MGH
grade_reason: Multiple independent attestations: the 1847 pamphlet's four witness statements, the Paris letter's account of the Boston trip, Nature's 1948 summary, and the later institutional recognitions — held at CORROBORATED on the retrospective documentary structure (the 1844 events reach us through 1847 publications).
earliest_attestation: Wells's 1847 pamphlet 'A History of the Discovery of the Application of Nitrous Oxide Gas, Ether, and Other Vapors, to Surgical Operations' with four witness statements (three medical students present at Boston, plus Daniel T. Curtis); his February 1847 Paris letter; Nature's 1948 centenary abstract.

sources.ref: Nature (1948 centenary): the Colton exhibition of 10 December 1844, Cooley's bruised leg, Wells's own tooth extraction the next day, the January 1845 Boston demonstration ending in 'charlatan' and 'humbug' cries, the 24 January 1848 Tombs Prison suicide under chloroform, the 1864 ADA and 1870 AMA discoverer declarations.

Scribd document summary (archival citations): the gas bag removed too soon, the patient's groan, 'a humbug affair'; Wells's Paris stay and 1847 pamphlet; Morton's unscrupulous handling of the credit dispute; the chloroform addiction and Tombs Prison suicide at 33.

ResearchGate summary of the 1847 sources: three physician signatories (Kennedy, Mignault, Taft) present at the Boston demonstration; Wells's letter in Galignani's Messenger and the Boston Atlas (2 April 1847); his 'experimented with both nitrous oxide and ether prior to 1845.'

competing_hypotheses: That the failed January 1845 demonstration proves nitrous oxide inadequate rather than underdosed — the patient later said he remembered no pain and didn't know when the tooth was extracted; modern reading: premature bag removal plus a difficult patient (obese, alcoholic — less responsive to nitrous).
That the 1840s 'discoverer' declarations (ADA 1864, AMA 1870) are retrospective institutional politics, not evidence — graded as claims about the controversy, not about the 1844 operations.
falsifiability: Contemporary proof that the 1844 extractions did not happen (e.g. Colton's or Riggs's denial on the record) — the 1847 witness statements would then be perjury, which no source alleges.

title: Bigaglia's first glass paperweight (1845, credited)
claim: Pietro Bigaglia, a member of an old Venetian family of glass artists, manufactured the first glass paperweight in 1845.
place: Venice, Italy — Pietro Bigaglia's manufactory
grade_reason: The credit is conventional in the collector literature but rests on trade tradition rather than a dated document or patent, so it stays below VERIFIED; the Venice→France chronology is carried as the cited telling, not absorbed as fact.
earliest_attestation: Collectors' and trade literature (Christopher Proudlove's account of the French/Venetian paperweight trade).

sources.ref: Christopher Proudlove (Free Online Library) — Pietro Bigaglia, 'a member of an old Venetian family of glass artists,' is 'generally credited with the manufacture of the first glass paperweight in 1845'; the Venetian millefiori technique traces to the 15th century

Scottish Antiques, 'Paperweights' — the inspiration is generally accepted as the Venetian glassmakers of Murano, working with composite fine glass canes (the millefiori basis) as early as the 16th century; interest mushroomed in the 1840s

competing_hypotheses: That the glasshouses of France (Baccarat, Saint-Louis, Clichy) developed the paperweight concurrently and independently in the early-mid 1840s — Antique Trader's telling has paperweights originating in France around 1845 (carried as a named competing tradition)
That the 'first' is unknowable because the earliest weights are unmarked — no single dated artifact settles priority, so the credit rests on collectors' literature, not a document
falsifiability: A datable glass paperweight securely earlier than 1845, or documentation that Bigaglia's family had no 1845 paperweight output — neither has surfaced.

title: The Hill & de la Rue envelope-folding machine, 1845
claim: Edwin Hill (brother of postal reformer Rowland Hill) and Warren de la Rue received the first British patent for an envelope-folding machine in 1845 — a steam-driven machine that creased and folded pre-cut diamond sheets into envelopes — and exhibited an improved version at the London Great Exhibition of 1851.
place: London, England — patent registered; improved machine exhibited at the Crystal Palace, 1851
grade_reason: Two institutional sources (Smithsonian National Postal Museum, Library of Congress) agree on the patentees, the year, and the machine's function; the 1851 exhibition is documented in both. Held below VERIFIED on the 1840/1845 date-fog in secondary sources.
earliest_attestation: The 1845 British patent registration itself.

sources.ref: Smithsonian National Postal Museum — 'Envelopes in the Machine Age' (1845 patent; Edwin Hill & Warren de la Rue; 1851 London Exposition; Russell Hawes 1853 US patent)
Library of Congress, Inside Adams — 'Opening the Envelope' (1845 steam-powered machine; 1851 improved version at the London Exposition; US patents 6,055 (1849) and 9,812 (1853))
Baylor University, Texas Collection — 'envelope history' (1845 steam machine; Crystal Palace 1851 alongside the Koh-i-Noor and Colt's prototype)

competing_hypotheses: The '1840' date that circulates for the Hill/de la Rue patent appears to conflate George Wilson's 1840 tiling patent with the 1845 Hill/de la Rue machine patent — carried as the honest correction, not a contradiction of the machine's existence

In America, Jesse Park & Cornelius Watson (patent 6,055, 1849) and Russell Hawes (patent 9,812, 1853) patented envelope machines independently — the British machine is the first registered, not the only one
falsifiability: A documented earlier envelope-machine patent would demote the 'first registered' claim; period accounts denying the 1851 Crystal Palace exhibition would need to surface.

title: The food that kept leaving (1845–1852)
claim: Throughout the Great Famine, Ireland continued to export food — grain, livestock, dairy, and other produce shipped to Britain — and London refused to bar those exports, as it had done on previous occasions of dearth. The exports are honestly bounded: they were significantly reduced compared to pre-famine years, imports exceeded exports after 1846, and the exported grain would have compensated for only about one-seventh of the potatoes destroyed by the blight (Ó Gráda 1999).
place: Dublin and the Irish ports — the export manifests; the decision at Westminster
grade_reason: Attested on two independent lines: the contemporary export manifests and parliamentary record (the refusal to bar exports 'as had been done on previous occasions'), and the modern quantitative historiography (Ó Gráda 1999:124 — the one-seventh bound; exports reduced vs prior years; imports > exports after 1846). Held below VERIFIED on the single-lineage trade statistics and the honestly approximate arithmetic. This record is the fence that keeps the DEBUNKED blight-only telling honest: the exports were real and damning, and they were not, by the math, the whole story either.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary: the export manifests and the parliamentary debates over barring exports (the refusal is the documented decision); the quantitative bound is Cormac Ó Gráda's 'Black '47 and Beyond' (1999:124), via the UCL textbook study.

sources.ref: Wikipedia — 'Great Famine (Ireland)' ('Large quantities of food were exported from Ireland during the famine, and the refusal of London to bar such exports, as had been done on previous occasions, was an immediate and continuing source of controversy')

History Education Research Journal (UCL Press) — the Irish/UK textbook study (Ó Gráda 1999:124 — exported grain ≈ one-seventh of potatoes lost; exports reduced; imports exceeded exports after 1846; Mitchel 1854 and the scholarly corrective Nally 2008)

competing_hypotheses: The nationalist maximalist reading (Mitchel 1854: the exports prove deliberate starvation policy) vs the scholarly corrective (Nally 2008; the textbook study) — both carried; the record grades the exports as real and the export-ban refusal as documented, while the 'exports could have fed everyone' arithmetic is the bounded part
The laissez-faire defense (Trevelyan: non-interference with free trade) — carried as the contemporary justification, graded as doctrine, not exoneration
falsifiability: Port records showing no food exports from Ireland 1845–1852, or an Order in Council barring them, would overturn this; the manifests and the debate record both exist.

title: The Franklin expedition, 1845-1848 - the voyage that never came home
claim: In May 1845 Sir John Franklin sailed from England with HMS Erebus and HMS Terror and 129 officers and men to complete the charting of the Northwest Passage. The ships were beset in the ice off King William Island from September 1846; Franklin died on 11 June 1847; the 105 survivors abandoned the ships on 22 April 1848 and attempted a march south toward Back's Fish River (the Great Fish River). None survived.
place: Off the north-west coast of King William Island, Nunavut (beset position 5 leagues NNW of Point Victory)
grade_reason: The expedition's own contemporary note documents the beset, the deaths, Franklin's death date, and the abandonment; McClintock's 1859 finds, the Beechey Island graves (1845-46 winter), and the Inuit testimony independently corroborate the sequence.
earliest_attestation: The Victory Point note - the expedition's own record, written 28 May 1847 and 25 April 1848, found in a cairn at Point Victory, King William Island, in May 1859 by Lt. William Hobson (McClintock's Fox expedition).

sources.ref: The Victory Point note (28 May 1847 / 25 April 1848) - the expedition's own words; the only written record the expedition left behind
McClintock's Fox expedition (1859) - cairn finds, boat, relics, first survey of King William Island's west coast
Admiralty sailing orders, Instructions Addressed to Captain Sir John Franklin (1845)
John Rae's 1854 report to the Admiralty - Inuit accounts of white men dying of starvation near the Back River; Franklin relics recovered
David C. Woodman, Unravelling the Franklin Mystery: Inuit Testimony (1991) - synthesis of the Inuit evidence

competing_hypotheses: Franklin's party died entirely of starvation and exposure on the march south (the traditional reading of the retreat-corridor evidence)
Small groups survived into the early 1850s and the Erebus was briefly re-manned and sailed to its final resting place - reasoned from Inuit testimony, unattested by documents

Cannibalism among the last survivors - reported by Inuit to John Rae in 1854 (the report that caused the Victorian scandal; Lady Jane Franklin and Charles Dickens rejected it); forensic support came later (Keenleyside et al. 1997 cut marks on bones); treated as a separate honestly-graded question, not part of this record
falsifiability: Surviving documents from the ships contradicting the beset/abandonment sequence, or Admiralty orders proving a different sailing date, would overturn this record.

title: The French classic period of glass paperweights (1845–1860)
claim: From about 1845 to about 1860 — the collectors' 'classic period' — the French glasshouses Baccarat, Saint-Louis, and Clichy (with Monot's Cristallerie de Pantin and lesser lights such as Grenelle and Saint-Mandé) produced the finest glass paperweights in the world: millefiori canes and lampwork flowers under domed crystal, exhibited to acclaim at the 1851 Crystal Palace Great Exhibition, after which the art all but disappeared for some eighty years.
place: Lorraine, France — Baccarat and Saint-Louis glassworks; Paris — Clichy
grade_reason: Multiply attested in collector, dealer, and museum literature (Corning, Art Institute of Chicago, Bergstrom-Mahler collections; 1851 exhibition record), but the period boundaries are conventions and most weights are unmarked, so it stays below VERIFIED.
earliest_attestation: The 1851 Great Exhibition at the Crystal Palace (contemporary exhibition record); the factories' own output histories (Baccarat founded 1764; Clichy founded by Louis-Joseph Maës 1842).

sources.ref: Antique Trader, 'The Zen of Glass Paperweights' — originated in France around 1845 (Baccarat, Saint Louis, Clichy) as affordable objets d'art; 'exhibited to great acclaim in London's Great Exhibition of 1851'; collected by kings, presidents, Colette, Truman Capote

L. H. Selman Fine Glass Paperweights, 'Why Collect' — by 1845 France was 'the undeniable paperweight center of the world'; after about 1860 'the art of paperweight making all but disappeared for eighty years'

Scottish Antiques, 'Paperweights' — French houses made the weights as 'demonstrations of their craftsmanship'; the Clichy manufactory employed some 300 workers to meet demand after the 1851 Crystal Palace success; French houses: Baccarat, Clichy, St Louis, Monot's Cristallerie de Pantin, Grenelle, St Mandé

competing_hypotheses: That English and American glasshouses were quick imitators whose output belongs to the same boom rather than a French monopoly — the French lead is undisputed but the boom was international

That the 1860 'end' is a collectors' convention rather than a hard stop — late-19th-century production continued at reduced volume, and the 20th century (Lalique, Whitefriars, Caithness) revived the art
falsifiability: Factory records or dated weights showing the 'big three' were not the leading producers of the 1845–1860 boom, or exhibition records showing paperweights absent from the 1851 Crystal Palace displays.

title: The Great Irish Famine, 1845–1852
claim: The Great Irish Famine (An Gorta Mór) ran 1845–1852: potato blight destroyed the staple crop across successive seasons, roughly one million people died of starvation and famine-related disease, and over one million more emigrated; Ireland's population fell from ~8.5 million on the eve of the famine to ~4.4 million by 1901, and has never recovered to its pre-famine level. 1847 — 'Black '47' — was the worst year.
place: Ireland — island-wide; worst in the western counties (Connacht, west Munster)
grade_reason: Multiple independent primary lines converge: the decennial census series (1841/1851/1901), contemporary constabulary and relief-commission returns, emigration shipping records, and the parish death registers. The toll's exact integer is honestly rounded; the collapse is not.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary: the blighted 1845 harvest (press reports, constabulary returns); the 1841 census (8.175M) as the pre-famine baseline. The demographic collapse is documented in the 1851 and 1901 censuses.

sources.ref: Wikipedia — 'Great Famine (Ireland)' (proximate cause blight; ~1M died, ~1M+ emigrated; 8.5M → 4.4M by 1901; 'Black '47'; exports controversy; quarter-acre clause)
Smithsonian Magazine — 'Scientists Finally Pinpoint the Pathogen That Caused the Irish Potato Famine' (1845 splotches; 1845 harvest halved; island population still below pre-famine levels today)

competing_hypotheses: The one-million-dead figure is the conventional rounded estimate; the exact toll is honestly ranged in the scholarship — the demographic loss (death + emigration + averted births) is the firmer number
The 'no recovery' population claim holds for the island as a whole; regional trajectories differ
falsifiability: Census records showing no population collapse 1841–1851, or shipping/relief records contradicting the emigration scale, would overturn this; the census series is the anchor and it is unambiguous.

title: DEBUNKED: the famine was caused solely by the potato blight
claim: The Irish Potato Famine (1845–1852) was caused solely by the potato blight — that is, the million deaths and mass emigration were a pure natural disaster with no significant human or political causes.
place: Ireland — the telling is about the whole island; the evidence is the British policy record at Westminster and Dublin Castle
grade_reason: Killed on the documents, three ways: (1) Ireland kept producing and exporting other food throughout the famine — 'large quantities of food were exported from Ireland during the famine, and the refusal of London to bar such exports, as had been done on previous occasions, was an immediate and continuing source of controversy'; (2) the relief doctrine was ideological, not logistical — Trevelyan in 'The Irish Crisis' (1848) called the calamity 'the judgement of God' sent to teach the Irish a lesson and warned it 'must not be too much mitigated,' locating 'the real evil' not in hunger but in 'the moral evil of the selfish, perverse and turbulent character of the people'; (3) the statute book made starvation administrative — the 1847 Gregory quarter-acre clause barred relief to anyone holding more than a quarter acre. The blight destroyed the crop; the policies decided who ate. Scope fenced: never the blight's reality (evt-potato-blight-herb1-001 VERIFIED), never the death toll (evt-irish-famine-001 VERIFIED), never the honest bound on the exports (Ó Gráda's one-seventh, carried in evt-famine-food-exports-1845-001).
earliest_attestation: The blight-only telling is the textbook shorthand of the later 19th century; Mitchel's 1861 counter ('The Almighty, indeed, sent the potato blight, but the English created the famine') is the earliest dated rebuttal in the record consulted.

sources.ref: Wikipedia — 'Great Famine (Ireland)' (blight as proximate cause; absentee landlordism and single-crop dependence; Whig laissez-faire; exports continued and London refused to bar them; quarter-acre clause)

Adams auction catalogue — Trevelyan's 'The Irish Crisis' (1848): 'the judgement of God sent the calamity to teach the Irish a lesson, that calamity must not be too much mitigated'; 'the real evil ... the moral evil of the selfish, perverse and turbulent character of the people'

History Education Research Journal (UCL Press) — 'The Great Irish Famine in Irish and UK history textbooks, 2010–2020' (Trevelyan's providentialism; Ó Gráda 1999:124 — exported grain ≈ one-seventh of potatoes lost; imports exceeded exports after 1846; the genocide thesis and the scholarly corrective, Nally 2008)

irisharoundtheworld.com — 'Irish Potato Famine: Ireland's Great Hunger, 1845 to 1852' (the Great Hunger naming argument; most famine historians reject the genocide label while condemning the response; Mitchel 1861; Coogan 2012)

competing_hypotheses: The genocide question: John Mitchel's 1861 'The Almighty, indeed, sent the potato blight, but the English created the famine'; Tim Pat Coogan's 'The Famine Plot' (2012) argues British policy meets the UN Genocide Convention definition; most famine historians reject the label while condemning the response — carried as the named open debate, next on this beat's docket, NOT graded here

The providentialist reading as sincere belief vs calculated cruelty: Peel's 1845–46 measures were 'constructive but limited' (Wikipedia), and individual officials (e.g., the Quaker relief committees, private charity) worked against the doctrine — the system, not every person in it, is what the grade kills

The exports-alone counter-claim is itself bounded: Ó Gráda (1999) — the exported grain would have compensated for only about one-seventh of the potatoes lost; imports exceeded exports after 1846 — carried honestly, not flattened
falsifiability: Documented evidence that Ireland produced no exportable food 1845–1852, that London barred food exports, and that relief policy was maximal and non-ideological, would overturn this. The export manifests, Trevelyan's own writings, and the statute book all point the other way.

title: 'Stephen Perry invented the rubber band alone' — DEBUNKED
claim: The telling that 'Stephen Perry invented the rubber band alone in 1845' — that the rubber band began with one man, Perry, and the 1845 patent is his alone.
place: London, England — where the telling places the solo invention (Perry's city)
grade_reason: One kill, and it is the patent document itself: British Patent 13880/1845 was granted jointly to Stephen Perry of St John's Wood AND Thomas Barnabas Daft of Birmingham. Every 'Perry alone' telling drops the co-patentee.
earliest_attestation: The telling's popular form: quiz and trivia sites crediting 'Stephen Perry' alone for the 1845 patent (e.g. the QuizzClub trivia card: 'The inventor Stephen Perry acquired the patent for what item in 1845?'; the WCSA 'On This Day' column naming Perry alone in its headline telling). The patent specification names Perry AND Thomas Barnabas Daft.

sources.ref: British Patent 13880/1845 — joint grant to Stephen Perry and Thomas Barnabas Daft, sealed 17 March 1845 (the killing document; cited via the rubber-band article's patent reference, todayinsci archive)
QuizzClub trivia, 'The inventor Stephen Perry acquired the patent for what item in 1845?' — the popular solo telling in its quiz-card form: Perry alone, 1845, no Daft
WCSA 'On This Day — March 17, 2021' — headline telling credits 'Stephen Perry (a British inventor and businessman)' alone for the first rubber band; the body names Messrs Perry and Co. but never Daft

competing_hypotheses: The scoped honest version — 'Perry was the London rubber manufacturer who patented and commercialized the band' — survives and is graded separately in evt-perry-daft-rubber-band-patent-1845-001
That Daft's contribution was minor or administrative — carried as an honest hedge; the patent grants them jointly regardless, so the solo telling dies either way
falsifiability: A re-examination of the 13880/1845 specification showing Daft's name absent, or documentary proof Daft was struck from the grant — the joint grant is on the record as sealed.

title: The Perry & Daft rubber-band patent (17 March 1845)
claim: British Patent 13880/1845 — sealed 17 March 1845 — granted jointly to Stephen Perry of St John's Wood, Middlesex, and Thomas Barnabas Daft of Birmingham, for 'improvements in springs to be applied to girths, belts, and bandages, and improvements in manufacture of elastic bands.' The elastic bands were cut as narrow rings from vulcanized rubber tube and sold by Perry's firm, Messrs Perry and Co., Rubber Manufacturers of London, advertised as useful for holding 'papers, letters, etc.'
place: London, England — Messrs Perry and Co., Rubber Manufacturers of London
grade_reason: The patent document exists, is multiply and consistently cited (patent-office records, trade histories, encyclopedia references), and names both grantees with the sealed date.
earliest_attestation: The patent specification itself: British Patent 13880/1845, granted to Stephen Perry and Thomas Barnabas Daft, sealed 17 March 1845.

sources.ref: British Patent 13880/1845 — specification granted to Stephen Perry (St John's Wood, Middlesex, gentleman) and Thomas Barnabas Daft (Birmingham, manufacturer), 'for improvements in springs to be applied to girths, belts, and bandages, and improvements in manufacture of elastic bands'; sealed 17 March 1845 (cited via the rubber-band article's patent reference, todayinsci archive)

WCSA 'On This Day — March 17, 2021: Stephen Perry received a patent for the first rubber band, in 1845' — Messrs Perry and Co., bands extruded into tube, cured, sliced widthwise; advertised for 'papers, letters, etc.'; 'Perry opened the UK's first rubber band factory'

WayneDaleNews, 'Stretched Tales of Elastic: The History of Ordinary Things' (2026) — 'In 1845, the modern rubber band was invented by Stephen Perry and Thomas Daft of London. They sliced narrow rings from a vulcanized rubber tube.'

competing_hypotheses: The scoped honest telling — 'Perry was the rubber manufacturer who patented and commercialized the band' — is what the quiz sites mean; it survives, and it is this record, not the solo-inventor version

That unvulcanized rubber bands existed before 1845 in some form (mid-19th-century non-vulcanized bands are reported in trade histories, though without a documented first) — carried as an ungraded caveat, not a rival invention claim
falsifiability: A showing that the 13880/1845 specification names Perry alone, or that the sealed patent is a misfiled/modern fabrication — neither is the case; the joint grant is on the document.

title: HERB-1: the blight strain identified (1845)
claim: The potato crop failures of 1845–1852 were caused by potato late blight, the oomycete Phytophthora infestans — and the exact historical strain is now identified: HERB-1, a unique 19th-century genotype distinct from all modern strains (including the long-suspected US-1), which spread from North America to Europe in 1845 from a Mexican Toluca Valley origin. The 1845 harvest was cut roughly in half; by 1846 it had fallen to about a quarter.
place: County Cork, Ireland — first Irish reports, summer 1845; the strain's origin: Toluca Valley, Mexico
grade_reason: Peer-reviewed primary science: Yoshida et al., eLife 2013 (DOI 10.7554/eLife.00731) — 11 historical + 15 modern genomes, HERB-1 a single low-diversity lineage, distinct from US-1, close relative of it, dispersed from a common ancestor outside Mexico in the early 1800s. Corroborated by contemporary 1845–46 field reports and the harvest-collapse figures. The natural half of the famine's causation is verified — which is precisely what makes the blight-only telling a half-truth rather than a truth.
earliest_attestation: 1845 field reports of splotched leaves and mushy tubers (e.g., the County Cork accounts); the scientific identification is Yoshida et al. 2013 — shotgun sequencing of 11 herbarium specimens (Kew, Munich, collected from 1845 on) against 15 modern strains.

sources.ref: Yoshida et al. 2013, eLife 2:e00731 — 'The rise and fall of the Phytophthora infestans lineage that triggered the Irish potato famine' (11 herbarium + 15 modern strains; HERB-1 unique, distinct from US-1; spread North America → Europe 1845)
Smithsonian Magazine — 'Scientists Finally Pinpoint the Pathogen That Caused the Irish Potato Famine' (1845 splotches; 1845 harvest halved, 1846 quartered; Kew 1847 specimens)
NPR/WEKU — 'How Genomics Solved The Mystery Of Ireland's Great Famine' (22 May 2013; the US-1 theory overturned; Burbano/Kamoun)

competing_hypotheses: The pre-2013 US-1-origin theory (a single US-1 strain dominated globally for 150 years) — superseded by the herbarium aDNA, carried as the corrected prior
Whether HERB-1's extinction and US-1's 20th-century replacement reflect selection or drift — open, stated in the paper as future work
falsifiability: A competing pathogen identified in 1840s herbarium potato tissue, or a demonstration that the herbarium genomes are contaminated, would overturn this; the 11-specimen consensus across two herbaria makes that structurally unlikely.

title: The Lundström safety match (1845–1858) — Sweden's commercial match
claim: The Lundström brothers of Jönköping, Sweden — Johan Edvard (1815–1888) and Carl Frans (1823–1917) — took Pasch's separated safety-match design and made it commercially successful: experimenting from 1845, a production plant on Lake Vättern by 1847, a prize-winning exhibit at the 1855 Paris World Exhibition, ~12 million matchboxes in 1858, and a path to the Jönköping match monopoly (Jönköpings & Vulcans Tändsticksfabriks AB, 1903; later Swedish Match). Johan Edvard Lundström left the business in 1863 and spent 1875–77 as a government inspector in the match industry, working to prevent and forbid the use of dangerous white phosphorus.
place: Jönköping, Sweden (Lundström match factory; original factory now a museum)
grade_reason: The 1845–47 development, the 1855 Paris award, and the 1858 output figure are consistently attested across sources; the Lundström-to-Swedish-Match lineage is documented. Patent-date details vary, so held at CORROBORATED.
earliest_attestation: Lundström workshop records, Jönköping, 1845 (secondary); Paris World Exhibition award 1855

sources.ref: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustaf_Erik_Pasch — Lundström brothers took Pasch's design; commercial success ~1855–60; 1855 Paris award
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johan_Edvard_Lundström — 1845 workshop start; 1847 Lake Vättern plant; 1855 Paris award; Lagerman's automatic match machine; inspector work 1875–77 against white phosphorus
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safety_matches — 1858 output ~12 million matchboxes; Jönköpings & Vulcans Tändsticksfabriks AB 1903; Coigent patent contest in France
Discover Magazine — 'They Invented It' (Fenella Saunders): 'In 1855 Johan Edvard Lundström of Sweden patented safety matches using less volatile red phosphorus'

competing_hypotheses: The French courts contested the Lundström patent (Coigent Père & Fils, Lyon) on the basis that the invention was known in Vienna before the brothers' patent — carried honestly as a contested priority claim

Discover Magazine dates the Lundström safety-match patent to 1855; the Wikipedia tradition centers the 1845–47 development and the 1855 Paris award. The date of the patent instrument is carried as secondary-level, not settled
falsifiability: Evidence that commercial safety-match production at scale predates the Lundström brothers, or that the 1855 Paris award went to another maker

title: Adolphe Sax patents the saxophone (28 June 1846) — and the twenty-year patent war
claim: Adolphe Sax invented the saxophone — a conical brass body with a single-reed mouthpiece, bridging brass power and woodwind agility — patented 28 June 1846 in France for use in orchestras and military bands; he then spent over twenty years in patent litigation that bankrupted him three times, and died in poverty in Paris in 1894 without ever hearing the jazz the instrument would define.
place: Paris (Sax's workshop; born Dinant, Belgium, 1814)
grade_reason: Multiple independent sources agree: the 28 June 1846 French patent; the design (conical brass + single reed, bridging brass and woodwind); Berlioz's 1842 approval; the French military's mid-1840s embrace; the 20+ years of patent litigation (the original opposition suit unresolved until 1854 — eight years — with Sax's patents ultimately declared valid and the opposition ordered to pay damages); the three bankruptcies (1852/56, 1873, 1877 — sources differ on the first date, fenced); the 1853–1858 lip cancer survived; the 1857 Paris Conservatoire post; the 1894 death in poverty in Paris, buried at Montmartre. The popular 'pure martyr' telling is fenced: Sax was also the plaintiff — he sued rivals for infringement — and his patents were upheld; the litigation costs, not theft, destroyed him.
earliest_attestation: The French patent of 28 June 1846; Berlioz's 1842 writings

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Adolphe Sax': 'On 28 June 1846 he patented the saxophone, intended for use in orchestras and military bands... Composer Hector Berlioz wrote approvingly of the new instrument in 1842... Legal troubles involving patents continued for over 20 years, with rival instrument makers attacking the legitimacy of his patents and Sax suing them for patent infringement. He was driven into bankruptcy three times: in 1852, 1873 and 1877... Sax suffered from lip cancer between 1853 and 1858 but made a full recovery. In 1894 he died of pneumonia in Paris, in poverty.'

Scribd, 'Saxophone's Absence in Orchestras': 'The original lawsuit in opposition to his patent application was not resolved until 1854, eight years after it was filed. Although Sax's patents were declared valid and the opposition was ordered to pay damages, the time and money that could have been spent creatively had been expended on endless legal battles.'

AV Club: 'rival instrument makers, several of whom either sued Sax for patent infringement or tried to delegitimize the patents he held. Legal battles over his designs dragged on for 20 years, and he was driven into bankruptcy three times. He died in poverty, never dreaming that when humanity eventually achieved musical perfection, it would come in the form of the saxophone riff from "Baker Street."'

Natalija Ugrina (Dinant): 'In 1841, a young Sax packed his creations and moved to Paris... His solution was the saxophone: a conical brass body like a trumpet, fitted with a single-reed mouthpiece like a clarinet. He patented it in 1846.' Rival makers 'accused him of stealing ideas, sabotaged his business, and filed endless lawsuits.' Lip cancer 1853, recovered; died 1894, Montmartre Cemetery.

falsifiability: A dated patent or instrument proving a saxophone predating June 1846, or court records contradicting the litigation/bankruptcy account

title: DEBUNKED: 'Ether Day was the first ever surgical anesthesia'
claim: The 16 October 1846 Ether Dome demonstration was the first ever use of inhaled anesthesia in surgery — the moment pain was abolished.
place: Boston (the monument and the dome)
grade_reason: Two independent prior uses precede it on the documentary record: Crawford Long's ether surgeries in Jefferson, Georgia (from 30 March 1842, documented by certificates and the patient's account, published 1849) and Horace Wells's nitrous-oxide dental use (December 1844, demonstrated publicly in Boston January 1845) — plus the recreational 'ether frolics' both traditions drew on. The event stays CORROBORATED; the superlative dies.
earliest_attestation: The 'first ever' reading is carried in granite on the Ether Monument (Boston Public Garden, 1868): 'First proved at Mass. General Hospital in Boston October AD MDCCCXLVI' — a claim Morton himself pushed and Mark Twain called a lie that would outlast the monument a million years.

sources.ref: The Conversation/MedicalXpress (republished): the monument's inscription quoted verbatim ('First proved at Mass. General Hospital in Boston October AD MDCCCXLVI'); the claim called 'untrue' — Long's 1842 use had six witnesses in his public office; Holmes's 'ether or either'; Twain's 'the lie it tells will outlast it a million years.'

Long's 1849 Southern Medical and Surgical Journal account (via the 1849 original at archive.org/NIH): the 30 March 1842 operation on James Venable, the 6 June 1842 second operation, the certificates of patient and witnesses — the documentary existence of pre-1846 surgical ether.

Harvard Countway ('Monument to E(i)ther'): 'Crawford W. Long may well have employed an anesthetic before either Morton or Wells but neglected to develop or promote the idea' — the priority verdict from the medical-history establishment.

competing_hypotheses: That Ether Day was the first DOCUMENTED, widely witnessed, and medically consequential demonstration — the version this grade does not kill (see evt-ether-dome-1846-001).
falsifiability: Proof that no earlier surgical use of an inhaled anesthetic occurred anywhere — impossible against Long's 1842 records and Wells's 1844–45 records.

title: Ether Day — the 16 October 1846 Ether Dome demonstration
claim: On 16 October 1846, in the Bulfinch Building's surgical amphitheater at Massachusetts General Hospital (Boston), dentist William T. G. Morton administered sulfuric ether to patient Edward Gilbert Abbott, after which surgeon John Collins Warren painlessly removed part of a tumor from Abbott's neck before a medical audience — the event known as Ether Day, and the first successful public demonstration of surgical ether anesthesia.
place: Massachusetts General Hospital (Bulfinch Building), Boston
grade_reason: The event is multiply attested by contemporary witnesses (surgeon, audience of physicians, press) and the preserved site; the 'first ever' superlative is graded separately (see evt-anesthesia-first-ever-001).
earliest_attestation: Contemporary newspaper accounts and Warren's same-evening journal entry; the amphitheater is preserved as the Ether Dome (National Historic Landmark).

sources.ref: Linda Hall Library: 'first successful public demonstration of surgical anesthesia' — Warren's journal excerpt (Mass. Historical Society); Abbott's 'neck's been scratched' report; the Wells-failure contrast in the same theater.
Russell Museum (MGH): the amphitheater's history — 8,000+ operations 1821–1867; Warren's 'no humbug' proclamation; the dome as meeting space today.

Edward Gilbert Abbott — Warren's same-evening journal, Abbott's post-operation report; the 'no Humbug' reference and its disputed origin (Warren later said he did not remember Wells's 1845 demo until Wells raised it in 1847).

competing_hypotheses: Warren's 'Gentlemen, this is no humbug' is attested in popular accounts; the exact conversations that morning were not stenographically recorded — only Warren's same-evening journal entry ('interesting operation,' Mass. Historical Society) is a contemporary note.
The patient was aware of the surgery and later said it felt as if his neck had been scratched — the claim graded is the demonstration's success, not unconsciousness in the modern sense.
falsifiability: A contemporary denial by a present surgeon, or evidence the operation was staged (e.g. Abbott's pain actually severe and documented at the time).

title: The 'First Thanksgiving' National-Origin Myth
claim: That the 1621 Plymouth harvest feast was 'the first Thanksgiving' and the founding of an annual national tradition leading directly to the American Thanksgiving holiday.
place: Plymouth, Massachusetts (site of the retrojected claim)
grade_reason: Scope fenced: the 1621 feast itself is CORROBORATED (evt-1621-feast-001) and the holiday is a real American tradition — what dies is the retrojection. The feast was never called a 'thanksgiving' by its participants; Separatists held no annual holidays (even Christmas was rejected); the 1623 rain thanksgiving is the first day identified as 'thanksgiving' in Plymouth primary sources; and the national holiday's documented origin is Hale's 1846-1863 campaign plus Lincoln's October 3, 1863 proclamation, not a continuous line from 1621.
earliest_attestation: The 1621 feast was re-baptized as 'the first Thanksgiving' in the Victorian era: Sarah Josepha Hale's campaign in Godey's Lady's Book (1846-1863), Abraham Lincoln's Proclamation of October 3, 1863, and the mass-circulation imagery of the 1880s-1910s (Jane G. Austin's fiction, Jennie Augusta Brownscombe's 1914 painting, Jean Leon Gerome Ferris's c. 1912-15 painting).

sources.ref: Sarah Josepha Hale's letter to Abraham Lincoln, September 28, 1863 (Library of Congress, Manuscript Division)
Abraham Lincoln's Thanksgiving Proclamation, October 3, 1863 (last Thursday of November)
Act of Congress, December 26, 1941 (Public Law 77-379) — Thanksgiving fixed as the fourth Thursday of November
Edward Winslow's letter, Mourt's Relation (1622) — what it does NOT say: no 'thanksgiving' label, no annual recurrence, no turkey centerpiece
Library of Congress blog, 'The Woman Who Helped Put Thanksgiving on the Calendar' (2024) — documents Hale's campaign and Lincoln's proclamation
Caleb Johnson's Mayflower History research: no buckles anywhere; hat buckles not fashionable until late 17th century; black clothing formal wear, everyday clothing colorful

competing_hypotheses: The 'first Thanksgiving' title is definition-dependent: Berkeley Hundred, Virginia (December 4, 1619) and St. Augustine, Florida (September 8, 1565) both have documented 'thanksgiving' observances predating 1621 — if a first is wanted, 1621 loses on chronology too

The myth as deliberate Civil-War nation-building rather than innocent error: Hale explicitly framed the holiday as a 'great Union Festival of America' to bind a divided country; the origin story served that civic purpose

The 1637 Mystic thanksgiving proclamation (Winthrop's Massachusetts Bay colony, after the Pequot massacre) — activist literature's counter-claim that the 'first official Thanksgiving' celebrated a massacre; attestation disputed and outside this record's scope, carried here as an ungraded footnote
falsifiability: A pre-1863 American source calling the 1621 feast 'the first Thanksgiving' as the start of an annual national tradition — none exists; the two 17th-century sources call it a feast, not a thanksgiving

title: Howe's 1846 lockstitch patent (U.S. 4,750)
claim: On 10 September 1846, Elias Howe Jr. of Massachusetts was granted U.S. Patent No. 4,750 for an improvement in sewing machines using a lockstitch design — eye-pointed needle, shuttle beneath the cloth forming the lockstitch, automatic feed — sewing about 250 stitches per minute.
place: Boston / Spencer, Massachusetts, USA (Howe's shop and patent filing)
grade_reason: The patent is a primary legal document with a fixed number and grant date, institutionally preserved.
earliest_attestation: U.S. Patent 4,750, granted 10 September 1846 (primary document); Smithsonian National Museum of American History photograph of the patent record

place: Edinburgh (Simpson); London/Buckingham (Snow, Victoria)
grade_reason: Simpson's 1847 presentation and practice, the Queen Street dinner-party account (multiple attendee retellings), Victoria's journal in her own words, and Snow's published anesthesia work — multiply attested; held at CORROBORATED on the retrospective biographical structure rather than a single contemporary document.

Laing Gordon (via Google Books): Simpson appointed Chair of Midwifery 1840; ether introduced to UK obstetrics 19 January 1847; the dinner-table trials; chloroform introduced 8 November 1847; the 1853 Victoria confinement making the practice 'generally accepted'; Simpson knighted 1866 — the first physician knighted for medicine.

Historic Geneva: Fanny Longfellow (1847), Emma Darwin (1847, 1848 — 'Get me the chloroform'), Caroline Post Swan (ether, 1851); Victoria's journal quote; the Genesis 3:16 Calvinist objection carried as vocal minority; Simpson's own prophecy that patients would force the profession's hand.

competing_hypotheses: That Victoria's 1853 confinement 'settled' the chloroform question — the acceptance was gradual (Emma Darwin used chloroform in 1847 and 1848; Caroline Post Swan tried ether in 1851); Victoria's use accelerated it but did not single-handedly end opposition (see fences).

That religious opposition (Genesis 3:16, 'in sorrow thou shalt bring forth children') was the decisive barrier — the record shows the opposition was a vocal minority (Calvinist critics in Scotland) plus legitimate medical caution about dosing (Hannah Green, 15, died of chloroform overdose in 1848).
falsifiability: Simpson's 1847 presentation record or Snow's casebooks shown to be misdated or fabricated; Victoria's journal entry disproven.

title: The Victory Point note - the only words the expedition left behind
claim: The Victory Point note is the single written record the Franklin expedition left behind: a pre-printed Admiralty form written in two parts. The first, dated 28 May 1847 and signed by Lt. Graham Gore and Mate Charles Des Voeux, reports the ships wintered in the ice and 'All well.' The second, added in the margins on 25 April 1848 and signed by Capt. James Fitzjames and Capt. Francis Crozier, records that the ships were deserted on 22 April 1848 after being beset since 12 September 1846, that Sir John Franklin died on 11 June 1847, that deaths had reached nine officers and fifteen men, and that the 105 survivors under Crozier would start the next day for Back's Fish River. It was found in May 1859 by Lt. William Hobson of McClintock's Fox expedition in a cairn at Point Victory on the north-west coast of King William Island - originally deposited in James Clark Ross's 1830 Victory Point cairn four miles north.

grade_reason: The physical document survives, its text is fully published, the signatures and Admiralty form are undisputed, and its contents are independently consistent with the Beechey Island graves, McClintock's cairn finds, and the Inuit testimony.
earliest_attestation: The note itself (1847-48) - the earliest surviving document; the finder was Lt. William Hobson, McClintock's Fox expedition, May 1859.

sources.ref: The Victory Point note itself - two-part Admiralty form, 28 May 1847 (Gore/Des Voeux) + 25 April 1848 (Fitzjames/Crozier), margins
McClintock's Fox expedition (1857-59) - Hobson's discovery at the Victory Point cairn, May 1859
Royal Museums Greenwich collection MSR/C/9 - the surviving document
James Clark Ross's 1830 cairn - the original deposition site, four miles north (Victory Point)

competing_hypotheses: The note's second part was written 25 April 1848 (the accepted reading); the surviving text does not record the precise hour - 'start on tomorrow' is the expedition's own phrasing
Graham Gore's original 1847 deposition was moved by Crozier's party from the Ross cairn to the Victory Point cairn where Hobson found it - McClintock's reconstruction, accepted but second-hand
falsifiability: A contemporaneous Franklin-expedition document contradicting its dates, or forensic proof the note is a later forgery, would overturn this record; none exists - the handwriting and the Admiralty form are undisputed.

title: Meucci's teletrofono — the 1871 caveat, the lapsed renewal, the 2002 recognition
claim: Antonio Meucci developed a 'teletrofono' (speaking telegraph): conceived in Havana c. 1849, demonstrated in New York in 1860, U.S. patent caveat filed December 28, 1871, lapsed after 1874 when he could not pay the $10 renewal; on June 11, 2002 the U.S. House of Representatives passed H. Res. 269 acknowledging his work in the invention of the telephone.

grade_reason: The caveat filing (1871), the lapsed renewal (1874), and the 2002 House resolution are all documented; the 1860 demonstration is attested in the resolution's preamble and museum record. Held below VERIFIED on the lost prototypes (the Western Union models vanished — the physical evidence is gone) and on the exact 1860 demonstration details.

In 1871, he filed a caveat... Due to financial hardships, Meucci could not renew his caveat. His role in the invention of the telephone was overlooked until the United States House of Representatives passed a Resolution on June 11, 2002, honoring Meucci's contributions and work.'

U.S. House of Representatives, H. Res. 269 (107th Congress), passed June 11, 2002 — preamble: 'if Meucci had been able to pay the $10 fee to maintain the caveat after 1874, no patent could have been issued to Bell'; resolved: 'the life and achievements of Antonio Meucci should be recognized, and his work in the invention of the telephone should be acknowledged.' competing_hypotheses: Judge Wallace's 1887 ruling (U.S. Government vs. Meucci): Meucci could not show his caveat contained the elements of an electric speaking telephone — Wallace called it an elaborate 'string telephone' (mechanical, not electrical) and found attempted fraud on investors. The non-binding caveat: H. Res. 269 was a sense-of-the-House resolution, not a legal finding — it 'acknowledged his work in the invention,' not that he was the inventor. The 'wrong laboratory' coincidence: the H. Res. 269 preamble notes Bell 'conducted experiments in the same laboratory where Meucci's materials had been stored' — carried as stated in the resolution, not as a proven misappropriation.
falsifiability: The 1871 caveat is a filed public document; a showing that no such caveat was filed, or that the 1860 demonstration is wholly unattested in period sources, would overturn this record.

title: 'Lightning never strikes the same place twice' (myth)

grade_reason: NOAA and NASA document repeated strikes on the same structures: the Empire State Building is hit about 23–25 times per year (NOAA; NASA's LIS climatology), was struck eight times in 24 minutes during one storm, and the Eiffel Tower about ten times a year — lightning seeks the tallest conductive path, so a spot struck once is proven to be an excellent target, not a spent one.
earliest_attestation: The folk saying in 19th-century English usage as a metaphor; the physical refutation from 20th-century strike records

For example, the Empire State Building is hit about 25 times per year.'

NASA Scientific Visualization Studio, 'Where Does Lightning Strike?' (2017): 'However, this common phrase is a myth. Lightning often strikes the same place repeatedly—especially tall, pointy, and isolated objects. According NOAA, the Empire State Building is hit approximately 23 times a year.' Note_on_grade_scope: the grade kills the 'nothing original' reading only — the translation movement was real and foundational, Galen and Hippocrates were the base texts, and the conduit story survives as PART of the truth, not the whole of it.
earliest_attestation: The claim lives in the modern secondary literature and popular 'dark ages' narratives, not in any ancient source

sources.ref: evt-ibn-al-nafis-001: pulmonary circulation, 1242 — an anatomical claim Galen got wrong, corrected 300 years before Servetus
evt-al-zahrawi-001: ~200 illustrated surgical instruments, c. 1000 — the first illustrated surgical manual
evt-bimaristan-001: waqf-endowed hospitals, 872-1284 — no ancient parallel at this institutional scale

Translation as scholarship: the 9th-century translation movement (Hunayn ibn Ishaq's circle) was itself research-grade work — new editions, corrections, syntheses — not 'just copying'; the conduit insult devalues even the transmission

Mirror-exaggeration: modern popular writers sometimes inflate individual attributions (every instrument 'invented,' every idea 'first') — the records above grade each on its own evidence and park VERIFIED where single-source, so the fence cuts both ways
falsifiability: It is already falsified: any ONE demonstrated original contribution collapses the 'nothing original' universal — this record carries four (pulmonary circulation, illustrated surgical instruments, the institutional hospital, the crankshaft/camshaft automata)

title: Joseph Swan's carbon-filament lamp — the priority the legend skipped (evidence chain corrected)
claim: Joseph Swan built and publicly demonstrated a working carbon-filament incandescent lamp before Edison — public demonstrations at Newcastle on 18 December 1878 (Chemical Society lecture), 17 January 1879 (repeat lecture, lamp shown in operation), and 3 February 1879 (Literary and Philosophical Society theatre, audience 700+, Sir William Armstrong presiding); British Patent No. 4933 granted 27 November 1880; installations followed at his Gateshead home, the Lit & Phil Library (20 October 1880), and the Savoy Theatre, London (December 1881).
place: Newcastle upon Tyne / Gateshead, England — the February 1879 lecture demonstration; Swan's Gateshead home, the first home lit by electric light
grade_reason: Attested by contemporary lecture reports (18 Dec 1878, 17 Jan 1879, 3 Feb 1879 — the last to 700+ with Armstrong presiding), the patent register (No. 4933, 27 Nov 1880), and institutional histories (Swan Electric Light Company 1881; Lit & Phil Library first public room lit by electricity 20 Oct 1880; Savoy Theatre Dec 1881 first public building lit entirely by electricity). Held at CORROBORATED rather than VERIFIED because the primary lecture reports were accessed here through secondary aggregators; the chain is strong but one layer removed. Supersedes evt-swan-incandescent-lamp-001, which carried the imprecise '1878 patent' shorthand.
earliest_attestation: Newcastle Chemical Society lecture, 18 December 1878; repeat lecture 17 January 1879; Literary and Philosophical Society of Newcastle upon Tyne public demonstration, 3 February 1879 (contemporary lecture reports and institutional histories).

sources.desc: Swan began experimenting with carbonized paper filaments in an evacuated glass bulb in 1850; working device by 1860, stalled by poor vacuum pumps; demos 18 Dec 1878 (lamp broke down), 17 Jan 1879 (successful repeat), 3 Feb 1879 (700+ audience, Armstrong presiding); filament made from paper strips coated with treacle and tar, fired in a pottery kiln
sources.ref: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Swan; W.P.E.H.S. historic supplement No. 65 — Joseph Swan biography (wpehs.org.uk/historicsupplements/Sup065JosephSwanBiog.pdf)

sources.desc: British Patent No. 4933 granted 27 November 1880 (not '1878'); Gateshead history page notes he 'did not receive a patent until 27 November 1880'; Arapostathis & Gooday (Patently Contestable, MIT Press 2013): Swan did not file until aware of Edison's patenting — priority rests on the dated demos and research
sources.ref: gatesheadhistory.com/joseph-swan.html; University of Reading working paper (centaur.reading.ac.uk/79610/1/Fundamental patents.pdf) citing Arapostathis & Gooday

sources.desc: Installations: Underhill (Gateshead home) — first house with working bulbs; Lit & Phil Library, Newcastle — first public room lit by electric light (20 Oct 1880); founded The Swan Electric Light Company, 1881; Savoy Theatre, London (Dec 1881) — first public building lit entirely by electricity using Swan's lamps
sources.ref: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Swan

competing_hypotheses: Swan's pre-1878 prototypes suffered from weak vacuum pumps, so his lamps were impractical until the late 1870s — the 1860s work establishes priority of experiment, not commercial readiness
Edison's improvements (thin high-resistance filament, better evacuation) were incorporated by Swan into his own lamps — the two programs converged, which is why the merger made commercial sense

Swan's patent paper-trail is messier than the demo record: Arapostathis & Gooday argue he did not file until he became aware of Edison's patenting — his priority rests on the dated public demonstrations and documented research, which is also what the academic record says won him the 1883 settlement
falsifiability: Archival evidence that the December 1878–February 1879 demonstrations did not occur or that Patent No. 4933 was never granted — against the lecture reports and the patent register.

title: The Canterbury Hall opens, 17 May 1852 — Morton's purpose-built hall
claim: On 17 May 1852 Charles Morton and Frederick Stanley opened the 700-seat Canterbury Hall at the Canterbury Arms, Upper Marsh, Lambeth — the purpose-built hall that became the model for the music-hall boom, described by historians as 'the most significant date in all the history of music hall'.

grade_reason: Multiple independent attestations converge: the licence records, the consistent 17 May 1852 opening date, the documented 1856 rebuild around the old hall, and the institutional record of the Theatres Trust — while the same record corrects the 'first music hall' flattening.
earliest_attestation: Morton's singing-room licences (1849–1851); contemporary press on the 1852 opening; Morton's own publicity, including the 1855–56 advertisements in The Times around the Theatres Act prosecutions

sources.ref: Theatres Trust theatrical database — Canterbury Hall: 'Charles Morton's Canterbury Hall was a key building in the history of music hall'; opening licences and history
Wikipedia / Charles Morton (impresario): Canterbury Hall 1852 (700 seats), New Canterbury December 1856 (1,500 seats)

falsifiability: Licence records or press contradicting the 17 May 1852 opening, the 700-seat capacity, or Morton's proprietorship.

title: Samuel Fox's Paragon rib patent (1852): the modern umbrella frame
claim: Samuel Fox patented the 'Paragon' umbrella rib in 1852 — a thin steel strip rolled into a U (trough) section, combining lightness with strength, inspired by the tubular construction of the Menai bridge; the Paragon frame became the industry standard for umbrella ribs. Fox founded Fox Umbrella Frames Ltd at Stocksbridge, Sheffield, in 1842, and became the world's largest umbrella-frame manufacturer.
place: Stocksbridge, Sheffield, England
grade_reason: The patent record itself is the primary evidence, multiply and independently described: the 1911 Britannica names the 1852 Paragon patent and its U-section form; Sangster's contemporary trade history describes the Paragon frame (half the weight of whalebone, equally strong; the Menai-bridge trough inspiration); the Hoyland Fox company history confirms the 1842 Stocksbridge founding and the Paragon name.
earliest_attestation: The 1852 patent record; 1911 Britannica 'Umbrella' entry

sources.ref: 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Umbrella' (public domain): 'One of the most notable inventions for combining lightness, strength and elasticity in the ribs of umbrellas was the Paragon rib patented by Samuel Fox in 1852... formed of a thin strip of steel rolled into a U or trough section'
William Sangster, Umbrellas and Their History (1868): the Paragon frame — half the weight of whalebone, equally strong; the trough form from the Menai tubular bridge

Hoyland Fox company history: Samuel Fox founded Fox Umbrella Frames Ltd in 1842 at Stocksbridge; first inventor of the U-shape ribs called 'Paragon'; became the world's largest umbrella-frame manufacturer
Digitized 19th-c. trade book (WSU digital collection): '1851, Fox's paragon frames were introduced' — introduction-vs-patent variance carried honestly

competing_hypotheses: Introduction-vs-patent date: one digitized trade book says '1851, Fox's paragon frames were introduced' — the 1852 patent date is the secure anchor; the one-year variance is carried honestly, not resolved
The pre-Paragon metal-rib step: Holland introduced metal (not whalebone/cane) ribs in 1850 — Fox's innovation was the rib section and manufacture, not the metal rib itself
falsifiability: The 1852 patent record proving to be misattributed, or a dated prior patent for a U-section steel umbrella rib

title: 'Charles Morton invented the music hall' — the invention credit, corrected
claim: Charles Morton invented the music hall — he was the inventor of music-hall entertainment as a form.
place: Canterbury Hall, Upper Marsh, Lambeth, London, England (the telling's location)
grade_reason: The Theatres Trust — the institutional authority on British theatres — states it outright: Canterbury 'was not, as is often said, 'the first music hall' and Morton was not 'the inventor' of music-hall entertainment.' The song-and-supper rooms predate 1852; the 1852 building was 'a fairly typical pub concert room.'
earliest_attestation: The invention credit is a later popular flattening; the Theatres Trust entry documents the correction with the full misdating history ('starting with a Select Committee report in 1866 and continuing to the latest edition of Grove's Dictionary of Music & Musicians')

sources.ref: Theatres Trust theatrical database — Canterbury Hall: 'It was not, as is often said, 'the first music hall' and Morton was not 'the inventor' of music hall entertainment, but the second Canterbury was, beyond argument, the first of the giant grand music halls'; misdating history traced to the 1866 Select Committee report through Grove's Dictionary
BBC 'What a Performance!' — music hall episode: taproom concerts as background diversion in early-19th-century pubs; mid-1830s 'song and supper rooms' as established institutions before Morton

The 'Father of the Halls' sobriquet as honorific: a founder's title that popular retellings flattened into an invention credit
falsifiability: Pre-1852 song-and-supper rooms are the falsifier that already exists: the invention credit requires nothing to have existed before the Canterbury; Evans's, the 'Free and Easys,' and the whole taproom-concert tradition did.

title: Pravaz's syringe: the Lyon half of the 1853 twin invention
claim: In 1853, Charles-Gabriel Pravaz of Lyon built a working hypodermic syringe — graduated glass cylinder, screw-driven piston, silver construction — and used it to inject coagulating solutions (perchloride of iron/mercury) via trocar into aneurysms, in sheep and then in practice — independently of Alexander Wood's same-year Edinburgh work, with no channel of transmission between the two.
place: Lyon, France
grade_reason: The simultaneity is agreed across the specialist literature (MDDI: 'independently invented virtually simultaneously in 1853'; ThoughtCo; the French 'Pravaz syringe' tradition). Held at CORROBORATED on the thinner primary documentation of Pravaz's own 1853 experiments relative to Wood's 1855 publication, and on the genuine French/Anglo split in the credit tradition.
earliest_attestation: The Pravaz syringe's entry into surgical use, mid-1850s; the 19th-century French surgical literature

sources.ref: MDDI Online, 'The Hypodermic Syringe: Greatest Medical Device of All Time?' — 'The first devices recognizable as hypodermic syringes were independently invented virtually simultaneously in 1853 by Scottish physician Alexander Wood and French surgeon Charles Gabriel Pravaz'

ThoughtCo, 'The History of Hypodermic Needles and Syringes' — the Pravaz syringe: silver construction, screw piston mechanism, graduated measurements; 'At about the same time, Charles Gabriel Pravaz, of Lyon, was making a similar syringe'

The Free Library, 'The early development of intravenous apparatus' — 'The French physician, Charles Gabriel Pravaz is widely but erroneously credited with the invention of the syringe and subcutaneous medication. His experiments... involved the use of a silver metal syringe and injection of perchloride of mercury via a trochar into arterial aneurysms in sheep'

competing_hypotheses: Pravaz's device was a trocar modification rather than a true syringe — Wood's all-glass instrument deserves the 'first true hypodermic syringe' title alone (the Anglo telling; rejected by the French 'Pravaz syringe' tradition and the simultaneity evidence)
Pravaz knew of Wood's work through the medical press (unattested — no channel documented)
falsifiability: Contemporary evidence of a documented channel of transmission from Edinburgh to Lyon in 1852–1853, or proof Pravaz's 1853 work postdated and depended on Wood's

title: The myth: Alexander Wood invented the hypodermic syringe (sole inventor, 1853)
claim: Alexander Wood was the sole inventor of the hypodermic syringe in 1853 — the lone genius of the glass tube.
place: Edinburgh, Scotland (Wood's practice, 19 Royal Circus)
grade_reason: The sole-inventor reading dies on three independent facts: (1) Charles-Gabriel Pravaz of Lyon built a working hypodermic syringe — graduated cylinder, screw piston, silver — in the same year, 1853, with no channel of transmission between the two men; (2) Francis Rynd's hollow-needle injection at Dublin's Meath Hospital came nine years earlier (3 June 1844, reported in the Dublin Medical Press, 12 March 1845 — 'the first known hypodermic injection'); (3) the deeper prior art — Anel's 1714 syringe, de Graaf's 17th-century metal syringe, Heron's ~180 BC piston-and-barrel syringe, Wren's 1656 quill-and-bladder injections. Wood's real, surviving contribution (the all-glass syringe, the 1855 neuralgia paper, subcutaneous morphine practice) is carried in the companion record — the lone-genius story is not.
earliest_attestation: Wikipedia, 'Alexander Wood (physician)': 'In 1853, he invented the first hypodermic needle that used a true syringe and hollow needle' — the telling being graded here

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Francis Rynd' — Dublin Medical Press 12 March 1845 report of the 3 June 1844 injection; 'the first known hypodermic injection'

MDDI Online, 'The Hypodermic Syringe: Greatest Medical Device of All Time?' — 'The first devices recognizable as hypodermic syringes were independently invented virtually simultaneously in 1853 by Scottish physician Alexander Wood and French surgeon Charles Gabriel Pravaz'
ThoughtCo, 'The History of Hypodermic Needles and Syringes' — Pravaz's screw mechanism and graduated syringe; Wood's all-glass syringe and 1855 neuralgia paper

The Free Library (anesthesia history), 'The early development of intravenous apparatus' — Pravaz 'widely but erroneously credited with the invention of the syringe'; Rynd's work; Wood's 1855 publication; Fordyce Barker 1856 US introduction
Wikipedia, 'Alexander Wood (physician)' — the sole-inventor telling being graded; Wood vs Hunter 'subcutaneous' vs 'hypodermic' dispute; Brunton 2000 priority paper

competing_hypotheses: The co-invention framing: Wood and Pravaz independently arrived at workable hypodermic syringes in the same year — the standard account in the specialist literature
The Rynd-first framing: Rynd's 1844 hollow-needle injection is the true beginning, with Wood and Pravaz refining it into syringes nine years later
The diffusionist framing: the 1853 devices were only the convergence point of centuries of syringe and hollow-needle development, so 'invention' is the wrong word entirely
falsifiability: Contemporary evidence that Pravaz's 1853 work was derivative of Wood's (a documented channel of transmission), or that Rynd's 1844 report was fabricated

title: Wood's real achievement: the all-glass syringe and the 1855 neuralgia paper
claim: In 1853, Alexander Wood of Edinburgh built an all-glass hypodermic syringe with a hollow needle, and in 1855 published 'A New Method of Treating Neuralgia by the Direct Application of Opiates to the Painful Points' (Edinburgh Medical and Surgical Review) — the first practical method of subcutaneous morphine injection for neuralgia, which Wood argued had 'a far wider application' beyond narcotics.
place: 19 Royal Circus, Edinburgh, Scotland
grade_reason: Wood's invention and publication are in the primary record (the 1855 paper and its preface, via Brown 1886) and in the secondary literature (Brunton 2000, 'A Question of Priority: Alexander Wood, Charles Hunter and the Hypodermic Method'); Hunter's 'hypodermic' coinage and the local-vs-general dispute are documented in the same record. Held at CORROBORATED: the surviving achievement is the method and the paper, not the sole-inventor title. The DEBUNKED companion record carries the myth's death; this record carries the man's real work.
earliest_attestation: Wood, A. (1855). 'A New Method of Treating Neuralgia by the Direct Application of Opiates to the Painful Points', Edinburgh Medical and Surgical Review; and the separately published preface quoted by his biographer Thomas Brown (1886)

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Alexander Wood (physician)' — 'In 1853, he invented the first hypodermic needle that used a true syringe and hollow needle'; Wood's 'subcutaneous' vs Hunter's 'hypodermic'; Wood vs Hunter local-vs-general dispute; Thomas Brown (1886) biography quotes
D. Brunton (2000). 'A Question of Priority: Alexander Wood, Charles Hunter and the Hypodermic Method'. Proceedings of the Royal College of Physicians of Edinburgh 30(4): 349–351

competing_hypotheses: Charles Hunter's reading was right — injections have a general, not local, effect, and the English term 'hypodermic' (coined by Hunter) names the method better than Wood's 'subcutaneous' (the contemporary dispute; the profession backed Hunter — carried in the record)
Fordyce Barker's 1856 US introduction, not Wood's 1855 paper, is the method's real diffusion event
falsifiability: Proof the 1855 paper's cases were fabricated, or evidence the all-glass syringe predates 1853 in Wood's hands

title: The Inuit testimony - the witnesses the searchers kept ignoring
claim: Inuit oral testimony is a primary evidentiary source for the Franklin expedition's fate: Inuit witnesses continuously located the expedition and its ships from the 1850s onward. Charles Francis Hall's 1869 witness In-nook-poo-zhe-jook described a ship sunk off the west coast of King William Island - the account that matches Terror Bay, where HMS Terror was found in 2016. John Rae's 1854 report (the £10,000 Admiralty-reward report) rested on Inuit accounts of starving white men near the Back River. Louie Kamookak of Gjoa Haven spent decades compiling Inuit oral history into a search geography that Parks Canada's teams credit as decisive in locating HMS Erebus in 2014. The testimony was repeatedly discounted by Victorian and modern searchers in favor of their own theories - and was right.
place: King William Island and the Queen Maud Gulf region, Nunavut
grade_reason: The geographic testimony is independently confirmed by two wreck discoveries at Inuit-indicated locations, and the institutional record (Parks Canada) explicitly credits Inuit oral history as decisive - but the testimony is a transmitted oral tradition, so it stays below VERIFIED.
earliest_attestation: John Rae's 1854 report to the Admiralty - Inuit accounts of the expedition's fate; the reward was paid.

sources.ref: John Rae's 1854 report to the Admiralty - Inuit accounts, Franklin relics; the £10,000 reward report
Charles Francis Hall's 1869 expedition - In-nook-poo-zhe-jook's account of a ship sunk off King William Island's west coast
David C. Woodman, Unravelling the Franklin Mystery: Inuit Testimony (1991) - the synthesis that argued the testimony had been right all along

Parks Canada, Wrecks of HMS Erebus and HMS Terror National Historic Site - published credit to Inuit oral history (Kamookak, Gjoa Haven and Cambridge Bay consultations); 'never gave up on the belief that Inuit oral histories were accurate'
Louie Kamookak's decades of oral-history compilation (Gjoa Haven) - the search geography behind the 2014 find

competing_hypotheses: The testimony is evidence but not proof: individual Inuit accounts conflate events, dates drift across retellings, and the oral tradition cannot substitute for the archaeological record - the testimony located the wrecks; the sonar and divers confirmed them
Some Victorian-era Inuit testimony was mistranslated or selectively reported (the Rae cannibalism controversy shows the transmission was politically fraught)
David Woodman's 1991 synthesis over-reads some accounts - the Inuit record is strongest on geography (where the ships were), weaker on chronology (when)
falsifiability: Showing that the 2014/2016 wreck positions came from search-technology alone with no Inuit input (contradicted by Parks Canada's own published credit), or that the 1869 Hall account describes a different ship, would weaken this record; it is held at CORROBORATED because individual accounts vary while the geographic consensus holds.

title: Göbel's 1854 lamp — the priority claim the courtroom killed
claim: Heinrich Göbel built a working incandescent electric lamp with a carbonized bamboo filament in New York in 1854 — beating Swan and Edison by decades.
place: New York, New York — the claimed site of the 1854 lamp (no contemporary site documentation)

Mass., 1893), Judge Colt ruled it 'extremely improbable that Henry Goebel constructed a practical incandescent lamp in 1854,' noting such claims rest on recollection 'to be received with great caution.' Add the documentary gap — no contemporary 1854 record of any kind — and the anachronistic bamboo-filament detail, and the claim dies twice. The grade kills the 1854 priority telling, never the court's careful words and never the real priority trail (de Moleyns 1841, Starr, Swan).

sources.ref: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Göbel

sources.desc: Göbel's 1854 claim surfaced decades after the fact via promotion and family testimony; no contemporary 1854 documentation; the bamboo-filament detail mirrors Edison's 1880 bamboo work
sources.ref: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Göbel

competing_hypotheses: Göbel did experiment with early electric lighting apparatus in the 1850s — the claim of a practical working lamp in 1854 is what dies, not any tinkering at all
The bamboo-filament detail of the Göbel telling suspiciously mirrors Edison's 1880 bamboo work, which is exactly the period the claim was being promoted — retrofitting, not memory
Göbel's advocates cite German-American commemorative literature and family testimony; the court record carries the rebuttal, which is why this grade is DEBUNKED rather than CLAIMED

title: The cannonballs in the road at Crimea
claim: Roger Fenton's 'Valley of the Shadow of Death' (Crimea, April 1855) exists in two plate variants — cannonballs on the road in one, off the road in the other — because Fenton's team moved the cannonballs onto the road for the more dramatic exposure.
