sources.ref: The two surviving 'Valley of the Shadow of Death' plates (April 1855)
Errol Morris, Believing Is Seeing (2011) — forensic essay on the plate order and the cannonball question

competing_hypotheses: The staging reading (Morris 2011): the off-road variant came first; Fenton's team rolled cannonballs onto the road for the famous shot — the valleys' visual rhyme with Tennyson demanded a better composition

The dispute: other photographic analyses (Groves and successors) argue the road-variant came first or that both are honest sequence exposures; Fenton's Crimean wagon (Marcus Sparling's van) logistics cut both ways
The neutral reading: two exposures of the same road taken minutes apart, cannonball displacement unexplained but not necessarily deliberate — hence CLAIMED, not DEBUNKED or CORROBORATED
falsifiability: A dated field note, letter, or exposure log from the Fenton/Sparling party fixing the sequence would move the grade; absent that, shadow-angle and ball-position analysis keep it contested.

title: The real 19th-century life of 'lions led by donkeys'
claim: The 'lions led by donkeys/asses' image predates the First World War by more than half a century, appearing in the Crimean War, the Franco-Prussian War, the Boxer Rebellion, and in print as early as 1855 — it was a 19th-century commonplace, not a 1914 German verdict.
place: Western Europe — the phrase's 19th-century print trail (London, Paris, Sevastopol)
grade_reason: Multiple independent 19th-century print attestations across three wars and three nations; the phrase's pre-WWI life is documented, even where the original coinage remains untraced.
earliest_attestation: The Daily Journal (American newspaper), August 1855, report of the Siege of Sevastopol: 'an army of lions led by donkeys' — attributed in the piece to the Russians. The Times of London wrote of the British Army in the Crimea, 'The Russians say we are lions led on by asses.'

sources.ref: The Daily Journal, August 1855 — Sevastopol report, 'an army of lions led by donkeys'
The Times, London — Crimean War ('lions led on by asses'); Franco-Prussian War reuse ('lions led by donkeys' of the French)
Francisque Sarcey, 'Paris During The Siege' (1871): 'You are lions led by jackasses' — The Times's utterance 'drummed into' the French troops
Colonel J. M. Grierson, 1901 report on the Russian contingent to the Boxer Rebellion: 'lions led by asses' (via Richard Connaughton)
Captain P. A. Thompson, 'Lions Led by Donkeys' (1927) — the phrase as a book title before Clark, subtitled 'Showing how victory in the Great War was achieved by those who made the fewest mistakes'

competing_hypotheses: The phrase may be Russian in origin — unclear; phrases.org.uk notes the origin is not established
Each war re-coined it independently as a natural metaphor, rather than inheriting it as a single coinage
The Evelyn Princess Blücher 1921 'invented by an Englishwoman in wartime Berlin' reading (Mackenzie Institute) — carried as an unattested alternative attribution
falsifiability: Evidence that every pre-1961 instance is misdated or fabricated would overturn this; the 1855, 1870-71, 1901, and 1927 instances are on the print record.

title: The Yellow River's 1855 avulsion — a river that changed seas
claim: On 1 August 1855 (19th day of the 6th month, Xianfeng 5), the Yellow River breached its northern bank at Tongwaxiang in present-day Lankao, Henan, diverting its course from the Yellow Sea (via the Huai system, Jiangsu) to the Bohai Sea via the old Daqing/Ji River course in Shandong. The 1855 event ended the river's 1128–1855 southern course (itself a man-made diversion of 1128, when the river captured the Huai); the 1855 shift was natural. The new delta has since migrated repeatedly (six large natural diversions 1889–1934, four artificial 1953–1996).
place: Tongwaxiang, Lankao, Henan — the 1855 breach point
grade_reason: The event is dated to the day in Qing records and independently corroborated by modern sediment-delta science (delta growth, mouth migrations, marine sediment provenance).
earliest_attestation: Qing administrative records of the Xianfeng 5 breach at Tongwaxiang, August 1855.

sources.ref: Fei et al. 2012, Limnology 13:117 (cited in the 1851–1855 floods chronology) — the breach sequence

MDPI Land 14(9):1826 — cultivated-land dynamics in the Yellow River Delta basin since 1855 (the 1855 Tongwaxiang breach into the Daqing course; the 1128 man-made diversion; the ten post-1855 mouth migrations)
Nature s41598-017-03140-x — clay-mineral record confirming the pre-1855 southern (Yellow Sea) course

Frontiers in Marine Science 2026 (doi:10.3389/fmars.2024.1490990) — Yellow River Delta coastline 1984-2024: three stages (rapid transformation, gradual slowdown, stabilization, ~15 yr each); abandoned Diaokou estuary eroding inland while the active Qingshuigou estuary progrades seaward — the 40-year observed modern analog of lobe switching: the abandoned lobe rots, the live one builds, in one generation of observation

MDPI Water 18(5):598 (published 28 Feb 2026) — four OSL-dated sediment cores of the shallow-buried abandoned Yellow River Delta (893–1855 AD): the 893 AD Yellow River avulsion triggered delta abandonment (893–1482 AD, fluvial-to-wave-controlled shift); Little Ice Age storm surges (1482–1855) further reworked the deposits — the delta the 1855 river abandoned had itself been abandoned 962 years earlier; the substrate's confession in two acts. Grade-neutral for the 1855 event (the breach date and geography unchanged) — appended as context for the river's serial abandonment habit

competing_hypotheses: The breach as a purely climatic event vs a maintenance-collapse event — the 1851–1855 high-water sequence is documented; the dyke state is the live sub-question
falsifiability: A published Qing record re-dating the breach would move the date; a sediment record contradicting the Bohai-first arrival would revise the geography.

title: The anti-Stratfordian claim — 'Shakespeare didn't write Shakespeare'
claim: William Shakespeare of Stratford-upon-Avon did not write the plays and poems attributed to him; a hidden aristocrat or courtier (Francis Bacon, Christopher Marlowe, Edward de Vere, Mary Sidney, Queen Elizabeth I, or another candidate) wrote them and used his name as a front.
place: Stratford-upon-Avon, England (the claim is about Stratford; the evidence is London's archives)
grade_reason: Four independent kills: (1) no contemporary ever expressed doubt and no contemporary document links any candidate to the authorship; (2) each leading candidate fails on the record — de Vere died in 1604 before The Tempest and other late plays, Marlowe died in 1593, and Meres (1598) lists de Vere and Shakespeare as separate writers; (3) at least 80 rival candidates cancel each other — every camp's proof is another camp's problem; (4) the whole thesis rests on argumentum ex silentio — absence of school records read as evidence of absence, a method scholars reject for every other period writer.
earliest_attestation: Delia Bacon, The Philosophy of the Plays of Shakespeare Unfolded (1856) — the first published alternative-authorship proposal

sources.ref: Delia Bacon, The Philosophy of the Plays of Shakespeare Unfolded (1856) — origin of the modern question
Wikipedia, 'Shakespeare authorship question' — documentary record, candidate problems, the 80-candidate count

New York Times survey of 265 American Shakespeare professors, 22 April 2007 — 6% 'yes' good reason to question, 11% 'possibly'; 61% 'a theory without convincing evidence', 32% 'a waste of time and classroom distraction'
Shakespeare Authorship Coalition, 'Declaration of Reasonable Doubt' — 3,348 signatories by 23 April 2016 (named fairly as the agnostic position)
James Shapiro, Contested Will (2010) — the question as 19th-century invention

competing_hypotheses: The mainstream position: the documentary record is sufficient and the 'authorship question' is a 19th-century invention (Shapiro, Contested Will, 2010)

The agnostic position: authorship is genuinely unsettled because no autograph manuscripts survive — the Shakespeare Authorship Coalition's 'Declaration of Reasonable Doubt' (3,348 signatories by the 2016 deadline, incl. 573 self-described academics)
falsifiability: Already falsifiable and falsified: a single contemporary link between any candidate and the plays would reopen the question — 170 years of searching has produced none.

title: Scott's 1860 phonoautogram — the first recorded human voice
claim: On 9 April 1860, a Parisian inventor's machine recorded a human voice on soot-covered paper — the singer singing a fragment of the French folk song 'Au Clair de la Lune' — and that physical trace survives, dated, and was played back audibly in 2008: the earliest recognizable recording of a human voice, made seventeen years before Edison's phonograph.
place: Paris, France (phonoautograph patent; phonautogram papers at the French Academy of Sciences / Paris patent office)
grade_reason: The artifact survives with Scott's own date on it; the 1857 patent documents the machine; and the 2008 virtual-stylus playback — by particle physicist Carl Haber at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, from First Sounds' recovered papers — turned the very tracings into audible sound, independently confirming that the sheet captured a human voice. Multiple independent lines (the paper, the patent, the playback) converge on the same event.
earliest_attestation: The dated phonautogram sheet itself, 9 April 1860, found among Scott's patent-office and French Academy of Sciences papers

sources.ref: Wikipedia — 'Phonautograph': French patent 25 March 1857 #17,897/31,470; 9 April 1860 'Au Clair de la Lune' recording; device not designed for playback; First Sounds / Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory 2008 digital conversion; 'prior to this point, the earliest known record of a human voice was thought to be an 1877 phonograph recording by Thomas Edison'

Symmetry Magazine (Dec 2009) — 'Physicist revives oldest recording of the human voice': Scott never intended playback; Carl Haber of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory pulled the sound from Scott's soot-covered paper in March 2008 — 'the earliest recording of the human voice ever successfully played back'

LiveScience — 'Edison Voice Recording Is Old, but Not Oldest': the December 2007 discovery in the Paris patent office by an American audio historian; the French Academy of Sciences cache; the Lawrence Berkeley digital mapping with a 'virtual stylus'; Scott's first phonautograms dated three years before the 1857 patent, indecipherable without the tuning-fork timing signal; the earliest recognizable recording of any sound is an 1859 tuning-fork recording at 435 Hz

Classical Net / NYT (Jody Rosen, 27 March 2008) — 'Researchers Play Tune Recorded Before Edison': Samuel Brylawski (former head of the Library of Congress recorded-sound division, not affiliated with the research group) — 'This is a historic find, the earliest known recording of sound'

competing_hypotheses: The singer is 'thought to be Scott' (NYT reporting) rather than positively identified — the recording's identity rides below the artifact's certainty

Scott dated his first phonautograms to 1853–54, but those carry no tuning-fork timing reference and remain indecipherable 'squawks'; the 1860 recording is the earliest INTELLIGIBLE one, not the earliest attempt
The earliest recognizable recording of any sound at all is an 1859 tuning-fork recording at 435 Hz — the 1860 is the earliest recognizable HUMAN VOICE
falsifiability: Proof that the 9 April 1860 sheet is a forgery, is misdated, or was fabricated later (e.g. by Edison-era agents) would collapse the record; independent dating of the paper/ink in the negative would reopen it

title: Lipman's pencil-with-eraser patent, US 19,783 (March 30, 1858)
claim: On March 30, 1858, Philadelphia stationer Hymen L. Lipman (born Kingston, Jamaica, 1817; America's first envelope manufacturer) was granted U.S. patent 19,783 for the 'Combination of Lead-Pencil and Eraser' — the first patent for a pencil with an attached eraser. Lipman sold the patent in 1862 to Joseph Reckendorfer for $100,000. Important design note: Lipman's patent was not the glued-on pink cap of modern memory — the specification embeds a groove of prepared india-rubber inside the pencil wood, exposed by cutting/sharpening the end, so a soiled point could be renewed 'as in the ordinary lead-pencil.'
place: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
grade_reason: The patent document is independently verifiable on Google Patents; the 1862 sale to Reckendorfer for $100,000 and the subsequent litigation are carried across reference sources; the embedded-core design detail comes straight from the specification's text.
earliest_attestation: U.S. Letters Patent 19,783 (March 30, 1858); Google Patents scan of the specification

sources.ref: U.S. Patent 19,783 — 'Combination of Lead-Pencil and Eraser' (March 30, 1858), specification text via Google Patents
Wikipedia, 'Hymen Lipman': patent date, 1862 sale to Reckendorfer for $100,000, 1875 Supreme Court invalidation; cites Petroski (1990)
Smithsonian Magazine, 'Happy Birthday to the Modern Pencil' (2017): Lipman's embedded-core design (chunk of rubber exposed by sharpening) vs the modern glued end; Lipman's envelope/postcard career

competing_hypotheses: The 1875 Supreme Court invalidation (separate record evt-reckendorfer-v-faber-1875-001) killed the patent's legal force, not its historical reality — the grant is undisputed.
Popular retellings date the patent 1868 (a Smithsonian article's own dating slip) — the patent document itself reads March 30, 1858.
falsifiability: The patent document itself is the evidence; a falsifying find would have to show the document is not what it purports to be.

title: Warner's can opener (US 19,063, 1858)
claim: Ezra J. Warner of Waterbury, Connecticut received US Patent 19,063 on 5 January 1858 for a can opener — a curved-handle tool combining a piercing 'bayonet' and a sawing 'sickle' blade that cut a jagged line around the can lid, kept from penetrating too deep by a metal guard.
place: Waterbury, Connecticut, USA
grade_reason: The patent itself is the primary source; the design details (bayonet + sickle, metal guard) are in the specification and multiply summarized.
earliest_attestation: US Patent 19,063 (5 January 1858)

sources.ref: US Patent 19,063 (5 January 1858), Ezra J. Warner — curved handle, long bayonet blade and interchangeable sliding shoe; bayonet pierces the lid, sickle saws around the edge

Researchpod, "Lifting the lid on the tin can opener" — 'Three years later, in 1858, a similar lever opener was patented in America by Ezra J. Warner'; the now-familiar construction: curved blade with a jaw and a projection with shoulders forming an efficient bearing or fulcrum

Google Arts & Culture / Tomato Museum, 'The History of the Can Opener' — Warner's US 19,063: used by the Northern Army during the American Civil War (1861–1865); dangerous for domestic use, production abandoned

title: The Carrington Event, 1–2 September 1859 (VERIFIED)
claim: On 1–2 September 1859, the Carrington Event — the most intense geomagnetic storm in recorded history — set telegraph systems sparking and pushed auroras to the tropics.
place: London, England (observation); global (storm effects)
grade_reason: Multiply attested: on 1 September 1859 at 11:18, Richard Carrington — sketching sunspots at his private observatory near London — saw two brilliant patches of white light erupt in a sunspot group, lasting about five minutes; Richard Hodgson independently observed the same — the first recorded white-light solar flare, published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society; ~17.6 hours later (unusually fast — typical CMEs take 2–4 days, suggesting an earlier CME had cleared the way), the coronal mass ejection struck Earth, producing the most intense geomagnetic storm in recorded history (estimated Dst −850 to −1760 nT, far beyond anything in the space age); auroras were reported globally — as far equatorward as Cuba, Hawaii, Jamaica, northern Australia, and Santiago; telegraph systems worldwide failed, sparked, and caught fire — operators received electric shocks, message paper ignited, and in Boston operators disconnected their batteries and kept sending messages on the storm's own geomagnetically induced current; Rocky Mountain miners woke at midnight and began cooking breakfast, believing dawn had come; compasses swung erratically and magnetometers worldwide registered extreme fluctuations. The modern-vulnerability corollary (a repeat would damage power grids and satellites) is graded separately as expert assessment, not as established fact about 1859.
earliest_attestation: Richard Carrington (and independently Richard Hodgson), 1 September 1859; published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society

sources.ref: Wikipedia: 'The Carrington Event was the most intense geomagnetic storm in recorded history, peaking on 1–2 September 1859 during solar cycle 10. It created strong auroral displays that were reported globally and caused sparking and even fires in telegraph stations.' The 1 September 1859 flare observed independently by Carrington and Hodgson — the first records of a solar flare.
The Watchers: Carrington's 11:18 observation, the five-minute brightening, Hodgson's independent observation, the 17.6-hour CME transit, Dst −850 to −1760 nT, erratic compasses.

Discover Magazine: the September 1, 1859 flare, the ~18-hour particle arrival, global telegraph disruption, equatorial auroras; Carrington's 'singular outbreak of light which lasted about five minutes.'

Energy Daily (July 2026): auroras to Cuba, telegraph paper on fire from Boston to Paris, operators sending messages with batteries disconnected on the storm's own current; Rocky Mountain miners mistaking aurora for dawn.

falsifiability: Contemporary telegraph/observatory records proven fabricated

title: The Crown's storm-glass distribution to fishing villages
claim: After the Royal Charter storm of October 1859, the Crown distributed storm glasses — 'FitzRoy's storm barometers' — to many small fishing communities around the British Isles, as part of FitzRoy's program to put forecasting instruments in working hands.
place: British Isles coastal fishing communities
grade_reason: Wikipedia's FitzRoy biography documents the Crown's distribution of the storm glasses to fishing communities after the 1859 storm; the program is consistent with FitzRoy's documented mission to put instruments in working hands (the warning cones, the telegraphed forecasts). Held at CORROBORATED rather than VERIFIED pending direct archival citation of the distribution manifests.
earliest_attestation: Board of Trade / Meteorological Department distribution records, via the secondary accounts

sources.ref: Wikipedia 'Robert FitzRoy': 'The 1859 storm resulted in the Crown distributing storm glasses, then known as "FitzRoy's storm barometers", to many small fishing communities around the British Isles.'

competing_hypotheses: The distribution as a purely symbolic gesture (the glasses' predictive failure, established in the storm-glass record, limits what the program could have achieved — but the distribution as an event is independently attested)
falsifiability: Board of Trade archives showing no such distribution program, or evidence the 'storm barometers' were never manufactured or sent

title: The Suez Canal opens (1869)
claim: On 17 November 1869, a 164 km sea-level waterway opened through the Isthmus of Suez, connecting the Mediterranean at Port Said to the Red Sea at Suez — built 1859–1869 by Ferdinand de Lesseps's Compagnie Universelle du Canal Maritime de Suez.
place: Isthmus of Suez, Egypt (Port Said → Suez)
grade_reason: Opening date, length, builder, and route converge across the company's own archives, contemporary press, and later documentary-heritage inscription.
earliest_attestation: The Compagnie Universelle's own construction records 1859–1869; contemporary press of the 17 November 1869 opening.

sources.ref: Compagnie Universelle du Canal Maritime de Suez — concession (1854/1856) and construction records 1859–1869
Contemporary press coverage of the 17 November 1869 opening ceremony at Port Said
UNESCO Memory of the World — Suez Canal Company archives (documentary heritage of the build)

competing_hypotheses: The canal's labor history is contested: the Egyptian corvée system supplied much of the workforce under terms that the 1856 firman capped — later French accounts minimized this, Egyptian nationalist accounts emphasize it
falsifiability: A contemporary survey showing a different route or length, or records showing the canal uncompleted by late 1869

title: The crystal skulls (ancient-artifact claim)
claim: Life-size quartz crystal skulls are genuine pre-Columbian (Aztec or Maya) artifacts, thousands of years old.
place: Eugène Boban's Paris curio shop (first appearance); British Museum / Smithsonian (the lab verdicts)
grade_reason: Electron microscopy reads 19th–20th-century manufacture on every tested skull: rotary disc tools, carborundum (synthesized 1890s), and no provenance before Boban's 1880s shop.
earliest_attestation: The British Museum skull first appears 1881 in Eugène Boban's Paris shop catalogue — no crystal skull is referenced anywhere before the 1860s

sources.ref: Sax, Meeks, Collon & Walsh, 'The origin of two purportedly pre-Columbian Mexican crystal skulls', J. Archaeol. Sci. 35 (May 2008): British Museum skull worked with a rotary disc tool and harsh abrasive (corundum/diamond); Smithsonian specimen with silicon carbide (carborundum, synthesized 1890s) — 'suggest[ed] ... made in the 1950s or later'
Jane MacLaren Walsh, Smithsonian — 2008 SEM examination of the Mitchell-Hedges skull: high-speed rotary tool marks; facial reconstruction (Gloria Nusse) showing European features
British Museum catalogue — the skull is 'probably European, 19th century AD' and 'not an authentic pre-Columbian artefact'
Sotheby's London 1943 — F.A. Mitchell-Hedges purchased the 'Skull of Doom' for £400 (not excavated at Lubaantun)

competing_hypotheses: Mitchell-Hedges's telling — the 'Skull of Doom' found at Lubaantun, 3,600 years old (undercut by the 1943 Sotheby's £400 purchase record)
Modern manufacture on old crystal (true of the material — quartz can't be dated by the carving — irrelevant to the manufacture date, which is what the tool marks read)
falsifiability: A crystal skull excavated in a documented, undisturbed pre-Columbian context — or any large skull bearing only pre-industrial tool marks

title: 'Edison made the first sound recording' — the misattributed superlative
claim: Thomas Edison made the first sound recording — the claim that the human voice was first captured in 1877 on Edison's tin-foil phonograph, and that Edison stands as the 'father of recorded sound' by virtue of the first recording.
place: Paris, France (the 1860 phonautogram's archive)
grade_reason: Three independent kills. (1) The artifact: a dated 9 April 1860 phonautogram of a human voice singing 'Au Clair de la Lune' survives in the French Academy of Sciences / Paris patent-office papers — seventeen years before Edison's machine existed. (2) The patent: Scott's phonoautograph patent of 25 March 1857 (#17,897/31,470) predates the tin-foil phonograph's December 1877 build entirely. (3) The playback: in March 2008, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's Carl Haber converted Scott's soot tracings into audible sound with a virtual stylus, independently confirming the sheet captured a human voice — a fact Scott himself never lived to hear. Edison's title as 'father of recorded sound' rests on the one thing he was first at: recording AND reproducing. The recording-only first is French, 1860, and unplayed for 148 years.
earliest_attestation: The 9 April 1860 'Au Clair de la Lune' phonautogram, in Scott's own papers (dated by his hand)

sources.ref: Wikipedia — 'Phonautograph': 'Prior to this point, the earliest known record of a human voice was thought to be an 1877 phonograph recording by Thomas Edison' — the sentence the 2008 recovery rewrote

LiveScience — 'Edison Voice Recording Is Old, but Not Oldest': December 2007 discovery of the phonautograms in the Paris patent office by an American audio historian; the 1860 'Au Clair de la Lune' recording 'predat[es] Edison's recording by a full two decades' (New Atlas summary of the finding)

New Atlas (28 March 2008) — 'Edison's first sound recording predated by 20 years': Scott's 1860 phonoautogram playback; Scott's 1878 self-published memoir railing against Edison for 'appropriating' his methods — 'the goal, Scott argued, was not sound reproduction, but "writing speech, which is what the word phonograph means"'
Symmetry Magazine (Dec 2009): 'Scott never intended to play back his recording... Edison would not invent the phonograph until 17 years later'

competing_hypotheses: The popular reading conflates 'first device that could play sound back' with 'first device that could record sound' — the two superlatives belong to two different inventors and two different decades

Edison's own misdated 'Aug 12, 1877' sketch (written 1917) fed the 1877-first framing; the Batchelor diary and the Kruesi build records point to early December 1877 for the working machine — a dating argument that is real but does not affect the debunk, which stands on 1860 alone
falsifiability: A pre-1860 recognizable human-voice recording attributed to Edison (or anyone) would not save the claim — the claim is specifically that EDISON was first; only proof that the 1860 sheet is fake or misdated would reopen it

title: Mouhot 'discovered' Angkor Wat — the discovery reading
claim: Henri Mouhot, the French naturalist, 'discovered' Angkor Wat in 1860 — he was the first person to find the lost temple in the jungle.
place: Angkor Wat — the temple whose 'discovery' is the claim
grade_reason: Two independent kills. (1) Angkor was never lost: the entire series of Angkor sites was always known to the Khmers, who continuously lived, worshipped, and farmed in and around the temple complexes — and Angkor Wat specifically stayed an active religious center into the present. (2) Westerners predated Mouhot by three centuries: the Portuguese trader Diogo do Couto wrote accounts c. 1550, the monk Antonio da Magdalena wrote of his visit in 1586, and Mouhot's own contemporary Father Bouillevaux published his account in 1858 after visiting at least five years before Mouhot's 1860 visit. The grade kills the 'discovery' reading, never the man's genuine achievement: Mouhot popularized Angkor in the West.
earliest_attestation: Mouhot's posthumously published 'Travels in Siam, Cambodia and Laos' (1863–64); the 'discovery' reading is the Western reception tradition — modern scholarship explicitly flags it as 'mistakenly credited'. Mouhot himself acknowledged predecessors in his own journals.

sources.desc: 'Mouhot is often mistakenly credited with "discovering" Angkor, although Angkor was never lost — the location and existence of the entire series of Angkor sites was always known to the Khmers and had been visited by several westerners since the 16th century.' Mouhot mentions in his journals that Father Charles Emile Bouillevaux had reported visiting at least five years before Mouhot; Bouillevaux published accounts in 1857/1858. Portuguese trader Diogo do Couto wrote accounts c. 1550; Antonio da Magdalena wrote of his visit in 1586. 'Mouhot did, however, popularise Angkor in the West.'
sources.ref: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Mouhot

sources.desc: 'Numerous western missionaries either saw or knew of Angkor at least three hundred years before Mouhot'; Diogo de Couto mid-16th c. 'accurately described both Angkor Wat and Angkor Thorn'; Père Chevruel early 17th c. called it 'as famous among the gentiles as St. Peter's at Rome'. 'Even though Henri Mouhot did not "rediscover" Angkor... he was the first westerner to generate a widespread interest in the ancient Khmer capital' — through detailed descriptions and illustrations.
sources.ref: rooneyarchive.net — 'In the footsteps of Henry Mouhot'

sources.desc: Bouillevaux, Voyage dans l'Indo-Chine 1848–1856 (Paris, 1858); Ma visite aux ruines cambodgiennes en 1850 (1874). Documents a published Western account of Angkor a full decade before Mouhot's journals appeared in print.
sources.ref: ecommons.cornell.edu — doctoral chapter on Mouhot (Bouillevaux citations)

sources.desc: 'Angkor was never lost to the Khmer people, who continuously lived, worshipped and farmed in and around the temple complexes. Moreover, other Western visitors, including missionaries like Bouillevaux, had described Angkor several years before Mouhot arrived in 1860.' What Mouhot did: 'make Angkor dramatically visible to European readers... at a specific moment when archaeological curiosity and imperial interest in Asia were expanding.' He became 'widely and inaccurately celebrated as Angkor's "discoverer".'
sources.ref: wondersofcambodia.com — 'Henri Mouhot and the Rediscovery of Angkor: Explorer, Myth and Legacy'

competing_hypotheses: Mouhot 'rediscovered' it for the West — this is this record's foil (his genuine achievement: making Angkor visible to the West through his Travels and engravings), not a defense of the discovery reading

The broader capital of Angkor did decline after the 15th century (population loss, court moving south) — that is a real, separate story (a future record), not evidence Angkor Wat was ever 'lost' or unknown
falsifiability: Evidence that no Khmer knew Angkor's location and no Westerner visited before 1860 — impossible against the documented record: Khmer continuous knowledge, do Couto c. 1550, da Magdalena 1586, Bouillevaux's 1858 published account.

title: The Pony Express (April 1860 – October 1861)
claim: The Pony Express was an American express mail service using relays of horse-mounted riders between St. Joseph, Missouri and Sacramento, California, operated by the Central Overland California and Pikes Peak Express Company (founders Alexander Majors, William B. Waddell, William H. Russell). It ran from 3 April 1860 to 26 October 1861 — about eighteen months. The ~1,900-mile route used relay stations every 10-15 miles (riders changed horses at stations, fresh riders every 75-100 miles), delivering mail in about ten days at an initial rate of $5 per half-ounce. Despite a heavy subsidy it was not a financial success: it went bankrupt within eighteen months, never winning the hoped-for U.S. government postal contract, and was made obsolete by the completion of the first transcontinental telegraph on 24 October 1861.
place: St. Joseph, Missouri (headquarters; eastern terminus of the route)
grade_reason: Multiply and independently attested: founders, dates, route, relay mechanics, the bankruptcy, and the telegraph terminus are all documented in company records, contemporary 1860-61 press, and modern institutional scholarship (NPS National Historic Trail, National Pony Express Association).
earliest_attestation: 1860 company advertisements and contemporary newspaper coverage; Patee House / Central Overland California and Pikes Peak Express Company records, St. Joseph

sources.ref: Pony Express company records and 1860-61 advertisements (Central Overland California and Pikes Peak Express Company)
Contemporary 1860-61 newspaper coverage of the service (founding, runs, demise)
U.S. National Park Service, Pony Express National Historic Trail — History & Culture
National Pony Express Association — historic trail and founders research
Smithsonian Magazine, 'Murder, Marriage and the Pony Express: Ten Things You Didn't Know About Buffalo Bill' (Lincoln 1860 election news carried Fort Kearney to Placerville in five days)
Pony Express — Wikipedia (infobox dates, founders, bankruptcy, telegraph terminus; secondary aggregator)

competing_hypotheses: The end date: some accounts give 24 October 1861 (the telegraph's completion) as the effective end, others 26 October 1861 as the formal last run — a two-day documentary variance, not a dispute
The 'sixteen months' vs 'eighteen months' shorthand found in some popular accounts — both round the April-1860-to-October-1861 span
falsifiability: Company ledgers showing the firm turned a profit, or documentary evidence of the U.S. government mail contract the founders sought — either would overturn the failure reading.

title: The long-lived Pony Express (myth)
claim: The popular image of the Pony Express as a long-running American mail institution — years or decades of lone heroic riders carrying the West's mail as a great national success — rather than what it was: an eighteen-month relay service that went bankrupt.
place: St. Joseph, Missouri (headquarters; the myth's eastern terminus)
grade_reason: Three independent kills from the attested record: (1) DURATION — the service ran about eighteen months (3 April 1860 to 26 October 1861), not a long era; (2) the LONE RIDER — the system was a relay: stations every 10-15 miles for fresh horses, fresh riders every 75-100 miles, ~190 stations total; (3) the SUCCESS — it went bankrupt within eighteen months despite a heavy subsidy, never won the government postal contract it was built to chase, and was killed within days of the transcontinental telegraph's completion on 24 October 1861.
earliest_attestation: The myth's components postdate the service: romanticization documented in the decades after 1861 (Wild West show from 1883, dime-novel pipeline)

sources.ref: Pony Express service record: 18 months of operation, relay-station mechanics, bankruptcy, telegraph terminus — see evt-pony-express-1860-001
Buffalo Bill — Wikipedia (Cody's Pony Express claim; historians' difficulty documenting it; the parent-firm errand theory)
Paul Fees (ret.) / True West Magazine, 'Did Buffalo Bill Cody Ever Ride for the Pony Express?' (the Gray debunk challenged: 'generally assumed, not without controversy')
Columbia Electronic Encyclopedia, 'Buffalo Bill' ('he claimed, apparently falsely, to have ridden for the pony express in 1860')

competing_hypotheses: The Buffalo Bill Cody rider question: Cody claimed to have ridden for the Pony Express at fourteen in 1860; historians have had difficulty documenting any of his claimed early jobs and he may have fabricated some for publicity — but Paul Fees (Buffalo Bill Center of the West) and others argue the Gray debunk overreaches, rider documentation is rare, and the association is 'generally assumed, not without controversy'. Graded CONTESTED, not part of this debunk

The sympathetic reading: the service's brevity is exactly what made it legendary — 'quickly became romanticized and became part of the lore of the Old West' is the documented phenomenon, not a refutation
falsifiability: Documentary evidence that the service ran for years beyond October 1861, or that the parent company profited from it — either would overturn this grade.

title: The secession declarations' own words
claim: The seceding states of the Lower South stated their reasons for secession in formal written declarations, and those declarations name slavery and hostility to slavery as their cause.
place: Charleston, South Carolina (the convention that adopted the first declaration)
grade_reason: The texts survive as contemporaneous primary documents and say what they say: South Carolina's lists the fugitive-slave clause, 'the right of property in slaves,' northern attacks on slavery as sinful, and a president 'hostile to slavery'; Mississippi's opens 'Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery — the greatest material interest of the world'; Texas's defends 'negro slavery' as the reason for its revolution from Mexico; none names tariffs or abstract constitutional principle as its cause.
earliest_attestation: The convention-adopted printed declarations themselves, winter 1860-61 (contemporaneous primary documents).

sources.ref: South Carolina, Declaration of the Immediate Causes (Dec 24, 1860)
Mississippi, Declaration of the Immediate Causes (Jan 9, 1861)
Georgia, Declaration of Immediate Causes (Jan 29, 1861)
Texas, Declaration of the Causes (Feb 1, 1861)

competing_hypotheses: Some upper-South ordinances (Virginia, North Carolina, Tennessee, Arkansas) emphasize federal 'coercion' of the seceded states — the chronology matters: they seceded after Fort Sumter, and their stated trigger differs from the Lower South's documents
Georgia's declaration includes some tariff/trade material, but its center of gravity is slavery — the documents are read as wholes, not by selective sentence
falsifiability: The declarations, on inspection, not naming slavery among their reasons — inspection shows they do.

title: The storm glass predicts the weather (myth)
claim: The storm glass (the camphor-liquid 'FitzRoy storm barometer') predicts the weather — its crystallization patterns foretell storms, frost, and fair weather.
place: London (Meteorological Office / Tomlinson's tests)
grade_reason: Charles Tomlinson tested FitzRoy's claims over several months in 1862 and concluded 'all of the phenomena were caused by changes in temperature and nothing else' — 'the storm glass acts as a rude kind of thermometer' — and recommended the Meteorological Office abandon it, which it did. In 2008, Allan Mills (Leicester) and Kazushige Nagashima (Meiji University) independently confirmed the crystals respond to temperature and are pure camphor. Modern experiments consistently find the glasses 'aren't very accurate' as forecasters.
earliest_attestation: FitzRoy's documented weather-reading chart for the storm glass (clear liquid = clear weather, cloudy = cloudy, dots = humid/foggy, stars = thunderstorms, etc.), promoted in the 1860s

sources.ref: New Scientist, 'Storm warning: Can crystal-gazing predict the weather?': Tomlinson 'decided to test FitzRoy's claims scientifically. Over several months in 1862, Tomlinson recorded the response of a storm glass to the weather... he reasoned that all of the phenomena were caused by changes in temperature and nothing else. "It may be fairly concluded that the storm glass acts as a rude kind of thermometer," Tomlinson wrote... left him recommending that the instrument be abandoned by the Meteorological Office. Tomlinson carried the day.' Also: 2008, Allan Mills (Leicester) and Kazushige Nagashima (Meiji University) 'confirmed that the crystals in the glass respond to temperature' and 'proved the crystals were pure camphor.'

Leeds City Museums, 'For All Seasons' exhibition (Admiral FitzRoy barometer): the storm glass 'holds a mixture of different chemicals in water which were thought to change in appearance in anticipation of different weather patterns. However, most modern experiments have found that the glasses aren't very accurate.'

FitzRoy's storm-glass reading chart (via the Constantinople storm-glass manual, reproducing FitzRoy's documented patterns): clear = clear weather, cloudy = cloudy, dots = humid/foggy, stars = thunderstorms, flakes = overcast/snow, bottom crystals = frost, top threads = wind — the specific predictive claims Tomlinson tested

competing_hypotheses: The storm glass as a barometer manqué (the riskyregencies account: early, poorly sealed glasses may have responded partly to air pressure like a barometer — even if so, the sealed modern instrument does not, and FitzRoy's specific weather-reading chart is still refuted)
The storm glass as a decorative curiosity (true of its modern commercial life, but irrelevant to the historical predictive claim)
falsifiability: A controlled trial showing storm-glass crystallization predicting weather changes independently of temperature — the exact trial Tomlinson ran in 1862, which found the opposite

title: Joseph Swan's carbon-filament lamp — the priority the legend skipped
claim: Joseph Swan built and demonstrated a working carbon-filament incandescent lamp before Edison — British patent 1878, public demonstration February 1879, commercial and public-building lighting thereafter.
place: Newcastle upon Tyne / Gateshead, England — the February 1879 lecture demonstration; Swan's Gateshead home, the world's first home lit by electricity
grade_reason: Attested by the patent registers, contemporary lecture reports, and institutional histories (Smithsonian, Science Museum Group): carbonized paper filaments by 1860, UK patent 1878, public demonstration February 1879, Savoy Theatre 1881 — the first public building in the world lit entirely by electricity. Held at CORROBORATED rather than VERIFIED because the primary patent documents and lecture reports were accessed here through secondary aggregators; the chain is strong but one layer removed.
earliest_attestation: Swan's 1878 UK patent; Smithsonian-recorded February 1879 Newcastle lecture demonstration.

sources.desc: Swan's career: 1860 carbonized paper filaments, 1878 UK patent, Feb 1879 Newcastle demonstration (Smithsonian), Swan's Gateshead home as first lit home, Lit & Phil Library and Savoy Theatre 1881 lighting, 1883 Ediswan merger
sources.ref: famousinventors.info — Joseph Swan biography; Smithsonian Institution; Science Museum Group

sources.desc: Swan's lamps independently satisfactory by 1878 alongside Edison's 1879 work; litigation resolved by the 1883 joint company
sources.ref: legaleraonline.com — 'Whose Electric Bulb Is It Anyway?'

competing_hypotheses: Swan's pre-1878 prototypes suffered from weak vacuum pumps, so his lamps were impractical until the late 1870s — the 1860s work establishes priority of invention, not commercial readiness
Edison's improvements (thin high-resistance filament, better evacuation) were incorporated by Swan into his own lamps — the two programs converged, which is why the merger made commercial sense
falsifiability: Archival evidence that Swan's 1878 patent did not exist or that the February 1879 demonstration was fabricated — against the patent registers and contemporary Newcastle lecture reports.

title: Localization of function (the genuine heir of phrenology's question)
claim: Cognitive functions are localized in distinct regions of the cerebral cortex: damage to a specific region produces a specific deficit — the lesion logic that built modern neuroscience.
place: Paris, France (Broca's 1861 presentation)
grade_reason: Multiple independent lines: lesion cases (Broca 1861, Wernicke 1874), cytoarchitectonic maps (Brodmann 1909, 52 areas), Penfield's intraoperative stimulation mapping (motor/sensory homunculi), split-brain work (Sperry, 1960s), and modern fMRI. Stops short of VERIFIED only because the full functional map remains incomplete (memory, consciousness unmapped).
earliest_attestation: Paul Broca, 'Remarques sur le siège de la faculté du langage articulé' (1861) — the Leborgne ('Tan') case: left inferior frontal gyrus lesion, lost articulate speech.

sources.ref: Paul Broca (1861), 'Remarques sur le siège de la faculté du langage articulé' — the Tan case
Carl Wernicke (1874), Der aphasische Symptomencomplex — sensory aphasia, superior temporal gyrus
Korbinian Brodmann (1909), Vergleichende Lokalisationslehre — 52 cytoarchitectonic areas
Wilder Penfield & Rasmussen (1950), The Cerebral Cortex of Man — stimulation mapping, homunculi

competing_hypotheses: Localization vs. equipotentiality/holism (Flourens, then Lashley 1929): the brain acts as a whole — carried as the genuine rival; the resolution was neither extreme (specialization AND distributed networks, per modern neuroimaging)
The neuron doctrine itself was the contested rival of the reticular theory (Golgi vs. Cajal, shared 1906 Nobel) — the anatomical half of the same argument
falsifiability: Consistent failure of focal lesions to produce consistent specific deficits, or whole-brain functional imaging showing no regional specialization for any cognitive function.

title: FitzRoy's storm-warning service, February 1861
claim: In February 1861, Vice-Admiral Robert FitzRoy's Meteorological Department of the Board of Trade issued the first telegraphed storm warnings to British harbor towns — cones and drums hoisted on warning masts — the origin of the shipping forecast and the longest-running national forecasting service in the world.
place: London (Board of Trade Meteorological Department)
grade_reason: Multiple independent sources agree on the trigger (the Royal Charter storm, 26 October 1859, 450+ lives lost off Anglesey), the approval (December 1859), the mechanism (fifteen telegraph stations reporting to London, cones and drums hoisted at harbor towns), and the February 1861 first warnings — and on the service's continuity into the modern shipping forecast.
earliest_attestation: The February 1861 telegraphed gale warnings themselves; FitzRoy's synoptic charts and the Board of Trade Meteorological Department records

sources.ref: phys.org, 'Royal Charter storm of 1859': FitzRoy had lobbied for a storm warning system since summer 1859; after the storm he demonstrated it could have been predicted; 'the new storm warning system was approved' in December 1859 and 'the first warning was issued in February 1861,' delivered by telegraph to harbor towns, which 'hoisted cones and drums on a mast'; the service became the shipping forecast, 'the longest running national forecasting service in the world'

maritime-executive.com, 'The Royal Charter Storm of 1859 and the Roots of the Marine Forecast': same account — December 1859 approval, February 1861 first warning, telegraph-to-harbor-towns with cones and drums; the first public weather forecast printed in The Times in August 1861

Wikipedia 'Robert FitzRoy': the 1859 Royal Charter loss inspired FitzRoy's prediction charts and the coined term 'weather forecast'; fifteen land stations telegraphed daily reports; 1860 storm-warning cones at principal ports; fishing fleet owners objected, the system was abandoned briefly after his 1865 death and reinstated in simplified form in 1874; the Crown distributed 'FitzRoy's storm barometers' to fishing communities

HM Coastguard/Maritime and Coastguard Agency: 'Rewind 101 years and Weather Shipping was broadcast over a telegraphic messaging system first developed in 1861 by Vice-Admiral Robert FitzRoy to issue weather warnings to ships'; the Royal Charter sinking, 26 October 1859, loss of over 450 lives, as the motivation

competing_hypotheses: The 1860 cone system as the true start (FitzRoy introduced storm-warning cones at principal ports in 1860; the February 1861 warnings were the first operational telegraphed gale warnings — the record's claim follows the standard 'first warning issued February 1861' dating)
The American Signal Corps program (1873) as the first government marine-weather service (later and separate; the British telegraphic system predates it by twelve years)
falsifiability: Board of Trade or Met Office archives showing no warning system existed before a later date, or that the February 1861 warnings were never sent

title: Reis's 'Telephon' — the 1861 public demonstrations
claim: In 1861, German physics teacher Johann Philipp Reis publicly demonstrated his 'Telephon' — an apparatus that converted sounds to electrical signals and transmitted speech, imperfectly — the first use of the word 'telefon/telephone' for such a device; he demonstrated widely but never sought a patent.
place: Frankfurt am Main, Germany
grade_reason: The 1861 demonstrations are attested in Reis's own published accounts and the Physical Society record, and the LoC carries the device, the term, and the no-patent fact together. Held below VERIFIED on the exact fidelity of what was transmitted (speech vs tones is the contested layer) and on the precise demonstration dates.
earliest_attestation: Reis's 1861 demonstrations before the Physical Society of Frankfurt and his published accounts; the apparatus and the term 'Telephon' in his own 1860s writings.

sources.ref: Library of Congress, 'Who is credited with inventing the telephone?' — 'Reis was a physics teacher in Germany who developed a device that transmitted speech (albeit badly) in the early 1860s. He called his apparatus a "telefon," the first time the term was used to refer to an apparatus that converts sounds to electrical signals. Reis demonstrated his device widely, but never sought a patent nor did he continue to further develop his idea.'

competing_hypotheses: The 'not a true telephone' reading: Reis's device transmitted music and some speech but handled consonants poorly — critics (then and now) argue it was a tone-transmitter, not a speech-transmitter. The LoC's own 'albeit badly' carries this honestly inside the CORROBORATED grade.

The priority-minimalist reading: Reis never patented and never commercialized; his work was a dead end rather than a link in the chain. The demonstrations are the fact; the influence on Bell is the argument (Bell knew of Reis's work — carried as documented awareness, not proven derivation).
falsifiability: Period documentation that Reis's 1861 demonstrations did not occur, or that the device never transmitted voice-like sounds, would overturn this record.

title: The 'states' rights, not slavery' cause claim
claim: The American Civil War (1861-1865) was fought mainly over 'states' rights' and not mainly over slavery.
place: Charleston, South Carolina (the Secession Convention, December 1860)
grade_reason: The seceding states' own Declarations of Immediate Causes — adopted as formal state acts — name slavery and hostility to slavery as their reasons; South Carolina's (Dec 24, 1860) lists northern states' refusal to return fugitive slaves, attacks on slavery as sinful, abolition societies, and a president 'hostile to slavery'; Mississippi's (Jan 1861) opens 'Our position is thoroughly identified with the institution of slavery'; the Confederacy's own vice-president, Alexander Stephens, said slavery was 'the immediate cause of the late rupture and present revolution' (Savannah, March 21, 1861). The 1861 evidence contradicts the postwar slogan.
earliest_attestation: The postwar Lost Cause literature of the 1870s (e.g. the Southern Historical Society Papers, founded 1869) re-framed the cause as states' rights; the 1861 secession documents themselves say slavery.

sources.ref: South Carolina, Declaration of the Immediate Causes Which Induce and Justify the Secession of South Carolina from the Federal Union (adopted Dec 24, 1860)
Mississippi, A Declaration of the Immediate Causes Which Induce and Justify the Secession of the State of Mississippi from the Federal Union (Jan 1861)
Alexander H. Stephens, 'Cornerstone Speech,' Savannah, March 21, 1861 (reported in the Savannah Republican; text public domain 1861)

Pew Research Center, 'Civil War at 150: Still Relevant, Still Divisive' (April 8, 2011; national survey March 30-April 3, 2011, n=1,507) — 48% said the war was mainly about states' rights, 38% mainly about slavery, 9% volunteered both equally
Charles B. Dew, Apostles of Disunion (UVA Press, 2001) — the secession commissioners' speeches; Dew documents his own change of mind from the states'-rights version he grew up on

competing_hypotheses: 'States' rights' as a legal doctrine was real — Southern leaders also appealed to the compact theory of the Constitution; but the right they defended with arms was the right to maintain slavery (the tariff argument fails: the secession declarations mention no tariff; South Carolina had seceded-threatened over a tariff in 1832 and knew how to name one)

The North's war aim in 1861 was union, not abolition (Lincoln said so himself, August 1862: saving the Union was the official object) — the record separates the secession cause (slavery, documented) from the Union war aim (union first, emancipation as the war's moral pivot)
Some historians stress economic and modernization rivalries; these remain subordinate — remove slavery and there is no secession, no secession means no war
falsifiability: The secession declarations naming economic or constitutional causes unrelated to slavery as their stated reasons — the actual documents do the opposite.

title: Lipman founds America's first envelope company
claim: Philadelphia stationer Hymen Lipman (1817-1893) founded the first envelope company in the United States — three years after he sold his 1858 pencil-with-attached-eraser patent to Joseph Reckendorfer for $100,000 (1862). The Smithsonian account adds that Lipman put adhesive on the back flap, devised an eyelet paper-binding method that preceded the stapler by two decades, and sold the first blank postcards in the US in 1873.
place: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
grade_reason: Three independent modern retellings (Wikipedia, Smithsonian Magazine, the Davison biography) agree on the 'first envelope company' claim, drawing on the 1893 obituary trail; the adhesive-flap and eyelet details come from the Smithsonian's Petroski-sourced account. Held below VERIFIED — the sources are biographical summaries, not the obituaries themselves.
earliest_attestation: Late-19th-century obituary trail (Philadelphia Inquirer obituary Nov 11, 1893; Paper Trade Journal Nov 18, 1893) and modern retellings drawing on them.

sources.ref: Wikipedia — 'Hymen Lipman' ('Three years later, he started the first envelope company in the US' [after the 1862 patent sale]; cites Philadelphia Magazine and Petroski 1990)
Smithsonian Magazine — 'Happy Birthday to the Modern Pencil' (Lipman as 'America's first envelope manufacturer'; adhesive back flap; eyelet binding before the stapler; first US blank postcards 1873)
George M. Davison — 'Hymen Lipman: Creator of the Attached-Eraser Pencil' (sold patent to Reckendorfer 1862; 'start the first envelope company in the U.S.')
Winterthur Museum, 'Every Trade Card Tells a Story' (early-1840s Lipman trade card; envelopes not yet listed — used to bound the factory's start to post-1843)

competing_hypotheses: Biographical retellings are secondhand — the Winterthur museum's trade-card research places his first envelope factory in 1843, suggesting the 'first envelope company' story has an earlier and later telling that may both point at the same Philadelphia stationery career
The exact founding date of the envelope company is not carried by the cited sources — graded as an open detail, not a settled date
falsifiability: A documented earlier American envelope company would demote the 'first' claim; Philadelphia city-directory evidence showing no envelope concern under Lipman's name in the 1860s would weaken it.

title: The Emancipation Proclamation as issued
claim: President Abraham Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation (preliminary Sept 22, 1862; final Jan 1, 1863) declared free all persons held as slaves in the states then in rebellion, authorized the enlistment of Black men in the Union armed forces, and turned emancipation into a war aim — but did not end slavery nationally (that took the Thirteenth Amendment, ratified December 1865).
place: Washington, D.C. (the White House, where Lincoln signed it)
grade_reason: The signed document survives in the National Archives with the scope and exemptions exactly as issued: it applied to the named states in rebellion (South Carolina, Mississippi, Florida, Alabama, Georgia, Texas, Arkansas, North Carolina), expressly exempted Tennessee, the 48 West Virginia counties, and named counties/parishes of Virginia and Louisiana under Union control, left the border states (Maryland, Delaware, Kentucky, Missouri) untouched, authorized Black enlistment (~200,000 served by war's end), and ended nothing nationally — slavery became illegal only with the Thirteenth Amendment's ratification in December 1865.
earliest_attestation: The signed proclamation itself (National Archives), January 1, 1863.

sources.ref: Emancipation Proclamation, final version, January 1, 1863 (National Archives, signed original)

Equal Justice Initiative, 'History of Racial Injustice: Emancipation Proclamation' — scope summary: rebel states only; exempted Tennessee, portions of Virginia and Louisiana; border states untouched; military-service provision; Thirteenth Amendment ratified Dec 6, 1865
Abraham Lincoln to Horace Greeley, August 22, 1862 — the Union-first war aim, stated by the author of the Proclamation

competing_hypotheses: The Proclamation's limits were real and deliberate: a war measure under Lincoln's commander-in-chief power, which he believed did not authorize abolition in loyal territory — the Thirteenth Amendment was needed precisely because the Proclamation could not reach the border states or survive a court challenge

The 'freed no one' shorthand is overstated: it freed the enslaved people already behind Union lines in the named areas and made every Union advance a liberation; the Proclamation's force was military and prospective, not a nullity
falsifiability: A version of the document applying to loyal territory or lacking the military-service provision — the National Archives copy has both the exemptions and the provision.

title: The Lincoln portrait that is really Calhoun
claim: The popular 1860s full-length standing portrait of Abraham Lincoln — Lincoln in frock coat and shawl beside a table of documents — is a composite image: Lincoln's head set on John C. Calhoun's body.
place: New York (printmaker William Pate)
grade_reason: Collection records (Lincoln Financial Foundation Collection, Indiana State Museum) document the image as a composite: Pate's engraving based on Ritchie's 1852 Calhoun, Calhoun's head replaced with Lincoln's, the table papers re-lettered from 'Strict Constitution / Free Trade / the Sovereignty of the States' to 'Constitution / Union / Proclamation of Freedom.' The most famous fake Lincoln portrait ever sold — photoshopped before Photoshop existed.
earliest_attestation: The engraving itself (mid-1860s), cataloged in the Lincoln Financial Foundation Collection, Indiana State Museum holdings.

sources.ref: Lincoln Financial Foundation Collection catalog records (items 71.2009.081.0474, .1455, .1466, .2605) — composite attribution, Ritchie 1852 source, document re-lettering details
Alexander H. Ritchie, engraving of John C. Calhoun (1852) — the source plate

competing_hypotheses: None substantive: the composite origin is multiply documented in collection records; the only open questions are the exact printmaker's variants (Pate, Pate & Lesch) and their dating (1863-1870 window)
falsifiability: Would require the Ritchie 1852 Calhoun plate and the Pate Lincoln plate to differ in body, background, and drapery — they are the same plate with the head swapped and the table documents re-lettered.

title: The staged Gettysburg sharpshooter
claim: Alexander Gardner's 'Home of a Rebel Sharpshooter' (Gettysburg, July 1863) is an unmanipulated documentary record: the dead Confederate soldier lies exactly where he fell.
place: Devil's Den, Gettysburg battlefield, Pennsylvania
grade_reason: Forensic photo-historical demonstration (Frassanito, Gettysburg: A Journey in Time, 1975) that the corpse in 'Home of a Rebel Sharpshooter' is the same man photographed ~40 yards away in 'A Sharpshooter's Last Sleep'; the body was moved to the stone-wall enclosure, a prop rifle added. Minority dissents (Pougher 1988, Groves 1998) are on the record but have not displaced the mainstream reading. The 'where he fell' caption is false.
earliest_attestation: The plate itself (July 1863) with Gardner's 1865 caption describing a Confederate sharpshooter who died a slow death thinking of family; Gardner also claimed the body and gun were still there when he returned in November 1863 — itself impossible, since no body lay unburied for months and no rifle would have escaped relic hunters.

sources.ref: William A. Frassanito, Gettysburg: A Journey in Time (1975) — six-plate analysis, blanket-drag route from the south edge of Devil's Den to the stone-wall enclosure
Frederic Ray, Civil War Times (1961) — first published suggestion that the same corpse appears in two locations
NARA / DOCSTEACH record for 'Home of a Rebel Sharpshooter': Gardner and O'Sullivan moved the corpse more than 40 yards to stage the exposure
Alexander Gardner, Photographic Sketch Book of the War (1865), vol. 1, plate 41 — the original caption
Richard D. Pougher (1988) — dissent via uniform/hair/facial analysis; James C. Groves (1998) — photographic analysis contradicting Frassanito

competing_hypotheses: The staged reading (Frassanito 1975, mainstream): the same corpse appears in 'A Sharpshooter's Last Sleep,' first exposed ~40 yards away; Gardner's crew (O'Sullivan, Gibson) dragged it by blanket to the stone-wall enclosure at Devil's Den, added a prop rifle, and exposed the second plate
The 1961 first flag (Frederic Ray, Civil War Times): same body in two locations — Ray made the match, Frassanito built the six-plate case

The dispute (Pougher 1988): material-culture analysis of uniforms, hair, facial features — two different bodies; Groves 1998: photographic analysis contradicting Frassanito. Both on record; mainstream photo-historiography still follows Frassanito
The rifle question: the weapon is not a sharpshooter's rifle — a prop either way; the man was likely an infantryman, not a sharpshooter
falsifiability: Already falsified: the corpse is identifiable as the same man in six plates (facial features, clothing, the blanket-drag route); proving the caption true would require the body to have fallen in the stone enclosure and the rifle to be a sharpshooter's arm.

title: Who wrote the Bixby letter: Lincoln or Hay
claim: Abraham Lincoln personally composed the November 21, 1864 condolence letter to Mrs. Bixby.
place: Executive Mansion, Washington, D.C.
grade_reason: Attribution to Lincoln rests on the signature and the contemporary publication; serious scholarship splits between Lincoln and his secretary John Hay, with no holograph or dated draft settling it.
earliest_attestation: Boston Evening Transcript, November 25, 1864 — the letter printed under Lincoln's name.

sources.ref: Michael Burlingame, Journal of the Abraham Lincoln Association: Hay-authorship argument — Hay's scrapbooks at Brown hold the letter's clipping among his own writings; 'beguile' recurs in Hay's writings; 'I cannot refrain from tendering' appears in Hay's 1864 letter to Quincy Gillmore
Aston University Centre for Forensic Linguistics (2018): n-gram tracing method devised for short texts identified John Hay as the author
Jean G. Pival (1988, for investigator Joe Nickell): stylistic study of vocabulary and syntax concluded the letter more closely resembled Lincoln's writing than Hay's

Edward Steers and Jason Emerson: Lincoln's authorship — stylistic match to the Gettysburg and Farewell addresses; Robert Todd Lincoln's 1917 letter to Isaac Markens records Hay saying he had 'no special knowledge of the letter'

competing_hypotheses: John Hay composed the letter for Lincoln's signature (Burlingame; Aston 2018 forensic linguistics)
Lincoln composed it himself (Pival 1988; Steers; Emerson)
Hay drafted it and Lincoln edited before signing (hybrid authorship)
falsifiability: A dated holograph in Lincoln's hand would verify Lincoln; a Hay manuscript draft predating November 21, 1864 would verify Hay

title: The Bixby letter's premise: five sons lost
claim: Lydia Bixby, the Boston widow addressed in the November 21, 1864 condolence letter, had lost five sons fighting for the Union — the letter's own premise ('a statement of the Adjutant General of Massachusetts that you are the mother of five sons who have died gloriously on the field of battle').
place: Boston, Massachusetts
grade_reason: Muster and service records show only two of the five sons were confirmed killed in battle; one was honorably discharged and the others deserted or died as prisoners — the Adjutant General's October 12, 1864 report, which the letter honestly quotes, was wrong.
earliest_attestation: William Schouler's report to the War Department, October 12, 1864 (forwarding Bixby's own claim of five sons dead).

sources.ref: William Schouler's report to the War Department, Oct 12, 1864

Michael Burlingame, research summarized in Smithsonian Magazine (2017): two sons died in battle, one honorably discharged, one deserted for certain, the fifth may have deserted; original letter destroyed by Bixby or discarded by the Transcript
Lapham's Quarterly: two sons killed in action, a third either deserted or died as a prisoner of war, a fourth honorably discharged, the fifth deserted
Baltimore Post-Examiner (2018): two killed, two deserted (one possibly to the Confederate Army), one honorably discharged

competing_hypotheses: Bixby deliberately deceived Schouler to gain aid (David R. Barbee's reading: 'a liar and a schemer')
Bixby genuinely believed she had lost five sons (wartime record confusion; she had reason to believe it at the time)
falsifiability: Muster rolls showing all five Bixby sons killed in action

title: The Bixby letter (Nov 21, 1864)
claim: A condolence letter signed 'A. Lincoln,' dated at the Executive Mansion November 21, 1864, was issued to Mrs. Lydia Bixby of Boston, Massachusetts; Massachusetts Adjutant General William Schouler delivered it to her on November 24, 1864, and its full text appeared in the Boston Evening Transcript's afternoon second edition of November 25, 1864.
place: Boston, Massachusetts
grade_reason: The letter's issue, its hand-delivery by Schouler, and its contemporary newspaper publication are multiply attested in contemporary records; only the original holograph is missing.
earliest_attestation: Boston Evening Transcript, afternoon second edition, November 25, 1864 (the text survives only through this newspaper printing; the original holograph has never been recovered).

sources.ref: Boston Evening Transcript, Nov 25, 1864 (afternoon second edition)
William Schouler papers / Massachusetts Adjutant General's report to the War Department, Oct 12, 1864
Lincoln Financial Foundation Collection, item 71.2009.081.1041 (print of the letter's text)

competing_hypotheses: The Transcript's printed text contains transcription errors versus the lost original
Delivery was deliberately delayed past the November 8 election to avoid the appearance of electioneering
falsifiability: A dated holograph differing from the published text, or proof the Transcript never printed it

title: 'McGill invented the brass fastener' — the first-inventor telling
claim: George W. McGill invented the brass paper fastener in 1866 — that the round-head brad with two split legs originated with him and his US 56,587 patent.
place: Washington, D.C. — McGill's residence at filing
grade_reason: The first-inventor telling rests on a single patent whose title and specification both say 'Improvement' — McGill claimed an advance, not the device class, and his T-strip construction is not the round-head brad.
earliest_attestation: No documented first-inventor attestation found this pass — the telling rests on the single patent document US 56,587.

sources.ref: US Patent 56,587 — 'Improvement in metallic paper-fasteners,' specification: 'certain new and useful Improvements in Paper-Fastenings'; claims a single metal strip bent into a T shape with pointed ends
Wikipedia 'Brass fastener' — 'A patent of the fastener was issued in 1866 to George W. McGill,' citing only US 56,587

competing_hypotheses: McGill's 1866 fastener is an early documented node in the brass-fastener lineage but not its origin: the patent's own title says 'Improvement in metallic paper-fasteners,' claiming an advance on an existing device class

grade_reason: DEBUNKED on two independent lines: (1) the 1868-1890s record shows a literary-parody form — Thompson's Ixion was a parodied Greek myth with puns, travesty roles, and topical farce, attested by the contemporary New York Times report and Gänzl's 2002 scholarly biography; (2) the strip turn is documented and dated: the 1893 Midway's hootchy-kootchy, the Minsky brothers' 1917 Mae Dix 'accident' (Morton Minsky's memoir), and the scholarly consensus that striptease became the dominant ingredient only by the mid-1920s.

sources.ref: Kurt Gänzl, 'Lydia Thompson: A Biography' (Routledge, 2002)
Robert C. Allen, 'Horrible Prettiness: Burlesque and American Culture' (UNC Press, 1991) — the scholarly anatomy of the form
Morton Minsky & Milt Machlin, 'Minsky's Burlesque' (Knopf, 1986) — the Mae Dix 1917 anecdote (single interested source, graded accordingly)

falsifiability: A 19th-century burlesque house's books showing striptease as the billed center of the show before 1893, or a contemporary review describing systematic clothing-removal as the act in the 1868-1890 era.

title: The giant that was carved in Chicago — the Cardiff Giant hoax, 1868–1869
claim: The Cardiff Giant — unearthed near Cardiff, New York, in October 1869 — was a genuine petrified prehistoric man (or an ancient statue of a giant).
place: Cardiff, New York — the Newell farm where the gypsum figure was buried and 'discovered' in October 1869
grade_reason: Killed by the hoaxer's own confession plus the documented manufacturing chain: Hull noticed blue-streaked gypsum resembling veins in an Iowa quarry, had a twelve-foot slab cut and shipped to Chicago, had stone-cutters carve a giant 'died in great pain' (right hand clutching stomach), aged it chemically, buried it at his cousin's farm, and had well-diggers 'find' it on cue. When Barnum built a rival replica and Hannum sued, Hull confessed; the judge ruled both exhibits were fakes. Confession + paper trail + court ruling: the petrified-man reading is dead.
earliest_attestation: The counter-attestation is the hoaxer's own: George Hull confessed to carving the 'giant' from a twelve-foot slab of Iowa gypsum, having it shaped by Chicago stone-cutters (Edward Burghardt and assistants, sworn to secrecy, needlepoint-mallet skin pores, chemically aged), shipping it to his cousin William Newell's farm near Cardiff, New York, burying it, and arranging its 'discovery' six months later. Hull's confession — made when banker David Hannum sued P. T. Barnum — is the hoax's death certificate.

sources.ref: BookBrowse, 'Why do we say There's a sucker born every minute?' — Hull's 1868 carving (Iowa gypsum, Chicago stone-cutters, needlepoint pores, chemical aging), the burial at William Newell's farm, the October 1869 'discovery,' the 25–50 cent admissions, the expert split

Medium / Skeptikai, 'The REAL Story Behind the Quote' — Hannum's purchase and Syracuse exhibit; Barnum's $50,000–$60,000 refused offers; Barnum's replica claimed as the true Giant; Hull's confession at trial; the judge's ruling that both were hoaxes

competing_hypotheses: The ancient-statue reading: some defenders held the figure was a genuine ancient sculpture (Jesuit-father work was proposed). This reading died with the hoax confession — a carved statue of 1868 is still a fraud when sold as antiquity.

The Genesis-apologetics reading: many visitors embraced the Giant because it seemed to prove Genesis 6:4 ('The Nephilim were on the earth'). This belief phenomenon is real and historically important — it is what made the hoax profitable — but it is a belief about the object, not evidence for the object.
falsifiability: Geological evidence that the Cardiff figure is fossilized tissue or a genuinely ancient artifact — against Hull's confession, the documented quarry-to-burial paper trail, and the court record.

title: The anonymous Ether Monument, 1868
claim: The Ether Monument (Boston Public Garden, unveiled 1868 — the first statue erected in the Public Garden) is a 40-foot Gothic memorial topped by a Good Samaritan sculpture that names NO discoverer of anesthesia — no Morton, no Wells, no Jackson, no Long — only biblical quotations about relieving pain ('Neither shall there be any more pain'). The anonymity was the settlement of a credit war no committee could decide.
place: Boston Public Garden
grade_reason: The monument is a standing, inspectable artifact; its namelessness is verifiable in person and in the Smithsonian/Mass. Historical Society record; the controversy context (Morton vs Jackson, the refused 5,000-franc half-prize, Twain's and Holmes's interventions) is multiply attested.
earliest_attestation: The monument itself, still standing in the Boston Public Garden; contemporary press and Oliver Wendell Holmes's 'ether or either' quip.

sources.ref: Smithsonian Magazine: the 40-foot monument, the nameless inscription ('The sculptor inscribed no names on the structure, only biblical quotations about the blessed work of alleviating pain'), 'the nation's only monument to a drug.'

Mass. Historical Society (Oct 2016 Object of the Month): 'the Ether Monument credited neither Morton nor Jackson, but rather was dedicated to "either"' — Holmes's line; Jackson's asylum years at McLean.

Somerville Times (Oct 2026): the 1868 unveiling as the Public Garden's first statue; 'The memorial doesn't mention the first men who practiced with the mysterious vapor... it simply praises ether and its wondrous contribution to mankind'; Jackson's 1873 commitment to McLean's double domes.

competing_hypotheses: That the anonymity was deliberate wisdom rather than deadlock — Holmes's 'To Ether!' joke read as intentional institutional neutrality.

That the monument's side inscription ('To commemorate the discovery that the inhaling of ether causes insensibility to pain. First proved at Mass. General Hospital in Boston October AD MDCCCXLVI') names a place and date — the 'First proved' clause is graded separately as DEBUNKED (evt-anesthesia-first-ever-001); the monument itself is real and CORROBORATED.
falsifiability: Discovery of a hidden name on the monument (the sculptor's inscription is physically checkable — it names no one) or a committee record showing a named dedication that was then altered.

title: Haeckel's embryo drawings were doctored
claim: Ernst Haeckel's embryo drawings (Anthropogenie, 1874) were doctored: he resized embryos to a common scale (erasing up to 10-fold size differences), eliminated limb buds and heart bulges, and omitted species names to exaggerate similarity — documented contemporaneously by Rütimeyer (1868) and forensically by Richardson et al. (1997, Anatomy and Embryology 196:91–106, photographic comparison across 39 species).
place: Jena, Germany (Haeckel's chair, 1865–1909)
grade_reason: The doctoring is multiply attested: a contemporary 1868 exposure, a 1997 photographic re-examination across 39 species, and Gould's scholarly assessment — fraud on the record, not a rumor.
earliest_attestation: L. Rütimeyer 1868 (contemporary critique, shown within months of the 1868 publication); Richardson, Hanken et al. 1997, Anatomy and Embryology 196:91–106

sources.ref: Richardson, Hanken, Gooneratne et al. 1997, Anatomy and Embryology 196:91–106 — 'There is no highly conserved embryonic stage in the vertebrates'; photographic comparison of the species Haeckel drew: resized embryos, erased limb buds and heart bulges, fudged scales, unnamed species

Rütimeyer 1868 — contemporary demonstration, within months of the 1868 publication, that Haeckel had altered the embryos to look more alike
Gould's assessment — Haeckel 'committed the academic equivalent of murder' (quoted in the secondary literature; the 'astonished and ashamed' century of textbook recycling)

competing_hypotheses: The 'mere schematics' defense — the drawings as idealized diagrams rather than fraudulent claims
That the drawings were accurate representations of the compared stages (refuted by the photographic record)
falsifiability: A photographic re-comparison showing Haeckel's plates faithful to the embryos at the stated stages; retraction of Richardson et al. 1997. Neither has occurred.

title: The 'Jonas Hanway invented the umbrella' telling
claim: Jonas Hanway (1712-1786), the London merchant and philanthropist, invented the umbrella — the schoolbook-and-quiz telling that credits him with the umbrella's invention.
place: London (the telling's claimed setting)
grade_reason: Two independent kills: (1) the umbrella predates Hanway by millennia — royal parasols in ancient Assyria and Egypt (iconographic record, conventionally ~4,000 years), waterproof Chinese oil-paper umbrellas (conventionally 11th c. BCE), the Roman umbraculum; (2) even in England, umbrellas preceded him — the Female Tatler of 12 December 1709 advertises a coffee-house umbrella borrowed by a Customs House gentleman, and General Wolfe writing from Paris in 1752 wonders the practice does not obtain in England. Hanway's documented achievement was popularization, never invention.
earliest_attestation: Popular biography/quiz shorthand, 19th-20th century (no 18th-century source)

sources.ref: 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Umbrella' (public domain): credits Hanway with having been 'the first Englishman who habitually carried an umbrella' — popularization, not invention
William Sangster, Umbrellas and Their History (1868; Project Gutenberg edition): Hanway's ~30 years of carrying (hence c. 1750), the derision, the hackney coachmen; Wolfe's 1752 Paris letter
The King's Parasol (aina.org, 2021): Egypt/Assyria origins, Chinese 11th-c.-BCE waterproof umbrellas, Hanway as popularizer ('men even called their umbrellas a Hanway')
acrosswalls.org Hanway notes: Female Tatler 12 Dec 1709 coffee-house umbrella announcement; John Macdonald's 1770 memoirs ('Frenchman, why don't you get a coach?')

competing_hypotheses: The telling conflates invention with popularization: Hanway may genuinely have been the first Englishman to carry an umbrella habitually, which popular memory shortened into 'invented'
The 'brought the umbrella to Britain' variant — dead on the Female Tatler 1709 evidence (a coffee-house umbrella in London 41 years before Hanway's first use), kept as a separate weaker claim
falsifiability: A credible 18th-century source attributing the umbrella's invention to Hanway, or proof that the ancient parasol records (Assyrian reliefs, Egyptian iconography, Chinese oil-paper umbrellas) are forgeries
