title: The QWERTY layout, 1868-1878
claim: The QWERTY keyboard arrangement emerged between 1868 and 1878 through documented, gradual iteration: Sholes's November 1868 first TypeWriter (28 keys, alphabetical, piano-style) built with Glidden, Soule and Densmore in Milwaukee and shipped to Edward Payson Porter's Telegraph College in Chicago; the April 1870 38-key machine built with Matthias Schwalbach; the August 1872 Scientific American engraving showing a four-row keyboard with a second row beginning QWE.TY; the 1873 sale of manufacturing rights to E. Remington & Sons; the Remington No. 1 (1874, commercially successful); and the Remington No. 2 (1878), which stabilized the modern QWERTY layout. The arrangement was shaped by feedback from early professional users — principally telegraph operators — not by a single design decision.
place: Milwaukee, Wisconsin (Sholes's workshop; machines shipped to Chicago)
grade_reason: The artifact's paper trail is multiply and independently documented — patents, dated machines, the 1872 engraving, Remington's production records — though the precise rationale for each key's placement remains honestly uncertain.
earliest_attestation: US Patent 79,265 to C. Latham Sholes, C. Glidden and S. W. Soule (23 June 1868); typewritten letters and subsequent Sholes patents (1870-1872)

sources.ref: Yasuoka, Koichi & Yasuoka, Motoko (2011). 'On the Prehistory of QWERTY.' ZINBUN 42:161-174, Kyoto University
New Scientist, 'The truth about the QWERTY keyboard' (article 2200664) — 1872 Scientific American engraving, Remington No. 1 (1874), 100,000+ machines by 1890
US Patent 79,265 — 'Type-Writing Machine' (Sholes, Glidden & Soule, 23 June 1868)

competing_hypotheses: The layout was a semi-random rearrangement of the original alphabetical keyboard, with no recoverable design rationale (Jan Noyes, Loughborough, ~1973: 'no obvious reason for the placement of letters')
Remington's engineers, not Sholes, finalized the arrangement (the QWERTUIOPY prototype and Sholes's demand that Y be reinstated between T and U suggest shared authorship)
The arrangement was partly a proprietary lock-in device: Remington trained typists on QWERTY, raising switching costs (Gizmodo/Smithsonian reading — commercial motive, not engineering motive)
falsifiability: Discovery of a Sholes-era document showing the full QWERTY arrangement predating 1868, or proof the 1868-1878 paper trail is misdated

title: The line the showman never said — Barnum and 'a sucker born every minute'
claim: P. T. Barnum said 'There's a sucker born every minute.' — the most famous sentence in show business, as his own philosophy.
place: New York City (Barnum's American Museum and the 1869–1870 Cardiff Giant affair); Syracuse, New York (Hannum's exhibit)
grade_reason: Four independent kills on the Barnum authorship. (1) THE BIOGRAPHER'S EMPTY SEARCH: Arthur H. Saxon — Barnum's own biographer, with every motive to confirm the line — tried to track down when Barnum said it and could not verify it; no contemporary account exists. (2) THE CHRONOLOGY: a variant of the saying was published in the European Magazine in January 1806, four years before Barnum was born. (3) THE COMPETING ATTRIBUTIONS: the Oxford Dictionary of American Quotations credits con man Joseph 'Paper Collar Joe' Bessimer; the common story credits banker David Hannum, stung by Barnum's rival Cardiff Giant. (4) THE INTERESTED WITNESS: the attribution to Barnum comes from circus competitor Adam Forepaugh's 1880s newspaper interview — a rival's discredit, not testimony. The line's own logic dies too: Barnum's business depended on patrons, not contempt for them.
earliest_attestation: No contemporary account exists of Barnum uttering the line — Barnum's biographer Arthur H. Saxon tried to track down an occasion and could not verify it: 'There's no contemporary account of it, or even any suggestion that the word "sucker" was used in the derogatory sense in his day. Barnum was just not the type to disparage his patrons.' The line first travels in late, second-hand attributions.

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'There's a sucker born every minute' — 'a quotation often associated with American showman P. T. Barnum (1810–1891), although there is no evidence that he actually said it'; Saxon's failed verification ('no contemporary account of it'); Bessimer per Oxford Dictionary of American Quotations; Hannum version via the Cardiff Giant affair; Forepaugh's 1880s attribution as likely discredit; the January 1806 European Magazine variant ('there vash von fool born every minute')
The Independent (Lafayette), 'Too Good To Be True' — Hannum's Syracuse exhibit, Barnum's refused $50,000–$60,000 offers, the replica, the 1870 judicial ruling that both were hoaxes

BookBrowse, 'Why do we say There's a sucker born every minute?' — Hull's gypsum carving (1868), the buried 'discovery' (1869), the pore-chiseling and chemical aging, the 25-cent admissions, the expert split

competing_hypotheses: The Hannum reading: the line was spoken by banker David Hannum — the Syracuse investor who owned the Cardiff Giant — about the crowds paying to see Barnum's rival replica after Barnum built his own giant and claimed Hannum's was the fake. This is the most common alternative attribution, but even it rests on late, contested accounts.
The Bessimer reading: the Oxford Dictionary of American Quotations points to Joseph 'Paper Collar Joe' Bessimer, the confidence man, as the probable originator.

The 1806 reading: a variant ('there vash von fool born every minute') appeared in the European Magazine and London Review in January 1806 — four years before Barnum was born — which kills Barnum's authorship by chronology alone, whoever actually coined it.
The Forepaugh reading: circus competitor Adam Forepaugh attributed the line to Barnum in an 1880s newspaper interview — plausibly a deliberate attempt to discredit his rival, not testimony.
falsifiability: A contemporary 1810–1891 document — letter, newspaper, memoir — quoting Barnum saying the line. Biographer Saxon's exhaustive search found none.

title: The myth: Wood's wife was the first morphine addict, killed by his syringe
claim: Rebecca Massey Wood — wife of Alexander Wood — was the first known intravenous morphine addict, and she died of a morphine overdose delivered by her husband's invention.
place: Dean Cemetery, Edinburgh (Wood family grave)
grade_reason: Two independent kills: (1) Richard Davenport-Hines, The Pursuit of Oblivion (2003, p. 68), calls it a myth — 'she outlived him, and survived until 1895'; (2) the Dean Cemetery gravestone records Rebecca Massey Wood's death on 6 February 1895 — eleven years after Wood's own death on 26 February 1884. The 1869 overdose death is impossible on the stone's own dates. What survives the grade: the genuine 19th-century phenomenon of iatrogenic morphine dependence that Wood's 1855 paper helped make possible — and the real tragedy that the legend smuggles, minus the wrong woman.
earliest_attestation: Wikipedia, 'Alexander Wood (physician)': 'It is, however, a false rumour that Rebecca Massey was the first known intravenous morphine addict and died of an overdose delivered by her husband's invention'

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Alexander Wood (physician)' — 'It is, however, a false rumour that Rebecca Massey was the first known intravenous morphine addict and died of an overdose delivered by her husband's invention; Richard Davenport-Hines says, "It is a myth: she outlived him, and survived until 1895."' — gravestone date 6 February 1895
Richard Davenport-Hines (2003). The Pursuit of Oblivion: A Global History of Narcotics. W.W. Norton, p. 68
C-SPAN3 Lectures in History, 'Drug Addiction in 19th-Century America' — the genuine 1840–1870 rise in opiate importation and the beginnings of hypodermic morphine use (the fenced real phenomenon)

competing_hypotheses: The anecdote is true in substance but wrong in the details — she developed dependence but survived (rejected: Davenport-Hines calls the whole thing a myth)
The legend conflates her with the genuine 19th-century wave of iatrogenic morphine dependence (the real phenomenon, the wrong woman)
falsifiability: A contemporary death certificate or burial record showing Rebecca Massey Wood died in 1869 of a morphine overdose

title: The transcontinental railroad completed at Promontory Summit, 10 May 1869 — VERIFIED
claim: On 10 May 1869 at Promontory Summit, Utah Territory, the Central Pacific and Union Pacific railroads were joined, completing the first continuous transcontinental railroad across the United States; the ceremony centered on the driving of the 'Last Spike' — a golden spike — with the moment signaled nationwide by telegraph.
grade_reason: VERIFIED: the joining at Promontory Summit on 10 May 1869 is one of the best-documented single days in 19th-century American history — multi-side contemporary attestation (both railroads' company records, the press, the telegraph log, the surviving ceremony artifacts including the golden spike itself). The timeline's first railroad-era record and the foil to the gauge folklore: the railways' own paperwork is how the real history is known.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary newspaper accounts, Union Pacific and Central Pacific company records, and the telegraph record of the ceremony — the 'DONE' signal sent over the wires at the moment of the driving.

sources.ref: Golden Spike National Historical Park, National Park Service — the 10 May 1869 joining, the ceremony, the Last Spike
Union Pacific company history — construction 1863–1869, Promontory Summit completion
Contemporary telegraph/press record of the ceremony — the 'DONE' signal

competing_hypotheses: The 'not really the first' note: transcontinental rail SERVICE was not fully seamless in 1869 (ferries across the Missouri and the Sacramento/San Joaquin bays remained, and the railheads had met at a gap-bridged point); what was completed was continuous RAIL across the continent — the claim is about the rails meeting, which happened that day.

The Stanford-swing detail: tradition holds Leland Stanford missed the spike on his first swing (the telegraph operator sent 'DONE' anyway). This is a ceremony anecdote, not a challenge to the completion — the rails met on 10 May regardless of the hammer work.
falsifiability: A Union Pacific or Central Pacific document showing the railheads joined on a different date, or that the ceremony did not occur, would overturn this; the contemporary record is dense and univocal.

title: The Kansas cattle towns' body count
claim: The five Kansas railhead cattle towns (Abilene, Ellsworth, Wichita, Caldwell, Dodge City) recorded 45 homicides across 15 town-years of peak cattle-trading seasons; Dodge City during its 1876-1886 cattle-trading period (with the open carry of sidearms banned) averaged fewer than two violent deaths per year; Dodge's most homicidal year had 5 killings, Deadwood's 4, Tombstone's 5.
place: Dodge City, Kansas (with Abilene, Ellsworth, Wichita, Caldwell as comparison set)
grade_reason: Multiply documented from independent directions: Dykstra's 1968 newspaper-and-record survey, the Smithsonian's 2018 corroborating account of Dodge's <2/year figure, Trimble's town-by-town maxima, and Roth's independent re-analysis — which disagrees on rates-per-denominator but confirms the absolute counts.
earliest_attestation: The towns' own coroners' records, newspapers, and court records of the 1870s-1880s, analyzed by Robert R. Dykstra (The Cattle Towns, 1968)

sources.ref: Robert R. Dykstra, The Cattle Towns (Knopf, 1968; repr. Univ. of Nebraska Press, 1983)

Smithsonian Magazine, 'How Dodge City Became a Symbol of Frontier Lawlessness' (2018): Dodge 1876-1886 averaged less than two violent deaths per year; none apparent Aug 1873-1875; open-carry ban from 1876; Harry Gryden's Police Gazette role
Randolph Roth, 'Homicide Rates in the American West' (Criminal Justice Research Center, Ohio State): Dodge City adults ~165 per 100,000/year 1876-1885 — the independent re-analysis
Marshall Trimble, 'Violence in Old West Towns,' True West magazine (Dodge 5, Deadwood 4, Tombstone 5 maxima; Tombstone gun ordinance)

competing_hypotheses: Randolph Roth's independent re-analysis using adult-male resident denominators finds higher rates than Dykstra's implication — Dodge City 1876-1885 at least ~165 per 100,000 adults per year; the absolute counts are agreed, the rate-per-denominator reading differs. Both agree the counts are far below the popular myth.
Transient populations were undercounted by the towns; the true resident denominator may have been smaller, which would raise the rate but not change the absolute body count.

Under-recording: not every violent death may have reached the coroner or the press, but the towns' records were kept closely and no alternative count has been produced that changes the order of magnitude.
falsifiability: Discovery of an independent contemporary count (coroner's ledgers, cemetery records, court dockets) for the same towns and years showing substantially higher totals.

title: The rotary opener that reached the kitchen (Lyman, 1870)
claim: William W. Lyman of Meriden, Connecticut patented the first practical domestic rotary can opener on 12 July 1870 (US Patent 105,346) — pierce the lid's center, set the butterfly-screw wheel, cut around; the design Baumgarten & Co. put into production from 1890 and that American kitchens actually held.
place: Meriden, Connecticut, USA
grade_reason: Patent date and design multiply attested (patent + museum collection history); the 'first widespread domestic opener' reading is the encyclopedia consensus but rests on secondary market history, hence CORROBORATED.
earliest_attestation: US Patent 105,346 (12 July 1870)

sources.ref: US Patent 105,346 (12 July 1870), William W. Lyman — circular rotation opener: pierce the lid's center, set the rotating blade with the butterfly screw, cut around the lid

Google Arts & Culture / Tomato Museum, 'The History of the Can Opener' — Lyman's 12 July 1870 patent (US 105,346); put into production by the Baumgarten Company since 1890; J. Osterhoudt's 1866 key-wind system (US 58,554) as the competing opener family

competing_hypotheses: J. Osterhoudt's 1866 key-wind opener (US 58,554) reaches ordinary hands earlier — the 'first domestic' title depends on whether a key stuck on the lid counts as the kitchen tool
Warner's 1858 lever was 'used by thousands of Americans, from Civil War soldiers to everyday grocers' — the domestic-vs-trade line is the fence, not the chronology
falsifiability: A dated domestic rotary opener in kitchen circulation before 1870, or proof the Baumgarten 1890 production date is wrong

title: The lawless Wild West (constant gunfights)
claim: The frontier towns of the American West, c. 1870-1890, were lawless places where gunfights in the streets were a daily or near-daily occurrence — the Hollywood version: every disagreement settled at high noon.
place: Dodge City, Kansas (control sample; Abilene, Ellsworth, Caldwell, Wichita as the comparison set)
grade_reason: The towns' own recorded body counts are two orders of magnitude below the myth — Dodge City averaged fewer than two violent deaths per year across its entire 1876-1886 cattle-trading period, 45 homicides total across five towns in fifteen years — and the myth's manufacture is itself documented: a paid Police Gazette sensationalist, magazine mythmaking from 1902, and Hollywood.
earliest_attestation: Harry Gryden's sensationalist dispatches from Dodge City to the National Police Gazette, c. 1878-1883 (myth construction); the underlying reality is attested in the towns' own records and contemporary newspapers (see evt-cattle-towns-bodycount-001)

sources.ref: Smithsonian Magazine, 'How Dodge City Became a Symbol of Frontier Lawlessness' (2018)
Robert R. Dykstra, The Cattle Towns (Knopf, 1968; repr. Univ. of Nebraska Press, 1983): 45 homicides in 15 years across five Kansas cattle towns
Marshall Trimble (Arizona's official historian), 'Violence in Old West Towns,' True West magazine: Dodge City 5 killings in its most homicidal year; Deadwood 4; Tombstone 5; Tombstone's gun ordinance
Terry L. Anderson and Peter J. Hill, The Not So Wild, Wild West (Stanford UP, 2004): property-rights and private-order institutions in the West

competing_hypotheses: Randolph Roth's re-analysis (Criminal Justice Research Center, Ohio State): computing on adult-male resident populations, Dodge City 1876-1885 carried at least ~165 homicides per 100,000 adults per year — high by modern standards, so the 'peaceful' reading needs the denominator stated. The DEBUNK targets daily gunfights and lawlessness, not danger.
Mining camps and boomtowns may have been more violent than the cattle towns; Dykstra's sample is the railhead cattle towns, not the whole West.

Hollywood's version draws on real but rare incidents (the OK Corral shootout, 26 Oct 1881, ~30 seconds, ~30 shots, Tombstone, Arizona — itself a gunfight between men defying a town gun ordinance) and inflates frequency, not the incidents themselves.
falsifiability: A documented town where coroners' ledgers, newspapers, and court records show dozens of gunfight deaths per year across multiple years — the paper trail Dykstra found to be absent.

title: The Great Chicago Fire (8-10 October 1871)
claim: The Great Chicago Fire burned 8-10 October 1871, destroying some 17,000-18,000 buildings across about 3.3 square miles, killing approximately 300 people, and leaving about 100,000 of the city's 300,000 residents homeless — one of the most devastating urban fires of the 19th century.
place: Chicago, Illinois (fire began at the O'Leary barn, DeKoven Street, Near West Side)
grade_reason: Multiply attested by contemporary primary sources: the 1871 Board of Police and Fire Commissioners' investigation report, contemporary newspaper coverage, and the city's own records. The commissioner's report estimated 17,000-18,000 buildings destroyed and ~300 dead; drought context documented (no measurable rain since early July, 13 weeks).
earliest_attestation: Contemporary: the Chicago Board of Police and Fire Commissioners' 1871 investigation report; Chicago newspaper coverage October 1871

sources.ref: Chicago Board of Police and Fire Commissioners, 1871 investigation report (commissioner's report: 17,000-18,000 buildings burned, ~300 dead; blamed poor building codes and insufficient fire-department funds)
Encyclopedia of Chicago / Chicago History Museum — Great Chicago Fire entry (dates, toll, drought context: no rain since early July)

Scott W. Berg, 'The Burning of the World: The Great Chicago Fire and the War for a City's Soul' (Pantheon) — the fire began in the barn of Patrick and Catherine O'Leary, DeKoven Street, evening of 8 Oct 1871
Chicago Tribune 150th-anniversary retrospective: 'the City Council officially exonerated Mrs. O'Leary and her cow in 1997, and the true cause may never be known'

competing_hypotheses: The death toll is an estimate: contemporary counts were imprecise, and bodies lost in the fire's core were never recovered — ~300 is the accepted figure, not a census
The fire's cause theories (Sullivan, Cohn, comet, cow) are all unproven; the official inquiry could not determine the cause
falsifiability: Contemporary official documentation, casualty lists, and property records exist in quantity; the event's core facts are not seriously contested

title: The foreign builders of Great Zimbabwe — the colonial myth
claim: Great Zimbabwe was built by non-African foreigners: Phoenicians, Arabs, the Queen of Sheba's people from the biblical Ophir, Egyptians, Vikings, Atlanteans — 'more civilized races' than the Africans who lived around it.
place: Great Zimbabwe, Masvingo, Zimbabwe
grade_reason: Two independent refutations (Randall-MacIver 1905 artifact analysis; Caton-Thompson 1929–31 stratigraphy) plus the Rhodesian establishment's documented 1970s censorship regime — museum staff instructed to withhold the African-origin evidence, Garlake and Summers driven out — because the archaeology would not cooperate; no credible archaeological support for the foreign reading has ever existed.
earliest_attestation: Carl Mauch 1871 (the 'Ophir' visit); formalized by James Theodore Bent, The Ruined Cities of Mashonaland (1892), and Hall & Neal, The Ancient Ruins of Rhodesia (1902)

sources.ref: Bent 1891 excavation report (British Association, Rhodes-funded): the 'bastard race' reading — white northern fathers, destroyed stratigraphy around the conical tower, discarded Arab/Persian trade beads
Hall & Neal 1902: Phoenician/Arabian authorship as the official colonial version; Hall's 1–3 m of discarded 'primitive' deposits (he was dismissed for the damage)
David Randall-MacIver, Medieval Rhodesia (1905): the first refutation — 'unquestionably African in every detail' — rejected by the colonial establishment
Gertrude Caton-Thompson, The Zimbabwe Culture: Ruins and Reactions (1931): stratigraphic excavation proving medieval Shona-culture construction

The 1970s Rhodesian censorship regime (Paul Sinclair testimony, 'None But Ourselves'; SA History Online): the Museums and Monuments director told archaeologists to withhold the African-origin evidence from the press; guidebooks, displays, and textbooks censored; Peter Garlake and Roger Summers departed — the myth's official version needed the state's help
Wikipedia 'Archaeology and racism' / Great Zimbabwe historiography summaries: the post-1980 archaeological consensus (Shona origin unchallenged)

competing_hypotheses: Hall's counter-position that later Shona occupation merely reused ruins built by earlier 'civilized' races — refuted by Caton-Thompson's stratigraphy showing continuity
The post-independence political-use caution: the site's name now names the country, so even true archaeology can carry national meaning — the grade is on the evidence, not the flag
falsifiability: Pre-11th-century sealed contexts with non-African construction technology or inscriptions; none have been found in 130+ years of excavation

title: The O'Leary cow that started the Great Chicago Fire (DEBUNKED)
claim: Mrs. Catherine O'Leary's cow kicked over a lantern while being milked in the O'Leary barn on the night of 8 October 1871, starting the Great Chicago Fire.
place: The O'Leary barn, DeKoven Street, Chicago (the fire's origin point, per the 1871 Board)
grade_reason: DEBUNKED — 219th DEBUNKED family. Three kills: (1) the story's own author, reporter Michael Ahern of The Chicago Republican, admitted more than 20 years later that he had concocted the cow tale because it made for a better story (reported Chicago Tribune, 1996); (2) the 1871 Board of Police and Fire Commissioners' investigation could not determine the cause — and the O'Learys testified under oath they were asleep when the fire broke out; (3) the Chicago City Council passed a resolution in October 1997 officially exonerating Catherine O'Leary and her cow. Historians (Ann Durkin Keating, North Central College) note the telling caught on through anti-Irish, anti-immigrant sentiment — a convenient scapegoat: Irish, Catholic, immigrant, a woman.
earliest_attestation: Chicago newspaper coverage, October 1871 — first reported by Michael Ahern of The Chicago Republican

sources.ref: Chicago Tribune, 9 Nov 1996 (ct-xpm-1997-10-07-9710080245 trail): Michael Ahern, reporter for The Chicago Republican, admitted more than 20 years after the fire that he concocted the cow tale because it made for a better story; Ann Durkin Keating on the anti-Irish/anti-immigrant scapegoating
Chicago City Council resolution, October 1997 — officially exonerated Mrs. O'Leary and her cow (Chicago Tribune ct-xpm-1997-10-07-9710080245)
1871 Board of Police and Fire Commissioners investigation report — cause could not be determined; the O'Learys testified under oath they were asleep
Richard Bales, 'The Great Chicago Fire and the Myth of Mrs. O'Leary's Cow' — the Sullivan theory and the myth's historiography

herhalfofhistory.com, 8 Oct 2026: the commissioner's report blamed poor building codes and insufficient fire-department funds; Catherine O'Leary's testimony ('I always milked my cows by daylight and never had a lamp of any kind or a candle about the barn'); she died 1895 of pneumonia, ~68
Parade, Oct 2026: the 1997 exoneration; Catherine O'Leary died 1895 without living to see her name cleared

competing_hypotheses: Daniel 'Peg Leg' Sullivan — the neighbor who first reported the fire — started it (Richard Bales, 'The Great Chicago Fire and the Myth of Mrs. O'Leary's Cow')
Louis M. Cohn's craps-game confession theory
The Biela's Comet fragment theory (the 1871 comet, also attached to the Peshtigo fire the same night)
The official position: the cause could not be determined — the honest unknown
falsifiability: The claim is killed by its own author's confession plus the official record; the fire's true cause remains undetermined — the grade kills the cow, not the uncertainty

title: Schliemann's excavation of Troy at Hisarlik (1871–1890)
claim: Heinrich Schliemann excavated the mound of Hisarlik in the Troad (1871–1890), identified it as the Troy of Homer's Iliad, and the site is broadly accepted as ancient Troy (Ilios/Ilion).
place: Hisarlik (Troy), Tevfikiye, Çanakkale Province, Turkey
grade_reason: The excavations happened and are multiply documented (his own reports, Ottoman records, the site's later excavation history); Calvert's priority is documented; Hisarlik's identification as Troy is the scholarly consensus — the ancient Greeks themselves placed Ilios there.
earliest_attestation: Frank Calvert's identification of Hisarlik (1850s–1860s); Schliemann's published excavation reports from 1874; Ottoman excavation firmans (including the 1870 dig that Ottoman officials penalized with a delayed 1871 permit).

sources.ref: Smithsonian, 'In Search of Troy' — 'Schliemann converted Hisarlik to Troy' (R. Aslan); Troy II layer dated 2500–2300 BCE; city of Homer's epic thought to correspond to Troy VI–VIIa
National Geographic — Schliemann assumed Homer's Troy lay at the mound's bottom; Homer's Troy c. 1200 BCE corresponds to layer VIIa; 150 workers, rail lines, poor record-keeping
Susan H. Allen, 'Finding the Walls of Troy: Frank Calvert and Heinrich Schliemann at Hisarlik' (UC Press, 1999) — Calvert's priority in identifying Hisarlik
Archaeology.org, Interactive Map of Troy (Troy II, ca. 2550–2300 BCE) — ten+ distinct settlements at the site

competing_hypotheses: The pre-Calvert Bunarbashi hypothesis placed Troy elsewhere (Pınarbaşı) — superseded
Whether a Trojan War happened at Hisarlik at all remains a separate CLAIMED question — the site is accepted, the war is not
falsifiability: Epigraphic or stratigraphic proof that Hisarlik is not ancient Ilios/Ilion — the Roman-period city's own inscriptions and the 2019 British Museum exhibition's consensus make this very unlikely

title: The gladiatorial 'thumbs down' death signal
claim: In the Roman arena, the crowd signaled death for a defeated gladiator with a thumbs-down gesture (thumbs-up meaning spare him).
place: The Colosseum (Flavian Amphitheatre), Rome
grade_reason: No Roman text specifies the direction of 'pollice verso' (Juvenal, Prudentius, Martial are all directionally silent), and the only surviving physical depiction of a gladiatorial thumb gesture shows the MERCY signal (pressed thumb, Cavillargues medallion). The modern thumbs-down=death mapping traces to Gérôme's 1872 painting, was contested in print within seven years (1879 pamphlet), and was re-imported by Gladiator (2000) — a 19th-century invention, not a Roman record.
earliest_attestation: The popular up/down mapping originates with Jean-Léon Gérôme's 1872 painting 'Pollice Verso'; the phrase 'pollice verso' itself is Roman (Juvenal Satires 3.36, Prudentius Contra Symmachum 2.1096).

sources.ref: Juvenal, Satires 3.36-38 ('verso pollice') — the thumb is 'turned', direction unspecified
Prudentius, Contra Symmachum 2.1096 ('converso pollice') — direction unspecified
Cavillargues medallion (Nîmes) — 'STANTES MISSI', shows the mercy gesture: closed fist with thumb pressed down; the only surviving physical evidence of a gladiatorial thumb gesture

Anthony Corbeill, Nature Embodied: Gesture in Ancient Rome (Princeton UP, 2004) — the death signal was most likely a thumb turned UP or outward (a sword thrust); mercy a thumb pressed down on a closed fist
Gérôme, 'Pollice Verso' (1872; Phoenix Art Museum) — sold to Alexander Turney Stewart for 80,000 francs, exhibited in New York; the source of the modern up=life/down=death mapping
1879 pamphlet 'Pollice Verso': To the Lovers of Truth in Classic Art (26 pages), incl. Gérôme's 8 Dec 1878 letter — the painting's accuracy was publicly contested immediately
Gladiator (2000, dir. Ridley Scott) — re-manufactured the gesture, with Commodus's thumbs-up sparing and thumbs-down killing, the Gérôme mapping again
Wikipedia, 'Pollice verso' — summary of the textual silence and the painting's cultural transmission

competing_hypotheses: Corbeill's reconstruction: death = thumb turned UP or outward (mimicking a sword thrust), mercy = thumb pressed down on closed fist — the best-supported scholarly reading, but still a reconstruction
The direction may have been regionally or editorially variable — no single universal gesture
falsifiability: A Roman-period depiction of the death gesture showing a downward thumb, or a text explicitly specifying a downward motion for the kill signal

title: Troy II as Homer's Troy — Schliemann's 'burnt city'
claim: Troy II — Schliemann's 'burnt city,' the layer from which 'Priam's Treasure' came — is the Troy of Homer's Iliad, the city besieged in the Trojan War.
place: Hisarlik (Troy), Tevfikiye, Çanakkale Province, Turkey
grade_reason: The stratigraphy is decisive: Troy II's burnt destruction dates c. 2300 BCE — over a thousand years before the Trojan War era — while the candidate Homeric layers (VI–VIIa, c. 1700–1180 BCE, VIIa showing violent destruction c. 1180 BCE) sit several layers above it. Schliemann's fixation on the bottom of the mound led him to dig through and destroy much of the real candidate layer on his way down.
earliest_attestation: Schliemann's reports from 1872 onward — his own identification, never shared by the stratigraphy.

sources.ref: Archaeology.org, Interactive Map of Troy (Troy II, ca. 2550–2300 BCE) — 'destroyed by a fire around 2300 B.C.'; treasures 'more than 1,000 years before the supposed events of the Trojan War'
Smithsonian, 'In Search of Troy' — the city of Homer's epic 'is thought to correspond to Troy VI-VIIa'
National Geographic — 'Homer's Troy, circa 1200 B.C., probably corresponds to layer VIIa, nowhere near the bottom'; Schliemann never recorded strata
Popular Archaeology interview — scholars split Troy VIh vs VIIa as 'Homer's' city (both c. 13th century BCE); Schliemann 're-found and mostly destroyed... Homer's imaginary Troy, not the Trojan War'
Smithsonian — Schliemann's methods 'savage and brutal': a 45-foot trench plowed through layers 'without proper record keeping'; Turkish archaeologists are still repairing the damage

competing_hypotheses: Troy VIh vs VIIa as 'Homer's city' (both c. 13th century BCE) — the honest scholarly split
The anti-stratigraphic reading: Homer's Troy as an imaginary composite, not a level (the 2019 British Museum exhibition's 'Troy: myth and reality' framing)
falsifiability: A Late Bronze Age date for the Troy II destruction horizon — radiocarbon and the ceramic sequence both forbid it

title: 'Priam's Treasure' — Schliemann's 1873 gold hoard
claim: The gold hoard Heinrich Schliemann reported discovering on 31 May 1873 at Troy is the personal treasure of Homer's King Priam — one single find, in the ruins of Homeric Troy, photographed on Sophia Schliemann and smuggled out in her shawl.
place: Hisarlik (Troy), Tevfikiye, Çanakkale Province, Turkey
grade_reason: Two independent kills: (1) STRATIGRAPHY — the treasure's layer (Troy II) dates c. 2400 BCE, roughly a thousand years before the Trojan War era, so it cannot be Priam's; (2) FRAUD — Traill (Anatolian Studies 2000) showed the 'single find' was an artificial composite assembled from several sources, with falsified findspot and date, and the Sophia-present/Sophia's-shawl stories were Schliemann's own inventions.
earliest_attestation: Schliemann's own reports (from 1874) — self-attested. No independent contemporary witness to the single-find story exists.

sources.ref: Traill, David (2000), '"Priam's Treasure": clearly a composite', Anatolian Studies 50:17–35 — the hoard is an artificial collection from several sources, not a single find; findspot and discovery date falsified; some photographed pieces appear in 1872 photos of earlier finds
Easton, D.F. (1998), 'Heinrich Schliemann: Hero or Fraud?', The Classical World 91(5):335–343

Archaeology.org, Interactive Map of Troy (Troy II, ca. 2550–2300 BCE) — the Troy II treasures 'date to around 2400 B.C., more than 1,000 years before the supposed events of the Trojan War' and 'cannot possibly be associated with any of Homer's heroes'
Smithsonian, 'In Search of Troy' — the Troy II layer dated 2500–2300 BCE, 'about 1,000 years earlier than the agreed upon time of Homeric Troy'; the treasure is 4,000+ years old goldwork

Wikipedia, 'Priam's Treasure' — the artefacts are 'likely to be a composite of multiple finds across the site rather than one hoard'; Schliemann falsified the finding circumstances; the Sophia's-shawl smuggling story was planted by Schliemann himself (citing Allen 1999)
Smithsonian/National Geographic — Schliemann smuggled the treasure out of Ottoman territory; the Ottoman government sued; he paid a 10,000 gold-franc fine and kept digging

competing_hypotheses: The gold is genuine Early Bronze Age metalwork (now in the Pushkin Museum, Moscow) — the objects are real, the millennium and the story are not
Some pieces may genuinely have come from one late-1873-season deposit (Traill grants a genuine core find, then shows Schliemann added to it)
falsifiability: An independent contemporary document confirming the single 31 May 1873 find in a Late Bronze Age context — none exists; Traill's 1872 photographs of the same pieces would need explaining

title: Reckendorfer v. Faber (92 U.S. 347, 1875) — the Supreme Court kills the eraser patent
claim: In Reckendorfer v. Faber, 92 U.S. 347 (1875), the U.S. Supreme Court declared Lipman's pencil-with-eraser patent invalid. The ruling: the patent was 'merely the combination of two things, without a new use' — 'A combination, to be patentable, must produce a different force, effect, or result in the combined forces or processes from that given by their separate parts... A combination, therefore, which consists only of the application of a piece of rubber to one end of the same piece of wood which makes a lead pencil is not patentable.' Lipman kept the $100,000 he got from Reckendorfer; Reckendorfer was left with nothing.
place: Washington, D.C. (U.S. Supreme Court)
grade_reason: The Supreme Court opinion is a primary published source; its holding is carried independently across the Wikipedia, Patent Plaques, QuizzClub/NYT lineage, and the static.case.law circuit record. No source disputes the outcome.
earliest_attestation: Reckendorfer v. Faber, 92 U.S. 347 (1875), opinion text; Case No. 11,625 circuit record (May 20, 1874)

sources.ref: Reckendorfer v. Faber, 92 U.S. 347 (Supreme Court of the United States 1875) — holding: combination of two known things with no new use is not patentable
Case No. 11,625 (20 Fed. Cas. 389) — circuit record: Woodruff, Circuit Judge, May 20, 1874
Patent Plaques blog, 'Pencil Patent Dispute?': quotes the decision's aggregation test; patent 19,783 image
QuizzClub/NYT lineage: Reckendorfer paid $100,000, sued Faber, lost everything; Lipman kept the money

competing_hypotheses: The circuit court had earlier weighed the same questions (Case No. 11,625, Woodruff, Circuit Judge, May 20, 1874) — the Supreme Court's 1875 ruling is the controlling one.
The ruling killed the patent, not the product: unpatentable combinations still sell — the pencil-with-eraser took decades to become standard anyway.
falsifiability: The published opinion is the evidence; an intact enforcement record after 1875 would contradict the invalidation.

title: 'Mr. Watson, come here' — the first intelligible telephone transmission, March 10, 1876
claim: On March 10, 1876, at 5 Exeter Place, Boston, Alexander Graham Bell transmitted the first intelligible sentence by telephone to his assistant Thomas Watson in the next room — 'Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you!' — as recorded in Bell's laboratory journal.
place: 5 Exeter Place, Boston, Massachusetts
grade_reason: The event is anchored in Bell's own laboratory journal — a contemporary primary record — and the date/place/persons are undisputed. Held below VERIFIED on the exact wording: the LoC itself notes the dispute between the journal's 'Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you!' and the Bell Company's later ceremonial 'Watson, come here, I want you!' (from the 1915 transcontinental call).
earliest_attestation: Bell's laboratory journal entry for March 10, 1876.

sources.ref: Library of Congress, 'Who is credited with inventing the telephone?' — 'it was March 10, 1876 that Bell declared to his assistant, "Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you!" over the lines of his working telephone, as he wrote in his laboratory journal. There is some dispute over the exact words used.'
HISTORY.com, 'First speech transmitted by telephone' (March 10, 1876) — the June 1875 precursor tests ('No intelligible words were transmitted, but sounds resembling human speech were heard').

competing_hypotheses: The wording variant: the Bell Company's house version — 'Watson, come here, I want you!' — quoted from the 1915 first transcontinental call ceremony, where an elderly Bell repeated the line. The journal's longer version is the period record; the shorter is the corporate memory.

The 'first' qualifier: 'first intelligible sentence' — the June 1875 tests transmitted sounds but no intelligible words (HISTORY.com). The March 10 transmission is the first documented intelligible sentence, not the first electrical speech-like sound.
falsifiability: Bell's laboratory journal for March 10, 1876 is extant; a showing that the entry is forged or misdated would overturn this record.

title: Alexander Graham Bell alone invented the telephone (the sole-inventor myth)
claim: That Alexander Graham Bell alone invented the telephone — the single-inventor reading of the telephone's origin carried by textbooks and popular history.
place: Boston, Massachusetts (the myth's home city)
grade_reason: Three independent kills on the 'alone': (1) Johann Philipp Reis publicly demonstrated his 'Telephon' transmitting speech in 1861 — fifteen years before Bell's patent (LoC: 'transmitted speech (albeit badly)... first time the term was used'); (2) Antonio Meucci demonstrated his teletrofono in New York in 1860 and filed a US patent caveat Dec 28, 1871, lapsed 1874 for the $10 renewal — recognized by H. Res. 269 (2002); (3) Elisha Gray's lawyer filed a telephone caveat on the SAME day as Bell's application, Feb 14, 1876, both built around a liquid transmitter. The telephone had multiple fathers; the patent had one winner.
earliest_attestation: The sole-inventor reading consolidated in the Bell Company's own histories and the schoolbook tradition after the patent wars; the competing inventors were in the record from the start (Reis 1861, Meucci 1871 caveat, Gray 1876 caveat).

sources.ref: Library of Congress, 'Who is credited with inventing the telephone?' — Bell credited 'since his patent and demonstrations... were successful' AND 'his invention did not come to be in isolation. There are many others who are often put forward as co-inventors, such as Antonio Meucci, Johann Reis and Elisha Gray.'

Wikipedia, 'Elisha Gray and Alexander Bell telephone controversy' — the Feb 14, 1876 same-day filings; Bell's application 5th entry, Gray's caveat 39th; both documents incorporating a liquid transmitter.

U.S. House of Representatives, H. Res. 269 (107th Congress), passed June 11, 2002 — 'the life and achievements of Antonio Meucci should be recognized, and his work in the invention of the telephone should be acknowledged'; preamble: 'if Meucci had been able to pay the $10 fee to maintain the caveat after 1874, no patent could have been issued to Bell.'
HISTORY.com, 'First speech transmitted by telephone' (March 10, 1876) — Bell's 1875 harmonic-telegraph work as the origin of the telephone ideas; the June 1875 tests.

competing_hypotheses: The 'practical inventor' defense (LoC's own framing): Bell's design was the first patented, and he carried it beyond the patent to a working, commercialized system — 'the father of the telephone' as builder-of-the-industry, not sole conceiver. This defense is honored in the fence, not in the grade: the record distinguishes the patent (VERIFIED, evt-bell-telephone-patent-001) from the 'alone' reading.

Canada's counter-motion (June 2002): ten days after H. Res. 269, the House of Commons of Canada unanimously passed a parliamentary motion stating Alexander Graham Bell was the inventor of the telephone — the national-pride counterweight, carried as belief ecology, not evidence.

The courtroom defense: the Bell Company survived 600+ patent challenges; the courts consistently ruled for Bell. A legal victory is a legal fact, not an invention fact — the suits tested patent validity, not the 'alone' reading.
falsifiability: Period evidence that Reis never demonstrated a working voice-transmission device before 1876, that Meucci's teletrofono never existed, AND that Gray's caveat was not filed Feb 14, 1876 — all three kills would have to fall — would reopen this record.

title: US Patent 174,465 — Bell's telephone patent, granted March 7, 1876
claim: United States Patent No. 174,465, titled 'Improvement in Telegraphy,' was granted to Alexander Graham Bell on March 7, 1876, covering an apparatus for 'transmitting vocal or other sounds telegraphically... causing electrical undulations.'
place: Washington, D.C. (U.S. Patent Office)
grade_reason: Surviving primary legal document: the patent grant is a matter of public record with an exact date, number, and title; the application-to-grant interval is documented in the Patent Office daybook.
earliest_attestation: The patent document itself, issued March 7, 1876 (application filed Feb 14, 1876).

sources.ref: Library of Congress, 'Who is credited with inventing the telephone?' — 'Bell was granted US Patent Number 174,465 for an "Improvement in Telegraphy" on March 7, 1876.'

HISTORY.com, 'First speech transmitted by telephone' — 'on March 7 he was awarded U.S. patent 174,465, which granted him ownership over both his telephone instruments and the concept of a telephone system.'

competing_hypotheses: The fraud allegation: on January 13, 1887 the U.S. government moved to annul Bell's patent on grounds of fraud and misrepresentation (backing Meucci's priority); the Supreme Court found the case viable and remanded for trial, but Meucci died in October 1889 and the patent expired in January 1893 — the case was discontinued as moot without reaching the underlying issue. Carried as the unresolved challenge, not a refutation of the grant itself.

The Wilber bribery allegation: examiner Zenas Fisk Wilber's 1886 affidavit claimed he took a $100 bribe to show Gray's caveat to Bell's lawyer — unproven, never adjudicated; carried inside evt-telephone-patent-race-001.
falsifiability: The patent document is extant and publicly recorded; only a finding that Patent 174,465 was never issued (or was issued to someone else) would overturn this — not plausible.

title: Bell's telephone offered to Western Union, fall 1876 (and declined)
claim: In the fall of 1876, Gardiner Hubbard, Alexander Graham Bell's chief backer, brought Bell's inventions to the Western Union Telegraph Company and its president William Orton, and Western Union declined to buy them.
place: New York City (Western Union headquarters)
grade_reason: Two lines: (1) Hubbard's own contemporary letters (16 Oct. and 16 Dec. 1876, to Gertrude Hubbard, Hubbard Papers) record the approach to Western Union — the event is attested in the year it happened; (2) the business history (W. Bernard Carlson, 'Entrepreneurship in the Early Development of the Telephone,' Business and Economic History v23 n2, pp. 161-192) reconstructs the fall-1876 offer and the turndown with Orton's documented business logic. Held below VERIFIED: the famous $100,000 figure does NOT come from the 1876 letters — it comes from Thomas A. Watson's 1926 memoir (p. 107), a fifty-year-late recollection (see also Bruce 1973, p. 229). The amount is fenced at CLAIMED inside this CORROBORATED record.
earliest_attestation: Hubbard's own letters to his wife, 16 Oct. and 16 Dec. 1876 (Hubbard Papers), mention taking Bell's 'inventions' to Western Union

sources.ref: W. Bernard Carlson, 'Entrepreneurship in the Early Development of the Telephone: How Did William Orton and Gardiner Hubbard Conceptualize this New Technology?' Business and Economic History, v23 n2, pp. 161-192 — fall-1876 offer; Orton's turndown; the two Hubbard-to-Gertrude letters (16 Oct., 16 Dec. 1876, Hubbard Papers) as the contemporary anchor; the $100,000 figure traced to Watson 1926, p. 107; Bruce 1973, p. 229
Thomas A. Watson, Exploring Life (1926), p. 107 — the $100,000 figure's earliest known source, a half-century-late recollection

competing_hypotheses: The sympathetic reading: the rejection was rational in 1876 — the telephone worked only over short distances, tied up an entire wire for one conversation (reducing telegraph throughput rather than raising it), and did not fit Western Union's core business of short business messages between cities. Carlson's account treats the decision as explicable rather than blind. The grade of the rejection as an event is unaffected.
falsifiability: Contemporary 1876 Western Union internal records showing no approach by Hubbard, or showing the approach accepted, would overturn this grade.

title: Dewey's real achievement: the standardized, commercialized card (1876)

place: Boston, Massachusetts — the Library Bureau's home
grade_reason: The commercial record converges: the 1876 ALA meeting agreed on standard card stock, Dewey ran the supply department, the Bureau sold cards, cabinets, and the 'approved library hand' system. Held below VERIFIED — the 'standard size agreed at the first ALA meeting' detail rides secondary sources, and the corporate founding date is honestly disputed (1876 vs 1879 vs 1888).

title: The 'Mask of Agamemnon' (Mycenae, 1876)
claim: The gold funeral mask found at Mycenae in 1876 is the death mask of Homer's King Agamemnon — the face Schliemann claimed in his telegram to have gazed upon.
place: Mycenae, Argolis, Greece (Grave Circle A)
grade_reason: The mask is a genuine 16th-century BCE gold artifact — but it dates 300 to 400 years before the Trojan War era, so it cannot be Agamemnon's. The telegram story's own provenance is disputed (reported as 'supposed to have told'; one account calls it a press invention), and Schliemann himself later conceded the attribution ('let's call him Schulze').

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Mask of Agamemnon' — 'modern archaeological research suggests that the mask dates to around the 16th century BC, pre-dating the period of the mythical Trojan War by 300–400 years'; found 1876 in Grave V, Grave Circle A; 'He is supposed to have told the king in a telegraph, "I have gazed upon the face of Agamemnon"'; Schliemann's late-life concession: 'So this is not Agamemnon... All right, let's call him Schulze'
Brewminate, 'The Legendary (or Not) Ancient Funerary Mask of Agamemnon' — 'the mask dates to about 1600 BC, predating the period of the legendary Trojan War by about 400 years'
Perceptivetravel / Tony Perrottet — the telegram story: 'Unfortunately, the story was invented by the press'

competing_hypotheses: Minority forgery/doctored-piece doubts (e.g. Calder) — named, held below: the mask's manufacture as a 16th-c. BCE artifact is secure, which is precisely what kills the attribution

falsifiability: A secure c. 1200 BCE date for the mask, or a contemporary inscription naming Agamemnon — neither exists

title: The Valentine's Day race — Bell's application and Gray's caveat, February 14, 1876
claim: On February 14, 1876, Bell's lawyer filed Bell's telephone patent application and Elisha Gray's lawyer filed Gray's telephone caveat on the same day at the U.S. Patent Office — Bell's the fifth entry of the day, Gray's the thirty-ninth; both documents incorporated a liquid transmitter.
place: Washington, D.C. (U.S. Patent Office)
grade_reason: Multiply attested in the patent-office record and the compiled histories: the same-day filings, the entry numbers (5th vs 39th), and the shared liquid transmitter are documented. Held below VERIFIED on the contested sequencing layer — the popular 'Bell arrived first' story is itself disputed (Evenson) — and on the unproven Wilber bribery allegation.
earliest_attestation: The Patent Office cash-receipts blotter and daybook entries of February 14, 1876 (Bell's fee entered before noon, Gray's that afternoon).

sources.ref: Library of Congress, 'Who is credited with inventing the telephone?' — 'the application for this patent was submitted on February 14, 1876. That same day, but just a few hours later, Elisha Gray applied for a caveat... Bell's was the fifth entry of that day, while Gray's was 39th.'

Wikipedia, 'Elisha Gray and Alexander Bell telephone controversy' — Gardiner Hubbard's lawyer filed Bell's application Feb 14, 1876; Gray's lawyer filed the caveat the same day; the fee-blotter sequencing (Bell before noon, Gray that afternoon; caveat not to the examiner until the next day); Evenson's finding that the popular 'Bell arrived an hour or two earlier' version did not happen.

competing_hypotheses: The popular version: 'Bell arrived at the patent office an hour or two before Gray, and Gray lost his rights as a result' — historian A. Edward Evenson's finding is that this did not happen (Gray's caveat arrived in the morning and sat in the in-basket; Bell's lawyer got the fee entered first). The popular version is the belief ecology; Evenson's is the archival reading.

The Wilber allegation: patent examiner Zenas Fisk Wilber swore in an 1886 affidavit that he accepted a $100 bribe to show Gray's caveat to Bell's lawyer Marcellus Bailey — never proven, never adjudicated; carried as an unresolved allegation, not a finding.

The legal-irrelevance reading: under the 1876 patent law (first-to-invent, not first-to-file), the day's sequencing should not have mattered at all — the interference proceedings should have tested invention dates, not filing order. The race mattered anyway, because the caveat system rewarded the fuller filing.
falsifiability: The Patent Office daybook for Feb 14, 1876 is the anchor; a showing that Gray's caveat was filed on a different date would overturn the same-day claim (the entries are numbered and dated).

title: 'An electrical toy' — the Western Union dismissal quote (misquotation)
claim: That Western Union president William Orton, on being offered Bell's telephone patent in 1876, dismissed it with the words 'an electrical toy' (in some tellings 'nothing but a toy') — the famous attributed quote of the Western Union telephone story.
place: New York City (the attributed scene)
grade_reason: Two kills from the archival record itself: (1) NO PERIOD ATTESTATION — the scholarly account of the 1876 decision (Carlson, citing the Hubbard Papers and Watson) contains no such wording; the quote has no primary-source lineage anywhere in the telephone literature — it exists only as unsourced pop-history embroidery, typically traceable to the Wikipedia-era Bell article ('the president of Western Union balked, countering that the telephone was nothing but a toy'); (2) the documented reasoning contradicts the caricature — Orton's actual documented logic (telephone's 20-mile range, one wire per conversation, mismatch with WU's short-business-message model) was specific and businesslike, not a sneer. The companion 'two years later he said $25 million would be a bargain' line rides the same unsourced rail and is fenced with it.
earliest_attestation: The wording circulates in modern pop retellings, commonly sourced (explicitly or implicitly) to the Wikipedia article on Alexander Graham Bell and its derivatives — not to any 1876 document, letter, memo, or contemporary report

sources.ref: W. Bernard Carlson, 'Entrepreneurship in the Early Development of the Telephone,' Business and Economic History v23 n2, pp. 161-192 — the scholarly reconstruction of the 1876 decision; contains the documented business logic and NO 'toy' wording

Pop retelling exemplars carrying the unattributed quote (the belief ecology): rismedia 'You've Come a Long Way Baby' (explicitly sourcing Wikipedia's Bell article: 'the president of Western Union balked, countering that the telephone was nothing but a toy. Two years later, he told colleagues that if he could get the patent for $25 million he'd consider it a bargain')

competing_hypotheses: The charitable transmission theory: the wording could paraphrase a real internal sentiment (Carlson documents Orton's actual 1876 business logic — short-range, wire-hogging, unsuited to WU's message business). But a paraphrase that hardened into a direct quotation is still a misquotation; the grade is about the attribution, not the sentiment. If a primary source for the exact wording ever surfaces, this record re-opens.
falsifiability: A period document — an 1876 letter, memo, or contemporary report — carrying the 'electrical toy' / 'nothing but a toy' wording from Orton or a Western Union decision-maker would overturn this grade.

title: The real doctor behind Holmes: Doyle's 1892 letter to Joseph Bell
claim: Sherlock Holmes's analytical method was modeled on the real Edinburgh surgeon Joseph Bell — Arthur Conan Doyle himself named Bell as Holmes's model in writing.
place: Edinburgh Royal Infirmary / Royal College of Surgeons of Edinburgh (letter archive)
grade_reason: An author's own dated letter naming his model — a primary document held in an institutional archive, corroborated the same year by Doyle's own published interview describing the ward observations first-hand. Two independent documentary lines; held below VERIFIED because 'modeled on' leaves room for the composite reality (Dupin, Littlejohn, Doyle himself) that the letter's own phrasing admits.
earliest_attestation: The 4 May 1892 letter, one of a set of seven Doyle letters held by the Library of the Royal College of Surgeons of Edinburgh: 'It is most certainly to you that I owe Sherlock Holmes, and though in the stories I have the advantage of being able to place him in all sorts of dramatic positions I do not think that his analytical work is in the least an exaggeration of some effects which I have seen you produce in the outpatient ward.' Corroborating contemporaneous attestation: Doyle's August 1892 Strand Magazine interview (to Harry How): 'I was clerk in Mr. Bell's ward... When everything was ready, I would show them in to Mr. Bell... His intuitive powers were simply marvellous.'

sources.ref: Arthur Conan Doyle to Joseph Bell, 4 May 1892 — one of seven Doyle letters held by the Library of the Royal College of Surgeons of Edinburgh
The Strand Magazine, August 1892 — Doyle interviewed at his home by Harry How: the ward-clerk account
Arthur Conan Doyle Encyclopedia, 'Joseph Bell' — letter and interview documentation

competing_hypotheses: The Littlejohn contribution: Edinburgh forensic expert Henry Littlejohn lectured Doyle in forensic science and worked with Bell on the Ardlamont (1893) and Ripper cases — a partial, co-model position
The self-portrait reading: Doyle himself was the doctor-observer; the Watson–Holmes dynamic mirrors the Doyle–Bell ward relationship
The pure-fiction position: Holmes is a composite of influences including Poe's Dupin — named honestly, but does not overturn the documentary Bell acknowledgment
falsifiability: Archival evidence (e.g., an earlier Doyle letter or diary) crediting a different sole model, or documentation that the 1892 letter is misdated or inauthentic.

title: Edison's tin-foil phonograph, December 1877 — the first machine that talked back
claim: In December 1877 Thomas Edison's shop built the first practical machine capable of BOTH recording and reproducing sound: the tin-foil cylinder phonograph — Edison speaking 'Mary had a little lamb' into the mouthpiece and the machine playing his words back — demonstrated at Scientific American's offices (reported 22 December 1877), patent filed 24 December 1877, granted 19 February 1878 as U.S. Patent 200,521.
place: Menlo Park, New Jersey (Edison's laboratory; Scientific American demonstration at the magazine's New York offices)
grade_reason: The build chain, the contemporary press account, and the patent record converge on the same device: Kruesi's 1–6 December 1877 build from Edison's 29 November sketch; the 22 December 1877 Scientific American demonstration with verbatim quotation; the 24 December 1877 patent filing and the 19 February 1878 grant (U.S. Patent 200,521). The Edison Speaking Phonograph Company was capitalized 24 January 1878. The reproduction half of the invention — playing sound back — is the superlative that survives Scott's 1860 recording-only priority.
earliest_attestation: The Scientific American account of 22 December 1877 ('Mr. Thomas A. Edison recently came into this office, placed a little machine on our desk, turned a crank, and the machine inquired as to our health...')

sources.ref: Library of Congress — 'History of the Cylinder Phonograph' (Inventing Entertainment): the August-12-vs-December dating argument; Charles Batchelor's diary (constructed 4 December, finished two days later); the 22 December 1877 Scientific American report; patent filed 24 December 1877, issued 19 February 1878; Charles Cros's April 18, 1877 paper as theory-only
Wikipedia — 'Phonautograph': 'Edison's 1877 phonograph was the first machine capable of both recording and replaying sound' — the surviving superlative

Schaeffer's History of Recording: Kruesi built the first practical machine 1–6 December from Edison's 29 November sketch (not 'Aug. 12,' misdated by Edison in 1917); patent 200,521 granted 19 February 1878 for cylinders wrapped with tin foil, 2–3 minute capacity

competing_hypotheses: The date of the first working test: Edison's later-stated 'August 12, 1877' vs the documentary record — John Kruesi built the first practical machine 1–6 December from Edison's 29 November sketch, and Charles Batchelor's diary confirms construction 4–6 December (the 'Aug. 12' date was written by Edison on another sketch in 1917 and is a misdate)
Charles Cros's April 18, 1877 paper: the only other recorded contemporary evidence of the idea — but it remained a theory, no working model was produced
falsifiability: Proof that a working record-and-playback machine predated December 1877 (e.g. a Cros working model) would overturn the 'first' superlative — none exists in the documentary record

title: The name "Silk Road" (and the single-road idea)
claim: The "Silk Road" is a single ancient trade road whose name dates to antiquity — the ancients knew it as one road under that name.
place: Berlin (publication place of Richthofen's China vol. 1, 1877)
grade_reason: The name is a documented 1877 German coinage; no pre-1877 source uses any general system name for the routes, and the routes themselves were a braided network, not one road.
earliest_attestation: Ferdinand von Richthofen, "China: Ergebnisse eigener Reisen und darauf gegründeter Studien", vol. 1 (Berlin: Dietrich Reimer, 1877), and his 1877 journal article on the Tarim-basin trade routes.

sources.ref: Richthofen, China vol. 1 (1877) — four uses of Seidenstrasse/Seidenstrassen; plus the 1877 article (English versions 1878 in Geographical Magazine and Popular Science Monthly)
D. C. Waugh, "Richthofen's 'Silk Roads': Toward the Archaeology of a Concept" (2007) — the coinage, the limited use, the later appropriation
Marinus of Tyre via Maes Titianus (1st c. CE), preserved in Ptolemy — the ancient route description Richthofen mapped (untitled); no ancient name for the system as a whole
Valerie Hansen, The Silk Road: A New History (2012) — many routes, not one road

competing_hypotheses: The coinage-vs-popularization nuance: some argue Richthofen merely 'popularized' the label and that earlier descriptions (e.g. Marinus) constitute an ancient naming — rejected on the evidence: Marinus described a route; he did not name a system, and no ancient administrative, legal, or literary text names the network as a whole

The jstage geographical society reading that a 'name' was first used in Marinus's account c. 100 CE — a minority phrasing that confuses a route description with a system name; the 1877 coinage of the general term is uncontested in the scholarly literature (Waugh 2007)
falsifiability: A pre-1877 text using 'Silk Road'/Seidenstrasse (or a calque) as a general system name would falsify the coinage; an ancient administrative or legal text naming the whole network as one entity would falsify the no-ancient-name leg

title: The telephone war of 1877-78 and the 1879 settlement (the foil)
claim: After declining Bell in 1876, Western Union built its own telephone operation — hiring Elisha Gray and Thomas Edison to develop rival telephony — fought Bell for the telephone business in 1877-78, and settled in 1879 by withdrawing from telephony, with Bell acquiring the Edison carbon-microphone technology from Western Union's camp. place: New York / the Bell vs Western Union litigation

title: The QWERTY slowdown myth
claim: The QWERTY keyboard layout was deliberately designed to slow typists down, so that the typewriter's typebars would not jam.
place: Milwaukee, Wisconsin (geography of the claim's subject — the 1870s design work)
grade_reason: Three independent kills: (1) no contemporary source attributes slowdown intent to Sholes — Yasuoka & Yasuoka (2011), working from his patents and typewritten letters, conclude he 'never intended to slow down the operator'; (2) the internal logic fails — the most common English digraphs T+H and E+R sit adjacent in QWERTY, and a 1949 statistical analysis found QWERTY has more close letter-pairs than a random layout; (3) the arrangement demonstrably emerged from operator feedback — the first professional users were telegraph operators who found the alphabetical layout unworkable, and the keys moved in response to how the machines were actually used.
earliest_attestation: 20th-century popular histories of the typewriter (no Sholes-era source states or implies slowdown as a design goal)

sources.ref: Yasuoka, Koichi & Yasuoka, Motoko (2011). 'On the Prehistory of QWERTY.' ZINBUN 42:161-174 — 'We don't agree it. Christopher Latham Sholes... did not arrange the typebars in such way. And he never intended to slow down the operator.'

New Scientist, 'The truth about the QWERTY keyboard' — T+H and E+R adjacency; 1949 statistical analysis (QWERTY has more close pairs than random); 'TYPE WRITER' top-row salesman story has no historical evidence

The lock-in reading: the layout persisted for commercial and training-economics reasons, which later writers retrofitted with a deliberate-design story
falsifiability: A Sholes-era document — letter, patent text, or workshop record — stating that slowing the operator was a design goal

title: Edison's Menlo Park system — the real achievement the legend mislabels
claim: Edison's real achievement was the first practical, complete incandescent electric lighting system — long-life lamp plus generators, distribution, and wiring — demonstrated at Menlo Park in December 1879 and commercialized with Pearl Street Station, New York, in September 1882.

This is the foil that survives the debunk of the solo-inventor myth: the legend is false about priority, true about the system.
