competing_hypotheses: Swan partisans note Swan lit his own home and the Savoy Theatre first (1881) — true, but a building wired to one circuit is not the city-scale system Edison's Pearl Street plant represented
The 'practical' reading has been overstretched in popular accounts into the first-inventor reading — that stretch is the myth; this record grades only the system
falsifiability: Evidence that a city-scale incandescent lighting system with central distribution predated Pearl Street (Sep 1882) — none is known; arc-lighting systems (Brush) and isolated Swan installations are the documented alternatives, and neither is a distributed incandescent system.

title: The French Panama effort, 1882–1889
claim: Ferdinand de Lesseps's Compagnie Universelle du Canal Interocéanique de Panama (founded 1879; construction 1882–May 1889) attempted the Panama Canal before the United States: a sea-level design stubbornly kept until the October 1887 conversion to a lock canal; by the 1889 bankruptcy the company had spent ~Fr 1.18 billion (≈ $235 million), excavated ~50–53 million cubic meters — about two-fifths of the final total — and lost roughly 20,000–22,000 workers, mostly to yellow fever and malaria.
place: Isthmus of Panama (Colon → Panama City)
grade_reason: Multiple independent aggregators converge on the dates, the spending, the excavation fraction, and the death-toll range; exact figures vary between sources so it stops short of VERIFIED.
earliest_attestation: Compagnie Universelle corporate records 1879–1889; contemporary French and American press coverage of the 1889 bankruptcy and the 1892–93 Panama Scandal trials.

sources.ref: NASA engineering analysis of the Compagnie Universelle effort (53M m³ of 75M m³ cost-baseline excavated; Fr 1.18B spent; ~16,500 lives)
History of the Panama Canal survey (1888 workforce ~20,000, nine-tenths Afro-Caribbean; ~22,000 dead 1881–1889; ~two-fifths complete; $234,795,000 spent)
Maritime Executive centenary survey (French effort 1881–1889, ~22,000 dead in the French period)
New Civil Engineer archive: the Panama canal (sea-level design kept until October 1887 lock conversion; Culebra landslides; FFr1bn spent)

competing_hypotheses: The older 'doomed from the start' reading (American press 1904 era, French 1892 tribunal): financiers manipulated de Lesseps's delusional rhetoric — vs. the NASA engineering analysis, which finds the project was set on a course to failure early but treats it as an engineering/management failure, not a fraud
falsifiability: Compagnie ledger evidence showing materially different expenditure/excavation, or contemporary records placing the lock-canal conversion at a different date

title: The Selden patent monopoly (1903–1911) and Ford's courtroom win
claim: The Selden patent (US 549,160, filed 8 May 1879, issued 5 November 1895) gave its holders — the Electric Vehicle Company and the Association of Licensed Automobile Manufacturers (ALAM, founded March 1903) — a working monopoly claim over gasoline automobiles in the United States from 1903 until the 9 January 1911 Second Circuit decision in Ford's favor, which held the patent valid only for Brayton-type two-stroke engines that the industry no longer used.
place: Rochester, New York (Selden's residence and filing origin)
grade_reason: Held at CORROBORATED rather than VERIFIED: the paper trail is complete and multiply attested (patent record 549,160; ALAM founding 1903; the 1903 suit against Ford; Judge Hough's 1909 decision; the 2d Cir. January 1911 opinion quoting the patent's 'inclosed crank chamber' as the Brayton-type improvement), but key details rest on secondary summaries (BPM Legal, EDN, Wikipedia) rather than the reporter's text read directly — the full 196 F. 615 opinion was cited, not read. Selden never built a commercial car; his own trial expert testified no working automobile used his engine design — the 'monopoly' was a licensing regime over a paper right, and the record grades it as exactly that.
earliest_attestation: US Patent 549,160, 'Road Engine,' issued to George Selden, 5 November 1895

sources.ref: US Patent 549,160 — inventor George Selden, Rochester, New York; filed May 8, 1879; issued November 5, 1895 (BPM Legal patent summary)

Wikipedia — 'Association of Licensed Automobile Manufacturers': ALAM formed March 1903; campaign threatening buyers of unlicensed cars; Judge Charles Merrill Hough upheld the patent 15 September 1909; court of appeals ruled for Ford 9 January 1911; ALAM declined to contest

EDN (originally posted 5 November 2012, edited 4 November 2019) — Selden sold the patent to the Electric Vehicle Company in 1899; ALAM brass 'Selden Patent' plates on licensed cars; eight-year legal fight; appeal won on the Brayton-vs-Otto engine argument

Jalopnik (14 October 2026) — 'Henry Ford Killed The Patent That Claimed To Own The Automobile': Winton's settlement, the EVC's enforcement, the 1911 verdict (patent valid only for Brayton two-stroke engines), patent expired two years later

competing_hypotheses: The older reading ('Ford beat the patent troll') treats Selden as a pure rent-seeker; the revisionist reading notes Selden did improve the Brayton engine for road use and that the trial court (Judge Hough, September 1909) found the patent infringed — the 1911 decision narrowed the claim's scope rather than invalidating it

The ALAM's 'don't buy a lawsuit' ad campaign vs. Ford's indemnification ads: a genuine 1903–1911 chilling effect on the industry, or marketing theater that Ford exploited for publicity — both attested, the magnitude unquantified
falsifiability: A court record showing the Selden patent enforced against a four-stroke Otto-engine automobile AFTER January 1911 would reopen the monopoly's end date; a Selden-built working road vehicle predating Benz would change the story's meaning but not its American-legal facts

title: The "America built the Panama Canal alone" myth
claim: The United States built the Panama Canal from scratch and on its own — the canal was an entirely American achievement, with no foreign effort before it and American hands doing the digging.
place: Isthmus of Panama (Colon → Panama City)
grade_reason: Three independent kills: (1) the purchase — the U.S. bought the defunct French company's works and assets outright ($40M to the French company, $10M to Panama), inheriting the excavated cut, the Panama Railroad, and the plant; (2) the hands — the American-era digging army was overwhelmingly West Indian (Barbados, Jamaica, Martinique, Guadeloupe); the silver roll bore the work and the dying (5,609 dead, only 350 white); (3) the design — the lock canal the Americans built was the conversion the French had already adopted in October 1887.
earliest_attestation: The American-era popular narrative, 1904–1914 onward (textbook shorthand, Roosevelt-era triumphalism); the corrective documentary record is continuous from the French period.

sources.ref: MIT Project Evaluation paper (US $10M to Panama + $40M to the French company; US construction cost $352M; 5,609 dead 1904–1914)
Smithsonian 1898 exhibition: U.S.-directed construction; crews from the West Indies began 1904, carving 100M m³ of rock and soil
History of the Panama Canal survey (1888 French workforce ~20,000, nine-tenths Afro-Caribbean; the sea-level-to-locks conversion October 1887)
Canal Zone labor-history survey: gold roll exclusively white, silver roll mainly Black Caribbean migrants; official toll 5,609, only 350 white

competing_hypotheses: The 'American completion' reading: the U.S. finished, paid for, and operates the canal — true, but a different claim than the from-scratch invention of it; kept as the honest form of the American credit
falsifiability: Records showing the French excavation was trivial or unusable (it was used — the Culebra cut and Gatun/Limón infrastructure carried forward), or U.S. payrolls showing an American-majority digging force (they show the opposite)

title: The 1883 Edison & Swan merger — the lawsuit that became a company
claim: After the British Edison Company sued Swan's company for incandescent-lamp patent infringement, the British suit was dropped in favor of a negotiated merger — creating the Edison and Swan United Electric Light Company in 1883 to exploit the two firms' complementary patents.
place: London, England — the joint company's formation; the British suit was dropped, not decided
grade_reason: Multiply and independently attested: the Manchester Guardian's 3 October 1883 report (via the MIT Press academic history), the 1979 Science centennial reassessment confirming the out-of-court settlement, and the company's own existence. The merger is the documentary proof that Swan's dated prior-research evidence could not be beaten in court — the suit was dropped precisely because it was tried in the record room and lost there.
earliest_attestation: Manchester Guardian, 3 October 1883 (via Arapostathis & Gooday, Patently Contestable, MIT Press 2013).

sources.desc: British Edison Company sued the Swan Company for infringement but, 'mindful of Swan's evidence of prior research and publication, switched to negotiating a merger deal' creating the Edison and Swan United Electric Lighting Company — reported in the Manchester Guardian, 3 Oct 1883
sources.ref: Arapostathis & Gooday, Patently Contestable (MIT Press 2013), via University of Reading working paper (centaur.reading.ac.uk/79610/1/Fundamental patents.pdf)

sources.desc: 1979 Science centennial piece confirms the out-of-court settlement in 1883 and the formation of the Edison and Swan company
sources.ref: Science 1979, vol 204 no 4388 (centennial reassessment, via iarchive.299792458.su)

competing_hypotheses: The folk version that Edison 'lost in court and was forced to merge' — the scholarly record is more careful: the suit was dropped for a negotiated deal, not decided against Edison; the forced-merger telling is graded as folk embellishment

The merger as pragmatic business: the two programs' improvements (Swan's, Edison's high-resistance filament and evacuation) had converged technically, so joint exploitation made commercial sense beyond the legal dispute
falsifiability: Contemporary company records showing no 1883 joint company, or a decisive courtroom verdict against Edison in Britain before October 1883.

title: The day of two noons — US standard time, 18 November 1883
claim: The American railroads adopted standard time at noon on 18 November 1883 — William F. Allen's five-zone plan (Intercolonial, Eastern, Central, Mountain, Pacific) approved by the General Time Convention in Chicago on 11 October 1883 — a full year before the International Meridian Conference met; the day was called 'the day of two noons' because cities reset their clocks at the new standard noon after having already observed local noon.
place: Chicago (General Time Convention, Grand Pacific Hotel, 11 Oct 1883)
grade_reason: Independently attested in the convention record, contemporary press coverage, and the Library of Congress legal-history account — the event (noon, 18 November 1883, Allen's plan, the telegraph synchronization) is documented from multiple sides; minor details vary between secondary accounts.
earliest_attestation: General Time Convention records (11 October 1883, Grand Pacific Hotel, Chicago); the contemporary newspaper instructions for resetting clocks; US Naval Observatory and Allegheny Observatory telegraph signals for synchronization

sources.ref: Library of Congress, In Custodia Legis: General Time Convention gathered at the Grand Pacific Hotel, Chicago, 11 October 1883; Allen's plan for five zones on the 75th/90th/105th/120th meridians; railroad clocks set to the new standard at noon on 18 November 1883; the US Naval Observatory and Allegheny Observatory telegraph signals; 'The Day of Two Noons' — noon struck twice in several cities

Wikipedia, 'Railway time': standard railway time introduced at noon 18 November 1883; Indianapolis Sentinel protest 17 November 1883; near-unanimous railroad support with Yale/Harvard observatory backing; federal law incorporation only in 1918

competing_hypotheses: The railroads' plan was the direct, sole ancestor of every American zone — boundaries later shifted by the ICC (1918) and have been revised since
Standard time was a railroad convention with no legal force at all — cities adopted it voluntarily; Congress did not legislate zone time until the Standard Time Act of 19 March 1918
falsifiability: Convention minutes or contemporary press records showing a different date or plan would move it; held at CORROBORATED because minor details (e.g., the exact 85% adoption figure, the 'day of two noons' coinage) rest on secondary synthesis, not primary documents.

title: 'The 1884 conference created the world's time zones'
claim: The 1884 International Meridian Conference created the world's time zones in a single meeting — that 41 delegates in Washington drew the zone system the world now uses.
place: Washington, D.C. (the conference that did not draw them)
grade_reason: Killed three ways: (1) the published resolutions draw no time zones at all — Resolution II adopts a meridian, Resolution IV recommends a universal day 'for purposes for which it may be found convenient,' and every resolution is framed as a proposal to governments, with no binding force; (2) the American zones predated the conference by a year — US railroads adopted standard time at noon on 18 November 1883, eleven months before the delegates met; (3) national adoption took decades afterward: France kept Paris Mean Time until 1891 and only aligned with Greenwich (minus 9 minutes 21 seconds, without naming it) in 1911 — 27 years later. No one drew the zones in Washington; everybody drew them at home, slowly.
earliest_attestation: The shorthand is the popular schoolbook version; the conference's own resolutions (Final Act, October 1884) are the contemporary refutation — no time zones appear in them

sources.ref: Published proceedings, Final Act (Gutenberg eBook 17759): Resolutions I–VII — no time-zone scheme, no binding act; Resolution IV's own wording limits the universal day to purposes 'for which it may be found convenient'

Library of Congress, In Custodia Legis: 'Whose Time is it Anyway? A Brief History of Standardized Time Zones in the United States' — General Time Convention, Grand Pacific Hotel Chicago, 11 October 1883; railroad clocks set to the new standard at noon on 18 November 1883; 'The Day of Two Noons'; five zones (Intercolonial, Eastern, Central, Mountain, Pacific)

Wikipedia, 'Railway time': standard railway time introduced at noon 18 November 1883; incorporated into US federal law only in 1918 (Standard Time Act, 19 March 1918). France: Paris Mean Time 1891; 1911 adopted Paris Mean Time delayed 9 min 21 s (equal to GMT without mentioning Greenwich). Germany: uniform time reckoning law 1 April 1893.

competing_hypotheses: The conference merely formalized what was already happening; the zones came from national adoption
The conference did real work — the Greenwich meridian vote and universal-day recommendation — but the zones themselves were adopted country by country over decades
falsifiability: Would require the conference's resolutions to include a time-zone scheme with country-by-country adoption, or a binding act of law — the published proceedings show neither.

title: The Home Insurance Building's hybrid frame: iron-dominant, steel-incorporating, bolted
claim: The Home Insurance Building's frame was a metal skeleton incorporating structural steel alongside wrought and cast iron; the frame carried the floors and helped carry the exterior walls — but masonry walls still carried some of the weight, and the metal frame was bolted rather than riveted.
place: LaSalle & Adams Streets, Chicago, Illinois (demolished 1931)
grade_reason: Multiple independent lines converge: the Chicago landmark report (official document) gives the precise 'incorporate structural steel' formulation; the structural-historical scholarship documents the iron-dominant hybrid frame and bolted connections; the construction-halt episode is independently attested (History.com, Wikipedia). Held at CORROBORATED rather than VERIFIED because the building is gone and the record rests on the scholarship's convergence, not on the artifact itself.
earliest_attestation: The building's documented design and construction: Jenney's metal skeleton of vertical columns and horizontal beams (1884–1885); city officials halted construction to investigate its safety — the inspection episode corroborates the novelty of the frame.

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Early skyscrapers' — 'Jenney's design was unusual in that it incorporated structural steel into the building's internal metal frame alongside the traditional wrought iron... some of the weight was still carried by masonry walls, and the metal frame was bolted, rather than riveted, together'

City of Chicago landmark report — 'the first skyscraper to incorporate structural steel in its skeleton frame'; 'the first in which the exterior became merely a curtain wall supported by the internal fireproofed framing'
History.com — city officials 'halted construction for a period of time so that they could ensure its safety' (1884–1885)
Wikipedia, 'Early skyscrapers' — 'The 1890 Rand McNally Building became the first entirely self-supporting, steel-framed skyscraper' (the contrast that bounds this record)

competing_hypotheses: The popular-steel version: the building was 'supported both inside and outside by a fireproof structural steel frame' (Wikipedia intro) — the version that feeds the textbook one-liner.

The measured version (accepted here): Jenney's design incorporated structural steel into the internal metal frame alongside traditional wrought iron; the frame took the floor loads and helped support the exterior walls; but some weight was still carried by masonry, and the frame was bolted, not riveted (Wikipedia 'Early skyscrapers', citing structural-historical scholarship). The Chicago landmark report's precise formulation is 'the first skyscraper to incorporate structural steel in its skeleton frame.'
falsifiability: Structural drawings or demolition records showing a full self-supporting riveted steel skeleton in 1885 (like the Rand McNally's 1890 frame) would overturn the measured version; the documented hybrid frame and bolted connections would have to be disproven.

title: The International Meridian Conference of 1884
claim: The International Meridian Conference assembled at Washington, D.C. in October 1884 — 41 delegates from 25 nations (26 invited, Denmark absent) — and on 13 October 1884 adopted Resolution II: the meridian through the centre of the transit instrument at the Greenwich Observatory would be the initial meridian for longitude, by 22 votes to 1 (San Domingo against), with Brazil and France abstaining. The conference also recommended a universal day — a mean solar day beginning at mean midnight at Greenwich — expressly for purposes 'for which it may be found convenient,' with no interference to local or standard time, and all resolutions were framed as proposals to the governments represented, not binding acts.
place: Washington, D.C. (Meridian Conference)
grade_reason: The event and its votes are documented in the conference's own published proceedings with full country-by-country tallies; the recommendation (not law) framing is in the resolution texts themselves.
earliest_attestation: The conference's own published proceedings: 'International Conference Held at Washington for the Purpose of Fixing a Prime Meridian and a Universal Day, October, 1884' (including the full vote tallies: ayes 22, noes 1, abstaining 2)

sources.ref: International Conference Held at Washington for the Purpose of Fixing a Prime Meridian and a Universal Day, October, 1884 — published proceedings (Project Gutenberg eBook 17759): resolutions I–VII with full vote tallies; Resolution II ayes 22 (Austria-Hungary, Mexico, Chili, Netherlands, Colombia, Paraguay, Costa Rica, Russia, Germany, Salvador, Great Britain, Spain, Guatemala, Sweden, Hawaii, Switzerland, Italy, Turkey, Japan, United States, Liberia, Venezuela), noes 1 (San Domingo), abstaining 2 (Brazil, France)
Wikipedia, 'International Meridian Conference' — 41 delegates, 26 invited nations (Denmark absent), resolutions adopted 22 October 1884, voting took place 13 October
Sandford Fleming's shipping-tonnage figures (72% of world shipping already using Greenwich vs 8% Paris) as presented to the conference — the practical case for Greenwich

competing_hypotheses: The conference fixed the prime meridian at Greenwich as a matter of binding international law
The conference was primarily about time zones and adopted them in the resolutions
falsifiability: The published proceedings themselves would have to be forgeries; the vote tallies are multiply cross-attested in the official record and in secondary histories of the conference.

title: Waterman's 1884 three-fissure feed
claim: Lewis Waterman's first pen-related patent, granted 12 February 1884, was for the 'three fissure feed' — a capillary-action ink feed that let air into the reservoir through narrow channels so ink flowed steadily without flooding; Waterman took over Frank Holland's abandoned 1883 pen company and fitted its pens with this feed, which is what made the Waterman pen the first reliably non-leaking, commercially dominant fountain pen.
place: New York City, USA — where Waterman assembled and sold the pens (behind a cigar shop, with a five-year guarantee)
grade_reason: The 'three fissure feed' scope of the 1884 patent is corroborated by Wikipedia's Lewis Waterman entry and the Holland-takeover narrative; held below VERIFIED because this pass relied on secondary transmission of the patent's claims rather than the specification itself.
earliest_attestation: US patent granted 12 February 1884 (the 'three fissure feed'); Ideal Pen Company founded 1884

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Lewis Waterman' — 'It was for this "three fissure feed" which his first pen-related patent was granted in 1884'; the Frank Holland 1883 takeover ('fitting the pens with a simplified feed of his own design'); National Inventors Hall of Fame 2006

Antique Trader, 'Putting pen to paper with distinction' — 'Waterman was granted a patent on February 12, 1884 for his "Fountain Pen"... Waterman's design limited airflow into the ink reservoir through the use of a small air channel'; Ideal Pen Company 1884, renamed L.E. Waterman 1888; spoon feed 1899 and the 1900 Exposition Universelle gold medal
ksgills.com, 'Lewis Waterman – Inventor of Fountain Pen' — names the lost-contract telling explicitly as 'just that — a legend'; describes the capillary-tube experiments with his brother Elijah

competing_hypotheses: That the famous lost-insurance-contract legend (a leaky pen spoiling a sale, Waterman losing the client while fetching a fresh contract) explains his invention — carried as apocrypha; Wikipedia marks it 'an apocryphal story' and trade histories note Waterman himself told it; the legend is the marketing, the feed is the fact

That Waterman founded the industry — he founded the Ideal Pen Company (1884, renamed L.E. Waterman 1888) and set the quality standard, but the pen trade already existed (Paul E. Wirt founded 1884, Holland's company 1883)
falsifiability: The patent specification itself (showing a feed, not a pen invention) is the evidence; the grade only falls if the 1884 patent proves to be for a complete new pen rather than the feed mechanism

title: 'Waterman invented the fountain pen' — the myth
claim: Lewis Waterman invented the fountain pen in 1884.
place: New York City, USA — where Waterman's pen company was founded
grade_reason: Two kills: (1) Petrache Poenaru registered a French patent for a self-inking portable pen on 25 May 1827 — 57 years before Waterman's; the first patent for a pen holding its own ink supply is Poenaru's, not Waterman's. (2) Waterman's own 1884 patent was for the 'three fissure feed' — a capillary-action feed that solved leaking — fitted onto pens of Frank Holland's abandoned 1883 company that Waterman took over; his patent is an improvement filing, not an invention filing.
earliest_attestation: The telling circulates in modern exam banks and trivia (e.g. testbook.com Kolkata Police Constable 2012 exam: 'Fountain Pen was invented by — Lewis E. Waterman'); pen-trade sites (ksgills.com 'Lewis Waterman – Inventor of Fountain Pen')

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Lewis Waterman' — 'It was for this "three fissure feed" which his first pen-related patent was granted in 1884'; Holland 1883 takeover context

Antique Trader, 'Putting pen to paper with distinction' — 'The first patent for a pen holding its own ink supply was issued in 1827 to Romanian Petrache Poenaru'; Waterman granted a patent 12 February 1884 for his 'Fountain Pen'; describes his capillary air-channel feed

Wikipedia, 'Petrache Poenaru' — French Ministry of the Interior registration 25 May 1827, code 3208, 'plume portable sans fin, qui s'alimente elle-meme avec de l'ancre' (citing 'Brevets d'Invention Nr. 3208' PDF, 25 May 1827)
testbook.com exam bank (Kolkata Police Constable 2012): 'Fountain Pen was invented by — Lewis E. Waterman' — the belief ecology: the telling as a test answer
ksgills.com, 'Lewis Waterman – Inventor of Fountain Pen' — the pen-trade telling in its bald form

competing_hypotheses: The honest scoped telling that survives: Waterman's 1884 three-fissure feed made the fountain pen the first reliably non-leaking, commercially dominant pen — Wikipedia's Waterman Pen Company entry hedges to 'invented the first truly functional fountain pen in the early 1880s'; the improvement was genuine, the primacy claim is not

Deeper predecessors: the 973 CE reservoir pen made for the Fatimid caliph al-Mu'izz (one-off commission, not a patent tradition) and Daniel Schwenter's 17th-century two-quill reservoir — named here as documented predecessors, each graded on its own evidence in future passes, never silently folded into the Waterman story
falsifiability: A pre-1884 patent or grant for a self-inking fountain pen stronger than Poenaru's 1827 brevet would deepen the kill, not weaken it; the grade only falls if the 1827 Poenaru patent is proven a fabrication and no other pre-1884 self-inking pen can be documented

title: The 'first skyscraper' was the Home Insurance Building (1885) — the definition-dependent title
claim: The Home Insurance Building in Chicago (designed by William Le Baron Jenney, completed 1885) was the world's first skyscraper — the unqualified textbook form of the claim.
place: LaSalle & Adams Streets, Chicago, Illinois (demolished 1931)
grade_reason: The building is real and its frame was an advance — but 'first skyscraper' is a title awarded by definition, and the academy has never agreed on the definition. Academic disagreement is documented (Wikipedia 'Early skyscrapers': 'there is academic disagreement over which building should be considered the first skyscraper'); the honor rotates by criterion (iron frame → 1797, curtain wall → 1864, steel → 1885, fully self-supporting steel → 1890). A contested title is CLAIMED, not CORROBORATED.
earliest_attestation: The building itself: designed by William Le Baron Jenney 1884, completed 1885, NE corner of LaSalle and Adams Streets, Chicago. The 'first skyscraper' title is a later historiographical attribution, not a contemporary claim.

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Early skyscrapers' — 'There is academic disagreement over which building should be considered the first skyscraper... various candidates exist depending on the criteria applied'; Home Insurance Building 'most often labeled the first skyscraper because of its innovative use of structural steel in a metal frame design'
Wikipedia, 'Home Insurance Building' — 10 stories, 138 ft (1885), 180 ft after 1891 addition; designed by William Le Baron Jenney; demolished 1931; construction begun May 1, 1884

City of Chicago landmark report (chicago.gov) — Jenney 'the first architect to use skeleton-frame construction'; Home Insurance 'the first skyscraper to incorporate structural steel in its skeleton frame'
History.com, 'Home Insurance Building' — the steel-frame design, the halted construction, the 138-ft height, and the building as the standard for skyscraper innovations

competing_hypotheses: The conventional-attribution position: the Home Insurance Building is 'most often labeled the first skyscraper' because of its innovative use of structural steel in a metal frame design (Wikipedia 'Early skyscrapers'; History.com; chicago.gov landmark report). Under a steel-frame-plus-height definition, the title holds.

The definition-dependence position: there is academic disagreement over which building should be considered the first skyscraper; 'identifying the first "true skyscraper" is not straightforward, and various candidates exist depending on the criteria applied' (Wikipedia 'Early skyscrapers', citing structural historians). Under an iron-frame definition, Ditherington (1797) wins; under curtain-wall, Oriel Chambers (1864); under entirely self-supporting steel, the Rand McNally (1890).

The Chicago-school-boosterism position: the 'first skyscraper' title did cultural work for Chicago's civic identity and the Chicago School narrative — the claim's persistence is partly historiographical, not purely technical.
falsifiability: A scholarly consensus definition of 'skyscraper' under which exactly one building satisfies all criteria, and under which no earlier candidate (Ditherington, Oriel Chambers, Equitable Life, Produce Exchange) qualifies, would resolve the dispute — but no such definition commands consensus, which is precisely why the grade is CLAIMED.

title: The hyper-radial order: the largest lighthouse lens ever put into use (Makapu'u Point, 1909)
claim: The hyper-radial order of Fresnel lens (focal length 1330 mm) is the largest lighthouse-lens size ever put into use: made from 1885 (Barbier test lens for the South Foreland trials; Chance Brothers' first in 1887), installed in about two dozen major landfall beacons worldwide; the Makapu'u Point hyper-radial (lit 1909) is the only such lens in U.S. service and has been the largest lens in U.S. service since 1909 — 12 feet tall, over a thousand prisms, displayed at the 1893 Chicago World's Fair before installation.
place: Makapu'u Point Light, Oahu, Hawaii, USA (the flagship hyper-radial)

Makapu'u, Cabo de Sao Vicente, Manora Point, Bishop Rock, Cabo de Santa Marta, Cape Race), the Makapu'u Point record ('only U.S. light with such a lens'; 'largest lens in U.S. service' since 1909; 12 ft; 1000+ prisms; 1893 Chicago fair), DVIDS/USCG ('world's largest lighthouse lens'; 19 nm range), and Foghorn Publishing ('largest lens in use in the United States, about 12 feet high'). Held below VERIFIED on the source-dependent production count.

Barbier (Paris) as test lens for the South Foreland trials; Chance Brothers first 1887; 'the largest ever put into use'; installed in about two dozen major landfall beacons (Makapu'u Point, Cabo de Sao Vicente, Manora Point Karachi, Bishop Rock, Cabo de Santa Marta, Cape Race); rendered obsolete by 1920s high-intensity lamps

Makapu'u Point Light — displayed at the 1893 Chicago World's Fair as 'the largest size ever made, off the chart of sixth through first Order'; 'only U.S. light with such a lens'; 'ever since its activation in 1909, it has had the distinction of having the largest lens in U.S. service'; 12 feet tall, over a thousand prisms

title: Smith's conductor's punch (1885)

title: The Mendenhall Order of 1893: metric standards become the fundamental standards of the United States
claim: In 1893, by the Mendenhall Order issued by T. C. Mendenhall (Superintendent of the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey), the United States adopted the international meter and kilogram as the fundamental standards for length and mass; the customary units — the yard, the pound, and their relatives — have been defined in relation to the meter and the kilogram ever since.
place: Washington, D.C., United States (the Mendenhall Order was an administrative act of the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey, not a place-bound event)
grade_reason: VERIFIED on multiple independent official and secondary records: the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey Report for 1893 carries the order; NIST Letter Circular 1136 states 'In 1893, metric standards, developed through international cooperation under the auspices of BIPM, were adopted as the fundamental standards for length and mass in the United States. Our customary measurements — the foot, pound, quart, etc. — have been defined in relation to the meter and the kilogram ever since'; the USMA transcribes the original order with the conversion tables (1 yard = 3600/3937 meter; 1 avoirdupois pound = 0.4535924277 kilogram). The reasons are independently documented: the imperial bronze yard No. 11 (an exact copy of the British imperial standard) had shown changes on comparison in 1876 and 1888 that could not be blamed on No. 11 alone, and the two-piece brass mint pound could not be density-tested without leakage risk and oxidized — so the Office of Weights and Measures had already been 'practically forced' to use the metric standards before the order formalized it.
earliest_attestation: The order itself, published in the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey Report for 1893.

sources.ref: Wikipedia — 'Mendenhall Order': the conversions 1 yard = 3600/3937 meter and 1 pound = 0.4535924277 kilogram; 'the Mendenhall order amounted to a formal announcement of a change that had already occurred in practice' — the Office of Weights and Measures had been 'practically forced' to use the metric standards because the imperial bronze yard No. 11 was unstable and the mint pound 'likewise unfit for use.'

NIST Letter Circular 1136 (1997 revision) — 'The U.S.A. and the Metric System': 'In 1893, metric standards, developed through international cooperation under the auspices of BIPM, were adopted as the fundamental standards for length and mass in the United States. Our customary measurements — the foot, pound, quart, etc. — have been defined in relation to the meter and the kilogram ever since.'

US Metric Association — transcription of the Mendenhall Order with the 1893 Report's yard/pound tables: the bronze yard No. 11's instability on 1876/1888 comparisons and the mint pound's two-piece leakage problem; 'the new metres and kilograms represented the most advanced ideas of standards, and it therefore seemed that greater stability in our weights and measures as well as higher accuracy would be secured by accepting the international metre and kilogram as fundamental standards.'

competing_hypotheses: The reading that the order changed nothing in daily life — true and fenced: it formalized a change already in practice; the public kept measuring in feet and pounds
The reading that the United States 'went metric' in 1893 — false as everyday practice; the 1975 Metric Conversion Act was deliberately voluntary and metric never became the common commercial system
falsifiability: If the Order had never been issued and U.S. customary units were still legally defined by the bronze yard and the mint pound rather than by metric prototypes, the claim would be false. The order's text survives in the official report and its conversions (1 yard = 3600/3937 meter; 1 pound = 0.4535924277 kilogram) were used by the Office of Weights and Measures thereafter.

title: "Edwin Seibels invented the vertical filing cabinet in 1893"
claim: Edwin Seibels, an insurance salesman, invented the vertical filing cabinet in 1893 — first and alone.
place: Chicago, Illinois (the 1892 Library Bureau prototype — the evidence that predates the claim)
grade_reason: The solo-inventor telling dies four ways: Seibels's own prototype dates to 1898, not 1893; the Library Bureau's Chicago office built a prototype for Dr. Rosenau in 1892 — six years earlier; the patent office denied Seibels (his application described 'a system that was an idea, not a device'); and the scholarly verdict is at least two inventors, likely more unrecorded.
earliest_attestation: 20th/21st-century popular histories, textbooks, and homework sites; Seibels's own 1898-prototype story (a later date than the telling claims).

sources.ref: Craig Robertson, The Filing Cabinet: A Vertical History of Information (University of Minnesota Press, 2021) — emergence in 1891; at least two inventors; Rosenau 1892 prototype; Seibels 1898 prototype; patent denied as 'an idea, not a device'
News@Northeastern interview with Craig Robertson (Oct 2021) — Dewey among contributors; emergence 1891
Wikipedia, 'Library Bureau' — 'In the 1890s, the Library Bureau introduced vertical filing'

Catherine Insler, 'The Day We Turned Paper Sideways' (Medium, Jan 2026) — belief ecology: 'In 1893, a young insurance man named Edwin Seibels was drowning in paper... created the world's first Vertical File'

University lecture notes, PSYC305A (2008) — belief ecology: 'The vertical filing system was invented in 1898 by Edwin G. Seibels (1866-1954). One of his original filing cabinets is in the Smithsonian museum.' (the Smithsonian conflation noted in the record)

competing_hypotheses: Seibels as one of several independent inventors (the Robertson multiple-inventor framing)
The '1893' date as a garbled reference to the Columbian Exposition year, borrowed by the popular telling
The Library Bureau's later institutional claim to the invention (marketing after the fact)
falsifiability: A dated 1893 Seibels prototype or filing predating the 1892 Rosenau/Library Bureau prototype would reopen the priority question.

title: 'America never adopted the metric system': the myth that mistakes the road signs for the statute books
claim: The United States has NEVER adopted the metric system — that metric units have never been the legally fundamental measurement standards of the country.
place: United States (a legal-fact claim, not a place-bound event)
grade_reason: Killed one way, conclusively, on the law: the Mendenhall Order of 1893 made the international meter and kilogram the fundamental standards of the United States — NIST's own words: 'Our customary measurements — the foot, pound, quart, etc. — have been defined in relation to the meter and the kilogram ever since.' The United States signed the Treaty of the Metre (Metric Convention) in 1875, received national prototype meters Nos. 27 and 21 in 1890, and in 1959 agreed with five other nations to define the inch as exactly 2.54 centimeters — a definition written in metric. 'The U.S. never adopted metric' confuses the commercial system on the road signs with the legal system in the statute books; the road signs are honestly fenced here, and the statute books say otherwise.
earliest_attestation: The shorthand version of the belief is standard textbook and journalistic framing; its strongest documentary form is the 'three countries' claim (U.S., Liberia, Myanmar) repeated in metric-advocacy journalism (e.g., The Collegian, 2026). The legal refutation is the Mendenhall Order text itself, 1893.

sources.ref: Wikipedia — 'Mendenhall Order': 1 yard = 3600/3937 meter; 1 pound = 0.4535924277 kilogram; the order 'amounted to a formal announcement of a change that had already occurred in practice.'

NIST Letter Circular 1136 (1997 revision): 'In 1893, metric standards... were adopted as the fundamental standards for length and mass in the United States. Our customary measurements... have been defined in relation to the meter and the kilogram ever since.'

The Collegian (2026): 'There are three countries in the world that do not formally use the metric system: Liberia, Myanmar and the United States' — and concedes the counter-argument: 'One could try to make the argument that the United States has technically implemented the metric system already — we've defined our units of measurement in terms of the meter since the Mendenhall Order of 1893. But that's not quite the same as common everyday usage.' Also carries: the 1975 Metric Conversion Act (voluntary), the 1988 Omnibus Act (metric 'the Preferred system'), the 1971 'A Metric America' report's ten-year plan.

Popular Science (Jason Schneider, June 2016): the history of the failed conversions — Gallup polling showed 45 percent of Americans opposed the metric switch in the late-1960s debate; the 1968 three-year study recommended a ten-year plan that Congress declined to make mandatory.

competing_hypotheses: The reading that 'adopted' means 'made the everyday commercial system' — on that reading the claim is TRUE and honestly fenced here: the 1975 Metric Conversion Act was deliberately voluntary, metric never became the common commercial system, and the U.S. remains one of three countries (with Liberia and Myanmar) not on metric for everyday use

The reading that the metric presence is cosmetic (labeling, science) — partly true as practice, but false as law: since 1893 the customary units themselves are legally defined BY the meter and kilogram, not merely convertible to them
falsifiability: The myth would stand if U.S. customary units were still legally defined by non-metric artifacts (the bronze yard, the mint pound). They are not: every customary unit is legally a defined fraction or multiple of an SI unit (the international yard and pound agreement, 1959, set 1 inch = 2.54 cm exactly; NIST states customary units have been defined in relation to the meter and kilogram since 1893).

title: The Dickson Experimental Sound Film (1894/95) - the first known sound film
claim: The Dickson Experimental Sound Film, made by W.K.L. Dickson in late 1894 or early 1895 at Edison's Black Maria studio, is the first known film with live-recorded sound - Dickson playing a violin into a wax-cylinder recording horn while two men dance to the music; selected for the National Film Registry in 2003.
place: Black Maria studio, West Orange, New Jersey (city precision)
grade_reason: The artifact survives and is independently documented: the 17-second restored film (Planquette's 'Song of the Cabin Boy' from Les Cloches de Corneville, 1877), the cylinder's ~2 minutes of sound including 23 seconds of violin music, the Library of Congress selection for preservation in 2003 as 'culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant,' and Musser's assessment (via the EMRO review) as 'the world's first known experiment in producing a motion picture with a recorded synchronized sound track.' Held below VERIFIED: the 'first known' is a claim about absence of predecessors, and the Kinetophone's no-true-sync caveat is fenced, not flattened - there is also no evidence of original-format exhibition. Three decades before Vitaphone, and thirty-two years before The Jazz Singer.
earliest_attestation: The surviving film strip and cylinder; no evidence it was ever exhibited in its original format.

sources.ref: Wikipedia - 'The Dickson Experimental Sound Film' (late 1894/early 1895; first known film with live-recorded sound; Kinetophone sync caveat; Black Maria; LOC National Film Registry 2003; resynchronized 2000)
EMRO - 'Edison: The Invention of the Movies (1891-1918)' (Musser: 'the world's first known experiment in producing a motion picture with a recorded synchronized sound track')

competing_hypotheses: The sync caveat: the Kinetophone was not a true sound-film system - there was no attempt to synchronize picture and sound throughout playback - so the film is the first known sound-film EXPERIMENT, not the first true sound film
falsifiability: An earlier film with documented live-recorded sound.

title: The Dreyfus Affair: arrest, trials, degradation, exoneration (1894-1906)
claim: The Dreyfus Affair (1894-1906): French artillery captain Alfred Dreyfus, an Alsatian Jew, was arrested in October 1894 on suspicion of passing military secrets to Germany, convicted of treason by a Paris court-martial on 22 December 1894, publicly degraded (5 January 1895) and deported to Devil's Island; in 1896 the new head of the army's intelligence Statistical Section, Georges Picquart, identified Major Ferdinand Walsin Esterhazy as the real author of the incriminating bordereau; after Zola's 'J'Accuse' (13 January 1898), the exposure of Colonel Henry's forged evidence (August 1898), a second court-martial at Rennes (August-September 1899) that still found Dreyfus guilty 'with extenuating circumstances,' a presidential pardon (19 September 1899), the Court of Cassation annulled the conviction on 12 July 1906, reinstated Dreyfus as a major, and awarded him the Legion of Honour.
place: Paris, France (court-martial, degradation, J'Accuse); Devil's Island, French Guiana (imprisonment); Rennes (1899 retrial)
grade_reason: Multiply attested by military-justice records across twelve years, the Court of Cassation's 1906 decision with its two stated 'new facts,' contemporary press (Zola's J'Accuse sold 200,000+ copies in an evening), and the physical forgery evidence (the Henry document, exposed 1898).
earliest_attestation: Contemporary French military-justice records, 1894-1906; the bordereau itself; the Court of Cassation's 1906 decision.

sources.ref: Court of Cassation, 12 July 1906 decision (annulment of the 1894 conviction; the two 'new facts')
Wikipedia 'Resolution of the Dreyfus affair': Rennes retrial 7 Aug 1899, guilty with extenuating circumstances, 10 years; pardon 19 Sept 1899; annulment 12 July 1906
history.com 'What Was the Dreyfus Affair': bordereau in the waste basket, Picquart's 1896 Esterhazy identification, Henry's forged evidence and suicide
Zola, 'J'Accuse...!', L'Aurore, 13 January 1898 (contemporary press)

competing_hypotheses: That the Rennes 1899 guilty verdict reflects a genuine military conviction rather than institutional self-protection: carried as the counterweight — two separate courts-martial convicted him.

That the 1906 annulment was a political act by a republican government rather than an evidentiary one: carried and weighed against the two 'new facts' (Esterhazy attribution + secret communication of the 'canaille de D...' document) on which the Court of Cassation grounded the decision.
That Dreyfus's acceptance of the 1899 pardon implied guilt: carried and rejected — the pardon required withdrawing his appeal; his name was not cleared until 1906.
falsifiability: Discovery that the court records are fabrications, or a contradicting authenticated document establishing a different sequence of events.

title: The Dreyfus guilty verdict: the bordereau was Esterhazy's, the evidence was forged
claim: Captain Alfred Dreyfus was guilty of the treason for which he was convicted on 22 December 1894 — that he personally authored the bordereau (the torn-up memorandum found in the German military attache's wastebasket) offering French military secrets to Germany.
place: Paris, France
grade_reason: Three independent kills: (1) the handwriting attribution was formally transferred to Esterhazy — Picquart's 1896 identification (petit bleu telegram, handwriting comparison) became one of the Court of Cassation's two stated 'new facts' in 1906; (2) the army's own counterintelligence officer, Colonel Hubert-Joseph Henry, manufactured forged evidence to support the conviction, confessed when exposed (30 August 1898), and killed himself the next day — the case's own builder admitted it was built on forgery; (3) the French state's highest court annulled the conviction on 12 July 1906. The 1899 Rennes retrial's guilty-with-extenuating-circumstances verdict is carried in competing hypotheses as the counterweight; it was itself the product of military pressure, and it was the verdict the 1906 court erased.
earliest_attestation: The 1894 court-martial record (the guilty verdict itself, 22 December 1894); refuted by the Court of Cassation, 12 July 1906.

sources.ref: Court of Cassation, 12 July 1906 decision: annulment grounded on (1) the bordereau's attribution to Esterhazy and (2) the secret communication of the 'canaille de D...' document
history.com 'What Was the Dreyfus Affair': Henry 'admitted that he had forged much of the evidence against Dreyfus and then Henry committed suicide'; 1906 exoneration
Wikipedia 'Resolution of the Dreyfus affair': the two 'new facts' (Esterhazy attribution; secret communication); Rennes guilty verdict with extenuating circumstances, 9 September 1899
Wikipedia 'Dreyfus affair': Esterhazy court-martial acquitted unanimously January 1898 after minutes of deliberation; Zola's J'Accuse in response

competing_hypotheses: That the 1894 handwriting experts were right and the later Esterhazy attribution is the error: carried and weighed — the 1894 experts' methods (including Bertillon's 'self-forgery' theory) were pseudo-scientific, and the 1906 Court of Cassation's 'new facts' included the formal attribution of the bordereau to Esterhazy.
That Esterhazy was Dreyfus's accomplice rather than his replacement: no documentary support; the 'petit bleu' telegram and the handwriting evidence place Esterhazy, not Dreyfus, at the center.

That the Henry forgery was an isolated excess by one officer, not proof the original conviction was wrong: carried honestly — but the forgery was manufactured specifically to shore up the case against Dreyfus, and the forger was the army's own counterintelligence officer.
falsifiability: An authenticated Dreyfus-authored copy of the bordereau, or forensic proof that the Esterhazy attribution is itself mistaken.

title: Edison 'invented the movies' — the solo-inventor reading
claim: Thomas Edison invented motion pictures — he was the sole inventor of the movies.
place: West Orange, New Jersey — the laboratory where the legend was written
grade_reason: The invention has too many fathers for one grave. W.K.L. Dickson, not Edison, did most of the 1889–1892 Kinetoscope development (Eastman Museum, 2021); the Kinetoscope was a single-viewer peep-show, and Edison initially disdained projection as financially nonviable — the shared-experience cinema came from the Lumières' 28 December 1895 paid screening (VERIFIED, evt-lumiere-first-screening-001); and motion photography predates Edison's lab entirely (Le Prince 1888, Marey 1882, Muybridge 1878). The grade kills the sole-inventor reading only — never the genuine Edison/Dickson system, never the commercial parlor achievement.
earliest_attestation: American popular and educational treatments crediting Edison as inventor, consolidated during his publicist-era dominance; the singular-inventor form is a later simplification, not a period claim.

sources.desc: George Eastman Museum (Todd Gustavson, Oct 2021): 'Most of the development was done by W. K. L. (William Kennedy Laurie) Dickson, an employee and official photographer of the Edison Manufacturing Company' — Dickson designed the Kinetograph and Kinetoscope; flexible Eastman nitrate film the substrate

Kinetoscope article: Edison's 1888 conception, Dickson's 1889–1892 development, the 20 May 1891 semi-public demo, the 14 April 1894 first commercial parlor exhibition (Holland Brothers, NYC, ten films), and the line 'Film projection, which Edison initially disdained as financially nonviable, soon superseded the Kinetoscope's individual exhibition model'
ASC Museum: the Kinetoscope's 1894 Paris demonstration at 20 boulevard Poissonnière as one of the Lumières' primary inspirations — the line of influence runs Edison-lab → Lyon, not the reverse

competing_hypotheses: The 'perfected/commercialized' defense: Edison's lab built the first commercially viable motion-picture system (Kinetograph/Kinetoscope, perforated 35mm film) — that is this record's foil (evt-kinetoscope-1894-001 CORROBORATED), not a defense of the sole-inventor reading

W.K.L. Dickson's role: the Eastman Museum and the Kinetoscope's own Wikipedia article attribute most of the 1889–1892 development work to Dickson, Edison's employee and official photographer — so even within the Edison-lab story the invention is collective
falsifiability: A single documented origin point with Edison as sole inventor — instead the record shows Louis Le Prince's Roundhay Garden Scene (1888), Marey's chronophotography (1882), Anschütz's Schnellseher (1891), and the Lumière public projection (1895), any one of which breaks the monopoly.

title: The Kinetoscope — 1894, the first commercially viable motion-picture system (peep-show, not projection)
claim: The Edison-lab Kinetograph/Kinetoscope system (1889–1894): William K.L. Dickson's motion-picture camera and peep-show viewer, first commercially exhibited 14 April 1894 at the Holland Brothers' parlor in New York City — the first commercially viable motion-picture system, single-viewer, not projected.
place: Broadway, New York City — the first Kinetoscope parlor
grade_reason: The system's essentials are multiply documented: Dickson's 1889–1892 development (Eastman Museum), the perforated 35mm film with sprocketed intermittent movement ('the first practical system of its type'), the April 1894 commercial parlor, and the Fred Ott sneeze as the first copyrighted movie. Held at CORROBORATED rather than VERIFIED on the internal lab chronology (1888 conception → 1891 tests), which rests on company records and retrospective testimony. The record fences the achievement honestly: peep-show, not projection — Edison initially disdained projection as financially nonviable.
earliest_attestation: The Holland Brothers' 1894 parlor opening; the Edison Manufacturing Co. product labels ('EDISON KINETOSCOPE MANUFACTURED BY EDISON MFG. CO., ORANGE, N.J.'); the Fred Ott sneeze copyright filing (January 1894, Library of Congress).

sources.desc: George Eastman Museum (Todd Gustavson, Oct 2021): Dickson's authorship, the Eastman nitrate-film substrate, 'the first practical system of its type'
Kinetoscope article: the 1888 Edison conception, the 1891 semi-public demo, the 14 April 1894 Holland Brothers commercial exhibition with ten films
Pre-cinema history timeline: Dickson and Heise filming Fred Ott's sneeze (1894) as a magazine publicity stunt, copyrighted as a 'photograph' — the first copyrighted movie

competing_hypotheses: The 20 May 1891 semi-public demonstration to the National Federation of Women's Clubs at the Edison laboratory is the earlier exhibition date; 14 April 1894 is the first COMMERCIAL exhibition
The 9 May 1893 Brooklyn Institute of Arts and Sciences unveiling (per the ASC Museum) sits between the two dates; the record carries all three honestly
falsifiability: Documentation that the April 1894 exhibition was not the first commercial motion-picture exhibition, or that the system did not use perforated 35mm film with intermittent movement.

title: The Browne Issue System (1895)
claim: Nina E. Browne, librarian at the Library Bureau in Boston, devised the first widely adopted card-and-pocket library charging system by 1895: each borrower's ticket and each book's card were filed together in date trays at checkout, the date was stamped in the book, and on return the borrower's card was handed back and the book card replaced in the book — after which no record of the transaction remained.
place: Library Bureau, Boston, Massachusetts
grade_reason: Multiply attested in library-history sources (Gorman, Queensland CLS manual, Sturges); the 1895 date rides on a single secondary transmission chain — held below VERIFIED.
earliest_attestation: Attested in Michael Gorman's Broken Pieces (ALA, 2011), Chapter 3 footnote 4; the State Library of Queensland Country Lending Service manual (2006) §3.1 describes the system in operational use; Sturges, Iliffe & Dearnley (2001) discuss its record-keeping privacy aspect.

sources.ref: Gorman, Michael (2011). Broken Pieces: A Library Life, 1941–1978. ALA. Ch. 3, 4th footnote.
State Library of Queensland, Country Lending Service (CLS) manual (2006), §3.1 'Issue systems'.
Sturges P., Iliffe U. & Dearnley J. 'Privacy in the Digital Library Environment' (2001), §2.3 'Record keeping in twentieth century libraries'.
Prytherch, Ray J. Harrod's Librarians' Glossary, 8th ed. (1995).

competing_hypotheses: The card-and-pocket form evolved gradually across several libraries and bureaus rather than from a single deviser (the 'folk technology' reading)
Browne's system was one node in the Library Bureau's commercial product line — the Bureau, not Browne alone, owns the 'invention'
falsifiability: A dated pre-1895 publication describing an identical book-card/borrower-ticket tray system, or archival evidence that Browne's 1895 system postdates the Newark implementation

title: The 'Einstein failed math' myth
claim: Albert Einstein failed mathematics in school — he was a poor student of math as a child.
place: Aarau, Switzerland (Aargau Cantonal School); Zurich (ETH)
grade_reason: DEBUNKED because the original documents show the opposite. Einstein's 1896 Matura certificate records 6s — the HIGHEST mark — in Algebra, Geometry, Descriptive Geometry, and Physics (5s in German, Italian, Chemistry, Natural History; a 3 in French). By age 15 he had mastered differential and integral calculus. The 'failure' is a two-part transmission accident: (1) the Aargau Cantonal School changed its grading scale mid-career — under the old system 1 was the highest and 6 the lowest; under the new, 6 was the highest — so biographers reading his grades as '1s turning into 6s' got the meaning exactly backwards; (2) he did fail the October 1895 ETH entrance exam — but in languages, botany, and zoology, not mathematics. Einstein himself refuted the story in letters and interviews: he never failed mathematics. The grade kills the myth, never the man's real struggles — French was his worst subject (3), and he was a rebellious, often frustrated student.
earliest_attestation: The misreading: Einstein's Aarau report cards showing grades of '1' (best under the old scale) and later '6' (best under the new scale) — read backwards by biographers who mixed the two scales. Popularized via Ripley's Believe It or Not (1935) and the comfort-myth circuit.

sources.ref: ETH-Bibliothek (Zurich) via ETH history holdings, as cited in 2026 analysis of the 1896 Matura certificate: final grades — Algebra 6, Geometry 6, Descriptive Geometry 6, Physics 6 (6 = highest under the new scale); 5s in German, Italian, Chemistry, Natural History; 4s in Geography, Art and Technical Drawing; 3 in French

factually.co fact-check (2026), 'What were Albert Einstein's actual grades in mathematics?': Aarau report cards show 6s in Algebra, Geometry, Descriptive Geometry, Physics; calculus mastery before age 15; the failed October 1895 entrance exam concerned botany, zoology, and languages, not mathematics

Historical analysis of the Aargau Cantonal School grading change: under the earlier system 1 was the highest grade and 6 the lowest; under the new system 6 was highest and 1 lowest — Einstein's algebra/geometry grades went from 1 to 6 because the scale flipped, not because his performance collapsed

ww2.jacksonms.gov article, 'Did Albert Einstein Fail Math': Einstein's documented excellence in mathematics and physics; Einstein refuted the myth in later letters and interviews, stating he never failed mathematics

competing_hypotheses: The 'real entrance exam' objection: Einstein DID fail the ETH Zurich entrance examination in October 1895. This is true — but the failure was in botany, zoology, and languages, not mathematics; he received his BEST results in mathematics and natural sciences, and failed because he sat the exam at 16, two years early.

The 'Munich years' objection: his grades at the Luitpold Gymnasium were merely good rather than perfect. The myth's specific claim is failing math — the Aarau records and ETH records both refute that reading.
falsifiability: A contemporaneous school report in which Albert Einstein received a failing grade in a mathematics subject.

title: The Lumière first paid public screening — 28 December 1895
claim: The first paid public film projection in history took place on 28 December 1895 at the Salon Indien du Grand Café, Paris — the Lumière brothers' Cinématographe screening of ten short films before a paying audience.
place: Salon Indien du Grand Café, 14 Boulevard des Capucines, Paris
grade_reason: The event is multiply documented: the original program listing the ten films (La Sortie de l'usine Lumière, La Voltige, La Pêche aux poissons rouges, Le Débarquement du congrès de photographie à Lyon, Les Forgerons, Le Jardinier (L'Arroseur arrosé), Repas de bébé, Le Saut à la couverture, Place des Cordeliers à Lyon, La Mer), the paid admission (one franc), and the continuous daily screenings that followed — the commercial cinema was born with a business ledger, not just a camera.
earliest_attestation: The original printed program of 28 December 1895; the Lumière company business records; the subsequent daily-screening accounts from the Salon Indien (January 1896 press coverage).

sources.desc: Program of the 28 December 1895 screening (ten films, ~50 seconds each) — published original program, via the IAFOR EuroMedia 2019 paper's reproduction and the Wikipedia Lumière article's sourced list

Smithsonian Magazine (Brigit Katz, 2018): the Sotheby's poster auction piece — <30 attendees against 100 chairs, the Cinématographe as camera-and-projector, and its inspiration in Edison's Kinetograph

The 22 March 1895 private screening (Society for the Development of the National Industry, one film, Léon Gaumont reportedly present) — the prior event that makes 28 December the first PAID public one, not the first demonstration

competing_hypotheses: The screening was 'the birth of cinema' in the shared-experience sense — the event as a premiere, not the invention of motion photography (Muybridge 1878, Marey 1882, Le Prince 1888, Edison's Kinetoscope 1894 are earlier motion pictures; the 22 March 1895 private Lumière screening of one film to a society audience precedes it)

The exact headcount on 28 December is honestly ranged across sources (<30 per the Smithsonian's Sotheby's-audio piece; ~35–40 in popular retellings; 100 chairs set up) — the variation is carried in the record, the date/venue/program/paid-admission are not in dispute
falsifiability: A documented paid public projection before 28 December 1895 (the Skladanowsky Bioskop at Berlin's Wintergarten, November 1895, is the named rival candidate and is carried in the competing hypotheses — it was not charged-admission projection in the Lumière sense and does not overturn the grade on the dated event).

title: 'Cinema is an invention without a future' — the Louis Lumière attribution
claim: Louis Lumière told Georges Méliès that the cinema was 'an invention without a future' (the famous 1895–96 warning, usually in the form: 'Jeune homme, remerciez-moi. Mon invention n'est pas à vendre... elle n'a aucun avenir commercial').
place: Paris — the legend's claimed scene
grade_reason: Three independent scholarly kills on the Louis-attribution. (1) The 'jeune homme' absurdity: James Leo Cahill's October 109 note — Louis Lumière (born 1864) was YOUNGER than Georges Méliès (born 1861); 'jeune homme' from Louis to Méliès makes no sense. (2) The absent Louis: Cahill again — Louis was not at the screening Méliès purportedly attended, so a direct address is unlikely 'even if the transaction occurred through the postal system.' (3) The father's claim: Tom Gunning, quoting Bernard Chardère, attributes the sentiment to Antoine Lumière — the attribution to Louis is, in Cahill's word, a 'misattribution.' The grade kills the Louis-to-Méliès utterance as documented fact, never the commercial pessimism itself (the Lumières' 1905 return to photography corroborates the mood) and never the Antoine hypothesis, which stays CLAIMED.
earliest_attestation: Maurice Bessy & Lo Duca, Georges Méliès: Mage (1945) — fifty years after the event; C.W. Ceram, Archaeology of the Cinema (1965) — the full 'Jeune homme' form, seventy years late.

sources.desc: James Leo Cahill, 'The Invention without a Future,' October 109 (Summer 2004), notes — via the USC cinema.usc.edu PDF: the passage is 'misattributed to Louis Lumière,' citing C.W. Ceram 1965; the 'jeune homme' absurdity (Louis b.1864, Méliès b.1861); Louis's absence from the screening; Gunning/Chardère's attribution to Antoine Lumière

World Records Journal: 'wherever this apocryphal quote is invoked' — the Lumières' supposed declaration characterized as apocryphal; the refusal of sale to Méliès out of respect for the magician's career

Wrong Reel Productions (on Godard's Le Mépris, 1963): the Lumière line 'The cinema is an invention without a future' written in Italian on the screening-room wall — the quote's canonization as legend, and its claimed origin: 'Lumière told fellow pioneer Georges Méliès when he was inquiring about the technology'

competing_hypotheses: The sentiment belongs to the father: Tom Gunning, quoting Bernard Chardère, attributes the commercial-pessimism sentiment to Antoine Lumière — the family patriarch, not Louis (CLAIMED — single-attribution, not independently documented)

The commercial pessimism was real regardless of who said it: the Lumières themselves treated the Cinématographe as a laboratory instrument, made 1,400+ views, and returned to still photography by 1905 — the documented behavior matches the sentiment even where the utterance fails
C.W. Ceram's Archaeology of the Cinema (1965) is the earliest traceable printed form of the full 'Jeune homme' version — the quote's documentary trail begins seventy years after the event
falsifiability: A contemporary (1895–96) source recording Louis Lumière saying it — none exists in the film-studies literature despite the quote's canonization.

title: Nobel's 1895 will
claim: On 27 November 1895, at the Swedish-Norwegian Club in Paris, Alfred Nobel signed his last will and testament, directing that the bulk of his estate (about 94% after taxes and individual bequests) be converted into a fund whose interest would be distributed annually as prizes to 'those who, during the preceding year, shall have conferred the greatest benefit to mankind' — in physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature, and peace. Nobel died 10 December 1896 in Sanremo, Italy, leaving no public explanation for the bequest.
place: Swedish-Norwegian Club, Paris
grade_reason: The signed document exists and is multiply attested; its terms are undisputed.
earliest_attestation: The will itself (27 November 1895), held by the Nobel Foundation; executed after Nobel's death 10 December 1896.

sources.ref: The will of Alfred Nobel, 27 November 1895 (Nobel Foundation holdings)
Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Alfred Nobel' — the will's terms and the five prizes

competing_hypotheses: The will was motivated by Nobel's documented pacifist sympathies and his friendship with Bertha von Suttner
The will was motivated by the 1888 obituary shock (see evt-nobel-obituary-inspired-prizes-001, DEBUNKED)
falsifiability: The will's text is a public document; a verified contradiction between its terms and this record would overturn it.

title: The train panic — audiences fled the Lumière screening in terror
claim: When the Lumières projected 'L'Arrivée d'un train en gare de La Ciotat,' the audience panicked — leapt up, ducked, fled the room in terror at the train rushing toward them (the founding legend of cinema's power, usually dated to the 28 December 1895 premiere).
place: Salon Indien du Grand Café, Paris — the legend's claimed scene
grade_reason: Two independent kills. (1) The wrong program: the train film was not in the 28 December 1895 program (the original program lists ten other films; it was first projected in January 1896, per the IAFOR paper and the film's own trivia record — sources disagree on whether it was filmed in summer 1895 (IMDb trivia) or 1896 (the IAFOR paper), but all agree it was absent from the December program; the third version dates to summer 1897). The panic story's claimed setting never happened. (2) The empty contemporary record: no major newspaper covered the December 1895 screening at all, and no 1895–96 account reports flight — the flight reports begin with Schönwald in 1916, twenty years late, and the mainstream historiography (the Loire–Péardinger chapter) notes film historians repeat the claim 'without examination,' providing 'neither evidence nor even references to contemporary sources.' The grade kills the panic and its placement, never the genuine astonishment — de Parville's captivated neighbor, Gorky's 1896 'plunge into the darkness' prose, and Gunning's roller-coaster thrill all survive untouched.
earliest_attestation: Post-war film histories (Sadoul 1959 et al.) — all decades after the event. No newspaper or eyewitness account from 1895–96 reports any flight.

sources.desc: IAFOR EuroMedia 2019 paper: the legend recreated, the original-program evidence that the train film was NOT in the 28 December program (filmed 1896, per the paper's reading), and the verdict 'this legend around the Lumière's view it's a fake'

Workers' Liberty 'Myths of cinema 2': no evidence of any flight; no major newspaper reported the screening; the earliest flight report is Schönwald 1916; the third version of the film shot summer 1897

Loiperdinger chapter (AMIA): 'The audience's terror in view of the arriving train is still passed on as a proven fact by film historians today' — but 'mainstream film historiography has provided neither evidence nor even references to contemporary sources'; Gregor/Patalas, Eisner, Sadoul, Chardère, Burch, Meusy all repeat the claim without sourcing

IMDb trivia: the panic legend 'identified as promotional embellishment'; the film not on the 1895 program; shot summer 1895, screened 1896; Gorky's 1896 poetic-terror review quoted as the literary form of the response

competing_hypotheses: The soft version: audiences were genuinely startled and astonished — Henri de Parville's 1896 account has one neighbor 'sprung to her feet' — wonder, not flight
The folk-festival version: film historian Tom Gunning's roller-coaster reading — the thrill of apparent danger known to be safe, not panic
falsifiability: A contemporary (1895–96) report of audience flight at a train-film projection — none exists despite the IAFOR paper's and Workers' Liberty's surveys of the record.

title: Hubert's company and the 'Ever Ready' brand
claim: Conrad Hubert's American Electrical Novelty and Manufacturing Company commercialized the flashlight, built the 'Ever Ready' brand (1905), and became the Eveready of the battery aisle.
place: New York City
grade_reason: The commercialization record is multiply attested: the NYPD testimonial distribution, the May 1898 Electrical Show at Madison Square Garden, the 'Ever Ready' trademark, the 1905 company rename, the 1914 National Carbon acquisition and 'Eveready' shortening — all consistently documented.
earliest_attestation: The 1899 'Ever Ready' catalogue (ThoughtCo); the January 1899 Ever-Ready flashlight advertisement referencing patent-infringement proceedings against rivals (Wikipedia).

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Eveready Battery Company': Hubert renamed the company 'The American Ever Ready Company' in 1905; it joined National Carbon Company in 1914 (trademark shortened to 'Eveready'); Hubert stayed on as president; National Carbon merged with Union Carbide in 1917; AA dry cell 1907, AAA 1911.
ThoughtCo: the 1899 Eveready catalogue advertising the new flashlight ('Let there be light' cover); Misell and Cowen-era background.

patentplaques-blog, 'Let There Be Light! – Invention of the Flashlight': the 1917 National Carbon naming contest for the flashlight — over 530,000 entries, four winners receiving $3,000 each for 'DAYLO'; the name was used 1917-1921 and discontinued after 1922.

competing_hypotheses: The company's founding date: given as 1896 (Wikipedia) and 1888 (ThoughtCo); one account (patentplaques-blog) has Hubert buying the operation from Joshua Lionel Cowen (later of Lionel trains) and renaming it, rather than founding it outright — the brand history is firm, the origin story is not
falsifiability: Company-registration records contradicting the 1905 rename or the 1914 National Carbon acquisition would overturn the branding timeline.

title: Why they were called 'flash' lights
claim: The word 'flashlight' (American) / 'torch' naming comes from the devices' first decade: weak zinc-carbon batteries and carbon-filament bulbs could only produce brief flashes of light, not sustained beams.
place: New York City
grade_reason: The technical mechanism (zinc-carbon cells that faded fast; carbon filaments that burned briefly) is independently attested by popular-science and collector histories, and the naming follows the behavior: users got flashes, not beams.
earliest_attestation: 1899 'Ever Ready' catalogue advertising the new flashlight (ThoughtCo).

sources.ref: Discover Magazine, 'They Invented it': 'Burdened with inefficient carbon-filament bulbs and weak batteries, early flashlights lasted only a few seconds when the user held down a tab or ring.'

ThoughtCo, 'The Invention of the Flashlight': the 1899 Eveready catalogue advertising the new flashlight carried the biblical quote 'let there be light' on the cover — the word 'flashlight' in commercial use within a year of the patent.
Collector account (CandlePowerForums): early users flashed the light briefly and switched off before the bulb blew; 1910 tungsten filaments then made sustained use practical.

competing_hypotheses: The name as pure marketing coinage by Hubert's company (the 'Ever-Ready' catalogue of 1899 used the word — but the catalogues describe an existing behavior, not a fresh invention of the term)
Collector lore adds that users 'flashed' the light to keep fragile carbon filaments from blowing — a behavior-level variant of the same mechanism
falsifiability: A pre-1898 published use of 'flashlight' for a portable electric lamp, or a contemporary document offering a different naming story, would overturn this.

title: The coal-bunker fire theory — the Maine's most probable cause
claim: The USS Maine was destroyed by an internal explosion: a spontaneous fire in a coal bunker — burning bituminous coal, prone to spontaneous combustion — ignited the adjacent 6-inch reserve magazines, which detonated the forward magazines on the night of 15 February 1898.
place: Havana Harbor, Cuba
grade_reason: The US Navy's own 1974–76 engineering investigation ('How the Battleship Maine Was Destroyed') — the most rigorous forensic study the ship ever received — concluded the internal coal-bunker fire was the most probable cause; the 1898 board's dismissal rested on a false claim ('never been a case of spontaneous combustion of coal on board the MAINE') contradicted by other US ships' known incidents. Held at CORROBORATED, not VERIFIED: the physical evidence is gone (wreck re-sunk 1912, photos inconclusive per National Geographic), and the Navy itself holds the cause 'unsettled.'
earliest_attestation: Dissenting US Navy officers at the time of the 1898 inquiry, who held that the magazines had been ignited by a spontaneous coal-bunker fire — the position the board declined to credit.

sources.ref: Adm. Hyman G. Rickover, 'How the Battleship Maine Was Destroyed' (1976, reissued 1995): Navy engineering investigation; concluded an internal explosion from a coal-bunker fire adjacent to the 6-inch reserve magazines was the most probable cause

Louis Fisher, 'Destruction of the Maine (1898)' (Law Library of Congress): the 1898 board claimed 'there had never been a case of spontaneous combustion of coal on board the MAINE' — but did not acknowledge that other US ships had experienced spontaneous combustion of coal in bunkers

Newspapers.com blog, 'The Sinking of the USS Maine' (1911 board + Rickover 1976): the 1911 investigation repeated the mine conclusion; the 1976 Rickover-led investigation concluded the explosions were caused by a coal-bunker fire adjacent to one of the ship's magazines

competing_hypotheses: The 1898 Sampson Board / 1911 Vreeland Board position: an external explosion from a mine (mechanism, not attribution) — the historical verdict, superseded on engineering grounds but never refuted by new physical evidence; the wreck was re-sunk in 1912 and cannot be re-examined.
The National Geographic computer-analysis position: photographic study of the twisted hull was inconclusive — the forensic trail genuinely ends where the cofferdam began.
falsifiability: A forensic re-examination of the wreck proving a mine blast (e.g., explosive residue consistent with a naval mine on the exterior plating) would overturn this; the wreck lies at 1,100 m depth north of Havana and has never been forensically re-examined since 1911.

title: The destruction of the USS Maine
claim: On the evening of 15 February 1898, the American battleship USS Maine (ACR-1) exploded and sank in Havana Harbor, Cuba, killing 266 of the 350 men aboard when her forward magazines detonated. She had been sent to Havana three weeks earlier, moored at buoy 4, to protect American interests during the Cuban War of Independence. The wreck was raised within a cofferdam in 1911 and re-sunk with military honors in deep water north of Havana in 1912; her main mast stands as a memorial at Arlington National Cemetery.
place: Havana Harbor, Cuba (moored at buoy 4)
grade_reason: The explosion, date, place, ship, and death toll are attested by the US Naval Court of Inquiry, the Spanish commission, the US Navy's casualty accounting, and the physical wreck — hostile and domestic traditions agreeing on the event itself.
earliest_attestation: The 1898 US Naval Court of Inquiry (Sampson Board), convened within weeks; Captain Sigsbee's reports; the Spanish naval commission's contemporaneous findings.

sources.ref: US Naval History and Heritage Command (DVIDS, 125th anniversary): explosion 15 Feb 1898 sank the ship, killing 266 sailors; the 1898 board ruled a mine detonated under the ship

Louis Fisher, 'Destruction of the Maine (1898)' (Law Library of Congress): 2 officers + 250 enlisted killed outright, 14 of the injured later died — 266 total; the 1898 board concluded a mine under the ship at frame 18
Smithsonian Magazine (Tom Miller, Feb 1998): 266 of 350 aboard killed; the 1976 Rickover investigation found the demise self-inflicted, likely a coal bunker fire

competing_hypotheses: The death toll is carried as 266 per the US Navy's official casualty accounting; Wikipedia carries 268 — the discrepancy is a counting convention, not a dispute about the event.

Whether the explosion's mechanism was external or internal is a separate, contested question graded in evt-maine-spanish-mine-001 and evt-maine-coal-bunker-fire-001 — this record covers only the event itself.
falsifiability: There is no live falsifier — the explosion is multiply and independently attested by hostile traditions (American board, Spanish commission, the wreck itself).

title: The Spanish mine that never was — 'Remember the Maine, to hell with Spain'
claim: Spain — a Spanish-placed mine, a Spanish-ordered sabotage — destroyed the battleship USS Maine in Havana Harbor on 15 February 1898, and the 'Remember the Maine — to hell with Spain!' war cry named the true culprit.
place: Havana Harbor, Cuba
grade_reason: Four independent kills: the 1898 board itself could not name any responsible person; no evidence of Spanish involvement exists after 128 years; Spain had no motive and its own commission read the explosion as internal; the 1976 Rickover engineering investigation — the US Navy's own — concluded an internal coal-bunker fire was the most probable cause.
