earliest_attestation: The 1898 American press cycle ('Spanish Treachery!' headlines; Hearst's New York Journal offering a reward for the 'Perpetrator of the Maine Outrage') and the wartime slogan itself — attestation of the belief, not of the fact.

sources.ref: Louis Fisher, 'Destruction of the Maine (1898)' (Law Library of Congress): the 1898 board 'was unable to obtain evidence fixing the responsibility for the destruction of the MAINE upon any person or persons'; Spain's commission, denied access to the wreck, concluded an internal explosion; the board ignored known spontaneous-combustion incidents on other US ships

Adm. Hyman G. Rickover, 'How the Battleship Maine Was Destroyed' (1976, reissued 1995): Navy engineering investigation concluding an internal coal-bunker fire — not a mine — was the most probable cause of the magazine explosion

NHHC (DVIDS, 125th anniversary, 2023): 'While the cause of the great tragedy remains unsettled, contemporary American popular opinion blamed Spain, and the Spanish-American War followed' — the Navy's own institution distinguishes the event from the attribution

Smithsonian Magazine (Tom Miller, Feb 1998): the Rickover team's finding that the demise was self-inflicted, likely a coal bunker fire; the external-blast position surviving only as 'there are those who still maintain it'

competing_hypotheses: The historical 1898–1911 position: the Sampson Board (March 1898) and the Vreeland Board (1911) both ruled an external explosion from a mine — but neither board ever fixed responsibility on Spain or any person; the boards graded the mechanism, the press and the war cry graded the attribution.
The pure-mechanism reading: an external explosion from a non-Spanish source — never attested by any evidence, and fenced here as a what-if, not a claim.
falsifiability: This claim has already met its falsifiers: (1) no evidence of Spanish involvement has surfaced in 128 years — no Spanish mine, no Spanish order, nothing in Spanish archives; (2) Spain had every reason to avoid the war it was about to lose, and its own commission — though denied access to the wreck — concluded an internal explosion; (3) the 1976 Navy engineering investigation found an internal coal-bunker fire the most probable cause; (4) even the 1898 board that the war cry leaned on could not fix responsibility on any person.

title: David Misell's tubular flashlight, 1898-1899
claim: English inventor David Misell designed and patented the first practical tubular dry-cell flashlight, 1898-1899.
place: New York City
grade_reason: Primary patent record corroborated by secondary industrial histories: the design (three D batteries front-to-back in a paper tube, bulb with rough brass reflector at the end), the filing and issue dates, and the assignment to Hubert's company are all consistently attested.
earliest_attestation: U.S. Patent 617,592, 'electric device', issued to David Misell 10 January 1899 (filed 12 March 1898, with Conrad Hubert as witness).

sources.ref: U.S. Patent 617,592 ('electric device'), issued to David Misell, 10 January 1899, filed 12 March 1898; tubular design with D batteries in a paper tube, assigned to the American Electrical Novelty and Manufacturing Company
Wikipedia, 'Eveready Battery Company': the flashlight 'designed by Misell was powered by "D" batteries laid front-to-back in a paper tube with the light bulb and a rough brass reflector at the end.'

CandlePowerForums, 'History of the First Tubular Flashlight': Misell applied for the patent 12 March 1898 with Hubert as witness; accepted 3 January 1899, issued 10 January 1899; first flashlights handmade from crude paper and fiber tubes; success at the May 1898 Electrical Show, Madison Square Garden.
ThoughtCo, 'The Invention of the Flashlight': Misell's portable light was designed in the now familiar tube-shape and used three D batteries placed in a line, with a lightbulb at one end of the tube.

competing_hypotheses: Misell's own earlier work: an 1895 portable electric lamp patent and an 1896 bicycle head-lamp — the 1898 tubular design descends from these, with Gustav Hitzelberger's workshop contribution (CandlePowerForums)

Earlier rival devices (the 'Acme Electric Lamp', Ohio Electric Works pocket lights) — documented products, but bulkier and less practical; the patent record favors Misell's tubular form as the modern prototype
falsifiability: An earlier patented tubular dry-cell design, or proof Misell's patents were fraudulently obtained, would overturn this; neither has surfaced in the patent record.

title: Seibels's 1898 prototype, the 1899 Globe-Wernicke cabinets, and the denied patent
claim: Edwin Seibels, an insurance salesman, built a vertical-filing prototype in 1898; a year later the Cincinnati company Globe-Wernicke produced five vertical filing cabinets, one of which survives in the Smithsonian Institution's National Museum of American History collection; Seibels's patent application was denied on the grounds that it described a system that was an idea, not a device.
place: National Museum of American History, Washington, DC (holds one of the five 1899 Globe-Wernicke cabinets)
grade_reason: Robertson's researched account; the surviving 1899 cabinet in the NMAH collection corroborates the Globe-Wernicke production leg — held below VERIFIED on the single-chain transmission of the denial, and the lecture notes' 'one of his original filing cabinets is in the Smithsonian' conflation (the NMAH cabinet is a Globe-Wernicke 1899 cabinet, not one of Seibels's) is corrected here.
earliest_attestation: Craig Robertson, The Filing Cabinet: A Vertical History of Information (University of Minnesota Press, 2021).

sources.ref: Craig Robertson, The Filing Cabinet: A Vertical History of Information (2021) — Seibels 1898 prototype; Globe-Wernicke's five 1899 cabinets; one in the Smithsonian NMAH collection; patent denied — 'his application described a system that was an idea, not a device'
University lecture notes, PSYC305A (2008) — earliest advertisement 1901

competing_hypotheses: The homework-site telling that Seibels 'was granted a patent' (uncited; contradicted by Robertson)
The lecture-note conflation that the Smithsonian cabinet is one of Seibels's own (Robertson: it is a Globe-Wernicke 1899 cabinet)
falsifiability: A granted Seibels vertical-file patent in the USPTO record would overturn the denial leg; a documented Seibels-made cabinet in the NMAH collection would overturn the Globe-Wernicke attribution.

title: The invention of bushido
claim: Bushido was the ancient, timeless code of honor followed by the samurai class throughout Japan's feudal history.
place: Tokyo — the samurai tradition the doctrine claims to describe
grade_reason: The coherent 'ancient code' has no premodern documentary existence: the term is scarcely used before the modern period (Friday 2007), and the canonical text was written in English in 1900 to make the samurai legible to Western readers; the modern invention is documented in Benesch 2014.
earliest_attestation: Nitobe Inazō, Bushido: The Soul of Japan — written in English for Western readers, published 1899/1900

sources.ref: Oleg Benesch, Inventing the Way of the Samurai: Nationalism, Internationalism, and Bushido in Modern Japan (Oxford University Press, 2014, Past & Present series) — the modern bushido tradition as a Meiji-and-later invention; Nitobe's 1900 English book as the tradition's founding act

Karl Friday (2007), cited via IJAPS 2011 — 'Japanese scarcely used the term Bushidō until the modern period, and there was little written discussion in premodern Japanese times as to what constituted the way of the warrior'

Jayson Chun, 'Bushido: The Last Samurai' (IJAPS Vol. 7 No. 3, 2011) — Nitobe a pacifist Quaker; the warrior code propagated by the Meiji government through education and mass media as a national myth to teach commoners 'the supposed militaristic values of the samurai'

Nitobe Inazō, Bushido: The Soul of Japan (1900) — the founding text itself, written in English for the West; seven virtues organized to parallel European chivalry, Stoicism, and Christian ethics (belief-ecology: Theodore Roosevelt bought dozens of copies)

competing_hypotheses: Warrior ethical norms existed in premodern Japan but were plural, situational, and never a single named code — the 'Way of the Horse and Bow' (kyūba no michi), Hagakure (1716) as one retainer's private notes, not a school code
The modern concept genuinely reflects an organic tradition that Nitobe and Benesch's critics say the modernists only named — graded against the near-absence of the term in premodern texts
falsifiability: A pre-1868 Japanese text naming and expounding 'bushido' as a coherent samurai-wide code

title: The "Conrad Hubert invented the flashlight" telling
claim: Conrad Hubert invented the flashlight.
place: New York City
grade_reason: Two independent kills: (1) U.S. Patent 617,592 for the tubular hand-held flashlight was issued 10 January 1899 to David Misell, filed 12 March 1898 and assigned to Hubert's company; (2) Hubert's own documented role is buyer/marketer — he purchased Misell's patents, workshop, and the unfinished tubular design in 1897-98 and commercialized the device.
earliest_attestation: Modern reference-work convention crediting Hubert; contradicted by the primary patent record.

sources.ref: U.S. Patent 617,592 ('electric device'), issued to David Misell, 10 January 1899, filed 12 March 1898; assigned to the American Electrical Novelty and Manufacturing Company

Wikipedia, 'Eveready Battery Company': 'On January 10, 1899, the company obtained U.S. Patent No. 617,592 (filed March 12, 1898) from David Misell, an inventor... Misell, the inventor of the tubular hand-held "electric device" (flashlight), assigned his invention over to Hubert's company.'

ThoughtCo, 'The Invention of the Flashlight': 'While Conrad Hubert might have known the flashlight was a bright idea, it was not his. British inventor David Misell... patented the original flashlight and sold those patent rights to the Eveready Battery Company.'; Hubert met Misell in 1897 and bought his patents, workshop, and the unfinished tubular design.
Discover Magazine, 'They Invented it': Misell 'assigned his patents to his employer, Conrad Hubert'; with Misell's help Hubert developed the first tubular flashlight.

competing_hypotheses: The reading Hubert 'invented' the flashlight in the loose sense of creating the commercial product line — true of the brand, not of the invention
An even earlier origin (Misell's unfinished tubular design derives from his own 1895-96 bicycle-lamp work — the patent file is the cleanest document, not the only ancestor)
falsifiability: A Hubert-signed patent, dated workshop drawing, or contemporary document showing the tubular design in Hubert's hand before Misell's 1898 application would restore the claim.

title: The 'Johan Vaaler invented the paper clip' myth
claim: Johan Vaaler, a Norwegian inventor, invented the paper clip — filing his patent in 1899 and receiving German (DRP 121,067) and US patents in 1901 — and the modern paper clip is his invention.
place: Sandvika, Norway (the 1989 monument site; Vaaler was an Oslo clerk)
grade_reason: DEBUNKED — 222nd DEBUNKED family. Two kills. (1) The Gem design predates and outlives Vaaler: the loop-within-a-loop paper clip (torsion principle) was in widespread use by 1900, never patented as a clip, and was the product of the Gem Manufacturing Co. in England (Design News; Scientific American). William Middlebrook's 1899 machine patent (US 636,272, Waterbury CT) illustrates a perfectly proportioned Gem — the invention predates Vaaler's filing in commerce, whatever the patent office shows. (2) Vaaler's design was NOT the Gem: it lacked the critical second loop — the papers were inserted by lifting the outer wire so the rest of the clip stood out at roughly ninety degrees, held by wire flexibility alone, poorly. It was never manufactured or sold, and his patents expired (Gizmodo; War History Online). Vaaler did not patent in his native Norway at all. The 1989 seven-meter Sandvika monument and the commemorative stamp honor Vaaler but both depict the Gem design, not his — the memorials themselves document the confusion.
earliest_attestation: Vaaler's patent documents (German DRP 121,067; US patent), 1901

sources.ref: Gizmodo, 'How the Humble Paperclip Became a Secret World War II Symbol': patents granted Germany + US 1901, none in Norway; Vaaler's design lacked the second loop, stood out at ~90°, held poorly, never manufactured, never sold; encyclopedias falsely credit him; the 23-foot 1989 statue and stamp depict the Gem, not his design

War History Online, 'Paperclip, WWII Resistance Mark': Vaaler's patents 1901 (Germany, US), not Norway; single-loop design lacked the second vital loop; never manufactured, patents expired; encyclopedias credit him falsely; monument + stamp depict the Gem

Design News, 'Lessons From Paper Clips': the classic loop-within-a-loop clip known as the Gem after the late-19th-century stationery firm Gem Ltd.; because no patent was taken out, other manufacturers copied and sold it
Scientific American, 'The Paper Clip' (via Early Office Museum): Gem-type paper clip in use by ~1892, never patented; Henry Petroski on the right wire + wire-bending machinery as preconditions

Answers.com Q&A page (accessed Oct 2026): 'The paperclip was invented in 1899 by Johan Vaaler. He received an American patent in 1901' — the misconception's canonical school-answer form, carried as belief ecology, not evidence

competing_hypotheses: Vaaler independently invented a wire fastener of his own design, while the Gem arose separately — both positions fenced as patent records: Vaaler's design is documented, the Gem's inventor is anonymous
Vaaler's patent predates the Gem's manufacture — killed by the Gem's documented trade use before 1899 (see evt-gem-paperclip-circa1900-001)
The Norwegian telling is national pride only — the patent file is real, so Vaaler is at least a documented paper-clip patentee, just not the inventor of the thing the world uses
falsifiability: Evidence that Vaaler's design was manufactured and sold before the Gem's documented trade use, or a patent showing Vaaler invented the loop-within-a-loop design before the Gem appeared in commerce.

title: Cows lying down means rain (myth)
claim: Cows lying down in a field is a sure sign that rain is on the way — cattle can sense approaching rain and lie down in anticipation.
place: England (UK Met Office survey — over 60% of the British public believe it)
grade_reason: The Met Office: 'there is no scientific evidence for it at all.' BBC Science Focus: 'there is no scientific evidence for this piece of weather folklore' — cows spend up to half their time lying down (rest, cud-chewing), so there is a 50:50 chance of seeing them down at any moment, rain or shine; herd mimicry makes whole-herd lying look meaningful. Live Science and Discover concur: no scientific evidence. The 2013 Arizona/Northern Missouri study found only a temperature link (cows stand in heat to cool, lie down in cold) — cold often precedes rain, but that is not rain-sensing and not the claim as stated.
earliest_attestation: The folk saying in long-standing British and American rural usage

sources.ref: BBC Science Focus Magazine, 'Is it true that cows lie down when it's about to rain?': 'According to a recent survey by the UK Met Office, over 60 per cent of the British public believe that cows lying down is a sure sign of rain.' And: 'In truth, however, there is no scientific evidence for this piece of weather folklore... cows spend up to half of their time lying down, either to rest or to chew their cud, so there's a 50:50 chance that they'll be lying down at any given moment, come rain or shine.' Also the 2013 US study (Arizona/Northern Missouri): cows stand in hot weather to cool off, lie down when colder — cold air often precedes rain.

Live Science, 'Do Cows Really Lie Down When It's About to Rain?': 'Not likely – cows lie down for many reasons, and there's no scientific evidence that rain is one of them. As the Farmer's Almanac says, "Cows lying down in a field more often means they're chewing their cud, rather than preparing for raindrops."'

Dairy Diary (UK), '7 Weather Folklore Sayings': 'Cows lie down when it is going to rain. Many believe that the sight of cows lying down means there is rain on the way but, according to the Met Office, there is no scientific evidence for it at all.'
Discover Magazine, 'Old Wives' Tales to Predict Weather': 'Cows lie down when rain is on the way. This claim lacks any scientific evidence, however.'

Fox Weather, 'Bovine barometers' (2021): Justin Rhinehart, UTenn beef cattle specialist — 'There may be some truth to it... I don't think we understand it enough to base a lot of planning around it... it may be something like, if you see all of your cows laying down in a field you might not want to mow hay and risk getting rained on.' Don't rule out pressure response, 'but it's also possible they are simply taking a nap.'

competing_hypotheses: Cows as temperature responders (the 2013 Arizona/Northern Missouri finding: cows stand longer in heat to cool off and lie down when colder; cold air often precedes rain — a weak indirect mechanism via temperature, not rain-sensing, and not the claim as stated)

Cows as barometers (the pressure-stomach theory — no evidence; Fox Weather's Rhinehart: behavior 'may be' a response to pressure, but 'I don't think we understand it enough to base a lot of planning around it')
falsifiability: A controlled study showing cattle lying-down behavior predicting rainfall independently of temperature, rest cycles, and herd mimicry

title: MYTH: John Cotton Dana invented the library's card-and-pocket checkout system
claim: The popular telling that John Cotton Dana invented the library book-card checkout — that the card-and-pocket system (book pocket, book card, date slip, borrower's card) began with Dana's Newark system about 1900, with no predecessor.
place: Newark Public Library, Newark, New Jersey (the telling's home; the refutation's geography is Boston 1895)
grade_reason: Nina E. Browne's card-and-pocket charging system dates to 1895 — five years before the Newark system's ~1900 debut — and Freedman's 1981 survey explicitly describes Newark as 'incorporating features of earlier systems'; the single-inventor telling cannot survive both facts.
earliest_attestation: The myth's vector: 'invented about 1900' tellings of the Newark system (e.g. Dean 2015 DHQ timeline), quiz-bank formulations crediting Dana, and the Newark system's own institutional memory.

sources.ref: Dean, Gabrielle (2015). DHQ timeline 'invented about 1900' formulation — the source of the single-inventor shorthand.
Freedman, Maurice J. (1981). 'Circulation Systems Past and Present' — Newark 'incorporating features of earlier systems' (the kill).
Gorman, Michael (2011). Broken Pieces, Ch. 3 fn 4 — Browne 1895 priority (the kill).
Browne Issue System article — 'replaced in America by the Newark and Detroit methods and others based on them' (the sequence).

competing_hypotheses: Dana's genuine contribution: the Newark system's borrower registration file, statistical reporting, and institutional popularization were real refinements — the DEBUNKED claim is the 'invented, no predecessor' form only
The two systems were developed in parallel ignorance of each other (no documentary proof of Dana reading Browne — the sequence is established, the transmission is not)
falsifiability: This record is already falsified-in-reverse: it would be un-DEBUNKED only if Browne's 1895 date collapses or Newark is shown to predate it — neither currently holds

title: The giant destrier — the draft-horse-sized medieval war horse
claim: The medieval knight's war horse — the destrier — was a huge animal, the size of a modern draft horse (17–18 hands high at the withers), a mount built to carry an armored man like a small tank.
place: England (171 excavated sites, AD 300–1650 — the study sample that killed the image)
grade_reason: The zooarchaeological sample (1,965 remains) shows medieval horses were small by modern standards: 16 hands rare even at the royal studs' zenith; none approached modern draft or police-horse sizes.
earliest_attestation: The modern draft-horse image: 20th-century film (shire horses cast as warhorses) and museum displays; not a medieval source

sources.ref: Ameen, C. et al., 'In search of the 'great horse': A zooarchaeological assessment of horses from England (AD 300–1650)', International Journal of Osteoarchaeology (2021), DOI 10.1002/oa.3038

Press coverage of the study, 10 Jan 2022: tallest Norman horse ~15 hands (Trowbridge Castle); 16 hands first appears in the 13th c. and was 'very rare' even at the 13th–14th c. royal stud zenith; horses of 16 and even 15 hands 'very rare'; none of the ~2,000 studied could serve as a modern police horse (UK minimum 16.2 hands)
Outram (Univ. of Exeter): 'High medieval destriers may have been relatively large for the time period, but were clearly still much smaller than we might expect for equivalent functions today'
Benkert (Univ. of Exeter): 'Neither size, nor limb bone robusticity alone, are enough to confidently identify warhorses in the archaeological record' — the study's own honesty fence

competing_hypotheses: Medieval documents describe destriers as 'great' (equus magnus) — a relative term, large for the contemporary stock, not draft-horse-sized in absolute terms
Selective royal studs (13th–14th c.) may have produced animals larger than the zooarchaeological mean; the English sample could underrepresent elite remounts
Regional variation across medieval Europe could put some warhorses above the English sizes without reviving the draft-horse picture
falsifiability: A securely-dated medieval European horse skeleton at 17 hands or above (1.73 m+) from a documented war-horse context

title: The Flannan Isles keepers' disappearance, December 1900
claim: Three lighthouse keepers — James Ducat, Thomas Marshall and Donald McArthur — vanished from the Flannan Isles lighthouse (Eilean Mòr, Outer Hebrides) between the last written log entries of 13 December and the arrival of the relief tender Hesperus on 26 December 1900; the steamer Archtor had already noted the light unlit on 15 December. Their bodies were never found.
place: Eilean Mòr, Flannan Isles, Outer Hebrides, Scotland
grade_reason: Multiple independent contemporary documentary sources (ship log, telegram, NLB investigation, relief-keeper account) attest the disappearance; the lighthouse itself is a documented, dated structure (designed David Alan Stevenson, first lit 7 December 1899). The cause is NOT part of this grade — held separately.
earliest_attestation: Archtor's log, 15 December 1900 (light not operational noted in poor weather); Captain Harvie's telegram to the NLB, 26 December 1900

sources.ref: Northern Lighthouse Board station page, 'Flannan Isles' (nlb.org.uk): discovery by Hesperus 26 Dec 1900; log 13 Dec; slate 14–15 Dec; everything in order; lamp ready to be lit; men disappeared afternoon of Saturday 15 December
Captain Harvie's telegram to the NLB, 26 December 1900 ('A dreadful accident has happened at the Flannans' — public domain)

Robert Muirhead's NLB investigation, 29 December 1900: Ducat and Marshall went down to the west landing; McArthur (the 'Occasional') left in shirtsleeves; damage to the west landing 'difficult to believe unless actually seen'; conclusion that an extra-large sea swept the men away while securing the mooring-rope box ~110 ft above sea level
Joseph Moore's relief-keeper account: kitchen utensils very clean (after dinner, contradicting later poetic invention)
Wikipedia, 'Flannan Isles Lighthouse' (secondary compilation with citations to Muirhead report, NLB, and period sources)

competing_hypotheses: Muirhead's wave theory (the NLB's official conclusion): the men went down to secure the west-landing rope box and were swept off by an extraordinary sea; refined by James Love's research (Marshall had previously been fined five shillings when equipment washed away — motive to go out; the cave-terminating geo at the west landing explains the violence of the water)
Accidental fall or a violent quarrel near the cliff edge by the west landing (psychology-based proposal, single-source, unattested)
Supernatural explanations (sea serpent, phantom ship, arranged escape, foreign spies) — graded separately in evt-flannan-keeper-myths-001
falsifiability: Any authenticated contemporary record placing any of the three keepers alive after 15 December 1900, or identified remains contradicting the disappearance.

title: TELLING (DEBUNKED): 'posh' = Port Out, Starboard Home
claim: TELLING (DEBUNKED): 'posh' is an acronym of 'Port Out, Starboard Home' — the Peninsular & Oriental Steam Navigation Company stamped wealthy Britain-India passengers' tickets P.O.S.H. for the cooler (more expensive) cabins.
place: London (P&O shipping and English print culture)
grade_reason: The OED, quoted verbatim by Ben Yagoda: 'However, no evidence has been found for the existence of such tickets.' Acronym etymologies for words predating the acronym era are, in Kory Stamper's phrase, by and large total horseshit — the genre is the tell.
earliest_attestation: The acronym story circulates in the 20th century; the word 'posh' predates it by a century

sources.ref: OED, 'posh' entry — 'no evidence has been found for the existence of such tickets' (quoted in Ben Yagoda, Gobsmacked! and benyagoda.substack.com); origin officially 'unknown', leading guess Romani money-slang
Kory Stamper (former Merriam-Webster lexicographer), via Yagoda — 'Acronymic etymologies are, by and large, total horseshit'

Cambridge UP excerpt (OUP researchers) — 'Posh ... has been mistakenly claimed to be a blend of 'Port Out, Starboard Home' ... The Oxford English Dictionary considers this etymology to be without foundation'

competing_hypotheses: Romani posh-houri ('halfpenny', then money) — the OED's leading guess
19th-c. slang 'posh' (money) expanding to 'fancy' — meaning the story has the direction backwards
falsifiability: A P&O ticket, ledger, or letter stamped P.O.S.H. in the stated sense

title: Landsteiner's ABO blood groups (1900–1901)
claim: Karl Landsteiner discovered the human ABO blood groups (A, B, O) — 1900 serum-mixing experiments, published 1901 — establishing the compatibility rules that made transfusion safe; AB followed (Decastello & Sturli, 1902); Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1930.
place: Vienna
grade_reason: The published experiment, the immediate AB extension, the 1907 independent confirmation, and the 1930 Nobel form converging independent lines; the serology is replicable to this day.
earliest_attestation: Landsteiner's 1901 paper; his 1900 laboratory experiments mixing staff blood samples

sources.ref: Karl Landsteiner, 'Zur Kenntnis der antifermentativen, lytischen und agglutinierenden Wirkungen des Blutserums und der Lymphe' (1901) — the A/B/O groups

News-Medical history of blood transfusion — 'In 1901, Karl Landsteiner, an Austrian physician discovered the first human blood groups... Landsteiner discovered blood groups A, B and O and established the basic principals of ABO compatibility'
Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1930, awarded to Karl Landsteiner 'for his discovery of human blood groups'

competing_hypotheses: Jan Jansky's 1907 independent classification (IV groups) — convergence, not contention
falsifiability: Proof the 1900–1901 experiments are misdated or the Nobel-cited discovery was made elsewhere first

title: The Newark Charging System (~1900)
claim: John Cotton Dana's Newark Public Library introduced its card-based circulation system about 1900: each book carried a book pocket with a book card (4"x2"), each checkout was stamped on a date slip pasted in the book, and the book card was filed in charging trays by date and call number against the borrower's registration — replacing ledger-based circulation and becoming, by the 1913 ALA survey, the most common named charging system in American libraries.
place: Newark Public Library, Newark, New Jersey
grade_reason: Contemporary operational documentation (Dana/Van de Carr 1908–12), the 1913 ALA adoption survey, and Freedman's 1981 survey converge on the system's existence, form, and dominance; the ~1900 origin date is secondary-attested.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary operational account: Dana & Van de Carr, Modern American library economy as illustrated by the Newark, N.J., Free Public Library, vol. 1, pt. 1 (Elm Tree Press, 1908–12), §2 'Lending and receiving books; the charging system'; 1913 ALA 'Summary of Reports on Charging Systems' lists Newark as the most common named system; Maurice J. Freedman, 'Circulation Systems Past and Present', Journal of Library Automation 14(4), Dec 1981.

sources.ref: Dana, J.C. & Van de Carr, S.C. Modern American library economy (1908–12), v.1 pt.1 §2.
American Library Association (1913). 'Summary of Reports on Charging Systems'. Papers and Proceedings of the 35th General Meeting.
Freedman, Maurice J. (1981). 'Circulation Systems Past and Present'. Journal of Library Automation 14(4):278–285.
Dean, Gabrielle (2015). 'The Shock of the Familiar: Three Timelines about Gender and Technology in the Library'. Digital Humanities Quarterly 9(2).
Wilson, Martha (1920). School Library Management. H.W. Wilson. (Newark procedure described)

competing_hypotheses: The Newark system was an adaptation of the Browne system and other earlier card systems, not a fresh invention (Freedman 1981: 'incorporating features of earlier systems')
The ~1900 date marks the Newark library's internal rollout, with the described procedure standardizing later (1908–12 publication)
falsifiability: A Newark library record showing card-based charging before Browne's 1895 system, or the 1908–12 Dana volume describing a different procedure

title: Stage versions of the rope trick — the legend's children, not its ancestors
claim: Twentieth-century stage magicians performed rope-rising effects — a rope made to stand or rise apparently without support — inspired by the Indian rope trick legend, not as survivals of an ancient classic feat.
place: India and the Western stage (the legend's two homes)
grade_reason: Lamont's single-scholar audit is the attestation: later stage performances of the trick were inspired by Wilkie's 1890 account. Held at CLAIMED — single-source, late — pending independent attestation of the lineage.
earliest_attestation: 20th-century stage-magic performances and exposure literature; Lamont 2004 traces their lineage to the post-1890 legend rather than to an ancient original.

sources.ref: Peter Lamont — 'The Rise of the Indian Rope Trick' (2004): 'later stage magic performances of the trick were inspired by Wilkie's account' (via Wikipedia's summary of Lamont's argument)

competing_hypotheses: Some stage versions preserve a genuine pre-1890 Indian rope-effect tradition (the simpler effects are real conjuring; only the classic full sequence is the hoax's child)
The stage versions are independent inventions with no lineage to the legend at all
falsifiability: A dated pre-1890 stage record of the classic full sequence (rigid rope, vanishing boy, falling limbs, restored boy) performed as described

title: Conklin's 1901 crescent filler — the first reliable self-filler
claim: Roy Conklin's US patent 685,258 (granted October 1901) covered the crescent filler: an internal rubber sac compressed by a pressure bar running through a slot in the barrel, attached to an external crescent-shaped hump; pressing and releasing the hump drew ink in without a separate dropper — the first reliable self-filling fountain pen. Conklin had founded the Self-Filling Fountain Pen Company (1898, with C. B. Gundy), renamed the Conklin Pen Manufacturing Co. (1901); Mark Twain lent his name to the pens; crescent fillers were produced through 1930.
place: Toledo, Ohio, USA — Conklin Pen Manufacturing Co.
grade_reason: The patent number, mechanism description, company history, Mark Twain endorsement, and 1930 production end are corroborated across the Vintage Pen Doctor, FountainPen.it, and Fountain Pen Network sources; held below VERIFIED on the one-day grant-date variance and the trade/collector transmission.
earliest_attestation: US patent 685,258, granted October 1901 (Roy Conklin); extensive marketing began 1904 per Geyer's Stationer

sources.ref: Vintage Fountain Pen Doctor, 'Conklin Crescent filling fountain pen' — Roy Conklin granted US patent 685258 on October 29, 1901; sac compressed via pressure bar through a barrel slot to an external hump; locking ring; marketing from 1904; Mark Twain convert by 1903

FountainPen.it, 'Conklin/en' — company born as Self-Filling Fountain Pen Co. 1898 (Roy Conklin + C. B. Gundy); Conklin Pen Manufacturing Co. 1901; 'the first working automatic filling system created for a pen'; crescent filler the first truly reliable automatic mechanism

Fountain Pen Network, 'Fountain Pen Chronology' — 1897: Roy Conklin begins working on fountain pens; 1901: Conklin Pen Manufacturing Co founded, patenting the crescent filler; 1915: Waterman introduces the lever filler; 1916: Parker introduces the button filler

competing_hypotheses: That the patent was granted 28 October vs 29 October 1901 — two collector sources differ by one day; carried as an honest one-day variance, both agree on October 1901

That Sheaffer's lever filler (1908 patent) displaced the crescent — true and honestly scoped: the crescent was first and most cumbersome; the lever was 'less efficient than the crescent filler, but far less cumbersome and more elegant' (Fountain Pen Network); the crescent's primacy survives the lever's victory
falsifiability: An earlier working self-filling patent predating 1901 (the 1897 Conklin-era claims and earlier 'automatic filling' patents are the audit surface); held below VERIFIED on the collector/trade transmission of this pass

title: Marconi's 1901 transatlantic 'S' (the contested reception)
claim: On 12 December 1901, at Signal Hill, St. John's, Newfoundland, Guglielmo Marconi received three faint clicks — the Morse letter 'S' — transmitted from his station at Poldhu, Cornwall, the first wireless reception across the Atlantic.
place: Signal Hill, St. John's, Newfoundland
grade_reason: Attested but not independently corroborated: the only witnesses are Marconi's own expedition party (Kemp, Paget), and Marconi refused a public demonstration at the time; the Antique Wireless Association's two-part technical review (2001) concluded modern propagation physics makes daytime reception at ~350 kHz over ~2,100 miles effectively impossible via the D-layer absorption Marconi could not have known about. Held at CLAIMED rather than DEBUNKED because the 1902 SS Philadelphia voyage, the 1902-03 Glace Bay night receptions, and the 1907 commercial transatlantic service prove the Atlantic was soon spanned by the same system — the anomaly is the December daylight, not the wireless itself.
earliest_attestation: Marconi's own diary, 12 Dec 1901 (signals logged at 12:30, 1:10, 2:20 Newfoundland time); Kemp and Paget as the on-site witnesses (Marconi's own men)

sources.ref: Antique Wireless Association, 'Did Marconi Receive Transatlantic Radio Signals in 1901?' Part 1 (pre-history, Poldhu, and the propagation critique: 'could hardly have picked a worse combination of frequency and time of day'; D-layer daytime absorption at AM broadcast frequencies)

Antique Wireless Association, Part 2 (conclusion): Marconi's diary — signals at 12:30, 1:10, 2:20 Newfoundland time; 'a rhythmic succession of the 3 dots corresponding to the letter S of the Morse code'; Anglo-American Telegraph Company's monopoly threat ended the Newfoundland experiments; SS Philadelphia follow-up voyage, Feb 1902

IEEE Engineering and Technology History Wiki, 'Reception of Transatlantic Radio Signals, 1901' (IEEE Milestone) — the institutional honor for the event; cited as a named position in competing hypotheses, not as independent evidence

competing_hypotheses: The reception was genuine: the claim stands on the diary + the expedition party's own reports, and Marconi did go on to span the Atlantic regularly at night (1902-03) and commercially (1907); one anomalous reception need not be impossible merely because the physics was unmodeled.
Marconi heard something real but not Poldhu — e.g., local atmospheric noise or spark-interference misread as the 'S' by a motivated listener; this is the classic motivated-perception alternative.

Marconi heard harmonics or secondary radiation from nearer spark equipment and attributed it to Poldhu; his refusal to demonstrate the reception publicly at the time is read by skeptics as significant.

The event happened but does not establish what is claimed: even if three clicks were heard, a non-replicated, single-party reception is not the same claim as 'the Atlantic was spanned' — the distinction between hearing clicks and a documented transatlantic service.
falsifiability: A second, independent contemporary party's log of the same signals at the same hour — or a verifiable public demonstration in the same conditions — would move the grade up; period evidence that the Poldhu transmitter was not keying at the logged times would move it down to DEBUNKED.

title: "Elementary, my dear Watson" — the line Doyle never wrote
claim: Sherlock Holmes said "Elementary, my dear Watson" in Sir Arthur Conan Doyle's original published stories (the canon of 56 short stories and four novels, 1887–1927).
place: London (221B Baker Street — the fictional setting) / the canon as published
grade_reason: Killed on two lines: (1) the negative — across every story Doyle wrote, the phrase never appears; Quote Investigator, Phrase Finder, and Sherlockian scholarship (Redmond's Quotations from Baker Street, 2009) agree; (2) the positive manufacture trail — the line is traceable through dated parodies and newspapers BEFORE the famous 1915 and 1929 landmarks, showing it condensed out of the press culture, not out of Doyle's pen.
earliest_attestation: Quote Investigator traces the components: 'Elementary' is said by Holmes in 'The Adventure of the Crooked Man' (1893) — Watson cries 'Excellent!' and Holmes answers 'Elementary,' said he — and 'my dear Watson' / 'Exactly, my dear Watson' appear elsewhere; the two fragments NEVER appear together in the canon. Exact-phrase print history: a 1901 Northampton Mercury parody ('Elementary, my dear Potson'), The Globe (London) 27 February 1908 (earliest exact print match), The Times Dispatch 24 August 1909 ('as Sherlock Holmes was wont to say' — already circulating as established folklore), Wodehouse's Psmith, Journalist (1915, book; serial in The Captain Oct 1909–Mar 1910: 'Elementary, my dear Watson, elementary,' murmured Psmith), and the 1929 film The Return of Sherlock Holmes (Clive Brook, first Holmes talkie) whose final lines put the phrase in Holmes's own spoken voice.

sources.ref: Quote Investigator, 'Quote Origin: Elementary, My Dear Watson' (2016-07-14) — full print-history trace: 1913 Everybody's Magazine, 1915 Wodehouse, 1922 NY Tribune, 1929 Clive Brook film
The Phrase Finder, 'Elementary my dear Watson' — 'one of the best known phrases that Sherlock Holmes never said'; nearest-miss citations (The Crooked Man, The Cardboard Box)
artwaste.land, 'The Phrase Holmes Never Said' — six-dated rise: canon (never), Gillette 1899 (unverified), Northampton Mercury 1901 parody, The Globe 1908, Wodehouse 1915, 1929 talkie
I Hear of Sherlock Everywhere, '“Elementary, my dear Watson” — The Birth of a Quotation' (2016-08) — Wodehouse serial Feb 1910, Times Dispatch 24 Aug 1909 pre-Wodehouse print occurrence

competing_hypotheses: The Gillette attribution: the line is often credited to William Gillette's 1899 stage play — but the line appears in NO published version of his script, so the attribution is unverifiable, not a documented origin
The collective-forgery reading (artwaste.land): the line 'condensed' out of turn-of-the-century parody and the popular press rather than being coined by one author
falsifiability: A citation of the exact phrase in any of the 56 stories or 4 novels as published by Doyle — the full canon is machine-searchable.

title: The 'Brontosaurus never existed' myth
claim: The popular claim 'Brontosaurus never existed — it was a scientific error from the start.' The animal was always real: Riggs 1903 performed a taxonomic sinking (synonymy under the priority rule), not a fraud exposure, and the type skeleton sat in museums throughout; the 2015 peer-reviewed reinstatement of the genus makes the 'never existed' version false twice over.
place: Como Bluff, Wyoming — the animal's type locality; the myth lived in textbooks and on a postage stamp
grade_reason: Two independent kills: (1) Riggs's 1903 paper says nothing about nonexistence — it moves excelsus into Apatosaurus on priority, and everyone including Riggs agreed the species was real; (2) Tschopp, Mateus & Benson 2015 (PeerJ 3:e857, ~300 pages, 477 characters, 81 specimens) reinstated Brontosaurus as a valid genus, adopted by the Paleobiology Database and modern mounts.
earliest_attestation: Riggs 1903 synonymy, as misread in popular science writing; the schoolbook shorthand 'Brontosaurus didn't exist' hardened through the 20th century

sources.ref: Riggs 1903: the synonymy sentence itself — 'the two genera may be regarded as synonymous. As the term Apatosaurus has priority, Brontosaurus will be regarded as a synonym.' — a filing decision, not a fraud exposure
Tschopp, E., Mateus, O. & Benson, R.B.J. (2015), PeerJ 3:e857, doi:10.7717/peerj.857 — the reinstatement; 'the famous genus Brontosaurus is considered valid by our quantitative approach'

Stephen Jay Gould, 'Bully for Brontosaurus' (1991, W.W. Norton): the stamp-era counterpoint — 'Brontosaurus and Apatosaurus are simply different names for the same dinosaur'; the issue is nomenclature, not existence

USPS 1989 four-dinosaur stamp issue (Tyrannosaurus, Stegosaurus, Pteranodon, Brontosaurus): public outrage, accusations of 'fostering scientific illiteracy,' demands for recall — the belief ecology that froze the myth into postage

competing_hypotheses: The myth's defense: 'the 2015 paper is contested, so the old belief is vindicated' — fails, because contesting genus rank does not resurrect 'never existed'; the bones were real either way
The true core the myth over-reads: Marsh DID mount a chimeric skull (Camarasaurus bones from three quarries) and the name DID lose on priority — the myth mistakes filing decisions for fabrication
falsifiability: A peer-reviewed demonstration that the 2015 Tschopp–Mateus–Benson analysis is methodologically unsound AND that the YPM 1980 holotype is non-diagnostic or fabricated — neither has been produced

title: The myth: Edison electrocuted Topsy to win the War of Currents
claim: Thomas Edison personally ordered the 1903 electrocution of the elephant Topsy as an anti-AC demonstration during the War of Currents against George Westinghouse.
place: Luna Park, Coney Island, Brooklyn, New York
grade_reason: Three independent kills: (1) agency — the execution was ordered by Topsy's owners Thompson & Dundy (their hanging plan was blocked by the SPCA; electrocution was the fallback; cyanide-laced carrots and strangulation were also attempted), not by Edison; (2) presence — Edison was never at Luna Park; the film was shot by his company's camera operator; (3) chronology — the War of Currents had ended by ~1892 (Edison General Electric + Thomson-Houston merger; Edison no longer attached to GE), so a 1903 execution could not have been a War-of-Currents weapon.
earliest_attestation: The myth is modern: its traceable vector is an unsourced 2008 Wired piece by Tony Long, per the electrotechnical-history record (brian.carnell.com); it has since circulated in pop culture, film, and some journalism (e.g., the Gizmodo 1903-framing piece) as an 'Edison did it' story.

sources.ref: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrocuting_an_Elephant — 'War of the currents misconception' section: execution was Thompson & Dundy's, Edison never visited Luna Park, 10 years after the war ended, Edison no longer attached to GE (1892 merger)

onthisday.com/photos/topsy-the-elephant-is-electrocuted — 'urban legend that Thomas Edison had ordered the elephant electrocuted ... This is false — the war between AC and DC took place ten years before the death of Topsy and Edison was never at Luna Park'

brian.carnell.com electrotechnical archive — 'Edison was not responsible ... nor did he participate in the euthanization'; the 2008 Wired article by Tony Long 'made this baseless claim without citing any evidence or sources'; the AC/DC dispute 'had largely ended with the creation of General Electric in 1892'

competing_hypotheses: The Edison Manufacturing Company filmed the event for commercial spectacle-footage reasons (one of many Edison 'actualities'), not propaganda — consistent with the company's newsreel business, and with no evidence of Edison's personal involvement

The myth's persistence reading: the 1903 film's genuine horror plus Edison's REAL 1888–1890 anti-AC campaign (Harold Brown's demonstrations, the 'Westinghoused' coinage, the AC electric chair) give the false story its plausibility
falsifiability: A document showing Edison ordered, directed, or was present at the execution — or evidence the War of Currents was still commercially live in 1903 — would overturn the grade.

title: The execution of Topsy the elephant, 4 January 1903
claim: On 4 January 1903 at Luna Park, Coney Island, New York, the female Asian elephant Topsy was publicly executed by electrocution on the orders of her owners, park proprietors Frederick Thompson and Elmer Dundy; the event was filmed by the Edison Manufacturing Company as 'Electrocuting an Elephant.'
place: Luna Park, Coney Island, Brooklyn, New York
grade_reason: Multiply attested contemporary event: period press, the surviving film, and institutional preservation in the Library of Congress.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary press reports, January 1903 (NYT: 'a rather inglorious affair'); the Edison Manufacturing film 'Electrocuting an Elephant' (1903), preserved in the U.S. Library of Congress.

sources.ref: The New York Times, 5 January 1903 ('a rather inglorious affair')
Edison Manufacturing Company, 'Electrocuting an Elephant' (1903), U.S. Library of Congress paper print collection
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrocuting_an_Elephant (event section, citing period press and LoC holdings)
onthisday.com/photos/topsy-the-elephant-is-electrocuted (compiled from period sources: owners' hanging plan blocked by the SPCA)

competing_hypotheses: The owners' stated motive (a dangerous animal that had killed three men, one of whom had burned her trunk with a cigar) as the full explanation
The publicity-motive reading: Thompson and Dundy had already been exploiting Topsy's reputation for park PR, and the staged execution drew ~1,500 spectators and press
falsifiability: Evidence that the execution did not occur as reported — e.g., proof the film depicts a different event, or period records contradicting the date, place, or owners' agency.

title: The Wrights' first powered, controlled flights, December 17, 1903
claim: At Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina, on December 17, 1903, Orville and Wilbur Wright made four sustained, powered, controlled, man-carrying flights (12 seconds/120 feet to 59 seconds/852 feet), photographed at the moment of liftoff and reported by telegram the same day — the first such flights in history. This is the timeline's first aviation record.
place: Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina (Wright Brothers National Memorial)
grade_reason: Contemporaneous photograph of the event, same-day documentary telegram, five named eyewitnesses, the brothers' own records, and the surviving aircraft — multiple independent primary lines.
earliest_attestation: Contemporaneous: the December 17, 1903 telegram to Bishop Milton Wright (Western Union via the Kitty Hawk weather bureau); the brothers' diaries; John T. Daniels' 5x7-inch glass-plate photograph of the first liftoff (negative deposited in the Library of Congress, 1949)

sources.ref: The December 17, 1903 telegram: 'Success four flights Thursday morning all against twenty-one mile wind... longest 57 seconds inform Press home Christmas' — contemporaneous documentary record of the flights the same morning

John T. Daniels photograph of Orville's liftoff, 10:35 a.m.: the famous image annotated by Smithsonian Magazine's photo analysis — the elevator position, the wing-warping cradle, the bench and footprints in the sand all consistent with a genuine, controlled liftoff (the machine had traveled only ~20 feet over the ground when the shutter tripped, and flew on)
Five named eyewitnesses from the Kill Devil Hills lifesaving station and town: John T. Daniels, W. S. Dough, A. D. Etheridge, W. C. Brinkley of Manteo, and Johnny Moore of Nags Head

The original 1903 Flyer itself, preserved: loaned to London's Science Museum 1928-1948 after the Smithsonian feud, returned 1948, installed in the Smithsonian's Arts and Industries Building — the artifact survives for inspection
NASA, Space History Photo: The Wright Brothers First Heavier-than-air Flight — confirms the flight parameters (12 s / 120 ft first flight; 59 s / 852 ft final flight; ~10 ft maximum altitude)

competing_hypotheses: Gustave Whitehead's claimed 1901 No. 21 flights in Connecticut (reason.com 2013 revival of a century-old newspaper claim): a single 1901 Bridgeport Herald report, no surviving machine, no photograph of a powered flight — the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum historians reject the case; the claim is documented in the record as the strongest rival and still lacks the Wrights' corroboration density

Alberto Santos-Dumont's 14-bis (October-November 1906, Paris): the first officially observed powered flight in Europe, taking off under its own power — the FAI/Brazilian priority position (see evt-santos-dumont-14bis-001); the record is genuine, the dispute is about what 'first' measures (Kitty Hawk's witnessed, controlled, photographed 1903 work vs. Bagatelle's publicly observed 1906 hops)
Clément Ader's 1890 Éole hop (20 cm, ~50 m, unconfirmed and uncontrolled): recorded here so the record shows what the Wright achievement had to beat — a hop is not a flight
falsifiability: A 1903-dated photograph of the Flyer elsewhere on December 17, or a published diary entry from one of the five eyewitnesses contradicting the flights — neither exists

title: The 1906 San Francisco Earthquake
claim: On 18 April 1906 at 05:12 local time, a ~Mw 7.9 strike-slip earthquake ruptured ~296 miles of the San Andreas Fault, shaking northern California from Eureka to the Salinas Valley at up to Mercalli XI (Extreme).
place: San Andreas Fault, northern California (epicenter debated; most recent USGS estimate near Mussel Rock, Daly City)
grade_reason: Instrumentally recorded on multiple continents' seismographs, contemporaneously reported, and investigated by the Lawson commission within two years.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary seismograms (Kobe, Göttingen, Bridston), USGS instrumental record, the 1908 Lawson report of the State Earthquake Investigation Commission

sources.ref: USGS / ANSS ComCat — Mw 7.9, epicenter 37.75N 122.55W, depth ~8 km
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1906_San_Francisco_earthquake (UTC time 1906-04-18 13:12:27; Mw 7.9; MMI XI; 05:12 local)
SEAONC Legacy Project — USGS relocated epicenter near Mussel Rock off Daly City; ~26 miles surface rupture; ~3,000 lives

competing_hypotheses: Epicenter offshore of the Golden Gate vs on the San Francisco peninsula (2018 USGS relocation)
falsifiability: Contemporary seismograms are the anchors; a demonstration that the 1906 records were misattributed would move this record

title: Santos-Dumont's 14-bis: the first officially observed powered flights in Europe, 1906

grade_reason: Officially observed by sporting authorities, publicly performed, contemporaneously reported in the press, prize-awarded — multiple independent contemporary attestations.

title: The 1906 San Francisco Firestorms

grade_reason: Converging independent sources: the Lawson report, contemporary Army reports, Genthe's photographs, the UC Berkeley Seismology Lab, and Hansen & Condon's 1989 document re-examination all place the fires as the dominant destroyer and the true death toll at ~3,000+, against the official 498.

title: The 1907 international reply coupon — the world's first prepaid-reply instrument

title: The twenty-six-year detention of Mary Mallon
claim: Mary Mallon was confined on North Brother Island from 1907 to 1910 and again from 1915 until her death in 1938 — the only identified typhoid carrier detained indefinitely.
place: North Brother Island, East River, New York City

The singularity of the punishment is the record's core: the only carrier confined indefinitely.

Wikipedia, 'Mary Mallon' — 1907 identification; first confinement 1907-1910; release on promise; 'Mrs. Brown' alias; 1915 Sloane Hospital outbreak and re-confinement; death 1938; 'the only one confined indefinitely'

Rosenau: 'it is not necessary to imprison the bacillus carrier. It is sufficient to restrict the activities of such an individual'

title: The 'only carrier' legend of Typhoid Mary
claim: Mary Mallon was the only healthy typhoid carrier — the one dangerous exception among well people.
place: New York City (identification, confinement on North Brother Island)
grade_reason: Three independent kills: (1) by Mallon's death in 1938, New York officials had identified more than 400 healthy typhoid carriers — and none had been forced into confinement (National Geographic; Wikipedia citing the carrier literature); (2) named contemporaries falsify the singularity directly — Frederick Moersch, a German-immigrant confectioner sent to North Brother Island in 1915, released in 1944 with a Brooklyn hospital job and state-paid rent; Alphonse Cotils, a Belgian baker banned from his bakery, given a suspended sentence in 1924 after a judge held he could not be imprisoned 'on account of his health'; Tony Labella, responsible for 87 cases and 2 deaths (later 35 more cases and 3 deaths after evading restrictions) — officials helped him find work outside the food industry; (3) the biology — up to 6% of people who have had typhoid become chronic carriers long after recovery (Stanford microbiologist Denise Monack, via Smithsonian), so carrier status was never unusual. What was unique about Mallon was the punishment, not the pathology: she was the only carrier confined indefinitely. The singularity claim is DEBUNKED; the confinement record stands as graded in evt-typhoid-mallon-confinement-001.
earliest_attestation: The 'one dangerous woman' framing: George Soper's identification work and his 1913 speech ('Since Typhoid Mary was discovered, the whole problem of carriers... has assumed an immense importance'); the press's 'Typhoid Mary' branding from 1907 onward

sources.ref: National Geographic, 'Typhoid Mary's tragic tale exposed the health impacts of super-spreaders' — 'at the time of Mallon's death, more than 400 healthy carriers of typhoid who had been identified by New York officials, and none had been forced into confinement'; 'at least 51 people caught typhoid through Mallon, and three died'

Wikipedia, 'Mary Mallon' — Frederick Moersch (North Brother 1915, released 1944, Brooklyn hospital job, state-paid rent); Alphonse Cotils (Belgian baker, 1924 suspended sentence, judge: cannot be imprisoned 'on account of his health'); Tony Labella (87 cases/2 deaths, then 35 cases/3 deaths after evading; helped into non-food work); 'over four hundred recorded cases of asymptomatic typhoid carriers' by her death, 'none of them were detained or quarantined for as long as she was'

Smithsonian Magazine, 'The Frightening Legacy of Typhoid Mary' — Leavitt's Typhoid Mary: Captive to the Public's Health; 'thousands across the country and hundreds in New York'; up to 6% of typhoid cases become long-term carriers (Monack, Stanford); Columbia's James Colgrove: 'the million-dollar question that nobody can answer' — why Mallon alone was imprisoned for life

Judith Walzer Leavitt, Typhoid Mary: Captive to the Public's Health (1996) — via secondary citation: Mallon's working-class immigrant status shaped public and scientific perceptions; health officials asked the wrong questions (how to stop her shedding bacilli rather than how to keep her from cooking)

competing_hypotheses: The fair defense of the legend: Mallon was the only carrier who refused to cooperate and kept cooking after promising to stop — so the singularity is moral, not biological (Leavitt's account notes the uncooperative framing; the counter: Tony Labella also evaded restrictions and was helped into non-food work, not confined)

The discrimination reading (Leavitt; Foss): Mallon's working-class Irish-immigrant-woman status shaped both public and scientific perception; had she been born twenty years earlier or later, Foss hypothesizes, she would not have been imprisoned

title: Frederick Cook's 1908 North Pole claim — the pole that wasn't reached (claimed 21 April 1908, disproven 21 December 1909)
claim: Frederick A. Cook claimed that he reached the North Pole on 21 April 1908, traveling by dogsled across the polar ice cap, and announced the achievement in September 1909 — days before Robert Peary announced his own 6 April 1909 claim. No verifiable proof of Cook's arrival at the Pole has ever been produced.
place: North Pole (claimed arrival point)
grade_reason: DEBUNKED as a reaching-of-the-Pole claim, by three independent findings: (1) the University of Copenhagen commission, 21 December 1909, examined Cook's submitted evidence and ruled his records did not contain proof he reached the Pole; (2) Cook never produced detailed original navigational records — he said they were in three boxes left with hunter Harry Whitney at Annoatok in April 1909, and those boxes were never recovered (Peary refused them aboard the Roosevelt); (3) modern analysis concludes Cook's 1908 journey did not venture far onto the Arctic Ocean before turning around — a formidable sledge journey, but not a polar one. Bryce (1996, 'Cook and Peary: The Polar Controversy, Resolved') concluded neither man reached the Pole. The claim dies; the expedition's genuine distance traveled is not denied.
earliest_attestation: Cook's announcement, September 1909, after two years out of contact.

sources.ref: Wikipedia 'Frederick Cook': announced September 1909 after two-year absence; claimed 21 April 1908; never produced detailed original navigational records ('three boxes' left with Harry Whitney at Annoatok, April 1909 — Whitney tried to bring them back aboard the Roosevelt, Peary refused, boxes never found); University of Copenhagen commission, 21 December 1909, ruled his records did not contain proof; National Geographic Society held Peary's papers and refused researchers access for decades
Explorersweb, 'Fakin' It: Exploration Hoaxes, Part I': Cook's claim largely discredited — 'he made a great journey but did not venture far out on the Arctic Ocean before turning around'
Wikipedia 'Peary's Expedition (1908-1909)', summarizing Bryce (1996) 'Cook and Peary: The Polar Controversy, Resolved': Bryce's conclusion — neither Cook nor Peary reached the Pole

History News Network, 'When Did Americans First Become Shocked by Lying': Cook claimed the 1908 arrival 'but he actually never got that far'; modern scholarship scrutinizing suppressed papers shows 'neither reached it, and both knew it'

competing_hypotheses: The Cook rehabilitation line: Cook's defenders argue his journey was formidable and that the lost records (the 'three boxes' left with Harry Whitney at Annoatok, April 1909) were genuine — but no scholar has produced those records, and the commission finding stands.

The sabotage line: Cook's supporters have long argued Peary's camp actively suppressed Cook's evidence (Peary refused to allow Whitney to bring Cook's boxes back aboard the Roosevelt; the National Geographic Society, which held Peary's papers, refused researchers access for decades). The suppression of access is documented; it does not supply Cook with proof he never submitted.
falsifiability: Verifiable original navigational records from Cook's 1908 sledge journey, independently corroborated — the very thing the 1909 commission asked for and never received.

title: Peary's 1909 North Pole claim — the expedition is documented; the exact point stays contested (6 April 1909)
claim: Robert E. Peary claimed he reached the North Pole on 6 April 1909, traveling by dogsled from the Roosevelt with Matthew Henson and four Inughuit men. The expedition itself is documented to the day; whether his party stood at the exact point 90 degN remains contested by serious scholarship.
place: North Pole (claimed arrival point, vicinity)
grade_reason: Split grade: the EXPEDITION is VERIFIED — the Roosevelt, the Cape Sheridan departure, the sledge journey, and the return are documented on Peary's own records and the Inughuit party's testimony. The EXACT-POINT claim ('stood at 90 degN on 6 April 1909') is CORROBORATED — not VERIFIED: the National Geographic Society's 1989 reanalysis (ocean-depth soundings + flag-pole shadow geometry) places the party within ~5 miles, which corroborates a near-Pole arrival; but Wally Herbert's 1989 expeditionary arithmetic (34-46 miles/day vs 6.3) and Bryce's 1996 resolution both argue the party fell short — and Peary's refusal to open his records to third-party review keeps the corroboration conditional. CORROBORATED is the honest grade for a contested near-hit: supported by one serious reanalysis, denied by two serious ones.
earliest_attestation: Peary's wired dispatch to The New York Times, September 1909, from the far north of Canada.

sources.ref: Wikipedia 'Peary's Expedition (1908-1909)': Herbert (The Noose of Laurels, 1989) — 34 mpd outbound / 46 return vs Cagni 6.3 mpd, conclusion ~50 miles short with falsified data; Bryce (1996) — neither reached, Peary ~160 km short; Crocker Land invention (1906 expedition diary: no land visible) named as Peary's documented fabrication for context

BBC Science Focus, 'Who really discovered the North Pole?': NGS 1989 reanalysis — photographs, ocean-depth soundings, data consistent with within 8 km of the true pole; Herbert 1968-69 crossing, Pole reached 6 April 1969

National Press Club, 'Club served as forum for debate over first to reach North Pole': NGS reanalysis — soundings put Peary within 60 miles at the continental shelf drop-off; flag-pole shadow geometry put the claim within five miles; 'good enough for government work'

HNN, 'North Pole pioneer Ralph Plaisted dies at 80': Cook announced 21 April 1908, Peary wired NYT days later claiming 6 April 1909; Peary declared Cook's claim fraudulent; modern conclusion — 'though both made formidable journeys, they more than likely never got close to the pole'

competing_hypotheses: The NGS reanalysis (1989): Gilbert M. Grosvenor's team used Peary's daily Arctic Ocean soundings (the seafloor depth dropping off at the continental shelf) plus a shadow-length analysis of Peary's flag-pole photographs to place the party within ~5 miles of the Pole — 'good enough for government work.' Support for the near-Pole reading.

The Herbert dissent (1989): Wally Herbert — who himself crossed the entire Arctic 1968-69 by dog team, reaching the Pole on 6 April 1969 — calculated from Peary's own records that Peary averaged 34 miles/day outbound and 46/day returning, versus his previous norm of ~6.3 miles/day (Cagni's best single day: 21.2 miles), and concluded Peary fell short by ~50 miles with falsified measurement data (The Noose of Laurels).
The Bryce resolution (1996): Robert M. Bryce concluded neither Cook nor Peary reached the Pole — Peary still had ~160 km to travel when he turned back.

The suppression fact: Peary refused to submit his records to any third-party review; the National Geographic Society, which held his papers, refused researchers access for decades. The paper trail was curated, not open — named as a fence, not a verdict.
falsifiability: A verified independent fix at 90 degN for 6 April 1909; or conclusive demonstration that Peary's sounding and photograph records cannot place him within the claimed radius — the NGS/Herbert dispute in evidence form.

title: The 1910 Halley cyanogen panic (DEBUNKED)
claim: When Earth passed through Halley's tail on 18–19 May 1910, the cyanogen gas in the tail would poison the atmosphere and kill all life.
place: New York, USA (panic epicenter); global (tail passage)
grade_reason: The panic is VERIFIED; the poisoning claim is DEBUNKED. Spectroscopic analysis (notably Yerkes Observatory) did find cyanogen in the tail — that part was real. Camille Flammarion warned it would 'impregnate the atmosphere and possibly snuff out all life on the planet,' and the New York Times ran the story. The public response is documented: sealed homes, gas masks, 'anti-comet pills' and 'anti-comet umbrellas' sold by street vendors, church prayer vigils. But other astronomers immediately dismissed the danger as nonsense — the gas was far too diffuse to have any effect — and on 18–19 May 1910 the Earth spent six hours passing through the tail with no ill effects whatsoever: no one sickened, no one died, the atmosphere unmeasurably changed. The anti-comet pills were later found to be merely quinine and sugar. The hoax layer (the 'Sacred Followers' virgin-sacrifice story) was also debunked. Mark Twain — born 30 November 1835, two weeks after the comet's perihelion, died 21 April 1910, the day after its next perihelion — really did bookend his life with the comet, as he predicted in his 1909 autobiography.
earliest_attestation: Camille Flammarion's warning, amplified by the New York Times, early 1910

sources.ref: History.com: the NYT's Flammarion story — cyanogen 'might impregnate the atmosphere and snuff out all life on the planet'; other scientists dismissed it as nonsense; the sealed homes, gas masks, churches, and 'anti-comet pills.'

Cook Islands education wiki: the 1910 approach (naked-eye ~10 April, perihelion 20 April, 0.15 AU); Flammarion's claim; the panicked buying; 'in reality, as other astronomers were quick to point out, the gas is so diffuse that the world suffered no ill effects.' The Sacred Followers hoax. Twain's 1835/1910 bookend.
FunFactz: Earth passed through the tail 18–19 May 1910; 'the cyanogen in the comet's tail had no measurable effect on Earth's atmosphere or life.'

falsifiability: Contemporary atmospheric measurements showing harm

title: Amundsen reaches the South Pole, 14 December 1911 — VERIFIED
claim: Roald Amundsen's Norwegian party reached the geographic South Pole on 14 December 1911 — the first humans to do so — beating Robert Falcon Scott's British Terra Nova party (which arrived c. 17 January 1912 and perished on the return) by roughly five weeks. This is the Race to the Pole, settled by the logs.
place: South Pole, Antarctica — the 1911 marker site (Polheim); longitude undefined at the pole
grade_reason: Double-attested by the two competitors themselves: Amundsen's logs, three days of sextant observations, and photographs — and the defeated party's own diary, which records finding Amundsen's tent and flag at the Pole. The Norwegian claim is thus corroborated by the British adversary's primary record, the strongest possible attestation structure. The search party's recovery of Scott's diary (12 November 1912) preserves the losing side's contemporaneous account.
earliest_attestation: Amundsen's expedition logs and sextant measurements (14–17 December 1911, three days of observations to fix the pole) + photographs; Scott's diary entry ('The Pole. Yes, but under very different circumstances from those expected... Great God! This is an awful place'), recovered by the search party 12 November 1912

sources.ref: Roald Amundsen, The South Pole: An Account of the Norwegian Antarctic Expedition in the Fram, 1910–1912 (1912) — logs, sextant observations 14–17 Dec 1911, photographs
Robert Falcon Scott's diary — the Pole entry (17 January 1912) recording the discovery of Amundsen's tent; recovered by the search party 12 November 1912
General survey consensus on the 14 December 1911 / 17 January 1912 dates and the five-week margin

competing_hypotheses: None on the outcome; Scott's defenders debate the causes of his failure (weather, logistics, pony/motor-sledge choices) — the audit keeps the cause debate separate from the arrival record
falsifiability: Sextant logs contradicting Amundsen's fix, or Scott's diary being a later fabrication — both examined repeatedly for a century without contradiction

title: The 'lost city discovered by Bingham, 1911' — the Machu Picchu discovery myth
claim: Machu Picchu was a lost city, unknown to the world until Yale explorer Hiram Bingham III discovered it on 24 July 1911.
place: Machu Picchu ridge, Urubamba Province, Peru
grade_reason: The site was inhabited and farmed when Bingham arrived; a previous visitor had signed a wall in 1902 (and Bingham's own journal credits Lizárraga as discoverer); it appeared on 19th-century maps; and Bingham himself believed he had found a different city (Vilcabamba). What Bingham genuinely did — the first archaeological survey and worldwide publicity — is the surviving truth, carried in the competing hypotheses, not the grade.
earliest_attestation: Bingham's own expedition accounts and the 1912-1913 National Geographic publicity; the 'lost city' framing is his and the press's, not the locals'.

sources.ref: Bingham's field journal for 24 July 1911 — 'Agustin Lizarraga is the discoverer of Machu Picchu.'
The 'Lizarraga 1902' charcoal inscription on the site (Temple of the Three Windows) — pre-dates Bingham by nine years

Expedition record: farmer-innkeeper Melchor Arteaga led Bingham and Sgt. Carrasco up the ridge (paid one sol); farmers Richarte and Álvarez were living in huts and farming cleared terraces at the top; Álvarez's 11-year-old son Pablito walked Bingham to the main ruins
1874 Göhring expedition map and 19th-century references (Berns 1867; von Hassel) — the site appears on maps decades before 1911
Bingham's own later statements that he believed Machu Picchu was Vilcabamba, the last Inca refuge — he was hunting a different city and remained convinced to the end of his life
Gonzales & Bauer 2021 (Ñawpa Pacha) — no Inca reference to a city called 'Machu Picchu' predates 1912; Bingham adopted the name from his guide's mountain; locals knew the site by another name

competing_hypotheses: The honest 're-discovery' framing: Bingham was the first to conduct an archaeological survey (1912, 1914-15 expeditions) and to bring the site to worldwide attention — a real scientific achievement, distinct from 'discovery'
Peru's 2011 centennial framed 1911 as the 'discovery' — the national narrative's political usefulness does not make the site lost in 1911

Bingham's defenders (e.g. Yale's Levin) frame the 1911 arrival as a 'breakthrough scientific discovery' of Machu Picchu 'and other undocumented sites' — a discovery of the archaeological record for science, not of the place
falsifiability: Contemporary evidence that no one lived at or knew of the site in 1911 — contradicted by the journal, the inscription, the farmers, and the maps

title: The fictional Flannan logbooks and the supernatural explanations
claim: The famous 'dramatic log entries' of the Flannan Isles keepers (12 Dec: severe winds and McArthur crying; 13 Dec: storm still raging, all three praying; 15 Dec: 'Storm ended, sea calm. God is over all') are authentic contemporary records, and the keepers were taken by supernatural means (a sea serpent, the Phantom of the Seven Hunters, arranged escape, or foreign spies).
place: Eilean Mòr, Flannan Isles, Outer Hebrides, Scotland
grade_reason: Journalist Mike Dash's investigation for the Fortean Times revealed the dramatic logbooks to be fictional, later additions to the story; the NLB's actual records show written log entries dated 13 December and slate particulars for 14–15 December with no such content, and no storms were reported in the area on 12–14 December. Gibson's poem scene is contradicted by Moore's first-hand account. No evidence supports the serpent, phantom-ship, spies, or arranged-escape claims.
earliest_attestation: Wilfrid Wilson Gibson's ballad 'Flannan Isle' (1912) — the overturned chair and uneaten meal; the dramatic log entries circulated later still

sources.ref: Mike Dash, Fortean Times investigation: the dramatic logbook entries are fictional, later additions (secondary investigation cited via periodical reporting)
Northern Lighthouse Board station page (nlb.org.uk): last written entries 13 Dec, slate 14–15 Dec, everything in order, lamp ready — no dramatic entries
Joseph Moore's relief-keeper account: 'The kitchen utensils were all very clean' — contradicts Gibson's overturned-chair/uneaten-meal scene

Wikipedia, 'Flannan Isles Lighthouse', 'Speculation and conjecture' + 'Later theories' sections (secondary compilation: Gibson 1912 poem; no reported storms 12–14 Dec; serpent/spies/phantom-ship/escape claims)

competing_hypotheses: The disappearance was caused by an extraordinary sea at the west landing — the NLB's documented conclusion (Muirhead, 29 December 1900), held in evt-flannan-isles-1900-001; this DEBUNKED family kills only the manufactured layers
The exact sequence of the keepers' last hours remains honestly unknown — no bodies, no witnesses; uncertainty is not evidence for any theory
falsifiability: Authenticated contemporary logbook pages bearing the dramatic entries, or any pre-1912 source attesting the sea-serpent/phantom-ship/espionage claims.

title: The whole nine yards: attestation (1946-1962)
claim: The phrase 'the whole nine yards' is attested in American print from the mid-20th century: 1946-51 in a Lexington, Kentucky newspaper; July 1956 and January 1957 in Kentucky Happy Hunting Ground (Kentucky Dept. of Fish and Wildlife Resources); 1962 in Michigan's Voices and a Car Life letter. A 1912 Kentucky 'whole six yards' variant shows the number was never fixed — it is a reified-number idiom, not a measurement.
place: Lexington / Kentucky print culture
grade_reason: Multiple independent dated prints in the documented antedating chain (Shapiro/Zimmer/Taylor-Blake); the six-yard variant independently corroborates the arbitrary-number reading.
earliest_attestation: Kentucky newspapers, 1912 ('the whole six yards'); the nine-yard form 1946-51 (Lexington, KY)

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Nine yards' — post-war usages 1946-51 (Lexington, KY), 1956/57 KHHG, 1962 Michigan's Voices / Car Life; 1912-1927 'six yards' variants
Fred R. Shapiro, Yale Alumni Magazine — the antedating sequence: 1962 (Goranson, Taylor-Blake) → 1956/57 KHHG (Taylor-Blake, verified by the Kentucky Afield editor)
Ben Zimmer, Visual Thesaurus 'Word Routes' — 'something of a Holy Grail among word sleuths'; no definitive origin story

competing_hypotheses: The phrase is a WWII-era coinage (falsified by the 1946-51 Kentucky prints, and by the 1912 six-yard variant which predates WWII entirely)
The number nine encodes a specific nine-yard object (falsified by the six-yard variant — the number moves, so it cannot be pinned to one object)
falsifiability: A securely dated, contextually confirmed earlier print of the idiomatic phrase

title: Titanic's wireless room: the distress calls that brought the Carpathia (1912)
claim: On the night of 14-15 April 1912, RMS Titanic's wireless operators Jack Phillips and Harold Bride transmitted distress calls — first Marconi's CQD, then also the international SOS at Bride's suggestion — that reached RMS Carpathia 58 miles away; the Carpathia altered course and rescued the survivors in the lifeboats (705). The disaster led to the Radio Act of 1912 mandating round-the-clock wireless watches aboard ships.
place: North Atlantic, Titanic wreck position (distress position transmitted was ~41°46'N 50°14'W, ~13 miles east of the actual wreck)
grade_reason: Multiple independent contemporary sources converge: Bride's sworn Senate testimony, Cottam's Carpathia reception and Rostron's diversion, the inquiries' published records, and the 1912 Radio Act itself as legislative consequence. The CQD-then-SOS sequence (Bride: 'Send S.O.S., it's the new call, and it may be your last chance to send it'), the 58-mile distance, the 705 survivors, and the California's silenced set are all multiply attested.
earliest_attestation: Bride's surviving testimony (U.S. Senate Inquiry, Day 2, Harold Bride); Carpathia operator Harold Cottam's reception log; contemporary press and inquiry records, April-May 1912

sources.ref: National Geographic, 'Why Titanic's first call for help wasn't an SOS signal' — Phillips/Bride as Marconi employees; CQD as the Marconi standard since 1904; SOS ratified 1908; 'Shut up! I am busy' to the Californian's ice warning

Wikipedia, 'Jack Phillips (wireless operator)' — 23:40 strike; distress sequence shortly after midnight (CQD, then SOS at Bride's suggestion); Carpathia contacted; power gone shortly after 02:00; last seen separating from Bride; body not recovered

U.S. Senate Inquiry, Day 2 — Harold Bride testimony (via Encyclopedia Titanica / secondary summaries) — the primary survivor's sworn account of the wireless room, the calls sent, and the ships contacted

competing_hypotheses: The minimal reading: wireless helped, but the rescue was a lifeboat story — the survivors were in boats when Carpathia arrived at ~4:00 am, four hours after the sinking; the wire located the boats, it did not save the ship (which is nobody's claim here).

The tragedy-was-worsened reading: Marconi's wireless monopoly and the backlog of passenger Marconigrams contributed to the disaster — Phillips's 'Shut up! I am busy' to the Californian's ice warning, and unsent ice warnings, are carried in the sources; the technology's failure mode is part of the record, not hidden from it.
falsifiability: No single falsifier is available; the record would be overturned by contemporaneous wireless logs showing no distress transmission from Titanic and no Carpathia diversion — the opposite is documented many times over.

title: Death Valley's 134°F (1913) as the reliable world record (disputed)
claim: The highest air temperature ever reliably measured on Earth is 134°F (56.7°C), recorded at Greenland Ranch, Death Valley, California, on 10 July 1913.
place: Greenland Ranch (Furnace Creek), Death Valley, California
grade_reason: The WMO lists 134°F as the official world record — but the word 'reliably' in the claim is exactly what the experts dispute. Weather historian Christopher Burt and climatologist William Reid (2016) concluded the reading was 'essentially not possible from a meteorological perspective' — the station's July peak ran 18°F above its monthly average while neighboring stations ran only 7–11°F above theirs — attributing it to observer error. A 2026 Bulletin of the AMS study estimated the true peak near 120°F. The WMO itself now describes Death Valley's 130°F readings of 2020 and 2021 as the highest 'since at least the 1930s.' The record survives by institutional inertia — 'a correction needs an owner, and this one has never found one' — not by surviving scrutiny. Official, but not corroborated as reliable.
earliest_attestation: The Greenland Ranch station log, 10 July 1913 (U.S. Weather Bureau)
