sources.ref: Smithsonian Magazine, 'How the Record for Hottest Temperature Ever Was Refuted' (on El Azizia): 'The WMO assessment is that the highest recorded surface temperature of 56.7°C (134°F) was measured on 10 July 1913 at Greenland Ranch (Death Valley) CA USA.' Notes Burt's skepticism of the Death Valley measurement as well.

Weather.com (2020): 'a detailed blog published in October 2016 by climatologist William Reid and weather historian Christopher Burt concluded the 134-degree Death Valley high in 1913 "was essentially not possible from a meteorological perspective, using an officially sanctioned USWB shelter and thermometer and following proper procedures observationally." They attributed these extreme temperatures in 1913 to observer error.'

Space Daily (2026): the Burt–Reid case — 'The monthly peak at Greenland Ranch was 18 degrees above its July average, while nearby stations were only 7 to 11 degrees above theirs'; 'A study published this year in the Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society pushed the point further, estimating that the true peak that day was about 120 degrees Fahrenheit'; the WMO 'has described Death Valley's much more recent readings of 130 degrees, reached in both 2020 and 2021, as the highest recorded anywhere in the world since at least the 1930s'; 'A correction needs an owner, and this one has never found one.'

WUOT/NPR (2020): 'Many experts are referring to Sunday's eye-catching high as being the hottest "reliably recorded" temperature, reflecting widespread doubts about the validity of the 1913 record of 134 degrees.' Burt: 'I look back at that record with a little bit of skepticism... he and a colleague "conclude with certainty that the actual hottest temperature ever reliably measured on Earth is 54°C (129.2°F), shared by Death Valley on June 30, 2013 and Mitribah, Kuwait on July 21, 2016."'

competing_hypotheses: The 1913 reading as valid (the WMO's standing position — the archive lists it; no committee has overturned it; the observer's other thermometers read higher, suggesting if anything an under-read)
The true modern maximum as the real record (Burt's position: 54°C/129.2°F, shared by Death Valley 30 June 2013 and Mitribah, Kuwait 21 July 2016 — the highest 'reliably measured' in the modern era)
falsifiability: A WMO committee ruling overturning the record (as happened with El Azizia 2012), or the discovery of the original instrument/observer logs resolving the discrepancy

title: The Palace Theatre's slow exit from vaudeville, 1927–1952
claim: New York's Palace Theatre (opened 24 March 1913, the flagship of American vaudeville — 'playing the Palace' the industry's pinnacle) played straight vaudeville until July 1932 — five years after The Jazz Singer — then a mixed vaudeville-before-film policy (last vaudeville accompaniment 12 November 1932), converted to a movie palace under RKO, flipped back to vaudeville-before-film on 7 January 1933, alternated formats for two years, showed films almost exclusively 1935–1949, and hosted vaudeville revivals in the 1950s (Judy Garland, 16 October 1951, 19 weeks).
place: Palace Theatre, 160 West 47th Street, New York City
grade_reason: The flagship's slow ending is multiply documented: Wikipedia's Palace Theatre article (specific weeks: last straight vaudeville July 9, 1932, featuring Louis Sobol; last accompaniment November 12, 1932, Nick Lucas and Hal Le Roy; reversion to vaudeville-before-film January 7, 1933), Playbill's theatre archive (1913 opening; Judy Garland's 16 October 1951 triumph and 19-week run), and BroadwayWorld's history (the RKO merger context; 1950s revivals by Sinatra, Kaye, Lewis, Hutton). The five-year gap between October 1927 and November 1932 is the myth's fatal measurement: vaudeville's flagship did not fall overnight.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary: 1913 opening coverage and Keith-Albee booking records; 1932 trade reporting (Variety); RKO business records; the theater's own later histories (Playbill's 'At This Theatre' archive).

sources.ref: Wikipedia — Palace Theatre (New York City): 1932 transition detail (last straight vaudeville July 9, 1932; last accompaniment Nov 12, 1932; Jan 7, 1933 reversion; 1935–1949 film-exclusive; two-year alternation)
Playbill — Palace Theatre 'At This Theatre' (opened 1913; Martin Beck/Keith/Albee; Judy Garland Oct 16, 1951, 19 weeks; 1950s personal-appearance revivals)
BroadwayWorld (2018) — Palace Theatre, the Valhalla of Vaudeville (1929 Kennedy-engineered KAO+RCA+FBO merger into RKO; combination bills tried on and off; 1950s revivals; Citizen Kane 1941 premiere)

competing_hypotheses: The 'death knell' dating: Wikipedia's vaudeville article gives the exclusive-cinema shift as 16 November 1932 vs the Palace article's 12 November 1932 last accompaniment — four-day variance, honestly carried
Whether the 1932 switch was corporate strategy (RKO's film-first economics) or audience-driven is an interpretive question, not part of the venue-facts grade
falsifiability: Documented evidence that the Palace ceased live vaudeville performance in 1928 (or before 1932), or that it never returned to mixed bills after November 1932.

title: The Christmas Truce of 1914
claim: In late December 1914, on the Western Front in Flanders, soldiers of the British Expeditionary Force and the Imperial German Army initiated a series of localized, unofficial truces: singing carols across the lines on Christmas Eve, meeting in no-man's-land on Christmas Day, exchanging gifts and food, posing for photographs together, and organizing joint burial parties for the dead. The truces were not universal (fighting continued in other sectors), were unofficial (high commands disapproved and issued anti-fraternization orders afterward), and made no difference to the war's course.
place: Frelinghien / Messines / Ploegsteert sector, Western Front, French-Belgian border
grade_reason: Multiply attested by independent primary sources on both sides — British and German letters, diaries, and war diaries written in December 1914, plus contemporary press and the subsequent official bans on fraternization, which confirm the event by trying to stop its recurrence.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary letters and diaries, December 1914 (both sides); war diaries; contemporary press (The Times, Daily Mirror) from late December 1914

sources.ref: Captain Robert Hamilton (Royal Warwickshire Regiment) diary — basis of 'Meet at Dawn, Unarmed' (co-authored by his grandson)
Lt. Kurt Zehmisch (134th Infantry Regiment) diary — among the best German-side accounts: orders that no shot be fired on the holy night and Christmas Day
Imperial War Museums collections — letters, diaries, and Ernie Williams's recorded interview (Messines sector kickabout testimony)
Michael Jürgs, Der kleine Frieden im großen Krieg (2003) — collation of German diary fragments
Dan Richards (IWM, head of documents and sound) on the truces as localized 'mini truces'
Smithsonian Magazine, 'The Story of the WWI Christmas Truce' — the 133rd Royal Saxon Regiment's War History on the Saxon-Scots fraternization

competing_hypotheses: Participation scale: contemporary reports speak of ~100,000 troops; the figure is an estimate, honestly ranged, not a count

How much was fraternization vs tacit mutual non-firing: Connelly (Kent) argues most men took part 'in this tacit manner rather than actively fraternized' — burial parties and ignoring each other vs. active mingling varied by sector
falsifiability: Contemporary evidence that no fraternization occurred along the front in December 1914 — no such evidence exists; the documentary record on both sides confirms it

title: The Christmas Truce Kickabouts (December 1914)
claim: During the Christmas truce of December 1914, in multiple sectors of the Western Front, British and German soldiers engaged in informal football kickabouts in no-man's-land — improvised games with real or makeshift balls (bully-beef tins, straw-stuffed sandbags), caps for goalposts, frozen ground, dozens to hundreds of men joining in, no teams, no officials, no kept score.
place: Western Front, French-Belgian border sectors (Frelinghien, Messines, Ploegsteert among the documented areas)
grade_reason: Independent attestation on both sides: Ernie Williams (IWM interview, Messines sector) — 'it wasn't a team game in any sense of the word... a kickabout... no score, no tally at all. It was simply a melee'; a Bedfordshire Regiment report of 'teams of about fifty a side played until this was unfortunately punctured'; Niemann's caps-as-goals account; Kurt Zehmisch's diary context. Multiple witnesses, multiple sectors, same shape of event.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary letters and diaries, December 1914 (both sides); IWM recorded interviews with veterans (e.g., Ernie Williams)

sources.ref: Ernie Williams, 19-year-old English soldier near Messines — recorded interview (IWM): 'From somewhere, somehow, this football appeared... it was just a general kickabout... There was no score, no tally at all. It was simply a melee.'
Bedfordshire Regiment report: 'a keen sportsman produced a ball, and teams of about fifty a side played until this was unfortunately punctured'
Lt. Johannes Niemann (133rd Saxon Infantry Regiment), regimental history: 'Suddenly a Tommy came with a football... We marked the goals with our caps... the Fritzes beat the Tommies 3-2'
Dan Richards (IWM, head of documents and sound): 'several smaller, much less formalised kickabouts took place in various parts of No Man's Land'
Prof. Mark Connelly (University of Kent): 'I think it highly likely that someone, somewhere did bring out a ball and a bit of a kick about took place'

competing_hypotheses: The exact number and location of kickabouts: estimates speak of 'around 15 games' across the frontline (Mirror/Pehr research) — an estimate, not a count
Which specific units played where: some unit identifications rest on single letters; the fact of kickabouts rests on multiple independent ones
falsifiability: Contemporary evidence that no football of any kind was played during the truce period — no such evidence exists; independent attestations on both sides confirm kickabouts

title: The Legend of the Organized Christmas Truce Football Match
claim: During the Christmas truce of 1914, British and German soldiers played an organized, regulation football fixture — eleven players a side, ninety minutes, officials, a definitive final score — the great Germany-3-2-England 'match' of popular legend.
place: Western Front, Flanders — the legendary fixture is placed variously and vaguely across the truce sectors
grade_reason: The organized-fixture reading dies on the evidence, not on skepticism. (1) THE HISTORIANS: Prof. Mark Connelly (Kent) — 'there is no absolute hard, verifiable evidence of a match'; IWM's Dan Richards — the one-big-organized-game idea 'is simply inaccurate, and many historians get quite prickly at its erroneous prominence.' (2) THE PHOTOGRAPH: the image most commonly used to illustrate the Christmas Truce football match was taken in Salonika, Greece, in 1915 — a year later, 1,600 miles from Flanders — and has nothing to do with the truce. (3) THE PADDING: elements of the legend were invented after the fact — poet Robert Graves reconstructed the encounter in a 1962 story, adding the sardonic fictional flourish of the 'Reverend Jolly' referee and the offside winning goal, which entered the legend as fact. (4) THE COUNTER-WITNESS: Ernie Williams, there at Messines, told the IWM it 'wasn't a team game in any sense of the word... There was no score, no tally at all. It was simply a melee.'
earliest_attestation: No contemporary attestation of a regulation fixture exists. The legend's paper trail runs through later retellings: the 2014 centenary popularization (Sainsbury's Christmas ad, the Premier League Christmas Truce Tournament, the UEFA-backed 2014 Ploegsteert memorial) — commemoration, not documentation.

sources.ref: Prof. Mark Connelly (University of Kent, Centre for War, Propaganda and Society): 'there is no absolute hard, verifiable evidence of a match' — CNN
Dan Richards (IWM, head of documents and sound): the one-big-organized-game idea 'is simply inaccurate'; the truces were localized 'mini truces'
The famous truce-football photograph: Salonika, Greece, 1915 — misattributed to Flanders 1914 (photo-historical correction, repeated across truce scholarship)
Robert Graves's 1962 fictional reconstruction — the 'Reverend Jolly' referee and offside-winner flourishes that entered the legend (Smithsonian)
Ernie Williams (IWM interview, Messines): 'no score, no tally at all. It was simply a melee' — direct counter-testimony to the scored-fixture legend

falsifiability: Already falsified: contemporary evidence of a regulation 11-a-side fixture with a kept score would overturn this — none has ever surfaced in 110 years of searching

title: The Endurance expedition and the all-28-survived rescue — VERIFIED
claim: The Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition (1914–1917): the Endurance was beset in the Weddell Sea pack ice in January 1915, abandoned 27 October 1915, and sank 21 November 1915; the 28 men of the Weddell Sea party drifted on ice floes, reached Elephant Island 15 April 1916, and were all — every one of the 28 — brought home alive after Shackleton's James Caird open-boat voyage to South Georgia (24 April–10 May 1916) and the Chilean Yelcho's rescue on 30 August 1916.
place: Endurance wreck site, Weddell Sea (found 5 March 2022 by Endurance22 at ~3,000 m; consistent with the drift account)
grade_reason: Multiply and independently attested primary record: the ship's logs, Hurley's glass-plate photographs of the sinking and the ice camps, Shackleton's own published account (South, 1919), Worsley's navigation notes for the James Caird, and multiple survivor memoirs — with external institutional corroboration (the Chilean navy's Yelcho under Captain Luis Pardo, whose government was formally thanked). The wreck's 2022 discovery at the predicted position closes the archaeological loop.
earliest_attestation: Frank Hurley's photographs (the sinking, 21 November 1915 — taken on glass plates at −30 °C) + the expedition's ship's logs + Shackleton's South (Heinemann, 1919)

sources.ref: Ernest Shackleton, South: The Story of Shackleton's Last Expedition, 1914–1917 (Heinemann, 1919) — the commander's published account
Frank Hurley's glass-plate photographs — the sinking (21 Nov 1915), Ocean Camp, the ice drift — developed under expedition conditions; National Library of Australia holdings
Endurance ship's logs + Frank Worsley's navigation notes (the James Caird voyage, 24 April–10 May 1916)

Wikipedia, 'Endurance (1912 ship)' — consolidated chronology: beset January 1915; abandoned 27 October 1915; sank 21 November 1915; Elephant Island 15 April 1916; James Caird departs 24 April 1916; South Georgia 10 May; Yelcho rescue 30 August 1916, 128 days after Shackleton departed

Australian Geographic, 2022 — Endurance22 expedition (Falklands Maritime Trust): wreck located 5 March 2022, 100 years to the day from Shackleton's 1922 burial; consistent with the 1915 sinking account

competing_hypotheses: No serious competing hypothesis disputes the outline; the exact dates of minor movements (ice-camp shifts, the sinking's hour) vary across survivor memoirs — the audit holds the dated milestones only where the logs and photographs converge
falsifiability: Photographs of the wreck contradicting Hurley's sinking position (the Endurance22 expedition's 2022 wreck discovery sits consistent with the 1915 sinking account)

title: Gallieni's taxis: the requisition and the run, 6–7 September 1914
claim: On the night of 6–7 September 1914, General Joseph Gallieni, military governor of Paris, requisitioned approximately 600–630 Paris taxis (chiefly Renault AG1 Landaulets, many from the G7 company) to transport roughly 3,000–6,000 soldiers of the French 7th Division (103rd and 104th Infantry Brigades) from Les Invalides to Nanteuil-le-Haudouin (~50 km). The drivers were paid by the meter; the French war ministry put the total bill at about 70,102 francs.
place: Les Invalides, Paris → Nanteuil-le-Haudouin (49.14033, 2.81303), ~50 km
grade_reason: Multiple independent contemporary sources: Gallieni's order, war-ministry accounts, the preserved taxi, participants' testimony, and the museum record all attest the requisition and the run.
earliest_attestation: Gallieni's requisition order and French military transport records, September 1914; contemporary press and participants' accounts

sources.ref: Musée de l'Armée, 'The Marne Taxi' (Google Arts & Culture): ~630 taxis requisitioned from Les Invalides, >3,000 soldiers transported ~60 miles; the preserved G7 Renault taxi
Express (2014), 'Taxi to the front and a place in history': French war ministry total Fr 70,102; first convoy ~250 taxis from La Villette via National Road 2; ~5,000 soldiers
Keegan, J., The First World War (1998) — standard scholarly treatment of the Marne and Gallieni's improvisation
Doughty, R., Pyrrhic Victory (2005) — French strategy and the 1914 campaign, the 7th Division's movement

competing_hypotheses: The higher figures (670+ taxis, 6,000 men) come from later popular accounts; the museum and war-ministry figures cluster at ~600–630 taxis and 3,000–5,000 men — carried as variance, honestly unresolved
Some accounts date the main run to the night of 7 September rather than 6–7; the operation spanned the night in any case
falsifiability: A Gallieni order countermanding the requisition, war-ministry accounts showing no taxi payments, or transport records placing the 103rd/104th brigades at the front by rail instead

title: The Taxis of the Marne decided the battle and saved Paris (the 'miracle' reading)
claim: The Paris taxis of September 1914 were decisive in the Allied victory at the First Battle of the Marne — the reinforcements they carried saved Paris and decided the battle.
place: Nanteuil-le-Haudouin — where the taxis arrived; the battle's decision happened elsewhere
grade_reason: Three independent kills: (1) scale — ~5,000 men in a battle of ~2 million; (2) most taxied troops were held in reserve; (3) the battle's decision is attributed by the campaign record to von Kluck's flank exposure, Joffre's counter-stroke, and the BEF wedge, not the taxi convoy.
earliest_attestation: French wartime press and the 'union sacrée' propaganda, autumn 1914; the reading persists in popular histories

sources.ref: Express (2014): 'In a battle involving two million men, 5,000 mattered little, especially as most of the taxied troops were held in reserve. The taxi-borne reinforcements were a flea bite, although the episode was artfully used by the French government to promote the idea that a "union sacrée" of soldiers and civilians had joined together'

Standard campaign histories (Keegan 1998; Doughty 2005): the Marne's decisive factors were von Kluck's exposed flank, Joffre's mass of manoeuvre, the BEF wedge, and Moltke's detached command — not the taxi-borne reinforcement

competing_hypotheses: The morale effect was real and is not graded here: the moonlit convoy genuinely heartened troops on the road, and the 'union sacrée' symbolism had genuine home-front value — the debunk kills the causal military claim, never the morale story
Counterfactual refinements (the 7th Division plugged a specific gap on 7–8 September) are honestly carried but do not survive the scale test as a battle-deciding factor
falsifiability: Divisional after-action records showing the taxi-borne brigades as the decisive force at the decisive point of the battle, or a battle-level analysis attributing the German withdrawal primarily to their arrival

title: Niemann's 3-2 Game at Frelinghien
claim: Lieutenant Johannes Niemann of the 133rd Saxon Infantry Regiment, opposite Scottish troops (Seaforth or Argyll & Sutherland Highlanders) at Frelinghien, described a football game during the Christmas truce: a Tommy arrived with a football, caps were laid down to mark the goals, the teams organized on the frozen ground, and 'the Fritzes beat the Tommies 3-2' — a real game with a claimed score, attested by one man.
place: Frelinghien, Western Front (opposite the British/Scottish line)
grade_reason: The most detailed single account of a truce football game — but it is ONE man's account, written up after the war and recalled in an interview in the 1960s, not a contemporary diary entry. Niemann honestly describes a real, organized-ish game on frozen mud with caps for goals and a 3-2 result. What the account does NOT support is the legend-form fixture: nothing about Niemann's game makes it an international, eleven-a-side, ninety-minute regulation match. Attested but single-source and late: CLAIMED, held below CORROBORATED.
earliest_attestation: Niemann's account in the 133rd Royal Saxon Regiment's War History; a later interview in the 1960s. Late relative to the event — the regimental history is a postwar compilation, not a 1914 diary entry.

sources.ref: Lt. Johannes Niemann (133rd Saxon Infantry Regiment), in the regiment's War History: 'Suddenly a Tommy came with a football, kicking already and making fun, and then began a football match... We marked the goals with our caps. Teams were quickly established for a match on the frozen mud, and the Fritzes beat the Tommies 3-2.'
Niemann's 1960s interview recounting the game (Smithsonian's summary: 'in the one detailed eyewitness account that survives — albeit in an interview not given until the 1960s')
Anonymous letter, The Times, 1 January 1915: a match with the 107th Saxon Infantry Regiment, same 3-2 score — parallel attestation, not independent confirmation

competing_hypotheses: Whether Niemann's game is the same event other units reported (the 107th Saxon letter to The Times, 1 Jan 1915, also claims a 3-2) or a separate one — the identical score suggests cross-contamination between accounts
The kilt anecdote (Niemann's description of the Highlanders' 'bottoms clearly visible') — carried as his account, not independently verified
falsifiability: A contemporary 1914 German or British document describing this exact game would raise it; evidence that Niemann was not at Frelinghien would kill it — neither exists

title: The Assassination at Sarajevo (28 June 1914)
claim: On the morning of 28 June 1914, in Sarajevo, Gavrilo Princip — a 19-year-old Bosnian Serb nationalist and one of seven conspirators armed by Serbian military intelligence — shot and killed Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his wife Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg, when their motorcar stopped on Franz Josef Street in front of Moritz Schiller's delicatessen.
place: Sarajevo — corner of Appel Quay and Franz Josef Street, in front of Moritz Schiller's delicatessen
grade_reason: Multiply attested contemporary event: the victims' deaths, the conspirators' trial records, eyewitness testimony, and the contemporary press all converge on the same morning.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary press, 28 June 1914; the trial of Princip and his co-conspirators (Sarajevo, October 1914; transcripts published by Vojislav Bogicevic, Sarajevski atentat, 1954)

sources.ref: Trial transcripts: Vojislav Bogicevic (ed.), Sarajevski atentat: stenogram glavne rasprave protiv Gavrila Principa i drugova, odrzane u Sarajevu 1914 (1954)
Joachim Remak, Sarajevo: The Story of a Political Murder (1959) — Princip waited outside Schiller's, where he spoke to a friend
David James Smith, One Morning in Sarajevo, June 28 1914 (2008)
Christopher Clark, The Sleepwalkers: How Europe Went to War (2012); NPR/WCMU 2014 interview on the day's events

competing_hypotheses: The extent of Serbian state involvement (the 'Black Hand' chain of command) remains a live historiographical debate — Clark's Sleepwalkers treatment vs. the maximalist Serbian-state reading
Whether the July Crisis made war inevitable after the assassination, or whether the assassination was merely the pretext the capitals were waiting for
falsifiability: Contemporary evidence that the shooting did not occur as documented (e.g., a different shooter, different date) — no such evidence exists in the record

title: The Sarajevo Motorcade Route and the Wrong Turn (28 June 1914)
claim: Franz Ferdinand's published motorcade route ran along the Appel Quay, with conspirators stationed along it; after Nedeljko Cabrinovic's grenade bounced off the Archduke's car (10-second fuse; it exploded under the following car), the plan changed — the drivers, not briefed on the change, continued on the original route, and at the corner with Franz Josef Street the chauffeur took the wrong turn, corrected on Governor Potiorek's orders, bringing the car to a halt directly in front of Schiller's delicatessen, where Princip was standing outside (having spoken with his friend Mihajlo Pusara) on the original route — the position he should have held all along.
place: Sarajevo — Appel Quay / Franz Josef Street corner
grade_reason: The route, the grenade attack, the drivers' unbriefed continuation, and Princip's position outside Schiller's are independently corroborated by trial testimony, eyewitnesses, and contemporary press; the exact words of the Potiorek–chauffeur exchange vary by account, held honestly at CORROBORATED.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary press, 28 June 1914; trial testimony (Remak 1959; trial transcripts via Trifkovic)

sources.ref: Roberta Strauss Feuerlicht (via Mike Dash, Smithsonian 2011): Schiller's delicatessen stood on the original route planned for the motorcade; the chauffeur's fatal uncertainty was caused by Oskar Potiorek shouting from the passenger seat that he should have stayed on Appel Quay
Joachim Remak (1959): the assassin waited outside Schiller's, where he spoke to a friend (Mihajlo Pusara) — cited via Dash/Trifkovic

Christopher Clark (NPR/WCMU, 2014): the motorcade route had been published; drivers carried on as before; the miscommunication took the royal couple 'right in front of Gavrilo Princip, one of the assassins who was stationed on the original path'

competing_hypotheses: The wrong turn as pure driver error (unfamiliar with the city) vs. as confusion caused by conflicting orders — accounts differ on who shouted what
Whether Princip had repositioned deliberately after the grenade failure or simply stayed at his post — the testimony supports the post, the 'dispersed disconsolate' version is later storytelling
falsifiability: Contemporary evidence that the motorcade route was secret, or that Princip was elsewhere at 10:55 — the published route and his trial statement ('in the vicinity of the Latin bridge') both contradict that

title: Shackleton's 'Men wanted for hazardous journey' advertisement — DEBUNKED
claim: Ernest Shackleton placed a famous newspaper recruitment advertisement for his Antarctic expedition reading: 'Men wanted for hazardous journey. Low wages, bitter cold, long hours of complete darkness. Safe return doubtful. Honour and recognition in event of success.' (Often said to have drawn ~5,000 applications.)
place: London, England — the claimed placement venue (the ad is about this city's newspapers)
grade_reason: Killed four times from the record itself: (1) no original has ever been found — citizen historians have searched since the early 2000s, the Antarctic Circle's $100 reward (plus Headland's case of Madeira, 2016) is unclaimed; Bob Headland (Scott Polar Research Institute): 'fairly convinced this haystack doesn't have a needle in it'; (2) the trail begins in print, not paper — Elmore 1944 and Watkins 1959, the latter dating the ad to 1900, years before the expedition; (3) the alternative date fails too — it did not run in The Times on 29 December 1913 (the paper's issues have been read and programmatically searched); (4) it made no sense for Shackleton to advertise — free press coverage gave him abundant applicants, and Frank Worsley (crew member) wrote his memoirs with no mention of an ad, recalling instead that he simply walked into the expedition's offices.
earliest_attestation: Carl Hopkins Elmore, Quit You Like Men (New York: Charles Scribner's Sons, 1944), p. 53 — a candidate earliest printed form; Julian Lewis Watkins, The 100 Greatest Advertisements 1852–1958 (1959), the vector that spread it to the advertising canon (claiming London papers, 1900 — years before the expedition it supposedly recruited)

sources.ref: South Georgia Heritage Trust, 'Men Wanted' (sght.org/timeline/men-wanted) — 'there are no facts to support this'; one of the first books to feature the ad was Watkins 1959, claiming London newspapers 1900, 'several years before Shackleton's hazardous journey'; other biographies claim The Times 29 December 1913 — 'it did not run on that day'; reward unclaimed; Frank Worsley made no mention of the ad; 'almost certainly a myth'

Smithsonian Magazine, 'Ernest Shackleton's Famous Job Ad ... Is Probably a Myth' — citizen historians searching since the early 2000s came up empty; Antarctic Circle $100 reward; Bob Headland (then-curator, Scott Polar Research Institute, Cambridge) 2004: 'This is a needle-in-a-haystack situation... I'm fairly convinced this haystack doesn't have a needle in it'; 2016: reward sweetened with a case of Madeira; still unclaimed

Discerning History, 'Shackleton's Ad – Men Wanted for Hazardous Journey' — the months covering Shackleton's preparations read and the paper programmatically searched, both empty; descendants' memories 'likely a recollection based on reading the ad rather than something they were actually told'; Worsley wrote his memoirs and did not record seeing an ad
Julian Lewis Watkins, The 100 Greatest Advertisements 1852–1958 (Dover, 1949/1959) p. 1 — the advertising-canon vector; dates the ad to 1900, impossible for the 1914 expedition
Campaign magazine, 1999 — ranked the ad 86th in its 100 best ads of the century — belief ecology: the ad industry's own canonization of a copy that likely never ran

Frank Worsley, Endurance: An Epic of Polar Adventure (1931) — the crew member's own memoir: no ad mentioned; he applied by walking into the offices — the negative-evidence anchor from inside the expedition

competing_hypotheses: The text may have originated as a genuine but unpublished draft — some defenders propose Shackleton or a colleague wrote it as copy that never ran; without any surviving draft or contemporary reference, this remains unfalsifiable speculation

The ad's persistence could reflect a genuine folk memory of a real but short-lived placement that escaped all archival survival — the counter is that the claimed venues (London newspapers, The Times) have complete archives, and programmatic searches of those exact issues came up empty
falsifiability: A single surviving newspaper clipping with masthead, date, and page — the Antarctic Circle's $100 reward (later plus a case of Madeira, 2016) has gone unclaimed for 20+ years

title: What Mata Hari's information was actually worth
claim: The intelligence Mata Hari actually transmitted — to Germany, and to France — was of negligible military value: she took German money (autumn 1915, ~20,000 francs, codename H21) and she did work for the French Deuxième Bureau, but no operation, battle, or casualty has ever been documented as a consequence of her information, and the case against her rested substantially on circumstantial and tampered evidence.
place: Madrid, Spain (German embassy station, Major Arnold Kalle) and Paris
grade_reason: Multiple independent lines converge on the negligible value of what she passed: the French could produce no definite evidence at trial, her own prosecutor later admitted doubts, Ladoux tampered with evidence against her, and the 1970s German releases document payment and codename without any military consequence.
earliest_attestation: German Foreign Ministry / III B documents (released 1970s); French military-justice dossier (1917, published 2017); MI5 surveillance files (released 2014).

sources.ref: MI5 release 2014: Zelle admitted conducting espionage for the German Secret Service, codename H21, payments of ~20,000 francs; invisible-ink vials in her hotel suite

German documents unsealed in the 1970s: autumn 1915 recruitment, Major Roepell / Walter Nicolai / Captain Hoffmann; historians: 'she may have merely accepted money from the Germans without actually carrying out any spy duties'
Wikipedia 'Mata Hari': Ladoux's evidence tampering; prosecutor André Mornet later expressed doubts about her guilt; Clunet denied cross-examination rights; conviction 'a foregone conclusion'
warhistoryonline.com: Ladoux arrested four days after her execution for double espionage (cleared, but the charge raised the frame-up question)

competing_hypotheses: That she was an effective German asset whose damage is simply undocumented: possible in principle, but the services' own released files (German 1970s releases, French 2017 dossier, MI5 2014) attach no consequence to her transmissions, and silence in the institutions' own damage files is expected evidence.

That she was primarily a French asset and the trial was a Deuxième Bureau cover-up: the Bureau did task her (she believed herself their agent, demanding a million francs); Ladoux's evidence-tampering and his own arrest for double espionage four days after her execution keep this live but unproven — the French files published in 2017 neither confirm nor fully close it.
falsifiability: A documented military consequence of her transmissions — an operation compromised, a unit's loss, an intercepted report with actionable content.

title: The Sykes-Picot Agreement, May 1916
claim: In May 1916, Britain and France secretly agreed to partition the Ottoman Arab lands into zones of direct control (blue/French, red/British) and spheres of influence (A/French, B/British), with Palestine as an international (brown) zone — the Sykes-Picot Agreement.
place: The Ottoman Arab provinces (the Levant and Mesopotamia covered by the 1916 map)
grade_reason: Multiply attested contemporary diplomatic documents — the Grey-Cambon letters, the signed map, the Russian and Italian assents — published and never denied as a document.
earliest_attestation: The letters themselves (1916); public exposure by the Bolsheviks, Moscow, 23 November 1917, reprinted in the Manchester Guardian, 26 November 1917: 'the British were embarrassed, the Arabs dismayed and the Turks delighted.'

sources.ref: Smithsonian Magazine, 'The Origins of the World War I Agreement That Carved Up the Middle East': terms set out in Grey's letter to Cambon, 16 May 1916; red/blue/brown zones; Bolshevik exposure 1917; affirmed at San Remo 1920, ratified by the League 1922
GlobalSecurity.org, 'Sykes-Picot Agreement - 1916' (negotiation background: Nicolson, Sykes, Picot; zones A/B, the Arab state or confederation formula)
Wikipedia, 'Sykes-Picot Agreement' (secondary; used for the assent trail: Russia via Sazonov-Paleologue, Italy 1917; publication dates 23/26 November 1917)

competing_hypotheses: The Lloyd George reading: an 'egregious,' 'foolish' document (he was indignant that Palestine was 'inconsiderately mutilated') — a blunder, not a master plan
The Antonius reading ('a shocking document'): imperial double-dealing against the McMahon-Hussein correspondence — perfidy, not partition craft
falsifiability: Proof the letters are forgeries or misattributed would overturn the record; none exists — the text is settled and was never denied as a document.

title: The claim that Sykes-Picot drew the modern Middle East's borders
claim: The borders of today's Middle Eastern states were drawn by the 1916 Sykes-Picot Agreement — the lines on the modern map are essentially the lines Sykes and Picot drew on their 1916 map.
place: The Ottoman Arab provinces (the Levant and Mesopotamia as partitioned in the 1916 map)
grade_reason: The 1916 lines were never implemented as drawn — Russia dropped out, France ceded Palestine and Mosul, the international Palestine zone never happened — and today's borders were drawn by the 1920-1926 settlement; the 1916 map bears no resemblance to the Middle East today.
earliest_attestation: The agreement itself: exchange of letters between Sir Edward Grey and Paul Cambon, 15-16 May 1916; publicly exposed by the Bolsheviks, Moscow, 23 November 1917 (reprinted in the Manchester Guardian, 26 November 1917).

sources.ref: The Cairo Review, 'A Century After Sykes-Picot' (centenary essay): 'many still believe the agreement set the borders of the modern Middle East. In fact, the map as drawn by Sykes and Picot bears no resemblance to the Middle East today.'

MERIP, Middle East Brief 103: 'the borders of today's Middle East were not actually drawn by colonial authorities via the Sykes-Picot Agreement... the lineup of states in the region has evolved, with some borders changed and others finally demarcated. Locals played important roles throughout.'
Nick Danforth, 'Forget Sykes-Picot. It's the Treaty of Sèvres That Explains the Modern Middle East,' Foreign Policy (cited in MERIP Brief 103)
Sara Pursley, ''Lines Drawn on an Empty Map': Iraq's Borders and the Legend of the Artificial State,' Jadaliyya, 2 June 2015 (cited in MERIP Brief 103)
James Barr, A Line in the Sand: The Anglo-French Struggle for the Middle East, 1914-1948 (W.W. Norton, 2012) — the counter-position: the pact survived to form the basis of the mandate division
Smithsonian Magazine, 'The Origins of the World War I Agreement That Carved Up the Middle East' (agreement terms: Grey-Cambon letter, 16 May 1916; zones A/B, blue/red/brown)

competing_hypotheses: Barr (2012, 'A Line in the Sand'): the pact survived the war to form the basis of the postwar mandate division — the Anglo-French partition logic and spheres persisted as the mandate system even where the literal lines did not

The symbolic reading: the agreement named the imperial method and became the region's shorthand for imposed borders, which is why the myth is so durable — ISIS's 2014 'end of Sykes-Picot' theater traded on the symbol, not the map
falsifiability: A demonstrable one-to-one correspondence between the 1916 map's boundaries and today's state borders would restore the claim; the existing comparisons (e.g., the Cairo Review's centenary overlay) show none.

title: Mata Hari: arrest, trial, and execution (1917)
claim: Margaretha Geertruida Zelle (born 7 August 1876, Leeuwarden, Netherlands), performing as the exotic dancer Mata Hari, was arrested in Paris on 13 February 1917 on suspicion of spying for Germany, tried by a French military court on 24 July 1917, convicted, and executed by firing squad at Vincennes on 15 October 1917.
place: Fort de Vincennes, Paris, France
grade_reason: Multiply attested by the French military-justice dossier, contemporary press, the firing-squad record, and the British MI5 surveillance files released in 2014.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary press and court records, 1917; the interrogation and trial records in the French military-justice dossier (published online by the French armed forces for the 2017 centenary).

sources.ref: French military-justice dossier on Mata Hari (interrogation transcripts, trial record, 1917)
MI5 release, 2014: surveillance files on Zelle (intelNews.org summary)
Wikipedia 'Mata Hari': arrest 13 February 1917 at the Hôtel Élysée Palace; trial 24 July; execution 15 October 1917

competing_hypotheses: That she was primarily a French agent caught in the wrong jurisdiction: she did work for French intelligence (recruited by the Deuxième Bureau), but this was used against her as evidence of her duplicity rather than for her.

That the entire trial was preordained regardless of evidence: her defense attorney Édouard Clunet was denied permission to cross-examine prosecution witnesses or examine his own directly, making the conviction, per many historians, a foregone conclusion.
falsifiability: Discovery that the arrest/trial/execution records are forgeries, or a contradicting civil record of her death on another date.

title: Mata Hari the 'master spy' who killed 50,000 men
claim: Mata Hari was a master German spy (agent H21) whose treason caused the deaths of at least 50,000 French soldiers — the charge on which she was convicted at her 24 July 1917 trial.
place: Paris, France (the court-martial)
grade_reason: The 50,000 figure has no evidentiary lineage — no name, no unit, no operation, no transmission was ever attached to it; it was pure prosecution rhetoric (Chatin), and no intelligence accounting exists. The master-spy reading is independently dead: the evidence against her was circumstantial and partly forged, and historians concur she transmitted no military information of consequence.
earliest_attestation: The 24 July 1917 military trial: the prosecution's charge sheet and Captain Chatin's argument; reported in Morain (1930) and the contemporary press.

sources.ref: Wikipedia 'Mata Hari': tried 24 July 1917 'accused of spying for Germany and consequently causing the deaths of at least 50,000 soldiers'; no definite evidence produced by French or British intelligence; prosecutor's evidence tampering (Ladoux); her own prosecutor André Mornet later admitted doubts
Captain Jean Chatin, trial jurist: 'collective assassination' of 'more than 50,000 men' (Morain 1930: 210), quoted in the City Research Online study of the Mata Hari trial

German documents unsealed in the 1970s: she entered German service autumn 1915 (codename H21, Major Roepell, III B chief Walter Nicolai, handler Captain Hoffmann); some historians argue she 'may have merely accepted money from the Germans without actually carrying out any spy duties'

warhistoryonline.com: trial accused her of passing information 'that had caused the deaths of 50,000 French soldiers' while 'neither French nor British Intelligence could provide concrete evidence that Hari was spying for Germany'

competing_hypotheses: That she was an ineffective German agent whose reports were worthless but who still took German money: German documents unsealed in the 1970s confirm she entered German service in autumn 1915 and was paid (20,000 francs), which is consistent with recruitment but not with master-spy effectiveness.

That she was a double agent who genuinely served both sides: her defenders and some historians argue she believed herself to be working for France; the French Deuxième Bureau did task her, and her Madrid telegram interception was real — but the content she passed was of negligible value.
falsifiability: A documented intelligence accounting tying her to specific casualties — a named unit, operation, or transmission with a casualty consequence.

title: The Mae Dix 'accident' at the National Winter Garden, 1917
claim: In 1917, on a hot night at the Minsky brothers' National Winter Garden on Houston Street, chorus performer Mae Dix walked offstage while still removing her costume — and when the crowd cheered she returned and kept removing it; the Minskys' first raid followed, and the 'accident' became the house's founding striptease legend.
place: National Winter Garden theatre, Houston Street at 2nd Avenue, New York City, USA
grade_reason: CORROBORATED on the memoir + the documented 1917 first-raid pattern + the scholarly consensus (the striptease became burlesque's dominant ingredient by the mid-1920s); held below VERIFIED because the anecdote's sole provenance is the family memoir — the interested party's own origin story.
earliest_attestation: Morton Minsky with Milt Machlin, 'Minsky's Burlesque' (Knopf, 1986) — the single interested source.

sources.ref: Morton Minsky & Milt Machlin, 'Minsky's Burlesque' (Knopf, 1986)
Wikipedia 'Minsky's Burlesque' / 'American burlesque' — the 1917 raid and the mid-1920s striptease dominance (secondary aggregators of the scholarly record)

competing_hypotheses: The incident was staged from the start by Billy Minsky (carried fairly: Morton Minsky's memoir says Billy ordered the accident repeated nightly, but the first night is framed as genuine accident — the memoir is the interested party telling on itself)
The 1917 anecdote is later industry folklore with no 1917 basis (carried fairly: no independent contemporary documentation has surfaced; the memoir is the sole provenance, published decades later)
falsifiability: The Minskys' license records showing no 1917 raid, or house payroll proving Mae Dix was not in the company that year.

title: Zimmermann's admission: 'I cannot deny it. It is true.' (March 1917)
claim: Confronted with the published Zimmermann telegram, Foreign Secretary Arthur Zimmermann publicly admitted it was genuine: at a press conference on 3 March 1917 he told an American journalist, 'I cannot deny it. It is true,' and on 29 March 1917 he admitted it before the Reichstag — ending the Hearst-press and pro-German lobby's forgery defense in a single sentence.
place: Berlin (press conference, then the Reichstag)
grade_reason: Multiply and independently attested in contemporary press on both sides of the Atlantic within days; the quote is stable across sources; the pro-German lobby's forgery defense collapsed on the record immediately after.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary press reports, March 1917: US newspapers, Reuters (Reichstag speech); the Hearst press's reversal documented

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Zimmermann Telegram' (citing press records): 3 March press conference — 'I cannot deny it. It is true'; 29 March Reichstag admission
Friends of the Intelligence Museum, 'The Zimmermann Telegram' (2017): Hale's question, the admission, the Reichstag lie about Carranza, the press reversal
CFR, 'Remembering the Zimmermann Telegram': the front-page publication, the authenticity questions, Zimmermann's 3 March answer settling them

competing_hypotheses: Zimmermann's admission as a tactical blunder (contemporary reading): he hoped Americans would see the proposal as conditional on US entry — carried fairly, though it concedes the authorship
The questioner, William Bayard Hale, was later shown to have been a paid German agent — the confession came to the most sympathetic possible audience, which makes the blunder worse, not better
falsifiability: Contemporary 1917 press records showing Zimmermann denied the telegram instead — no such record exists; the admission is quoted in multiple independent papers

title: 'The telegram alone brought America into the war' — the sole-cause myth
claim: The Zimmermann telegram, by itself, brought the United States into World War I — i.e., without the telegram the US would not have declared war in April 1917.
place: Washington, D.C. (Congress, declaration of war)
grade_reason: Four independent kills on the SOLE-cause reading. (1) CHRONOLOGY: the US had already severed diplomatic relations with Germany on 3 February 1917 over the resumed unrestricted submarine warfare — before the telegram was published (1 March). (2) THE TELEGRAM FAILED ITS OWN TEST: Wilson released it hoping to pressure Congress into arming merchant ships; antiwar senators filibustered the measure anyway (CFR) — the telegram moved the public but not the votes it was deployed for. (3) THE BRITISH TREATED IT AS A TIMED WEAPON, not a self-evident trigger: Hall held the 17 January decrypt five weeks (Foreign Office 5 February, Page 23 February) until the moment it would land hardest. (4) THE HISTORIANS' VERDICT: HISTORY.com's 'accelerated... coupled with the submarine attacks' — the shared-cause consensus; Wilson's 2 April war address made submarine warfare the case, and the March sinkings of US ships (Algonquin, Vigilancia, City of Memphis) were the immediate pressure.
earliest_attestation: The sole-cause reading's popular form: Barbara Tuchman, The Zimmermann Telegram (1958), and the schoolbook/YouTube-shorts telling downstream of it

sources.ref: CFR, 'Remembering the Zimmermann Telegram': relations severed 3 Feb over the U-boat war; the telegram 'failed to advance Wilson's immediate goal' of arming merchant ships
HISTORY.com, 'The Secret History of the Zimmermann Telegram': 'the march to war was no doubt accelerated' — 'coupled with the submarine attacks, it finally turned the U.S. government'
Tuchman, B., The Zimmermann Telegram (1958): the 'last straw' reading that built the popular sole-cause telling
Friends of the Intelligence Museum, 'The Zimmermann Telegram' (2017): Hall's five-week hold; the Mexico cover story; Zimmermann's admissions; the Carranza lie

competing_hypotheses: The telegram as the decisive last straw (Tuchman's 1958 reading): it converted a divided public and gave Wilson the 'overt act' — graded CORROBORATED as an accelerator, never as a sole cause
The telegram as irrelevant (minority): the U-boat war and the March sinkings were sufficient — carried fairly, though it understates the telegram's documented effect on Congress and the press
falsifiability: Contemporary 1917 evidence that Wilson and Congress treated the telegram, not the U-boat war, as the casus belli — e.g., a war address citing the telegram as the cause (the 2 April address centered submarine warfare)

title: The Zimmermann telegram, 16 January – 1 March 1917
claim: On 16 January 1917 German Foreign Secretary Arthur Zimmermann sent a coded telegram to Heinrich von Eckardt, the German minister in Mexico City, proposing a German-Mexican military alliance in the event the United States entered WWI: 'make war together, make peace together, generous financial support and understanding on our part that Mexico is to reconquer the lost territory in Texas, New Mexico and Arizona.' It also announced the 1 February resumption of unrestricted submarine warfare and instructed Eckardt to invite Japan to adhere via the Mexican president. The British Admiralty's Room 40 intercepted and decoded it on 17 January 1917 (Nigel de Grey, with William Montgomery; German diplomatic code 13040). After a cover story that it had been 'stolen in deciphered form in Mexico,' the text was published 1 March 1917.
place: Berlin (origin) → intercepted at Room 40, London (51.50, -0.13) → delivered to Eckardt, Mexico City (19.43, -99.13)
grade_reason: Multiple independent contemporary lines: the Room 40 decode (Hall's own logs), the State Department cable relay records, the photographed original in the UK National Archives, the published text of 1 March 1917, and Zimmermann's own public admission of authorship (3 March 1917).
earliest_attestation: The intercepted telegram itself, 16-17 January 1917; photographed German original held at The National Archives (UK); Room 40 decode sheets

sources.ref: The National Archives (UK): photographed German original of the Zimmermann telegram
HISTORY.com, 'The Secret History of the Zimmermann Telegram': 16 Jan handoff to Gerard; decoded 17 Jan by Nigel de Grey; Hall's cover story; published 1 March
Council on Foreign Relations, 'Remembering the Zimmermann Telegram and the U.S. Entry Into World War I': State Department cable routing; Wilson's release to newspapers; armed-ships filibuster
Tuchman, B., The Zimmermann Telegram (1958, Pulitzer 1959): the standard documentary account of the intercept, decode, and publication

competing_hypotheses: The popular telling treats the telegram as the sole trigger of US entry; the documentary timeline (severed relations 3 February over the U-boat war, published text 1 March) carries the shared-cause reading
Some accounts date de Grey's full decode to later in January; the 17 January partial decode is the documented watershed
falsifiability: A proven forgery finding on the National Archives original, Room 40 logs showing no such decode, or State Department cable records showing no such transmission

title: Sundback's Separable Fastener (1917) — the modern zipper
claim: Gideon Sundback's 1917 'Separable Fastener' (US patent 1,219,881) — the interlocking-tooth slide fastener with slider — is the modern zipper: the first cheap, reliable, mass-producible design.
place: Meadville, Pennsylvania (Hookless Fastener Company; Talon from 1937)
grade_reason: The patent is a public document; the 1915 patent model sits in the Smithsonian; the production and sales records of the Hookless Fastener Company are multiply attested.
earliest_attestation: US Patent 1,219,881 (1917), with the 1915 patent model held by the Smithsonian National Museum of American History

sources.ref: US Patent 1,219,881, 'Separable Fastener' (Gideon Sundback, 1917)
Smithsonian National Museum of American History — Sundback's Modern Slide Zipper Patent Model, 1915
Pennsylvania Center for the Book / Penn State — 'Zip It Up: Talon Zippers' (2009), citing Robert Friedel, Zipper: An Exploration in Novelty (1994)

competing_hypotheses: Priority for the first working zipper goes to Whitcomb Judson's 1893 clasp locker (the idea, not the teeth — judged fair: Judson pioneered the sliding fastener concept)
The invention is a continuous line rather than one patent: Howe 1851, Judson 1893, Sundback's 1913 Hookless and 1917 Separable — the 1917 patent as the culmination, not the genesis
falsifiability: A dated prior-art patent or commercial product with interlocking teeth and a slider predating Sundback's 1913-1917 work

title: The 'female Cher Ami' myth (DEBUNKED by 2021 DNA)
claim: Cher Ami, the famous WWI homing pigeon, was female (a hen).
place: Smithsonian National Museum of American History, Washington D.C. (where the bird is displayed)
grade_reason: DEBUNKED by DNA. The original U.S. Army Signal Corps report described Cher Ami as a black check hen, and the 'female hero pigeon' telling persisted for a century — amplified by Rose Wilder Lane's 1919 Ladies' Home Journal piece describing a male French pigeon (the stories contradicted each other from the start) and by the American Legion Weekly's 1919 description of 'her' exhaustion. The Smithsonian had long classified the bird as male. In 2021, DNA testing by the Smithsonian and the National Zoo confirmed Cher Ami was a cock bird, settling the century-long controversy. The bird's heroism is unaffected — the grade is on the sex claim only.
earliest_attestation: U.S. Army Signal Corps report, 1918 (described the bird as a 'black check hen')

sources.ref: Smithsonian Magazine (NMAH, July 2021): the Signal Corps' original 'black check hen' report; the media blurring of the bird's sex; the August 1919 Ladies' Home Journal (male French pigeon) vs American Legion Weekly ('her' exhaustion) contradiction; the 2021 DNA confirmation of a cock bird.

FunFactz: 'Wartime Signal Corps records described Cher Ami as a hen, but the Smithsonian had always classified him as male. In 2021, DNA testing conducted by the Smithsonian and its National Zoo confirmed Cher Ami was a cock bird, resolving a century-long controversy.'

falsifiability: DNA evidence of the bird's sex

title: Cher Ami's flight for the Lost Battalion (4 October 1918)
claim: On 4 October 1918, the homing pigeon Cher Ami carried Major Whittlesey's message from the surrounded Lost Battalion 25 miles to division headquarters in 25 minutes, despite being shot through the breast, blinded in one eye, and nearly losing the leg carrying the message — and the message halted the friendly-artillery barrage, contributing to the relief of the battalion's survivors.
place: Argonne Forest, France (Charlevaux ravine to division HQ)
grade_reason: The flight is VERIFIED across Signal Corps records, contemporary press, and the Smithsonian's holdings. On 4 October 1918, Major Charles W. Whittlesey's ~554 men of the 77th Division were surrounded in the Argonne; two pigeons had already been shot down; Cher Ami — the last bird — carried the message 'We are along the road parallel 276.4. Our own artillery is dropping a barrage directly on us. For heaven's sake stop it.' The bird flew ~25 miles in ~25 minutes despite a breast wound, a blinded eye, and a nearly-severed leg with the capsule dangling from the tendons. The message reached headquarters and the barrage was lifted; 194 men walked out on 7–8 October. Cher Ami received the French Croix de Guerre with Palm and has been displayed at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History since 1921. The bird's sex is fenced separately (see evt-cher-ami-female-myth-001) — it does not affect this grade.
earliest_attestation: U.S. Army Signal Corps records, October 1918; contemporary press from April 1919

sources.ref: Smithsonian Magazine (NMAH, July 2021): the 4 October 1918 flight — Whittlesey's message text, the severed leg with the capsule on the tendons, the relief on the night of October 7; the 1919 media sensation and the sex controversy.
Library of Congress research guide (Pigeons in War): the 4 October 1918 date, the 194 survivors, the Croix de Guerre with Palm; the 1870 Paris siege context (800 pigeons, 40,000 messages).
FunFactz: 25 miles in 25 minutes; the breast wound, blinded eye, and severed leg; the capsule on the tendons; the wooden leg; the 1931 Racing Pigeon Hall of Fame induction.

falsifiability: Signal Corps records contradicting the flight

title: The Smithsonian's claim that Langley's 1903 Aerodrome was the first flight-capable man-carrying aircraft
claim: That the Smithsonian Institution was correct (1918-1942) to display Langley's Great Aerodrome as the first man-carrying aeroplane capable of free flight — i.e., that Langley's 1903 machine, as Langley built and launched it, had been demonstrated capable of sustained powered flight before the Wrights' December 1903 flights.
place: Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C. (site of the 1918-1942 display and the 1942 retraction)
grade_reason: The 'evidence' was a 1914 flight of a substantially modified machine (new floats, different engine, rerigged bracing, altered wings/controls) flown by a litigant with motive; the Smithsonian itself published the retraction in 1942. A modified replica is not the 1903 aircraft.
earliest_attestation: Albert F. Zahm's 1913 Smithsonian report and the Institution's 1918 display label; Orville Wright's documented refutation (his papers catalog the Curtiss modifications); Charles G. Abbott's October 26, 1942 Smithsonian statement

sources.ref: Air & Space Forces Magazine, 'The Aerodrome Fraud' — Hallion's account: Walcott lent Curtiss the Aerodrome; Curtiss 'essentially used this as the base for a whole new machine, adding many components, including pontoons for takeoff... rerigged the bracing and ultimately put in a new engine'; the result 'bore only a vague visual similarity to the 1903 machine'; the Smithsonian displayed it under Zahm's claim that Langley 'developed and built the first man-carrying aeroplane capable of free flight'

Orville Wright's papers documenting Curtiss's modifications in exhaustive detail; his 1928 decision to send the original 1903 Flyer to the London Science Museum: 'I have sent our original 1903 machine to the British National Museum because of the hostile and unfair attitude shown towards us by the officials of the Smithsonian Institution'

Scientific American, July 1925 'Our Point of View': the editors on Orville's decision — the Smithsonian had Langley 'retrofitted to prove it could have flown — if only it hadn't failed — and used that to award him the credit'; the display 'misleading'; Langley 'definitely did not beat the Wright brothers'

Air & Space Forces Magazine, 'Orville Wright Plays Hardball' — the 20-year London exile; Abbott's 1942 report 'acknowledging the injury done the Wrights and repudiating any claims to the Great Aerodrome's airworthiness'; the Flyer came home in 1948 — nine months after Orville's death in January 1948

Fred C. Kelly, 'The Wright Brothers: A Biography Authorized by Orville Wright' (1943) — carries the full text of Abbott's October 26, 1942 apology/statement, giving the retraction its widest distribution

competing_hypotheses: The Aéro-Club de France / Santos-Dumont priority position: Langley's 1896 model flights were genuine unmanned successes, so the Aerodrome's failure was an airframe-launch problem rather than an aerodynamic one — carried honestly, but models are not man-carrying aircraft

The 'capable of flight' defense: Albert F. Zahm's 1913 Smithsonian report argued Langley built the first machine *capable* of flight — 'not the same as the first that actually flew,' as one contemporary account put it; the record notes this is a distinction without an airworthiness test
falsifiability: A pre-December-17-1903 test showing the unmodified 1903 Aerodrome in sustained powered free flight — none exists; Langley's two 1903 attempts (October 7, December 8) both ended in the Potomac

title: The 19th Amendment ratified, August 1920
claim: The Nineteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution — 'The right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of sex' — passed the Senate on 4 June 1919 (56–25), was ratified by Tennessee as the 36th state on 18 August 1920 (the House carried it by a single vote, 49–47, after 24-year-old Rep. Harry T. Burn switched at his mother Febb Burn's urging), and was certified in effect on 26 August 1920 by Secretary of State Bainbridge Colby.
place: Nashville, Tennessee (state capitol; final ratifying vote)
grade_reason: Multiple independent contemporary sources converge: Congress's own record, the state journal, and the federal certification. The Febb Burn letter story is the best-documented explanation of Burn's switch and is multiply attested in Tennessee sources.
earliest_attestation: Congressional Record, 66th Congress (1919); Journal of the Tennessee House of Representatives, 1920; Colby proclamation 26 Aug 1920

sources.ref: National Archives: the 19th Amendment (text) and the Colby certification of 26 August 1920
Congressional Record, 66th Congress — Senate vote 4 June 1919
Journal of the Tennessee House of Representatives, 1920 (pp. 91–92, the 18 August ratification vote)
Tennessee State Museum: 'The War of the Roses in Tennessee' (Senate 13 Aug 1920 vote 25–4; House proceedings)

competing_hypotheses: The Tennessee vote has minor variant tallies in popular accounts (50–49 vs 49–47 on different motions); the single-vote margin is uncontested in all versions

The 'de jure victory vs de facto exclusion' framing (historians of the 1920 centennial: the amendment as landmark AND as unfinished): the universality question is graded in a separate record, evt-19th-amendment-universal-001
falsifiability: A 36th-state ratification from a different state or a different date would break the record — none exists

title: The first artificial transmutation — Rutherford 1919
claim: In 1919 Ernest Rutherford achieved the first artificial transmutation of one element into another: bombarding nitrogen-14 with alpha particles produced oxygen-17 and a proton (alpha + 14N -> 17O + p) — the experiment that actually did what the alchemists had promised for sixteen centuries.
place: University of Manchester, England — the 1917-19 alpha-bombardment experiments
grade_reason: The 1919 experiment is multiply documented — the papers, the scintillation data, the Manchester laboratory record — and Blackett's 1924-25 cloud-chamber series furnished conclusive photographic proof of the nitrogen-to-oxygen reaction. The gold-making successors (1941, 1980) independently confirm the principle.
earliest_attestation: Rutherford's 1919 Philosophical Magazine papers reporting proton emission under alpha bombardment of nitrogen; conventional credit fixed to 1919 with Blackett's 1924-25 cloud-chamber photographs (Proc. R. Soc.) as the conclusive demonstration.

sources.ref: Rutherford, 'Collision of alpha Particles with Light Atoms' series, Philosophical Magazine (1919) — proton emission observed under alpha bombardment of nitrogen
Blackett, cloud-chamber photographs 1924-25 (Proc. R. Soc. 1925) — ~400,000 tracks; two-forked tracks confirming nitrogen captures the alpha particle, ejects a proton, and leaves oxygen

Krivit, 'Who Started the Ernest Rutherford Transmutation Myth' (2019) — documents that Rutherford's 1919 papers did not themselves identify the residual atom; the Nobel Prize biography page silently dropped its 'first to deliberately transmute one element into another' phrasing without crediting Blackett
Sherr, Bainbridge & Anderson, Physical Review 60:147 (1941) — mercury + neutrons -> radioactive gold; the first actual gold-making
Aleklett, Morrissey, Loveland, McGaughey & Seaborg, Phys. Rev. Lett. 44:1488 (1980) — bismuth bombarded with heavy ions -> a few thousand gold atoms; Seaborg senior author

Scientific American, 'Fact or Fiction?: Lead Can Be Turned into Gold' — Loveland: ~$5,000/hr Bevalac beam time, ~a day used; Seaborg: 'more than one quadrillion dollars per ounce' vs ~$560/oz gold in 1980
Discover Magazine, 'Turning Lead Into Gold' — McMillan 1937 deuteron-beam artificial gold isotopes (first cyclotron-made gold); decades of accelerator gold before 1980

competing_hypotheses: The Krivit correction: Rutherford's 1919 papers established proton emission but did NOT identify the residual atom — the scintillator could not do it; the transmutation proof properly belongs to Blackett's 1924-25 cloud-chamber photographs. The Nobel Prize site's silent retraction is the institutional tell. The 1919 EVENT is verified either way; only the credit-line is contested
Rutherford's satellite model of the nucleus misdescribed the mechanism even where the event was right — the reaction happened, the theory around it was wrong
falsifiability: The 1919 scintillation data and Blackett's ~400,000 cloud-chamber tracks are the evidence; their retraction or exposure as artifacts would unmake the record. Nothing of the sort is on the horizon.

title: The tribunal dockets as measured denominator
claim: When a regime loses a war intact and its archives are seized whole, the denominator is measured, not guessed. The Nuremberg IMT published 42 volumes of transcript with prosecution document books built from the regime's own captured files; the Tokyo IMTFE left ~48,000 pages of transcript; the victor's archivists catalogued what the defeated had filed while they expected to win. Against that measured baseline, systematic silence reads as VIII.f-pattern: what a regime documented when it thought it would never answer for it is the expectation, and the gaps are the evidence. The Constantinople courts-martial of 1919–20 are the counter-exhibit: the empire that tried the Armenian massacres dissolved, its archives scattered across three continents, and the baseline there stays a guess — VIII.d retains jurisdiction. The tribunal dockets are the VIII.g rule's regime-baseline measured at full strength.
place: Nuremberg, Palace of Justice (regime-baseline exhibit); Constantinople (scattered-baseline exhibit)
grade_reason: Method demonstration record: the transcripts are published, multiply held, and built from captured archives — the denominator is auditable, not asserted.
earliest_attestation: The Constantinople courts-martial proceedings 1919–1920 (published proceedings, incomplete survival); the Nuremberg IMT transcript 1945–1946 (42 vols., published contemporaneously)

sources.ref: Nuremberg IMT transcript, 42 vols. (1945–1946) + prosecution document books built from captured German archives
Tokyo IMTFE transcript (~48,000 pages, 1946–1948)
Constantinople courts-martial 1919–1920 (Armenian massacres tried in the empire's own courts; archives scattered with the empire's dissolution)

competing_hypotheses: The 'victor's justice' reading: tribunals are political theater and the archives were cherry-picked by the prosecutors — the baseline is the prosecution's, not the regime's
The destroyed-archives reading: what was burned or hidden before capture is unknown, so the measured denominator is partial — the denominator is never whole
The procedure-not-truth reading: transcripts record what was said in court, not what happened — the docket is a performance archive, and the performance has its own baseline
falsifiability: A demonstrated case where a tribunal's seized-archive baseline was substantially fabricated — cherry-picking at scale proven against the surviving originals — would demote this exhibit from measurement back to guess.

title: Versailles Article 231 — the clause itself
claim: Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles (signed 28 June 1919; Part VIII, Section I, 'Reparation — General Provisions') is the opening clause of the treaty's reparations section. Its text: 'The Allied and Associated Governments affirm and Germany accepts the responsibility of Germany and her allies for causing all the loss and damage to which the Allied and Associated Governments and their nationals have been subjected as a consequence of the war imposed upon them by the aggression of Germany and her allies.' The clause contains no word 'guilt'; it names 'Germany and her allies' (not Germany alone); and it sits immediately above Article 232, which recognizes that Germany's resources are inadequate for complete reparation — i.e. Article 231 establishes legal liability while Article 232 limits the financial obligation.
place: Palace of Versailles, Versailles, France
grade_reason: The signed, published treaty text is a public primary document; the clause's wording, position (Part VIII Section I), and companion Article 232 are all on the page.
earliest_attestation: The treaty text itself, 28 June 1919 (public document; League of Nations Treaty Series vol. 225).

sources.ref: Treaty of Versailles, Part VIII, Section I, Articles 231–232 (Great War Primary Documents Archive transcription)
League of Nations Treaty Series, vol. 225 (treaty deposit)

competing_hypotheses: The drafters secretly intended a moral condemnation: the clause's 'aggression' language reads as blame — but the drafting history (the American authors' memoranda) shows the intent was explicitly to create a legal basis for reparations while constraining them, not to extract a confession

The clause is meaningless because Germany would have paid regardless — a legal-realist reading; the team's position is that the clause's function was to make civilian-damage reparations lawful under the pre-armistice understanding (the Lansing note of 5 November 1918), which was its actual legal work
falsifiability: A discovered earlier or official text of the treaty omitting or altering the clause's wording, or treaty drafts showing the final wording was never adopted — the authenticated published text is the record

title: The Treaty of Versailles (1919)
claim: A peace treaty between Germany and the Allied and Associated Powers, signed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles on 28 June 1919 and entering into force on 10 January 1920, imposing territorial, military, economic, and reparations terms.
place: Hall of Mirrors, Palace of Versailles
grade_reason: Multiple independent primary and contemporary sources converge: the signed originals, Allied and German government records, and the treaty's registration in the League of Nations Treaty Series.
earliest_attestation: The signed treaty text itself, 28 June 1919 (440 articles); contemporary Allied and German records.

sources.ref: Treaty of Versailles, signed text (28 June 1919), Hall of Mirrors
Margaret MacMillan, Paris 1919: Six Months That Changed the World (2001/2002)
League of Nations Treaty Series, registration of the treaty

competing_hypotheses: The treaty's severity and causal role in later events are historiographical debates — named here as interpretation, not as rival event records
No serious dispute over the signing as an event
falsifiability: The signed originals and the League of Nations registration would have to be forgeries — an impossibility given the multi-government documentary trail.

title: The 'war guilt clause' reading of Article 231 (myth)
claim: Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles assigned sole moral blame ('war guilt') to Germany alone for World War I.
place: Hall of Mirrors, Palace of Versailles
grade_reason: Two independent kills: (1) the text itself — the word 'guilt' never appears, and the article names 'Germany and her allies' (plural) as a legal hook for reparations, with Article 232 capping payment to civilian damage; (2) the identical clause in the Austrian and Hungarian treaties drew no war-guilt reading at all — the 'war guilt clause' label is a Weimar-era propaganda coinage, documented by Marks (1978).
earliest_attestation: Treaty of Versailles, Article 231 (28 June 1919) — foil record evt-versailles-article-231-001; the 'war guilt' reading from Weimar-era German publications, early 1920s

sources.ref: Treaty of Versailles, Article 231 (signed text): 'The Allied and Associated Governments affirm and Germany accepts the responsibility of Germany and her allies for causing all the loss and damage to which the Allied and Associated Governments and their nationals have been subjected as a consequence of the war imposed upon them by the aggression of Germany and her allies.' — the word 'guilt' does not appear
Treaty of Versailles, Article 232: payment limited to civilian damage and Germany's capacity to pay

Sally Marks, 'The Myths of Reparations', Central European History Vol. 11, No. 3 (Sept 1978): Article 231 was designed to lay a legal basis for reparations; the same clause mutatis mutandis appeared in the treaties with Austria and Hungary, neither of which read it as a war-guilt declaration

ISS Forum Article Review No. 429 on Marks: the 'war guilt clause' myth 'propagated in the early 1920s by Weimar officials and opinion makers... continues to find its way into histories of the peace settlement'
René Albrecht-Carrié (May 1940): Article 231 'gave rise to an unfortunate controversy, unfortunate because it served to raise a false issue'
Wolfgang Mommsen: Austria and Hungary 'understandably paid no attention to this aspect of the draft treaty'

competing_hypotheses: E.H. Carr (1939): even as a legal device the clause was a political blunder — 'in the passion of the moment' the Allies 'failed to realize that this extorted admission of guilt could prove nothing, and must excite bitter resentment in German minds' (the clause's wisdom is a separate question from its wording)

The actual responsibility for the war's outbreak is a separate historiographical debate (Fischer vs Joll and successors) — this record grades only the reading of Article 231, never the war-guilt question itself
falsifiability: A signed 1919 instrument in which Article 231 contains the word 'guilt' or assigns blame to Germany alone, or a contemporary (1919) Allied or German legal document reading it that way.

title: The 'war guilt clause' reading of Versailles Article 231
claim: Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles — commonly called the 'war guilt clause' — formally required Germany to confess sole moral guilt for starting World War I.
place: Quai d'Orsay, Paris, France (Paris Peace Conference drafting)
grade_reason: The clause contains no word 'guilt', names 'Germany and her allies' rather than Germany alone, sits as the legal preamble of the reparations section above the limiting Article 232, was drafted by the moderate Americans (Dulles/Davis) precisely to constrain — not maximize — liability, and the historical consensus (Marks 1978; the commission's own record) is that guilt was never attached to the article; the 'confession' reading is the Weimar propaganda industry's product, not the text's.
earliest_attestation: The German delegation's May–June 1919 protest notes and the German 'war guilt' press campaign of 1919 onward (the reading is born in protest, not in the clause).

sources.ref: Treaty of Versailles, Article 231 text (contains no 'guilt'; 'Germany and her allies')
Sally Marks, 'The Myths of Reparations,' Central European History vol. 11 no. 3 (1978): 'Article 231, which was designed to lay a legal basis for reparations, in fact makes no mention of war guilt.'
John Foster Dulles and Norman Davis authorship of the clause as a liability-limiting legal instrument (Dulles later regretted the wording as aggravating German opinion)
Treaty of Saint-Germain and Treaty of Trianon: identical responsibility clauses accepted by Austria and Hungary without a 'war guilt' controversy — the control sample

competing_hypotheses: The Fischer thesis (1961): the German government bore primary responsibility for the July crisis — a historiographical claim about war origins, separate from the treaty's legal clause; the DEBUNKED grade here covers only the reading of Article 231, never the war-guilt debate as history

The intentionalist reading: Germany's allies accepted parallel clauses without protest — if Article 231 were a sole-confession demand, Austria and Hungary would have objected too; they didn't, which is evidence for the liability reading

The minimalist reading: the clause was window dressing and Germany would have owed reparations anyway — a legal-realist position; the record keeps the clause's intended function as the mainstream position without adjudicating its causal power
falsifiability: A drafting-history document from the Reparation Commission showing Dulles, Davis, or their principals intended a moral confession of sole war guilt rather than a legal basis for reparations — the American authors' memoranda show the opposite intent, so the grade stands unless such a document surfaces

title: The 'all women got the vote in 1920' reading
claim: The 19th Amendment gave all American women the right to vote in 1920 — the universal version of the suffrage victory story.
place: United States (national scope)
grade_reason: The universality reading dies on four documented fronts: the amendment's own text (a negative prohibition, not an affirmative grant — the 15th-Amendment pattern); Native American women were not even citizens until the 1924 Indian Citizenship Act, and states barred them for decades more; Chinese Americans could not naturalize until the Magnuson Act of 1943; Black women in the South faced poll taxes, literacy tests, white primaries, and violence until the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
earliest_attestation: The universal shorthand is a popular/educational framing, not a documentary source — it is what the record grades

sources.ref: National Geographic, '100 years of suffrage' (2020): 'Native Americans — men and women — weren't even citizens until 1924; Chinese Americans had to wait until 1943. The real watershed moment for many minority women would be Congress's passage of the Voting Rights Act of 1965.'

Martha S. Jones (quoted in National Geographic): the same Jim Crow machinery keeping Black men from the polls would keep Black women from them; 'There's good evidence that the promoters of the 19th Amendment were counting on that assumption.'

Harvard Radcliffe Institute, 'The Long 19th Amendment' (unit 5): after 1920, Black women in the South blocked by white primaries, 'literacy tests,' and violence; Native women ineligible until the 1924 Indian Citizenship Act; poll taxes in thirteen states; unnaturalized immigrant women barred entirely

Democracy Docket, 'The Complicated Legacy of the 19th Amendment': the amendment 'did nothing to protect women of color from disenfranchising laws that were legal at the time'; Native Americans not citizens until 1924; state-level bans persisted (Arizona/New Mexico until 1948 court rulings, Utah until 1957)
The 19th Amendment text itself (National Archives): a negative prohibition — 'shall not be denied or abridged... on account of sex' — creating no affirmative grant and removing no other barrier

competing_hypotheses: The 'partial victory' framing: the amendment as a genuine landmark — roughly 26 million women became eligible, over 8 million voted on 2 Nov 1920 — AND as unfinished. The record agrees with the landmark half and grades the universal half.
