claim: The Jazz Singer (1927) was the first motion picture with synchronized sound - that no film before October 1927 carried synchronized sound of any kind.
place: Warner's Theater, Times Square, New York City (the premiere that owns the myth)
grade_reason: Killed three ways by the surviving record: (1) Don Juan premiered 14 months earlier (6 August 1926) as the first feature-length film with a synchronized Vitaphone musical score and sound effects - it was staged and shot as a silent film, but its soundtrack was synchronized sound throughout; (2) Lee de Forest's Phonofilms were commercial sound-on-film shorts from 1923, with 20 Phonofilm outfits on theatrical roadshows by 1924 (Case/Sponable system); (3) the Dickson Experimental Sound Film (1894/95) is the first known film with live-recorded sound, in the National Film Registry since 2003. The grade kills ONLY the flat 'first' - never The Jazz Singer's genuine first (first feature with synchronized dialogue sequences - VERIFIED in evt-jazz-singer-1927-001), never its industry impact, never the talkie era's conventional start.
earliest_attestation: The 'first sound film' telling is retrospective popular history; the 1927 premiere's own publicity never claimed primacy in sound - it claimed a dialogue breakthrough.

sources.ref: Wikipedia - 'Don Juan (1926 film)' (6 August 1926 premiere; first feature-length film with synchronized Vitaphone score and sound effects, no spoken dialogue)

MoMA - 'Audience breathless as Vitaphone and talkies make debuts' (archival feature; the 6 August 1926 Warner's Theatre premiere: first synchronized score in history, Hays shorts, New York Philharmonic)
Gizmodo - 'The First Feature-Length Vitaphone-Synchronized Film Delighted Audiences 84 Years Ago' (sound-on-disc explained; Vitaphone the last and most successful sound-on-disc process)
cinemontage.org - 'When Movies Learned to Talk' (Phonofilm: Case/Sponable Aeo Light; 20 outfits on roadshows by 1924; Lauste 1910 sound-on-film)
Wikipedia - 'The Dickson Experimental Sound Film' (1894/95; first known film with live-recorded sound; Kinetophone; LOC National Film Registry 2003; never exhibited in original format)

competing_hypotheses: The conventional-marker defense: 'first talkie' is shorthand for 'the film that made sound commercially unstoppable' - true of The Jazz Singer's industry impact (1928 studio conversions, Western Electric's order book), but it does not make the chronology true

The 'real talkie' scope defense: 'talkie' means synchronized spoken dialogue in a feature, and The Jazz Singer is the first of those - this defense survives the grade and is carried in the foil record evt-jazz-singer-1927-001
falsifiability: A complete catalog proving no synchronized-sound film or phonograph-record film existed before October 1927 - which the surviving Phonofilms, Don Juan discs, and the Dickson cylinder all contradict.

title: The Jazz Singer premieres — the talkie era's conventional start
claim: The Jazz Singer premiered on 6 October 1927 at Warner's Theater, New York City, as the first feature-length film with sequences of synchronized spoken dialogue (Vitaphone sound-on-disc) — the conventional marker of the talkie era's beginning.
place: Warner's Theater, Times Square, New York City (approximate venue pin)
grade_reason: Multiply attested: the AFI catalog, the Library of Congress (National Film Registry essay), the National Museum of American History, and contemporary 1927 trade/newspaper coverage all fix the 6 October 1927 New York premiere, the Vitaphone sound-on-disc system, and the first-feature synchronized-dialogue status (distinguished from Don Juan's 1926 non-dialogue synchronization). The irony fenced into the timeline: the 'killer' of vaudeville's overnight myth starred Al Jolson — vaudeville's own headliner — and grew out of the vaudeville tradition itself.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary: Warner Bros. trade press and New York newspaper coverage, October 1927; the film print itself (surviving, National Film Registry).

sources.ref: American Film Institute catalog — The Jazz Singer (1927), New York premiere 6 October 1927
Library of Congress — The Jazz Singer described as the first feature film to include sequences of synchronized spoken dialogue (National Film Registry)
National Museum of American History — Jolson's 'Wait a minute...' premiere account (audience reaction noted, not treated as box-office data)
Men's Journal (9 Oct 2026, 99th-anniversary piece) — AFI premiere date, Vitaphone system detail
EBSCO — The Jazz Singer Premieres as the First Talkie (research starter; premiere reception and 1928 record run)

competing_hypotheses: 'First talkie' in the strict sense is defended by Don Juan (1926, synchronized music/effects, no dialogue) and earlier sound shorts — the record distinguishes 'first synchronized dialogue feature' from 'first synchronized sound of any kind'

The film was not an immediate unanimous sensation: EBSCO's record notes lukewarm critical reception at premiere, with attendance building through Warner Bros.' national press campaign into 1928 — the legend of the gasping crowd is later compression
falsifiability: Documented evidence that a feature-length film with sequences of synchronized spoken dialogue premiered publicly before 6 October 1927, or that The Jazz Singer's premiere post-dated that day.

title: The 'talkies killed vaudeville overnight' myth
claim: The arrival of the talkies (synchronized-sound film, from The Jazz Singer's October 1927 premiere) killed American vaudeville overnight — that live vaudeville effectively ended in 1927–1928.
place: Palace Theatre, New York City (venue of the five-year evidence gap)
grade_reason: Killed three ways. (1) THE CLOCK: The Jazz Singer premiered October 1927; vaudeville's flagship house, the Palace, played straight vaudeville until July 1932 and mixed bills until 12 November 1932 — five years of receipts the 'overnight' telling cannot account for, then flipped BACK to vaudeville-before-film in January 1933. (2) THE CORPORATE RECORD: on 23 October 1928 RCA merged Keith-Albee-Orpheum (700+ theatres, 15,000 acts booked) with Film Booking Offices to form RKO — vaudeville's owners chose film for Photophone sound-on-film market-making; the industry moved on corporate strategy, not a technological thunderbolt. (3) THE MULTIPLE CAUSES: Britannica gives three causes (Great Depression, radio's growth, motion pictures); the American Vaudeville Museum traces the fade from WWI through phonographs and silent film, free network radio and cheap talkies only after the 1929 collapse — and small-time vaudeville lingered into the early 1950s. Scope fenced via note_on_grade_scope: kills the overnight monocause ONLY — never The Jazz Singer's genuine impact, never RKO's film pivot, never the real decline, never the Palace's eventual conversion. The 188th DEBUNKED family on this timeline.
earliest_attestation: No documented single origin found for the 'overnight' telling; it circulates as popular shorthand (schoolbook framing, podcast/retrospective narration). The scholarly record has always told it slower: Britannica's three-cause account; the American Vaudeville Museum's 'began fading during WWI... by 1932 big-time dead except a handful... small time lingered into the early 1950s'.

sources.ref: Britannica — Vaudeville: 'Vaudeville declined due to the Great Depression, the growth of radio, and the advent of motion pictures' (three-cause account)
Wikipedia — Palace Theatre (New York City): 1932 transition detail
Wikipedia — RKO Pictures / Keith-Albee-Orpheum: RCA announced FBO+KAO merger 23 October 1928; Sarnoff engineered it for RCA Photophone market-making; KAO's 700+ theatres and 15,000 booked acts

American Vaudeville Museum / Frank Cullen (sites.arizona.edu) — the slow decline: crested 1910s, fading WWI through phonographs/silent film 1920s, free network radio + cheap talkies after the 1929 collapse; small-time vaudeville lingered into the early 1950s
Wikipedia — Vaudeville: 'There was no abrupt end to vaudeville... the form was clearly sagging by the late 1920s'; Palace's exclusive-cinema shift (Nov 1932) as the 'death knell'

competing_hypotheses: The monocausal reading's defensible remnant: talkies were one real cause among several (Britannica: Depression + radio + motion pictures) — the documented reality is multi-causal, not overnight
The economic-structural reading: the vaudeville chains themselves chose film (the October 1928 RKO merger converted KAO's 700+ houses to film-first) — the industry moved, not just the audience

The slow-decline reading: big-time vaudeville was gone by 1932 except a handful of venues, small-time lingered into the early 1950s (Frank Cullen, American Vaudeville Museum) — this is the record, and it kills the 'overnight' version without denying talkies' role
falsifiability: Documented evidence that no substantial live vaudeville performance occurred in the United States after 1928 — one ledger line from the Palace Theatre alone would falsify this; the record has years of them.

title: US Business Reply Mail introduced in 1928
claim: The U.S. Post Office Department introduced Business Reply Mail (together with bulk mail) in 1928: a permit system under which a mailer distributes reply cards, envelopes, self-mailers, cartons, or labels pre-printed with the 'BUSINESS REPLY MAIL' legend, a permit imprint, and a unique ZIP+4; the customer returns them with no postage affixed, and the permit holder pays postage plus a per-piece fee only on the pieces actually returned. The 1928 introduction is attested in the Winton M. Blount Postal History Symposium presentation by Diane DeBlois and Robert Dalton Harris (Smithsonian National Postal Museum, 8 December 2022): 'Business Reply & Bulk Mail introduced 1928.'
place: Washington, D.C. — U.S. Post Office Department
grade_reason: The 1928 introduction is attested in a Smithsonian National Postal Museum-affiliated postal-history symposium paper; the modern mechanics (postage + per-piece fee on returned pieces only) are VERIFIED-level in the USPS Domestic Mail Manual itself; held at CORROBORATED because the 1928 departmental origin document was not inspected this pass.
earliest_attestation: DeBlois & Harris, 'Big Mail: from Public Good to Private Profit,' 12th Winton M. Blount Postal History Symposium, Smithsonian National Postal Museum, 8 December 2022

sources.ref: Diane DeBlois & Robert Dalton Harris, 'Big Mail: from Public Good to Private Profit,' Twelfth Winton M. Blount Postal History Symposium, Smithsonian National Postal Museum, 8 December 2022 — slides state 'Business Reply & Bulk Mail introduced 1928'

USPS Domestic Mail Manual 505, Return Services — BRM service enables a permit holder to receive First-Class and Priority Mail back and 'pay postage and a per piece fee only for the pieces returned'; permit holder 'guarantees payment' of postage plus per-piece fee on all returned BRM including blank/empty pieces

The Stamp Forum, 'Business Reply Mail' thread — philatelic evidence of BRM in use: postage-due stamps affixed by the post office to collect postage + BRM fee from the permit holder (e.g. 1931 items at 2 cents postage + 1 cent fee); airmail BRM cards documented

competing_hypotheses: That 1928 is the introduction of the SERVICE as a formal permit system — the informal precursors ('return postage guaranteed' courtesy envelopes) predate it; the 1928 date marks the system, not the idea
That the symposium slide misdates — the exact Post Office Department order was not inspected this pass; a dated 1928 departmental order would move this to VERIFIED
falsifiability: A Post Office Department order establishing business reply mail before 1928, or evidence that no such service existed until a later year

title: The Italia airship disaster, 25 May – 12 July 1928
claim: On 25 May 1928, the Italian N-class semi-rigid airship Italia (N-4, designed by Umberto Nobile) crashed on the Arctic pack ice northeast of Svalbard while returning from the North Pole. The control car was smashed open and torn from the keel; nine survivors and one dead crewman were left on the ice, while the envelope rose again with six men aboard and was never found. The survivors dyed their 2.4×2.4 m silk tent red for visibility, radio operator Giuseppe Biagi transmitted SOS from 25 May, the signal was picked up on 3 June by a 21-year-old Soviet radio amateur (Nikolai Schmidt, Vokhma, on a home-made receiver), and after 48 days on the ice the remaining survivors were rescued — Nobile by the Swedish pilot Einar Lundborg on 23 June, the rest by the Soviet icebreaker Krasin on 12 July. Roald Amundsen disappeared on 18 June in the French Latham 47 while flying to join the rescue. Seventeen people died (crew and rescuers); eight survived.
place: Arctic pack ice ~120 km northeast of Nordaustlandet, Svalbard (crash site; the ice drifted during the 48 days on it)
grade_reason: Multiple independent primary and contemporary sources converge on the event: the expedition's own logs and Biagi's radio record, the international rescue participants' accounts (Norwegian, Swedish, Finnish, Soviet, French, Italian), contemporary press, and the 1929 commission's report. Only the sub-claims (exact coordinates, crash causes) vary — the event itself does not.
earliest_attestation: The expedition's own records and Biagi's radio log (25 May 1928 onward); the support ship Città di Milano's records; contemporary international press coverage (e.g., TIME, 23 July 1928); the Italian Commission of Inquiry report, Rivista Marittima, January 1930

sources.ref: Wikipedia 'Italia (airship)': the N-4 design, the three polar flights, the 23–25 May timeline (pole 24 May 00:24, crash 25 May morning), the control car torn from the keel, nine survivors + Pomella dead on the ice, six carried off with the envelope (never found), the red-dyed 2.4×2.4 m silk tent, Biagi's SOS from 25 May, Schmidt's 3 June reception (21-year-old Soviet amateur, Vokhma, home-made lamp-regenerative circuit), radio contact 9 June, Maddalena spotting the tent 20 June, Lundborg ordered to rescue Nobile first (23 June) and crashing on his return, Malmgren's 15–16 June death on the march, Krasin rescues 12 July, Amundsen's 18 June disappearance in the Latham 47, 17 dead / 8 survivors total

Leone & Robotti, 'The Polar Expedition of the Airship Italia (1928): A Chapter in the History of Physics,' Physics in Perspective 27 (2025), 340–402: the Red Tent position 81°14′N 25°25′E; Schmidt's SOS reception 3 June after nine days of failed attempts; Krasin rescue 12 July; Amundsen's 18 June disappearance; the INGV space-weather analysis of the failed radio propagation

naplesldm.com, 'Nobile' page: the one-seat Fokker ('the plane would never take off with the weight of even one more person'), Lundborg's return-flight crash, Nobile's 1930 book defending himself ('he had been ordered off the ice'), the 1929 inquiry finding him largely responsible, his resignation, the USSR years, the 1945 rehabilitation board and rank reinstatement
Wikipedia 'Umberto Nobile': cleared of all charges in 1945, reinstated at major general, promoted to lieutenant general with back pay to 1928

competing_hypotheses: The exact crash coordinates: Wikipedia gives ~81°14′N 28°14′E; a 2025 Physics in Perspective paper gives 81°14′N 25°25′E (the position the survivors calculated). The two longitudes differ by ~3°, well within the 'close to' hedging of both sources; the ice drifted under the survivors for 48 days, so no exact pin is honest

The causes of the crash remain controversial and are NOT settled by this record: Hugo Eckener's criticism (Nobile should never have climbed above the cloud layer), the sleep-deprivation analysis (Bendrick 2016; Bendrick & Alessandrini 2019), ice damage to propellers and envelope, possible gas-cell rupture
Whether Biagi's SOS was heard by the support ship's radio earlier (Pedretti intercepted a fragment on 29 May that was not acted on) — the documented first effective reception is Schmidt's, 3 June
falsifiability: Contemporary ship, radio, or commission records showing the crash did not occur on 25 May 1928, or that the envelope with six men was recovered — i.e., the primary documentary record contradicting the event

title: 'No postage necessary' means free — DEBUNKED
claim: The legend 'NO POSTAGE NECESSARY' on business reply mail means the mail travels free — that nobody pays for the postage. This is false. In the United States, the USPS Domestic Mail Manual (DMM 505) requires the BRM permit holder to guarantee payment of the applicable First-Class or Priority Mail postage, plus a per-piece fee, on ALL returned BRM — including incomplete, blank, or empty cards and envelopes — and to pay an annual permit fee. Under Royal Mail's Business Reply and Freepost services the licensee is billed per returned item (Freepost Standard/Plus, Business Reply Standard/Plus, Freepost Name licences). The Dutch antwoordnummer system bills the recipient the costs plus a fee; New Zealand freepost bills only when the permit number and recipient address match. In every system, 'no postage necessary' is a sender-facing instruction about affixing stamps, not a statement about who pays.
place: United States (USPS system; Royal Mail, Dutch PostNL, NZ Post analogues cited)
grade_reason: The permit holder's payment obligation is stated explicitly and unconditionally in the USPS Domestic Mail Manual — postage plus per-piece fee on every returned piece, blanks included — with Royal Mail, Dutch, and New Zealand analogues independently confirming the licensee/recipient pays; the 243rd DEBUNKED family.
earliest_attestation: USPS Domestic Mail Manual 505, Return Services (current); the 'NO POSTAGE NECESSARY' legend itself on BRM pieces

sources.ref: USPS Domestic Mail Manual 505, Return Services (DMM 505.1) — 'The permit holder guarantees payment of the applicable First-Class Mail or Priority Mail postage, plus a per piece fee, on all returned BRM' including 'any incomplete, blank, or empty BRM cards and envelopes'; annual permit fee; 'pay postage and a per piece fee only for the pieces returned'

engineersealstamps.com, 'No Postage Necessary Meaning: Business Reply Mail' — 'The permit holder pays everything: the returned piece's postage plus a per piece fee' per DMM 505.1.1 (annual permit fee, per piece fees, account maintenance fee)

postgrid.co.uk, 'Freepost and Business Reply Envelopes' — Royal Mail Business Reply: 'you need to pay the postage cost to Royal Mail while receiving these responses'; 'Freepost means free for the person who posts the envelope, not for you'; four services: Business Reply Standard/Plus, Freepost Standard/Plus, Freepost Name

Wikipedia, 'Freepost' — Netherlands: recipient pays costs plus a fee when no stamp used; New Zealand: permit number and recipient address must match for the recipient to be billed; UK: Freepost Name licence lets the public send free 'using any envelope,' the licence holder billed

competing_hypotheses: The surviving honest reading: 'no postage necessary' as a SENDER-facing instruction is accurate — the sender affixes no stamp and pays nothing; the DEBUNKED part is the extension to 'nobody pays'

That 'free to you' appears in Royal Mail marketing (Freepost Standard) — accurate for the sender, and Royal Mail's own licence documents show the licensee billed; the marketing line and the billing documents agree once read together
falsifiability: A postal regulation under which returned business reply mail costs the permit holder nothing — which would require rewriting the DMM's payment-guarantee clause itself

title: The 'Nobile abandoned his men' charge, 1928 (myth)
claim: Umberto Nobile cowardly abandoned his men in June 1928 by having himself rescued first from the Italia crash site — deserting them on the ice.
place: The Red Tent crash site, Arctic pack ice northeast of Svalbard (where the rescue priority was decided)
grade_reason: The charge dies on the documents: Lundborg was ORDERED to take Nobile first; the Fokker had exactly one spare seat ('the plane would never take off with the weight of even one more person'); Nobile was the worst-injured mobile case (broken leg, broken arm, cracked rib, head wound) — triage, not desertion; Lundborg crashed on his return flight, so the promised follow-up failed mechanically, not by Nobile's choice; and the fascist-era blame was formally withdrawn — the 1945 review cleared him of all charges, restored his rank, and promoted him with back pay to 1928.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary press and poetry, July 1928 (e.g., the NYT-reported Soviet poem of 16 July 1928); the Italian Commission of Inquiry report, Rivista Marittima, January 1930; Nobile's own 1930 defense (With the Italia to the North Pole); the 1945 rehabilitation

sources.ref: Wikipedia 'Italia (airship)': 'Swedish pilot Einar Lundborg is ordered to rescue Nobile first, but crashes his plane when he returns for more survivors and is trapped on the ice with the others' (23 June chronology); Nobile's injuries (broken leg, right arm, cracked rib, head wound); 'the Italian fascist government blamed Nobile for the crash and was the victim of a smear campaign in the press'

naplesldm.com, 'Nobile' page: Lundborg 'said truthfully that the plane would never take off with the weight of even one more person'; Nobile's 1930 book: 'he had been ordered off the ice'; the NYT-reported Soviet poem (16 July 1928) calling him 'The Fascist general who took the Cross to the pole but deserted his men'; the 1945 board of inquiry that officially 'rehabilitated' him and reinstated his rank

Wikipedia 'Umberto Nobile': 'In 1945, the Italian air force cleared Nobile of all charges related to the Italia crash, and not only reinstated him at his former rank as major general, but promoted him to lieutenant general and awarded him back pay dating to 1928'

Peroni, Irene, 'Into thin air' (thefreelibrary.com): 'A new inquiry in 1945 had cleared him of the accusations that had cost him his job and his title of general was restored'; the Amundsen-Nobile feud and the rumor-driven hostility toward Nobile

competing_hypotheses: The 1929 Italian Commission of Inquiry's criticism of Nobile's expedition leadership and crash management — a separate historical judgment about competence, NOT the desertion charge; this record kills only the cowardice/desertion reading, and reports the commission's criticism honestly without grading it here

The charge was sincerely felt by many at the time (the Soviet poet's 'Fascist general who took the Cross to the pole but deserted his men,' NYT 16 July 1928; the Narvik crowds' hostility) — sincerity of feeling is belief ecology, not evidence; the feeling is reported, the fact is graded
The rescue priority was genuinely controversial: a captain-is-last norm clashed with the evacuation order. The controversy is real; the desertion reading of it is not
falsifiability: A contemporary order or account showing Nobile requested to leave first for his own safety against the orders of his superiors, or evidence that the Fokker could have carried additional men and he refused them

title: The Parry-Lord oral-formulaic thesis: the song before the book
claim: The Homeric epics were composed in the oral tradition using a system of traditional formulae — poems tens of thousands of lines long made without writing.
place: Yugoslavia (Bosnia) — the 1933–1935 Parry–Lord fieldwork with the guslars
grade_reason: Three independent lines converge. (1) Parry's 1928 analysis showed the noun-epithet formulae ('swift-footed Achilles,' 'cloud-gathering Zeus') are a complete metrical system for the dactylic hexameter — a utilitarian composition technology for composing-in-performance, not decoration. (2) The 1933–35 fieldwork found the living mechanism: the Yugoslav guslars, illiterate bards who recomposed the story each performance; Avdo Mededovic's songs 'Osmanbey and Pavicevic Luka' and 'The Wedding of Smailagic Meho' ran over 12,000 lines each — contemporary analogues to a Homeric bard. (3) The archaic linguistic strata and formulaic density of the Homeric text resist written-composition explanations. Held at CORROBORATED, not VERIFIED: the field is live — analyst vs unitarian, dictation and transitional-text theories, and the exact road from song to the 6th-century Athenian text remain contested.
earliest_attestation: Milman Parry's 1928 Harvard doctoral work (L'epithete traditionnelle dans Homere; Les formules et la metrique d'Homere); the 1933–1935 Yugoslav fieldwork with Albert Lord (then his graduate student); Lord's The Singer of Tales (Harvard, 1960); the Milman Parry Collection of Oral Literature at Harvard Library (the digitized shellacs).

sources.ref: LA Review of Books, 'The Darwin of the Classics': Parry's theory and fieldwork as 'scientific discovery'-grade research; Lord's Singer of Tales (1960) bringing Parry 'bedrock status'; the guslars, the gusle, the 12,000-line songs of Avdo Mededovic; the Milman Parry Collection shellacs digitized at Harvard

Gale Power Search course document ('Was Homer an Oral Poet?'): Wolf 1795 and the analyst/unitarian split; Parry's mid-20th-century publications as the bridge to the 'monumental, but traditional, composer'; the formula as 'a group of words regularly employed under the same metrical conditions'; 'swiftfooted Achilles' and 'cloudgathering Zeus' as stock phrases

Vectree knowledge map, 'Milman Parry and the theory of oral-formulaic composition': the singer-as-performer (not writer); the guslars; recomposition per performance; formulae as 'utilitarian building blocks' for the dactylic hexameter's temporal constraint

competing_hypotheses: The unitarian monumental-composer thesis (Whitman, Kirk): one great poet shaped the tradition into the epics we have — compatible with the formulaic mechanism; oral does not mean anonymous
The dictation / transitional-text theories: a singer dictating to a scribe at writing's arrival — an alternative road from song to the fixed text
The Analyst position (Wolf, Prolegomena 1795): the poems as stitchings of shorter lays — the seams are real; the dispute is whether the stitching was a poet's or a tradition's
falsifiability: A written compositional draft tradition for the epics (authorial manuscripts, dated revisions in a single hand from the 8th c. BCE), or a demonstration that the Yugoslav analogues' recomposition-in-performance mechanism cannot produce the observed formulaic density and metrical regularity.

title: The 1929 crash (Black Thursday to Black Tuesday)
claim: In late October 1929 the New York stock market collapsed in a run of record selling days — Black Thursday (24 October) and Black Tuesday (29 October) — driven by forced selling of margin positions, wiping out much of the decade's paper gains and opening the financial chapter of the Great Depression.
place: New York Stock Exchange, 11 Wall Street, New York City
grade_reason: Multiple independent attestations: the exchange's own trading records, same-day newspaper reporting, and a half-century of scholarship built on them.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary newspaper reporting and NYSE trading records, October 1929

sources.ref: John Kenneth Galbraith, The Great Crash 1929 (1955) — the classic documented account of the bubble, the crash mechanics, and the aftermath
NYSE trading records, October 1929 (volumes, dates, price data)
Wikipedia: The Great Crash, 1929 (survey of the event and historiography)
HISTORY.com, '1929 Stock Market Crash: Did Panicked Investors Really Jump From Windows?' (2019, updated 2025) — crash context and Galbraith's statistics

competing_hypotheses: The monocausal reading: the crash caused the Great Depression

The Friedman–Schwartz reading (A Monetary History of the United States, 1963): the Depression's depth came from the Federal Reserve's contraction of the money supply and the banking collapse, with the crash as trigger rather than cause
falsifiability: Exchange records showing the October 1929 selloff did not occur on those dates or at those volumes would overturn the record

title: The Wall Street suicide wave of 1929 (myth)
claim: The popular image of a mass epidemic of ruined Wall Street brokers and speculators throwing themselves from office windows in the days and weeks after the October 1929 crash.
place: Wall Street financial district, Manhattan, New York City (geography of the claim)
grade_reason: Five independent kills from the contemporary record: Galbraith's suicide statistics, the medical examiner's refutation, the falsified London window reports, the misdated Churchill body, and the documented humor-to-myth pipeline.
earliest_attestation: London newspaper reports of window-jumpers; Will Rogers's newspaper quip (25 Oct 1929); Churchill's Daily Telegraph account (9 Dec 1929)

sources.ref: John Kenneth Galbraith, The Great Crash 1929 — on the suicide statistics: Oct/Nov 1929 suicides were among the lowest of any month that year, higher in the summer before the crash; on the London reports: no substance; 'In memory, some of these tragedies may have been moved back a year or two to the time of the stock market crash'

HISTORY.com, '1929 Stock Market Crash: Did Panicked Investors Really Jump From Windows?' (2019, updated 2025) — Norris's refutation, the Churchill/Matthies incident, the Borowski/Cutler/Stewart/Schwitzgebel/Motiska/Betts/Lytle cases, Galbraith's 17.0 → 21.3 per 100k figures

Wikipedia: The Great Crash, 1929 — 'London newspapers reported that ruined speculators were throwing themselves from windows but Galbraith asserts there was no substance to these claims of widespread suicides'
Charles Norris, NYC chief medical examiner, mid-November 1929 public refutation: 44 suicides in the prior four weeks in Manhattan vs 53 over the same period in 1928

competing_hypotheses: The literal-yes position (e.g., Morgan Housel): isolated suicides did happen — Borowski, Cutler, Stewart, Schwitzgebel, Motiska, Betts, Lytle are documented. The graded claim is the mass EPIDEMIC, which the statistics kill

The time-displacement reading: the real Depression-era suicide rise (17.0 to 21.3 per 100,000, 1929 to 1932) is being remembered as happening in October 1929 — the myth keeps the rise, but moves it two years early
falsifiability: Manhattan suicide data for October–November 1929 showing a spike above comparable prior periods (the Norris comparison reversed) would overturn this grade

title: The Salt March (Dandi March), March–April 1930
claim: From 12 March to 6 April 1930, M.K. Gandhi led 78 volunteers on a 240-mile (387 km) march from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi, Gujarat, where on the morning of 6 April he broke the British salt laws by making salt from seawater — inaugurating the Civil Disobedience Movement; the ensuing satyagraha saw 60,000+ Indians jailed.
place: Dandi, Gujarat, India (march terminus; route Sabarmati Ashram, Ahmedabad → Dandi)
grade_reason: Multiply and contemporaneously attested — the march was covered by the world press and newsreels as it happened, and its dates, route, and scale are uncontested in the historiography.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary 1930 press and newsreel coverage (the march was deliberately staged for the cameras); Gandhi's own writings; the Salt March Wikipedia record carries the standard account.

sources.ref: Wikipedia — 'Salt March': 24-day march 12 March–6 April 1930, 78 trusted volunteers, 387 km Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi; salt broken 8:30 am 6 April; 60,000+ jailed; 'the British did not make immediate major concessions'
Drishti IAS — 'Dandi March 1930': 12 March–6 April 1930, 78 followers, 241-mile march, Gandhi arrested 5 May, Dharasana 21 May under Sarojini Naidu, Gandhi released January 1931
Outlook Traveller — Dandi March route: Gandhi picked up salt at dawn on 6 April 1930 as a symbolic act of breaking British law; memorial at Dandi

competing_hypotheses: The march's immediate political yield was thin — the British made no major concessions at first; its victory was mobilizational, not legislative
The 78-marcher figure describes the starting column from Sabarmati; thousands joined along the route, so 'the march' as a mass event is larger than the founding cohort
falsifiability: Contemporary 1930 records contradicting the dates, the route, or the 78-volunteer starting figure

title: 'The Salt March ended the salt tax' — the seventeen-year gap
claim: Mahatma Gandhi's 1930 Salt March ended the British salt tax in India — the tax was abolished as a result of the march.
place: Dandi, Gujarat, India (where the reading locates the victory)
grade_reason: The tax outlived the march by seventeen years. The abolition paper trail runs through 1946–1947, not 1930: Gandhi had to formally request abolition again on 6 April 1946; Rowlands issued an abolition order that Viceroy Wavell vetoed; the Interim Government (Nehru; Finance Minister Liaquat Ali Khan) finally abolished the tax in March 1947, with the monopoly ceasing October 1946 and the duty from January 1947.
earliest_attestation: The popular reading lives in schoolbook shorthand, the 1982 film 'Gandhi''s victory framing, and Indian exam-prep culture — where 'Government monopoly in salt ended immediately after the Salt Satyagraha' is a standard FALSE distractor (GKToday). No primary source dates abolition to 1930.

sources.ref: Wikipedia — 'History of the salt tax in British India': 'The Dandi March was only partially successful... the salt tax continued'; Gandhi's 6 April 1946 formal request to Sir Archibald Rowlands; Rowlands's abolition order vetoed by Viceroy Lord Wavell; tax continued in force until March 1947, abolished by the Interim Government of India (Nehru; Finance Minister Liaquat Ali Khan)

Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi — 'Gandhiji's Correspondence with the Government, 1944-47' (freedomopedia PDF): 'Salt monopoly shall cease as from the first day of October 1946, and the duty on salt as from the first day of January 1947'

GKToday UPSC Prelims bank — 'Government monopoly in salt ended immediately after the Salt Satyagraha' carried as a FALSE statement: 'the government monopoly did not end immediately after the Salt Satyagraha in 1930, and salt taxes were abolished only in 1946 when Jawaharlal Nehru became head of Interim Government'

competing_hypotheses: The march won a limited concession at the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (5 March 1931) — Indians in coastal villages could make salt for domestic use — which the popular memory upgraded into full abolition
The tax's abolition was eventually real, just seventeen years late — the memory compresses the 1930–1947 arc into a single victory
falsifiability: A 1930–1931 abolition order for the Indian salt tax in the statute books — which does not exist; the paper trail runs the other way

title: Dord, the ghost word (1934–1947): the dictionary that printed a word that never existed
claim: For thirteen years (1934–1947), Webster's New International Dictionary, Second Edition, contained the word 'dord' — a ghost word, a non-word accidentally created when a chemistry editor's 3x5 slip reading 'D or d, cont./density.' was misread as the single word 'dord' (headwords were typed with spaces between letters). It appeared on page 771 defined as a noun meaning 'density' in physics and chemistry; an editor caught it on 28 February 1939, and it was excised in 1947.
place: Springfield, Massachusetts (G. and C. Merriam Company)
grade_reason: The error's entire lifecycle is documented by the institution that made it: the original slip (31 July 1931, Patterson, 'D or d, cont./density.'), the mechanism (headwords typed with spaced letters made 'D or d' read as 'Dord'), the printed entry (1934, p. 771, between Dorcopsis and doré), the 28 February 1939 discovery (an editor noticed the missing etymology), and the 1947 removal — all attested in Gove's letter to American Speech, Merriam-Webster's own retrospective, the Smithsonian account, and Wikipedia. Held at CORROBORATED rather than VERIFIED only because the primary-file evidence is carried through Gove's and the company's own retrospective accounts, not an independent external archive.
earliest_attestation: G. and C. Merriam Company's own files: Austin M. Patterson's 31 July 1931 slip ('D or d, cont./density.'); the 1934 printed entry 'dord (dôrd), n. Physics & Chem. Density.'; Philip Babcock Gove's letter to American Speech (c. 1954) reconstructing the whole chain; Merriam-Webster's own retrospective ('Dord: How a Non-Word Made it into the Dictionary').

sources.ref: Wikipedia — 'Dord': ghost word accidentally created by G. and C. Merriam staff in Webster's New International Dictionary 2nd ed. (1934); defined 'density' in physics and chemistry; Patterson's 31 July 1931 slip 'D or d, cont./density.'; appeared p. 771; caught 28 Feb 1939; removed 1947; Gove's American Speech letter.

Smithsonian Magazine (Kat Eschner, 28 Feb 2017): 'As "Dord" Shows, Being in the Dictionary Doesn't Always Mean Something's a Word' — Merriam-Webster's 'only one'; the 1939 discovery; Gove's 'probably too bad, for why shouldn't dord mean density?'

Merriam-Webster — 'Dord: How a Non-Word Made it into the Dictionary': the company's own account — W2 weighed 17 pounds, 250 editors and consultants; the entry had no etymology, no examples; the Austin M. Patterson slip story retold by the house.

competing_hypotheses: Whether the error lived until 1940 or 1947 in print (bound books began appearing without it in 1940, but the entry was not fully removed until 1947 — both on the record; copies printed in between vary)
Gove's 'probably too bad' shrug — 'why shouldn't dord mean density?' — carried as the house's own verdict, not an evidential position
falsifiability: The Merriam-Webster archive could contradict the slip story — it does the opposite: the company tells the story itself. Proof that 'dord' was a genuine in-use word before 1931 would overturn the ghost-word reading (no such attestation exists; Gove's investigation found no etymology, no examples, no file evidence).

title: The workers entombed in Hoover Dam's concrete
claim: Construction workers who fell into wet concrete during Hoover Dam's construction (1931-1936) were left there, entombed in the dam's structure.
place: Hoover Dam, Black Canyon, Arizona-Nevada border
grade_reason: Killed four ways: the dam was built as interlocking blocks poured in shallow lifts, not a monolithic pour; a body inside a block would create a structural weak spot (decay leaves a void); the documented 1933 W.A. Jameson form-collapse victim's body was recovered after sixteen hours, not left; and mid-1980s interviews with surviving workers found no witness to any purposeful burial. The genuine entombment belongs to Montana's Fort Peck Dam (1938 slide: eight died, six bodies still entombed) - the dams got mixed up in the retelling.
earliest_attestation: Undocumented oral/worker lore; the stories surface in mid-1980s interviews with surviving construction workers (Todd King, University of Nevada) - none of the interviewees witnessed a burial.

sources.ref: Gizmodo - 'Who is buried in the Hoover Dam?' (the 1933 Jameson accident, Todd King interviews, Fort Peck correction, structural argument)
Cracked - '6 Historical Myths You've Lapped Up As Fact' (Fort Peck mix-up, 1986 worker rumors)
Construction Knowledge - 'The Men Who Built Hoover Dam' (96 deaths, death-benefit incentive, 8-inch lifts, no bodies)
Boulder City 2020 Community Guide - Hoover Dam (officially 96 died; none buried in the dam)
National Historic Landmark summary - Hoover Dam (gradual pour techniques made burial impossible)

competing_hypotheses: The 96-death official toll undercounts deaths in scope: Six Companies' death-benefit contract gave the company an incentive to move dying men offsite, so offsite deaths went unrecorded - the toll's scope is contested, not the entombment
The Fort Peck Dam mix-up: six bodies genuinely entombed at Montana's Fort Peck Dam (1938 slide) migrated into Hoover Dam lore - the real entombment happened at a different dam
falsifiability: Ground-penetrating radar or coring revealing human remains inside the dam's concrete, or a contemporary (1931-1936) site record documenting a body left in a pour.

title: Hoover Dam built, 1931-1936
claim: Hoover Dam (authorized as Boulder Dam) was built in Black Canyon on the Arizona-Nevada border by Six Companies, Inc. under a 1931 contract: roughly 3.25 million cubic yards of concrete poured in interlocking blocks, dedicated by President Franklin D. Roosevelt on 30 September 1935, completed 1936; 96 workers died during construction per the official count.
place: Hoover Dam, Black Canyon, Arizona-Nevada border
grade_reason: Multiply attested: the authorizing act, the contract record, the Bureau's construction documentation, the block-pour method, and the 1935 dedication converge on the dates, the builder, the method, and the 96-death official count.
earliest_attestation: Boulder Canyon Project Act (1928); Six Companies contract (March 1931); Bureau of Reclamation construction records; contemporary press coverage.

sources.ref: National Historic Landmark summary - Hoover Dam (construction 1931, dedication 1935, 96 deaths, $49M, renamed 1947, NHL 1985)
Construction Knowledge - 'The Men Who Built Hoover Dam' (96 deaths, 8-inch lifts, block-pour method)
Boulder City 2020 Community Guide - Hoover Dam (Boulder Canyon Project Act 1928, Black Canyon site, dedication 30 Sept 1935)

competing_hypotheses: The 96-death count is contested in scope: the death-benefit contract gave Six Companies an incentive to move dying men offsite, so offsite deaths went unrecorded - the count is official, not exhaustive

The 'concrete still curing today' telling: the cooling-pipe engineering (river water, then chilled water, through embedded pipes) is real; the 'still curing ninety years later' reading is the myth built on it (fenced, not graded here)
falsifiability: Bureau of Reclamation construction records showing a different contractor, different dates, or a monolithic (non-block) pour method.

title: The Vitaphone disc's afterlife (1931–mid-1930s)
claim: After the format war, sound-on-disc lived on as an exhibition medium: Warner Bros. recorded and edited optically from mid-1931 but dubbed the finished soundtracks to discs for theaters with Vitaphone projection equipment, and most Hollywood studios pressed dubbed disc sets for disc-only houses into the mid-1930s.
place: United States exhibition circuit — the disc-only small-town and late-converting houses
grade_reason: Attested in the Vitaphone secondary record: the mid-1931 recording switch, the 'both sound-on-film and sound-on-disc versions' spin as the retirement was announced, and the continuing dubbed-disc supply driven by theaters that could not afford to replace disc-only equipment. Held below VERIFIED on the single-source-lineage (the fandom wiki and Wikipedia carry the same account) and the approximate end date.
earliest_attestation: The practice is documented in the Vitaphone secondary record (the mid-1931 Warner announcement and its 'both versions' spin); no single primary contract set has been located by this run — an honest gap, carried in the grade.

sources.ref: Wikipedia — 'Vitaphone' (mid-1931 switch; 'A significant number of theater owners... financially unable or unwilling to replace their sound-on-disc-only equipment... This practice continued, although on an ever-dwindling scale, into the mid-1930s.')
Warner Bros. Entertainment Wiki (fandom) — 'Vitaphone' (same account; the retirement spin as 'doing the entire movie industry a favor')
shootonline.com — 'Sound Comes to Hollywood' (the Vitaphone brand synonymous with talkies by 1928; small-town exhibitor economics)

competing_hypotheses: The afterlife was longer than documented in aggregate: individual theaters' disc use may have stretched further than the 'mid-1930s' secondary-literal reading

The driver was contractual as well as technical: exhibitors had invested heavily in Vitaphone equipment and were financially unable or unwilling to replace it — the studios supplied dubbed discs as required, which is itself the Format Reader's point: installed base outvotes best engineering
falsifiability: Documented evidence that no dubbed disc sets were pressed after 1931, or that disc-only theaters converted immediately, would overturn this; the theater-owner economics (recent heavy Vitaphone investment) make the tail structurally expected.

title: The Polish break of Enigma (1932) and the Pyry transfer (1939)
claim: In December 1932 (between Christmas and New Year, per Rejewski's account), Marian Rejewski of the Polish Cipher Bureau (Biuro Szyfrow) reconstructed the internal wiring of the German military Enigma machine using permutation theory plus German cipher documents obtained by French intelligence (Captain Gustave Bertrand's source inside the German cipher office, Hans-Thilo Schmidt, 'Asche'). With Jerzy Rozycki and Henryk Zygalski, the Poles then read German military Enigma traffic daily from ~January 1933, building the cyclometer, Zygalski's perforated sheets, and the electromechanical bomba kryptologiczna (Nov 1938). On 25 July 1939 at Pyry, south of Warsaw — five weeks before WWII — Poland handed Britain (Alastair Denniston, Alfred Dillwyn Knox, Humphrey Sandwith) and France (Bertrand, Braquenie) the full documentation, the cryptanalytic machines, and Enigma replicas. Britain, which had concluded Enigma unbreakable and made zero pre-war progress, began reading Enigma within months of the war's outbreak, on Polish foundations.
place: Pyry, south of Warsaw (Biuro Szyfrow facility); Warsaw
grade_reason: Multiply attested across independent sources: the three principals' accounts, Bertrand's French records, British GCCS documentation of the Pyry handover and its fruits, and Bletchley's own 2002 plaque. The breakthrough date is retrospective testimony, so CORROBORATED is the honest ceiling.
earliest_attestation: Rejewski's own published accounts (1967, 1976); Gustave Bertrand's intelligence records; British GCCS records of the Pyry meeting and of manufacturing perforated sheets from Polish documentation (mid-Dec 1939); the 2002 Bletchley Park plaque commemorating Rejewski, Rozycki, and Zygalski 'in first breaking the Enigma code.'

sources.ref: Rejewski's accounts (1967/1976): break between Christmas 1932 and New Year using permutation equations + French-supplied documents; AVA company built the Enigma replicas

Wikipedia (Marian Rejewski): Pyry meeting 25 July 1939 — Denniston, Knox, Sandwith; Bertrand, Braquenie; full documentation + replicas; British manufactured at least two sets of perforated sheets, reading Enigma within months of the war
Bletchley Park 2002 plaque: commemorates Rejewski, Rozycki, Zygalski 'in first breaking the Enigma code' — their work 'greatly assisted the Bletchley Park code breakers'

competing_hypotheses: The retrospective-date caution: the December-1932 breakthrough date rests substantially on Rejewski's own later accounts (1967/1976), not on a dated contemporary intercept log — the transfer and the daily reads are the multiply-attested parts; the grade sits at CORROBORATED, not VERIFIED, for exactly this reason

The counterfactual 'Britain would have broken it anyway': Bletchley had excellent people and resources, but as of July 1939 it had nothing on military Enigma — Knox's team thought it could not be read at scale; the claim is untestable and fenced as speculation
falsifiability: Contemporary Polish, French, or British documents showing the 1932 break did not occur, or that Pyry handed over nothing material; or German records showing the 1933 reads did not happen.

title: DEBUNKED: 'Alan Turing single-handedly broke the Enigma'
claim: The popular version — most concentrated in the 2014 Oscar-nominated film 'The Imitation Game' — that Alan Turing single-handedly broke the Enigma code is false. The military Enigma was first broken by Marian Rejewski and the Polish Cipher Bureau in December 1932 — seven years before Bletchley Park's wartime program began — and Poland handed Britain the complete solution (documentation, machines, replicas) at Pyry on 25 July 1939, when Britain had made zero pre-war progress. Turing's genuine, major contributions — the Bombe (built with Gordon Welchman's diagonal board), Banburismus, and the breaking of naval Enigma (Shark) — belong to the wartime industrial phase of a break that already existed. Colossus (the Lorenz-cipher machine) belongs to Bill Tutte, Max Newman, and Tommy Flowers, not Turing. Twenty-ninth DEBUNKED family.
place: Bletchley Park, UK (where the myth is set); Warsaw/Pyry (where the break happened)
grade_reason: Direct chronological contradiction: the documented 1932 break and 1939 transfer precede Turing's Enigma work by years, and Britain's own records confirm it received the solution rather than inventing it. The 'single-handedly' reading has no source; the Polish-first record has three governments' paper trails.
earliest_attestation: The same documentary trail as evt-polish-enigma-break-001 (Pyry attendee lists, GCCS records, the 2002 Bletchley plaque) precedes every Turing Enigma claim by seven years; Turing's own wartime papers document the Bombe and Banburismus as later-stage work.

sources.ref: The Pyry attendee record and British GCCS manufacturing of perforated sheets from Polish documentation (mid-Dec 1939) — Britain receiving the solution, per the same sources as evt-polish-enigma-break-001
Bletchley Park 2002 plaque: 'in first breaking the Enigma code' — the institution's own commemoration of the Polish priority

competing_hypotheses: The charitable reading: 'Turing broke Enigma' as shorthand for 'Turing was central to the Allied codebreaking effort' — the record grades what is said (single-handed invention of the break), not what might have been meant

The pro-Bletchley emphasis: that the wartime scale of reading (thousands of messages daily, the bombes, Ultra's distribution) was the decisive achievement — true as a claim about scale, and fenced off from this grade, which targets only the first-break attribution
falsifiability: Documents showing Turing reconstructed the military Enigma independently before or without the 1939 Polish transfer — none exist; the British records show the transfer was the starting point.

title: The Akron rubber workers' sit-downs (1934–36) — the tactic Flint inherited
claim: In early 1936, Akron, Ohio's rubber workers carried out some of the first major sit-down strikes in the United States — the tactic pioneered at General Tire in 1934, used at Firestone in January 1936 and Goodyear in February 1936 — proving the tactic and making the Flint sit-down possible.
place: Akron, Ohio — the rubber plants
grade_reason: CORROBORATED — held below VERIFIED because the priority-chain details (the 1934 origin, exact sit-down dates in Jan–Feb 1936, the baseball-game origin story) ride through secondary aggregators and institutional summaries rather than a single converged primary archive; what is multiply attested: the General Tire 1934 origin (Ohio History Connection + labor historian Daniel Nelson), the Firestone 29 January 1936 sit-down over Clayton Dicks (APWU + Brecher), and the Goodyear February 1936 sit-downs and month-long picket ending in the 22 March 1936 settlement (Ohio History Connection + Zinn Education Project + Wikipedia).
earliest_attestation: The actions were contemporaneously documented — local press, the fledgling United Rubber Workers (created September 1935), the Summit County Central Labor Council's 1936 role, and the Ohio History Connection's historical-marker program all converge.

sources.ref: Ohio History Connection (Remarkable Ohio marker 32-77): 'Five Depression-era strikes against many of Akron's rubber companies culminated in a giant sit-down strike against Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company... in February and March of 1936'; the URW, created September 1935, 'used the tactic of being at work but not working that had been pioneered by rank-and-file workers in a successful 1934 strike against the General Tire and Rubber Company'; the strike was 'one of the earliest successes for the Committee for Industrial Organization (CIO)'

APWU 'Labor History: Akron Rubber Workers Innovate Strike Tactics': 'In January 1936, at the Firestone Tire and Rubber Co.... workers sat down on Jan. 29, 1936, occupying the plant for three days until Dicks was reinstated with back pay. On Feb. 16, 1936, workers at Goodyear also participated in a sit-down strike after the company announced plans to lay off workers, increase work hours, and reduce pay.'

Zinn Education Project, 'Feb. 16, 1936: Akron Rubber Strike': 'On Feb. 16, 1936, rubber workers began a sit-down strike at Goodyear Tire and Rubber Co. in Akron, Ohio' — the sit-down defined as workers quitting work but occupying their places so the factory owners could not send in strikebreakers

Jeremy Brecher, 'Akron rubber workers' struggles, 1933-1936' (libcom.org): the detailed chronology — Goodrich tire department sit-down Feb 8, 1936 ('stopping it completely within six hours, and management rapidly capitulated'); Feb 14, 1936: '137 tire builders in Department 251-A of Goodyear's Plant No.2... shut off the power and sat down'

competing_hypotheses: The 'General Tire 1934 was the true origin' refinement — some accounts treat the 1934 General Tire action as the first American sit-down proper, with 1936 as the first sustained campaign — is carried honestly: the priority chain is General Tire 1934 → Firestone/Goodyear 1936, all Akron, all before Flint.

The Zinn Education Project's dating nuance (the Goodyear sit-down 'Feb. 16, 1936' vs the brecher-derived 'Feb. 14' account of 137 tire builders shutting off the power) is carried as a source variance on days, never on the month — February 1936 is uncontested.
falsifiability: A showing that the 1934 General Tire action and the January–February 1936 Akron sit-downs did not involve workers occupying the workplace while refusing to work would reverse the verdict; the contemporary accounts describe exactly that.

title: The RCA–Farnsworth patent interference (1934–1939)
claim: In 1934 the Radio Corporation of America brought patent interference proceedings (Interference No. 64,027) against Philo Farnsworth's television patents, asserting Vladimir Zworykin's priority; the U.S. Patent Office decided the interference for Farnsworth in February 1935, RCA's 1936 appeal failed, and in 1939 RCA took a license to Farnsworth's patents — paying him about $1 million in royalties — before launching television to the public at the New York World's Fair.
place: Washington, D.C. (U.S. Patent Office, Interference No. 64,027)
grade_reason: The legal outcome is multiply attested: the February 1935 interference decision for Farnsworth (Tolman testimony, 1922 sketch), RCA's failed 1936 appeal, and the 1939 license — reported by independent secondary sources (Wikipedia, MIT Technology Review, JDSupra, learnbright). Held below VERIFIED because the royalty figure (~$1M) and the 1931 $100,000 buyout offer ride secondary aggregators rather than the agreement's own terms.
earliest_attestation: U.S. Patent Office Interference No. 64,027 (1934–1935): Examiner's decision February 1935 (Tolman's preserved sketch of Farnsworth's spring-1922 blackboard drawing, teacher's testimony); RCA appeal 1936; 1939 license agreement

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Philo Farnsworth': interference brought by RCA in 1934, decided February 1935; Tolman's sketch of the spring-1922 blackboard drawing; RCA appealed in 1936 and lost; Farnsworth received royalties from RCA
MIT Technology Review, 'Who Really Invented Television?' (Sept 2000): the Sarnoff–Zworykin collaboration; the April 1930 Green Street lab visit; Westinghouse bankers' pressure to sell
LearnBright, 'Philo T. Farnsworth': Farnsworth won the case in 1935, ruling upheld on appeal; 'RCA licensed the patents in 1939 and paid Farnsworth a million dollars for them'
JDSupra, 'The Top Ten Patent Wars — Television (#10)': 'after taking a million-dollar license from Farnsworth after losing the interference proceedings'

competing_hypotheses: The royalty-figure reading: the 'about $1 million' total traces to secondary aggregators (learnbright.org, JDSupra); a strict reader would demand the 1939 agreement's own terms — the legal outcome (license after lost interference) is firmer than the figure.

The Sarnoff-business reading: the 1939 license was a business decision (clearing the patent thicket before the World's Fair launch), not an admission of non-inventorship — RCA's litigation was good-faith patent defense by the era's standards, and the interference record says priority, not 'theft'.

The 1931-offer reading: the famous $100,000 buyout offer (refused by Farnsworth, who wanted royalties) is attested only in secondary recountings — it belongs to the story's color, not its legal core; the interference record stands without it.

The appeal-scope reading: RCA's 1936 appeal and its loss concern the interference on Claim 15's count; RCA continued television development under license — the legal episode ended the priority fight, not the engineering competition.
falsifiability: The Patent Office decision and the appeal loss are matters of legal record; a showing that the 1939 license was not taken — i.e., period RCA financial records with no Farnsworth royalty line — would overturn the agreement leg. The ~$1M figure, riding secondary sources, could be revised downward or upward without moving the legal grade.

title: 'YKK invented the zipper' — the manufacturer, not the inventor (DEBUNKED)
claim: The Japanese company YKK — the letters stamped on most of the world's zippers — invented the zipper. The documents say otherwise: YKK (Yoshida Kogyo K.K.) was founded January 1, 1934 by Tadao Yoshida in Tokyo as a zipper MANUFACTURER, seventeen years after Sundback's 1917 separable-fastener patent and eleven years after Goodrich coined the name. YKK overtook the inventor's own company (Talon, the former Hookless Fastener Co.) for the American market in the 1970s-80s; it conquered zipper MANUFACTURE, not zipper INVENTION.
place: Tokyo, Japan (YKK headquarters; founded in Nihonbashi, Tokyo)
grade_reason: The founding date (1934) is documented by the company and independent sources; the 1917 Sundback patent and 1923 Goodrich naming are public records. A 1934 manufacturer cannot invent a 1917 device.
earliest_attestation: The chronological impossibility is itself the attestation: Sundback 1917 / Goodrich 1923 predate Yoshida 1934 by 17 and 11 years

sources.ref: YKK Corporation corporate history — founded January 1, 1934, Tadao Yoshida, Tokyo
Smithsonian Magazine — 'One Japanese Company Makes Half of the World's Zippers' (2015): Sundback's 1917 patent precedes Yoshida by 17 years
Pennsylvania Center for the Book / Penn State — 'Zip It Up: Talon Zippers' (2009): YKK overtook Talon for the American market in the 1980s

competing_hypotheses: YKK independently advanced zipper technology (its machine-building and quality systems are genuine innovations — manufacturing genius, not invention priority)
falsifiability: A Yoshida zipper patent or product predating 1917 — none exists; the company's own history begins in 1934

title: The 1937 New York City burlesque license-kill
claim: In April 1937, a police raid on Abe Minsky's New Gotham Theater in Harlem — a stripper caught working without a G-string — gave New York City License Commissioner Paul Moss the criminal conviction he needed, and he then refused to renew the licenses of all of New York City's burlesque theaters, driving them to close.
place: New York City, USA (the burlesque houses; the April 1937 raid at the New Gotham Theater, Harlem)
grade_reason: CORROBORATED on converging secondary documentation: the State Court of Appeals ruling that Moss needed a criminal conviction (the precondition), the April 1937 G-string raid and ensuing conviction (the trigger), the license revocation plus the citywide non-renewals (the weapon), the no-stripper reopening code and the wave of closures (the effect), and the post-election advertising bans on the words 'burlesque' and 'Minsky' (the afterword). Held below VERIFIED because the actual 1937 license orders and the conviction record are not yet in hand — stated honestly.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary 1937 press coverage (e.g. the August 27, 1937 Evening Independent burlesque-column item); the full campaign sequence as documented in the secondary histories

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Minsky's Burlesque' (secondary aggregator: the 1935 complaints, the Court of Appeals ruling, the April 1937 raid, the license revocation and non-renewals, the no-stripper code, the advertising bans)
Wikipedia, 'American burlesque' (secondary aggregator: La Guardia's 1937 clampdown, burlesque 'effectively put out of business' in NYC by the early 1940s, lingering elsewhere)

Sidney Pullen, 'Burlesque: The Other Side of Vaudeville,' American Vaudeville Museum / UA Collections (citing Robert C. Allen 1991: theaters refused renewal 'because of burlesque's supposed moral deviance')
Evening Independent (St. Petersburg), Aug 27, 1937, p. 20 — contemporary press on the post-raid scene ('burlesque followers,' the Oriental theater dark)

competing_hypotheses: The 1935-1937 pressure was driven as much by citizens' groups and anti-vice clergy as by City Hall (carried fairly: the 1935 citizens' complaints predate Moss's decisive move and are the campaign's documented opening)

The license refusals were legally a renewal decision rather than a revocation (carried fairly: Moss refused RENEWALS; only Abe Minsky's own license was revoked outright — the mechanism was refusal, not a ban statute)
falsifiability: The actual 1937 license docket showing renewals granted to strippers-included burlesque houses, or a court record overturning the conviction that grounded the refusals

title: The 'Invented Once, in the Fertile Crescent' Claim
claim: Agriculture was invented exactly once in human history — in the Fertile Crescent — and then spread outward from that single origin to every other farming society in the world.
place: The Fertile Crescent (the claimed single hearth)
grade_reason: The single-origin model fails on its own requirement: other centers hold earlier or overlapping dates with unrelated domesticated species (New Guinea taro/banana/yam ~10 ka; Chinese rice; Mesoamerican maize) — a single invention cannot produce independent, contemporaneous, species-distinct agricultures.
earliest_attestation: V. Gordon Childe, Man Makes Himself (1936) — the Neolithic Revolution model; the postwar diffusionist tradition that made the Fertile Crescent the single hearth.

sources.ref: V. Gordon Childe, Man Makes Himself (1936) — the Neolithic Revolution; single-hearth model
J. G. Hawkes, The Diversity of Crop Plants (1983) — 'Agriculture began not once but several times, more or less simultaneously'

Denham et al., Origins of agriculture at Kuk Swamp in the highlands of New Guinea, Science (2003) — taro/banana cultivation 10,220-9,910 cal BP, 'agriculture at Kuk as early as anywhere in the world' (Spriggs)
UNESCO World Heritage listing, Kuk Early Agricultural Site (2008) — criterion iv: 'one of the few places in the world where archaeological evidence suggests independent agricultural development'

Centers-of-origin synthesis (Vavilov center data, 2003 map): Fertile Crescent ~11,000 BP; Yangtze/Yellow River basins ~9,000 BP; New Guinea Highlands 9,000-6,000 BP; Central Mexico 5,000-4,000 BP; northern South America 5,000-4,000 BP; sub-Saharan Africa 5,000-4,000 BP; eastern North America 4,000-3,000 BP — overlapping dates, unrelated species

competing_hypotheses: The demic-diffusion 'wave of advance' model (Ammerman & Cavalli-Sforza 1984) — TRUE for Europe specifically: Near Eastern farming genuinely spread across Europe; this record does not touch it. Regional diffusion is real; world single-origin is not.
Contact-era crop diffusion (maize, wheat, rice moving by trade/colonialism) — real diffusion of specific species, not diffusion of the invention of agriculture.
falsifiability: Demonstration that all crop traditions trace to a single botanical lineage and chronology would reopen the claim; the domesticated species are distinct (wheat, rice, maize, taro, banana, potato, sorghum) at overlapping dates — ruled out.

title: The Berlin Olympic Games, 1936
claim: The Games of the XI Olympiad were held in Berlin 1–16 August 1936, with 3,963 athletes from 49 nations; American sprinter Jesse Owens won four gold medals — 100 metres, 200 metres, long jump, and 4x100 metre relay — in Adolf Hitler's Berlin.
place: Olympiastadion, Berlin, Germany
grade_reason: Multiply documented event — official report, IOC archive, contemporary press, newsreel, and the physical stadium all converge; Owens's four golds are among the best-recorded results in sports history.
earliest_attestation: The Official Report of the Organising Committee for the XIth Olympiad, Berlin 1936 (1937); IOC records; contemporary newsreel footage

sources.ref: Organising Committee, Official Report of the Games of the XI Olympiad, Berlin 1936 (1937)
International Olympic Committee — Berlin 1936 results archive
Britannica — Jesse Owens and the 1936 Berlin Olympics
Mark Dyreson, 'From Civil Rights to Scientific Racism: American Responses to the Legend of Jesse Owens and the Berlin Olympics' (Centre for Olympic Studies symposium, Oct 1994, Weber State)

competing_hypotheses: The games as Nazi stagecraft — a propaganda triumph that laundered the regime (the 'Nazi Olympics' reading)
The games as the moment the regime's racial ideology was publicly embarrassed by Owens's victories (the 'defeat on their own stage' reading)
falsifiability: The Official Report, IOC archive, and newsreel record would all have to be fabrications; no serious historian disputes the games' occurrence.

title: The Dvorak-superiority claim
claim: The Dvorak Simplified Keyboard is scientifically proven to be faster than QWERTY, and QWERTY's survival is therefore proof of an inefficient market lock-in.
place: Washington, DC (US Patent Office, 1936 patent; Navy and GSA studies)
grade_reason: The layout's existence is documented (1936 patent), but the 'scientifically proven faster' claim is attested-only and contested: its flagship evidence is an unpublished Navy study directed by the layout's own inventor; the 1956 GSA study found QWERTY typists as fast or faster; Liebowitz & Margolis (1990) concluded there is 'no scientifically acceptable evidence that Dvorak offers any real advantage over QWERTY.' The lock-in parable built on the superiority claim collapses with it.
earliest_attestation: Dvorak & Dealey, US Patent 2,040,248 (1936); the superiority claim's evidentiary base is the unpublished 1940s US Navy typing study

sources.ref: Liebowitz, Stan J. & Margolis, Stephen E. (1990). 'The Fable of the Keys.' Journal of Law and Economics, vol. XXXIII (April 1990) — Dvorak's own direction of the Navy study; GSA 1956 parity finding; ergonomic studies show 2.3%, 5%, 6.2% — 'no clear advantage'
US Patent 2,040,248 — Dvorak & Dealey, 'Typewriter keyboard' (1936)
Finkelstein, Seth. 'The Fable of the Fable' — rebuttal defending Dvorak, carried as the competing position

competing_hypotheses: The Finkelstein rebuttal ('The Fable of the Fable'): Liebowitz & Margolis attack Dvorak rather than engaging path-dependence theory generally, and dismiss real switching-cost barriers too quickly — the defense of Dvorak from the Dvorak side, named fairly
The retraining-cost position: even small layout advantages cannot justify the cost of retraining the installed base — QWERTY's persistence is efficient regardless of which layout is marginally faster
The agnostic position: the ergonomic literature is simply too thin and too old for either layout to claim proven superiority
falsifiability: A published, peer-reviewed, independently replicated typing trial showing Dvorak typists substantially and consistently faster than QWERTY typists

title: The Flint sit-down strike (1936–37) — the 44 days that unionized the auto industry
claim: The Flint sit-down strike — autoworkers occupying General Motors' Fisher Body plants in Flint, Michigan — ran from 30 December 1936 to 11 February 1937 (44 days), and ended with GM formally recognizing the United Automobile Workers as the collective bargaining representative, the victory that unionized the American auto industry.
place: Flint, Michigan — the Fisher Body plants
grade_reason: VERIFIED — the ninety-eighth family-adjacent event record: multiple independent contemporary lines converge (UAW records, GM records, Governor Frank Murphy's administration papers, national press): 30 Dec 1936 occupation, 44 days, the 'Battle of the Running Bulls' (January 1937), and the 11 February 1937 agreement with formal UAW recognition.
earliest_attestation: The strike itself was contemporaneously documented — national press, the UAW's own records, Governor Frank Murphy's administration papers, and GM's corporate records all converge on the dates and the recognition outcome.

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Flint sit-down strike': 'Date: December 30, 1936 – February 11, 1937; Location: Flint, Michigan; Result: Recognition of the UAW' — 'thousands of workers occupied the plants for 44 days, from December 30, 1936 to February 11, 1937'; Governor Frank Murphy 'refused to use force against the strikers, and sent in the Michigan National Guard to protect the workers from police and company guards, until an agreement was reached'

This Day In Automotive History, 'February 11, 1937: The Flint Sit-Down Strike Ends, UAW Recognized': the 44-day standoff ended 11 Feb 1937 when GM recognized the UAW — 'the first time a major U.S. automaker formally accepted an industrial union'; the 'Battle of the Running Bulls' police attempt to retake a plant, January 1937

Workers World (Martha Grevatt), 'The Occupy that won the union' (75th-anniversary retrospective, 2012): the sit-down began Dec. 30, 1936, ended in victory Feb. 11, 1937; workers won UAW recognition and the first industry contract; notes the misconception that the strike was spontaneous — it was the product of organized preparation

title: The Hitler–Owens 'Snub' at Berlin 1936
claim: Adolf Hitler personally snubbed Jesse Owens at the 1936 Berlin Olympics — deliberately refusing to meet, greet, or congratulate him because he was Black.
place: Olympiastadion, Berlin, Germany
grade_reason: Three independent kills: (1) Hitler congratulated German winners only on day one, the IOC told him to congratulate all or none, and he then congratulated nobody and left the stadium before Owens's first race — there was no personal encounter to refuse; (2) the one documented exchange was a wave returned — sports reporter Paul Gallico saw it in Berlin, and Owens himself confirmed it in the Pittsburgh Press two weeks later; (3) Owens's own lifelong verdict, stated plainly: the man who did not snub him was Hitler — 'Hitler didn't snub me, it was Roosevelt who snubbed me. The president didn't even send me a telegram.'
earliest_attestation: Rumors in Berlin during the games, per Mark Dyreson (1994); the cinematic version (Owens crossing the line cut against Hitler leaving) is decades later

sources.ref: Britannica — 'Was Jesse Owens Snubbed by Adolf Hitler at the Berlin Olympics?'
Paul Gallico, sports reporting from Berlin, 1936 (contemporary account of Owens below the honor box; Hitler's seated return salute)
Pittsburgh Press, 24 August 1936 — Owens: 'before he left I was on my way to a broadcast and passed near his box. He waved at me and I waved back'
Professor Buzzkill — 'Hitler, Jesse Owens, and the 1936 Berlin Olympics' (IOC president de Baillet-Latour's all-or-none instruction; Hitler's absence after day one)
ThoughtCo — 'Did Hitler Snub Jesse Owens at the Berlin Olympics?' (Hitler left before Owens competed; German crowds' ovations)
Mark Dyreson, 'From Civil Rights to Scientific Racism: American Responses to the Legend of Jesse Owens and the Berlin Olympics' (LA84 digital library, 1994)

competing_hypotheses: The documentary-edit tradition: Owens crossing the finish line cut against Hitler leaving the stadium — an editing choice read as a snub (the film is real; the causation is the myth)

falsifiability: Contemporary film or photography of Hitler refusing an offered greeting from Owens, or any statement by Owens himself that he felt personally snubbed in Berlin — the subject's own repeated, public, lifelong denials are the record's strongest evidence.

title: The '10% of the brain' myth
claim: Human beings use only 10 percent of their brains; 90 percent of the brain's tissue is unused and available to be unlocked.
place: Cambridge, Massachusetts (Harvard — James's lecture halls; Thomas's attribution point)
grade_reason: Every line of modern neuroscience contradicts it: fMRI/PET show activity across the whole brain over a day; the brain consumes ~20% of resting energy on ~2% of body mass; damage to essentially any region produces impairment; there is no unused 90% of tissue to unlock.
earliest_attestation: Lowell Thomas's 1936 foreword to Dale Carnegie's 'How to Win Friends and Influence People': 'Professor William James of Harvard used to say that the average man develops only ten percent of his latent mental ability.'

sources.ref: Lowell Thomas foreword to Dale Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People (1936)

William James, 'The Energies of Men' (1906 lecture; Science, 1907): 'we are only half awake... making use of only a small part of our possible mental and physical resources' — no percentage, and about energy/potential, not tissue
1929 World Almanac self-help advertisement: 'Scientists and psychologists tell us we use only about TEN PERCENT of our brain power' (pre-1936 circulation of the figure)

Barry Beyerstein, 'Whence Cometh the Myth that We Only Use Ten Percent of our Brains?' in Mind Myths (1999) — the archival hunt; Einstein Archives could locate no Einstein statement of the claim (apocryphal attribution)
BPS Research Digest, 'Great myths of the brain: We only use 10 per cent' — survey data and myth history

competing_hypotheses: The claim was always a statement about untapped cognitive potential, not about unused tissue (James's original meaning; the ambiguity is what let the myth survive)

Related misattributions: Wilder Penfield's cortical-stimulation 'silent areas' were sometimes blamed (he mapped unexplored cortex, not unused cortex); Karl Lashley's 1920s-30s rat lesion work suggested equipotentiality in the damaged cortex, misread as spare capacity
falsifiability: A documented region of the human brain, present in healthy adults, whose removal or destruction produces no functional, cognitive, or metabolic change whatsoever — repeatedly observed across subjects.

title: Han van Meegeren's forged Vermeers
claim: Between 1936 and 1943 the Dutch painter Han van Meegeren (1889–1947) produced a series of forged 'Vermeer' paintings — including The Supper at Emmaus (1936–37) and Christ with the Woman Taken in Adultery (1941–42) — on genuine 17th-century canvases, using period pigments hardened with 20th-century phenol-formaldehyde resin, and sold them as rediscovered Vermeers.
place: Amsterdam, Netherlands (arrest, demonstration painting, trial)
grade_reason: The forger's own 1945 confession, his courtroom demonstration painting produced under observation, the Coremans commission's chemistry (Bakelite/Albertol resins — 20th-century materials — plus a resin bottle found in his studio), the 12 Nov 1947 forgery/fraud conviction, and the museum provenance records all converge on the same event.
earliest_attestation: The forger's own confession, May 1945; the courtroom demonstration painting Jesus among the Doctors, painted under observation July–Dec 1945

sources.ref: Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen — Boijmans Studies (new findings on van Meegeren's forgeries, reported 2025): the 1937 purchase, the Bredius authentication, the post-war unmasking
NPR — 'How Mediocre Dutch Artist Cast The Forger's Spell' (Edward Dolnick, 2008): the Emmaus sale, the Goering transaction (137 looted paintings traded), the unmasking via Nazi paperwork

Coremans commission (1945–47, led by Paul B. Coremans, Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium): phenol-formaldehyde resins Bakelite and Albertol identified in the paint; resin bottle found in van Meegeren's studio
essentialvermeer.com — list of known forgeries with sale prices (Emmaus 520,000–550,000 guldens; Adulteress 1,650,000 guldens)
Amsterdam Regional Court record, Room 4, 29 Oct–12 Nov 1947: forgery and fraud conviction, one-year sentence; van Meegeren died 30 Dec 1947 (via Wikipedia, citing trial sources)

competing_hypotheses: Lopez's revision (2008): van Meegeren's 'I duped Goering to teach the Nazis a lesson' narrative was a trial-defense construction; the sale was an ordinary business transaction — the propagandistic works he painted for the German-installed government and donations to Nazi causes complicate the patriot story
Whether Bredius's 1937 authentication was honest scholarly error or eagerness fed by nationalist desire for a great Vermeer (carried as interpretation, not adjudicated)
falsifiability: Genuine 17th-century material signatures in the Emmaus paint — no Bakelite, no Albertol, no anachronistic pigments — would overturn the forgery finding

title: The Atanasoff–Berry Computer (1937–1942)
claim: The Atanasoff–Berry Computer (ABC), built by John Vincent Atanasoff and Clifford Berry in the basement of the physics building at Iowa State College (1937–1942), was a working electronic digital computer — binary arithmetic, vacuum-tube switching, regenerative capacitive memory kept separate from computation — and the documented prior art from which the ENIAC inventors derived the automatic electronic digital computer. John Mauchly visited Ames for five days in June 1941 as Atanasoff's houseguest, studied the machine in detail with the schematics, and helped Berry work on it.
place: Basement of the physics building, Iowa State College, Ames, Iowa
grade_reason: Multiple independent lines converge: Atanasoff's own design manuscript and the 1939–40 grant trail, Mauchly's documented 1941 visit (both men's testimony), the 1997 working replica proving the engineering was real, and a federal court's factual findings. Held below VERIFIED because the priority narrative runs largely through the trial record and later biographies rather than contemporaneous engineering journals — the ABC's own press coverage at the time was effectively nil.
earliest_attestation: Atanasoff's 35-page design manuscript (1939–40), reviewed by Mauchly in June 1941; the 1967–73 trial record formalizes the machine's priority role.

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Atanasoff–Berry computer' — binary + vacuum tubes + separate memory; dismantled 1948; 1997 Delwyn Bluhm/John Gustafson working replica ($350,000)

hhuc.hotbed.a2hosted.com, 'Name the First Electronic Digital Computer?' — 1939 prototype timeline ($650 grant, Berry hired spring 1939, working by end of 1939); Mauchly's May/June 1941 five-day visit, schematics review, denied copy request, machine 'mostly complete and functional'

thingshavehistory.com, 'The Atanasoff-Berry Computer, or the basement machine that unmade ENIAC' — June 1941 visit via Computer History Museum; binary arithmetic, electronic switching, memory separate from computation as the architecture
