The near-miss reading (Shurkin): the ABC was a clever near-miss — a special-purpose linear-equation solver, never fully operational (the binary card punch/reader stayed the lingering issue), influential rather than first — carried fairly; the record's claim is prior art and influence, not a production computer
falsifiability: Contemporaneous evidence that Mauchly's June 1941 visit did not occur, or that the machine's documented binary/electronic features postdate ENIAC — the trial record's 77 witnesses run the other way.

title: 'La Guardia's 1937 ban killed burlesque'
claim: La Guardia's 1937 action against burlesque was a ban that killed burlesque — the form died in 1937.
place: New York City, USA (the telling's home address; the form survived elsewhere)
grade_reason: DEBUNKED on three independent lines: (1) it was never a ban — it was a license campaign: the State Court of Appeals had ruled Moss could not revoke without a criminal conviction, and the weapon was the refusal to renew licenses, not a prohibition statute; (2) it did not kill burlesque — it killed burlesque in New York City: the Minskys opened productions in Miami, Chicago, and New Orleans, road shows toured the country, Harold Minsky's Follies ran six years at the Dunes in Las Vegas from 1957, the form lingered into the 1970s, and neo-burlesque revived it in the late 1990s; (3) the New York houses were offered a choice — reopen under the no-stripper code — and it was the economics of the compliant shows, not the law, that closed them ('business under the new code was so bad that many closed their doors for good'). Scope fenced: kills the flat 'ban = national death' reading, never the April 1937 raid, never the license refusals, never the no-stripper code, never New York burlesque's genuine collapse, never the advertising restrictions on the words 'burlesque' and 'Minsky'.
earliest_attestation: The telling itself is a modern shorthand (pop-history one-liners, the 'La Guardia banned burlesque' formulation); no contemporary source describes a 1937 ban statute.

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Minsky's Burlesque' (secondary aggregator: the no-ban, license-refusal mechanism; the Minskys 'finished in New York' — in New York)

UNLV Special Collections / ONE article, 'Minsky's Burlesque' (institutional: family opened productions in Miami, Chicago, and New Orleans; road shows; Harold Minsky's six-year Follies run at the Dunes, Las Vegas, beginning 1957)
Wikipedia, 'American burlesque' (secondary aggregator: 'Burlesque lingered on elsewhere in the U.S.'; the form's 'final shabby demise' only in the 1970s)

competing_hypotheses: The compression is fair as New York City history: the city's burlesque really did collapse under the license-kill, and the form's afterlife elsewhere was a different thing (carried fairly: NYC burlesque's death is not in dispute — only the word 'ban' and the national flat reading are)

The license action was effectively a ban in practice, since no compliant house could survive economically (carried fairly: the no-stripper code's economics did the closing — but a choice under bad economics is not a prohibition, and the distinction is the record)
falsifiability: A 1937 New York City statute criminalizing burlesque performance per se (rather than the documented license-refusal campaign), or evidence that no burlesque-form performance continued anywhere in the United States after 1937.

title: The Supper at Emmaus as a genuine Vermeer
claim: The Supper at Emmaus — bought by Museum Boijmans (Rotterdam) in 1937 for 520,000 guilders after Abraham Bredius authenticated it in The Burlington Magazine as 'the masterpiece of Johannes Vermeer of Delft' — is a genuine painting by Johannes Vermeer (1632–1675).
place: Rotterdam, Netherlands (Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen)
grade_reason: Three independent kills: (1) the painter's own confession (May 1945) plus his courtroom re-demonstration under observation; (2) the Coremans commission's chemistry — phenol-formaldehyde resins Bakelite and Albertol, 20th-century inventions, in paint supposedly three centuries old, with a resin bottle found in his studio; (3) the museum record itself: Boijmans withdrew the Vermeer attribution after the confession.
earliest_attestation: Abraham Bredius's authentication in The Burlington Magazine, 1937

sources.ref: Coremans commission (1945–47, Paul B. Coremans): Bakelite + Albertol resins identified in the paint; resin bottle found in van Meegeren's studio (via Wikipedia, citing commission sources)
Van Meegeren's confession (May 1945) + the courtroom demonstration painting Jesus among the Doctors, painted under observation July–Dec 1945
Amsterdam Regional Court record, 29 Oct–12 Nov 1947: forgery and fraud conviction; collaboration charges dropped because the 'Vermeer' sold to Goering was not Dutch cultural property
Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen: the painting displayed as the collection's highlight 1937–1945, the Vermeer attribution withdrawn after the confession (Boijmans Studies, reported 2025)

NPR (Dolnick, 2008): the unmasking came from Goering's meticulous paperwork tracing the Adulteress back to van Meegeren — 'Most forgers fool one person too few... that never happened with van Meegeren'

competing_hypotheses: The 1937 authentication was honest scholarly error: Bredius, the foremost Vermeer scholar of the age, genuinely saw a Vermeer where none was (the standard reading)

The acceptance was eagerness: the painting was exactly the 'missing' religious-period Vermeer that scholarship predicted should exist — 'they only had to look like the Vermeer that he had introduced into the accepted works' (Dolnick, 2008)
falsifiability: Contemporaneous 17th-century provenance for the canvas, or paint analysis showing no 20th-century materials, would reopen the attribution

title: The Roman-chariot-rut origin of standard gauge — DEBUNKED
claim: The world's standard railroad gauge of 1,435 mm (4 ft 8 1/2 in) descends from the ruts left by Roman chariots and war wagons — the story that George Stephenson's gauge, and the whole modern railway system, preserves the Roman wheel standard through two millennia of road vehicles that kept running in the same ruts.
grade_reason: DEBUNKED as a transmission claim — the 81st DEBUNKED family. Three independent kills: (1) no documented chain: nothing in Stephenson's workshop practice, letters, or the 1846 Royal Commission record (48 witnesses, 35 for Stephenson's gauge) invokes Roman ruts; (2) the actual workshop history is recoverable and Roman-free: 4 ft 8 in Killingworth/Stockton & Darlington edge-rail practice, the half inch added to reduce binding on curves (the summarize.tech railway-gauge video summarizes this; the 'arbitrary five feet' version is quadibloc); (3) tramway gauges in Stephenson's own district varied widely — 4 ft, 4 ft 4 in, 4 ft 7 1/2 in, 5 ft — which is exactly what you expect from local workshop practice and exactly not what you expect from a preserved imperial standard. Snopes categorizes the legend 'false.' The grade kills the LINEAGE, not the gauge: 1,435 mm is real, Stephenson's choice is real, and the Evans/Pompeii measurements (Roman vehicles ~4 ft 9 in) stand as honestly-documented coincidence, carried in competing hypotheses.
earliest_attestation: The legend 'has circulated since at least 1937' (Standard-gauge railway, Wikipedia, citing earlier folklore histories); a model-railroading writer traces the Roman-rut supposition to references in 1914 and 1958 (quadibloc). The specific form — Roman ruts → Stephenson → standard gauge — is modern folklore with no ancient attestation.

sources.ref: Standard-gauge railway, Wikipedia — Origins section: legend 'circulated since at least 1937'; Snopes categorized 'false'; tramway gauge table (4 ft to 5 ft variants)
Trains magazine reader answer, reprinted in power-eng 'Dimensions in Time – Revisited' — Stephenson's 4 ft 8 in choice, the Gauge Wars, the Royal Commission (48 witnesses, 35 in favor), the 1846 Act
Trains.com, 'Track gauge: Different degrees of separation' — Walton W. Evans's Pompeii rut measurements (~4 ft 9 in center-to-center), Charles E. Lee on horse-sized optima
quadibloc.com, 'Gauge is Not Scale — Does Ancient Rome Come into the Picture?' — the 1914/1958 folklore references; the 'arbitrary five feet' workshop reconstruction

competing_hypotheses: The honest middle (Snopes' 'partly true, but for trivial and unremarkable reasons'): horse-drawn vehicles in Stephenson's Northumberland were roughly 5 ft outside-to-outside because that is about the width that fits a carthorse between the shafts (Charles E. Lee's 'optimal size of a road vehicle relative to the indivisible size of a horse'). Stephenson started from a tramway-scale vehicle ~5 ft wide, not from any Roman document or measurement. A vague horse-width resemblance is not a lineage.

Trains magazine's version of the truth (March 2000 reader answer, reprinted power-eng): Stephenson selected 4 ft 8 in as a 'narrow' gauge for his own railways; other companies chose other gauges (Surrey Iron 4 ft, GWR 7 ft 1/4 in); the Royal Commission heard 48 witnesses and the 1846 Gauge Act fixed 4 ft 8 1/2 in by statute — a political-economic decision, not an archaeological one.

The Evans corroboration (Trains.com, from the 1870s Pompeii excavations): Roman road vehicles did often run at roughly 4 ft 9 in center-to-center — later archaeology confirmed a Roman common vehicle gauge close to modern values. This is convergence on a horse-sized optimum, not transmission: no documentary chain connects Roman ruts to Stephenson's workshop, and Stephenson never cited any such source.
falsifiability: A contemporary document (pre-1846) in which Stephenson, his associates, or the gauge commission cite Roman wheel ruts as the basis for the gauge would reverse the verdict. Two centuries of railway archives have produced none.

title: The nylon toothbrush (1938) — the end of animal bristles
claim: In 1938, DuPont introduced the first toothbrush with synthetic nylon bristles (Dr. West's Miracle-Tuft Toothbrush), ending the centuries-long dependence on animal-hair bristles.
place: Wilmington, Delaware, USA (DuPont)
grade_reason: The 1938 introduction is multiply and independently attested across dental histories, broadcast archives, and the company's own record; the date does not wander.

Dental-history convention: nylon invented mid-1930s; the first nylon toothbrush appeared on the market in 1938; softer nylon bristles by the 1950s (dental-history timelines)
The post-nylon arc: the 1939 Swiss electric toothbrush; the 1960 US Broxodent (Squibb); the 1961 GE rechargeable cordless — the same documentary tradition, carried comparatively

title: The Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact (23 August 1939)

Contemporary world press coverage, 24 August 1939

title: 'RCA invented television' (the Sarnoff claim)
claim: Electronic television was invented by RCA — David Sarnoff's Radio Corporation of America — and specifically by RCA's engineer Vladimir Zworykin, the 'father of television'; the independent inventor Philo Farnsworth contributed nothing original to electronic TV.
place: Flushing Meadows, Queens, New York (1939 World's Fair RCA pavilion)
grade_reason: The U.S. Patent Office decided Interference No. 64,027 against RCA in February 1935 — Farnsworth, not Zworykin, had priority on the electrical image — RCA's 1936 appeal lost, and RCA took a Farnsworth license in 1939 (about $1 million in royalties). A company that licenses the invention from the priority winner did not invent it; the World's Fair story was the marketing of a licensee.
earliest_attestation: RCA publicity around the 1939 New York World's Fair television launch; Sarnoff-era corporate claims that RCA 'invented television'

sources.ref: MIT Technology Review, 'Who Really Invented Television?' (Sept 2000): Zworykin's April 1930 visit to Farnsworth's Green Street lab ('Dr. Zworykin was there for three days, and he saw everything' — Pem Farnsworth); Farnsworth built an image dissector before his eyes; Sarnoff–Zworykin collaboration

Wikipedia, 'Philo Farnsworth': patent interference brought by RCA in 1934, decided February 1935 (Tolman's 1922 sketch; spring-1922 blackboard drawing testimony); RCA appealed in 1936 and lost; Farnsworth received royalties from RCA; Zworykin's 1930 visit to Farnsworth's lab before leaving Westinghouse, Westinghouse team made copies of the Image Dissector

JDSupra, 'The Top Ten Patent Wars — Television (#10)': 'RCA used its marketing might, after taking a million-dollar license from Farnsworth after losing the interference proceedings, and claimed to the world that it had invented television through a much-hyped launch at the 1939 New York World's Fair'

competing_hypotheses: The corporate-invention reading: RCA's television was the genuine system innovation — Zworykin's Iconoscope, RCA's engineering organization, and the 1939 launch deserve the invention title even if Farnsworth had priority on one patent; invention and industrialization are graded separately.

The Zworykin-independence reading: Zworykin's 1923 Westinghouse application represents independent invention, and his 1930 lab visit added nothing material — RCA's interference case was good faith, and Farnsworth's priority was a legal accident of Tolman's preserved sketch.

The mechanical-priority reading: true television priority belongs to the mechanical pioneers (Baird's 1926 public demonstration, Jenkins) and 'electronic television' is a category drawn to favor Farnsworth; the corporate-vs-lone-inventor framing is the wrong fight.

The Farnsworth-skeptical reading: Farnsworth's image dissector was a technical dead end (required blinding illumination, no storage), and the eventual television camera descended from Zworykin's storage principle — so the commercial victor deserves the historical title.
falsifiability: A pre-1934 RCA laboratory record showing a working Zworykin electronic television camera transmitting an electronic image independently of anything seen at Farnsworth's Green Street lab — or a showing that Interference No. 64,027 was decided on grounds other than Farnsworth's priority — would reopen the grade.

claim: On 23 August 1939, alongside the public Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, Ribbentrop and Molotov signed a Secret Additional Protocol dividing Eastern Europe into German and Soviet spheres of influence: the Baltic states (Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania) with Lithuania's northern boundary as the sphere line; Poland along the Narew-Vistula-San rivers; and Bessarabia noted as a Soviet interest — the document to be treated as 'strictly secret'.

US Department of State, 'Nazi-Soviet Relations, 1939-1941' (1948) — full verbatim publication of the protocol

title: The fifty-year denial of the secret protocol (1939-1989)
claim: The secret protocol of 23 August 1939 never existed — it was a Western forgery, and the Soviet Union's official position denying its existence (maintained from 1939 to 1989) was correct.
place: Moscow (the denial's issuing authority)
grade_reason: Killed twice: (1) the captured German Foreign Office microfilms of the signed originals, published verbatim by the US State Department in 1948, predate any possible Cold War fabrication and were examined by the FRG in 1989; (2) Moscow itself abandoned the denial in 1989 — the Yakovlev commission's findings and the 24 December 1989 Congress declaration confirming and denouncing the secret protocols, followed by the 1992 declassification of the Soviet copy.

sources.ref: US Department of State, 'Nazi-Soviet Relations, 1939-1941' (1948) — the 1948 publication that made the denial's factual position untenable
Stalin (ed.), 'Falsifiers of History' (1948) — the Soviet counter-narrative

title: Aeroelastic flutter: the mechanism that killed Galloping Gertie
claim: The destructive final oscillation of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge on 7 November 1940 was aeroelastic flutter: the slender 8-foot plate-girder deck, displaced by the wind, shed motion-induced vortices whose aerodynamic forces fed energy back into the twist — a self-excited oscillation with effectively negative damping, in a fundamental antisymmetric torsion mode that had not manifested until ~45 minutes before the collapse. title: The paper clip as Norway's WWII resistance symbol

title: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapses (7 November 1940)
claim: The first Tacoma Narrows suspension bridge ('Galloping Gertie'), opened 1 July 1940, collapsed into Puget Sound on the morning of 7 November 1940 after violent torsional oscillations in ~42 mph winds; the center span fell around 11:00–11:10 AM. No people died; the only casualty was Tubby, a cocker spaniel left in a car on the deck. The collapse was filmed (Barney Elliott, Harbine Monroe) and studied by a Federal Works Agency commission in 1941.
place: Tacoma Narrows, Washington, USA
grade_reason: Multiply attested by contemporary film, the federal commission report, newspapers, and the state DOT's own historical record.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary: the Elliott/Monroe film (November 1940), newspaper coverage, and the Federal Works Agency Board of Engineers report (1941)

title: The Tacoma Narrows 'resonance' explanation (the textbook myth)

place: Tacoma Narrows, Washington, USA
grade_reason: Two independent kills: (1) the physics — the wind was a steady ~42 mph, not a periodic forcing at the natural frequency; the destructive motion was torsional flutter, a self-excited oscillation with negative aerodynamic damping (Billah & Scanlan 1991); (2) the amplitude record — Feldman 2003 showed 'no resonance behavior in the amplitude as a function of wind velocity' for the torsional mode, and the 1941 federal board had already judged ordinary vortex resonance 'very improbable.'

falsifiability: A measurement showing the wind's periodic forcing matched the bridge's natural torsional frequency at the moment of failure — the 1941 board and all subsequent analyses find the opposite

title: De Mestral invents the hook-and-loop fastener (1941–1954)

The name etymology may be post-hoc branding lore — carried as the company's own telling, not independently verified

title: The 'Alexander son of Simon' ossuary (1941 Kidron find; the Simon-of-Cyrene identification pressed October 2026)

title: The curse of Tamerlane: opening the tomb in June 1941 unleashed the invasion of the USSR
claim: Opening Timur's tomb in June 1941 released a supernatural curse — announced by the inscribed warning 'whomsoever opens my tomb shall unleash an invader more terrible than I' — that caused Nazi Germany's invasion of the Soviet Union (Operation Barbarossa) on 22 June 1941; the curse was lifted when Timur was reburied in November 1942, before Stalingrad.
place: Gur-e Amir mausoleum, Samarkand, Uzbekistan (the legend's scene)
grade_reason: Two independent kills. (1) The inscribed warning does not exist: the coffin's interior carries a simple Islamic prayer, the jade slab a genealogy — Semenov's translation found no curse; the 'warning' came from a 19th-century legend book, and even the 1941 team's own men attributed the curse idea to a grave-robber deterrent. (2) The causal mechanism is impossible: Operation Barbarossa was planned since July 1940 and formally ordered by Directive No. 21 on 18 December 1940 — six months BEFORE the tomb was opened. The June 1941 timing is post hoc ergo propter hoc, the purest specimen on the timeline.
earliest_attestation: No ancient or Timurid-era curse text exists. The modern legend's first detailed Soviet publication was a 1990 Zvezda Vostoka article; it was popularized by Aleksandr Fetisov's 2004 documentary (cameraman Malik Qayumov's interview). The 1941 'warning' the legend leans on came from a 19th-century Jangnoma book of local legends, not an ancient manuscript.

Yale Avalon Project, Nuremberg Judgement on the Aggressive War Against the USSR (citing captured OKW file 446-PS) — Directive No. 21 issued 18 December 1940, 'issued more than six months in advance of the attack'; planning since July 1940 under 'Operation Otto'; preparations complete by 15 May 1941. The three-old-men scene (multiple accounts): men handed Sadriddin Ayni a manuscript warning of a curse — but it was the Jangnoma, a 19th-century book of local legends, not an ancient script; Ayni 'shooed them away with a stick' and attributed the curse idea to a post-Timur legend invented to deter grave robbers; Qayumov's 2004 retelling (Persian-script warning he could not read; Ayni's son Kamal confirmed the men, disputed details)

competing_hypotheses: The 2004 Qayumov retelling's emphasis (the teahouse warning, the lights going out) — atmosphere, not evidence; the electrician found no cause, and foul smells attend exhumations generally (cf. the Tutankhamun-curse parallel cited on the Wikipedia page)
The 'coincidence deserves respect' reading: the June 20-to-June 22 timing genuinely spooked people, including expedition members — belief was real; but real belief is not a causal mechanism
falsifiability: The claim is already falsified twice over; reviving it would require either (a) the production of the inscribed warning in the tomb or coffin (it has been translated: it isn't there), or (b) evidence that Barbarossa's planning postdated June 1941 (it predates it by eleven months).

title: The Venona Project
claim: From 1 February 1943 to 1 October 1980, the US Army's Signal Intelligence Service (later the NSA) ran a counterintelligence program at Arlington Hall that decrypted and translated approximately 2,900–3,000 Soviet intelligence cables (NKVD/KGB/GRU, mostly 1942–1946), revealing extensive Soviet espionage in the United States during and after World War II. The decrypts were declassified and publicly released beginning 11 July 1995.
place: Arlington Hall, Virginia (project headquarters)
grade_reason: Multiple independent primary lines converge: the NSA's own released summary history, the 1995/1996 declassification releases, the FBI's published history, and the 1999 Haynes & Klehr archival study; the one-time-pad reuse blunder (~35,000 duplicate key pages) is cryptographically documented.
earliest_attestation: The project itself was secret until 1995; the earliest PUBLIC attestation of its existence by name is MI5 officer Peter Wright's memoir 'Spycatcher' (1987), followed by the official 11 July 1995 release ceremony hosted by DCI John M. Deutch at CIA headquarters.

sources.ref: NSA, 'Venona — Summary History' (18 May 1995, internal summary released with the 1995 materials): project ran 1 Feb 1943 – 1 Oct 1980; ~2,200 translations published; KGB NY 1944 traffic 49% readable; worked with GCHQ from 1948
CIA/DVIDS, 'Venona Officially Released to the Public (11 Jul 1995)': SSA began 1 Feb 1943 on Clarke's order; collection began 1939; Weisband tip 1948; ~2,900 messages shared by the 1996 conference

John Earl Haynes & Harvey Klehr, 'Venona: Decoding Soviet Espionage in America' (Yale University Press, 1999), Chapter 1: Clarke's separate-peace motive; the 349 Americans with covert ties; the compartmentalization that kept McCarthy-era demagogues mixing 'accurate information about betrayal by men such as Harry White and Alger Hiss with falsehoods about Acheson and Marshall'

Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan, tribute to Meredith Gardner, Congressional Record vol. 145 (S8293): NSA 'spent four decades deciphering what Moscow intended to be an unbreakable Soviet cipher'; the decrypts 'finally revealed publicly in 1995'

competing_hypotheses: The 1945 Soviet knowledge of the break (Weisband, Philby) means some decrypted traffic may have been seeded as disinformation — no confirmed case of a fabricated Venona message has been produced, but the possibility is the standard caveat in the literature

The ~3,000 decrypted messages represent a small and possibly unrepresentative fraction of the hundreds of thousands of intercepted cables — the project sees only what the 1942 duplicate pads made readable
falsifiability: Authenticated Soviet archival records showing the decrypted plaintexts do not match the originals, or proof the 1995 releases were forged; neither has ever been produced — 'no one has ever challenged their authenticity' (Frederick M. Hess review, Free Library)

title: DEBUNKED: 'ENIAC was the first electronic computer'
claim: The claim that ENIAC (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer) was the first electronic computer is false. The invention of the automatic electronic digital computer was legally assigned by a federal court to John Vincent Atanasoff, whose Atanasoff–Berry Computer predates ENIAC by years; John Mauchly examined Atanasoff's machine in detail during a five-day visit to Ames, Iowa, in June 1941, three years before ENIAC's construction began. Seventy-third DEBUNKED family.
place: Moore School of Electrical Engineering, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia (where the claim was built); U.S. District Court, Minneapolis (where it was unmade)
grade_reason: A federal court, after 135 days of testimony and 77 witnesses, found as fact that the ENIAC inventors derived the subject matter of the electronic digital computer from Atanasoff's earlier machine — which the ENIAC camp's own John Mauchly had studied on site in 1941.
earliest_attestation: The 'ENIAC = first computer' claim enters the press with the 1946 unveiling; the counter-evidence enters the legal record with Honeywell v. Sperry Rand, filed 26 May 1967, decided 19 Oct 1973.

sources.ref: Honeywell, Inc. v. Sperry Rand Corp., 180 U.S.P.Q. 673 (D. Minn. 1973) — Wikipedia summary of the ruling: ENIAC patent invalidated; inventors derived the subject matter from the ABC; Atanasoff should have legal recognition as the inventor of the first electronic digital computer
Gizmodo, 'Why Was the Computer Never Patented?' — the longest federal trial to date: 77 witnesses, ~33,000 exhibits, four grounds for invalidation including derivation
Chronicle of Higher Education, 'An Ancient Feud: Who Invented the Computer?' — Mauchly's June 1941 five-day Ames visit; Atanasoff's charge of borrowing; ENIAC operational 1946
Associated Press obituary (Roanoke Times, 17 June 1995) — 'waited more than 30 years to receive credit'; National Medal of Technology 1990; prototype completed 1939

competing_hypotheses: The general-purpose reading: ENIAC was the first general-purpose, programmable, fully electronic digital computer publicly demonstrated (1946) — the ABC was a special-purpose equation solver never put into full production, and a court ruling on patent priority is not a ruling on historical firstness

The Colossus-first reading: Colossus Mark 1 (Dec 1943) ran before ENIAC — counter: special-purpose cipher machines, fenced to Dr. Rowan Ashmore's cipher beat; the general-purpose distinction is where the comparison lives
falsifiability: Contemporaneous documentation that Eckert and Mauchly developed the electronic digital computer independently of Atanasoff's machine and the 1941 visit — the 1973 court's factual findings run the other way.

title: TELLING (DEBUNKED): the whole nine yards = WWII ammo belt
claim: TELLING (DEBUNKED): 'The whole nine yards' comes from the length of a World War II fighter plane's machine-gun ammunition belt — nine yards of belt, hence 'give 'em the whole nine yards.'
place: Kentucky print culture (where the phrase is documented)
grade_reason: The documented prints (1946-51 Lexington KY, 1956/57 KHHG) predate the theory's reach, and the 1912 'whole six yards' variant shows the number was never fixed to any nine-yard object — a belt of exactly nine yards cannot explain 'six yards.'
earliest_attestation: The WWII-belt story circulates in print from the late 20th century; the phrase is documented in print from 1946-51

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Nine yards' — the antedating chain vs. the ammunition-belt theory
Fred R. Shapiro, Yale Alumni Magazine — 'every theory must be assessed in light of the dated documentation — or lack thereof'

competing_hypotheses: The kilt-cloth theory (nine yards in a kilt)
The cement-mixer theory (nine cubic yards in a truck) — both die on the same dates
An unattested older nautical or textile origin
falsifiability: A WWII-era document connecting the phrase to ammunition belts, antedating the 1946-51 Kentucky prints

title: The cryptonym caveat
claim: A decrypted Venona cable names a person. The NSA's cryptanalysts assigned real names to the Soviet cryptonyms, and the identifications are settled. (The methodological caveat every historian of Venona must carry: the transcripts identify about 349 Americans with a covert relationship to Soviet intelligence, but fewer than half have been matched to real-name identities; the cryptonym-to-person match is a method, not a conviction.)
place: Arlington Hall, Virginia (the identifications' working room)
grade_reason: Corroborated by convergent independent lines (defectors, FBI files, confessions, post-1991 Russian archival releases), but held below VERIFIED because the identifications are inherently inferential: the same person sometimes had different cryptonyms, the same cryptonym was sometimes reused, and the flagship matches are disputed on the record.
earliest_attestation: The decrypted translations themselves (1946 onward), cross-filed against FBI investigative records and defector testimony; the NSA's published decryption-rate table (1942: 1.8%; 1943: 15.0%; 1944: 49.0%; 1945: 1.5%)

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Venona project' (citing the NSA): 'To what extent the various individuals referred to in the messages were involved with Soviet intelligence is a topic of minor historical dispute... most of the individuals mentioned in the Venona decrypts were probably either clandestine assets and/or contacts'; decryption-rate table: 1942 1.8%, 1943 15.0%, 1944 49.0%, 1945 1.5%; 'Out of some hundreds of thousands of intercepted encrypted texts, it is claimed under 3,000 have been partially or wholly decrypted'

Haynes & Klehr, 'Venona' (Yale, 1999), Ch. 1: the decrypted cables 'identify 349 citizens, immigrants, and permanent residents of the United States who had had a covert relationship with Soviet intelligence agencies'; 'less than half could be identified by their real names and nearly two hundred remained hidden behind cover names'; the same-cover-name cases: 'Muse' (unidentified OSS woman), 'Source No. 19' (claimed as Hopkins, Benes, or Duggan by different authors), 'Bibi', 'Donald', 'Quantum', 'Pers', 'Mole'

competing_hypotheses: The maximalist reading (cryptonym = identified agent) used in some popular accounts — the NSA's own decryption-rate table argues against overconfidence
The minimalist reading (the codenames prove nothing) — rejected by the convergent lines: defector testimony, confessions, and later Soviet-archival evidence that confirm many matches
falsifiability: Independent primary evidence (Soviet archives, trial records, confessions) contradicting a specific cryptonym match — which is exactly how the disputed matches are adjudicated in the literature

title: The 'peaceful handover' myth of decolonization
claim: The European empires ended peacefully — independence was granted by the colonizers rather than taken by the colonized, without war or systematic violence on the colonizers' part.
place: Cape Town, South Africa (the 'Wind of Change' speech, 3 Feb 1960 — the myth's emblematic telling; the claim itself spans the decolonizing world, 1947-1990)
grade_reason: Four independent kills from the colonizers' own paper trails. (1) Kenya: the 1952-1960 Emergency's detention/torture system, exposed by the Hanslope Park 'migrated archives' (~8,800 files from 37 colonies) and settled by the British government itself — £19.9M to 5,228 Kenyans in 2013 (Elkins 'Imperial Reckoning', 2005; Anderson 'Histories of the Hanged', 2005). (2) Malaya: the 1948-1960 counterinsurgency — the Briggs Plan's forced resettlement of ~half a million people into ~600 'New Villages' and the Batang Kali killings of 11-12 Dec 1948 (24 unarmed civilians, Scots Guards; covered up for decades). (3) Algeria: the 1 Nov 1954 - 19 Mar 1962 war that France legally called 'operations for the maintenance of order' for 37 years, renamed the 'guerre d'Algérie' only by Law 99-882 of 18 Oct 1999; 350,000-400,000 Algerian dead by census comparison (Stora 2005; Algerian official figure 1.5M), systematic torture documented (Vidal-Naquet; Branche 2001). (4) India 1947: ~15 million displaced and 0.5-2 million killed at the empire's exit (Satia/Stanford; Dalrymple). The blanket 'peaceful handover' reading is disproven by the colonizers' own archives, courts, and legislatures.
earliest_attestation: The postwar 'orderly withdrawal' narrative — emblematically Harold Macmillan's 'Wind of Change' speech to the South African parliament, Cape Town, 3 February 1960, framing the end of empire as an accommodating inevitability rather than a contested fight.

sources.ref: Caroline Elkins, 'Imperial Reckoning' (2005) — the Kenya detention-camp system (Pulitzer Prize, history)
David Anderson, 'Histories of the Hanged' (2005) — the Kenya Emergency's executions and the colonial state's paper trail
Brill, 'Architecture of Denial' — the Hanslope Park migrated archives (~8,800 files from 37 former colonies) and the Mau Mau court case
2013 UK Mau Mau settlement — £19.9M to 5,228 Kenyans (Foreign Secretary William Hague's statement)
'Malayan Emergency', English Wikipedia — Briggs Plan resettlement (~500k-1M into ~600 New Villages), Batang Kali 11-12 Dec 1948 (24 unarmed civilians, Scots Guards, cover-up)
French Law 99-882 of 18 Oct 1999 (Journal Officiel) — substituting 'guerre d'Algérie' for 'opérations effectuées en Afrique du Nord'
Stora/Eldridge via Perlego, 'The Algerian War, The Algerian Revolution' — census-comparison death toll 350,000-400,000 (Algerian official figure 1.5M), 'war without a name' until 1999
Priya Satia (Stanford historian) on the Partition of India — ~15M displaced, 0.5-2M killed
UN Digital Library — UNGA Resolution 1514 (XV), 14 Dec 1960: 89-0-9 vote record (the anti-colonial powers' own paper trail, adopted against the abstentions of the colonial powers)

competing_hypotheses: The mixed-record reading — that many transfers were negotiated and comparatively non-violent (much of French sub-Saharan Africa in 1960, Ghana 1957, the Caribbean independences) — is carried honestly: it is true of those cases and is what makes the BLANKET claim false rather than every-transfer false. The grade kills the blanket, not the exceptions.

The 'orderly wind-down' historiography (British 'transfer of power' school, early Macmillan-era framing) — carried as the scholarly form of the myth; the post-2011 archival releases (Hanslope Park migrated archives) are the evidence it has not survived.

The Algerian-state casualty figure of 1.5 million 'martyrs' is carried as the official national figure, not the scholarly range (350,000-400,000 per census comparisons, Stora 2005) — the grade holds on either number; the myth dies on the war's existence, not its exact toll.
falsifiability: Archival proof that the cited counterinsurgency campaigns, death tolls, and cover-ups never happened — e.g. the 2013 Mau Mau settlement and the Hanslope Park files being forgeries, or the French 1999 law having been unnecessary because a war had already been declared.

title: The withheld 1948 Peace Prize (Gandhi)
claim: The Nobel Peace Prize was not awarded in 1948, the year Mohandas Gandhi was assassinated (30 January 1948); the Norwegian Nobel Committee stated that 'there was no suitable living candidate.' The non-award is understood as the withheld Gandhi prize — posthumous award was possible at the time (Dag Hammarskjold received the 1961 Peace Prize posthumously), and the formal ban on posthumous awards came only in 1974.
place: Oslo
grade_reason: The non-award and the stated reason are documented fact; the Gandhi reading is the near-universal standard interpretation, supported by the 1961 posthumous award showing the committee could have honored him.
earliest_attestation: The Norwegian Nobel Committee's 1948 announcement; the 1961 posthumous Hammarskjold award; the 1974 statute change.

sources.ref: Norwegian Nobel Committee, 1948 — the non-award and the 'no suitable living candidate' statement
The 1961 posthumous Nobel Peace Prize to Dag Hammarskjold (the practice before the 1974 statute change)

competing_hypotheses: The committee's stated reason taken literally: 1948 had no living candidate the committee deemed suitable, Gandhi included
falsifiability: Committee minutes or correspondence from 1948 naming a different rationale for the non-award would refine the record.

title: The 1949 Roland Doe case: the best-documented possession dossier
claim: From January to April 1949, a fourteen-year-old boy from Cottage City, Maryland (later moved to St. Louis), documented under the pseudonyms 'Roland Doe' and 'Robbie Mannheim', was the subject of a series of Catholic exorcisms authorized by Archbishop Joseph Ritter and performed by Jesuit priests including Fr. William S. Bowdern, with Fr. Raymond J. Bishop keeping a diary (reportedly ~26 pages). The family's Lutheran minister referred them to Catholic help; forty-eight witnesses are said to have observed episodes, nine of them Jesuits (per Thomas B. Allen). Mid-1949 newspapers printed anonymous reports of the case. William Peter Blatty used the events in The Exorcist (1971). In December 2021, The Skeptical Inquirer reported the boy's identity as Ronald Edwin Hunkeler (1935–2020). Fr. Walter H. Halloran, one of the last surviving eyewitnesses, refused to go on record affirming a possession.
place: Cottage City, Maryland (family home); St. Louis, Missouri (St. Louis University Hospital; Alexian Brothers Hospital)
grade_reason: The documentary event is multiply attested: a contemporary priest's diary, mid-1949 newspaper reports, a 1993 documentary book built from the diary and interviews, archdiocesan authorization, and named dissenting witnesses (Halloran). The grade covers the file — who wrote it, who corroborates, who dissents. The possession itself is ungraded, per the attestation rule.
earliest_attestation: Bishop's diary (contemporary, surfaced publicly in the 1980s); the mid-1949 anonymous newspaper reports; Thomas B. Allen's Possessed (1993), built from the diary and interviews

sources.ref: Fr. Raymond J. Bishop's diary (contemporary, ~26 pages; published via Thomas B. Allen, Possessed, 1993)
Mid-1949 anonymous newspaper reports (the source thought to be the family's former pastor, Luther Miles Schulze)
Wikipedia, 'Exorcism of Roland Doe' — summarizes the diary record, Ritter's authorization, Halloran's refusal to affirm, the 2021 Skeptical Inquirer identification
Skeptical Inquirer, December 2021 — reports the identity as Ronald Edwin Hunkeler (1935–2020)
William Peter Blatty, The Exorcist (1971) — the cultural transmission of the case, not evidence for it

competing_hypotheses: The case as genuine possession: the Church treated the phenomena as real enough to authorize ~30 rites over Holy Week; the Church never issued a formal declaration of possession

The case as adolescent disturbance plus suggestion and cryptomnesia: Halloran himself 'expressed his skepticism about potential paranormal events before his death' (per Wikipedia, citing Allen); the entity is never adjudicated here
The case as the founding text of modern exorcism culture: Blatty's novel and the 1973 film transmitted the dossier to 100M+ viewers — graded as cultural transmission, not as evidence
falsifiability: Production of Bishop's diary showing the episodes were fabricated or never recorded; contemporary archdiocesan files showing no Ritter authorization; demonstration that the mid-1949 newspaper reports were hoaxes. This record claims the documentary trail, never the possession.

title: Dogon Sirius knowledge (Sirius Mystery)
claim: The Dogon people of Mali possessed inexplicable knowledge of Sirius B (invisible companion, ~50-year orbit, extreme density) — evidence of extraterrestrial contact (Robert Temple, The Sirius Mystery, 1976).
place: Bandiagara plateau, Mali (Dogon country)
grade_reason: Dutch anthropologist Walter van Beek's 1991 fieldwork found no Dogon outside Griaule's informant circle had ever heard of sigu tolo or po tolo, and none knew Sirius as a double star; astronomy is marginal in Dogon ritual life. Earlier critics (Goody 1967; Douglas 1968; Clifford 1983; Ridpath 1978) had already flagged the single-informant methodology. The extraterrestrial leap was Temple's, not Griaule's — and it rests on data that cannot be reproduced.
earliest_attestation: Marcel Griaule & Germaine Dieterlen's 1950 publication on Dogon cosmology, based largely on conversations with one informant (Ogotemmêli)

sources.ref: The Sirius Mystery article: Temple's claim, van Beek's findings, Brosch's cultural-transfer explanation, Ridpath's 1978 critique
badarchaeology.com: van Beek's 1991 fieldwork, single-informant problem, Sigu tolo/to polo identifications

competing_hypotheses: Cultural transfer: Western astronomical knowledge reached the Dogon via French expeditions (e.g., the 1893 Deslandres eclipse expedition), missionaries, or Griaule's own conversations — Noah Brosch's 'Sirius Matters' argument
Griaule's data was an artifact of his method: single-informant interviews through an interpreter, an enthusiastic amateur astronomer rationalizing confused lore (van Beek 1991; Ridpath 1978)
The lore is genuine Dogon cosmology that never was about Sirius B at all (Sigu tolo ≠ Sirius; to polo ≠ Sirius B) and got retrofitted by Western writers
falsifiability: Dated Dogon artifacts or records predating Western contact that unambiguously describe Sirius B's orbit and density would reopen the question. None exists; the claimed '400-year-old artifacts' have never been produced for examination.

title: The Fermi paradox (the argument, not the evidence)
claim: In 1950, over lunch at Los Alamos, Enrico Fermi asked 'Where is everybody?' — pointing at the tension between the high estimated number of habitable planets and the absence of observed extraterrestrials. The argument was formalized by Michael Hart ('An Explanation for the Absence of Extraterrestrials on Earth', 1975) and Frank Tipler (1980). It is a reasoning tool about scale versus silence, not evidence for or against extraterrestrial life.
place: Los Alamos, New Mexico (origin of the anecdote)
grade_reason: The argument's existence, its 1950 origin anecdote, and its 1975/1980 formalizations are multiply documented. The paradox is graded as an argument — it proves nothing about whether anyone is out there.
earliest_attestation: Recollections of Fermi's 1950 lunch conversation (published in various memoirs); Hart, QJRAS 16 (1975)

sources.ref: Michael H. Hart, 'An Explanation for the Absence of Extraterrestrials on Earth', Quarterly Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society 16 (1975)
Frank J. Tipler, 'Extraterrestrial Intelligent Beings Do Not Exist', QJRAS 21 (1980)
Recollections of the 1950 Fermi lunch (Herb York; Emil Konopinski, 'Where is Everybody?', Physics Today, 2003)

competing_hypotheses: The paradox dissolves: its premises (how common life is, how detectable it would be) are speculative — garbage in, paradox out
The 'zoo hypothesis' and non-interference: they are there and watching (untestable; SPECULATION)
The paradox holds force: at least one civilization should have colonized the galaxy in the time available — the silence is genuinely puzzling
falsifiability: The argument cannot be falsified as an argument; its conclusion ('somebody should be here') would be settled by a confirmed technosignature, which does not exist

title: Bette Nesmith Graham invents correction fluid (Mistake Out / Liquid Paper)

place: Dallas, Texas
grade_reason: CORROBORATED — 246th family's foil record. Multiply attested by independent secondaries (NYT 2018 'Overlooked No More', USPTO 'Perseverance, thy name is Bette', MPL, Wikipedia, East Texas Historical Association); held below VERIFIED because the 1951/1956 invention-date variance is unresolved and no contemporary 1951 document was inspected this pass.

sources.ref: NYT 'Overlooked No More: Bette Nesmith Graham, Who Invented Liquid Paper' (2018-07-11)
USPTO, 'Perseverance, thy name is Bette'
Minneapolis Public Library, 'Bette Nesmith Graham, Inventor of Liquid Paper' — 1951 kitchen-blender origin, 'Mistake Out', 1967: 1M+ units/year, sold to Gillette 1979 ~$48M
East Texas Historical Association (Sosebee 2022): born 1924, executive secretary, son Michael Nesmith of the Monkees

The 'fired for a typing error' origin story varies across tellings (fired 1958 for putting her company name on bank letterhead per Wikipedia; for a typing error per the viral video telling) — the firing itself is multiply attested, the exact trigger is not
falsifiability: A dated pre-1951 commercial correction-fluid product with the same formulation purpose, or contemporary evidence that Graham's 1951 kitchen experiments postdate a documented competitor's invention.

title: The 1952 Cuyahoga River fire (the big one)
claim: The 1952 Cuyahoga River fire was a genuinely large blaze — the biggest of the river's documented fires — causing over $1.3 million (some accounts say $1.5 million+) in damage. It is the fire whose photographs the nation actually saw: Time's 1 August 1969 article about the 1969 fire illustrated it with this blaze's picture.
place: Cuyahoga River, Cleveland, Ohio
grade_reason: The 1952 blaze is multiply attested as the large one — the $1.3M+ damage figure converges across accounts — and its photographs are the documented source of the Time 1969 illustration; held below VERIFIED on the damage figure's source variance ($1.3M vs $1.5M+) and thin primary-record citation in the secondary coverage.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary 1952 Cleveland press and photographs — the famous Cuyahoga-fire photographs come from THIS fire, not 1969

sources.ref: Smithsonian Magazine: Time's 1 Aug 1969 article used 'an accompanying photo from an incident in 1952' — the 1952 fire's image as the myth's visual fuel
Discover Magazine: the 1952 fire 'caused more than $1.5 million in damage [Cleveland Plain-Dealer]'
Zweiglist retrospective ('When the Cuyahoga River Burned'): 'the massive 1952 Cuyahoga River blaze that caused upwards of $1.3 million in damages'
Water Tech Online (40th anniversary): the 1952 fire in the thirteen-fire sequence

competing_hypotheses: The damage figure is honestly ranged: Smithsonian and the Zweiglist retrospective give 'upwards of $1.3 million'; Discover and the YouTube-era summaries give '$1.5 million+'. The order of magnitude, not the decimal, is the point — hence CORROBORATED, not VERIFIED.
falsifiability: Cleveland archive records showing the 1952 fire caused only minor damage — against every account, which agrees the 1952 blaze was the century's big one.

title: The Ipuwer-as-Exodus-plagues telling
claim: The Admonitions of Ipuwer (Papyrus Leiden I 344) are an Egyptian eyewitness record of the ten plagues of Exodus: 'the river is blood' describes the first plague, and the text's chaos imagery corroborates the biblical narrative. (Claim form; adjudicated.)

Habermehl (2018, Eighth International Conference on Creationism): the Admonitions preserve a genuine Egyptian memory of the plagues
