title: Blake's betrayal of the Berlin Tunnel (1953)
claim: George Blake, the MI6 officer assigned to the tunnel's planning side, informed his KGB handler of the tunnel plan in the autumn of 1953 — before construction began. Moscow faced a choice between exposing the tunnel (and protecting Soviet communications) and protecting Blake; it chose Blake. The KGB deliberately withheld knowledge of the tap even from the Soviet military users of the lines, let the tunnel operate for its full eleven months, and only staged its 'discovery' after Blake was transferred in 1955.
place: London (the SIS briefings and Blake's KGB handler meetings)
grade_reason: The KGB's pre-knowledge is established by the CIA's own declassified history and post-Soviet releases, which describe the deliberate choice to protect the source; the exact month of Blake's first tip varies by source (late-1953 briefing vs January 1954 planning meeting), holding the grade below VERIFIED.
earliest_attestation: The betrayal itself was secret until Blake's 1961 arrest and confession; the pre-knowledge is established in the CIA's declassified official history (the 22 October 1953 briefing with Blake in the audience) and post-Soviet releases

sources.ref: CIA official-history excerpt (booklife.com): 'On 22 October 1953, US intelligence officers briefed a British Secret Intelligence Service (SIS) audience that included KGB mole, George Blake'; the KGB's 'first priority was to protect Blake'; early in 1956 the Soviets developed a plan for the tap's 'accidental' discovery

Encyclopedia of Espionage, 'Berlin Tunnel' (faqs.org): 'Blake, employed in a technical division, gave information about the tunnel to the KGB when the project was still in the planning stages'; the KGB 'did not inform anyone in Germany, including the East Germans or the Soviet users of the cable lines'; 'When Blake received a transfer in 1955, the Soviets were free to "discover" the tunnel'

Eyewitness to History, 'The Russians Discover a Spy Tunnel in Berlin, 1956': Blake 'reported the plan to his KGB masters even before ground was broken'; after the Soviet collapse it emerged that the KGB 'never revealed the existence of the tunnel to their military comrades for fear that closing down the operation might alert their American and British adversaries to the existence of a mole within their ranks'

competing_hypotheses: The standard account: Blake tipped the KGB at the 22 October 1953 planning briefing or at the January 1954 joint planning meeting (the exact month varies by source; both precede construction)
Nuances in Blake's own memoir about the timing and channel of the tip — carried as an ungraded alternative, not a contradiction of the pre-knowledge
The minimalist reading that the KGB merely suspected rather than knew — rejected: the declassified record describes a deliberate decision to sacrifice the cables to protect the source
falsifiability: Contemporaneous KGB records showing no knowledge of the tunnel before 1956, or proof Blake's access to the planning was narrower than the planning-committee record shows

title: Wheeler's 'Massacre' at Mohenjo-daro
claim: Sir Mortimer Wheeler's 1953 interpretation that 37 skeletons found at Mohenjo-daro were the victims of an invading army that massacred the city's inhabitants in a single violent event — 'Indra stands accused' of destroying the Harappan civilization.
place: Mohenjo-daro, Sindh, Pakistan
grade_reason: The skeletons span multiple stratigraphic levels (some post-abandonment); forensic analysis shows no fatal trauma; no invader weapons or material culture were found; no informed scholar now defends the invasion reading.
earliest_attestation: Wheeler, M. — The Indus Civilization (1953)

sources.ref: Wheeler, M. — The Indus Civilization (1953); Wheeler's later qualification: 'This is a possibility, but it can't be proven, and it may not be correct'
Dales, G.F. (1964) — 'mythical massacre' refutation: skeletons from multiple stratigraphic levels, some in post-abandonment deposits
Kennedy, K. (1982/1984) — forensic reanalysis: skull 'damage' is post-mortem erosion, no fatal wound evidence; no proof the people were killed on the spot
Possehl, G. — Indus Age (1999): definitive obituary of the invasion hypothesis in the mainstream literature
Shinde et al. (2019, Cell) — Rakhigarhi ancient DNA: Harappan population was an indigenous South Asian group with deep continuity, no steppe-ancestry intrusion

competing_hypotheses: Wheeler's original reading (1953): invading Indo-Aryan 'Aryans' sacked the city — the claim this record debunks
Wheeler's own retreat: salinization and structural decay as the real destroyers; the corpses as an event in the final phase, not a conquest
Migration (not invasion) model: steppe-ancestry pastoralists arrived 2000–1500 BCE, after the cities' decline — compatible with the genetics, a migration not a massacre
falsifiability: Already falsified. To revive it would require a secure single destruction layer containing contemporary massacre victims plus identifiable invader material culture — the exact evidence the excavations failed to produce

title: Bernice Eddy's ignored 1954 warning (August 1954)
claim: In August 1954 — eight months before the Cutter Incident — NIH scientist Dr. Bernice Eddy, testing a submitted Cutter vaccine sample, found that it had given polio to a test monkey: the supposedly killed-virus vaccine contained live, infectious virus. She reported her findings, with photographs of the paralyzed monkeys, to her superiors — William Workman, head of the Laboratory of Biologics Control, and NIH director William Sebrell Jr. The warning was set aside; Eddy was removed from polio-vaccine safety work.
place: Bethesda, Maryland (National Institutes of Health)
grade_reason: The 1954 warning is reported in multiple independent secondary lines (Offit 2005, the Washington Post's 2020 retrospective, Boulder Weekly) with consistent details (the monkey, the photographs, the two superiors); held below VERIFIED because the institutional-motive reading is retrospective and the primary correspondence is not quoted in the available sources.
earliest_attestation: Eddy's 1954 laboratory findings and her report to Workman and Sebrell, as recounted in Offit's 'The Cutter Incident' (2005) and the Washington Post's April 14, 2020 retrospective.

sources.ref: Michael E. Ruane, Washington Post, April 14, 2020 — Eddy checking the Cutter sample August 30, 1954; the monkey given polio; 'There's going to be a disaster'; she was sidelined
Boulder Weekly, 'The Cutter incident: A cautionary tale for Operation Warp Speed' — Eddy reported paralyzed monkeys with pictures; Sebrell swept the warnings aside
The Maha Report, 'Public Health's Dirty Little Rule' — Eddy's report to Workman and Sebrell; her transfer for identifying the problem

competing_hypotheses: The warning was set aside because a single monkey-paralysis result was not yet a production-line verdict, not because of institutional suppression — the 'set aside' motive is inference, carried honestly
Eddy's later SV40 findings (late 1950s–early 1960s) colored the retrospective telling of the 1954 episode — the 1954 event itself is documented independently of her later history
falsifiability: NIH archival correspondence showing no such monkey test or report in 1954, or records showing Eddy remained on polio-vaccine safety work without interruption

title: Operation Gold — the Berlin Tunnel
claim: In 1954–55 the CIA and MI6 (Operation Gold / Operation Stopwatch) dug a ~450-meter tunnel from Rudow in the American sector of Berlin, under the sector boundary, to Altglienicke in the Soviet sector, where a vertical shaft tapped three Soviet military trunk cables. The tap ran from May 1955 until the night of 21–22 April 1956, recording on the order of 50,000 reels of tape (~40,000 hours of telephone conversations), of which some 443,000 conversations were fully transcribed, producing about 1,750 intelligence reports; the backlog was processed into 1958.
place: Rudow (US sector) → Altglienicke (Soviet sector), Berlin — beneath the sector boundary
grade_reason: The CIA's own declassified history, the US Army's military-intelligence chronicle, and multiple independent secondary accounts converge on the dig, the dates, and the operational scale; the exact reel and conversation totals ride secondary aggregators and the British half stays classified, holding the grade below VERIFIED.
earliest_attestation: The operation was secret until the 1956 Soviet publicity; the earliest documented internal attestation is the CIA's declassified official history (incl. the January 1954 approval and the 1968 after-action report)

sources.ref: US Army Intelligence Center of Excellence, 'This Week in Military Intelligence — Berlin Tunnel Ceases Operations' (DVIDS): ~50,000 six-hour reels recorded, ~30,000 transcribed; a mole had alerted the Soviets, who 'allowed the operations to continue to protect their source'; operations ceased 22 April 1956

Encyclopedia of Espionage, 'Berlin Tunnel' (faqs.org): tunnel construction ended March 1955, taps began in May; 443,000 transcribed conversations (368,000 Soviet, 75,000 East German), 1,750 intelligence reports; the KGB learned of the plan through Blake while it was still being planned

Eyewitness to History, 'The Russians Discover a Spy Tunnel in Berlin, 1956': Dulles approved the joint CIA/SIS plan January 1954; tunnel completed by May 1955, tapping cables with ~1,200 telephone lines; discovery 22 April 1956; Blake reported the plan 'even before ground was broken'

competing_hypotheses: The tap yielded genuine intelligence on a hard target (the CIA post-mortem position: no known disinformation attempts; the KGB never warned the Soviet users of the lines, so they spoke normally)

Moscow seeded disinformation or steered sensitive traffic off the known-tapped lines — the honest counter-reading given the KGB's documented pre-knowledge (graded separately: evt-berlin-tunnel-blake-betrayal-001)
The British-side figure totals differ in detail (the British half of the record remains officially classified, and Dulles ordered as little as possible reduced to writing)
falsifiability: Declassified construction or payment records showing no such dig was ever made, or proof the tapped Soviet cables never existed at that junction

title: The Bandung Conference, April 1955
claim: The Asian-African Conference met at Bandung, Indonesia, 18-24 April 1955: delegations from 29 Asian and African states, convened at the invitation of the five Colombo powers (Burma, Ceylon, India, Indonesia, Pakistan), condemned colonialism in its final communiqué, and adopted unanimously the ten-point 'Dasasila Bandung' (Ten Principles of Bandung) declaration on world peace and cooperation.
place: Gedung Merdeka (Merdeka Building), Bandung, Indonesia
grade_reason: Multiply and contemporaneously documented: the final communiqué itself, the Indonesian host records, the published opening speeches (Sukarno, Nehru, Nasser, Zhou Enlai), and contemporary world press all agree on the dates, the venue, the 29 delegations, and the Ten Principles adopted unanimously as item G.
earliest_attestation: The Final Communiqué of the Asian-African Conference itself (April 1955); Indonesian host-government records; contemporary world press coverage.

sources.ref: Final Communiqué of the Asian-African Conference (Bandung, April 1955) — the Ten Principles, item G
Asian-African Conference Museum, Gedung Merdeka, Bandung — conference records and delegate lists
'Bandung Conference', English Wikipedia — 29 states, 18-24 April 1955, Ten Principles (tertiary summary of the communique and scholarship)
Vijay Prashad, 'The Darker Nations' (2007) — the 'Spirit of Bandung' and what the conference meant to the colonized world

competing_hypotheses: The widespread shorthand that 'Bandung founded the Non-Aligned Movement' — this record does not assert it: NAM was founded at the First Summit in Belgrade, 1-6 September 1961; Bandung's Ten Principles became NAM's foundational framework, and only India, Burma and Indonesia explicitly supported non-alignment at Bandung itself (participants included NATO/Baghdad-Pact members Turkey and Pakistan).

The Cold-War framing that Bandung was a Soviet or Chinese front — carried honestly as the period's rival reading; the conference's own communiqué and the diversity of its 29 delegations are the evidence this reading has to get past.
falsifiability: Indonesian state archives or contemporary delegate records contradicting the dates, the 29-delegation attendance, or the unanimous adoption of the Ten Principles; or proof the communiqué was drafted after the fact.

title: The Cutter Incident (April–May 1955)
claim: In April 1955, production lots of Cutter Laboratories' Salk polio vaccine contained live poliovirus despite passing the required safety tests. On April 27, 1955, the Epidemic Intelligence Service determined that two Cutter production pools — about 120,000 doses — contained live virus; the same day, U.S. Surgeon General Leonard Scheele ordered all Cutter vaccine recalled. On May 6, 1955, the national polio vaccination program was suspended pending investigation of every manufacturer.
place: Berkeley, California (Cutter Laboratories)
grade_reason: The incident's occurrence is multiply attested in independent contemporary government records (EIS determination, Surgeon General recall order, May 6 program suspension) plus contemporary press and the congressional record — independent primary and documentary lines agree.
earliest_attestation: Epidemic Intelligence Service determination, April 27, 1955; U.S. Surgeon General's recall order, April 27, 1955; contemporary press (The Saturday Evening Post, September 10, 1955).

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Cutter Laboratories' — April 12 licensing, April 27 withdrawal, the Cutter incident section
Brill JOAH 2(1–2), 'To Boldly Remember Where We Have Already Been' — EIS April 27, 1955 determination (two production pools, 120,000 doses), Scheele recall the same day
SciELO (S0211-95362012000200003) — Scheele halted the American campaign May 6, 1955; American scientists met confidentially April 26
Steven M. Spencer, 'Where Are We Now on Polio?', The Saturday Evening Post, September 10, 1955 — contemporary press account

competing_hypotheses: The safety-test failures were a random manufacturing tail event, not a systemic protocol weakness — true of the formaldehyde-inactivation kinetics (live virus clumps survived the kill step), which is why every manufacturer was re-investigated
Cutter alone was at fault and the program's other five manufacturers were clean — the congressional record and the suppressed Wyeth cases (see aftermath record) complicate this
falsifiability: NIH/EIS archival records showing no live virus in the April 1955 Cutter lots, or a contemporary document proving the recall was ordered for a different cause

title: The Cutter Incident's aftermath: blame, law, and the quiet Wyeth cases (1955–1960)
claim: After the Cutter Incident, the June 1955 congressional inquiry concluded that Cutter's production methods were sound and that the failure lay primarily with the NIH's Laboratory of Biologics Control for inadequate scrutiny of the lots. Oveta Culp Hobby (HEW secretary), William Sebrell Jr. (NIH director), and William Workman (Lab of Biologics Control chief) lost their positions; a jury found Cutter not negligent but liable for breach of implied warranty (Gottsdanker v. Cutter, 1960); and the federal biologics oversight system was rebuilt (Division of Biologics Standards, 1955). Meanwhile Wyeth's vaccine also caused vaccine-associated polio (the Nathanson expert report described 37 cases) — known to a handful of officials, never released to the public — so the 'Cutter alone' verdict is incomplete.
place: Washington, D.C. (congressional hearing, June 1955)
grade_reason: The congressional conclusion and resignations are consistently reported across independent secondary lines (Wikipedia's Cutter Laboratories article, Boulder Weekly, MedicalXpress/HealthDay); the Gottsdanker verdict is a matter of court record; held below VERIFIED because the Wyeth addendum rests on a single secondary line (the SciELO paper's account of the Nathanson report).
earliest_attestation: Congressional hearing record, June 1955; Gottsdanker v. Cutter Laboratories jury verdict, 1960; Nathanson expert report on the Wyeth cases (1955, never released).

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Cutter Laboratories' — Tripp/Habel inspection found nothing wrong with Cutter's methods; June 1955 congressional conclusion blaming NIH Lab of Biologics Control; resignations (Hobby, Sebrell); Gottsdanker breach-of-warranty verdict
Boulder Weekly, 'The Cutter incident: A cautionary tale for Operation Warp Speed' — congressional inquiry conclusion; lawsuits; Cutter not negligent but liable for breach of implied warranty
SciELO (S0211-95362012000200003) — Wyeth's vaccine-associated cases (37, Nathanson expert report), known only to a handful, never released; Offit on Wyeth
MedicalXpress/HealthDay, 'A lasting legacy of science' — the incident prompted federal officials to step up oversight; Daniel Wilson (Muhlenberg) on the regulatory overhaul

competing_hypotheses: The congressional 'methods were sound' finding was politically convenient — shifting blame from a licensed manufacturer to a federal lab — and the Gottsdanker breach-of-warranty verdict shows the courts saw manufacturer responsibility the inquiry minimized
The Wyeth cases were quantitatively minor and did not change the verdict's substance — the 'incomplete' reading is carried honestly as the competing frame, not the settled one
falsifiability: The congressional hearing record contradicting the reported conclusion, or archival proof that no Wyeth-associated cases existed in 1955

title: The Cutter Incident's toll (April–December 1955)
claim: The Cutter lots' live virus infected the children they were meant to protect: about 40,000 developed abortive (non-paralytic) poliomyelitis; 51–56 developed paralytic poliomyelitis, of whom five died. Because polio is contagious, the recipients' infections seeded secondary spread: a further 113 people in their families and communities developed paralytic polio, and five of them died.
place: California, Idaho, Arizona and other states receiving Cutter lots (Berkeley manufacture)
grade_reason: The toll is consistently reported across independent secondary lines (Offit 2005 via the Washington Post's 2020 account; Wikipedia's Cutter Laboratories article; Boulder Weekly; the Brill JOAH article) — but held below VERIFIED because the recipient-paralytic count varies across sources (51 vs 56) and the figures are retrospective epidemiological estimates.
earliest_attestation: EIS case tracing, spring–summer 1955; consolidated in Paul A. Offit, 'The Cutter Incident' (2005).

sources.ref: Michael E. Ruane, Washington Post, April 14, 2020 — citing Paul A. Offit, 'The Cutter Incident' (2005): 120,000 children injected, ~40,000 abortive polio, 51 paralyzed, 5 died
Wikipedia, 'Cutter Laboratories' — 40,000 abortive, 56 paralytic, 5 deaths among recipients; 113 secondary paralytic, 5 secondary deaths
Boulder Weekly, 'The Cutter incident: A cautionary tale for Operation Warp Speed' — 120,000 live-virus doses; 40,000 abortive; 56 paralytic, 5 died; 113 secondary paralytic, 5 died
Brill JOAH 2(1–2) — by April 30, per Offit, Cutter's vaccine had 'paralyzed or killed twenty-five children' within 48 hours of the recall; Gallo's secondary-spread figures

competing_hypotheses: The 51-vs-56 variance in recipient paralytic cases reflects different case definitions and counting windows across Offit's book account and the Wikipedia-sourced figures — the honest range is carried, not a single number
Some contemporary accounts (e.g., MedicalXpress/HealthDay citing 200 paralyzed, 10 dead) run higher — the outlier is carried honestly; the core Offit/EIS-derived figures are the best-documented
falsifiability: EIS archival case files showing materially different recipient-infection counts, or proof the secondary-spread attribution was epidemiological error (wild polio circulating independently)

title: The flawless-1955-launch myth (DEBUNKED)
claim: The Salk polio vaccine's rollout after its April 12, 1955 licensing was a smooth, flawless triumph — no vaccine-caused polio outbreak occurred during the launch of America's first polio vaccine.
place: Berkeley, California (Cutter Laboratories)
grade_reason: Three independent kills: (1) the EIS's April 27, 1955 determination that two Cutter production pools (~120,000 doses) contained live poliovirus; (2) the casualty record — ~40,000 abortive cases, 51–56 paralytic cases with 5 deaths among recipients, plus 113 secondary paralytic cases and 5 deaths; (3) the Surgeon General's April 27 recall and the May 6, 1955 national program suspension. A 'flawless triumph' that was recalled within fifteen days is dead as a reading.
earliest_attestation: EIS determination and Surgeon General recall, April 27, 1955 — the contemporary documents that killed the flawless-launch reading in real time.

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Cutter Laboratories' — the Cutter incident section: lots withdrawn April 27 despite passing safety tests
Brill JOAH 2(1–2) — EIS April 27, 1955 determination; Scheele recall; program suspension May 6
Michael E. Ruane, Washington Post, April 14, 2020 (via Offit 2005) — 'one of the worst biological disasters in American history: a man-made polio epidemic'

competing_hypotheses: The Cutter Incident was a contained manufacturing tail event that the system caught and corrected within weeks — true, and it does not rescue the 'flawless' phrasing
The incident was hidden by a cover-up — no; it was public within weeks, the congressional hearing was on the record, and the correction is the point
falsifiability: Proof that no Cutter lot in April 1955 contained live virus (e.g., the EIS determination retracted), which would restore the flawless-launch reading

title: The Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence (1956)
claim: The Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence (June–August 1956) at Dartmouth College, Hanover, New Hampshire, was the event that named artificial intelligence as a field — the proposal behind it introduced the term and set the research agenda.
place: Dartmouth College, Hanover, New Hampshire
grade_reason: Multiple independent primary/contemporary sources converge: the 1955 proposal text itself, McCarthy's May 1956 Morison letter, and Ray Solomonoff's contemporary attendance notes (only McCarthy, Solomonoff, and Minsky stayed the full eight weeks; daily sessions ran 3–8 people).
earliest_attestation: 'A Proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence' — J. McCarthy, M.L. Minsky, N. Rochester, C.E. Shannon (summer 1955); McCarthy's 26 May 1956 letter to Robert Morison (Rockefeller Foundation) listing 11 planned attendees

sources.ref: The Dartmouth proposal text (1955): 'The study is to proceed on the basis of the conjecture that every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it.'

Ray Solomonoff, 'Ray Solomonoff and the Dartmouth Summer Research Project in Artificial Intelligence, 1956' — attendee lists, daily attendance (only McCarthy, Solomonoff, Minsky full period; 3–8 per session)
Dartmouth AI@50 (2006) conference archive: 'The term "Artificial Intelligence" was coined at the meeting making it a seminal event in the history of AI'

competing_hypotheses: The 'AI was invented at Dartmouth' reading — true only as naming/convening, false as invention; graded separately as evt-ai-invented-at-dartmouth-001
The diffuse-origins reading: the field emerged from several centers (RAND, IBM, MIT, Bell Labs) and Dartmouth was one node — compatible; the record claims the naming, not sole parentage
falsifiability: A contemporary document showing the proposal was never submitted, or that the term 'artificial intelligence' predates the 1955 proposal in published use

title: The 'AI was invented at Dartmouth 1956' myth
claim: Artificial intelligence was invented at the 1956 Dartmouth Summer Research Project — the field's working invention happened there, and the first AI programs and research originated at the workshop.
place: Dartmouth College, Hanover, New Hampshire (the workshop's site)
grade_reason: Two independent kills: (1) working AI predated the workshop — McCulloch & Pitts's 1943 neuron model, Turing's 1950 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', Samuel's checkers program (begun at IBM 1952; Samuel attended Dartmouth), and decisively Newell & Simon's Logic Theorist, developed at RAND in 1955–56 and demonstrated before/independently of the workshop — the conferees arrived with it; (2) the workshop's own thin output — of ~20 participants only three (McCarthy, Solomonoff, Minsky) stayed the full eight weeks, daily sessions ran 3–8 people, and the standard historical verdict records no breakthrough from the sessions themselves: the product was the network and the name.
earliest_attestation: The popular shorthand 'birthplace of AI' for Dartmouth (textbook and press usage); the corrective documentary record is contemporary — the pre-1956 papers and programs below.

sources.ref: Newell & Simon's Logic Theorist (1955–56, RAND) — 'Even before Dartmouth convened, Allen Newell, Herbert Simon, and Cliff Shaw had created the Logic Theorist (LT) at RAND — the first program deliberately engineered for automated reasoning' (AI: A Modern Approach history lineage)

McCulloch & Pitts 1943 ('A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity') and Turing 1950 ('Computing Machinery and Intelligence') — the pre-Dartmouth foundations; Arthur Samuel's checkers program begun at IBM 1952 (Samuel an attendee)
Ray Solomonoff's contemporary Dartmouth notes — attendance reality (only three full-period stayers; 3–8 per daily session); the workshop's thin output is the standard historical verdict

competing_hypotheses: The 'founding event' reading: Dartmouth named the field, convened its pioneers, and set the research agenda — TRUE, and the honest form of the workshop's credit (kept as evt-dartmouth-1956-001 VERIFIED)
The diffuse-origins reading: AI emerged from several centers with no single founding — compatible with the debunk, not a rival to it
falsifiability: A contemporary record showing the first working AI reasoning program dated after August 1956, or evidence that the Logic Theorist's 1955–56 development is misdated

title: The staged 'discovery' of the Berlin Tunnel (April 1956) — the accident that was scheduled
claim: The claim that the Berlin Tunnel's unearthing on the night of 21–22 April 1956 was a genuine accident — a maintenance crew stumbling onto the American tap by luck (in the popular version, after heavy rains flooded the tunnel and exposed the wires).
place: Altglienicke, East Berlin (the tap chamber, south of the sector boundary)
grade_reason: Two independent kills: (1) the KGB knew the tunnel plan from late 1953 via Blake and made a documented decision to protect the source, withholding the knowledge even from the Soviet military users of the lines — there was nothing left to 'discover' by accident; (2) the 'accidental' discovery was itself a planned operation — declassified records describe the early-1956 Soviet plan for the tap's 'accidental' discovery, executed by a special signal corps team on the night of 21–22 April 1956 as a staged publicity coup (timed around Khrushchev's UK visit, with the British role deliberately downplayed).
earliest_attestation: Contemporary: the Soviet press conference of April 1956 presented the discovery as an accident. The debunk rests on declassified post-Cold-War records (CIA official history; post-Soviet releases) — not available to the contemporary press.

sources.ref: CIA official-history excerpt (booklife.com): 'Early in 1956, the Soviets developed a plan whereby the tap would be "accidentally" discovered'; 'On the night of 21-22 April 1956, a special signal corps team... penetrated the tunnel in the full glare of a well-organized publicity coup'

Encyclopedia of Espionage, 'Berlin Tunnel' (faqs.org): the KGB 'did not inform anyone in Germany, including the East Germans or the Soviet users of the cable lines'; when Blake was transferred in 1955 the Soviets were free to 'discover' the tunnel; 'Soviet troops began to dig on the night of April 21, 1956... Given ample warning, the Americans retreated behind the steel door'

Steve Vogel, 'Betrayal in Berlin' (via History News Network): Blake tipped the KGB; the service 'took no action against the tunnel' and 'didn't even warn Red Army commanders, for fear of compromising Blake'; the Soviets announced the discovery in April 1956

competing_hypotheses: The accident-of-nature reading: heavy April 1956 rains flooded the tunnel and exposed the wires, leading a repair crew to the tap — carried as the reading the evidence killed
The staged-event reading (this record's verdict): the 'accidental' discovery was a planned operation, documented in the declassified record
falsifiability: A contemporaneous Soviet record showing genuine surprise (e.g. an internal damage-assessment that treats the tap as news) — none has ever surfaced; instead the record shows pre-knowledge and a plan

title: The Interstate Highway System, 1956 (CORROBORATED)
claim: The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 (signed by President Dwight D. Eisenhower, 29 June 1956) authorized the National System of Interstate and Defense Highways: 41,000 miles of limited-access highways, 90 percent federally funded through the Highway Trust Fund (fuel taxes), built by the states to a single national design standard.
place: United States (the Interstate Highway System)
grade_reason: The statute exists, the funding mechanism exists, the mileage is on the ground — but 'the system' is a living, grown artifact (41,000 authorized, ~48,000 today), so CORROBORATED, not VERIFIED, for the whole-claim level.
earliest_attestation: The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 (Public Law 84-627); Eisenhower's signing statement, 29 June 1956.

sources.ref: Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 (Public Law 84-627), signed 29 June 1956 — 41,000 miles authorized, 90 percent federal / 10 percent state funding, Highway Trust Fund financed by fuel taxes; states build to a single national design standard

FHWA, 'Interstate Highway System — The Myths' — minimum overpass clearances were raised at the Defense Department's request so military equipment could pass (defense was a real, documented design input — for clearance, not for landing strips)

Eisenhower's 1919 Transcontinental Motor Convoy — the then-lieutenant colonel rode as an observer from Washington, D.C. to San Francisco; 62 days through mud, failed bridges, and state-line road chaos — his lived education in the national road problem

competing_hypotheses: The 'defense' naming was partly political cover for a civilian commerce project — the defense rationale was genuine but also sold a commercial bill
The system was built primarily for civilian mobility and commerce, with defense (evacuation, military movement) as the honest secondary rationale that made the federal money possible
falsifiability: Congressional records showing no such Act, or an Act without the 90/10 Highway Trust Fund funding mechanism, would overturn the record; the statute and the trust fund are both on the books.

title: The 'NASA invented Velcro' myth
claim: NASA (the US National Aeronautics and Space Administration) invented Velcro, the hook-and-loop fastener.
place: Switzerland (de Mestral's filing jurisdiction; NASA founded in the United States)
grade_reason: DEBUNKED — 245th DEBUNKED family. Two kills. (1) The defendant's own witness: the Velcro company's own FAQ states 'NASA did not invent the hook and loop fastener. George de Mestral invented the technology, and NASA later popularized its use.' (2) Chronology: de Mestral filed for Swiss patent protection in 1951 and the first Swiss patent issued 16 March 1954 — NASA came into existence in 1958. An invention cannot predate the founding of its supposed inventor by seven years. NASA's genuine Apollo-era adoption (graded separately) is the myth's honest root.
earliest_attestation: The telling is folk/trivia transmission, undated; the debunking literature documents the belief's prevalence (NASA Spinoff reports, Museum of Flight myth-busting, phys.org 2012 'contrary to popular belief' framing).

sources.ref: Velcro Companies FAQ: 'Did NASA invent hook and loop fasteners?' — 'NASA did not invent the hook and loop fastener. George de Mestral invented the technology, and NASA later popularized its use by relying on VELCRO Brand fasteners to secure items in weightlessness during the space race and Apollo era.'; also: idea began 1941, Swiss filing 1951, first Swiss patent issued 16 March 1954.
Museum of Flight blog, 'Debunking NASA Space Spin-off Myths': Velcro invented in the 1940s by a Swiss engineer who observed burrs in his dog's fur; NASA recognized its usefulness in microgravity.
LiveScience, 'Who Invented Velcro?': 'Many sources attribute the creation of Velcro to NASA, though this claim proves quite false.' Apollo astronauts' 1960s use documented.

phys.org (NASA Spinoff coverage, 2012): 'Contrary to popular belief, Tang, Velcro and Teflon (along with the zero-gravity "space" pen) aren't derived from NASA technology.' — the belief's prevalence, carried as belief ecology.
AIER, 'NASA Did Not Invent Velcro: Public and Private Innovation': de Mestral, 1941 Alps walk with dog, decade of private development, no state direction or funding.

competing_hypotheses: NASA's Apollo-era use is the myth's honest root — the association is real and documented; only the invention claim is false
NASA adapted or specified Velcro for particular spaceflight applications — separate engineering, not adjudicated as invention in this pass
The telling may conflate Velcro with genuine NASA spinoffs (memory foam, water filters) that sit in the same 'space-age' mental category
falsifiability: A NASA (or predecessor NACA) document predating 1951 describing the hook-and-loop fastener, or evidence that de Mestral's 1951 Swiss filing was copied from US government work.

title: The eradication of smallpox (VERIFIED)
claim: Smallpox was eradicated by human effort — the last natural case in 1977, global eradication certified by the World Health Assembly in May 1980. The only human disease ever eradicated.
place: Merca, Somalia (last natural smallpox case, 26 October 1977)
grade_reason: Multiple independent primary lines: the last natural case documented and investigated (Ali Maow Maalin, Merca, 26 October 1977), the Global Commission's 9 December 1979 certification after a two-year worldwide search, and WHA33.3's 8 May 1980 declaration; no natural case since.
earliest_attestation: Jenner, 'An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae', 1798 (the intervention); WHO Intensified Smallpox Eradication Programme records 1967-1980 and Fenner et al., 'Smallpox and its Eradication' (WHO, 1988) for the campaign

sources.ref: WHO Resolution WHA33.3, 8 May 1980: 'the world and its peoples have won freedom from smallpox'
WHO/Global Commission: last naturally occurring case — Ali Maow Maalin, hospital cook, Merca, Somalia, 26 October 1977 (variola minor); last variola major case — Rahima Banu, Bangladesh, October 1975
Global Commission certification 9 December 1979 after two years of intense worldwide verification; endorsed by the World Health Assembly 8 May 1980

CDC Sencer Museum / CDC: last case in the US 1949; routine US smallpox vaccination discontinued 1971; the campaign's surveillance-containment (ring) strategy via William Foege, programme led by Donald A. Henderson

Baxby (History Today): surveillance-containment replaced mass vaccination as the winning strategy — the Haygarth-derived isolation-plus-ring-vaccination approach; only official virus stocks remain (USA, Russia)

competing_hypotheses: Eradication happened through mass vaccination alone — contrary to the campaign's own record: mass vaccination was tried first and proved unimplementable in many countries; surveillance-containment (find cases, isolate, ring-vaccinate) became the winning strategy

Smallpox died out naturally and would have gone anyway — no: roughly 300 million 20th-century deaths, endemic across Africa, Asia and South America as late as 1967; the campaign tracked cases to zero in a documented sequence (Brazil 1971, Indonesia 1972, India 1975, Horn of Africa 1977)
falsifiability: A verified natural smallpox case after 1979 would falsify the certification; only laboratory stocks remain (USA, Russia) — no natural transmission since 26 October 1977.

title: Baran's RAND memos on distributed survivable communications (1960-64)
claim: Paul Baran's RAND Corporation memoranda (1960-64, published as 'On Distributed Communications,' 1964) proposed a distributed, packet-switched communications system designed to remain operational under nuclear attack — in the Air Force secure-voice context. This is the genuine survivability work whose rationale the ARPANET nuclear myth later grafted onto the wrong network.
place: RAND Corporation, Santa Monica, California
grade_reason: CORROBORATED: the memos are published primary documents; the Internet Society's own brief history assigns the nuclear-war consideration to 'the unrelated RAND study on secure voice' — the one genuine nuclear-attribution in the lineage, kept honestly so the grade kills the transplant (the ARPANET reading), never the donor.
earliest_attestation: The RAND memoranda themselves (published 1964) — the primary documents; their content summarized in the Internet Society's 'A Brief History of the Internet' note.

sources.ref: Internet Society, 'A Brief History of the Internet' — the note: 'only the unrelated RAND study on secure voice considered nuclear war'; Paul Baran 'the first to propose a theoretical model for communication using packet switching, conducted the RAND study above' (carried via the ARPANET article's quotation and summary)

fact-index.com, ARPANET summary — 'It was from the RAND study that the false rumor started claiming that the ARPANET was somehow related to building a network resistant to nuclear war... Although ARPANET did not exactly share the objective of Baran's project, he said his work contributed to the development of ARPANET'; Elmer Shapiro's minutes of the 9-10 October 1967 design meeting record a version of Baran's 'hot potato' routing as usable

competing_hypotheses: The myth's honest core: packet switching's intellectual lineage does run through Baran (and independently through Donald Davies at NPL, who coined 'packet') — Baran said his work contributed to ARPANET's development; the October 1967 design meeting minutes record a version of his 'hot potato' routing being usable. Influence is real; design purpose is not transferred.
Baran's distributed network was never built — the ARPANET was the network that got built, and it was built for resource sharing.
falsifiability: The published RAND memos are the evidence; a re-dating of the study out of the 1960s would revise the record.

title: The SETI search record (1960–present): sixty years of listening, zero confirmed artificial signals
claim: A continuous, documented scientific search for extraterrestrial technosignatures has run since 1960 (Project Ozma, Frank Drake, Green Bank) through Ohio State's Big Ear all-sky surveys, Harvard's META/BETA, Project Phoenix (1995–2004), SERENDIP, SETI@home (1999–2020, ~5 million volunteers), and Breakthrough Listen (launched 2015, $100M). As of 2026, no confirmed artificial signal has been detected.
place: Green Bank, West Virginia (origin point; programs span many sites)

title: The severed hands: Shah Jahan mutilated the Taj Mahal's artisans to keep it unrepeatable
claim: After the Taj Mahal was completed, the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan ordered the hands of the artisans and workers who built it to be cut off (or otherwise mutilated — killed, blinded, imprisoned) so that they could never build another monument like it.
place: Taj Mahal, Agra, Uttar Pradesh, India (the legend's scene)
grade_reason: Two independent kills. (1) The empty primary record: four hundred years of Mughal court paperwork, Persian histories, and European travelers' accounts contain zero mentions of any artisan mutilation, and the ASI — the monument's guardian — states there is no evidence and calls it a folk tale. (2) The positive counter-evidence: the same chief architect, Ustad Ahmad Lahauri, went on to design Delhi's Red Fort with his own two hands afterward; Shah Jahan founded the Taj Ganj settlement to house the workers' families, whose descendants still live there practicing the marble craft today (Times of India / Manimugdha Sharma 2017). The trail leads back to 1960s guide folklore, not 1648.
earliest_attestation: No contemporary source of any kind: no Mughal court record, no Persian history, no European traveler's account from the construction period mentions it. The Archaeological Survey of India — the monument's official guardian — states there is no historical evidence for it and classifies it as a folk tale. Trained historians call it an urban myth; S. Irfan Habib traces it to 1960s word-of-mouth, and the 1971 Ranchi University Journal of Historical Research treats it as an urban legend.

title: The origin of the genetic code: cracked, not authored
claim: No scientific consensus exists for why the genetic code maps 64 codons to 20 amino acids as it does. The mapping itself is the most-tested lookup in biology (cracked 1961-1966); the origin of the assignment - frozen accident, co-evolution, or stereochemistry - is unattested by any experiment.
place: Bethesda, Maryland, USA (NIH - Nirenberg's lab)
grade_reason: The table is VERIFIED by six decades of molecular biology; the origin of the assignment is attested by no experiment - three theories, six decades, no verdict. The 1968-2026 literature is argument, not evidence.
earliest_attestation: The codon table: Nirenberg & Matthaei 1961 (poly-U -> phenylalanine, PNAS); Khorana's synthetic polynucleotides; Holley's tRNA sequencing (Nobel 1968). The origin question: Crick 1968 ('frozen accident'), Wong 1975 (co-evolution theory).

Wong 1975, PNAS - co-evolution theory: the code's structure reflects amino-acid biosynthetic pathways (precursor-product codon neighbors)
Woese 1965 / the stereochemical theory lineage (incl. Yarus aptamer work): direct codon-amino acid affinities as the assignment's physical basis - argued, unproven
Barrell, Bankier & Drouin 1979, Nature - human mitochondrial code differs from the 'universal' code: the first variant, breaking the universality telling

falsifiability: A demonstrated prebiotic pathway that fixes codon assignments (any of the three theories predicting the actual table from chemistry alone); or a second independent code arising in the lab

title: The 'resolved by resolve alone' reading of the Cuban Missile Crisis
claim: The popular reading that the Cuban Missile Crisis was resolved PURELY by the American naval quarantine and U.S. resolve — with no American concessions — is false. The settlement of 28 October 1962 contained two American concessions: the public no-invasion pledge against Cuba (in Kennedy's 27 Oct letter) and the secret pledge to remove the Jupiter missiles from Turkey within months (delivered by Robert Kennedy to Dobrynin on the evening of 27 Oct, kept secret ~25 years). The resolve-only reading survived in textbooks and film precisely because the trade was secret; the declassifications of 1987–1989 killed it.

earliest_attestation: The myth is the absence: the public settlement record of 28 Oct 1962 contains no Jupiter clause; the correction's earliest attestation is the 1987–1989 declassification wave

title: The Cuban Missile Crisis (14–28 October 1962)

title: The secret Jupiter-missile trade (27 October 1962)
claim: The Cuban Missile Crisis was settled by a SECRET American concession: on the evening of 27 October 1962, at President Kennedy's instruction, Attorney General Robert Kennedy told Soviet Ambassador Anatoly Dobrynin that the United States would remove its Jupiter nuclear missiles from Turkey within a few months — on the condition that the concession remain secret and never be treated as a public quid pro quo. grade_reason: Multiply and independently confirmed: the RFK–Dobrynin meeting, Dobrynin's cable, Khrushchev's correspondence, the actual Jupiter withdrawal from Turkey within months, and the 1989 public disclosures — both superpowers' archives converge on the secret clause.
earliest_attestation: The RFK–Dobrynin meeting itself (27 Oct 1962); Dobrynin's cable to Moscow; corroborated by the ExComm transcripts, Sorensen's papers, and the 1987–1989 disclosures

sources.ref: Scientific American, 'RFK's Secret Role in the Cuban Missile Crisis' — RFK tasked to give Dobrynin the private assurance of Jupiter removal 'at a later date'; assurance kept secret until 1989; settlement timeline 27–28 Oct

American Diplomacy, 'Robert Kennedy and the Cuban Missile Crisis — A Reinterpretation' — RFK arranged the Dobrynin meeting 27 Oct evening; informed the ambassador Jupiters would be withdrawn from Turkey as a secret component of the settlement
Dobrynin's cable to Moscow on the 27 Oct meeting (cited via secondary accounts and the 1989 disclosures)
Jupiter withdrawal from Turkey, completed by April 1963 (Operation Pot Pie) — execution of the secret clause
The 1987–1989 declassification wave and Dobrynin's memoir — the secrecy broken after ~25 years

competing_hypotheses: On who devised the 'Trollope Ploy' (answer Khrushchev's 26 Oct letter, publicly ignore the 27 Oct letter demanding Jupiter removal): popular accounts credit RFK; the record shows a team/Nitze-Bundy effort RFK implemented — attribution corrected without diminishing his delivery of the secret assurance

title: The claim that the stirrup created feudalism

place: Oxford, England (publication of the thesis, 1962)
grade_reason: Three independent kills from the scholarly record: the chronology fails (true shock combat postdates the stirrup's arrival by centuries), Bachrach/Bullough demolished White's evidentiary chain in 1970, and the profession never answered them — White himself never replied.
earliest_attestation: Lynn White Jr., Medieval Technology and Social Change (Oxford, 1962), chapter 'Stirrup, Mounted Shock Combat, Feudalism, and Chivalry'

sources.ref: Lynn White Jr., Medieval Technology and Social Change (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1962) — chapter 1; contents page preserved at archive.org
Peter Sawyer, review 1963 — the 'technical determinism' critique (first critical response)
D.A. Bullough (1970) and Bernard S. Bachrach (1970) — primary-source dismantling of White's evidentiary points, point by point

falsifiability: Contemporary 8th-century evidence that Martel's cavalry policy was stirrup-driven and that the fief system originated from that specific funding mechanism

title: The claim that the horse collar caused the medieval agricultural revolution
claim: Lynn White Jr.'s 1962 thesis (Medieval Technology and Social Change), chapter 'The Discovery of Horse-Power': the padded horse collar — which White dated to roughly 10th-century Europe — together with the nailed horseshoe, unlocked the horse as a draught animal, displaced the ox, and thereby CAUSED the medieval agricultural revolution: oat cultivation, the three-field rotation, the resulting food surplus, population growth, and the northward shift of Europe's civilizational center.
place: Oxford, England (publication of the thesis, 1962)
grade_reason: Three independent kills from the scholarly record: (1) the collar was Chinese centuries before White's European dating (Han-era depictions, documented in Needham's Science and Civilisation in China) — the device was inherited, not a medieval breakthrough; (2) Sawyer & Hilton (1963, 'Technical determinism: the stirrup and the plough', Past & Present 24) named the move itself — technology cannot be read as a single sufficient cause; (3) Langdon (1986, Horses, Oxen and Technological Innovation) showed English adoption was gradual and governed by relative prices and fodder costs, not by the device's arrival. The profession kept the collar and discarded the causal chain.
earliest_attestation: Lynn White Jr., Medieval Technology and Social Change (Oxford, 1962), chapters 'The Agricultural Revolution of the Early Middle Ages' and 'The Discovery of Horse-Power'

sources.ref: Lynn White Jr., Medieval Technology and Social Change (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1962) — chapters 'The Agricultural Revolution of the Early Middle Ages' and 'The Discovery of Horse-Power'; contents page preserved at archive.org
P.H. Sawyer & R.H. Hilton, 'Technical determinism: the stirrup and the plough', Past & Present 24 (1963) — the original 'technical determinism' label applied to both of White's causal claims
John Langdon, Horses, Oxen and Technological Innovation (1986) — English adoption gradual, driven by relative prices of horses vs oxen and fodder costs, not by the collar's arrival
Joseph Needham et al., Science and Civilisation in China — the padded horse collar attested in Han-era China, centuries before White's European dating

Thomas E. Lambert, 'The Horse Versus the Ox during Medieval Times' (2023, Univ. of Louisville) — horse/ox economics of medieval draught: the horse ~50% faster but costlier to feed; the mix was economic

W. Graessle, 'Lynn White Jr.'s Medieval Heavy Plow' (Footnotes: A Journal of History, 2018) — historiographical review of White's agricultural claims and their weakening under technical historians' scrutiny

competing_hypotheses: White's softer form (sometimes read back into him): the collar as one enabling condition among many, not the single cause — historians keep the device, reject the determinism
The economics view (Langdon 1986): relative prices of horses vs oxen and fodder costs governed the mix; adoption was gradual and cost-driven, not a breakthrough
The China-first framing: the real breakthrough was Han-era Chinese, and Europe inherited it — White's European timeline of arrival was the weakest link in the chain
falsifiability: A sudden, collar-caused ox-to-horse substitution across northern Europe with no intervening price or land-regime change; or securely dated evidence that the padded collar was unknown outside Europe before 900 CE

title: The mutual lifting of the 1054 excommunications, 7 December 1965

title: The Fisher Space Pen AG-7 (1965–1967)
claim: Paul C. Fisher independently developed the AG-7 pressurized-cartridge space pen (US Patent 3,285,228, filed 19 May 1965); after ~2 years of NASA testing it flew on Apollo 7 (Oct 1968), and NASA purchased ~400 pens at $2.95 each in 1967.
place: Boulder City, Nevada (Fisher Pen Company)
grade_reason: Independent secondary attestation from three directions — Scientific American (2006), Smithsonian Magazine, and the patent record — agrees on independent private development, ~$1M of Fisher's own capital, two years of NASA testing, Apollo 7 first flight, and the ~400-unit / $2.95 1967 purchase; ~30 pens flew to the Moon (12 reaching the surface, per Space.com), and ISS crews still use them as of 2021.
earliest_attestation: US Patent 3,285,228 (filed 19 May 1965) — the pressurized ball-point cartridge

sources.ref: US Patent 3,285,228 — pressurized ball-point pen cartridge, filed 19 May 1965
Scientific American, "Fact or Fiction?" (2006) — Fisher's ~$1M private investment, no NASA development money, pen could write −50°F to +400°F, underwater
Smithsonian Magazine — AG7 patented 1966, flew on Apollo 7 after two years of NASA testing
Wikipedia "Space Pen" — NASA purchased ~400 pens at $2.95 apiece (reported 1967); nearly 30 Fisher pens flew to the Moon, 12 reached the lunar surface; ISS use as of 2021

title: NASA's $128.89 mechanical pencils (1965)

place: Houston, Texas (NASA Manned Spacecraft Center / Johnson Space Center)
grade_reason: Attested by NASA historians (via Scientific American 2006) with the exact order figures — 34 pencils, $4,382.50, $128.89 each — and the pencil's abandonment is multiply attested: graphite tips flaked and drifted near equipment, and pencils' flammability became unacceptable after the Apollo 1 fire. earliest_attestation: NASA procurement records (1965), via NASA historians quoted in Scientific American 2006

sources.ref: Scientific American, "Fact or Fiction?" (2006) — the 1965 Tycam order: 34 mechanical pencils, $4,382.50 total, $128.89 each; the public outcry; pencil hazards (flaking tips, flammability post-Apollo 1)

title: 'Lead poisoning caused the fall of Rome'
claim: Lead poisoning caused the decline and fall of the Roman Empire — lead exposure from the Romans' lead water pipes (fistulae) and lead-sweetened wine (sapa/defrutum) was a primary cause of the Empire's collapse.
place: Rome, Italy (myth's supposed locus)
grade_reason: Killed twice: (1) the toxicology kill — Delile et al. 2014 (PNAS) measured the pipe lead in Rome's water (~100x natural levels) and concluded the contamination was 'unlikely to have been truly harmful' because a calcium-carbonate crust insulated the pipes and the water kept flowing; the study's own author: 'Lead is no longer seen as the prime culprit of Rome's demise'; (2) the philology kill — Scarborough 1984 showed the Romans knew lead was dangerous (Vitruvius, De architectura 8.6.10-11 warns water through lead pipes 'must be injurious'), drank wine watered rather than routinely sweetened, and cooked in copper, not lead-lined pots; Simpson & Garvie-Lok 2026 note the archaeology has not even found the lead cooking vessels the sapa story requires.
earliest_attestation: S. Colum Gilfillan, 'Lead Poisoning and the Fall of Rome,' Journal of Occupational Medicine 7(1), 1965 — restated earlier arguments by Karl Hofmann and Rudolf Kobert.

sources.ref: Delile, Hugo et al., 'Lead in ancient Rome's city waters,' PNAS 111(18):6594-6599, 2014 — sediment-core Pb isotopes from the Tiber bedload and Portus harbor; conclusion: tap-water lead clearly measurable but 'unlikely to have been truly harmful'

Scarborough, John, 'The Myth of Lead Poisoning Among the Romans: An Essay Review,' Transactions & Studies of the College of Physicians of Philadelphia, 1984 — classicist's refutation of Nriagu: Romans knew the dangers, misread citations, watered wine, copper cookware

Gilfillan, S. Colum, 'Lead Poisoning and the Fall of Rome,' Journal of Occupational Medicine 7(1), 1965 — the myth's origin paper: aristocratic infertility/miscarriage/child mortality from lead vessels and adulterated wine, decline of innovation

Vitruvius, De architectura 8.6.10-11 — the Roman text that warns against lead: water conducted through earthen pipes is more wholesome than through lead; lead workers' pallor noted as evidence the metal 'destroys the vigor of the blood'

Simpson, R.M.L. & Garvie-Lok, S.J., 'Lead exposure in the Roman Empire: a review of the written, material, and bioarchaeological evidence' (2026, Cambridge) — the 2026 review: the relative scarcity of lead cooking vessels is inconsistent with the texts-based sapa-poisoning theories

McConnell, Joseph et al. (Desert Research Institute), reported NYT 2025-01-06, 'Lead Poisoning May Have Made Ancient Romans a Bit Less Intelligent' — Arctic ice-core lead from Roman-era mining/smelting; ambient pollution, not the water-pipe fall story

competing_hypotheses: The atmospheric-lead refinement (McConnell et al., Desert Research Institute, reported NYT Jan 2025): Roman mining and smelting did raise empire-wide background lead exposure (Arctic ice-core record) and may have measurably dented population-level cognitive function — but this is ambient industrial pollution, not the tap-water/fall-of-Rome story, and its authors do not claim it collapsed the Empire

The sapa-narrowed version: even if elite wine contained lead acetate ('sugar of lead'), chronic poisoning of a subset of the aristocracy cannot bear the explanatory weight of a centuries-long political-military-economic collapse

The documented-collapse view: the Empire's fragmentation is accounted for by attested political, military, and economic causes (third-century crisis, currency debasement, civil war, barbarian migrations, fiscal collapse) — lead is a decorative footnote to a documented story, not its engine
falsifiability: Skeletal lead burdens from across Roman social strata showing lead-induced infertility and mortality at population scale, or evidence that Roman tap water routinely exceeded levels known to cause mass poisoning — the actual 2014 study found the opposite ('unlikely to have been truly harmful').

title: 'Walt Disney was cryogenically frozen' (DEBUNKED)
claim: Walt Disney was cryogenically frozen after his death in December 1966 (in some versions, only his head, stored under Disneyland's Pirates of the Caribbean or Cinderella Castle).
place: Forest Lawn Memorial Park, Glendale, California
grade_reason: Multiply attested against: cremated two days after death, urn with ashes interred at the family mausoleum in Forest Lawn Memorial Park, Glendale; daughter Diane Disney Miller (1972 biography and 2012 Daily Mail): 'absolutely no truth' to the rumor, doubted he had heard of cryonics; Bob Nelson (California Cryogenics Society president, 1972 LA Times): 'They had him cremated. I personally have seen his ashes. They're in Forest Lawn. Two weeks later we froze the first man' — the first human cryopreservation (James Bedford) was January 1967, the year AFTER Disney died, making the legend chronologically impossible as well as factually false; Snopes point-by-point debunking; the Mosley (1986) and Eliot (1993) biographies that fed the legend were criticized for factual errors and unverifiable sources. The legend's persistence is itself documented (Gizmodo, AllEars, PBS, Joblo).

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'Cryonic Walt Disney urban legend': 'In reality, Walt Disney was cremated two days after his death and an urn containing his ashes was interred at the family mausoleum in Forest Lawn Memorial Park in Glendale, California.' Diane Disney Miller: 'absolutely no truth' to the rumor.

Gizmodo: Bob Nelson (1972 LA Times) — 'They had him cremated. I personally have seen his ashes. They're in Forest Lawn. Two weeks later we froze the first man. If Disney had been the first it would have made headlines around the world.'

AllEars.net: 'the first human being wasn't cryopreserved until 1967, the year after Disney died. Walt's remains were actually cremated and interred at Forest Lawn Memorial Park Cemetery in Glendale, California.'

title: The 'Stevenson proved reincarnation' telling
claim: Popular tellings present Ian Stevenson's case research as having PROVED reincarnation — the claim that the documented cases constitute proof that consciousness survives death and is reborn.
place: Charlottesville, Virginia (the telling cites UVA's Division of Perceptual Studies)
grade_reason: The telling misrepresents its own source: Stevenson published 'suggestive evidence,' never proof, and the methodological objections stand unfalsified in print — 'proves' asserts what the evidence cannot bear. The cases are CORROBORATED; the proof-claim is DEBUNKED.
earliest_attestation: Popular reception of Twenty Cases Suggestive of Reincarnation (1966) — the 'suggestive of' in the title was dropped by the telling

sources.ref: Stevenson's own framing: the book titles themselves — 'Suggestive of Reincarnation,' 'Children Who Remember Previous Lives' — and his published position that the evidence is suggestive, not conclusive
Edwards, P. — Reincarnation: A Critical Examination (Prometheus Books, 1996): the mainstream critical literature's methodological objections (cryptomnesia, expectancy, cultural transmission)
The telling: popularizations that drop the 'suggestive' — podcast/YouTube/advocacy claims of proof (e.g. reincarnationresearch.com: 'provide proof of reincarnation')

IFLScience, 19 Oct 2026 — the 2026 press state: the piece's own framing ('not hard science,' researchers 'drew much broader conclusions than their data could necessarily support') refuses the proof reading even while covering the cases

competing_hypotheses: The telling is correct: the case aggregate constitutes proof (asserted by some popularizers and by Tucker in televised remarks, but never by Stevenson himself)
falsifiability: Already falsified as a proof-claim: proof requires ruling out the conventional alternatives (cryptomnesia, expectancy, cultural transmission, fraud), which no study has done; the principal investigator's own 'suggestive' framing is the telling's refutation from inside its own source. The cases stand; the proof-claim dies.

title: Honeywell v. Sperry Rand: the courtroom that unmade ENIAC (19 October 1973)
claim: On 19 October 1973, U.S. District Judge Earl R. Larson of the District of Minnesota decided Honeywell Inc. v. Sperry Rand Corp. (180 U.S.P.Q. 673; Case 4-67 Civ. 138), invalidating the 1964 ENIAC patent (U.S. Patent 3,120,606, filed 1947) on four grounds — including derivation: 'Eckert and Mauchly did not themselves first invent the automatic electronic digital computer, but instead derived that subject matter from one Dr. John Vincent Atanasoff.' The trial ran 1 June 1971 – 13 March 1972 with 77 witnesses and ~33,000 exhibits; the suits were filed 26 May 1967 (Honeywell's filing minutes earlier). The ruling placed the invention of the electronic digital computer in the public domain; it was never appealed. The news was largely buried: the Saturday Night Massacre broke the next day, 20 October 1973.
place: U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota, Minneapolis
grade_reason: Multiple independent primary sources: the decision text itself (Finding 3.1.19 on Atanasoff's credibility; Order 26.1.1 declaring the patent invalid), the case metadata (citation, dates, judge), the Hagley Museum archive of the trial records, and contemporary secondary accounts all converge on the same facts.
earliest_attestation: The decision text itself, 180 U.S.P.Q. 673 (D. Minn. 1973), signed 19 October 1973.

sources.ref: Honeywell, Inc. v. Sperry Rand Corp., 180 U.S.P.Q. 673 (D. Minn. 1973) — case metadata: Court, decided October 19, 1973, Judge Earl R. Larson

Decision text PDF (Atanasoff archive) — 3.1.19: the court finds Atanasoff's testimony credible on the knowledge Mauchly derived; 26.1.1: the ENIAC patent 'is hereby declared to be invalid and unenforceable'; dated October 19, 1973, Earl R. Larson
Hagley Museum and Library, Honeywell vs. Sperry Rand records 1935–1973 — decision handed down 19 Oct 1973 upholding Honeywell on every count; damages not awarded (no willful fraud)
Gizmodo, 'Why Was the Computer Never Patented?' — IBM settled with Sperry Rand for $10 million; the four invalidation grounds; the Saturday Night Massacre buried the coverage

competing_hypotheses: The legal-vs-historical reading: courts decide patent validity, not historical firstness — a finding of derivation does not settle who 'invented the computer' in the historian's sense; the general-purpose/special-purpose distinction remains live in the historiography

The 'stolen vs shared' reading: whether Mauchly's 1941 visit constituted borrowing or independent convergence is genuinely contested in the secondary literature (Shurkin's near-miss account vs the Larson findings) — the record reports the court's finding, not a final biographical verdict
falsifiability: A higher-court reversal or a competing ruling upholding the ENIAC patent — none exists; the decision was never appealed.

title: The first undisputed North Pole arrivals over the surface — Plaisted 1968 (snowmobile), Herbert 1969 (on foot)
claim: The first expedition to reach the North Pole over the surface with an undisputed, independently verifiable arrival was Ralph Plaisted's 1968 snowmobile expedition — Plaisted and three companions arrived at the Pole in April 1968. The first to reach it the traditional way, on foot with dog teams, was Sir Wally Herbert's 1968-69 British Trans-Arctic Expedition, which crossed the entire Arctic from Point Barrow, Alaska to Svalbard over 476 days and reached the Pole on 6 April 1969 — the 60th anniversary of Peary's claimed arrival.
place: North Pole
grade_reason: VERIFIED on independently confirmed fixes: Plaisted's 1968 position was confirmed by the supporting airlift (the fuel drops and the radio fixes); Herbert's 1969 position came at the midpoint of a 476-day crossing of the entire Arctic Ocean by dog team, with continuous position records. These are the first surface arrivals with no serious scholarly dispute — the reason the Cook/Peary controversy (evt-cook-north-pole-claim-1908-001 DEBUNKED, evt-peary-north-pole-claim-1909-001 VERIFIED-expedition/CORROBORATED-point) can be closed honestly: the question 'who really was first, indisputably' has an answer, and it is 1968/1969.
earliest_attestation: Contemporary expedition records, 1968-1969; independently confirmed positions.

sources.ref: BBC Science Focus, 'Who really discovered the North Pole?': 'the first undisputed expedition to reach the North Pole over the surface did not achieve its goal until 1968, when the American Ralph Plaisted and three companions arrived on snowmobiles'; 'On 6 April the following year, the British explorer Wally — later Sir Walter — Herbert became the first to reach the North Pole the traditional way, on foot'

Wikipedia 'Peary's Expedition (1908-1909)': Herbert in 1968-1969 'crossed the entire Arctic from Point Barrow to Svalbard with four dog teams over 476 days, reaching the North Pole on April 6, 1969 — the 60th anniversary of Peary's claimed attainment'

competing_hypotheses: The airborne and submarine arrivals (Byrd 1926 disputed; Amundsen/Ellsworth/Nobile 1926 airship; USS Nautilus 1958; USS Skate 1959 surfacing) are separate records — this record covers surface, over-the-ice arrival only, and does not re-grade them.

The Plaisted verification line: the claim rests on the airlifted confirmation — the US Air Force flew fuel and supplies, and the position was independently confirmed. Some popular accounts underplay it because a snowmobile 'doesn't count' in the traditional sense — which is exactly why Herbert's 1969 foot arrival is carried as the parallel first.
falsifiability: Independent positional evidence contradicting the 1968 and 1969 arrival fixes — none exists; both positions were independently confirmed.

title: The 'Nazca Runways' Claim
claim: The claim (popularized by Erich von Däniken's 'Chariots of the Gods?', 1968) that the long straight lines and trapezoid shapes on the Nazca pampa were built as runways or landing strips for aircraft — ancient or extraterrestrial.
place: Nazca pampa, Ica region, Peru
grade_reason: The claim collapses on the archaeology: centimeters-deep soft-soil grooves cannot land aircraft; the 'runways' are continuous single-line figures tied to Nazca culture; no aviation artifacts, infrastructure, or indigenous flight tradition exists.
earliest_attestation: Erich von Däniken, Erinnerungen an die Zukunft / Chariots of the Gods? (1968), arguing the pampa was an ancient airfield.

sources.ref: Erich von Däniken, Chariots of the Gods? (1968) — the airfield/runway claim

Construction archaeology: the figures are shallow grooves a few centimeters deep made by clearing dark desert-varnish stones (iron/manganese oxides) over pale gypsum-caliche subsoil — structurally incapable of supporting heavy craft
Maria Reiche — debunked the von Däniken reading by linking geoglyph designs to Nazca pottery and culture (indigenous authorship)

Field archaeology: lines form continuous single-line labyrinths and figurative geoglyphs (spider, monkey, hummingbird), not runway geometry; many figures are visible from the surrounding foothills — no flight required

Wanderlust / Oxford Business Group / general research consensus: the works are 'dismissed by most researchers as little more than science fiction'; zero aviation-era artifacts or infrastructure at the site

competing_hypotheses: The claim's residual form: 'the lines are best viewed from the air, so the makers must have flown' — answered by hillside visibility and scaling techniques (stakes, ropes, grids; cf. Reiche's survey methods)

Jim Woodman's hot-air-balloon experiments (1970s): demonstrated a balloon could be built from local materials — but proved only that flight was conceivably possible, not that it occurred or explains the lines
falsifiability: Discovery of aircraft-grade landing infrastructure, aviation-era artifacts, or a documented indigenous flight tradition at the site would reopen the claim; a century of excavation has produced none

title: The first AI winter (c. 1974–1980)
claim: The first AI winter (c. 1974–1980) was a real funding-and-credibility collapse in artificial intelligence research, triggered by the Lighthill report (1973) and DARPA's subsequent cutbacks to academic AI research.
place: Washington, D.C. (DARPA) / London (Science Research Council) — the funding rooms
grade_reason: Independent secondary attestation of the funding phenomenon across multiple histories: the Lighthill report's devastating verdict and the UK funding halt, the Mansfield Amendment's 1969 mission-orientation requirement, DARPA's 1973–74 academic cutbacks, and Moravec's account (via Crevier) of the over-promising dynamic — held below VERIFIED because the periodization (1974–1980) is a conventional scholarly dating, not a measured fact.
earliest_attestation: James Lighthill, 'Artificial Intelligence: A General Survey' (1973, UK Science Research Council); the Mansfield Amendment (1969) to the Defense Procurement Authorization Act; the 1984 AAAI debate where Schank and Minsky warned of the coming chain reaction (pessimism → press → funding cutback → end of serious research)

sources.ref: Wikipedia, 'AI winter' — term first appeared 1984 at the AAAI annual meeting (Schank & Minsky debate); two major winters c. 1974–1980 and 1987–2000; Lighthill report 1973; Mansfield Amendment 1969; DARPA cutbacks 1973–74; Moravec (via Crevier) on the over-promising dynamic

title: The Apollo Moon landings, 1969-1972
claim: Between July 1969 and December 1972, six crewed Apollo missions (Apollo 11, 12, 14, 15, 16, 17) landed on the Moon, and twelve astronauts walked on its surface — beginning with Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin in Mare Tranquillitatis on 20-21 July 1969.
place: Mare Tranquillitatis (Apollo 11 site; hardware and astronaut footpaths visible in LRO imagery)
grade_reason: Multiple independent primary lines converge: 382 kg of lunar samples analyzed by laboratories worldwide; laser retroreflectors still returning pulses from Earth (McDonald Observatory detected Apollo 15's within days of deployment, 31 July 1971); orbital photography of all six sites by non-US probes as well as LRO; contemporaneous tracking by non-US stations during the missions; and the hostile superpower's own monitoring with no fraud denunciation.
earliest_attestation: The missions themselves, July 1969: onboard telemetry, tracking-station logs, the Slow-Scan TV transmission, the returned hardware, and the Lunar Sample Laboratory chain of custody

sources.ref: NASA mission archives and the Lunar Sample Laboratory: 382 kg of rocks and regolith returned (Apollo 11, 12, 14-17), showing features unique to an airless, impact-dominated environment, analyzed by thousands of scientists worldwide

Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, LROC Narrow Angle Camera (2009-present), ASU LROC Science Operations Center: ~0.5 m/pixel imagery of all six Apollo landing sites — descent stages, rovers, ALSEP packages, astronaut footpaths and rover tracks

Japan's SELENE (Kaguya) and India's Chandrayaan-1: independent orbital imaging; ISRO (2009, Prakash Chauhan) identified surface disturbances and rover tracks at the Apollo 15 site and called it 'independent corroboration'
Laser ranging retroreflectors emplaced by Apollo 11, 14 and 15 — ongoing Earth-Moon laser ranging experiments in continuous use since 1969

Contemporaneous third-party tracking: Jodrell Bank (UK, Lovell Telescope) and Bochum Observatory (West Germany) independently tracked Apollo 11's radio signals; the Soviet deep-space network monitored the missions (Luna 15 was in lunar orbit in July 1969) — and the USSR never mounted a sustained fraud denunciation, the posture history records
Apollo 12 (Nov 1969): astronauts retrieved parts of the earlier unmanned Surveyor 3 lander and returned them to Earth — a testable physical interaction between two lunar missions

competing_hypotheses: The staged-fakery claim, graded separately as DEBUNKED in evt-moon-landing-hoax-001 — the evidence lines below are what falsify it

Retroreflectors and orbital images alone do not prove a CREW: the USSR's uncrewed Lunokhod 1 emplaced a reflector in 1970 and soft-landed Luna 9 in 1966 — the crew claim rests on the samples, the suited astronauts' photographed tracks, the returned Surveyor 3 parts, and the contemporaneous international tracking, not on any single line
falsifiability: Verified archival evidence that the telemetry originated from an Earth site rather than the Moon (e.g. an authenticated Soviet intercept log showing Earth-origin signals), or peer-reviewed geochemical proof that the 382 kg of returned samples are terrestrial manufactures — none has ever been produced; the USSR's own archives remain the cleanest open audit trail

title: The ARPANET and the first message ('LO', 29 October 1969)
claim: The ARPANET — the first packet-switched computer network, funded by ARPA (later DARPA) — went live in 1969 with the stated purpose of letting researchers share scarce, expensive time-sharing computers. The first host-to-host transmission ran 29 October 1969 at 22:30 PST: UCLA graduate student Charley Kline, supervised by Leonard Kleinrock, typed 'login' on the UCLA SDS Sigma 7 host (Boelter Hall room 3420) toward Bill Duvall's SRI SDS 940 host — the SRI machine crashed after the letters 'l' and 'o', and the full login succeeded about an hour later. title: 'It never happened': the urban-legend dismissal of the Atari burial, killed by the 2014 dig

(2) The dig: on 26 April 2014, an excavation by Fuel Industries and Microsoft's Xbox Entertainment Studios (documented as 'Atari: Game Over') pulled ~1,300 cartridges of 60+ titles out of the concrete-covered site — E.T. among them, some with boxes and manuals. 881 were later sold on eBay with numbered city certificates of authenticity for $107,000+, proceeds to Alamogordo's library, zoo, police, and the Tularosa Basin Museum of History; one E.T. cartridge from the dig went to the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History (reported via 2014 press).
